Frontend and Full Stack

How the browser builds a page, frontend tooling, React and Next.js, client data fetching, frontend-backend contracts, browser auth and security, web performance, testing, shipping frontends, one feature built end to end, and frontend and full-stack interviews.

Part 69 — How the Browser Builds a Page

For most of this book the browser has been a client at the far end of the wire. It sent a request, your NestJS application answered, and the story ended at the last byte of the response. In this Volume the story keeps going. The browser takes those bytes and, in a few hundred milliseconds, turns them into a page a person can read, tap and buy from. Every decision your API makes about headers, payload shape, cookies and timing shows up somewhere in that process, and very often it shows up as "the page feels slow" or "the button jumps when I try to click it".

Part 3 — How the Web Works sketched the outline: DNS, connection, HTML, sub-resources, JavaScript, API calls (see 3.6). Part 11 — Networking and HTTP went deep on the wire itself: caching headers (11.11), TLS (11.12), CORS (11.13) and an end-to-end request trace (11.14). This Part starts where those stop. We open the browser up and follow the bytes through the HTML parser, the style engine, layout, paint and the compositor. Then we look at the parts of HTML, CSS and JavaScript that a backend engineer must understand to build or review a screen, the storage the browser gives you and what must never go in it, accessibility as an engineering discipline, and the DevTools panels that let you see all of this happening. We finish by tracing a real product page from its first byte to the moment a user can click "Add to cart", with an annotated network waterfall.

Throughout, every concept ends with a Backend side (NestJS) block. That block answers one question: what must the API do so that the page is correct and fast?

69.1 From URL to pixels: the rendering pipeline

Concept

A browser turns a URL into pixels through a fixed sequence of stages. First it navigates: it decides this is a page load, finds the server, and requests the HTML document. Then it parses the HTML into a tree of objects called the DOM (Document Object Model). In parallel it parses CSS into a second tree-like structure called the CSSOM (CSS Object Model). It combines the two into a render tree that contains only the things that will be drawn, with their final computed styles. It runs layout to work out the exact position and size of every box. It paints those boxes into lists of drawing commands, and finally it composites the painted layers together on the GPU to produce the frame you see.

This sequence is often called the critical rendering path. "Critical" because nothing appears on the screen until the first pass through it finishes. Every byte, every blocking script and every stylesheet you put in front of that first pass delays the moment the user sees anything at all.

The pipeline does not run once. It runs again whenever something changes: JavaScript adds a row to an order table, a font finishes loading, a user resizes the window, a CSS animation moves a toast. Knowing which stage a change forces the browser to redo is the difference between a page that scrolls at 60 frames per second and one that stutters.

Why does it exist?

HTML, CSS and JavaScript arrive as text, in pieces, over a network that might be fast fibre or a congested train-station 4G connection. The browser cannot wait for everything before drawing. It must start work on the first bytes, discover what else it needs as early as possible, and draw something useful the moment it has enough. The staged pipeline exists to make that possible:

  • Streaming parsing means the browser can build the top of the DOM while the bottom of the HTML is still on the wire.
  • Separating DOM and CSSOM means structure and style can be fetched and parsed in parallel.
  • Separating layout from paint from compositing means a change that only affects colour does not have to recompute geometry, and a change that only moves a layer does not have to repaint anything.

Mental model

Imagine a newspaper print shop at 03:00. Reporters send articles in one paragraph at a time (the HTML stream). A typesetter turns each paragraph into lines of type as it arrives (parsing into the DOM). The style guide says which headlines are bold and which columns are narrow (the CSSOM). An editor combines the type and the style guide into a page plan, leaving out anything marked "do not print" (the render tree). The layout desk measures where each column and photo goes on the page (layout). The printers ink each sheet (paint). Finally, the sheets are stacked and bound together (compositing).

If the style guide is late, the editor refuses to plan any page, because printing the paper in the wrong fonts and then reprinting it would be worse than waiting. That is exactly why CSS blocks rendering. If someone changes one headline's colour, only the printers redo work. If someone adds a new paragraph in the middle, the layout desk must re-measure everything below it. If someone just slides a finished sheet across the table, nobody reinks anything; that is compositing.

How it works

The full pipeline, in order:

flowchart LR
    nav["Navigation: DNS, TCP, TLS, GET html"] --> bytes["HTML bytes"]
    bytes --> tok["Tokenizer"]
    tok --> dom["DOM tree"]
    css["CSS bytes"] --> cssom["CSSOM"]
    dom --> sty["Style: compute styles per node"]
    cssom --> sty
    sty --> rt["Render tree: visible nodes only"]
    rt --> layout["Layout: geometry of every box"]
    layout --> paint["Paint: display lists per layer"]
    paint --> raster["Raster: pixels in tiles"]
    raster --> comp["Composite: GPU draws the frame"]

Step 1: navigation. When the user presses Enter, the browser process decides whether the input is a URL or a search, checks for a service worker that controls the URL, and starts the request. The network part (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP) is covered in Part 11 — Networking and HTTP. What matters here is the cost: on a mobile connection with a 150 ms round-trip time, a cold connection with TLS 1.3 needs roughly DNS (one round trip, often cached) plus TCP (one round trip) plus TLS (one round trip) before the first request byte leaves. That is 300 to 450 ms of nothing before your server even sees the request. Once the response headers arrive, the browser checks Content-Type. If it is text/html, it hands the stream to a renderer process for that site. If it is application/json or application/pdf, the page load becomes a download or a viewer instead.

Step 2: parsing HTML into the DOM. The HTML parser reads bytes, decodes them into characters using the charset (from the Content-Type header, or a <meta charset> in the first 1,024 bytes), splits characters into tokens (start tag, end tag, text, comment) and builds DOM nodes from those tokens. HTML parsing is forgiving by specification: an unclosed <p> or a stray </div> does not stop the page, the parser repairs the tree using well-defined rules. That is why invalid HTML "works" but sometimes produces a DOM you did not expect, for example a <div> placed inside a <p> closes the paragraph early.

The parser works on a stream. With an HTML response that is sent in chunks, the browser builds the <head> and the first part of <body> while the rest is still arriving. This is why sending the top of the page early (streaming, or "early flush") is so effective.

Step 3: the preload scanner. The main parser must stop when it meets a classic <script src> without defer or async, because that script may call document.write() and change everything after it. To avoid wasting that waiting time, browsers run a second, lightweight preload scanner (also called the speculative parser). It races ahead through the raw HTML, finds URLs in <link rel="stylesheet">, <script src>, <img src> and <img srcset>, and starts fetching them early. It cannot see resources that only JavaScript creates, or images that are only referenced from CSS background-image, or anything rendered later by a client-side framework. That limitation will matter in the worked example in 69.11.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Net as Network
    participant Main as MainParser
    participant Scan as PreloadScanner
    participant JS as ScriptEngine
    Net->>Main: first 14 KB of HTML
    Main->>Main: build head nodes
    Main->>Scan: blocked on classic script app.js
    Scan->>Net: fetch styles.css, hero.avif, vendor.js early
    Net-->>JS: app.js arrives
    JS->>JS: execute app.js
    JS-->>Main: resume parsing
    Net-->>Main: rest of HTML
    Main->>Main: DOM complete, fire DOMContentLoaded

Step 4: CSS into the CSSOM. Each stylesheet is parsed into rules: selectors plus declarations. The CSSOM is not a copy of the DOM; it is the set of rules, organised so the style engine can quickly find which rules match a given element. Two important behaviours:

  • CSS is render-blocking. The browser will not paint the first frame until all stylesheets found in the <head> (that apply to the current media) have loaded and parsed. This avoids a flash of unstyled content followed by a jarring re-layout.
  • CSS can be parser-blocking indirectly. A classic script after a stylesheet waits for that stylesheet, because the script might read computed styles such as getComputedStyle(el).width. So a slow CSS file delays scripts that come after it, which delays the rest of the parse.

Step 5: style calculation and the render tree. For every DOM node, the style engine finds the matching CSS rules, resolves the cascade (69.4) and computes final values: font-size: 1.25rem becomes 20px, width: 50% stays relative until layout. Nodes that are not rendered do not enter the render tree (in Chromium this structure is called the layout tree): everything in <head>, elements with display: none, <script> elements. Nodes with visibility: hidden are in the tree; they take space but are not painted. Pseudo-elements such as ::before are added even though they are not in the DOM.

Step 6: layout. Layout (also called reflow) walks the render tree and computes geometry: the x and y position, width and height of every box, line breaks in every paragraph, the size of every flex item and grid track. Layout is inherently global. Change the width of a container and every child inside it may need new line breaks. Insert a 40-pixel banner at the top of the body and everything below moves down by 40 pixels.

Step 7: paint. Paint does not produce pixels directly. It produces display lists: ordered drawing commands such as "fill rectangle at (0, 64, 1280, 400) with #f5f5f5", "draw text run 'Ergonomic Office Chair' at (24, 96)", "draw image hero.avif into this rectangle". The page is split into layers at this point. Elements with a 3D transform, will-change: transform, a <video>, a position: fixed header or an animated opacity often get their own layer.

Step 8: raster and composite. Raster threads turn display lists into pixels, in tiles of a few hundred pixels square, usually on the GPU. The compositor thread then stacks the layers in the right order, applies transforms and opacity, and hands the final frame to the display. The compositor runs on its own thread. That is why a page can still scroll smoothly while the main thread is busy with JavaScript, as long as scrolling does not need the main thread (for example, no non-passive wheel or touchmove listeners blocking it).

The most important practical consequence is the cost ladder. When something changes, the browser restarts the pipeline from the earliest affected stage:

flowchart TB
    change["Something changed"] --> q1{"Geometry changed? width, height, top, font-size, adding nodes"}
    q1 -->|"yes"| L["Style, then Layout, then Paint, then Composite: most expensive"]
    q1 -->|"no"| q2{"Only appearance? color, background, box-shadow"}
    q2 -->|"yes"| P["Style, then Paint, then Composite"]
    q2 -->|"no"| q3{"Only transform or opacity on its own layer?"}
    q3 -->|"yes"| C["Composite only: runs on the compositor thread"]
    q3 -->|"no"| S["Style recalc only"]

The frame budget makes this concrete. A 60 Hz display shows a new frame every 16.7 ms. A 120 Hz phone shows one every 8.3 ms. Out of that budget the browser needs a few milliseconds for its own housekeeping, so your JavaScript plus style plus layout plus paint for one frame must fit in roughly 10 ms on a 60 Hz screen. A full layout of a complex product listing page with 2,000 DOM nodes on a mid-range Android phone can take 15 to 40 ms by itself. Animate top on such a page and you will drop frames. Animate transform: translateY() and the compositor does it without touching layout or paint at all.

A last, critical detail: forced synchronous layout. Normally the browser batches style and layout work and does it once per frame. But if JavaScript writes a style and then immediately reads a geometric property (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect(), scrollTop), the browser has to run layout right now to give a correct answer. Do this in a loop and you get layout thrashing:

// BAD: each iteration writes then reads, forcing a full layout 200 times.
const rows = document.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>('.order-row');
rows.forEach((row) => {
  row.style.height = `${row.offsetHeight + 8}px`; // read after previous write = forced layout
});

// GOOD: read everything first, then write everything. One layout total.
const heights = Array.from(rows, (row) => row.offsetHeight); // reads, one layout
rows.forEach((row, i) => {
  row.style.height = `${heights[i] + 8}px`;                  // writes, batched
});

With 200 rows on a phone, the first version can easily take 300 ms. The second takes a few milliseconds.

Two more milestones finish the page load:

  • DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is fully parsed and all defer and module scripts have run. Images and stylesheets may still be loading.
  • load fires when everything the page references (images, iframes, stylesheets, synchronous scripts) has finished loading.

Neither milestone means "the user sees the content" or "the user can interact". That is why modern measurement uses user-centric metrics: First Contentful Paint (FCP), when the first text or image appears; Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), when the biggest content element (usually the hero image or the main heading) is painted; Interaction to Next Paint (INP), how long the page takes to respond visually to clicks and key presses; and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), how much the page jumps around. Part 76 — Web Performance covers them in depth. For now remember the "good" thresholds Google uses: LCP at or under 2.5 s, INP at or under 200 ms, CLS at or under 0.1.

Practical example

A customer opens https://shop.example.com/products/ergonomic-office-chair on a mid-range phone over 4G. Here is what the pipeline does, with plausible timings:

Time (ms) Stage What happens
0 Navigation Enter pressed, no service worker, DNS cached from an earlier visit
0 to 310 Connection TCP and TLS 1.3 to the CDN edge, about two round trips at 150 ms
310 to 520 Server time CDN misses, origin renders HTML (database query, product API call)
520 First byte Head of the HTML arrives; parser starts, preload scanner finds app.css, app.js, hero.avif
520 to 800 CSS fetch 38 KB of compressed CSS over the existing connection
830 Style, layout, paint First frame: header, title, price. FCP
800 to 1,400 Image fetch 110 KB AVIF hero image
1,450 Paint Hero image painted. LCP
900 to 1,600 JS fetch 160 KB compressed JavaScript (defer)
1,600 to 2,050 Script Parse, compile, execute, React hydration: one 380 ms long task
2,050 Interactive "Add to cart" handler attached

Notice that the user sees the price at 830 ms but cannot add to cart until 2,050 ms. If they tap at 1,800 ms, nothing happens: the button looks ready but is not. That gap is invisible in server logs and is exactly the kind of thing this Part teaches you to see.

React / Next.js example

With the Next.js 14 App Router, a page is a server component by default. It renders to HTML on the server and streams that HTML to the browser, so the parser can start immediately. A <Suspense> boundary lets the slow part (reviews from a separate service) stream in later without holding back the shell.

// app/products/[slug]/page.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router; in Next.js 15 params is a Promise)
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
import Image from 'next/image';
import { Reviews } from './reviews';

type Product = { id: string; name: string; priceMinor: number; currency: string;
  image: { url: string; width: number; height: number; alt: string } };

async function getProduct(slug: string): Promise<Product | null> {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/v1/products/by-slug/${slug}`, {
    next: { revalidate: 60 }, // cache this fetch for 60 s on the Next.js server
  });
  if (res.status === 404) return null;
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`product API ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  const product = await getProduct(params.slug);
  if (!product) notFound();

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      {/* priority: preloads the image and sets fetchpriority=high, so the LCP image is found early */}
      <Image src={product.image.url} width={product.image.width} height={product.image.height}
             alt={product.image.alt} priority />
      <p>{new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: product.currency })
            .format(product.priceMinor / 100)}</p>
      {/* The shell above is flushed first; reviews stream in when ready */}
      <Suspense fallback={<p aria-busy="true">Loading reviews...</p>}>
        <Reviews productId={product.id} />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}

What reaches the browser is HTML in two chunks: first everything outside the <Suspense> boundary plus the fallback, then, when Reviews resolves, a second chunk containing the reviews markup and a tiny inline script that swaps it into place. The parser and the preload scanner start on chunk one while the server is still waiting on the reviews service.

Backend side (NestJS)

The browser can only start its pipeline when bytes arrive, so the most valuable thing a backend can do for rendering is send useful bytes early and label them correctly. When NestJS serves HTML itself (server-rendered templates, an admin page, a status page), two techniques help:

  1. 103 Early Hints: before the final response is ready, tell the browser which critical resources to fetch. Node.js has response.writeEarlyHints() since v18.11, and Chrome supports Early Hints for preload and preconnect since version 103.
  2. Early flush: write the <head> immediately, then await the slow data, then write the body. The browser fetches CSS while your database query runs.
// product-page.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Param, Res, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Response } from 'express';
import { ProductService } from './product.service';
import { renderHead, renderProductBody } from './templates';

@Controller('products')
export class ProductPageController {
  constructor(private readonly products: ProductService) {}

  @Get(':slug')
  async page(@Param('slug') slug: string, @Res() res: Response): Promise<void> {
    // 1. 103 Early Hints: the browser starts these fetches during our DB query.
    res.writeEarlyHints({
      link: [
        '</assets/app.3f9c1a.css>; rel=preload; as=style',
        '<https://img.shop-cdn.example>; rel=preconnect',
      ],
    });

    // 2. Look up the product before committing to a 200 status.
    const product = await this.products.findBySlug(slug); // ~8 ms, indexed lookup
    if (!product) throw new NotFoundException();

    res.status(200);
    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/html; charset=utf-8'); // charset in the header, not just meta
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300');

    // 3. Early flush: head goes out now, the browser starts on CSS immediately.
    res.write(renderHead({ title: product.name }));

    // 4. Slower work (recommendations, ~120 ms) happens while the browser parses the head.
    const related = await this.products.related(product.id, 8);
    res.end(renderProductBody(product, related));
  }
}

Things the backend must get right, which this code shows:

  • Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 in the header. Without a charset, the browser may have to restart parsing when it meets <meta charset> later.
  • Decide the status code before the first res.write(). Once bytes are flushed, headers are sent, so a 404 or 500 discovered later cannot be reported with the right status. That is why the product lookup happens before the flush and only the "nice to have" data comes after.
  • Watch the compression middleware. The compression package for Express buffers output; with streaming you need it to flush per write (it adds a res.flush() method) or let the CDN or load balancer compress.

When Next.js is the frontend and NestJS is a JSON API behind it, the same idea applies one level down: the API's latency is part of the server-render time, so a slow GET /v1/products/by-slug/:slug delays the first byte of HTML for every user. Measure it as part of the page budget, not as an isolated endpoint.

Production scenario

A furniture retailer serves 1.8 million product page views per day. Their HTML is rendered by Next.js and cached at the CDN for 60 s. CDN hit rate is 92 %. On a hit, time to first byte (TTFB) at the 75th percentile is 90 ms; on a miss it is 640 ms, of which 410 ms is the Next.js server waiting on three sequential API calls to NestJS services (product, price, stock). The rendering pipeline on a mid-range phone adds about 900 ms after the first byte before LCP.

The team's LCP at p75 is 2.3 s on hits and 2.9 s on misses. The cheapest fix was not in the browser at all: running the three API calls in parallel with Promise.all cut the miss TTFB to 310 ms and brought p75 LCP on misses to 2.5 s. The lesson that repeats through this Part: the backend's latency is the first stage of the browser's pipeline.

Failure scenario

At 11:20 on a sale day, conversion on product pages dropped 18 % within ten minutes of a deploy. Server metrics were perfect: TTFB unchanged, error rate flat. The on-call backend engineer was about to declare "not us" when a frontend colleague opened DevTools, recorded a Performance trace and saw it: the first paint now happened at 3.4 s instead of 0.9 s.

The deploy had added a third-party A/B testing snippet as a classic <script src> in the <head>, placed above the main stylesheet. The vendor's server in another region was answering in 2.1 s under sale-day load. Because the script was parser-blocking, the HTML parser stopped at it. The preload scanner had already started the stylesheet fetch, but nothing could render until the script downloaded and executed. Every user stared at a white screen for over two seconds.

The fix was a one-line change to load the snippet with async and to give it a 1 s timeout through the vendor's own loader. The postmortem added two rules: no synchronous third-party script in <head>, ever, and every deploy runs a synthetic Lighthouse check against a product page with a budget on FCP.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Wrong Content-Type: serving HTML as text/plain shows the source code; serving JSON as text/html from an error handler can open an XSS hole if the body contains user input. Always set it explicitly, and send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
  • Charset declared late: a <meta charset> after the first 1,024 bytes, or a mismatch with the header, can cause a parse restart or garbled text ("â‚¹" instead of the rupee sign).
  • Server buffering defeats streaming: a reverse proxy with response buffering (NGINX proxy_buffering on) or a compression layer that waits for the whole body turns an early flush into a late one.
  • Status after flush: errors discovered after streaming starts cannot change the status code; the page must render an error state inside a 200 response, which monitoring might count as success.
  • Layout thrashing in a loop: a read-after-write pattern inside a list renderer turns one layout into hundreds.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior engineer treats the page load as one pipeline with the backend as stage one. Before arguing about React rendering or image formats, they ask: how long until the first byte, how long until the browser knows about the critical CSS and the LCP image, and what blocks the parser? They know that a 200 ms win in TTFB is a 200 ms win in every later metric, and that a parser-blocking script can wipe out any backend optimisation.

They refuse to measure page speed with server metrics alone, and they refuse to accept "it's fast on my machine": a developer laptop with a fast CPU and wired internet is four to six times faster at JavaScript than the median phone. They profile with CPU throttling and network throttling turned on.

They also keep the cost ladder in mind when reviewing frontend code. An animation of height, top or width gets a comment asking for transform. A loop that reads offsetHeight after setting styles gets flagged for thrashing. To a product manager they would say: "The page has to be built in stages. Our job is to make the first stage short and to never block the later ones."

Common mistakes

  • Treating load as "page ready". Users judge speed by when content appears (FCP, LCP) and when the page responds (INP), not by load.
  • Putting scripts in <head> without defer or async. This stops the parser and delays everything; 69.6 covers the right attributes.
  • Animating layout properties. Animating top or height re-runs layout every frame; use transform and opacity.
  • Ignoring TTFB because "the API is only 300 ms". For a server-rendered page that 300 ms is directly in front of FCP.
  • Rendering the LCP image only through JavaScript or CSS backgrounds. The preload scanner cannot find it, so it is fetched late.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through what happens between receiving HTML bytes and seeing pixels. Expected answer: parse HTML into the DOM (with a preload scanner fetching resources ahead), parse CSS into the CSSOM, compute styles, build the render tree of visible nodes, run layout for geometry, paint into display lists per layer, rasterise, composite on the GPU. Why it matters: it shows whether the candidate can reason about where time goes. Follow-ups: why does CSS block rendering? What does display: none versus visibility: hidden do to the render tree?
  2. Why is animating transform cheaper than animating left? Expected answer: left changes geometry and forces layout and paint every frame; transform on a composited layer only changes how the compositor draws an existing layer, on a separate thread. Follow-up: what does will-change: transform do and what does it cost (memory for an extra layer)?
  3. What is layout thrashing and how do you fix it? Expected answer: interleaving style writes with geometry reads, forcing synchronous layout repeatedly. Fix by batching reads before writes, or by using requestAnimationFrame to schedule writes.
  4. What is the preload scanner and what can it not see? Expected answer: a secondary parser that discovers resource URLs in raw HTML while the main parser is blocked; it cannot see resources created by JavaScript, CSS background images, or content rendered client-side.
  5. The API is fast but the page is slow. Where do you look first? Expected answer: a DevTools Performance trace and Network waterfall: render-blocking resources, parser-blocking scripts, late-discovered LCP image, long main-thread tasks.

Practical exercise

Build a tiny NestJS endpoint that serves an HTML product page in two ways: (a) wait for all data, then res.send() the whole page; (b) send 103 Early Hints for the stylesheet, flush the <head> immediately, sleep 300 ms to simulate a slow recommendation query, then send the body. Load both in Chrome with network throttling set to a slow 4G preset and record a Performance trace for each.

Acceptance criteria:

  • You can point to the "Parse HTML" tasks in the Performance panel and show that in version (b) parsing starts about 300 ms earlier.
  • In the Network panel, the stylesheet request in version (b) starts before the HTML response finishes.
  • You can explain why the product-not-found check must happen before the first res.write().
  • You write down FCP for both versions from the Performance panel's Timings track.

69.2 HTML that matters: semantic elements and forms

Concept

HTML is the structure of a page. Each element carries meaning, not just appearance. A <button> is something you press, an <a href> is something that navigates, a <nav> is a block of site navigation, an <h1> is the main heading, a <form> collects input and sends it to a server. Using the element that matches the meaning is called semantic HTML.

Semantic elements come with behaviour the browser provides for free: a <button> is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, and submits its form; an <a href> can be opened in a new tab, bookmarked and crawled; a <label> makes clicking its text focus the input; an <input type="email"> brings up the right mobile keyboard and validates the format. A <div onClick> has none of that. You have to rebuild each behaviour in JavaScript, and in practice nobody rebuilds all of it.

Forms deserve special attention from backend engineers, because a plain HTML form is a fully working HTTP client. With zero JavaScript, a <form method="post" action="/checkout/address"> builds a request body, sets a Content-Type, sends a POST and follows the response, including redirects. Many frontend bugs (double orders, lost input, the "Confirm Form Resubmission" dialog) come from not knowing what that default behaviour is.

Why does it exist?

Without semantics, a page is a pile of boxes that only humans with good eyesight and a mouse can use. Semantics let three other consumers understand the page:

  1. Assistive technology. Screen readers build their interface from elements: "heading level 1, Ergonomic Office Chair", "button, Add to cart", "navigation landmark". See 69.9.
  2. The browser itself. Keyboard navigation, form autofill, password managers, reader mode, translation and "open in new tab" all rely on real elements.
  3. Machines. Search engine crawlers, link previews and price comparison bots read headings, links and structured data.

Forms exist because the web needed a way to send user input to servers long before JavaScript existed. That default behaviour is still there, under every React form, and it still fires unless you stop it.

Mental model

Imagine a building. Semantic HTML is the signage and the standard fittings: doors that look like doors and have handles, lifts with numbered buttons and Braille, fire exits marked as exits. A <div> styled to look like a button is a painting of a door on a wall. It looks right in a photo, but you cannot walk through it, a blind visitor cannot find it, and the fire marshal (the browser's accessibility and keyboard features) does not know it exists.

A form is a pre-printed envelope with the address already written on it. Fill in the fields, press submit, and the post office (the browser) delivers it with the correct stamp (Content-Type) to the address in action. If you want to deliver it yourself by courier (fetch), you must first stop the post office from also delivering it (event.preventDefault()).

How it works

Semantic structure of a typical product page:

<body>
  <a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to content</a>
  <header>
    <nav aria-label="Primary">
      <ul><li><a href="/chairs">Chairs</a></li><li><a href="/desks">Desks</a></li></ul>
    </nav>
  </header>
  <main id="main">
    <article>
      <h1>Ergonomic Office Chair</h1>
      <p><data value="1249900">Rs 12,499</data></p>
      <form method="post" action="/cart/items">
        <input type="hidden" name="sku" value="CHR-ERG-001">
        <label for="qty">Quantity</label>
        <input id="qty" name="qty" type="number" min="1" max="10" value="1" inputmode="numeric">
        <button type="submit">Add to cart</button>
      </form>
      <section aria-labelledby="reviews-h"><h2 id="reviews-h">Reviews</h2></section>
    </article>
  </main>
  <footer>...</footer>
</body>

Each landmark (header, nav, main, footer) shows up in a screen reader's landmark list. Headings form an outline (h1 then h2, no skipped levels) that users jump through. The "Add to cart" form works even if JavaScript fails to load.

What a form submission does, step by step:

  1. Triggering. A submit happens when the user clicks a submit button, presses Enter in a single-line text input while the form has a submit button (this is called implicit submission), or JavaScript calls form.requestSubmit(). A <button> inside a form with no type attribute is type="submit" by default. This single rule causes many accidental submits: a "Show password" or "Apply coupon" button with no type submits the whole checkout form.
  2. Validation. Unless the form has novalidate, the browser checks constraints: required, type="email", min, max, minlength, maxlength, pattern. If anything fails, it shows a native message, focuses the first invalid field, and does not send anything. This is a convenience for users, never a security control; anyone can send a request with curl.
  3. The submit event fires. Calling event.preventDefault() here stops the browser's own submission. Every single-page app does this and then calls fetch.
  4. Building the body. The browser collects every successful control: enabled, has a name, and (for checkboxes and radios) is checked. Disabled fields are not sent. An unchecked checkbox sends nothing at all, not false. A readonly field is sent.
  5. Encoding. With method="get" the fields become the query string: /search?q=chair&sort=price. With method="post" the body is encoded per enctype: the default application/x-www-form-urlencoded (sku=CHR-ERG-001&qty=2), multipart/form-data for file uploads (required for <input type="file">), or text/plain (rarely useful).
  6. Navigation. The browser sends the request as a navigation and renders whatever comes back. If the server answers with a redirect, the browser follows it.
  7. Refresh behaviour. If the response to a POST is a page (200), pressing refresh offers to re-send the POST, the classic "Confirm Form Resubmission" dialog. That is how duplicate orders happen. The fix is Post/Redirect/Get (PRG): answer the POST with 303 See Other pointing at a result page, so refresh only repeats the harmless GET.
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant B as Browser
    participant API as NestJS
    U->>B: click Place order
    B->>B: constraint validation passes
    B->>API: POST /checkout/place-order, urlencoded body
    API->>API: create order 8812, idempotency key stored
    API-->>B: 303 See Other, Location /orders/8812
    B->>API: GET /orders/8812
    API-->>B: 200 order confirmation page
    U->>B: presses refresh
    B->>API: GET /orders/8812 again, harmless

Attributes that make forms usable and correct:

Attribute Example What it does
autocomplete autocomplete="email", "postal-code", "cc-number", "one-time-code" Lets the browser and password managers fill fields correctly; one-time-code enables SMS code autofill on phones
inputmode inputmode="numeric" Shows a numeric keypad without the quirks of type="number" (spinners, scroll-to-change)
type email, tel, url, date, search Right keyboard on mobile plus basic validation
name name="shipping.postalCode" The key in the submitted body; no name means not submitted
required, pattern, min, max pattern="[1-9][0-9]{5}" Native validation; mirror server-side rules, never replace them
enctype multipart/form-data Required to upload files
formaction, formmethod on a second submit button One form, two actions (for example "Save draft" versus "Submit")

Practical example

A checkout address step has an "Apply coupon" button and a "Continue to payment" button in the same form. A developer wired the coupon button with an onClick handler and no type. In production, every click on "Apply coupon" applied the coupon and submitted the form, moving the user to payment with half-filled address fields. The backend saw a burst of 400 Bad Request responses for missing postalCode. The fix was one attribute: <button type="button">. The backend fix was to return field-level errors (69.9) so the page could show what was missing instead of a generic toast.

React / Next.js example

In a React single-page form, you control submission yourself, but you still use the native form so that Enter submits, the browser validates, and password managers recognise the fields. React 18's useId creates stable ids for label and error association, even with server rendering.

// AddressForm.tsx  (React 18)
import { useId, useState, type FormEvent } from 'react';

type FieldErrors = Partial<Record<'fullName' | 'postalCode', string>>;

export function AddressForm({ onSaved }: { onSaved: (addressId: string) => void }) {
  const id = useId();
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState<FieldErrors>({});
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);

  async function handleSubmit(e: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
    e.preventDefault();                      // stop the browser's own POST navigation
    if (submitting) return;                  // ignore a second Enter or double click
    setSubmitting(true);
    const body = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(e.currentTarget)); // only named, enabled fields
    try {
      const res = await fetch('/api/v1/addresses', {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify(body),
      });
      if (res.status === 422) { setErrors((await res.json()).fieldErrors); return; }
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      onSaved((await res.json()).id);
    } finally {
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <label htmlFor={`${id}-name`}>Full name</label>
      <input id={`${id}-name`} name="fullName" autoComplete="name" required
             aria-invalid={!!errors.fullName} aria-describedby={`${id}-name-err`} />
      <p id={`${id}-name-err`}>{errors.fullName}</p>

      <label htmlFor={`${id}-pin`}>PIN code</label>
      <input id={`${id}-pin`} name="postalCode" autoComplete="postal-code" inputMode="numeric"
             pattern="[1-9][0-9]{5}" required aria-invalid={!!errors.postalCode}
             aria-describedby={`${id}-pin-err`} />
      <p id={`${id}-pin-err`}>{errors.postalCode}</p>

      <button type="button" onClick={() => alert('coupon')}>Apply coupon</button>
      <button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>Continue to payment</button>
    </form>
  );
}

With the Next.js 14 App Router, you can go further and let the form work without client JavaScript using a Server Action: <form action={saveAddress}> where saveAddress is an async function marked 'use server'. The browser submits a real POST; after hydration, React intercepts it and sends it with fetch instead. Next.js 14 bundles a React canary build that also exports useFormStatus from react-dom for a pending state; in plain React 18 that hook does not exist (it is stable in React 19).

Backend side (NestJS)

A NestJS API used by HTML forms must accept form encodings, not just JSON. By default NestFactory.create() with the Express adapter registers both a JSON and a URL-encoded body parser, so application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies arrive in @Body(). Every value arrives as a string, so the DTO must transform types.

// checkout.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Headers, Post, Res, UsePipes, ValidationPipe } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Response } from 'express';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';
import { IsInt, IsString, Matches, Max, Min } from 'class-validator';
import { CheckoutService } from './checkout.service';

export class PlaceOrderForm {
  @IsString() @Matches(/^[A-Z0-9-]{3,32}$/) sku!: string;
  @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(10) qty!: number;  // form fields are strings: "2" -> 2
  @IsString() @Matches(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/) idempotencyKey!: string; // hidden input rendered with the page
}

@Controller('checkout')
export class CheckoutController {
  constructor(private readonly checkout: CheckoutService) {}

  @Post('place-order')
  @UsePipes(new ValidationPipe({ transform: true, whitelist: true }))
  async placeOrder(
    @Body() form: PlaceOrderForm,
    @Headers('accept') accept: string | undefined,
    @Res() res: Response,
  ): Promise<void> {
    // The hidden idempotency key turns a double submit into a replay of the same order.
    const order = await this.checkout.placeOrder(form, form.idempotencyKey);

    if (accept?.includes('application/json')) {
      res.status(201).json({ id: order.id, status: order.status }); // fetch() callers
      return;
    }
    // Plain HTML form: Post/Redirect/Get. 303 forces the follow-up to be a GET.
    res.redirect(303, `/orders/${order.id}`);
  }
}

The points that make the frontend correct:

  • Return 303, not 302, after a form POST. Browsers historically turn 302 into a GET anyway, but 303 states it explicitly and is the documented status for PRG.
  • Accept the idempotency key as a field. Render a fresh UUID into a hidden input when the page is generated. A double click, a refresh or a retry then reuses the key, and the service returns the original order instead of creating a second one (see Part 15 — API Design (REST first), 15.12 Idempotency, for the storage side).
  • Expect strings and missing fields. An unchecked checkbox is simply absent, so @IsOptional() plus a default of false is correct; @IsBoolean() on a form field will always fail, because the value is the string "on".
  • Return field-level errors with status 422 (or 400) so the page can attach each message to its input.
  • Set a body size limit. multipart/form-data uploads should go through a dedicated interceptor with explicit limits (see Part 33 — File Storage and Uploads), not the global parser.

Production scenario

A grocery-delivery site processes about 40,000 orders per day. Their analytics showed 0.6 % of orders were exact duplicates placed within 10 seconds of each other, about 240 per day, each one needing a manual refund and an apologetic support ticket. Session replays showed three causes: users double-tapping "Place order" on slow 3G, users pressing Enter twice, and users refreshing the confirmation page that was rendered directly in the POST response.

The fix was layered. Frontend: disable the button on submit and ignore re-entry. HTML: switch to PRG with a 303 redirect. Backend: require an idempotency key from a hidden field and enforce a unique constraint on (customer_id, idempotency_key). Duplicates fell to under 5 per day, all from users genuinely ordering twice.

Failure scenario

A team rebuilt their login page as a polished React component. Inputs were custom <div contenteditable> elements styled beautifully, and the "Sign in" control was a <div role="button" onClick>. Within a week, support tickets doubled. Password managers no longer filled credentials because there was no <input type="password"> and no <form>. Pressing Enter did nothing. iOS users could not paste their password. Screen reader users heard "group" with no name.

The backend team noticed first, oddly: login attempts per successful login went from 1.3 to 2.6, and password reset requests tripled, because users who relied on password managers could not remember their passwords. The rollback restored a plain <form> with <input type="email" autocomplete="username"> and <input type="password" autocomplete="current-password">, and the numbers recovered the same day.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Button default type: any <button> inside a <form> without type="button" submits it.
  • Disabled versus readonly: disabled fields are excluded from the body; a disabled "price" field is not sent, a readonly one is (and must never be trusted).
  • Checkbox absence: unchecked boxes send nothing; the server must treat "missing" as "false".
  • Multiple values: <select multiple> or several checkboxes with the same name send repeated keys (tag=a&tag=b); Object.fromEntries(formData) keeps only the last one, so use formData.getAll('tag').
  • GET forms leak data: a search form with method="get" puts every field in the URL, server logs, browser history and the Referer header. Never use GET for anything sensitive.
  • Back-forward cache: pressing Back can restore a form page from the back-forward cache with the previous values, including a "submitting" spinner that never stops if your state assumed a fresh load.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior reaches for the native element first and asks "what does the browser already do here?" before writing any handler. They see a <form> as an HTTP client with well-defined behaviour and design the endpoint to support it: accept form encoding, validate strings, return 303 after writes, expect retries.

They view double submission as a backend problem with a frontend helper, not the other way round. Disabling the button reduces duplicates, but only an idempotency key and a unique constraint eliminate them, because the network can always retry. To a product manager: "We can make the button harder to press twice, but only the server can guarantee one click equals one order."

They also insist that a page's core action works with the network flaky and JavaScript late: a server-rendered form that posts and redirects is the most robust checkout you can build, and frameworks like Next.js Server Actions exist precisely to keep that robustness while adding a nicer client experience.

Common mistakes

  • Using <div onClick> instead of <button>. You lose keyboard support, focus, form submission and the accessible role.
  • Using <button> for navigation or <a href="#"> for actions. Links navigate, buttons act; mixing them breaks middle-click, history and screen reader expectations.
  • Forgetting event.preventDefault(). The page navigates away and the fetch is cancelled, so the API sees an aborted request or nothing at all.
  • Rendering a page directly in response to a POST. Refresh then re-submits; use PRG.
  • Trusting hidden or readonly fields. A hidden price field is a field the user can change with DevTools in five seconds.
  • Removing name or autocomplete from inputs in a redesign, breaking autofill and password managers.

Interview questions

  1. What does a plain HTML form do on submit, without JavaScript? Expected answer: runs constraint validation, collects successful controls, encodes them per method and enctype, sends a navigation request to action, follows redirects and renders the response. Follow-up: which controls are left out? (Disabled, unnamed, unchecked.)
  2. Why use 303 after a form POST? Expected answer: Post/Redirect/Get, so refreshing repeats only a GET and cannot re-submit the order. Follow-up: what else protects against duplicates? (Idempotency key with a unique constraint.)
  3. Why is <button> better than a styled <div>? Expected answer: focusable, keyboard activation, form submission, accessible role and name, all built in.
  4. A user reports the checkout jumps to payment when they apply a coupon. What do you suspect? Expected answer: a button inside the form with no type, defaulting to submit.
  5. How does a NestJS endpoint receive a form-encoded body and what types does it get? Expected answer: Express's URL-encoded parser fills @Body(); all values are strings, so the DTO must use @Type(() => Number) or similar with transform: true.
  6. When is method="get" the right choice for a form? Expected answer: for safe, bookmarkable queries like search and filters; never for writes or sensitive data.

Practical exercise

Build an order "Place order" flow that works with JavaScript disabled. A NestJS endpoint renders a page with a form containing a hidden idempotency key. The POST handler validates a form-encoded body, creates the order idempotently and answers with a 303 to the confirmation page. Then add a React enhancement that intercepts the submit, sends JSON, and disables the button while pending.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With JavaScript disabled in DevTools (Command Menu, "Disable JavaScript"), the order can be placed and refreshing the confirmation page does not create a second order.
  • Double-clicking the button with JavaScript enabled creates exactly one order row in PostgreSQL.
  • Sending the same request twice with curl and the same idempotency key returns the same order id.
  • The coupon button does not submit the form.

69.3 The head: meta tags, preload and preconnect

Concept

The <head> element holds information about the page rather than content on the page. It is small, often under 3 KB, but it controls how the page is decoded, how it is sized on a phone, what appears in a browser tab and a link preview, and, most importantly for speed, which resources the browser fetches first.

The parts that matter to engineers fall into three groups:

  • Document setup: <meta charset="utf-8">, the viewport meta tag, <title>, <html lang>.
  • Metadata for other systems: <meta name="description">, Open Graph tags for link previews, <link rel="canonical">, <meta name="robots">.
  • Resource hints: preconnect, dns-prefetch, preload, modulepreload, prefetch, and the fetchpriority attribute. These tell the browser about work it will need to do before it discovers that work on its own.

Why does it exist?

By the time the parser reaches the <body>, the browser has already made decisions it cannot easily undo: which character encoding to use, how wide the layout viewport is, which stylesheets block the first paint. The <head> is where you make those decisions explicit.

Resource hints exist because the browser discovers resources late. A web font is referenced inside a CSS file, which is referenced from the HTML. The browser only learns about the font after downloading and parsing the CSS. An image served from a separate CDN domain needs its own DNS, TCP and TLS setup, which the browser only starts when it finds the first image. On a 150 ms round-trip mobile network, each of those discoveries can cost 300 to 600 ms. A hint lets you start that work at the first byte of HTML.

Mental model

Imagine a chef receiving a dinner order (the HTML). Without hints, the chef reads the recipe, sees "saffron", walks to the store, comes back, reads further, sees "fresh basil", walks to the store again. Resource hints are a note stapled to the top of the order: "You'll need saffron and basil, and the fish supplier's phone line is slow, so call them now." preconnect is calling the supplier to open the line. preload is ordering the exact ingredient. prefetch is ordering something for tomorrow's menu, at low priority.

How it works

A production <head> for a product page, with each line explained:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en-IN">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">                                   <!-- must be in the first 1024 bytes -->
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Ergonomic Office Chair | Shop</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Mesh back, adjustable lumbar support, 5-year warranty.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://shop.example.com/products/ergonomic-office-chair">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://img.shop-cdn.example/chair-1200x630.jpg">

  <!-- Open connections early to origins we will certainly use -->
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://img.shop-cdn.example">
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://api.shop.example.com" crossorigin>

  <!-- Fetch late-discovered critical resources now -->
  <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-var.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
  <link rel="preload" as="image" href="https://img.shop-cdn.example/chair-800.avif"
        imagesrcset="https://img.shop-cdn.example/chair-400.avif 400w, https://img.shop-cdn.example/chair-800.avif 800w"
        imagesizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw" fetchpriority="high">

  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.3f9c1a.css">   <!-- render-blocking, keep it small -->
  <script type="module" src="/assets/app.81bd2e.js"></script> <!-- modules are deferred -->
  <link rel="modulepreload" href="/assets/vendor.c41a77.js">
</head>

Line by line, what the browser does:

  1. <meta charset="utf-8"> tells the decoder which encoding to use. It must appear within the first 1,024 bytes; otherwise the browser may guess, then re-parse when it finds the tag. The Content-Type header's charset wins over the meta tag when both exist.
  2. Viewport meta. Without width=device-width, mobile browsers lay the page out on a virtual 980-pixel-wide canvas and shrink it, so text is tiny and media queries (69.4) never match the phone's real width. Do not add maximum-scale=1 or user-scalable=no; they block pinch zoom, which is an accessibility failure.
  3. <title> and lang. The title is the tab label, the bookmark name, the search result headline and the first thing a screen reader announces. lang tells screen readers which pronunciation rules to use and lets the browser offer translation.
  4. preconnect performs DNS, TCP and TLS to an origin now, so the first real request skips those round trips. The crossorigin attribute matters: browsers keep separate connection pools for credentialed and anonymous (CORS) requests, so a preconnect without crossorigin does not help a fetch() with CORS mode or a font load, and one with crossorigin does not help a plain <img>. Chrome closes a preconnected socket that is not used within about 10 seconds, and each preconnect costs CPU and a TLS handshake, so limit them to two or three origins you will use in the first second.
  5. dns-prefetch does only the DNS lookup. It is cheaper than preconnect and fine for origins you might use later.
  6. preload fetches a specific resource at high priority without executing or applying it. The as attribute is mandatory in practice: it sets priority, the Accept header and the right cache matching. Without a correct as, the browser downloads the resource twice, once for the preload and once when it is really needed. Fonts must be preloaded with crossorigin even on your own origin, because font requests are always made in CORS mode. If a preloaded resource is not used within a few seconds of the load event, Chrome logs a console warning that the resource "was preloaded using link preload but not used within a few seconds".
  7. fetchpriority="high" on an <img> or a preload raises its priority. Images normally start at low priority until layout shows they are in the viewport; for the LCP image this boost can save hundreds of milliseconds.
  8. modulepreload is preload for ES modules: it fetches, parses and compiles the module and puts it in the module map, so the import graph does not discover its dependencies one round trip at a time.
  9. prefetch fetches something for a likely next navigation at the lowest priority, into the HTTP cache. Good for the checkout bundle while the user is on the cart page.
flowchart LR
    html["HTML head parsed at 520 ms"] --> pc["preconnect img CDN: DNS, TCP, TLS in parallel"]
    html --> pl["preload font and hero image at high priority"]
    html --> css["stylesheet: render blocking"]
    css --> fp["first paint about 830 ms"]
    pc --> img["hero image request skips 300 ms of setup"]
    pl --> img
    img --> lcp["LCP about 1450 ms"]

The same hints can come from the server as HTTP headers, which arrive even earlier than the HTML body:

HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
Link: </assets/app.3f9c1a.css>; rel=preload; as=style
Link: <https://img.shop-cdn.example>; rel=preconnect

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Link: </fonts/inter-var.woff2>; rel=preload; as=font; type="font/woff2"; crossorigin

A quick decision table:

Hint Use it for Cost if wrong Typical count
preconnect Third-party origin used in the first second (image CDN, API on another origin) Wasted handshake, CPU, socket 1 to 3
dns-prefetch Origins used later (analytics, chat widget) Negligible Any
preload Late-discovered critical resource: web font, LCP image set in CSS, critical script imported by another Steals bandwidth from more important resources; double download with wrong as 1 to 4
modulepreload Deep ES module graph Same as preload Main chunk dependencies
prefetch Next likely page's resources Wasted bytes on metered connections A few
fetchpriority="high" The LCP image Starves other high-priority resources if overused 1

Practical example

A product page loads its Inter font from /fonts/inter-var.woff2, referenced inside app.css. On a throttled 4G profile the waterfall shows: HTML at 520 ms, CSS finishes at 800 ms, the font request only starts at 810 ms and finishes at 1,150 ms. Text is invisible or swaps visibly until then. Adding a preload with as="font" and crossorigin moves the font request start to 530 ms, in parallel with the CSS, and it finishes at 870 ms. Text renders in the final font on the first paint. Cost: one line in the head.

React / Next.js example

The Next.js 14 App Router manages the <head> for you through the Metadata API, and its built-in components emit the right hints.

// app/layout.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router)
import type { Metadata, Viewport } from 'next';
import { Inter } from 'next/font/google';
import './globals.css';

// next/font downloads the font at build time, self-hosts it, preloads it
// and generates a size-adjusted fallback to reduce layout shift.
const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'], display: 'swap' });

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  metadataBase: new URL('https://shop.example.com'),
  title: { default: 'Shop', template: '%s | Shop' },
  description: 'Office furniture delivered in 48 hours.',
};

// Next.js 14 moved viewport settings out of `metadata` into a separate export.
export const viewport: Viewport = { width: 'device-width', initialScale: 1 };

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en-IN" className={inter.className}>
      <body>{children}</body>
    </html>
  );
}

A page can add its own metadata with export async function generateMetadata({ params }), which runs on the server and can call the API for the product name and Open Graph image. next/image with the priority prop adds a preload and high fetch priority for the LCP image. The App Router's bundled React canary also exposes preconnect() and preload() from react-dom, which insert the matching <link> tags from inside any component; in plain React 18 these functions are not available.

Backend side (NestJS)

When the backend or a BFF knows which resources a page needs, it can send them as Link headers or as 103 Early Hints, so the browser starts before it parses a single byte of HTML. A small NestJS middleware can attach Link headers for every HTML page:

// link-hints.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Injectable()
export class LinkHintsMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  private readonly hints: string[];

  constructor(config: ConfigService) {
    // The build writes hashed asset names to config; never hard-code hashes.
    const css = config.getOrThrow<string>('ASSET_MAIN_CSS');      // e.g. /assets/app.3f9c1a.css
    const imgCdn = config.getOrThrow<string>('IMAGE_CDN_ORIGIN'); // e.g. https://img.shop-cdn.example
    this.hints = [`<${css}>; rel=preload; as=style`, `<${imgCdn}>; rel=preconnect`];
  }

  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction): void {
    if (req.method === 'GET' && req.accepts('html')) {
      res.writeEarlyHints({ link: this.hints }); // 103, only useful if every proxy passes it on
      res.setHeader('Link', this.hints.join(', ')); // also on the final 200 for CDNs that cache hints
    }
    next();
  }
}

What the API must get right for the head to work:

  • The API origin and CORS mode. If the page calls https://api.shop.example.com with fetch and CORS, a preconnect to it needs crossorigin. If you can serve the API from the same origin (for example /api/* routed by the CDN or load balancer), you avoid both the extra connection and CORS preflights entirely (see Part 11 — Networking and HTTP, 11.13).
  • Metadata endpoints must be fast. generateMetadata in Next.js awaits your API before the head can be sent. A 400 ms product lookup there is 400 ms in front of the first byte. Cache it, or share the request with the page body (Next.js memoises identical fetch calls within one render).
  • Know your path to the browser. 103 responses must survive every hop. Some load balancers and CDNs strip or ignore informational responses; check with curl -v --http2 against the real public URL before relying on them.

Production scenario

A travel site served images from images.travel-cdn.example and fonts from a third-party font host. Their p75 LCP on mobile was 3.1 s. A field trace showed two cold connections started only after CSS parsing: one to the font host (310 ms of setup) and one to the image CDN (290 ms). Adding two preconnect tags and self-hosting the fonts removed one origin entirely and moved the other's setup to overlap with the HTML download. p75 LCP dropped to 2.4 s. They then tried adding preload for six images "to be safe"; LCP went back up to 2.7 s because the six images competed for bandwidth with the CSS. They kept a single preload for the actual LCP image.

Failure scenario

A team added <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/brand.woff2" as="font"> to speed up text rendering. The waterfall in DevTools then showed the font downloaded twice, 96 KB each time, and the console said the preloaded resource was not used. The missing piece was crossorigin. Font fetches always use CORS mode, while a preload without crossorigin was made in no-CORS mode, so the cache entries did not match. Every page view wasted 96 KB, and on slow connections the second download delayed text rendering further than before the "optimisation". Adding crossorigin (and type="font/woff2") fixed it. The postmortem added a CI check that runs Lighthouse and fails on the "preloaded resource not used" warning.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Preload without as or with the wrong as: double download, wrong priority.
  • Font preload without crossorigin: double download even on the same origin.
  • Over-preloading: every preload is high priority; preloading eight resources is the same as preloading none, except you also delayed the CSS.
  • Preloading responsive images without imagesrcset: the browser preloads the wrong size, then downloads the right one.
  • Too many preconnects: each costs a TLS handshake on a constrained phone CPU; unused ones are closed after about 10 seconds.
  • Viewport tag missing: mobile renders a shrunken desktop page; media queries never fire.
  • Charset mismatch between header and meta: the header wins, so a server sending charset=iso-8859-1 breaks every non-ASCII character regardless of the meta tag.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the head as a priority list, not a dumping ground. They ask: what does the first paint need (CSS, maybe a font), what is the LCP element, and which origins will the page connect to in the first second? Then they hint exactly those, verify in the waterfall that the hints moved request start times, and remove hints that did not help. They know a hint is a promise to the browser; a broken promise costs bandwidth.

They prefer removing an origin to preconnecting to it: self-hosting fonts, serving the API under the same origin, and putting images on the same CDN as the HTML. To a product manager: "Each extra domain on the page is a phone call the browser has to make before it can fetch anything from there. We can make the call early, but it is better to need fewer calls."

Common mistakes

  • Copy-pasting hints from a blog post without checking that the resources and origins match the page.
  • Preloading everything "for performance", which reorders priorities and slows the first paint.
  • Forgetting crossorigin on font preloads and on preconnects for CORS API calls.
  • Blocking zoom in the viewport tag.
  • Hard-coding hashed asset names in server-side hints instead of reading the build manifest.
  • Leaving <title> identical on every page, which hurts search, tabs, history and screen reader users.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between preload, prefetch and preconnect? Expected answer: preconnect opens a connection (DNS, TCP, TLS) to an origin; preload fetches a specific resource needed for the current page at high priority; prefetch fetches a resource likely needed for a future navigation at low priority. Follow-up: when would preload make a page slower?
  2. Why does a font preload need crossorigin on the same origin? Expected answer: font requests are made in CORS mode; without matching mode, the preload and the real request do not share a cache entry, so it downloads twice.
  3. What does the viewport meta tag do? Expected answer: tells mobile browsers to use the device width as the layout viewport so pages are not shrunk from a 980-pixel canvas and media queries work.
  4. What are 103 Early Hints and what can break them? Expected answer: an informational response with Link headers sent before the final response so the browser can preload and preconnect during server think time; proxies, load balancers or CDNs that do not forward 1xx responses break them.
  5. How do you decide which image gets fetchpriority="high"? Expected answer: the LCP element, identified from a Performance trace or Lighthouse; only one.

Practical exercise

Take a page you own (or a sample Next.js app) and record the Network panel with a slow 4G preset and "Disable cache" ticked. Note the start time of the font request, the LCP image request and the first request to each third-party origin. Add at most one preconnect, one font preload and fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image. Record again.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A before-and-after table of request start times showing each hint moved its target earlier.
  • No resource appears twice in the waterfall, and the console has no "preloaded but not used" warnings.
  • LCP in the Performance panel improves, or you can explain from the waterfall why it did not.
  • You can show, with curl -sI, the Link headers your NestJS middleware adds to an HTML response.

69.4 CSS essentials: box model, cascade, flexbox, grid and responsive design

Concept

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) decides how every element looks and where it sits. Four ideas cover most of what a backend engineer needs to read and review CSS with confidence:

  • The box model. Every element is a rectangle made of content, padding, border and margin.
  • The cascade and specificity. Many rules can target the same element; the cascade is the algorithm that decides which declaration wins.
  • Layout systems. Flexbox arranges items along one direction (a row or a column). Grid arranges items in two dimensions (rows and columns at once).
  • Responsive design. Media queries and container queries change styles depending on the screen or the container size, so one page works on a 360-pixel phone and a 1,920-pixel monitor.

Why does it exist?

HTML gives structure; without CSS every page would be one long column of default-styled text. CSS separates presentation from structure, so the same HTML can be styled differently for phones, printers and dark mode, and so a design system can change a brand colour in one place.

The cascade exists because styles come from several sources at once: the browser's default stylesheet, your site's stylesheets, component libraries, inline styles, and user settings such as a larger default font. Something has to decide who wins, predictably. When engineers do not understand that algorithm, they fight it with !important and ever-longer selectors, and the stylesheet becomes impossible to change safely.

Mental model

Imagine every element as a framed picture on a wall. The picture is the content, the matting around it is padding, the frame is the border, and the empty wall you leave around the frame is margin. "How wide is this picture?" depends on whether you measure only the picture (content-box) or the whole thing including matting and frame (border-box).

The cascade is a set of house rules with a clear chain of authority. The museum's default rules (browser styles) apply unless the curator (your stylesheet) overrides them; a specific note on one picture beats a general note for a whole room; and among equally specific notes, the latest one wins.

Flexbox is a bookshelf: books line up in one row and you decide how they share the leftover space. Grid is a chessboard: you define rows and columns first, then place pieces on squares.

How it works

1. The box model. By default, width sets only the content width. A card with width: 300px; padding: 16px; border: 1px solid is actually 334 pixels wide, which is why layouts overflow by a few pixels. Nearly every modern stylesheet starts with:

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; } /* width now includes padding and border */

Two more rules trip people up. Vertical margins between block elements collapse: a 24-pixel bottom margin above a 16-pixel top margin produces a 24-pixel gap, not 40. And display decides the box type: block takes the full width and starts on a new line, inline flows inside text and ignores width and height, inline-block flows like text but accepts a size, and display: flex or grid turns an element into a layout container for its children.

2. The cascade. When several declarations set the same property on the same element, the browser decides in this order:

  1. Origin and importance: browser defaults, then user styles, then author (your) styles; !important declarations reverse that order.
  2. Inline styles (style="...") beat stylesheet rules.
  3. Cascade layers (@layer): later-declared layers beat earlier ones, and unlayered styles beat all layered ones.
  4. Specificity: a score of three numbers (IDs, classes and attributes and pseudo-classes, element types and pseudo-elements), compared left to right.
  5. Order of appearance: the last declaration wins.

Specificity examples:

Selector Specificity (id, class, type) Notes
button (0, 0, 1) Element type
.btn (0, 1, 0) One class beats any number of types
.checkout .btn.primary (0, 3, 0) Three classes
#pay-now (1, 0, 0) One id beats any number of classes
:where(.card) .title (0, 1, 0) :where() contributes zero
:is(#a, .b) span (1, 0, 1) :is() takes the most specific argument

Inheritance is separate from the cascade: some properties (color, font-family, line-height) inherit from the parent when nothing sets them; others (margin, border, width) do not.

3. Flexbox and grid.

/* Flexbox: one direction. A header with logo left, cart right. */
.site-header { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 16px; }

/* Grid: two dimensions. A product listing that fits as many 220px+ columns as possible. */
.product-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
  gap: 24px;
}

/* Grid with named areas: the product page layout. */
.product-page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 380px;
  grid-template-areas: "gallery buybox" "details buybox";
}
.gallery { grid-area: gallery; } .buybox { grid-area: buybox; } .details { grid-area: details; }
Need Use Why
Items in a row or column, sizes driven by content (nav bar, button group, toolbar) Flexbox One axis; items share space with flex: 1, flex-shrink, flex-wrap
Rows and columns that must align across items (product grid, dashboard, page layout) Grid Tracks are defined by the container, so items line up in both directions
Centre one thing in a box Either: display: grid; place-items: center Shortest reliable recipe
Text wrapping around an image Floats The only remaining good use of float
Overlays, badges, sticky headers position: absolute, sticky, fixed Out of normal flow

4. Responsive design. A media query applies rules when the viewport (or device) matches a condition. Mobile-first stylesheets write the small-screen styles as the default and add complexity as the screen grows:

.product-page { display: block; }                       /* phones: one column */
@media (min-width: 768px) {                              /* tablets and up */
  .product-page { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 380px; }
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {               /* respect OS accessibility setting */
  * { animation-duration: 0.01ms !important; transition-duration: 0.01ms !important; }
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --bg: #111; --fg: #eee; } }

Container queries (supported in all evergreen browsers since 2023) apply rules based on the size of a containing element rather than the viewport, which is what component libraries usually want: a product card that switches to a horizontal layout when its column is wider than 400 pixels, wherever it is placed.

.card-slot { container-type: inline-size; }
@container (min-width: 400px) { .product-card { display: flex; gap: 16px; } }

Relative units do much of the responsive work: rem (relative to the root font size, respects user font settings), %, vw and vh (viewport width and height), dvh (dynamic viewport height, which accounts for mobile browser toolbars appearing and disappearing), fr (a fraction of free grid space) and clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 1.5rem) for fluid type.

flowchart TB
    decl["Competing declarations for one property"] --> o{"Origin and importance"}
    o -->|"tie"| inl{"Inline style?"}
    inl -->|"tie"| lay{"Cascade layer order"}
    lay -->|"tie"| spec{"Specificity: ids, classes, types"}
    spec -->|"tie"| ord["Order of appearance: last wins"]
    o -->|"decided"| win["Winning value"]
    inl -->|"decided"| win
    lay -->|"decided"| win
    spec -->|"decided"| win
    ord --> win

Practical example

An order-history table looks fine on desktop but overflows horizontally on phones, so the whole page scrolls sideways. In DevTools, the Elements panel's Computed tab shows the table's min-width is 920 pixels because each of its eight columns has white-space: nowrap. The fix is responsive, not a JavaScript hack: below 768 pixels, render each order as a stacked card using grid (grid-template-columns: auto 1fr), keeping the table markup for larger screens. Alternatively, wrap the table in a container with overflow-x: auto so only the table scrolls and the page does not.

React / Next.js example

In a Next.js 14 app, CSS Modules give each component locally scoped class names, which removes most specificity fights because classes never collide across components.

// components/ProductCard.tsx  (Next.js 14, CSS Modules)
import Image from 'next/image';
import styles from './ProductCard.module.css';

export type ProductCardProps = {
  name: string; price: string;
  image: { url: string; width: number; height: number; alt: string };
};

export function ProductCard({ name, price, image }: ProductCardProps) {
  return (
    <article className={styles.card}>
      {/* width and height let the browser reserve space before the image loads (see 75.5) */}
      <Image src={image.url} width={image.width} height={image.height} alt={image.alt}
             sizes="(max-width: 600px) 50vw, 220px" className={styles.thumb} />
      <h3 className={styles.name}>{name}</h3>
      <p className={styles.price}>{price}</p>
    </article>
  );
}
/* components/ProductCard.module.css  -- compiled to unique names like ProductCard_card__x7Kq2 */
.card { display: grid; gap: 8px; padding: 12px; border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; }
.thumb { width: 100%; height: auto; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; object-fit: cover; }
.name { font-size: 1rem; line-height: 1.4; display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 2;
        -webkit-box-orient: vertical; overflow: hidden; }   /* two lines max, never grows */
.price { font-weight: 600; }

Backend side (NestJS)

CSS can only reserve the right space if it knows the dimensions of what is coming. The API should give the frontend the facts it needs to lay out content before every byte arrives:

// product-image.dto.ts and the listing response
import { ApiProperty } from '@nestjs/swagger';

export class ProductImageDto {
  @ApiProperty() url!: string;            // CDN URL, already resized variants
  @ApiProperty() width!: number;          // intrinsic pixel width, from the upload pipeline
  @ApiProperty() height!: number;         // intrinsic pixel height
  @ApiProperty() alt!: string;            // human-written alt text (see 75.9)
}

export class ProductCardDto {
  @ApiProperty() id!: string;
  @ApiProperty() name!: string;
  @ApiProperty() priceMinor!: number;     // integer minor units: 1249900 = Rs 12,499.00
  @ApiProperty() currency!: string;
  @ApiProperty({ type: ProductImageDto }) image!: ProductImageDto;
  @ApiProperty({ maxLength: 120 }) badge!: string | null; // null, never a missing key
}
  • Store intrinsic image dimensions at upload time (read them once with an image library in the upload worker) and return them in every product response. Without them, the frontend cannot set width and height or aspect-ratio, and every image causes a layout shift.
  • Bound text lengths in the API contract (product names at most 120 characters, for example) so designers can size containers and line-clamp safely.
  • Return stable shapes. Always send badge: null rather than omitting the key; a component that sometimes renders a badge and sometimes does not should still reserve the same space, and that is much easier when the contract is explicit.

Production scenario

An e-commerce company's design system had grown for four years in one global stylesheet of 410 KB uncompressed (58 KB with Brotli). The CSS Overview and Coverage panels in DevTools showed that 81 % of the rules were unused on the product page. Style recalculation for the product page took 34 ms on a mid-range phone, partly because of selectors like .page .content div > ul li a span. Moving to CSS Modules per component and a small global layer brought product page CSS to 14 KB compressed and style recalculation to 9 ms. Because CSS is render-blocking, the smaller file also moved first paint 180 ms earlier on slow 4G.

Failure scenario

On a Friday afternoon, a developer fixed a misaligned button in the admin panel by adding .btn { margin-top: 4px !important; } to the shared stylesheet. The admin panel and the customer checkout shared that stylesheet. On Monday, the payment page's "Pay now" button, which used a .btn class inside a fixed-height footer, was pushed 4 pixels down and clipped by overflow: hidden. On some Android phones the visible part of the button was 6 pixels tall. Payment conversion on Android dropped 7 % over the weekend before anyone noticed. The fix took one minute. The prevention took longer: scoped CSS per app, a lint rule banning !important outside a utilities layer, and visual regression tests on the checkout (Part 77 — Frontend Testing and Quality).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • content-box surprises: padding added to a width: 100% element overflows its parent unless box-sizing: border-box is set.
