  • Margin collapse: spacing between sections is smaller than expected; flex and grid containers do not collapse their children's margins.
  • !important wars: each fix requires a stronger override, and the cascade becomes unpredictable.
  • Long unbroken strings: an order id or email address without spaces overflows a narrow card; use overflow-wrap: anywhere.
  • Flex items not shrinking: a flex child's default min-width: auto prevents it from shrinking below its content width; set min-width: 0 on the child that contains long text.
  • 100vh on mobile: includes the area under the browser toolbar, so "full-screen" panels are cut off; use 100dvh.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior does not try to memorise CSS; they understand its algorithms well enough to predict results and debug with DevTools' Computed tab, which shows the winning declaration and every overridden one. They value scoping (CSS Modules, a design-system component library, cascade layers) over clever selectors, because the real cost of CSS is the fear of changing it.

They pick flexbox for one-dimensional alignment, grid for page and listing layouts, and they review layout code by asking "what happens with a 200-character product name, a missing image, a 320-pixel screen and a user with 150 % font size?" They also see the backend's role: an API that supplies image dimensions, bounded strings and stable shapes is what makes a robust layout possible.

Common mistakes

  • Using !important to win a specificity battle instead of fixing the selector or using a layer.
  • Styling by ID or deep descendant chains, which creates high specificity that nobody can override cleanly.
  • Fixed pixel heights on text containers, which clip content when text wraps or fonts are larger.
  • Designing desktop-first and squeezing down, leaving phones with overflow and tiny tap targets.
  • Forgetting min-width: 0 on flex children with long text.

Interview questions

  1. Explain the cascade. In what order does the browser decide which declaration wins? Expected answer: origin and importance, inline styles, cascade layers, specificity, then order of appearance. Follow-up: how do :where() and @layer help a design system?
  2. What is the difference between content-box and border-box? Expected answer: whether width includes padding and border; border-box makes sizes predictable.
  3. When would you choose grid over flexbox? Expected answer: when items must align in two dimensions or the container defines the tracks; flexbox for one-axis, content-driven arrangements.
  4. What is the difference between a media query and a container query? Expected answer: media queries respond to the viewport or device; container queries respond to the size of a containing element, which suits reusable components.

Practical exercise

Build an order-history page that renders a table at 768 pixels and above and stacked cards below, using only CSS (one HTML structure, or a component that renders the same data with a media or container query). Feed it data from a NestJS endpoint that includes one order with a 60-character unbroken reference string.

Acceptance criteria:

  • No horizontal page scroll at 360, 768 and 1,280 pixels wide (check with DevTools device toolbar).
  • The long reference wraps without overflowing.
  • Setting the browser default font size to 24 px does not clip any text.
  • No !important in your stylesheet.

69.5 Layout shift: why a CSS change moves the page

Concept

A layout shift happens when an element that is already visible changes position between two frames without the user asking for it. The text you were reading jumps down 200 pixels; the "Cancel order" button moves into the place where "Confirm" was a moment ago. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) is the Core Web Vital that measures it. A score at or under 0.1 is "good"; above 0.25 is "poor".

Layout shifts are caused by content whose size the browser did not know when it first laid out the page: images and videos without dimensions, ads and embeds, late-arriving banners, web fonts that render text at a different size, and content inserted above what the user is looking at. They are a direct consequence of the pipeline in 69.1: every time new information arrives, layout runs again, and anything below the change moves.

Why does it exist?

The metric exists because layout shift is not just ugly; it causes wrong actions. Users tap the wrong button, lose their reading position, or dismiss a dialog they meant to accept. On a checkout page, a shift can turn "Apply coupon" into "Place order". Google uses CLS as a ranking signal and in the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX), which makes it a business metric as well as a user experience one.

The underlying mechanism exists because HTML and CSS were designed for documents whose size flows from content. If the browser does not know an image is 800 by 800 pixels, it lays it out as 0 pixels tall, then lays everything out again when the image header arrives.

Mental model

Imagine reading a printed menu while a waiter keeps sliding new pages into the middle of it. Every insertion pushes the page you were reading further down. If the waiter had left blank, correctly sized pages in place from the start, nothing would move when the real pages arrived. Reserving space is leaving those blank pages.

How it works

  1. The browser lays out the page with what it knows. An <img> without width, height or an aspect-ratio gets a height of zero until its size is known.
  2. New information arrives: an image's header reveals its dimensions, a font finishes loading, JavaScript inserts a "Free delivery over Rs 499" banner, an API response fills an empty list.
  3. Layout runs again and elements move.
  4. For each frame, the browser computes a layout shift score for unexpected movement: impact fraction (how much of the viewport the moving elements cover, before and after) multiplied by distance fraction (how far they moved, relative to the viewport's largest dimension). A banner that pushes content covering 75 % of the viewport down by 25 % of its height scores 0.75 multiplied by 0.25, about 0.19, already "needs improvement" from one event.
  5. Shifts within 500 ms of a discrete user input (click, tap, key press) are excluded, because the user caused them. Scrolling does not count as input for this purpose.
  6. CLS is the largest session window of shifts: shifts less than 1 second apart are grouped, each window lasts at most 5 seconds, and the worst window is the page's CLS.
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Parser
    participant L as Layout
    participant N as Network
    participant JS as Script
    P->>L: first layout, hero img height 0
    L-->>P: price at y 120 px
    N-->>L: hero image header, 800 by 800
    L->>L: relayout, price moves to y 520 px, shift
    N-->>L: web font loaded, wider glyphs
    L->>L: title wraps to 2 lines, shift
    JS->>L: insert promo banner at top
    L->>L: everything moves down 48 px, shift

The common causes and their fixes:

Cause Why it shifts Fix
Image or video without dimensions Height unknown until the file header arrives width and height attributes (the browser derives aspect-ratio), or CSS aspect-ratio
Ad slots, iframes, embeds Third party decides size late Reserve a min-height for the slot; never collapse an empty slot above content
Content injected above existing content Banners, cookie notices, "app install" bars Reserve space in the server-rendered HTML, overlay with position: fixed, or insert below the fold
Web fonts Fallback and web font have different metrics, text rewraps font-display: optional, or a size-matched fallback with size-adjust (Next.js next/font does this)
Client-rendered data Empty container, then a list of 20 items Skeletons with the same height as real content; or render the data on the server
Animations of layout properties Changing top or height moves neighbours Animate transform instead; transforms do not affect layout of other elements
Late CSS A non-blocking or lazily loaded stylesheet restyles visible content Keep above-the-fold styles in the render-blocking CSS

Practical example

A product listing page shows 24 cards. Each image is an <img src> with CSS width: 100% and no height. On a slow connection, the page first renders 24 cards each about 80 pixels tall (title plus price), then grows each card by about 220 pixels as images arrive, in random order. Measured CLS: 0.42. Adding width="800" height="800" to each <img> (values from the API) plus height: auto in CSS lets the browser compute the aspect ratio before loading. CLS drops to 0.02. No JavaScript changed.

React / Next.js example

Two patterns cover most of it in React and Next.js 14: next/image (which requires width and height, or fill inside a sized container) and skeletons that match the final size.

// app/orders/OrderList.tsx  (client component, React 18)
'use client';
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

type Order = { id: string; placedAt: string; totalLabel: string; status: string };
const ROW_HEIGHT = 72; // matches .order-row min-height in CSS, so skeleton and data are the same size

export function OrderList() {
  const [orders, setOrders] = useState<Order[] | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const ctrl = new AbortController();
    fetch('/api/v1/orders?limit=10', { signal: ctrl.signal })
      .then((r) => r.json())
      .then((body: { items: Order[] }) => setOrders(body.items))
      .catch(() => { /* aborted on unmount, or show an error state; Part 72 covers this properly */ });
    return () => ctrl.abort();
  }, []);

  if (!orders) {
    // Reserve the space of 10 rows: when data arrives, nothing below this list moves.
    return <ul aria-busy="true" style={{ minHeight: ROW_HEIGHT * 10 }}>
      {Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => <li key={i} className="order-row skeleton" />)}
    </ul>;
  }
  return <ul>{orders.map((o) => (
    <li key={o.id} className="order-row">{o.id} {o.placedAt} {o.totalLabel} {o.status}</li>
  ))}</ul>;
}

The better fix for data that is known at request time is not to fetch it on the client at all: render the list in a server component so it is in the first HTML and never shifts. Part 72 — Client State, Data Fetching and Caching covers the client-side cases properly with TanStack Query.

For fonts, next/font generates a fallback @font-face with size-adjust, ascent-override and descent-override computed from the real font, so swapping from the fallback to the web font barely moves any text.

Backend side (NestJS)

Most layout shift fixes need information only the backend has, at the moment the HTML is generated:

  • Image dimensions in every response (69.4). This is the single most effective backend contribution to CLS.
  • Know the page size up front. A list endpoint that returns a predictable limit lets the frontend reserve the right number of rows. Return totalCount or hasMore so the frontend knows whether to reserve space for a "Load more" button.
  • Decide personalised slots on the server. If a "Free delivery unlocked" banner depends on the user's cart, expose it in the same request that renders the page (or a BFF call made during server rendering) instead of a separate client-side call that inserts the banner after first paint.
// page-slots.controller.ts: one call returns every slot the page must reserve
import { Controller, Get, Req, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request } from 'express';
import { OptionalAuthGuard } from '../auth/optional-auth.guard';
import { PromoService } from './promo.service';

@Controller('v1/page-slots')
export class PageSlotsController {
  constructor(private readonly promos: PromoService) {}

  @Get('product')
  @UseGuards(OptionalAuthGuard)
  async productSlots(@Req() req: Request & { user?: { id: string } }) {
    const banner = await this.promos.bannerFor(req.user?.id); // ~3 ms, Redis-backed
    return {
      // Always present, so the page can reserve 48 px even when there is nothing to show.
      topBanner: banner ? { text: banner.text, href: banner.href } : null,
      topBannerHeightPx: 48,
    };
  }
}

Production scenario

A news-style marketplace homepage had a CLS of 0.31 at p75 in CrUX. The Performance panel's Layout Shifts track showed three clusters: a cookie consent bar inserted at the top by a consent manager script (0.12), 12 product images without dimensions (0.11) and a font swap on the headline (0.06). The team overlaid the consent bar with position: fixed at the bottom, added dimensions from the API to every image, and switched the headline font to font-display: optional with a metric-matched fallback. CLS dropped to 0.04 at p75 within the 28-day CrUX window, and the click-through rate on the first product row rose 3 %, because users stopped tapping the wrong card.

Failure scenario

A food-delivery app added a "Your order is arriving in 5 minutes" live banner at the top of the restaurant menu page, inserted by a WebSocket message. On busy evenings the banner appeared while users were scrolling and tapping "Add" buttons. Each insertion shifted the entire menu down 56 pixels. Support received complaints of wrong items in carts, and the backend saw a spike in DELETE /cart/items within 3 seconds of POST /cart/items, about 4,000 per evening. The fix moved the banner into a fixed-position toast that overlays the bottom of the screen without affecting layout. Undo-within-3-seconds requests fell by 85 %.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shifts after user input are excluded only for 500 ms: an accordion that opens after a 700 ms API call counts as an unexpected shift.
  • Infinite scroll: appending items below the viewport is fine; inserting "new items" at the top while the user reads is not.
  • Lazy-loaded images above the fold have no space reserved if dimensions are missing, and arrive late too, so they shift twice as visibly.
  • Responsive images with different aspect ratios per breakpoint (art direction with <picture>) need per-source dimensions, or the reserved box is wrong.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats unreserved space as a bug, not a polish item. In code review they check every image for dimensions, every async slot for a reserved size and every insertion for its position relative to the user's view. They know lab tools (Lighthouse) only see shifts during load, while users experience shifts during the whole visit, so they check field data from real-user monitoring or CrUX. They push personalisation decisions to the server so the first HTML is already the final layout, and they ask the backend for the dimensions and stable shapes that make reservation possible.

Common mistakes

  • Omitting width and height on images because "CSS sets the width".
  • Inserting banners and notices at the top of the page after first paint.
  • Skeletons that are a different height from the real content, which only moves the shift later.
  • Animating height for expand and collapse instead of animating transform or using grid-template-rows: 0fr to 1fr transitions inside a reserved container.

Interview questions

  1. What is CLS and how is a layout shift scored? Expected answer: the largest session window of unexpected layout shifts; each shift scores impact fraction multiplied by distance fraction; shifts within 500 ms of user input are excluded; good is at most 0.1. Follow-up: why does lab CLS often differ from field CLS?
  2. Name four causes of layout shift and the fix for each. Expected answer: images without dimensions, late-injected content, web fonts, ad and embed slots; dimensions or aspect-ratio, reserved space or overlays, size-matched fallbacks or font-display: optional, min-height slots.
  3. How can the backend reduce CLS? Expected answer: return image dimensions, stable response shapes, predictable page sizes, and decide personalised content during server rendering.
  4. Why does animating transform not cause layout shift while animating top on a relatively positioned element can? Expected answer: transforms do not affect the layout of other elements and are not counted as layout shifts; changes that alter geometry can move other elements.

Practical exercise

Create a product listing page that fetches 24 products from a NestJS endpoint and renders cards with images, a top promo banner from a separate endpoint, and a custom web font. Measure CLS with the Performance panel (Layout Shifts track) and Lighthouse under slow 4G and 4x CPU throttling.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Starting CLS is above 0.1 and you can name each shift's source from the Layout Shifts track.
  • After adding dimensions from the API, reserving the banner slot and fixing the font fallback, CLS is under 0.05.
  • The DevTools Rendering drawer's "Layout Shift Regions" option shows no blue flashes during load.

69.6 Script loading: classic, defer, async and modules

Concept

How a <script> tag is written decides when its file is downloaded, when it runs, and whether the HTML parser has to stop for it. There are four forms that matter:

  • Classic script <script src="app.js">: download and execute immediately, and the parser waits for both.
  • defer <script defer src="app.js">: download in parallel with parsing, execute after the document is parsed, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded.
  • async <script async src="widget.js">: download in parallel, execute as soon as it arrives, in whatever order downloads finish, pausing the parser while it runs.
  • Module <script type="module" src="app.js">: an ES module with import and export; deferred by default, can also be async, always strict mode, fetched with CORS.

Why does it exist?

Classic scripts block because of document.write(). A script can write raw HTML into the stream at the point where it appears, so the parser cannot safely continue past a script it has not run. That made sense in 1997; today almost no script needs it, but the browser must still assume it might. defer and async exist so you can tell the browser "this script will not document.write, keep parsing". Modules exist to give the browser a native dependency system instead of global variables and concatenated files.

Mental model

Imagine a tour guide (the parser) walking a group through a museum, reading each placard aloud. A classic script is a placard that says "stop and wait here until the curator arrives from the other building and gives a speech". defer is "the curator will give a speech at the end of the tour; keep walking". async is "the curator will interrupt the tour the moment they arrive, wherever you are". A module is a deferred curator who brings a list of colleagues who must also arrive first.

How it works

gantt
    title Script loading relative to HTML parsing
    dateFormat X
    axisFormat %s
    section Classic
    Parse HTML      :a1, 0, 3
    Download script :a2, 3, 7
    Execute script  :a3, 7, 9
    Parse rest      :a4, 9, 12
    section Defer
    Parse HTML      :b1, 0, 8
    Download script :b2, 2, 6
    Execute after parse :b3, 8, 10
    section Async
    Parse HTML      :c1, 0, 5
    Download script :c2, 2, 5
    Execute on arrival :c3, 5, 7
    Parse rest      :c4, 7, 9
Form Blocks parser Execution order When it runs Good for
Classic in <head> Yes, download and run Document order Immediately Almost nothing today; tiny inline config only
Classic at end of <body> Yes, but little left to parse Document order When reached Legacy pages
defer No Document order After parsing, before DOMContentLoaded Your application bundle
async Only while executing Arrival order, unpredictable As soon as downloaded Independent third-party scripts (analytics)
type="module" No (deferred by default) Document order After parsing Modern application code
type="module" async Only while executing Arrival order As soon as the module graph is ready Independent modules
Inline <script> Yes (waits for pending stylesheets) Document order Immediately Small bootstrapping data; defer is ignored on inline classic scripts

Details that matter in production:

  1. A classic script waits for earlier stylesheets. It might read computed styles, so it cannot run until preceding CSS is parsed. A slow CSS file therefore also delays a classic script and the rest of the parse.
  2. Module graphs are discovered lazily. The browser fetches app.js, parses it, finds import './cart.js', fetches that, finds its imports, and so on: one network round trip per level of the graph. That is why bundlers still exist (Part 70 — Frontend Tooling and TypeScript in the Browser) and why <link rel="modulepreload"> helps.
  3. Modules are fetched with CORS. A module served from a CDN on another origin needs Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the response, and must be served with a JavaScript MIME type (text/javascript). Browsers refuse to execute a module served as text/plain or application/octet-stream, with a "Strict MIME type checking is enforced for module scripts" console error.
  4. Download is not the only cost. A 160 KB compressed bundle is often 550 to 650 KB of JavaScript after decompression. On a mid-range phone, parse and compile plus first execution of that much code commonly takes 400 to 900 ms of main-thread time. Network throttling alone hides this; CPU throttling reveals it.
  5. Dynamic import() loads a module on demand and returns a promise. Frameworks use it for code splitting by route or component.

Practical example

A product page has four scripts: the app bundle, a vendor chunk, an analytics script from a third party, and a chat widget. The right arrangement is: app and vendor as type="module" (or defer, in order, vendor first) so they never block parsing and run in dependency order; analytics as async because nothing depends on it; the chat widget loaded by your own code after the load event or on the first user interaction, because it is 300 KB of JavaScript that 2 % of visitors use. That alone moved the chat widget's 280 ms long task out of the window where users first try to tap.

React / Next.js example

Next.js generates and orders its own framework and page scripts. For anything you add, next/script (Next.js 13 and 14) controls the loading strategy explicitly:

// app/layout.tsx or a page  (Next.js 14 App Router)
import Script from 'next/script';

export function ThirdPartyScripts() {
  return (
    <>
      {/* afterInteractive (default): injected after hydration starts; fine for analytics */}
      <Script src="https://analytics.example/a.js" strategy="afterInteractive" />

      {/* lazyOnload: injected during browser idle time after load; for chat and feedback widgets */}
      <Script src="https://chat.example/widget.js" strategy="lazyOnload"
              onLoad={() => console.info('chat widget ready')} />

      {/* beforeInteractive: only in the root layout, for scripts that must run before hydration,
          such as a consent manager. Use rarely: it delays your app. */}
    </>
  );
}

For your own heavy components, next/dynamic (or React.lazy with <Suspense> in plain React 18) splits them into separate chunks:

import dynamic from 'next/dynamic';
// The 3D product viewer (220 KB) is only fetched when this component renders, never on first load.
const ProductViewer3D = dynamic(() => import('./ProductViewer3D'), {
  ssr: false, loading: () => <p>Loading 3D view...</p>,
});

Backend side (NestJS)

When NestJS (or the same container as your API) serves the built frontend assets, three headers decide whether scripts load quickly and at all:

// main.ts: serving a built SPA from NestJS
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import type { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);

  // Hashed files (app.81bd2e.js) never change content: cache for a year, immutable.
  app.useStaticAssets(join(__dirname, '..', 'web', 'assets'), {
    prefix: '/assets/',
    maxAge: '365d',
    immutable: true,
    setHeaders: (res, path) => {
      if (path.endsWith('.js')) res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/javascript; charset=utf-8');
      // Only needed if pages on another origin load these as modules:
      res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', 'https://shop.example.com');
    },
  });

  // index.html must always be revalidated, or users keep pointing at old hashed bundles.
  app.useStaticAssets(join(__dirname, '..', 'web'), { index: false, maxAge: 0, etag: true });
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();
  • Content-Type: text/javascript for every .js and .mjs file. A misconfigured static server or object store serving application/octet-stream breaks module scripts completely.
  • Long-lived immutable caching only for content-hashed filenames, and no-cache (or max-age=0 with an ETag) for the HTML that references them (see Part 11 — Networking and HTTP, 11.11). Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends covers what happens to users on the old version during a deploy.
  • CORS on cross-origin modules: if the CDN origin differs from the page origin, module scripts need Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and fonts need it too.

Production scenario

A ticketing site moved its application bundle from a classic <script> at the end of <body> to type="module" in the <head>, plus modulepreload for its three largest chunks. On a slow 4G profile, the bundle request now started at 540 ms (when the head arrived) instead of 1,100 ms (when the parser reached the end of the body), and hydration finished 480 ms earlier at p75. Separately, they moved a session-replay vendor script from synchronous to async and then to "load after first interaction", which removed a 190 ms long task from the first second.

Failure scenario

At 09:05 a platform team migrated static assets from NGINX to an object storage bucket behind the CDN. The upload script did not set content types, so every .js object was stored as application/octet-stream. The site's HTML used <script type="module">. Within minutes, every page rendered its server-rendered HTML and then nothing worked: no add to cart, no search, no menus. The console showed "Failed to load module script: Expected a JavaScript module script but the server responded with a MIME type of application/octet-stream". Backend dashboards were green; API traffic simply dropped by 70 %, because the client code that made API calls never ran. The fix was re-uploading with explicit Content-Type and purging the CDN. The lesson: a drop in API traffic with no errors is often a frontend that failed to boot.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • async scripts that depend on each other run in random order and fail intermittently, depending on which one downloads first.
  • Mixing defer and inline scripts: an inline script that uses a library loaded with defer runs before the library exists.
  • document.write from a third-party script loaded asynchronously is ignored by browsers, with a console warning, which silently breaks old ad tags.
  • A module that throws during evaluation stops every module that imports it; one bad import can take down the whole app.
  • Chunk load errors after a deploy: an old tab requests chunk.a1b2.js, which no longer exists, and gets the HTML 404 page; Part 78 covers keeping old assets around.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior sees every script tag as a scheduling decision with a cost in download, parse, compile and execution time, and every third-party script as a dependency on someone else's uptime running with full access to the page. Their defaults: application code as modules or defer, third parties async or deferred until interaction, nothing synchronous in the head. They budget JavaScript in kilobytes and main-thread milliseconds, not just requests. They also make sure the backend serves scripts with the right MIME type, caching and CORS, because those failures break the page while every server metric stays green.

Common mistakes

  • Putting a classic <script src> in <head> "so it runs early".
  • Using async for scripts that depend on each other.
  • Loading heavy widgets on page load when they are only used after a click.
  • Measuring JavaScript cost by bytes over the wire only, ignoring parse and execution on slow CPUs.
  • Serving assets without correct Content-Type or with long caching on unhashed file names.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between defer and async? Expected answer: both download in parallel without blocking the parser; defer runs after parsing in document order, async runs on arrival in any order and pauses the parser while executing. Follow-up: which one for an analytics script, and which for your app bundle?
  2. Why do module scripts fail with a MIME type error and how do you fix it on the backend? Expected answer: browsers enforce a JavaScript MIME type for modules; set Content-Type: text/javascript on the server, CDN or object store.
  3. Why is a 160 KB script slower on a phone than a 160 KB image? Expected answer: the script must be decompressed, parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread; the image is decoded off the main thread and does not block interaction.
  4. What does modulepreload solve? Expected answer: the round-trip-per-level discovery of an ES module graph, by fetching and compiling dependencies early.

Practical exercise

Create a page with three scripts: a.js logs and sets window.A, b.js uses window.A, and c.js is independent. Load them as classic, defer, async and modules, and use the Network panel's throttling plus the "Block request URL" option to delay or block each.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A written table of observed execution order for each form, matching the rules above.
  • You can reproduce the async race where b.js fails, and fix it.
  • Serving c.js as a module with Content-Type: text/plain from a NestJS route reproduces the MIME type error, and fixing the header resolves it.

69.7 The main thread, the browser event loop and long tasks

Concept

Each page (more precisely, each renderer and its frames) has one main thread. It runs your JavaScript, handles input events, computes styles, runs layout and paints. While it is busy with one thing, it cannot do any of the others. A long task is any task that occupies the main thread for more than 50 ms. During a long task, clicks wait, typing lags and animations that need the main thread freeze.

The browser schedules work on the main thread with an event loop, like Node.js does (see Part 10 — Operating Systems and the Node.js Runtime, 10.16 and 10.17). The difference is that the browser's loop also has to produce frames: between tasks it decides whether to render, and rendering competes for the same thread as your code.

Why does it exist?

JavaScript was designed to run on the same thread as the DOM so that scripts never see a half-updated page and never need locks. That simplicity is why the DOM is easy to program and why one slow function can freeze a page. The event loop is how the browser shares that single thread fairly between network callbacks, timers, user input and rendering. Long tasks are the measurable symptom of the sharing going wrong, and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) is the Core Web Vital that measures how badly it hurts users: the time from a click or key press to the next frame that shows a response, with "good" at or under 200 ms.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant with a single chef who also has to plate and send every dish. Orders (tasks) arrive on tickets. After each ticket, the chef must immediately handle any "quick follow-ups" pinned to it (microtasks), and roughly every 16 ms a runner shouts "plates out!" (a rendering opportunity). If the chef spends 400 ms on one elaborate dish, nothing goes out, new customers wave for attention (input events) and are ignored, and the dining room sees a frozen kitchen. The fix is never "a faster chef" alone; it is splitting the elaborate dish into steps so the runner can take plates out in between, or handing prep work to a kitchen assistant in another room (a Web Worker).

How it works

One turn of the browser event loop:

  1. Pick one task from a task queue: a parsed HTML chunk, a setTimeout callback, a fetch response callback, a click event handler, a message from a worker. Browsers keep several queues and prioritise input over timers.
  2. Run it to completion. Nothing can interrupt synchronous JavaScript.
  3. Microtask checkpoint. Run every queued microtask (promise reactions, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver callbacks), including microtasks queued by microtasks, until the queue is empty.
  4. Maybe render. If it is time for a new frame (about every 16.7 ms at 60 Hz) and something changed, run the rendering steps: requestAnimationFrame callbacks, style, layout, paint, then hand off to the compositor. If the page is hidden, rendering is skipped.
  5. Idle. If there is time left before the next frame and nothing urgent, run requestIdleCallback callbacks.
  6. Repeat.
flowchart TB
    task["Run one task to completion: event handler, timer, fetch callback"] --> micro["Drain all microtasks: promise then, queueMicrotask"]
    micro --> frame{"Time for a frame and something changed?"}
    frame -->|"yes"| raf["requestAnimationFrame callbacks"]
    raf --> render["Style, Layout, Paint, then Compositor"]
    render --> idle{"Spare time before next frame?"}
    frame -->|"no"| idle
    idle -->|"yes"| ric["requestIdleCallback"]
    idle -->|"no"| task
    ric --> task

Browser versus Node.js:

Aspect Browser Node.js
Task sources DOM events, input, timers, network, postMessage, parsing libuv phases: timers, poll (I/O), check (setImmediate), close
Microtasks Promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver Promises, queueMicrotask, plus process.nextTick which runs before promises
Rendering Built into the loop, about every 16.7 ms None
Main cost of blocking Frozen UI, bad INP All requests on that process stall, latency spikes for every user
setTimeout minimum Clamped to 4 ms after 5 nested levels; throttled to 1 s or more in background tabs About 1 ms, no nesting clamp
Escape hatch for CPU work Web Workers worker_threads
Exclusive APIs requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback setImmediate, process.nextTick

The most important shared rule: microtasks starve everything. A promise chain that keeps scheduling more promise work never gives the loop a chance to render or handle input, in both runtimes. In the browser, that looks like a frozen tab; in Node, like an unresponsive server.

What creates long tasks in real pages:

  • Hydration: React walking the whole server-rendered tree, attaching event handlers, often 150 to 600 ms on phones for a large page.
  • Parsing big JSON: JSON.parse of a 5 MB response takes roughly 40 to 80 ms on a mid-range phone, plus the time to render what it contains.
  • Rendering large lists: 2,000 table rows produce 2,000 component renders plus a big layout.
  • Third-party scripts: tag managers, A/B testing, chat widgets.
  • Synchronous storage: localStorage.getItem on a large value blocks (69.8).

Measuring them:

// Report long tasks and long animation frames from real users (Chromium browsers).
const longTasks = new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (entry.duration > 100) {
      navigator.sendBeacon('/api/v1/rum/long-task', JSON.stringify({
        page: location.pathname, durationMs: Math.round(entry.duration),
        startMs: Math.round(entry.startTime),
      }));
    }
  }
});
longTasks.observe({ type: 'longtask', buffered: true });
// 'long-animation-frame' (Chrome 123+) also attributes the time to specific scripts.

Breaking up long tasks: yield to the event loop between chunks of work so input and rendering can run.

// Yield control so pending input and rendering can run between chunks.
function yieldToMain(): Promise<void> {
  // scheduler.yield() exists in Chromium (Chrome 129+); fall back to a macrotask elsewhere.
  const s = (globalThis as { scheduler?: { yield?: () => Promise<void> } }).scheduler;
  if (s?.yield) return s.yield();
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 0));
}

export async function indexOrdersForSearch(orders: { id: string; items: string[] }[]) {
  const index = new Map<string, string[]>();
  let lastYield = performance.now();
  for (const order of orders) {
    for (const item of order.items) {
      const key = item.toLowerCase();
      index.set(key, [...(index.get(key) ?? []), order.id]);
    }
    if (performance.now() - lastYield > 40) {   // keep each slice under the 50 ms long-task line
      await yieldToMain();
      lastYield = performance.now();
    }
  }
  return index;
}

Note that await Promise.resolve() would not yield: it is a microtask, so the loop never reaches input or rendering.

Practical example

An admin "Orders" screen loads 5,000 orders in one 6.2 MB JSON response and renders them into a table. On an office laptop: JSON.parse 35 ms, React render 410 ms, layout 180 ms, one 625 ms long task. Typing in the search box above the table lags by half a second per keystroke because each keystroke filters and re-renders 5,000 rows. Three changes fix it: the API paginates to 50 rows with a cursor, the table virtualises rows (Part 71 — React Fundamentals for Backend Engineers), and filtering happens on the server. The longest task drops to 38 ms.

React / Next.js example

React 18 can keep input responsive while expensive re-renders happen, by marking them as non-urgent. useDeferredValue lets the input update immediately while the filtered list catches up; React's concurrent renderer works in small slices and yields to the browser between them.

// ProductSearch.tsx  (React 18)
import { memo, useDeferredValue, useMemo, useState } from 'react';

type Product = { id: string; name: string };

const Results = memo(function Results({ query, products }: { query: string; products: Product[] }) {
  const matches = useMemo(
    () => products.filter((p) => p.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase())).slice(0, 200),
    [query, products],
  );
  return <ul>{matches.map((p) => <li key={p.id}>{p.name}</li>)}</ul>;
});

export function ProductSearch({ products }: { products: Product[] }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);     // lags behind during heavy renders
  const stale = query !== deferredQuery;
  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} aria-label="Search products" />
      <div style={{ opacity: stale ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
        <Results query={deferredQuery} products={products} />
      </div>
    </>
  );
}

useTransition and startTransition do the same for state updates you trigger yourself, such as switching a tab. These tools make React yield between components; they do not make a single slow component or a single 300 ms loop faster. That still needs less work, chunking, or a Web Worker.

Backend side (NestJS)

The backend decides how much work lands on the main thread. Every byte of JSON is parsed on it, and every item becomes DOM. The API should make the cheap path the default:

// orders.controller.ts: bounded, shaped responses for UI lists
import { Controller, Get, Query } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Type } from 'class-transformer';
import { IsIn, IsInt, IsOptional, IsString, Max, Min } from 'class-validator';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

export class ListOrdersQuery {
  @IsOptional() @Type(() => Number) @IsInt() @Min(1) @Max(100) limit = 25; // hard upper bound
  @IsOptional() @IsString() cursor?: string;                              // keyset pagination
  @IsOptional() @IsString() q?: string;                                   // filter on the server
  @IsOptional() @IsIn(['summary', 'full']) view: 'summary' | 'full' = 'summary';
}

@Controller('v1/orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get()
  async list(@Query() query: ListOrdersQuery) {
    // 'summary' returns 6 fields per order (about 300 bytes) instead of 40 (about 4 KB).
    const page = await this.orders.list(query);
    return { items: page.items, nextCursor: page.nextCursor, hasMore: page.nextCursor !== null };
  }
}
  • Cap page sizes (@Max(100)), so no client can request 5,000 rows by accident.
  • Offer summary views for lists and full views for detail pages.
  • Filter, sort and aggregate on the server where the index is (see Part 15 — API Design (REST first), 15.5 Pagination). Totals computed in SQL cost 2 ms; computed in the browser over 5,000 rows they cost a long task.
  • Send preformatted values sparingly: a totalLabel string saves the client a few microseconds but couples the API to one locale; usually return minor units plus currency and format with Intl.NumberFormat on the client.

Production scenario

A logistics dashboard showed 3,000 live shipment rows updated over a WebSocket at 20 messages per second. Each message triggered a full re-render of the table: about 70 ms per update, so the main thread was busy over 100 % of the time and clicks took 1 to 2 seconds to respond. INP at p75 was 1,400 ms. The team batched updates on a 500 ms interval, virtualised the table to render only the 40 visible rows, and moved the backend to send a version per shipment so the client could skip unchanged rows. Main-thread busy time fell to 12 % and INP to 160 ms.

Failure scenario

A food-delivery checkout used a client-side "address autocomplete" that downloaded a 9 MB JSON file of all street names for the city on first focus of the address field, then parsed and indexed it on the main thread. On a 2019 budget Android phone the parse alone took 240 ms and the indexing 1.9 s, during which the page was frozen. Users tapped "Place order" repeatedly; when the thread freed up, the queued taps were processed and some orders were sent twice (only the idempotency key saved them, 69.2). The fix moved autocomplete to a server endpoint (GET /v1/addresses/suggest?q=) backed by a PostgreSQL trigram index, returning 8 suggestions in about 12 ms.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Microtask loops: recursive promise chains starve rendering; the tab freezes without any long-task entry pointing at an obvious event handler.
  • await does not yield to rendering: awaiting an already-resolved promise continues in the same turn.
  • Background tabs: timers are throttled to once per second, and Chrome's intensive throttling can reduce chained timers to once per minute after 5 minutes hidden; polling loops slow down silently.
  • Input queued during a long task is delivered afterwards, so users trigger double actions.
  • Web Workers cannot touch the DOM; they communicate by postMessage, which copies data (structured clone) unless you transfer ownership of an ArrayBuffer.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the main thread like a single-threaded server with a 50 ms SLO per task: anything above it is an incident in miniature. They measure with a throttled CPU, look for long tasks in the Performance panel and in real-user data, and fix the biggest ones first. Their first instinct is to do less (smaller payloads, fewer DOM nodes, server-side filtering), then to do it later (defer, lazy load, yield), and only then to do it elsewhere (Web Workers). They recognise the parallel with Node: a 300 ms synchronous loop in a NestJS handler freezes every request on that process, and a 300 ms loop in a click handler freezes every interaction on that page.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking async functions run in the background. They run on the same thread; only the waiting is asynchronous.
  • Loading entire datasets into the browser and filtering there.
  • Profiling on a fast laptop without CPU throttling.
  • Using await Promise.resolve() to "yield", which never lets rendering run.
  • Re-rendering a whole list for every real-time update instead of batching and updating only changed rows.

Interview questions

  1. How does the browser event loop differ from Node's? Expected answer: both run one task then drain microtasks, but the browser adds rendering steps (rAF, style, layout, paint) between tasks and prioritises input; Node has libuv phases, process.nextTick and no rendering. Follow-up: what does a microtask loop do in each?
  2. What is a long task and why 50 ms? Expected answer: a main-thread task over 50 ms; it leaves no room to respond to input within about 100 ms, which users perceive as lag.
  3. How would you break up a long task? Expected answer: chunk the work and yield with scheduler.yield() or a macrotask, use React transitions for rendering work, or move pure computation to a Web Worker.
  4. What is INP and what usually makes it bad? Expected answer: time from a user interaction to the next paint, at the 98th percentile of interactions on a page; long tasks, heavy event handlers and large re-renders.
  5. What can the backend do to reduce main-thread work? Expected answer: smaller, paginated, shaped responses; server-side filtering and aggregation; fewer round trips that each trigger re-renders.

Practical exercise

Build an orders page that first loads 5,000 orders from a NestJS endpoint and renders them, with a search box that filters on each keystroke. Record a Performance trace with 6x CPU throttling and note the longest task and the input delay when typing. Then implement server-side pagination and filtering (limit at most 100, cursor, q) and useDeferredValue for the input.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Before: at least one task over 300 ms and visible typing lag in the trace.
  • After: no task over 50 ms during typing, and each keystroke's interaction in the Performance panel's Interactions track is under 200 ms.
  • The API rejects limit=5000 with a 400 response from the ValidationPipe.

69.8 Browser storage: cookies, Web Storage, IndexedDB and the Cache API

Concept

The browser gives every origin (scheme plus host plus port, for example https://shop.example.com) several places to keep data on the user's device:

  • Cookies: small name-value pairs the browser sends automatically with matching HTTP requests. Set by the server with Set-Cookie or by JavaScript with document.cookie.
  • localStorage: a synchronous string key-value store that persists until cleared. Shared by all tabs of the origin.
  • sessionStorage: the same API, but scoped to one tab and cleared when that tab closes.
  • IndexedDB: an asynchronous, transactional database of structured objects with indexes, able to hold hundreds of megabytes.
  • Cache API: a store of HTTP Request and Response pairs, used mainly by service workers for offline pages and assets.

Why does it exist?

HTTP is stateless (Part 3 — How the Web Works), so cookies were invented to let servers recognise a returning browser. Cookies travel on every request, so they are a terrible place for anything large; Web Storage was added for client-only data like a remembered filter. Apps that work offline or cache large datasets needed a real database (IndexedDB) and a programmable HTTP cache (Cache API). Each exists for a different job, and most storage bugs come from using one for another's job.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel guest. Cookies are the wristband: small, shown automatically at every door, and anyone who steals it can enter. localStorage is a notebook left in the room: handy, but any visitor allowed in the room can read it. sessionStorage is a sticky note that goes in the bin when you check out of this one visit. IndexedDB is a locked filing cabinet in the room with folders and an index. The Cache API is a shelf of photocopies of documents you fetched from the front desk, so you do not have to walk downstairs again.

How it works

Store Capacity (typical) API Sent to server Readable by page JavaScript Lifetime Use for
Cookie 4 KB per cookie; Chrome allows about 180 per domain Set-Cookie, document.cookie Yes, every matching request No if HttpOnly Expires or Max-Age, or session Session ids, CSRF tokens, consent flags
localStorage About 5 MB per origin Synchronous, strings only No Yes Until cleared UI preferences, non-sensitive drafts
sessionStorage About 5 MB per origin Synchronous, strings only No Yes Until tab closes Per-tab wizard state
IndexedDB Large: a share of free disk, often hundreds of MB to GB Asynchronous, transactions, structured clone No Yes Until cleared or evicted Offline data, large client caches
Cache API Shares the IndexedDB quota Asynchronous, caches.open() No Yes, including service workers Until cleared or evicted Offline assets and pages

Key mechanics:

  1. Cookies ride on every request. A 3 KB cookie on the .shop.example.com domain is sent with every image, CSS and API request to every subdomain: on a page with 80 requests over HTTP/1.1, that is 240 KB of upload. HTTP/2 header compression (HPACK) reduces repeated cost but not the first request. Server limits are real: Node.js rejects request headers over 16 KB by default with 431 Request Header Fields Too Large, and NGINX's default buffers produce 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large.
  2. Cookie attributes decide who can read and send them: HttpOnly (invisible to JavaScript), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite=Lax|Strict|None (whether cross-site requests carry it), Domain and Path (scope), Max-Age (lifetime). Part 75 — Auth and Security in the Browser covers the security model in depth.
  3. Web Storage is synchronous. localStorage.getItem blocks the main thread; reading a 2 MB value on a slow phone can take tens of milliseconds, and the first access may load the whole store from disk.
  4. Everything JavaScript can read, an XSS bug can read. One injected script can dump localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB and non-HttpOnly cookies and send them anywhere. Only HttpOnly cookies are out of its reach.
  5. Quotas and eviction. navigator.storage.estimate() reports usage and quota. Under storage pressure, browsers evict "best-effort" origins, least recently used first, unless the origin has navigator.storage.persist(). Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention deletes all script-writable storage for a site after 7 days without user interaction.

What must never go in browser storage readable by JavaScript: passwords; long-lived refresh tokens or session tokens (use HttpOnly cookies); full card numbers or CVV (PCI DSS forbids storing CVV anywhere after authorisation); API secrets or keys with server-side power; personal data you would not be comfortable losing in a breach (government ids, health information). Also never trust anything read back from storage: the user can edit all of it in the Application panel.

flowchart TB
    q1{"Must the server see it on each request?"} -->|"yes"| q2{"Is it a credential?"}
    q2 -->|"yes"| c1["HttpOnly Secure SameSite cookie"]
    q2 -->|"no"| c2["Small cookie, minimal Path and Domain"]
    q1 -->|"no"| q3{"Large, structured or offline?"}
    q3 -->|"yes, data"| idb["IndexedDB"]
    q3 -->|"yes, HTTP responses"| cache["Cache API via service worker"]
    q3 -->|"no"| q4{"Per tab only?"}
    q4 -->|"yes"| ss["sessionStorage"]
    q4 -->|"no"| ls["localStorage, non-sensitive only"]

Practical example

An e-commerce app stores: the session id in an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax cookie; the "grid or list view" preference in localStorage; the multi-step return-request wizard's progress in sessionStorage, so two tabs with two returns do not overwrite each other; the last 200 viewed products in IndexedDB for an offline "recently viewed" page; and the app shell (HTML, CSS, JS) in the Cache API through a service worker. The cart lives on the server, keyed by the session, so it follows the user across devices.

React / Next.js example

Server rendering has no window, so reading localStorage during render crashes on the server or causes a hydration mismatch (the server HTML says "grid", the client says "list"). React 18's useSyncExternalStore handles this cleanly with a server snapshot:

// useLocalPreference.ts  (React 18, safe with Next.js server rendering)
'use client';
import { useCallback, useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';

function subscribe(onChange: () => void) {
  window.addEventListener('storage', onChange);       // fires when another tab changes it
  return () => window.removeEventListener('storage', onChange);
}

export function useLocalPreference(key: string, fallback: string) {
  const value = useSyncExternalStore(
    subscribe,
    () => { try { return localStorage.getItem(key) ?? fallback; } catch { return fallback; } },
    () => fallback,                                    // server snapshot: always the fallback
  );
  const set = useCallback((next: string) => {
    try { localStorage.setItem(key, next); } catch { /* quota exceeded or storage disabled */ }
    window.dispatchEvent(new StorageEvent('storage', { key })); // notify this tab too
  }, [key]);
  return [value, set] as const;
}

On the server side of Next.js 14, cookies() from next/headers reads request cookies inside server components, Route Handlers and Server Actions, and can set them in Server Actions and Route Handlers. That is the right channel for anything the server needs during rendering.

Backend side (NestJS)

The backend owns cookies and can instruct the browser to wipe storage. A login and logout pair shows both:

// session.controller.ts  (requires app.use(cookieParser()) in main.ts)
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post, Req, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { SessionService } from './session.service';
import { LoginDto } from './login.dto';

@Controller('v1/session')
export class SessionController {
  constructor(private readonly sessions: SessionService) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(204)
  async login(@Body() dto: LoginDto, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
    const session = await this.sessions.create(dto);    // random 32-byte id, stored server side
    res.cookie('sid', session.id, {
      httpOnly: true,            // invisible to document.cookie and to XSS
      secure: true,              // HTTPS only
      sameSite: 'lax',           // not sent on cross-site POSTs
      path: '/',
      maxAge: 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 7, // 7 days, in milliseconds for Express
    });
  }

  @Post('logout')
  @HttpCode(204)
  async logout(@Req() req: Request, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
    await this.sessions.revoke(req.cookies?.sid);
    res.clearCookie('sid', { path: '/', httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' });
    // Ask the browser to delete cached responses, cookies and all storage for this origin.
    res.setHeader('Clear-Site-Data', '"cache", "cookies", "storage"');
  }
}
  • Keep cookies small and scoped. One session id of about 40 bytes; no user profiles or feature flags in cookies. Set Path and avoid parent-domain cookies unless every subdomain truly needs them.
  • Use Clear-Site-Data on logout for shared-device safety; it is supported in Chromium and Firefox, and partially in Safari, so do not rely on it alone.
  • Mark user-specific API responses Cache-Control: private, no-store so they do not end up in the HTTP cache or a service worker cache on a shared machine.

Production scenario

A media site set analytics, A/B testing and personalisation cookies on .example.com. Over two years the average request carried 6.8 KB of cookies. Their image CDN on img.example.com received those cookies on every image request, which disabled caching at one CDN tier keyed on cookies and added 120 ms per image on 3G. Moving images to a cookieless domain and trimming cookies to under 1 KB cut median page weight by 310 KB of upload per page view and raised CDN hit rate from 71 % to 96 %.

Failure scenario

On a Tuesday morning, 4 % of logged-in users suddenly got a blank error page on every request: NGINX was answering 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large. A marketing tool had started writing a new cookie per campaign, and long-time users had accumulated 30 of them. The backend team's dashboards showed nothing, because the requests never reached NestJS. Support could only tell users to clear cookies. The fix was a cookie allow-list at the edge, raising large_client_header_buffers temporarily, and a monitor on response code 400 and 431 at the load balancer split by cookie header size.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • localStorage throws in some private modes or when storage is disabled, and on setItem when the quota is exceeded; always wrap it in try and catch.
  • Cross-tab overwrite: two tabs write the same localStorage key; the storage event only fires in other tabs.
  • Stale schema: a stored object from last year's app version lacks new fields; version the stored data.
  • Third-party storage partitioning: embedded iframes from other sites get partitioned or blocked storage in modern browsers, breaking old embed-based login flows.
  • Eviction: IndexedDB data can disappear under disk pressure; treat it as a cache unless persistence is granted.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior asks three questions for any piece of client-side data: who must read it (server, page, both), what happens if an attacker reads it, and what happens if it disappears. Credentials go in HttpOnly cookies, user-owned business data goes on the server, and the browser keeps only caches and preferences that can be lost without harm. They watch cookie size like they watch payload size, because it is paid on every request and its failures happen before the application sees anything.

Common mistakes

  • Storing JWTs or refresh tokens in localStorage, readable by any XSS.
  • Putting large or numerous cookies on the parent domain.
  • Trusting values read from storage (prices, roles, feature flags) without server validation.
  • Reading localStorage during server render, causing crashes or hydration mismatches.
  • Never versioning stored data, so a new release crashes on old shapes.

Interview questions

  1. Where would you store a session token in a browser app and why? Expected answer: an HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite cookie, because JavaScript (and therefore XSS) cannot read it; pair it with CSRF protection. Follow-up: what are the tradeoffs versus a token in memory?
  2. What is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage? Expected answer: same API; localStorage is shared across tabs and persists, sessionStorage is per tab and cleared when it closes.
  3. When would you use IndexedDB over localStorage? Expected answer: large or structured data, asynchronous access, offline support, transactions and indexes.
  4. How can cookies break a site without any application error? Expected answer: oversized headers rejected by proxies (400 or 431), cookies disabling CDN caching, cookies sent to every subdomain.

Practical exercise

Implement login and logout in NestJS with an HttpOnly session cookie and Clear-Site-Data on logout. In the frontend, store a view preference in localStorage and a wizard step in sessionStorage. Use the DevTools Application panel to inspect each.

Acceptance criteria:

  • document.cookie in the Console does not show the session cookie, but the Application panel does, with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax ticked.
  • After logout, the Application panel shows the session cookie and localStorage cleared (in Chromium).
  • Sending 20 KB of cookies with curl to the NestJS server reproduces a 431 response.

69.9 Accessibility as engineering

Concept

Accessibility (often written a11y: "a", 11 letters, "y") means people can use your product regardless of disability: blindness and low vision, deafness, motor impairments that make a mouse impossible, cognitive differences, or a temporary condition like a broken wrist. About 1 in 6 people worldwide lives with a significant disability (WHO estimate). Accessibility is also a legal requirement in many markets, including the Americans with Disabilities Act in the US and the European Accessibility Act, which applies to e-commerce from June 2025. The common technical standard is WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines), usually at level AA.

The browser exposes the page to assistive technology through the accessibility tree: a parallel tree to the DOM in which each meaningful node has a role (button, link, heading, textbox), an accessible name ("Add to cart"), a state (expanded, checked, invalid, disabled) and sometimes a value. A screen reader reads that tree, not your pixels.

Why does it exist?

Without it, a screen reader user hears "button, button, button, image, link" and cannot shop. A keyboard-only user cannot reach the "Pay" button. A low-vision user cannot read light-grey text on white. These are not edge cases; they are customers who leave. Accessibility also overlaps with quality for everyone: keyboard support helps power users, captions help people in noisy places, good contrast helps everyone in sunlight, and semantic structure helps search engines and automated tests (Testing Library's getByRole queries the same tree).

Mental model

Imagine your page described over the phone to someone who cannot see it. The accessibility tree is that description. If you used a <div> instead of a <button>, the description says "some text" instead of "a button labelled Add to cart". If you moved focus nowhere after opening a dialog, the person on the phone is still standing in the previous room while you talk about a new one.

How it works

  1. The browser builds the accessibility tree from the DOM and CSS. Native elements bring roles automatically: <button> is a button, <a href> a link, <h2> a heading level 2, <input type="checkbox"> a checkbox, <nav> a navigation landmark. Elements hidden with display: none or aria-hidden="true" are removed.
  2. The accessible name is computed in a fixed order: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then native labelling (<label for>, alt on images, the text content of a button or link), then title as a last resort.
  3. ARIA attributes add or override semantics when no native element exists: role="tablist", aria-expanded="true", aria-controls, aria-invalid, aria-describedby. The first rule of ARIA: if a native element does the job, use it. ARIA changes what is announced, never behaviour; role="button" on a <div> does not make it focusable or respond to Enter.
  4. Keyboard navigation. Tab and Shift+Tab move between focusable elements in DOM order. Enter activates links and buttons; Space activates buttons and checkboxes; arrow keys move within composite widgets (menus, tabs, radio groups); Escape closes dialogs and menus. tabindex="0" adds an element to the tab order, tabindex="-1" makes it focusable by script only, and positive values break the natural order and should never be used. :focus-visible shows a focus ring for keyboard users without showing it on mouse clicks.
  5. Focus management. When the UI changes context, the code must move focus: into a dialog when it opens (and back to the trigger when it closes), to the new page's heading after a client-side route change, to the first invalid field after a failed submit.
  6. Live regions announce changes without moving focus: role="status" (or aria-live="polite") for "Added to cart", role="alert" for urgent errors.
  7. Contrast. WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (24 px, or about 18.7 px bold) and for UI component boundaries and focus indicators. #767676 on white is about 4.5:1, the lightest grey that passes for body text.

How a screen reader reads a page: NVDA or JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, TalkBack on Android. Users rarely listen top to bottom. They jump by headings (the H key in NVDA), by landmarks, by form fields or by links, pulling up lists of each. In a form, the reader announces each field as "PIN code, edit text, required, invalid entry, Enter a 6-digit PIN code". That sentence is built entirely from the label, the input type, required, aria-invalid and aria-describedby.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant SR as ScreenReader
    participant AT as AccessibilityTree
    participant App as Page
    U->>SR: press H for next heading
    SR->>AT: next node with role heading
    AT-->>SR: heading level 1, Ergonomic Office Chair
    U->>SR: Tab to next control
    SR->>AT: focused node
    AT-->>SR: button, Add to cart
    U->>App: press Enter
    App->>AT: status region text Added to cart
    AT-->>SR: live region changed, polite
    SR-->>U: Added to cart

Practical example

A "Cancel order" flow opens a confirmation dialog. Accessible behaviour: the dialog has role="dialog" with a name from its heading; focus moves into it on open; Tab stays inside it; Escape closes it; the page behind is inert; focus returns to the "Cancel order" button on close; the result ("Order 8812 cancelled") is announced by a status region. The native <dialog> element with showModal() provides most of that for free: the rest of the page becomes inert, Escape closes it and modern browsers restore focus to the previously focused element.

React / Next.js example

// CancelOrderDialog.tsx  (React 18, native <dialog>)
import { useId, useRef, useState } from 'react';

export function CancelOrder({ orderId, onCancel }: { orderId: string; onCancel: () => Promise<void> }) {
  const dialogRef = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);
  const titleId = useId();
  const [status, setStatus] = useState('');

  async function confirm() {
    await onCancel();
    dialogRef.current?.close();              // focus returns to the trigger button
    setStatus(`Order ${orderId} cancelled`); // announced politely by the status region
  }

  return (
    <>
      <button type="button" onClick={() => dialogRef.current?.showModal()}>Cancel order</button>
      <dialog ref={dialogRef} aria-labelledby={titleId}>
        <h2 id={titleId}>Cancel order {orderId}?</h2>
        <p>Your refund will be issued to the original payment method within 5 to 7 days.</p>
        {/* showModal() focuses the first focusable element: the safe choice goes first */}
        <button type="button" onClick={() => dialogRef.current?.close()}>Keep order</button>
        <button type="button" onClick={confirm}>Yes, cancel</button>
      </dialog>
      <p role="status">{status}</p>
    </>
  );
}

In a Next.js App Router app, client-side navigation does not reload the page, so the screen reader is not told a new page has loaded. Next.js includes a route announcer that reads the new page's <title> (or first <h1>) on navigation, which is one more reason every page needs a distinct title (69.3).

Backend side (NestJS)

Accessible forms need the API to say which field is wrong and why, in words a person can understand. Configure the ValidationPipe to return field-level errors in a stable shape:

// main.ts: field-level validation errors the UI can attach to inputs
import { BadRequestException, ValidationPipe, type ValidationError } from '@nestjs/common';

export const validationPipe = new ValidationPipe({
  whitelist: true,
  transform: true,
  exceptionFactory: (errors: ValidationError[]) =>
    new BadRequestException({
      type: 'validation_error',
      title: 'Some fields need attention',
      fieldErrors: Object.fromEntries(
        errors.map((e) => [e.property, Object.values(e.constraints ?? {})[0] ?? 'Invalid value']),
      ),
    }),
});
// app.useGlobalPipes(validationPipe);

With fieldErrors.postalCode = "Enter a 6-digit PIN code", the frontend sets aria-invalid and renders the message in the element referenced by aria-describedby, and moves focus to the first invalid field. Write constraint messages for humans in DTOs (@Matches(/^[1-9][0-9]{5}$/, { message: 'Enter a 6-digit PIN code' })), and return product alt text, captions and transcripts as content fields, written by people, not generated from file names. Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts covers the full error contract.

Production scenario

A retailer received a legal demand letter citing 14 WCAG failures on checkout. An audit with axe DevTools and manual screen reader testing found: icon-only buttons without names ("button" announced for the cart, search and close icons), a custom dropdown for delivery slots unusable by keyboard, error messages shown only as red borders, focus lost after the coupon form re-rendered, and grey placeholder text at 2.9:1 contrast used as labels. The fixes took one sprint: aria-label on icon buttons, a native <select>, field errors from the API linked with aria-describedby, focus restoration, real <label> elements, darker text. Checkout completion for keyboard and screen reader users, tracked by a small usability panel, went from 3 of 10 to 9 of 10, and overall checkout errors fell 6 % because clearer error messages helped everyone.

Failure scenario

A team shipped a redesigned order-tracking page where the status updated live: "Packed", then "Out for delivery". The status was a styled <div> updated by React. A blind customer called support three times asking whether their insulin delivery had shipped; the page had changed, but nothing was announced, and the screen reader still read the old text it had cached in browse mode. The fix was a role="status" region for the current status and a real <ol> for the timeline with aria-current="step" on the active step. The team added an automated check with @axe-core/playwright to the CI journey tests (Part 77 — Frontend Testing and Quality).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Icon-only buttons without aria-label are announced as just "button".
  • outline: none without a replacement makes keyboard focus invisible.
  • Placeholder used as a label disappears on typing and usually fails contrast.
  • Toasts that vanish after 3 seconds may never be read; use a status region and enough time.
  • Disabled submit buttons cannot be focused, so screen reader users cannot discover why they cannot proceed; prefer enabled buttons that show errors.
  • Focus lost on re-render: replacing a list or form with new DOM drops focus back to <body>.
  • Infinite scroll makes the footer unreachable by keyboard.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats accessibility like security: a property of the system built in from the start, tested automatically where possible and manually where not. Automated tools such as axe and Lighthouse catch about a third of issues (missing names, contrast, invalid ARIA); keyboard testing and a screen reader pass catch the rest. Their defaults are native elements, visible focus, labelled controls, managed focus, and errors that say what to do. They know the backend shapes accessibility through error messages, alt text and content fields. To a product manager: "If a customer can't use the checkout with a keyboard, that's a checkout outage for them, and in many countries a legal risk for us."

Common mistakes

  • Adding ARIA to fix non-semantic markup instead of using the right element.
  • Removing focus outlines for aesthetics.
  • Using colour alone to show errors or order status.
  • Generic messages like "Invalid input" with no field association.
  • Testing only with Lighthouse and never with a keyboard or screen reader.

Interview questions

  1. What is the accessibility tree and how is an element's accessible name computed? Expected answer: the browser's semantic representation of the page for assistive tech; name from aria-labelledby, aria-label, native labels or content, then title. Follow-up: why does role="button" on a <div> not make it a button?
  2. How do you make a modal dialog accessible? Expected answer: dialog role and name, focus moved in, focus contained, Escape closes, background inert, focus restored; native <dialog> with showModal() provides most of this.
  3. What contrast ratios does WCAG AA require? Expected answer: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text and UI components.
  4. How does the API help accessibility? Expected answer: field-level, human-readable error messages; alt text and captions as content; stable error shapes.

Practical exercise

Make an address form and a cancel-order dialog fully operable by keyboard and screen reader, with errors from a NestJS ValidationPipe exceptionFactory. Test with VoiceOver (Cmd+F5 on macOS) or NVDA, and with the DevTools Accessibility pane and Lighthouse.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every control is reachable with Tab in a logical order and shows a visible focus ring.
  • Submitting invalid data moves focus to the first invalid field, and the screen reader announces its label, "invalid entry" and the API's message.
  • The dialog traps focus, closes with Escape and returns focus to its trigger.
  • Lighthouse accessibility score is 100 and axe reports zero violations, and you can name one issue you found manually that neither tool reported.

69.10 DevTools for backend engineers: Network, Performance and Application panels

Concept

Browser DevTools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on macOS, in Chrome and Edge; Firefox and Safari have equivalents) is the browser's own observability stack. For a backend engineer three panels do most of the work:

  • Network: every request the page made, with timing phases, headers, payloads, priorities and who triggered it. It is the browser-side equivalent of a distributed trace's client spans.
  • Performance: a recording of the main thread, network, frames, layout shifts and interactions over time. It is a CPU profiler and a frame timeline in one.
  • Application: storage (cookies, Web Storage, IndexedDB, Cache API), service workers and the web app manifest.

Why does it exist?

Server logs end at the last byte you sent. Everything after that, including requests the browser never made, requests it made twice, and JavaScript that froze the page, is invisible from the backend. Most "the API is slow" tickets turn out, in DevTools, to be queueing behind other requests, a chain of dependent calls, or a long task delaying the callback. DevTools turns arguments about blame into evidence.

Mental model

Imagine your backend has a flight recorder for every request: when it was queued, when it got a connection, how long the server thought, how long the bytes took. The Network panel is that recorder for the browser's side of the conversation. The Performance panel is the cockpit video: what the pilot (the main thread) was doing every millisecond, and when the passengers (users) pressed buttons.

How it works

Network panel. Open it before loading the page, tick Disable cache for cold-load testing, choose a throttling preset, and reload.

  • Columns: Name, Status, Type, Initiator, Size, Time and Waterfall by default. Right-click the header to add Priority, Protocol (h2, h3), Remote Address and Connection ID (which requests shared a connection).
  • Size shows bytes transferred and, on hover, the decompressed resource size; "(memory cache)", "(disk cache)" or "(ServiceWorker)" means no network transfer.
  • Timing tab for a request breaks down its phases:
Phase Meaning If it is large, suspect
Queueing Waiting before the browser starts the request Lower priority than other requests, or HTTP/1.1 limit of 6 connections per host
Stalled Waiting for a connection or a cache lock Connection limits, proxy negotiation
DNS Lookup Resolving the host New origin; use fewer origins or preconnect
Initial connection, SSL TCP and TLS handshakes New connection; keep-alive, HTTP/2, preconnect
Request sent Uploading the request Large bodies or cookies
Waiting for server response Time to first byte: network round trip plus server time Your backend, or the CDN miss path
Content Download Receiving the body Payload size, bandwidth, compression

If the server sends a Server-Timing header, its entries appear in the Timing tab next to these phases.

  • Initiator column and tab show what caused each request: the parser (HTML line number), a script (with a stack trace), or another request. Holding Shift while hovering a row highlights its initiators in green and the requests it caused in red, which makes request chains obvious.
  • Filters: domain:api.shop.example.com, status-code:500, larger-than:100k, method:POST, has-response-header:set-cookie, -domain:*.analytics.example (a leading - negates).
  • Tools: right-click a request for Copy as cURL (replay it from a terminal against staging), Block request URL (simulate a failed dependency), Override content or Override headers (test a header change locally without deploying), and Save all as HAR (attach to a ticket; HAR files contain cookies and tokens, so scrub them).

Performance panel. Click Record and reload, with CPU throttling set to 4x or 6x to approximate a mid-range phone. The recording shows:

  • Network track: requests as bars, aligned with main-thread work.
  • Timings track: FCP, LCP, DOMContentLoaded and load markers, plus your own performance.mark() and performance.measure() entries.
  • Main track: a flame chart of tasks; long tasks have a red corner and red striping beyond 50 ms. Purple is style and layout, green is paint, yellow is scripting.
  • Layout shifts and Interactions tracks: each shift with the elements that moved; each click or key press with its input delay, processing time and presentation delay (the parts of INP).
  • Bottom-Up and Call Tree tabs: which functions consumed the most self time.

Recent Chrome versions also open the panel on a live metrics view that shows LCP, CLS and INP as you use the page, alongside field data from the Chrome UX Report when available.

Application panel. Under Storage, inspect and edit cookies (with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite and partition columns), local and session storage, IndexedDB databases and Cache Storage. Storage at the top shows usage per type and a Clear site data button. Service workers offers "Update on reload", "Bypass for network" and "Offline" toggles, which is how you reproduce "users still see the old version" bugs (Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends). Back/forward cache runs a test that tells you why a page cannot be restored instantly on Back, often an unload listener or Cache-Control: no-store on the HTML.

flowchart LR
    sym["Symptom: page slow or broken"] --> net["Network: what was requested, when, by whom"]
    net --> ttfb{"Long Waiting for server response?"}
    ttfb -->|"yes"| be["Backend: Server-Timing, traces, slow queries"]
    ttfb -->|"no"| chain{"Late start or chained requests?"}
    chain -->|"yes"| init["Initiator chain: hints, batching, server render"]
    chain -->|"no"| perf["Performance: long tasks, layout, paint"]
    perf --> app["Application: cookies, storage, service worker"]

Practical example

A ticket says "order history takes 4 seconds". In the Network panel, GET /v1/orders shows Waiting for server response 180 ms and Content Download 20 ms, so the API is not the problem. The Initiator chain shows it started at 2.9 s, triggered from app.js, which itself finished downloading at 1.1 s. The Performance panel shows a 1.6 s long task in between: the app was parsing a 2.4 MB translation file before mounting. The fix was loading only the active locale. The API team closed the ticket with a screenshot of the Timing tab.

React / Next.js example

User Timing marks put your own milestones on the Performance panel's Timings track, and Next.js 14 exposes Web Vitals from real users through useReportWebVitals:

// app/web-vitals.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router, client component rendered in the root layout)
'use client';
import { useReportWebVitals } from 'next/web-vitals';

export function WebVitals() {
  useReportWebVitals((metric) => {
    // metric.name is one of 'TTFB', 'FCP', 'LCP', 'CLS', 'INP' (and 'FID' in older versions)
    const body = JSON.stringify({ name: metric.name, value: metric.value, id: metric.id,
      page: location.pathname });
