    navigator.sendBeacon('/api/v1/rum/vitals', body); // survives page unload
  });
  return null;
}

// Anywhere in client code: custom milestones visible in the Performance panel.
export function markCartReady() {
  performance.mark('cart-ready');
  performance.measure('cart-time-to-ready', { start: 0, end: 'cart-ready' });
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The most useful thing a backend can add for DevTools users is a Server-Timing header, which turns "Waiting for server response: 640 ms" into a breakdown everyone can see:

// server-timing.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Response } from 'express';
import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class ServerTimingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const started = process.hrtime.bigint();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap(() => {
        const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - started) / 1e6;
        const dbMs: number = res.locals.dbMs ?? 0; // accumulated by the data layer for this request
        // Shown in DevTools Network, Timing tab. Never put secrets or SQL in descriptions.
        res.setHeader('Server-Timing', `app;dur=${ms.toFixed(1)}, db;dur=${dbMs.toFixed(1)}`);
        // Lets cross-origin pages read the timing values from JavaScript (Resource Timing API).
        res.setHeader('Timing-Allow-Origin', 'https://shop.example.com');
      }),
    );
  }
}

Also expose a request id (X-Request-Id, see Part 43 — Observability: Logs, Metrics and Traces) so a request seen in DevTools can be found in your logs and traces, and make sure CORS exposes it with Access-Control-Expose-Headers if frontend code needs to read it. Be deliberate about Server-Timing in production: durations are harmless, but descriptions that name internal services or queries leak architecture.

Production scenario

A payments team added Server-Timing with auth, db, psp (payment service provider) and app entries to the checkout API. Within a week, frontend engineers stopped filing "checkout API slow" tickets without evidence; they attached screenshots showing psp;dur=1840 during a provider incident, which routed the problem to the right team in minutes instead of hours.

Failure scenario

An engineer debugging a customer issue exported a HAR file from the customer's session and attached it to a public issue tracker. The HAR contained the customer's session cookie and an Authorization header. Security rotated the session within an hour, but the lesson stuck: HAR files are credentials. The team now uses Chrome's sanitized HAR export (which omits sensitive data by default in recent versions), scrubs any HAR before sharing, and keeps session lifetimes short.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Cache enabled while testing hides cold-load problems; Disable cache only applies while DevTools is open.
  • Throttling presets are approximations; they add latency per request but do not model packet loss or real radio behaviour.
  • Preserve log is needed to see requests across redirects and full-page form posts (69.2).
  • Service workers can answer requests without touching the network, showing "(ServiceWorker)" in Size; use "Bypass for network" when debugging the backend.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior opens DevTools before opinions form. They read a waterfall like a trace: find the critical path, find the gaps, find who started what. They profile on a throttled CPU, compare with field data, and they make the backend legible to the browser with Server-Timing and request ids, because the fastest way to resolve a cross-team incident is a shared screen showing the same evidence.

Common mistakes

  • Testing on an unthrottled laptop with a warm cache.
  • Reading only the Time column instead of the Timing phases.
  • Ignoring the Initiator column, so request chains go unnoticed.
  • Sharing raw HAR files.
  • Concluding "backend is fine" from TTFB alone, without checking what the page did with the response.

Interview questions

  1. A request shows 900 ms in the Time column. How do you find where the time went? Expected answer: the Timing tab phases: queueing and stalled (browser), DNS, connection and TLS (network setup), waiting (round trip plus server), download (size and bandwidth); Server-Timing breaks the server part down further.
  2. How do you find request chains? Expected answer: the Initiator column and tab, Shift-hover in the waterfall, and the Network track in a Performance recording.
  3. What is Server-Timing and what must you be careful about? Expected answer: a response header whose metrics appear in DevTools and the Resource Timing API; avoid leaking internal details, and add Timing-Allow-Origin for cross-origin access from JavaScript.
  4. Why record performance with CPU throttling? Expected answer: median phones are several times slower at JavaScript than developer laptops; long tasks invisible on a laptop dominate on phones.

Practical exercise

Add the ServerTimingInterceptor to a NestJS API with a database timing counter. Load a page that calls it, with Disable cache, a slow 4G preset and 4x CPU throttling.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The Timing tab shows app and db entries for each API request.
  • You can identify, with Shift-hover, at least one request started by another request's callback.
  • A Performance recording shows FCP and LCP markers and a custom performance.measure entry, and you can name the longest task and its source script.

69.11 Worked example: tracing a product page from first byte to interactive

Concept

This section puts the whole Part together. We load one product page cold, read the network waterfall and the performance trace, explain every gap using 69.1 to 69.10, and decide which fixes belong to the frontend and which to the backend. Part 76 — Web Performance takes the optimisation much further; the goal here is to read a page load fluently.

The setup

A Next.js 14 App Router storefront in front of NestJS services. Page: https://shop.example.com/products/ergonomic-office-chair. The HTML is server-rendered on a CDN miss; the stock badge and reviews are fetched by client components after hydration. Test profile in DevTools: Disable cache, a slow 4G preset (about 150 ms round trip, 1.6 Mbps down) and 4x CPU throttling, roughly Lighthouse's mobile profile.

The annotated waterfall

#   Request                               Prio     Start  TTFB   End    Transfer  Notes
1   GET /products/ergonomic-office-chair  Highest      0   720    850    26 KB   [A] DNS 40, TCP 150, TLS 150; Server-Timing app;dur=230, api;dur=190
2   /_next/static/css/app.3f9c1a.css      Highest    735   890   1030    18 KB   [B] found by preload scanner, same h2 connection
3   /_next/static/media/inter.woff2       High       735   905   1150    48 KB   preloaded by next/font, crossorigin
4   (preconnect) img.shop-cdn.example                735               -          DNS, TCP, TLS overlap with HTML download
5   chair-800.avif                        High       760  1060   1690   110 KB   [C] next/image priority, fetchpriority=high
6   /_next/static/chunks/main-app.js      High       740   900   1500    62 KB   framework runtime
7   /_next/static/chunks/page.js          High       740   910   1820   142 KB   [D] page code, about 520 KB after decompression
8   analytics.js (third party, async)     Low       1900  2300   2380    38 KB   next/script afterInteractive
9   GET /api/v1/products/123/stock        High      2420  2690   2700   0.3 KB   [E] initiator page.js, useEffect after hydration
10  GET /api/v1/products/123/reviews      High      2700  3020   3060    14 KB   [F] initiator: request 9 callback, a chain

Main thread: FCP 1,090 | LCP 1,720 | long task 1,840 to 2,400 (hydration, 560 ms) | DCL 2,410
User-visible: price at 1,090 | hero at 1,720 | Add to cart works at 2,400 | stock badge 2,760 | reviews 3,120
flowchart LR
    html["HTML, first byte 720 ms"] --> css["CSS, done 1030 ms"]
    html --> img["Hero image, done 1690 ms"]
    html --> js["page.js, done 1820 ms"]
    css --> fcp["FCP 1090 ms"]
    img --> lcp["LCP 1720 ms"]
    js --> hyd["Hydration long task 560 ms"]
    hyd --> stock["GET stock, done 2700 ms"]
    stock --> rev["GET reviews, done 3060 ms"]

Reading it, letter by letter

[A] First byte at 720 ms. About 340 ms is connection setup (DNS 40, TCP 150, TLS 150) before the request leaves. Then half a round trip each way (150 ms total) plus 230 ms of server time. Server-Timing says 190 of those 230 ms were API calls from Next.js to NestJS. The NestJS trace shows three sequential calls: product (60 ms), price (70 ms), related items (60 ms). They do not depend on each other. Backend fix: run them with Promise.all in the page, or add one aggregated BFF endpoint (Part 73 — Next.js and Rendering Strategies). Expected server time: about 100 ms.

[B] CSS at 1,030 ms, FCP at 1,090 ms. The preload scanner found the stylesheet in the first HTML chunk and fetched it on the existing HTTP/2 connection, so no new handshake. CSS is render-blocking (69.1), so FCP waits for it: CSS end plus about 60 ms of style, layout and paint on a throttled CPU. Healthy.

[C] LCP at 1,720 ms. The hero image request started at 760 ms, early, because next/image with priority put a preload in the head and the image origin was preconnected (69.3). The image is 110 KB; at 1.6 Mbps shared with JavaScript downloads, that takes most of a second. Frontend fix: serve a 600-pixel variant to phones via sizes (about 55 KB). LCP is already under 2.5 s, so this is a nice-to-have.

[D] Interactive at 2,400 ms. The page code finished downloading at 1,820 ms, then executed and hydrated in one 560 ms long task (69.7). A user tapping "Add to cart" at 2,000 ms waits until 2,400 ms for the handler and then for the next paint: an INP of roughly 450 ms, "needs improvement". The Bottom-Up tab attributes 210 ms to a 3D viewer component imported on the page but used only after a click. Frontend fix: next/dynamic for the viewer (69.6), making it a separate chunk; hydration drops to about 330 ms.

[E] Stock badge at 2,760 ms. The stock request's initiator is page.js, inside a useEffect, so it cannot start until hydration finishes. Stock is above the fold and changes slowly enough to cache for 30 s. Backend and frontend fix: fetch stock during server rendering, with the NestJS endpoint sending Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=30. The badge arrives in the HTML; the reserved slot (69.5) no longer shifts.

[F] Reviews at 3,120 ms. Shift-hover on request 10 shows request 9 highlighted in green as its initiator: the reviews fetch was written inside the stock fetch's .then(). That is a client-side waterfall costing a full round trip for no reason. Fix: fetch reviews on the server inside a <Suspense> boundary so they stream after the shell (69.1), or at least in parallel with stock.

Backend side (NestJS)

The backend changes from this trace, in priority order:

Change Where Expected effect
Parallelise product, price and related calls Next.js server code or a BFF endpoint Server time 230 to about 110 ms; every later milestone moves 120 ms earlier
Cacheable stock endpoint with s-maxage=30 NestJS stock controller Stock rendered in HTML; one client request removed
Server-Timing on every API (already present) Global interceptor Keeps the next investigation short
Reviews endpoint returns first page only (limit=10, cursor) NestJS reviews controller 14 KB to 5 KB; less parsing during streaming
Image dimensions and alt in product response (already present) Product DTO No CLS from the gallery

After the fixes

                      Before     After
First byte            720 ms     600 ms
FCP                   1,090 ms   970 ms
LCP                   1,720 ms   1,450 ms
Hydration long task   560 ms     330 ms
Interactive           2,400 ms   2,050 ms
Stock visible         2,760 ms   970 ms (in HTML)
Reviews visible       3,120 ms   1,300 ms (streamed)
Client API requests   2          0 on load
CLS                   0.04       0.01

Failure scenario

Before this investigation, the same page had a two-week "performance war" between teams. The backend team showed p95 API latency of 80 ms and declared the API fast. The frontend team showed a Lighthouse score of 61 and blamed the API. Both were right about their own numbers and wrong about the cause. The waterfall settled it in one meeting: the API calls were fast but sequential on the server and chained on the client, and the biggest delay to interactivity was hydration of code nobody used on load. Neither team's dashboard could show that alone.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior reads a page load as one critical path that crosses the network, the server and the main thread. They annotate it, assign each gap to a cause, and fix the largest gaps first regardless of which team owns them. They know that the backend's best contributions are often not "make the endpoint faster" but "make fewer, parallel, cacheable calls available at server-render time".

Interview questions

  1. Given a waterfall, how do you find the critical path to LCP? Expected answer: follow the LCP element's request back through its initiators to the HTML; anything on that chain (TTFB, render-blocking CSS, late discovery) delays LCP; requests off the chain matter only through bandwidth and main-thread contention.
  2. Why did moving the stock fetch to the server help so much? Expected answer: it removed a dependency on JavaScript download and hydration and a client round trip, and allowed CDN caching.
  3. How would you prove to a skeptical backend team that the problem is partly theirs? Expected answer: Server-Timing breakdown plus backend traces showing sequential calls, side by side with the waterfall.

Practical exercise

Pick a real page you own. Record a cold load with the profile above, export the waterfall into a table like the one in this section, label every gap with a letter, write one sentence of cause for each, and propose one frontend and one backend fix.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every request on the critical path to LCP and to "interactive" is explained.
  • At least one request chain is identified with the Initiator view.
  • One backend change is implemented and the after-numbers are recorded with the same profile.

Senior Checklist — Part 69

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can walk through navigation, parsing, DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint and compositing, and say which stage a given change re-runs
  • I can explain what the preload scanner finds and what it misses
  • I know what a plain HTML form submits, how it encodes it, and why a form POST should answer with 303
  • I can write a correct <head> with charset, viewport, preconnect and preload, and spot a double download
  • I can predict which CSS declaration wins and choose between flexbox and grid
  • I can find and fix the causes of layout shift, and I return image dimensions from the API
  • I can choose between classic, defer, async and module scripts, and serve them with the right MIME type and caching
  • I can explain the browser event loop versus Node's and break up a long task
  • I know which browser storage to use for what, and what must never go into storage readable by JavaScript
  • I can make a form and a dialog keyboard and screen reader accessible, with field-level errors from NestJS
  • I can read a Network waterfall, the Timing phases and the Initiator chain, and I add Server-Timing to my APIs

Part 69 — Key Takeaways

  • The backend is the first stage of the rendering pipeline: every millisecond of time to first byte delays every later milestone.
  • CSS blocks rendering and classic scripts block parsing; nothing else should.
  • The preload scanner finds resources in raw HTML only, so put the LCP image and critical assets where it can see them.
  • Layout is the expensive stage; animate transform and opacity, and never interleave style writes with geometry reads.
  • A plain HTML form is a complete HTTP client; use native elements, type="button" for non-submit buttons, and Post/Redirect/Get with idempotency keys.
  • Resource hints are promises to the browser: one wrong as or a missing crossorigin means a double download.
  • Unreserved space is a bug; layout shift is fixed with dimensions and stable shapes the API provides.
  • The main thread is single-threaded like Node: tasks over 50 ms freeze input, and the cure is less work, later work, or work elsewhere.
  • Anything JavaScript can read, XSS can read; credentials belong in HttpOnly cookies and cookies must stay small.
  • Accessibility is built from semantics, focus and words; the API's error messages and alt text are part of it.
  • DevTools turns blame into evidence: read Timing phases and Initiator chains, and make your backend visible with Server-Timing and request ids.

Part 70 — Frontend Tooling and TypeScript in the Browser

A NestJS service has a simple relationship with its tooling. You write TypeScript, tsc (or nest build, which calls tsc or SWC) turns it into JavaScript in dist/, and Node.js runs that JavaScript on a machine you control. Nobody downloads your dist/ folder over a 4G connection. Nobody runs it on a five-year-old phone. Nobody can read your process.env from the outside.

A frontend breaks all three of those assumptions. The code you write runs on millions of machines you do not control, in browsers you did not choose, after travelling across a network that charges you in milliseconds for every kilobyte. And every byte you ship is public: anyone can press F12 and read it. That is why the frontend world has so much tooling, and why that tooling looks strange to a backend engineer the first time: a dev server that does not bundle, a production build that does, environment variables that are frozen into files, source maps that can leak your source code, a TypeScript compiler that is used only to check types and never to produce output.

Part 4 — Linux and the Command Line covered npm, lock files and semantic versioning (4.6). Part 5 — Git Basics and the Development Workflow covered the branch-and-pull-request workflow. Part 69 — How the Browser Builds a Page showed what the browser does with scripts once they arrive: defer, async, modules and the cost of parsing and executing JavaScript on the main thread (69.6, 69.7). This Part sits between those. It explains what happens from the moment you save a .tsx file to the moment a hashed, minified, compressed bundle sits on a CDN, and it shows how one TypeScript codebase can feed both a NestJS API and a React web app without the two drifting apart.

We will cover why browsers need a build step at all, how transpilers turn TypeScript and JSX into JavaScript for a chosen set of browsers, what bundlers and dev servers (Vite, esbuild, webpack, Turbopack) actually do, how hot module replacement works, how tree shaking and code splitting decide what each user downloads, why every "secret" in a frontend bundle is public, how source maps and minification interact with production debugging, how to configure TypeScript for the browser and share types with the backend, how monorepos with pnpm workspaces and Turborepo or Nx hold it all together, and how ESLint, Prettier and pre-commit checks keep it clean. We finish with a decision table for choosing a frontend stack and a worked pnpm monorepo with apps/api (NestJS), apps/web (React) and packages/contracts.

As in the rest of this Volume, every concept ends with a Backend side (NestJS) block: what the API, or the backend team, must do so that the frontend build is correct, fast and safe.

70.1 Why browsers need a build step

Concept

A build step is a program that runs on your machine or in CI before deployment and turns the code you write into the code the browser runs. For a backend you already have one: tsc compiles src/ to dist/. For a frontend the build step does more, because the gap between "what developers want to write" and "what browsers can efficiently download and execute" is wider.

Developers want to write TypeScript, JSX (<OrderCard order={order} />), hundreds of small files that import each other, imports of npm packages by bare name (import { z } from 'zod'), CSS modules, images imported as values, and modern syntax. Browsers natively understand JavaScript, HTML and CSS, ES modules loaded by URL (not by package name), and whatever syntax and APIs their particular version supports. The build step closes that gap: it transpiles (TypeScript and JSX to JavaScript, new syntax to older syntax), bundles (many files into a few), resolves (bare package names into real files), optimises (removes unused code, minifies, compresses) and fingerprints (adds a content hash to every file name so it can be cached forever).

Why does it exist?

Five separate problems, each of which alone would justify a build step:

  1. TypeScript and JSX are not JavaScript. No browser runs .ts or .tsx. Type annotations must be stripped and JSX must become function calls (jsx('div', {...})). Node.js 22.6+ can strip simple TypeScript types with a flag and Node 23.6+ does it by default, but browsers do not, and JSX is not part of any standard.
  2. Modules over the network are slow. Browsers do support ES modules (69.6), but each import is discovered only after the importing file is downloaded and parsed. A real React app has 1,500 to 4,000 modules once you include node_modules. Loading them one by one, level by level, even over HTTP/2, takes many round trips. On a 150 ms mobile connection, a dependency graph eight levels deep costs at least 1.2 s in discovery alone.
  3. Bare imports do not resolve. import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query' means nothing to a browser. It needs a URL. Import maps can map names to URLs, but you still need something to find the right file inside node_modules, read its package.json exports field and choose the browser build.
  4. Old browsers. Your users are not all on the latest Chrome. Safari on an iPhone that can no longer update, an embedded browser inside a banking app, a corporate Windows machine with an old Edge: each supports a different set of syntax and APIs. Writing for the lowest common denominator by hand would mean giving up ?., ??, async/await and class fields.
  5. Size is user-visible latency. Every kilobyte is downloaded over a mobile network and then parsed and compiled on a slow CPU (69.7). Comments, long variable names, whitespace, unused functions in a library and development-only warnings all cost the user time. A build step removes them.

Without a build step you get one of two bad outcomes: a codebase written in plain old JavaScript with globals and script tags (how much of the web worked before 2015), or a page that loads 3,000 files one by one and runs development-mode React in production.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen. Chefs work with whole ingredients, scraps, notes on the recipe, measuring spoons and tasting spoons. The customer receives a plated dish: trimmed, portioned, arranged so it can be eaten quickly, with no measuring spoons on the plate. The build step is the pass between kitchen and dining room. It throws away what the customer does not need (types, comments, unused code), combines components into portions that can be delivered in one trip (bundles), and labels each plate with a unique ticket so the waiter never serves yesterday's version (content hashes).

The kitchen also has a tasting mode for the chef, which is very different from service: dishes are prepared one component at a time, half-assembled, and adjusted in seconds. That is the dev server. It optimises for "see my change in 50 ms", not for "smallest download".

How it works

A frontend build is a pipeline. Different tools implement different stages, but the stages are the same everywhere:

flowchart LR
    src["Source: .ts .tsx .css .svg"] --> resolve["Resolve imports to files"]
    resolve --> transform["Transform: strip types, JSX, down-level syntax"]
    transform --> mgraph["Module graph"]
    mgraph --> shake["Tree shake unused exports"]
    shake --> chunk["Split into chunks"]
    chunk --> minify["Minify and mangle"]
    minify --> hash["Content hash file names"]
    hash --> out["dist: index.html plus hashed assets"]
    out --> cdn["CDN with immutable caching"]

Step by step, for a Vite + React app:

  1. Entry. The build starts from index.html, finds <script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx">, and treats main.tsx as the entry module.
  2. Resolve. For every import, the bundler finds the file. Relative paths are easy. Bare names (react) go through Node-style resolution: look in node_modules/react/package.json, read its exports map, pick the browser or import or default condition, and also honour any path aliases you configured.
  3. Load and transform. Each file is read and transformed. TypeScript types are stripped (by esbuild in Vite 2 to 7, by Oxc in Vite 8), JSX becomes jsx() calls from react/jsx-runtime, CSS is processed, an imported logo.svg becomes a URL string.
  4. Build the module graph. The bundler now knows every module and every import edge. This graph is the core data structure of every bundler.
  5. Tree shake. Starting from the entry, the bundler marks which exports are actually used and drops the rest (70.5).
  6. Chunk. Modules are grouped into output files. Dynamic import() calls create split points, so the admin dashboard does not ship to every shopper (70.5).
  7. Minify. Whitespace and comments go, local variable names become one letter, if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production') blocks that were replaced with if (false) are removed entirely.
  8. Hash and emit. Each output file is named after a hash of its content: assets/index-B7xQ2kLm.js. index.html is rewritten to reference those names. Because the name changes whenever the content changes, the files can be cached for a year with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, while index.html itself is revalidated on every load (Part 11 — Networking and HTTP, 11.11).

Here is what that means in numbers for a typical mid-size e-commerce SPA (React 18, React Router, TanStack Query, zod, a date library, an icon set, about 220 source files):

Measure Unbundled dev server Production build
Modules in the graph about 1,900 (including node_modules) same graph
Files the browser requests 300 to 600 on first load (dependencies pre-bundled) 6 to 15
JavaScript transferred 4 to 7 MB, uncompressed, with dev warnings 180 to 260 KB gzip for the first route
React build development (extra checks, about 3x slower) production
Source available in DevTools yes, original files only through source maps

The "1,900 modules become 10 files and 220 KB" line is the whole reason the build step exists.

A note on import maps. Browsers since 2023 (Chrome 89, Firefox 108, Safari 16.4) support <script type="importmap">, which maps bare names to URLs:

<script type="importmap">
  { "imports": { "zod": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/zod@3.23.8/+esm" } }
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { z } from 'zod'; // resolved through the import map
</script>

That solves bare imports, and for a small internal page with three dependencies it is a fine choice with no build at all. It does not solve TypeScript, JSX, the module waterfall, tree shaking or minification. Rails 7 uses this approach ("no-build" with importmap-rails) precisely for server-rendered apps with little JavaScript. For a React app with thousands of modules, it does not scale.

Practical example

An order tracking page in a food delivery app is written as 14 source files: main.tsx, App.tsx, routes/track.tsx, components/StatusTimeline.tsx, components/RiderMap.tsx, api/client.ts, api/orders.ts, hooks/useOrderStatus.ts, plus styles and icons. It imports React, React DOM, TanStack Query, zod and a map library.

Without a build, the browser would need a TypeScript compiler (it has none), would fail on the first import React from 'react', and even with an import map would request roughly 420 files. With a build:

  • index-Cj3k9P1a.js, 61 KB gzip: React, React DOM, the router, the app shell.
  • track-D9f2LmQe.js, 18 KB gzip: the tracking route, TanStack Query, zod schemas.
  • RiderMap-A1b2C3d4.js, 94 KB gzip: the map library, loaded only when the map scrolls into view.
  • index-Bq7rT0aZ.css, 9 KB gzip.

On a mid-range phone over 4G the first two files arrive in about 450 ms and execute in about 180 ms. The map chunk arrives later, off the critical path.

React / Next.js example

The source you write for that page uses all the things the browser cannot run directly:

// src/routes/track.tsx  (React 18, Vite)
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';
import { useParams } from 'react-router-dom';
import { useOrderStatus } from '../hooks/useOrderStatus';   // TypeScript module
import { StatusTimeline } from '../components/StatusTimeline';
import type { OrderStatus } from '@shop/contracts';         // type-only, erased at build

// Split point: the bundler emits RiderMap as its own chunk.
const RiderMap = lazy(() => import('../components/RiderMap'));

export default function TrackOrderRoute() {
  const { orderId } = useParams<{ orderId: string }>();
  const { data, isPending, error } = useOrderStatus(orderId!);

  if (isPending) return <p aria-busy="true">Loading your order...</p>;
  if (error) return <p role="alert">We could not load this order. Pull down to retry.</p>;

  const status: OrderStatus = data.status;
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Order {data.displayId}</h1>
      <StatusTimeline status={status} events={data.events} />
      {status === 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY' && (
        <Suspense fallback={<div style={{ height: 320 }} aria-hidden="true" />}>
          <RiderMap riderId={data.riderId} />
        </Suspense>
      )}
    </main>
  );
}

After the build, the type annotations and the import type line are gone, the JSX is calls to jsx() and jsxs(), lazy(() => import('../components/RiderMap')) points to ./RiderMap-A1b2C3d4.js, and the whole module is merged with its neighbours into track-D9f2LmQe.js. With Next.js 14 the same transformation happens inside next build, using SWC for transforms and webpack for bundling by default; Turbopack takes over bundling as an opt-in in Next.js 15 and as the default from Next.js 16.

Backend side (NestJS)

When the built SPA is served by your NestJS application (common for admin panels and internal tools, where a separate CDN setup is overkill), the backend must understand the shape of a build output: one HTML entry that must never be cached for long, many hashed files that should be cached forever, and client-side routes that do not exist as files. @nestjs/serve-static handles this:

// app.module.ts
import { Module } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ServeStaticModule } from '@nestjs/serve-static';
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { OrdersModule } from './orders/orders.module';

@Module({
  imports: [
    OrdersModule,
    ServeStaticModule.forRoot({
      rootPath: join(__dirname, '..', '..', 'web', 'dist'),
      // Do not let the SPA fallback swallow API routes. NestJS 11 (Express 5,
      // path-to-regexp v8) uses '/api/{*path}'; NestJS 10 and earlier used '/api*'.
      exclude: ['/api/{*path}'],
      serveStaticOptions: {
        // Unknown paths like /orders/123 return index.html, so the client router can handle them.
        fallthrough: true,
        setHeaders: (res, filePath) => {
          if (filePath.endsWith('index.html')) {
            res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-cache'); // always revalidate the entry
          } else if (filePath.includes('/assets/')) {
            res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable');
          }
        },
      },
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

Three things the backend owns here:

  • The SPA fallback must not hide API 404s. A request to /api/v1/ordrs (typo) must return a JSON 404, not index.html with status 200. Otherwise the frontend's JSON parser fails with Unexpected token '<' and the real error is invisible.
  • Missing assets must 404, not fall back to HTML. If /assets/track-OLDHASH.js is requested after a deploy, returning index.html produces a confusing "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module" or a MIME type error. The fallback should apply only to paths without a file extension.
  • Caching follows the hash. Immutable for assets/, no-cache for index.html. Get this backwards and users run yesterday's bundle against today's API.

Production scenario

A logistics company ran its dispatcher console as a single 2.4 MB JavaScript file built by a hand-written Gulp script in 2016: concatenation plus Uglify, no modules, no hashing, served with Cache-Control: max-age=3600. Every deploy produced an hour of support tickets because some browsers kept the old file while the API had already changed. Load time on the warehouse tablets was 6 to 8 s.

They moved to Vite with React and TypeScript. The production build produced 14 hashed files; the dispatcher's first route was 210 KB gzip; the map and reporting screens loaded on demand. Load time on the same tablets fell to 1.9 s, and because file names now changed with content and index.html was revalidated, stale-bundle tickets after deploys went to zero. The build took 38 s in CI, compared with 3 minutes for the old Gulp pipeline.

Failure scenario

At 16:40 on a Friday a team shipped a new internal returns dashboard. In staging it worked. In production every page showed a blank screen and the console said Uncaught ReferenceError: process is not defined.

The cause: a shared utility file, written for the NestJS backend, read process.env.FEATURE_RETURNS_V2 directly. Webpack 4, which the team's older apps used, automatically polyfilled process for the browser, so this had always "worked". The new app was built with Vite, which does not polyfill Node globals and only replaces import.meta.env.* and an explicit list of define keys. Staging worked because the developer had a define: { 'process.env': {} } hack in a local config file that was never committed.

The fix took ten minutes: read feature flags from a runtime config endpoint instead of process.env, and add an ESLint no-restricted-globals rule for process in browser code. The lesson took longer to learn: code that runs in the browser is not Node.js, and the build tool decides which Node-isms silently "work". Webpack 5 removed automatic Node polyfills for exactly this reason.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Development and production differ. Dev servers serve unbundled modules with development React; production is bundled, minified and tree-shaken. Bugs that only appear after minification (code that relies on function.name, which mangling changes) or after tree shaking (a side effect in an "unused" import) never show in dev.
  • Case-insensitive file systems. import './orderCard' when the file is OrderCard.tsx works on macOS and Windows and fails on the Linux CI runner or Docker build.
  • Node globals in shared code: process, Buffer, __dirname, require do not exist in the browser; behaviour depends on the bundler.
  • Packages without a browser build: a library that ships only CommonJS or depends on fs will either fail to build or bloat the bundle with polyfills.
  • Unhashed asset names cached at the CDN keep serving old code after a deploy.
  • A build that "succeeds" with type errors: most bundlers do not type-check (70.2), so a green build does not mean correct types.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the frontend build as part of the production system, not a developer convenience. The build output is the artefact that ships, so it is reviewed, measured and reproducible like a Docker image (Part 44 — Docker for Backend Engineers). They ask: what is the size of the first-route JavaScript, and is it in a budget? Which browsers do we support, and who decided? Is the build deterministic from the lock file? Does a green build also mean a green type check?

They also refuse the opposite extreme. A two-page internal status page does not need a bundler, a framework and a monorepo; server-rendered HTML with a small <script type="module"> and an import map is simpler and will still work in ten years. To a product manager they would say: "The build step is what lets us write the app quickly and still send phones a small, fast download. We keep it simple and measure what it produces."

Common mistakes

  • Treating the dev server as a preview of production. Always test the production build (vite build && vite preview, or next build && next start) before release.
  • Shipping development builds. A missing NODE_ENV=production in a custom webpack setup ships React's development build, about 3x slower and much larger.
  • Long-caching unhashed files or short-caching hashed ones.
  • Sharing backend utility files with the frontend without checking for Node-only globals and modules.
  • Assuming the build checks types. It usually does not; run tsc --noEmit separately.

Interview questions

  1. Browsers support ES modules. Why do we still bundle? Expected answer: module discovery is a waterfall (one round trip per level of the import graph), thousands of small files have per-request overhead, bare imports do not resolve without a tool, and bundling enables tree shaking, minification and hashed caching. Why it matters: shows the candidate understands the network cost, not just "because everyone does". Follow-up: when would you skip bundling? (Small pages, import maps, few dependencies.)
  2. What does a content hash in a file name buy you? Expected answer: the URL changes whenever content changes, so the file can be cached forever with immutable, and only the HTML entry needs revalidation. Follow-up: what happens to a user with the old index.html open during a deploy? (Old chunk names; keep previous assets available, see Part 78.)
  3. What are the stages of a frontend build? Expected answer: resolve, transform, build the module graph, tree shake, chunk, minify, hash, emit.
  4. Your SPA shows Unexpected token '<' when parsing an API response. What happened? Expected answer: the server returned HTML (often the SPA fallback index.html or a proxy error page) where JSON was expected; fix the routing so API paths never fall through to the SPA.
  5. Why does code that worked with webpack 4 fail with process is not defined in Vite or webpack 5? Expected answer: webpack 4 polyfilled Node globals automatically; newer tools do not, so Node-specific code must not run in the browser.

Practical exercise

Create a Vite React TypeScript app (npm create vite@latest web -- --template react-ts), add an order list route and a lazily loaded order detail route, then build it.

Acceptance criteria:

  • You can list every file in dist/assets/, its gzip size (gzip -c file | wc -c), and which source modules ended up in each.
  • You can explain why the order detail route is a separate file.
  • You serve dist/ from a NestJS app with ServeStaticModule, and verify with curl -I that index.html has Cache-Control: no-cache, hashed assets have immutable, /orders/42 returns the HTML, and /api/does-not-exist returns a JSON 404.

70.2 Transpiling: TypeScript, JSX and browser targets

Concept

Transpiling means converting source code in one language or language version into another at the same level of abstraction. In a frontend build it does three jobs: removes TypeScript types, turns JSX into function calls, and rewrites modern syntax that your oldest supported browser does not understand into older syntax.

The crucial idea for a backend engineer is that, in frontend builds, transpiling and type checking are separated. The tools that produce the JavaScript you ship (esbuild, SWC, Babel, Oxc) strip types without checking them, one file at a time, extremely fast. The TypeScript compiler tsc is run separately, with noEmit: true, only to report type errors. This is different from a typical NestJS project, where tsc both checks and emits.

A browser target is the list of browsers (and versions) your output must run in. The transpiler uses it to decide which syntax to rewrite. A polyfill is code that adds a missing API at runtime (for example Array.prototype.at in Safari 15.3). Transpilers rewrite syntax; they do not add APIs. Polyfills are a separate decision.

Why does it exist?

Type checking needs the whole program: to know whether order.total.amount is valid, the checker must read the Order type, which might come from another file, which imports from a package. That is slow. On a 2,000-file React app, tsc --noEmit commonly takes 20 to 45 s on a laptop. Stripping types does not need the whole program: you can look at one file, delete the annotations, and you are done. esbuild does this for the same 2,000 files in well under a second.

If the dev server had to type-check before every refresh, you would wait 20 s for each change. So the ecosystem split the jobs: fast per-file transpiling on every save, slower whole-program type checking in the editor (the TypeScript language server), in a background watcher, and in CI.

Targets exist because "JavaScript" is not one thing. Optional chaining (a?.b) arrived in Chrome 80 (2020) and Safari 13.1. Class static blocks in Safari 16.4. Top-level await in Safari 15. If 3 % of your shoppers are on a browser that does not understand a syntax feature, the entire bundle fails to parse for them: not one broken feature, a completely blank page.

Mental model

Imagine translating a contract. A lawyer reads the whole contract and checks every clause against every other clause and against the law (type checking): slow, needs the full document. A typist removes the margin notes, reformats it for the printer and replaces modern abbreviations with full words the recipient will understand (transpiling): fast, can work page by page. You want the typist working on every draft, instantly. You want the lawyer to review before it is signed (CI).

Browser targets are the recipient's reading level. A polyfill is a glossary stapled to the back for words the recipient's dictionary does not contain.

How it works

flowchart TB
    file["OrderCard.tsx"] --> fast["Fast transpiler: esbuild, SWC, Babel or Oxc"]
    fast --> js["OrderCard.js: types gone, JSX as jsx calls, syntax lowered to target"]
    js --> bundler["Bundler"]
    proj["Whole project plus node_modules types"] --> tsc["tsc --noEmit"]
    tsc --> report["Type errors only, no output files"]
    report --> ci["CI gate and editor squiggles"]

The transpilers.

Tool Written in Used by Notes
tsc TypeScript (a Go-native port, TypeScript 7, was previewed in 2025 as tsgo with about 10x faster checking) Type checking everywhere; emitting for Node backends Whole-program; the only one that checks types
esbuild Go Vite 2 to 7 (dev transforms, dependency pre-bundling, minification), many libraries Per-file; no type checking; very fast
SWC Rust Next.js 12+ (transforms and minification), @vitejs/plugin-react-swc, NestJS CLI optional builder Per-file; Babel-compatible plugin model in Rust
Babel JavaScript Older webpack setups, @vitejs/plugin-react (for Fast Refresh and plugins), React Compiler Slowest, most plugins
Oxc Rust Vite 8 (through Rolldown), oxlint Per-file transformer, parser, minifier

Because these tools see only one file at a time, a few TypeScript features cannot be compiled correctly by them:

  • const enum across files: the value must be inlined from another file, which a per-file tool cannot read.
  • Re-exporting a type without type: export { OrderStatus } from './types'. If OrderStatus is only a type, the per-file tool does not know and emits a runtime re-export of something that does not exist.
  • Namespaces merging across files.

The tsconfig option isolatedModules: true makes tsc report an error for exactly these cases, so code that type-checks will also transpile correctly per file. TypeScript 5.0 added verbatimModuleSyntax: true, which is stricter and simpler: any import or export without the type modifier is kept in the output exactly as written, and any with type is removed. It forces you to write import type { Order } from './types', which is exactly what a per-file transpiler needs. Vite's TypeScript templates enable it.

JSX. With React 17 and later, the "automatic runtime" is standard. tsconfig has "jsx": "react-jsx", and the transpiler turns:

<OrderCard order={order} compact />

into:

import { jsx as _jsx } from 'react/jsx-runtime';
_jsx(OrderCard, { order: order, compact: true });

The older "jsx": "react" setting produced React.createElement(...) and required import React from 'react' in every file.

Targets. You tell the build which browsers to support, and the transpiler lowers any syntax newer than that. Each tool expresses this differently:

Tool How you set the target Default
Vite 5 and 6 build.target 'modules': browsers with native ES modules, dynamic import and import.meta (about Chrome 87, Safari 14)
Vite 7 and later build.target 'baseline-widely-available': Chrome 107, Edge 107, Firefox 104, Safari 16
esbuild --target=es2020,chrome100,safari15 esnext (no lowering)
Next.js browserslist in package.json Chrome 64, Edge 79, Firefox 67, Opera 51, Safari 12 (Next.js 14)
Babel and webpack browserslist (.browserslistrc or package.json) defaults query

browserslist is a shared format: "browserslist": ["> 0.5%", "last 2 versions", "not dead"] resolves against usage data from caniuse to a concrete list of browser versions.

Polyfills are separate. If you call structuredClone() or Array.prototype.findLast() and your target includes Safari 15.3, no transpiler will save you; the function simply does not exist there. Options: avoid the API, add a specific polyfill (core-js/actual/array/find-last), or use @vitejs/plugin-legacy, which builds a second legacy bundle with Babel and core-js and serves it only to browsers that do not support modules, using <script nomodule>. The legacy bundle is usually 30 to 60 % larger and takes as long again to build, so you pay only if you need it.

Where type checking goes. Since the bundler will not do it, you add it explicitly:

{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.app.json",
    "build": "tsc -b && vite build",
    "preview": "vite preview"
  }
}

The Vite React TypeScript template runs tsc -b (build mode with project references, still emitting nothing because noEmit is set in each referenced config) before vite build. In a monorepo with Turborepo (70.9) you usually make typecheck its own task so it can run in parallel with tests and be cached separately. During development, vite-plugin-checker can run tsc --watch in a worker and show errors as an overlay in the browser without slowing HMR.

Practical example

A checkout team supports "the last two versions of every major browser plus Safari 15 on iOS", because 4 % of their iPhone shoppers are stuck on iOS 15 devices. They set build.target: ['es2020', 'safari15', 'chrome100', 'firefox100'] in Vite.

Effects measured on their 230 KB gzip bundle:

  • Optional chaining, nullish coalescing and async/await are kept as-is (all supported by Safari 15). No size change.
  • Class static blocks used in one library were lowered to plain assignments: plus 0.3 KB.
  • Top-level await in a config module failed the build with "Top-level await is not available in the configured target environment". They removed it and loaded config in an async bootstrap function instead.
  • Array.prototype.at() (Safari 15.4+) was used in the cart. The transpiler did not touch it, and 0.6 % of iOS users got TypeError: items.at is not a function until they added a three-line helper.

That last one is the classic trap: targets cover syntax, not APIs.

React / Next.js example

A Vite config that sets targets deliberately and uses the SWC-based React plugin for faster transforms:

// vite.config.ts  (Vite 6 or 7)
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react-swc'; // SWC for JSX and Fast Refresh; @vitejs/plugin-react uses Babel

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  build: {
    // Syntax newer than these is lowered. APIs are NOT polyfilled.
    target: ['es2020', 'safari15', 'chrome100', 'firefox100', 'edge100'],
    cssTarget: ['safari15'], // CSS nesting and similar are lowered for Safari 15
  },
  esbuild: {
    // Drop console.debug calls and debugger statements in production builds only.
    pure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' ? ['console.debug'] : [],
    drop: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' ? ['debugger'] : [],
  },
});

For Next.js the target lives in package.json, and SWC reads it:

{
  "browserslist": ["chrome >= 100", "edge >= 100", "firefox >= 100", "safari >= 15", "ios_saf >= 15"]
}

Backend side (NestJS)

Choosing targets is a data decision, and the backend has the data. Every API request carries a User-Agent header (and, from Chromium browsers, Sec-CH-UA client hints). A small middleware that counts browser families and major versions into a metric answers "can we drop Safari 14?" with numbers instead of opinions:

// browser-usage.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { Counter, register } from 'prom-client';

const browserRequests =
  (register.getSingleMetric('api_browser_requests_total') as Counter<string>) ??
  new Counter({
    name: 'api_browser_requests_total',
    help: 'API requests by browser family and major version',
    labelNames: ['family', 'major'],
  });

// Deliberately coarse parsing: we need families and majors, not perfect detection.
const PATTERNS: Array<[string, RegExp]> = [
  ['edge', /Edg\/(\d+)/],
  ['chrome', /Chrome\/(\d+)/],
  ['firefox', /Firefox\/(\d+)/],
  ['safari', /Version\/(\d+)[\d.]* .*Safari\//],
];

@Injectable()
export class BrowserUsageMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, _res: Response, next: NextFunction): void {
    const ua = req.headers['user-agent'] ?? '';
    const hit = PATTERNS.find(([, re]) => re.test(ua));
    const [family, major] = hit ? [hit[0], ua.match(hit[1])?.[1] ?? 'unknown'] : ['other', 'unknown'];
    // Cap label cardinality: bucket very old majors together.
    browserRequests.inc({ family, major: Number(major) < 90 ? 'old' : major });
    next();
  }
}

Register it only on browser-facing routes (consumer.apply(BrowserUsageMiddleware).forRoutes('v1/orders', 'v1/cart')) so server-to-server calls do not skew the numbers. After two weeks, a Grafana panel shows that Safari 14 is 0.4 % of checkout traffic, and the team can make the call with the product manager instead of guessing. The same data tells you when a polyfill can be deleted.

The backend's second job is not to make the frontend's target harder: an API that returns BigInt-sized numbers as JSON numbers, or dates in a non-ISO format that only some Date parsers accept, pushes compatibility problems into the browser. Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts covers these wire formats.

Production scenario

A travel booking site had browserslist: "defaults" and Babel with useBuiltIns: 'usage' and core-js 3. Their main bundle was 410 KB gzip, of which 71 KB was core-js polyfills for features every browser in their real traffic already supported. Their API's browser metric showed 99.2 % of bookings came from browsers released in the last four years.

They changed the target to chrome >= 100, safari >= 15, firefox >= 100 and removed the global polyfill injection, adding two specific polyfills that were still needed. The bundle fell to 322 KB gzip, the transpile step in CI went from 74 s to 21 s, and p75 Interaction to Next Paint on mobile improved by 40 ms because there was less JavaScript to parse at startup. The 0.8 % of users on older browsers got a server-rendered "please update your browser, or call us" page with the phone number, which the business accepted.

Failure scenario

On a Monday at 10:15, support tickets spiked from users of a corporate travel portal: "blank page". All tickets came from one enterprise customer. Error tracking showed nothing at all, because the error tracker itself was in the bundle that failed to parse.

A dependency upgrade had pulled in a new version of a date library that used class static blocks. The project's Vite 5 build.target was the default 'modules', which includes Chrome 87. The customer's managed laptops were pinned to Chrome 91, which does not support static blocks (added in Chrome 94). The entire bundle threw SyntaxError: Unexpected token '{' at parse time.

The immediate fix was setting build.target: ['es2020', 'chrome87'], which made esbuild lower the static blocks. The longer-term fixes: a tiny inline script in index.html, outside the bundle, that reports window.onerror for syntax errors to a NestJS endpoint, so parse failures are visible; and a CI step that runs the production build through the es-check tool against the declared target.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Syntax errors kill the whole bundle, including your error reporting. Report parse errors from a separate tiny inline script.
  • Dependencies are not always transpiled. Some setups skip node_modules for speed. Vite's production build does lower dependencies to build.target, but pre-bundled dev dependencies may differ.
  • const enum from a library compiled with isolatedModules off can break silently; prefer union string types (type Status = 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED') in shared code.
  • Type-only imports without import type produce runtime imports of things that do not exist, typically "does not provide an export named X" in the browser.
  • Decorators: TypeScript's experimentalDecorators (used by NestJS, TypeORM, class-validator) differ from TC39 standard decorators (TypeScript 5.0+). Sharing decorated classes with a browser build invites trouble; share plain types or zod schemas instead (70.8).
  • Polyfills loaded twice: once by you and once inside a library, growing the bundle and sometimes conflicting.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior writes the supported browser list down, with a date and an owner, and derives it from real traffic, not from a default. They know a target is a cost decision: each older browser supported costs bundle size and build complexity for everyone else. They keep type checking as a separate, mandatory CI gate and never rely on the bundler for it. They avoid TypeScript features that need whole-program compilation (const enum, namespaces) in code that a per-file tool will see. And they make sure the one failure mode that hides itself, a parse error that takes out the error reporter, is reported by something outside the bundle.

Common mistakes

  • Believing the target polyfills APIs. It lowers syntax only.
  • Leaving the default target forever without checking it against real traffic.
  • Turning off isolatedModules because it "complains", then hitting runtime import errors.
  • Running tsc to emit files in a Vite project, producing a stray .js next to every .ts that the bundler may pick up instead of the source.
  • Relying on the error tracker to catch syntax errors in the bundle that contains the error tracker.

Interview questions

  1. Why do frontend builds separate transpiling from type checking? Expected answer: type checking needs the whole program and is slow; transpiling can be done per file in milliseconds, so it runs on every save while type checking runs in the editor and CI. Follow-up: what tsconfig options make per-file transpiling safe? (isolatedModules, verbatimModuleSyntax.)
  2. What is the difference between a build target and a polyfill? Expected answer: the target controls which syntax is rewritten; a polyfill adds missing runtime APIs. Follow-up: how would you decide which polyfills you still need?
  3. A dependency upgrade made the page blank for one customer. How do you investigate? Expected answer: check for a parse-time SyntaxError in that customer's browser version, compare the dependency's syntax with the build target, lower the target or pin the dependency, and add parse-error reporting outside the bundle.
  4. Why is const enum risky in a codebase built with esbuild or SWC? Expected answer: the value must be inlined from another file, which a per-file tool cannot read.
  5. How do you choose which browsers to support? Expected answer: from real traffic data and business impact, written down with an owner, revisited periodically.

Practical exercise

In a Vite React TypeScript project, add a class with a static { } block and a call to [1, 2, 3].at(-1). Build twice: once with build.target: 'esnext' and once with build.target: ['es2020', 'chrome87'].

Acceptance criteria:

  • You can show, in the built JavaScript, that the static block is rewritten in the second build and untouched in the first.
  • You can show that .at(-1) is untouched in both, and explain why.
  • You add verbatimModuleSyntax: true and fix every error it reports, explaining for one of them what would have gone wrong at runtime.
  • You add the BrowserUsageMiddleware to a NestJS app and produce a /metrics output with at least two browser families.

70.3 Bundlers and dev servers: Vite, esbuild, webpack and Turbopack

Concept

A bundler takes your entry file, follows every import to build the module graph (70.1), and writes a small number of optimised output files. A dev server serves your app to the browser during development and updates it when you save a file. Historically one tool did both. The big change of the last five years is that the fastest tools now treat development and production differently.

Four names cover most of what you will meet:

  • webpack (v5 since 2020): the long-time standard. Bundles everything, in development and production, through a highly configurable system of loaders and plugins. Next.js used it by default up to version 15.
  • esbuild (Go, 2020): an extremely fast bundler and transpiler with a deliberately small feature set. Rarely used alone for apps; used inside other tools.
  • Vite (v1 2020, v5 2023, v6 late 2024, v7 mid 2025, v8 with Rolldown): a dev server that does not bundle your source during development and a production build that does. It is the default for new React SPAs since Create React App was deprecated in February 2025.
  • Turbopack (Rust): the bundler built by Vercel for Next.js, based on fine-grained incremental computation. Opt-in for next dev in Next.js 13.4 and 14, stable for development in Next.js 15, and the default for both next dev and next build in Next.js 16.

You will also meet Rollup (Vite's production bundler up to Vite 7, strong at tree shaking and library builds), Rolldown (a Rust rewrite of Rollup's ideas that replaces both Rollup and esbuild inside Vite 8) and Rspack (a Rust implementation of webpack's API, 1.0 in 2024, for teams with large webpack configs who want speed without a rewrite).

Why does it exist?

Bundling solves the network problem (70.1), but it creates a development problem. A webpack dev server must build the entire graph before it can serve the first page. On a 3,000-module app that is 30 to 90 s on start and 1 to 3 s after each save, because even an incremental rebuild has to re-emit the bundle that contains the changed file. Developers save files hundreds of times a day. Three seconds per save is a quarter of an hour of waiting every day, and it breaks concentration.

Vite's insight was that during development the network is localhost, so the module waterfall that makes unbundled ES modules slow in production barely matters. Let the browser request modules natively, transform each one only when it is requested, and the dev server starts in under a second regardless of app size. Only third-party dependencies, which often consist of hundreds of internal files or ship as CommonJS, are pre-bundled once.

Turbopack took a different route to the same goal: keep bundling in development (so dev matches production more closely), but make it incremental at the level of individual functions, caching every intermediate result so a change recomputes only what depends on it.

Mental model

Imagine a magazine print shop. The webpack way rebinds the whole issue every time an editor changes a sentence. The Vite way, during editing, hands editors loose pages as they ask for them and binds only the final print run. The Turbopack way keeps a ledger of which sentence fed which page, so a change reprints exactly the affected lines.

How it works

Vite in development.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant V as ViteDevServer
    participant E as Transformer
    participant D as DepCache
    B->>V: GET /
    V-->>B: index.html with HMR client injected
    B->>V: GET /src/main.tsx
    V->>E: transform main.tsx on demand
    E-->>V: JS with rewritten imports
    V-->>B: main.tsx as ES module
    B->>V: GET /node_modules/.vite/deps/react.js
    V->>D: pre-bundled on first start
    D-->>V: react as one ESM file
    V-->>B: react.js with long cache
    B->>V: GET /src/routes/track.tsx
    V->>E: transform only when requested
    V-->>B: track.tsx as ES module
  1. Dependency pre-bundling. On first start, Vite scans your source for bare imports, then bundles each dependency (React, TanStack Query, lodash-es) into a single ESM file in node_modules/.vite/deps/. This converts CommonJS to ESM and collapses packages with hundreds of internal modules (lodash-es has over 600) into one request. Vite 2 to 7 use esbuild for this; Vite 8 uses Rolldown. Results are cached until the lock file or config changes.
  2. On-demand source transforms. Your own files are served as native ES modules. When the browser requests /src/routes/track.tsx, Vite transforms that one file (strip types, JSX, rewrite import 'react' to /node_modules/.vite/deps/react.js?v=hash) and responds. A route you never open is never transformed.
  3. Caching. Pre-bundled dependencies are served with Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable; source modules use 304 Not Modified revalidation, so a reload re-sends only changed files.

Vite in production. vite build uses a real bundler: Rollup up to Vite 7, Rolldown from Vite 8. This dual approach has one real cost: the dev server and the production build are different programs, so a few bugs appear only in production (a CommonJS interop edge case, a different chunk order, a module with side effects that tree shaking removes). That inconsistency is one of the reasons Vite 8 moved both dev pre-bundling and production bundling onto Rolldown.

webpack. Everything is a module, and everything that is not JavaScript is turned into JavaScript by a loader (ts-loader or babel-loader for TypeScript, css-loader for CSS). Plugins hook into the compilation for everything else: HtmlWebpackPlugin writes index.html, MiniCssExtractPlugin extracts CSS files, DefinePlugin replaces constants. The dev server (webpack-dev-server) builds the whole graph into memory and serves it. webpack 5 added a persistent filesystem cache (cache: { type: 'filesystem' }) that cuts warm starts by 60 to 90 %, and Module Federation, which lets separately deployed apps load each other's modules at runtime (the basis of most "micro-frontend" setups).

esbuild alone is a command:

# Bundle, minify, split chunks and write source maps in about a second for a mid-size app.
npx esbuild src/main.tsx --bundle --minify --sourcemap --splitting --format=esm \
  --target=es2020,safari15 --outdir=dist/assets --define:process.env.NODE_ENV=\"production\"

It has no HMR (it has a --watch mode and a simple --serve with live reload), and code splitting works only with --format=esm. That is why apps use esbuild through Vite rather than directly, while small libraries, CLIs and Lambda functions often use it alone.

Turbopack computes the build as a graph of small cached functions ("parse this file", "resolve this import", "chunk this route"). On a change it invalidates only the functions whose inputs changed. It bundles per route on demand in development, so opening /checkout does not compile /admin. It is not a general-purpose bundler you configure for any app; it is built into Next.js and configured through next.config.js.

Typical numbers for a 2,000-module React app on a 2023 laptop (they vary a lot with plugins and machine; treat them as orders of magnitude):

Tool Dev server cold start Update after save Production build
webpack 5 with babel-loader 25 to 45 s (8 to 12 s with warm filesystem cache) 1 to 3 s 90 to 150 s
Rspack 1.x 3 to 6 s 100 to 300 ms 10 to 25 s
Vite 6 or 7 (Rollup build) under 1 s to start; first page 2 to 4 s while modules transform 20 to 80 ms 30 to 60 s
Vite 8 (Rolldown build) similar to Vite 7 20 to 80 ms 5 to 15 s
Next.js 16 with Turbopack 1 to 3 s per first route visit under 100 ms 20 to 45 s for the whole app
esbuild alone no dev server rebuild 50 to 200 ms with --watch 1 to 3 s

Practical example

A merchant dashboard on Create React App (webpack 4 underneath) took 52 s to start and 2.5 s per change. The two-day Vite migration: move index.html to the root with <script type="module" src="/src/index.tsx">, rename process.env.REACT_APP_* to import.meta.env.VITE_* (70.6), replace CRA's proxy field with server.proxy, add vite-plugin-svgr for SVG-as-component imports CRA did implicitly, and remove one dynamic require(). Dev start went to 0.8 s, updates to about 40 ms, the production build from 140 s to 34 s, and the bundle shrank 11 % from better tree shaking.

React / Next.js example

A Vite config for a React SPA that talks to a NestJS API on another port, with the dev proxy that removes the need for CORS in development:

// apps/web/vite.config.ts  (Vite 6 or 7)
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { fileURLToPath, URL } from 'node:url';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  resolve: {
    alias: { '@': fileURLToPath(new URL('./src', import.meta.url)) }, // matches tsconfig paths (76.8)
  },
  server: {
    port: 5173,
    strictPort: true, // fail instead of silently moving to 5174 and breaking cookie and CORS assumptions
    proxy: {
      // Browser calls /api/... on :5173; Vite forwards to NestJS on :3000. Same origin, no CORS.
      '/api': { target: 'http://localhost:3000', changeOrigin: true },
      // Server-Sent Events and WebSockets for live order status (Part 35)
      '/realtime': { target: 'ws://localhost:3000', ws: true },
    },
  },
  build: { outDir: 'dist', sourcemap: 'hidden' }, // 'hidden': maps generated but not referenced (76.7)
  preview: { port: 4173 },
});

In Next.js 14 you opt into Turbopack for development only:

{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "next dev --turbo",
    "build": "next build",
    "start": "next start"
  }
}

In Next.js 15 the flag is --turbopack (with --turbo still accepted), and in Next.js 16 Turbopack is the default for both commands, with --webpack to opt out. A custom webpack() function in next.config.js is ignored by Turbopack, which is the main migration cost for older Next.js apps.

Backend side (NestJS)

The dev server topology decides what the API must do in development, and getting it wrong creates bugs that only exist on laptops.

With a proxy (recommended), the browser sees one origin (http://localhost:5173). Cookies set by NestJS on /api/auth/login are first-party, SameSite=Lax works, and the API needs no CORS configuration at all in development. Production usually looks the same, with a CDN or load balancer routing /api/* to NestJS, so dev mirrors prod.

Without a proxy, the browser on :5173 calls :3000 directly. That is cross-origin (different port means different origin), so NestJS must enable CORS, and cookies need credentials: 'include' on every fetch. Keep that configuration explicit and development-only:

// main.ts
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  const config = app.get(ConfigService);
  app.setGlobalPrefix('api'); // matches the '/api' proxy prefix, so paths are identical in dev and prod

  // Only for setups without a dev proxy. Never use origin: true or '*' together with credentials.
  const devOrigins = config.get<string>('CORS_DEV_ORIGINS'); // e.g. "http://localhost:5173"
  if (config.get('NODE_ENV') !== 'production' && devOrigins) {
    app.enableCors({
      origin: devOrigins.split(','),
      credentials: true,
      exposedHeaders: ['X-Request-Id', 'Retry-After'], // headers the frontend must be able to read
    });
  }

  app.enableShutdownHooks();
  await app.listen(config.get<number>('PORT', 3000));
}
bootstrap();

Two backend details matter with proxies: changeOrigin: true rewrites the Host header, so NestJS sees localhost:3000 (fine for most apps, wrong if you build absolute URLs from Host; use a configured public base URL instead), and the proxy adds X-Forwarded-For, so trust it only in development or behind your real load balancer (Part 11 — Networking and HTTP covers forwarded headers).

Production scenario

An online grocery company with 14 frontend engineers logged rebuild durations and found 41 minutes per engineer per day spent waiting on webpack 5 (a 3,400-module app, 2.1 s average update). Their config had eight custom loaders and relied on Module Federation. Rspack accepted it with two changes, brought updates to 180 ms and production builds from 2 min 40 s to 22 s. They chose it over a Vite rewrite because it was a one-week migration rather than a six-week one.

Failure scenario

A Vite app worked perfectly in development and passed all tests. After deploy, the order history page threw TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'default').

The page imported a CommonJS charting library. In development, esbuild's pre-bundling interop exposed module.exports one way; in production, Rollup's @rollup/plugin-commonjs produced a slightly different shape, and the code's Chart.default.render(...) only worked with one of them. Nobody had run vite build && vite preview before merging.

The fix was a one-line import change. The process fix was a CI job that builds, starts vite preview and runs the Playwright smoke tests against the production bundle (Part 77 — Frontend Testing and Quality), not the dev server.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Dev and production bundlers differ (Vite up to 7): CommonJS interop, chunk ordering and side-effect removal can behave differently. Always test the production build.
  • First page load in a big Vite app is slow (hundreds of on-demand transforms). It is a one-time cost per session; server.warmup in Vite 5.1+ pre-transforms listed files.
  • Pre-bundle cache stale after linking a local package (for example a workspace package changed outside Vite's watch). vite --force rebuilds it.
  • strictPort: false silently moves to the next port; your proxy, CORS allow-list or OAuth redirect URI then points at the wrong one.
  • Custom webpack config ignored by Turbopack in Next.js; features that relied on it break silently in dev.
  • Proxy timeouts: long-polling and SSE endpoints proxied through the dev server need ws: true or longer timeouts, or the stream drops every 2 minutes in development only.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior picks the bundler that the framework already chose (Next.js gives you Turbopack or webpack; a React SPA gets Vite) and spends their energy elsewhere. They do not hand-roll a webpack config in a new project in 2026. For an existing large webpack codebase they weigh a compatible speed-up (Rspack) against a rewrite (Vite) by migration cost, not by benchmark headlines. They measure developer wait time, because it is real money: 30 minutes a day across 20 engineers is more than a full-time salary.

They also insist that CI tests the artefact that ships: the production bundle, served the way production serves it. "It works in vite dev" is not evidence.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a bundler by benchmark instead of by framework fit and migration cost.
  • Never running the production build locally.
  • Enabling CORS with origin: true and credentials: true "just for dev" and shipping it to production.
  • Using Node-only libraries in browser code and expecting the bundler to polyfill them.

Interview questions

  1. Why does Vite start in under a second when webpack takes 40 s on the same app? Expected answer: Vite does not bundle source in development; it serves native ES modules and transforms each file on request, and pre-bundles dependencies once with a fast tool. webpack builds the whole graph first. Follow-up: what does that cost? (Dev and prod differ; slow first page on very large apps.)
  2. What is dependency pre-bundling and why does Vite need it? Expected answer: converting CommonJS dependencies to ESM and collapsing many-file packages into one request, so the browser does not make hundreds of requests for one library.
  3. When would you choose Rspack over migrating to Vite? Expected answer: large existing webpack configuration, custom loaders, Module Federation; Rspack keeps the config and gives most of the speed.
  4. How do you avoid CORS in local development? Expected answer: a dev server proxy so the browser sees one origin, matching production routing.
  5. What is the main migration risk when moving a Next.js app to Turbopack? Expected answer: custom webpack configuration and loaders are not used; equivalent configuration must be found or the feature replaced.

Practical exercise

Take an existing React app (or the one from 70.1) and measure: dev server cold start, time from save to visible change, and production build time. Then add a Vite server.proxy for /api pointing at a NestJS app.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A table with the three timings, measured three times each.
  • The browser's Network panel shows API calls to localhost:5173/api/... and no CORS preflight OPTIONS requests.
  • A login endpoint in NestJS sets an HttpOnly cookie that the browser sends on the next /api call without any CORS configuration.
  • vite build && vite preview runs the same flows successfully.

70.4 Hot module replacement

Concept

Hot module replacement (HMR) swaps a changed module into the running page without a full reload. You edit the padding on the order summary card, press save, and within 50 ms the card updates while the cart still holds its three items, the checkout form keeps what you typed, and the modal stays open. A full reload would lose all that state.

React Fast Refresh is React's HMR integration. It re-renders edited components while keeping their useState and useReducer state, as long as the edit does not change the component's hook order. Next.js has it built in; in Vite it comes from @vitejs/plugin-react or @vitejs/plugin-react-swc.

Why does it exist?

Frontend work is iterative and visual. Reaching the screen you are working on often takes clicks: log in, add items, go to checkout, open the coupon dialog. With full reloads, every CSS tweak costs those clicks again. HMR keeps the app in the state you set up and changes only the code you edited. It is the single biggest contributor to frontend developer speed after a fast dev server.

Mental model

Imagine changing a tyre on a moving car without stopping. A full reload is pulling over, switching off the engine, changing the tyre, and starting the journey again from home. HMR replaces exactly one tyre while the car keeps rolling, and only if the car was designed with a hub that allows it. A module that declares "I can be replaced in place" is that hub, called an HMR boundary. If the changed module has no such hub anywhere above it, the only option left is to stop the car: a full page reload.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant FS as FileSystem
    participant V as DevServer
    participant C as HmrClient
    participant R as ReactRefresh
    FS->>V: OrderSummary.tsx changed
    V->>V: invalidate module, walk importers to nearest boundary
    V->>C: WebSocket update for OrderSummary.tsx with timestamp
    C->>V: import OrderSummary.tsx?t=1730800000
    V-->>C: freshly transformed module
    C->>R: accept callback with new module
    R->>R: re-render OrderSummary, keep hook state
  1. Watch. The dev server watches the file system. When OrderSummary.tsx changes, it invalidates that module's transform cache.
  2. Find the boundary. It walks up the importers of the changed module until it finds one that accepts updates, meaning it called import.meta.hot.accept() (Vite) or module.hot.accept() (webpack). React plugins inject this automatically into files that export only React components.
  3. Notify. It sends a message over a WebSocket to the HMR client script injected into the page.
  4. Re-import. The client imports the new version of the module with a cache-busting query (?t=timestamp), so the browser fetches fresh code.
  5. Apply. The boundary's accept callback runs. For React Fast Refresh, React re-renders every mounted instance of the changed components with the new function body, keeping their state.
  6. Fallback. If no boundary is found (for example the change is in main.tsx, or in a module that exports both a component and a constant), the client does a full reload.

A module can also clean up after itself before being replaced, which matters for anything with side effects:

// src/realtime/orderSocket.ts  (Vite)
const socket = new WebSocket(`${location.origin.replace('http', 'ws')}/realtime/orders`);
export { socket };

if (import.meta.hot) {
  // Without this, every save opens another socket and the old ones keep running.
  import.meta.hot.dispose(() => socket.close(1000, 'hmr'));
  import.meta.hot.accept();
}

The if (import.meta.hot) block is removed entirely from production builds, because import.meta.hot is replaced with undefined and the dead branch is eliminated.

Rules that decide whether Fast Refresh keeps state:

  • A file must export only React components to be a refresh boundary. Export a component and a helper constant from the same file, and every edit triggers a full reload. eslint-plugin-react-refresh has an only-export-components rule for this.
  • Editing hooks order (adding a useState above another) resets that component's state.
  • Class components are remounted, not refreshed.
  • Edits to non-component modules (an API client, a zod schema) propagate up to the components that import them, which re-render with the new code.

Practical example

Styling the "Payment failed, retry?" banner at step 3 of checkout takes about 40 s of clicking to reach each time. With Fast Refresh each change appears in 30 to 60 ms with the checkout still on step 3: over 150 saves, 5 minutes instead of 100.

React / Next.js example

Keep components and non-component exports in separate files so every component file is a clean refresh boundary:

// src/checkout/PaymentFailedBanner.tsx: exports only a component, so edits keep state
import { useState } from 'react';
import { PAYMENT_RETRY_LIMIT } from './checkout.constants'; // constants live elsewhere

type Props = { attempt: number; onRetry: () => Promise<void> };

export function PaymentFailedBanner({ attempt, onRetry }: Props) {
