  const [retrying, setRetrying] = useState(false); // preserved across edits by Fast Refresh

  if (attempt >= PAYMENT_RETRY_LIMIT) {
    return <p role="alert">Payment failed again. Please try another card.</p>;
  }
  return (
    <div role="alert" className="banner banner--error">
      <p>Your payment did not go through.</p>
      <button
        disabled={retrying}
        onClick={async () => {
          setRetrying(true);
          try { await onRetry(); } finally { setRetrying(false); }
        }}
      >
        {retrying ? 'Retrying...' : 'Retry payment'}
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}
// src/checkout/checkout.constants.ts: non-component exports, no JSX
export const PAYMENT_RETRY_LIMIT = 3;

Next.js has Fast Refresh built in for both the Pages Router and the App Router (for client components). Server components in the App Router are re-rendered on the server and the new result is streamed in, which keeps client state in client components below them.

Backend side (NestJS)

HMR touches the backend in two ways.

First, HMR multiplies connections. A module that opens a WebSocket or EventSource at import time opens a new one on every save unless it disposes the old one. A developer saving 200 times an hour can leave 200 open SSE connections against a shared development or staging API, and a NestJS gateway that loads per-connection state (subscriptions, Redis pub/sub channels) will feel it. Cap connections per user on the server, which is good production hygiene anyway:

// order-status.gateway.ts  (@nestjs/websockets with socket.io)
import { WebSocketGateway, OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect } from '@nestjs/websockets';
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Socket } from 'socket.io';

const MAX_SOCKETS_PER_USER = 5;

@WebSocketGateway({ namespace: '/realtime/orders' })
export class OrderStatusGateway implements OnGatewayConnection, OnGatewayDisconnect {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(OrderStatusGateway.name);
  private readonly perUser = new Map<string, Set<string>>();

  handleConnection(client: Socket): void {
    const userId = client.handshake.auth?.userId as string | undefined; // set after auth middleware
    if (!userId) { client.disconnect(true); return; }
    const sockets = this.perUser.get(userId) ?? new Set<string>();
    if (sockets.size >= MAX_SOCKETS_PER_USER) {
      this.logger.warn(`user ${userId} exceeded ${MAX_SOCKETS_PER_USER} sockets; closing oldest`);
      const oldest = sockets.values().next().value as string;
      client.nsp.sockets.get(oldest)?.disconnect(true);
      sockets.delete(oldest);
    }
    sockets.add(client.id);
    this.perUser.set(userId, sockets);
  }

  handleDisconnect(client: Socket): void {
    for (const [userId, sockets] of this.perUser) {
      if (sockets.delete(client.id) && sockets.size === 0) this.perUser.delete(userId);
    }
  }
}

(In a multi-instance deployment this map must live in Redis; Part 35 — Real-Time Systems covers that.)

Second, the backend has its own reload loop. nest start --watch restarts the whole Node process on each change (2 to 6 s for a mid-size app). The NestJS docs have a webpack HMR recipe (module.hot.accept() with module.hot.dispose(() => app.close()) in main.ts); the SWC builder (nest start --watch -b swc) is usually fast enough without it. During each restart the dev proxy sees ECONNREFUSED, so the frontend should retry idempotent reads rather than show a fatal error.

Production scenario

HMR is a development feature, but it can leak into production. Vite and Next.js strip the HMR client automatically; a hand-written webpack config with HotModuleReplacementPlugin left in the production config does not, and one retailer found it as 2 million failed WebSocket attempts to localhost per day in their real-user monitoring.

Failure scenario

A team's staging environment started returning 503 from the notifications service every afternoon. The service's Redis instance hit its maxclients limit of 10,000. Each SSE connection to the notifications endpoint subscribed to a Redis pub/sub channel on its own connection.

The source: 12 developers pointing their local frontends at the shared staging API. The notifications client opened an EventSource at module import time with no import.meta.hot.dispose. Every save in any file that the notification module's importers touched re-executed the module and opened a new stream; old streams stayed open until the tab closed. By mid-afternoon, about 9,000 orphaned streams were open from 12 laptops.

Fixes: dispose() in the client module, a per-user connection cap in the NestJS gateway, and a shared Redis subscriber that multiplexes channels instead of one Redis connection per SSE client.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mixed exports (component plus constant) make every edit a full reload.
  • Module-level side effects (sockets, intervals, global event listeners, analytics init) run again on each update unless disposed.
  • State shape changes (renaming a useState value's fields) keep the old state object, so the component renders with stale shapes until you reload.
  • HMR WebSocket blocked by a corporate proxy or a remote dev environment behind HTTPS: set server.hmr.clientPort or server.hmr.protocol: 'wss' in Vite.
  • Backend restarts during HMR show as transient network errors in the frontend.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats "this file keeps doing full reloads" as a code smell: it usually means mixed responsibilities or import-time side effects, which also hurt testability. They keep side effects inside effects or explicit init() functions with cleanup, and they cap per-user connections on the backend, because a development habit can become a staging outage and a buggy client a production one.

Common mistakes

  • Opening sockets, timers or listeners at module scope without HMR disposal.
  • Exporting constants and hooks from component files, breaking Fast Refresh.
  • Leaving HMR plugins in a production webpack config.
  • Pointing many local frontends at a shared staging backend without connection limits.
  • Assuming HMR state is real state: always do a full reload before declaring a UI bug fixed.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through what happens between saving a file and seeing the change with HMR. Expected answer: file watcher, invalidate module, walk importers to an accepting boundary, WebSocket message, client re-imports with a timestamp query, accept callback applies it; full reload if no boundary. Follow-up: what makes a React file a boundary?
  2. Why does Fast Refresh sometimes reset component state? Expected answer: hook order changes, class components, or the file exports non-components so it is not a boundary and a parent remounts.
  3. What is import.meta.hot.dispose for? Expected answer: cleaning up side effects (sockets, timers, listeners) of the old module instance before the new one runs.
  4. How can frontend development habits cause a backend incident? Expected answer: leaked long-lived connections from HMR re-execution against shared environments; mitigate with client disposal and server connection caps.

Practical exercise

In a Vite React app, create a module that opens an EventSource to a NestJS SSE endpoint (@Sse('orders/stream')) at import time and logs messages.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Without dispose, saving the module five times leaves six open connections, visible in the Network panel and in a NestJS counter of active streams.
  • With import.meta.hot.dispose(() => source.close()), the count stays at one.
  • You move a constant out of a component file and show, with a counter in useState, that edits now keep state where previously they reloaded the page.

70.5 Tree shaking and code splitting at build time

Concept

Tree shaking is the removal of exported code that nothing imports. If your app imports debounce from a utility library that exports 300 functions, tree shaking keeps debounce (and whatever it calls) and drops the other 299. The name comes from shaking a tree so the dead leaves fall off.

Code splitting is dividing the bundle into several files (chunks) so each page downloads only the code it needs. The shopper on a product page does not download the admin reports screen or the 3D product viewer until they need it. At build time, the bundler decides the chunk boundaries; at run time, the browser fetches chunks on demand.

Both decide the same thing from opposite directions: tree shaking decides what code exists in the output at all, and code splitting decides when each piece of it is downloaded.

Why does it exist?

JavaScript cost is paid twice: in network time and in main-thread time to parse, compile and execute (69.7). Libraries are written for everybody, so they contain much more than any one app uses. Apps grow screens that most users never visit. Without tree shaking you ship whole libraries. Without code splitting every user pays for every screen. A typical e-commerce SPA with neither optimisation ships 900 KB to 1.5 MB of gzip JavaScript; with both, the first route is often 150 to 250 KB.

Mental model

Imagine packing for a trip from a big wardrobe. Tree shaking is leaving behind every item you will never wear on this trip, however nice it is. Code splitting is packing a carry-on with what you need on day one and having the rest shipped to the hotel only when your itinerary says you will need it. Both depend on knowing your itinerary in advance: if a bag might contain something with a hidden purpose (a side effect), you cannot safely leave it behind.

How it works

Tree shaking depends on static ES module syntax. import { debounce } from 'lodash-es' and export function debounce can be analysed without running any code, so the bundler can build a precise graph of which exports are used. CommonJS (require, module.exports) is dynamic: module.exports[name] = fn is decided at run time, so bundlers can rarely shake it. That is why lodash (CommonJS) costs about 24 KB gzip whatever you import from it, while lodash-es costs about 1 KB for debounce.

flowchart LR
    entry["main.tsx"] --> utils["utils/index.ts barrel"]
    utils --> money["formatMoney: used"]
    utils --> dates["formatDate: used"]
    utils --> csv["exportCsv: unused"]
    utils --> chart["chartHelpers: unused"]
    chart --> lib["chart library 180 KB"]
    money --> keep["kept in bundle"]
    dates --> keep
    csv --> drop["dropped if side-effect free"]
    lib --> drop

The catch is side effects. A module has a side effect if importing it does something: registers a polyfill, adds a global CSS rule, patches a prototype, starts a timer. If a module might have side effects, the bundler must keep it even when none of its exports are used, because removing it would change behaviour. Two hints let bundlers drop more:

  • "sideEffects" in package.json: "sideEffects": false promises that no file in the package has import-time side effects. An array lists the exceptions: "sideEffects": ["*.css", "./src/polyfills.ts"]. webpack, Rollup, Rolldown and esbuild all honour it.
  • /*#__PURE__*/ annotations before a call (const Icon = /*#__PURE__*/ createIcon(...)) tell the minifier the call has no side effects, so if Icon is unused the call can be dropped.

Barrel files (an index.ts that re-exports everything in a folder) are where tree shaking most often struggles. In production a bundler can shake a barrel when the package is marked side-effect free. But in a Vite dev server every module in the barrel is still requested and transformed, so importing one icon from an icon library's barrel can load 1,500 modules in development. Next.js 13.5+ has experimental.optimizePackageImports (and applies it by default to libraries like lucide-react and date-fns) to rewrite barrel imports into direct ones.

Code splitting happens at split points. Every dynamic import() creates one:

flowchart TB
    entryc["index chunk: React, router, app shell, 62 KB gz"] --> home["home route chunk, 14 KB gz"]
    entryc --> pdp["product route chunk, 21 KB gz"]
    entryc --> checkout["checkout route chunk, 33 KB gz"]
    pdp --> viewer["3D viewer chunk, 220 KB gz, on click"]
    checkout --> pay["payment SDK chunk, 48 KB gz, on step 3"]
    pdp --> shared["shared: price formatting, zod schemas, 9 KB gz"]
    checkout --> shared
  1. The bundler follows static imports to build the entry chunk.
  2. Each import('./routes/Checkout') starts a new chunk containing that module and its static imports not already in a parent chunk.
  3. Modules used by several chunks are moved into shared chunks so they are downloaded once.
  4. The bundler writes a small runtime that fetches a chunk by its hashed name when import() runs, and Vite injects <link rel="modulepreload"> for a chunk's own dependencies so they load in parallel instead of in a waterfall.

You can steer the grouping. Rollup (Vite up to 7) has build.rollupOptions.output.manualChunks; webpack has optimization.splitChunks. A common use is a separate vendor chunk for large, rarely-changing libraries, so a deploy that changes only your code does not invalidate the cached React chunk.

Split too much and you create a request waterfall: chunk A loads, then discovers chunk B, then C. Split too little and the first route carries code for every screen. A practical rule: split by route, split anything over about 30 KB gzip that is not needed for first paint (editors, charts, maps, payment SDKs), and stop there.

Measure, do not guess. rollup-plugin-visualizer (Vite), webpack-bundle-analyzer and @next/bundle-analyzer render a treemap of what is inside each chunk. size-limit or a simple script that fails CI when the entry chunk exceeds a budget keeps it from creeping back (Part 76 — Web Performance covers budgets).

Practical example

A pharmacy app's first-route bundle was 480 KB gzip. The treemap showed:

Culprit Size gzip Fix After
moment with all locales 72 KB date-fns with direct imports, or Intl.DateTimeFormat 6 KB
lodash (CommonJS) 24 KB lodash-es or native methods 2 KB
Icon library through a barrel without sideEffects 96 KB direct imports icons/Pill 4 KB
Rich text editor in the static graph of the product page 110 KB lazy(() => import('./ReviewEditor')) 0 KB on first route
Payment SDK imported in the app shell 48 KB load in the checkout payment step 0 KB on first route

Total first-route JavaScript fell to 188 KB gzip. On a mid-range Android phone, main-thread script time at startup dropped from 1.1 s to 420 ms.

React / Next.js example

Route-level splitting with React Router and lazy, plus a vendor chunk that changes rarely:

// src/router.tsx  (React 18, React Router 6.4+)
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';
import { createBrowserRouter } from 'react-router-dom';
import { AppShell } from './AppShell';      // static: part of the entry chunk
import { RouteError } from './RouteError';

const Home = lazy(() => import('./routes/Home'));
const Product = lazy(() => import('./routes/Product'));
const Checkout = lazy(() => import('./routes/Checkout')); // payment SDK lives in here, not in the shell

const page = (el: JSX.Element) => <Suspense fallback={<div className="route-skeleton" />}>{el}</Suspense>;

export const router = createBrowserRouter([
  {
    path: '/', element: <AppShell />, errorElement: <RouteError />, // catches failed chunk loads too
    children: [
      { index: true, element: page(<Home />) },
      { path: 'p/:slug', element: page(<Product />) },
      { path: 'checkout', element: page(<Checkout />) },
    ],
  },
]);
// vite.config.ts (excerpt, Vite up to 7: Rollup output options)
build: {
  rollupOptions: {
    output: {
      // React and the router change a few times a year; keep them in their own long-cached chunk.
      manualChunks(id) {
        if (/node_modules\/(react|react-dom|react-router|react-router-dom|scheduler)\//.test(id)) return 'vendor-react';
      },
    },
  },
},

Next.js splits by route automatically: each page.tsx in the App Router is its own entry, and next/dynamic (shown in 69.6) splits components inside a page. Server components never ship their code to the browser at all, which is the most effective tree shaking there is.

Backend side (NestJS)

Two backend responsibilities follow from splitting.

Data does not belong in the bundle. Teams often import a 180 KB countries.json, a product category tree or a list of pincodes straight into the frontend. It is then parsed on every page load and re-downloaded on every deploy because the chunk hash changes. Serve it from the API with HTTP caching instead:

// reference-data.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header, Headers, Res, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Response } from 'express';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { ReferenceDataService } from './reference-data.service';

@Controller('v1/reference')
export class ReferenceDataController {
  constructor(private readonly refs: ReferenceDataService) {}

  @Get('countries')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=86400, stale-while-revalidate=604800')
  async countries(@Headers('if-none-match') ifNoneMatch: string | undefined, @Res() res: Response) {
    const countries = await this.refs.countries(); // from PostgreSQL, cached in memory for 1 h
    const body = JSON.stringify(countries);
    const etag = `"${createHash('sha1').update(body).digest('base64url')}"`;
    if (ifNoneMatch === etag) return res.status(HttpStatus.NOT_MODIFIED).end();
    res.setHeader('ETag', etag);
    res.type('application/json').send(body); // about 9 KB gzip, fetched only on the address step
  }
}

Old chunks must stay reachable. A user who loaded the app before a deploy has an entry chunk that references Checkout-OLDHASH.js. If the deploy deleted it, their next navigation fails with "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module" (Vite) or ChunkLoadError (webpack). Keep the previous one or two releases' assets in the bucket or container, and return a real 404 for missing assets, never the SPA's index.html. Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends covers the full deploy story; the errorElement above is the client half of it, offering a reload.

Production scenario

A fashion retailer added a "complete the look" carousel to the product page using a new design-system package. The product page chunk grew from 41 KB to 167 KB gzip; nobody noticed until p75 LCP on mobile went from 2.3 s to 2.9 s and the conversion dashboard showed a 3 % drop on product pages. The treemap showed the whole design-system package, all 90 components, inside the chunk: its package.json had no sideEffects field and its index.js was a barrel. Adding "sideEffects": ["*.css"] to the package brought the chunk to 52 KB. The team then added a CI budget of 60 KB gzip for that chunk.

Failure scenario

The same design-system team, wanting to be thorough, set "sideEffects": false in the next release. Their components imported their own styles with import './Button.css'. In development everything looked perfect, because the dev server loads every module it is asked for. In the production build, the bundler believed the CSS imports had no effect, since nothing used their exports, and dropped them. At 09:30 the release went live and every button and input on the checkout page was unstyled: grey system buttons, no spacing, a "Pay now" button that looked disabled. Payments fell by a third in 20 minutes before a rollback.

The correct value was the array form, ["*.css"]. The process fix: a Playwright visual snapshot of checkout against the production build in CI (Part 77 — Frontend Testing and Quality).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Wrong sideEffects claims drop CSS imports and polyfills silently in production only.
  • CommonJS dependencies defeat tree shaking; check for an ESM build (module or exports.import in their package.json).
  • Over-splitting creates waterfalls of small chunks; watch the Network panel's initiator chain.
  • Vendor chunk instability: one changed dependency changes the vendor hash and invalidates the whole cached chunk for everyone.
  • Chunk load failures after deploys or on flaky networks need an error boundary with a retry or reload.
  • Dynamic import paths built from variables (import(`./locales/${lang}.ts`)) make the bundler include every matching file as a chunk; fine for 6 locales, bad for 600 files.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior reads a bundle treemap the way they read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan: the biggest box is where the time goes, and guesses are usually wrong. They set a budget for the first route and enforce it in CI, because bundle size only ever grows by small, reasonable-looking additions. They split by route and by heavy feature, not by every component. They push data out of the bundle and into cacheable API responses, and they treat "keep old chunks available" as part of the deploy contract, not an afterthought.

Common mistakes

  • Importing a whole library for one function (import _ from 'lodash').
  • Putting large data files into the bundle instead of fetching them.
  • Setting "sideEffects": false on a package that imports CSS.
  • Splitting every component, producing hundreds of tiny chunks.
  • Deleting old assets on deploy, breaking every open tab.

Interview questions

  1. Why can bundlers tree-shake ES modules but not CommonJS? Expected answer: ESM imports and exports are static and analysable at build time; CommonJS exports are assigned at run time. Follow-up: what does sideEffects add on top?
  2. What is a split point and what does it cost? Expected answer: a dynamic import() that becomes a separate chunk, fetched on demand; it costs a request and possible waterfall when the code is needed.
  3. Your product page bundle doubled after adding one component. How do you find out why? Expected answer: bundle analyzer treemap, look for a barrel import or a package without side-effect hints, check whether a heavy dependency is statically imported.
  4. What happens to users with an open tab during a deploy that deletes old chunks, and how do you prevent it? Expected answer: dynamic imports 404, navigation fails; keep previous assets for a grace period and catch chunk errors with a reload prompt.
  5. When would you create a manual vendor chunk? Expected answer: when large, rarely-changing libraries would otherwise be re-downloaded on every deploy.

Practical exercise

Add rollup-plugin-visualizer to a Vite app, build it, and open the treemap.

Acceptance criteria:

  • You identify the three largest modules in the entry chunk and their gzip sizes.
  • You move at least one heavy, non-critical component behind lazy() and show the entry chunk shrinking.
  • You add a CI check (a script reading dist/assets/*.js gzip sizes) that fails when the entry chunk exceeds a chosen budget.
  • You move one static JSON data file out of the bundle into a NestJS endpoint with ETag and Cache-Control, and show a 304 on the second load.

70.6 Environment variables in frontends

Concept

In a backend, an environment variable is read at run time: NestJS's ConfigService reads process.env.DATABASE_URL when the process starts, on a server only your team can access (Part 4 — Linux and the Command Line, 4.5). In a frontend build, "environment variables" are usually something else entirely: values that the build tool replaces with string literals at build time, so they become part of the JavaScript file that every visitor downloads.

That gives two rules that every full-stack engineer must know by heart:

  1. Build-time values are frozen. Changing an environment variable after the build changes nothing; you must rebuild.
  2. Every value in a frontend bundle is public. There is no such thing as a secret environment variable in browser code. If the browser can use it, anyone can read it.

Why does it exist?

The browser has no process.env. There is no operating system environment it can read from your server. The build tool bridges the gap by substituting values during the build, which is simple and fast: no extra request at startup, and dead-code elimination can remove branches like if (import.meta.env.DEV) entirely.

The prefixes exist as a safety net. Vite only exposes variables starting with VITE_ to client code, Next.js only NEXT_PUBLIC_, and Create React App only REACT_APP_. Without a prefix, a careless process.env.DATABASE_URL in a component would have pulled your database password into the bundle. The prefix makes exposure an explicit decision. It does not make the exposed value secret.

Mental model

Imagine printing a flyer. Whatever you write on it before the print run (the build) is on every copy, and every person who picks one up can read it. You cannot change the phone number on flyers already in people's hands; you have to print again. A runtime config is a QR code on the flyer that points to a web page: you can change the page without reprinting, but anyone can still scan it and read it. Neither is a place for the combination to your safe.

How it works

flowchart LR
    envfile[".env.production: VITE_API_URL, VITE_MAPS_KEY"] --> build["vite build"]
    build --> bundle["index-Hash.js contains the literal strings"]
    bundle --> cdn["CDN: public to the world"]
    secret["PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY: no VITE_ prefix"] -. "not exposed" .-> build
    server["Server or container start"] --> runtime["GET /api/public-config"]
    runtime --> browser["Browser reads config at boot"]
    cdn --> browser

Vite. Variables are loaded from .env, .env.local, .env.[mode] and .env.[mode].local (later files win; actual process environment variables win over all files). Only VITE_-prefixed names (configurable with envPrefix) are exposed, through import.meta.env. Built-ins: import.meta.env.MODE, DEV, PROD, SSR, BASE_URL. At build time, import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL is replaced with the literal "https://api.shop.example". Types come from an augmentation file:

// src/vite-env.d.ts
/// <reference types="vite/client" />
interface ImportMetaEnv {
  readonly VITE_API_URL: string;
  readonly VITE_MAPS_BROWSER_KEY: string; // referrer-restricted browser key, public by design
}
interface ImportMeta { readonly env: ImportMetaEnv }

Next.js. Variables prefixed NEXT_PUBLIC_ are inlined into client bundles at next build. Variables without the prefix are available only in server code (server components, Route Handlers, Server Actions, getServerSideProps), and those are read at run time when the page renders dynamically. Two traps: dynamic lookups such as process.env[name] are not inlined, and a page that is statically rendered at build time freezes even server-side values into the HTML. The server-only package (import 'server-only') makes the build fail if a module meant for the server is imported into a client component.

webpack. DefinePlugin does the same text substitution: new DefinePlugin({ 'process.env.API_URL': JSON.stringify(url) }).

What "public" really means. After a build, run:

# Everything in dist is what the world can read.
grep -rhoE '(sk_live|AKIA)[A-Za-z0-9_]{8,}' dist/ || echo "no Stripe secret or AWS access key patterns"
grep -rho 'https://[a-z0-9.-]*\.internal[^"]*' dist/ | sort -u   # internal hostnames leaking?

Some values are designed to be public and safe in a bundle, because the provider protects them another way: a Stripe publishable key (pk_live_...), a Google Maps browser key restricted by HTTP referrer, a Firebase web config (protected by security rules), a Sentry DSN (write-only ingestion, rate-limited). Anything that grants access to your systems or bills you per call without such protection (a Stripe secret key sk_live_..., an AWS key, an internal service token, an OpenAI or LLM API key, an admin API key) must stay on the server.

Runtime configuration solves the "frozen" problem, not the "public" problem. Instead of baking VITE_API_URL into the build, the app fetches /config.json or reads window.__APP_CONFIG__ injected into index.html by the server at start-up. Then one build can be promoted from staging to production unchanged. Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends covers "build once, deploy many" in detail.

Practical example

A food delivery web app needs four configuration values:

Value Where it lives Why
API base URL runtime config (/api/public-config) or same-origin /api Differs per environment; same build promoted through stages
Maps browser key VITE_MAPS_BROWSER_KEY, restricted to *.food.example referrers Public by design; the restriction is the protection
Geocoding server key NestJS only, called through /api/geocode Bills per call with no referrer restriction; would be abused within hours
Feature flags runtime, from the flag service through the API Must change without a rebuild

React / Next.js example

A typed, validated config module for a Vite SPA that reads runtime configuration once at boot and fails loudly if it is wrong:

// src/config.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

const PublicConfig = z.object({
  apiBaseUrl: z.string().url(),
  mapsBrowserKey: z.string().min(10),
  sentryDsn: z.string().url().optional(),
  features: z.record(z.boolean()).default({}),
});
export type PublicConfig = z.infer<typeof PublicConfig>;

let config: PublicConfig | undefined;

export async function loadConfig(): Promise<PublicConfig> {
  const res = await fetch('/api/public-config', { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000) }); // never hang boot
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`config ${res.status}`);
  config = PublicConfig.parse(await res.json()); // a broken config fails at boot, not on the payment step
  return config;
}

export function getConfig(): PublicConfig {
  if (!config) throw new Error('getConfig() called before loadConfig()');
  return config;
}
// src/main.tsx
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { loadConfig } from './config';
import { App } from './App';

loadConfig()
  .then(() => createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(<App />))
  .catch(() => {
    document.getElementById('root')!.innerHTML =
      '<p role="alert">We could not start the app. Please refresh the page.</p>';
  });

In Next.js, read server-only values directly in server code and pass only what the client needs as props:

// app/checkout/page.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router, server component)
import 'server-only';
import { PaymentStep } from './PaymentStep'; // client component

export default async function CheckoutPage() {
  // Read at request time on the server (this page is dynamic because it uses cookies elsewhere).
  const publishableKey = process.env.STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY!; // public by design
  // process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY stays in server code and Route Handlers only.
  return <PaymentStep publishableKey={publishableKey} />;
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The backend owns the public config endpoint and every secret the frontend must not hold.

// public-config.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { FeatureFlagsService } from '../flags/feature-flags.service';

@Controller('public-config')
export class PublicConfigController {
  constructor(private readonly config: ConfigService, private readonly flags: FeatureFlagsService) {}

  @Get()
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=60') // short: flags may change; CDN can absorb load
  async get() {
    // Explicit allow-list. Never spread process.env or the whole config object into a response.
    return {
      apiBaseUrl: this.config.getOrThrow<string>('PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL'),
      mapsBrowserKey: this.config.getOrThrow<string>('MAPS_BROWSER_KEY'),
      sentryDsn: this.config.get<string>('SENTRY_BROWSER_DSN'),
      features: await this.flags.publicFlags(), // only flags marked safe for clients
    };
  }
}

For anything that needs a real secret, the browser calls your API and your API calls the provider. That proxy is also where you add authentication, rate limiting and caching, which a key in the browser can never have:

// geocode.controller.ts: the browser never sees GEOCODING_SERVER_KEY
import { Controller, Get, Query, UseGuards, BadRequestException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { GeocodingService } from './geocoding.service';

@Controller('geocode')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class GeocodeController {
  constructor(private readonly geocoding: GeocodingService) {}

  @Get()
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 30, ttl: 60_000 } }) // 30 lookups per minute per user (@nestjs/throttler v5+)
  async lookup(@Query('q') q?: string) {
    if (!q || q.length < 3 || q.length > 200) throw new BadRequestException('q must be 3 to 200 chars');
    return this.geocoding.lookup(q); // uses the server key, caches results in Redis for 24 h
  }
}

Production scenario

A grocery chain ran the same React build across three environments using runtime config served by NestJS. Promotion from staging to production became "copy the same dist/ artefact"; build time per release fell from three builds of 4 minutes to one, and a whole class of "staging works, production broken" bugs (caused by builds with different inlined values) disappeared. The /api/public-config endpoint served about 4,000 requests per minute at peak, 97 % from the CDN cache with its 60 s max-age.

Failure scenario

At 14:05 a developer added VITE_REFUNDS_API_TOKEN to a back-office web app so a new "issue refund" button could call the payments service directly, "just until the backend endpoint is ready". The app was internal but its bundle sat on the public CDN. At 19:40 an automated scanner that crawls JavaScript bundles for tokens found it. Between 20:10 and 21:30, 214 refunds totalling a little over 3 lakh rupees were issued to accounts the attacker controlled.

The token was revoked at 21:32 after an alert on refund volume. The postmortem's actions: no service tokens in any VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable, enforced by a CI step that greps the build output for known token formats and fails the build; refunds only through a NestJS endpoint with role checks and an audit log (Part 40 — Security covers both); and a reminder printed in the team handbook: internal app does not mean private bundle.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Changing an env var without rebuilding changes nothing for build-time values.
  • Dynamic access (import.meta.env[name], process.env[name]) is not replaced; it is undefined in the browser.
  • Statically rendered Next.js pages freeze server-side values read at build time.
  • .env.local committed by accident puts developer secrets into the repository; keep *.local in .gitignore.
  • Different values in CI and locally produce bundles that behave differently; print the resolved mode and public values in the build log.
  • Spreading config into a response (return this.config) leaks every server secret through a "public" endpoint.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior classifies every configuration value before it is added: public-by-design, environment-specific, or secret. Public values can be inlined or served. Environment-specific values come from runtime config so one artefact moves through every stage. Secrets live only in the backend, behind authentication, rate limits and audit logs. They do not argue about whether a token is "probably safe because the app is internal"; the bundle is a public document. To a product manager: "If the browser can use a key, the whole internet can. So anything that can cost money or move data goes through our server."

Common mistakes

  • Putting secret keys in VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables.
  • Rebuilding per environment when the only difference is a URL.
  • Assuming obfuscation or minification hides values. A minified string is still a string.
  • Exposing a config endpoint without an allow-list.
  • Not validating config at boot, so a missing value fails later on a critical step.

Interview questions

  1. How does import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL get its value, and when? Expected answer: Vite replaces it with a literal string at build time from .env files and the build environment; it is not read in the browser at run time. Follow-up: how would you change the API URL without rebuilding?
  2. Why is there no such thing as a secret in a frontend bundle? Expected answer: the bundle is downloaded by every visitor and readable by anyone; minification does not hide strings.
  3. Which keys are safe in the browser? Expected answer: keys designed for it and protected by other means (publishable payment keys, referrer-restricted keys, DSNs); never keys that authorise access or billing.
  4. How do you call a third-party API that needs a secret key from a web app? Expected answer: through a backend endpoint that holds the key, authenticates the user, rate-limits and caches.
  5. What is the difference between NEXT_PUBLIC_X and X in Next.js? Expected answer: the first is inlined into client bundles at build time; the second is available only in server code, read at render time for dynamic pages.

Practical exercise

Build a Vite app with VITE_API_URL set and search dist/ for the value. Then replace it with runtime config from a NestJS /api/public-config endpoint.

Acceptance criteria:

  • grep shows the literal URL in the first build and not in the second.
  • The same dist/ folder works against two different NestJS instances returning different apiBaseUrl values.
  • A CI script fails the build when dist/ contains a string matching sk_live_ or AKIA.
  • The config endpoint returns only allow-listed fields, verified by a NestJS e2e test.

70.7 Source maps, minification and debugging production bundles

Concept

Minification rewrites JavaScript to be as small as possible while behaving the same: whitespace and comments removed, local names shortened to one letter (mangling), constant expressions folded, unreachable branches deleted. Compression (gzip or Brotli) then shrinks the minified file further on the wire.

A source map is a separate JSON file that maps every position in the minified output back to a file, line and column in your original source. With it, DevTools and error trackers can show OrderSummary.tsx:42 instead of index-B7xQ2kLm.js:1:48213. Source maps let you ship small, unreadable code and still debug it.

Why does it exist?

Size, again. A real entry chunk might be 640 KB of JavaScript as written by the bundler. Minified it is about 230 KB; gzip brings it to about 72 KB; Brotli to about 62 KB. Minification alone usually removes 55 to 70 % of the bytes and, just as important, reduces parse time, which scales with the size of the uncompressed source.

The cost is debuggability. A production error from a minified bundle reads TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'a') at n (index-B7xQ2kLm.js:1:48213). Every file is on line 1, every function is n or t. Without source maps, production frontend errors are close to useless.

Mental model

Imagine a book translated into dense shorthand to save paper. The shorthand edition is what you sell. The source map is the translator's index: "shorthand page 1, character 48,213 corresponds to chapter 7, paragraph 42 of the original". You do not print the index in every copy; you keep it in the office, so when a reader reports "something is wrong at character 48,213", you can find the original sentence.

How it works

flowchart LR
    src["OrderSummary.tsx line 42"] --> build["Bundler and minifier"]
    build --> js["index-B7xQ2kLm.js, one long line"]
    build --> map["index-B7xQ2kLm.js.map"]
    js --> browser["Browser runs minified code"]
    browser --> err["Error at 1:48213"]
    err --> tracker["Error tracker or symbolication service"]
    map --> tracker
    tracker --> readable["OrderSummary.tsx:42 in formatTotal"]

Minifiers. esbuild (Vite's default up to Vite 7, very fast), Terser (JavaScript, slightly smaller output, 5 to 20x slower; build.minify: 'terser' in Vite, the default in webpack 5 through TerserPlugin), SWC (Next.js 13+), and Oxc (Vite 8). Differences in output size between them are usually 1 to 3 %.

Source map format (v3). A .map file is JSON:

{
  "version": 3,
  "file": "index-B7xQ2kLm.js",
  "sources": ["../../src/checkout/OrderSummary.tsx", "../../node_modules/react/cjs/react.production.min.js"],
  "sourcesContent": ["import { formatMoney } from '../money';\n..."],
  "names": ["formatTotal", "order", "items"],
  "mappings": "AAAA,SAASA,EAAYC,GACnB..."
}

mappings encodes, with base64 VLQ numbers, "generated column X maps to source file S, line L, column C, name N". sourcesContent embeds your original source code, so the map works even without access to the repository. That is convenient and it is also your entire frontend source code, comments included.

How a map is found. The minified file ends with a comment //# sourceMappingURL=index-B7xQ2kLm.js.map, or the server sends a SourceMap: /maps/index-B7xQ2kLm.js.map response header. DevTools fetches the map only when DevTools is open, so normal users never download it. The map is typically 2.5 to 4 times the size of the minified file.

The options that matter.

Tool Setting Map file written Reference comment in JS Use
Vite build.sourcemap: true yes yes Public maps (open-source, internal tools)
Vite build.sourcemap: 'hidden' yes no Upload to error tracker, do not serve publicly
Vite build.sourcemap: 'inline' inside the JS as a data URL yes Never in production: doubles the download
webpack devtool: 'hidden-source-map' yes no Same as Vite hidden
webpack devtool: 'nosources-source-map' yes, without sourcesContent yes Readable stack traces without exposing source
Next.js productionBrowserSourceMaps: true yes, served publicly yes Off by default; error-tracker plugins usually upload hidden maps instead

The production debugging workflow.

  1. Build with hidden maps.
  2. Upload the maps to your error tracker (Sentry, Datadog, Bugsnag, or your own service), tagged with the release (the git SHA). Newer tooling injects a debug ID into both the JS file and its map so they can be matched without relying on file names.
  3. Delete the .map files from the artefact before uploading it to the CDN, or serve them only on an internal network.
  4. When an error arrives, the tracker finds the map for that release and file, maps each stack frame and shows the original code.

For one-off debugging, Chrome DevTools can attach a map manually: in the Sources panel, right-click the minified file and choose "Add source map...", pointing it at a URL reachable from your machine (for example an internal artefact store). The {} "pretty print" button helps when you have no map at all.

Practical example

A user reports that applying coupon WELCOME10 at checkout shows a blank screen. The error tracker shows TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'percent') at index-B7xQ2kLm.js:1:48213. With the release's hidden map uploaded, the same frame reads src/checkout/applyCoupon.ts:27 in discountFor with the line return coupon.rule.percent * subtotal. The API had returned a fixed-amount coupon with rule: null and amountMinor: 10000. A two-minute diagnosis instead of an afternoon.

React / Next.js example

A Vite build that produces hidden maps, uploads them in CI, and removes them from the deployable artefact:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/build-web.sh: run in CI after tests pass
set -euo pipefail
RELEASE="web@${GITHUB_SHA}"

pnpm --filter web exec vite build --sourcemap hidden   # maps written, no sourceMappingURL comment

# Upload maps to the private symbolication store, keyed by release.
aws s3 cp apps/web/dist/assets/ "s3://shop-sourcemaps/${RELEASE}/" \
  --recursive --exclude '*' --include '*.map'

# Never ship maps to the public CDN.
find apps/web/dist -name '*.map' -delete
echo "built ${RELEASE}; $(ls apps/web/dist/assets/*.js | wc -l) JS files, maps uploaded privately"

In the app, send errors with the release so the backend can find the right maps:

// src/errors/report.ts
const RELEASE = import.meta.env.VITE_RELEASE; // set to web@<sha> at build time; public and harmless

export function reportError(error: unknown): void {
  const err = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error));
  const body = JSON.stringify({ release: RELEASE, message: err.message, stack: err.stack, url: location.href });
  // sendBeacon survives page unload; fall back to fetch with keepalive.
  if (!navigator.sendBeacon('/api/client-errors', new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' }))) {
    void fetch('/api/client-errors', { method: 'POST', body, keepalive: true, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } });
  }
}

Backend side (NestJS)

If you run your own error collection, the backend symbolicates. The source-map library (Mozilla, v0.7) does the lookup; maps come from a private bucket, never from the public CDN:

// client-errors.service.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { SourceMapConsumer, type RawSourceMap } from 'source-map';
import { SourcemapStore } from './sourcemap.store'; // reads s3://shop-sourcemaps/<release>/<file>.map, LRU-cached

const FRAME = /(https?:\/\/[^\s)]+\/assets\/([^/:]+\.js)):(\d+):(\d+)/; // Chrome and Firefox frame formats

@Injectable()
export class ClientErrorsService {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(ClientErrorsService.name);
  constructor(private readonly maps: SourcemapStore) {}

  async symbolicate(release: string, stack: string): Promise<string[]> {
    const out: string[] = [];
    for (const line of stack.split('\n').slice(0, 20)) {        // cap work per report
      const m = FRAME.exec(line);
      if (!m) { out.push(line.trim()); continue; }
      const [, , file, lineNo, colNo] = m;
      const raw: RawSourceMap | null = await this.maps.get(release, `${file}.map`);
      if (!raw) { out.push(`${line.trim()} (no map for ${release})`); continue; }
      const pos = await SourceMapConsumer.with(raw, null, (c) =>
        c.originalPositionFor({ line: Number(lineNo), column: Number(colNo) - 1 }), // columns are 0-based in maps
      );
      out.push(pos.source ? `${pos.source}:${pos.line}:${pos.column} in ${pos.name ?? '<anonymous>'}` : line.trim());
    }
    return out;
  }
}

The controller in front of it should be rate-limited with @nestjs/throttler, accept a small body (an error storm from one buggy release can send thousands of reports per second), and log the release so a bad deploy is visible as a spike for one release value. Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends covers correlating these browser errors with backend traces.

Production scenario

A marketplace with 1.2 million daily sessions receives about 30,000 frontend error reports per day, 95 % of them from browser extensions and ad blockers. Release-tagged, symbolicated stacks let them group by original source location; the top three groups each mapped to one line of their code and were fixed in a day. Their maps total about 9 MB per release, stored privately for 90 days at negligible cost.

Failure scenario

After a CI refactor, every production error in the tracker pointed to nonsense: React internals for code that was clearly in the checkout, or lines in the middle of comments. Engineers lost two days chasing a "bug in React" that did not exist.

The cause: the pipeline built the app twice, once for tests with source maps and once for deployment, and uploaded the maps from the first build. The two builds were not byte-identical (one had a different VITE_RELEASE value inlined, which shifted every column after it), so every mapping was off. The fix was to build once, upload maps from that exact build, and deploy those exact files. Debug IDs, which tie a JS file to its map by an ID injected into both, make this mistake impossible.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Public maps with sourcesContent publish your full source, including comments, internal URLs and commented-out code.
  • Maps from a different build produce confident but wrong stack traces.
  • inline maps in production double or triple download size.
  • Minifier-sensitive code: logic that depends on function.name or constructor.name breaks after mangling (common with class-based "type" checks and some dependency injection libraries).
  • Third-party scripts produce Script error. with no stack unless loaded with crossorigin and served with CORS headers.
  • Huge error bursts from one bad release can overload a self-hosted collector; sample and rate-limit.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats source maps as sensitive build artefacts, like debug symbols for a native binary: generated for every release, stored privately, tied to the exact build, and never served to the public unless the source is public anyway. They insist on "build once, deploy the same bytes" so maps and code always match. They also make sure the release identifier flows from the bundle to the error report to the backend logs, so the first question in a frontend incident ("which release?") answers itself.

Common mistakes

  • Turning source maps off entirely to "protect the code", then debugging blind.
  • Leaving .map files on the public CDN by default.
  • Uploading maps from a different build than the one deployed.
  • Not tagging errors with a release.
  • Pretty-printing and guessing instead of setting up symbolication once.

Interview questions

  1. What is in a source map, and why might it be sensitive? Expected answer: mappings from generated to original positions, original file names, symbol names and often the full original source in sourcesContent. Follow-up: how do you keep readable stack traces without exposing source? (Hidden maps uploaded privately; or nosources maps.)
  2. What does hidden mean in build.sourcemap: 'hidden'? Expected answer: maps are generated but the JS has no sourceMappingURL comment, so browsers do not look for them.
  3. Your error tracker shows wrong source lines. What do you check? Expected answer: whether maps came from the same build and release as the deployed files.
  4. How much does minification save and what else does it change? Expected answer: typically 55 to 70 % before compression; it also mangles names and removes dead code, which can break code that relies on names.

Practical exercise

Build a Vite app with sourcemap: 'hidden', throw an error from a nested function, and capture the minified stack trace.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The deployed JS contains no sourceMappingURL comment and no .map file is reachable over HTTP.
  • A NestJS endpoint using SourceMapConsumer turns the stack into original file, line and function names.
  • Rebuilding with a different inlined value and reusing the old maps produces wrong lines, which you explain.

70.8 TypeScript configuration for frontends

Concept

tsconfig.json controls two different things in a frontend project: how strictly your code is checked, and which environment the checker assumes (which global types exist, how imports are resolved, how JSX is understood). Because the bundler, not tsc, produces the output (70.2), a frontend tsconfig is almost entirely about checking: noEmit: true, with options chosen to describe the browser and the bundler accurately.

The same codebase often also needs to share types with the backend: the shape of an order, the allowed status values, the request body of "place order". Doing that well means understanding how a frontend tsconfig differs from a NestJS one.

Why does it exist?

Types are only as good as the environment they describe. If the checker thinks process and Buffer exist (because @types/node was pulled in by some dependency), it will happily approve browser code that crashes (the 70.1 incident). If it does not know that import.meta.env exists, every config read is an error. If it resolves imports differently from the bundler, it will report errors that the build does not have, or miss ones it does. And without strict options, the most common production crash in frontends, reading a property of undefined, passes type checking.

Mental model

Imagine a building inspector. You must tell them which building code applies (browser or server), which floor plan to use (how imports resolve), and how strict to be. An inspector using the wrong code approves a design that collapses; one who is not strict signs off on missing handrails. tsconfig is the inspector's brief.

How it works

A frontend config for a Vite React app, close to what create-vite generates, with the options that matter annotated:

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "lib": ["ES2022", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],
    "types": ["vite/client"],
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "noEmit": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "allowImportingTsExtensions": true,
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] }
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
  • lib: ["ES2022", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"] declares the browser globals (window, fetch, HTMLInputElement) and the language features available. A NestJS config has no DOM.
  • types: ["vite/client"] limits which @types/* packages are loaded automatically. Without it, TypeScript includes every package in node_modules/@types, so @types/node (pulled in transitively by almost anything) makes process.env.X type-check in browser code, and makes setTimeout return NodeJS.Timeout instead of number. Portable code uses ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>.
  • moduleResolution: "bundler" (TypeScript 5.0+) resolves imports the way Vite, webpack and esbuild do: package.json exports are honoured and extensionless relative imports are allowed. NestJS projects use "node10" (formerly "node") with CommonJS, or "nodenext" for native ESM.
  • strict: true turns on strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes and the rest. Non-negotiable for new code.
  • noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes items[0] and pricesBySku[sku] typed as T | undefined. It catches the "first item of an empty list" crash. It is not part of strict; turn it on explicitly.
  • exactOptionalPropertyTypes distinguishes "property missing" from "property set to undefined", which matters for PATCH request bodies where sending "coupon": undefined (dropped by JSON.stringify) and "coupon": null (an explicit removal) mean different things.
  • paths affects only type checking. The bundler needs the same alias (resolve.alias in Vite, or vite-tsconfig-paths), Vitest reads Vite's config, Jest needs moduleNameMapper. On the NestJS side, tsc does not rewrite aliases in emitted JavaScript, so a backend using paths needs tsconfig-paths at run time or a tool such as tsc-alias after the build, or it fails with Cannot find module '@/orders/...' in production.

Vite's template splits configuration with project references: a root tsconfig.json with "files": [] and "references" to tsconfig.app.json (browser code, DOM, vite/client) and tsconfig.node.json (vite.config.ts, which runs in Node and needs @types/node). tsc -b checks both, each in the right environment.

Frontend and backend configs side by side:

Option apps/web (Vite React) apps/api (NestJS 10 or 11) Why they differ
module / moduleResolution ESNext / bundler commonjs / node10 Bundler resolves for the browser; Node loads CommonJS
lib ES2022, DOM ES2021 or later, no DOM Different global environment
experimentalDecorators, emitDecoratorMetadata off on NestJS DI, TypeORM and class-validator need legacy decorators and metadata
noEmit true false (emits dist) The bundler emits for the web; tsc or SWC emits for Node
jsx react-jsx not set
strict true true (Nest's CLI default is looser; tighten it)

Sharing types with the backend. The two configs differ enough that sharing code is risky, but sharing types and schemas is easy and valuable:

  • Share plain TypeScript types and string union enums (type OrderStatus = 'PENDING' | 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED'), and zod schemas if you want runtime validation at both ends. These compile under both configs.
  • Import them with import type in the frontend, so they vanish from the bundle when they are only types.
  • Do not import NestJS DTO classes or TypeORM entities into the frontend. They carry decorators that need experimentalDecorators, pull class-validator, class-transformer or typeorm into the bundle (hundreds of KB), and describe your database, not your API.
  • Types are compile-time promises, not runtime guarantees. The API can still send something else. Validate at the boundary (Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts goes deep on OpenAPI clients, zod and contract testing).

Practical example

A team turned on noUncheckedIndexedAccess in a 600-file app. It produced 214 errors. About 180 were genuine "this might be undefined" cases that needed a guard or a default; 11 of them were real bugs that had already caused production errors, including const primary = order.addresses[0].city on accounts with no saved address and PRICES[sku].amount for SKUs removed from the catalogue. The migration took two days, done one folder at a time.

React / Next.js example

A component that consumes shared types and benefits from the strict options:

// apps/web/src/orders/OrderRow.tsx
import type { OrderSummary, OrderStatus } from '@shop/contracts'; // type-only: erased from the bundle

const STATUS_LABEL = {
  PENDING: 'Awaiting payment',
  PAID: 'Preparing',
  SHIPPED: 'On the way',
  DELIVERED: 'Delivered',
  CANCELLED: 'Cancelled',
} satisfies Record<OrderStatus, string>; // adding a status in contracts breaks this until a label is added

export function OrderRow({ order }: { order: OrderSummary }) {
  const firstItem = order.items[0]; // OrderItem | undefined thanks to noUncheckedIndexedAccess
  return (
    <tr>
      <td>{order.displayId}</td>
      <td>{STATUS_LABEL[order.status]}</td>
      <td>{firstItem ? firstItem.name : 'No items'}{order.items.length > 1 ? ` +${order.items.length - 1}` : ''}</td>
      <td>{new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: order.currency })
            .format(Number(order.totalMinor) / 100)}</td>
    </tr>
  );
}

The satisfies operator (TypeScript 4.9+) checks that the object covers every status without widening its type, so the backend adding 'RETURNED' to OrderStatus fails the frontend type check until someone writes a label.

Backend side (NestJS)

The NestJS side implements the same shared types, so the compiler checks that the API and the client agree:

// apps/api/src/orders/dto/order-summary.dto.ts
import type { OrderSummary, OrderStatus } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ApiProperty } from '@nestjs/swagger';

// The DTO class stays in the backend (decorators, Swagger metadata);
// "implements" makes tsc fail if it drifts from the shared contract.
export class OrderSummaryDto implements OrderSummary {
  @ApiProperty() id!: string;
  @ApiProperty() displayId!: string;
  @ApiProperty({ enum: ['PENDING', 'PAID', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED'] }) status!: OrderStatus;
  @ApiProperty({ description: 'Integer minor units as a string, e.g. "129900"' }) totalMinor!: string;
  @ApiProperty() currency!: string;
  @ApiProperty({ type: () => [Object] }) items!: OrderSummary['items'];
  @ApiProperty() placedAt!: string; // ISO 8601 with offset
}

Note totalMinor: string. PostgreSQL numeric and bigint columns come back from the pg driver as strings by default (TypeORM and Sequelize pass that through), because JavaScript numbers cannot represent every value exactly. Make the contract say so, rather than declaring number and hoping.

Production scenario

A B2B ordering portal shared a contracts package between NestJS and React. Over six months, tsc in CI caught 37 contract mismatches before merge: renamed fields, new enum values without UI labels, optional fields made required. Each would otherwise have been a runtime error found by a customer. The type check for both apps took 48 s in CI, cached by Turborepo when neither app nor the contracts package changed (70.9).

Failure scenario

On a Saturday at 11:00, the order history page started crashing for every user with TypeError: order.total.toFixed is not a function. The shared type said total: number. A backend refactor had replaced a hand-written query with a TypeORM find() on an entity whose total column was numeric(12,2). The pg driver returned "1299.00" as a string, exactly as it always does for numeric; the old query had cast to float8. TypeScript was satisfied on both sides because the entity property was declared number, and nothing checked at run time.

The fix: declare the column honestly (@Column({ type: 'numeric', precision: 12, scale: 2 }) total!: string or use a column transformer), send money as integer minor units in a string field, and validate API responses on the client with a zod schema in development and tests. Types describe what you believe; only runtime validation checks it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • @types/node leaking into browser code hides Node-only globals behind green type checks; set types.
  • Aliases configured in only one place work in the editor and fail in the bundler, the test runner or the NestJS runtime.
  • Shared types that import from backend packages drag typeorm or @nestjs/common into the frontend's type check and sometimes into its bundle.
  • skipLibCheck: true hides type errors inside .d.ts files, including your own built contracts package; check the package itself in its own build.
  • any from res.json(): fetch returns Promise<any>, which silently disables checking for everything downstream. Parse into a known type at the boundary.
  • Numeric and bigint columns arrive as strings from pg; the type must match reality.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior configures TypeScript to describe the real runtime accurately, browser or Node, and as strictly as the team can sustain, with noUncheckedIndexedAccess included. They share types and schemas, never classes with decorators, and they let implements and satisfies turn contract drift into compile errors on both sides. They also remember that the type system ends at the network boundary: anything that arrives over HTTP is unknown until validated.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving strict off in a new project "to move faster".
  • Importing entity or DTO classes into the frontend.
  • Declaring number for numeric and bigint columns.
  • Configuring path aliases only in tsconfig.
  • Trusting res.json() as the declared type without validation.

Interview questions

  1. What does moduleResolution: "bundler" do and why not use it in NestJS? Expected answer: it mirrors how bundlers resolve imports, including exports and extensionless paths; NestJS output is run by Node, which resolves CommonJS or native ESM differently. Follow-up: what breaks if the frontend uses node10?
  2. Why set types in a browser tsconfig? Expected answer: to stop @types/node and other ambient types from making Node globals look valid in browser code.
  3. What does noUncheckedIndexedAccess catch that strict does not? Expected answer: indexed reads possibly being undefined, the most common source of "cannot read properties of undefined".
  4. How do you share types between NestJS and React safely? Expected answer: a contracts package with plain types or zod schemas, import type on the frontend, implements on backend DTOs, no decorated classes or entities shared, runtime validation at the boundary.
  5. Why can a fully type-checked frontend still crash on an API field type? Expected answer: types are erased at run time; the API may send a different shape (for example numeric as string), and only runtime validation catches it.

Practical exercise

Take a React app and a NestJS app in one repository. Create a shared OrderSummary type.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The web tsconfig has strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, types: ["vite/client"] and moduleResolution: "bundler", and process.env.X in a component is a type error.
  • The NestJS DTO implements OrderSummary; renaming a field in the shared type breaks both builds.
  • A satisfies Record<OrderStatus, string> map in the UI fails type checking when a new status is added.
  • The web bundle contains no code from class-validator, typeorm or @nestjs/* (checked with the bundle treemap).

70.9 Monorepos: workspaces, Turborepo and Nx, and a shared contracts package

Concept

A monorepo is one Git repository that holds several projects, for example a NestJS API, a React web app, an admin app and shared packages. It is a repository layout, not an architecture: the API and the web app still build, deploy and scale independently.

Three layers of tooling make it work:

  1. Workspaces (npm 7+, Yarn, pnpm) let the package manager install all projects with one lock file and link local packages to each other, so apps/web can depend on packages/contracts as if it were published to npm.
  2. A task runner (Turborepo, Nx) understands the dependency graph between projects, runs tasks such as build, test and lint in the right order and in parallel, and caches their results so unchanged projects are not rebuilt.
  3. Shared packages, most importantly a contracts package that holds the types and schemas both the NestJS API and the React app use.

Why does it exist?

With the API and web app in separate repositories, a contract change is a three-step dance: change the API, publish a types package, bump the version in the web repo. In between, the two disagree, and nobody's CI notices. In one repository, one pull request changes the contract, the API and the UI together, and CI type-checks both against the new contract before anything merges.

Without a task runner, though, a monorepo gets slow. Running every build and every test on every pull request turns a 4-minute pipeline into a 25-minute one as projects multiply. Task graphs and caching keep CI proportional to what changed.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant group with three kitchens in one building and a shared pantry. Workspaces are the pantry: one stock list, every kitchen draws from it, and the house sauce made in-house is on the same shelf as bought ingredients. The task runner is the head chef's board: "the sauce must be made before the pasta station starts; the dessert station does not depend on either; if nothing in the sauce recipe changed since yesterday, use yesterday's batch."

How it works

Workspaces. With pnpm, the root declares which folders are packages:

# pnpm-workspace.yaml
packages:
  - "apps/*"
  - "packages/*"

A package depends on a sibling with the workspace: protocol: "@shop/contracts": "workspace:*". pnpm symlinks apps/web/node_modules/@shop/contracts to packages/contracts. With npm workspaces the root package.json has "workspaces": ["apps/*", "packages/*"] and local packages are linked into the root node_modules.

The important difference is strictness. npm and Yarn Classic hoist everything into one flat root node_modules, so apps/web can import a package it never declared because apps/api happened to install it: a phantom dependency. It works on your laptop and breaks when the web app is built alone in Docker. pnpm keeps each package's node_modules limited to what it declared (with symlinks into a content-addressable store, which also saves disk: a monorepo that needs 2.1 GB with npm often needs 600 to 800 MB with pnpm). pnpm 10 also stopped running dependencies' install scripts by default unless allow-listed in onlyBuiltDependencies, which closes a common supply-chain attack path (Part 40 — Security).

Useful commands:

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile          # CI: fail if pnpm-lock.yaml does not match package.json files
pnpm --filter web dev                   # run a script in one package
pnpm --filter "web..." build            # build web and everything it depends on
pnpm --filter "...[origin/main]" test   # test packages changed since main, plus their dependents
pnpm add zod --filter @shop/contracts   # add a dependency to one package

Task graph and caching. Turborepo reads each package's scripts and a root turbo.json:

{
  "$schema": "https://turbo.build/schema.json",
  "tasks": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["dist/**"] },
    "typecheck": { "dependsOn": ["^build"] },
    "lint": {},
    "test": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["coverage/**"] },
    "dev": { "cache": false, "persistent": true }
  }
}

(Turborepo 2.0 renamed the top-level pipeline key to tasks.) "^build" means "build my dependencies first". So turbo run build produces this graph:

flowchart LR
    contractsBuild["contracts: build"] --> apiBuild["api: build"]
    contractsBuild --> webBuild["web: build"]
    contractsBuild --> apiTest["api: test"]
    contractsBuild --> webTest["web: test"]
    contractsBuild --> webTypes["web: typecheck"]
    lintAll["lint: all packages in parallel"]

Before running a task, Turborepo computes a hash of its inputs: the package's source files, its resolved dependencies from the lock file, the hashes of the tasks it depends on, the task configuration, and declared environment variables. If the hash was seen before, it restores the outputs and the logs from the cache (local in .turbo/cache, or a remote cache shared by CI and developers) in a fraction of a second. A pull request that only touches apps/web rebuilds nothing in apps/api.

Nx offers the same core (a project graph, nx affected -t lint test build to run only what changed, local and remote caching), plus code generators and a lint rule, @nx/enforce-module-boundaries, that forbids imports across tagged boundaries (for example "web must not import from api"). Turborepo is smaller and configuration-light; Nx does more and asks more. Both work with pnpm workspaces.

The contracts package. It must be consumable by two very different builds: NestJS (CommonJS, run by Node) and Vite (ESM, bundled). The simplest robust setup builds it with tsup (an esbuild-based library bundler) into both formats with declarations:

{
  "name": "@shop/contracts",
  "version": "0.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "sideEffects": false,
  "main": "./dist/index.js",
  "module": "./dist/index.mjs",
  "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
  "exports": {
    ".": {
      "types": "./dist/index.d.ts",
      "import": "./dist/index.mjs",
      "require": "./dist/index.js"
    }
  },
  "scripts": {
    "build": "tsup src/index.ts --format cjs,esm --dts --clean",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"
  },
  "dependencies": { "zod": "^3.23.8" },
  "devDependencies": { "tsup": "^8.3.0", "typescript": "^5.6.0" }
}

An alternative, the "internal package" pattern, points exports straight at ./src/index.ts and lets each consumer compile it. Vite and Next.js (with transpilePackages) handle that well; a NestJS build with plain tsc does not compile TypeScript inside node_modules, so for a NestJS consumer the built package is the safer choice.

Practical example

A team of 11 has apps/api, apps/web, apps/admin and packages/contracts, packages/ui, packages/eslint-config. Before Turborepo, CI ran everything: 19 minutes per pull request. After: a PR touching only apps/admin runs admin's lint, typecheck, test and build, with everything else restored from the remote cache, in 3 min 40 s. A PR touching packages/contracts rebuilds and tests everything, correctly, in 14 minutes. The remote cache hit rate across all CI runs settled at 71 %.

React / Next.js example

The web app declares the dependency and imports both types and runtime schemas:

{
  "name": "web",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": {
    "@shop/contracts": "workspace:*",
    "@tanstack/react-query": "^5.59.0",
    "react": "^18.3.1",
    "react-dom": "^18.3.1"
  }
}
// apps/web/src/api/orders.ts
import { OrderSummarySchema, type OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import { z } from 'zod';

const OrderListSchema = z.object({ items: z.array(OrderSummarySchema), nextCursor: z.string().nullable() });

export async function fetchOrders(cursor?: string): Promise<{ items: OrderSummary[]; nextCursor: string | null }> {
  const url = new URL('/api/v1/orders', location.origin);
  if (cursor) url.searchParams.set('cursor', cursor);
  const res = await fetch(url, { credentials: 'same-origin', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000) });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`orders ${res.status}`);
  return OrderListSchema.parse(await res.json()); // the network boundary: unknown until validated
}

For a Next.js app in the same monorepo consuming the source-only pattern, add transpilePackages: ['@shop/contracts'] to next.config.js.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API consumes the same package and, in Docker, must be built from the monorepo without copying the whole repository into the image. turbo prune creates a minimal subset containing only the API and its workspace dependencies, with a pruned lock file:

# apps/api/Dockerfile, built from the repository root: docker build -f apps/api/Dockerfile .
FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS prune
WORKDIR /repo
RUN corepack enable
COPY . .
RUN pnpm dlx turbo@2 prune api --docker   # writes out/json (manifests) and out/full (sources)

FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS build
WORKDIR /repo
RUN corepack enable
COPY --from=prune /repo/out/json/ ./                  # manifests only: install layer cached until they change
COPY --from=prune /repo/out/pnpm-lock.yaml ./pnpm-lock.yaml
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
COPY --from=prune /repo/out/full/ ./
RUN pnpm dlx turbo@2 run build --filter=api           # builds contracts first, then api
RUN pnpm --filter api deploy --prod /out              # api plus production deps, workspace packages copied in

FROM node:20.18.1-alpine3.20 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /out ./
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/main.js"]

(corepack ships with Node 20 and 22; newer Node versions may need npm i -g corepack first. pnpm 10's deploy requires inject-workspace-packages=true in .npmrc, or the --legacy flag.) Part 44 — Docker for Backend Engineers explains the multi-stage pattern; the monorepo-specific part is pruning and pnpm deploy, which turn a 1.4 GB "copy everything" image into roughly 190 MB.

Production scenario

A payments company moved its checkout web app, NestJS API and shared contracts from three repositories into one pnpm and Turborepo monorepo. Contract-related production incidents (field renamed in the API, UI not updated, or the reverse) went from five in the previous half-year to zero in the next, because every such change now failed typecheck in the same pull request. The tradeoff they accepted: a contracts change triggers every app's pipeline, and CODEOWNERS on packages/contracts requires one backend and one frontend reviewer.

Failure scenario

On a Tuesday the production web app started calling the staging payment gateway's public endpoint. Payments failed with "invalid merchant". The deploy pipeline had restored apps/web's build output from the Turborepo remote cache.

The web app's vite.config.ts read a non-prefixed PAYMENT_ENV variable through process.env and inlined it with define. Turborepo automatically includes framework-prefixed variables such as VITE_* in the hash, but not arbitrary names. PAYMENT_ENV was not listed in the task's env, so the staging build and the production build had the same hash, and production received the cached staging bundle.

The fix: list it ("build": { "env": ["PAYMENT_ENV"], ... }), and better, remove per-environment values from the build entirely in favour of runtime config (70.6). Turborepo 2's strict environment mode, which only passes declared variables to tasks, would have turned this into a loud build failure instead of a silent wrong value.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Phantom dependencies with hoisting work locally and fail in isolated builds; pnpm's strict layout surfaces them early.
  • Undeclared inputs (environment variables, files outside the package, generated code) make cache hits wrong.
  • Circular workspace dependencies (contracts importing from api) break the task graph; lint against them.
  • Version skew: two apps on different React or TypeScript majors in one repo; pnpm catalogs (pnpm 9.5+) or a single root version keeps them aligned.
  • A huge repo with no caching makes every PR slow; the monorepo then gets blamed for a missing task runner.
  • Deploy coupling: one repo does not mean one deploy. Keep pipelines per app.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior chooses a monorepo for the contract, not for fashion: the value is that one change to an API shape is type-checked against every consumer before merge. They pick pnpm for strictness and disk usage, add Turborepo (or Nx when the team wants generators and boundary rules), declare every task input, and keep deploys independent per app. They refuse "shared utils" packages that grow into a dumping ground; shared packages have an owner and a narrow purpose: contracts, UI components, lint config.

Common mistakes

  • Sharing backend code (entities, services) instead of contracts.
  • Running every task on every PR without a task graph and cache.
  • Not declaring environment variables as task inputs.
  • One deploy for the whole repo.
  • Using npm hoisting and discovering phantom dependencies in Docker.

Interview questions

  1. What does "dependsOn": ["^build"] mean in Turborepo? Expected answer: run the build task of every workspace dependency before this package's task. Follow-up: what goes into the cache hash?
  2. What is a phantom dependency and how does pnpm prevent it? Expected answer: importing a package you did not declare because hoisting put it in reach; pnpm's non-flat node_modules makes undeclared packages unresolvable.
  3. How would you make a shared contracts package consumable by both NestJS and Vite? Expected answer: build CJS and ESM outputs with declarations and an exports map, or source-only consumed by bundlers with NestJS compiling it some other way; no decorators, no backend imports.
  4. How do you keep monorepo CI fast? Expected answer: affected-only task execution, remote caching, correct inputs and outputs, and parallelism.
  5. How do you build one app's Docker image from a monorepo? Expected answer: prune to the app and its dependencies (turbo prune --docker), install from the pruned lock file, build, pnpm deploy --prod.

Practical exercise

Create a pnpm workspace with apps/api, apps/web and packages/contracts, and add Turborepo.

Acceptance criteria:

  • pnpm turbo run build builds contracts before both apps; a second run is fully cached (FULL TURBO in the output).
  • Changing only a file in apps/web rebuilds only web.
  • Adding an undeclared import of a package used only by api into web fails to resolve.
  • The API Docker image built with turbo prune and pnpm deploy is under 250 MB and starts.

70.10 Linting, formatting and pre-commit checks

Concept

A linter (ESLint) analyses code for likely bugs and agreed rules: a promise that is never awaited, a React hook called conditionally, an import that crosses a forbidden boundary. A formatter (Prettier) rewrites code into one canonical layout: indentation, quotes, line breaks. They do different jobs, and since ESLint deprecated its formatting rules in v8.53 (they moved to @stylistic), the standard split is ESLint for correctness and Prettier for layout. Pre-commit checks run a fast subset of both on the files you are committing, before the commit is created.

Why does it exist?

Code review time is expensive and should be spent on design and behaviour, not on spaces versus tabs or on spotting a missing await by eye. A formatter ends layout debates permanently.
