A linter catches whole classes of bugs mechanically, including some the type checker cannot: react-hooks/exhaustive-deps finds effects that read stale values; @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises finds repository.save(order) without await in NestJS and queryClient.invalidateQueries() dropped on the floor in React.

Mental model

Imagine a publishing house. The formatter is the typesetter: every book gets the same fonts and margins, and nobody argues about it. The linter is the copy editor with a checklist: dangling sentences, contradictions, banned words. The pre-commit hook is the copy editor glancing at the pages you just changed before they leave your desk. CI is the final proofread that every manuscript gets, no exceptions.

How it works

ESLint 9 flat config. ESLint 9 made eslint.config.js (an array of config objects) the default; the old .eslintrc format is deprecated and removed in ESLint 10. One root config can serve the whole monorepo, with per-folder blocks for browser and Node code:

// eslint.config.mjs (repository root; ESLint 9.22+ for defineConfig, typescript-eslint v8)
import js from '@eslint/js';
import tseslint from 'typescript-eslint';
import reactHooks from 'eslint-plugin-react-hooks';
import reactRefresh from 'eslint-plugin-react-refresh';
import prettier from 'eslint-config-prettier';
import globals from 'globals';
import { defineConfig } from 'eslint/config';

export default defineConfig(
  { ignores: ['**/dist/**', '**/coverage/**', '**/.turbo/**'] },
  js.configs.recommended,
  tseslint.configs.recommendedTypeChecked,
  {
    languageOptions: { parserOptions: { projectService: true, tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname } },
    rules: {
      '@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises': 'error',  // unawaited promises: lost writes, silent failures
      '@typescript-eslint/switch-exhaustiveness-check': 'error',
    },
  },
  {
    files: ['apps/web/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
    languageOptions: { globals: globals.browser },
    plugins: { 'react-hooks': reactHooks, 'react-refresh': reactRefresh },
    rules: {
      ...reactHooks.configs.recommended.rules,             // rules-of-hooks, exhaustive-deps
      'react-refresh/only-export-components': 'warn',      // keeps Fast Refresh boundaries clean (76.4)
      'no-restricted-globals': ['error', 'process', 'Buffer'],
      'no-restricted-imports': ['error', { patterns: [
        { group: ['@nestjs/*', 'typeorm', 'class-validator', '**/apps/api/**'], message: 'Browser code must not import backend code. Use @shop/contracts.' },
      ] }],
    },
  },
  { files: ['apps/api/**/*.ts'], languageOptions: { globals: globals.node } },
  prettier, // last: turns off any rule that conflicts with Prettier's formatting
);

projectService: true (typescript-eslint v8) finds the right tsconfig for each file automatically, which is what makes type-aware rules such as no-floating-promises possible. They are slower: a type-aware lint of a 2,000-file repo can take 40 to 90 s against 8 to 15 s without type information, which is why they belong in CI and the editor rather than in every pre-commit run on large repos.

Prettier 3. A tiny config and a check in CI:

{ "singleQuote": true, "printWidth": 110, "trailingComma": "all" }

prettier --check . fails CI if any file is not formatted; prettier --write fixes. eslint-config-prettier disables ESLint rules that would fight it. Faster all-in-one alternatives exist (Biome for linting and formatting, oxlint for linting) and are worth evaluating for large repos, but ESLint plus Prettier remains the default most teams and plugins target.

Pre-commit with husky and lint-staged.

pnpm add -D -w husky lint-staged
pnpm exec husky init        # husky v9: adds "prepare": "husky" and creates .husky/pre-commit
echo "pnpm exec lint-staged" > .husky/pre-commit
{
  "lint-staged": {
    "*.{ts,tsx}": ["eslint --max-warnings=0", "prettier --write"],
    "*.{json,md,yaml,css}": ["prettier --write"]
  }
}

lint-staged runs the commands only on staged files, so the hook takes 1 to 5 s instead of a minute. Whole-project checks (tsc, type-aware lint, tests) are too slow for a pre-commit hook and run in CI, optionally also in a pre-push hook.

flowchart LR
    save["Save file"] --> editor["Editor: ESLint and Prettier on save"]
    editor --> commit["git commit"]
    commit --> hook["Pre-commit: lint-staged on staged files, about 3 s"]
    hook --> push["git push"]
    push --> ci["CI: prettier --check, full lint, typecheck, tests"]
    ci --> merge["Merge allowed"]

Hooks are a convenience, not a control: git commit --no-verify skips them, and they do not run for commits made in the web UI. CI is the gate (Part 47 — CI/CD).

Practical example

In a NestJS and React monorepo, enabling no-floating-promises reported 63 errors. In the API: an auditLog.record() call in an exception filter without await (audit entries lost when the request ended first), and this.events.emit() inside a transaction callback whose failure was never observed. In the web app: 14 onClick={() => mutation.mutateAsync(...)} handlers whose rejections became unhandled promise rejections instead of error toasts. Each was a real bug or a silent failure.

React / Next.js example

The fix pattern for floating promises in a React handler, which the rule forces you to make explicit:

// apps/web/src/orders/CancelOrderButton.tsx
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { cancelOrder } from '../api/orders';

export function CancelOrderButton({ orderId }: { orderId: string }) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  const mutation = useMutation({
    mutationFn: () => cancelOrder(orderId, crypto.randomUUID()), // idempotency key per attempt (Part 15.12)
    onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] }), // returned promise: awaited by TanStack Query
  });

  return (
    <button
      disabled={mutation.isPending}
      // mutate() (not mutateAsync) returns void and routes errors to mutation.error, so nothing floats.
      onClick={() => mutation.mutate()}
    >
      {mutation.isPending ? 'Cancelling...' : 'Cancel order'}
    </button>
  );
}

Next.js 14 ships eslint-config-next and runs ESLint during next build (configurable with eslint.ignoreDuringBuilds); Next.js 16 removed the automatic lint step from next build, so lint must be its own CI task.

Backend side (NestJS)

The same root config lints the API, and the type-aware rules matter even more there, because an unawaited promise in a request handler is a write that may never happen:

// apps/api/src/orders/orders.service.ts (excerpt)
async cancel(orderId: string, userId: string): Promise<void> {
  await this.dataSource.transaction(async (em) => {
    const order = await em.findOneOrFail(Order, { where: { id: orderId, userId }, lock: { mode: 'pessimistic_write' } });
    order.status = 'CANCELLED';
    await em.save(order);
    // Without await, a failure here would surface after the transaction committed, unobserved.
    await em.insert(OutboxEvent, { type: 'order.cancelled', payload: { orderId } });
  });
}

Keep the backend's formatting identical to the frontend's (one Prettier config at the root), so a full-stack pull request is not half reformatting.

Production scenario

A team with 30 engineers adopted Prettier and the flat ESLint config in one pass. They formatted the entire repository in a single dedicated commit, added that commit's SHA to .git-blame-ignore-revs so git blame skips it (Part 5 — Git Basics and the Development Workflow), and only then turned on the CI check. Review comments about style dropped to nearly zero within a month, and median review time on frontend pull requests fell from 26 to 17 hours.

Failure scenario

A different team added a pre-commit hook that ran eslint --fix and prettier --write on every file touched by a commit, not just changed lines, in a legacy codebase that had never been formatted. A developer fixing a one-line bug in the coupon calculation committed a 1,400-line diff: the one-line fix plus 1,399 lines of reformatting. The reviewer approved the "formatting" without seeing that the fix had also flipped a >= to >, so coupons stopped applying on orders of exactly the minimum value. Support took three days to connect complaints about "my coupon doesn't work at exactly 500 rupees" to the change.

The lesson: introduce formatting as a single dedicated commit, never mixed with behaviour changes, and keep feature diffs minimal so reviewers can see what changed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Hooks skipped with --no-verify or by GUI tools; CI must re-run every check.
  • Type-aware lint too slow for pre-commit on large repos; keep it in CI and the editor.
  • ESLint and Prettier fighting when eslint-config-prettier is missing or not last.
  • Mixed .eslintrc and flat config during migration; ESLint 9 ignores .eslintrc unless ESLINT_USE_FLAT_CONFIG=false.
  • Auto-fix on whole legacy files produces unreviewable diffs.
  • prepare scripts in Docker: husky in prepare fails in images without .git; install production deps with --ignore-scripts (Part 44).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior automates everything that is not judgement. Formatting is not judgement: Prettier decides. A handful of high-value lint rules (no-floating-promises, the React hooks rules, import boundaries, no Node globals in browser code) catch real bugs and are non-negotiable; long lists of stylistic rules are not worth the friction. Pre-commit hooks are kept fast and treated as a courtesy; CI is the authority. And they protect reviewers: formatting changes and behaviour changes never share a commit.

Common mistakes

  • Using ESLint for formatting and Prettier on top, so they fight.
  • Slow pre-commit hooks that people learn to skip.
  • Relying on hooks instead of CI.
  • Reformatting whole files inside feature commits.
  • Turning on every rule and drowning real errors in warnings; use --max-warnings=0 with a small, meaningful rule set.

Interview questions

  1. Why separate linting from formatting? Expected answer: they solve different problems; formatters are deterministic layout, linters find bugs and enforce agreed rules; combining them causes conflicts. Follow-up: how do you stop them fighting? (eslint-config-prettier.)
  2. Name a lint rule that catches bugs the type checker misses. Expected answer: no-floating-promises, react-hooks/exhaustive-deps, rules-of-hooks.
  3. What should run in a pre-commit hook and what should not? Expected answer: fast checks on staged files (lint and format); whole-project type checks and tests in CI.
  4. How do you introduce Prettier to a large existing codebase? Expected answer: one dedicated formatting commit, .git-blame-ignore-revs, then enforce in CI.

Practical exercise

Set up a root eslint.config.mjs for a monorepo with apps/api and apps/web, plus Prettier, husky and lint-staged.

Acceptance criteria:

  • An unawaited repository.save() in the API and an unawaited mutateAsync() in the web app both fail lint.
  • import { Entity } from 'typeorm' in apps/web fails lint with your custom message.
  • The pre-commit hook completes in under 5 s for a two-file commit.
  • CI runs prettier --check . and full lint, and a commit made with --no-verify that breaks formatting fails CI.

70.11 Choosing a frontend stack: Vite SPA vs Next.js vs plain server-rendered pages

Concept

Most teams that build a web product choose between three shapes:

  • Vite SPA: a single-page application. The server (CDN) sends a nearly empty index.html and a JavaScript bundle; React renders everything in the browser and calls your NestJS API for data.
  • Next.js: a React framework that renders on the server (and at build time) as well as in the browser, with routing, data fetching, caching and a Node server or serverless runtime of its own. Part 73 — Next.js and Rendering Strategies goes deep on how.
  • Plain server-rendered pages: HTML produced by your backend with templates (Handlebars, EJS or Pug through NestJS's @Render(), or another server framework), with a little JavaScript for interactivity, often loaded as a module or with a library such as htmx or Alpine.js.

The tooling in this Part applies differently to each. A Vite SPA uses all of it. Next.js hides most of the bundler behind its own CLI. Server-rendered pages may need no bundler at all.

Why does it exist?

Because the cost profiles are different. An SPA is cheap to host (static files) but shows nothing until JavaScript runs, which hurts first load on slow phones and complicates SEO. Next.js gives fast first paint and SEO but adds a server tier you must run, monitor and scale. Server-rendered pages are the simplest and fastest to first byte, but rich interactivity gets awkward as screens grow. Choosing by fashion rather than by these costs is how teams end up running a Node rendering tier for an internal admin tool, or shipping a 400 KB SPA for a marketing page.

Mental model

Imagine three ways to serve food. The SPA is a meal kit: cheap to deliver, but the customer cooks before eating. Next.js is a restaurant: food arrives ready, but you run a kitchen with staff and opening hours. Server-rendered pages are a canteen: simple, fast, limited menu. Each is right for someone.

How it works

flowchart TB
    q1{"Do pages need SEO or fast first paint for anonymous users?"}
    q1 -->|"no: behind login"| q2{"Rich, app-like interactivity?"}
    q1 -->|"yes"| q3{"Mostly content with little interactivity?"}
    q2 -->|"yes"| spa["Vite SPA plus NestJS API"]
    q2 -->|"no: forms and tables"| ssr["Server-rendered pages from the backend"]
    q3 -->|"yes"| ssr2["Server-rendered or static pages"]
    q3 -->|"no: product pages, checkout, personalised"| nextjs["Next.js in front of NestJS"]
Criterion Vite SPA Next.js (App Router) Server-rendered pages
First paint on a slow phone Slow: waits for JS (often 2 to 4 s) Fast: HTML from server or cache Fastest: HTML straight from the backend
SEO for public pages Weak without prerendering Strong Strong
Hosting Static files on S3 + CDN, cents per day Node server, serverless or edge; a tier to operate Your existing backend
Build tooling you own Vite config, all of this Part Mostly next.config.js Little or none
Rich interactivity Excellent Excellent Limited; grows awkward
Secrets and server logic in the frontend tier None (all in NestJS) Server components, Route Handlers can hold secrets (BFF) Backend already holds them
Team skills needed React React plus server rendering, caching semantics Backend templates
Typical fit Dashboards, admin, logged-in apps Storefronts, marketing plus app, SEO-critical pages Internal tools, simple CRUD, emails, status pages

Backend side (NestJS)

Each shape asks something different of the API:

  • Vite SPA: the API is called from the browser. It must handle cookies or tokens for browser auth (Part 75 — Auth and Security in the Browser), CORS if on another origin (or better, same-origin routing through the CDN), and response shapes that the browser can render without extra round trips.
  • Next.js: the API is mostly called server-to-server from the Next.js tier. Latency between Next.js and NestJS lands directly in time to first byte (69.1), so co-locate them and parallelise calls. The Next.js server can act as a backend-for-frontend that aggregates several NestJS endpoints.
  • Server-rendered pages: NestJS renders HTML itself, with @Render('orders/list') and a view engine configured through app.setViewEngine() on the Express platform. No separate frontend build or contract package is needed for those pages.

Production scenario

An electronics retailer ran its whole site as a Vite SPA: storefront, account area and an internal merchandising tool. Product pages had p75 LCP of 3.6 s on mobile and organic search traffic was flat. They moved only the storefront (home, category, product pages) to Next.js with cached server rendering, kept the logged-in account area as part of the Next.js app with client components, and left the merchandising tool as a Vite SPA because it is behind login, used on desktops, and nobody searches for it. LCP on product pages fell to 1.9 s. The tool stayed cheap: static files on S3.

Failure scenario

A team building a four-screen internal returns approval tool chose Next.js "because it's the standard". Six months later, they were running a Node server tier with autoscaling, debugging cache invalidation for pages that were only ever viewed by logged-in staff, and paying for a server that served 300 users. A rewrite to server-rendered pages inside the existing NestJS service took two weeks and removed a deployment, a container and an on-call surface.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior chooses per surface, not per company. Public, SEO-sensitive, first-load-sensitive pages justify server rendering and its operational cost. Logged-in, interaction-heavy tools are well served by an SPA on a CDN. Simple internal CRUD is often best as server-rendered HTML from the service that owns the data. They ask: who loads this page, on what device, how often, does search matter, and who will operate the extra tier at 02:00?

Interview questions

  1. When would you choose a Vite SPA over Next.js? Expected answer: logged-in, interaction-heavy apps where SEO does not matter and static hosting is attractive. Follow-up: what does the SPA cost you on first load?
  2. What new operational responsibilities come with Next.js? Expected answer: a server or serverless rendering tier to deploy, scale and monitor, caching layers to understand, and server-to-server latency to the API.
  3. When are plain server-rendered pages the best choice? Expected answer: simple internal tools and content pages with little interactivity, especially when the backend already owns the data.

70.12 Worked example: a pnpm monorepo with NestJS, React and shared contracts

Concept

We now put the Part together in one repository: apps/api (NestJS 10), apps/web (React 18 with Vite), and packages/contracts (zod schemas and the types inferred from them). The goal: one pull request can change an API shape, and CI proves that both the API and the UI agree with it before merge.

The layout

shop/
├── package.json             root: scripts, devDependencies for lint, format, turbo
├── pnpm-workspace.yaml      apps/*, packages/*  (76.9)
├── pnpm-lock.yaml
├── turbo.json               build, typecheck, lint, test tasks  (76.9)
├── eslint.config.mjs        one flat config for all packages  (76.10)
├── .prettierrc.json
├── .husky/pre-commit        pnpm exec lint-staged
├── apps/
│   ├── api/                 NestJS: depends on @shop/contracts
│   │   ├── src/orders/...
│   │   ├── tsconfig.json    commonjs, decorators, strict
│   │   └── Dockerfile       turbo prune + pnpm deploy  (76.9)
│   └── web/                 Vite React: depends on @shop/contracts
│       ├── src/...
│       ├── tsconfig.app.json  bundler resolution, DOM, strict  (76.8)
│       └── vite.config.ts     proxy /api to :3000, hidden source maps  (76.3)
└── packages/

        ├── src/index.ts
        └── package.json     exports map  (76.9)

    contracts["packages/contracts: zod schemas and types"] --> api["apps/api: NestJS validates requests with the schemas"]
    contracts --> web["apps/web: React validates responses with the schemas"]

packageManager pins the pnpm version; Corepack and pnpm/action-setup read it, so every developer and CI runner uses the same one.

The contracts package

// packages/contracts/src/index.ts  (zod 3.23)
import { z } from 'zod';

export const OrderStatusSchema = z.enum(['PENDING', 'PAID', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED']);
export type OrderStatus = z.infer<typeof OrderStatusSchema>;

// Money as integer minor units in a string: exact, and safe beyond 2^53.
export const MinorUnitsSchema = z.string().regex(/^\d+$/, 'integer minor units');

export const OrderItemSchema = z.object({
  sku: z.string().min(1),
  name: z.string().min(1),
  quantity: z.number().int().positive(),
  unitPriceMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
});
export type OrderItem = z.infer<typeof OrderItemSchema>;

export const OrderSummarySchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  displayId: z.string(),
  status: OrderStatusSchema,
  totalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
  currency: z.string().length(3),
  items: z.array(OrderItemSchema),
  placedAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),
});
export type OrderSummary = z.infer<typeof OrderSummarySchema>;

export const OrderListResponseSchema = z.object({
  items: z.array(OrderSummarySchema),
  nextCursor: z.string().nullable(),
});
export type OrderListResponse = z.infer<typeof OrderListResponseSchema>;

export const CancelOrderRequestSchema = z.object({ reason: z.enum(['CHANGED_MIND', 'TOO_SLOW', 'OTHER']) });
export type CancelOrderRequest = z.infer<typeof CancelOrderRequestSchema>;

No NestJS, no React, no TypeORM: only zod, which runs in both places. The schemas are the single source of truth; the types are derived from them, so they cannot disagree.

The API side

A small validation pipe uses the shared schemas, following the "object schema validation" pattern from the NestJS documentation:

// apps/api/src/common/zod-validation.pipe.ts
import { BadRequestException, PipeTransform } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { ZodType } from 'zod';

export class ZodValidationPipe<T> implements PipeTransform<unknown, T> {
  constructor(private readonly schema: ZodType<T>) {}

  transform(value: unknown): T {
    const result = this.schema.safeParse(value);
    if (!result.success) {
      // One error shape for the frontend to map onto form fields (Part 74 covers error contracts).
      throw new BadRequestException({
        code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED',
        issues: result.error.issues.map((i) => ({ path: i.path.join('.'), message: i.message })),
      });
    }
    return result.data;
  }
}
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Headers, HttpCode, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Post, Query, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CancelOrderRequestSchema, type CancelOrderRequest, type OrderListResponse } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get()
  list(@CurrentUser() userId: string, @Query('cursor') cursor?: string): Promise<OrderListResponse> {
    return this.orders.listForUser(userId, cursor, 20); // return type is checked against the contract
  }

  @Post(':id/cancel')
  @HttpCode(202)
  cancel(
    @CurrentUser() userId: string,
    @Param('id', new ParseUUIDPipe()) id: string,
    @Headers('idempotency-key') idempotencyKey: string,
    @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(CancelOrderRequestSchema)) body: CancelOrderRequest,
  ): Promise<void> {
    return this.orders.cancel({ userId, orderId: id, reason: body.reason, idempotencyKey });
  }
}

OrdersService.listForUser maps entities to OrderSummary explicitly, converting numeric columns to minor-unit strings and timestamps to ISO strings, so the database shape never leaks into the contract (70.8). The Promise<OrderListResponse> return type means a renamed field in the contract is a compile error in the API.

The web side

// apps/web/src/orders/useOrders.ts
import { useInfiniteQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderListResponseSchema, type OrderListResponse } from '@shop/contracts';

async function fetchOrderPage(cursor: string | null, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<OrderListResponse> {
  const qs = cursor ? `?cursor=${encodeURIComponent(cursor)}` : '';
  const res = await fetch(`/api/v1/orders${qs}`, { credentials: 'same-origin', signal });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`orders ${res.status}`);
  return OrderListResponseSchema.parse(await res.json()); // the same schema the API was built against
}

export function useOrders() {
  return useInfiniteQuery({
    queryKey: ['orders'],
    queryFn: ({ pageParam, signal }) => fetchOrderPage(pageParam, signal),
    initialPageParam: null as string | null,
    getNextPageParam: (last) => last.nextCursor,
  });
}

The OrderRow component from 70.8 renders each item with its satisfies Record<OrderStatus, string> label map. Part 72 — Client State, Data Fetching and Caching covers the TanStack Query side in depth.

Numbers for this repository on a 2023 laptop: pnpm install cold 38 s, warm 4 s; contracts build 0.6 s; API build (nest build with tsc) 9 s; web production build 21 s, producing a 71 KB gzip entry chunk; turbo run typecheck 26 s cold and 0.3 s fully cached.

CI

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }             # turbo --affected compares against the base branch
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4            # reads "packageManager" from package.json
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm exec prettier --check .
      - run: pnpm turbo run lint typecheck test build --affected
        env:
          TURBO_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TURBO_TOKEN }}   # remote cache shared with other runs
          TURBO_TEAM: ${{ vars.TURBO_TEAM }}

--affected (Turborepo 2.1+) runs tasks only for packages changed in the pull request and their dependents. Part 47 — CI/CD covers the deploy stages that follow; Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends covers deploying the web build.

A breaking change caught in CI

A backend engineer renames displayId to orderNumber in packages/contracts, updates the API mapper, and opens a pull request. Because contracts changed, Turborepo runs typecheck for every dependent package. The web job fails in 26 s:

web:typecheck: src/orders/OrderRow.tsx(16,22): error TS2339: Property 'displayId' does not exist on type
web:typecheck:   '{ id: string; orderNumber: string; status: "PENDING" | "PAID" | ... }'.
web:typecheck: ERROR: command finished with error: command (apps/web) pnpm run typecheck exited (2)

The engineer now has three honest options instead of a production incident: update the UI in the same pull request; add orderNumber alongside displayId and remove the old field later (the expand-and-contract approach from Part 25 — Backward Compatibility: APIs, Schemas, Events and Clients, needed anyway because old browser tabs and the mobile app still expect displayId); or decide the rename is not worth it. Without the shared package, the first sign would have been "Order undefined" on every order card in production.

Failure drills

  • Contracts package not rebuilt. If a developer runs pnpm --filter web dev without building contracts first, the web app imports a stale dist/. Fix: a dev task in turbo.json with dependsOn: ["^build"], or tsup --watch in contracts during development.
  • Backend-only import leaks into web. Someone imports @nestjs/common in a shared helper. The no-restricted-imports rule (70.10) fails lint before the bundle grows by 200 KB.
  • Turbo cache serves a wrong build. Covered in 70.9: declare every environment input, prefer runtime config.
  • Docker image includes the whole monorepo. turbo prune api --docker plus pnpm deploy keeps the image to the API and its real dependencies.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The value of this setup is not the tools; it is the feedback loop. A contract change produces a red build in under a minute, in the same pull request, with an error message that names the exact line in the UI that disagrees. The senior keeps that loop fast (caching, affected-only runs), honest (runtime validation at both ends, not just types) and narrow (contracts contain only shapes, never backend logic). They also remember what the type check cannot see: clients already in the field. Shared types prevent drift inside the repository; compatibility rules from Part 25 still govern what is already deployed.

Practical exercise

Build this repository from scratch.

Acceptance criteria:

  • pnpm verify passes from a clean clone in under 3 minutes, and a second run in under 20 seconds thanks to caching.
  • Renaming a field in packages/contracts fails typecheck in both apps/api and apps/web with errors pointing at the exact lines.
  • Sending {"reason": "BORED"} to POST /api/v1/orders/:id/cancel returns a 400 with code: "VALIDATION_FAILED" and an issues array.
  • The web production build's entry chunk is under 90 KB gzip and contains no @nestjs, typeorm or class-validator code.
  • The API Docker image is under 250 MB.

Senior Checklist — Part 70

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain why browsers need a build step even though they support ES modules
  • I know that frontend bundlers transpile without type checking, and I run tsc --noEmit as a separate CI gate
  • I can set browser targets from real traffic data and know that targets lower syntax but do not polyfill APIs
  • I can explain how Vite's dev server differs from its production build, and I test the production bundle before release
  • I can make a module HMR-safe with import.meta.hot.dispose and cap per-user connections on the backend
  • I can read a bundle treemap, fix a barrel or CommonJS import, and set a first-route budget in CI
  • I never put a secret in a VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable, and I can serve runtime config from NestJS with an allow-list
  • I can produce hidden source maps, upload them privately per release, and symbolicate a minified stack trace
  • I can write a browser tsconfig with strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, types and moduleResolution: "bundler"
  • I can share types between NestJS and React without sharing decorated classes or entities
  • I can set up a pnpm workspace with Turborepo, declare task inputs correctly, and build one app's Docker image from it
  • I can configure ESLint 9 flat config with type-aware rules, Prettier, and fast pre-commit hooks, with CI as the real gate
  • I can choose between a Vite SPA, Next.js and server-rendered pages for a given surface and defend the choice

Part 70 — Key Takeaways

  • The build step exists because of five real problems: TypeScript and JSX, the module waterfall, bare imports, old browsers and bytes on slow phones.
  • Frontend bundlers transpile one file at a time and do not check types; a green build is not a green type check.
  • Build targets rewrite syntax, not APIs; choose them from the browser data your API already sees.
  • Vite is fast in development because it does not bundle your source there; always test the production build, which is a different program.
  • HMR re-executes modules; anything with side effects must dispose of them, and the backend should cap connections anyway.
  • Tree shaking needs ES modules and honest sideEffects hints; code splitting by route and by heavy feature keeps the first route small.
  • Every value in a frontend bundle is public. Secrets live only in the backend, behind auth, rate limits and audit logs.
  • Source maps are sensitive build artefacts: generate them hidden, store them privately per release, and build once so they always match.
  • Configure TypeScript to describe the browser accurately and strictly, and remember that types end at the network boundary.
  • A monorepo earns its keep by type-checking one contract against every consumer in the same pull request; a task graph and correct cache inputs keep it fast.
  • Automate formatting and a few high-value lint rules, keep hooks fast, and let CI be the gate.
  • Pick the frontend shape per surface: SPA for logged-in tools, Next.js for public and SEO-critical pages, server-rendered HTML for simple internal screens.

Part 71 — React Fundamentals for Backend Engineers

Most backend engineers meet React sideways. A bug report says "the order page shows the wrong total after applying a coupon", and the stack trace ends in OrderSummary.tsx. It looks like TypeScript you know, then it gets strange: the function runs again and again, a variable you set does not change the screen, an API call fires twice in development, typed text jumps to another row, and "Place order" creates two orders on a slow phone.

None of that is magic. React is a small number of rules applied very consistently, and each has a reason a backend engineer can understand in backend terms: a component is a serializer, state is a row React keeps for you, re-rendering is a reconciliation job, and an effect is a resource you must release.

Part 69 — How the Browser Builds a Page showed what the browser does with HTML, CSS and JavaScript (including forms in 69.2 and long tasks in 69.7). Part 70 — Frontend Tooling and TypeScript in the Browser showed how .tsx becomes a bundle, how Fast Refresh works (70.4) and how packages/contracts shares zod schemas between NestJS and React (70.12). This Part covers what React does with your components once the bundle has loaded, and ends with a worked checkout form wired to a NestJS API.

The baseline is React 18 (29.2 and 29.3), what most production codebases and Next.js 14 run. React 19 (stable since December 2024) adds the use API, Actions, useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, ref as a prop and <Context> as a provider; each is called out where it matters. The React Compiler (1.0, October 2025) automates much of the memoisation in 71.6 and 71.12.

As in the rest of this Volume, every concept ends with a Backend side (NestJS) block: what the API must do so that the React code above it can be simple, correct and fast.

71.1 Components, props and JSX: thinking in components for an order page

Concept

A component is a TypeScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns a description of some UI. That description is written in JSX, a syntax extension that looks like HTML inside TypeScript. Props (short for properties) are the single argument to that function: a plain object of inputs the parent passes down.

type Props = { displayId: string; status: 'PENDING' | 'PAID' | 'SHIPPED' };

export function OrderHeader({ displayId, status }: Props) {
  return (
    <header className="order-header">
      <h1>Order {displayId}</h1>
      <span className={`badge badge--${status.toLowerCase()}`}>{status}</span>
    </header>
  );
}

That is the whole idea. A React app is a tree of these functions. The root component renders children, which render their own children, down to plain elements like <h1> and <span>. Data flows down the tree through props. Events flow up through callback props (onCancel, onSubmit).

JSX is not HTML. It compiles to function calls: <h1>Order {displayId}</h1> becomes jsx('h1', { children: ['Order ', displayId] }) (the React 17+ automatic runtime; older code used React.createElement). Those calls return plain objects called React elements. A component never touches the DOM; it returns descriptions, and React decides what to change.

Why does it exist?

Before component frameworks, a page was server HTML plus jQuery scripts that found elements by selector and mutated them. On an order page where the total appears in four places and a status change must update a badge, a timeline, the buttons and the title, every mutation was manual, and forgetting one produced a page showing "Shipped" in the header and "Cancel order" in the footer.

Components solve two problems. UI as a function of data: you describe the screen for a given order and React makes the DOM match. Encapsulation: OrderTimeline owns its markup and behaviour behind a typed interface (its props), like a NestJS service.

Mental model

Imagine a NestJS serializer. Given an Order entity it returns an OrderResponseDto, calls smaller serializers for nested objects, never writes to the database, and returns the same output for the same input however often it is called.

A React component is that serializer with a UI description as output. It must be pure during rendering: no network calls, no writes to globals, no Math.random(). React may call it once or a hundred times and relies on the same answer for the same inputs.

How it works

flowchart TB
    page["OrderPage: owns orderId, fetches order"] --> header["OrderHeader: displayId, status"]
    page --> timeline["StatusTimeline: events"]
    page --> items["LineItemList: items"]
    items --> row1["LineItemRow: sku 1"]
    items --> row2["LineItemRow: sku 2"]
    page --> summary["PriceSummary: subtotal, discount, total"]
    page --> actions["OrderActions: status, onCancel"]
    actions --> dialog["CancelDialog: onConfirm"]
  1. Your code returns elements. OrderPage returns <OrderHeader displayId="A7K2Q9P" status="SHIPPED" /> among others. JSX attributes become props. Children between tags become props.children.
  2. React walks the tree. For every element whose type is a function (a component), React calls that function with the props and gets more elements back. For every element whose type is a string ('h1', 'div'), it is a host element: something the DOM will contain.
  3. The result is a tree of host elements. On the first render React creates DOM nodes for all of them and inserts them into the page. This is called mounting.
  4. Later renders produce a new tree. React compares it with the previous tree (71.3) and applies only the differences to the DOM.

Some JSX rules that trip backend engineers:

  • Capitalisation matters. <orderHeader /> is treated as an unknown HTML tag called orderheader; <OrderHeader /> calls your function.
  • Expressions, not statements, go inside {}. {order.total} works. {if (x) ...} does not. Use {x && <Badge />}, a ternary, or compute a variable before return.
  • {0 && <Badge />} renders 0. && returns its left side when it is falsy, and React renders numbers. Write {count > 0 && <Badge />}.
  • Text is escaped. {order.note} with <script> inside renders as literal text. React escapes everything you interpolate, which is why XSS in React needs dangerouslySetInnerHTML or a href="javascript:..." (Part 75 — Auth and Security in the Browser).

Practical example

"Thinking in components" is the skill of looking at a screen and drawing boxes. For an order details page, a senior draws them by responsibility and by data ownership, not by visual size:

Component Props in Owns state? Why it is its own component
OrderPage orderId from the URL Yes: the loaded order, loading and error The only place that talks to the API
OrderHeader displayId, status No Reused on order list cards
StatusTimeline events[] No Complex markup, tested alone
LineItemList / LineItemRow items[] / one item No List rendering with keys (71.3)
PriceSummary money fields as strings, currency No Formatting rules for money in one place
OrderActions status, onCancel, onReturn Yes: "is the dialog open" UI state that nobody else needs
CancelDialog onConfirm, onClose Yes: chosen reason Focus trap, accessibility (69.9)

The rule of thumb: most components should take props and return JSX, with no state and no API calls. A few components near the top own data. This is the frontend version of "controllers are thin, services own logic, DTOs are dumb".

React / Next.js example

The page and two of its pieces, in React 18 with TypeScript, using the shared contract types from @shop/contracts (70.12):

// src/orders/PriceSummary.tsx: presentational, no state, no fetching
import type { OrderView } from '@shop/contracts';

const fmt = (minor: string, currency: string) =>
  new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency }).format(Number(minor) / 100);

type Props = Pick<OrderView, 'subtotalMinor' | 'discountMinor' | 'totalMinor' | 'currency'>;

export function PriceSummary({ subtotalMinor, discountMinor, totalMinor, currency }: Props) {
  const hasDiscount = discountMinor !== '0'; // compare strings, never parse money twice
  return (
    <dl className="price-summary">
      <dt>Subtotal</dt><dd>{fmt(subtotalMinor, currency)}</dd>
      {hasDiscount && (<><dt>Discount</dt><dd>-{fmt(discountMinor, currency)}</dd></>)}
      <dt>Total</dt><dd><strong>{fmt(totalMinor, currency)}</strong></dd>
    </dl>
  );
}
// src/orders/OrderDetails.tsx: composes the page from small components
import type { OrderView } from '@shop/contracts';
import { OrderHeader } from './OrderHeader';
import { StatusTimeline } from './StatusTimeline';
import { LineItemList } from './LineItemList';
import { PriceSummary } from './PriceSummary';
import { OrderActions } from './OrderActions';

type Props = { order: OrderView; onCancel: (reason: string) => Promise<void> };

export function OrderDetails({ order, onCancel }: Props) {
  return (
    <article aria-labelledby="order-title">
      <OrderHeader displayId={order.displayId} status={order.status} />
      <StatusTimeline events={order.events} />
      <LineItemList items={order.items} />
      <PriceSummary
        subtotalMinor={order.subtotalMinor} discountMinor={order.discountMinor}
        totalMinor={order.totalMinor} currency={order.currency}
      />{/* explicit props: {...order} would pass every field at runtime */}
      {order.allowedActions.includes('CANCEL') && <OrderActions onCancel={onCancel} />}
    </article>
  );
}

PriceSummary never computes a total, and OrderActions renders only when the server allows cancelling. Neither knows how the order was fetched (71.4 and Part 72 — Client State, Data Fetching and Caching cover that).

In the Next.js 14 App Router, OrderDetails and PriceSummary could be server components (the default there) because they have no state or event handlers; only OrderActions would need 'use client'. Part 73 — Next.js and Rendering Strategies covers that boundary.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API response shape decides the component tree. Return raw entities and "can this order be cancelled?" gets copied into three components, each slightly different from the real rule. Shape the response for the screen and keep rules on the server:

// apps/api/src/orders/order-view.mapper.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { OrderView } from '@shop/contracts';
import { Order } from './order.entity';
import { OrderPolicy } from './order.policy';

@Injectable()
export class OrderViewMapper {
  constructor(private readonly policy: OrderPolicy) {}

  toView(order: Order, now = new Date()): OrderView {
    return {
      id: order.id,
      displayId: order.displayId,
      status: order.status,
      currency: order.currency,
      subtotalMinor: order.subtotalMinor.toString(), // bigint column -> string, exact
      discountMinor: order.discountMinor.toString(),
      totalMinor: order.totalMinor.toString(),
      items: order.items.map((i) => ({
        sku: i.sku, name: i.name, quantity: i.quantity, unitPriceMinor: i.unitPriceMinor.toString(),
      })),
      events: order.events.map((e) => ({ status: e.status, at: e.createdAt.toISOString() })),
      // The rule lives here, once. The UI just reads the list.
      allowedActions: this.policy.allowedActions(order, now), // e.g. ['CANCEL'] within 30 min of payment
    };
  }
}

Three backend habits make component code simpler:

  • Send derived business facts, not raw inputs to rules. allowedActions, isReturnable, estimatedDeliveryAt. The UI should never re-implement your cancellation window.
  • Send money as strings in minor units, with the currency. The component formats; it never adds. Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts covers money, dates and IDs on the wire.
  • One endpoint per screen region that loads together. If OrderPage must call five endpoints before it can render, you have built a network waterfall. A view endpoint, or a BFF (Part 73), turns it into one round trip.

Production scenario

A food delivery app's order page was one 1,400-line component that re-rendered entirely on every rider location ping (every 4 s), making the chat input lag 120 to 200 ms per keystroke on mid-range Android phones.

Splitting it into 14 components took two sprints. The rider map received only riderLocation; the chat owned its own input state. Pings then re-rendered one component (71.12 explains why), and input lag fell under 16 ms.

Failure scenario

At 19:40 on a Friday, customers started cancelling orders that were already out for delivery. The backend rejected none of them.

The cause was two layers of "the UI decides". The OrderActions component showed the Cancel button when status !== 'DELIVERED'. A new status OUT_FOR_DELIVERY had been added on the backend that afternoon, the frontend had not been updated, so the button appeared. And the cancel endpoint had no guard of its own, because "the button is hidden when you can't cancel".

The fix was the pattern above: the server computes allowedActions, the UI renders from it, and the cancel endpoint checks the same policy and returns 409 Conflict with code: "ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE" when it is violated. The UI is a hint; the server is the rule.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • {count && ...} renders 0 on the page when the count is zero.
  • Unknown enum values from the API (a new status) fall through switch statements and render nothing, or the wrong thing. Always have a default branch (Part 74 covers unknown enums).
  • Impure render: Date.now() or Math.random() in render gives different output each call and causes hydration mismatches in server rendering (Part 73).
  • Mutating props (props.items.sort()) changes the parent's data in place; React will not notice, and other components see a reordered array. Copy first: [...items].sort(...) or items.toSorted(...).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior draws the component tree before writing code, marks the few boxes that own data, and keeps props narrow: PriceSummary gets four fields, not the whole order. In review they look for business logic hiding in JSX conditions (status === 'PAID' && Date.now() - paidAt < 1800000) and move it behind the API.

Common mistakes

  • One giant component per page, which re-renders everything and is impossible to test.
  • Re-implementing backend rules in JSX conditions, which drift as soon as the backend changes.
  • Calling fetch directly inside the component body, which runs on every render (71.4 shows the right place).
  • Defining a component inside another component's body. The inner function is a new type on every render, so React unmounts and remounts it each time, losing its state and DOM.

Interview questions

  1. What does JSX compile to, and what does a component actually return? Expected answer: calls to jsx() (or React.createElement in the classic runtime) that return plain element objects describing type and props. The component does not create DOM. Why it matters: explains why components can be called repeatedly and why they must be pure. Follow-up: what is the difference between a component and an element?
  2. Why must components be pure during rendering? Expected answer: React may call them many times (Strict Mode, concurrent rendering, re-renders) and may discard a render; side effects in render would run unpredictably. Follow-up: where do side effects go then? (Event handlers and effects.)
  3. Why is defining a component inside another component a bug? Expected answer: the inner component's identity changes every render, so React remounts it and loses state.
  4. Where should "can this order be cancelled?" be computed? Expected answer: on the server, returned as data and enforced again on the write endpoint.

Practical exercise

Take an existing order or product page from any app (or the NestJS order API from Part 15) and draw its component tree.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A diagram with every component, its props, and a mark on the ones that own state or fetch data. No more than two components fetch.
  • A PriceSummary component that formats money from string minor units and renders a discount row only when the discount is not "0".
  • The NestJS order endpoint returns an allowedActions array computed by one policy class, and the cancel endpoint enforces the same policy with 409.

71.2 State and re-rendering: useState and how React decides what to re-render

Concept

State is data a component remembers between renders and that changes what is shown: whether the cancel dialog is open, the text in a search box, the step of a checkout. You declare it with the useState hook:

const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);

useState returns the current value and a setter. Calling the setter does not change the variable you are holding; it asks React to re-render the component, which means calling the component function again. In that next call, useState returns the new value.

A component re-renders for exactly three reasons:

  1. Its own state changed (a setter was called with a new value).
  2. Its parent re-rendered (by default, all children re-render with it).
  3. A context it reads changed (71.5).

Props changing is not a separate reason: props only change when the parent re-renders.

Hooks are functions whose names start with use that let a component use React features (state, effects, context). They have two rules: call them only at the top level of a component or custom hook (never inside if, loops or nested functions), and call them only from React functions. React identifies each hook by its call order, so the order must be the same on every render. eslint-plugin-react-hooks enforces both rules; treat its errors as compile errors.

Why does it exist?

A component is a function, and its local variables vanish when it returns. A click handler that sets let isOpen = true changes nothing React knows about, and the next render resets it. React needs storage outside your function, tied to one component instance, and a signal to re-run it. useState is both.

Mental model

Imagine React keeps a table with one row per mounted component instance, keyed by tree position, and one slot per hook call. The first useState(false) stores false in slot 0. setIsOpen(true) does not touch your running code; it queues true for slot 0 and schedules "re-run this component", where useState reads slot 0 and returns true.

That is why hooks must be called in the same order: React knows "the second hook call of this component instance", not your variable names.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant H as ClickHandler
    participant R as React
    participant C as Component
    participant D as DOM
    U->>H: clicks Cancel order
    H->>R: setIsOpen true
    H->>R: setReason null
    Note over R: both updates queued, one render scheduled
    R->>C: call OrderActions with new state
    C-->>R: new elements
    R->>R: diff against previous elements
    R->>D: commit only the changes
    D-->>U: dialog visible

React's work happens in two phases:

  1. Trigger. A setter is called. React compares the new value with the current one using Object.is. If they are the same, React may skip the render entirely (it "bails out").
  2. Render phase. React calls your component (and, by default, all components below it) to get a new element tree. This is pure computation. Nothing on screen has changed yet. In React 18's concurrent features (startTransition), this phase can be paused, resumed or thrown away.
  3. Commit phase. React compares the new tree with the old one (reconciliation, 71.3) and applies the minimum DOM changes: change a text node, toggle an attribute, insert a dialog. Then it runs effects (71.4).
  4. Paint. The browser lays out and paints (69.1).

Rules that follow from this mechanism:

  • State is a snapshot. Inside one render, isOpen is a constant. Calling setCount(count + 1) three times in one handler sets it to count + 1 once, because count is the same value in all three calls. Use the updater form when the new value depends on the old: setCount((c) => c + 1) three times adds three.
  • Batching. React groups several setter calls into one render. React 17 batched only inside React event handlers; React 18 with createRoot batches everywhere, including after await, in timeouts and in native listeners. flushSync from react-dom forces an immediate render in the rare case you need it.
  • Replace, do not mutate. React detects changes by identity (Object.is), not by deep comparison. cart.items.push(item); setCart(cart) passes the same object, so React bails out and the screen does not update. Create a new object: setCart({ ...cart, items: [...cart.items, item] }).
  • Re-rendering is not slow by default. Calling a function that returns 40 elements takes microseconds. A typical component renders in 0.05 to 0.5 ms. Rendering becomes a problem only when one update re-renders thousands of components or one component does heavy work in render (71.12).

Practical example

A cart quantity stepper should keep only UI state locally and treat the server as the source of truth for the cart:

Data Where it lives Why
Cart lines, prices, totals Server, fetched and cached (Part 72) Taxes, promotions, stock: only the server knows
Quantity being edited, before it is sent useState in the stepper Pure UI, nobody else needs it
"Saving..." indicator useState or the mutation's pending flag Pure UI
Coupon code text in the input useState or the form library (71.7) Pure UI until submitted

The test for "should this be state?": if you can compute it from props or other state during render, it is not state. totalItems = items.reduce(...) is computed, not stored. Storing it creates two sources of truth that will eventually disagree.

React / Next.js example

// src/cart/QuantityStepper.tsx  (React 18)
import { useState } from 'react';

type Props = {
  sku: string;
  quantity: number;               // from the server's cart
  maxQuantity: number;            // from the server: stock and per-order limits
  onChange: (sku: string, quantity: number) => Promise<void>;
};

export function QuantityStepper({ sku, quantity, maxQuantity, onChange }: Props) {
  const [saving, setSaving] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

  async function update(next: number) {
    if (next < 1 || next > maxQuantity || saving) return;
    setSaving(true);              // batched with the next line into one render
    setError(null);
    try {
      await onChange(sku, next);  // parent sends PATCH and refreshes the cart from the response
    } catch {
      setError('Could not update quantity. Please try again.');
    } finally {
      setSaving(false);           // after await: still batched in React 18
    }
  }

  return (
    <div className="stepper" aria-busy={saving}>
      <button type="button" aria-label="Decrease" disabled={saving || quantity <= 1}
        onClick={() => update(quantity - 1)}>-</button>
      <output aria-live="polite">{quantity}</output>
      <button type="button" aria-label="Increase" disabled={saving || quantity >= maxQuantity}
        onClick={() => update(quantity + 1)}>+</button>
      {error && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

Notice what is not in state: the quantity. It comes from the server via props, so the stepper never shows a number the server did not confirm (Part 72 shows optimistic updates as a deliberate alternative).

Lazy initial state. useState(expensive()) calls expensive() on every render and throws the result away after the first. Pass a function to run it once: useState(() => JSON.parse(sessionStorage.getItem('draft') ?? '{}')).

Strict Mode. In development, <StrictMode> calls your component function twice per render (and React 18 also mounts, unmounts and re-mounts every component once, see 71.4) to surface impure code. A console.log in render printing twice is expected in development, not a bug.

Backend side (NestJS)

The frontend can keep little state only if write endpoints return what the screen needs next. A PATCH returning 204 forces the UI to guess new totals or make a second GET (80 to 150 ms on mobile). Return the recomputed resource:

// apps/api/src/cart/cart.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Patch, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { UpdateCartLineSchema, type CartView, type UpdateCartLine } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { CartService } from './cart.service';

@Controller('v1/cart')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class CartController {
  constructor(private readonly cart: CartService) {}

  @Patch('lines/:sku')
  @HttpCode(200)
  async updateLine(
    @CurrentUser() user: AuthUser,
    @Param('sku') sku: string,
    @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(UpdateCartLineSchema)) body: UpdateCartLine,
  ): Promise<CartView> {
    // The service clamps quantity to stock and per-order limits, reprices, re-applies promotions,
    // and returns the whole cart so the UI replaces its copy in one step.
    return this.cart.updateLineAndView(user.id, sku, body.quantity);
  }
}

Return maxQuantity per line so the stepper can disable "+" without guessing stock, and a cart version so stale writes from another tab get 409 (Part 21 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control).

Production scenario

An electronics retailer kept subtotal, discount and total in useState and recomputed them in the browser. On carts with "buy 2 get 1" plus a percentage coupon, the browser applied them in a different order than the pricing service: 1.8 % of checkouts showed a cart total that differed from the payment page by up to 12 %, and those sessions converted at half the normal rate.

The fix deleted 300 lines of client pricing; the PATCH returned the repriced cart (median 38 ms) and the mismatch rate went to zero.

Failure scenario

A support agent reported that clicking "Add note" on an order sometimes showed the note and sometimes did not. The code:

function addNote(text: string) {
  order.notes.push({ text, at: new Date().toISOString() }); // mutates the object in state
  setOrder(order);                                           // same reference: React bails out
}

setOrder received the same reference, Object.is returned true, and React skipped the render. The note appeared only when something else re-rendered the component. The fix: setOrder({ ...order, notes: [...order.notes, newNote] }), plus the react-hooks lint rules turned on as errors.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale closures: a handler created in render N captures state from render N. A setTimeout that reads count five seconds later reads the old value. Use the updater form or a ref (71.5).
  • Setting state during render for something that is not derived causes an infinite loop ("Too many re-renders").
  • Copying props into state (useState(props.quantity)) only uses the prop on mount; later prop changes are ignored. Either read the prop directly or reset with a key (71.3).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior keeps state minimal and close to where it is used, asking of each value: who owns it? Server-owned data goes in a server cache (Part 72), computable data is computed, shared data is lifted to the nearest common parent (71.10). They design for re-renders being cheap rather than trying to prevent them everywhere.

Common mistakes

  • Mutating state objects and wondering why the screen does not update.
  • Reading state right after setting it and expecting the new value (setStep(2); console.log(step) prints the old one).
  • Storing derived values (totals, filtered lists, "isValid") in state.
  • Duplicating server data into local state and then trying to keep the two in sync with effects.

Interview questions

  1. What happens, step by step, when you call a state setter? Expected answer: the update is queued; React compares with Object.is and may bail out; it schedules a render of that component and its children; render phase computes new elements; commit applies DOM changes; effects run. Why it matters: it explains batching, snapshots and why mutation does not work. Follow-up: what changed about batching in React 18?
  2. Why does setCount(count + 1) called three times only add one? Expected answer: count is a snapshot constant for that render; use the updater function.
  3. What are the rules of hooks, and why do they exist? Expected answer: top level only, React functions only; React identifies hooks by call order.
  4. When does a component re-render? Expected answer: own state change, parent re-render, consumed context change. Follow-up: does a prop change cause a re-render? (Only via the parent re-rendering.)

Practical exercise

Build a QuantityStepper against a NestJS PATCH /v1/cart/lines/:sku endpoint.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The endpoint returns the full repriced cart including maxQuantity per line; a "buy 2 get 1" rule is applied server-side.
  • The component holds no copy of the quantity or totals in state; it renders the server's numbers.
  • Clicking "+" five times quickly results in at most one in-flight request at a time (the button is disabled while saving).
  • A deliberate bug that mutates the cart array is shown not to re-render, then fixed with an immutable update.

71.3 Reconciliation and keys

Concept

Reconciliation is how React turns "here is the new element tree" into "here are the DOM changes". After every render, React compares the new tree with the previous one and works out the smallest set of operations: update this text, change that attribute, insert this node, remove that one.

A key is a string or number you give to items in a list so React can match each item in the new list with the same item in the old list. Keys answer one question: "is this the same thing as before, or a different thing?"

{items.map((item) => <LineItemRow key={item.sku} item={item} />)}

Keys are also how React decides whether a component keeps its state. Same type at the same position with the same key means "same component instance, keep state and DOM". Anything else means "throw the old one away, mount a new one".

Why does it exist?

Comparing two arbitrary trees optimally is an O(n³) problem. For a page with 3,000 elements that is 27 billion operations: impossible at 60 frames per second. React uses two assumptions to make it O(n):

  1. Elements of different types produce different trees. If a <div> becomes a <section>, or <OrderSummary> becomes <OrderSkeleton>, React does not compare their insides. It destroys the old subtree (and its state) and builds the new one.
  2. The developer can mark which children are stable across renders with keys. Without keys, React can only compare children by position.

Without keys, prepending one item to a 500-row list looks like 500 changed rows plus one new one, and any state inside the rows (an expanded panel, typed text) stays at the position, attached to the wrong item.

Mental model

Imagine a sync job copying the orders table into a search index. Match rows by position and one insert at the top rewrites everything; match by primary key and it is one insert. Keys are primary keys for list items: stable, unique within the list, owned by the data.

How it works

flowchart TB
    start(["Compare old and new element at one position"]) --> sameType{"Same type?"}
    sameType -->|"No"| replace["Unmount old subtree, state lost, mount new"]
    sameType -->|"Yes"| sameKey{"Same key?"}
    sameKey -->|"No"| replace
    sameKey -->|"Yes"| host{"Host element or component?"}
    host -->|"Host like div"| attrs["Update changed DOM attributes, recurse into children"]
    host -->|"Component"| rerender["Keep state, call function with new props, recurse"]

For a list of children:

  1. React builds a map from key to old child.
  2. For each new child, it looks up the old child with the same key. If found and the type matches, it is moved if needed and updated; its state and DOM node are kept.
  3. Old children whose keys are not in the new list are unmounted.
  4. New keys are mounted.

Consequences:

  • Index as key (key={index}) is the same as no key for reordering purposes: it matches by position. It is acceptable only when the list is static, never reordered, filtered or prepended, and items have no state.
  • Random keys (key={Math.random()} or crypto.randomUUID() in render) are the worst option: every render, every key is new, so every row is unmounted and remounted. All state is lost and the DOM is rebuilt each time.
  • Keys must be unique among siblings only, not globally. Two different lists can both have an item with key "A7K2Q9P".
  • Keys are not passed as props. props.key is undefined inside the child. If the child needs the ID, pass it separately.
  • A key on any component forces identity. <CheckoutForm key={cartId} /> means "when cartId changes, this is a different form": React unmounts the old one and mounts a fresh one with fresh state. This is the cleanest way to reset a component, far better than an effect that resets ten state variables.

Practical example

An admin order-line editor has a "note" textarea per row and can be sorted by price. With key={index}, an agent types "gift wrap" into the coffee machine's row, sorts, and the textarea stays at its position next to a different SKU; the note is saved against the wrong line. With key={line.sku} (or a line ID), React moves the DOM node with its content.

For lines that do not exist on the server yet (added in the UI, not saved), generate a client ID once, when the item is created, not during render:

function addLine(product: Product) {
  setDraftLines((lines) => [{ clientId: crypto.randomUUID(), sku: product.sku, quantity: 1 }, ...lines]);
}

React / Next.js example

Two key patterns: stable list keys, and a key used to reset a form when the order changes.

// src/admin/OrderLinesEditor.tsx  (React 18)
import { useState } from 'react';
import type { OrderLine } from '@shop/contracts';

type DraftLine = OrderLine & { clientId: string };

export function OrderLinesEditor({ initialLines }: { initialLines: OrderLine[] }) {
  // clientId is created once per line, here or when a line is added; never in render.
  const [lines, setLines] = useState<DraftLine[]>(() =>
    initialLines.map((l) => ({ ...l, clientId: l.id ?? crypto.randomUUID() })),
  );
  const [sortBy, setSortBy] = useState<'name' | 'price'>('name');

  const sorted = [...lines].sort((a, b) =>
    sortBy === 'name' ? a.name.localeCompare(b.name) : Number(a.unitPriceMinor) - Number(b.unitPriceMinor),
  ); // derived during render, not stored

  return (
    <>
      <select value={sortBy} onChange={(e) => setSortBy(e.target.value as 'name' | 'price')}>
        <option value="name">Name</option>
        <option value="price">Price</option>
      </select>
      <ul>
        {sorted.map((line) => (
          <li key={line.clientId}> {/* stable identity: state and DOM follow the line */}
            {line.name}
            <textarea aria-label={`Note for ${line.name}`} defaultValue={line.note ?? ''} />
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}
// src/admin/OrderEditPage.tsx: reset all form state when navigating between orders
export function OrderEditPage({ order }: { order: OrderView }) {
  // Without the key, moving from order A to order B would keep A's draft lines in state,
  // because useState only reads its initial value on mount.
  return <OrderLinesEditor key={order.id} initialLines={order.items} />;
}

React's console warnings about missing or duplicate keys are bugs, not noise: duplicate keys make React drop or duplicate rows.

Backend side (NestJS)

Keys are only as good as the IDs the API returns. Three backend rules:

  • Every item in every list response has a stable, unique ID. Not a position, not a value that can change (a product name), not a composite the client must assemble. If line items are identified by (order_id, sku), return that identity as a field or return a line ID.
  • IDs are stable across requests. An API that generates a fresh UUID per response for "virtual" rows (computed fee lines, promotional freebies) forces remounts on every refetch. Derive them deterministically: fee:delivery, promo:BUY2GET1:sku-123.
  • Pagination does not duplicate items. Offset pagination over a table receiving inserts shifts rows between pages, so page 2 repeats the last item of page 1. In an infinite list that is a duplicate key, and React may drop a row. Use cursor pagination (Part 15 — API Design (REST first), 15.5):
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.repository.ts  (TypeORM)
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { Order } from './order.entity';

@Injectable()
export class OrdersRepository {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  // Keyset pagination on (placed_at, id): stable under concurrent inserts, no duplicates across pages.
  async pageForCustomer(customerId: string, limit: number, after?: { placedAt: Date; id: string }) {
    const qb = this.ds.getRepository(Order).createQueryBuilder('o')
      .where('o.customer_id = :customerId', { customerId })
      .orderBy('o.placed_at', 'DESC').addOrderBy('o.id', 'DESC')
      .take(limit + 1); // one extra row tells us whether a next page exists
    if (after) {
      qb.andWhere('(o.placed_at, o.id) < (:placedAt, :id)', after);
    }
    const rows = await qb.getMany();
    return { items: rows.slice(0, limit), hasMore: rows.length > limit };
  }
}

With an index on (customer_id, placed_at DESC, id DESC), each page is a 1 to 3 ms index range scan regardless of how deep the customer scrolls.

Production scenario

A restaurant dashboard listed incoming orders newest-first, each card with a "prep notes" input, keyed by index. At peak a new order arrived every 20 to 40 s, shifting cards while notes stayed in place; cooks saw notes "jump" to other orders about 30 times a night across 400 restaurants. key={order.id} fixed it, and commit time per new order fell from 22 ms to 3 ms.

Failure scenario

A checkout page wrapped its content in a conditional layout:

return isMobile ? <div className="sheet"><CheckoutForm /></div> : <section><CheckoutForm /></section>;

On tablets, rotation crossed the breakpoint, the wrapper changed from section to div, and React unmounted the form: every typed field vanished, and tablet abandonment at the address step rose 4 %. The fix kept the same element type and changed only className.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Index keys with filtering: filtering a list shifts positions exactly like sorting does.
  • Duplicate keys from the API (a join that returns one row per tag) make React silently drop children.
  • Keys from mutable fields (email, name) remount the row when the field is edited, losing focus mid-typing.
  • Conditional wrappers that change element type unmount everything below.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats keys as primary keys: key={index} on anything dynamic and random keys anywhere are blocking review comments. They use key deliberately to reset components, and push identity into the API with stable IDs and cursor pagination.

Common mistakes

  • Using the array index as key for lists that sort, filter, prepend or contain inputs.
  • Generating keys during render.
  • Expecting props.key to be readable in the child.
  • Resetting state with an effect when a key change would do it in one line.
  • Changing wrapper element types conditionally and losing all child state.

Interview questions

  1. Why does React need keys, and what happens with index keys when you prepend an item? Expected answer: keys let React match children across renders; with index keys every position appears changed, causing extra updates and state attached to the wrong item. Follow-up: when is an index key acceptable? (Static lists without state.)
  2. What are React's two heuristics that make reconciliation O(n)? Expected answer: different types mean different trees; keys identify stable children.
  3. How do you reset all state in a form when the user switches from editing order A to order B? Expected answer: give the form key={orderId}.
  4. Why can offset pagination cause bugs in an infinite list? Expected answer: inserts shift rows, so items repeat across pages, producing duplicate keys and dropped or duplicated rows; use cursors.

Practical exercise

Build a list of 50 orders, each with a text input, that can be sorted and that receives a new order at the top every 5 seconds.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With key={index}, you can demonstrate typed text moving to a different order after an insert or sort.
  • With key={order.id}, the text stays with its order.
  • The React DevTools Profiler shows fewer components rendered per insert with stable keys.
  • The NestJS endpoint uses keyset pagination on (placed_at, id) and a test proves that inserting 10 orders between page fetches produces no duplicate IDs.

71.4 Effects: useEffect done right

Concept

An effect is code that synchronises a component with something outside React: a WebSocket, a browser API (document.title, IntersectionObserver, a timer), a third-party widget (a map, a chart, a payment SDK), or analytics. You declare it with useEffect:

useEffect(() => {
  const source = new EventSource(`/api/v1/orders/${orderId}/events`);
  source.onmessage = (e) => onStatus(JSON.parse(e.data));
  return () => source.close(); // cleanup
}, [orderId]);                 // dependencies

The function runs after React has committed the render to the screen. It may return a cleanup function. The dependency array lists every reactive value the effect uses (props, state, values derived from them). React re-runs the effect after a render where any dependency changed, running the previous cleanup first. On unmount, the last cleanup runs.

The official React documentation puts it well: effects are an escape hatch for synchronising with external systems. If no external system is involved, you probably do not need an effect.

Why does it exist?

Rendering must be pure (71.1), yet apps must open sockets, set timers and drive non-React code. Event handlers handle side effects caused by a user action ("clicked Pay, so send the payment"). Some side effects are caused by being on screen ("while tracking is visible, keep a live connection"), and there is no event for that. Effects fill that gap.

Mental model

Imagine a NestJS provider with OnModuleInit and OnModuleDestroy: open the Kafka consumer on init, close it on destroy. An effect is that lifecycle per component instance and per set of inputs. But the better model is not "on mount do X"; it is "keep X in sync with these values", like a Kubernetes controller reconciling desired state: for this orderId there should be exactly one open stream.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant R as React
    participant E as Effect
    participant X as EventSourceA
    participant Y as EventSourceB
    R->>R: commit render with orderId A
    R->>E: run setup for A
    E->>X: open stream for order A
    R->>R: commit render with orderId B
    R->>E: run cleanup for A
    E->>X: close stream A
    R->>E: run setup for B
    E->>Y: open stream for order B
    R->>R: component unmounts
    R->>E: run cleanup for B
    E->>Y: close stream B
  1. Render returns elements, and the effect function is recorded, not run.
  2. Commit updates the DOM. The browser usually paints.
  3. Effects run after paint (for useEffect). React compares each dependency with the previous render's value using Object.is. If any changed (or on first mount), it runs the previous cleanup, then the new setup.
  4. Unmount runs the final cleanup.

Dependency array forms:

Form Runs setup Typical use
useEffect(fn, [a, b]) On mount and when a or b changes Almost everything
useEffect(fn, []) Once on mount (twice in dev Strict Mode) Subscriptions that depend on nothing reactive
useEffect(fn) After every render Rarely correct

useLayoutEffect has the same signature but runs after DOM changes and before the browser paints. Use it only to measure layout and adjust before the user sees a flicker (positioning a tooltip). It blocks paint, so keep it short.

Strict Mode double-mount (React 18+, development only). React mounts each component, runs all effect cleanups, then runs the effects again: setup, cleanup, setup. It simulates a component being hidden and shown again (React 19.2's <Activity> does this for real) and exposes effects without proper cleanup. If you see two sockets in development, fix the cleanup; do not remove Strict Mode.

Effects you do not need. Most incorrect effect code is one of these, and the fix is to delete the effect:

  • Deriving data: useEffect(() => setTotal(sum(items)), [items]) renders twice and briefly shows a stale total. Compute const total = sum(items) in render.
  • Responding to a user event: useEffect(() => { if (submitted) postOrder(); }, [submitted]) turns a click into a state flag into a side effect. Call postOrder() in the click handler.
  • Resetting state when a prop changes: use a key (71.3).
  • Notifying a parent of a state change: call the parent's callback in the same event handler that changed the state.

Why most data fetching should not be hand-written effects

Fetching in an effect looks simple and is the most common source of bugs in React apps. A correct hand-written fetch effect must handle all of this:

// src/orders/useOrderOnce.ts: what a "correct" hand-written fetch effect needs (React 18)
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { OrderViewSchema, type OrderView } from '@shop/contracts';

type State =
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error }
  | { status: 'success'; order: OrderView };

export function useOrderOnce(orderId: string): State {
  const [state, setState] = useState<State>({ status: 'loading' });

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();           // 1. cancel on change or unmount
    setState({ status: 'loading' });                     // 2. reset when orderId changes
    fetch(`/api/v1/orders/${orderId}`, { signal: controller.signal, credentials: 'include' })
      .then(async (res) => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`); // 3. fetch does not reject on 4xx/5xx
        return OrderViewSchema.parse(await res.json());     // 4. types end at the network boundary
      })
      .then((order) => setState({ status: 'success', order }))
      .catch((error: unknown) => {
        if (controller.signal.aborted) return;           // 5. ignore results for a stale orderId
        setState({ status: 'error', error: error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error)) });
      });
    return () => controller.abort();                     // 6. cleanup closes the race
  }, [orderId]);

  return state;
}

And it still lacks caching, deduplication across components, retries with backoff, refetch on focus, invalidation after mutations, pagination and server rendering support: each a day of work and a source of bugs.

Without step 5, there is a race condition: the user clicks order A, then quickly order B. Request A is slow (900 ms), request B is fast (120 ms). B's response arrives and renders, then A's arrives and overwrites it. The page now says "Order B" in the URL and shows order A's items. This is the frontend version of a lost update.
