Effects also create waterfalls: the parent's effect fetches the order, renders, then the child's effect fetches the restaurant, renders, then the grandchild fetches rider location. Each round trip waits for the previous render. On a 150 ms mobile RTT that is 450 ms before the page is complete, against 150 ms if all three started together.

So the rule in modern React is:

  • Client-side SPA: use a data-fetching library. TanStack Query (useQuery, useMutation) is the default; SWR and RTK Query are alternatives. Part 72 — Client State, Data Fetching and Caching covers them in depth.
  • Next.js App Router: fetch in server components or route loaders, not in client effects (Part 73).
  • React 19: the use(promise) API reads a promise inside render and suspends until it resolves, with Suspense showing a fallback (71.11). The promise must come from a cache or a parent (a server component, a router loader, a library); creating a new promise during a client render loops forever. In React 18, Suspense for data only works through libraries that implement it (TanStack Query's useSuspenseQuery, Relay, Next.js).

Hand-written fetch effects are acceptable for one-off, non-shared, non-cached reads in small apps, and only with all six steps above.

Practical example

Correct uses of effects on an order tracking page:

Need External system Effect?
Live status updates while the page is open EventSource to NestJS SSE Yes, with close() in cleanup
Tab title shows "(Out for delivery) Order A7K2Q9P" document.title Yes, restore on cleanup
Rider location on a Mapbox map Map SDK instance Yes, create in setup, map.remove() in cleanup
"Order viewed" analytics event Analytics SDK Yes, but beware double-firing in dev; the backend must dedupe
Load the order HTTP API No: data library or server component
Show "Delivered" banner when status becomes DELIVERED None No: derive from status during render
Send a POST when "Confirm received" is clicked HTTP API No: event handler

React / Next.js example

A live order status subscription with correct cleanup, reconnection handled by the browser, and a stable callback:

// src/tracking/useOrderStatusStream.ts  (React 18)
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { OrderStatusEventSchema, type OrderStatusEvent } from '@shop/contracts';

export function useOrderStatusStream(orderId: string, onEvent: (e: OrderStatusEvent) => void) {
  // Keep the latest callback in a ref so the stream is not reopened when the parent
  // passes a new function on every render (77.5 covers refs).
  const onEventRef = useRef(onEvent);
  useEffect(() => { onEventRef.current = onEvent; });

  useEffect(() => {
    const source = new EventSource(`/api/v1/orders/${orderId}/events`, { withCredentials: true });
    const handler = (msg: MessageEvent<string>) => {
      const parsed = OrderStatusEventSchema.safeParse(JSON.parse(msg.data));
      if (parsed.success) onEventRef.current(parsed.data); // ignore unknown shapes, never crash
    };
    source.addEventListener('status', handler as EventListener);
    // EventSource reconnects by itself and sends Last-Event-ID; nothing to do on error here.
    return () => {
      source.removeEventListener('status', handler as EventListener);
      source.close(); // without this, Strict Mode and HMR leave orphaned streams (76.4)
    };
  }, [orderId]); // one stream per order; reopened only when the order changes
}

Backend side (NestJS)

Effects create traffic patterns the backend must be ready for.

Duplicate requests. Strict Mode runs every effect twice on mount in development, and remounts happen in production too. Reads must be safe to repeat; any write triggered from an effect needs a client-generated ID the server dedupes on, or belongs in an event handler.

Cancelled requests. AbortController.abort() closes the connection. The server keeps working unless it notices. For expensive endpoints (search, reports), stop work when the client goes away:

// apps/api/src/search/search.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Query, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Response } from 'express';
import { SearchService } from './search.service';

@Controller('v1/search')
export class SearchController {
  constructor(private readonly search: SearchService) {}

  @Get('orders')
  async orders(@Query('q') q: string, @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response) {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    // The response 'close' event fires when the connection ends. If we have not finished
    // writing yet, the browser went away (user typed another letter, navigated away).
    // Listen on res, not req: since Node 16, req 'close' fires once the body is read.
    res.on('close', () => { if (!res.writableFinished) controller.abort(); });
    // Pass the signal down to anything that accepts one: fetch to another service,
    // or cancel a long PostgreSQL query with pg_cancel_backend via the driver.
    return this.search.searchOrders(q, { signal: controller.signal });
  }
}

Aborted requests show as 499 in nginx logs; a spike usually means a frontend refetching on every keystroke without debouncing.

Long-lived connections need cleanup on both sides. An SSE endpoint should send a heartbeat every 15 to 30 s so proxies keep the connection, and release resources on close. @Sse() returns an Observable that Nest unsubscribes on disconnect, so the teardown is where your Redis unsubscribe goes:

// apps/api/src/orders/order-events.controller.ts
import { Controller, MessageEvent, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Sse, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, interval, map, merge } from 'rxjs';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { OrderEventsBus } from './order-events.bus';

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class OrderEventsController {
  constructor(private readonly bus: OrderEventsBus) {}

  @Sse(':id/events')
  stream(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string): Observable<MessageEvent> {
    const updates = new Observable<MessageEvent>((subscriber) => {
      const off = this.bus.subscribe(id, (evt) => subscriber.next({ type: 'status', id: evt.seq, data: evt }));
      return () => off(); // teardown runs when the browser closes the EventSource
    });
    const heartbeat = interval(20_000).pipe(map(() => ({ type: 'ping', data: '' })));
    return merge(updates, heartbeat);
  }
}

Setting id on each event lets the browser send Last-Event-ID on reconnect so the server can replay missed events (Part 35 — Real-Time Systems: WebSockets, SSE and Pub/Sub). React 19 apps can also render <title> in any component instead of syncing document.title in an effect.

Production scenario

A grocery app's tracking page opened an SSE stream in an effect with [order] as its dependency, and order was a new object after every 10 s poll. The stream closed and reopened six times a minute per customer: with 25,000 evening trackers, the SSE gateway took 2,500 new connections per second, each with JWT verification and a Redis subscribe, and CPU went from 20 % to 85 %. Depending on [order.id] fixed it.

Failure scenario

On launch day of a new checkout, the payments team saw 3 % of payment intents created twice. The PaymentStep component created a payment intent in an effect:

useEffect(() => { api.createPaymentIntent(cartId).then(setIntent); }, [cartId]);

Production has no Strict Mode double-mount, so it seemed safe. But the parent showed a skeleton while the cart revalidated on tab focus, which unmounted and remounted PaymentStep: one new intent per refocus. Customers switching to their banking app and back created several, and two were sometimes confirmed.

The fixes: the backend made POST /payment-intents idempotent per cart version (Idempotency-Key: cart:{id}:v{version}, Part 15.12), returning the same intent for the same cart; the frontend moved intent creation to the "Continue to payment" click handler and cached the result per cart version.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Object or function dependencies recreated each render make the effect run every render. Depend on primitive fields (order.id), or stabilise with useMemo/useCallback/refs (71.5, 71.6).
  • Missing dependencies (silenced with // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps) leave the effect using stale values. The lint rule is right far more often than the developer.
  • Async functions as the effect: useEffect(async () => ...) returns a promise, not a cleanup; React warns. Define an async function inside and call it.
  • Race conditions between overlapping requests; always abort or ignore stale results.
  • Effects that set state unconditionally without dependencies cause infinite render loops.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior asks of every effect: "Which external system is this synchronising with?" No answer means no effect. Otherwise they check that cleanup exactly undoes setup, dependencies are complete and primitive, and the effect survives running twice. In a real app they use TanStack Query or the framework's loaders instead of fetch effects.

On the backend, they assume every effect-driven request may be duplicated, cancelled or reopened, because it will be.

Common mistakes

  • Fetching in effects without abort, causing race conditions.
  • Using effects to derive state or to react to clicks.
  • Disabling the exhaustive-deps lint rule instead of fixing the dependency.
  • Missing cleanup for sockets, timers, listeners and SDK instances.
  • Creating server-side resources (payment intents, carts) in effects without idempotency.

Interview questions

  1. When should you use useEffect, and when not? Expected answer: to synchronise with an external system (sockets, browser APIs, third-party widgets); not for derived data, user events or resetting state. Why it matters: misuse causes most React bugs. Follow-up: name three effects you would delete.
  2. Why does my effect run twice in development? Expected answer: React 18 Strict Mode mounts, unmounts and remounts to verify cleanup; fix cleanup, not Strict Mode.
  3. Describe the race condition in fetch-in-effect code and how to fix it. Expected answer: overlapping requests resolve out of order; abort with AbortController in cleanup or ignore stale results.
  4. Why prefer a data library over hand-written fetch effects? Expected answer: caching, deduplication, retries, invalidation, focus refetch, Suspense and SSR support; fewer races and waterfalls.
  5. How does an SSE endpoint in NestJS release resources when the browser navigates away? Expected answer: the @Sse() Observable is unsubscribed on disconnect; teardown logic releases subscriptions; heartbeats keep proxies from closing idle streams.

Practical exercise

Build an order tracking page that subscribes to a NestJS SSE endpoint.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Switching between three orders leaves exactly one open stream in the Network panel, in development with Strict Mode on.
  • The NestJS controller logs subscribe and unsubscribe; counts match after navigating away.
  • A hand-written fetch effect for the order shows the race condition with an artificial 900 ms delay on one order, then fixes it with AbortController.
  • The same page rewritten with a data library (Part 72) has no fetch inside any useEffect.

71.5 useRef, useReducer and useContext

Concept

Three hooks cover most needs beyond useState and useEffect:

  • useRef(initial) returns a mutable object { current: initial } that survives re-renders and does not cause a re-render when changed. It has two uses: holding a reference to a DOM node (<input ref={inputRef} />, then inputRef.current.focus()), and holding a mutable value that is not displayed (a timer ID, the latest callback, an idempotency key for the current checkout attempt).
  • useReducer(reducer, initialState) is useState for state with several fields that change together according to rules. You describe changes as actions ({ type: 'COUPON_APPLIED', totals }) and a pure reducer function computes the next state: (state, action) => newState. It returns [state, dispatch].
  • useContext(SomeContext) reads a value provided by the nearest <SomeContext.Provider value={...}> above in the tree, without passing it through every intermediate component's props. It is how the current user, theme, locale or feature flags reach deep components.

Why does it exist?

useRef: some values must persist across renders without triggering them (a timer ID in state would re-render for nothing; in a local variable it is lost), and some operations are imperative by nature: focus an input, scroll to an error, hand a DOM node to a map SDK.

useReducer: a checkout has a step, address, coupon, totals, payment status and error. With six useState calls, "coupon applied" must call four setters correctly in every handler, and forgetting one creates impossible states. A reducer puts every transition in one pure, unit-testable function.

useContext: without it, the current user is passed through Layout, Page, OrderList and OrderCard just to reach ReorderButton. This prop drilling pollutes every intermediate interface.

Mental model

  • useRef is an instance field on a class: this.timerId. You can read and write it freely, and nothing reacts to the change.
  • useReducer is a state machine with an event log, exactly like the order status machine in your backend: PENDING + PAYMENT_CAPTURED -> PAID. Events go in, the reducer decides the next state, illegal transitions are refused in one place. If you have used CQRS or event sourcing (@nestjs/cqrs), the reducer is the aggregate's apply method.
  • useContext is NestJS dependency injection, scoped to a subtree. A provider at the top registers a value; any component below asks for it by token (the context object) and gets the nearest one. Like DI, it is convenient and it hides dependencies, so use it for genuinely cross-cutting things.

How it works

useRef. React returns the same ref object every render; writing ref.current mutates it without React knowing. For DOM refs, React sets ref.current to the node during commit and to null on unmount. Read and write refs in effects and event handlers, not during render, where they may be stale.

Passing a ref to your own component: in React 18, function components cannot receive ref as a prop; you wrap them in forwardRef((props, ref) => ...). In React 19, ref is an ordinary prop for function components (function TextField({ ref, ...props })), and forwardRef is no longer needed (it still works and will be deprecated later). React 19 also lets a ref callback return a cleanup function.

useReducer.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Address
    Address --> Coupon: ADDRESS_SAVED
    Coupon --> Coupon: COUPON_APPLIED or COUPON_REJECTED
    Coupon --> Payment: CONTINUE_TO_PAYMENT
    Payment --> Placing: PLACE_ORDER
    Placing --> Placed: ORDER_PLACED
    Placing --> Payment: ORDER_FAILED
    Payment --> Address: EDIT_ADDRESS
    Placed --> [*]
  1. dispatch(action) queues the action, like a setter.
  2. On the next render, React calls reducer(currentState, action) for each queued action.
  3. If the result is the same object (Object.is), React may bail out; otherwise it re-renders.
  4. The reducer must be pure: no API calls, no Date.now(), no mutation. Side effects happen in event handlers that dispatch before and after (PLACE_ORDER, then ORDER_PLACED or ORDER_FAILED).

dispatch has a stable identity across renders, so you can pass it to children or effects without memoisation.

useContext.

  1. createContext(defaultValue) creates a context object. The default is used only when there is no provider above.
  2. <Ctx.Provider value={v}> makes v available below. In React 19 you can write <Ctx value={v}> directly; Ctx.Provider still works.
  3. useContext(Ctx) returns the nearest provider's value and subscribes the component: when the provider's value changes (by Object.is), every component that reads that context re-renders, even if it uses only one field and even if a memo parent sits between them.
  4. React 19 adds use(Ctx), which reads context like useContext but can be called conditionally (inside if or after an early return).

The performance trap is point 3. value={{ user, flags, cart }} is a new object every provider render, so every consumer re-renders every time, and a cart change re-renders components that only read user. Memoise the value and split contexts by change frequency; for fast-changing global client state, a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux Toolkit) beats context (Part 72).

Practical example

On a checkout page:

Need Hook Why
Focus the first invalid field after submit useRef on the input Imperative DOM operation
Idempotency key for this "Place order" attempt useRef Must persist across renders, must not re-render, must not change on retry
The latest onEvent callback for an SSE subscription useRef Avoids reopening the stream (71.4)
Step, address, coupon, totals, payment status, error useReducer Several fields that change together by rules
Current user, currency, locale useContext Needed in many places, changes rarely
Feature flag newCouponFlow useContext Cross-cutting, loaded once per session
Cart line items Neither: server cache (Part 72) Server-owned data

React / Next.js example

A checkout reducer, tested without React:

// src/checkout/checkoutReducer.ts: pure, no React import needed
import type { Address, CartTotals } from '@shop/contracts';

export type CheckoutState =
  | { step: 'address'; address: Address | null; totals: CartTotals }
  | { step: 'coupon'; address: Address; coupon: string | null; totals: CartTotals; couponError: string | null }
  | { step: 'payment' | 'placing'; address: Address; coupon: string | null; totals: CartTotals; error: string | null }
  | { step: 'placed'; orderId: string };

export type CheckoutAction =
  | { type: 'ADDRESS_SAVED'; address: Address; totals: CartTotals }      // totals include delivery fee
  | { type: 'COUPON_APPLIED'; coupon: string; totals: CartTotals }
  | { type: 'COUPON_REJECTED'; message: string }
  | { type: 'CONTINUE_TO_PAYMENT' }
  | { type: 'PLACE_ORDER' }
  | { type: 'ORDER_PLACED'; orderId: string }
  | { type: 'ORDER_FAILED'; message: string };

export function checkoutReducer(state: CheckoutState, action: CheckoutAction): CheckoutState {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'ADDRESS_SAVED':
      return { step: 'coupon', address: action.address, coupon: null, totals: action.totals, couponError: null };
    case 'COUPON_APPLIED':
      if (state.step !== 'coupon') return state;                  // illegal transition: ignore
      return { ...state, coupon: action.coupon, totals: action.totals, couponError: null };
    case 'COUPON_REJECTED':
      if (state.step !== 'coupon') return state;
      return { ...state, couponError: action.message };
    case 'CONTINUE_TO_PAYMENT':
      if (state.step !== 'coupon') return state;
      return { step: 'payment', address: state.address, coupon: state.coupon, totals: state.totals, error: null };
    case 'PLACE_ORDER':
      if (state.step !== 'payment') return state;                 // a second click while placing is a no-op
      return { ...state, step: 'placing', error: null };
    case 'ORDER_PLACED':
      return state.step === 'placing' ? { step: 'placed', orderId: action.orderId } : state;
    case 'ORDER_FAILED':
      return state.step === 'placing' ? { ...state, step: 'payment', error: action.message } : state;
  }
}

Because the state is a discriminated union, TypeScript stops you from reading state.totals when step is 'placed'. Impossible states cannot be represented.

A session context, split from the fast-changing cart and memoised:

// src/session/SessionContext.tsx  (React 18; in React 19 <SessionContext value={...}> also works)
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo, type ReactNode } from 'react';
import type { SessionView } from '@shop/contracts';

type Session = { user: SessionView['user']; flags: SessionView['flags']; currency: string };
const SessionContext = createContext<Session | null>(null);

export function SessionProvider({ session, children }: { session: SessionView; children: ReactNode }) {
  // New object only when the session itself changes, not on every render of the provider.
  const value = useMemo(
    () => ({ user: session.user, flags: session.flags, currency: session.currency }),
    [session],
  );
  return <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</SessionContext.Provider>;
}

export function useSession(): Session {
  const ctx = useContext(SessionContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('useSession must be used inside <SessionProvider>'); // fail loudly in dev
  return ctx;
}

A DOM ref is equally small: const postcodeRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null), <input ref={postcodeRef} />, then postcodeRef.current?.focus() in the submit handler when the server rejects the postcode, so keyboard and screen-reader focus lands on the problem (69.9). React Hook Form does this for you (71.7).

Backend side (NestJS)

The client reducer mirrors a server state machine; it does not replace it. The checkout reducer refuses PLACE_ORDER unless the step is payment, but a second tab, a replayed request or a script can still call the API. The backend must enforce the same transitions and say clearly when one is illegal:

// apps/api/src/orders/order-state.ts
import { ConflictException } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { OrderStatus } from '@shop/contracts';

const allowed: Record<OrderStatus, OrderStatus[]> = {
  PENDING: ['PAID', 'CANCELLED'],
  PAID: ['SHIPPED', 'CANCELLED'],
  SHIPPED: ['DELIVERED'],
  DELIVERED: [],
  CANCELLED: [],
};

export function assertTransition(from: OrderStatus, to: OrderStatus): void {
  if (!allowed[from].includes(to)) {
    // 409 with a machine-readable code: the UI maps it to a message and refetches the order.
    throw new ConflictException({ code: 'INVALID_ORDER_TRANSITION', from, to });
  }
}

Apply it inside the transaction that updates the row, with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a conditional UPDATE orders SET status = $2 WHERE id = $1 AND status = $3 that checks the affected row count, so two concurrent transitions cannot both succeed (Part 21 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control).

Context needs one cheap bootstrap endpoint. Session context is loaded once at app start. Make that one request carry everything cross-cutting, and make sure no cache stores it:

// apps/api/src/session/session.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { SessionView } from '@shop/contracts';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { FlagsService } from '../flags/flags.service';

@Controller('v1/me')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class SessionController {
  constructor(private readonly flags: FlagsService) {}

  @Get()
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-store') // per-user: never in a CDN or shared cache
  async me(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser): Promise<SessionView> {
    return {
      user: { id: user.id, name: user.name, roles: user.roles },
      flags: await this.flags.evaluateFor(user.id),   // e.g. { newCouponFlow: true }
      currency: user.currency,
    };
  }
}

Roles in the session context are for showing or hiding UI only. Every endpoint still checks authorisation (Part 75 — Auth and Security in the Browser).

Production scenario

A B2B ordering portal put user, permissions, cart, notifications and a "last activity" timestamp (updated on every mouse move for idle detection) into one context with a new value object each render. All 1,100 consumers re-rendered on every mouse move: 40 to 70 ms commits, and visible typing lag.

The fix: the timestamp moved to a useRef (it was never displayed), the context split into SessionContext and CartContext, and both values were memoised. Mouse-move commits went to zero; typical commits fell to 2 to 5 ms.

Failure scenario

A payment step stored its idempotency key in useState, regenerated in the click handler. A customer on a train clicked "Pay", the request timed out while the server was still processing, and the retry click sent a fresh key: the server saw a new operation and charged the card twice.

The key must identify the attempt, not the click: a ref created once per cart version, reused for every retry, replaced only after a definitive answer. 71.8 builds this properly.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Reading ref.current in render shows stale values and breaks under concurrent rendering.
  • Reducers with side effects (calling the API inside the reducer) run twice in Strict Mode and may run for renders React discards.
  • Context without a provider silently returns the default value; prefer a null default and a hook that throws.
  • Context value recreated every render re-renders every consumer.
  • One giant context couples unrelated updates; split by change frequency.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior writes the reducer first, as a pure function with unit tests, the way they would write a domain aggregate before its controller. Refs are for imperative escape hatches and values that are never displayed; context is for slow-changing, truly global values.

They also hold a firm line: the client state machine is UX. The server state machine is the truth, and it must refuse illegal transitions with a precise, documented error.

Common mistakes

  • Six useState calls for a multi-step form with rules scattered across handlers.
  • Putting server data into context and building a homemade cache on top of it.
  • Generating idempotency keys per click instead of per attempt.
  • Passing a new object as the context value every render.
  • Using refs to store values that are rendered, then wondering why the screen is stale.

Interview questions

  1. When would you choose useReducer over useState? Expected answer: several related fields that change together, transitions with rules, wanting a pure testable function, or next state depending on previous state in complex ways. Follow-up: how do side effects fit? (Dispatch before and after them in event handlers.)
  2. What is the difference between a ref and state? Expected answer: both persist across renders; changing state re-renders, changing a ref does not; refs are for non-rendered values and DOM access.
  3. Why can context cause performance problems, and how do you fix them? Expected answer: every consumer re-renders when the value changes; memoise the value, split contexts, or use a store with selectors.
  4. How do you pass a ref to a custom input component in React 18 vs React 19? Expected answer: forwardRef in 18; ref is a regular prop in 19.
  5. If the client reducer prevents placing an order twice, why does the server still need to check? Expected answer: other tabs, retries, scripts and bugs bypass the client; the server enforces transitions atomically.

Practical exercise

Implement the checkout reducer above and its NestJS counterpart.

Acceptance criteria:

  • At least 10 unit tests for the reducer, including every illegal transition returning the same state object.
  • A SessionProvider with a memoised value; the React Profiler shows that updating the cart does not re-render a component that only reads useSession().user.
  • The NestJS order service rejects an illegal transition with 409 and code: "INVALID_ORDER_TRANSITION", and a concurrency test with two simultaneous transitions results in exactly one success.
  • After a server field error, focus moves to the invalid input (verified with a Testing Library assertion on document.activeElement).

71.6 useMemo, useCallback and custom hooks

Concept

useMemo(compute, deps) caches the result of a calculation between renders and recomputes it only when a dependency changes. useCallback(fn, deps) caches a function itself, so the same function object is returned until a dependency changes. useCallback(fn, deps) is exactly useMemo(() => fn, deps).

Both exist for two reasons: to skip expensive work during re-renders, and to keep referential identity stable, so that a child wrapped in memo or an effect with that value in its dependencies does not see a "new" value every render.

A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks. It lets you extract stateful logic (subscribe to a stream, debounce a value, manage an idempotency key) into a reusable, testable unit. Custom hooks share logic, not state: two components calling useDebouncedValue each get their own independent state.

Why does it exist?

Every render re-runs every line of the component. Two situations hurt: expensive derived data (filtering 8,000 products or grouping 2,000 orders on every keystroke in an unrelated input, 10 to 50 ms each time), and identity churn: an inline object or arrow function is new every render, so a memo child re-renders anyway and an effect depending on it re-runs (the SSE churn story in 71.4).

Custom hooks replaced the higher-order components and render props of pre-2019 React, which nested deeply and were hard to type. A custom hook is just a function.

Mental model

useMemo is a single-entry cache in front of a pure function, keyed by its dependencies, like a memoised getter on a NestJS request-scoped provider. It is not a guarantee: React may throw the cache away (the docs reserve the right), so the code must still be correct without it. Use it for performance, never for correctness.

A custom hook is a NestJS provider you inject into components: it encapsulates behaviour behind a small interface. useOrderStatusStream(orderId, onEvent) hides EventSource, refs and cleanup, the way an OrderEventsClient hides Kafka.

How it works

  1. On the first render, useMemo calls compute(), stores the result and the dependency values in the hook slot, and returns the result.
  2. On later renders, React compares each dependency with the stored one (Object.is). If all are equal, it returns the stored result without calling compute. If any differ, it recomputes and stores.
  3. useCallback stores the function you passed and returns the stored one while dependencies are equal.
  4. Memoisation only helps if someone uses the stable identity: a memo component, a dependency array, or a context value. A useCallback passed to a plain <button onClick> does nothing useful; the DOM element does not care about identity.

Costs: memoisation is not free. Each useMemo stores values, compares dependencies on every render, and adds code. Wrapping a 0.01 ms calculation in useMemo makes it slower. Measure first (71.12).

The React Compiler (stable 1.0 in October 2025, works with React 17, 18 and 19; React 19 has the runtime built in, older versions need react-compiler-runtime) is a Babel/SWC build plugin that analyses your components and inserts memoisation automatically, at a finer grain than you would by hand. In a codebase with the compiler on, most hand-written useMemo, useCallback and memo become unnecessary, and the compiler requires that your code follows the rules of React (pure renders, no mutation of props or state). Without the compiler, the guidance below applies.

Custom hooks follow the rules of hooks (top level, React functions only) and can return anything: a value, a tuple, an object of functions. Name them useSomething so the lint rules check them.

When to use which:

Situation Tool
Expensive pure calculation (> about 1 ms measured) depending on props or state useMemo
Object or array passed to a memo child or used in an effect dependency useMemo
Callback passed to a memo child or used in an effect dependency useCallback
Callback passed to a DOM element Nothing
Cheap calculation Nothing
Latest callback inside a long-lived subscription useRef pattern (71.4) or React's useEffectEvent (stable in React 19.2)
Repeated hook combination in 2+ components Custom hook

Practical example

A pharmacy branch screen holds 6,000 SKUs on the client for offline stock lookups. Without useMemo, opening the cart drawer re-filters all of them (14 ms on a mid-range phone); keyed on [query, inStockOnly, products], it costs 0.4 ms. For most catalogues, though, the right answer is server search, debounced on the client with a custom hook, as below.

React / Next.js example

Two custom hooks and a component that uses them, with memoisation where it pays:

// src/hooks/useDebouncedValue.ts
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, delayMs = 250): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delayMs); // external system: a timer
    return () => clearTimeout(t);                              // cancel if value changes first
  }, [value, delayMs]);
  return debounced;
}
// src/hooks/useIdempotencyKey.ts: one key per logical attempt, survives re-renders and retries
import { useCallback, useRef } from 'react';

export function useIdempotencyKey() {
  const keyRef = useRef<string | null>(null);
  const get = useCallback(() => (keyRef.current ??= crypto.randomUUID()), []);  // lazily create
  const reset = useCallback(() => { keyRef.current = null; }, []);              // after a final answer
  return { get, reset };
}
// src/catalog/ProductSearch.tsx  (React 18, TanStack Query v5 for the request; Part 72 covers it)
import { memo, useCallback, useMemo, useState } from 'react';
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useDebouncedValue } from '../hooks/useDebouncedValue';
import { searchProducts, type ProductHit } from '../api/catalog';

const ResultList = memo(function ResultList(
  { hits, onAdd }: { hits: ProductHit[]; onAdd: (sku: string) => void },
) {
  return <ul>{hits.map((h) => <li key={h.sku}>{h.name} <button onClick={() => onAdd(h.sku)}>Add</button></li>)}</ul>;
});

export function ProductSearch({ addToCart }: { addToCart: (sku: string) => Promise<void> }) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');
  const [drawerOpen, setDrawerOpen] = useState(false);
  const q = useDebouncedValue(query.trim(), 250);           // 1 request per pause, not per keystroke

  const { data, isFetching } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['product-search', q],
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => searchProducts(q, signal),    // signal aborts superseded requests
    enabled: q.length >= 2,
    staleTime: 30_000,
  });

  const hits = useMemo(() => (data?.items ?? []).filter((h) => h.inStock), [data]); // stable array
  const onAdd = useCallback((sku: string) => { void addToCart(sku); }, [addToCart]); // stable for memo

  return (
    <>
      <input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)} aria-label="Search products" />
      <button type="button" onClick={() => setDrawerOpen((o) => !o)}>Cart</button>
      {isFetching && <span aria-live="polite">Searching...</span>}
      <ResultList hits={hits} onAdd={onAdd} /> {/* skips re-render when only drawerOpen changes */}
      {drawerOpen && <aside>{/* cart drawer */}</aside>}
    </>
  );
}

Note that onAdd is only stable if the parent passes a stable addToCart; memoisation is a chain, and one unstable link breaks it. That fragility is the main argument for the React Compiler.

Backend side (NestJS)

Debouncing on the client is a courtesy; rate limiting on the server is the guarantee. A 250 ms debounce turns "wireless headphones" (19 keystrokes) into 2 or 3 requests instead of 19. But old clients, scripts and bugs will still send every keystroke. Protect the search endpoint with @nestjs/throttler and make it cheap:

// apps/api/src/catalog/catalog.controller.ts  (@nestjs/throttler v5+)
import { Controller, Get, Header, Query, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle, ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { ProductSearchQuerySchema, type ProductSearchQuery, type ProductSearchResponse } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { CatalogService } from './catalog.service';

@Controller('v1/catalog')
@UseGuards(ThrottlerGuard)
export class CatalogController {
  constructor(private readonly catalog: CatalogService) {}

  @Get('search')
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 20, ttl: 10_000 } })   // 20 searches per 10 s per client
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=30')       // identical queries from many users hit the CDN
  search(@Query(new ZodValidationPipe(ProductSearchQuerySchema)) q: ProductSearchQuery): Promise<ProductSearchResponse> {
    // q.text is 2..64 chars, q.limit is capped at 50: the UI never needs more than one screen of hits.
    return this.catalog.search(q.text, q.limit);
  }
}

And compute aggregates on the server. Shipping 40,000 orders so the browser can useMemo "revenue by day" costs 8 MB and 60 ms of main-thread work; a GROUP BY date_trunc('day', placed_at) returns 90 rows in milliseconds. The best memoisation is work the client never does.

Production scenario

An admin analytics page computed seven chart series from 25,000 rows in render, so every tooltip hover re-ran them (180 ms). useMemo cut hover renders to 6 ms; the real fix moved the aggregations to a NestJS endpoint over a PostgreSQL materialised view, taking the payload from 5.4 MB to 38 KB and load from 3.1 s to 0.6 s.

Failure scenario

A developer added useCallback to every function in a checkout component "for performance", including one that read the selected delivery slot:

const placeOrder = useCallback(() => api.placeOrder({ cartId, slotId }), [cartId]); // slotId missing

The lint rule had been disabled for the file. The callback captured the first render's slotId, so customers who changed their slot had orders placed for the original one: about 600 orders over two days.

The fix restored the dependency, made react-hooks/exhaustive-deps an error repo-wide, removed most useCallback calls (no measurable benefit), and showed the chosen slot in the confirmation the API returned.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Missing dependencies in useMemo/useCallback produce stale values: correctness bugs disguised as optimisations.
  • Unstable dependencies (an inline object) make memoisation recompute every render: cost with no benefit.
  • Memoising cheap work adds overhead and noise.
  • Relying on useMemo for correctness (for example to keep a generated ID stable) breaks if React discards the cache; use useRef or useState for that.
  • Custom hooks that hide effects with surprising network traffic; name them for what they do (useOrderStatusStream, not useOrder).
  • Debounce without abort still lets an old slow response overwrite a newer one; abort or key the request by query (as the data library does).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior memoises when the Profiler says so or when identity matters for a memo child or an effect. With the React Compiler on, they remove manual memoisation over time. They extract custom hooks when a pattern appears twice, name them for their side effects, and test them with renderHook (Part 77).

They push heavy computation to the backend when the data comes from the backend anyway, because a GROUP BY on an indexed table beats any amount of client-side memoisation.

Common mistakes

  • Wrapping everything in useCallback without a memo consumer.
  • Disabling exhaustive-deps to make the warning go away.
  • Using useMemo to cache server data instead of a data library.
  • Custom hooks that are just one useState with a new name, adding indirection without value.
  • Shipping 40,000 rows for a client-side aggregation.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback? Expected answer: useMemo caches a computed value, useCallback caches a function; useCallback(fn, d) equals useMemo(() => fn, d). Follow-up: when is useCallback useless? (When nothing depends on the function's identity.)
  2. What does the React Compiler change? Expected answer: automatic, fine-grained memoisation at build time; manual memo hooks become mostly unnecessary; code must follow the rules of React.
  3. Do two components using the same custom hook share state? Expected answer: no; each call has its own state. Share state through lifting, context or a store.
  4. Your search box sends a request per keystroke. What do you change on both sides? Expected answer: client debounce plus abort of superseded requests; server rate limit, input bounds, result cap and caching.

Practical exercise

Build a product search against a NestJS endpoint with 50,000 products in PostgreSQL.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Typing a 15-character query sends at most 3 requests, and superseded requests show as cancelled in the Network panel.
  • The endpoint is throttled (a script sending 50 requests in 2 s receives 429 with Retry-After) and validates text length and limit.
  • A pg_trgm GIN index makes the search query run in under 20 ms (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) output included).
  • The Profiler shows that toggling the cart drawer does not re-render ResultList; removing the useCallback shows that it does.
  • useDebouncedValue and useIdempotencyKey have unit tests using renderHook and fake timers.

71.7 Forms: controlled and uncontrolled inputs, validation, React Hook Form with zod

Concept

A form in React can manage its inputs in two ways:

  • Controlled input: React state is the source of truth. The input's value comes from state, and every keystroke calls onChange, which sets state, which re-renders the input with the new value.

    const [postcode, setPostcode] = useState('');
<input value={postcode} onChange={(e) => setPostcode(e.target.value)} />

  • Uncontrolled input: the DOM is the source of truth. You give an initial defaultValue and read the current value when you need it: from a ref, or from FormData on submit.

    <input name="postcode" defaultValue={saved?.postcode ?? ''} />
// on submit: new FormData(event.currentTarget).get('postcode')

Validation happens in three places with three different jobs: the browser's built-in constraint validation (required, type="email", pattern, 69.2), a client-side schema for fast, specific feedback, and the server, which is the only validation that counts.

React Hook Form (RHF 7) registers inputs as uncontrolled, so typing does not re-render the form, and tracks errors and submission state. zod defines a schema once and gives both runtime validation and a static type (z.infer). @hookform/resolvers/zod connects them, and the same schema in @shop/contracts validates the request in NestJS (70.12).

Why does it exist?

Forms are where most frontend bugs and support tickets live: values lost on navigation, errors before the user has typed, "Something went wrong" for a server rejection, a button that submits twice.

Controlled inputs give full control (live formatting, dependent fields) at the cost of a re-render per keystroke for the state owner; with 25 fields owned at the top, each keystroke re-renders all 25. Uncontrolled inputs are faster and closer to HTML, but reacting to each change is harder.

Libraries exist because the bookkeeping is large (per-field errors, touched and dirty flags, validation timing, focus on the first error, field arrays, mapping server errors) and hand-written versions behave differently on every screen.

Mental model

A controlled input is synchronous replication: React state is the primary and every DOM change is copied into it. An uncontrolled input is primary-only: read the DOM when you need a value. Validation layers form a NestJS pipeline: browser checks reject malformed input, the client schema is a bypassable ValidationPipe, and server validation is the database constraint, the only layer you trust.

How it works

flowchart LR
    user["User types"] --> input["Input element"]
    input -->|"on blur or change"| rhf["React Hook Form store"]
    rhf -->|"resolver"| schema["zod schema in contracts"]
    schema -->|"field errors"| rhf
    rhf -->|"valid data on submit"| api["POST to NestJS"]
    api -->|"same zod schema plus business rules"| nest["ZodValidationPipe and service"]
    nest -->|"422 with issues and paths"| mapErr["setError per field"]
    mapErr --> rhf
    nest -->|"201 created"| done["Next step"]

RHF's model:

  1. useForm({ resolver, defaultValues, mode }) creates a form store held in a ref, not in React state. register('postcode') returns { name, ref, onChange, onBlur } to spread on a native input; RHF reads the DOM through the ref, so typing does not re-render your component.
  2. formState (errors, isSubmitting, isDirty, touchedFields) is a proxy: your component re-renders only when a piece of formState it actually reads changes.
  3. mode decides when validation runs: 'onSubmit' (default), 'onBlur', 'onTouched' (first blur, then every change), 'onChange' or 'all'. 'onTouched' is the best checkout default: quiet while typing the first time, immediate while fixing.
  4. handleSubmit(onValid) prevents the browser submit, validates, focuses the first invalid field, and holds isSubmitting true while your onValid runs.
  5. setError('address.postcode', { type: 'server', message }) attaches a server error to a field; setError('root.server', ...) attaches a form-level one (read as errors.root?.server).
  6. For components that do not expose a native input (a date picker, a custom select), Controller or useController wraps them as controlled inputs inside RHF.

zod's model:

  • z.object({...}) describes the shape; .safeParse() returns { success, data | error }; z.infer<typeof Schema> gives the type, so form values and the API request share one type; .refine / .superRefine add cross-field rules.
  • Inputs always produce strings. Use z.coerce.number() or RHF's valueAsNumber for numeric fields.

React 19 forms. Actions let you write <form action={fn}>, where fn receives the FormData, may be async and runs in a transition. useActionState(action, initialState) returns [state, formAction, isPending] (named useFormState in the canary build Next.js 14 bundles); useFormStatus() from react-dom gives a nested button { pending }; uncontrolled fields reset after success. They suit simple forms and Next.js Server Actions (Part 73); RHF remains the usual choice for complex client forms.

Practical example

A delivery address form: name, phone, address lines, city, postcode, and a "save to address book" checkbox. Rules: phone is a 10-digit Indian mobile number; postcode is 6 digits; the postcode must be serviceable, which only the server knows.

Rule Where it is checked Feedback timing
Required fields Browser required + zod On blur after first touch
Phone and postcode format zod regex (shared) On blur, then on change
Max lengths (match DB columns) zod + DB varchar(n) On change
Postcode is serviceable Server only After submit, mapped to the postcode field
Address belongs to this user (when editing) Server only 404 or 403, shown as a form error

React / Next.js example

The shared schema (zod 3.23, also valid in zod 4):

// packages/contracts/src/address.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const AddressSchema = z.object({
  fullName: z.string().trim().min(2, 'Enter your full name').max(80),
  phone: z.string().trim().regex(/^[6-9]\d{9}$/, 'Enter a 10-digit mobile number'),
  line1: z.string().trim().min(3, 'Enter house number and street').max(120),
  line2: z.string().trim().max(120).optional().default(''),
  city: z.string().trim().min(2).max(60),
  postcode: z.string().trim().regex(/^\d{6}$/, 'Postcode must be 6 digits'),
  saveToBook: z.boolean().default(false),
});
export type Address = z.infer<typeof AddressSchema>;

The form, with React Hook Form 7 and @hookform/resolvers:

// src/checkout/AddressForm.tsx  (React 18, react-hook-form 7, @hookform/resolvers)
import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
import { zodResolver } from '@hookform/resolvers/zod';
import { AddressSchema, type Address } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ApiError, applyServerErrors } from '../api/errors';

type Props = { initial?: Partial<Address>; onSaved: (a: Address) => Promise<void> };

export function AddressForm({ initial, onSaved }: Props) {
  const { register, handleSubmit, setError, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } = useForm<Address>({
    resolver: zodResolver(AddressSchema),
    defaultValues: { fullName: '', phone: '', line1: '', line2: '', city: '', postcode: '', saveToBook: false, ...initial },
    mode: 'onTouched',                                   // quiet until the first blur
  });

  const onValid = async (values: Address) => {
    try {
      await onSaved(values);                             // POST /v1/checkout/address
    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof ApiError && applyServerErrors(e, setError)) return; // field errors mapped
      setError('root.server', { type: 'server', message: 'Could not save the address. Please try again.' });
    }
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onValid)} noValidate> {/* noValidate: one consistent error UI */}
      <label htmlFor="fullName">Full name</label>
      <input id="fullName" autoComplete="name" {...register('fullName')} aria-invalid={!!errors.fullName}
        aria-describedby="fullName-err" />
      <p id="fullName-err" role="alert">{errors.fullName?.message}</p>

      <label htmlFor="phone">Mobile number</label>
      <input id="phone" type="tel" inputMode="numeric" autoComplete="tel-national" {...register('phone')}
        aria-invalid={!!errors.phone} aria-describedby="phone-err" />
      <p id="phone-err" role="alert">{errors.phone?.message}</p>

      {/* line1, line2, city follow the same pattern */}

      <label htmlFor="postcode">Postcode</label>
      <input id="postcode" inputMode="numeric" autoComplete="postal-code" {...register('postcode')}
        aria-invalid={!!errors.postcode} aria-describedby="postcode-err" />
      <p id="postcode-err" role="alert">{errors.postcode?.message}</p>

      <label><input type="checkbox" {...register('saveToBook')} /> Save to address book</label>

      {errors.root?.server && <p role="alert">{errors.root.server.message}</p>}
      <button type="submit" disabled={isSubmitting}>{isSubmitting ? 'Saving...' : 'Continue'}</button>
    </form>
  );
}

The server-error mapper, which relies on a stable error contract:

// src/api/errors.ts
import type { FieldValues, Path, UseFormSetError } from 'react-hook-form';

export type ApiIssue = { path: string; message: string; code?: string };
export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(public status: number, public code: string, public issues: ApiIssue[] = [], public requestId?: string) {
    super(code);
  }
}

// Returns true if at least one issue was attached to a field.
export function applyServerErrors<T extends FieldValues>(err: ApiError, setError: UseFormSetError<T>): boolean {
  let mapped = false;
  err.issues.forEach((issue, i) => {
    if (!issue.path) return;
    setError(issue.path as Path<T>, { type: 'server', message: issue.message }, { shouldFocus: i === 0 });
    mapped = true;
  });
  return mapped;
}

As controlled inputs with top-level useState, every keystroke would re-render all fields: on a 20-field form on a mid-range phone, 20 to 40 renders per second while typing, against zero with RHF.

Backend side (NestJS)

The form can only show precise server errors if the API returns them in one predictable shape with field paths that match the form's field names. Reuse the shared schema for syntax, then check business rules and return them in the same shape:

// apps/api/src/checkout/checkout-address.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Post, UnprocessableEntityException, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AddressSchema, type Address, type CartTotals } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { ServiceabilityService } from '../logistics/serviceability.service';
import { CheckoutService } from './checkout.service';

@Controller('v1/checkout')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class CheckoutAddressController {
  constructor(private readonly serviceability: ServiceabilityService, private readonly checkout: CheckoutService) {}

  @Post('address')
  async setAddress(
    @CurrentUser() user: AuthUser,
    @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(AddressSchema)) address: Address, // 400 VALIDATION_FAILED with issues on syntax
  ): Promise<{ totals: CartTotals }> {
    const area = await this.serviceability.lookup(address.postcode); // cached, about 2 ms
    if (!area.serviceable) {
      // Semantic rule: same issue shape, path matches the form field name exactly.
      throw new UnprocessableEntityException({
        code: 'ADDRESS_NOT_SERVICEABLE',
        issues: [{ path: 'postcode', code: 'NOT_SERVICEABLE', message: 'We do not deliver to this postcode yet' }],
      });
    }
    // Delivery fee depends on the area, so the response carries recomputed totals for the next step.
    return { totals: await this.checkout.setAddress(user.id, address, area) };
  }
}

Backend rules for forms:

  • Validate everything again on the server, with the same schema where possible. The client schema is a UX feature.
  • One error shape for syntax (400) and business rules (422): { code, issues: [{ path, code, message }], requestId }. Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts formalises this as RFC 7807 problem details.
  • Paths match field names, including nesting (address.postcode) and arrays (items.2.quantity), which RHF understands. Messages are safe to show; internals go to logs under the requestId.
  • Column limits and schema limits match. If line1 is varchar(120), the schema says .max(120). Otherwise the client accepts what the database rejects with a 500.

Production scenario

A pharmacy delivery app validated addresses with mode: 'onChange', so "Postcode must be 6 digits" appeared after the first digit, and the step had 9 % abandonment. Switching to 'onTouched', adding autoComplete attributes and mapping the server's "not serviceable" error to the postcode field (instead of a generic toast) brought it to 5.5 %. The backend change was 15 lines: a 422 with a path instead of a 400 with a sentence.

Failure scenario

A team added a landmark field to the form and its zod schema, but the NestJS DTO used class-validator with forbidNonWhitelisted: true. Every submit failed with 400 property landmark should not exist, shown as "Could not save the address" with no field highlighted. Checkout conversion dropped 30 % for 50 minutes until rollback.

The fix: the schema moved to @shop/contracts so API and form cannot disagree without a type error in the same pull request (70.12), and a CI contract test posts the form's default values to the API (Part 74).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Switching an input from uncontrolled to controlled (value={undefined} then value="x") triggers a React warning and loses the cursor position; always give controlled inputs a defined value ('', not undefined).
  • Number inputs return strings; "0" vs "" vs NaN need explicit handling.
  • Browser autofill sets values without key events; RHF reads the DOM so it sees them, but some custom controlled inputs miss them.
  • Server errors for fields not on screen (a hidden field, a different step) must fall back to a form-level message.
  • Editing a record that changed on the server while the form was open; use a version and handle 409.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior designs a form from its error states backwards: what can go wrong per field, where the user sees it, what the API returns for it. They use RHF for anything non-trivial, controlled inputs only where live formatting needs them, and one schema shared with the backend. "Something went wrong" on a form is a bug in the API contract.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting client validation and skipping server checks.
  • Validating on every change from the first keystroke.
  • Generic error toasts for field-level problems.
  • Duplicating the schema in the form and the API, then letting them drift.
  • Making every field controlled with top-level state in a large form.

Interview questions

  1. Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs: what is the difference and when would you choose each? Expected answer: controlled means React state is the source of truth and every keystroke re-renders; uncontrolled means the DOM holds the value and you read it on demand. Choose controlled for live formatting or dependent UI, uncontrolled (often via RHF) for performance and simplicity. Follow-up: how does RHF avoid re-renders?
  2. Why validate on both client and server? Expected answer: client for fast feedback, server because clients can be bypassed; the server is authoritative.
  3. How do you map a server validation error onto the right field? Expected answer: a stable error contract with field paths that match form names; setError per issue; a form-level fallback.
  4. What do React 19 Actions and useActionState add to forms? Expected answer: form actions that receive FormData, run in a transition with a pending state, integrate with Server Actions, and reset uncontrolled fields after success. Version: React 19 (Next.js 14 used canary APIs under different names).

Practical exercise

Build the address form with a shared zod schema and a NestJS endpoint.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The same AddressSchema is imported by the React form and the NestJS controller.
  • Submitting postcode 999999 (configured as not serviceable) shows the server's message under the postcode field and moves focus there.
  • A curl request with a 500-character line1 gets a 400 with an issue whose path is line1, and the database column limit matches the schema.
  • Typing into one field does not re-render the other fields (verified with the Profiler or a render counter).

71.8 Double-submit protection and idempotency from the form

Concept

A double submit is one intention ("place this order") reaching the server as several requests: double taps, Enter plus click, impatient retries, client-library retries, or the browser re-sending after a network change.

Protection is layered, and only the last layer is a guarantee:

  1. UI guard: disable the button and ignore re-entry while the submission is in flight.
  2. Attempt identity: send an idempotency key that identifies this attempt, the same key on every retry of it.
  3. Server idempotency: the server records the key and returns the original result for repeats (Part 15 — API Design (REST first), 15.12 Idempotency).
  4. Database constraint: a unique constraint that makes a duplicate physically impossible even if everything above fails.

Part 69.2 showed the plain HTML version with a hidden input and Post/Redirect/Get. This section is the React version.

Why does it exist?

Because "disable the button" is not enough, for four reasons:

  • Timing: in React 18 a click is a "discrete" event, so setSubmitting(true) in the handler commits before the next click is processed. But a guard set after an await (async validation, fetching a payment token) leaves a gap, and so do two triggers (Enter and a click).
  • Remounts (a route change, a parent showing a skeleton) forget "submitting" state; retries after timeouts follow requests that may already have succeeded; and other clients (a second tab, a script) are outside the UI's control.

Mental model

Imagine a lift button. Pressing it ten times calls one lift, because the controller records "lift requested for floor 3", not "button pressed". The button light (the UI guard) is feedback; the floor number (the idempotency key) is what makes repeats collapse into one.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant F as CheckoutForm
    participant A as NestJS
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    U->>F: clicks Place order
    F->>F: guard ref set, button disabled, key K reused for this attempt
    F->>A: POST /v1/orders with Idempotency-Key K
    A->>DB: reserve K and insert order
    Note over F,A: response lost, client times out after 15 s
    F-->>U: Still working, retrying
    F->>A: POST /v1/orders with Idempotency-Key K again
    A->>DB: K already completed
    A-->>F: 201 same order with Idempotent-Replayed true
    F-->>U: Order placed, one order only

The client side, step by step:

  1. Create the key per attempt: on the first submit for a given cart version, generate crypto.randomUUID() and keep it (71.5); every retry reuses it.
  2. Guard synchronously: check and set a ref flag at the very start of the handler, before any await. State drives the disabled button; the ref closes the gap.
  3. Send the key as an Idempotency-Key header with the request.
  4. Handle outcomes by meaning:
    • 201/200: success. Clear the key, navigate to the confirmation page with replace so Back does not return to a live form.
    • 409 with Retry-After (key in progress): wait and retry with the same key.
    • Network error or timeout: the outcome is unknown. Retry with the same key, or show "Checking your order..." and retry; never generate a new key.
    • 4xx that ends the attempt (payment declined, validation): show the error and clear the key, because the next submit is a new attempt with possibly different data.
    • 422 "key reused with a different body": a client bug; log it with the request ID.
  5. Change the key when the request content changes. Editing the address after a failed attempt makes the next submit a different operation, so clear the key after any final error.

Practical example

Situation UI behaviour Key Server response
Double click Second click ignored by guard Same One request only
Enter key + click Guard ref blocks the second Same One request only
Timeout after 15 s, user taps Retry "Retrying..." Same Original order replayed
Card declined, user picks another card Error shown, form re-enabled New New attempt
User opens checkout in two tabs Each tab its own key Different Second fails on cart version or stock, by design
Component remounts mid-request Guard lost Key lost unless stored per cart version Server replay or unique constraint catches it

The last row is why the key often lives in sessionStorage keyed by cart ID and version, not only in a ref: it survives a remount or a reload during the attempt.

React / Next.js example

A usePlaceOrder hook that implements the client side, used by the payment step:

// src/checkout/usePlaceOrder.ts  (React 18)
import { useCallback, useRef, useState } from 'react';
import { placeOrder, ApiTimeoutError } from '../api/orders';
import { ApiError } from '../api/errors';

type Result = { ok: true; orderId: string } | { ok: false; message: string };
const keyStorage = (cartId: string, version: number) => `idem:checkout:${cartId}:v${version}`;

function getAttemptKey(cartId: string, version: number): string {
  const k = keyStorage(cartId, version);
  let key = sessionStorage.getItem(k);                     // survives remounts and reloads
  if (!key) { key = crypto.randomUUID(); sessionStorage.setItem(k, key); }
  return key;
}

export function usePlaceOrder(cartId: string, cartVersion: number) {
  const inFlight = useRef(false);                          // synchronous guard, no render needed
  const [pending, setPending] = useState(false);           // drives the disabled button and label

  const submit = useCallback(async (paymentMethodId: string): Promise<Result> => {
    if (inFlight.current) return { ok: false, message: 'Already placing your order' };
    inFlight.current = true;                               // set before the first await
    setPending(true);
    const key = getAttemptKey(cartId, cartVersion);
    try {
      for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= 3; attempt++) {
        try {
          const order = await placeOrder({ cartId, cartVersion, paymentMethodId }, key, { timeoutMs: 15_000 });
          sessionStorage.removeItem(keyStorage(cartId, cartVersion)); // final answer: attempt is over
          return { ok: true, orderId: order.id };
        } catch (e) {
          const retryable = e instanceof ApiTimeoutError || (e instanceof ApiError && e.status === 409 && e.code === 'IDEMPOTENCY_IN_PROGRESS');
          if (!retryable || attempt === 3) throw e;
          await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1000 * attempt)); // same key, backoff 1 s then 2 s
        }
      }
      throw new Error('unreachable');
    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof ApiError && e.status >= 400 && e.status < 500 && e.status !== 409) {
        sessionStorage.removeItem(keyStorage(cartId, cartVersion)); // declined or invalid: next submit is new
        return { ok: false, message: e.issues[0]?.message ?? 'Your order could not be placed.' };
      }
      // Unknown outcome (timeouts exhausted, 5xx): keep the key so the next try replays, not duplicates.
      return { ok: false, message: 'We could not confirm your order yet. Please check My Orders before trying again.' };
    } finally {
      inFlight.current = false;
      setPending(false);
    }
  }, [cartId, cartVersion]);

  return { submit, pending };
}

The API helper sends the header and enforces a timeout with AbortSignal.timeout (supported in all current browsers):

// src/api/orders.ts (excerpt)
export async function placeOrder(body: PlaceOrderRequest, key: string, opts: { timeoutMs: number }) {
  let res: Response;
  try {
    res = await fetch('/api/v1/orders', {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Idempotency-Key': key },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
      credentials: 'include',
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(opts.timeoutMs),       // aborts the request after the timeout
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof DOMException && e.name === 'TimeoutError') throw new ApiTimeoutError();
    throw e;
  }
  if (!res.ok) throw await toApiError(res);              // parses { code, issues, requestId }
  return OrderCreatedSchema.parse(await res.json());
}

RHF's isSubmitting, and React 19's isPending (useActionState) and pending (useFormStatus), drive the disabled button; none of them replaces the ref guard or the idempotency key.

Backend side (NestJS)

The server side is the guarantee. Part 15.12 builds the full IdempotencyInterceptor with Redis reservation, fingerprinting and replay. What the browser adds:

  • CORS must expose the headers the client reads if the web app and API are on different origins: exposedHeaders: ['Idempotent-Replayed', 'Retry-After', 'X-Request-Id'], and Idempotency-Key must be in allowedHeaders (it is a non-simple header, so it triggers a preflight; Part 11.13).
  • Require the key on money endpoints. Reject POST /v1/orders without one with 400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED; otherwise one old client version silently bypasses the protection.
  • Back it with a constraint, so even a Redis outage cannot produce two orders:
-- Duplicate orders become impossible, not just unlikely.
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN idempotency_key uuid;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_idem_uq
  ON orders (customer_id, idempotency_key)
  WHERE idempotency_key IS NOT NULL;
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts (excerpt)
import { BadRequestException, Body, Controller, Headers, Post, UseGuards, UseInterceptors } from '@nestjs/common';
import { PlaceOrderRequestSchema, type PlaceOrderRequest, type OrderCreated } from '@shop/contracts';
import { IdempotencyInterceptor } from '../common/idempotency.interceptor'; // from Part 15.12
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Post()
  @UseInterceptors(IdempotencyInterceptor)            // replays completed keys, 409 for in-progress
  async place(
    @CurrentUser() user: AuthUser,
    @Headers('idempotency-key') key: string | undefined,
    @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(PlaceOrderRequestSchema)) body: PlaceOrderRequest,
  ): Promise<OrderCreated> {
    // Require a UUID key on every money endpoint; old clients without one fail loudly, not silently.
    if (!key || !/^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$/i.test(key)) {
      throw new BadRequestException({ code: 'IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED' });
    }
    // Inside one transaction: check cart version, reserve stock, insert order with the key.
    // A unique violation on orders_customer_idem_uq is caught and turned into a replay of the existing order.
    return this.orders.placeFromCart(user.id, body, key);
  }
}
  • Check the cart version. PlaceOrderRequest carries cartVersion; if the cart changed since the page loaded (another tab added an item), return 409 CART_CHANGED with the fresh cart, rather than placing an order for contents the user did not review.
  • Payment providers need the key too. Pass a derived key to the payment provider's own idempotency mechanism (most card APIs accept one), so a retry inside your service cannot double-charge either.

Production scenario

A food delivery platform found 0.4 % duplicate orders (same customer, restaurant and items within 60 s), about 1,900 a day: 55 % retries after client timeouts, 30 % double taps missed because the guard was set after an async address check, 15 % two tabs.

After per-attempt keys in sessionStorage, a ref guard before any await, server replay and the unique index, duplicates fell to 0.02 %, almost all genuine reorders.

Failure scenario

At 21:05 during a cricket final, a promotion drove checkout traffic to 6x normal and order-service p99 rose from 400 ms to 9 s. The mobile web client timed out at 10 s, showed "Something went wrong", re-enabled the button and generated a new key per click. In 25 minutes 3,200 customers got two or more orders, and the duplicate load pushed latency higher still: a retry storm built by the UI.

The changes: keys per attempt; unknown outcomes show "Checking your order..." and poll GET /v1/orders?cartId=...; a 20 s timeout with a progress message after 5 s; and server load shedding with 503 and Retry-After before latency reaches the client timeout (Part 42 — Performance Engineering).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Guard set after an await leaves a window for a second submit.
  • Key per click turns every retry into a new operation.
  • Key never rotated after the request content changes returns the old result for a different order (the server should 422 on fingerprint mismatch).
  • Key lost on remount if stored only in component state; use a ref plus sessionStorage keyed by cart version.
  • Client library auto-retries (axios-retry, TanStack Query mutation retry) on POST without a key create duplicates; only retry POST with a key.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior asks the mantra about the submit button: can it duplicate, time out after succeeding, partially succeed? They model the attempt lifecycle (new, in flight, succeeded, failed definitively, unknown), map every HTTP outcome to one state, and make "unknown" honest, because "try again" when the order might exist is how retry storms and double charges start. The UI guard is UX; the key plus a constraint is correctness.

Common mistakes

  • Only disabling the button.
  • Generating the key on each click or on each render.
  • Showing a retry button after a timeout without checking whether the order exists.
  • Retrying POST automatically without a key.

Interview questions

  1. A customer was charged twice after double-tapping "Pay". Walk through the layers you would add. Expected answer: synchronous UI guard, per-attempt idempotency key reused on retries, server-side idempotency with replay, unique constraint, idempotency key forwarded to the payment provider. Why it matters: each layer covers a different failure. Follow-up: where do you store the key so a remount does not lose it?
  2. What should the UI do when a place-order request times out? Expected answer: treat the outcome as unknown; retry with the same key or check order status; do not invite a fresh submit with a new key.
  3. When should the client generate a new key? Expected answer: after a definitive answer (success, or a 4xx that ends the attempt) or when the request content changes.

Practical exercise

Implement usePlaceOrder against a NestJS POST /v1/orders with the Part 15.12 interceptor.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A Playwright test that double-clicks "Place order" produces exactly one order row.
  • With the API delayed by 20 s and the client timeout at 15 s, the client retries with the same key and the database contains one order.
  • A card decline clears the key; the next submit sends a new key.
  • Removing the interceptor (simulating a Redis outage) still produces one order, because of the unique index, and the duplicate request receives the existing order.
  • The browser can read Retry-After and Idempotent-Replayed in a cross-origin setup.

71.9 Lists, tables and large lists: virtualisation

Concept

Rendering a list in React is array.map returning elements with keys (71.3). For tables, use real <table>, <thead>, <th scope="col"> and <tbody> elements, so screen readers can announce "row 4 of 50, column Status" (69.9).

The problem starts with size. Every row becomes DOM nodes, and each node costs memory, style calculation, layout and paint. A list of 10,000 orders with 8 cells each is over 80,000 DOM nodes. Virtualisation (also called windowing) renders only the rows that are visible in the scroll area, plus a few extra above and below (the overscan), and fakes the rest of the scroll height with an empty spacer. As you scroll, rows leaving the viewport are unmounted and rows entering it are mounted. 10,000 rows become about 30 rendered rows.

Why does it exist?

Measured on a mid-range Android phone (2023), rendering an order table with 8 columns:

Rows rendered DOM nodes First render + layout Memory Scroll
50 about 500 25 ms small smooth
1,000 about 9,000 450 ms +40 MB some jank
10,000 about 90,000 4 to 6 s, one long task +350 MB unusable; tab may be killed
10,000 virtualised about 400 30 ms +15 MB (data only) smooth

Backend engineers recognise the shape: it is SELECT * without LIMIT. Most of the cost is not React; it is the browser's layout and paint work on nodes nobody is looking at.

Mental model

Imagine a database cursor over a large result set. You do not materialise ten million rows in memory; you fetch the window you need. A virtualised list is a cursor over DOM: the data may be all in memory, but only the window on screen is materialised as elements. Pagination is the same idea one level lower, on the network.

How it works

flowchart TB
    scroll["Scroll container, fixed height 600 px"] --> spacer["Inner spacer, height = rows x estimated row height"]
    spacer --> visible["Rows 120 to 140 rendered, translated to their offsets"]
    scroll -->|"scroll event, scrollTop 5760"| calc["Virtualizer computes first and last visible index"]
    calc -->|"index 120 to 132 plus overscan 8"| visible
    visible -->|"measureElement reports real heights"| calc
  1. The scroll container has a fixed height (600 px) and overflow: auto.
  2. Inside it, a spacer element is as tall as all rows would be: count x estimatedSize (10,000 x 48 px = 480,000 px), so the scrollbar looks right.
  3. On scroll, the virtualizer reads scrollTop, finds which indices fall in the visible range, adds overscan, and returns that small list of "virtual items", each with an index, start offset and size.
  4. You render only those items, positioned with transform: translateY(start).
  5. For variable-height rows, each rendered row is measured after mount, and the virtualizer corrects offsets.

@tanstack/react-virtual (version 3) is the headless library most teams use: it calculates, you render. react-window and react-virtuoso are alternatives. Before reaching for any of them, consider two cheaper options:

  • Paginate or load more. If users look at 50 orders at a time, show 50. Infinite scroll with a data library (Part 72) still loads only what is scrolled to.
  • content-visibility: auto in CSS lets the browser skip layout and paint for off-screen sections while keeping them in the DOM (searchable with Ctrl+F). It helps for hundreds of rows, not tens of thousands.

Practical example

An operations dashboard for a delivery company lists today's orders for a city: 6,000 to 15,000 rows, filtered and sorted on the server, with live status updates. Agents scroll and use keyboard navigation. The team chose virtualisation (users genuinely scan the full list), cursor-loaded pages of 200 rows from the API, and fixed row heights (48 px) because fixed heights make the virtualizer exact and cheap.

React / Next.js example

// src/ops/OrdersTable.tsx  (React 18, @tanstack/react-virtual 3)
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { useVirtualizer } from '@tanstack/react-virtual';
import type { OpsOrderRow } from '@shop/contracts';

const ROW_HEIGHT = 48;

export function OrdersTable({ rows, onEndReached }: { rows: OpsOrderRow[]; onEndReached: () => void }) {
  const parentRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);

  const virtualizer = useVirtualizer({
    count: rows.length,
    getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current,
    estimateSize: () => ROW_HEIGHT,   // exact here: fixed-height rows
    overscan: 8,                      // render 8 extra rows each side to avoid blank flashes
  });

  const items = virtualizer.getVirtualItems();
  const lastIndex = items[items.length - 1]?.index ?? -1;
  useEffect(() => {
    if (lastIndex >= rows.length - 20) onEndReached(); // prefetch the next page early; not in render
  }, [lastIndex, rows.length, onEndReached]);

  return (
    <div ref={parentRef} role="table" aria-rowcount={rows.length} style={{ height: 600, overflow: 'auto' }}>
      <div style={{ height: virtualizer.getTotalSize(), position: 'relative' }}>
        {items.map((item) => {
          const row = rows[item.index]!;
          return (
            <div key={row.id} role="row" aria-rowindex={item.index + 1}   /* stable key: the order ID */
              style={{ position: 'absolute', top: 0, left: 0, right: 0, height: item.size,
                       transform: `translateY(${item.start}px)` }}>
              <span role="cell">{row.displayId}</span>
              <span role="cell">{row.status}</span>
              <span role="cell">{row.restaurantName}</span>
              <span role="cell">{row.etaMinutes} min</span>
            </div>
          );
        })}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Notes that matter: the key is the order ID, not item.index, so a live update that reorders rows keeps identity; aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex tell assistive technology the real size; and onEndReached should be idempotent, because it fires on several renders (a data library's fetchNextPage ignores calls while a page is loading). For variable heights, pass ref={virtualizer.measureElement} and data-index={item.index} on each row.

Backend side (NestJS)

A virtualised list is only as good as the API that feeds it:

  • Cursor pagination with a capped limit (71.3 showed the keyset query). Accept limit up to 200 for this screen and reject more; a client asking for 50,000 rows is a bug or an attack.
  • Slim rows. The list needs 6 fields, not the full order with items and addresses. A list-specific DTO cut one team's payload from 2.1 KB to 160 bytes per row: 200 rows went from 420 KB to 32 KB.
  • Do not compute exact totals by default. SELECT count(*) over a 40-million-row table with filters can take seconds. Return hasMore, or an estimate, and compute exact counts only on request or from a maintained counter.
