  • Exports are jobs, not lists. "Download all 80,000 orders as CSV" belongs in a background job (Part 36 — Background Jobs and Schedulers) that produces a file and a signed URL, not in a JSON endpoint the table calls with limit=80000.
// apps/api/src/ops/ops-orders.query.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const OpsOrdersQuerySchema = z.object({
  city: z.string().min(2).max(40),
  status: z.enum(['PLACED', 'PREPARING', 'PICKED_UP', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED']).optional(),
  cursor: z.string().max(200).optional(),          // opaque, base64 of (placed_at, id)
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(200).default(100),
});
// The controller returns { items: OpsOrderRow[], nextCursor: string | null } with 6 fields per row.

Production scenario

The ops dashboard above initially loaded the whole city in one request: 14,000 rows, 9.8 MB of JSON, JSON.parse 120 ms, React render plus layout 3.4 s on agents' laptops, and each live status update re-rendered the full table (900 ms). After virtualisation, slim rows and 200-row pages: first page 32 KB, first render 28 ms, live updates re-render one row's component in under 2 ms.

Failure scenario

After virtualising the order list, support agents reported "orders are missing". They were not: agents used the browser's Ctrl+F to find an order number, and virtualised rows that are not mounted do not exist in the DOM, so the browser could not find them. Printing the page also printed only 20 rows.

The fixes were product decisions, not code tricks: a real search box that queried the API by order number (faster than scrolling anyway), a "Print" button that generated a server-side PDF, and a note in the team's design guidelines that any virtualised list must ship with a search box.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Ctrl+F, printing and "select all" see only mounted rows.
  • Variable row heights with a bad estimate cause the scrollbar to jump; measure rows or keep heights fixed.
  • Scroll restoration on Back navigation needs the scroll offset and loaded pages to be restored together.
  • Live updates that insert above the viewport shift content down; anchor on the visible item.
  • Keyboard focus on a row that scrolls out of view is lost when the row unmounts; manage focus by index.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior first asks whether users need a long list at all. Search, filters and pagination are often better UX and much cheaper. When a long list is real, they virtualise, use fixed heights if the design allows, keep keys as IDs, and design the API as a cursor over slim rows with hard limits. They do not let the frontend become the place where a 50,000-row export is assembled.

Common mistakes

  • Rendering thousands of rows and blaming React for the slowness.
  • Virtualising a 40-row list, adding complexity and breaking Ctrl+F for nothing.
  • Using the virtual index as key for data that reorders.
  • Fetching everything so that client-side filtering "feels fast".

Interview questions

  1. How does list virtualisation work? Expected answer: a scroll container with a full-height spacer; compute visible indices from scrollTop and row sizes; render only those plus overscan, positioned by offset; measure variable heights. Follow-up: what breaks? (Ctrl+F, printing, focus, scroll restoration.)
  2. When would you not virtualise? Expected answer: small lists, when pagination or search serves the user better, or when in-page search and printing are essential.
  3. What does the API need to provide for a 15,000-row ops table? Expected answer: cursor pagination, capped limits, slim row DTOs, no expensive exact counts by default, and exports as background jobs.

Practical exercise

Render 20,000 orders from a NestJS endpoint, first naively, then virtualised.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A Performance panel recording for both versions, with first-render time and DOM node count.
  • The virtualised table renders fewer than 60 row components at any time and scrolls at 60 fps.
  • The API rejects limit=1000 with 400 and returns pages of slim rows with an opaque cursor.
  • A search box finds an order that is not currently rendered.

71.10 Component patterns: composition, lifting state up, container and presentational components

Concept

Four patterns account for most of how real React code is organised:

  • Composition: components accept other elements as props, most often children, instead of knowing about every possible child. A Card renders whatever is inside it; a Dialog takes title, children and actions slots.
  • Lifting state up: when two sibling components need the same state, move it to their closest common parent and pass it down as props, with callbacks to change it. One source of truth.
  • Container and presentational components: a container knows where data comes from (calls hooks, handles loading and errors); a presentational component only renders props. The split is a convention, not an API.
  • Custom hooks as the container's engine: in modern code the "container" is often a thin component calling a custom hook (useOrder, usePlaceOrder) and passing results to presentational children.

Why does it exist?

Without composition, generic components grow props for every case (showHeader, headerIcon, footerButtons, footerAlign) until they are unmaintainable. Without lifting state, siblings each keep their own copy of a value and fall out of sync: the coupon input thinks a coupon is applied while the price summary does not. Without a container/presentational split, every component fetches its own data, testing requires a network mock for every leaf, and changing the API touches 40 files.

Composition also solves prop drilling more often than context does: instead of passing user through five layers, the top component builds <Header avatar={<Avatar user={user} />} />, and the intermediate layers only pass an element through.

Mental model

Composition is dependency injection: Dialog does not construct its buttons; the caller injects them. Lifting state up is moving a value from two services' private caches into one shared repository. Container and presentational map directly to controller and view, or to a NestJS service and its DTO serializer: one layer talks to the outside world, the other is pure and trivially testable.

How it works

flowchart TB
    container["CheckoutContainer: useCart, usePlaceOrder"] -->|"cart, totals, onApplyCoupon"| layout["CheckoutLayout: slots"]
    layout --> couponBox["CouponBox: code, error, onApply"]
    layout --> priceBox["PriceSummary: totals"]
    layout --> payBox["PayButton: pending, onPay"]
    couponBox -->|"onApply code"| container
    payBox -->|"onPay"| container
  1. Data flows down from the container as props.
  2. Events flow up through callback props (onApply, onPay).
  3. State lives at the lowest common owner. The applied coupon affects both CouponBox and PriceSummary, so it lives in the container (or, better, in the server's cart response the container holds).
  4. Layout components use slots. CheckoutLayout takes summary, main and footer elements and arranges them, knowing nothing about checkout.

A fifth pattern you will meet: compound components, where a parent shares implicit state with its children through context (<Tabs><Tabs.List /><Tabs.Panel /></Tabs>). Headless UI libraries (Radix UI, React Aria, Headless UI) use it to give you accessible behaviour without styling.

Practical example

The coupon field and the price summary on a checkout page. Version 1 (wrong): CouponBox holds appliedCoupon in its own state and calls the API; PriceSummary holds its own totals from the first cart load. After applying a coupon, the box shows "SAVE10 applied" and the summary still shows the old total.

Version 2 (lifted): the container owns the cart (from the server cache), CouponBox receives appliedCoupon and onApply, PriceSummary receives totals. Applying calls the API, the API returns the repriced cart, the container updates it, and both children re-render from the same data.

React / Next.js example

// src/ui/Dialog.tsx: composition with slots (presentational, reusable everywhere)
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

type Props = { title: string; children: ReactNode; actions: ReactNode; onClose: () => void };

export function Dialog({ title, children, actions, onClose }: Props) {
  return (
    <div role="dialog" aria-modal="true" aria-labelledby="dlg-title" className="dialog">
      <h2 id="dlg-title">{title}</h2>
      <div className="dialog__body">{children}</div>
      <footer className="dialog__actions">{actions}</footer>
      <button type="button" aria-label="Close" onClick={onClose} className="dialog__close">x</button>
    </div>
  );
}
// src/orders/CancelOrderContainer.tsx: container owns data and the mutation
import { useState } from 'react';
import { useCancelOrder } from './useCancelOrder';   // custom hook wrapping the mutation (Part 72)
import { Dialog } from '../ui/Dialog';
import { CancelReasonPicker, type Reason } from './CancelReasonPicker'; // presentational

export function CancelOrderContainer({ orderId, onDone }: { orderId: string; onDone: () => void }) {
  const [reason, setReason] = useState<Reason | null>(null);          // lifted: picker and button both need it
  const { cancel, isPending, error } = useCancelOrder(orderId);

  return (
    <Dialog
      title="Cancel this order?"
      onClose={onDone}
      actions={
        <button type="button" disabled={!reason || isPending}
          onClick={async () => { if (reason && (await cancel(reason))) onDone(); }}>
          {isPending ? 'Cancelling...' : 'Cancel order'}
        </button>
      }
    >
      <CancelReasonPicker value={reason} onChange={setReason} />
      {error && <p role="alert">{error.message}</p>}
    </Dialog>
  );
}

Dialog and CancelReasonPicker can be tested and shown in Storybook with plain props. CancelOrderContainer is the only piece that needs a mocked API (Part 77 — Frontend Testing and Quality).

Backend side (NestJS)

Containers map to data sources, so the API's granularity decides how many containers a screen needs and how many requests it makes:

  • One container, one view endpoint for regions that always load together (the checkout summary: cart, totals, addresses, available payment methods). A GET /v1/checkout/view that aggregates in the service is one round trip instead of four.
  • Separate endpoints for regions with different freshness: live order status (SSE, 71.4) is separate from the order details (cacheable for minutes).
  • Mutations return the state the container needs next (71.2), so lifted state is replaced from one response.
  • Consistent error shapes let one custom hook map errors for every container (71.7).
// apps/api/src/checkout/checkout-view.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { CheckoutView } from '@shop/contracts';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { CheckoutViewService } from './checkout-view.service';

@Controller('v1/checkout')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class CheckoutViewController {
  constructor(private readonly view: CheckoutViewService) {}

  @Get('view')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-store')
  get(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser): Promise<CheckoutView> {
    // Loads cart, saved addresses and payment methods in parallel (Promise.all), prices once:
    // about 25 ms server time, one 4 KB response, instead of four client round trips.
    return this.view.forUser(user.id);
  }
}

When several frontends need different aggregations, this logic moves into a BFF (Part 73 — Next.js and Rendering Strategies) rather than into a growing list of screen-specific endpoints in a domain service.

Production scenario

A food delivery app's restaurant page had every card (menu item, offer banner, rating widget) fetch its own data: 38 requests on page load, with a waterfall four levels deep. Time to a complete page on 4G was 3.9 s. Refactoring into three containers (restaurant header, menu, offers) backed by two view endpoints cut it to 6 requests and 1.4 s, and made 30 of the components pure enough to snapshot in Storybook.

Failure scenario

The checkout "Place order" button was disabled until termsAccepted was true. The terms checkbox lived in one component with its own state; the button lived in another, which kept its own termsAccepted copy synced by an effect from a shared event emitter. Under a slow render on one Android WebView, the effect ran late: the checkbox showed ticked, the button stayed disabled for a few seconds, and some customers left. Lifting termsAccepted into the checkout container and passing it to both removed the emitter, the effect and the bug.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lifting state too high (into the app root) re-renders large trees on every change; lift to the lowest common owner.
  • Containers inside presentational components quietly bring fetching back into leaves.
  • Slot props recreated every render defeat memo on the layout; usually harmless, occasionally measurable (71.12).
  • Compound components used outside their parent throw or misbehave; give them a clear error like useSession in 71.5.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior keeps one owner per piece of state and lets the rest of the tree be pure. They reach for composition before context, and for a container-plus-hook before scattering fetches. They also shape the API around the containers they intend to build: a screen with three containers should need about three requests, not thirty.

Common mistakes

  • Duplicating state in siblings and syncing it with effects or event emitters.
  • Boolean prop explosions on generic components instead of slots.
  • Every leaf fetching its own data.
  • Building an endpoint per component instead of per screen region.

Interview questions

  1. Two sibling components need the same value. What do you do? Expected answer: lift it to the closest common parent and pass it down with a change callback; if it is server data, keep it in the server cache both read from. Follow-up: when would context or a store be better?
  2. What is the container/presentational split, and why does it help testing? Expected answer: containers handle data and side effects, presentational components render props; presentational ones need no mocks.
  3. How does composition reduce prop drilling? Expected answer: the top component builds the element that needs the data and passes the element down, so intermediate layers do not need the data.
  4. How should API granularity relate to the component tree? Expected answer: one request per region that loads together, separate streams for different freshness, mutations returning next state.

Practical exercise

Refactor a checkout page where the coupon box and price summary hold separate copies of totals.

Acceptance criteria:

  • One container owns the cart; both children are presentational and receive props.
  • A Dialog with slots is reused for "Remove item" and "Cancel order" without new boolean props.
  • The page makes one GET /v1/checkout/view request on load, and a coupon apply makes one POST whose response updates both children.
  • Presentational components have tests with no network mocks.

71.11 Error boundaries and Suspense

Concept

An error boundary is a component that catches errors thrown while rendering the components below it and shows a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole page. Suspense is a component that shows a fallback (a skeleton, a spinner) while something below it is not ready yet: a lazily loaded code chunk, or data read through a Suspense-enabled source.

Both are declarative boundaries in the tree. You place them where you want failure or loading to be contained: "if the recommendations widget breaks, the rest of the order page keeps working", "while the payment chunk loads, show a skeleton for that panel only".

Why does it exist?

Since React 16, an uncaught error during rendering unmounts the entire React root. The user sees a blank white page. One undefined.toFixed() in a "You may also like" carousel takes down the checkout. Before boundaries, every component had to defend itself; with them, you decide the blast radius in a few places.

Suspense exists because loading states were scattered: five data sources meant five spinners popping in at different times, shifting layout (69.5). Suspense lets a parent show one skeleton for a region and lets frameworks stream server HTML region by region (Part 73).

Mental model

An error boundary is a try/catch around a subtree's rendering, or a bulkhead on a ship: water in one compartment does not sink the vessel. In NestJS terms it is an exception filter scoped to part of the tree, turning a crash into a well-formed fallback response.

Suspense is a loading barrier: like Promise.all for a region, with a placeholder shown until the region's promises resolve.

How it works

flowchart TB
    root["App root"] --> pageBoundary["ErrorBoundary: page level"]
    pageBoundary --> layout["OrderPage layout"]
    layout --> detailsSuspense["Suspense: details skeleton"]
    detailsSuspense --> details["OrderDetails reads order"]
    layout --> recBoundary["ErrorBoundary: recommendations, fallback renders nothing"]
    recBoundary --> recSuspense["Suspense: carousel skeleton"]
    recSuspense --> recs["Recommendations lazy chunk"]

Error boundaries.

  1. A boundary is a class component with static getDerivedStateFromError(error) (return state that switches to the fallback) and optionally componentDidCatch(error, info) (log it, with info.componentStack). There is still no hook equivalent in React 18 or 19; most teams use the react-error-boundary package, which wraps the class.
  2. When a component below throws during render, in a lifecycle method or in a constructor, React finds the nearest boundary above, renders its fallback, and unmounts the broken subtree.
  3. Boundaries do not catch errors in event handlers, in asynchronous code (setTimeout, promise callbacks), during server rendering, or in the boundary itself. For event handlers, use try/catch and show an inline error. To send an async error to a boundary, set it in state and throw it during render; react-error-boundary provides useErrorBoundary().showBoundary(error) for exactly this.
  4. In React 19, createRoot accepts onCaughtError and onUncaughtError options, a single place to report every error to your monitoring tool (Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends), and React logs each error once instead of twice.

Suspense.

  1. A component suspends when it cannot render yet. React then shows the nearest <Suspense fallback> above it and retries when the awaited thing resolves.
  2. What can suspend: React.lazy(() => import('./PaymentPanel')) code chunks (since React 16.6); data from Suspense-enabled libraries in React 18 (TanStack Query's useSuspenseQuery, Relay, Next.js server components); and in React 19, use(promise) with a cached promise.
  3. A plain useEffect fetch does not suspend; it only sets state.
  4. Transitions change the behaviour. If an update wrapped in startTransition (or a router navigation, which most routers wrap) causes a suspend, React keeps showing the old UI with an isPending flag instead of replacing already visible content with a fallback. That avoids the "page flashes to skeleton on every tab click" problem.
  5. Siblings inside one boundary are revealed together; nested boundaries reveal progressively, outer first.

Practical example

An order details page:

Region Error boundary fallback Suspense fallback
Whole page "Something went wrong" with a Retry button and request ID none
Order details and timeline "Could not load this order" with Retry Skeleton matching final layout
Live tracking map (lazy chunk, 180 KB) Static text ETA, no map Map-sized grey box
Recommendations Render nothing Small skeleton
Support chat widget (third party) "Chat unavailable, call us" none

The rule: wrap each independent region, choose a fallback the user can act on, and make skeletons the same size as the content to avoid layout shift.

React / Next.js example

// src/orders/OrderPageShell.tsx  (React 18, react-error-boundary 4, TanStack Query v5)
import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';
import { ErrorBoundary, type FallbackProps } from 'react-error-boundary';
import { QueryErrorResetBoundary, useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { fetchOrderView } from '../api/orders';
import { OrderDetails } from './OrderDetails';
import { OrderSkeleton } from './OrderSkeleton';
import { reportClientError } from '../observability/report';

const TrackingMap = lazy(() => import('./TrackingMap'));          // separate chunk (76.5)

function OrderRegion({ orderId }: { orderId: string }) {
  const { data } = useSuspenseQuery({ queryKey: ['order', orderId], queryFn: () => fetchOrderView(orderId) });
  return <OrderDetails order={data} onCancel={async () => {}} />;  // data is never undefined here
}

function OrderError({ error, resetErrorBoundary }: FallbackProps) {
  const requestId = (error as { requestId?: string }).requestId;  // from the API error (77.7)
  return (
    <div role="alert">
      <p>We could not load this order.</p>
      {requestId && <p>Reference: <code>{requestId}</code></p>}
      <button type="button" onClick={resetErrorBoundary}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  );
}

export function OrderPageShell({ orderId }: { orderId: string }) {
  return (
    <QueryErrorResetBoundary>
      {({ reset }) => (
        <ErrorBoundary FallbackComponent={OrderError} onReset={reset} resetKeys={[orderId]}
          onError={(error, info) => reportClientError(error, info.componentStack)}>
          <Suspense fallback={<OrderSkeleton />}>
            <OrderRegion orderId={orderId} />
          </Suspense>
          <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Live map unavailable. ETA is shown above.</p>}>
            <Suspense fallback={<div className="map-placeholder" style={{ height: 320 }} />}>
              <TrackingMap orderId={orderId} />
            </Suspense>
          </ErrorBoundary>
        </ErrorBoundary>
      )}
    </QueryErrorResetBoundary>
  );
}

resetKeys={[orderId]} clears the error when the user navigates to a different order; QueryErrorResetBoundary makes "Try again" refetch instead of re-throwing the cached error. In the Next.js App Router, error.tsx and loading.tsx files create these boundaries per route segment for you (Part 73).

Backend side (NestJS)

A fallback is only useful if it carries information the user and support can act on. The API should make every error identifiable and classifiable:

// apps/api/src/common/http-exception.filter.ts
import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpException, HttpStatus, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request, Response } from 'express';

@Catch()
export class AllExceptionsFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  private readonly logger = new Logger('HTTP');

  catch(exception: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost): void {
    const ctx = host.switchToHttp();
    const req = ctx.getRequest<Request>();
    const res = ctx.getResponse<Response>();
    const requestId = (req.headers['x-request-id'] as string) ?? crypto.randomUUID();
    const status = exception instanceof HttpException ? exception.getStatus() : HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR;
    const body = exception instanceof HttpException ? exception.getResponse() : { code: 'INTERNAL' };

    if (status >= 500) this.logger.error({ requestId, path: req.url, err: exception });
    res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', requestId);  // expose it via CORS exposedHeaders if cross-origin
    res.status(status).json({ ...(typeof body === 'object' ? body : { message: body }), requestId });
  }
}

Three more backend duties:

  • Status codes the UI can branch on. 404 renders "Order not found" (no retry), 401 redirects to login, 409 refetches, 429 and 503 retry after Retry-After, 500 shows the boundary with the request ID. A 200 with { "error": ... } defeats all of this.
  • A client error intake. componentDidCatch/onError reports go somewhere: a monitoring service, or a POST /v1/client-errors endpoint with @Throttle and a body size limit, because a broken bundle on 100,000 devices will report in a loop.
  • Do not stream half a page you cannot finish. With streaming SSR (Part 73), headers are sent before all data is ready; the backend must keep slow dependencies out of the first chunk or give them timeouts.

Production scenario

A marketplace added a top-level boundary plus per-widget ones. About 0.3 % of sessions hit a caught error, mostly in a third-party reviews widget; before, each was a blank page, after, 92 % continued to checkout.

Failure scenario

A Monday deploy added discountLabel.toUpperCase() to the cart line component. For free-gift lines the API sent discountLabel: null, and with no boundary below the root, React unmounted the whole app: a blank page for about 7 % of carts during a promotion. The on-call engineer saw a healthy backend and spent 40 minutes looking at the API.

Fixes: boundaries around the cart and each checkout step, the shared zod schema parsing the response (so null vs string was caught at the network boundary and reported precisely, 71.4), and an alert on client error rate per release (Part 78).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Errors in event handlers are not caught; wrap async handlers and show inline errors.
  • A boundary that throws in its fallback escalates to the next boundary up.
  • Retry loops: "Try again" that re-renders without refetching hits the same cached error.
  • Suspense fallback flashes on fast networks; keep old UI with transitions, or show skeletons only after about 200 ms.
  • Creating promises during render for use (React 19) creates a new promise every render and suspends forever; cache promises outside render.
  • Lazy chunk load failures after a deploy (old HTML, deleted chunk) throw a ChunkLoadError; catch it in a boundary and offer a reload (Part 78 tells that incident story).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior draws failure and loading boundaries on the page design, not after the first incident. Every independent region gets a boundary with an actionable fallback, skeletons match final layout, and all caught errors are reported with the request ID and release version. They treat error responses as part of the contract: status codes that mean something, a request ID on every response, and a body the UI can trust.

Common mistakes

  • No boundary below the root, so any render error is a blank page.
  • One boundary around everything, so a broken widget hides the whole page.
  • Expecting boundaries to catch async or event handler errors.
  • Spinners per component instead of region-level Suspense.
  • Errors reported without a request ID or release, impossible to correlate with backend logs.

Interview questions

  1. What does an error boundary catch, and what does it not catch? Expected answer: errors during render, lifecycle methods and constructors below it; not event handlers, async code, SSR or itself. Follow-up: how do you route an async error to a boundary? (Set state and throw in render, or showBoundary.)
  2. What can suspend in React 18 vs React 19? Expected answer: 18: React.lazy and Suspense-enabled libraries or frameworks; 19 adds use(promise) with cached promises.
  3. Why do transitions matter for Suspense? Expected answer: they keep the current UI visible with a pending flag instead of replacing it with a fallback.
  4. What should an API return so an error fallback is useful? Expected answer: meaningful status codes, a consistent error body, and a request ID header and field.

Practical exercise

Add boundaries and Suspense to an order page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Forcing a render error in the recommendations widget leaves the rest of the page usable.
  • The order region shows a skeleton of the same height as the content, and "Try again" refetches.
  • Every caught error is reported once with release version and the API's request ID, visible in NestJS logs for the same request.
  • A 404 from the API renders "Order not found" without a retry button.

71.12 Performance basics: unnecessary renders, memoisation tradeoffs and the React Profiler

Concept

React performance problems come in three kinds:

  1. Too many renders: one update re-renders far more components than changed (a keystroke re-rendering a 2,000-row table).
  2. Too expensive renders: one component does heavy work in render (sorting 20,000 items, formatting 5,000 dates with a new Intl.DateTimeFormat each time).
  3. Too much DOM: the browser's layout and paint work dominates (71.9).

The browser has about 16 ms per frame at 60 Hz, and users notice input delay above about 100 ms. Interaction to Next Paint (INP), a Core Web Vital, measures that delay on real devices; under 200 ms is "good" (Part 76 — Web Performance).

The React Profiler measures which components rendered, how long each took and why. It exists as a tab in React DevTools and as a <Profiler> component you can put in code.

Why does it exist?

React's default is safe: when a component re-renders, its children re-render too. That is cheap for most trees. Without measurement, teams either ignore real problems or wrap everything in memo, which adds complexity and hides bugs (71.6). The Profiler turns "it feels slow" into "OrderRow rendered 2,000 times in a 140 ms commit because its onSelect prop changed".

Mental model

Think of a re-render like a cache invalidation that cascades through dependent views. The goal is not zero invalidations; it is invalidating only what depends on the change. The Profiler is EXPLAIN ANALYZE for a commit: it shows the plan React actually executed and where the time went.

How it works

Techniques, in the order a senior tries them:

  1. Measure first. React DevTools > Profiler > record, perform the slow interaction, stop. The flamegraph shows each commit; the ranked view lists the slowest components. Enable "Record why each component rendered while profiling" in the Profiler settings to see "props changed: onSelect" or "parent rendered". Use a production build for real numbers: development builds are 2 to 5 times slower. For profiling production, alias react-dom$ to react-dom/profiling in the bundler.
  2. Move state down. If typing in a search box re-renders the whole page, the input's state lives too high. Put it in the component that uses it.
  3. Lift content up (children as props). A component with frequently changing state that wraps an expensive subtree can receive the subtree as children; the children are created by the parent, so they do not re-render when the wrapper's state changes.
  4. Split context by change frequency (71.5).
  5. Memoise at the boundary. Wrap the expensive child in memo and make its props stable (useMemo, useCallback, or primitive props). memo(Component, arePropsEqual?) skips rendering when props are shallowly equal.
  6. Make renders cheaper. Hoist constants and formatters out of render, precompute on the server, use useMemo for heavy derived data.
  7. Defer non-urgent work with useDeferredValue or startTransition (69.7 shows an example), so input stays responsive while a big list catches up.
  8. Reduce DOM: virtualise (71.9).
  9. Turn on the React Compiler (71.6) and delete manual memoisation it makes redundant.

Memoisation tradeoffs:

Choice Benefit Cost
No memoisation Simple code, nothing to keep in sync Children re-render with parents
memo on a leaf rendered 2,000 times Large: skips most renders Shallow compare per render; useless if any prop is unstable
useCallback everywhere Usually none Noise, dependency bugs, stale closures
React Compiler Automatic, fine-grained Build plugin; code must follow the rules of React

Practical example

An order management screen: a filter bar, a 300-row virtualised table (71.9) and a details side panel. Selecting a row took 140 ms. The Profiler showed every visible row (40) and the filter bar re-rendering on selection, because selectedId lived at the page level and each row received onSelect={() => setSelectedId(row.id)}, a new function per render. Each row also built an Intl.NumberFormat in render.

Changes: hoisting the formatter to module scope (row render 1.1 ms to 0.2 ms), passing isSelected (boolean) and a stable onSelect(id) callback to memo(OrderRow), and moving the filter bar's input state into the filter bar. Selection commits fell to 9 ms, with 2 rows (old and new selection) and the panel rendering.

React / Next.js example

// src/ops/OrderRow.tsx  (React 18)
import { memo } from 'react';
import type { OpsOrderRow } from '@shop/contracts';

const money = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' }); // once, not per render

type Props = { row: OpsOrderRow; isSelected: boolean; onSelect: (id: string) => void };

export const OrderRow = memo(function OrderRow({ row, isSelected, onSelect }: Props) {
  return (
    <div role="row" aria-selected={isSelected} onClick={() => onSelect(row.id)}>
      <span role="cell">{row.displayId}</span>
      <span role="cell">{row.status}</span>
      <span role="cell">{money.format(Number(row.totalMinor) / 100)}</span>
    </div>
  );
});
// src/ops/OrdersScreen.tsx: stable callback, primitive props, measured with <Profiler>
import { Profiler, useCallback, useState, type ProfilerOnRenderCallback } from 'react';
import type { OpsOrderRow } from '@shop/contracts';
import { OrderRow } from './OrderRow';

const onRender: ProfilerOnRenderCallback = (id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration) => {
  // actualDuration: time spent rendering this commit; baseDuration: estimated time without memoisation.
  if (actualDuration > 16) navigator.sendBeacon('/api/v1/rum/slow-commit',
    JSON.stringify({ id, phase, actualDuration: Math.round(actualDuration), baseDuration: Math.round(baseDuration) }));
};

export function OrdersScreen({ rows }: { rows: OpsOrderRow[] }) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const onSelect = useCallback((id: string) => setSelectedId(id), []); // setter is stable, so [] is correct

  return (
    <Profiler id="OrdersTable" onRender={onRender}>
      {rows.map((r) => <OrderRow key={r.id} row={r} isSelected={r.id === selectedId} onSelect={onSelect} />)}
    </Profiler>
  );
}

<Profiler> is disabled in normal production builds (its callback does not fire) unless you use the profiling build; sample it on a small percentage of sessions if you enable it in production, because it adds overhead.

Backend side (NestJS)

The backend influences render cost more than most backend engineers expect:

  • Stable data means fewer renders. TanStack Query and similar libraries use structural sharing: after a refetch, unchanged objects keep their old references, so memo rows whose data did not change skip rendering. That only works if the API returns the same data in the same shape: deterministic ordering (ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC, never unordered), no per-response timestamps like serverTime inside every row, and no random IDs for computed rows (71.3).
  • 304 is the cheapest response. For polled resources, send an ETag and Cache-Control: private, no-cache. The Express adapter in NestJS generates weak ETags for JSON responses by default, and returns 304 Not Modified when the browser sends a matching If-None-Match. A 304 has no body to download or parse, and the cache keeps its existing objects.
  • Payload size is main-thread time. Parsing JSON costs roughly 1 ms per 100 to 200 KB on a mid-range phone, before React touches it. Slim list DTOs (71.9) and server-side aggregation (71.6) are render optimisations.
  • A RUM endpoint for slow commits (like the sendBeacon above) should be cheap, unauthenticated or token-light, throttled and sampled; it should never be on the critical path.
// apps/api/src/orders/orders-poll.controller.ts (excerpt)
@Get('active')
@Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache')   // revalidate every time; Express adds a weak ETag
listActive(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser) {
  return this.orders.activeForCustomer(user.id); // ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC: deterministic
}

Production scenario

A cloud kitchen's order board polled every 5 s and re-rendered all 120 cards each time (35 to 60 ms on cheap tablets, laggy touch). The API stopped adding fetchedAt to every card and ordered results deterministically, so structural sharing kept unchanged cards identical; the poll returned 304 when nothing changed (70 % of polls); cards were wrapped in memo. Poll commits dropped to 0 ms (304) or 3 to 5 ms.

Failure scenario

A team chasing a slow checkout wrapped everything in memo and useCallback. Commit times barely moved: the real cost was parsing a 1.2 MB response and sorting 8,000 delivery slots every render. Worse, a custom arePropsEqual comparing only id stopped slots updating when availability changed, and 140 customers picked full slots before payment rejected them.

The Profiler would have pointed at the sort in five minutes. The fixes: the API returned only the next 3 days of slots (40 KB), the sort moved to SQL, the custom comparator was deleted, and the team adopted "no memoisation without a Profiler screenshot in the pull request".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Profiling development builds exaggerates costs and changes the ranking.
  • Custom arePropsEqual comparators that skip fields cause stale UI.
  • memo with children props almost never helps: JSX children are new objects every render.
  • Strict Mode double rendering in development doubles render counts; do not count it as a production problem.
  • The Profiler measures React, not the browser: long layout or paint shows in the Performance panel (69.10), not in the React Profiler.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior profiles first, in a production build, on a representative device; fixes structure (state placement, context splits, virtualisation) before memoising measured hot spots; and checks the backend's share, because payload size, deterministic responses and 304s are often the cheapest render optimisation.

Common mistakes

  • Optimising without measuring.
  • Memoising everything, then debugging stale closures.
  • Unstable props (inline objects, arrow functions) to memo children, making memo pointless.
  • Doing heavy work in render that belongs on the server or in useMemo.
  • Ignoring the browser's layout cost while tuning React render times.

Interview questions

  1. A keystroke in a search box makes the page lag. How do you investigate and fix it? Expected answer: profile in a production build; check which components render and why; move state down, memoise the expensive subtree with stable props, defer the list with useDeferredValue, virtualise, or move filtering to the server. Follow-up: how would you confirm the fix with real users? (INP from RUM.)
  2. When does memo help and when does it not? Expected answer: helps for expensive components re-rendered with equal props; useless with unstable props or children; harmful with incorrect custom comparators.
  3. What do actualDuration and baseDuration mean in the Profiler API? Expected answer: time spent rendering the committed update vs estimated time to render the whole subtree without memoisation.
  4. How can the backend reduce React render work? Expected answer: deterministic responses for structural sharing, ETag and 304 for polls, slim payloads, server-side aggregation and sorting.

Practical exercise

Profile and fix a slow order selection interaction in a 300-row table.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Before-and-after Profiler screenshots from a production build, with commit times and rendered component counts.
  • Selection renders at most the two affected rows and the details panel.
  • The poll endpoint returns 304 when nothing changed, verified in the Network panel, and unchanged rows do not re-render after a 200 poll.
  • A pull request description that explains each memoisation with a measured number.

71.13 Worked example: a checkout form with address, coupon and payment steps

Concept

We now assemble the Part into one feature: a three-step checkout for a grocery delivery app, built with React 18, React Hook Form 7, zod and TanStack Query v5 on top of the NestJS API used throughout this Volume.

Requirements, written the way a senior would write them before coding:

  • Steps: address, then coupon (optional), then payment and "Place order". The user can go back to edit the address from the payment step.
  • Server is the truth for money. Every change that affects price (address changes the delivery fee, coupon changes the discount) returns recomputed totals from the API. The UI never adds numbers.
  • One order per attempt, even with double taps, timeouts and retries (71.8).
  • Precise errors: field errors under the field, business errors (postcode not serviceable, coupon expired) mapped to the right input, and an honest "unknown outcome" state.
  • Numbers: checkout view loads in one request under 300 ms p95; each step transition under 400 ms p95 on 4G; zero duplicate orders in the double-click test; no render of the whole page on keystrokes.

The flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant W as CheckoutPage
    participant A as NestJS
    participant P as PostgreSQL
    W->>A: GET /v1/checkout/view
    A-->>W: cart, version 7, totals, saved addresses
    U->>W: submits address
    W->>A: POST /v1/checkout/address
    A->>P: store address, price delivery fee, version 8
    A-->>W: totals with delivery fee, version 8
    U->>W: applies coupon SAVE50
    W->>A: POST /v1/checkout/coupon with version 8
    A-->>W: totals with discount, version 9
    U->>W: Place order, twice by accident
    W->>A: POST /v1/orders, Idempotency-Key K, version 9
    A->>P: insert order with K in one transaction
    A-->>W: 201 order A7K2Q9P
    W-->>U: confirmation page, navigated with replace

The cart version is the thread through the whole flow. Every pricing change increments it. Every write sends the version it was based on. The idempotency key is scoped to the version (71.8), so a coupon change after a failed payment attempt automatically starts a new attempt.

The contracts

Additions to @shop/contracts (zod 3.23), next to AddressSchema from 71.7:

// packages/contracts/src/checkout.ts
import { z } from 'zod';
import { AddressSchema } from './address';
import { MinorUnitsSchema } from './money';

export const CartTotalsSchema = z.object({
  subtotalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
  deliveryFeeMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
  discountMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
  totalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
  currency: z.string().length(3),
});
export type CartTotals = z.infer<typeof CartTotalsSchema>;

export const CheckoutViewSchema = z.object({
  cartId: z.string().uuid(),
  version: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
  totals: CartTotalsSchema,
  savedAddresses: z.array(AddressSchema.extend({ id: z.string() })).max(20),
  appliedCoupon: z.string().nullable(),
});
export type CheckoutView = z.infer<typeof CheckoutViewSchema>;

export const ApplyCouponSchema = z.object({
  code: z.string().trim().toUpperCase().regex(/^[A-Z0-9]{4,16}$/, 'Enter a valid code'),
  cartVersion: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
});
export type ApplyCoupon = z.infer<typeof ApplyCouponSchema>;

export const PricedCartSchema = z.object({ version: z.number().int(), totals: CartTotalsSchema, appliedCoupon: z.string().nullable() });
export type PricedCart = z.infer<typeof PricedCartSchema>;

export const PlaceOrderRequestSchema = z.object({
  cartId: z.string().uuid(),
  cartVersion: z.number().int().nonnegative(),
  paymentMethodId: z.string().min(1).max(64),
});
export type PlaceOrderRequest = z.infer<typeof PlaceOrderRequestSchema>;

The API side

Endpoint Purpose Key behaviour
GET /v1/checkout/view Everything the page needs in one request (71.10) Cache-Control: private, no-store
POST /v1/checkout/address Validate, check serviceability, price delivery (71.7) 422 with path: "postcode" when not serviceable
POST /v1/checkout/coupon Apply a coupon, reprice 422 with path: "code"; 409 CART_CHANGED on stale version; throttled
DELETE /v1/checkout/coupon Remove the coupon, reprice Returns the priced cart
POST /v1/orders Place the order (71.8) Requires Idempotency-Key; unique index; 409 CART_CHANGED

The coupon endpoint shows the patterns that are new in this example: optimistic concurrency on the cart version, business errors with field paths, and rate limiting against code guessing.

// apps/api/src/checkout/coupon.controller.ts  (@nestjs/throttler v5+)
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle, ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { ApplyCouponSchema, type ApplyCoupon, type PricedCart } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { CouponService } from './coupon.service';

@Controller('v1/checkout/coupon')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, ThrottlerGuard)
export class CouponController {
  constructor(private readonly coupons: CouponService) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(200)
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 } })  // 10 attempts a minute: stops brute-forcing codes
  apply(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser, @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(ApplyCouponSchema)) body: ApplyCoupon): Promise<PricedCart> {
    // In one transaction:
    //   UPDATE carts SET coupon_code = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3
    //   0 rows updated -> 409 { code: 'CART_CHANGED', cart: <fresh priced cart> }
    //   coupon invalid -> 422 { code: 'COUPON_REJECTED', issues: [{ path: 'code', code: 'EXPIRED', message: 'This code expired on 31 Oct' }] }
    //   otherwise reprice and return { version, totals, appliedCoupon }
    return this.coupons.apply(user.id, body.code, body.cartVersion);
  }
}

The conditional UPDATE ... WHERE version = $3 is the backend twin of the client's version thread: if another tab changed the cart, the write affects zero rows and the client gets a fresh cart to show, instead of a coupon applied to contents the user never saw (Part 21 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control).

The checkout container

The page loads the view with a data library, then hands it to a flow component keyed by cart ID (71.3), so a different cart always starts with fresh state. The flow owns the reducer from 71.5.

// src/checkout/CheckoutPage.tsx  (React 18, TanStack Query v5)
import { useReducer, useState } from 'react';
import { useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';
import { useSuspenseQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import type { CheckoutView, PricedCart } from '@shop/contracts';
import { fetchCheckoutView, saveAddress } from '../api/checkout';
import { checkoutReducer, type CheckoutState } from './checkoutReducer';  // 77.5
import { AddressForm } from './AddressForm';                              // 77.7
import { CouponStep } from './CouponStep';
import { PaymentStep } from './PaymentStep';
import { PriceSummary } from './PriceSummary';

export function CheckoutPage() {
  const { data: view } = useSuspenseQuery({ queryKey: ['checkout-view'], queryFn: fetchCheckoutView });
  return <CheckoutFlow key={view.cartId} view={view} />;  // wrapped in Suspense and an ErrorBoundary (77.11)
}

function CheckoutFlow({ view }: { view: CheckoutView }) {
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(checkoutReducer, { step: 'address', address: null, totals: view.totals } as CheckoutState);
  const [version, setVersion] = useState(view.version);                   // latest server cart version

  const onPriced = (cart: PricedCart) => setVersion(cart.version);         // every pricing response moves it

  if (state.step === 'placed') return null;                               // navigation already happened
  return (
    <div className="checkout">
      <main>
        {state.step === 'address' && (
          <AddressForm initial={view.savedAddresses[0]} onSaved={async (address) => {
            const cart = await saveAddress(address, version);                 // throws ApiError on 422
            onPriced(cart);
            dispatch({ type: 'ADDRESS_SAVED', address, totals: cart.totals });
          }} />
        )}
        {state.step === 'coupon' && (
          <CouponStep cartVersion={version} applied={state.coupon}
            onApplied={(cart) => { onPriced(cart); dispatch({ type: 'COUPON_APPLIED', coupon: cart.appliedCoupon ?? '', totals: cart.totals }); }}
            onContinue={() => dispatch({ type: 'CONTINUE_TO_PAYMENT' })} />
        )}
        {(state.step === 'payment' || state.step === 'placing') && (
          <PaymentStep cartId={view.cartId} cartVersion={version} error={state.error}
            onStart={() => dispatch({ type: 'PLACE_ORDER' })}
            onResult={(r) => {
              if (r.ok) { dispatch({ type: 'ORDER_PLACED', orderId: r.orderId }); navigate(`/orders/${r.orderId}`, { replace: true }); }
              else dispatch({ type: 'ORDER_FAILED', message: r.message });
            }} />
        )}
      </main>
      <aside><PriceSummary {...state.totals} /></aside>   {/* totals only ever come from a server response */}
    </div>
  );
}

Three design points. The version is held separately from the reducer because every server response carries it, whatever step we are in. PriceSummary renders state.totals, which only ever comes from a server response. And the confirmation page is reached with replace: true, so the Back button does not return to a live payment form (71.8).

The coupon step

A small form, also with React Hook Form, so server errors land under the input:

// src/checkout/CouponStep.tsx
import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
import { zodResolver } from '@hookform/resolvers/zod';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { ApplyCouponSchema, type PricedCart } from '@shop/contracts';
import { applyCoupon } from '../api/checkout';
import { ApiError, applyServerErrors } from '../api/errors';                // 77.7

const FormSchema = ApplyCouponSchema.pick({ code: true });               // version comes from props
type Form = z.infer<typeof FormSchema>;

type Props = { cartVersion: number; applied: string | null;
               onApplied: (cart: PricedCart) => void; onContinue: () => void };

export function CouponStep({ cartVersion, applied, onApplied, onContinue }: Props) {
  const { register, handleSubmit, setError, formState: { errors, isSubmitting } } =
    useForm<Form>({ resolver: zodResolver(FormSchema), defaultValues: { code: '' }, mode: 'onSubmit' });

  const onValid = async ({ code }: Form) => {
    try {
      onApplied(await applyCoupon({ code, cartVersion }));
    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof ApiError && e.code === 'CART_CHANGED') {
        setError('root.server', { message: 'Your cart changed in another tab. Prices have been updated.' });
        return;                                    // the api helper also refreshes the checkout view cache
      }
      if (e instanceof ApiError && applyServerErrors(e, setError)) return; // e.g. "This code expired on 31 Oct"
      setError('root.server', { message: 'Could not apply the code. Please try again.' });
    }
  };

  return (
    <section aria-labelledby="coupon-h">
      <h2 id="coupon-h">Have a coupon?</h2>
      <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onValid)} noValidate>
        <label htmlFor="code">Coupon code</label>
        <input id="code" autoComplete="off" autoCapitalize="characters" {...register('code')}
          aria-invalid={!!errors.code} aria-describedby="code-err" />
        <p id="code-err" role="alert">{errors.code?.message ?? errors.root?.server?.message}</p>
        <button type="submit" disabled={isSubmitting}>{isSubmitting ? 'Applying...' : 'Apply'}</button>
      </form>
      {applied && <p>{applied} applied.</p>}
      <button type="button" onClick={onContinue}>Continue to payment</button>
    </section>
  );
}

Typing in the coupon field re-renders nothing (uncontrolled registration); the summary in the sidebar re-renders once, when the server's new totals arrive.

The payment step

The step uses usePlaceOrder from 71.8, which owns the synchronous guard, the per-attempt key stored per cart version, timeouts and retries with the same key:

// src/checkout/PaymentStep.tsx
import { useState } from 'react';
import { usePlaceOrder } from './usePlaceOrder';                          // 77.8

type Props = { cartId: string; cartVersion: number; error: string | null;
               onStart: () => void; onResult: (r: { ok: true; orderId: string } | { ok: false; message: string }) => void };

export function PaymentStep({ cartId, cartVersion, error, onStart, onResult }: Props) {
  const [method, setMethod] = useState<string>('upi');                     // pure UI state, local
  const { submit, pending } = usePlaceOrder(cartId, cartVersion);

  return (
    <form onSubmit={async (e) => { e.preventDefault(); onStart(); onResult(await submit(method)); }}>
      <fieldset disabled={pending}>
        <legend>Payment method</legend>
        <label><input type="radio" name="pm" value="upi" checked={method === 'upi'} onChange={() => setMethod('upi')} /> UPI</label>
        <label><input type="radio" name="pm" value="card" checked={method === 'card'} onChange={() => setMethod('card')} /> Card</label>
      </fieldset>
      {error && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
      <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>{pending ? 'Placing your order...' : 'Place order'}</button>
    </form>
  );
}

A double tap calls submit twice; the second call returns immediately from the ref guard, and the reducer ignores a second PLACE_ORDER because the step is already placing. If the user is slow and the first request times out, usePlaceOrder retries with the same key and the server replays the original order. If the outcome stays unknown, the message points to "My Orders" rather than inviting a new attempt.

What can go wrong, and where it is handled

Failure Layer that handles it User sees
Postcode not serviceable API 422 path postcode, RHF setError Message under postcode, focus moved
Coupon expired API 422 path code "This code expired on 31 Oct" under the input
Cart changed in another tab Conditional UPDATE, 409 CART_CHANGED "Your cart changed", fresh totals
Double tap on Place order Ref guard, reducer, key, unique index One order
Timeout after the server committed Same-key retry, server replay Confirmation page
Payment declined 402/422 from API, key cleared Error, can choose another method
A widget throws while rendering Error boundary around the step (71.11) Step fallback with request ID
Coupon guessing script @Throttle 10/min 429 with Retry-After

Tests and acceptance criteria

Part 77 — Frontend Testing and Quality builds the full test suite; the minimum for this feature:

  • Reducer unit tests: every legal and illegal transition (71.5).
  • Component tests with MSW mocking the API: a 422 for the postcode shows the message under the field; a 409 CART_CHANGED on the coupon shows the notice and new totals; typing the coupon re-renders neither the address nor the summary.
  • API tests: the coupon endpoint returns 409 for a stale version and 429 after 10 attempts; POST /v1/orders without a key returns 400.
  • One Playwright journey against a real NestJS and PostgreSQL in Docker: complete all three steps with a double click on "Place order", then assert exactly one row in orders for the cart.
  • Profiler check: no commit over 16 ms on a mid-range Android profile during typing.

What a senior would change at scale: move the checkout aggregation into a BFF if mobile and web need different shapes (Part 73), generate the API client from OpenAPI or keep the zod contracts as the single source (Part 74), and add real-user monitoring of step timings and error codes so a regression in "postcode not serviceable" rates shows up as a dashboard alert, not a support queue (Part 78).

Senior Checklist — Part 71

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can split a page into components by data ownership and keep most of them pure and presentational
  • I can explain what triggers a re-render, why state is a snapshot, and why mutation does not update the screen
  • I choose keys from stable data IDs, use key to reset components, and know why the API must return stable IDs and cursor pages
  • I write effects only to synchronise with external systems, with cleanup that survives Strict Mode's double mount
  • I use a data library or the framework for fetching instead of hand-written effects, and I can describe the race they prevent
  • I know when useReducer, useRef and useContext fit, and I keep context values memoised and split by change frequency
  • I memoise only with a measured reason, and I know what the React Compiler changes
  • I can build a form with React Hook Form and a shared zod schema, and map server field errors onto inputs
  • I protect submits with a synchronous guard, a per-attempt idempotency key, server replay and a unique constraint
  • I can virtualise a long list and design the cursor-paginated, slim API behind it
  • I place error boundaries and Suspense boundaries per independent region with actionable fallbacks
  • I can profile a slow interaction in a production build and fix it structurally before adding memo
  • I know which APIs need React 19 (use, Actions, useActionState, useFormStatus, ref as a prop) and which work in React 18

Part 71 — Key Takeaways

  • A component is a pure function from props and state to a UI description; React, not your code, changes the DOM.
  • State is a snapshot per render; setters schedule a new render, and React detects changes by identity, so replace objects instead of mutating them.
  • Keys are primary keys for list items: stable IDs from the API, never indexes for dynamic lists, never random values.
  • Effects synchronise with external systems and must clean up; most data fetching belongs in a data library or the framework.
  • useReducer makes client state machines explicit, but the server must enforce the same transitions atomically.
  • Memoisation is a measured optimisation, not a habit; the React Compiler is making most of it automatic.
  • Forms need one shared schema, server-authoritative validation and an error contract with field paths.
  • Double-submit protection is layered: UI guard, per-attempt idempotency key, server replay and a database constraint.
  • Large lists are a DOM problem first: virtualise, and make the API a capped cursor over slim rows.
  • Error boundaries set the blast radius of a render failure; Suspense sets the shape of loading; both belong in the page design.
  • Profile before optimising, and remember the backend's share: payload size, deterministic responses and 304s cut render work.
  • Most of React's correctness depends on the API being honest: stable IDs, server-computed money, clear status codes and a request ID on every response.

Part 72 — Client State, Data Fetching and Caching

72.1 Server state vs client state: why API data in a global store goes wrong

Concept

Every value a React app holds belongs to one of two families.

Server state is data whose source of truth lives on a server: orders, products, stock levels, the cart, the customer profile. The browser never owns it. It holds a copy, taken at some moment, that other actors can change at any time: a warehouse worker marks the order shipped, a support agent issues a refund, the same customer cancels from their phone. Server state is asynchronous (you must ask for it), shared (many screens and many users read it) and always potentially out of date.

Client state is data the browser owns outright: whether the filter drawer is open, which tab is selected, the text typed into a half-finished form, the theme, a queue of toasts waiting to be shown. Nobody else can change it, it is available synchronously, and it is never stale because there is nothing to be stale against.

In practice it helps to split client state further, because each kind has a natural home:

Kind Example on an order list page Owner Natural home
Server state The orders, their statuses, the cart count badge The API and its database A server-state cache (TanStack Query, RTK Query, SWR)
URL state Status filter, date range, sort order, search text The address bar useSearchParams (React Router) or searchParams (Next.js)
Local UI state "Cancel" dialog open, row expanded One component useState / useReducer (Part 71 — React Fundamentals for Backend Engineers)
Form state Cancel reason being typed The form React Hook Form (71.7)
Global client state Toast queue, list density preference, dismissed banners The tab or the device Context, Zustand or Redux Toolkit (72.9)

The rule of this section is short: server state is a cache, so manage it with a cache. Putting API responses into a general-purpose global store and treating that store as the truth is the single most common architectural mistake in React apps.

Why does it exist?

The distinction exists because the two families have opposite problems.

Client state has a coordination problem: several components need the same value and must change it consistently. A store solves that.

Server state has a freshness problem. Once you copy server data into the browser, you inherit every question a backend cache answers (Part 27 — Caching and Redis): when does this copy expire, who invalidates it after a write, what happens when two requests for the same key are in flight, when is memory released, and what does the user see while a refresh is running. A general store answers none of these. If you put orders into Redux or a Context and fetch them once, you have built a cache with no TTL, no invalidation, no deduplication and no eviction, and you will rebuild each of those features by hand, one bug at a time.

What goes wrong in practice:

  1. Staleness with no expiry. Orders loaded at login are shown for the whole session. The order shipped two hours ago; the screen still says "Paid".
  2. Duplicate copies that drift. The list holds order A7K2Q9P as PAID, the detail page fetched it again and holds CANCELLED, the header badge holds a count from login. Three copies, three answers.
  3. Hand-rolled loading flags. ordersLoading, ordersError, orderDetailLoading, cancelPending, multiplied by every resource. Each flag is a chance for a stuck spinner.
  4. Race conditions. Two components dispatch the same fetch; responses arrive out of order and the older one wins (71.4 described the effect version of this race).
  5. Memory that never shrinks. A store keeps every page the user ever visited. A B2B buyer with 1,800 orders scrolls the history and the tab holds 3 MB of JSON forever.
  6. Leaks across users. The store is not cleared on logout, and on a shared counter terminal the next person sees the previous customer's orders.

Mental model

Imagine your NestJS service read the whole orders table into a Map at startup and served every request from it, forever. Nobody would accept that design on the backend: you would put Redis in front of PostgreSQL with a key per query, a TTL, explicit invalidation after writes and a single-flight lock to stop stampedes (Part 27.5).

A server-state library is exactly that Redis layer, running inside the browser tab. The query key is the Redis key. The query function is the loader that reads from the source of truth. The stale time is the TTL. invalidateQueries is DEL after a write. The global store, by contrast, is the Map loaded at startup. It is a perfectly good tool for client state, which has no source of truth elsewhere, and a bad one for data that does.

How it works

A useful classification test is one question: "Can anything other than this browser tab change this value?" If yes (the server, a worker, another device, another user, another tab), it is server state.

flowchart TB
    q1{"Can anything other than this tab change it?"} -->|"Yes"| srv["Server state: cache it with a query library"]
    q1 -->|"No"| q2{"Should a shared or reloaded link restore it?"}
    q2 -->|"Yes"| url["URL state: search params"]
    q2 -->|"No"| q3{"Is it a form being edited?"}
    q3 -->|"Yes"| frm["Form state: React Hook Form"]
    q3 -->|"No"| q4{"Do distant components need it?"}
    q4 -->|"No"| loc["Local state: useState or useReducer"]
    q4 -->|"Yes"| glb["Global client state: Context, Zustand or Redux Toolkit"]

What a server-state cache does that a store does not:

  1. Keys data by the request that produced it. ['orders', 'list', { status: 'PAID' }] and ['orders', 'detail', 'a1b2...'] are separate entries with separate lifetimes.
  2. Tracks freshness per entry. Each entry records when it was fetched. After its stale time it is still shown, but the next trigger (a component mounting, the tab regaining focus, the network reconnecting) refetches it in the background.
  3. Deduplicates. Ten components asking for the same key while a request is in flight share one request.
  4. Garbage-collects. When no component uses an entry for a while (five minutes by default in TanStack Query), it is deleted.
  5. Exposes status, not flags. Every entry has a status (pending, error, success) and a fetch status (fetching, paused, idle), so loading UI is derived, not hand-maintained.
  6. Gives writes a way to invalidate. After a mutation, you mark related keys stale and they refetch if on screen.

What stays in a store is small: UI preferences, ephemeral global UI, and sometimes a long-lived client-side domain model (a drawing canvas, an offline-first editor) that genuinely has no server truth until it is saved.

Practical example

The "My Orders" page of a grocery delivery app, classified:

Value Classification Why
List of orders with status Server state Riders, warehouses and support change it
Count in the "Active orders" badge Server state Derived from server data; do not keep a separate counter
Status filter PAID, range 30d URL state A support agent asks the customer to share the link; it must reproduce the view
"Cancel order" dialog open for order A7K2Q9P Local state One component, gone on close
Cancel reason being chosen Form state Validated, submitted once
Compact vs comfortable row density Global client state, persisted A device preference
"Your refund is on its way" toast queue Global client state Triggered from many places, shown in one

Notice what is not in a global store: the orders. Teams that put them there usually also put the filter there, which breaks the back button and shared links, and the badge count, which drifts from the list.

React / Next.js example

The store-shaped version most teams start with (Redux Toolkit 2):

// src/orders/ordersSlice.ts  (the anti-pattern: server data as store truth)
import { createAsyncThunk, createSlice } from '@reduxjs/toolkit';
import { OrderListResponseSchema, type OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';

export const loadOrders = createAsyncThunk('orders/load', async () => {
  const res = await fetch('/api/v1/orders', { credentials: 'include' });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`orders ${res.status}`);
  return OrderListResponseSchema.parse(await res.json());
});

type OrdersState = { items: OrderSummary[]; loading: boolean; error: string | null; loadedOnce: boolean };
const initialState: OrdersState = { items: [], loading: false, error: null, loadedOnce: false };

const ordersSlice = createSlice({
  name: 'orders',
  initialState,
  reducers: {},
  extraReducers: (b) => {
    b.addCase(loadOrders.pending, (s) => { s.loading = true; s.error = null; });
    b.addCase(loadOrders.fulfilled, (s, a) => { s.items = a.payload.items; s.loading = false; s.loadedOnce = true; });
    b.addCase(loadOrders.rejected, (s, a) => { s.loading = false; s.error = a.error.message ?? 'failed'; });
  },
});
export default ordersSlice.reducer;
// Missing: expiry, refetch on focus, dedupe, cancellation, pagination, invalidation after cancel,
// eviction, per-filter entries, clearing on logout. Each becomes a hand-written reducer case.

The same need expressed as server state (TanStack Query v5):

// src/orders/RecentOrders.tsx  (React 18, TanStack Query v5)
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderListResponseSchema } from '@shop/contracts';

async function fetchRecentOrders(signal: AbortSignal) {
  const res = await fetch('/api/v1/orders?limit=5', { credentials: 'include', signal });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`orders ${res.status}`);
  return OrderListResponseSchema.parse(await res.json());
}

export function RecentOrders() {
  const { data, isPending, isError } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['orders', 'list', { limit: 5 }],          // the cache key
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetchRecentOrders(signal),   // the loader; signal aborts on unmount
    staleTime: 30_000,                                    // fresh for 30 s, then refetched on next trigger
  });

  if (isPending) return <p>Loading your orders...</p>;
  if (isError) return <p role="alert">We could not load your orders.</p>;
  return <ul>{data.items.map((o) => <li key={o.id}>{o.displayId}: {o.status}</li>)}</ul>;
}

Fewer lines, and every missing feature in the first version is a default or one option in the second. The rest of this Part explains each of those options, because defaults you do not understand are bugs you have not met yet.

Backend side (NestJS)

A client cache can only be as correct as the API lets it be. Five things the API owes a server-state cache:

  1. Stable IDs on every resource (71.3), so cached entries and list rows can be matched across responses.
  2. A version or updatedAt on every mutable resource, so the client can tell which of two copies is newer. This matters the moment real-time events and optimistic updates meet (72.6, 72.8).
  3. Mutations that return the updated resource. A 200 with the new order lets the client write it straight into the cache instead of refetching.
  4. Compatible shapes between list and detail. If the list item is a strict subset of the detail, the detail page can show the list's copy instantly while the full record loads.
  5. Honest HTTP cache headers. Per-user data must not be cached by shared caches, and must not be cached by the browser in a way that hides fresh data from the query library (72.4).

This Part extends the shared contract from Part 70.12 with two fields:

// packages/contracts/src/index.ts  (zod 3.23; OrderSummarySchema from 76.12 with two new fields)
export const OrderSummarySchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  displayId: z.string(),
  status: OrderStatusSchema,
  totalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
  currency: z.string().length(3),
  items: z.array(OrderItemSchema),
  placedAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),
  version: z.number().int().nonnegative(),           // new: increments on every change to the order row
  updatedAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),  // new: for "updated 2 min ago" and debugging
});
export type OrderSummary = z.infer<typeof OrderSummarySchema>;

On the backend, TypeORM's @VersionColumn() increments the column on every save(); for raw UPDATE statements, increment it explicitly (SET version = version + 1). The controller sets cache headers that keep shared caches out and let the browser revalidate:

// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts  (excerpt)
import { Controller, Get, Header, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get(':id')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache') // browser may store it, but must revalidate; CDNs must not store it
  findOne(@CurrentUser() userId: string, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string): Promise<OrderSummary> {
    return this.orders.findForUser(userId, id); // 404 for another user's order, never 403 (no existence leak)
  }
}

Production scenario

A B2B dental supplies marketplace loaded the buyer's entire order history into a Redux slice at login: one GET /v1/orders?all=true. For a typical clinic that was 40 orders; for hospital buyers it was 1,800 orders and 3.4 MB of JSON, taking 1.9 s at p95 and blocking the dashboard. Statuses were refreshed only on full page reload, so buyers who kept the tab open all day (most of them) saw "Processing" on orders that had shipped in the morning. "Where is my order" support tickets made up 31 % of all contacts.

The team moved orders to TanStack Query with cursor pages of 20 (72.7), staleTime: 30_000 and refetch on focus. The dashboard request became 22 KB and 120 ms at p95. Buyers saw shipped status within 30 s of returning to the tab, and later within 2 s once status events were pushed over SSE (72.8). "Where is my order" tickets fell to 18 % of contacts in six weeks. The Redux store kept three slices: UI preferences, the toast queue and a draft purchase-order builder.

Failure scenario

At 10:40 a support agent cancelled order A7K2Q9P on the customer's behalf because a product was out of stock. The customer's laptop had the orders page open since 08:15, with orders in a Context loaded once on mount. At 11:05 the customer clicked "Track", saw "Paid, preparing", and called support again. The agent said it was cancelled; the customer refreshed and saw "Cancelled"; trust dropped and the call took 9 minutes.

Worse, the same Context held the order list, and the "Cancel order" button read the stale status. Several customers clicked "Cancel" on orders that had already shipped, got a 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE with no explanation, and assumed the site was broken.

The post-incident review named the root cause precisely: the UI treated a copy as the truth and had no rule for when the copy expires. The fix was not "refresh more often"; it was moving server data into a cache with freshness rules, invalidation after the user's own writes, and pushed events for other people's writes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Derived server state stored separately, such as a cart count kept in a store and incremented locally, drifts from the server's cart after a failed add or an add from another device. Derive it from the cart query.
  • Filters in a store instead of the URL break the back button, shared links and reloads.
  • Server data copied into useState "to edit it" stops receiving updates. Copy only into a form's default values, keyed by the resource version so a newer version resets the form (71.3).
  • Logout without clearing caches leaks one user's data to the next on shared devices (72.10).
  • Multiple tabs each have their own cache. A cancel in tab 1 is invisible to tab 2 until it refetches. Refetch on focus, a BroadcastChannel message or pushed events close the gap.
  • Huge "load everything" endpoints created to fill a store become the slowest endpoint in the API.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior classifies before choosing tools. They ask "who else can change this?" and "should a link reproduce this?" for each value, and the tool choice falls out of the answers. They refuse to let a global store become a second database: if a reviewer sees orders or products in a Redux slice, the first question is "what invalidates this?"

They also see that the backend shapes how hard this is. An API with versions on resources, mutation responses that return the new resource, and stable IDs makes the client cache simple. An API that returns 204 No Content from every write and has no version field forces the client to refetch everything and guess which copy is newer.

To a product manager: "The screen shows a copy of the order. We are choosing how old that copy may get and how quickly it updates after a change. Thirty seconds on focus is cheap; two seconds needs live updates and costs a little more infrastructure."

Common mistakes

  • Fetching once into a global store and never expiring it.
  • Storing the same entity in several places (list slice, detail slice, badge counter) that drift apart.
  • Keeping filter and sort state in a store instead of the URL.
  • Copying query data into useState and editing the copy, which silently stops updates.
  • Adding loading/error flags per resource by hand instead of using a library's status.
  • Building "load everything" endpoints to feed a store.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between server state and client state, and why does it matter for tool choice? Expected answer: server state has a remote source of truth, is async, shared and can be stale; client state is owned by the browser and synchronous. Server state needs caching semantics (keys, freshness, dedupe, invalidation, garbage collection) that general stores lack. Why it matters: most data bugs in React apps come from managing server data as if it were client data. Follow-up: where does a status filter belong? (The URL.)
  2. A teammate puts the product catalogue in Redux "for performance". What do you ask? Expected answer: what invalidates it, how stale can it be, how much memory, what happens on price changes and on logout; propose a query cache with a long stale time instead.
  3. How do you decide whether a value belongs in the URL? Expected answer: if reloading, sharing a link or pressing Back should restore it.
  4. What does the API need to provide so the client can cache correctly? Expected answer: stable IDs, versions or updatedAt, mutation responses returning the new resource, consistent list and detail shapes, correct Cache-Control.
  5. Two tabs are open; the user cancels in one. What does the other show and how do you fix it? Expected answer: the stale status until refetch; refetch on focus, BroadcastChannel, or server-pushed events.

Practical exercise

Take an existing page that keeps API data in a Context or store.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A table classifies every value on the page into the five kinds above, with the reason.
  • Filters move to the URL; reloading and sharing the link reproduce the view.
  • API data moves to TanStack Query; the store or Context shrinks to genuine client state.
  • After a support-side status change in the database, returning to the tab shows the new status within the configured stale time, without a manual reload.
  • The NestJS order endpoints return version and updatedAt, and GET /v1/orders/:id sends Cache-Control: private, no-cache.

72.2 TanStack Query: queries, query keys and deduplication

Concept

TanStack Query (formerly React Query) is a server-state cache for the browser. This Part uses v5 (@tanstack/react-query 5.x, React 18+). Its core pieces:

  • QueryClient: one per app (per tab). It owns a query cache: a map from a hashed query key to a query object holding data, error, status and timestamps.
  • useQuery: a hook that subscribes a component to one query. You give it a query key (an array that identifies the data) and a query function (an async function that fetches it and throws on failure).
  • Observers: every mounted useQuery is an observer of its query. Many observers can share one query.
const { data, error, status, fetchStatus } = useQuery({
