  queryKey: ['orders', 'detail', orderId],
  queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetchOrder(orderId, signal),
});

v5 accepts only the object form shown above. The positional overloads from v4 (useQuery(key, fn, options)) were removed, and the same applies to queryClient methods such as invalidateQueries({ queryKey }). Old blog posts with positional arguments will not compile against v5.

Why does it exist?

Part 71.4 listed what a correct hand-written fetch effect needs (abort, reset on input change, non-2xx handling, runtime validation, ignoring stale responses) and what it still lacks: caching, deduplication across components, retries, refetch on focus, invalidation after writes, pagination and server rendering support. TanStack Query exists to provide all of that once, tested, for every request in the app. You write the query function (how to fetch) and the key (what it is); the library decides when to fetch, when to reuse, and when to throw away.

Mental model

Imagine a read-through Redis cache in a NestJS service: getOrCompute(key, loader, ttl). On a hit, return the cached value. On a miss, call the loader, store the result, return it. If two requests miss at the same moment, a single-flight lock makes the second wait for the first's result instead of calling the loader again.

useQuery is getOrCompute with three differences. The "TTL" (staleTime) does not delete the value; it only marks it as due for a background refresh. The value is pushed to every subscribed component whenever it changes. And entries with no subscribers are deleted after gcTime, the way Redis evicts keys under a TTL.

The query key is the Redis key. If two different things share a key, one overwrites the other. If one thing has two keys, you have two copies that drift. Key design is cache design.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant H as HeaderBadge
    participant P as OrderPage
    participant QC as QueryClient
    participant API as NestJS
    H->>QC: observe key orders detail 42
    QC->>API: GET /v1/orders/42
    P->>QC: observe key orders detail 42
    Note over QC: same key in flight, no second request
    API-->>QC: 200 order 42
    QC-->>H: data, status success
    QC-->>P: data, status success
    P->>QC: unmount, observer removed
    Note over QC: H still observes, entry kept

Step by step, for one useQuery call:

  1. Hash the key. The key array is turned into a deterministic string. Object properties are sorted, so { status: 'PAID', range: '30d' } and { range: '30d', status: 'PAID' } hash the same. Array order matters: ['orders', 42] is not [42, 'orders']. Properties whose value is undefined are dropped, so { status: undefined } equals {}.
  2. Find or create the query in the cache for that hash.
  3. Attach an observer for this component. The observer decides what the component needs to re-render for; by default it tracks which result properties you actually read (data, isFetching...) and re-renders only when those change.
  4. Decide whether to fetch. If there is no data, fetch. If there is data and it is stale and a trigger fired (this observer just mounted, the window regained focus, the network reconnected), refetch in the background while returning the cached data. 72.3 covers the triggers.
  5. Deduplicate. If a fetch for this query is already in flight, the new observer joins it. One request serves all observers.
  6. Call the query function with a context object: { queryKey, signal, meta }. signal is an AbortSignal the library aborts if every observer unmounts before the request finishes, or if you call queryClient.cancelQueries for the key.
  7. Store the result. On success, the data is merged into the previous data with structural sharing: unchanged parts of the JSON keep their old object references, so memoised rows for unchanged orders do not re-render (71.12). On failure, retries run (72.3), then the error is stored.
  8. Notify observers, which re-render.

Query keys should come from one place per domain, a key factory, so every reader and every invalidation uses the same shape:

// src/orders/orderKeys.ts
import type { OrderListFilters } from '@shop/contracts';

export const orderKeys = {
  all: ['orders'] as const,
  lists: () => [...orderKeys.all, 'list'] as const,
  list: (filters: OrderListFilters) => [...orderKeys.lists(), filters] as const,
  details: () => [...orderKeys.all, 'detail'] as const,
  detail: (id: string) => [...orderKeys.details(), id] as const,
};
// invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() }) matches every list, whatever the filters,
// because matching is by prefix: ['orders', 'list'] is a prefix of ['orders', 'list', {...}].

Prefix matching is what makes the hierarchy useful. Every queryClient method that takes filters (invalidateQueries, cancelQueries, setQueriesData, removeQueries) matches all keys that start with the given key, unless you pass exact: true.

Three more options shape a query:

  • enabled: false stops automatic fetching, for dependent queries (enabled: !!customerId).
  • select: transforms the cached data for this observer only (select: (d) => d.items.filter(o => o.status === 'PAID')). The cache keeps the full response; select runs on the client and saves no bytes on the wire.
  • queryOptions(...): a v5 helper that bundles key, function and options into one typed object, reusable in useQuery, prefetchQuery and getQueryData with the data type inferred.

Practical example

On an order detail screen, three components need order 42: the header ("Order A7K2Q9P, Paid"), the timeline and the "Cancel order" button. With hand-written effects that is three requests and three possibly different answers. With one query key from the factory it is one request, one cached copy, and every component re-renders together when the status changes. If the user goes back to the list and returns within the five-minute garbage-collection window, the detail renders instantly from cache and refreshes in the background if stale.

React / Next.js example

App setup, one QueryClient per tab, created once:

// src/main.tsx  (React 18, TanStack Query v5, Vite SPA)
import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { ReactQueryDevtools } from '@tanstack/react-query-devtools';
import { App } from './App';

const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: { staleTime: 30_000 }, // app-wide default; individual queries override it (78.3)
  },
});

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(
  <StrictMode>
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <App />
      <ReactQueryDevtools initialIsOpen={false} /> {/* tree-shaken out of production builds */}
    </QueryClientProvider>
  </StrictMode>,
);

A reusable query definition and two consumers:

// src/orders/orderQueries.ts
import { queryOptions, useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderSummarySchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { apiGet } from '../api/http';
import { orderKeys } from './orderKeys';

export const orderDetailQuery = (id: string) =>
  queryOptions({
    queryKey: orderKeys.detail(id),
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => apiGet(`/v1/orders/${id}`, OrderSummarySchema, signal),
  });

export const useOrder = (id: string) => useQuery(orderDetailQuery(id));

// Elsewhere: a component that only needs the status re-renders only when status changes,
// because select returns a primitive and the observer compares results.
export const useOrderStatus = (id: string) =>
  useQuery({ ...orderDetailQuery(id), select: (o) => o.status });

The shared apiGet helper is the one place that knows about credentials, errors and validation:

// src/api/http.ts
import type { ZodType } from 'zod';
import { ApiError } from './errors'; // { status, code, issues, requestId } from 77.7

export async function apiGet<T>(path: string, schema: ZodType<T>, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api${path}`, { credentials: 'include', signal });
  if (!res.ok) {
    const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));               // error bodies are not always JSON
    throw new ApiError(res.status, body.code ?? `HTTP_${res.status}`, body.issues ?? [],
      body.requestId ?? res.headers.get('X-Request-Id') ?? undefined);
  }
  return schema.parse(await res.json()); // a contract mismatch throws here, not deep in a component
}

Install @tanstack/eslint-plugin-query: its exhaustive-deps rule flags query functions that use a variable missing from the key, which is the bug in the failure scenario below.

Backend side (NestJS)

A query key is a client-side name for one GET. The backend makes that mapping clean in three ways.

Canonical query parameters. The client should build keys from the same normalised filter object it sends as query parameters. The server should treat equivalent requests identically: defaults applied (range missing means 30d), multi-value filters order-insensitive (status=PAID,SHIPPED equals status=SHIPPED,PAID), unknown parameters rejected rather than ignored. One schema in @shop/contracts does both jobs:

// packages/contracts/src/index.ts  (continued)
export const OrderListFiltersSchema = z.object({
  status: OrderStatusSchema.optional(),
  range: z.enum(['30d', '6m', 'all']).default('30d'),
}).strict(); // unknown query params are a 400, not silently ignored
export type OrderListFilters = z.infer<typeof OrderListFiltersSchema>;
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts  (excerpt)
@Get()
@Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache')
list(
  @CurrentUser() userId: string,
  @Query(new ZodValidationPipe(OrderListQuerySchema)) q: OrderListQuery, // filters + cursor + limit (78.7)
): Promise<OrderListResponse> {
  return this.orders.listForUser(userId, q);
}

Deterministic responses. Structural sharing only helps if unchanged data serialises identically. An API that adds generatedAt: new Date() to every list response, or returns items in an unstable order when timestamps tie, makes every refetch look like a change: every row re-renders. Sort by a total order (placed_at DESC, id DESC) and keep per-response metadata in headers.

Purpose-built small reads. select does not shrink the payload. If the header badge needs "3 active orders", a GET /v1/orders/summary returning { active: 3 } (one indexed count(*) on a partial index WHERE status IN ('PENDING','PAID','SHIPPED'), about 1 ms) beats downloading the first page of orders to count them.

Production scenario

A food delivery web app's home screen had nine widgets (greeting, wallet balance, active order, loyalty points, saved addresses...), and each called GET /v1/me in its own effect to read one field. On an evening peak of 52,000 page loads per minute that was about 7,800 RPS to /v1/me, each doing a JWT check and a PostgreSQL read (2 to 4 ms). Moving to one useQuery({ queryKey: ['me'] }) with select per widget cut it to one request per page load, about 870 RPS. Database CPU on the primary dropped from 46 % to 31 % in the evening, and the home screen's last widget appeared 400 ms sooner on 4G, because nine parallel requests had been competing for the same six HTTP/1.1 connections to the API origin.

Failure scenario

An internal support console showed a customer's orders. The query key was ['orders'] and the query function read the customer ID from the route:

useQuery({ queryKey: ['orders'], queryFn: () => fetchOrders(customerId) }); // customerId missing from key

An agent opened customer A, then customer B. The key did not change, so TanStack Query returned the cached data for ['orders']: customer A's orders under customer B's name. With staleTime: 60_000, no refetch happened for a minute. An agent read out a delivery address belonging to someone else before noticing. It was reported as a data-protection incident.

The fix had three layers: the key became orderKeys.list({ customerId, ...filters }); the ESLint exhaustive-deps rule for queries was turned on as an error; and the backend added a response header X-Customer-Id, which the console's apiGet compared with the requested customer and threw on mismatch, a cheap guard against the whole class of bug.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A variable used in queryFn but missing from the key returns another entity's data. The most dangerous query bug.
  • Unstable values in keys (a Date created during render, a full object with functions) create a new cache entry each render: an endless refetch loop. Put only serialisable, stable values in keys.
  • Two keys for one resource (['order', id] here, ['orders', 'detail', id] there) cause two copies and missed invalidations. Use the factory.
  • select returning a new object each time makes the component re-render on every cache notification; return primitives or memoise the selector with useCallback.
  • enabled: false with no data leaves status: 'pending' forever; render based on isLoading (which is isPending && isFetching) or handle the disabled case explicitly.
  • Query functions that return undefined are an error in v5; return null for "nothing".
  • A schema parse failure is a thrown error like any other, so it is retried three times by default. Make contract errors non-retryable (72.3).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats the key factory as the schema of the client cache and reviews it like a Redis key-naming convention: hierarchical, prefix-matchable, containing every input. They insist the key and the request parameters are built from the same normalised object, so the cache cannot disagree with the URL.

They keep the query function thin and boring: one HTTP call, one schema parse, throw on non-2xx. Business logic does not belong there. And they remember that deduplication is per tab: ten open tabs are still ten clients to the API, so the backend's rate limits and caches must assume that.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving inputs out of the key because "the component only ever shows one".
  • Inline string keys scattered across files instead of a factory.
  • Using select to avoid building a small endpoint, downloading kilobytes to read one number.
  • Creating the QueryClient inside a component without useState, so it is recreated on every render and the cache is lost.
  • Copying data into useState and rendering the copy.
  • Using v4 positional signatures and cacheTime with v5.

Interview questions

  1. How does TanStack Query deduplicate requests? Expected answer: queries are keyed by a hashed key; observers of the same key share one query, and a fetch already in flight is joined rather than repeated. Why it matters: it replaces hand-written single-flight logic. Follow-up: is deduplication shared across tabs? (No; each tab has its own QueryClient and cache.)
  2. What must go into a query key? Expected answer: every value the query function depends on, as serialisable, stable data; usually built by a factory for prefix invalidation.
  3. What is structural sharing and why does it matter for performance? Expected answer: new data is merged with old so unchanged subtrees keep their references; memoised components for unchanged items skip rendering. It needs deterministic API responses.
  4. Why does select not reduce network cost, and what would you do instead? Expected answer: it runs on cached data after download; add a small purpose-built endpoint.
  5. What changed in the v5 API surface? Expected answer: object-only signatures, cacheTime renamed gcTime, isLoading for status renamed isPending, keepPreviousData replaced by placeholderData: keepPreviousData, query-level onSuccess/onError callbacks removed, useErrorBoundary renamed throwOnError, initialPageParam required for infinite queries.

Practical exercise

Build the order detail screen with three components reading the same order.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Network panel shows one GET /api/v1/orders/:id when all three mount together.
  • All keys come from orderKeys; the ESLint query plugin is enabled and fails the build when a query function uses a variable not in its key.
  • A component using select: (o) => o.status does not re-render when only updatedAt changes (verified with the React Profiler).
  • The NestJS list endpoint rejects an unknown query parameter with 400 VALIDATION_FAILED and treats a missing range the same as range=30d.
  • Two consecutive identical list responses serialise byte-for-byte identically.

72.3 Stale time, garbage-collection time, background refetch and retries

Concept

Two timers decide the life of every cached query, and they are constantly confused.

  • staleTime (default 0) is how long data counts as fresh after it was fetched. While fresh, nothing triggers a refetch: new components mounting, the tab regaining focus, all of them read the cache silently. Once stale, the data is still shown, but the next trigger refetches it in the background.
  • gcTime (default 5 minutes) is how long an inactive query (one with no mounted observers) stays in memory before it is garbage-collected. It has nothing to do with freshness. A query that is on screen is never collected, however old.

In v4 gcTime was called cacheTime. v5 renamed it because "cache time" made people think it controlled how long data is reused without refetching, which is staleTime's job. If you see cacheTime in code, it is v4 or a migration that was not finished.

Background refetch is how stale data becomes fresh without a spinner: the cached value stays on screen, isFetching becomes true, and the new data replaces it when it arrives. Retries are how a failed fetch gets more chances before the query reports an error: by default 3 retries for queries, with exponential backoff, and 0 retries for mutations.

Why does it exist?

There are only two ways to keep a copy in sync with a source of truth: the source tells you when it changes (push, 72.8) or you ask again at sensible moments (pull). TanStack Query's triggers are a good default answer to "sensible moments": when a new screen needs the data, when the user comes back to the tab (they may have been away for an hour), and when the network returns. staleTime stops those triggers from firing pointlessly; gcTime stops memory from growing with every screen visited; retries absorb the transient failures that are normal on mobile networks.

Mental model

Imagine a supermarket shelf with "best before" and "remove from shelf" dates. Best before is staleTime: before it, sell without a second thought; after it, still sell, but order a fresh batch the next time someone looks. "Remove from shelf if nobody has picked it up" is gcTime: it applies only to items nobody is holding. An item in someone's basket (a mounted component) is never removed, however old.

How it works

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Fetching: first observer mounts
    Fetching --> Fresh: success
    Fetching --> Failed: error after retries
    Fresh --> Stale: staleTime elapsed
    Stale --> Refetching: mount, focus, reconnect or interval
    Refetching --> Fresh: success, data replaced
    Refetching --> Failed: error, old data kept
    Fresh --> Inactive: last observer unmounts
    Stale --> Inactive: last observer unmounts
    Inactive --> Stale: observer mounts again within gcTime
    Inactive --> [*]: gcTime elapsed, entry deleted

The refetch triggers, all on by default and each a per-query option:

Trigger Option v5 behaviour
A new observer mounts refetchOnMount Refetch if stale; 'always' ignores freshness
Tab becomes visible again refetchOnWindowFocus Listens to visibilitychange only (v4 also used focus, which fired on every devtools click)
Network comes back refetchOnReconnect Driven by the browser online event via onlineManager
Timer refetchInterval Off by default; paused in hidden tabs unless refetchIntervalInBackground: true
Explicit refetch(), invalidateQueries Always fetches

Retries follow retry (default 3) and retryDelay (default Math.min(1000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000)): 1 s, 2 s, 4 s. A query against a dead API therefore shows its error after about 7 s plus four request durations. During retries the query stays pending (or keeps its old data) and exposes failureCount and failureReason, so the UI can say "Still trying..." instead of spinning silently.

Two rules make retries safe. Retry only failures that can succeed on a second attempt (network errors, timeouts, 502/503/504, 429 after a wait), never a 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 or 422, nor a contract parse error. And remember that every retry is extra load arriving exactly when the server is already struggling (Part 31 — Reliability Engineering, 31.3 and 31.4).

Practical example

Choosing staleTime per data type is a product decision with a backend cost:

Data staleTime Reasoning
Product catalogue, categories 5 to 10 min Changes rarely; a minute's lag is harmless
Customer profile (/v1/me) Infinity + invalidate on edit Only this user changes it, through this app
Order list 30 s Changes through other actors; pushed events cover urgent changes (72.8)
Live order status on tracking page 0 + SSE Freshness is the feature
Stock and price at checkout 0, and the server rechecks on submit The UI hint can lag; the server decides (71.13)
Feature flags 60 s Rollouts tolerate a minute; kill switches use a push channel

gcTime rarely needs tuning. Raise it (say 30 min) for data users navigate back to often, so Back renders instantly. Lower it for very large responses on memory-poor devices.

React / Next.js example

App-wide defaults that encode the retry rules:

// src/api/queryClient.ts  (TanStack Query v5)
import { QueryCache, QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { ZodError } from 'zod';
import { ApiError } from './errors';
import { toast } from '../ui/toast';

export function isRetryable(error: unknown): boolean {
  if (error instanceof ZodError) return false;                       // contract mismatch: retrying cannot fix it
  if (error instanceof ApiError) return error.status === 429 || error.status >= 500;
  return true;                                                       // network error, timeout: worth another try
}

export const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  queryCache: new QueryCache({
    // v5 removed onError from useQuery; global side effects live on the cache.
    // Only toast when a background refetch fails and old data is still on screen.
    onError: (error, query) => {
      if (query.state.data !== undefined) toast.warn('Could not refresh. Showing the last saved data.');
    },
  }),
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: {
      staleTime: 30_000,
      gcTime: 5 * 60_000,
      retry: (failureCount, error) => isRetryable(error) && failureCount < 2, // at most 2 retries
      retryDelay: (attempt, error) =>
        error instanceof ApiError && error.status === 429
          ? 5_000                                                    // rate limited: back off hard
          : Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 8_000) + Math.random() * 500, // jitter spreads the herd
    },
    mutations: { retry: 0 },                                         // writes retry only with an idempotency key (78.6)
  },
});

Per-query overrides where the table says so:

// src/catalog/useCategories.ts and src/session/useMe.ts
export const useCategories = () =>
  useQuery({ queryKey: ['categories'], queryFn: ({ signal }) => apiGet('/v1/categories', CategoriesSchema, signal),
    staleTime: 10 * 60_000, gcTime: 30 * 60_000 });

export const useMe = () =>
  useQuery({ queryKey: ['me'], queryFn: ({ signal }) => apiGet('/v1/me', MeSchema, signal),
    staleTime: Infinity }); // refetched only when a profile mutation invalidates ['me']

Backend side (NestJS)

Pull-based freshness puts a predictable, bursty load on the API. Design for it:

  • Focus refetches arrive in waves. A push notification ("Your order is out for delivery") makes tens of thousands of users switch back to the tab within seconds, and every stale query on the visible page refetches. Make those GETs cheap: indexed, small, and answerable with 304 Not Modified (72.4).
  • Retries need signals. Send Retry-After on 429 and 503 so clients back off for the right time; @nestjs/throttler returns 429 through ThrottlerGuard, and a load-shedding guard (Part 31.8) should return 503 early rather than queue work it will time out on.
  • GETs must be safe to repeat. Every GET will be sent twice at some point (retries, Strict Mode, two tabs). Never write in a GET handler; "mark notifications as seen on read" belongs in a POST.
  • Errors must be classifiable. The client's isRetryable depends on honest status codes: a validation failure returned as 500 gets retried; a database timeout returned as 400 does not. Map exceptions deliberately in the exception filter (71.11).

Production scenario

A food delivery app sent "Your rider is 2 minutes away" pushes at dinner peak. Each tap brought the web tab back to the foreground. With staleTime: 0, the visible tracking page refetched six queries on every focus. At 19:05 on a Friday, 58,000 users came back within about 10 s: roughly 35,000 RPS against an API sized for 9,000. p99 rose from 120 ms to 2.4 s, retries tripled the load, and the tracking page showed errors to people whose orders were fine.

The fix combined both sides. The client set staleTime: 30_000 on everything except the live status (fed by SSE and so never needing focus refetches), cut retries to 2 with jitter, and skipped retries on 4xx. The backend made the five static-ish queries answer 304 from a version check that cost one indexed lookup. Peak focus traffic fell to about 6,000 RPS, 80 % of which were 304s of under 200 bytes.

Failure scenario

During a PostgreSQL failover the API returned 503 for 40 s. Each page had four queries, each with the v5 default of 3 retries, and users who saw the error page pressed "Try again", which called refetch() on all four, each again with 3 retries. Load on the recovering primary was about 4.5x normal when it came back, its connection pool saturated, and the outage stretched to 6 minutes as the herd kept it down. This is a textbook retry storm (Part 31.3).

The changes: at most 2 retries, exponential backoff with jitter, Retry-After: 10 on 503 honoured by the client, and the "Try again" button disabled for the Retry-After period with a countdown. The next failover recovered in 55 s.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • gcTime shorter than the time users spend away makes Back show a spinner instead of instant data.
  • staleTime: Infinity without invalidation shows stale data for the whole session; every Infinity needs a named invalidation path.
  • Hidden tabs with refetchIntervalInBackground: true poll all night on laptops left open; multiply by every open tab.
  • Retries on non-idempotent work disguised as a GET duplicate side effects.
  • Long retry sequences with no UI feedback look like a frozen page; show failureCount.
  • A refetch that fails after earlier success leaves status: 'error' and the old data; a component that checks isError first throws away good data (72.11).
  • Server rendering: on the server, TanStack Query defaults retry to 0 and gcTime to Infinity; do not copy client tuning into SSR prefetch code blindly.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior picks staleTime from a freshness requirement ("how wrong may this be, for how long?") and states it in the code review. They treat refetch triggers as load generators and do the arithmetic: focus refetches per minute equal active tabs times queries per page times the fraction of stale queries. They allow retries only where the server can tell transient from permanent failure, and they want backoff with jitter on every client, because a thundering herd is still a herd when it lives in browsers.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing staleTime with gcTime (or with v4's cacheTime) and setting the wrong one.
  • Leaving staleTime: 0 everywhere, which turns every mount and focus into requests.
  • Retrying 4xx and parse errors three times before showing the error.
  • Disabling refetchOnWindowFocus globally because it "makes too many requests", instead of raising staleTime.
  • Polling with refetchInterval when push already exists, or polling fast in background tabs.

Interview questions

  1. Explain staleTime and gcTime. Why did v5 rename cacheTime? Expected answer: staleTime is freshness, deciding whether triggers refetch; gcTime is how long inactive queries stay in memory. The rename stopped people reading "cache time" as freshness. Follow-up: what does the user see with staleTime: 0 and gcTime: 5 min when they navigate back? (Cached data instantly, plus a background refetch.)
  2. What triggers a background refetch in v5? Expected answer: new observer mount, window visibility, reconnect, interval, explicit refetch or invalidation; only when stale except explicit calls and 'always'.
  3. How would you configure retries for an API client? Expected answer: retry only transient failures, cap at 2 or 3, exponential backoff with jitter, honour Retry-After, no retries for mutations without idempotency keys.
  4. Why can client defaults cause a backend outage? Expected answer: focus refetch waves and retries multiply load during incidents; staleTime and backoff bound it.

Practical exercise

Configure the app-wide QueryClient and simulate failures with the network throttled to "Fast 4G".

Acceptance criteria:

  • A 404 shows an error immediately with no retries; a 503 retries twice with jittered backoff, visible as "Still trying (attempt 2)".
  • Switching tabs away and back within 30 s causes zero requests; after 30 s, only queries on the current screen refetch.
  • Navigating away and back within gcTime renders cached data instantly and refetches in the background without a spinner.
  • The NestJS API returns Retry-After on 429 and 503, and the client waits at least that long before retrying.

72.4 Cache layers end to end: query cache, HTTP cache and the backend cache

Concept

When a React component asks for an order, the answer can come from up to six caches: the TanStack Query cache in memory, a service worker's Cache API, the browser's HTTP cache, a CDN, a Redis cache in the NestJS service, and PostgreSQL's own buffer cache. Each has its own key, its own lifetime and its own invalidation rule. Invalidating one layer does nothing to the others. A refetch from the query cache can still be answered by a stale browser cache or a stale Redis entry.

Why does it exist?

Each layer earns its place: the query cache avoids re-rendering spinners, the HTTP cache avoids bytes, the CDN avoids trips to the origin, Redis avoids database work (Part 27). But a user-visible staleness bug happens when one layer is invalidated and the next one down is not. Seniors therefore think of freshness as a budget across layers, not a property of one cache.

Mental model

Imagine asking a colleague for the latest sales figure. They check their notes (query cache); if those are old, they check the printout on their desk (browser cache); if that is old, they ring the regional office (CDN), who check their spreadsheet (Redis) before asking finance (PostgreSQL). Telling your colleague "your notes are out of date" helps only if the printout, the regional office and the spreadsheet are also current, or at least not older than you can tolerate.

How it works

flowchart LR
    comp["Component"] --> qc["Query cache, staleTime"]
    qc -->|"refetch"| sw["Service worker, if any"]
    sw --> hc["Browser HTTP cache, Cache-Control"]
    hc --> cdn["CDN, s-maxage"]
    cdn --> api["NestJS"]
    api --> rds["Redis, TTL"]
    rds --> pg["PostgreSQL"]
  1. The query cache decides whether to call the query function at all (72.3).
  2. fetch() goes through a service worker if one is registered (Part 78 covers them).
  3. The browser HTTP cache applies Cache-Control from the last response. With max-age=60, any fetch within 60 s is served from disk without contacting the server, and JavaScript sees an ordinary 200. With no-cache, the browser always revalidates, sending If-None-Match with the stored ETag; on 304 it serves the stored body, and again JavaScript sees a 200 with the full body (Part 11.11).
  4. A CDN stores responses marked public or with s-maxage. Per-user API data must be private so shared caches never store it.
  5. Redis in the API (Part 27.2) serves cache-aside reads with a TTL.
  6. PostgreSQL is the truth.

The worst-case staleness a user can see is roughly the sum of the lifetimes of every layer that was not invalidated by the write. A 30 s staleTime, a 60 s max-age and a 120 s Redis TTL add up to three and a half minutes, even though each looked harmless on its own.

Layer Who invalidates on a write Recommended for per-user order data
Query cache The client, invalidateQueries or setQueryData staleTime 30 s, invalidated by the user's own mutations
Browser HTTP cache Nobody: it obeys headers only Cache-Control: private, no-cache with an ETag
CDN Purge API, slow and global Do not cache: private
Redis The API, in the same code path as the write Delete or update the key after the transaction commits
PostgreSQL Not applicable The truth

Practical example

The order list endpoint answers GET /v1/orders?status=PAID for one customer. The right header set is Cache-Control: private, no-cache plus an ETag. The query cache absorbs re-mounts; the browser revalidates cheaply; a 304 costs about 150 bytes instead of 22 KB; the CDN never sees personal data; the API owns Redis invalidation. When the user cancels an order, client-side invalidation is enough, because every layer below either revalidates or was updated by the write.

React / Next.js example

Nothing in the query function changes, which is the point: fetch hides 304 handling. Two client options matter only when the server's headers are wrong and cannot be fixed quickly:

// src/api/http.ts  (excerpt): a temporary guard while a backend header fix ships
export async function apiGetNoStore<T>(path: string, schema: ZodType<T>, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<T> {
  // cache: 'no-store' bypasses the browser HTTP cache entirely for this request:
  // no stored response is used and none is written. 'no-cache' would revalidate instead.
  const res = await fetch(`/api${path}`, { credentials: 'include', signal, cache: 'no-store' });
  if (!res.ok) throw await toApiError(res); // { code, issues, requestId } from 77.8
  return schema.parse(await res.json());
}

Use it as a stopgap, not a default: no-store throws away cheap 304 revalidation.

Backend side (NestJS)

Express, under NestJS's default platform, already computes a weak ETag from every JSON body and answers 304 when If-None-Match matches. That saves bandwidth but not work: the handler still ran the queries and serialised the response before Express hashed it. For hot endpoints, compute the validator before loading data, from a cheap aggregate:

// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts  (excerpt; Express platform)
import { Controller, Get, Query, Req, Res, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { OrderListQuerySchema, type OrderListQuery, type OrderListResponse } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { hashQuery } from '../common/hash-query'; // stable sha1 of the normalised query object
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { OrdersService } from './orders.service';

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly orders: OrdersService) {}

  @Get()
  async list(
    @CurrentUser() userId: string,
    @Query(new ZodValidationPipe(OrderListQuerySchema)) q: OrderListQuery,
    @Req() req: Request,
    @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response,
  ): Promise<OrderListResponse | undefined> {
    // One index-only lookup: max(updated_at) and count for this customer (about 0.3 ms).
    const stamp = await this.orders.listStamp(userId);
    const etag = `W/"o:${userId}:${stamp.maxUpdatedAt}:${stamp.count}:${hashQuery(q)}"`;
    res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache');
    res.setHeader('ETag', etag);
    if (req.headers['if-none-match'] === etag) {
      res.status(304);
      return undefined;                       // no list query, no serialisation, no body
    }
    return this.orders.listForUser(userId, q); // 3 to 8 ms with joins and mapping
  }
}
-- The stamp query, served from an index on (customer_id, updated_at)
SELECT max(updated_at) AS max_updated_at, count(*) AS count
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1;

Including count catches deletions that do not move max(updated_at). Redis entries for the same list must be deleted in the same service method that cancels the order, after the transaction commits (Part 27.5 covers the race between delete and a concurrent read-repopulate).

Production scenario

A grocery app's order list endpoint served 4,200 RPS at evening peak, mostly from focus refetches and back navigation, at 22 KB per response. After switching to private, no-cache with the pre-computed ETag, 78 % of requests ended in 304. Egress fell from about 92 MB/s to 21 MB/s, median API CPU per request from 6 ms to 0.9 ms, and on the client nothing re-rendered for unchanged lists, because structural sharing found identical data.

Failure scenario

A developer added @Header('Cache-Control', 'max-age=60') to GET /v1/orders to "reduce load". Ten minutes after the deploy, customer support saw a wave of complaints: "I cancelled, but it still says Paid". The cancel mutation worked and called invalidateQueries; TanStack Query dutifully refetched; the browser served the 40-second-old response from its HTTP cache without contacting the server. Every layer did what it was told. Some customers cancelled twice and got 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE for the second attempt.

The header was reverted within the hour. The postmortem added a contract test asserting private, no-cache on every per-user endpoint, and a lint rule rejecting max-age in @Header decorators outside the catalogue module.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • max-age on per-user data makes client invalidation useless for that window.
  • public or missing private on authenticated responses lets a CDN or corporate proxy serve one user's data to another (Part 11.11).
  • ETag from the body only still runs the expensive query on every request.
  • Redis cache not invalidated by the write means the client's refetch gets the old value from the API: correct client code, stale screen.
  • Service worker caching API responses with a "stale-while-revalidate" recipe copied from a blog serves stale orders after the user's own writes.
  • Weak vs strong ETags: W/ validators are fine for If-None-Match; range requests need strong ones, which JSON APIs rarely use.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior draws the layers for each endpoint and writes down, per layer, its lifetime and who invalidates it. Anything personal is private. Anything the user can change is no-cache with a validator, so the browser never holds back fresh data. Server caches are invalidated in the write path, not by hoping for TTLs. And they add up the worst-case staleness and compare it with the product requirement, because users experience the sum.

Common mistakes

  • Fixing client staleness with max-age, which makes it worse.
  • Using no-store everywhere, losing cheap revalidation.
  • Forgetting that fetch turns 304 into 200 and building client logic around 304 that never runs.
  • Invalidating the query cache but not Redis, or the reverse.
  • No test for cache headers, so one decorator change ships a privacy bug.

Interview questions

  1. A user cancels an order, the client invalidates the list, and the old status still shows. Where do you look? Expected answer: browser HTTP cache (max-age), service worker, CDN, the API's Redis cache; check response headers and X-Cache-style diagnostics in the Network panel.
  2. What Cache-Control should a per-user, frequently changing JSON endpoint send? Expected answer: private, no-cache with an ETag; why: no shared caching, always revalidate, cheap 304s.
  3. How do you make a 304 save database work and not just bandwidth? Expected answer: compute the validator from a cheap aggregate or version before running the main query.
  4. How do you reason about end-to-end staleness? Expected answer: sum the lifetimes of every layer not invalidated by the write, and compare with the requirement.

Practical exercise

Instrument the order list across all layers.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With DevTools open, a focus refetch of an unchanged list shows a 304 in the Network panel and no React commit in the Profiler.
  • After a cancel, the next list response is a 200 with the new status within one round trip; a test fails if Cache-Control on any /v1/orders route contains max-age or public.
  • The NestJS handler skips the list query on a matching If-None-Match (verified by a query counter in an integration test).
  • The cancel service method deletes the customer's Redis list keys after commit, with a test proving the next read misses the cache.

72.5 Mutations and invalidation

Concept

A mutation is a write: create, update, delete, or any action that changes server state (cancel an order, apply a coupon). In TanStack Query v5 it is useMutation:

const mutation = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (input: UpdateNoteInput) => updateDeliveryNote(input),
  onSuccess: (order) => { /* update the cache */ },
});
// mutation.mutate(input), mutation.mutateAsync(input), mutation.isPending, mutation.error, mutation.reset()

Unlike a query, a mutation does not run by itself, is not cached by key, and is not retried by default. Its job is to send the write and then bring the query cache back in line with the server, in one of two ways:

  • Invalidate: queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey }) marks matching queries stale and refetches those currently on screen. Simple, always correct, costs a round trip.
  • Write the response into the cache: queryClient.setQueryData(key, data) replaces the cached value with the server's answer. Instant, no extra request, correct only if the response has exactly the cached shape.

Most real mutations do both: write the returned resource into its detail entry, invalidate the lists that might contain it.

v5 renamed the mutation's isLoading to isPending (status 'pending'), matching queries.

Why does it exist?

After a write, every cached query that includes the changed data is wrong. Without a rule for fixing them, the user edits the delivery note and the order page still shows the old one, or the list shows a count that no longer matches. Hand-written code fixes the one screen the developer was looking at and misses the other three. Mutations give writes a single place to say "these keys are affected", using the same key factory as reads (72.2).

Mental model

Imagine the two strategies a backend uses after UPDATE orders: cache-aside delete (DEL order:42, the next read repopulates from PostgreSQL) and write-through (SET order:42 <new row>). Invalidation is cache-aside delete with an immediate re-read for anything on screen. setQueryData from the response is write-through. Write-through is faster but trusts that you wrote exactly what a read would have returned.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant M as useMutation
    participant QC as QueryClient
    participant API as NestJS
    U->>M: mutate note for order 42
    M->>API: PATCH /v1/orders/42 note, expectedVersion 7
    API-->>M: 200 order 42 version 8
    M->>QC: setQueryData orders detail 42
    M->>QC: invalidateQueries orders list
    QC->>API: GET /v1/orders, only for lists on screen
    API-->>QC: 200 page with version 8
    QC-->>U: every view shows the new note
  1. mutate(variables) calls mutationFn(variables). The mutation's status becomes pending.
  2. On success, onSuccess(data, variables, context) runs. If it returns a promise, the mutation stays pending until that promise settles. Returning the invalidateQueries promise keeps the button's spinner on until the lists have refetched, so the user never sees the old list after a "saved" message.
  3. invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() }) matches by prefix. Matching queries are marked stale. Those with mounted observers are refetched now (refetchType: 'active', the default); inactive ones refetch when next used. refetchType: 'none' only marks them stale; 'all' refetches inactive ones too.
  4. On failure, onError(error, variables, context) runs; onSettled runs after either outcome.

Callbacks can be passed in two places. Callbacks on useMutation({...}) always run. Callbacks passed to mutate(vars, { onSuccess }) run only if the component is still mounted when the mutation finishes. Put cache updates in the first; put UI reactions (close the dialog, navigate) in the second.

mutate swallows errors into mutation.error; mutateAsync returns a promise that rejects, so wrap it in try/catch or you get unhandled rejections.

Practical example

A customer edits the delivery note on order A7K2Q9P ("Leave with the concierge"). Affected cached data: the order detail (['orders', 'detail', id]), any order list containing it (['orders', 'list', ...]), and nothing else. The API returns the updated order, so the detail is written directly and lists are invalidated. If the customer is on the detail page, one PATCH and zero extra GETs update what they see; the list refetches when they navigate back, because it was marked stale while inactive.

React / Next.js example

// src/orders/useUpdateDeliveryNote.ts  (TanStack Query v5)
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderSummarySchema, type OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import { apiSend } from '../api/http';
import { orderKeys } from './orderKeys';

type Input = { orderId: string; note: string; expectedVersion: number };

export function useUpdateDeliveryNote() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: ({ orderId, note, expectedVersion }: Input) =>
      apiSend('PATCH', `/v1/orders/${orderId}`, { note, expectedVersion }, OrderSummarySchema),
    onSuccess: (order: OrderSummary) => {
      // Write-through: the response is a full OrderSummary, validated by the same schema as reads.
      queryClient.setQueryData(orderKeys.detail(order.id), order);
      // Cache-aside for lists: returning the promise keeps isPending true until lists are fresh.
      return queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() });
    },
  });
}
// src/orders/DeliveryNoteForm.tsx  (excerpt)
const update = useUpdateDeliveryNote();
const onSubmit = (note: string) =>
  update.mutate(
    { orderId: order.id, note, expectedVersion: order.version },
    { onSuccess: () => setEditing(false) }, // UI reaction: runs only if this form is still mounted
  );
// <button disabled={update.isPending}>{update.isPending ? 'Saving...' : 'Save'}</button>
// {update.error instanceof ApiError && update.error.code === 'VERSION_CONFLICT' && <p>This order changed. Reload?</p>}

apiSend is the write twin of apiGet (72.2): JSON body, credentials: 'include', an optional Idempotency-Key header (72.6), ApiError on non-2xx, schema parse on success.

Backend side (NestJS)

Mutations are only cheap on the client if the API returns enough to update the cache:

  • Return the updated resource (200 with the body) from updates and actions, in the same shape as the read endpoint. A 204 No Content forces a refetch for every write.
  • Use the version for optimistic concurrency. The client sends the version it edited; the server updates only if it still matches and returns 409 VERSION_CONFLICT otherwise, in the { code, issues, requestId } shape.
  • Make side effects visible. If cancelling an order also changes the wallet balance, either return both or document which keys the client must invalidate. Hidden side effects are where stale screens come from.
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.service.ts  (TypeORM, excerpt)
async updateNote(userId: string, orderId: string, note: string, expectedVersion: number): Promise<OrderSummary> {
  // TypeORM's PostgreSQL driver returns [rows, rowCount] for UPDATE/DELETE through query().
  const [rows] = (await this.ds.query(
    `UPDATE orders
        SET delivery_note = $3, version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
      WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2 AND version = $4
    RETURNING *`,
    [orderId, userId, note, expectedVersion],
  )) as [OrderRow[], number];
  if (rows.length === 0) {
    const exists = await this.ds.query('SELECT version FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2', [orderId, userId]);
    if (exists.length === 0) throw new NotFoundException({ code: 'ORDER_NOT_FOUND' });
    throw new ConflictException({ code: 'VERSION_CONFLICT', issues: [], currentVersion: exists[0].version });
  }
  return this.mapper.toSummary(rows[0]); // same mapper as GET, so the client can setQueryData safely
}

The conditional UPDATE ... WHERE version = $4 is one round trip and needs no explicit lock: PostgreSQL's row lock during the update serialises concurrent writers, and the loser matches zero rows (Part 21 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control).

Production scenario

An admin console called queryClient.invalidateQueries() with no filter after every mutation "to be safe". The dashboard kept 14 queries active (KPIs, charts, three tables). Each status change by an operations agent triggered 14 refetches, several of them aggregate queries costing 80 to 200 ms of database time. With 120 agents making about 6 changes per minute each, that was 10,000 extra requests per minute and a reporting replica at 70 % CPU. Scoping invalidation to orderKeys.lists() and ['kpis', 'orders'] cut it to 2 refetches per change and replica CPU to 25 %.

Failure scenario

The "update delivery note" endpoint originally returned { id, note, version } rather than a full order. A developer wrote setQueryData(orderKeys.detail(id), response). TypeScript did not complain because the mutation's return type was any from an untyped helper. The detail page re-rendered with an object that had no items, and order.items.map threw. The error boundary showed "Something went wrong" for every customer who edited a note, about 2,000 people in the first hour.

Fixes: the mutation response was parsed with OrderSummarySchema, so a shape mismatch fails in mutationFn (an error state, not a corrupted cache); the API returned the full summary; and apiSend became generic over the schema so any could no longer leak.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Writing a partial response into the cache corrupts it; parse with the read schema or merge explicitly with setQueryData(key, (old) => old && { ...old, ...patch }).
  • Invalidating too broadly turns each click into a refetch storm; too narrowly leaves stale screens. Use the key hierarchy.
  • Infinite lists refetch every loaded page when invalidated (72.7); patch them with setQueriesData when you know the change.
  • Callbacks in mutate() do not run after unmount; cache updates placed there are silently skipped.
  • mutateAsync without catch produces unhandled promise rejections.
  • Double submit: isPending disables the button after a render; a fast double tap can still fire twice. Use the ref guard and idempotency key from 71.8.
  • A mutation that succeeds on the server but times out on the client has an unknown outcome; refetch the affected keys before letting the user retry.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

For each mutation the senior lists the affected keys, the same way they would list cache keys to evict after a database write. They prefer write-through from a validated response for the resource itself, scoped invalidation for collections and aggregates, and they make the API return what the client needs to do that. They insist on the version check so two agents editing the same order do not silently overwrite each other.

Common mistakes

  • Returning 204 from every write, forcing refetches.
  • Global invalidateQueries() after every mutation.
  • Cache updates inside mutate() callbacks instead of the hook's options.
  • Trusting an untyped response in setQueryData.
  • No version check, so last write wins without anyone noticing.

Interview questions

  1. Invalidate or setQueryData after a mutation: how do you choose? Expected answer: setQueryData when the response is exactly the cached shape for a known key; invalidate for lists, aggregates and anything derived; often both. Follow-up: why return the invalidate promise from onSuccess? (To keep the mutation pending until fresh data is shown.)
  2. What is the difference between callbacks on useMutation and on mutate? Expected answer: the latter run only if the component is mounted; use the former for cache work.
  3. How does the server prevent lost updates between two editors? Expected answer: optimistic concurrency with a version in the WHERE clause and a 409 on mismatch.
  4. What does refetchType control? Expected answer: whether invalidated queries refetch now: active ones (default), all, or none.

Practical exercise

Implement "edit delivery note" end to end.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Saving on the detail page makes exactly one PATCH and zero GETs; navigating back to the list triggers one list refetch.
  • Two browser sessions editing the same order: the second save gets 409 VERSION_CONFLICT and a "This order changed" message.
  • A mocked response missing items fails the mutation with a parse error and leaves the cache unchanged.
  • The save button stays in "Saving..." until list invalidation completes.

72.6 Optimistic updates, rollback and idempotency keys from the client

Concept

An optimistic update shows the result of a write before the server confirms it, and undoes it if the server says no. The heart icon fills the instant you tap it; the request goes out in the background; if it fails, the heart empties again with a message.

TanStack Query v5 supports two styles:

  • Optimistic via the UI: render mutation.variables while mutation.isPending, without touching the cache. On error the pending variables simply disappear. Simple, local to one component (or several, via useMutationState).
  • Optimistic via the cache: in onMutate, cancel in-flight fetches, snapshot the current cache value, write the expected value, and return the snapshot as context; in onError, restore it; in onSettled, invalidate to reconcile with the truth.

An idempotency key from the client is a unique ID generated once per user intent and sent with every attempt of that write (Idempotency-Key: 7f3c...), so the server can recognise retries and return the original result instead of applying the write twice (Part 15.12). Optimistic UIs retry more, so they need it more.

Why does it exist?

On a 4G connection a write takes 150 to 600 ms; on a congested one, seconds. For frequent, low-risk actions (wishlist, mark as read, reorder a list, toggle a setting) that delay makes the app feel broken. Optimism removes the wait for the common case (the write almost always succeeds) at the cost of handling the rare failure honestly.

Idempotency keys exist because the client cannot tell "the request failed" from "the response was lost". After a timeout, a retry without a key may cancel twice, pay twice or create two orders.

Mental model

Imagine writing a cheque into your ledger in pencil the moment you hand it over, then inking it when the bank clears it, or erasing it if it bounces. You need the pencil entry to be distinguishable (a pending marker), you need to remember what the line said before (the snapshot), and you must not erase entries the bank added in the meantime (newer server data). The idempotency key is the cheque number: if the bank sees the same number twice, it pays once.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant M as useMutation
    participant QC as QueryClient
    participant API as NestJS
    U->>M: tap heart on SKU 991
    M->>QC: cancelQueries wishlist
    M->>QC: snapshot, then setQueryData saved true
    QC-->>U: heart filled at once
    M->>API: PUT /v1/wishlist/items/991
    alt server accepts
        API-->>M: 200 count 12
        M->>QC: onSettled invalidates wishlist
    else server rejects
        API-->>M: 422 WISHLIST_FULL
        M->>QC: onError restores snapshot
        QC-->>U: heart empty, message shown
    end

Cache-style optimistic update, in order:

  1. onMutate(variables) runs before mutationFn.
  2. await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey }). Without this, a background refetch that started before the tap can land after the optimistic write and overwrite it with old data: the heart flickers back.
  3. Snapshot: const previous = queryClient.getQueryData(key) (or getQueriesData({ queryKey }) for several list variants).
  4. Write the expected state with setQueryData (or setQueriesData).
  5. Return { previous }. It arrives as the third argument of onError and onSettled.
  6. onError(error, variables, context) restores context.previous, and tells the user.
  7. onSettled invalidates the key so the cache ends up matching the server either way.

Ordering and retries need two more tools:

  • scope: { id } (v5): mutations with the same scope ID run one at a time, in order. Tapping the heart three times quickly sends PUT, DELETE, PUT in sequence rather than racing, so the final server state matches the final tap.
  • Retries with a stable key: generate the idempotency key when the user acts, pass it in variables, and every retry of that mutation reuses it. Only then is retry: 2 on a mutation safe.

When not to be optimistic: payments, placing orders, anything with limited stock, anything with a low success rate, and anything whose failure the user would not notice in time to act. A heart that unfills is fine; a "Paid" badge that reverts is not.

Practical example

The wishlist heart on a product grid: the success rate is above 99.8 % (failures are network loss or the 500-item limit), the action is trivially reversible, and it appears on every product card. It is the textbook case for optimism.

Order cancellation is a borderline case, and the worked example in 72.12 handles it carefully: the server rejects about 4 % of cancels because the order shipped in the meantime, so the optimistic state is shown as "Cancelling..." rather than a final "Cancelled", and the rollback explains why.

The backend can often make the idempotency question disappear by designing naturally idempotent endpoints: PUT /v1/wishlist/items/:sku ("this SKU is saved") and DELETE /v1/wishlist/items/:sku can be repeated any number of times with the same result. Keys are needed for writes that are not naturally idempotent: POST /v1/orders, POST /v1/orders/:id/reorder, payments.

React / Next.js example

// src/wishlist/useToggleWishlist.ts  (TanStack Query v5)
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { WishlistSchema, type Wishlist } from '@shop/contracts';
import { apiSend } from '../api/http';
import { toast } from '../ui/toast';

const wishlistKey = ['wishlist'] as const;

export function useToggleWishlist(sku: string) {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    scope: { id: `wishlist:${sku}` },                    // rapid taps on one SKU run in order
    mutationFn: (save: boolean) =>
      apiSend(save ? 'PUT' : 'DELETE', `/v1/wishlist/items/${sku}`, undefined, WishlistSchema),
    onMutate: async (save) => {
      await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: wishlistKey });       // stop older refetches landing later
      const previous = queryClient.getQueryData<Wishlist>(wishlistKey); // snapshot for rollback
      queryClient.setQueryData<Wishlist>(wishlistKey, (old) =>
        old && {
          ...old,
          skus: save ? [...new Set([...old.skus, sku])] : old.skus.filter((s) => s !== sku),
        });
      return { previous };
    },
    onError: (_error, _save, context) => {
      if (context?.previous) queryClient.setQueryData(wishlistKey, context.previous);
      toast.error('Could not update your wishlist. Please try again.');
    },
    onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: wishlistKey }), // converge on the truth
  });
}

For a non-idempotent write, the key is created at intent time and travels in the variables:

// src/orders/useReorder.ts  (excerpt): POST creates a new order, so it needs a key
const reorder = useMutation({
  mutationFn: ({ orderId, idempotencyKey }: { orderId: string; idempotencyKey: string }) =>
    apiSend('POST', `/v1/orders/${orderId}/reorder`, {}, OrderCreatedSchema, { idempotencyKey }),
  retry: (count, error) => isRetryable(error) && count < 2, // safe only because the key is stable
});

// In the click handler: one key per user intent, reused by every automatic retry.
const onReorder = () => reorder.mutate({ orderId, idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID() });

A second component (a header badge counting "items being saved") can read pending mutations anywhere in the tree with useMutationState({ filters: { status: 'pending' }, select: (m) => m.state.variables }).

Backend side (NestJS)

Optimistic clients send more retries and more out-of-order writes than pessimistic ones. The backend's job is to make every write safe to repeat:

// apps/api/src/wishlist/wishlist.controller.ts
import { Controller, Delete, HttpCode, Param, Put, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Wishlist } from '@shop/contracts';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { WishlistService } from './wishlist.service';

@Controller('v1/wishlist/items')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class WishlistController {
  constructor(private readonly wishlist: WishlistService) {}

  @Put(':sku')
  @HttpCode(200)
  save(@CurrentUser() userId: string, @Param('sku') sku: string): Promise<Wishlist> {
    return this.wishlist.add(userId, sku); // INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, then return the list
  }

  @Delete(':sku')
  @HttpCode(200)
  remove(@CurrentUser() userId: string, @Param('sku') sku: string): Promise<Wishlist> {
    return this.wishlist.remove(userId, sku); // deleting an absent row is still success
  }
}
-- Repeating the PUT is harmless: the primary key absorbs duplicates.
CREATE TABLE wishlist_items (
  customer_id uuid NOT NULL,
  sku         text NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, sku)
);
INSERT INTO wishlist_items (customer_id, sku) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

For non-idempotent POSTs, require Idempotency-Key and apply the IdempotencyInterceptor from Part 15.12 (reserve the key in Redis, fingerprint the request, store and replay the response, back it with a unique constraint). For a browser on another origin, add Idempotency-Key to CORS allowedHeaders and expose Idempotent-Replayed so the client can tell a replay from a fresh result (71.8).

Production scenario

A fashion marketplace's product grid showed 48 cards per page, each with a heart. Before optimism, a tap showed a spinner for the request duration: median 210 ms, p95 900 ms on mobile. After moving to optimistic updates with scope, perceived latency was zero, and wishlist adds per session rose 14 %. The error rate stayed at 0.15 %, mostly offline taps, each rolled back with a message. Because PUT/DELETE were naturally idempotent, retries and duplicates needed no key storage.

Failure scenario

The first optimistic version skipped cancelQueries. The wishlist query had refetchOnWindowFocus on. A user returned to the tab (refetch started, 400 ms on their connection) and tapped a heart 100 ms later. The optimistic write filled the heart; 300 ms later the refetch landed with the pre-tap list and emptied it; then onSettled invalidated and it filled again. Users saw hearts flicker and tapped again, which removed the item. Support tickets called it "the wishlist forgets things".

Adding await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: wishlistKey }) in onMutate and scope per SKU removed both the flicker and the double-toggle.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • No cancelQueries: an in-flight refetch overwrites the optimistic state.
  • Snapshot rollback overwrites newer data: if a pushed event updated the entry after the snapshot, restoring the snapshot erases it. Roll back by reverting only the field you changed, or invalidate instead (72.12 shows this).
  • Rapid repeated actions race without scope; the last response to arrive wins, not the last tap.
  • Optimistic writes to several keys (list and detail) must all be snapshotted and restored.
  • Retried mutations without a stable key duplicate non-idempotent writes.
  • Keys generated in mutationFn change on every retry, which defeats them; generate at intent time.
  • Offline: paused optimistic mutations may sit for minutes (72.10); the UI must show them as pending, not done.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks three questions before approving an optimistic update: what is the success rate, what does the user lose if it reverts, and can the server make this write idempotent by design? High, little, yes: go optimistic. Otherwise show a pending state and wait for the server. They keep optimistic state visibly provisional when the stakes are higher ("Cancelling..."), and they always end with invalidation so the cache converges on the truth whatever happened in between.

Common mistakes

  • Optimistic updates for money and stock.
  • Skipping cancelQueries and the snapshot.
  • Rolling back without telling the user why their action vanished.
  • Generating a new idempotency key per retry.
  • Retrying non-idempotent mutations with no key.
  • Forgetting onSettled invalidation, leaving the optimistic guess as permanent truth.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through an optimistic update with rollback in TanStack Query. Expected answer: onMutate cancels queries, snapshots, writes the expected state and returns the snapshot; onError restores; onSettled invalidates. Why it matters: each step prevents a specific bug (overwrite, lost rollback, permanent guess). Follow-up: when would you use variables instead of the cache?
  2. Why does a client need idempotency keys, and when are they unnecessary? Expected answer: lost responses make retries ambiguous; unnecessary when the endpoint is naturally idempotent (PUT/DELETE of a state).
  3. How do you stop rapid toggles from ending in the wrong state? Expected answer: serialise with scope, or debounce to the final intent, and make server writes order-insensitive.
  4. When would you refuse an optimistic update? Expected answer: low success rate, irreversible or costly actions, payments, stock-limited actions.

Practical exercise

Build the wishlist heart with optimistic updates.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With network throttled to 3G, the heart fills within one frame of the tap.
  • With the API returning 422 WISHLIST_FULL, the heart reverts and a message explains why.
  • Five rapid taps produce five ordered requests and a final server state equal to the final UI state.
  • A focus refetch started before the tap does not overwrite the optimistic state.
  • The reorder mutation sends the same Idempotency-Key on every retry, and the NestJS integration test proves a replayed request creates one order.

72.7 Pagination and infinite scroll from the client

Concept

Part 15.5 designed pagination on the API side: offset pages for small admin tables, cursor (keyset) pages for anything large or changing. This section is the other end of that contract.

From the client, there are two shapes:

  • Numbered pages ("Page 3 of 12"): one ordinary useQuery per page, with the page number in the key. v5's placeholderData: keepPreviousData keeps page 2 on screen while page 3 loads, instead of flashing a spinner. (v4 had a keepPreviousData: true option; v5 replaced it with the imported keepPreviousData function passed to placeholderData.)
  • Infinite lists ("Load more" or scroll to load): one useInfiniteQuery whose cached value is a list of pages. Each page is fetched with a page parameter (for cursor APIs, the previous page's nextCursor).
useInfiniteQuery({
  queryKey,
  queryFn: ({ pageParam, signal }) => fetchPage(pageParam, signal),
  initialPageParam: null as string | null,            // required in v5
  getNextPageParam: (lastPage) => lastPage.nextCursor, // null or undefined means "no more pages"
});
// data.pages, data.pageParams, fetchNextPage(), hasNextPage, isFetchingNextPage

Why does it exist?

An order history, a product feed or a notification list can hold thousands of rows. Loading everything costs seconds and megabytes; numbered pages are awkward on phones. Infinite lists load 20 rows, then 20 more as the user approaches the end. The client must remember which pages it has, which cursor comes next, whether a request is already running, and what to do when filters change. useInfiniteQuery holds all of that as one cache entry.

Mental model

Imagine reading a Kafka topic with a consumer that stores its offset. Each poll returns a batch and the position to continue from; you never ask for "batch number 7", you ask for "after offset X". A cursor is that offset for an API, and useInfiniteQuery is the consumer that keeps the batches and the next offset together. Change the filter and you are reading a different topic: new key, new consumer, starting from the beginning.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant S as Sentinel
    participant IQ as useInfiniteQuery
    participant API as NestJS
    IQ->>API: GET /v1/orders?status=PAID&limit=20
    API-->>IQ: 20 items, nextCursor c1
    U->>S: scrolls near the end
    S->>IQ: fetchNextPage
    IQ->>API: GET /v1/orders?status=PAID&limit=20&cursor=c1
    API-->>IQ: 20 items, nextCursor c2
    U->>S: scrolls again
    IQ->>API: same request with cursor c2
    API-->>IQ: 7 items, nextCursor null
    Note over IQ: hasNextPage false, sentinel stops
  1. First page: the query function is called with initialPageParam.
  2. Next page: fetchNextPage() calls getNextPageParam(lastPage, allPages). If it returns null or undefined, hasNextPage is false and nothing is fetched. Otherwise the query function runs with that cursor and the page is appended.
  3. One fetch at a time: calling fetchNextPage while a fetch is running is ignored by default, so a scroll sentinel firing repeatedly is safe. Still guard with hasNextPage && !isFetchingNextPage to avoid wasted renders.
  4. Filters are part of the key. A new filter is a new cache entry starting at page one; switching back within gcTime restores the old pages instantly.
  5. Refetch replays every page. When an infinite query is refetched (focus, invalidation), v5 refetches all loaded pages, sequentially, from the first, recomputing each cursor from the fresh previous page. That keeps the list consistent, but 15 loaded pages means 15 sequential requests.
  6. maxPages (v5) caps how many pages are kept. With maxPages: 5 and getPreviousPageParam, the list keeps a sliding window and can fetch backwards when the user scrolls up.

The cursor contract the client depends on:

Rule Why the client needs it
nextCursor is opaque and null at the end The client never builds cursors, and knows when to stop
Total, stable order (placed_at DESC, id DESC) No duplicates or gaps between pages (71.3)
Cursor bound to its filters A cursor from status=PAID used with status=SHIPPED is rejected, not silently wrong
Capped limit (max 50) One client cannot request 10,000 rows
No total count count(*) on large filtered sets is slow (Part 15.5); show "Load more", not "page 3 of 120"

Practical example

The "My Orders" page loads 20 orders, shows a skeleton row at the end, and fetches more when that row scrolls within 400 px of the viewport. Filters (status, date range) live in the URL; changing one swaps to another cached list. A customer with 300 orders who scrolls to the bottom triggers 15 requests of about 60 ms each over a minute of scrolling, instead of one 1.4 s request for everything. With maxPages: 10, at most 200 orders sit in memory; beyond that, rows are also virtualised (71.9).

React / Next.js example

The list hook, keyed by the normalised filters:

// src/orders/useOrderList.ts  (TanStack Query v5)
import { useInfiniteQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderListResponseSchema, type OrderListFilters } from '@shop/contracts';
import { apiGet } from '../api/http';
import { orderKeys } from './orderKeys';

export function useOrderList(filters: OrderListFilters) {
  return useInfiniteQuery({
    queryKey: orderKeys.list(filters),
    queryFn: ({ pageParam, signal }) => {
      const qs = new URLSearchParams({ range: filters.range, limit: '20' });
      if (filters.status) qs.set('status', filters.status);
      if (pageParam) qs.set('cursor', pageParam);
      return apiGet(`/v1/orders?${qs}`, OrderListResponseSchema, signal);
    },
    initialPageParam: null as string | null,
    getNextPageParam: (last) => last.nextCursor,     // null ends the list
    maxPages: 10,                                     // keep at most 200 rows in the cache
    staleTime: 30_000,
  });
}

A sentinel that loads more when it nears the viewport, using IntersectionObserver in an effect (an external browser API, so an effect is right, 71.4):

// src/ui/LoadMoreSentinel.tsx  (React 18)
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';

type Props = { onVisible: () => void; disabled: boolean };

export function LoadMoreSentinel({ onVisible, disabled }: Props) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  const cb = useRef(onVisible);
  useEffect(() => { cb.current = onVisible; });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (disabled || !ref.current) return;
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      (entries) => { if (entries[0]?.isIntersecting) cb.current(); },
      { rootMargin: '400px 0px' },                    // start loading 400 px before the end
    );
    observer.observe(ref.current);
    return () => observer.disconnect();
  }, [disabled]);

  return <div ref={ref} aria-hidden="true" style={{ height: 1 }} />;
}

// Usage: a real button stays for keyboard and screen-reader users, and when observers fail.
// <LoadMoreSentinel disabled={!hasNextPage || isFetchingNextPage} onVisible={() => fetchNextPage()} />
// <button onClick={() => fetchNextPage()} disabled={!hasNextPage || isFetchingNextPage}>Load more</button>

Rendering flattens pages and drops duplicates by ID, a cheap safety net if the API ever returns an overlapping row:

const orders = useMemo(() => {
  const seen = new Map<string, OrderSummary>();
  for (const page of data?.pages ?? []) for (const o of page.items) seen.set(o.id, o);
  return [...seen.values()];
}, [data]);

Backend side (NestJS)

The query schema extends the filters from 72.2 and caps the limit:

// packages/contracts/src/index.ts  (continued)
export const OrderListQuerySchema = OrderListFiltersSchema.extend({
  cursor: z.string().max(512).optional(),
  limit: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(50).default(20), // query strings arrive as text
});
export type OrderListQuery = z.infer<typeof OrderListQuerySchema>;

The cursor codec from Part 15.5 (HMAC-signed base64url of { t, i }) gains one field: a short hash of the filters. Decoding a cursor whose filter hash does not match the request throws 400 CURSOR_FILTER_MISMATCH, which turns a subtle "wrong rows" bug into a loud error. The query uses a composite index per common filter:

-- One index serves "all statuses" and "status = X" lists for a customer.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_status_placed_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, status, placed_at DESC, id DESC);

SELECT id, display_id, status, total_minor, currency, placed_at, version, updated_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = $1
  AND status = $2
  AND placed_at >= now() - interval '30 days'
  AND (placed_at, id) < ($3, $4)            -- strictly after the cursor row
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;                                   -- one extra row says whether nextCursor is needed

Each page is an index range scan of 21 rows, 1 to 3 ms at any depth. Because infinite queries refetch every loaded page on invalidation, this per-page cost multiplies: keep it flat.

Production scenario

A pharmacy app's order history let users scroll indefinitely. Analytics showed 6 % of sessions loaded more than 10 pages, and those were long-time customers on low-end Android phones. Without maxPages, a 40-page session held 800 orders with line items, about 9 MB of JS heap, and scroll jank reached 120 ms frames. With maxPages: 10, row virtualisation, and slimmer list rows (items count instead of full line items), heap stayed under 2 MB and frames under 16 ms.

Failure scenario

The first release invalidated orderKeys.lists() after every cancel. A heavy user had 25 pages loaded. Invalidation refetched all 25, one after another, at about 90 ms each: 2.3 s with isFetching true, while the list re-rendered page by page and the scroll position jumped twice. During a sale weekend, cancels spiked and this pattern produced 40 % of all list traffic.

The fix: after a cancel, patch the one order in place across every cached list with setQueriesData (72.12), and invalidate only the detail and the summary counts. Lists refetch naturally on focus after their staleTime, now capped at 10 pages.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Missing initialPageParam is a type error in v5; code copied from v4 will not compile.
  • Offset pagination under inserts duplicates or skips rows (71.3); dedupe by ID at render as a guard, fix with cursors.
  • Filter not in the key shows pages from the previous filter appended to the new one.
  • Cursor expiry: if cursors embed a signature with a key rotation, old cursors fail; return 400 with a code the client handles by resetting the list.
  • Status filters and live changes: an order in a "Paid" list that ships is now outside the filter. Decide whether it disappears (refetch) or stays with its new badge until the next refresh (patch); users usually prefer it to stay.
  • Scroll restoration: navigating to a detail and back must restore the same pages and position; keep the query cached (gcTime) and store scroll offset per key.
  • Sentinel without a button locks keyboard and screen-reader users out of more content.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats the cursor as an API contract with the same care as a field name: opaque, signed, bound to filters, with a documented end marker. On the client they bound memory (maxPages, virtualisation) and avoid full invalidation of deep lists, preferring targeted patches. They also push back on "page N of M" in product designs for large lists, because the count query costs more than the page.

Common mistakes

  • Building cursors on the client from the last row's fields.
  • Invalidating deep infinite lists after every small change.
  • No maxPages for feeds users scroll for minutes.
  • Using useQuery with an accumulating array in state to fake infinite scroll.
  • Asking for totals on cursor APIs.

Interview questions

  1. How does useInfiniteQuery refetch, and why does it matter for the backend? Expected answer: it refetches all loaded pages sequentially from the first; deep lists cost N requests, so pages must be cheap and invalidation targeted. Follow-up: what does maxPages change?
  2. What should a cursor pagination contract guarantee? Expected answer: opaque cursor, null at end, total stable order, filter binding, capped limit.
  3. How do you avoid flashing a spinner when moving between numbered pages? Expected answer: placeholderData: keepPreviousData in v5.
