  4. An order in a filtered list changes status. What should happen? Expected answer: a product decision; patch in place with the new badge, or refetch and remove; explain the tradeoff.

Practical exercise

Build the infinite order history.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Initial render makes one request with limit=20; scrolling to the end loads the next page once per sentinel crossing.
  • Changing the status filter starts a new list; switching back within 5 minutes shows the old pages instantly.
  • A cursor from one filter sent with another returns 400 CURSOR_FILTER_MISMATCH.
  • With maxPages: 10, the cache never holds more than 10 pages (checked in Devtools).
  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) for page 30 shows an index range scan with fewer than 30 buffers read.

72.8 Real-time data in the UI: polling, SSE and WebSockets, merged into the cache

Concept

Pull-based freshness (72.3) is enough for most data. For order status on a tracking page, a kitchen ticket board or a support queue, users expect changes within a second or two. The browser has three ways to get them:

  • Polling: ask on a timer. In TanStack Query, refetchInterval.
  • Server-Sent Events (SSE): one long-lived HTTP response that the server writes events into; the browser API is EventSource. One direction (server to client), automatic reconnection, plain HTTP.
  • WebSockets: a full-duplex connection; the browser API is WebSocket. Both directions, binary or text, no automatic reconnection.

Part 35 — Real-Time Systems covers the server side of all three (35.1 to 35.4) and fan-out with pub/sub (35.5). This section is about the browser: opening and closing connections correctly, and merging pushed events into the query cache, so pushed data and fetched data never become two competing truths.

Why does it exist?

Without push, the order page learns that the rider picked up the food only when the user refocuses the tab or a poll runs. Without merging, pushed events update one widget's local state while the cached list and detail still show the old status: the header says "Out for delivery", the list says "Preparing". The cache must stay the single source the UI reads, with events as one of its writers.

Mental model

Imagine a CDC (change data capture) consumer keeping a read model up to date from a stream of row changes. Each event carries the row's version; the consumer applies it only if it is newer than what it has; if it falls too far behind or misses events, it rebuilds from a snapshot. The query cache is the read model, the SSE stream is the change feed, and invalidation is "rebuild from snapshot".

How it works

Choosing a transport from the browser's point of view (server tradeoffs are in Part 35.1):

Need Polling SSE WebSocket
Server to client updates, seconds of latency acceptable Good, simplest Good Overkill
Server to client, sub-second Wasteful Best fit Fine
Client sends frequent messages (chat, collaborative edit) No No, use normal POSTs Best fit
Works through every proxy and HTTP stack Yes Mostly; needs buffering off Needs upgrade support
Reconnection Not needed Built in, with Last-Event-ID You write it
Auth Cookies or headers Cookies only, no custom headers Cookies, or a ticket in the URL or first message
Hidden tab behaviour Timers throttled, paused by default in TanStack Query Keeps streaming Keeps running; may be dropped on mobile

Two kinds of events, and the merge rule for each:

  1. Payload events carry the new state ({ orderId, status, version }). Apply with setQueryData / setQueriesData only if event.version is greater than the cached version. Duplicates and out-of-order events (common after reconnects and replays, Part 35.10) are then harmless.
  2. Signal events say only "something changed" ({ type: 'orders-changed' }). Respond with invalidateQueries. Simpler and always correct, but every client refetches at once: a fan-out of N events becomes N GETs.
flowchart TB
    evt["SSE event: order 42, SHIPPED, version 9"] --> parse{"Valid against schema?"}
    parse -->|"No"| drop["Ignore and log"]
    parse -->|"Yes"| known{"Order 42 in any cached list or detail?"}
    known -->|"No"| inval["Invalidate order lists"]
    known -->|"Yes"| newer{"Event version greater than cached?"}
    newer -->|"No"| skip["Skip: duplicate or out of order"]
    newer -->|"Yes"| patch["Patch detail and every list page with setQueriesData"]

Connection lifecycle in the browser:

  • EventSource reconnects by itself after a dropped connection, waiting the retry: value the server sent (default about 3 s), and sends Last-Event-ID with the last id: it saw. It stops only if the server answers with a non-200 status or a wrong content type, at which point readyState becomes CLOSED (2) and you must reconnect yourself.
  • After any reconnect, events may have been missed. If the server can replay from Last-Event-ID, nothing to do; if it cannot (gap too old), it should send a reset event and the client invalidates.
  • HTTP/1.1 allows about six connections per origin per browser, shared across all tabs. Each open EventSource holds one. With seven tabs open, every other API request from that origin queues forever. Serve SSE over HTTP/2 (100 or more streams per connection), or keep one stream per browser with a leader tab and BroadcastChannel.
  • WebSocket has no reconnection. Reconnect on close with exponential backoff and jitter, resubscribe, and refetch to catch up.
  • Background tabs: Chrome throttles timers in hidden tabs, to once a minute after five minutes, so polling there is unreliable by design. Mobile browsers may close connections when the app is backgrounded; on visibilitychange back to visible, check readyState and refetch.

Practical example

The order list page opens one SSE stream per customer (GET /v1/orders/events), not one per order row. Events carry { orderId, status, version, updatedAt }. When order A7K2Q9P ships, the server publishes one event; the client patches that order in the detail cache and in every cached list page, and the row's badge changes within about 500 ms of the warehouse scan. A brand-new order placed on another device arrives as an unknown ID, which invalidates the lists so it appears at the top.

For a simpler internal dashboard, polling is the right answer: refetchInterval: 15_000, paused in background tabs, stopped once all orders are terminal.

React / Next.js example

Polling that stops by itself (v5's refetchInterval accepts a function of the query):

useQuery({
  ...orderDetailQuery(orderId),
  refetchInterval: (query) =>
    query.state.data && ['DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED'].includes(query.state.data.status) ? false : 10_000,
});

The SSE hook that merges events into the cache:

// src/orders/useOrderEvents.ts  (React 18, TanStack Query v5)
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useQueryClient, type InfiniteData } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderEventSchema, type OrderListResponse, type OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import { orderKeys } from './orderKeys';

export function useOrderEvents() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();

  useEffect(() => {
    const source = new EventSource('/api/v1/orders/events', { withCredentials: true });

    const apply = (msg: MessageEvent<string>) => {
      const parsed = OrderEventSchema.safeParse(JSON.parse(msg.data));
      if (!parsed.success) return;                                   // unknown shape: ignore, never crash
      const e = parsed.data;
      const patch = (o: OrderSummary) =>
        o.id === e.orderId && e.version > o.version ? { ...o, status: e.status, version: e.version, updatedAt: e.updatedAt } : o;

      let found = false;
      queryClient.setQueryData<OrderSummary>(orderKeys.detail(e.orderId), (old) => {
        if (old) found = true;
        return old && patch(old);
      });
      queryClient.setQueriesData<InfiniteData<OrderListResponse>>({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() }, (old) => {
        if (!old) return old;
        return { ...old, pages: old.pages.map((p) => ({ ...p, items: p.items.map((o) => {
          if (o.id === e.orderId) found = true;
          return patch(o);
        }) })) };
      });
      if (!found) void queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() }); // new order elsewhere
    };

    const reset = () => void queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.all }); // gap too old to replay
    source.addEventListener('order', apply as EventListener);
    source.addEventListener('reset', reset);
    return () => { source.removeEventListener('order', apply as EventListener); source.removeEventListener('reset', reset); source.close(); };
  }, [queryClient]);
}

Unchanged orders keep their object identity (patch returns o itself), so structural sharing and memoised rows skip re-rendering everything except the changed row.

Backend side (NestJS)

The event contract, shared with the client:

// packages/contracts/src/index.ts  (continued)
export const OrderEventSchema = z.object({
  orderId: z.string().uuid(),
  status: OrderStatusSchema,
  version: z.number().int().nonnegative(),   // the same version column as OrderSummary
  updatedAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),
});
export type OrderEvent = z.infer<typeof OrderEventSchema>;

The stream endpoint, one per customer, with replay and a reset signal:

// apps/api/src/orders/order-events.controller.ts
import { Controller, Headers, MessageEvent, Sse, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, concat, from, interval, map, merge, mergeMap, of } from 'rxjs';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { OrderEventsBus, type StoredOrderEvent } from './order-events.bus';

const toMessage = (e: StoredOrderEvent): MessageEvent => ({ type: 'order', id: e.streamId, data: e.payload });

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
export class OrderEventsController {
  constructor(private readonly bus: OrderEventsBus) {}

  @Sse('events')
  stream(
    @CurrentUser() userId: string,
    @Headers('last-event-id') lastEventId: string | undefined, // sent by EventSource on reconnect
  ): Observable<MessageEvent> {
    // Replay what the browser missed, or tell it to refetch if the gap is too old.
    const replay = from(this.bus.replaySince(userId, lastEventId)).pipe(
      mergeMap((r) => (r.ok ? from(r.events.map(toMessage)) : of<MessageEvent>({ type: 'reset', data: '' }))),
    );
    const live = this.bus.subscribe(userId).pipe(map(toMessage)); // teardown unsubscribes on disconnect
    const heartbeat = interval(20_000).pipe(map((): MessageEvent => ({ type: 'ping', data: '' })));
    // An event published while replay runs may arrive twice; the client's version guard absorbs it.
    return merge(concat(replay, live), heartbeat);
  }
}

replaySince reads a per-customer Redis Stream with XRANGE from the last ID (kept for 15 minutes with MAXLEN); subscribe wraps Redis pub/sub or XREAD BLOCK and unsubscribes in its teardown when the browser disconnects (Part 35.5, 35.9). The version in each payload comes from the same UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 that changed the order, published after commit via the outbox (Part 30.10), so events can never claim a version the database does not have.

Production scenario

A meal-kit company's order list polled every 10 s while visible. At 30,000 concurrent viewers that was 3,000 RPS of list requests, 95 % returning unchanged data, and status changes still took 5 s on average to appear. Moving to one SSE stream per customer cut list traffic to under 200 RPS (initial loads and focus refetches), held 30,000 idle connections at about 4 KB each on two gateway pods, and brought median status latency to 600 ms from warehouse scan to badge.

Failure scenario

After the SSE release, a support team (who kept eight or more order tabs open) reported that "the whole admin hangs". Each tab held one EventSource, the admin API was still served over HTTP/1.1 through an old load balancer listener, and Chrome's limit of six connections per origin was exhausted by streams. The seventh tab's API calls sat in "Stalled" in the Network panel indefinitely.

The immediate fix was enabling HTTP/2 on the listener, which multiplexes all streams on one connection. The longer-term fix was a leader-tab pattern: one tab holds the EventSource and rebroadcasts events to the others on a BroadcastChannel, with a new leader elected when it closes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Out-of-order and duplicate events after reconnects; the version guard makes them no-ops.
  • Events arriving before the initial fetch finds nothing to patch; the fetch that follows already includes the change, so dropping is correct.
  • Pushed events vs optimistic updates: an event can land between onMutate and the server's reply; roll back by field and version, not by snapshot (72.12).
  • Six-connection limit on HTTP/1.1, shared by all tabs.
  • Proxy buffering delivers events in bursts or not at all; disable buffering, send heartbeats every 15 to 30 s (Part 35.8).
  • Session expiry: EventSource cannot refresh tokens; a 401 closes it permanently. Detect readyState === 2 and reconnect after the auth refresh (Part 75).
  • Signal-event fan-out: one "orders changed" event to 30,000 clients produces 30,000 GETs within a second; send payloads or add jittered delay.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps the query cache as the only thing components read, and makes push one more writer with the same rules as mutations: versioned, idempotent, convergent. They pick the least powerful transport that meets the latency requirement (polling, then SSE, then WebSocket) and count connections per browser and per pod before shipping. And they always ask what happens after a gap: replay, or reset and refetch.

Common mistakes

  • Storing pushed data in component state next to a cache that disagrees.
  • Applying events without version checks.
  • One stream per list row instead of one per page or user.
  • WebSockets for one-way updates, then hand-writing reconnection that SSE has built in.
  • Ignoring the hidden-tab and mobile background cases.

Interview questions

  1. How do you merge server-pushed events into a TanStack Query cache safely? Expected answer: validate, patch with setQueryData/setQueriesData only when the event version is newer, invalidate when the entity is unknown or after a replay gap. Why it matters: the cache stays the single source of truth. Follow-up: payload events vs signal events?
  2. SSE or WebSocket for live order status? Expected answer: SSE: one direction, auto reconnect with Last-Event-ID, plain HTTP; WebSocket if the client must stream messages.
  3. What is the six-connection problem? Expected answer: HTTP/1.1 per-origin connection limits shared across tabs; long-lived streams starve other requests; use HTTP/2 or one stream per browser.
  4. What should happen after a reconnect? Expected answer: replay from the last event ID if possible, otherwise a reset event and invalidation.

Practical exercise

Add live status to the order list.

Acceptance criteria:

  • One EventSource per tab, closed on unmount (verified with Strict Mode on).
  • A status change in the database appears on the list row within 1 s without a GET.
  • Sending the same event twice, or an older version after a newer one, changes nothing.
  • Killing the API for 30 s and restoring it: the stream reconnects with Last-Event-ID, and missed changes appear, or a reset triggers one refetch.
  • An unknown order ID in an event causes exactly one list invalidation.

72.9 Client state stores: Context, Zustand and Redux Toolkit

Concept

Once server state lives in a query cache and filters live in the URL, what remains is genuine global client state: preferences, a toast queue, a multi-step wizard's progress, rows selected across pages for a bulk action, an in-browser editor's document. Three tools dominate:

  • React Context (built in): passes a value down the tree. Every component that reads the context re-renders when the provider's value changes (71.5).
  • Zustand (about 1 KB gzip): a store that lives outside React. Components subscribe with a selector and re-render only when the selected slice changes.
  • Redux Toolkit (RTK): the official way to write Redux. A single store, state changed only by dispatching actions to reducers written with createSlice, excellent devtools, middleware. It ships RTK Query, a server-state cache comparable to TanStack Query, for teams already on Redux.

Why does it exist?

Passing a value through six layers of props is noisy and brittle. Context fixes that for values that change rarely. For values that change often and are read in many places, Context's "everyone re-renders" behaviour becomes a performance problem, and a store with selectors fixes it. For large apps with many developers, Redux adds a strict, inspectable structure: every change is a named action you can log, replay and test.

Mental model

  • Context is NestJS dependency injection scoped to a subtree: ask for a token, get the nearest provider's value.
  • Zustand is a singleton service with an event emitter: anyone can call its methods, and listeners decide whether the change concerns them.
  • Redux is event sourcing in miniature (Part 30.16): actions are events, reducers fold them into state, and the devtools can replay the log.

How it works

flowchart LR
    subgraph Ctx
        pv["Provider value changes"] --> c1["Every consumer re-renders"]
    end
    subgraph Zus
        zs["setState"] --> sel["Each subscriber runs its selector"]
        sel --> cmp{"Selected value changed?"}
        cmp -->|"Yes"| rr["That component re-renders"]
        cmp -->|"No"| nr["No render"]
    end
    subgraph Rdx
        da["dispatch action"] --> rd["Reducers return new state"]
        rd --> us["useSelector compares, re-renders on change"]
    end

Zustand v5 specifics. create<State>()((set, get) => ({ ... })) returns a hook. useStore((s) => s.density) subscribes to one field. A selector that returns a new object or array each time ((s) => ({ a: s.a, b: s.b })) looks changed on every check; in v5, which is built on React's useSyncExternalStore, that can cause an infinite render loop. Wrap such selectors in useShallow from zustand/react/shallow. The persist middleware (zustand/middleware) saves the store to localStorage or sessionStorage via createJSONStorage, with partialize to choose fields and version plus migrate for schema changes.

Redux Toolkit specifics. configureStore sets up the store with devtools and serialisability checks; createSlice generates actions and a reducer using Immer, so "mutating" code in reducers produces immutable updates. RTK 2 and React Redux 9 add useSelector.withTypes<RootState>() for typed hooks. RTK Query defines endpoints with createApi and fetchBaseQuery; caching uses tags (providesTags, invalidatesTags) rather than key prefixes; unused data is kept for keepUnusedDataFor seconds (default 60); refetchOnFocus needs setupListeners(store.dispatch); optimistic updates use onQueryStarted with api.util.updateQueryData and patch.undo(). Infinite query endpoints were added in RTK 2.6.

The decision:

Situation Choose Why
Current user, locale, theme, feature flags Context Rare changes, read everywhere
A few fast-changing global UI values (toasts, selection, drawer) Zustand Selector subscriptions, no provider, tiny
Large team, complex client-side workflows, need for action logs and replay Redux Toolkit Structure, devtools, middleware
Already on Redux and need server-state caching RTK Query Same store and devtools, tag invalidation
Not on Redux and need server-state caching TanStack Query Richer infinite queries, persistence and offline support
State used by one component or one subtree useState / useReducer No library at all

Practical example

On the order list page the global client state is small: the row density preference (persisted per device), a toast queue (any component can push, one component renders), and, in the admin version, a set of selected order IDs that must survive paging and filter changes for a bulk "Export CSV" action. That is a 30-line Zustand store. The orders themselves stay in TanStack Query.

React / Next.js example

// src/state/uiStore.ts  (Zustand v5)
import { create } from 'zustand';
import { createJSONStorage, persist } from 'zustand/middleware';

type Toast = { id: string; kind: 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'; text: string };
type UiState = {
  density: 'comfortable' | 'compact';
  toasts: Toast[];
  selectedOrderIds: Set<string>;
  setDensity: (d: UiState['density']) => void;
  pushToast: (t: Omit<Toast, 'id'>) => void;
  dismissToast: (id: string) => void;
  toggleSelected: (id: string) => void;
};

export const useUiStore = create<UiState>()(
  persist(
    (set) => ({
      density: 'comfortable',
      toasts: [],
      selectedOrderIds: new Set(),
      setDensity: (density) => set({ density }),
      pushToast: (t) => set((s) => ({ toasts: [...s.toasts, { ...t, id: crypto.randomUUID() }] })),
      dismissToast: (id) => set((s) => ({ toasts: s.toasts.filter((t) => t.id !== id) })),
      toggleSelected: (id) => set((s) => {
        const next = new Set(s.selectedOrderIds);           // new Set so subscribers see a change
        next.has(id) ? next.delete(id) : next.add(id);
        return { selectedOrderIds: next };
      }),
    }),
    {
      name: 'ui-prefs',
      version: 1,
      storage: createJSONStorage(() => localStorage),
      partialize: (s) => ({ density: s.density }),         // persist the preference only, never toasts or IDs
    },
  ),
);

// Components subscribe to exactly what they read:
// const density = useUiStore((s) => s.density);
// const { toasts, dismissToast } = useUiStore(useShallow((s) => ({ toasts: s.toasts, dismissToast: s.dismissToast })));

The same orders API in RTK Query, for a team already on Redux:

// src/state/ordersApi.ts  (Redux Toolkit 2, RTK Query)
import { createApi, fetchBaseQuery } from '@reduxjs/toolkit/query/react';
import type { OrderListFilters, OrderListResponse, OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';

export const ordersApi = createApi({
  reducerPath: 'ordersApi',
  baseQuery: fetchBaseQuery({ baseUrl: '/api/v1', credentials: 'include' }),
  tagTypes: ['Order'],
  endpoints: (build) => ({
    getOrders: build.query<OrderListResponse, OrderListFilters>({
      query: (filters) => ({ url: '/orders', params: filters }),
      providesTags: (res) => [{ type: 'Order', id: 'LIST' }, ...(res?.items ?? []).map((o) => ({ type: 'Order' as const, id: o.id }))],
    }),
    cancelOrder: build.mutation<OrderSummary, { id: string; filters: OrderListFilters; key: string }>({
      query: ({ id, key }) => ({ url: `/orders/${id}/cancel`, method: 'POST', body: { reason: 'CHANGED_MIND' }, headers: { 'Idempotency-Key': key } }),
      async onQueryStarted({ id, filters }, { dispatch, queryFulfilled }) {
        const patch = dispatch(ordersApi.util.updateQueryData('getOrders', filters, (draft) => {
          const o = draft.items.find((x) => x.id === id);
          if (o) o.status = 'CANCELLED';                       // Immer draft: write as if mutable
        }));
        try { await queryFulfilled; } catch { patch.undo(); }   // rollback on failure
      },
      invalidatesTags: (_res, _err, { id }) => [{ type: 'Order', id }],
    }),
  }),
});
export const { useGetOrdersQuery, useCancelOrderMutation } = ordersApi;

Backend side (NestJS)

Client stores touch the backend in three places:

  • Cross-device preferences belong on the server. If density or default filters should follow the user to their phone, persist them with PUT /v1/me/preferences and load them into the query cache; the store holds only device-local choices.
  • Never treat store contents as authority. A role: 'admin' in a store decides which buttons render, nothing else; every endpoint enforces permissions with guards (Part 75 covers why hiding a button is not authorization).
  • Bulk actions from client selections must be bounded and re-checked. A "cancel 300 selected orders" request carries IDs the server must re-authorise one by one, cap (say 100 per request), and process idempotently:
// packages/contracts/src/index.ts  (continued)
export const BulkExportRequestSchema = z.object({
  orderIds: z.array(z.string().uuid()).min(1).max(100), // the server's cap, enforced at the edge
});
-- The service filters IDs by ownership in one query; foreign IDs are silently excluded, never leaked.
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 AND id = ANY($2::uuid[]);

Production scenario

A logistics customer portal had grown to 118 Redux slices over four years; 41 of them held API data with hand-written loading flags and "last fetched" timestamps. Migrating API data to TanStack Query and the rest to three Zustand stores and two Contexts removed about 9,000 lines of reducers and thunks (to 2,100), cut the main bundle by 31 KB gzip, and closed 23 open "stale data" bugs, most of which simply stopped existing because their slices were deleted.

Failure scenario

A team upgraded Zustand from v4 to v5 on a Friday. The order page's toolbar used useUiStore((s) => ({ density: s.density, setDensity: s.setDensity })). In v4 this re-rendered on every store change, which nobody noticed. In v5 it threw "Maximum update depth exceeded" on load, and the error boundary replaced the whole page. Error tracking showed 100 % of order-page sessions failing for 25 minutes until rollback.

The fix was one wrapper, useShallow(...), and a lint rule flagging object-literal selectors without it. The postmortem also noted that no test rendered the toolbar with the real store; a single component test (Part 77) would have caught it in CI.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Module-level stores in Next.js server rendering are shared across all requests on the server: one user's data can leak into another's HTML. Create stores per request and provide them through Context (Part 73).
  • Persisted stores rehydrate after first render, so the first frame shows defaults; render a neutral state until hydrated, or use sessionStorage only for non-visual state.
  • Schema changes to persisted state without version and migrate crash on old saved data.
  • Context value recreated each render re-renders every consumer (71.5).
  • Sets and Maps in Redux break serialisability checks; use arrays or records.
  • PII in localStorage survives logout and is readable by any script on the origin (69.8); persist preferences, not personal data.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior shrinks global client state first, by moving server data to a query cache and view state to the URL, then picks the lightest tool that fits what remains. They choose Redux for organisational reasons (a large team that benefits from enforced structure and action logs), not because "real apps use Redux". And they treat every persisted store as a schema with versions, because data saved on a user's device is data you must migrate.

Common mistakes

  • A global store as a second copy of server data.
  • Context for fast-changing values read across the app.
  • Object-literal selectors without useShallow in Zustand v5.
  • Persisting everything, including tokens, PII and transient UI.
  • Using both RTK Query and TanStack Query in one app for overlapping data.

Interview questions

  1. When would you pick Context, Zustand or Redux Toolkit? Expected answer: Context for rarely changing cross-cutting values; Zustand for small, fast-changing global UI state with selector subscriptions; Redux Toolkit for large apps needing structure, devtools and middleware. Follow-up: where does server data go in each case? (A query cache, or RTK Query on Redux.)
  2. Why does Context cause extra re-renders, and how do stores avoid it? Expected answer: every consumer re-renders on value change; stores notify subscribers who compare selected slices.
  3. How does RTK Query invalidate compared with TanStack Query? Expected answer: tags (providesTags/invalidatesTags) instead of key prefixes.
  4. What can go wrong with a module-level store in server rendering? Expected answer: shared across requests, leaking data between users.

Practical exercise

Replace a Context that holds fast-changing UI state with a Zustand store.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The React Profiler shows that toggling density re-renders only components that read density.
  • Only density appears in localStorage; toasts and selections do not.
  • A version bump with a migrate function upgrades an old saved shape without errors.
  • The bulk export endpoint rejects 101 IDs with 400 VALIDATION_FAILED and silently excludes IDs owned by other customers.

72.10 Offline and flaky networks: timeouts, retries, AbortController and honest stale data

Concept

Mobile networks fail in four ways, and the client must handle each:

  1. Offline: no connectivity. Requests fail immediately with a TypeError: Failed to fetch.
  2. Slow: 300 to 2,000 ms round trips on congested 3G or 4G.
  3. Hanging: the request is sent and nothing comes back. fetch has no default timeout; a request can sit for minutes.
  4. Lying: the browser says online (navigator.onLine === true) behind a hotel captive portal or a dead Wi-Fi uplink.

The tools: timeouts on every request (AbortSignal.timeout), cancellation (AbortController, and AbortSignal.any to combine signals), bounded retries with backoff (72.3), TanStack Query's network mode and paused queries and mutations, a persisted cache for instant start-up, and a UI that shows stale data honestly instead of pretending it is live.

Why does it exist?

A spinner that never ends is the worst possible UI: the user cannot tell whether to wait, retry or give up. A blank error page that discards the orders loaded two minutes ago is nearly as bad. Users on trains, in lifts and in basements are a large share of real traffic, and the difference between "your data, 3 minutes old, reconnecting" and "something went wrong" is the difference between a working app and a support ticket.

Mental model

Imagine your NestJS service calling a payment gateway (Part 31.2). You would never call it without a timeout, you would retry only safe calls with backoff, and you would serve degraded but useful answers when it is down (Part 31.10). In the browser, your API is the unreliable dependency, and the phone's radio is the flaky network. Apply the same reliability toolbox from the other side.

How it works

Combining the library's cancellation signal with a timeout:

// src/api/http.ts  (apiGet with a deadline; AbortSignal.any needs Chrome 116+, Firefox 124+, Safari 17.4+)
export class ApiTimeoutError extends Error {}

export async function apiGet<T>(path: string, schema: ZodType<T>, signal?: AbortSignal, timeoutMs = 10_000): Promise<T> {
  const deadline = AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs);                 // aborts with a 'TimeoutError' DOMException
  const combined = signal ? AbortSignal.any([signal, deadline]) : deadline;
  let res: Response;
  try {
    res = await fetch(`/api${path}`, { credentials: 'include', signal: combined });
  } catch (e) {
    if (deadline.aborted) throw new ApiTimeoutError(`GET ${path} timed out after ${timeoutMs} ms`); // retryable
    throw e;                                                       // AbortError from the library: not an error to show
  }
  if (!res.ok) throw await toApiError(res);
  return schema.parse(await res.json());
}

TanStack Query's networkMode decides what happens without a connection:

networkMode Queries when offline Mutations when offline Use when
'online' (default) Do not start; fetchStatus: 'paused'; resume on reconnect Paused, resumed in order on reconnect Normal API-backed apps
'offlineFirst' Try once (a service worker or HTTP cache may answer), then pause retries Same Apps with a service worker cache
'always' Fetch regardless, fail normally Same Local-first data, or when online detection is unreliable

Online state comes from onlineManager, which listens to the browser's online and offline events. A query can be status: 'success' and fetchStatus: 'paused': it has data, it wanted to refetch, and it is waiting for the network. That combination is the "showing saved data" state.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Fetching: trigger while online
    Idle --> Paused: trigger while offline
    Paused --> Fetching: online event
    Fetching --> Idle: success or final error
    Fetching --> Paused: went offline during retries

A persisted cache writes the query cache to storage and restores it at start-up, so a returning user sees their orders instantly, marked as saved, while fresh data loads. PersistQueryClientProvider from @tanstack/react-query-persist-client with createSyncStoragePersister (@tanstack/query-sync-storage-persister, for localStorage) or createAsyncStoragePersister (for IndexedDB through a small wrapper) does this. Three rules: gcTime must be at least the persister's maxAge or restored entries are collected immediately; set buster to the app version so a deploy with changed schemas discards old caches; and clear it on logout.

Practical example

A customer opens "My Orders" on an underground train. The persisted cache renders the list from 40 minutes ago in under 100 ms, with a banner "Saved at 08:12. Reconnecting...". The status query is paused, not failing. They tap "Cancel" on an order; the mutation is paused and the row shows "Cancel queued, will send when you are back online". At the next station the network returns, onlineManager fires, the paused mutation runs with its original idempotency key, and the list refetches. The server says the order shipped 10 minutes ago: 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE, and the row explains it.

React / Next.js example

// src/main.tsx  (excerpt, TanStack Query v5 persistence)
import { PersistQueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query-persist-client';
import { createSyncStoragePersister } from '@tanstack/query-sync-storage-persister';
import { queryClient } from './api/queryClient';

const persister = createSyncStoragePersister({ storage: window.localStorage, key: 'rq-cache' });

// queryClient defaults include gcTime: 24 * 60 * 60_000 so restored entries survive (gcTime >= maxAge).
<PersistQueryClientProvider
  client={queryClient}
  persistOptions={{
    persister,
    maxAge: 24 * 60 * 60_000,
    buster: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,               // new deploy, new cache
    dehydrateOptions: { shouldDehydrateQuery: (q) => q.queryKey[0] === 'orders' && q.state.status === 'success' },
  }}
  onSuccess={() => queryClient.resumePausedMutations()}     // send writes queued before a reload
>
  <App />
</PersistQueryClientProvider>;

Paused mutations restored after a reload have no function attached, so register defaults by key: queryClient.setMutationDefaults(['orders', 'cancel'], { mutationFn: cancelOrder }), and give the cancel mutation mutationKey: ['orders', 'cancel'].

Honest staleness in the UI:

// src/ui/FreshnessBanner.tsx
import { useIsRestoring, onlineManager } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';

export function FreshnessBanner({ updatedAt, failed }: { updatedAt: number; failed: boolean }) {
  const online = useSyncExternalStore(onlineManager.subscribe.bind(onlineManager), () => onlineManager.isOnline());
  const restoring = useIsRestoring();
  if (restoring || (online && !failed)) return null;
  const at = new Date(updatedAt).toLocaleTimeString([], { hour: '2-digit', minute: '2-digit' });
  return <p role="status">Showing orders saved at {at}. {online ? 'Could not refresh, retrying.' : 'Reconnecting...'}</p>;
}
// <FreshnessBanner updatedAt={query.dataUpdatedAt} failed={query.isError} />

Logout must clear every layer: queryClient.clear(), persister.removeClient(), and the persisted Zustand stores.

Backend side (NestJS)

Offline clients change the backend's assumptions:

  • Writes can arrive hours late. A queued cancel replays when the phone reconnects. Idempotency records (Part 15.12) must live at least as long as the client's offline window: 24 hours, not 5 minutes. Business rules are evaluated at replay time, so a late cancel of a shipped order is a clean 409, not a corruption.
  • Server deadlines must be shorter than client timeouts. If the browser gives up at 10 s, a handler still working at 25 s is wasted work and a likely duplicate when the user retries. A timeout interceptor returns 503 with Retry-After first:
// apps/api/src/common/timeout.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor, ServiceUnavailableException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, TimeoutError, catchError, throwError, timeout } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class TimeoutInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    return next.handle().pipe(
      timeout(8_000),                                                     // below the browser's 10 s deadline
      catchError((err) => {
        if (!(err instanceof TimeoutError)) return throwError(() => err);
        ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse().setHeader('Retry-After', '5');   // tell clients when to retry
        return throwError(() => new ServiceUnavailableException({ code: 'UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT', issues: [] }));
      }),
    );
  }
}

The RxJS timeout stops waiting, not the work; pass an AbortSignal or a PostgreSQL statement_timeout down to really stop it (Part 31.2).

  • Small, compressible responses matter more on slow links than CPU does: 22 KB gzip is 0.3 s on a 600 kbps connection; 400 KB is 5 s.

Production scenario

A pharmacy delivery app's analytics showed 9 % of sessions spent at least one minute offline or on a "lying" connection, concentrated in commuter hours. Before the changes, those sessions hit endless spinners (no timeouts) and blank error screens. After adding 10 s deadlines, persisted order caches, paused mutations and the freshness banner, "app not working" reviews in the store fell by 60 % in a quarter, and support calls asking "did my cancel go through?" fell by half, because queued writes were visible as queued.

Failure scenario

A pharmacy chain ran the web app on shared in-store tablets for customers checking prescriptions and orders. The persisted query cache was not cleared on logout. A customer logged out; the next customer opened the app and, for the 300 ms before the auth check redirected to login, saw the previous customer's orders, including medicine names, restored from localStorage. A customer took a screenshot and complained to the regulator.

The fixes: logout cleared the query cache, the persister and all stores; the buster included a hash of the user ID so a different user could never restore another's cache; persistence excluded queries tagged as sensitive (meta: { persist: false }); and the shared-device mode disabled persistence entirely.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • navigator.onLine is true behind captive portals; rely on request timeouts, not the flag, to detect a dead network.
  • Retries multiply timeouts: 10 s timeout with 2 retries and backoff is about 33 s before an error. Tell the user after the first timeout, keep trying in the background.
  • TimeoutError vs AbortError: a timeout is a failure to show and retry; a library abort (unmount, superseded request) is not an error at all.
  • Paused mutations after a reload need setMutationDefaults or they cannot resume.
  • Persisted caches with changed schemas crash on restore; buster plus schema parsing on read protect you.
  • Offline writes conflict: a queued edit to an order changed elsewhere must hit the version check (72.5), not overwrite.
  • Quota limits: localStorage is about 5 MB per origin and synchronous; large caches belong in IndexedDB.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior designs for the network the users actually have, not the office Wi-Fi: every request has a deadline, every retry is bounded and safe, every screen has a "showing saved data" state, and queued writes are visible. They align timeouts across layers (browser above API above database) and make idempotency windows match offline windows. And they treat persisted caches as personal data at rest, with clearing and scoping rules.

Common mistakes

  • No timeout on fetch.
  • Showing an error page when stale data exists.
  • Trusting navigator.onLine.
  • Persisting caches without a buster or logout clearing.
  • Short idempotency TTLs that expire before queued writes replay.
  • Server handlers that outlive the client's patience.

Interview questions

  1. How do you add a timeout to fetch that also respects the library's cancellation? Expected answer: AbortSignal.timeout(ms) combined with the query signal through AbortSignal.any; distinguish TimeoutError from AbortError. Follow-up: browser support? (Recent evergreen browsers; polyfill or a manual controller for older ones.)
  2. What does networkMode: 'online' do? Expected answer: pauses queries and mutations while offline and resumes them on reconnect; fetchStatus becomes paused.
  3. What must the backend change when clients can queue writes offline? Expected answer: idempotency records that outlive the offline window, rules evaluated at replay time, version checks for conflicts.
  4. How do you show stale data honestly? Expected answer: keep rendering cached data, label it with dataUpdatedAt, show reconnecting or failed-refresh status, never replace it with an error page.

Practical exercise

Make "My Orders" survive a bad network.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With DevTools "Offline", a reload shows the persisted list within 200 ms with a "saved at" banner.
  • A cancel tapped offline shows as queued, survives a page reload, and is sent once on reconnect with the original idempotency key.
  • A request to an endpoint delayed by 30 s fails at 10 s with a retryable timeout; the NestJS interceptor returns 503 UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT at 8 s.
  • Logging out and in as another user never shows the first user's data, verified by a Playwright test.

72.11 Loading, empty and error states as a design requirement

Concept

Every region of a screen that shows server data has more states than "loading" and "done". For an order list, at least these:

State What the user should see TanStack Query v5 signal
First load, nothing cached Skeleton rows the size of real rows isPending && isFetching (isLoading)
Data The list data defined
Refreshing in background The list, with a subtle indicator at most data and isFetching
Empty, never had any "No orders yet" and a link to shop data with no items, default filters
Empty because of filters "No paid orders in the last 30 days" and "Clear filters" data with no items, non-default filters
Error, nothing to show Explanation, "Try again", a reference ID isError and no data
Refresh failed, old data shown The list plus "Could not refresh" isError and data
Offline, waiting The list plus "Reconnecting" fetchStatus === 'paused'
Loading more / end of list Row skeleton at the end / "That is all your orders" isFetchingNextPage / !hasNextPage
Placeholder while switching pages The previous page, dimmed isPlaceholderData

v5 naming matters here: status is 'pending' | 'error' | 'success'; isPending means "no data yet" and stays true for a disabled query that never runs; isLoading is isPending && isFetching, a real first load in progress. v4's isLoading meant what v5 calls isPending, and v4's isInitialLoading is now isLoading.

The point of this section is the title: these states are requirements. They belong in the design, in the acceptance criteria and in the tests, not in whatever the developer improvised at 6 p.m.

Why does it exist?

On good office Wi-Fi the happy path is all anyone sees, so the other states go unbuilt. Real users see them constantly: first loads on 3G, empty accounts, filters that match nothing, outages, tunnels. A missing state is not neutral. A spinner where a skeleton should be causes layout shift (69.5). An empty state shown during loading tells customers their orders are gone. An error page that replaces good data hides information the user had a second ago.

Mental model

Imagine a NestJS controller that handles only the 200 case and lets every other outcome become a generic 500. You would not ship it: each status class (2xx, 4xx, 5xx, timeouts) needs a deliberate response. A UI region is the same: each data state needs a deliberate rendering, and "the happy path plus a spinner" is the frontend's catch-all 500.

How it works

The order of checks is the whole trick: data first, then error, then loading.

flowchart TB
    start{"Is data defined?"} -->|"Yes"| empty{"Any items?"}
    empty -->|"Yes"| list["Render list, plus banner if refresh failed or paused"]
    empty -->|"No"| filt{"Non-default filters?"}
    filt -->|"Yes"| fe["Filtered-empty: offer to clear filters"]
    filt -->|"No"| ne["True empty: first-order call to action"]
    start -->|"No"| err{"isError?"}
    err -->|"Yes"| ep["Error with retry and request ID"]
    err -->|"No"| sk["Skeleton rows"]
  1. If there is data, render it, whatever else is true. Add a banner for a failed refresh or a paused fetch.
  2. Distinguish true empty from filtered empty. They need different words and different actions.
  3. Only without data does an error become the main content, and it must say what happened in human words, offer a retry, and show the requestId (71.11) so support can find the trace.
  4. Only without data and without error do you show a skeleton. Size skeleton rows like real rows to avoid layout shift, and delay them about 200 ms so fast responses never flash a skeleton at all.

Suspense is the other style (71.11): useSuspenseQuery lets a <Suspense> boundary show the skeleton and an error boundary show the error, so the component only renders the success case. It needs the same rules: refresh failures with existing data do not throw to the boundary, and empty states are still yours to design.

Practical example

The design spec for "My Orders" lists the ten states in the table above with copy and layout for each. The acceptance criteria include one test per state using mocked API responses (MSW, Part 77). The product manager signs off on the filtered-empty copy ("No cancelled orders in the last 6 months. Clear filters") because it is a real screen people will see thousands of times a day.

React / Next.js example

// src/orders/OrderListBody.tsx  (React 18, TanStack Query v5)
import type { UseInfiniteQueryResult, InfiniteData } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import type { OrderListFilters, OrderListResponse, OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ApiError } from '../api/errors';
import { FreshnessBanner } from '../ui/FreshnessBanner';
import { OrderRowsSkeleton } from './OrderRowsSkeleton'; // rows sized like real rows (75.5)

type Props = {
  query: UseInfiniteQueryResult<InfiniteData<OrderListResponse>, Error>;
  orders: OrderSummary[];
  filters: OrderListFilters;
  onClearFilters: () => void;
  renderRow: (o: OrderSummary) => JSX.Element;
};

export function OrderListBody({ query, orders, filters, onClearFilters, renderRow }: Props) {
  if (query.data) {                                                 // 1. data first, always
    const filtered = filters.status !== undefined || filters.range !== '30d';
    return (
      <>
        <FreshnessBanner updatedAt={query.dataUpdatedAt} failed={query.isError} />
        {orders.length === 0 ? (
          filtered
            ? <p>No orders match these filters. <button onClick={onClearFilters}>Clear filters</button></p>
            : <p>No orders in the last 30 days. <a href="/shop">Start shopping</a></p>
        ) : (
          <ul aria-busy={query.isFetchingNextPage}>{orders.map(renderRow)}</ul>
        )}
        {!query.hasNextPage && orders.length > 0 && <p>That is all your orders for this period.</p>}
      </>
    );
  }
  if (query.isError) {                                              // 2. error only when nothing to show
    const ref = query.error instanceof ApiError ? query.error.requestId : undefined;
    return (
      <div role="alert">
        <p>We could not load your orders.</p>
        <button onClick={() => query.refetch()}>Try again</button>
        {ref && <p>Reference: <code>{ref}</code></p>}
      </div>
    );
  }
  return <OrderRowsSkeleton count={6} />;                           // 3. first load
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The UI can only distinguish states the API distinguishes:

  • Empty is a 200. GET /v1/orders with no matches returns { items: [], nextCursor: null }, never 404. A 404 on a collection reads as an error and triggers retries.
  • "Never ordered" needs a fact the list cannot give. A filtered-empty list says nothing about older orders. The GET /v1/orders/summary endpoint (72.2) returns { active: 0, allTime: 37 }, so the empty state can say "No orders in the last 30 days. Show all 37 orders".
  • Errors carry code, issues and requestId (70.12, 77.7), so the client maps codes to copy (ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE becomes "This order has already shipped") and support can search logs by reference.
  • 401 is handled once, globally: an expired session redirects to login rather than painting an error in every region.
  • 503 with Retry-After lets the error state say "Back in a few seconds" and retry on time.

Production scenario

A grocery app audited its top ten screens against a state checklist and found 41 missing states. Building them took two sprints. Afterwards, sessions that hit any error state but continued shopping rose from 38 % to 61 %, mostly because refresh failures stopped replacing lists with error pages, and "my orders disappeared" contacts went to zero (see the failure below).

Failure scenario

The order list rendered if (!data?.pages[0].items.length) return <EmptyOrders />. While loading, data was undefined, the optional chain produced undefined, and !undefined is true: every customer saw "You have no orders yet" for 300 to 2,000 ms on every visit. On slow connections it looked permanent. Within a day support had 600 contacts asking where their orders had gone, and some customers re-placed orders they thought were lost.

The fix was the data-first decision order above, plus a component test per state. The team added a lint-style review rule: no !data?. checks in render.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Checking isError before data throws away good data after a failed refresh.
  • Empty state during loading from optional chaining, as above.
  • Disabled queries sit in isPending forever; show their own "choose a customer first" state.
  • Spinners for fast responses flash for 50 ms; delay skeletons about 200 ms.
  • Skeletons of the wrong size cause layout shift when data arrives.
  • Error copy from raw server messages leaks internals and is untranslatable; map codes to copy.
  • Partial failure: one region failing must not blank the page; give each independent region its own boundary (71.11).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks for the state table before the code: "What does this show on first load, empty, filtered-empty, error, stale, offline?" They make those states part of the definition of done and the test suite, and they push the API to provide the facts the states need (an allTime count, error codes, request IDs). The happy path is one row of ten.

Common mistakes

  • Building only the happy path and a spinner.
  • One generic "Something went wrong" for every failure.
  • Treating empty as an error on the API or in the UI.
  • Not testing states with mocked responses.

Interview questions

  1. In what order should a component check query state, and why? Expected answer: data, then error, then loading; refetch errors keep old data, and showing an error page would discard it.
  2. What is the difference between isPending and isLoading in v5? Expected answer: isPending means no data yet (including disabled queries); isLoading is isPending && isFetching.
  3. How should an API represent an empty collection? Expected answer: 200 with an empty list and nextCursor: null, plus summary facts when the UI needs them.
  4. How do you keep a skeleton from hurting CLS? Expected answer: size it like real content, reserve space, delay it for fast responses.

Practical exercise

Write one component test per state in the table for the order list.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Ten tests with MSW handlers, one per state, all passing.
  • A refetch failure with existing data keeps the list and shows the banner.
  • No "no orders" text ever appears before the first response (asserted with a delayed handler).
  • The summary endpoint returns allTime, and filtered-empty copy uses it.

72.12 Worked example: an order list with filters, infinite scroll, live status and an optimistic cancel

Requirements

We now assemble the Part into one screen: "My Orders" for a grocery delivery web app (React 18, Vite, React Router 6, TanStack Query v5, zod), on the NestJS API used throughout this Volume.

  • Filters (status, date range) live in the URL; reload, Back and shared links reproduce the view.
  • Infinite scroll over cursor pages of 20, at most 10 pages cached, with a "Load more" button for keyboard users.
  • Live status: changes made elsewhere (warehouse, rider, support, another device) appear within 1 s, through one SSE stream per tab.
  • Optimistic cancel: the row shows "Cancelling..." at once; on success it becomes "Cancelled"; if the order shipped meanwhile, it reverts with an explanation, without erasing newer data.
  • Numbers: first page under 300 ms p95 on 4G from a warm connection; list response under 25 KB; status updates under 1 s p95; zero duplicate cancels under double taps, retries and offline replays.

The flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant W as OrderListPage
    participant QC as QueryCache
    participant A as NestJS
    participant P as PostgreSQL
    W->>A: GET /v1/orders?status=PAID&range=30d&limit=20
    A-->>W: 20 orders, nextCursor
    W->>A: open SSE /v1/orders/events
    U->>W: Cancel order 42, version 7
    W->>QC: optimistic CANCELLED, version stays 7
    W->>A: POST /v1/orders/42/cancel, Idempotency-Key K
    A->>P: UPDATE where status in PENDING or PAID, version 8
    A-->>W: 200 order 42 CANCELLED version 8
    W->>QC: write response, version 8
    A-->>W: SSE order 42 CANCELLED version 8
    Note over QC: same version, event ignored

The contract

Built up across this Part in @shop/contracts: OrderSummarySchema with version and updatedAt (72.1), OrderListFiltersSchema and OrderListQuerySchema (72.2, 72.7), OrderEventSchema (72.8), and CancelOrderRequestSchema from 70.12. One change to 70.12's endpoint: POST /v1/orders/:id/cancel now returns 200 with the updated OrderSummary instead of 202 with no body, so the client can write the result straight into the cache.

Backend: the cancel endpoint

// apps/api/src/orders/orders.service.ts  (TypeORM, excerpt)
async cancel(input: { userId: string; orderId: string; reason: CancelReason }): Promise<OrderSummary> {
  return this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
    const [rows] = (await m.query(
      `UPDATE orders
          SET status = 'CANCELLED', cancel_reason = $3, version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
        WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2 AND status IN ('PENDING', 'PAID')
      RETURNING *`,
      [input.orderId, input.userId, input.reason],
    )) as [OrderRow[], number];                         // [rows, rowCount] for UPDATE in TypeORM's pg driver

    if (rows.length === 0) {
      const [current] = await m.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2', [input.orderId, input.userId]);
      if (!current) throw new NotFoundException({ code: 'ORDER_NOT_FOUND', issues: [] });
      if (current.status === 'CANCELLED') return this.mapper.toSummary(current); // repeat cancel: same answer
      throw new ConflictException({
        code: 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE',
        issues: [{ path: 'status', message: `Order is already ${current.status.toLowerCase()}` }],
        currentVersion: current.version,
      });
    }
    const order = this.mapper.toSummary(rows[0]);
    // Outbox row in the same transaction; a relay publishes it to the customer's Redis stream (Part 30.10).
    await m.query(`INSERT INTO outbox (topic, aggregate_id, payload) VALUES ('order.status', $1, $2)`,
      [order.id, JSON.stringify({ orderId: order.id, status: order.status, version: order.version, updatedAt: order.updatedAt })]);
    return order;
  });
}

The conditional UPDATE makes the state transition atomic: a rider app marking the order SHIPPED at the same instant either wins (cancel gets 409) or loses (the ship update must then check status itself). A repeat cancel of a cancelled order returns the same result, so the endpoint is idempotent by state; the controller still requires Idempotency-Key and applies the IdempotencyInterceptor from Part 15.12, with a 24-hour record TTL for offline replays (72.10). The list endpoint keeps the ETag/304 handling from 72.4 and the cursor query from 72.7.

Frontend: filters in the URL

// src/orders/useOrderFilters.ts  (React Router 6)
import { useSearchParams } from 'react-router-dom';
import { OrderListFiltersSchema, type OrderListFilters } from '@shop/contracts';

export function useOrderFilters() {
  const [params, setParams] = useSearchParams();
  // strip(): ignore unrelated params such as utm_source; the API's schema stays strict.
  const parsed = OrderListFiltersSchema.strip().safeParse(Object.fromEntries(params));
  const filters: OrderListFilters = parsed.success ? parsed.data : { range: '30d' };
  const setFilters = (next: Partial<OrderListFilters>) => {
    const merged = { ...filters, ...next };
    const qs = new URLSearchParams({ range: merged.range });
    if (merged.status) qs.set('status', merged.status);
    setParams(qs, { replace: false });                  // each filter change is a history entry: Back works
  };
  return { filters, setFilters, clear: () => setParams({}) };
}

Frontend: the optimistic cancel

A small helper patches one order everywhere it is cached, the same way the SSE hook does (72.8):

// src/orders/orderCache.ts
import type { InfiniteData, QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import type { OrderListResponse, OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import { orderKeys } from './orderKeys';

export function patchOrder(qc: QueryClient, id: string, fn: (o: OrderSummary) => OrderSummary) {
  qc.setQueryData<OrderSummary>(orderKeys.detail(id), (old) => old && fn(old));
  qc.setQueriesData<InfiniteData<OrderListResponse>>({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() }, (old) => old && {
    ...old,
    pages: old.pages.map((p) => ({ ...p, items: p.items.map((o) => (o.id === id ? fn(o) : o)) })),
  });
}

export function findOrder(qc: QueryClient, id: string): OrderSummary | undefined {
  const detail = qc.getQueryData<OrderSummary>(orderKeys.detail(id));
  if (detail) return detail;
  for (const [, data] of qc.getQueriesData<InfiniteData<OrderListResponse>>({ queryKey: orderKeys.lists() })) {
    const hit = data?.pages.flatMap((p) => p.items).find((o) => o.id === id);
    if (hit) return hit;
  }
  return undefined;
}
// src/orders/useCancelOrder.ts  (TanStack Query v5)
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderSummarySchema, type CancelOrderRequest } from '@shop/contracts';
import { apiSend } from '../api/http';
import { isRetryable } from '../api/queryClient';
import { findOrder, patchOrder } from './orderCache';

type Vars = { orderId: string; reason: CancelOrderRequest['reason']; idempotencyKey: string };

export function useCancelOrder() {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationKey: ['orders', 'cancel'],                  // lets paused cancels resume after reload (78.10)
    mutationFn: ({ orderId, reason, idempotencyKey }: Vars) =>
      apiSend('POST', `/v1/orders/${orderId}/cancel`, { reason }, OrderSummarySchema, { idempotencyKey }),
    retry: (count, error) => isRetryable(error) && count < 2, // safe: same key on every retry
    onMutate: async ({ orderId }) => {
      await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] });  // no in-flight refetch may overwrite the guess
      const before = findOrder(qc, orderId);
      patchOrder(qc, orderId, (o) => ({ ...o, status: 'CANCELLED' })); // version unchanged: still provisional
      return { before };
    },
    onSuccess: (order) => patchOrder(qc, order.id, (o) => (order.version >= o.version ? order : o)),
    onError: (_err, { orderId }, ctx) => {
      // Field-level, version-aware rollback. If an SSE event moved the order to SHIPPED (version 8)
      // while we waited, do NOT restore the version 7 snapshot over it.
      const before = ctx?.before;
      if (!before) return;
      patchOrder(qc, orderId, (o) =>
        o.version === before.version && o.status === 'CANCELLED' ? { ...o, status: before.status } : o);
    },
    onSettled: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders', 'summary'] }), // counts only; lists are patched
  });
}

Lists are patched, not invalidated, so a customer with 10 pages loaded does not trigger 10 sequential refetches (72.7). The detail and lists converge anyway through the SSE event and the next focus refetch.

Frontend: the page

// src/orders/OrderListPage.tsx  (React 18)
import { useMemo } from 'react';
import { useMutationState } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import type { OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import { useOrderFilters } from './useOrderFilters';
import { useOrderList } from './useOrderList';           // 78.7
import { useOrderEvents } from './useOrderEvents';       // 78.8
import { useCancelOrder } from './useCancelOrder';
import { OrderListBody } from './OrderListBody';         // 78.11
import { LoadMoreSentinel } from '../ui/LoadMoreSentinel';
import { ApiError } from '../api/errors';
import { OrderFilters, StatusBadge } from './components'; // presentational (77.10)

export function OrderListPage() {
  const { filters, setFilters, clear } = useOrderFilters();
  const query = useOrderList(filters);
  useOrderEvents();                                      // one stream per tab, merged into the cache
  const cancel = useCancelOrder();
  const cancelling = new Set(useMutationState({
    filters: { mutationKey: ['orders', 'cancel'], status: 'pending' },
    select: (m) => (m.state.variables as { orderId: string }).orderId,
  }));

  const orders = useMemo(() => {
    const seen = new Map<string, OrderSummary>();
    for (const p of query.data?.pages ?? []) for (const o of p.items) seen.set(o.id, o);
    return [...seen.values()];
  }, [query.data]);

  const renderRow = (o: OrderSummary) => (
    <li key={o.id}>
      {o.displayId} <StatusBadge status={o.status} pending={cancelling.has(o.id)} /> {/* "Cancelling..." */}
      {(o.status === 'PENDING' || o.status === 'PAID') && (
        <button disabled={cancelling.has(o.id)}
          onClick={() => cancel.mutate({ orderId: o.id, reason: 'CHANGED_MIND', idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID() })}>
          Cancel
        </button>
      )}
    </li>
  );

  return (
    <main>
      <OrderFilters value={filters} onChange={setFilters} />
      {cancel.error instanceof ApiError && cancel.error.code === 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE' && (
        <p role="alert">{cancel.error.issues[0]?.message ?? 'This order can no longer be cancelled.'}</p>
      )}
      <OrderListBody query={query} orders={orders} filters={filters} onClearFilters={clear} renderRow={renderRow} />
      <LoadMoreSentinel disabled={!query.hasNextPage || query.isFetchingNextPage} onVisible={() => query.fetchNextPage()} />
      {query.hasNextPage && (
        <button onClick={() => query.fetchNextPage()} disabled={query.isFetchingNextPage}>Load more</button>
      )}
    </main>
  );
}

The idempotency key is created in the click handler, once per intent. The button is disabled while that order's cancel is pending, and the key makes any double tap that slips through harmless on the server.

Failure drills

Drill Expected behaviour Mechanism
API down for 60 s List stays, banner "Could not refresh", retries twice then waits for focus Data-first rendering, bounded retries (72.3, 72.11)
SSE dropped by a proxy restart Reconnects in about 3 s with Last-Event-ID; missed changes replayed or reset refetches EventSource reconnect, replay window (72.8)
Cancel while the warehouse ships the order Row shows "Cancelling...", SSE moves it to "Shipped", cancel returns 409, rollback skipped, message explains Version-aware rollback
Double tap on Cancel One request; any second request replays the first result Disabled button, idempotency key, state-idempotent endpoint
Cancel tapped offline, page reloaded Cancel queued, resumed on reconnect with the same key; 409 if it shipped meanwhile Paused mutations, setMutationDefaults, 24 h idempotency TTL (72.10)
Filter changed while a page loads Old request aborted, new list from page one Key per filter, query signal
10 pages loaded, then a cancel One POST, no list refetch patchOrder instead of invalidation
Log out and in as someone else No trace of the first user's orders queryClient.clear(), persister removed

Numbers

Measured on a staging copy with 2 million orders: first page GET 38 ms p95 server time and 21 KB gzip; 304 on unchanged focus refetches in 71 % of cases at 0.9 ms of API CPU; status event from database commit to row badge 420 ms p50, 850 ms p95; optimistic cancel feedback within one frame; cancel conflict rate in production 3.8 %, every one rolled back correctly in the version-aware drill.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

Every piece of this screen is a cache-coherence decision. Fetched pages, pushed events, optimistic guesses and server responses all write to the same cache, and they stay consistent because they obey one rule: a write applies only if it is newer, by version, than what is there. The backend makes that rule possible by versioning every order change in the same statement that makes it and publishing events with that version through an outbox. The frontend makes it safe by never restoring old snapshots over newer data, never invalidating what it can patch, and never letting the network's bad moments erase what the user could already see.

Practical exercise

Build the screen and its API end to end.

Acceptance criteria:

  • All eight failure drills pass, scripted in Playwright against the NestJS API with a seeded PostgreSQL (Part 77 covers the setup).
  • A database-side status change appears on the row in under 1 s without any list GET.
  • The cancel-versus-ship race, forced with a delayed cancel handler, ends with "Shipped" and an explanatory message, never "Paid".
  • The URL fully describes the view; copying it into a new tab reproduces filters and first page.
  • With 10 pages loaded, a cancel produces exactly one network request besides the summary refetch.

Senior Checklist — Part 72

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can classify every value on a screen as server, URL, local, form or global client state, and put each in its natural home
  • I can design a query key factory, and I know that a variable missing from a key returns someone else's data
  • I can explain staleTime vs gcTime (and why v5 renamed cacheTime), the v5 refetch triggers, and safe retry rules
  • I can trace a stale screen through every cache layer and set Cache-Control: private, no-cache with a cheap ETag
  • I choose between setQueryData and invalidateQueries per mutation, and the API returns the updated resource with a version
  • I can write an optimistic update with cancelQueries, snapshot, rollback and onSettled invalidation, and know when to refuse one
  • I generate idempotency keys once per intent and know when a naturally idempotent endpoint makes them unnecessary
  • I can build cursor-based infinite scroll with useInfiniteQuery, maxPages and a filter-bound cursor contract
  • I can merge SSE or WebSocket events into the cache with version guards and recover from replay gaps
  • I can choose between Context, Zustand, Redux Toolkit and RTK Query, and avoid the Zustand v5 selector trap
  • Every request I write has a timeout, and my screens show stale data honestly when the network fails
  • I treat loading, empty, filtered-empty, error, stale and offline states as requirements with tests

Part 72 — Key Takeaways

  • Server state is a cache of someone else's truth; manage it with a cache library, not a global store.
  • Filters belong in the URL, preferences in a small store, and API data in the query cache.
  • The query key is the cache key: include every input, build keys from one factory, and invalidate by prefix.
  • staleTime controls freshness and gcTime controls memory; v5 renamed cacheTime to gcTime to end the confusion.
  • Refetch triggers and retries are load generators; bound them with staleTime, jittered backoff and honest status codes.
  • Invalidating the query cache is useless if the browser, CDN or Redis still holds stale copies; send private, no-cache with an ETag.
  • Mutations should get the updated resource back with a version, so the client can write through instead of refetching.
  • Optimistic updates need cancelQueries, a rollback that never overwrites newer data, and a final invalidation.
  • Idempotency keys are created once per user intent and reused by every retry and offline replay.
  • Infinite queries refetch every loaded page; patch deep lists, cap them with maxPages, and keep pages cheap.
  • Pushed events, fetched pages and optimistic guesses stay consistent when every write is applied only if its version is newer.
  • Render data first, then errors, then loading; a failed refresh must never erase what the user could already see.

Part 73 — Next.js and Rendering Strategies

Part 70 — Frontend Tooling and TypeScript in the Browser ended with a choice between a Vite SPA, Next.js and plain server-rendered pages (70.11). Parts 71, 72 built React screens and a client-side data layer on the assumption that the browser does the rendering. This Part removes that assumption. In Next.js the same React component can run at build time, on a server for each request, at the edge, or in the browser, and the choice decides your time to first byte (TTFB), your server bill, what search engines see and how stale a page can get.

The baseline is Next.js 14 with the App Router and React 18. Where Next.js 15 or 16 changed behaviour (async params and cookies(), fetch no longer cached by default, the move from route segment config to "use cache", middleware.ts becoming proxy.ts, Turbopack as the default bundler), the text says so at the point it matters. The NestJS API, @shop/contracts, ZodValidationPipe, the { code, issues, requestId } error shape and the TanStack Query setup from Part 72 are reused unchanged.

73.1 Rendering strategies: client-side, server-side and static rendering

Concept

Rendering means turning data plus components into HTML the browser can paint. The question is where and when that happens:

  • Client-side rendering (CSR): the server sends a nearly empty HTML shell plus JavaScript. The browser downloads and runs the bundle, the bundle calls the API, and React builds the DOM. Every Vite SPA in Parts 71, 72 works this way.
  • Server-side rendering (SSR): for each request, a server runs the React components, fetches data, and sends complete HTML. The browser paints it immediately, then downloads JavaScript and hydrates it (attaches event handlers to the existing DOM, 73.10).
  • Static site generation (SSG): the HTML is rendered once, at build time, and served as a file from a CDN to every visitor until the next build.

Two more strategies are refinements of these: incremental static regeneration (ISR), which re-renders static pages in the background after a time limit or on demand, and streaming, which sends server HTML in chunks as each part's data arrives. Both are in 73.2.

None of these is "the modern way". Each moves work to a different place and time, and each has a bill: latency, server CPU, freshness or SEO.

Why does it exist?

Because the three things you want from a page pull against each other:

  1. Fast first paint, which needs HTML that exists before the user asks (static) or is produced near them quickly (SSR in-region).
  2. Fresh, personal data, which needs work at request time with the user's cookies (SSR or CSR).
  3. Cheap operation, which wants no per-request server work at all (static, or CSR from a CDN).

A product page needs 1 and is mostly the same for everyone. A cart needs 2 and is different for everyone. An internal admin table needs neither SEO nor first-paint speed for anonymous users. One strategy for all three is either slow, expensive or stale somewhere. Frameworks like Next.js exist so you can choose per route, and in the App Router per component.

Mental model

Imagine a bakery. SSG is bread baked at 05:00 and stacked on the shelf: instant to hand over, identical for everyone, and yesterday's if nobody bakes again. SSR is a sandwich made to order: exactly what you asked for, but you wait while it is made and the kitchen needs staff for every customer. CSR is a meal kit: the shop hands you a box at once, but you cook at home, and on a weak stove (a cheap phone) dinner is late. ISR is the shelf with a rule: "if a loaf has been out more than 5 minutes, hand it over anyway but bake a fresh one for the next customer". Streaming is the waiter bringing the starter while the main course is still in the oven.

How it works

The same product page, three ways. Numbers are typical for a mid-range Android phone on 4G (round trip about 80 ms) with the Next.js server and NestJS in the same region as the user.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant CDN as CDN
    participant N as NextServer
    participant API as NestJS
    Note over B,API: CSR
    B->>CDN: GET /p/sonic-toothbrush
    CDN-->>B: empty shell, 2 KB, TTFB 40 ms
    B->>CDN: GET main.js 180 KB gzip
    B->>API: GET /v1/products/sonic-toothbrush
    API-->>B: JSON, LCP about 2.6 s
    Note over B,API: SSR
    B->>N: GET /p/sonic-toothbrush
    N->>API: product, price, stock in parallel
    API-->>N: 3 responses, 70 ms
    N-->>B: full HTML, TTFB about 260 ms, LCP about 1.3 s
    Note over B,API: SSG
    B->>CDN: GET /p/sonic-toothbrush
    CDN-->>B: full HTML from cache, TTFB 40 ms, LCP about 0.9 s

Step by step, what each costs:

  1. CSR. TTFB is tiny because the shell is static. But nothing meaningful paints until the JavaScript has downloaded (180 KB gzip is about 600 KB parsed), compiled and run (300 to 900 ms of main-thread time on a mid-range phone, Part 69 — How the Browser Builds a Page, 69.7), and then the data request has made its own round trip. The LCP element appears only after that chain: often 2.5 to 4 s. Crawlers that do not run JavaScript see an empty page; Googlebot does run it, but in a deferred second wave, and other crawlers and link-preview bots (Slack, WhatsApp, X) usually do not.
  2. SSR. The server does the data fetching close to the API (1 to 5 ms between them in one VPC instead of 80 ms per call from a phone), renders React to HTML (20 to 80 ms of CPU for a typical product page), and sends it. TTFB rises to the sum of API time plus render time plus network. The browser paints as soon as the HTML and critical CSS arrive. JavaScript still downloads and hydrates afterwards; until then the page is visible but buttons do nothing (the "uncanny valley" between paint and interactive).
  3. SSG. All of that work happened once at next build. The CDN serves a file. TTFB is the CDN's (20 to 60 ms at a nearby edge), and the server sees no traffic at all for that page. The price is freshness: the page shows data as of the build.

The decision matrix the rest of this Part keeps returning to:

CSR SSR SSG ISR (73.2) Streaming SSR (73.2)
TTFB 20 to 60 ms (shell) 150 to 600 ms (API + render) 20 to 60 ms (CDN) 20 to 60 ms on hit 50 to 150 ms (shell first)
LCP on mid-range 4G phone 2.5 to 4 s 1.2 to 2 s 0.8 to 1.5 s 0.8 to 1.5 s 1 to 1.8 s
Server CPU per view None (API calls only) Full render every request None One render per revalidation Full render every request
Freshness Live Live As of build Bounded: revalidate window or on-demand Live
Personalisation Full, in browser Full, on server None (or client islands) None (or client islands) Full
SEO and link previews Weak Strong Strong Strong Strong (bots wait for the stream)
Failure when the API is down Page shell loads, data errors Page errors (500) Page still served Stale page still served Shell served, sections error
Scales with traffic by API capacity Render servers + API CDN CDN Render servers + API

The last two rows matter most to a backend engineer. SSR multiplies your render tier and API load by your page views. Static and ISR pages survive API outages, because the CDN keeps serving the last good HTML.

Practical example

A grocery delivery storefront has these pages:

  • Home and category pages: same for everyone in a city, changed by merchandisers a few times a day, high traffic from search and ads. Static, refreshed by ISR.
  • Product page: same for everyone, but price and stock change. Static shell with ISR every few minutes, plus a small client-rendered stock badge if stock must be live.
  • Cart and checkout: different for every user, must be exact. Rendered on the client (or SSR without caching) from the user's session.
  • Order history: personal, behind login, not indexed. Either SSR per request with cookies, or CSR.
  • Admin dashboard for warehouse staff: behind login, desktop, interactive. CSR, possibly a separate Vite SPA (70.11).

The point is the shape: one site, four strategies, chosen per page by who sees it, how fresh it must be, and whether search matters. 73.12 turns this into a decision table.

React / Next.js example

In the Next.js 14 App Router you rarely say "SSR" or "SSG" explicitly. Next.js decides at build time whether each route can be static (rendered once) or must be dynamic (rendered per request), based on what the code does. You can also force it with route segment config, exported constants in a page.tsx or layout.tsx.

// apps/web/app/p/[slug]/page.tsx  (Next.js 14, App Router)
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
import { ProductViewSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { AddToCartButton } from './AddToCartButton'; // a client component (79.4)

export const revalidate = 300; // static, re-rendered at most every 5 min (ISR, 79.2)

async function getProduct(slug: string) {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.CATALOG_API_URL}/v1/products/${slug}`, {
    next: { revalidate: 300, tags: [`product:${slug}`] }, // Data Cache entry (79.7)
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),                  // never let a build or render hang
  });
  if (res.status === 404) return null;
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`catalog ${res.status}`); // nearest error.tsx renders (79.3)
  return ProductViewSchema.parse(await res.json());      // same zod contract as the API
}

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  const product = await getProduct(params.slug);
  if (!product) notFound();
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>{product.name}</h1>
      <p>{formatInr(product.priceMinor)}</p>
      <AddToCartButton sku={product.sku} />
    </main>
  );
}
