const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' });
function formatInr(minor: string) { return inr.format(Number(minor) / 100); } // fixed locale: no hydration drift (79.10)

Three things decide whether this page is static or dynamic in Next.js 14:

Code in the route Effect
fetch with default options or next: { revalidate: N } Cached; page can stay static
fetch(..., { cache: 'no-store' }) or next: { revalidate: 0 } Page becomes dynamic
Calling cookies(), headers() or reading searchParams Page becomes dynamic (it depends on the request)
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' Always dynamic, every request
export const dynamic = 'force-static' Always static; cookies() and headers() return empty values
export const dynamic = 'error' Static, and the build fails if anything dynamic is used

next build prints the verdict per route: ○ (Static), ● (SSG) for pages prerendered with generateStaticParams, and λ (Dynamic) in early 14.x releases (shown as ƒ (Dynamic) in later releases). Read that table in every pull request that touches data fetching; a route that silently flipped from static to dynamic just moved from the CDN to your servers.

Next.js 15 changed the default. In 15, fetch is no longer cached unless you ask (cache: 'force-cache' or next: { revalidate }), and params, searchParams, cookies() and headers() are Promises you must await. A route that does not use request data is still prerendered at build time in 15; it is the per-request data cache that stopped being implicit. 73.5 and 73.7 cover the details.

Backend side (NestJS)

The rendering strategy changes who calls your API and how often:

  • CSR: every visitor's browser calls NestJS. You need browser auth (cookies, Part 75 — Auth and Security in the Browser), CORS or same-origin routing (Part 11 — Networking and HTTP, 11.13), and enough capacity for peak page views times API calls per page.
  • SSR: the Next.js server calls NestJS once or more per page view, server to server. Latency between them lands straight in TTFB, so put them in the same region and VPC, reuse connections (keep-alive, Part 11.9), and give every call a timeout. A page that calls three endpoints sequentially at 60 ms each spends 180 ms before rendering starts; in parallel it spends 60.
  • SSG and ISR: NestJS is called at build time and on each revalidation, not per view. A catalogue of 40,000 products built at deploy means 40,000 calls in a few minutes; rate limits and connection pools on the catalogue service must allow that burst, or the build must prerender only the popular pages (73.5).

Whatever the strategy, the API should send honest cache headers. A public catalogue endpoint can say Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 so a CDN in front of it absorbs browser CSR traffic; a personal endpoint must say private, no-cache (72.4). Next.js's own Data Cache ignores those response headers; it follows the options on the fetch call, which is a common surprise (73.7).

Production scenario

An online pharmacy ran a Vite SPA. Search traffic landed on product pages; p75 LCP on mobile was 3.4 s and 22 % of visitors from ads left before the page painted. They moved product and category pages to Next.js with ISR (revalidate = 600 plus on-demand revalidation on price change), kept the account area client-rendered, and left the API alone.

After the change: p75 TTFB on product pages 52 ms (CDN hit rate 96 %), p75 LCP 1.4 s, bounce from ads down to 13 %. The Next.js tier rendered about 40 pages a minute for revalidations, on two small containers. The catalogue API's traffic actually fell by 70 %, because browsers no longer called it on every product view.

Failure scenario

A fashion retailer moved its home page to SSR "for freshness" so that a "Recommended for you" carousel could be personalised. The home page called five NestJS endpoints per request, two of them sequentially. On a sale morning at 09:00, traffic went from 300 to 4,500 page views per second in two minutes. Each view now meant five API calls and 60 ms of render CPU; the 12-pod Next.js deployment saturated its CPUs, p99 TTFB went from 400 ms to 9 s, and the load balancer's 10 s timeout started returning 504s on the most important page of the year.

Before the change, the same home page had been a static file. The fix was to make the page static with ISR again and render the personalised carousel as a client component that called a cached recommendations endpoint after paint. TTFB returned to 45 ms; the carousel arrived 300 ms after first paint, which nobody minded.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A single cookies() call in a shared layout makes every page under it dynamic: the whole site moves from the CDN to your servers on one line.
  • Build-time API failure: SSG pages built while the API returned errors are baked in until the next build. Fail the build on non-2xx, never render an error page as static output.
  • Huge static builds: 200,000 product pages at 50 ms each is almost 3 hours of build. Prerender the top pages, render the rest on first request (73.5).
  • CSR and bots: link previews in chat apps show a blank title and no image for a CSR page, which hurts sharing even if Google indexes it.
  • SSR without timeouts turns one slow dependency into a slow page for everyone, and holds render-server memory while it waits.
  • Static pages and personal data: anything rendered into static HTML is visible to every visitor. A "Hello, Priya" in a static layout is a privacy incident, not a cosmetic bug.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks four questions per page before choosing: Is it the same for everyone? How stale may it be, and who notices? Does search or link sharing matter? What happens to it when the API is down? "Same for everyone, a few minutes stale is fine" means static or ISR, with personal bits rendered on the client. "Different per user and must be exact" means request-time rendering, client or server. They prefer the option that keeps the CDN in front, because a CDN is the cheapest, most reliable server you will ever run. And they read SSR as a cost: a render tier that scales with page views, with its own on-call.

To a product manager: "Static pages are instant and survive outages, but show data a few minutes old. Server-rendered pages are fresh but slower and cost money per view. We'll make the shared parts static and load the personal parts in the browser."

Common mistakes

  • Choosing SSR for everything "for SEO" when the page is the same for everyone and ISR would be faster and cheaper.
  • Choosing CSR for public landing pages and losing link previews and first-paint speed.
  • Not reading the build output, so nobody notices a page became dynamic.
  • Rendering personal data into static or cached HTML.
  • Sequential server-side API calls that add their latencies into TTFB.

Interview questions

  1. Compare CSR, SSR and SSG on TTFB, LCP and server cost. Expected answer: CSR has tiny TTFB but late LCP (JS then data); SSR has higher TTFB (API plus render) but early paint and per-request CPU; SSG has CDN TTFB and early paint with no per-request cost but data as of build. Follow-up: which survives an API outage? (SSG/ISR.)
  2. How does Next.js App Router decide whether a route is static or dynamic? Expected answer: by usage of dynamic functions (cookies, headers, searchParams), uncached fetch, and route segment config like dynamic and revalidate; the build output shows the result.
  3. Why might moving a page from static to SSR cause an outage? Expected answer: every page view now costs render CPU and API calls; peak traffic hits origin instead of the CDN.
  4. A page needs SEO and a personalised section. What do you do? Expected answer: static or ISR for the shared content, client component (or streamed dynamic section) for the personal part, with reserved space to avoid layout shift.
  5. What changed about fetch caching in Next.js 15? Expected answer: it is not cached by default; you opt in with cache: 'force-cache' or next.revalidate; request APIs became async.

Practical exercise

Build one product page three ways in a Next.js 14 app: CSR (a client component fetching in TanStack Query), SSR (dynamic = 'force-dynamic') and SSG/ISR (revalidate = 300). Throttle DevTools to "Fast 4G" with 4x CPU slowdown.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A table of TTFB, LCP and total JavaScript transferred for each version, measured with Lighthouse in three runs each.
  • The next build output shows the expected ○, ● or ƒ/λ marker for each route.
  • With the NestJS catalogue stopped, the ISR page still loads and the SSR page shows the route's error.tsx.
  • curl -s of each URL shows whether the product name is in the initial HTML.

73.2 Incremental static regeneration and streaming

Concept

Incremental static regeneration (ISR) keeps the speed of static pages while bounding staleness. A page is rendered once and cached; after its revalidate window passes, the next request still gets the cached (stale) page, and Next.js re-renders it in the background. When the new render succeeds, it replaces the cached copy. This is the stale-while-revalidate pattern from HTTP (Part 11.11) applied to whole pages. On-demand revalidation skips the timer: your code calls revalidatePath('/p/sonic-toothbrush') or revalidateTag('product:sonic-toothbrush') when the data changes, and the next request triggers the re-render.

Streaming sends server-rendered HTML in pieces. The server sends the page shell (header, layout, skeletons) as soon as it can, keeps the HTTP response open, and sends each slow section as its data resolves, with a tiny inline script that swaps the skeleton for real content. In the App Router, every <Suspense> boundary (Part 71 — React Fundamentals for Backend Engineers, 71.11) and every loading.tsx file is a streaming point.

Why does it exist?

ISR exists because SSG's freshness problem gets worse as sites grow. Rebuilding 40,000 product pages to change one price is absurd, and a rebuild per price change is impossible at a hundred price changes an hour. ISR lets each page refresh on its own schedule or on its own event.

Streaming exists because SSR's TTFB is held hostage by its slowest dependency. If a product page needs product details (40 ms), price (50 ms) and reviews (400 ms), non-streaming SSR sends nothing until all three finish. With streaming, the browser gets the header and product details at about 60 ms, paints them, and the reviews arrive when ready.

Mental model

Imagine a newspaper stand. ISR is the stand that keeps yesterday's paper on display until someone buys one, and then sends a runner to fetch today's edition for the next customer. The first customer after the deadline gets yesterday's paper; everyone after gets today's. On-demand revalidation is the editor phoning the stand: "big story, replace the stack now".

Streaming is a restaurant that serves bread and water the moment you sit down, then each course as the kitchen finishes it, instead of making you wait at an empty table until dessert is ready.

How it works

ISR, time-based, with revalidate = 300:

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant N as NextServer
    participant C as PageCache
    participant API as NestJS
    U->>N: GET /p/sonic at 10:00
    N->>C: lookup
    C-->>N: HIT, rendered 09:58
    N-->>U: cached HTML, x-nextjs-cache HIT
    U->>N: GET /p/sonic at 10:04
    N->>C: lookup
    C-->>N: STALE, older than 300 s
    N-->>U: stale HTML immediately
    N->>API: background re-render fetches data
    API-->>N: new price
    N->>C: store new HTML and RSC payload
    U->>N: GET /p/sonic at 10:04 plus 2 s
    C-->>N: HIT, fresh
    N-->>U: new HTML
  1. At build time (or on first request for paths not prebuilt, 73.5), Next.js renders the page and stores both the HTML and the RSC payload (the serialised React Server Component tree used for client-side navigation, 73.4) in the Full Route Cache (73.7).
  2. Requests within the window are served from cache. Next.js sets the response header x-nextjs-cache: HIT and, for CDNs, Cache-Control: s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate (Next.js 15 adds an explicit long stale-while-revalidate value controlled by the expireTime config).
  3. The first request after the window gets the stale page (x-nextjs-cache: STALE) and triggers one background re-render. Concurrent requests during the re-render also get stale; Next.js does not start a second render for the same path on the same server.
  4. If the re-render throws (API down, validation error), the old page stays in the cache and the next request after the window tries again. Errors in background regeneration never replace good pages with error pages. This is what makes ISR pages survive outages.
  5. On-demand: revalidateTag('product:sonic') marks every Data Cache entry with that tag, and every route that used them, as stale. The next request re-renders. In Next.js 14 and 15 that next request receives the fresh page (it waits for the render); pages are not re-rendered eagerly in the background when you call revalidateTag.

Streaming, with one <Suspense> boundary around reviews:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant N as NextServer
    participant API as NestJS
    B->>N: GET /p/sonic
    N->>API: product and reviews in parallel
    API-->>N: product in 40 ms
    N-->>B: chunk 1 shell, product, reviews skeleton at 60 ms
    Note over B: browser paints header and product
    API-->>N: reviews in 400 ms
    N-->>B: chunk 2 reviews HTML plus swap script at 420 ms
    N-->>B: response ends

Under the hood this is HTTP chunked transfer encoding (Part 11.10) on HTTP/1.1, or a stream of DATA frames on HTTP/2. React's server renderer (renderToReadableStream / renderToPipeableStream) emits the shell first, then each resolved Suspense boundary as a hidden <div> plus an inline <script> that moves it into place. The browser can start fetching CSS and JavaScript referenced in chunk 1 while the server is still waiting on reviews.

The big consequence: the HTTP status code and headers are sent with the first chunk. Once the shell is out, the response is a 200. If the reviews section later calls notFound() or throws, Next.js cannot change the status; it renders the error boundary inside the stream (and for notFound() injects a <meta name="robots" content="noindex">). Anything that should decide the status code (product exists or not, user allowed or not) must run before the first Suspense boundary, in the page body that is awaited before streaming starts.

Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines the two: a static shell served from cache instantly, with dynamic holes streamed in the same response. It was experimental in Next.js 14 (experimental.ppr), incremental opt-in per route in 15 (ppr: 'incremental' plus export const experimental_ppr = true), and in Next.js 16 it became the default model under cacheComponents: true. Treat it as the direction of travel, not a 14-era tool.

Practical example

A category page "Electric toothbrushes" lists 48 products. Merchandisers change ordering twice a day; prices change through the pricing service maybe 30 times a day across the category; stock changes constantly.

  • The listing uses ISR with revalidate = 600 as a safety net and on-demand revalidateTag('category:electric-toothbrushes') whenever the catalogue service publishes a change to any product in it.
  • Stock is not rendered into the page at all; a small client component asks a cached stock endpoint for the 48 SKUs after paint (73.13).
  • The "Customers also viewed" rail is personalised; it streams inside a <Suspense> boundary on a dynamic product page, or is a client component on a static one.

With this split, a price change reaches the page in about 2 seconds (event, revalidation, next request re-renders), the page is served from cache 97 % of the time, and stock is never stale by more than the stock endpoint's 15-second cache.

React / Next.js example

ISR with time-based and on-demand revalidation, plus a streamed section:

// apps/web/app/c/[category]/page.tsx  (Next.js 14)
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { CategoryPageSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ProductGrid } from './ProductGrid';
import { Bestsellers, BestsellersSkeleton } from './Bestsellers';

export const revalidate = 600;          // safety net: at most 10 min stale even if an event is lost
export const dynamicParams = true;      // categories not prebuilt are rendered on first request, then cached

export default async function CategoryPage({ params }: { params: { category: string } }) {
  const res = await fetch(
    `${process.env.CATALOG_API_URL}/v1/catalog/categories/${params.category}/products?limit=48`,
    { next: { revalidate: 600, tags: ['catalog', `category:${params.category}`] }, signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000) },
  );
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`catalog ${res.status}`); // throws: ISR keeps the previous good page
  const page = CategoryPageSchema.parse(await res.json());

  return (
    <main>
      <h1>{page.title}</h1>
      <ProductGrid products={page.products} />
      {/* Not on the critical path: streamed when ready, skeleton sized to avoid layout shift (75.5) */}
      <Suspense fallback={<BestsellersSkeleton />}>
        <Bestsellers category={params.category} />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}
// apps/web/app/c/[category]/Bestsellers.tsx  (server component, may be slow)
export async function Bestsellers({ category }: { category: string }) {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.CATALOG_API_URL}/v1/catalog/categories/${category}/bestsellers`, {
    next: { revalidate: 3_600, tags: [`bestsellers:${category}`] },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1_500),
  });
  if (!res.ok) return null;             // optional section: degrade silently rather than fail the page
  const items: { sku: string; name: string }[] = await res.json();
  return <ul>{items.map((i) => <li key={i.sku}>{i.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}
export function BestsellersSkeleton() { return <div style={{ minHeight: 240 }} aria-busy="true" />; }

On a static ISR page, the Suspense boundary still matters during the background render and on cache misses, and it keeps a slow optional section from blocking the cached shell on dynamic pages. The on-demand trigger (a Route Handler NestJS calls on change) is in 73.6 and 73.13.

Backend side (NestJS)

ISR moves your API's load from "per page view" to "per revalidation", which changes what NestJS must be good at:

  • Bursts after invalidation. revalidateTag('catalog') on a site with 1,200 cached category pages means the next request to each one re-renders it, and each render calls the catalogue API. Popular pages re-render within seconds: a few hundred calls arrive at once. Tag narrowly (category:<slug>, product:<slug>), not with one global tag.
  • Errors must be errors. ISR keeps the old page only if the render throws. An API that returns 200 with an empty list during a database failover produces a perfectly valid, empty category page that gets cached for 10 minutes. Return 503 on dependency failure and let the frontend throw.
  • Streaming needs bounded dependencies. Every streamed section holds the HTTP response and a slot in the Next.js server open until it finishes. A 30-second reviews endpoint keeps thousands of responses open at peak. Give NestJS endpoints that feed optional sections a tight server-side timeout (Part 31 — Reliability Engineering, 31.1) and expect the frontend to drop the section.
  • Change events. On-demand revalidation needs the backend to say what changed. The catalogue service should publish a domain event (ProductPriceChanged { sku, categorySlugs }) after the transaction commits, and something must turn it into a signed call to the Next.js revalidation endpoint (73.13).

Production scenario

A home-goods marketplace with 160,000 product pages used revalidate = 3600 and nothing else. Price errors reported by customers ("the page said ₹1,499, checkout said ₹1,899") ran at about 40 a day, because a price change took up to an hour to appear. They added on-demand revalidation: the pricing service emitted events to Kafka, a small NestJS consumer called the Next.js revalidation Route Handler with the affected product:<slug> tags, batched every 2 seconds.

Median time from price change to page update fell from 31 minutes to 3 seconds. Background renders rose from about 4,000 an hour to about 9,000 an hour, still trivial for three containers. Price-mismatch tickets dropped to one or two a week, all from customers who had the old page open in a tab, which the checkout's server-side repricing already handled.

Failure scenario

At 01:40 a database failover on the catalogue service caused 90 seconds of errors. The catalogue controller had a try/catch that "helpfully" returned { products: [] } on any exception, so the error rate dashboard stayed green. During those 90 seconds, about 300 category pages hit their revalidation window, re-rendered against the empty response, and cached "No products found" for 10 minutes. Organic search traffic that landed on those pages bounced; Googlebot happened to crawl 40 of them and briefly dropped them from results.

The fix had three parts: the controller stopped swallowing errors and returned 503 with the standard error shape; the Next.js page threw on non-2xx and on an empty product list for a category that the catalogue said was non-empty (page.totalCount > 0 && page.products.length === 0); and an alert fired on the ratio of empty category renders.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The first visitor after expiry gets stale data by design. If that is unacceptable for a field (stock at checkout), it must not be in an ISR page.
  • ISR per server, not per cluster: with several self-hosted replicas and the default file-system cache, each replica regenerates and stores its own copy, and revalidateTag called on one replica does not reach the others (73.11).
  • CDN in front of ISR: the CDN caches according to s-maxage. revalidateTag clears Next.js's cache, not CloudFront's; the CDN keeps the old copy until its own TTL expires unless you also purge it (Part 46 — Cloud Architecture, 46.8).
  • Status code locked after the first chunk: notFound() inside a streamed section returns a 200 with a not-found UI.
  • Buffering proxies (some nginx configs, compression middleware, corporate proxies) collect the whole stream before forwarding it, silently turning streaming into slow SSR. Set X-Accel-Buffering: no for nginx, or disable proxy buffering for the Next.js upstream.
  • Many tiny Suspense boundaries cause content to pop in piece by piece and shift layout; group sections that load together.
  • Background regeneration that keeps failing means a page can be very stale with no visible error. Monitor regeneration failures, not just page errors.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats ISR as a cache with a freshness budget and an invalidation path, exactly like the Redis caches in Part 27 — Caching and Redis. Time-based revalidation is the safety net; on-demand revalidation is the mechanism. They tag narrowly so invalidation is cheap, and they make sure the data source fails loudly so stale-but-good is kept instead of fresh-but-wrong. For streaming, they decide which data determines the status code and keep it outside Suspense, then put each slow, optional section behind a boundary with a timeout and a skeleton that reserves its space.

Common mistakes

  • Using only time-based revalidation with a long window and then shortening it to "fix" freshness, which multiplies renders.
  • One global tag that invalidates the whole site on every change.
  • APIs returning empty 200s on failure, which ISR happily caches.
  • Calling notFound() inside a Suspense boundary and expecting a 404.
  • Assuming revalidateTag purges the CDN.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through what happens on the first request after an ISR page's revalidate window. Expected answer: stale page served immediately, background re-render, replace on success, keep old on failure; next request gets fresh. Follow-up: what if the re-render throws? (Old page kept, retried next time.)
  2. Time-based vs on-demand revalidation: when do you use each? Expected answer: time-based as a bound and safety net; on-demand for event-driven freshness; both together in production.
  3. Why can't a streamed page return 404 after streaming starts? Expected answer: status and headers go out with the first chunk; decide existence before the first Suspense boundary.
  4. What does the backend have to do differently for an ISR frontend? Expected answer: fail with real error codes, handle revalidation bursts, publish change events, keep catalogue endpoints cacheable.
  5. How would you debug "the page is still showing the old price"? Expected answer: check x-nextjs-cache, the tag used, whether revalidation reached every replica, the CDN TTL, and the browser's router cache (73.7).

Practical exercise

Add ISR and streaming to a category page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • curl -sI shows x-nextjs-cache: HIT on a repeat request, STALE after the window, and HIT again two seconds later.
  • Stopping the catalogue API and waiting past the window still serves the old page; the server logs one regeneration error per attempt.
  • A POST to the revalidation endpoint with a valid signature makes the next request show the new price.
  • With the bestsellers endpoint delayed by 3 s, the page's LCP element paints in under 1 s and the bestsellers section arrives later without layout shift (CLS under 0.05).

73.3 The App Router: routes, layouts and special files

Concept

The App Router (stable since Next.js 13.4, the default in 14) maps folders under app/ to URL segments. A folder becomes a public route only when it contains a page.tsx. Other reserved file names in the same folder add behaviour to that segment:

File What it does
page.tsx The UI for this URL; makes the segment routable
layout.tsx Wraps this segment and all children; persists across navigation between children (state kept, not re-rendered)
template.tsx Like a layout, but re-mounted on every navigation (fresh state, effects re-run)
loading.tsx Wraps the page in a <Suspense> boundary with this as the fallback; enables streaming and instant navigation feedback
error.tsx Wraps the page in an error boundary; must be a client component; receives error and reset
not-found.tsx Rendered when notFound() is called in this segment
global-error.tsx Error boundary for the root layout itself; must render its own <html> and <body>
route.ts A Route Handler: an HTTP endpoint instead of a page (73.6); cannot sit next to page.tsx

Folder name conventions add the rest: [slug] is a dynamic segment, [...slug] a catch-all, [[...slug]] an optional catch-all, (shop) a route group that organises files and layouts without appearing in the URL, _components a private folder that is never routed, @cart a parallel route slot rendered alongside the page, and (.)p/[slug] an intercepting route (for example, opening a product in a modal over the listing).

Why does it exist?

The older Pages Router (pages/, still supported) treated each page as one unit fetched by getServerSideProps or getStaticProps. Shared chrome such as a header with a cart count re-rendered on every navigation, data fetching could only happen at the page level, and loading and error states were hand-built per page. The App Router makes the segment the unit: each level of the URL can own its layout, data, loading state and error boundary, and navigation re-renders only the segments that changed.

Mental model

Imagine a set of nested picture frames. The outer frame (root layout) holds the site header and footer. Inside it, the (shop) frame holds the category sidebar. Inside that, the page is the picture. When you navigate from one product to another, only the picture is swapped; the frames stay on the wall, with any open drawer or typed search text still in place. loading.tsx is a placeholder card the framer slots in while the next picture is being fetched; error.tsx is a "sorry, this picture is damaged" card that replaces only the picture, not the frames.

How it works

A storefront's app/ directory:

apps/web/app/
├── layout.tsx                 root: <html>, <body>, header, Providers (79.4)
├── global-error.tsx
├── (shop)/
│   ├── layout.tsx             category nav; static
│   ├── page.tsx               home  ->  /
│   ├── c/[category]/
│   │   ├── page.tsx           /c/electric-toothbrushes  (ISR, 79.2)
│   │   └── loading.tsx
│   └── p/[slug]/
│       ├── page.tsx           /p/sonic-toothbrush
│       ├── error.tsx
│       └── not-found.tsx
├── (account)/
│   ├── layout.tsx             requires session (79.9)
│   ├── orders/page.tsx        /orders  (dynamic)
│   └── cart/page.tsx          /cart    (client-rendered cart, 79.13)
└── api/
    ├── revalidate/route.ts    POST /api/revalidate  (79.6)
    └── bff/cart/route.ts      GET  /api/bff/cart    (79.8)

For a request to /p/sonic-toothbrush, Next.js composes the segments into one React tree, in this nesting order per segment:

RootLayout
  └ (shop)/layout
      └ ErrorBoundary  (p/[slug]/error.tsx)
          └ Suspense   (loading.tsx, if present)
              └ NotFoundBoundary (not-found.tsx)
                  └ page.tsx

First load returns HTML (plus the RSC payload inlined in <script> tags so React can hydrate without refetching). Client-side navigation through <Link> or router.push() does not fetch HTML. The router requests the RSC payload for the new URL (a request with the RSC: 1 header and a _rsc query parameter), receives only the segments that differ from the current page, and patches the tree. Layouts that are shared between the old and new URL are not re-rendered on the server or remounted on the client.

Prefetching: in production, <Link> prefetches routes as the link enters the viewport. For a static route the whole RSC payload is prefetched; for a dynamic route only the part down to the nearest loading.tsx is prefetched, so the click shows the loading state instantly and the rest streams. Prefetched payloads live in the client-side Router Cache (73.7). prefetch={false} turns it off per link; in development nothing is prefetched, which is why production feels faster than next dev.

Practical example

The product page needs four states: found, not found, failed, and loading during navigation. With the App Router, each is a file. notFound() in the page renders not-found.tsx with a real 404 status (it runs before streaming starts). A thrown error renders error.tsx inside the (shop) layout, so the header and category navigation still work and the user can click away. Navigation from a category page shows loading.tsx instantly because the dynamic part was not prefetched.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/(shop)/p/[slug]/error.tsx  (must be a client component)
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';

export default function ProductError({ error, reset }: { error: Error & { digest?: string }; reset: () => void }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    // In production, Next.js replaces server error messages with a generic one and gives a digest
    // that matches the server log line. Report the digest, never the raw server message.
    console.error('product page error', error.digest);
  }, [error]);
  return (
    <section role="alert">
      <h2>We could not load this product.</h2>
      <p>Reference: <code>{error.digest}</code></p>
      <button onClick={() => reset()}>Try again</button> {/* re-renders the segment */}
    </section>
  );
}
// apps/web/app/(shop)/p/[slug]/page.tsx  (metadata excerpt, Next.js 14)
import type { Metadata } from 'next';
import { getProduct } from '@/lib/catalog.server'; // the fetch from 79.1, wrapped in React cache() (79.4, 79.7)

export async function generateMetadata({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }): Promise<Metadata> {
  const product = await getProduct(params.slug); // deduplicated with the page's own call
  return product
    ? { title: `${product.name} | Shop`, openGraph: { images: [product.imageUrl] } }
    : { title: 'Product not found' };
}

Next.js 15 change: params and searchParams are Promises. The 15 version of the signatures is { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> } followed by const { slug } = await params;. Next.js 15 still allowed synchronous access with a deprecation warning to ease migration; Next.js 16 removed it. The official codemod (npx @next/codemod@canary next-async-request-api .) rewrites most call sites.

Backend side (NestJS)

The router's behaviour shapes your API traffic:

  • Prefetching multiplies requests. A category page with 48 product links prefetches each product route as the user scrolls. For static or ISR product pages that is cheap (served from cache). For dynamic product pages, each prefetch is a server render, and each render calls NestJS. One page view can become 48 renders and 150 API calls.
  • generateMetadata and the page call the same data. Inside one render they share the result if the fetch is identical or wrapped in cache() (request memoisation, 73.7). If one passes a different header or URL, NestJS sees two calls per view.
  • Error digests correlate with your logs. Propagate an x-request-id from the Next.js server to NestJS on every call and log it with the digest, so "Reference: 3846270981" in a support ticket leads to the NestJS trace (Part 43 — Observability, 43.2).
  • 404 vs 500 must be distinguishable. notFound() should run only when NestJS says the product does not exist (404 with code: 'PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND'); any other failure should throw so the page shows the error boundary and ISR keeps the old copy.

Production scenario

A furniture retailer's category pages linked to dynamic product pages (they read a region cookie for delivery dates). After launching infinite scroll, each category visit rendered on average 31 product pages through prefetching, of which users clicked 1.4. The product render tier grew from 6 to 22 pods in a month and the catalogue API's RPS tripled.

They made product pages ISR (delivery dates moved into a small client component reading the region from a cookie in the browser), so prefetches became cache hits. The render tier went back to 6 pods; time from click to content stayed under 100 ms because the prefetched payload was already in the Router Cache.

Failure scenario

A team moved the site header, with its live cart count, into the root layout.tsx and fetched the cart there with cookies(). Every route in the app, including the home page and 40,000 product pages, became dynamic in the next build. Nobody read the build output. On deploy, CDN hit rate fell from 95 % to 0 % within the TTL, origin traffic went up twentyfold, and the Next.js autoscaler hit its maximum at 11:20. The rollback restored the static routes; the fix moved the cart count into a client component (73.13).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • error.tsx does not catch errors in the layout.tsx of the same segment; it sits inside that layout. Errors in a layout are caught by the parent segment's error.tsx, and errors in the root layout only by global-error.tsx.
  • Layouts do not re-render on navigation, so a layout cannot read the current pathname or search params on the server. Use a client component with usePathname() for "active link" styling.
  • template.tsx resets state on every navigation: useful for per-page analytics, harmful if used by accident for a layout with a form.
  • Route groups with multiple root layouts cause a full page reload when navigating between them.
  • Parallel routes need default.tsx for slots that have no match on hard navigation; Next.js 16 made a missing default a build error.
  • Prefetching in development is off, so performance problems from prefetch storms appear only in production.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior uses the folder structure as the architecture diagram: route groups separate the public, cacheable storefront from the personal, dynamic account area, and each group's layout declares what it may depend on. They check that shared layouts never read request data unless every page beneath them is meant to be dynamic. They budget prefetch traffic like any other load and choose static or ISR for heavily linked pages so prefetches are free.

Common mistakes

  • Reading cookies in the root layout, making the whole site dynamic.
  • Calling notFound() for every API error, turning outages into 404s that search engines de-index.
  • Showing error.message from server errors, which is replaced by a generic message in production anyway; use the digest.
  • Forgetting loading.tsx on dynamic routes, so clicks feel dead until the server finishes.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between layout.tsx and template.tsx? Expected answer: layouts persist and keep state across child navigation; templates re-mount. Follow-up: where would you put a cart drawer's open state? (Layout, or a client store.)
  2. What does a client-side navigation fetch in the App Router? Expected answer: the RSC payload for the changed segments, not HTML; shared layouts are reused.
  3. Why might error.tsx not catch an error thrown in a layout? Expected answer: it is rendered inside that layout; the parent segment's boundary catches it.
  4. How does prefetching affect backend load, and how do you control it? Expected answer: links in the viewport trigger route prefetches; dynamic routes render on the server; use static or ISR routes, loading.tsx boundaries, or prefetch={false}.

Practical exercise

Build the (shop) and (account) route groups from the tree above.

Acceptance criteria:

  • next build shows all (shop) routes as static or SSG and all (account) routes as dynamic.
  • A missing product returns HTTP 404 with the custom not-found.tsx; a NestJS 500 shows error.tsx with a digest that appears in the Next.js server log alongside the request id sent to NestJS.
  • Navigating between two products keeps the category sidebar's scroll position and does not refetch the layout (verified in the Network panel by the RSC request contents).
  • With production build and scrolling a category page, the Network panel shows prefetch requests answered from cache, not new renders.

73.4 Server components and client components: the boundary

Concept

In the App Router every component is a React Server Component (RSC) by default. Server components run only on the server, at build time or per request. They can be async, await data directly, read environment secrets and files, and import server-only libraries. Their code never reaches the browser. They cannot use state, effects, event handlers or browser APIs.

A file that starts with the directive 'use client' defines a client component boundary. That module, and every module it imports, becomes part of the JavaScript bundle sent to the browser. Client components are still rendered to HTML on the server for the first load (so they are not "client-only"), then hydrated in the browser where they can use useState, useEffect, onClick, window and TanStack Query.

The boundary is one-directional for imports: a server component can import and render a client component; a client component cannot import a server component. It can, however, receive already-rendered server components as children or other props.

Why does it exist?

In a classic SSR React app, every component is shipped to the browser and hydrated, even those that only ever render static text from data. A product description rendered from Markdown pulls a 60 KB Markdown parser into the bundle just to produce HTML that was already in the page. Server components let that work happen once on the server, with only the result sent. Data fetching also moves next to the component that needs it, server-side, close to the API, with no client-server waterfall.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant. Server components are the kitchen: they have the knives, the fridge and the supplier phone numbers (secrets, database, APIs), and they send out finished plates (rendered output). Customers never see the kitchen. Client components are the condiments and the bell on the table: small things that must be in the customer's hands to work. You do not send the whole kitchen to the table so the customer can add salt. And whatever you put on the plate, the customer can see: never plate the supplier invoices.

How it works

flowchart TB
    page["page.tsx, server"] --> desc["ProductDescription, server, renders Markdown"]
    page --> gallery["Gallery, client, swipe state"]
    page --> buy["AddToCartButton, client, onClick"]
    page --> reviews["Reviews, server, async fetch"]
    buy --> qty["QuantityStepper, client, imported by a client module"]
    page --> drawer["CartDrawer, client"]
    drawer -->|"children prop"| promo["PromoBanner, server, rendered before passing"]
  1. On the server, React renders the tree. Server components execute and produce output. For each client component it meets, React records a reference ("module AddToCartButton, chunk app/p/[slug]/page-4f2a.js, with these props") instead of running it as a server component.
  2. The result is the RSC payload: a compact serialised description of the tree, with server output inlined and client components as references plus their serialised props.
  3. For the first load, Next.js also renders the full tree, client components included, to HTML (classic SSR) and inlines the RSC payload in the page.
  4. In the browser, React loads the client chunks referenced in the payload and hydrates only those parts. Server component output is plain HTML that needs no JavaScript.
  5. Props across the boundary must be serialisable by React: strings, numbers, booleans, null, plain objects, arrays; recent React versions also handle Date, Map, Set, BigInt and Promises. Functions and class instances cannot cross, with one exception: Server Actions (functions marked 'use server', 73.6), which cross as references the client can call.
  6. Everything passed as a prop is in the page source. The serialised props are visible in the HTML and in the RSC payload of every client navigation.

Which side should a component live on:

Needs Server component Client component
Fetch data, read secrets, call internal APIs Yes No (call a Route Handler or API instead)
Large rendering libraries (Markdown, syntax highlighting, date formatting) Yes, zero client cost Shipped to every user
useState, useEffect, event handlers No Yes
Browser APIs (window, localStorage, geolocation) No Yes
React Context providers and consumers No Yes
TanStack Query, Zustand No Yes

The rule seniors teach: push 'use client' to the leaves. Keep pages and layouts as server components; make the smallest interactive pieces client components.

Practical example

On the product page, the description (Markdown), the specs table and the reviews list are server components: they only display data. The image gallery (swipe state), the quantity stepper and "Add to cart" button (state, clicks, a mutation), and the cart drawer (open state, TanStack Query for the live cart) are client components. The page passes the server-rendered promo banner into the client drawer as children, so the drawer can show it without the banner's code or data fetch moving into the client bundle.

React / Next.js example

The providers: a client component that creates TanStack Query per browser tab, and a fresh client per server request, which avoids the cross-request leak warned about in Part 72 — Client State, Data Fetching and Caching (72.9).

// apps/web/app/providers.tsx
'use client';
import { isServer, QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

function makeQueryClient() {
  return new QueryClient({
    defaultOptions: { queries: { staleTime: 30_000 } }, // >0 so data prefetched on the server is not refetched at once
  });
}

let browserClient: QueryClient | undefined;
function getQueryClient() {
  if (isServer) return makeQueryClient();        // new per request: never share user data between requests
  return (browserClient ??= makeQueryClient());  // one per tab, survives re-renders and Suspense
}

export function Providers({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const queryClient = getQueryClient();
  return <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>{children}</QueryClientProvider>;
}
// apps/web/app/layout.tsx  (server component; renders the client Providers around server children)
import { Providers } from './providers';
export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en-IN">
      <body><Providers>{children}</Providers></body>
    </html>
  );
}

A server-only data module, guarded so it can never be bundled for the browser:

// apps/web/lib/catalog.server.ts
import 'server-only';                       // build error if any client component imports this file
import { cache } from 'react';
import { ProductViewSchema, type ProductView } from '@shop/contracts';

const BASE = process.env.CATALOG_API_URL!;  // not NEXT_PUBLIC_: never inlined into client bundles (76.6)

export const getProduct = cache(async (slug: string): Promise<ProductView | null> => {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}/v1/products/${slug}`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CATALOG_SERVICE_TOKEN}` }, // service credential stays on the server
    next: { revalidate: 300, tags: [`product:${slug}`] },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000),
  });
  if (res.status === 404) return null;
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`catalog ${res.status}`);
  return ProductViewSchema.parse(await res.json());
});

And the client leaf receives only what it needs:

// apps/web/app/(shop)/p/[slug]/AddToCartButton.tsx
'use client';
import { useAddToCart } from '@/cart/useAddToCart'; // TanStack Query mutation with idempotency key (78.6, 79.13)

export function AddToCartButton({ sku }: { sku: string }) {   // a string, not the whole product object
  const add = useAddToCart();
  return (
    <button disabled={add.isPending}
      onClick={() => add.mutate({ sku, quantity: 1, idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID() })}> {/* one key per click, reused by retries (78.6) */}
      {add.isPending ? 'Adding...' : 'Add to cart'}
    </button>
  );
}

To prefetch personal data on the server and hand it to TanStack Query on the client, a dynamic page can prefetchQuery into a per-request QueryClient and wrap the client subtree in <HydrationBoundary state={dehydrate(queryClient)}>. The client's useQuery with the same key then starts with that data instead of a spinner. Use this for dynamic, personal pages; on static pages it would bake personal data into cached HTML.

Backend side (NestJS)

Server components make the Next.js server a trusted client of NestJS, which changes the API contract:

  • Service-to-service auth. Server components can call NestJS with a service token or forward the user's session cookie (73.8). Browser-callable endpoints and server-only endpoints should be distinguishable, with internal endpoints not exposed on the public load balancer.
  • Return view models, not entities. Whatever the server component passes to a client component is serialised into the page. If NestJS returns a Customer entity with riskScore and internalNotes, one careless prop leaks them. Shape responses with explicit DTOs and ClassSerializerInterceptor with @Exclude()/@Expose(), or zod schemas from @shop/contracts that strip unknown keys on both sides.
  • Smaller responses help render time. Server components parse and render every byte NestJS returns. A 400 KB product response with every variant's every image costs 15 to 30 ms of server parse and render per view on SSR pages.

Production scenario

A recipe-and-grocery site rendered recipe pages as client components that pulled in a Markdown parser, a syntax highlighter for ingredient tables and a date library: 310 KB of gzipped JavaScript on a page whose interactive parts were a "save" button and an "add ingredients to cart" button. Moving the page to server components with two client leaves cut JavaScript to 128 KB, cut p75 INP on low-end Android from 380 ms to 160 ms (Part 76 — Web Performance), and made the page render on the server in 35 ms instead of hydrating 900 DOM nodes of static text.

Failure scenario

A developer building an account page wrote <ProfileCard customer={customer} />, where ProfileCard was a client component (it had an "edit" toggle) and customer was the raw NestJS response from an internal endpoint. That endpoint, meant only for staff tools, included riskScore, fraudFlags and lastSupportNote. Nothing showed on screen, but every field was in the RSC payload in the HTML. A customer viewing source posted a screenshot of their own "fraudFlags: [chargeback_2024]" on social media three weeks later.

The fix: a dedicated GET /v1/me/profile endpoint returning a CustomerProfileView with six fields; the client component typed its prop as that view; import 'server-only' on the internal client; and a test that renders the page and asserts the HTML contains none of a list of sensitive field names. React's experimental taint APIs (experimental_taintObjectReference, enabled in Next.js with experimental.taint: true) can also refuse to pass marked objects to client components, but they are a seatbelt, not a design.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • 'use client' high in the tree (on a layout to use one hook) turns every imported module below into client code and can double the bundle.
  • A shared utility module that reads server env vars, imported by a client component, compiles with undefined values in the browser; server-only turns this into a build error.
  • Third-party components that use hooks but lack 'use client' fail when imported into a server component; wrap them in a one-line client module.
  • Non-serialisable props (class instances, functions) fail at build or render time with "Only plain objects can be passed to Client Components".
  • Context does not cross into server components: a server component cannot read a theme or cart context; pass values as props or read them from the request.
  • Prefetching personal data into a static page with HydrationBoundary caches one user's data for everyone.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats the boundary like an API boundary, because it is one: props are a public response body. They push 'use client' to small leaves, pass IDs and view models rather than domain objects, and guard server modules with server-only. They see server components as a way to delete client JavaScript and client-server waterfalls, not as a reason to put business logic in the frontend tier: rules still live in NestJS, and server components only fetch, compose and render.

Common mistakes

  • Marking pages or layouts 'use client' out of habit from the Pages Router or Vite.
  • Passing whole API responses to client components.
  • Fetching in a client effect data that a server component could have fetched next to the API.
  • Creating a module-level QueryClient or store used on the server, leaking data between requests.

Interview questions

  1. What runs where for a client component in the App Router? Expected answer: rendered to HTML on the server for first load, then hydrated and run in the browser; its code is in the bundle. Follow-up: so why is it called a client component? (It is the part that runs on the client; server components never do.)
  2. Can a client component render a server component? Expected answer: not by importing it, but it can receive one as children or a prop that the server rendered.
  3. What can and cannot be passed as props across the boundary? Expected answer: serialisable values; no functions except Server Actions; and everything passed is visible to the user.
  4. How do you prevent server-only code from reaching the bundle? Expected answer: import 'server-only', no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix for secrets, reviewing the bundle analyser.
  5. How would you combine server components with TanStack Query? Expected answer: per-request client on the server, prefetchQuery, dehydrate, HydrationBoundary, same keys on the client, non-zero staleTime; only for dynamic pages.

Practical exercise

Refactor a product page that is entirely 'use client' into server components with client leaves.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The page, layout, description and reviews have no 'use client'; only gallery, stepper, add-to-cart and cart drawer do.
  • First-load JavaScript for the route, as shown in the next build output, falls by at least 30 %.
  • catalog.server.ts imports server-only, and importing it from a client component fails the build.
  • A test fetches the rendered HTML and asserts that no field outside the ProductView schema appears in it.

73.5 Data fetching on the server: fetch, route segment config and static params

Concept

In the App Router, server components fetch data by calling await fetch(...) (or any async function) directly in the component. Next.js extends the standard fetch with two options that connect it to its caches:

  • cache: 'force-cache' | 'no-store': whether the response is stored in the Data Cache (73.7), a persistent server-side cache of fetch results that survives across requests and, on most hosts, across deployments.
  • next: { revalidate: number | false, tags: string[] }: how long the cached entry stays fresh (seconds; false means indefinitely) and which tags can invalidate it on demand.

Route segment config sets defaults for a whole route segment through exported constants in page.tsx or layout.tsx: dynamic, dynamicParams, revalidate, fetchCache, runtime, preferredRegion and maxDuration. generateStaticParams tells Next.js which values of a dynamic segment ([slug]) to prerender at build time.

The defaults moved between versions, which is why this section always names one:

Behaviour Next.js 14 Next.js 15 Next.js 16 with cacheComponents: true
fetch with no cache option Cached (force-cache) unless something dynamic came first Not cached Not cached; wrap code in "use cache" to cache
GET Route Handlers Static by default if they read no request data Dynamic by default Dynamic by default
params, searchParams, cookies(), headers() Synchronous Promises (sync access deprecated) Promises only
Opt into dynamic without reading request data unstable_noStore() await connection() from next/server await connection()
Route segment dynamic, revalidate, fetchCache Supported Supported Replaced by "use cache" and cacheLife

Why does it exist?

Without a framework cache, every server render calls the API afresh, and SSR load equals page views times API calls. The extended fetch lets each data dependency declare its own freshness, so one page can combine product data cached for 5 minutes, a category tree cached for an hour and an uncached stock figure. Route segment config exists for the cases where you need to state the route's behaviour explicitly instead of letting Next.js infer it, which is most production cases: inference is how routes silently flip from static to dynamic.

Mental model

Imagine each fetch as an order slip handed to a clerk who keeps a filing cabinet. The slip says either "use the file if it is younger than 5 minutes" (revalidate: 300), "always phone the supplier" (no-store), or "file it under 'product:sonic' so the manager can pull it later" (tags). Route segment config is a sign on the office door: "this office only serves pre-printed forms" (force-static) or "every customer gets a fresh phone call" (force-dynamic).

How it works

  1. During a render, each fetch computes a cache key from the URL and options (method, headers, body). With caching enabled, a fresh hit returns the stored body without a network call; a stale hit returns the stored body and refreshes it in the background; a miss calls the origin and stores the result.
  2. In Next.js 14, the route's ISR interval is the lowest revalidate among the route's segment config and its fetches. A page with revalidate = 3600 that contains one fetch with revalidate: 60 regenerates every 60 seconds.
  3. Using cookies(), headers(), searchParams, no-store or revalidate: 0 makes the route dynamic: rendered per request. Cached fetches inside a dynamic route still hit the Data Cache, so a dynamic page can be cheap if most of its data is cached.
  4. generateStaticParams runs at build time and returns the param sets to prerender. With dynamicParams = true (the default), other values render on first request and are then cached like ISR pages; with dynamicParams = false, they return 404. Returning an empty array prerenders nothing at build and caches every page on first visit.
  5. Non-fetch data sources (a database driver, a gRPC client, a vendor SDK) do not go through the Data Cache. In 14 and 15, wrap them with unstable_cache(fn, keyParts, { revalidate, tags }) from next/cache; in 16, mark the function with "use cache" (73.7). React's cache() only deduplicates within one render (73.7); it does not persist anything.

Waterfalls are the main performance trap. Awaits that run one after another add their latencies into TTFB:

Sequential:   product 60 ms ─▶ price 70 ms ─▶ related 60 ms      = 190 ms before render
Parallel:     product 60 ms
              price   70 ms   ──────────────────────────────────  = 70 ms before render
              related 60 ms

Nested server components create waterfalls too: a parent that awaits data before rendering a child that awaits its own data is sequential by construction. Start independent requests together with Promise.all, or start them in the parent and pass the promises down.

Practical example

A catalogue of 40,000 products, of which the top 2,000 get 85 % of traffic. The product route uses generateStaticParams to prerender those 2,000 at build (about 90 seconds at 25 concurrent renders) and leaves dynamicParams = true, so the long tail renders on first request and is cached. Category data is cached for an hour with tag catalog-tree; product data for 5 minutes with tag product:<slug>; the "delivery by" estimate depends on the visitor's region cookie and is a client component, keeping the page static.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/(shop)/p/[slug]/page.tsx  (Next.js 14)
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
import { getProduct, getPrice, getRelated } from '@/lib/catalog.server';

export const revalidate = 300;
export const dynamicParams = true;   // long tail rendered on demand, then cached (must be explicit, see below)
export const dynamic = 'error';      // fail the build on cookies()/headers(); also flips the dynamicParams default to false

export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.CATALOG_API_URL}/v1/catalog/top-products?limit=2000`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CATALOG_SERVICE_TOKEN}` },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`top-products ${res.status}`); // fail the build, do not ship empty pages
  const { slugs } = (await res.json()) as { slugs: string[] };
  return slugs.map((slug) => ({ slug }));
}

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  // Start all three at once: TTFB pays for the slowest, not the sum.
  const [product, price, related] = await Promise.all([
    getProduct(params.slug),
    getPrice(params.slug),
    getRelated(params.slug).catch(() => []),   // optional data must not fail the page
  ]);
  if (!product) notFound();
  return <ProductView product={product} price={price} related={related} />;
}

Caching a non-fetch source (here a search SDK) in Next.js 14 or 15. Note that the function's arguments are part of the cache key automatically; values captured from the surrounding scope are not:

// apps/web/lib/search.server.ts  (Next.js 14/15)
import 'server-only';
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache';
import { searchClient } from './search-client'; // vendor SDK, not fetch

export const getFacets = unstable_cache(
  async (category: string) => searchClient.facets({ category }), // category is an argument: part of the key
  ['facets-v2'],                                                // bump when the return shape changes
  { revalidate: 900, tags: ['facets'] },
);

Next.js 15 version of the same page signature: { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> } with const { slug } = await params;, and in 15 each fetch inside getProduct must say cache: 'force-cache' or next: { revalidate: 300 } to be cached; with no option it is fetched on every render (though the page itself is still prerendered at build if nothing dynamic is used).

Backend side (NestJS)

The NestJS catalogue service needs endpoints and limits shaped for these patterns:

  • A slug-listing endpoint for generateStaticParams, returning only slugs (40 KB for 2,000 products, not 40 MB of product bodies), ordered by popularity.
  • Build bursts are legitimate traffic. A build renders 2,000 pages with 3 calls each in about 90 seconds: roughly 70 RPS of uncacheable reads. Exempt the build's service token from ThrottlerGuard limits with a custom shouldSkip or a separate throttler profile, or the build fails at random with 429s.
  • Next.js ignores your Cache-Control for its Data Cache. s-maxage=60 on a NestJS response does not make Next.js cache it for 60 seconds; the fetch options do. Keep sending honest headers anyway: CDNs and browsers calling the same endpoint use them.
  • Make the fast path explicit. Per-request server calls should hit indexed lookups that return in 1 to 5 ms. A product endpoint that runs a 40 ms query is invisible on a cached page and terrible on a dynamic one.
// apps/api/src/catalog/catalog.controller.ts  (excerpt)
import { Controller, Get, Header, Query, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { SkipThrottle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { TopProductsQuerySchema, type TopProductsQuery } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { ServiceTokenGuard } from '../auth/service-token.guard';
import { CatalogService } from './catalog.service';

@Controller('v1/catalog')
export class CatalogController {
  constructor(private readonly catalog: CatalogService) {}

  @Get('top-products')
  @UseGuards(ServiceTokenGuard)        // internal: only the web tier's build and render calls this
  @SkipThrottle()                      // build bursts are expected; the guard limits who can do it
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'private, max-age=0')
  async topProducts(@Query(new ZodValidationPipe(TopProductsQuerySchema)) q: TopProductsQuery) {
    // SELECT slug FROM products WHERE active ORDER BY views_30d DESC LIMIT $1  (index on views_30d)
    return { slugs: await this.catalog.topSlugs(q.limit) };
  }
}

Production scenario

A sports-goods site's product page awaited product, then price, then stock, then reviews, each in its own nested server component. p50 server time was 240 ms and p95 610 ms, since every slow call delayed all later ones. Rewriting the page to start all four in Promise.all at the top and moving reviews behind a <Suspense> boundary cut p50 to 85 ms and p95 to 190 ms. They then cached product and price with revalidate: 120 and tags, which brought the median dynamic render (the page read a region cookie) to 22 ms, because only the stock call reached NestJS.

Failure scenario

To speed up a personalised home page, a developer cached recommendations with unstable_cache:

const user = await getSessionUser();                       // reads cookies()
const recs = await unstable_cache(
  async () => fetchRecommendations(user.id),               // user.id captured from scope, NOT in the key
  ['home-recs'],
  { revalidate: 600 },
)();

The first visitor after deploy filled the entry with their recommendations, and for 10 minutes every visitor saw them, including "Buy again: Pregnancy test kit". It was reported within 20 minutes. The fix passed user.id as an argument (so it became part of the key), and the team added a lint rule banning closures inside unstable_cache calls. The deeper lesson: any server cache keyed by something other than all of its inputs is a cross-user leak waiting to happen, exactly like the query keys in 72.2.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mixing revalidate values across fetches: the lowest one sets the route's regeneration interval in 14.
  • generateStaticParams calling a slow or rate-limited API makes builds flaky; give it a timeout and fail loudly.
  • dynamicParams = false with a stale build returns 404 for products added since the deploy.
  • Large fetch responses are not stored in the Data Cache: Next.js skips items over 2 MB and logs a warning, so a big catalogue response is fetched on every render.
  • POST requests used for reads (GraphQL) are not cached by fetch in Route Handlers or after dynamic APIs; use unstable_cache around the call if you need it.
  • dynamic = 'force-static' makes cookies() return empty values instead of failing: authenticated content renders as logged-out without an error. Prefer dynamic = 'error' to make violations fail the build.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior states caching intent explicitly on every fetch and every route, rather than relying on defaults that changed between 14 and 15. They prefer dynamic = 'error' on pages meant to be static so the build enforces it. They draw the data dependencies of a page and refuse sequential awaits for independent data. And they ask whether the Next.js tier should talk to a database at all: usually not. NestJS owns the data and its rules; the web tier fetches through the API, with a cache key that includes every input.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on Next.js 14's implicit fetch caching, then upgrading to 15 and watching API traffic multiply.
  • Sequential awaits in a page or in nested components.
  • Caching per-user data with a key that omits the user.
  • Prerendering every product at build instead of the popular ones.

Interview questions

  1. How do you make one fetch cached for 5 minutes and another uncached in the same page? Expected answer: per-fetch options, next: { revalidate: 300 } and cache: 'no-store'; the uncached one makes the route dynamic. Follow-up: what decides the route's revalidation interval in 14? (The lowest revalidate.)
  2. What do generateStaticParams and dynamicParams control? Expected answer: which params are prerendered at build, and whether others render on demand or 404.
  3. How do you cache a database or SDK call in Next.js 14/15? Expected answer: unstable_cache with arguments in the key, revalidate and tags; "use cache" in 16.
  4. What changed in data fetching defaults in Next.js 15? Expected answer: fetch and GET Route Handlers uncached by default; async request APIs; connection() for opting into dynamic.

Practical exercise

Optimise a dynamic product page with four data dependencies.

Acceptance criteria:

  • All independent fetches start in one Promise.all; a test with each mocked endpoint delayed by 100 ms shows server render under 150 ms.
  • Every fetch has an explicit cache option and a timeout, and a lint rule or code search proves it.
  • generateStaticParams prerenders the top 500 products; the 501st renders on first request and is a cache hit on the second (x-nextjs-cache: HIT).
  • A per-user cached function takes the user id as an argument; a test with two users proves they get different results.

73.6 Server Actions and Route Handlers

Concept

Server Actions are async functions marked with 'use server' that run on the server but can be called from client code or used as a form's action. Next.js gives each one an ID and exposes it as an HTTP endpoint: calling it sends a POST to the current page with a Next-Action header, the serialised arguments as the body, and gets back the return value, plus an updated RSC payload if the action revalidated anything. They were stable in Next.js 14.

Route Handlers are files named route.ts that export functions named after HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS). They receive a Web Request (or NextRequest) and return a Web Response (or NextResponse). They are plain HTTP endpoints living in the Next.js app, for webhooks, BFF proxies, OAuth callbacks and anything that is not a React render.

Why does it exist?

Mutations from a React page used to need three things: an API endpoint, a client-side fetch with loading and error handling, and code to refresh the page's data afterwards. Server Actions collapse that for the common case: a form posts to a server function that can validate, call the backend, and revalidate the affected cache in one step, and the form works even before JavaScript has loaded (progressive enhancement). Route Handlers exist because not every caller is a React component: NestJS needs an endpoint to trigger revalidation, a payment provider needs a webhook URL, and client components sometimes need a same-origin proxy.

Mental model

Imagine a Server Action as a direct phone line from a form on the page to a clerk in the back office: the customer picks up and speaks, the clerk does the work and updates the noticeboard. It feels private, but the line has a public number: anyone who learns it can dial. A Route Handler is the shop's public service window with a sign above it: "Deliveries: POST here". Both are doors into your server, and both need a lock.

How it works

A Server Action invoked from a form:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant N as NextServer
    participant API as NestJS
    B->>N: POST /p/sonic with Next-Action header and form data
    N->>N: check Origin matches Host
    N->>N: run action, validate with zod
    N->>API: POST /v1/stock-alerts with user token and Idempotency-Key
    API-->>N: 201 created
    N->>N: revalidatePath or revalidateTag
    N-->>B: action result plus fresh RSC payload
    Note over B: page updates without a full reload
  1. At build time, Next.js finds functions marked 'use server' (a whole file or a single function body), assigns each an ID, and replaces client imports with a reference that knows how to POST to it.
  2. On call, the client sends the arguments serialised by React. If JavaScript has not loaded, a <form action={serverAction}> submits as a normal HTML form post, and the action still runs.
  3. Next.js compares the Origin header to the Host (or X-Forwarded-Host) header and rejects mismatches, a built-in CSRF defence; extra trusted origins go in serverActions.allowedOrigins (under experimental in the 14 and 15 config). The request body is limited to 1 MB by default (serverActions.bodySizeLimit).
  4. Values captured in a closure from a server component are encrypted into the action reference so they cannot be read by the client; they can still be replayed, so never treat them as a security token.
  5. If the action calls revalidatePath or revalidateTag, the response carries the re-rendered RSC payload, and the client-side Router Cache is invalidated (73.7). redirect() inside an action redirects; cookies().set() sets a cookie and also refreshes the router.
  6. Next.js 15 made unused actions dead-code-eliminated and their IDs non-deterministic and rotated between builds, which reduces discoverability. It does not make them private: every exported Server Action is a public HTTP endpoint. Authenticate, authorise and validate inside every action, every time.

Route Handlers are simpler: a request comes in, your function returns a Response. In Next.js 14, a GET handler that reads no request data (request, cookies(), headers()) is treated as static and its response cached at build; in 15, GET handlers are dynamic unless you export dynamic = 'force-static'. Handlers are not part of the React tree, so React's cache() and fetch memoisation do not apply to them.

When to use which:

Need Use
A form or button on a Next.js page that changes data and refreshes the page Server Action
Reading data for rendering Server component fetch, not an action (actions are dispatched one at a time and are POSTs)
Webhook from NestJS or a payment provider Route Handler
Same-origin proxy so client components can call NestJS with the session cookie Route Handler or rewrites (73.8)
An endpoint for mobile apps or third parties NestJS, not Next.js

Practical example

A product that is out of stock shows "Notify me when back in stock". It is a form with one email field (prefilled for logged-in users) posted to a Server Action. The action validates the email with the zod schema from @shop/contracts, calls NestJS with the user's access token and an idempotency key, and returns { ok: true } or the API's { code, issues }. With JavaScript disabled or not yet loaded on a slow phone, the form still posts and the page re-renders with the confirmation.

Separately, the catalogue service in NestJS calls POST /api/revalidate on the web tier whenever a price changes, with an HMAC signature over the body; the Route Handler verifies the signature and calls revalidateTag for the affected tags.

React / Next.js example

The Server Action:

// apps/web/app/(shop)/p/[slug]/actions.ts
'use server';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { StockAlertRequestSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { getSession } from '@/lib/session.server';     // verifies the session cookie (79.9)

export type ActionState = { ok: boolean; code?: string; issues?: { path: string; message: string }[] };

export async function requestStockAlert(_prev: ActionState, formData: FormData): Promise<ActionState> {
  const parsed = StockAlertRequestSchema.safeParse({ sku: formData.get('sku'), email: formData.get('email') });
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return { ok: false, code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', issues: parsed.error.issues.map((i) => ({ path: i.path.join('.'), message: i.message })) };
  }
  const session = await getSession();                   // anonymous allowed here, but identify if present
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/v1/stock-alerts`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      ...(session ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${session.accessToken}` } : {}), // the USER's token, not a service token
      'Idempotency-Key': String(formData.get('idempotencyKey') ?? randomUUID()), // generated once per form render
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(parsed.data),
    cache: 'no-store',
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3_000),
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    const body = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));    // { code, issues, requestId } from NestJS
    return { ok: false, code: body.code ?? 'UPSTREAM_ERROR', issues: body.issues ?? [] };
  }
  return { ok: true };
}

The form, using useFormState from react-dom (the name in the React canary bundled with Next.js 14; it is useActionState from react in React 19 and Next.js 15):

// apps/web/app/(shop)/p/[slug]/StockAlertForm.tsx
'use client';
import { useFormState, useFormStatus } from 'react-dom';
import { requestStockAlert, type ActionState } from './actions';

function Submit() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();                  // disables during submit: no double posts (77.8)
  return <button disabled={pending}>{pending ? 'Saving...' : 'Notify me'}</button>;
}

export function StockAlertForm({ sku, idempotencyKey }: { sku: string; idempotencyKey: string }) {
  const [state, formAction] = useFormState<ActionState, FormData>(requestStockAlert, { ok: false });
  if (state.ok) return <p role="status">We will email you when it is back.</p>;
  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input type="hidden" name="sku" value={sku} />
      <input type="hidden" name="idempotencyKey" value={idempotencyKey} />
      <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" required /></label>
      {state.issues?.map((i) => <p key={i.path} role="alert">{i.message}</p>)}
      <Submit />
    </form>
  );
}

The revalidation Route Handler:

// apps/web/app/api/revalidate/route.ts
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';
import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache';
import { RevalidateRequestSchema } from '@shop/contracts';   // { tags: string[] }, max 100 tags

export const runtime = 'nodejs';                              // needs node:crypto
export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';

export async function POST(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const raw = await request.text();                           // sign the exact bytes, not re-serialised JSON
  const sig = Buffer.from(request.headers.get('x-signature') ?? '', 'hex');
  const expected = createHmac('sha256', process.env.REVALIDATE_SECRET!).update(raw).digest();
  if (sig.length !== expected.length || !timingSafeEqual(sig, expected)) {
    return Response.json({ code: 'BAD_SIGNATURE', issues: [] }, { status: 401 });
  }
  const parsed = RevalidateRequestSchema.safeParse(JSON.parse(raw));
  if (!parsed.success) return Response.json({ code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', issues: parsed.error.issues }, { status: 400 });
  for (const tag of parsed.data.tags) revalidateTag(tag);     // Next.js 16: revalidateTag(tag, 'max')
  return Response.json({ revalidated: parsed.data.tags.length, at: Date.now() });
}

The NestJS side signs the same raw body with the shared secret and calls this endpoint after the price transaction commits (73.13 shows the publisher).

Backend side (NestJS)

Server Actions and Route Handlers sit between the browser and NestJS, so the API must not relax because "the call comes from our own server":

  • Authenticate the user, not the web tier. Actions should forward the user's access token or session (73.8). If the web tier calls NestJS with an all-powerful service token for user operations, every authorisation check moves into the frontend tier, and one missing check is an IDOR (Part 40 — Security, 40.5).
  • Idempotency keys still matter. A Server Action can be retried by the browser, double-submitted, or replayed. Generate the key when the form is rendered and send it as Idempotency-Key; NestJS deduplicates it as in Part 15 — API Design (REST first) (15.12).
  • One error shape. Return { code, issues, requestId } from NestJS so the action can map issues[].path to form fields without bespoke parsing per endpoint.
  • Revalidation calls need limits. The revalidation endpoint is a cache-busting button: authenticate it with an HMAC or mTLS, cap the number of tags per call, and batch events (every 1 to 2 seconds) so a bulk price import of 20,000 SKUs is 50 calls, not 20,000.

Production scenario

A grocery app used Server Actions for "add to list" and "save address" on server-rendered account pages. Because the forms worked before hydration, the share of users who tapped a button that did nothing (measured as a click followed by a second identical click within 2 seconds) fell from 6 % to under 1 % on low-end phones, where hydration took 2 to 3 seconds. Each action revalidated only its own tag (addresses:<userId>), keeping the follow-up render to one NestJS call.

Failure scenario

An order-history page had a "Cancel" button wired to a Server Action:

'use server';
export async function cancelOrder(orderId: string) {
  await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/internal/orders/${orderId}/cancel`, {
    method: 'POST', headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.WEB_SERVICE_TOKEN}` },
  });
  revalidatePath('/orders');
}

The page only rendered the button for the logged-in user's own cancellable orders, so the developer assumed the action was safe. It used the web tier's service token, and the internal NestJS endpoint trusted that token for any order. A security researcher noticed the Next-Action header in DevTools, replayed the request with other order IDs and cancelled three test orders in another account. The report came through the bug bounty, not an incident, by luck.
