The fix: the action calls getSession() and passes the user's access token; NestJS's public POST /v1/orders/:id/cancel checks ownership with its own guard; the internal endpoint was removed from the web tier's reach. The team added a review rule: no Server Action may use a service token for a user-scoped operation.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Actions are public endpoints: hiding the button is not authorisation (Part 75 covers the browser side).
  • Large uploads through actions hit the 1 MB default body limit; use presigned uploads straight to object storage (Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts) rather than raising the limit to 50 MB on your render servers.
  • Actions run one at a time per client, so using them for reads makes parallel data loading sequential.
  • Different builds on different replicas produce different action IDs in 15; a page rendered by version A posting to a replica running version B fails with "Failed to find Server Action". Deploys need version-aware routing or a draining strategy (73.11).
  • Static GET Route Handlers in 14 cache the response at build: a "current time" or "feature flags" handler returns build-time data forever.
  • Webhooks without signature checks let anyone purge your cache in a loop, turning a cached site into an SSR load test.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior uses Server Actions for page-local mutations where progressive enhancement and automatic revalidation pay off, and keeps all business rules and authorisation in NestJS. They treat every action and every Route Handler as an endpoint that will be called by an attacker with arbitrary arguments: validate with the shared zod schema, authenticate with the user's own credentials, send an idempotency key. Endpoints that other clients need (mobile, partners) belong in NestJS, not in Route Handlers that only the web tier deploys.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting that only your UI can call an action.
  • Using a service token for user operations from the web tier.
  • Fetching data with Server Actions from client components.
  • Comparing HMAC signatures with === instead of timingSafeEqual.
  • Forgetting useFormStatus or a pending state, inviting double submits.

Interview questions

  1. How is a Server Action invoked over the wire, and what does that imply for security? Expected answer: POST to the page with a Next-Action header and serialised arguments; it is a public endpoint, so authenticate, authorise and validate inside it. Follow-up: what CSRF protection does Next.js give? (Origin vs Host check; allowedOrigins.)
  2. When would you use a Route Handler instead of a Server Action? Expected answer: webhooks, non-React callers, proxies, OAuth callbacks, GET endpoints.
  3. How do you trigger ISR revalidation from NestJS safely? Expected answer: signed request to a Route Handler, verify with timingSafeEqual, narrow tags, batching, call after commit.
  4. What changed for Route Handlers in Next.js 15? Expected answer: GET handlers are no longer cached by default.
  5. Why should a Server Action forward the user's token rather than use a service token? Expected answer: so NestJS enforces ownership; otherwise a single missing check in the web tier is an IDOR.

Practical exercise

Implement the stock-alert action and the revalidation endpoint.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With JavaScript disabled, the stock-alert form submits and shows the confirmation.
  • Submitting twice with the same idempotency key creates one alert in PostgreSQL.
  • Calling the action from curl with another user's session cannot affect that user's data (NestJS returns 403 or 404).
  • The revalidation endpoint returns 401 for a bad signature, 400 for more than 100 tags, and after a valid call the next product page request shows the new price.

73.7 Next.js caching layers and how to invalidate each

Concept

A Next.js 14 App Router app has four caches of its own, stacked between the user and your NestJS API. Each stores something different, lives in a different place and is cleared by a different action:

  1. Request memoisation: during one server render, identical GET fetch calls (same URL and options) run once and share the result. React's cache() does the same for any function you wrap.
  2. Data Cache: fetch results stored on the server across requests, users and (on most hosts) deployments, governed by revalidate and tags (73.5).
  3. Full Route Cache: the rendered HTML and RSC payload of static routes, produced at build or on revalidation (73.2).
  4. Router Cache: an in-memory cache of RSC payloads in the browser tab, filled by visits and prefetches (73.3).

Outside Next.js sit two more you already know: the CDN cache (Part 46 — Cloud Architecture, 46.8) and the browser HTTP cache (Part 11.11). Behind NestJS sits Redis (Part 27 — Caching and Redis). "The page shows old data" can come from any of these six layers, and fixing the wrong one changes nothing.

Why does it exist?

Each layer removes a different cost. Memoisation stops the page, its layout and generateMetadata from calling the same endpoint three times in one render. The Data Cache stops every render from calling NestJS at all. The Full Route Cache stops the server from rendering at all. The Router Cache stops the browser from asking the server at all when the user clicks Back or a prefetched link. The price is the classic one: every cache is a place where data can be stale and needs an invalidation path.

Mental model

Imagine a newspaper. The reporter checks a fact once and uses it in three articles in the same edition (memoisation). The newsroom keeps a filing cabinet of facts checked earlier today (Data Cache). The printing press keeps printed copies of today's edition (Full Route Cache). The reader keeps the copy they already bought on the kitchen table (Router Cache). If a price was wrong, correcting the filing cabinet does not change the copies already printed, and reprinting does not change the copy on the reader's table. You must know which copy the reader is looking at.

How it works

flowchart LR
    tab["Router Cache, browser tab"] -->|"miss or refresh"| cdn["CDN cache"]
    cdn -->|"miss"| frc["Full Route Cache, static routes"]
    frc -->|"miss or dynamic route"| render["Server render"]
    render --> memo["Request memoisation, one render"]
    memo -->|"first call"| dc["Data Cache, fetch results"]
    dc -->|"miss or stale"| api["NestJS API"]
    api --> redis["Redis"]
    api --> pg["PostgreSQL"]

The layers in Next.js 14, side by side:

Layer Where Stores Lifetime Invalidated by Opt out
Request memoisation Server, per render Return values of identical GET fetches and cache() calls One request Nothing needed Not using fetch; passing your own signal
Data Cache Server, persistent Fetch responses Until revalidate expires or a tag/path is revalidated revalidateTag, revalidatePath, time cache: 'no-store'
Full Route Cache Server, persistent HTML + RSC payload of static routes Until revalidated or redeployed Revalidating its data, redeploy Dynamic rendering
Router Cache Browser tab memory RSC payloads per segment Session; 30 s for dynamic pages, 5 min for static or fully prefetched pages (14.x defaults) router.refresh(), revalidatePath/revalidateTag/cookies().set() inside a Server Action, hard reload Cannot be disabled in 14; staleTimes from 14.2

Four mechanics trip people up:

  1. Memoisation is narrower than it looks. It applies only to GET fetches inside the React tree (server components, generateMetadata, generateStaticParams), not to Route Handlers. A fetch that passes its own signal, such as the AbortSignal.timeout(2_000) used throughout this Part, opts out of fetch memoisation by design, because React assumes someone else controls that request's lifetime. That is one more reason the data functions in 73.4 are wrapped in React's cache(), which deduplicates regardless of the fetch options inside.
  2. The Data Cache ignores HTTP headers. Cache-Control: no-store from NestJS does not stop Next.js 14 from caching a fetch with default options. In 14, a fetch that carries an Authorization or Cookie header is still cached unless an uncached request or a dynamic function came before it in the tree. Personal fetches must say cache: 'no-store' explicitly.
  3. Who calls revalidation matters for the browser. revalidateTag in a Server Action invalidates the server caches and the calling user's Router Cache, and returns fresh RSC in the same response. The same call in a Route Handler (a webhook from NestJS) clears the server caches only; users who already have the page in their Router Cache keep seeing it until the 30 s or 5 min timer expires, they navigate with a hard reload, or the app calls router.refresh().
  4. Redeploys clear the Full Route Cache but not necessarily the Data Cache. On Vercel the Data Cache survives deployments. Self-hosted, it lives in .next/cache on the container's disk, so each new container starts empty unless you configure a shared cache handler (73.11).

Version changes. Next.js 14.2 added experimental.staleTimes: { dynamic, static } to tune the Router Cache. Next.js 15 changed the default for dynamic pages to 0 s (page segments are refetched on every navigation; Back and Forward still restore from the cache, and layouts are still reused). Next.js 16 with cacheComponents: true replaces fetch-level options with the "use cache" directive plus cacheLife() and cacheTag() from next/cache, adds updateTag() (Server Actions only, read-your-own-writes: the caller waits for fresh data) and requires a cache profile as the second argument of revalidateTag(tag, 'max'), which then serves stale while revalidating.

Practical example

A customer cancels an order. Which layers hold the old "Paid" status, and what clears each?

  • The order page is dynamic (it reads the session cookie), so there is no Full Route Cache entry and no Data Cache entry, as long as the order fetch uses no-store.
  • The customer's Router Cache holds the order list visited 10 seconds ago. Navigating back to /orders within 30 seconds (Next.js 14) shows "Paid" with a Cancel button.
  • The CDN should hold nothing, because the response is private, no-store.

So the fix belongs in exactly one place: perform the cancel in a Server Action that calls revalidatePath('/orders'), or call router.refresh() after a client-side mutation.

React / Next.js example

The cancel as a Server Action, clearing the caller's Router Cache along with the server caches:

// apps/web/app/(account)/orders/actions.ts  (Next.js 14)
'use server';
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';
import { getSession } from '@/lib/session.server';

export async function cancelOrder(orderId: string, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const session = await getSession();
  if (!session) return { ok: false as const, code: 'UNAUTHENTICATED' };
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/v1/orders/${encodeURIComponent(orderId)}/cancel`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${session.accessToken}`, 'Idempotency-Key': idempotencyKey,
               'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ reason: 'CHANGED_MIND' }),
    cache: 'no-store',
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3_000),
  });
  if (!res.ok) return { ok: false as const, code: ((await res.json().catch(() => ({}))) as { code?: string }).code ?? 'UPSTREAM_ERROR' };
  revalidatePath('/orders');            // server caches for /orders AND this user's Router Cache
  revalidatePath(`/orders/${orderId}`); // the detail page too
  return { ok: true as const };
}

Tuning the Router Cache from 14.2 on, and the same product loader written for Next.js 16's model:

// apps/web/next.config.js  (Next.js 14.2+; still experimental in 15)
module.exports = {
  experimental: { staleTimes: { dynamic: 0, static: 180 } }, // personal pages never reused from the tab cache
};
// apps/web/lib/catalog.server.ts  (Next.js 16, cacheComponents: true)
import 'server-only';
import { cacheLife, cacheTag } from 'next/cache';
import { ProductViewSchema } from '@shop/contracts';

export async function getProduct(slug: string) {
  'use cache';                      // arguments (slug) are part of the cache key automatically
  cacheLife('minutes');             // built-in profile; replaces next.revalidate
  cacheTag(`product:${slug}`);      // replaces next.tags
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.CATALOG_API_URL}/v1/products/${slug}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000) });
  if (res.status === 404) return null;
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`catalog ${res.status}`);
  return ProductViewSchema.parse(await res.json());
}

Inside a "use cache" function you cannot call cookies() or headers(); request data must be read outside and passed in as an argument, which makes it part of the key. That rule is the framework enforcing the lesson of the unstable_cache leak in 73.5.

Backend side (NestJS)

  • Own the tag vocabulary. Put tag builders in @shop/contracts (cacheTags.product(slug), cacheTags.category(slug)) so the web tier that tags fetches and the NestJS publisher that revalidates them cannot drift apart. A typo in a tag fails silently: nothing is ever invalidated.
  • Personal responses say so. Send Cache-Control: private, no-store on user-scoped endpoints. Next.js ignores it, but CDNs, proxies and browsers do not, and it documents intent for whoever writes the fetch.
  • Mutations return the new state. A 200 with the updated resource and its version (72.5) lets a Server Action or client patch the UI without a second read that might hit a stale layer.
  • The publisher purges what Next.js cannot. After calling the revalidation endpoint, the same NestJS job can call CloudFront CreateInvalidation for the handful of hottest paths, or the CDN TTL for HTML can be capped low (73.11).

Production scenario

An electronics retailer kept getting "old price" tickets after adding on-demand revalidation. The on-call engineer wrote a runbook that walks the layers from the outside in:

Check Tool What it told them
Browser Router Cache Hard reload vs client navigation Hard reload showed the new price: tab cache, not server
CDN Age and x-cache response headers Age: 241, Hit from cloudfront: CDN holding a 4-minute-old copy
Full Route Cache x-nextjs-cache from origin, bypassing CDN HIT with fresh content
Data Cache Server log of tag revalidation Tag revalidated 3 s after the change
NestJS and Redis GET the API directly Correct price

Next.js had set s-maxage=600 on the ISR page, so CloudFront held it for up to 10 minutes regardless of revalidation. They capped the CloudFront cache policy's maximum TTL for HTML at 30 seconds, leaving hashed assets at a year. Origin requests for HTML rose from about 40 to about 90 per second, all served from the Full Route Cache in under 5 ms, and old-price tickets stopped.

Failure scenario

A food-delivery app on Next.js 14.1 implemented "Cancel order" as a client component calling NestJS through the BFF proxy, then router.push('/orders'). The cancel succeeded, but the list page came out of the Router Cache, visited 12 seconds earlier, still showing "Preparing" with a Cancel button. Customers pressed Cancel again, got 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE ("already cancelled"), assumed the app was broken and called support. Tickets about "cancel not working" ran at about 150 a day before anyone connected them to the 30-second Router Cache, which 14.1 did not let them configure.

The fix moved the mutation into a Server Action with revalidatePath('/orders'). The team also added a test that cancels, navigates back within 5 seconds and asserts the new status, because the bug never appeared in next dev, where prefetching and the Router Cache behave differently.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Webhook revalidation leaves open tabs stale until their Router Cache expires; pages that must reflect external changes quickly need polling, SSE (72.8) or router.refresh() on focus.
  • Back and Forward always restore from the Router Cache, even in Next.js 15 with dynamic: 0.
  • Self-hosted replicas each have their own Data Cache and Full Route Cache; a revalidation reaches one replica unless the cache handler is shared (73.11).
  • Fetch responses over 2 MB are not stored in the Data Cache, silently making a page call the API on every render.
  • revalidatePath('/p/[slug]', 'page') revalidates every product page at once: a thundering herd against the catalogue API.
  • Cookies and auth headers in a cached fetch in Next.js 14 can store one user's response for everyone if nothing dynamic ran first.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps a diagram of every cache between the user and PostgreSQL, with the owner, TTL and invalidation path of each, exactly as for Redis in Part 27. For every piece of data they ask: which layers may hold it, how stale may it be in each, and what event clears each one? Personal data is kept out of every shared layer by construction (no-store, private), not by care. Mutations that a user must see immediately go through Server Actions or are followed by router.refresh(). And they debug from the outside in, because the closest cache to the user is usually the one serving the stale copy.

Common mistakes

  • Revalidating the Data Cache and forgetting the CDN that sits in front of it.
  • Expecting a webhook's revalidateTag to update pages already open in users' tabs.
  • Relying on NestJS Cache-Control headers to control Next.js's Data Cache.
  • Tag names written as string literals in two codebases.

Interview questions

  1. Name the four Next.js caches and how to clear each. Expected answer: request memoisation (per render, nothing to clear), Data Cache (revalidateTag/revalidatePath, time), Full Route Cache (revalidating its data, redeploy), Router Cache (router.refresh(), revalidation inside a Server Action, hard reload). Follow-up: which survives a redeploy on Vercel? (The Data Cache.)
  2. A user cancels an order and the list still shows it as active. Where do you look? Expected answer: the Router Cache first; then whether the order fetch is accidentally cached; fix with a Server Action that revalidates or router.refresh().
  3. Why does revalidateTag from a Route Handler behave differently from the same call in a Server Action? Expected answer: only the action's response can carry fresh RSC and invalidate the caller's Router Cache.
  4. How does Next.js 16 change caching? Expected answer: explicit "use cache" with cacheLife and cacheTag, arguments as keys, no request APIs inside, updateTag for read-your-writes, revalidateTag(tag, profile).
  5. How do you make a CDN in front of ISR respect on-demand revalidation? Expected answer: cap the CDN TTL for HTML, purge hot paths from the publisher, or route revalidation-sensitive pages around the CDN.

Practical exercise

Instrument a product page and an order list so you can see each cache.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A runbook table like the one above, filled with real header values from your app for one product page.
  • After a price change and webhook revalidation, a hard reload shows the new price within 5 s; a client navigation shows it within the staleTimes.static window you configured.
  • Cancelling an order and pressing Back within 5 s shows the cancelled status (Playwright test against next start, not next dev).
  • A code search proves every fetch that sends a user token sets cache: 'no-store'.

73.8 The backend-for-frontend (BFF) pattern: Next.js in front of NestJS

Concept

A backend-for-frontend (BFF) is a server-side layer built for one frontend and usually owned by the team that builds it. It aggregates calls to several backend services into one response shaped for a screen, keeps tokens and service credentials on the server, translates backend errors into what the UI needs, and hides internal service topology from the browser. It does not own business rules or data; those stay in the services.

A Next.js app is already a server, so it is a natural BFF. Server components aggregate data for rendering (73.5), Server Actions handle page mutations (73.6), and Route Handlers or rewrites give client components a same-origin path to the API. The question is not whether Next.js can be the BFF, but how much it should do and when a separate API gateway is still needed.

Why does it exist?

General-purpose APIs are shaped around resources; screens are shaped around tasks. An order-details screen needs the order, its items, the shipment, the rider's location and the payment status. Called from a phone, that is five requests over 80 ms round trips, five sets of CORS preflights if the API is on another origin, a token stored in JavaScript to authorise them, and five error shapes to handle. A BFF makes those calls inside the data centre in parallel (1 to 5 ms each), returns one view model, and keeps the token in an HttpOnly cookie that only the BFF reads.

Mental model

Imagine a personal shopper in a department store. You give them one list; they visit the shoe, shirt and tie departments, which are next door to each other, and bring back one bag. But the shopper does not set prices or decide refund policy; if they started doing that, two shoppers would quote two prices for the same shirt.

How it works

Three ways the browser can reach NestJS from a Next.js app:

flowchart LR
    b["Browser"] -->|"1 direct, CORS"| gw["api.shop.example, NestJS"]
    b -->|"same origin"| next["Next.js, shop.example"]
    next -->|"2 rewrites proxy"| gw
    next -->|"3 Route Handler or server component, aggregates"| svc1["Cart service"]
    next --> svc2["Pricing service"]
    next --> svc3["Orders service"]
  1. Direct calls from client components to api.shop.example. Simple and keeps Next.js out of the hot path, but needs CORS with credentials (Part 11.13), cookies scoped to the parent domain, and the API must be public.
  2. rewrites in next.config.js proxy /api/v1/* on the web origin to NestJS. The browser sees one origin, so no CORS and cookies flow naturally. Next.js adds no logic; it forwards. Destinations are resolved at build, so the API URL is baked into the build (73.11).
  3. Route Handlers (and server components) that read the session cookie, call one or more services with the user's token, and return a view model. This is the full BFF, and the token-handler pattern: the browser holds only an HttpOnly session cookie; access tokens never reach JavaScript (Part 75 — Auth and Security in the Browser).
Direct rewrites proxy Route Handler BFF
CORS Needed Not needed Not needed
Token in browser JavaScript Often No (cookie forwarded) No
Aggregation and shaping No No Yes
Extra hop latency None 1 to 3 ms in-region 1 to 3 ms plus your code
Next.js tier in the failure path No Yes Yes
Best for Public, cacheable APIs Existing APIs, quick same-origin Screens needing several services

When to keep (or add) a separate API gateway in front of NestJS:

Situation Recommendation
One web app, one NestJS monolith Next.js server components and a few Route Handlers; no gateway
Web plus mobile apps plus partner API Gateway for auth, rate limits, API keys and WAF; Next.js BFF calls services through it or inside the VPC
Many teams and microservices Gateway for routing and cross-cutting policy; one BFF per frontend
Strict compliance (PCI scope) Keep payment calls off the web tier; browser talks to the payment provider's hosted fields directly

Practical example

The cart drawer (a client component, 73.4) needs items, prices after promotions and a delivery-fee estimate, from the cart and pricing services. Instead of three browser calls, it calls GET /api/bff/cart on the same origin. The Route Handler reads the session cookie, calls both services in parallel with the user's token, tolerates a pricing timeout by falling back to list prices with a promotionsUnavailable flag, and returns a 2 KB CartView. TanStack Query on the client caches it under ['cart'] (Part 72).

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/api/bff/cart/route.ts  (Next.js 14)
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
import { CartViewSchema, ServiceCartSchema, PromotionsSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { getSession } from '@/lib/session.server';
import { toCartView } from '@/lib/cart-view';

export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';                 // personal: never a static GET handler (79.6)
const PRIVATE = { 'Cache-Control': 'private, no-store' };

export async function GET(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const session = await getSession();
  const guestCartId = cookies().get('cart_id')?.value;    // anonymous carts keyed by an opaque id
  const requestId = request.headers.get('x-request-id') ?? crypto.randomUUID();
  const headers: Record<string, string> = { 'x-request-id': requestId };
  if (session) headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${session.accessToken}`;
  else if (guestCartId) headers['x-cart-id'] = guestCartId;
  else return Response.json(CartViewSchema.parse({ items: [], count: 0, subtotalMinor: '0', promotionsUnavailable: false }), { headers: PRIVATE });

  const [cartRes, promos] = await Promise.all([
    fetch(`${process.env.CART_API_URL}/v1/cart`, { headers, cache: 'no-store', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1_500) }),
    fetch(`${process.env.PRICING_API_URL}/v1/promotions/applicable`, { headers, cache: 'no-store', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(800) })
      .then(async (r) => (r.ok ? PromotionsSchema.parse(await r.json()) : null))
      .catch(() => null),                                // optional: degrade, do not fail the cart
  ]);
  if (!cartRes.ok) {
    const status = cartRes.status === 401 ? 401 : 502;   // never leak upstream 500 bodies to the browser
    return Response.json({ code: status === 401 ? 'UNAUTHENTICATED' : 'CART_UNAVAILABLE', issues: [], requestId }, { status, headers: PRIVATE });
  }
  const cart = ServiceCartSchema.parse(await cartRes.json());
  return Response.json(CartViewSchema.parse(toCartView(cart, promos)), { headers: PRIVATE }); // display shaping only
}

toCartView only reshapes and formats; the totals come from the cart service, which applied promotions itself. And the plain proxy for everything else:

// apps/web/next.config.js
module.exports = {
  async rewrites() {
    return [{ source: '/api/v1/:path*', destination: `${process.env.API_URL}/v1/:path*` }]; // read at build time
  },
};

Backend side (NestJS)

With a BFF in front, every request to NestJS comes from a handful of web-tier IP addresses, which breaks assumptions:

  • Rate limit by user, not by IP. ThrottlerGuard keys on the client IP by default; behind a BFF all customers share a few IPs and one busy minute throttles everyone. Override getTracker and register the guard so it runs after authentication:
// apps/api/src/common/user-throttler.guard.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ThrottlerGuard } from '@nestjs/throttler';

@Injectable()
export class UserThrottlerGuard extends ThrottlerGuard {
  protected async getTracker(req: Record<string, any>): Promise<string> {
    // Authenticated: per user. Anonymous: the original client IP from X-Forwarded-For,
    // which Express only trusts after app.set('trust proxy', 1) on a NestExpressApplication.
    return req.user?.id ? `user:${req.user.id}` : `ip:${req.ips?.[0] ?? req.ip}`;
  }
}
  • Trust the forwarded headers deliberately. Configure trust proxy for exactly the hops you control, or any client can forge X-Forwarded-For and pick its own rate-limit bucket.
  • Propagate x-request-id from the BFF and log it, so one cart drawer error traces through the BFF into both services (Part 43 — Observability).
  • Keep resource APIs generic. Do not add GET /v1/web-cart-drawer; the BFF composes screens, the services expose resources that mobile and partners can reuse.
  • Keep internal endpoints internal. Services the BFF calls should listen on an internal load balancer; the public gateway exposes only what browsers and apps may call.

Production scenario

An order-tracking page made six browser calls (order, items, shipment, rider location, payment, help articles), two of which depended on the first. On a 4G connection p75 time to complete data was 2.1 s. A Route Handler BFF aggregated them inside the VPC: the dependent calls now cost 3 ms each instead of 80 to 150 ms. p75 fell to 640 ms, and NestJS saw the same number of calls, just from closer.

Failure scenario

A web team put a "web-only 5 % welcome discount" calculation into the BFF's cart view to ship before a campaign, because the pricing service's team was busy. Three weeks later the mobile app showed one total, the web cart another, and checkout (which priced through the pricing service) a third. Over a weekend 2,300 orders were placed where the web cart had shown a lower total than the one charged. Refunds cost more than the campaign earned. The discount moved into the pricing service, and the team wrote down a rule: the BFF may format, aggregate and hide; it may not calculate anything that a backend also calculates.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The BFF becomes a single point of failure for every API call when all browser traffic goes through it; size and monitor it like an API tier.
  • Header forwarding by copy-paste (headers: request.headers) forwards Host, Cookie and Content-Length to the wrong service; forward an allow-list.
  • Missing timeouts in a BFF hold one Node.js process's sockets and memory per slow upstream call; a 30 s upstream stall can exhaust the web tier.
  • rewrites to an internal URL resolved at build break "build once, deploy many" across staging and production.
  • Streaming responses (SSE, 72.8) through rewrites or a buffering proxy may be held until they end; test them, or let the browser connect to the stream endpoint directly.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior uses Next.js as a thin BFF: aggregation, view shaping, token handling and error translation, with every call timed out and every optional dependency allowed to fail. Business rules, pricing and authorisation stay in NestJS, because the BFF is one client among several. They add a separate gateway when there are several kinds of clients or teams, not because a diagram looks more complete with one. A BFF in a different region from the API is a latency bug.

Common mistakes

  • Putting business logic in the BFF "just for the web".
  • Rate limiting by IP behind a proxy, which throttles all users at once.
  • Copying all request headers to upstream calls.
  • Exposing access tokens to client JavaScript when the BFF could hold them server-side.

Interview questions

  1. What belongs in a BFF and what does not? Expected answer: aggregation, view shaping, token handling, error translation; not business rules, pricing or authorisation decisions. Follow-up: what happens when you break the rule? (Clients disagree on totals.)
  2. Direct calls, rewrites or Route Handlers: how do you choose? Expected answer: direct for public cacheable APIs; rewrites for same-origin forwarding without logic; Route Handlers when aggregation or token handling is needed.
  3. Why does rate limiting break behind a BFF and how do you fix it? Expected answer: all requests share the BFF's IPs; key by user id, trust forwarded headers only from known proxies.
  4. When do you still need an API gateway with Next.js as BFF? Expected answer: multiple client types, partner APIs, cross-cutting policy, many services and teams.
  5. How does a BFF improve security for a browser app? Expected answer: tokens stay server-side behind an HttpOnly cookie; internal services are not exposed; error details are filtered.

Practical exercise

Build GET /api/bff/cart and the UserThrottlerGuard.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The cart drawer makes one request; the Network panel shows no request to any service origin.
  • With the pricing service delayed by 2 s, the BFF answers within 900 ms with promotionsUnavailable: true.
  • With the cart service returning 500, the browser receives 502 CART_UNAVAILABLE with a requestId that appears in both the BFF and NestJS logs, and no upstream stack trace.
  • A load test with 200 virtual users behind one IP is throttled per user, not as a group.

73.9 Edge vs Node runtime, middleware, and where auth checks run

Concept

Next.js server code runs in one of two runtimes:

  • The Node.js runtime (the default): a normal Node.js process with every Node API, native modules, TCP sockets, node:crypto, the PostgreSQL and Redis drivers, and most npm packages.
  • The Edge runtime: a lightweight V8 isolate (the same engine without Node.js around it) that offers Web-standard APIs only: fetch, Request, Response, Web Crypto (crypto.subtle), streams, TextEncoder, URL. No file system, no native modules, no raw TCP. It starts in milliseconds and, on platforms that support it, runs in many locations close to users.

A route chooses with export const runtime = 'edge' (or 'nodejs') in its segment config.

Middleware is a single file, middleware.ts at the project root (or in src/), whose exported middleware(request) function runs before every request it matches: before routing, before the Full Route Cache, before static pages are served. It can redirect, rewrite, set headers and cookies, or return a response directly. In Next.js 14, middleware always runs on the Edge runtime. Next.js 15.5 made the Node.js runtime stable for middleware (export const config = { runtime: 'nodejs' }), and Next.js 16 renamed the file to proxy.ts with an exported proxy function on the Node.js runtime, keeping middleware.ts only as a deprecated Edge option.

Why does it exist?

Some decisions must happen before any page renders, for every request: redirect a logged-out user away from /orders, send / to /en-in based on Accept-Language, assign an A/B test bucket cookie, block a bad bot. Doing these inside each page repeats code and runs after rendering has started. Middleware gives one choke point. The Edge runtime exists because those decisions are small and latency-sensitive: a few milliseconds near the user beats a round trip to one region.

Mental model

Imagine an office building. Middleware is the receptionist in the lobby: quick, checks that you have a badge, points you to the right floor, turns away people without one. The receptionist does not check whether you may open a specific filing cabinet on the fifth floor; that lock is on the cabinet itself (NestJS's guard and the ownership check in SQL). And if someone finds a side door, the lobby check never happens, which is why the cabinets have locks too.

How it works

Where auth decisions sit for a request to /orders/ord_42:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant M as Middleware
    participant P as OrdersPage
    participant D as SessionDAL
    participant API as NestJS
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    B->>M: GET /orders/ord_42, cookie session
    M->>M: verify JWT signature and expiry locally
    M-->>B: 307 to /login if missing or invalid
    M->>P: continue
    P->>D: requireSession
    D->>D: verify JWT again, cached per request
    P->>API: GET /v1/orders/ord_42 with Bearer token
    API->>API: JwtAuthGuard, roles
    API->>PG: SELECT where id and customer_id match
    PG-->>API: row or nothing
    API-->>P: 200 or 404
  1. Middleware: the optimistic check. Is there a session cookie, and is its signature valid and unexpired? That needs no network call if the token is a JWT verified against cached public keys (JWKS). If not, redirect to login. This is a user-experience check, not the security boundary.
  2. The data access layer (DAL): the real check in the web tier. Every server component, Server Action and Route Handler that touches user data calls getSession() or requireSession() itself. Next.js documentation recommends this explicitly, for two reasons: a matcher can miss a path, and layouts do not re-render on client navigation (73.3), so a check placed only in a layout does not run for every page.
  3. NestJS: the authority. The API verifies the token in a guard and enforces ownership in the query (WHERE customer_id = $2). Whatever the web tier does or forgets, the API refuses data the user may not see.

Choosing a runtime:

Need Node.js runtime Edge runtime
PostgreSQL, Redis, gRPC or other TCP clients Yes No
node:crypto, fs, sharp, most vendor SDKs Yes No (Web Crypto only)
Calls to a NestJS API in one region Best: deploy next to the API Pays the distance per call
Redirects, rewrites, headers, cookie checks without backend calls Works Best: tiny and close to users
Cold start Hundreds of ms on serverless A few ms
Code size Large bundles fine Platform limits (low single-digit MB on Vercel)

The trap with Edge is distance. An Edge function running in Sydney that calls a NestJS API in Mumbai pays about 120 ms per call; three sequential calls cost more than rendering the whole page on a Node server next to the API. Edge wins only when the work needs no backend, or the data is replicated to the edge too.

Practical example

The storefront uses middleware for three things only: redirect unauthenticated users away from (account) routes, set an A/B bucket cookie on first visit (so server and client render the same variant, 73.10), and add security headers. Every account page calls requireSession() before fetching. Every NestJS endpoint under /v1/orders uses a JWT guard and ownership filtering. The middleware matcher excludes _next/static, images and the public storefront, so the 95 % of traffic that hits cached product pages never runs middleware at all.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/middleware.ts  (Next.js 14, Edge runtime; in 16 this file is proxy.ts exporting proxy())
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose';         // jose runs on Web Crypto; jsonwebtoken does not

const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${process.env.AUTH_ISSUER}/.well-known/jwks.json`)); // keys cached per isolate

export async function middleware(req: NextRequest) {
  const token = req.cookies.get('session')?.value;
  if (token) {
    try {
      await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, { issuer: process.env.AUTH_ISSUER, audience: 'shop-web', clockTolerance: 5 });
      return NextResponse.next();
    } catch { /* expired, wrong key or forged: fall through to login */ }
  }
  const login = new URL('/login', req.url);
  login.searchParams.set('next', req.nextUrl.pathname);      // the login page allows only relative paths
  return NextResponse.redirect(login);
}

export const config = {
  matcher: ['/orders/:path*', '/cart', '/account/:path*'],   // the storefront never pays for middleware
};
// apps/web/lib/session.server.ts  (the data access layer used by 79.6 and 79.8)
import 'server-only';
import { cache } from 'react';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose';

const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${process.env.AUTH_ISSUER}/.well-known/jwks.json`));

export const getSession = cache(async () => {                 // once per request, however many components ask
  const token = cookies().get('session')?.value;              // Next.js 15+: (await cookies()).get(...)
  if (!token) return null;
  try {
    const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, { issuer: process.env.AUTH_ISSUER, audience: 'shop-web' });
    return { userId: String(payload.sub), roles: (payload.roles as string[] | undefined) ?? [], accessToken: token };
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
});

export async function requireSession() {
  const session = await getSession();
  if (!session) redirect('/login');                           // throws; nothing after this runs
  return session;
}

An account page then starts with const session = await requireSession(); before any fetch, and passes session.accessToken to NestJS. Token refresh, rotation and logout are covered in Part 75.

Backend side (NestJS)

NestJS issues the cookie the web tier reads and remains the authority:

// apps/api/src/auth/auth.controller.ts  (excerpt)
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post, Res } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Response } from 'express';
import { LoginRequestSchema, type LoginRequest } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { AuthService } from './auth.service';

@Controller('v1/auth')
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly auth: AuthService) {}

  @Post('login')
  @HttpCode(204)
  async login(@Body(new ZodValidationPipe(LoginRequestSchema)) body: LoginRequest,
              @Res({ passthrough: true }) res: Response): Promise<void> {
    const { accessToken } = await this.auth.login(body);      // RS256 JWT, 15 min, kid header for key rotation
    res.cookie('session', accessToken, {
      httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge: 15 * 60 * 1000,
    });
  }
}

This is the simplest working shape: one short-lived cookie, set by NestJS. Part 75 hardens it for production. The Next.js BFF becomes the only thing that sets cookies (__Host-session for the access token, __Secure-refresh scoped to /api/auth, and a __Host-csrf token). NestJS returns tokens only to the BFF, and refresh rotation keeps users signed in past 15 minutes (75.2, 75.3, worked end to end in 75.10). The verification rules below stay the same.

  • Publish a JWKS endpoint (/.well-known/jwks.json) with the public keys and a kid per key, so middleware and the DAL verify locally and keys can rotate without a deploy of the web tier.
  • Keep tokens short-lived. Local verification cannot see revocation; a 15-minute access token bounds how long a logged-out or banned session passes the web tier's checks. NestJS can additionally check a revocation list in Redis for sensitive operations.
  • Enforce ownership in the query, not just in a guard: SELECT ... WHERE id = $1 AND customer_id = $2 returns nothing for someone else's order, and the API answers 404.

Production scenario

A travel marketplace's middleware called NestJS GET /v1/auth/session on every request to check login, and its matcher was the default (everything). Static assets, images and prefetches all ran it: about 3,000 session checks per second, each a 40 to 90 ms round trip from the edge location to the API region. Replacing the call with local JWT verification against a cached JWKS and narrowing the matcher to account routes cut middleware time from 95 ms p50 to 1.5 ms, took 3,000 RPS off the auth service, and improved TTFB on every page, including static ones that had been waiting on the auth call.

Failure scenario

In March 2025, CVE-2025-29927 showed that a crafted x-middleware-subrequest header made self-hosted Next.js skip middleware entirely (fixed in 20.3.5, 13.5.9, 14.2.25 and 15.2.3). One retailer's back-office reports at /admin/exports were protected only by a role check in middleware; the page fetched data from NestJS with the web tier's service token. Within days of the advisory, a scanner sent the header and downloaded a customer export. Nothing in the API logs looked wrong: the requests carried a valid service token.

The response: upgrade Next.js the same day, strip x-middleware-subrequest at the load balancer, add requireSession() with a role check in the admin layout and in each admin data function, and replace the service token with the staff user's own token so NestJS's RolesGuard made the decision. Middleware went back to being what it should have been: a redirect for convenience.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Matcher gaps: '/orders' does not match /orders/ord_42; locale prefixes and trailing slashes create more gaps. The DAL check catches what the matcher misses.
  • Middleware on static assets when the matcher is too broad: every image request pays for it.
  • node:crypto in Edge middleware fails; use Web Crypto or jose, or the Node.js middleware runtime in 23.5 and later.
  • Redirect loops when /login itself is matched and redirects to /login.
  • Revoked sessions still pass local JWT verification until expiry.
  • Clock skew between the token issuer and the edge location rejects fresh tokens; allow a few seconds (clockTolerance).
  • Edge functions far from the API turn a fast redirect layer into a slow data layer.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior places auth in three layers and knows which one is the boundary: middleware for convenience, the web tier's DAL for correct rendering, NestJS for enforcement. They never let a check exist only in middleware or only in a layout. They choose the Edge runtime for small, backend-free decisions and the Node.js runtime, deployed next to the API, for anything that fetches. And they count middleware as per-request cost on every matched path, so they keep its matcher narrow and its work local.

Common mistakes

  • Authorisation only in middleware, bypassable by a bug or a matcher gap.
  • Auth checks only in a layout, which does not re-run on client navigation.
  • Network calls from middleware on every request.
  • Using jsonwebtoken in Edge middleware and discovering at build or runtime that it needs Node's crypto.
  • Service tokens for user-scoped reads, which make the web tier the only authorisation layer.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between the Edge and Node.js runtimes in Next.js? Expected answer: Edge is a V8 isolate with Web APIs only, fast start, near users; Node has full APIs and drivers. Follow-up: when is Edge slower? (When it calls a backend far away.)
  2. Where should authentication and authorisation checks live in a Next.js plus NestJS app? Expected answer: optimistic check in middleware, verified session in a DAL used by every data access, enforcement and ownership in NestJS.
  3. Why is a layout a bad place for an auth check? Expected answer: layouts are not re-rendered on client navigation between child pages.
  4. What did CVE-2025-29927 teach about middleware? Expected answer: it can be bypassed; never make it the only check; defence in depth.
  5. How can middleware verify a session without calling the auth service? Expected answer: signed JWT verified against a cached JWKS, short expiry, kid for rotation.

Practical exercise

Implement layered auth for the (account) route group.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Logged-out requests to /orders and /orders/anything redirect to /login?next=...; next=https://evil.example is ignored by the login page.
  • Deleting middleware.ts entirely still leaves every account page unable to show data without a valid session (DAL check).
  • Calling NestJS directly with user A's token for user B's order returns 404.
  • Middleware p95 under 5 ms under load, with no network calls in its trace.

73.10 Hydration and hydration errors

Concept

Hydration is the step where React, in the browser, takes HTML that the server already rendered and makes it interactive. It renders the client components again in memory, walks the existing DOM in step, attaches event listeners and runs effects, without recreating the DOM nodes. The precondition is strict: the first client render must produce exactly the same output as the server render. When it does not, React reports a hydration mismatch (a hydration error).

Server components are not hydrated; they have no client code. Only the client component islands (73.4) are.

Why does it exist?

Server rendering gives fast, visible HTML, but HTML alone cannot respond to clicks. Throwing it away and rendering from scratch in the browser would waste the server's work and cause a flash. Hydration reuses the server's DOM and only adds behaviour. It is cheaper than rendering, but not free: React still runs every client component once on the main thread.

Mental model

Imagine furniture delivered already assembled, with the instruction manual. The electrician (React) walks through the room with the manual, wiring each lamp where the manual says it is. If the manual says a lamp is on the left and it is on the right, the electrician cannot guess; they tear that part of the room down and rebuild it from the manual. The room still ends up correct, but slower, with a visible flash.

How it works

  1. The server renders the tree to HTML and inlines the RSC payload (73.4).
  2. The browser paints the HTML. The page is visible but not interactive.
  3. Client chunks download; React calls hydrateRoot on the document.
  4. React renders the client components and compares the result with the DOM it finds, node by node.
  5. On a match, it attaches listeners; effects (useEffect) run afterwards, and only then can state differ from the server.
  6. On a mismatch, React 18 logs an error in development ("Text content does not match server-rendered HTML", "Hydration failed because the initial UI does not match what was rendered on the server") and recovers by client-rendering: it discards the server HTML up to the nearest <Suspense> boundary and renders that subtree from scratch. With no boundary above the mismatch, the whole root is client-rendered. In production the message is short, and the recovery is reported through onRecoverableError. React 19 prints one error with a diff of the mismatched content.
  7. Selective hydration (React 18): with Suspense boundaries, React hydrates in chunks and, if the user clicks inside a boundary that is not hydrated yet, hydrates that one first.

Common causes and fixes:

Cause Example Fix
Time and time zone new Date(iso).toLocaleString() on a UTC server vs an IST browser Format with an explicit timeZone both sides, or render relative times after mount
Locale defaults toLocaleString() with no locale; Node's ICU differs from the browser's Always pass a locale (73.1 uses en-IN)
Randomness Math.random(), crypto.randomUUID() for element ids useId() for ids; decide random values on the server and pass them as props
Browser-only branches typeof window !== 'undefined' ? a : b in render Same render both sides; switch in useEffect or useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot
Browser storage Reading localStorage during render useSyncExternalStore, or read in an effect
Invalid HTML nesting <div> inside <p>, <a> inside <a> The browser's parser repairs the DOM, so it no longer matches; fix the markup
Outside modification Browser extensions adding attributes to <body>, CDN HTML rewriting suppressHydrationWarning on <html>/<body> only; disable HTML rewriting at the CDN
Separately decided flags A/B variant chosen on server and client independently Decide once (middleware cookie, 73.9) and read the same value both sides

Practical example

The order history page shows "Delivered at 11:40 PM" for each order. The server runs in UTC; customers are in India (UTC+05:30). The fix is to make the server and browser format the same instant in the same zone, by using the customer's time zone from their profile (sent by NestJS) on both sides. "Delivered 3 minutes ago" cannot be correct on both sides at all, because time passes between the server render and hydration, so it renders the absolute time first and switches to relative after mount.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/components/DeliveredAt.tsx
'use client';
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

const fmt = (timeZone: string) =>
  new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-IN', { timeZone, dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short' });

export function DeliveredAt({ iso, timeZone }: { iso: string; timeZone: string }) {
  const absolute = fmt(timeZone).format(new Date(iso));     // identical on server and client: same zone, same locale
  const [relative, setRelative] = useState<string | null>(null);
  useEffect(() => {                                          // runs only after hydration
    const mins = Math.round((Date.now() - Date.parse(iso)) / 60_000);
    if (mins < 60) setRelative(`${mins} min ago`);
  }, [iso]);
  return <time dateTime={iso} title={absolute}>{relative ?? absolute}</time>;
}

A value that exists only in the browser, read without a mismatch:

// apps/web/components/useRecentlyViewed.ts
'use client';
import { useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';

const subscribe = (cb: () => void) => { window.addEventListener('storage', cb); return () => window.removeEventListener('storage', cb); };

export function useRecentlyViewedCount(): number {
  return useSyncExternalStore(
    subscribe,
    () => JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('recently_viewed') ?? '[]').length, // client snapshot
    () => 0,                                                                   // server snapshot, also used while hydrating
  );
}

For a component that cannot render on the server at all (a map widget touching window on import), load it with next/dynamic and { ssr: false } from inside a client component, and give the placeholder a fixed size so it does not shift the layout (69.5).

Backend side (NestJS)

  • Send instants, not formatted strings. ISO 8601 in UTC with the Z suffix (2026-11-04T18:10:00Z). The frontend formats; the backend never sends "11:40 PM" built in its own zone.
  • Store and expose the user's time zone as an IANA name (Asia/Kolkata) on the profile, so server and browser can format identically.
  • Deterministic ordering. ORDER BY delivered_at DESC, id DESC. Without a tie-breaker, PostgreSQL may return rows with equal timestamps in a different order on the server's request and a client refetch, which reorders rows under the user and, with HydrationBoundary data plus an immediate refetch, causes flicker.
  • No per-request randomness in responses that the server and client might fetch separately ("shuffled recommendations"); seed it with a stable value such as the A/B bucket or the date.

Production scenario

A grocery app's product listing hydrated 1,900 DOM nodes of client components on every category page because the whole grid was one 'use client' module. On a Moto G-class phone, hydration took 1.1 s of main-thread time, and taps on "Add" in the first second were queued, giving a p75 INP of 420 ms. Converting the grid to server components with a small client AddButton per tile cut hydration to 280 ms and INP to 170 ms (Part 76 — Web Performance). Adding a Suspense boundary around the below-the-fold "Recently viewed" rail let React hydrate the visible grid first.

Failure scenario

An order-tracking page rendered the delivery time with new Date(order.deliveredAt).toLocaleString('en-IN'). In development, server and browser shared the laptop's IST time zone, so nothing was wrong. In production, the server ran in UTC. Every order page hit a text mismatch in the page header, outside any Suspense boundary, so React 18 discarded the server HTML for the whole root and client-rendered it, on every visit. The page flashed, p75 LCP went from 1.2 s to 2.9 s, and the error tracker received 400,000 "Hydration failed" events a day, which the team muted as "noise" for two weeks.

The fix passed timeZone from the profile into an explicit Intl.DateTimeFormat, added a Suspense boundary around the order body so any future mismatch would be contained, and turned hydration errors into an alert with a threshold instead of a muted issue. The CI pipeline now runs Playwright with timezoneId: 'Asia/Kolkata' against a server started with TZ=UTC, which reproduces the bug class.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale HTML with a new bundle: a CDN serving HTML from the old deploy with JavaScript from the new one produces mismatches across the page (73.11).
  • suppressHydrationWarning works one level deep, on one element's text and attributes; using it widely hides real bugs.
  • Mismatches outside Suspense client-render the whole root; boundaries contain the damage.
  • Translation extensions rewrite text nodes and can break hydration and later updates; there is no complete fix, only resilience.
  • Heavy client trees hydrate slowly even when correct; the fix is fewer client components, not faster hydration.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior sees hydration as a contract: the server and browser must compute the same first render from the same inputs. Anything that differs between them (clock, time zone, locale, storage, randomness, flags) is either passed in explicitly from the server or deferred until after mount. They treat hydration errors as real production errors with alerts, because each one costs a full client re-render and the user sees it. And they reduce hydration work structurally, by keeping client components small (73.4).

Common mistakes

  • Formatting dates without an explicit time zone and locale.
  • Branching on typeof window during render.
  • Muting hydration errors in the error tracker.
  • Sprinkling suppressHydrationWarning instead of fixing the cause.
  • Testing only with the server and browser in the same time zone.

Interview questions

  1. What is hydration, and what must be true for it to succeed? Expected answer: React attaching to server HTML by rendering the same tree on the client; the first client render must match the server output. Follow-up: what does React 18 do on a mismatch? (Client-renders up to the nearest Suspense boundary, or the whole root.)
  2. Give four causes of hydration mismatches and their fixes. Expected answer: time zones, locale defaults, randomness, browser-only branches, storage reads, invalid nesting, extensions; explicit inputs, useId, effects, useSyncExternalStore, valid HTML.
  3. How do server components change hydration cost? Expected answer: they are not hydrated, so only client islands cost main-thread time.
  4. What can the backend do to prevent hydration bugs? Expected answer: send UTC instants and the user's IANA time zone, stable sort orders, deterministic responses.

Practical exercise

Break and fix hydration on an order history page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Run the server with TZ=UTC and a Playwright browser with timezoneId: 'Asia/Kolkata'; capture the hydration error in the console.
  • After the fix, the same test passes with no hydration errors in the console, and the rendered time matches the profile's time zone.
  • A <div> nested in a <p> is caught by a test that fails on any console error during hydration.
  • Hydration main-thread time for the page, measured in the Performance panel with 4x CPU slowdown, is recorded before and after converting at least one large client component to a server component.

73.11 Deploying Next.js: static export, Node server, serverless and containers

Concept

next build can produce three kinds of output, and each one supports a different subset of what this Part has used:

  • Static export (output: 'export' in next.config.js): plain HTML, CSS and JS in out/, hosted on S3 plus CloudFront or any static host. No server at all.
  • Node.js server: next start, or output: 'standalone', which copies only the files and node_modules the server needs into .next/standalone with a server.js. You run it in a container on ECS, Kubernetes or a VM.
  • Serverless: each route runs as a function on demand, on Vercel or through adapters such as OpenNext on AWS Lambda.
Feature Static export Node server (container) Serverless
SSG pages Yes Yes Yes
ISR, revalidateTag No Yes (shared cache handler for several replicas) Yes (platform cache)
Server Actions, dynamic Route Handlers, cookies No Yes Yes
Middleware No Yes Yes
Default next/image optimisation No (needs a loader or unoptimized) Yes, uses your pods' CPU Yes
Cost shape Storage plus CDN Pods running 24/7 Per invocation; cold starts

Why does it exist?

Because sites differ. A documentation site or a marketing site needs no server, and static export makes it nearly free and impossible to overload. A storefront with ISR, auth and Server Actions needs a server process. Teams that already run NestJS on Kubernetes usually want the web tier in the same place, with the same observability, rather than a second platform.

Mental model

Imagine publishing a cookbook. Static export is printing copies and shipping them to shops. A Node server is running a restaurant: always staffed, cooks anything to order. Serverless is a catering service that hires cooks per event: no idle staff, but the first cook takes a while to arrive.

How it works

flowchart LR
    user["Browser"] --> cf["CloudFront"]
    cf -->|"/_next/static, hashed, 1 year"| s3["S3 static assets"]
    cf -->|"HTML, RSC, actions"| alb["ALB"]
    alb --> web1["Next.js pod 1"]
    alb --> web2["Next.js pod 2"]
    web1 --> cache["Redis, shared cache handler"]
    web2 --> cache
    web1 --> api["NestJS, internal ALB"]
    web2 --> api

What a self-hosted, multi-replica deployment must solve:

  1. One cache for all replicas. The default ISR and Data Cache live in memory and on each pod's disk. Configure cacheHandler (stable from Next.js 14.1) to a shared store such as Redis and set cacheMaxMemorySize: 0, or each pod regenerates on its own schedule and revalidateTag reaches only one pod.
  2. Same build everywhere. Build one image per commit and promote it through environments. Set generateBuildId to the commit SHA, and set NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY to the same value for every pod so closures encrypted by one pod decrypt on another.
  3. Version skew during deploys. During a rolling deploy, a page from version A can request a chunk or post a Server Action to a pod running version B. Keep previous builds' /_next/static files available (upload them to S3 and never delete on deploy), and prefer blue/green or short rolling windows. Next.js reloads the page when it detects a new deployment on navigation.
  4. Runtime configuration. NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables and rewrites destinations are fixed at build (70.6). Server-only process.env reads in server components happen at runtime. Keep environment-specific values server-side, or render them into the page from the server.
  5. Lifecycle. Readiness probe on a dynamic /api/health Route Handler; on SIGTERM, the pod should stop receiving traffic before it exits (a preStop sleep of 5 to 10 s lets the load balancer deregister it), so in-flight streams and actions finish.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/next.config.js  (Next.js 14.1+)
module.exports = {
  output: 'standalone',
  cacheHandler: require.resolve('./cache-handler.js'),  // implements get/set/revalidateTag against Redis
  cacheMaxMemorySize: 0,                                // no per-pod in-memory copy that could diverge
  generateBuildId: async () => process.env.GIT_SHA ?? 'local',
};
# apps/web/Dockerfile  (multi-stage; in a pnpm monorepo also set outputFileTracingRoot)
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
RUN corepack enable
COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
COPY . .
ARG GIT_SHA
ENV GIT_SHA=$GIT_SHA NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1
RUN pnpm next build

FROM node:20-alpine AS run
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=3000 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
COPY --from=build /app/public ./public
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/.next/static ./.next/static
USER app
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

The standalone image for a typical storefront is 150 to 250 MB instead of over 1 GB with full node_modules, and starts in about a second.

Backend side (NestJS)

  • The build calls the API. generateStaticParams and static pages fetch from NestJS during next build in CI, so CI needs network access to a catalogue API with production-like data, or prerendering must be limited and the rest rendered on demand.
  • Web and API deploy independently. During a deploy, old web pods call the new API and new web pods call the old API. Keep API changes additive and backward compatible (Part 25 — Backward Compatibility: APIs, Schemas, Events and Clients).
  • Keep-alive and pools. Each Next.js pod is an HTTP client of NestJS; enable keep-alive to avoid a new TCP and TLS handshake per server-side fetch, and size NestJS for the web tier's concurrency at peak.

Production scenario

A retailer moved its storefront from Vercel to ECS Fargate next to its NestJS services to cut cost and API latency. Six 1 vCPU / 2 GB tasks served 1,800 requests per second at peak behind CloudFront (93 % CDN hit rate). Server-side calls to NestJS dropped from 25 ms (cross-provider) to 2 ms (same VPC), p75 TTFB on dynamic pages fell from 310 ms to 140 ms, and the monthly bill for the web tier dropped by about 60 %. The price: they now ran the cache handler, autoscaling, image optimisation CPU and version-skew handling themselves.

Failure scenario

The same team's first launch used the default file-system cache. With six replicas, each pod held its own ISR copy of every page. When a price changed, the revalidation webhook hit one pod. For the next 10 minutes, a customer refreshing the product page saw the new price on one request in six and the old price on the rest, depending on which pod the load balancer chose. Support received screenshots of both prices "seconds apart". A shared Redis cache handler made the six pods agree, and a synthetic check now fetches one product page from every pod after each revalidation and compares the price.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Static export silently drops features: the build fails on cookies(), Server Actions or ISR, and teams discover this late.
  • Image optimisation on pods can eat CPU during traffic spikes; offload it to a CDN image service with a custom loader if needed.
  • Deleting old static assets on deploy produces ChunkLoadError for users with open tabs (Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends).
  • Serverless cold starts of 300 ms to 1 s on rarely used routes; Edge or warm pools help.
  • Memory: each pod's in-memory caches and in-flight streams grow with traffic; set container limits with headroom and watch for OOMKilled restarts.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior picks the deployment by the features the app actually uses: static export when no page needs a server, a managed platform when the team wants zero infrastructure, containers when the rest of the system already runs there and the team can own a shared cache and version-skew handling. They treat the Next.js tier as a stateless service with shared state outside it, like any NestJS service in Part 44 — Docker for Backend Engineers and Part 45 — Kubernetes for Backend Engineers.

Common mistakes

  • Running several replicas with the default per-pod cache.
  • Building separate images per environment because of NEXT_PUBLIC_ values.
  • Deleting the previous build's assets on every deploy.
  • No preStop delay, cutting off streams and actions during rollouts.

Interview questions

  1. What breaks when you self-host Next.js with three replicas and default settings? Expected answer: per-pod ISR and Data Cache, revalidation reaches one pod; fix with a shared cacheHandler, cacheMaxMemorySize: 0. Follow-up: and Server Actions? (Same encryption key and build across pods.)
  2. When is static export the right choice? Expected answer: no per-request logic, no ISR, no actions; marketing, docs, a Vite-like SPA.
  3. How do you handle version skew during a Next.js deploy? Expected answer: keep old assets, consistent build ID, blue/green or short rolls, client reload on new deployment.

Practical exercise

Containerise the storefront and run three replicas behind a local load balancer. Acceptance criteria: the image is under 300 MB; a revalidation call changes the price seen on all three replicas within 3 s; a rolling restart during a 100 RPS load test produces zero 5xx.

73.12 Decision table: a rendering strategy per page type

Concept

The rendering strategy is a per-page decision, made from four questions asked in 73.1: Is it the same for everyone? How stale may it be? Does search or sharing matter? What should happen when the API is down? This section turns the Part into one table that a team can apply in design review.

How it works

flowchart TB
    q1{"Same content for every visitor?"} -->|"yes"| q2{"Changes more often than a deploy?"}
    q2 -->|"no"| ssg["SSG"]
    q2 -->|"yes"| isr["ISR with tags plus time safety net"]
    q1 -->|"no"| q3{"Needs SEO or link previews?"}
    q3 -->|"yes"| ssr["Dynamic SSR, stream slow parts"]
    q3 -->|"no"| q4{"Behind login, highly interactive?"}
    q4 -->|"yes"| csr["Client rendering in a server-rendered shell"]
    q4 -->|"no"| dyn["Dynamic server components, no-store"]
    isr --> islands["Personal bits as client components"]
Page Strategy Next.js 14 setup Freshness Personal parts Why
Home, category ISR revalidate = 600, tags per category Seconds via on-demand Client components after paint High traffic, SEO, same for all
Product page ISR, prebuild top N generateStaticParams, dynamicParams = true, dynamic = 'error' Seconds via product:<slug> tag Stock badge, delivery estimate on client SEO, survives API outages
Search results Dynamic SSR with cached fetches Reads searchParams; facets via unstable_cache Live None or client Infinite query space, some SEO
Cart Client-rendered in static shell Client component plus TanStack Query via BFF Live All of it Personal, exact, no SEO
Checkout Dynamic, no-store requireSession(), Server Actions Live, repriced server-side All of it Correctness over speed
Order history Dynamic server components requireSession(), no-store, staleTimes.dynamic: 0 Live All of it Personal, behind login
Order tracking Dynamic shell, live client island Server-rendered order, SSE client component (72.8) Sub-second Live status Status changes constantly
Admin dashboard CSR, separate app or (admin) group Client components or a Vite SPA (70.11) Live All of it Desktop, internal, interactive
Help articles, blog SSG Static, rebuilt or revalidated on publish On publish None Rarely changes

Backend side (NestJS)

Each row implies an API shape: ISR rows need cacheable catalogue endpoints, change events and a slug-listing endpoint; client rows need same-origin access, private, no-store and per-user rate limits; dynamic rows need 1 to 5 ms indexed lookups because they sit in TTFB on every view.

Failure scenario

A team that skipped this review made every page dynamic "to be safe" when migrating from the Pages Router. Their Next.js tier needed 40 pods where 6 would have done, and a catalogue API incident took the whole storefront down, because no page had a cached copy to fall back on.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior writes the strategy, revalidation path and failure behaviour next to each route in the design document, then enforces it with route segment config (dynamic = 'error' on static pages) and reads the build output in review. The default for anything public is cached; request-time rendering has to justify its cost.

Common mistakes

  • One strategy for the whole site.
  • Personal data in ISR pages.
  • Deciding strategy by framework fashion rather than by the four questions.

Interview questions

  1. Pick a rendering strategy for product, cart, order history and admin pages, and justify each. Expected answer: as in the table; follow-up: what changes if product prices are personalised per customer segment? (Move price to a client or streamed dynamic section, or segment-specific static variants keyed by a cookie set in middleware.)
  2. How do you stop a static page from silently becoming dynamic? Expected answer: dynamic = 'error', build output review, a CI check.

Practical exercise

Fill in the table for your own product's ten busiest pages, including the NestJS endpoint each depends on and what users see when it is down. Acceptance criteria: every row has a revalidation path and a failure behaviour, and the next build output matches the table.

73.13 Worked example: an ISR product listing with a client-rendered personal cart

Requirements

Assemble the Part into one feature for the storefront: the category page /c/electric-toothbrushes and the cart in the site header.

  • The listing is the same for everyone, must be indexed and shareable, and must survive a catalogue outage.
  • A price change appears on the listing within 5 s p95; the page is never more than 10 minutes stale even if events are lost.
  • The header shows the visitor's cart count; "Add to cart" updates it at once, never adds twice on a double tap, and never makes the listing dynamic.
  • Numbers: listing TTFB under 100 ms p75 from the CDN; LCP under 1.5 s on a mid-range 4G phone; cart count visible within 400 ms of first paint.

The flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant CDN as CloudFront
    participant N as NextServer
    participant API as NestJS
    participant PUB as Publisher
    B->>CDN: GET /c/electric-toothbrushes
    CDN-->>B: static HTML, 45 ms
    B->>N: GET /api/bff/cart with session cookie
    N->>API: GET /v1/cart with Bearer token
    API-->>N: cart
    N-->>B: CartView, private, no-store
    Note over API,PUB: later, a price changes
    API->>PUB: product.price_changed after commit
    PUB->>N: POST /api/revalidate, signed, tags batched
    N->>N: revalidateTag category and product
    B->>CDN: next visitor
    CDN->>N: miss after short CDN TTL
    N->>API: re-render fetches new prices
    N-->>B: fresh HTML

The contract

From @shop/contracts: CategoryPageSchema (73.2), CartViewSchema (73.8), RevalidateRequestSchema (73.6) and the shared tag builders cacheTags.product(slug) and cacheTags.category(slug) (73.7). The listing page and the revalidation Route Handler are the ones already written in 73.2 and 73.6; the cart BFF is 73.8.

Backend: the revalidation publisher

// apps/api/src/catalog/revalidation.publisher.ts
import { Injectable, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { OnEvent } from '@nestjs/event-emitter';
import { Interval } from '@nestjs/schedule';
import { createHmac } from 'node:crypto';
import { cacheTags } from '@shop/contracts';

type PriceChanged = { slug: string; categorySlugs: string[] };

@Injectable()
export class RevalidationPublisher {
  private readonly log = new Logger(RevalidationPublisher.name);
  private readonly pending = new Set<string>();             // a Set dedupes 300 changes to one category tag

  @OnEvent('product.price_changed')                         // emitted by the outbox relay, after commit (Part 30)
  onPriceChanged(e: PriceChanged) {
    this.pending.add(cacheTags.product(e.slug));
    for (const c of e.categorySlugs) this.pending.add(cacheTags.category(c));
  }

  @Interval(2_000)                                          // batch: a 20,000-SKU import becomes a few calls a tick
  async flush() {
    const tags = [...this.pending].slice(0, 100);           // the Route Handler accepts at most 100
    if (tags.length === 0) return;
    tags.forEach((t) => this.pending.delete(t));
    const body = JSON.stringify({ tags });
    const sig = createHmac('sha256', process.env.REVALIDATE_SECRET!).update(body).digest('hex');
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`${process.env.WEB_INTERNAL_URL}/api/revalidate`, {
        method: 'POST', body, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'x-signature': sig },
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3_000),
      });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`revalidate ${res.status}`);
    } catch (err) {
      tags.forEach((t) => this.pending.add(t));             // retry next tick; revalidate = 600 is the backstop
      this.log.warn(`revalidation failed, ${tags.length} tags requeued: ${String(err)}`);
    }
  }
}

The queue is in memory, so a crash loses at most 2 seconds of tags; the page's revalidate = 600 bounds the damage. The internal URL reaches any web pod because the cache handler is shared (73.11).

Frontend: the personal cart on the client

// apps/web/cart/useCart.ts  (TanStack Query v5)
'use client';
import { useMutation, useQuery, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { CartViewSchema, type CartView } from '@shop/contracts';

export const cartKey = ['cart'] as const;

export function useCart() {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: cartKey,
    queryFn: async ({ signal }) => {
      const res = await fetch('/api/bff/cart', { signal });   // same origin: session cookie sent, no CORS
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`cart ${res.status}`);
      return CartViewSchema.parse(await res.json());
    },
    staleTime: 15_000,
  });
}

type AddVars = { sku: string; quantity: number; idempotencyKey: string };

export function useAddToCart() {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: async ({ sku, quantity, idempotencyKey }: AddVars) => {
      const res = await fetch('/api/v1/cart/items', {          // rewrites proxy to NestJS (79.8)
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Idempotency-Key': idempotencyKey },
        body: JSON.stringify({ sku, quantity }),
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5_000),
      });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`add ${res.status}`);
    },
    retry: 2,                                                  // safe: same key on every retry
    onMutate: async ({ quantity }) => {
      await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: cartKey });
      const before = qc.getQueryData<CartView>(cartKey);
      if (before) qc.setQueryData<CartView>(cartKey, { ...before, count: before.count + quantity });
      return { before };
    },
    onError: (_e, _v, ctx) => { if (ctx?.before) qc.setQueryData(cartKey, ctx.before); },
    onSettled: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: cartKey }),
  });
}

The header's CartCount is a client component that renders useCart().data?.count inside a badge with a fixed width, so the count arriving after paint causes no layout shift. The AddToCartButton from 73.4 creates the idempotency key in its click handler. Nothing in the listing reads cookies, so next build still marks it static, and dynamic = 'error' keeps it that way.

Failure drills

Drill Expected behaviour Mechanism
Catalogue API down for 5 minutes Listing served from cache; revalidation errors logged, old page kept ISR keeps the last good render (73.2)
Catalogue returns empty 200 during failover Render throws on totalCount > 0 with no products; old page kept Loud failure contract (73.2)
Publisher crashes mid-batch Up to 2 s of tags lost; pages correct within 10 minutes revalidate = 600 safety net
Cart service down Listing unaffected; header badge hidden, "Add" shows an error toast Client island, BFF 502 (73.8)
Double tap on "Add" One line item Disabled button, idempotency key
Six web pods, one receives the webhook All pods serve the new price Shared cache handler (73.11)
Someone adds cookies() to the layout Build fails dynamic = 'error'

Numbers

On a staging copy with 40,000 products: CDN hit rate 96 %; listing TTFB 45 ms p75 on a hit and 140 ms on an origin hit from the Full Route Cache; LCP 1.2 s p75 on a throttled mid-range phone; cart badge at 310 ms after first paint; price change to fresh listing 2.8 s p50 and 4.6 s p95 (2 s batch, revalidation, 30 s CDN TTL cap only for visitors who hit the CDN copy); the catalogue API served about 12 calls per second for revalidation renders instead of 1,500 per second of browser traffic.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The page is split by who sees what. Everything shared is rendered once and cached at every layer, with an event-driven invalidation path and a time-based backstop. Everything personal is fetched by the browser through a same-origin BFF, so it never touches a shared cache. The backend's job is to make both halves safe: fail loudly so caches keep good data, publish change events after commit, return per-user data as private, no-store, and deduplicate retries with idempotency keys.

Practical exercise

Build the feature end to end. Acceptance criteria: every drill in the table passes in a scripted run; curl of the listing shows prices in the HTML and no customer data; next build marks the listing static; the numbers above are measured and recorded for your environment.

Senior Checklist — Part 73

  • I understand the concept
