  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can compare CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR and streaming on TTFB, LCP, server cost, freshness, SEO and outage behaviour
  • I can read next build output and explain why a route is static or dynamic, and I enforce intent with dynamic = 'error'
  • I know which data decides the status code and keep it outside the first Suspense boundary
  • I push 'use client' to the leaves and treat props across the boundary as a public response body
  • I state caching intent on every fetch, start independent requests in parallel, and key every cached function by all its inputs
  • I can name the four Next.js caches, plus the CDN, and clear each one, including in Next.js 15 and 16
  • I treat every Server Action and Route Handler as a public endpoint: validate, authenticate with the user's token, send an idempotency key
  • I keep the BFF thin: aggregation, shaping and token handling, never business rules
  • I place auth in middleware for convenience, in a data access layer for correctness, and in NestJS for enforcement
  • I can diagnose and prevent hydration mismatches from time zones, locales, randomness and invalid HTML
  • I can self-host Next.js on several replicas with a shared cache handler, consistent builds and version-skew handling
  • I can choose a rendering strategy per page type and defend it in design review

Part 73 — Key Takeaways

  • Rendering strategy is a per-page choice between latency, server cost, freshness and SEO; there is no modern default.
  • Static and ISR pages are the cheapest and most reliable pages you will ever serve, and they survive API outages.
  • ISR is a cache with a freshness budget: on-demand tags as the mechanism, a time window as the safety net, narrow tags always.
  • An API that returns an empty 200 on failure poisons every cache in front of it; fail loudly so stale-but-good is kept.
  • The HTTP status is sent with the first streamed chunk; decide existence and access before the first Suspense boundary.
  • One cookies() call in a shared layout can move a whole site from the CDN to your servers; read the build output.
  • Everything passed to a client component is in the page source; pass IDs and view models, guard server code with server-only.
  • Next.js 15 stopped caching fetch by default and made request APIs async; Next.js 16 moved caching to "use cache".
  • "Old data on screen" can come from six layers; debug from the browser inward and clear the right one.
  • Server Actions are public POST endpoints; authorise with the user's own token in NestJS, never with a service token.
  • Middleware is a receptionist, not a lock; real authorisation lives in a data access layer and in the API.
  • Hydration needs identical first renders on server and client; pass time zone, locale and random values in explicitly.

Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts

Parts 70–73 kept assuming something they never fully examined: that the browser and the API agree. @shop/contracts (70.9, 70.12) gave both sides one set of zod schemas, the ApiError class (71.7) parsed one error shape, and every fetch in Parts 72, 73 ended with Schema.parse(await res.json()). That works well inside one repository, built and deployed by one team, on the day of the build. It stops working the moment there is a second consumer in another repository, a browser tab that has been open since Monday, a mobile app on last quarter's release, or a field that means something slightly different on each side.

This Part is about the agreement itself: how it is written down (OpenAPI, zod, tRPC routers, GraphQL schemas), how each side checks it (generated clients, validation at both ends, contract tests), how the awkward data types travel (dates, money, large integers, enums), how errors, uploads and downloads are shaped, and how you change any of it while old clients are still running. Part 15 — API Design and Part 25 — Backward Compatibility covered the rules from the server's side; Part 16 — GraphQL and gRPC covered the protocols. Here the frontend is in the loop, and the questions are "what does the UI do with this?" and "what breaks in a browser that is already open?".

The stack is the one the volume has used: NestJS 10 with @shop/contracts (zod 3.23), React 18, Next.js 14 App Router, TanStack Query v5. The error shape { code, issues, requestId } from 71.7 becomes a full RFC 9457 problem document in 74.6, without breaking any code written so far.

74.1 Why contracts break between frontend and backend teams

Concept

A contract between a frontend and a backend is everything one side relies on the other to do: the URL and method, the request body, the response fields and their types, the status codes, the headers (ETag, Retry-After, X-Request-Id), the error shape, the meaning of each value (is total before or after tax?), the ordering of lists, and the timing (does POST /orders return before or after payment is captured?). Only part of that is ever written down. The rest lives in people's heads and in the code that happens to work today.

A contract breaks when one side changes something the other relies on, and the other side does not change at the same moment. Because the frontend and backend are deployed separately, and because browsers keep running old code long after you deploy new code, "at the same moment" is never true. There is always a window where version N of one side talks to version N+1 of the other.

The cost of "just change the field name" is therefore not one pull request. It is the size of that window multiplied by every consumer in it.

Why does it exist?

Contracts break for organisational reasons first and technical reasons second:

  1. Different owners, different calendars. The API team ships twice a day; the web team ships on Tuesdays; the mobile team ships every two weeks and users update over a month. Each team's change is safe for its own release and unsafe for someone else's.
  2. Implicit agreements. The UI sorts by placedAt because the API happened to return newest first. Nobody wrote "newest first" anywhere. A query planner change in PostgreSQL (a new index, Part 20 — Database Indexing) flips the order, and the API team never knew they had promised it.
  3. Types that lie. A hand-written TypeScript interface in the web app says totalMinor: string. The API sends a number for orders created by an old code path. TypeScript checks nothing at runtime, so the error appears three components later as "1999".padStart is not a function, or worse, as a wrong total.
  4. Semantic drift. The field keeps its name and type but changes meaning: deliveryEta was "when the rider will arrive" and becomes "when the kitchen will finish". Every type check passes. The UI is now wrong.
  5. Clients you cannot update. A browser tab, a cached service worker, an installed mobile app, a partner's integration, a BFF pod that has not rolled yet. Part 25.5 and 25.6 cover these from the server's side; this Part looks at them from the client.

Mental model

Imagine two people building a bridge from opposite banks of a river. They agreed on the height in a meeting and each went back to their own bank. If one side raises the deck by 30 cm to clear a new boat, their half is now perfect and the bridge is broken. A contract is the drawing both sides build from. Contract checks are surveyors who measure both halves against the drawing every day. And compatibility rules are the rule that you may widen your half or add a lane, but you may not move where the two halves meet without building a temporary ramp first.

How it works

The life of one innocent rename, displayId to orderNumber on GET /v1/orders, with three consumers:

sequenceDiagram
    participant BE as API team
    participant API as OrdersAPI
    participant W as WebTab
    participant M as MobileApp
    participant P as MerchantPortal
    BE->>API: deploy v41, field renamed
    W->>API: GET /v1/orders from bundle built last week
    API-->>W: orderNumber present, displayId missing
    Note over W: cards show Order undefined
    M->>API: GET /v1/orders from app release 5.2
    API-->>M: same body
    Note over M: strict JSON decoder throws, screen empty
    P->>API: GET /v1/orders via generated client
    API-->>P: same body
    Note over P: CSV export column blank, nobody notices for 9 days

What happened, step by step:

  1. The API team renamed the field in the DTO and the mapper. Their unit and e2e tests passed, because their tests asserted the new name.
  2. The web app in the same monorepo was updated in the same pull request (70.12 shows how the shared package makes that a compile error). But the web deployment lags: CDN caches, open tabs and the Tuesday release mean the old bundle stays live for days.
  3. The mobile app parses JSON into a strict model. A missing required key throws. The screen shows its generic error state.
  4. The merchant portal, in another repository, uses a client generated from last month's openapi.json. Its types still say displayId. It does not crash; it silently renders blank cells.

The total cost: a rollback or a hotfix, a mobile release that cannot be hurried through app review, nine days of bad exports, and a postmortem. The change that would have been safe is the expand and contract sequence from Part 25 — Backward Compatibility (25.2): add orderNumber next to displayId, move every consumer over, measure that nobody reads displayId any more, then remove it.

Where contracts usually break, in the order you meet them:

Break Example Caught by types in a monorepo? Caught by a spec diff? Caught by a consumer contract test?
Field renamed or removed displayId to orderNumber Yes, for code built from the same commit Yes Yes, if the consumer reads it
Type changed totalMinor number to string Yes Yes Yes
Required became optional placedAt missing for drafts Partly (only if the schema says so) Yes Yes
New enum value status: 'PARTIALLY_REFUNDED' No Warning (25.7) Only if a pact uses it
New required request field POST /orders now needs channel Yes Yes Yes
Error shape or code changed 409 became 422 No Yes, if errors are documented Yes, if the error case is in a pact
Ordering, pagination or meaning newest first becomes oldest first No No Rarely
Header removed ETag dropped by a new proxy No Only if documented Only if asserted

The bottom rows are why this Part is not only about tools. Tools catch shape. Meaning and behaviour are caught by writing them down, naming them in the contract, and testing them on purpose.

Practical example

A food delivery company has apps/api (NestJS), apps/web (Next.js), an iOS and Android app, and a restaurant tablet app maintained by a different team. The tablet app shows incoming orders sorted by acceptBy. A backend engineer adds a priority field and changes the list endpoint to sort by priority first "because the web app needs it". The web app and the API ship together. The tablet app, which relied on the order without anyone writing it down, now shows a 30-minute-old order below a new one, and restaurants miss acceptance deadlines. Nothing in any type check, spec diff or log looked wrong. The fix was a sort query parameter defaulting to the old order, and one line in the OpenAPI description: "Default order: acceptBy ascending. Stable."

React / Next.js example

The single most effective defence on the frontend is to treat every response as unknown until parsed, at one place, with a schema. The 70.12 code already does this; the important part is what happens when parsing fails:

// apps/web/src/api/parse.ts
import type { ZodType } from 'zod';
import { reportContractViolation } from '../telemetry/contract';

export class ContractError extends Error {
  constructor(public endpoint: string, public issues: { path: string; message: string }[], public requestId?: string) {
    super(`Contract violation on ${endpoint}`);
  }
}

// One choke point: every response goes through here.
export function parseResponse<T>(schema: ZodType<T>, endpoint: string, body: unknown, res: Response): T {
  const result = schema.safeParse(body);
  if (result.success) return result.data;
  const issues = result.error.issues.map((i) => ({ path: i.path.join('.'), message: i.message }));
  const requestId = res.headers.get('X-Request-Id') ?? undefined;
  // Report the drift with the build version, so the API team sees "web@a91f3c fails on items.3.status".
  reportContractViolation({ endpoint, issues, requestId, build: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BUILD_ID });
  throw new ContractError(endpoint, issues, requestId); // the nearest error boundary shows a real error state
}

Two decisions are hidden in those lines. First, a contract violation is reported, not just thrown: a counter per endpoint and per build turns "some users see blank cards" into a dashboard line that moves at the minute of the API deploy. Second, the schema decides what counts as a violation. A schema that rejects unknown enum values or extra properties makes every additive backend change a frontend outage; 74.3 and 74.7 cover how to make schemas strict where it protects you and tolerant where it does not.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API's part of the bargain:

  • Write the implicit promises down. Default sort order, page size limits, which fields can be null, what total includes, which errors each endpoint can return. If it is not in the OpenAPI description or the contracts package, the frontend should not rely on it, and the backend cannot know they do.
  • Additive by default. New fields optional, new endpoints instead of changed ones, old fields kept until measured unused (Part 25.2).
  • Know your consumers. Log a client identifier and build version on every request (the web app sends X-Client: web and X-Client-Version: a91f3c; 74.9 shows the interceptor). Without that, "is anyone still using displayId?" has no answer.
  • Fail loudly on the server, tolerate on the client. Validate requests strictly (reject unknown fields on input, 74.3) and evolve responses tolerantly (add, never remove or retype without a version).

Production scenario

A grocery platform with 14 frontend and backend teams counted contract-caused incidents over a year: 23. Thirteen were removed or renamed fields, four were type changes, three were new enum values that crashed strict mobile decoders, two were changed default orders, and one was a status code change (404 to 410) that a frontend treated as "retry". After adding a committed, diffed OpenAPI spec (74.2), runtime response validation with telemetry on the web (above), and Pact for the two highest-traffic consumers (74.10), the next year had five, all semantic or ordering changes. Median time from API deploy to detection fell from 6 hours (customer complaints) to 4 minutes (contract violation alert).

Failure scenario

At 11:40 on a Friday the checkout team deployed an API change that made deliverySlot.end nullable, to support "deliver anytime today" slots. The web checkout's zod schema said z.string().datetime({ offset: true }). For the 6 % of orders with the new slot type, parse threw, the checkout page's error boundary rendered "Something went wrong", and customers could not pay. The web app's contract telemetry fired within two minutes, but the alert routed to the web team's channel, and the web team had not deployed anything. They spent 35 minutes looking for their own bug.

The fixes were organisational as much as technical: contract violation alerts now name the endpoint and are routed to the owning API team; the spec diff in CI marks "required became nullable" as breaking (Part 25.7 lists it); and the change was redone as a new slotType: 'WINDOW' | 'ANYTIME' field with end still present for windowed slots.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The same commit is not the same deployment. Types prove the code in one commit agrees; production runs several commits at once.
  • A BFF is a consumer too. The Next.js tier in 73.8 parses NestJS responses; during a rolling deploy, old BFF pods talk to new API pods.
  • Cached responses outlive deploys. An ISR page rendered from the old shape (73.2) or a TanStack Query cache persisted to storage (72.10) holds data in the old contract after the API changed.
  • Serialisation libraries change shapes quietly. Upgrading class-transformer or switching NestJS from Express to Fastify can change how undefined, Date and BigInt serialise.
  • Proxies are part of the contract. A CDN that strips ETag, or a WAF that rewrites error bodies as HTML, changes what the browser receives without touching your code.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior assumes there is always more than one version of every client running, and designs every change for that. They ask, before any API change: who consumes this, how long do their old versions live, and how will we know when they are gone? They insist that the contract includes behaviour (ordering, nullability, error codes, idempotency) and not just field names. They want three layers of defence, because each catches what the others miss: types for the code you build, a spec diff for the API you publish, and runtime validation with telemetry for what actually arrives.

To a product manager: "Renaming a field is a five-minute change and a three-week migration, because the phone apps and open browser tabs still use the old name. We'll add the new name now and remove the old one when our dashboards show nobody uses it."

Common mistakes

  • Treating the monorepo type check as the whole safety net, forgetting deployed clients.
  • Hand-written frontend interfaces that nobody updates, so the types describe the API as it was.
  • Casting responses with as Order instead of parsing them, so drift becomes a crash far from the cause.
  • Relying on undocumented behaviour, such as default ordering or a field always being present.
  • Routing contract alerts to the consumer's team instead of the producer's.

Interview questions

  1. Why do contracts break even in a monorepo with shared types? Expected answer: types check one commit; production runs several versions at once (open tabs, mobile releases, rolling pods, caches). Follow-up: what closes that gap? (Expand and contract, a spec diff against what is deployed, and consumer contract tests.)
  2. Which kinds of contract break are not caught by types or a spec diff? Expected answer: semantic changes, ordering, pagination behaviour, timing, headers stripped by proxies. Why it matters: they need documentation and targeted tests.
  3. How would you find out whether any client still uses a field? Expected answer: client and version headers logged per request, field-level usage where possible (GraphQL makes it easy, REST needs a deprecation period and telemetry), plus Pact's list of consumers.
  4. What should a web app do when a response fails validation? Expected answer: fail at one choke point with a typed error, show an honest error state, report it with endpoint, build and request id to the owning team.
  5. Explain expand and contract for a field rename. Expected answer: add the new field, write both, migrate consumers, measure old-field usage to zero, then remove.

Practical exercise

Take one real endpoint your web app uses and list every assumption the UI makes about it: fields, types, nullability, ordering, page size, headers, error codes, and timing.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The list has at least 12 items, and each is marked "written in the contract", "tested", or "implicit".
  • Every implicit item is either added to the OpenAPI description or removed from the UI's assumptions.
  • The web app parses that endpoint's responses through one parseResponse choke point that reports violations with the build version.
  • A staging deploy of the API that removes one field produces a contract violation event within one minute.

74.2 OpenAPI from NestJS and generated typed clients

Concept

OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of an HTTP API: paths, methods, parameters, request bodies, responses, error schemas and security schemes, in JSON or YAML. Part 15.14 showed how NestJS produces one code-first with @nestjs/swagger, and Part 25.7 showed how to diff it in CI. This section is about the other end: turning that document into a typed client the frontend actually calls, so that the browser code cannot send a request or read a field the document does not describe.

Three families of generator matter for a React app:

  • Types only: openapi-typescript turns the spec into TypeScript types (paths, components). A tiny typed fetch wrapper, openapi-fetch, uses those types so client.GET('/v1/orders/{id}', ...) checks the path, parameters and response at compile time. No generated runtime code per endpoint.
  • Full SDK and hooks: orval (and similar tools such as @hey-api/openapi-ts) generate one function per operation, and optionally TanStack Query hooks, zod schemas and MSW mock handlers, from the same spec.
  • Classic SDK generators: openapi-generator (typescript-fetch, typescript-axios) produce class-based clients, common for mobile and partner SDKs (Part 15.14).

Why does it exist?

Hand-written API calls are transcription. Someone reads the docs or the controller and types fetch('/v1/order/' + id) with a typo, the wrong method, a missing header or a field name from last month. Every consumer repeats that work, and every repetition drifts. A generated client makes the spec the build dependency: if the API removes displayId, regenerating the client turns every use of it into a compile error in the consumer's repository, before deploy. It also gives non-TypeScript and other-repository consumers what @shop/contracts gives the monorepo.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant that prints its menu from the kitchen's recipe system every morning. Waiters (the frontend) take orders only from the printed menu, so they never promise a dish that was dropped yesterday. Types only is a menu card; you still write the order slip yourself, but you cannot write a dish that is not on the card. A full SDK is a handheld ordering device with a button per dish, a photo, and a fake kitchen for training (the MSW mocks). Either way, if the kitchen changes a recipe, tomorrow's menu changes, and the waiter's device refuses the old dish.

How it works

flowchart LR
    dto["NestJS DTOs or zod contracts"] --> gen["generate-openapi script"]
    gen --> spec["openapi.json, committed"]
    spec --> diff["oasdiff against main"]
    spec --> ot["openapi-typescript"]
    spec --> orv["orval"]
    ot --> types["schema.d.ts in apps/web"]
    types --> of["openapi-fetch client"]
    orv --> hooks["typed functions, Query hooks, zod, MSW mocks"]
    spec --> mobile["openapi-generator for mobile and partners"]
  1. Produce the spec from the code in a script that boots the Nest application without listening (Part 25.7 shows scripts/generate-openapi.ts). Commit openapi.json so changes appear as reviewable diffs.
  2. Make the spec honest. Every response type declared (@ApiOkResponse({ type: OrderSummaryDto })), every error documented (@ApiResponse({ status: 409, type: ProblemDto })), required correct, enums named (enumName: 'OrderStatus' so generators emit one shared type instead of one per property), nullable: true where values can be null. The @nestjs/swagger CLI plugin ("plugins": ["@nestjs/swagger"] in nest-cli.json) reads TypeScript types and class-validator decorators, so required and constraints follow the DTO automatically.
  3. Generate in the consumer, pinned to a spec version. The web app runs openapi-typescript ./openapi.json -o src/api/schema.d.ts against the spec of the API version it targets. In the monorepo, that is the committed file; in another repository, a spec downloaded from a release artefact, never from a running server's /api/docs-json (which changes under you).
  4. Check generation in CI. Regenerate and git diff --exit-code, so nobody hand-edits generated code and nobody forgets to regenerate.
  5. Use the client everywhere. A lint rule (no-restricted-globals for fetch in src/features/**) keeps raw fetch calls out of feature code.

What the spec can express and what it cannot:

Concern In OpenAPI 3.0 / 3.1 Notes
Field names, types, required Yes The core of every generator
Nullable 3.0: nullable: true; 10.1: type: ['string', 'null'] Generators differ; test both null and missing
Enums Yes Open or closed is only a convention; see 74.7
Formats (uuid, date-time, date) Yes Mostly documentation; few generators validate them
Money as decimal string type: string, pattern Write the pattern; generators will not infer it
Error shapes per status Yes Only if declared on every operation
Headers (ETag, Retry-After) Yes Usually forgotten; declare the ones the UI reads
Default ordering, semantics Only in description Text, but reviewable and diffable

Practical example

The merchant portal is a separate React app in another repository, owned by the merchant team. It shows a restaurant's orders and lets staff mark them ready. It cannot import @shop/contracts from the shop monorepo, and should not: it would couple its build to another team's source. Instead, the API's CI publishes openapi.json for each release as a versioned artefact (orders-api-openapi@2.14.0). The portal pins that version, generates schema.d.ts, and upgrades in a deliberate pull request. When the API added estimatedReadyAt, the portal saw it in the regenerated types the next morning; when an API pull request tried to remove notes, the API's own spec diff failed before the portal ever saw it.

React / Next.js example

Types-only generation and the openapi-fetch client:

# apps/web: regenerate types from the committed spec (openapi-typescript 7)
pnpm exec openapi-typescript ../api/openapi.json -o src/api/schema.d.ts
// apps/web/src/api/client.ts  (openapi-fetch 0.12)
import createClient, { type Middleware } from 'openapi-fetch';
import type { paths } from './schema';           // generated: every path, parameter and response type
import { toApiError } from './errors';

const contractHeaders: Middleware = {
  async onRequest({ request }) {
    request.headers.set('X-Client', 'web');
    request.headers.set('X-Client-Version', process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BUILD_ID ?? 'dev'); // 80.9
    return request;
  },
  async onResponse({ response }) {
    if (!response.ok) throw await toApiError(response.clone()); // one error shape, 80.6
    return response;
  },
};

export const api = createClient<paths>({ baseUrl: '/api', credentials: 'same-origin' });
api.use(contractHeaders);
// apps/web/src/orders/useOrder.ts
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { OrderSummarySchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { api } from '../api/client';

export function useOrder(id: string) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: ['orders', id],
    queryFn: async ({ signal }) => {
      // Path and params are checked against the spec: '/v1/order/{id}' or a missing id fails to compile.
      const { data } = await api.GET('/v1/orders/{id}', { params: { path: { id } }, signal });
      return OrderSummarySchema.parse(data); // types say what the spec promises; parse proves what arrived
    },
  });
}

Generated types are compile-time only, which is why the last line still parses. If the web app is outside the monorepo and has no zod schemas, orval can generate them from the same spec:

// orval.config.ts  (orval 7)
import { defineConfig } from 'orval';

export default defineConfig({
  orders: {
    input: './openapi/orders-api-2.14.0.json',   // a pinned release artefact, not a live URL
    output: {
      target: './src/api/generated/orders.ts',
      client: 'react-query',                     // one useQuery or useMutation hook per operation
      mode: 'tags-split',                        // one file per OpenAPI tag
      mock: true,                                // MSW handlers with fake data for tests (Part 77)
      override: { mutator: { path: './src/api/http.ts', name: 'http' } }, // our fetch wrapper: headers, errors
    },
  },
  ordersZod: {
    input: './openapi/orders-api-2.14.0.json',
    output: { target: './src/api/generated/orders.zod.ts', client: 'zod' }, // runtime schemas for responses
  },
});

The tradeoff between the two: openapi-typescript with openapi-fetch adds about 6 KB to the bundle and nothing per endpoint, and you write your own TanStack Query hooks (Part 72's patterns, unchanged). orval writes the hooks for you, but generated hooks bake in query keys, options and error types you may want to control, and a 200-endpoint spec generates a lot of code. Teams with careful query-key design (72.2) often keep their own hooks and generate only types and zod schemas.

Situation Generate Keep by hand
Web app in the API's monorepo, zod contracts already shared Nothing for TypeScript; the spec only for other consumers Hooks, query keys
Separate-repository React app, small team Types (openapi-typescript) plus openapi-fetch Hooks, query keys, response zod schemas for key endpoints
Separate-repository app with dozens of endpoints and little caching subtlety orval functions, hooks, zod and MSW mocks Query-key factory override, error mapping
Mobile apps, partners, other languages openapi-generator SDKs from a released spec Retry and auth policy
Public API with unknown consumers A published SDK per language, semantically versioned Nothing: the SDK is the product

The question in every row is the same: which part of the client is pure transcription of the spec (generate it), and which part encodes decisions the spec does not know about, such as freshness, retries and how errors appear in the UI (write it by hand).

Backend side (NestJS)

The generated client is exactly as good as the spec. The API's responsibilities:

// apps/api/src/orders/dto/order-summary.dto.ts
import { ApiProperty, ApiPropertyOptional } from '@nestjs/swagger';

export enum OrderStatusDto { PENDING = 'PENDING', PAID = 'PAID', SHIPPED = 'SHIPPED', DELIVERED = 'DELIVERED', CANCELLED = 'CANCELLED' }

export class OrderSummaryDto {
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'uuid' }) id!: string;
  @ApiProperty({ example: 'DK-20481' }) displayId!: string;
  @ApiProperty({ enum: OrderStatusDto, enumName: 'OrderStatus', description: 'Open enum: clients must handle unknown values (80.7)' })
  status!: OrderStatusDto;
  @ApiProperty({ pattern: '^\\d+$', example: '129900', description: 'Integer minor units as a string' }) totalMinor!: string;
  @ApiProperty({ minLength: 3, maxLength: 3, example: 'INR' }) currency!: string;
  @ApiProperty({ format: 'date-time', description: 'UTC instant, ISO 8601 with offset' }) placedAt!: string;
  @ApiPropertyOptional({ type: String, format: 'date-time', nullable: true }) deliveredAt!: string | null;
  @ApiProperty({ description: 'Optimistic concurrency token (78.5)' }) version!: number;
}
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts (excerpt)
@ApiTags('orders')
@Controller('v1/orders')
export class OrdersController {
  @Get(':id')
  @ApiOkResponse({ type: OrderSummaryDto, headers: { ETag: { schema: { type: 'string' } } } })
  @ApiNotFoundResponse({ type: ProblemDto, description: 'NOT_FOUND' })              // ProblemDto: 80.6
  @ApiResponse({ status: 429, type: ProblemDto, headers: { 'Retry-After': { schema: { type: 'integer' } } } })
  get(@Param('id', new ParseUUIDPipe()) id: string) { return this.orders.get(id); }
}

Rules that keep the generated client trustworthy:

  • One response DTO per shape, never Object or any, which generate {} or unknown and silently disable type checking in every consumer.
  • nullable and required deliberately. deliveredAt above is required and nullable: always present, sometimes null. That is easier for clients than "sometimes missing".
  • enumName on every enum, so OrderStatus is one named schema in components.schemas, reused by every operation and generator.
  • Errors declared per operation, with the problem schema from 74.6, so generated clients type the error branch too.
  • Stable operationIds. Generators name functions after them (ordersControllerGet by default from @nestjs/swagger). Set operationIdFactory in SwaggerModule.createDocument options, for example (controllerKey, methodKey) => methodKey, or a rename in the controller renames every consumer's function.

If the API validates with zod (the ZodValidationPipe path from 70.12) rather than class-validator DTOs, @nestjs/swagger cannot see the schemas. 74.3 shows how to emit OpenAPI from the zod contracts instead, so there is still one source of truth.

Production scenario

An e-commerce company had four frontends calling the same NestJS API: web, admin, merchant portal and a support console. Before generation, a quarterly audit found 61 distinct hand-written request helpers, 9 of which called endpoints that no longer existed (they returned 404, caught and swallowed). After adopting a committed spec with openapi-typescript and openapi-fetch in all four, plus operationIdFactory for stable names, regeneration on API upgrade took under a minute per app. In the first quarter the compile step flagged 17 uses of deprecated fields and 3 calls to removed endpoints, all fixed before deploy.

Failure scenario

A team generated their client in the web app's postinstall script, fetching the spec from the staging API's /api/docs-json. On Monday the API team deployed a staging branch that renamed a query parameter. The web team's next CI run regenerated the client from staging, type-checked against it, and shipped to production, where the API still had the old parameter name. Order search silently ignored its filter for 40 minutes; customers saw every order instead of the ones they searched for.

Generation is a dependency like any other: pin it to a reviewed spec version, commit the output or the spec, and never generate from a live server during a build.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • additionalProperties: false in generated runtime validators turns every new response field into a parse failure. Configure the generator or post-process schemas to allow unknown keys on responses.
  • Polymorphic responses (oneOf with a discriminator) generate poorly in many tools. Prefer a type field and separate schemas the generator understands, and test the output.
  • Global prefix and versioning missing from generated paths: generate from an app configured exactly like main.ts (setGlobalPrefix, enableVersioning).
  • Huge specs (500+ operations) make orval output slow to type-check; split by tag or generate only the operations a frontend uses.
  • Date formats generated as Date by some generators while JSON carries strings: the type says Date, the value is a string. Keep string types and convert explicitly (74.7).
  • Swagger UI in production exposing every internal endpoint; gate it (Part 15.14).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior sees the spec as the published artefact of the API, not documentation: it is versioned, reviewed in pull requests, diffed in CI, and consumed by pinned generators. They prefer the smallest generator that removes transcription (types plus a typed fetch) and keep control of caching and query keys in hand-written hooks. They insist that types and runtime validation are separate jobs: generated types say what was promised; zod says what arrived. And they keep one source of truth: either DTOs or zod schemas produce the spec, never both by hand.

Common mistakes

  • Generating from a live server instead of a committed or released spec.
  • Undeclared error responses, so every generated client types errors as unknown.
  • any or Object response types that generate empty schemas.
  • Default operationIds that change when a controller method is renamed.
  • Trusting generated types as runtime guarantees.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between openapi-typescript with openapi-fetch and a full SDK generator like orval? Expected answer: types-only plus a tiny typed fetch versus generated functions and hooks per operation; bundle size, control over query keys and caching, regeneration noise. Follow-up: when would you pick each?
  2. Why should a generated client be pinned to a spec version? Expected answer: regenerating from a moving target changes behaviour with no reviewable diff; production may run a different API version than staging.
  3. Do generated types make runtime validation unnecessary? Expected answer: no; they are erased at runtime and describe the promise, not the response. Parse at the network boundary.
  4. What makes an OpenAPI spec bad for code generation? Expected answer: untyped responses, missing errors, unnamed inline enums, unstable operationIds, wrong required and nullable, missing global prefix.
  5. How does a separate-repository frontend consume the API contract safely? Expected answer: versioned spec artefacts, pinned generation, deliberate upgrade PRs, and a consumer contract test (74.10).

Practical exercise

Generate a client for the orders API in the web app with openapi-typescript and openapi-fetch, and migrate three hand-written calls to it.

Acceptance criteria:

  • openapi.json is generated by a script, committed, and regenerating it in CI with no code change produces no diff.
  • src/api/schema.d.ts is regenerated in CI and git diff --exit-code passes.
  • Calling api.GET('/v1/orders/{id}') without params.path.id, or with a path that does not exist in the spec, fails tsc.
  • The 404 and 429 responses of GET /v1/orders/{id} are typed with the problem schema in schema.d.ts.
  • Renaming the controller method does not change the generated operation name.

74.3 Shared zod schemas: validating at both ends

Concept

Part 70.9 created @shop/contracts, a package of zod schemas and the types inferred from them, consumed by both the NestJS API and the React app. This section is about using it well: which schema validates what, at which end, how strictly, and how it fits with class-validator and OpenAPI.

The rule is short. The server validates everything it receives, because it trusts nobody. The client validates everything it receives, because it trusts nothing to stay the same. Both use the same schema definitions, so they cannot disagree about what valid means, but they apply them with different strictness: strict on input, tolerant on output.

Why does it exist?

Without a shared schema, there are three definitions of an order: the class-validator DTO on the server, a hand-written TypeScript interface in the web app, and a form validation schema in the checkout page. They drift. The form allows 200 characters in addressLine1, the DTO allows 120, the database column is varchar(120), and a customer with a long address gets "Something went wrong" (71.7 tells this exact story). A single schema removes the drift between definitions. Validating at both ends then removes the drift between deployed versions: the server rejects bad input with a precise error, and the client detects a response that no longer matches before it renders nonsense.

Mental model

Imagine a customs form printed by one office and used at both borders. The exporting country checks the form before the lorry leaves (client validation: helpful, catches mistakes early, but the driver could have forged it). The importing country checks it again at arrival (server validation: the one that counts). Because both use the same printed form, they never argue about which box means what. But the importing border is strict about what goes in ("no undeclared goods"), while the exporter, reading the import receipt, only cares that the boxes it needs are filled ("ignore any extra stamps").

How it works

flowchart LR
    form["Checkout form, RHF plus zodResolver"] -->|"UX only"| req["CreateOrderRequestSchema"]
    req --> wire1["POST /v1/orders JSON"]
    wire1 --> pipe["ZodValidationPipe, strict"]
    pipe --> svc["OrdersService"]
    svc --> mapper["mapper to OrderSummary"]
    mapper --> wire2["201 JSON"]
    wire2 --> parse["OrderSummarySchema.parse, tolerant"]
    parse --> cache["TanStack Query cache"]
  1. Three kinds of schema, not one. A request schema (CreateOrderRequestSchema) describes what the client sends. A response schema (OrderSummarySchema) describes what the server returns. A form schema describes what the user types, which often differs: a confirm-email field, a quantity typed as a string, a card number that never reaches your API. Derive forms from requests (.extend, .pick, .omit), never the other way round.
  2. Strict input. z.object by default strips unknown keys: they are silently removed from the parsed output. .strict() makes unknown keys an error, and .passthrough() keeps them. On the server, request schemas should be .strict(): a client sending giftMessag (a typo) or a field the server does not know yet should get a 400 naming the key, not a silent drop.
  3. Tolerant output. On the client, response schemas use the default strip mode: a new field from a newer API is removed from the parsed value and the UI carries on. Enums need extra care, because an unknown value fails z.enum even in strip mode (74.7).
  4. Wire types without transforms. Keep @shop/contracts describing the JSON exactly: strings for dates, money and large IDs. If a schema has a .transform (string to Date) or z.coerce, its input type and output type differ (z.input<typeof S> versus z.output<typeof S>), and a server that returns z.infer<typeof S> would claim to send a Date, which JSON cannot carry. Put transforms in each side's own code, after parsing.
  5. Query strings are strings. GET /v1/orders?limit=20 arrives as { limit: '20' }. The server's query schema may use z.coerce.number().int().max(100); that coercion belongs to a server-side query schema, not to the shared response types.

The tradeoff with class-validator, the NestJS default:

class-validator + class-transformer DTOs zod schemas in @shop/contracts
Where it runs Server (decorators and reflect-metadata) Server, browser, Next.js server, edge, workers
NestJS integration Built in: ValidationPipe({ whitelist, forbidNonWhitelisted, transform }) A small custom pipe (70.12) or nestjs-zod
OpenAPI generation @nestjs/swagger CLI plugin reads it directly Needs @asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi, nestjs-zod, or zod 4's z.toJSONSchema()
Types for the frontend Classes cannot be imported into a browser bundle cleanly z.infer types and runtime schemas, about 13 KB gzip for zod 3
Unknown keys whitelist: true strips, forbidNonWhitelisted: true rejects Strip by default, .strict() rejects
Composition Inheritance, PartialType, PickType from @nestjs/swagger .extend, .pick, .partial, .merge, z.discriminatedUnion
Best for API-only teams, OpenAPI-first consumers TypeScript on both ends, monorepo, forms sharing rules

Neither is wrong. What is wrong is having both describe the same payload by hand. Pick one source per payload and generate the other artefacts from it.

Practical example

The checkout form (71.13) posts an address. AddressSchema lives in @shop/contracts with line1: z.string().trim().min(1).max(120) and postcode: z.string().regex(/^\d{6}$/). The form uses zodResolver(AddressFormSchema), where AddressFormSchema = AddressSchema.extend({ saveForLater: z.boolean() }). The server's pipe uses AddressSchema.strict(). The response, { totals: CartTotals }, is parsed on the client with CartTotalsSchema. When a later API version adds totals.deliveryFeeWaivedReason, old browsers strip it and keep working; new browsers show it.

React / Next.js example

// packages/contracts/src/orders.ts  (zod 3.23)
import { z } from 'zod';
import { AddressSchema } from './address';
import { MinorUnitsSchema } from './money';   // z.string().regex(/^\d+$/), 76.12

export const CreateOrderRequestSchema = z.object({
  cartId: z.string().uuid(),
  cartVersion: z.number().int().nonnegative(),  // optimistic concurrency (78.5)
  address: AddressSchema,
  paymentMethodId: z.string().min(1),
  expectedTotalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,         // server refuses if the price moved (77.13)
});
export type CreateOrderRequest = z.infer<typeof CreateOrderRequestSchema>;

// Response: tolerant by default (unknown keys stripped on parse).
export const OrderCreatedSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  displayId: z.string(),
  totalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
  currency: z.string().length(3),
});
export type OrderCreated = z.infer<typeof OrderCreatedSchema>;
// apps/web/src/checkout/AddressStep.tsx (excerpt)
'use client';
import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
import { zodResolver } from '@hookform/resolvers/zod';
import { AddressSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { z } from 'zod';

const AddressFormSchema = AddressSchema.extend({ saveForLater: z.boolean().default(false) }); // form-only field
type AddressForm = z.infer<typeof AddressFormSchema>;

export function AddressStep({ onSave }: { onSave: (a: AddressForm) => Promise<void> }) {
  const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } =
    useForm<AddressForm>({ resolver: zodResolver(AddressFormSchema), mode: 'onTouched' });
  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSave)} noValidate>
      <input {...register('line1')} autoComplete="address-line1" aria-invalid={!!errors.line1} />
      {errors.line1 && <p role="alert">{errors.line1.message}</p>}
      {/* postcode, city, saveForLater ... same pattern */}
    </form>
  );
}

The client schema prevents a round trip for "postcode must be 6 digits". It does not replace the server check: the browser's JavaScript is the user's to change.

Backend side (NestJS)

The strict server pipe, an upgrade of 70.12's ZodValidationPipe that rejects unknown keys and reports them by path:

// apps/api/src/common/zod-validation.pipe.ts
import { BadRequestException, PipeTransform } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ZodObject, type ZodRawShape, type ZodType } from 'zod';

export class ZodValidationPipe<T> implements PipeTransform<unknown, T> {
  private readonly schema: ZodType<T>;
  constructor(schema: ZodType<T>, opts: { strict?: boolean } = { strict: true }) {
    // Objects become strict on input: an unknown key is a 400, not a silent drop.
    this.schema = opts.strict && schema instanceof ZodObject ? ((schema as ZodObject<ZodRawShape>).strict() as unknown as ZodType<T>) : schema;
  }
  transform(value: unknown): T {
    const result = this.schema.safeParse(value);
    if (result.success) return result.data;
    throw new BadRequestException({
      code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED',
      issues: result.error.issues.map((i) => ({
        path: i.path.join('.'),
        code: i.code === 'unrecognized_keys' ? 'UNKNOWN_FIELD' : i.code.toUpperCase(),
        message: i.message,
      })),
    }); // the ProblemDetailsFilter (80.6) wraps this into application/problem+json
  }
}

.strict() applies to the top-level object only; nested objects in the shared schemas that must also reject unknown keys should be declared .strict() in a server-side variant. Teams usually keep a short strictRequest() helper that walks the shape for request schemas.

To publish OpenAPI from the same zod schemas, register them with @asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi in the spec script, so non-TypeScript consumers and generated clients (74.2) get the same contract:

// apps/api/scripts/generate-openapi.ts  (@asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi 7)
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { OpenAPIRegistry, OpenApiGeneratorV3 } from '@asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { CreateOrderRequestSchema, OrderCreatedSchema, OrderSummarySchema, ProblemSchema } from '@shop/contracts';

const registry = new OpenAPIRegistry();
const Order = registry.register('OrderSummary', OrderSummarySchema);    // becomes components.schemas.OrderSummary
const Problem = registry.register('Problem', ProblemSchema);            // 80.6

registry.registerPath({
  method: 'post', path: '/v1/orders', operationId: 'createOrder', tags: ['orders'],
  request: {
    headers: z.object({ 'idempotency-key': z.string().uuid() }),        // required header, Part 15.12
    body: { content: { 'application/json': { schema: CreateOrderRequestSchema } } },
  },
  responses: {
    201: { description: 'Created', content: { 'application/json': { schema: OrderCreatedSchema } } },
    422: { description: 'PRICE_CHANGED, INSUFFICIENT_STOCK', content: { 'application/problem+json': { schema: Problem } } },
  },
});
registry.registerPath({
  method: 'get', path: '/v1/orders/{id}', operationId: 'getOrder', tags: ['orders'],
  request: { params: z.object({ id: z.string().uuid() }) },
  responses: { 200: { description: 'Order', content: { 'application/json': { schema: Order } } } },
});

const doc = new OpenApiGeneratorV3(registry.definitions).generateDocument({
  openapi: '3.0.3', info: { title: 'Shop API', version: process.env.API_VERSION ?? '0.0.0' },
});
writeFileSync('openapi.json', JSON.stringify(doc, null, 2) + '\n');

The cost is that paths are registered by hand next to the controllers, so a route can exist without a registration. A test that boots the app, lists routes from the HTTP adapter, and fails if any v1 route is missing from the registry closes that gap. nestjs-zod's createZodDto(schema) is the other common route: it wraps a zod schema in a class that @nestjs/swagger can read, keeping registration on the controller itself.

Production scenario

A pharmacy platform consolidated three address definitions into one zod schema used by the web form, the Next.js BFF, the NestJS pipe and (through generated OpenAPI) the Android app. Address-related 500s, previously about 40 a day from database length violations, went to zero. Parse cost was measured on a mid-range Android phone: 0.4 ms for a 20-order page, 18 ms for a 2,000-row admin export preview, which moved to a Web Worker. The web bundle grew by 13 KB gzip for zod, which they accepted for the checkout and account routes only, via code splitting (Part 70.5).

Failure scenario

A team added giftMessage to the order form and the request schema in one pull request, then deployed the web app at 10:00 and the API at 12:00 because of a release train. For two hours the old API parsed requests with the default strip mode and dropped giftMessage without a word. 1,140 orders shipped without the customer's message, and the API logs showed nothing because nothing had failed.

Two rules came out of the postmortem. Request fields roll out provider first: the API must accept a field before any client sends it. And request schemas are strict: had the old API returned 400 UNKNOWN_FIELD giftMessage, the web canary would have failed loudly at 10:01 and been rolled back.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • .default() on response schemas hides a missing field from monitoring: the UI shows the default and nobody learns the API stopped sending it.
  • z.coerce in shared schemas accepts "abc" as NaN for numbers before .int() catches it, and accepts "" as 0; coerce only query and form strings, on the side that needs it.
  • Transforms leaking into types: a shared .transform(Number) makes the API's z.infer return type a number while the client parses strings; use z.input and z.output deliberately.
  • Huge responses: parsing 10,000 rows costs tens of milliseconds on a phone. Paginate (72.7), or validate a sample in production and everything in tests.
  • Recursive or deeply nested schemas need z.lazy, and generators may emit them poorly.
  • Different zod versions in web and API (3 and 4) can make shared schemas behave differently; pin one version at the workspace root.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps the shared package to wire shapes and pure rules (length, pattern, enum membership), and keeps business rules that need data (is this postcode serviceable, is this coupon valid) on the server, returned as 422 issues in the same shape. They make input strict and output tolerant, deploy request changes provider first and response removals consumer first, and treat every .default(), .catch() and .transform() in a shared schema as a decision to review. Asked "class-validator or zod?", they answer "whichever produces one source of truth for this team", and they will not accept two hand-maintained definitions of the same payload.

Common mistakes

  • Validating only on the client because "the form already checks it".
  • Default strip mode on server input, silently dropping fields during deploy skew.
  • Strict parsing of responses, so every additive API change breaks old browsers.
  • Putting transforms and coercions in shared wire schemas.
  • Sharing entity classes or TypeORM models instead of wire schemas (70.9).

Interview questions

  1. Why validate the same payload on both client and server? Expected answer: client for UX and drift detection on responses; server for trust. Follow-up: which can you skip? (Neither on input; client response validation can be sampled for very large payloads.)
  2. What does zod do with unknown keys by default, and what should a server do? Expected answer: strips them; a server should reject unknown keys on input with .strict(), while clients tolerate unknown keys on responses.
  3. class-validator or zod for a NestJS API with a React frontend? Expected answer: tradeoffs in the table; key point is one source of truth plus generated OpenAPI.
  4. Why should shared schemas avoid transforms? Expected answer: input and output types diverge; JSON cannot carry Date or bigint; each side converts after parsing.
  5. In what order do you deploy a new required request field? Expected answer: API accepts it as optional first, then clients send it, then the API makes it required once old clients are gone.

Practical exercise

Move the order creation payload to one zod schema used by the checkout form, the NestJS pipe and the web response parser, and publish it in openapi.json.

Acceptance criteria:

  • POST /v1/orders with an extra key returns 400 with an issue { path: 'giftMessag', code: 'UNKNOWN_FIELD' }.
  • A response with an extra field parses on the client without error, and the field is absent from the parsed value.
  • The form schema is derived from the request schema with .extend or .pick; no field rule is written twice.
  • openapi.json contains CreateOrderRequest and OrderSummary generated from the zod schemas, and a test fails if a v1 route is missing from the registry.

74.4 tRPC: end-to-end type safety and what it couples

Concept

tRPC is a library for TypeScript-only stacks where the server defines procedures (typed functions with zod-validated input) grouped into a router, and the client calls them through a proxy whose types are inferred directly from the server's router type. There is no spec and no code generation. Rename a procedure or a field on the server, and the client fails to compile at once, because the client's types are the server's types, imported with import type.

Over the wire it is plain HTTP and JSON: a query is a GET /trpc/orders.byId?input=..., a mutation is a POST /trpc/orders.cancel, and the default link batches several calls made in the same tick into one request. The version used here is tRPC v11, which integrates with TanStack Query v5 through @trpc/tanstack-react-query.

Why does it exist?

Because for one team writing both ends in TypeScript, the REST ceremony (resource URLs, a spec, generation, a fetch wrapper) is overhead that buys little. tRPC removes it: write a function on the server, call it on the client, with autocompletion and type errors across the network boundary. Teams building internal tools, admin panels and early-stage products ship noticeably faster with it.

Mental model

Imagine a house intercom versus a public phone line. The intercom (tRPC) connects rooms in one house: no dialling codes, no directory, you press "kitchen" and talk. It is the fastest way to talk inside the house, and useless for calling the neighbour. A public phone line (REST with OpenAPI) needs numbers and a directory, but anyone can call, from any kind of phone. And if you rewire the intercom, every handset in the house must be replaced at the same time, including the one in the guest room that a visitor (an open browser tab) is still holding.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as ClientComponent
    participant L as httpBatchLink
    participant S as tRPCHandler
    participant P as Procedures
    C->>L: orders.byId id 42, cart.get
    Note over L: same tick, batched
    L->>S: GET /trpc/orders.byId,cart.get?batch=1&input=...
    S->>P: run input parsers, then resolvers
    P-->>S: two results or TRPCErrors
    S-->>L: JSON array, one entry per call
    L-->>C: typed data per hook
  1. The server builds procedures with t.procedure.input(schema).query(fn) or .mutation(fn), and composes them with t.router. Middlewares (t.procedure.use) add auth and context.
  2. It exports only the router's type: export type AppRouter = typeof appRouter.
  3. The client creates a client with createTRPCClient<AppRouter> and a link (httpBatchLink, or httpLink without batching). The generic carries every procedure's input and output types.
  4. At runtime, input is validated by the server's zod schema; errors are TRPCErrors with codes such as UNAUTHORIZED, NOT_FOUND, BAD_REQUEST, mapped to HTTP statuses (401, 404, 400).
  5. Nothing is validated on the client: output types are compile-time inference from the resolver's return type.

Practical example

An internal warehouse dashboard (apps/ops) is built by four engineers who also own the inventory endpoints it uses. It has no other consumers and is deployed with the API in one pipeline. tRPC is a good fit: procedures like stock.adjust and picklists.today are written once and consumed with full types. The customer-facing order API, used by web, mobile and the merchant portal, stays REST with OpenAPI.

React / Next.js example

The client side with the v11 TanStack Query integration:

// apps/ops/src/trpc.ts  (tRPC 11, TanStack Query 5)
import { createTRPCClient, httpBatchLink } from '@trpc/client';
import { createTRPCContext } from '@trpc/tanstack-react-query';
import type { AppRouter } from '@shop/api/trpc';   // type-only: no server code enters the bundle

export const { TRPCProvider, useTRPC } = createTRPCContext<AppRouter>();

export const trpcClient = createTRPCClient<AppRouter>({
  links: [
    httpBatchLink({
      url: '/trpc',
      maxURLLength: 2_000,                          // split batches before the URL gets too long for proxies
      headers: () => ({ 'X-Client': 'ops', 'X-Client-Version': import.meta.env.VITE_BUILD_ID }),
    }),
  ],
});
// apps/ops/src/stock/StockRow.tsx
import { useMutation, useQuery, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useTRPC } from '../trpc';

export function StockRow({ sku }: { sku: string }) {
  const trpc = useTRPC();
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  const stock = useQuery(trpc.stock.bySku.queryOptions({ sku }));      // input and output fully typed
  const adjust = useMutation(trpc.stock.adjust.mutationOptions({
    onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: trpc.stock.bySku.queryKey({ sku }) }),
  }));
  if (!stock.data) return null;
  return (
    <tr>
      <td>{sku}</td>
      <td>{stock.data.onHand}</td>
      <td><button onClick={() => adjust.mutate({ sku, delta: -1, reason: 'DAMAGED' })}>-1</button></td>
    </tr>
  );
}

The app wraps its tree in <QueryClientProvider> and <TRPCProvider trpcClient={trpcClient} queryClient={queryClient}>. Everything from Part 72 (stale time, invalidation, optimistic updates) still applies, because tRPC produces ordinary query keys and query options.

Backend side (NestJS)

tRPC has no official NestJS integration. The robust approach is to mount its Express adapter in main.ts and pass Nest-managed services into the tRPC context:

// apps/api/src/trpc/router.ts
import { initTRPC, TRPCError } from '@trpc/server';
import { z } from 'zod';
import type { StockService } from '../inventory/stock.service';

export type Context = { userId: string | null; roles: string[]; stock: StockService; requestId: string };
const t = initTRPC.context<Context>().create();

const staff = t.procedure.use(({ ctx, next }) => {
  if (!ctx.userId || !ctx.roles.includes('warehouse')) throw new TRPCError({ code: 'FORBIDDEN' });
  return next({ ctx: { ...ctx, userId: ctx.userId } });          // narrowed: userId is a string below
});

export const appRouter = t.router({
  stock: t.router({
    bySku: staff.input(z.object({ sku: z.string().min(1) })).query(({ ctx, input }) => ctx.stock.get(input.sku)),
    adjust: staff
      .input(z.object({ sku: z.string().min(1), delta: z.number().int().min(-1000).max(1000), reason: z.enum(['DAMAGED', 'COUNT', 'RETURN']) }))
      .mutation(({ ctx, input }) => ctx.stock.adjust({ ...input, actorId: ctx.userId, requestId: ctx.requestId })),
  }),
});
export type AppRouter = typeof appRouter;
// apps/api/src/main.ts (excerpt)
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { createExpressMiddleware } from '@trpc/server/adapters/express';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';
import { appRouter } from './trpc/router';
import { StockService } from './inventory/stock.service';
import { SessionVerifier } from './auth/session-verifier';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  const stock = app.get(StockService);          // Nest DI still owns the services
  const sessions = app.get(SessionVerifier);
  app.use('/trpc', createExpressMiddleware({
    router: appRouter,
    createContext: async ({ req }) => {
      const user = await sessions.verify(req.headers.cookie);   // same session check as the Nest guards
      return { userId: user?.id ?? null, roles: user?.roles ?? [], stock, requestId: String(req.headers['x-request-id'] ?? randomUUID()) };
    },
  }));
  await app.listen(3000);
}
void bootstrap();

What the backend loses by doing this, and must replace:

  • Nest guards, interceptors, pipes and exception filters do not run for /trpc. Auth, rate limiting, logging, idempotency and error mapping must be rebuilt as tRPC middlewares or Express middleware.
  • No OpenAPI. Mobile and partners cannot consume procedures without a separate REST surface.
  • Per-endpoint metrics blur. A batched request carries several procedures; HTTP-level dashboards see /trpc/stock.bySku,picklists.today. Record metrics per procedure in a tRPC middleware.
  • Caching is manual. Queries are GETs, so they can be cached, but only if you set Cache-Control per procedure (tRPC's responseMeta option on the adapter).

When end-to-end types are worth the coupling:

Question tRPC fits REST + OpenAPI (or GraphQL) fits
Consumers One or two TypeScript apps you own Web, mobile, partners, other languages
Repository Monorepo, client can import the router type Several repositories
Release cadence API and client released together Independent releases
Long-lived clients Short (internal tool, reload is fine) Open tabs for days, mobile for months
Cross-cutting policy Small, can live in tRPC middleware Nest guards, interceptors, gateway policies
Team boundary Same team owns both ends Different teams negotiate the contract

Production scenario

A logistics start-up built its dispatcher console and API with tRPC: 140 procedures, 6 engineers, one pipeline. Feature lead time from idea to production was about 40 % shorter than on their older REST services, mostly because there was nothing to document or generate. Two years later they launched a driver app in Kotlin and a customer API for enterprise accounts. They kept tRPC for the console and added a REST surface with OpenAPI for the new consumers, sharing the zod schemas and services underneath. The tRPC layer stayed a thin adapter over the same services, which is what made the split cheap.

Failure scenario

The same console team renamed orders.assignRider to dispatch.assign on a Thursday afternoon, updated the client, and deployed both. Dispatchers keep the console open for whole shifts. For the next six hours, every dispatcher with the old tab open got NOT_FOUND from tRPC when assigning a rider, rendered as a generic toast. They thought the system was down and assigned riders by phone.

End-to-end types had done their job: the code in the repository agreed perfectly. Nothing protected the deployed tabs. The fix was the same as for REST: keep the old procedure as an alias for one release, add a build-version check that prompts long-lived tabs to reload (74.9), and show NOT_FOUND on a procedure as "This page is out of date. Reload" rather than a generic error.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Type-checking cost: the client's tsc now type-checks the server's router, and through it the server's service types. Large routers make editor and CI type checks slow; keep resolver return types explicit and narrow (return view models, not TypeORM entities).
  • Leaking server types: returning an entity from a resolver exposes every column to the client and couples the UI to the database schema (73.4 makes the same point for server components).
  • Batch failure modes: one slow procedure in a batch delays every result in it; use splitLink to send slow or streaming procedures separately.
  • URL length limits on batched GETs: proxies commonly reject URLs above 8 KB; set maxURLLength.
  • Serialisation: Date, Map and bigint do not survive JSON. tRPC supports a transformer such as superjson on both ends, which changes the wire format to something only tRPC clients read.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior sees tRPC as an excellent intercom and a poor public phone. They use it where one team owns both ends, clients are short-lived or reload easily, and nobody outside TypeScript needs the API. They keep procedures as thin adapters over services that a REST controller could also call, so adding a public surface later is a few days and not a rewrite. And they remember that end-to-end types end at the deploy boundary: open tabs, BFF pods and caches still run old code, so renames still need aliases and reload prompts.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing tRPC for an API that mobile or partners will need, then building a second API in a hurry.
  • Assuming tRPC removes the need for compatibility rules.
  • Returning ORM entities from resolvers.
  • Forgetting that Nest guards and filters do not apply to the mounted adapter.
  • Using superjson and then needing a non-tRPC consumer.

Interview questions

  1. What does tRPC give you that OpenAPI generation does not, and what does it cost? Expected answer: zero-step type sharing and instant feedback; it costs language lock-in, no spec for other consumers, tight coupling of client build to server types, and manual cross-cutting concerns. Follow-up: how do you add a mobile client later? (REST controllers over the same services and zod schemas.)
  2. Does tRPC protect you from breaking changes? Expected answer: only at compile time for code built together; deployed clients still break, so aliases, additive changes and reload prompts are still needed.
  3. How would you integrate tRPC into a NestJS app? Expected answer: mount the Express or Fastify adapter, inject Nest services into the context, rebuild auth, logging and rate limits as tRPC middleware.
  4. What problems does request batching introduce? Expected answer: blurred metrics and logs, slowest-procedure latency for the whole batch, URL length limits, harder HTTP caching.

Practical exercise

Add a tRPC router for two internal warehouse procedures to the NestJS API and call them from a small React app.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The client imports only type AppRouter; the client bundle contains no server code (check the bundle analyser).
  • Calling stock.adjust without the warehouse role returns HTTP 403 with tRPC code FORBIDDEN.
  • A tRPC middleware records latency per procedure, visible in metrics even for batched calls.
  • Renaming a procedure on the server fails the client's tsc; a deployed old client receives NOT_FOUND and shows a "reload" message.

74.5 GraphQL clients and codegen for the frontend

Concept

Part 16 — GraphQL and gRPC built the GraphQL server: schema, resolvers, DataLoaders, complexity limits and persisted-query safelists. This section is the browser's side. A GraphQL client sends operations (queries, mutations, subscriptions) written in the GraphQL language and caches the results. The two clients you will meet most in React are:

  • Apollo Client (version 3): a normalised cache. Every object with a __typename and an id is stored once, under a key such as Order:42, and every query that contains that object reads it from there.
  • urql (version 4): a document cache by default, which caches whole query results and invalidates results that contain a __typename after a mutation on that type. Its optional Graphcache exchange adds normalised caching.

Codegen makes the contract typed: GraphQL Code Generator reads the server's schema plus the operations written in your components and generates a TypeScript type for each operation's variables and result. The schema is the contract; the operations are each screen's declared use of it.

Why does it exist?

GraphQL lets each screen ask for exactly the fields it needs, which is its strength (no over-fetching, one round trip for nested data) and its contract risk (every screen has a different shape). Without codegen, the result of a query is any, and the frontend is back to hand-written interfaces. Without a normalised cache, a mutation that changes an order's status must find and update every cached query that contains that order. Clients and codegen exist to make "ask for any shape" safe to consume.

Mental model

Imagine a library with a request desk. With REST, you borrow fixed bundles ("the order bundle", "the items bundle"). With GraphQL, you hand in a request slip listing exactly the pages you want. Codegen is a clerk who checks every slip against the library catalogue before you leave home, so you never ask for a page that does not exist. A normalised cache is your home filing cabinet that stores each page once, by catalogue number: when the library sends a corrected page 42, every folder at home that referenced page 42 shows the correction.

How it works

flowchart LR
    nest["NestJS code-first resolvers"] --> sdl["schema.gql, committed"]
    sdl --> inspect["graphql-inspector diff in CI"]
    sdl --> codegen["graphql-codegen client preset"]
    docs["Operations in components"] --> codegen
    codegen --> typed["Typed documents in src/gql"]
    codegen --> manifest["persisted-documents.json"]
    manifest --> safelist["Server safelist, Part 16"]
    typed --> apollo["Apollo Client normalised cache"]
  1. NestJS's code-first GraphQL module writes the schema to a file (autoSchemaFile: 'schema.gql', sortSchema: true for stable diffs). Commit it, like openapi.json.
  2. Components write operations with the generated graphql() function. The client preset of GraphQL Code Generator scans them and generates a typed document per operation, so useQuery(OrderDetailQuery) knows its result type.
  3. Fragments colocate data needs with components: OrderCard declares fragment OrderCard_order on Order { id displayId status }, and the page query spreads it. The preset's fragment masking stops a parent from reading fields only the child asked for, so removing a field from a child's fragment cannot silently break the parent.
  4. The same codegen run can emit a persisted documents manifest: a hash per operation. CI uploads it to the server's safelist (16.2), and the client sends hashes instead of query text.
  5. At runtime, Apollo normalises each response into its cache by __typename and id (or keyFields), merges paginated lists with type policies, and re-renders every component watching a changed object.

The TanStack Query comparison, because Part 72 built on it:

TanStack Query with REST Apollo Client urql (default)
Cache unit One entry per query key (72.2) One entry per object (Order:42) One entry per query document and variables
After a mutation You invalidate or setQueryData Objects in the response update everywhere Results containing the mutated __typename refetch
Pagination useInfiniteQuery and cursors (72.7) typePolicies with merge, relayStylePagination Graphcache resolvers, or manual
Bundle size (gzip, approx.) 13 KB 33 KB 7 KB core
Best for REST or tRPC APIs Data-heavy apps with shared entities Smaller apps, simpler caching

Practical example

The order details page shows the order header, its items, the rider and a "similar products" strip, from one GraphQL query. When the rider app marks the order delivered, the web receives a subscription event (or refetches), the response contains { __typename: 'Order', id: '42', status: 'DELIVERED' }, and Apollo updates the header on the details page, the row in the order list and the badge in the navigation at once, because all three read Order:42.

React / Next.js example

The codegen configuration and a typed query:

// apps/web/codegen.ts  (@graphql-codegen/cli 5, client preset)
import type { CodegenConfig } from '@graphql-codegen/cli';

const config: CodegenConfig = {
  schema: '../api/schema.gql',                 // the committed schema, never a live endpoint in CI
  documents: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
  ignoreNoDocuments: true,
  generates: {
    './src/gql/': {
      preset: 'client',
      presetConfig: { persistedDocuments: true }, // emits persisted-documents.json for the safelist
      config: {
        enumsAsTypes: true,                    // string unions, so unknown values do not need a runtime enum
        scalars: { DateTime: 'string', BigInt: 'string', Money: 'string' }, // wire types, converted in code (80.7)
      },
    },
  },
};
export default config;
// apps/web/src/orders/OrderDetail.tsx  (Apollo Client 3)
'use client';
import { useQuery } from '@apollo/client';
import { graphql } from '../gql';

const OrderDetailQuery = graphql(`
  query OrderDetail($id: ID!) {
    order(id: $id) {
      id
      displayId
      status
      totalMinor
      currency
      items { sku name quantity }
    }
  }
`);

export function OrderDetail({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const { data, loading, error } = useQuery(OrderDetailQuery, { variables: { id }, errorPolicy: 'all' });
  if (loading && !data) return <OrderSkeleton />;
  if (!data?.order) return <OrderError error={error} />;   // error.graphQLErrors[i].extensions.code, 80.6
  return <OrderView order={data.order} />;                 // data.order is fully typed from the schema
}
// apps/web/src/gql/client.ts
import { ApolloClient, HttpLink, InMemoryCache } from '@apollo/client';
import { relayStylePagination } from '@apollo/client/utilities';

export const apollo = new ApolloClient({
  link: new HttpLink({ uri: '/graphql', credentials: 'same-origin' }),
  cache: new InMemoryCache({
    typePolicies: {
      Order: { keyFields: ['id'] },
      Query: { fields: { orders: relayStylePagination(['status']) } }, // pages merged per status filter
    },
    possibleTypes: { PaymentMethod: ['Card', 'Upi', 'Wallet'] },       // needed for fragments on interfaces and unions
  }),
});

The equivalent urql client is new Client({ url: '/graphql', exchanges: [cacheExchange, fetchExchange] }), with useQuery({ query: OrderDetailQuery, variables: { id } }) from urql.

Backend side (NestJS)

What the GraphQL server must do so clients and codegen stay correct:

// apps/api/src/graphql.module.ts (excerpt)
import { ApolloDriver, type ApolloDriverConfig } from '@nestjs/apollo';
import { GraphQLModule } from '@nestjs/graphql';

export const Gql = GraphQLModule.forRoot<ApolloDriverConfig>({
  driver: ApolloDriver,
  autoSchemaFile: 'schema.gql',   // committed; CI fails if regeneration changes it unexpectedly
  sortSchema: true,               // stable order, so the diff shows only real changes
  introspection: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production',
});
  • Diff the schema in CI. graphql-inspector diff between schema.gql on main and on the branch classifies changes as breaking, dangerous or safe. "Dangerous" includes adding an enum value or a union member, which strict clients may not handle.
  • Deprecate, measure, remove. @Field({ deprecationReason: 'Use orderNumber' }) marks a field in the schema; codegen and IDEs show it struck through. GraphQL's advantage over REST is that you can measure field usage per operation (16.4), so "is anyone still reading displayId?" has an exact answer.
  • Errors use the same catalogue as REST. Throw GraphQLError with extensions: { code: 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE', issues, requestId }, so the frontend maps codes the same way for both protocols (74.6).
  • IDs are strings. GraphQL's ID is serialised as a string, which avoids the large-integer problem of 74.7 by construction.

Production scenario

A marketplace web app moved its seller dashboard from 30 REST calls per page load to 4 GraphQL queries with fragments. p75 time to complete data fell from 1.9 s to 750 ms on 4G. Codegen caught 41 field mismatches in the first month, mostly fields the old hand-written types had and the schema did not. The persisted-documents manifest, uploaded in CI, let the server reject every operation not shipped in a real build, which removed a class of abusive queries entirely.

Failure scenario

The payments team added PayLater to the PaymentMethod union and deployed. The web's checkout used a fragment with ... on Card and ... on Upi and a switch on __typename with no default branch. For customers with a pay-later method saved, the component returned undefined, React rendered nothing, and the "Pay" button never appeared. Conversion fell 3 % before anyone connected it to the API deploy. The schema diff had flagged "union member added" as dangerous; nobody read warnings. Warnings on unions and enums consumed by checkout now block merge unless a frontend reviewer approves, and every __typename switch has a default branch that renders a safe fallback.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Missing id in a selection stops Apollo normalising that object; updates elsewhere no longer reach it. Select id everywhere (a lint rule in @graphql-eslint enforces it).
  • Partial data with errors: a 200 response can carry data and errors together. With errorPolicy: 'none' (Apollo's default), the data is discarded; choose the policy per screen.
  • Custom scalars (DateTime, BigInt) arrive as strings; mapping them to Date in codegen types without a runtime conversion makes the types lie.
  • Cache growth: a normalised cache keeps every object ever seen; long-lived dashboards need cache.evict and cache.gc().
  • Introspection-based codegen in CI against a live server reintroduces the moving-target problem from 74.2.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior picks GraphQL for the frontend when screens need many related entities and several clients need different shapes, and they accept the price: a bigger client, a cache with its own rules, and a server that must be bounded (Part 16). They commit the schema, generate types from operations, colocate fragments, and ship a persisted-documents manifest with every build. Because GraphQL tells them exactly which operations read which fields, they evolve it by deprecation and measured removal rather than by versions.

Common mistakes

  • Writing operations as untyped strings with gql and no codegen.
  • Forgetting id in selections, breaking normalisation.
  • No default branch for __typename and enum switches.
  • Treating automatic persisted queries as a safelist (16.2).
  • Choosing Apollo for a small app whose data does not share entities across screens.

Interview questions
