  1. Normalised cache versus per-query cache: what changes after a mutation? Expected answer: normalised caches update every view of the object automatically if the mutation returns it with id; per-query caches need invalidation or manual updates. Follow-up: when is the normalised cache wrong? (Lists that should gain or lose items; you still update them.)
  2. What does codegen generate from, and why not from a live server? Expected answer: the committed schema plus the operations in the code; live servers change under you.
  3. How do you safely add a member to a union that web and mobile consume? Expected answer: treat it as dangerous, ensure every client has a default branch, release clients first or gate the new member behind a capability.
  4. How does GraphQL make field removal safer than REST? Expected answer: per-operation field usage is observable; deprecate, measure to zero, remove.

Practical exercise

Add GraphQL Code Generator with the client preset to the web app and convert the order details page to a typed query with a fragment per child component.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Removing displayId from schema.gql fails codegen or tsc with the operation name and file in the message.
  • persisted-documents.json is produced in CI and the server rejects an operation not in it.
  • Changing an order's status through a mutation updates the details page and the order list without a refetch.
  • A response containing an unknown __typename in a union renders a fallback, not nothing.

74.6 Error contracts: one shape, mapped to fields, banners and toasts

Concept

An error contract is the agreement about what a failed request looks like and what the client may do about it. Since 70.12 this volume has used { code, issues: [{ path, code, message }], requestId }. This section makes it a full problem details document as defined by RFC 9457 (which replaced RFC 7807 in 2023), with media type application/problem+json:

{
  "type": "https://errors.shop.example/order-not-cancellable",
  "title": "Order cannot be cancelled",
  "status": 409,
  "detail": "Order DK-20481 has already shipped.",
  "instance": "/v1/orders/1d6c.../cancel",
  "code": "ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE",
  "issues": [],
  "requestId": "req_01JC8W5Y2Q"
}

type, title, status, detail and instance are the standard members. code, issues and requestId are extension members, which the RFC allows. Part 15.9 built the same idea with errors and correlationId; this volume keeps issues and requestId because every frontend helper since 77.7 already reads them. The names matter less than having one set of names across every endpoint, every service and every protocol.

The other half of the contract is the presentation rule: which errors become a message under a field, which become a banner at the top of a form, which become a toast, which redirect, and which are retried silently.

Why does it exist?

Without one shape, every call site parses errors its own way, and three bad things happen. Users see raw strings (Unexpected token < in JSON at position 0, Request failed with status code 500). Field-level problems ("we do not deliver to this postcode") become generic toasts, and conversion drops (71.7's pharmacy story). And support cannot find the failing request because nothing on screen identifies it. A single shape plus a single client-side classifier makes every new endpoint's errors display correctly with no new UI code.

Mental model

Imagine a hospital triage desk. Every patient arrives with the same intake form (the problem document). The triage nurse (the client classifier) reads two boxes, the category code and the body part, and sends the patient to the right place: a sprained finger to the minor injuries room (a field message), a broken leg to orthopaedics (a form banner), an expired appointment back to reception (redirect to login), and a patient brought in by someone else without any form (an HTML page from a load balancer) straight to the general ward with a reference number.

How it works

flowchart TB
    res["Response or thrown error"] --> net{"Network error, timeout or abort?"}
    net -->|"yes"| offline["Offline or timeout state, retry with same key"]
    net -->|"no"| json{"Content-Type is problem+json or json?"}
    json -->|"no, e.g. HTML 502"| generic["UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE, status only"]
    json -->|"yes"| parse["ProblemSchema.safeParse"]
    parse --> code{"Classify by status and code"}
    code -->|"issues with paths"| field["setError per field, focus first"]
    code -->|"401 UNAUTHENTICATED"| auth["Refresh once, else go to login"]
    code -->|"409 VERSION_CONFLICT"| reload["Dialog: this changed, reload"]
    code -->|"429 RATE_LIMITED"| wait["Wait Retry-After, then retry"]
    code -->|"known business code"| banner["Form banner with mapped copy"]
    code -->|"5xx or unknown"| toast["Toast with requestId"]
  1. Transport first. fetch rejects only on network failure or abort; a 500 is a resolved Response. AbortSignal.timeout rejects with a DOMException named TimeoutError (71.8).
  2. Do not assume JSON. A gateway timeout, a WAF block or a CDN error page arrives as HTML. Check Content-Type before res.json().
  3. Parse the problem tolerantly. code is an open string: a new code from a newer API must still produce a sensible default treatment.
  4. Classify once, centrally, into a small set of UI treatments. Feature code receives the treatment, not the raw response.
  5. Translate on the client by code. Server title and detail are English fallbacks. For a multilingual UI, the client maps code (and issue codes with params) to its own copy; it never parses English text.

The presentation table the web team and API team agree on:

Status code example UI treatment Automatic retry
400 VALIDATION_FAILED with issue paths Message under each field, focus first No
401 UNAUTHENTICATED Silent refresh once (Part 75), then login with return URL Once, after refresh
403 FORBIDDEN Full-page "no access" or hidden action No
404 NOT_FOUND Page-level not found (notFound() in Next.js) No
409 VERSION_CONFLICT Dialog: "This order changed. Reload?" No
409 / 422 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE, PRICE_CHANGED Form or action banner with mapped copy No
422 ADDRESS_NOT_SERVICEABLE with issues[0].path = 'postcode' Message under postcode No
429 RATE_LIMITED Inline "Too many attempts, try in 30 s" Yes, after Retry-After
502 / 503 / 504 UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE Keep stale data, toast or inline retry, show requestId Yes, with backoff (72.3)
500 INTERNAL Toast "Something went wrong. Ref req_01JC..." Queries yes, mutations only with an idempotency key

Practical example

A customer applies a coupon at checkout. The API returns 422 with code: 'COUPON_REJECTED' and issues: [{ path: 'couponCode', code: 'EXPIRED', message: 'This code expired on 31 Oct', params: { expiredAt: '2026-10-31' } }]. The classifier sees an issue with a path, React Hook Form puts the message under the coupon field, and the Hindi UI renders its own translation of EXPIRED using params.expiredAt. The same response from a mobile app is shown natively, from the same codes.

React / Next.js example

The shared schema and the classifier:

// packages/contracts/src/problem.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const IssueSchema = z.object({
  path: z.string(),                                     // matches form field names: 'address.postcode', 'items.2.quantity'
  code: z.string(),                                     // open: 'EXPIRED', 'TOO_LONG', 'NOT_SERVICEABLE'
  message: z.string(),                                  // safe English fallback
  params: z.record(z.union([z.string(), z.number()])).optional(),
});
export const ProblemSchema = z.object({
  type: z.string().default('about:blank'),
  title: z.string(),
  status: z.number().int(),
  detail: z.string().optional(),
  instance: z.string().optional(),
  code: z.string(),                                     // open string; known codes listed in KnownErrorCodes
  issues: z.array(IssueSchema).default([]),
  requestId: z.string().optional(),
});
export type Problem = z.infer<typeof ProblemSchema>;
export const KnownErrorCodes = ['VALIDATION_FAILED', 'UNAUTHENTICATED', 'FORBIDDEN', 'NOT_FOUND', 'VERSION_CONFLICT',
  'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE', 'PRICE_CHANGED', 'RATE_LIMITED', 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE', 'INTERNAL'] as const;
// apps/web/src/api/errors.ts  (extends 77.7's ApiError without changing its constructor)
import { ProblemSchema, type Problem } from '@shop/contracts';

export type ApiIssue = Problem['issues'][number];
export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(public status: number, public code: string, public issues: ApiIssue[] = [], public requestId?: string,
              public title?: string, public retryAfterSec?: number) { super(code); }
}

export async function toApiError(res: Response): Promise<ApiError> {
  const requestId = res.headers.get('X-Request-Id') ?? undefined;
  const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get('Retry-After')) || undefined;  // needs exposedHeaders under CORS
  const type = res.headers.get('Content-Type') ?? '';
  if (!type.includes('json')) {                                           // HTML from a proxy, empty body, etc.
    return new ApiError(res.status, res.status >= 500 ? 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE' : `HTTP_${res.status}`, [], requestId);
  }
  const parsed = ProblemSchema.safeParse(await res.json().catch(() => null));
  if (!parsed.success) return new ApiError(res.status, `HTTP_${res.status}`, [], requestId);
  const p = parsed.data;
  return new ApiError(p.status, p.code, p.issues, p.requestId ?? requestId, p.title, retryAfter);
}

export type Treatment =
  | { kind: 'fields'; issues: ApiIssue[] } | { kind: 'reauth' } | { kind: 'reload' }
  | { kind: 'wait'; seconds: number } | { kind: 'banner'; code: string } | { kind: 'toast'; requestId?: string };

export function classify(e: ApiError): Treatment {
  if (e.issues.some((i) => i.path)) return { kind: 'fields', issues: e.issues };
  if (e.status === 401) return { kind: 'reauth' };
  if (e.code === 'VERSION_CONFLICT') return { kind: 'reload' };
  if (e.status === 429) return { kind: 'wait', seconds: e.retryAfterSec ?? 30 };
  if (e.status < 500 && e.code in errorCopy) return { kind: 'banner', code: e.code };
  return { kind: 'toast', requestId: e.requestId };                      // unknown codes degrade safely
}

export const errorCopy: Record<string, string> = {
  ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE: 'This order has already shipped, so it can no longer be cancelled.',
  PRICE_CHANGED: 'Prices in your cart changed. Please review the new total.',
};

applyServerErrors from 71.7 handles the fields case unchanged. A Server Action (73.6) returns the same problem shape as its state instead of throwing, so forms that post through actions use the same classifier.

Backend side (NestJS)

One global filter produces every error body, including those from pipes, guards and the throttler:

// apps/api/src/common/problem-details.filter.ts
import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpException, HttpStatus, Logger } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ThrottlerException } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import type { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { DomainError } from './domain-error';                      // code + httpStatus, Part 15.9

const BASE = 'https://errors.shop.example/';

@Catch()
export class ProblemDetailsFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  private readonly log = new Logger('Problem');
  catch(err: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const req = host.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const res = host.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const requestId = String(req.headers['x-request-id'] ?? '');
    let status: number = HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR;
    let code = 'INTERNAL', title = 'Something went wrong', issues: unknown[] = [];

    if (err instanceof DomainError) ({ httpStatus: status, code, message: title } = err);
    else if (err instanceof ThrottlerException) { status = 429; code = 'RATE_LIMITED'; title = 'Too many requests'; }
    else if (err instanceof HttpException) {
      status = err.getStatus();
      const body = err.getResponse() as { code?: string; issues?: unknown[]; message?: string } | string;
      code = typeof body === 'object' && body.code ? body.code : HttpStatus[status] ?? `HTTP_${status}`;
      issues = typeof body === 'object' && Array.isArray(body.issues) ? body.issues : [];
      title = typeof body === 'object' && typeof body.message === 'string' ? body.message : err.message;
    }
    if (status >= 500) this.log.error(`unhandled ${requestId}`, err instanceof Error ? err.stack : String(err)); // details only in logs
    res.status(status).type('application/problem+json').json({
      type: BASE + code.toLowerCase().replace(/_/g, '-'), title, status, code, issues, requestId,
      instance: req.originalUrl,
    });
  }
}

Rules on the API side:

  • Paths in issues match form field names, including nesting and array indexes (71.7).
  • Codes are a catalogue, versioned in @shop/contracts and documented per operation in OpenAPI (74.2). Adding a code is additive; changing which status or code an existing case returns is breaking.
  • Never put internals in title or detail. Stack traces, SQL and upstream bodies go to logs under the requestId.
  • CORS exposes the headers the classifier reads: exposedHeaders: ['X-Request-Id', 'Retry-After', 'Idempotent-Replayed'] (71.8).
  • The BFF translates, it does not invent. 73.8's BFF returns 502 CART_UNAVAILABLE in the same shape; it never forwards an upstream HTML page.

Production scenario

A travel booking site measured its checkout errors: 38 % of all error toasts were field-level problems shown as generic messages. After moving to one problem shape with paths, a central classifier, and a copy table keyed by code, field errors appeared under fields, the copy table covered 31 codes, and checkout completion rose 2.1 points. Support tickets that included a request reference went from 9 % to 64 %, and median time to diagnose a reported checkout failure fell from 50 minutes to 8.

Failure scenario

On a sale night the load balancer's idle timeout fired on slow POST /v1/orders requests and returned its own 504 HTML page. The web's old error helper called res.json() unconditionally, which threw SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'. The checkout caught it as a generic error and, because it was not an ApiError, the retry logic treated it as a network failure and retried immediately, without the original idempotency key (a code path written before 71.8). 214 customers were charged twice. The fixes: check Content-Type before parsing, classify non-JSON 5xx as UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE, reuse the same idempotency key on every retry of an intent, and align the load balancer's timeout with the API's own deadline.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Empty bodies: 204, 304 and some 502s have no body; res.json() throws.
  • Errors inside successful responses: GraphQL errors with 200, batch endpoints with per-item failures (Part 15.7). Use the same code and issues shape per item.
  • Paths that no longer match the form after a UI rename; unmatched issues should fall back to the form banner, not disappear.
  • Translated server messages that the client also translates, producing mixed languages; pick one owner of copy.
  • Rate-limit 429 without Retry-After, or with it but not exposed through CORS, so clients retry in a tight loop.
  • Status code drift between services behind one BFF (404 versus 410 versus 422 for the same case); the catalogue decides.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior designs errors as a product surface with a contract, not as an afterthought. One shape everywhere, codes as a catalogue, paths that match fields, a request reference on every error, and a presentation table agreed between the API and web teams. They classify in one place so feature code never parses responses. They care most about the errors nobody designed: HTML from proxies, empty bodies, timeouts, and unknown codes from a newer API, and they make every one of those degrade to a safe, honest message.

Common mistakes

  • res.json() without checking Content-Type.
  • Branching on English message text instead of code.
  • Generic toasts for field errors.
  • Leaking stack traces or upstream bodies in error responses.
  • Different error shapes from pipes, guards and the throttler because only some go through the filter.

Interview questions

  1. What is RFC 9457 and which members would you add? Expected answer: problem details for HTTP APIs, application/problem+json, standard type, title, status, detail, instance; extensions for a machine code, field issues and a requestId. Follow-up: how is type used? (Stable URI identifying the problem kind, can link to documentation.)
  2. How do you map a server validation error onto a form field? Expected answer: issue paths that match form names, setError per issue, banner fallback for unmatched paths.
  3. The UI shows "Unexpected token <". What happened and how do you fix it? Expected answer: a non-JSON error page from a proxy; check Content-Type, classify as upstream unavailable, align timeouts.
  4. Which errors should a client retry automatically? Expected answer: network errors, 429 after Retry-After, 502 to 504 with backoff; mutations only with an idempotency key; never 4xx business errors.
  5. How do you localise API errors? Expected answer: client maps code and issue codes with params to its own copy; server text is a fallback.

Practical exercise

Make every error from the NestJS API a problem document and add the classifier to the web app.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Validation, domain, throttler, guard and unknown errors all return application/problem+json with code, issues and requestId.
  • A test sends a request through a proxy that returns HTML 502; the UI shows the upstream-unavailable message with no JSON parse error.
  • Every code in KnownErrorCodes has an entry in the presentation table and a test that checks its treatment.
  • An unknown code from a stubbed newer API renders a toast with the request reference.

74.7 Dates, money, IDs and enums across the wire

Concept

JSON has six value types: string, number, boolean, null, object and array. It has no date, no decimal, no 64-bit integer and no enum. Every one of those must be encoded into a JSON type by the server and decoded by the client, and each side must agree on the encoding. When they do not, the result is rarely a crash. It is a delivery date one day early, a total off by one paisa, an order ID that points at someone else's order, or a status badge that silently disappears.

This section fixes the wire encoding for each awkward type, as this volume's @shop/contracts has used since 76.12, and explains why:

Value Wire encoding Example Client decodes with
Instant (something happened at a moment) ISO 8601 string, UTC, with Z "2026-11-05T09:30:00.000Z" new Date(s), display with Intl.DateTimeFormat and an explicit timeZone
Calendar date (no time, no zone) YYYY-MM-DD string "2026-11-07" Keep as a string, or split into parts; never new Date(s)
Wall-clock time at a place Local time plus IANA zone { "opensAt": "09:00", "timeZone": "Asia/Kolkata" } Intl with that timeZone
Duration Integer seconds "prepSeconds": 900 Arithmetic on numbers
Money Integer minor units as a string, plus ISO 4217 currency { "totalMinor": "129900", "currency": "INR" } String or BigInt arithmetic, Intl.NumberFormat for display
ID Opaque string "id": "1d6c0b6e-...", "riderId": "1849302284551208961" Never parsed, compared or sorted as a number
Count or size below 2^53 JSON number "itemCount": 3 Number
Enum String from a documented set, open on responses "status": "SHIPPED" Known values mapped, unknown to a fallback
Absent versus empty Field present with null means "known empty"; missing means "not sent" "deliveredAt": null .nullable() versus .optional()

Why does it exist?

Because each JavaScript default is wrong for at least one of these types:

  • new Date('2026-11-07') is parsed as UTC midnight; displayed in New York (UTC-5) it is 6 November. new Date('2026-11-07T09:00') without an offset is parsed as local time. Same function, two rules.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so prices as JSON numbers invite float arithmetic and rounding drift between client and server.
  • JSON numbers become IEEE 754 doubles, exact only up to 2^53 - 1 (9,007,199,254,740,991). JSON.parse('{"id":1849302284551208961}').id is 1849302284551208960. The last digits change, silently.
  • An unknown string in a z.enum fails the whole parse; an unknown value in a switch with no default renders nothing.

Mental model

Imagine shipping goods across a border where the paperwork only has plain text boxes. You write the weight as "12.500 kg", not "about 12", because the receiver must not guess the precision. You write the delivery day as "7 November" and not "Friday at midnight in our time zone", because the receiver lives in a different zone. You copy the parcel's serial number letter by letter, because the receiver must never "round" it. And you write the category from an agreed list, with an agreed rule for "category not on my list: put it in the miscellaneous pile and tell the office".

How it works

Dates and time zones. Decide what kind of time each field is:

  1. Instants (placedAt, deliveredAt, cutoffAt) are points on the global timeline. PostgreSQL stores them as timestamptz (always UTC internally). node-postgres returns a JS Date, and JSON.stringify calls toISOString(), which emits UTC with Z. The client displays them in a chosen zone: the user's (Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone) for "when did I order", or the store's for "when does the kitchen close".
  2. Calendar dates (deliveryDate, dateOfBirth) have no time and no zone. PostgreSQL's date type is right, but node-postgres parses date columns into a JS Date at midnight in the server's time zone by default, which then serialises as the previous day's UTC instant on a server east of UTC. Register a type parser that keeps the string. On the client, keep it a string; to format it, build the date at noon UTC and format with timeZone: 'UTC', or use the parts directly.
  3. Wall-clock rules ("same-day delivery if ordered before 18:00 in the store's city") belong on the server. The server computes the instant (cutoffAt: "2026-11-05T12:30:00.000Z") and sends it; the client does not reimplement time zone rules.
  4. Relative values go stale. "Arrives in 12 minutes" is wrong after any cache, retry or slow render. Send an absolute instant (etaAt) and let the client compute the countdown. If the client's clock may be wrong, estimate the offset from the response Date header and correct the countdown.

Money. The server owns every calculation: line totals, discounts, tax, delivery fees and rounding. It sends results in integer minor units (paise, cents, yen) as strings, with the currency, because currencies have different exponents: INR and USD have 2 decimal places, JPY has 0, KWD has 3. Intl.NumberFormat knows each currency's digits (resolvedOptions().maximumFractionDigits). The client converts minor units to a decimal string by inserting the point, then formats. Where the client must add amounts (an optimistic cart badge), it uses BigInt, never floats, and replaces the result with the server's total as soon as it arrives.

IDs and large integers. IDs are strings on the wire, always, even when the database column is bigint. UUIDs are strings already. Snowflake-style IDs (64-bit, time-ordered) exceed 2^53 from day one: Twitter added id_str to its API in 2010 for exactly this reason. node-postgres returns bigint (int8) columns as strings by default, and TypeORM bigint columns are typed string, so the safe path is to keep them strings end to end. Never parseInt an ID, never sort by it on the client, never build one from parts. Note that JSON.stringify throws TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt if a mapper leaks a bigint value.

Enums. A response enum is open: the server will add values over time, and clients built before that must degrade, not crash. A request enum is closed: the server rejects values it does not know. In code, that means the shared contract keeps OrderStatusSchema = z.enum([...]) for requests and for the server's output types, while each client reads responses through a tolerant wrapper that maps unknown values to 'UNKNOWN' and reports them.

Null and missing. "deliveredAt": null means "not delivered"; a missing deliveredAt means "this server did not send the field" (an older version, or a sparse fieldset). Make response fields required and nullable where possible, so "missing" always signals a contract problem. For PATCH, missing means "do not change" and null means "clear", as in JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396, Part 15.8).

flowchart LR
    pg["PostgreSQL: timestamptz, date, bigint, numeric"] --> map["NestJS mapper: toISOString, date string, bigint to string, minor units"]
    map --> json["JSON wire: strings with fixed formats"]
    json --> zod["Client zod parse: formats checked, enums opened"]
    zod --> view["View: Intl.DateTimeFormat with timeZone, Intl.NumberFormat with currency"]

Practical example

A grocery app in three countries shows an order card: "Placed 5 Nov, 15:00 · Delivery Sat 7 Nov · Total ₹1,299.00 · Shipped". The API sends placedAt as an instant, deliveryDate as a calendar date, totalMinor: "129900" with currency: "INR", status: "SHIPPED" and storeTimeZone: "Asia/Kolkata". The card formats placedAt in the store's zone (so a customer travelling in London still sees the time the store saw), shows deliveryDate without any zone conversion, and formats money with the currency's own digits. When the API later adds status: "OUT_FOR_DELIVERY", old app versions show a neutral "In progress" badge until they update.

React / Next.js example

Client-side decoders and formatters, used by every component:

// apps/web/src/wire/decode.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

// Open enum: known values pass through, unknown become 'UNKNOWN' and are reported once per value.
const seenUnknown = new Set<string>();
export function openEnum<T extends string>(schema: z.ZodEnum<[T, ...T[]]>, name: string) {
  const known = new Set<string>(schema.options);
  return z.string().transform((v): T | 'UNKNOWN' => {
    if (known.has(v)) return v as T;
    if (!seenUnknown.has(`${name}:${v}`)) { seenUnknown.add(`${name}:${v}`); console.warn(`unknown ${name}: ${v}`); } // telemetry in production
    return 'UNKNOWN';
  });
}

// Money: integer minor units (string) to a display string, exact for any size.
export function formatMoney(minor: string, currency: string, locale = 'en-IN'): string {
  const nf = new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: 'currency', currency });
  const digits = nf.resolvedOptions().maximumFractionDigits ?? 2;          // INR 2, JPY 0, KWD 3
  const neg = minor.startsWith('-'); const abs = (neg ? minor.slice(1) : minor).padStart(digits + 1, '0');
  const decimal = digits === 0 ? abs : `${abs.slice(0, -digits)}.${abs.slice(-digits)}`;
  // format() accepts a decimal string in current browsers (exact); older engines convert to Number,
  // which is still exact for amounts below 2^53 minor units.
  return nf.format(`${neg ? '-' : ''}${decimal}` as `${number}`);
}

// Optimistic sums use BigInt, never floats.
export const addMinor = (a: string, b: string) => (BigInt(a) + BigInt(b)).toString();

// Calendar date: format without any time zone shift.
export function formatCalendarDate(ymd: string, locale = 'en-IN'): string {
  const [y, m, d] = ymd.split('-').map(Number);
  return new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { weekday: 'short', day: 'numeric', month: 'short', timeZone: 'UTC' })
    .format(new Date(Date.UTC(y, m - 1, d, 12)));                          // noon UTC: no zone can move the day
}

export const formatInstant = (iso: string, timeZone: string, locale = 'en-IN') =>
  new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short', timeZone }).format(new Date(iso));

This Part adds three fields to OrderSummarySchema in @shop/contracts, all required and nullable where they can be empty: deliveryDate: z.string().date().nullable() (YYYY-MM-DD, zod 3.23+), deliveredAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }).nullable() and storeTimeZone: z.string() (an IANA name). The web's read schema only opens the enum:

// apps/web/src/orders/schema.ts
import { OrderStatusSchema, OrderSummarySchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { openEnum } from '../wire/decode';

export const OrderSummaryRead = OrderSummarySchema.extend({
  status: openEnum(OrderStatusSchema, 'OrderStatus'),  // the server's type stays closed; the reader is open
});
export type OrderSummaryView = z.infer<typeof OrderSummaryRead>;

export const statusLabel = {
  PENDING: 'Awaiting payment', PAID: 'Confirmed', SHIPPED: 'On the way', DELIVERED: 'Delivered',
  CANCELLED: 'Cancelled', UNKNOWN: 'In progress',     // the fallback is a designed state, not an accident
} satisfies Record<OrderSummaryView['status'], string>;

In a server component, pass timeZone and locale explicitly to these formatters; otherwise server and browser format differently and hydration fails (73.10).

Backend side (NestJS)

The mapper is where the encoding is decided, once:

// apps/api/src/orders/order.mapper.ts
import type { OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';
import type { OrderEntity } from './order.entity';

export function toOrderSummary(o: OrderEntity): OrderSummary {
  return {
    id: o.id,                                    // uuid string
    displayId: o.displayId,
    status: o.status,                            // typed as OrderStatus: the server only emits known values
    totalMinor: o.totalMinor,                    // bigint column, already a string from node-postgres
    currency: o.currency,
    placedAt: o.placedAt.toISOString(),          // timestamptz -> UTC 'Z'
    deliveryDate: o.deliveryDate,                // date column kept as 'YYYY-MM-DD' by the type parser below
    deliveredAt: o.deliveredAt ? o.deliveredAt.toISOString() : null,  // required and nullable
    storeTimeZone: o.store.timeZone,             // 'Asia/Kolkata'
    version: o.version,                          // 78.1
    updatedAt: o.updatedAt.toISOString(),        // 78.1
  };
}
// apps/api/src/db/pg-types.ts  (imported once, before the DataSource initialises)
import { types } from 'pg';

types.setTypeParser(types.builtins.DATE, (v: string) => v);   // keep calendar dates as strings
// INT8 (bigint) is already returned as a string by default; do not change that to Number.

The entity side, with TypeORM:

// apps/api/src/orders/order.entity.ts (excerpt)
@Entity('orders')
export class OrderEntity {
  @PrimaryColumn('uuid') id!: string;
  @Column({ name: 'total_minor', type: 'bigint' }) totalMinor!: string;     // TypeORM maps bigint to string
  @Column({ type: 'char', length: 3 }) currency!: string;
  @Column({ name: 'placed_at', type: 'timestamptz' }) placedAt!: Date;
  @Column({ name: 'delivery_date', type: 'date', nullable: true }) deliveryDate!: string | null;
  @Column({ name: 'delivered_at', type: 'timestamptz', nullable: true }) deliveredAt!: Date | null;
  @Column({ type: 'text' }) status!: OrderStatus;
  @VersionColumn() version!: number;
  @UpdateDateColumn({ name: 'updated_at', type: 'timestamptz' }) updatedAt!: Date;
  @ManyToOne(() => StoreEntity, { eager: true }) store!: StoreEntity;
}

With Sequelize, DataTypes.BIGINT and DataTypes.DECIMAL values also come back as strings from PostgreSQL, and DataTypes.DATEONLY returns 'YYYY-MM-DD' strings, so the same mapper rules apply.

The cutoff rule computed in SQL, in the store's zone, and sent as an instant:

-- Same-day delivery cutoff: 18:00 local time in the store's zone, today, as a UTC instant.
SELECT s.id,
       ((now() AT TIME ZONE s.time_zone)::date + time '18:00') AT TIME ZONE s.time_zone AS cutoff_at
FROM stores s
WHERE s.id = $1;

now() AT TIME ZONE zone gives the local wall-clock timestamp; adding 18:00 to its date and converting back with AT TIME ZONE zone returns a timestamptz, which the mapper serialises with toISOString(). Daylight saving changes are handled by PostgreSQL's time zone database, not by the client.

Production scenario

An international flower delivery site had 0.8 % of orders arrive "on the wrong day" according to customers. Investigation found that the web's delivery-date picker sent "2026-02-14T00:00:00.000Z" (an instant from toISOString() of local midnight) instead of "2026-02-14". For customers west of UTC, local midnight was already 14 February in UTC; for customers east of UTC, it was 13 February. After switching the field to a calendar date string on both ends, plus a z.string().date() check in the request schema, wrong-day complaints fell to 0.05 %, the rate of genuine courier errors.

Failure scenario

A cart redesign calculated the "You save" line and the total on the client from list prices and a 15 % promotion, with Math.round(price * 0.85), to make the cart feel instant. The pricing service rounded half-to-even per line and summed. For about 4 % of carts, the totals differed by one minor unit. Checkout sent expectedTotalMinor from the client's total, and the API correctly refused with 422 PRICE_CHANGED. Customers saw "Prices in your cart changed" with no visible change and abandoned at three times the normal rate.

The fix was the rule already in this book: the client displays money computed by the server (73.8's failure scenario is the BFF version of the same mistake). The cart now shows the previous server total with a subtle loading state until the repriced cart arrives, typically 120 ms later.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Daylight saving gaps and overlaps: 02:30 does not exist on some spring dates and occurs twice on some autumn dates; never construct local times on the client from offsets.
  • toLocaleString() without arguments uses the runtime's locale and zone, which differ between Node.js on the server and the browser (73.10).
  • Negative money (refunds, credits) must survive formatting; test "-500".
  • Currency changes per order: a marketplace cart may mix sellers; totals in different currencies must not be summed by anyone.
  • IDs in URLs are fine as strings; IDs in <input type="number"> or in JSON numbers from a third-party API are not. Map them at the BFF.
  • Unknown enum values in request echoes: a client that sends back a status it received (PATCH { status }) can send 'UNKNOWN'; never round-trip display-only values.
  • Empty string as "no value" from forms: convert "" to null at the form boundary, or z.string().min(1) will reject it with a confusing message.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior refuses to let any value cross the wire in a format that can be misread. Instants are UTC strings, calendar dates are date strings, money is minor units in strings with a currency, IDs are opaque strings, enums are open on responses, and every response field is required and nullable rather than sometimes missing. They put each conversion in exactly one place on each side (the server mapper and the client decoder) so components never meet raw wire values. And they keep calculations on the server: the client formats, the server computes.

To a product manager: "We send dates and prices in a strict format so a customer in another time zone never sees the wrong delivery day, and the price in the cart is always the price we charge."

Common mistakes

  • new Date('YYYY-MM-DD') for calendar dates.
  • Money as JSON numbers, or float arithmetic on prices in the browser.
  • Numeric IDs from bigint columns or third-party APIs.
  • Closed enums on the client, crashing or rendering nothing on a new value.
  • Server and client formatting dates with different implicit time zones.
  • Optional response fields where required-and-nullable was meant.

Interview questions

  1. How do you send a delivery date and a delivery deadline? Expected answer: the date as YYYY-MM-DD (calendar date, no zone); the deadline as a UTC instant computed by the server in the store's zone. Follow-up: what goes wrong with new Date('2026-11-07')? (Parsed as UTC midnight, shown as the previous day west of UTC.)
  2. Why send money as integer minor units in a string? Expected answer: exact, no float drift, safe beyond 2^53, currency exponent explicit with the currency code; server computes, client formats.
  3. What happens to a 64-bit ID in JSON.parse? Expected answer: it becomes a double and loses precision above 2^53; send IDs as strings.
  4. How should a web client handle an enum value it does not know? Expected answer: map to a designed fallback state, report it, never crash; the server must still reject unknown values on input.
  5. Null versus missing: what is the difference and why does it matter? Expected answer: null is a known empty value; missing means not sent; required-nullable responses make missing a detectable contract error, and PATCH uses missing as "no change".

Practical exercise

Audit the order summary contract for wire encodings and fix every field that is ambiguous.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A test renders an order with deliveryDate: "2026-11-07" under TZ=America/Los_Angeles and TZ=Asia/Tokyo and both show 7 November.
  • formatMoney is tested for INR, JPY and KWD, negative amounts and "900719925474099312".
  • A response with status: "RETURN_REQUESTED" renders the fallback badge and emits one telemetry event.
  • The API returns a bigint ID column as a string, and a test fails if any response DTO field is a JS bigint or a number above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.
  • node-postgres returns date columns as strings, verified by an integration test against PostgreSQL.

74.8 Uploads and downloads from the browser

Concept

Part 33 — File Storage and Uploads built the server side: object storage, presigned PUT and POST, multipart uploads, the files table with its status machine, scanning and CDN delivery. This section is the contract between that machinery and a browser: which endpoints the page calls in which order, what each returns, how the page shows progress, how it resumes after a dropped connection, and how a download reaches the user with the right file name and permissions.

An upload from the browser is never one request. It is a small protocol: ask the API for permission, send the bytes somewhere (usually straight to S3, not through NestJS), tell the API you finished, and wait until the file is processed. Each step is a contract with its own failure modes.

Why does it exist?

Because the naive version, <input type="file"> posted as multipart/form-data to a NestJS endpoint, has three problems at real sizes. The API pod becomes a byte pipe, holding a connection and memory for the whole upload (Part 33.5). The user sees no progress for a 300 MB video and assumes the page froze. And when a phone on a train loses signal at 80 %, the upload starts again from zero. Direct-to-storage uploads, progress events and resumable protocols fix those, but only if the browser and the API agree on every step.

Mental model

Imagine sending a large parcel through a courier depot. You do not carry it to the head office. You ask the head office for a shipping label (the presigned URL, valid for 15 minutes and for one size of parcel). You drop the parcel at the depot yourself (the upload to S3). For a very heavy load you split it into numbered boxes, and if your van breaks down you only resend the boxes the depot has not signed for (multipart and resume). Then you phone the head office to say "delivered" (the complete call), and they inspect it before it goes on the shelf (scanning and processing).

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant API as NestJS
    participant S3 as S3
    participant W as Worker
    B->>API: POST /v1/uploads name, size, type, purpose
    API-->>B: uploadId, presigned POST url and fields, maxBytes, expiresAt
    B->>S3: POST form with file, XHR progress events
    S3-->>B: 204
    B->>API: POST /v1/uploads/uploadId/complete
    API->>S3: HeadObject, size and type check
    API-->>B: 202 status UPLOADED
    S3->>W: object created event
    W->>API: status PROCESSED or REJECTED
    B->>API: GET /v1/uploads/uploadId until PROCESSED
  1. Initiate. The page sends file metadata. The API checks the user may upload for that purpose (product photo, prescription, invoice), validates declared size and type, inserts a files row with status PENDING, and returns a presigned POST with a content-length-range condition, because a presigned POST is the only way to cap size on a browser upload (33.7).
  2. Upload with progress. fetch has no upload progress events. Use XMLHttpRequest and its upload.onprogress event, which reports loaded and total bytes. Cancel with xhr.abort(), wired to an AbortSignal so it fits the rest of the code.
  3. Complete. The page tells the API the upload finished. The API does not trust that: it checks the object exists and matches the declared size with HeadObject, then moves the row to UPLOADED.
  4. Wait for processing. Scanning and thumbnails take seconds. The page polls GET /v1/uploads/{id} with backoff, or receives a push event (72.8), until the status is PROCESSED or REJECTED.
  5. Resume large files. Above roughly 100 MB, use S3 multipart upload: the API returns presigned URLs per part (8 to 16 MB each). The browser uploads 3 to 4 parts in parallel, reads each part's ETag response header (the bucket's CORS must expose it, 33.6), and records finished parts in IndexedDB keyed by a file fingerprint (name, size, lastModified). After a reload, it asks the API which parts S3 already has (the API calls ListParts) and uploads only the rest. The tus protocol and its tus-js-client library offer the same resume semantics against a tus server, if you prefer a standard over S3-specific code.

Downloads are simpler, but the contract still matters:

Download Mechanism Contract detail
Public images, product media CDN URL in the response Immutable versioned keys, long Cache-Control (33.9)
Private file, small or large GET /v1/files/{id}/download returns 302 to a presigned GET API checks ownership first; presign with ResponseContentDisposition for the file name
Generated export (CSV of 200,000 orders) Long-running job, then a presigned link 202 plus a job resource (Part 15.16); never generate in the request
Inline viewing (PDF invoice in a tab) Same as private, with inline disposition Correct Content-Type; nosniff

The browser's download attribute on <a> is ignored for cross-origin URLs, so the file name must come from the Content-Disposition header that S3 returns, which the presigned URL controls. Non-ASCII names need the filename*=UTF-8''... form (RFC 6266). Avoid downloading large files through fetch into a Blob and URL.createObjectURL: the whole file sits in the tab's memory, and a 600 MB export crashes mobile browsers.

Practical example

A pharmacy app asks customers to upload a prescription photo (2 to 12 MB from a phone camera) before checkout. The page requests an upload slot for purpose: 'PRESCRIPTION', shows a progress bar during the direct upload, calls complete, and then shows "Checking your prescription..." while a worker scans the file and a pharmacist's queue picks it up. Checkout is allowed once the file is PROCESSED. A pharmacist later downloads it through a 302 to a presigned URL valid for 60 seconds, logged with their user ID.

React / Next.js example

The upload contract in @shop/contracts and a progress-aware uploader:

// packages/contracts/src/uploads.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const UploadPurposeSchema = z.enum(['PRESCRIPTION', 'PRODUCT_PHOTO', 'RETURN_EVIDENCE']);
export const InitiateUploadRequestSchema = z.object({
  purpose: UploadPurposeSchema,
  fileName: z.string().min(1).max(200),
  contentType: z.enum(['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/heic', 'application/pdf']),
  sizeBytes: z.number().int().positive().max(20 * 1024 * 1024),
});
export const InitiateUploadResponseSchema = z.object({
  uploadId: z.string().uuid(),
  url: z.string().url(),
  fields: z.record(z.string()),                         // presigned POST form fields, sent as-is
  expiresAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),
});
export const UploadStatusSchema = z.object({
  uploadId: z.string().uuid(),
  status: z.string(),                                   // open: PENDING, UPLOADED, SCANNING, PROCESSED, REJECTED
  rejectionCode: z.string().nullable(),
});
// apps/web/src/uploads/uploadWithProgress.ts
export function postFormWithProgress(url: string, form: FormData, onProgress: (pct: number) => void, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
    xhr.open('POST', url);
    xhr.upload.onprogress = (e) => { if (e.lengthComputable) onProgress(Math.round((e.loaded / e.total) * 100)); };
    xhr.onload = () => (xhr.status >= 200 && xhr.status < 300 ? resolve() : reject(new Error(`storage ${xhr.status}`)));
    xhr.onerror = () => reject(new TypeError('network'));        // same shape as a failed fetch
    xhr.onabort = () => reject(new DOMException('Aborted', 'AbortError'));
    signal?.addEventListener('abort', () => xhr.abort(), { once: true });
    xhr.send(form);
  });
}

export async function uploadPrescription(file: File, onProgress: (pct: number) => void, signal?: AbortSignal) {
  const slot = await api.initiateUpload({ purpose: 'PRESCRIPTION', fileName: file.name, contentType: file.type as 'image/jpeg', sizeBytes: file.size });
  const form = new FormData();
  Object.entries(slot.fields).forEach(([k, v]) => form.append(k, v));  // policy fields first
  form.append('file', file);                                            // S3 requires the file as the last field
  await postFormWithProgress(slot.url, form, onProgress, signal);
  await api.completeUpload(slot.uploadId);                               // the API verifies with HeadObject
  return slot.uploadId;                                                  // the caller polls status until PROCESSED
}

api.initiateUpload and api.completeUpload are thin wrappers over the generated client (74.2) that parse with the schemas above. Validate size and type on the client before initiating, for fast feedback, knowing the presigned policy is the real limit.

Backend side (NestJS)

The NestJS endpoints follow Part 33.14; the contract-specific rules are:

  • Return everything the browser needs in one response: URL, fields, expiry and the upload ID. The browser should never construct S3 keys.
  • Make complete idempotent. A retried complete on an UPLOADED row returns the same 202; on a missing object it returns 409 UPLOAD_NOT_FOUND, not 500.
  • Expire abandoned slots. A PENDING row older than its expiresAt becomes EXPIRED, and an S3 lifecycle rule aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a day, or orphaned parts cost storage forever (33.10).
  • CORS on the bucket, not just the API: AllowedOrigins for the web origin, AllowedMethods: ["POST", "PUT"], ExposeHeaders: ["ETag"] for multipart.
  • Downloads authorise, then redirect. GET /v1/files/{id}/download checks ownership against the files row, then returns 302 to a 60-second presigned GET signed with ResponseContentDisposition: 'attachment; filename="prescription.jpg"'. Never cache that redirect (Cache-Control: private, no-store).

Production scenario

A second-hand marketplace let sellers upload up to 10 photos per listing. Uploads went through NestJS as multipart form data; at the evening peak, 18 % of API memory was upload buffers and p99 latency for unrelated endpoints rose to 2.3 s. Moving to presigned POST with XHR progress removed upload traffic from the API entirely (about 1.4 TB a day), p99 for other endpoints returned to 180 ms, and listing completion rose 6 % once sellers could see per-photo progress.

Failure scenario

A video-review feature accepted clips up to 500 MB through a single presigned PUT. On mobile networks, 31 % of uploads over 200 MB failed and restarted from zero; some users tried four times and gave up. Support tickets said "upload stuck at 87 %". The team switched to multipart with 16 MB parts, three in parallel, progress stored in IndexedDB and ListParts-based resume. Completion for large clips rose from 69 % to 96 %. The first rollout still failed for every user: the bucket's CORS configuration did not expose ETag, so the browser could read no part ETags and CompleteMultipartUpload was impossible. It was caught in the canary within 20 minutes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Presigned URL expired because the user picked a file, then went for coffee: initiate when the upload starts, not when the dialog opens, and re-initiate on 403 from storage.
  • file.type is empty or wrong for some formats (HEIC on older browsers); the server's scan decides the real type.
  • Tab closed after upload, before complete: the object exists, the row is PENDING. A storage event or sweeper should reconcile it (33.8).
  • Double complete from a retry: idempotent by status.
  • Download links shared in chats: short expiry, and authorisation at the redirect, not in the link.
  • Corporate proxies that block direct S3 hosts; offer a fallback through a CloudFront distribution on your own domain.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps bytes away from the API, treats every upload as a small protocol with explicit states, and designs each step to be retried safely. They choose the simplest mechanism that fits the file sizes and networks they actually see: presigned POST for photos and documents, multipart with resume only when large files on mobile justify the code. They make progress and processing states visible to the user, because an upload with no feedback is indistinguishable from a broken page.

Common mistakes

  • Streaming large uploads through NestJS.
  • Using fetch and showing a spinner instead of progress for large files.
  • Trusting the client's "complete" without checking the object.
  • Forgetting bucket CORS and ExposeHeaders: ETag.
  • Downloading big files into a Blob instead of letting the browser stream them.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through a browser upload of a 10 MB photo with a size limit. Expected answer: initiate, presigned POST with content-length-range, XHR with progress, complete with HeadObject, poll processing status. Follow-up: why not a presigned PUT? (Cannot cap size, only fix it.)
  2. How do you resume a 400 MB upload after the tab reloads? Expected answer: multipart, part URLs, record finished parts locally, ListParts on resume, upload missing parts, then complete.
  3. How do you give a private file a correct download name? Expected answer: authorise, redirect to a short-lived presigned GET with ResponseContentDisposition; download attribute does not work cross-origin.
  4. What happens if the complete call is never made? Expected answer: orphaned object and a PENDING row; reconcile with storage events or a sweeper, and lifecycle rules for incomplete multipart uploads.

Practical exercise

Build the prescription upload end to end.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The API never receives file bytes; the Network panel shows the upload going to the storage host.
  • A progress bar updates at least every 500 ms on a throttled "Slow 4G" profile, and Cancel aborts the request.
  • A file above 20 MB is rejected by storage even if the client-side check is removed.
  • Complete is idempotent, and calling it for an object that does not exist returns 409 UPLOAD_NOT_FOUND.
  • A private download arrives with the original file name, and the presigned link stops working after 60 seconds.

74.9 Versioning and rollout with a frontend in the loop

Concept

Part 25 — Backward Compatibility covered versioning from the API's side: URI and header versions, the N-1 rule, mixed-version windows during rolling deploys, and mobile clients (25.2 to 25.6). With a frontend in the loop, the window is wider and stranger than a rolling deploy:

  • Open tabs run the JavaScript bundle they loaded, sometimes for days. A dispatcher or an admin may never reload.
  • Mobile and web release on different schedules. The web may be on today's build while 20 % of Android users are on a release from three months ago.
  • Caches hold old responses and pages: ISR pages (73.2), persisted query caches (72.10), service workers.
  • Feature flags mean two users on the same build see different UIs and may call the API in different ways.

Versioning with a frontend in the loop is the practice of knowing which client versions exist, keeping the API compatible with all of them, telling old clients when they must reload or update, and rolling out changes in an order that never leaves a client calling something that is not there.

Why does it exist?

Because "we deployed the web and the API together" is a statement about servers, not about users. During every deploy, and for days after, some users run the previous frontend. An API change that is correct for the new frontend can break the old one, and a frontend change that is correct for the new API can break against an old BFF pod or a cached response. Without measurement, nobody knows how long the old versions live, so removals are guesses.

Mental model

Imagine a city changing which side of the road the buses stop on. You cannot move every bus stop and every timetable overnight, because some buses are mid-route and some drivers are on holiday with old maps. So you put up the new stops next to the old ones, run both for a while, count how many buses still use the old stops, and only remove them when the count reaches zero. For drivers who never update their map, you put a sign at the old stop: "This stop has moved. Please collect a new map."

How it works

flowchart LR
    tabs["Open tabs: web builds N, N-1, N-2"] --> api["API supports a window of client versions"]
    mobile["Mobile releases 5.0 to 5.4"] --> api
    bff["BFF pods: old and new during rollout"] --> api
    api --> metrics["Requests by X-Client and X-Client-Version"]
    metrics --> decide{"Old version traffic below threshold?"}
    decide -->|"yes"| remove["Contract step: remove old field or endpoint"]
    decide -->|"no"| wait["Keep both, nudge reload or update"]

The mechanisms, in the order a team usually adopts them:

  1. Identify every request. The web sends X-Client: web and X-Client-Version: <build id> (74.2's middleware); mobile sends its app version; the BFF sends its own build. The API records them as metric labels with bounded cardinality (the last 20 builds, others bucketed as old).
  2. Advertise the current version. Responses carry X-App-Version: <latest web build> (or the web polls a small /version.json). When a tab sees a newer version, it switches client-side navigations to full page loads at the next route change, and after a threshold (for example, 30 minutes older) shows a non-blocking "A new version is available. Reload" bar. That pulls the tail of old tabs in from days to hours.
  3. Deprecate in the protocol. Deprecated endpoints and fields are marked in OpenAPI (deprecated: true) and, at runtime, endpoints send the Deprecation header (RFC 9745) and a Sunset header (RFC 8594) with the removal date. The web logs both in development and reports them in telemetry, so a team learns they depend on something scheduled for removal.
  4. Enforce a minimum only when you must. When a removal is unavoidable (a security fix, a legal change), the API rejects clients below a minimum with a problem document, code: 'CLIENT_OUTDATED', and the clients' classifier (74.6) turns that into "Please reload" on web or "Please update" on mobile. This is a last resort, not a release habit.
  5. Order the deploys. The expand and contract rule from Part 25, applied to who ships first:
Change Ship first Then Remove old after
New optional response field API Clients start reading it Not applicable
New request field API accepts it (optional) Clients send it API may require it when old clients are gone
New response enum value Clients with a fallback (74.7) API emits it Not applicable
Renamed response field API sends both Clients read the new name Old-name usage at zero by version metrics
Removed endpoint Clients stop calling it API returns 410 Gone with a problem body Then delete
Changed meaning A new field or endpoint; never change meaning in place Clients migrate As for a rename
  1. Flags agree on both ends. A feature flag that changes how the UI calls the API must be evaluated the same way by the UI and the API: one flag service, one sticky bucketing key (the user ID), and an API that accepts both the old and the new call for as long as the flag is not at 100 % plus the old-tab window. OpenFeature (@openfeature/web-sdk and @openfeature/server-sdk) gives both sides one evaluation API over whatever provider you use.

Next.js adds two specifics. Server Action IDs change between builds, so an old tab posting to an action that the new build no longer has gets an error ("Failed to find Server Action. This request might be from an older or newer deployment."); treat that like CLIENT_OUTDATED and reload. And the deploymentId option in next.config.js lets a platform route an old tab's requests to the matching deployment (skew protection, as Vercel offers); self-hosted, you keep old static assets and short rollout windows (73.11).

Practical example

The web team ships a new checkout behind a flag at 10 % of users. The new checkout calls POST /v1/orders with deliverySlotId; the old one sends deliveryWindow. The API accepts both for the whole rollout. At 100 %, the API's version metrics show deliveryWindow requests falling: 4 % after one day (open tabs and the 10-day-old mobile release), 0.3 % after a week, 0 from web after nine days. The mobile app takes six more weeks. Only then does the API stop accepting deliveryWindow, and it does so with 400 CLIENT_OUTDATED, not a validation error.

React / Next.js example

The reload nudge, driven by a response header:

// apps/web/src/version/useVersionCheck.ts
'use client';
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

const BUILD = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BUILD_ID!;
let latestSeen: { version: string; at: number } | null = null;

// Called from the API client's onResponse middleware (80.2) for every response.
export function noteServerVersion(res: Response) {
  const v = res.headers.get('X-App-Version');                   // exposed via CORS if cross-origin
  if (v && v !== BUILD && latestSeen?.version !== v) latestSeen = { version: v, at: Date.now() };
}

export function useVersionCheck(nudgeAfterMs = 30 * 60_000) {
  const [stale, setStale] = useState(false);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => setStale(!!latestSeen && Date.now() - latestSeen.at > nudgeAfterMs), 60_000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, [nudgeAfterMs]);
  return stale;  // the layout renders a "New version available. Reload" bar; route changes become full loads
}

The API client also treats code === 'CLIENT_OUTDATED' and the Server Action skew error as a reason to reload immediately after saving any form draft locally (72.10).

Backend side (NestJS)

One interceptor records versions, advertises the current one, and enforces minimums from configuration:

// apps/api/src/common/client-version.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import type { Request, Response } from 'express';
import { Counter } from 'prom-client';
import { ClientOutdatedError } from './errors';                   // DomainError: 400, code CLIENT_OUTDATED

const requests = new Counter({ name: 'api_requests_by_client_total', help: 'Requests by client and version', labelNames: ['client', 'version'] });

@Injectable()
export class ClientVersionInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  constructor(private readonly config: ConfigService) {}

  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    const client = String(req.headers['x-client'] ?? 'unknown');
    const version = String(req.headers['x-client-version'] ?? 'unknown');
    const known: string[] = this.config.get('RECENT_WEB_BUILDS', '').split(',');   // bounded label values
    requests.inc({ client, version: client === 'web' && !known.includes(version) ? 'old' : version });

    const blocked: string[] = this.config.get('BLOCKED_CLIENT_VERSIONS', '').split(',').filter(Boolean);
    if (blocked.includes(`${client}@${version}`)) throw new ClientOutdatedError(client, version);

    res.setHeader('X-App-Version', this.config.get('LATEST_WEB_BUILD', ''));
    return next.handle();
  }
}

Deprecated endpoints add Deprecation and Sunset headers with a small decorator-plus-interceptor or directly with @Header('Sunset', 'Sat, 31 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT'), and are marked deprecated: true in OpenAPI through @ApiOperation({ deprecated: true }). CORS exposedHeaders must include X-App-Version, Deprecation and Sunset for a cross-origin web app to read them.

Production scenario

A B2B ordering portal measured its version tail for the first time. 48 hours after each web deploy, 3.1 % of requests still came from the previous build and 0.6 % from builds older than that, mostly from warehouse terminals that were never closed. One terminal was on a build 41 days old. After adding the X-App-Version reload nudge and switching to full page loads on route change when stale, the 48-hour tail fell to 0.4 %, and the oldest active build was 3 days old. Removals that used to wait "a month to be safe" now waited a measured week.

Failure scenario

A team rolled out a redesigned "Edit delivery address" flow behind a flag evaluated in the browser with a client-side SDK. The API checked the same flag through its own SDK, keyed on the session ID instead of the user ID. For users whose two evaluations disagreed, the UI sent the new payload to an API that expected the old one, and 9 % of address edits failed with 400 VALIDATION_FAILED for two days. Nobody noticed in testing, where both flags were forced on. The fix: one bucketing key (user ID) on both sides, an API that accepts both payloads for the flag's whole lifetime, and a dashboard of flag-variant mismatches.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Persisted client caches (72.10) restore data in an old shape after an app update; version the persisted cache key with the contract version and drop it on mismatch.
  • Service workers can serve an old bundle indefinitely; Part 78 covers update flows.
  • ISR pages rendered with the old contract keep calling removed endpoints from their client islands until revalidated.
  • High-cardinality version labels (one per commit) can blow up a metrics backend; bound them.
  • Forced reloads that lose user input: save drafts before reloading.
  • Clock-based sunsets that nobody watches: alert two weeks before a Sunset date while traffic still uses the endpoint.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior thinks in version populations, not deploys: at any time there is a distribution of client versions, and every change must work across it. They measure that distribution, shrink its tail with reload nudges and update prompts, and only remove things when the numbers say nobody depends on them. They evaluate flags consistently on both ends and keep the API tolerant of every variant still in use. And they keep the hard cut, CLIENT_OUTDATED, for emergencies.

Common mistakes

  • Removing a field the day after the web deploy, forgetting open tabs and mobile.
  • No client version in requests, so removals are guesses.
  • Flags evaluated differently by the UI and the API.
  • Forced upgrades as a routine release tool.
  • Treating Next.js Server Action skew errors as generic failures.

Interview questions

  1. How long must the API support an old web build? Expected answer: as long as measured traffic says it is in use; shrink the window with reload nudges, full loads on navigation and short rollouts. Follow-up: and mobile? (Months; a minimum-version gate only for emergencies.)
  2. In what order do you deploy a renamed response field across web, mobile and API? Expected answer: API sends both, clients migrate, measure old usage to zero per client version, remove.
  3. How do feature flags interact with API contracts? Expected answer: the API must accept every variant's calls while any client can send them; evaluate flags with one key on both sides.
  4. What do the Deprecation and Sunset headers do? Expected answer: signal at runtime that an endpoint is deprecated and when it will be removed, so clients can report and migrate.
  5. What happens to an open Next.js tab after a deploy that removes a Server Action? Expected answer: the action request fails because its ID is unknown; detect it and reload, keep old assets and short rollouts, or use skew protection.

Practical exercise

Add version telemetry and a reload nudge to the web app and API.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A Grafana panel shows requests by client and version, with old web builds bucketed.
  • A tab left open across a deploy shows the reload bar within 31 minutes, and the next route change is a full page load.
  • An endpoint marked deprecated returns Deprecation and Sunset headers, and the web reports them in telemetry.
  • Adding web@<build> to BLOCKED_CLIENT_VERSIONS makes that build show "Please reload" without losing a half-filled form.

74.10 Contract testing between web and API

Concept

A consumer-driven contract test records what a consumer actually sends and reads, and replays it against the provider. Part 25.7 introduced Pact for service-to-service calls: the consumer writes a test against a Pact mock server, the test produces a pact file, a Pact Broker stores it, and the provider's CI verifies every relevant pact against a running instance of itself. This section applies it to the pair this volume cares about, the web app and the NestJS API, and adds what is specific to browsers: pacts generated from the real frontend client, verification against the web versions that are still in users' tabs, and the deploy gate (can-i-deploy) on both sides.

Contract tests sit between the other tools in this Part:

Tool Proves Blind spot
Shared types (70.9, 80.3) Code in one commit agrees Deployed versions; other repositories
Spec diff (74.2, 32.7) The published API did not break its own promise What consumers actually rely on; undocumented behaviour
Runtime validation with telemetry (74.1) What arrives in production matches Only after deploy
Consumer contract tests (this section) The provider still satisfies what each deployed consumer version uses Fields and cases nobody wrote an interaction for
End-to-end tests (Part 77) One journey works with both sides running Slow, few paths, one version pair

Why does it exist?

The spec diff answers "did the API break its promise?" It cannot answer "did the API break the merchant portal?", because the promise may be wider or narrower than what the portal uses. A field the spec marks optional may be one the portal cannot live without; a field the spec marks required may be one nobody reads, so removing it would be harmless. End-to-end tests answer the question for one pair of versions on one path, slowly. Consumer contract tests answer it for every consumer and every deployed version, in seconds, and they tell the API team who their consumers are.

Mental model

Imagine every tenant in a building writing down exactly which pipes and sockets their flat uses, and handing the list to the building manager. Before any renovation, the manager checks the plan against every tenant's list, including tenants who are away on holiday but still have a lease. The building's blueprint (the OpenAPI spec) shows every pipe; the tenant lists show which pipes matter to whom.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant WCI as WebCI
    participant BR as PactBroker
    participant ACI as ApiCI
    participant PROD as Production
    WCI->>WCI: Vitest consumer tests with real API client
    WCI->>BR: publish pact, version 7e21c0a, branch main
    ACI->>BR: fetch pacts for main and deployed or released
    ACI->>ACI: verify against API build 3b9f412
    ACI->>BR: publish verification results
    WCI->>BR: can-i-deploy web 7e21c0a to production
    BR-->>WCI: yes, verified with deployed API
    WCI->>PROD: deploy web
    WCI->>BR: record-deployment web 7e21c0a production
  1. Consumer tests use the real client. The web's Pact tests call the same functions the UI uses (the openapi-fetch client of 74.2 and its parsers) against the Pact mock server. If the UI's client changes what it sends or reads, the pact changes with it.
  2. Assert only what the UI reads. Matchers (like, eachLike, regex, uuid) describe types and formats, not exact values. A pact that pins every field of the response makes harmless API changes fail.
  3. Publish with version and branch. The pact is tagged with the web build's Git SHA and branch.
  4. Provider verification in the API's CI fetches the pacts selected by consumer version selectors, typically { mainBranch: true } (what consumers are about to ship) and { deployedOrReleased: true } (what is in production now). Provider states ("order 1d6c exists for user u1") are set up by state handlers that seed the database.
  5. Deploy gates on both sides. Before deploying either app, CI runs can-i-deploy against the target environment. The broker checks its matrix of verified version pairs. After deploying, CI runs record-deployment.
  6. Old tabs count as releases. record-deployment replaces the previous deployed version. For a web app whose old builds live on in open tabs, also run record-release for each build, and record-support-ended once version telemetry (74.9) shows its traffic is gone. Then deployedOrReleased covers every build still in use, not just the newest.

Messages work the same way. The order-status events streamed to the browser over SSE (72.8, and Part 79) can be covered with Pact's message pacts (MessageConsumerPact), where the consumer asserts the event payloads it handles and the provider verifies that its event builders produce them.

Practical example

The web app has 14 interactions with the orders API: list, get, cancel, create, and their important error cases (404, 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE, 422 PRICE_CHANGED, 400 VALIDATION_FAILED). The merchant portal has 6. The API's verification job runs 20 interactions against a test instance with a PostgreSQL container in 40 seconds. When an API engineer proposes changing 409 to 422 for non-cancellable orders, the web's interaction for that case fails verification, and the conversation about whether the change is worth it happens in the pull request, not in an incident.

React / Next.js example

A web consumer test, run by Vitest, using the real client:

// apps/web/src/api/orders.pact.test.ts  (@pact-foundation/pact 12, PactV3)
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { MatchersV3, PactV3 } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { createApi } from './client';               // createClient<paths>({ baseUrl }) plus middleware (80.2)
import { getOrder, cancelOrder } from '../orders/api';
import { ApiError } from './errors';

const { like, regex, uuid, eachLike, integer } = MatchersV3;
const pact = new PactV3({ consumer: 'web', provider: 'orders-api', dir: './pacts' });
const ORDER_ID = '1d6c0b6e-2f3a-4c55-9d1e-8a7b6c5d4e3f';

describe('web -> orders-api', () => {
  it('reads an order the way the order page does', () =>
    pact
      .given('order exists', { orderId: ORDER_ID, userId: 'u1', status: 'PAID' })
      .uponReceiving('a request for one order')
      .withRequest({ method: 'GET', path: `/v1/orders/${ORDER_ID}`, headers: { 'X-Client': 'web' } })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': regex('application/json.*', 'application/json; charset=utf-8') },
        body: {                                     // only the fields OrderSummaryRead and the page use
          id: uuid(ORDER_ID),
          displayId: like('DK-20481'),
          status: like('PAID'),                     // open enum: type only, no fixed value set
          totalMinor: regex('^\\d+$', '129900'),    // integer minor units as a string (80.7)
          currency: regex('^[A-Z]{3}$', 'INR'),
          placedAt: regex('^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}T.*Z$', '2026-11-05T09:30:00.000Z'),
          version: integer(3),
          items: eachLike({ sku: like('TB-SONIC-01'), name: like('Sonic toothbrush'), quantity: integer(1) }),
        },
      })
      .executeTest(async (mock) => {
        const order = await getOrder(createApi(mock.url), ORDER_ID);   // parses with OrderSummaryRead
        expect(order.status).toBe('PAID');
      }));

  it('shows the not-cancellable error as the UI expects', () =>
    pact
      .given('order exists', { orderId: ORDER_ID, userId: 'u1', status: 'SHIPPED' })
      .uponReceiving('a cancel for a shipped order')
      .withRequest({ method: 'POST', path: `/v1/orders/${ORDER_ID}/cancel`, body: { reason: 'CHANGED_MIND' } })
      .willRespondWith({
        status: 409,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/problem+json' },
        body: { code: 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE', status: 409, title: like('Order cannot be cancelled'), issues: [] },
      })
      .executeTest(async (mock) => {
        const err = await cancelOrder(createApi(mock.url), ORDER_ID, 'CHANGED_MIND', 'key-1').catch((e) => e);
        expect(err).toBeInstanceOf(ApiError);
        expect((err as ApiError).code).toBe('ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE');   // the classifier's input (80.6)
      }));
});

The idempotency key header is deliberately not asserted with a fixed value; if the API made it required, a separate interaction asserts that the client sends one ('Idempotency-Key': uuid() in the request headers). The X-Client header is asserted because the API's version metrics rely on it.

Mocks used in component tests (MSW, Part 77) drift from reality in the same way hand-written types do. Two habits keep them honest: build MSW fixtures through the same zod schemas (OrderSummarySchema.parse(fixture) in the fixture module), and generate them from the spec where possible (orval's mock: true, 74.2).

Backend side (NestJS)

Provider verification runs as a Jest test that boots the real Nest application against a test database:

// apps/api/test/pact/orders.provider.pact.spec.ts
import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing';
import type { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Verifier } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { AppModule } from '../../src/app.module';
import { ProblemDetailsFilter } from '../../src/common/problem-details.filter';
import { seedOrder, testAccessToken } from '../fixtures';

describe('orders-api provider verification', () => {
  let app: INestApplication;
  beforeAll(async () => {
    const mod = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] }).compile();
    app = mod.createNestApplication();
    app.useGlobalFilters(new ProblemDetailsFilter());             // same wiring as main.ts, or the errors differ
    await app.listen(0);
  });
  afterAll(() => app.close());

  it('satisfies every selected consumer pact', async () => {
    const ds = app.get(DataSource);
    await new Verifier({
      provider: 'orders-api',
      providerBaseUrl: await app.getUrl(),
      pactBrokerUrl: process.env.PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL,
      pactBrokerToken: process.env.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN,
      providerVersion: process.env.GIT_SHA,
      providerVersionBranch: process.env.GIT_BRANCH,
      publishVerificationResult: process.env.CI === 'true',
      consumerVersionSelectors: [{ mainBranch: true }, { deployedOrReleased: true }],
      enablePending: true,                                        // new pacts warn until first verified
      stateHandlers: {
        'order exists': async (params) => {
          const p = params as { orderId: string; userId: string; status: string };
          await seedOrder(ds, p);                                 // TRUNCATE + INSERT in the test schema
        },
      },
      requestFilter: (req, _res, next) => {                       // authenticate as the state's user
        req.headers.authorization = `Bearer ${testAccessToken('u1')}`;
        next();
      },
    }).verifyProvider();
  }, 120_000);
});

Things the API team owns in this setup:

  • Provider states are an API. Name them for business facts ("order exists" with parameters), keep handlers small, and never let them call external services.
  • Wire the test app like production: global prefix, filters, pipes, interceptors. Otherwise verification checks a different API from the one deployed. Exporting a configureApp(app) function used by both main.ts and tests removes the duplication.
  • Gate deploys. The API's pipeline runs can-i-deploy --pacticipant orders-api --version $GIT_SHA --to-environment production before deploying and record-deployment after.
  • Bi-directional option. If running the provider for verification is impractical, PactFlow's bi-directional contract testing compares consumer pacts with the provider's published OpenAPI spec instead. It is cheaper and weaker: it trusts the spec to match the code, which 74.2's response validation in e2e tests must then guarantee.

The broker commands in CI:

# web pipeline
pnpm --filter web test:pact                                    # writes apps/web/pacts/web-orders-api.json
pact-broker publish apps/web/pacts --consumer-app-version "$GIT_SHA" --branch "$GIT_BRANCH"
pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant web --version "$GIT_SHA" --to-environment production
# ... deploy ...
pact-broker record-deployment --pacticipant web --version "$GIT_SHA" --environment production
pact-broker record-release --pacticipant web --version "$GIT_SHA" --environment production   # old tabs keep it alive
# when version telemetry shows a build has no traffic (80.9)
pact-broker record-support-ended --pacticipant web --version "$OLD_SHA" --environment production

When not to bother: a single web app that lives in the API's monorepo, deploys with it in one pipeline, and has a measured old-tab tail of hours gains little from Pact over shared schemas, a spec diff and the reload nudge of 74.9. Pact earns its broker, its provider states and its extra CI minutes when there are consumers in other repositories, consumers on their own release trains, or consumer versions that must stay supported for weeks.

Production scenario

A food delivery company ran Pact between its web app, two mobile apps, a restaurant tablet app and the orders API: 7 consumers, 112 interactions. Verification took 70 seconds per API pull request. In a year, can-i-deploy blocked 26 API deploys; 19 were genuine breaks for a deployed consumer version (most often a mobile release still in support), and 7 were over-specified pacts that asserted exact values. After a pact review guideline ("type matchers by default, exact values only for codes and enums the UI branches on"), false failures dropped to about one a quarter.

Failure scenario

A web team adopted Pact and published pacts only from main, and the API verified only { mainBranch: true }. A Tuesday API change removed items[].imageUrl, which the web's main branch had stopped using a week earlier. Verification passed. But production still ran the previous web build, which rendered order thumbnails from imageUrl, and the web's own deploy was frozen for a release. Order history showed broken images for 30 hours.
