  • Refreshing on every 401, including 403s and revoked sessions, which creates refresh loops.
  • No single-flight, so ten parallel requests produce ten rotations and a reuse alarm.
  • Relying on setTimeout for proactive refresh in background tabs and sleeping laptops.
  • No grace window on rotation, turning ordinary tab races into "logged out on every device".
  • Logout that clears cookies but not the client cache, leaving the previous user's orders in memory for the next person at a shared computer.
  • Calling "logout everywhere" done after revoking refresh tokens, while access tokens stay valid for 15 more minutes on every API.

Interview questions

  1. How do you prevent multiple tabs from racing on refresh-token rotation? Expected answer: single-flight per tab with a shared promise, across tabs with the Web Locks API, an "already fresh" short circuit on the server, and a short grace window that returns the same child pair. Follow-up: what does the server see without these? (Reuse of a rotated token, which looks like theft.)
  2. What is refresh token reuse detection, and how can it hurt legitimate users? Expected answer: a used token presented again revokes the family; concurrent legitimate refreshes trigger it unless the client serialises and the server allows grace.
  3. How long after "log out everywhere" can a stolen access token still be used, and how do you shorten it? Expected answer: up to its lifetime (15 minutes); an epoch or denylist check in the API makes it immediate, at the cost of a Redis read per request.
  4. Proactive or reactive refresh in a browser? Expected answer: reactive on 401 plus refresh on navigation, optionally on visibilitychange; timers are throttled in background tabs and stop during sleep.
  5. Why does the 401 need a machine-readable reason? Expected answer: the client must distinguish "expired, refresh" from "revoked, log out" without guessing, or it loops or logs users out unnecessarily.
  6. How do you make a mutation safe to retry after a refresh? Expected answer: idempotency key reused on the retry, re-sendable body, retry once only.

Practical exercise

Implement authFetch, AuthBroadcastListener, the grace window and the epoch check.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With three tabs open and the access cookie deleted in DevTools, triggering a refetch in all three produces exactly one rotation in the refresh_tokens table.
  • Replaying a used refresh token from curl 30 seconds after rotation revokes the family and every open tab lands on /login?reason=REFRESH_REUSED within one second.
  • "Log out everywhere" from a phone session makes the laptop's next GET /api/v1/orders return 401 SESSION_REVOKED without a refresh attempt.
  • A checkout submitted 20 minutes after the form was loaded succeeds after one transparent refresh, and the order table contains one order for that idempotency key.

75.4 OIDC for single-page apps: authorization code with PKCE, and why the implicit flow is dead

Concept

Part 40.4 and 40.5 explained OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect from the server's side: the roles, scopes, ID tokens, discovery and the state and nonce checks. This section answers the browser question: when the login is done by an external identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Google), how does a browser app run the flow safely, and who ends up holding the tokens?

The answer in 2026 is the authorization code flow with PKCE for every browser-based client, and the recommended architecture, per the IETF's OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications guidance, is that the browser does not hold the tokens at all: a BFF runs the flow as a confidential client and gives the browser a session cookie. A pure SPA can still run code plus PKCE itself as a public client, with tighter rules on refresh tokens. The implicit flow, which returned tokens directly in the URL, is deprecated by the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (RFC 9700, January 2025) and removed in the OAuth 2.1 draft.

Why does it exist?

Early SPAs could not keep a client secret (anything in a bundle is public, Part 70.6) and could not easily make cross-origin POSTs to a token endpoint before CORS was widespread. The implicit flow worked around both: the authorization server redirected back with #access_token=... in the URL fragment, and JavaScript picked it up. It had four structural problems:

  1. Tokens in the URL end up in browser history, can leak through the Referer header and through analytics scripts that record the full URL, and are visible to every script on the page.
  2. No proof that the token was meant for this client: an attacker could inject a token obtained elsewhere (token injection), because nothing bound the response to the browser that started the flow.
  3. No refresh tokens, so apps "renewed" by loading the authorization server in a hidden iframe with prompt=none, which relied on the identity provider's cookie being sent in a third-party context.
  4. That iframe trick broke when Safari (Intelligent Tracking Prevention) and Firefox (Total Cookie Protection) blocked or partitioned third-party cookies. Chrome still allows them by default after Google abandoned its deprecation plan in 2025, but a login design that fails in two of three engines is not a design.

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) fixed the original reason for implicit: it lets a public client use the code flow safely without a secret.

Mental model

Imagine collecting a parcel from a depot. In the implicit flow, the depot hands your parcel to the courier at your door, who leaves it on the doorstep in full view of the street. In the code flow, the courier leaves a collection slip instead (the code), and you fetch the parcel yourself from the counter (the token endpoint). PKCE adds one more step: before you ordered, you wrote a secret word on a piece of paper and gave the depot only a fingerprint of it (the challenge). At the counter you must show the original paper (the verifier). Someone who steals the collection slip from your doorstep cannot collect the parcel, because they never had the paper.

How it works

The PKCE mechanics, which are the same for an SPA and a BFF:

  1. The client generates a code verifier: a random string of 43 to 128 characters (32 random bytes, base64url-encoded, gives 43).
  2. It computes the code challenge: BASE64URL(SHA-256(verifier)), and sends it with code_challenge_method=S256 in the authorization request, together with a random state (CSRF protection for the callback) and a random nonce (bound into the ID token).
  3. The user signs in at the identity provider, which stores the challenge with the issued authorization code and redirects to the exact registered redirect_uri with ?code=...&state=... (and iss=... when the provider supports RFC 9207, which defends against mix-up between several providers).
  4. The client checks state, then POSTs the code and the verifier to the token endpoint. The provider hashes the verifier, compares it with the stored challenge, and only then returns tokens.
  5. The client validates the ID token (signature, iss, aud, exp, nonce) and creates its session.

The BFF variant, which this volume uses:

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant BFF as NextBFF
    participant IDP as IdentityProvider
    participant API as NestJSAuth
    B->>BFF: GET /api/auth/oidc/start?next=/orders
    BFF->>BFF: create verifier, challenge, state, nonce
    BFF-->>B: 302 to IdP authorize, Set-Cookie oidc transaction
    B->>IDP: GET /authorize with challenge, state, nonce
    IDP-->>B: login page, user signs in
    IDP-->>B: 302 to /api/auth/oidc/callback?code&state
    B->>BFF: GET callback, oidc cookie sent because SameSite Lax
    BFF->>IDP: POST /token with code, verifier, client secret
    IDP-->>BFF: id_token, access_token
    BFF->>API: POST /v1/auth/oidc with id_token
    API-->>BFF: app access token and refresh token
    BFF-->>B: 303 to /orders, Set-Cookie session and refresh

Notice what the browser holds at every step: a transaction cookie for a few minutes, then the same two HttpOnly cookies as a password login (75.2). The identity provider's tokens never reach JavaScript. And NestJS issues the app's own session after verifying the ID token, so password login, Google login and enterprise SSO all end in one session model, one refresh flow (75.3) and one logout.

The choices side by side:

Implicit (dead) SPA with code plus PKCE BFF with code plus PKCE
Client type Public Public Confidential (has a secret or private key)
Tokens visible to JavaScript Yes, in the URL Yes, in memory or storage No
Refresh tokens No Yes, must rotate or be sender-constrained (RFC 9700) Yes, held server-side
Renewal Hidden iframe, broken by cookie blocking Refresh token Refresh token on the server
Works with third-party cookies blocked No Yes Yes
Needs a server No No Yes, the Next.js tier
XSS outcome Token theft Token theft (75.1) Session riding only

Practical example

A B2B ordering platform sells to clinics and hospital groups. Small clinics sign in with email and password; hospital groups require single sign-on with their own Microsoft Entra ID or Okta tenant. The platform's Next.js BFF runs one OIDC client per enterprise tenant (discovered from the issuer URL stored for that customer), and every path ends at NestJS issuing the platform's own token pair. When a hospital group disables an employee in Entra ID, the next refresh at the platform (within 15 minutes) re-checks the identity link and the user's status, and the employee loses access, without the platform holding Entra's refresh tokens at all.

React / Next.js example

The BFF side, with openid-client version 6 (the functional API, built on Web Crypto):

// apps/web/app/api/auth/oidc/start/route.ts  (Next.js 14, Node.js runtime)
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import * as oidc from 'openid-client';
import { getOidcConfig } from '@/lib/oidc.server';
import { safeNextPath } from '@/lib/safe-redirect';
import { sealTransaction } from '@/lib/seal.server';

export async function GET(req: NextRequest) {
  const config = await getOidcConfig();                         // oidc.discovery(...) once, cached per process
  const codeVerifier = oidc.randomPKCECodeVerifier();
  const state = oidc.randomState();
  const nonce = oidc.randomNonce();
  const url = oidc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
    redirect_uri: `${process.env.APP_ORIGIN}/api/auth/oidc/callback`, // exact, registered, never from the request
    scope: 'openid email profile',
    code_challenge: await oidc.calculatePKCECodeChallenge(codeVerifier),
    code_challenge_method: 'S256',
    state,
    nonce,
  });
  const res = NextResponse.redirect(url);
  res.cookies.set(`__Host-oidc-${state.slice(0, 8)}`,           // one cookie per attempt: two tabs do not collide
    await sealTransaction({ codeVerifier, state, nonce, next: safeNextPath(req.nextUrl.searchParams.get('next')) }),
    { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge: 600 });
  return res;
}
// apps/web/app/api/auth/oidc/callback/route.ts
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import * as oidc from 'openid-client';
import { getOidcConfig } from '@/lib/oidc.server';
import { unsealTransaction } from '@/lib/seal.server';
import { setAuthCookies } from '@/lib/auth-cookies';
import { setCsrfCookie } from '@/lib/csrf.server';
import { exchangeIdToken } from '@/lib/auth-api.server';

export async function GET(req: NextRequest) {
  const state = req.nextUrl.searchParams.get('state') ?? '';
  const cookieName = `__Host-oidc-${state.slice(0, 8)}`;
  const tx = await unsealTransaction(req.cookies.get(cookieName)?.value);
  if (!tx || tx.state !== state) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/login?reason=oidc_state', process.env.APP_ORIGIN));

  // Rebuild the callback URL from configuration: behind a proxy, req.url may say http://10.0.3.7:3000.
  const callbackUrl = new URL(`${process.env.APP_ORIGIN}/api/auth/oidc/callback${req.nextUrl.search}`);
  const tokens = await oidc.authorizationCodeGrant(await getOidcConfig(), callbackUrl, {
    pkceCodeVerifier: tx.codeVerifier,
    expectedState: tx.state,
    expectedNonce: tx.nonce,
    idTokenExpected: true,
  });
  const pair = await exchangeIdToken(tokens.id_token!);          // NestJS verifies again and issues the app session
  const res = NextResponse.redirect(new URL(tx.next, process.env.APP_ORIGIN), 303);
  setAuthCookies(res.cookies, pair);                             // same cookies as a password login (81.10)
  setCsrfCookie(res.cookies, pair.sessionId);
  res.cookies.set(cookieName, '', { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/', maxAge: 0 });
  return res;
}

sealTransaction encrypts and authenticates the small transaction object (AES-GCM through Web Crypto, or jose's EncryptJWT) so the verifier is not readable or forgeable by anyone who sees the cookie. safeNextPath is the open-redirect guard from 75.9. If token exchange throws (an expired code, a reused code after the back button), catch it and redirect to /login?reason=oidc_failed rather than showing a stack trace.

For a pure SPA with no server tier (a Vite app on S3, Part 78), use a maintained certified library such as oidc-client-ts, keep its state in sessionStorage rather than localStorage, and require the provider to rotate refresh tokens. The PKCE pieces it does for you are small enough to show:

// What a browser PKCE implementation does internally (Web Crypto, all modern browsers)
function base64url(bytes: Uint8Array): string {
  return btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes)).replace(/\+/g, '-').replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/=+$/, '');
}

export async function createPkcePair(): Promise<{ verifier: string; challenge: string }> {
  const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));             // 43 characters
  const digest = await crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(verifier));
  return { verifier, challenge: base64url(new Uint8Array(digest)) };
}

Never write the whole flow yourself; the validation steps (issuer, audience, nonce, iss response parameter, algorithm allow-lists) are where hand-written clients fail.

Backend side (NestJS)

NestJS turns a verified external identity into the platform's session. Part 40.5 covered account linking rules (never merge accounts by email alone); the endpoint the BFF calls looks like this:

// apps/api/src/auth/oidc.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post, UseGuards, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { BffClientGuard } from './bff-client.guard';
import { IdentityService } from './identity.service';
import { SessionIssuer } from './session-issuer';

const Body_ = z.object({ idToken: z.string().min(20).max(8_000) });
const jwks = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${process.env.IDP_ISSUER}/.well-known/jwks.json`)); // cached, kid-aware

@Controller('v1/auth/oidc')
@UseGuards(BffClientGuard)                                        // only the Next.js tier may call this (81.10)
export class OidcController {
  constructor(private readonly identities: IdentityService, private readonly sessions: SessionIssuer) {}

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(200)
  async exchange(@Body(new ZodValidationPipe(Body_)) body: z.infer<typeof Body_>) {
    const { payload } = await jwtVerify(body.idToken, jwks, {
      issuer: process.env.IDP_ISSUER, audience: process.env.IDP_CLIENT_ID, clockTolerance: 30,
    }).catch(() => { throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'OIDC_TOKEN_INVALID', status: 401, title: 'Sign-in failed' }); });
    const user = await this.identities.findOrLink('idp', String(payload.sub), payload); // (provider, subject) is the key
    if (user.status !== 'active') throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'ACCOUNT_DISABLED', status: 401, title: 'Account disabled' });
    return this.sessions.issueFamily(user, { amr: payload.amr, via: 'oidc' }); // same pair shape as password login
  }
}

Discovery documents publish jwks_uri; read it from discovery rather than assuming the /.well-known/jwks.json path, which differs between providers. Other API-side rules:

  • Register exact redirect URIs, one per environment. No wildcards, no "any path under the domain".
  • Key the user link on (issuer, sub), never on email; email is mutable and, at some providers, unverified.
  • Record amr and acr (how the user authenticated, for example mfa) in the session, so step-up checks (75.5) can require a recent strong login.

Production scenario

A clinic software vendor ran an SPA with oidc-client-ts and silent renew through a hidden iframe, with one-hour access tokens. After a Safari release tightened tracking prevention, 22 % of their users (everyone on Safari, including every iPad at reception desks) were logged out every hour on the hour, mid-appointment. Moving to a Next.js BFF as a confidential client with server-held refresh tokens took six weeks, removed the iframe and its 400 ms renew cost, and made the session behave identically in every browser. The identity provider's token endpoint load dropped too: one refresh per user per 15 minutes from the BFF, instead of one per tab.

Failure scenario

At 10:12 on launch day for enterprise SSO, logins for the first hospital customer failed with "state mismatch" for about one in five staff. The transaction cookie was a single __Host-oidc name. Staff habitually opened the platform in several tabs from a bookmarks bar; each tab, redirected to login, started its own flow and overwrote the shared transaction cookie. Whichever tab finished first succeeded; the others came back with a state that no longer matched.

The fix was the per-attempt cookie name shown above, keyed by a prefix of state, plus a cleanup that deletes stale transaction cookies on success. A second issue appeared the same week: the identity provider was configured for response_mode=form_post, so the callback was a cross-site POST, and the SameSite=Lax transaction cookie was not sent at all. Switching back to the default query response mode fixed it; the alternative, SameSite=None on the transaction cookie, would also have worked but reopens it to cross-site requests.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Back button after the callback replays a used code; the token endpoint returns invalid_grant. Treat it as "already signed in or start again", not an error page.
  • Redirect URI mismatch behind a proxy: building the callback from req.url gives an internal host or http. Always build it from configuration.
  • Clock skew between the identity provider and your servers rejects fresh ID tokens; allow 30 to 60 seconds.
  • Popup-based login breaks when Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin severs window.opener; use same-origin-allow-popups on the page that opens the popup, or use a full redirect.
  • Logout at the provider: clearing your cookies does not end the provider's session, so the next "Sign in" is instant. Use RP-initiated logout (end_session_endpoint, built with oidc.buildEndSessionUrl) when users expect a full sign-out, for example on shared clinic computers.
  • Multiple providers need the iss check on the authorization response, or a mix-up attack can send a code from one provider to another's token endpoint.
  • Embedded webviews (in-app browsers inside social apps) are blocked by Google and others for OAuth; detect and ask the user to open the system browser.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior does not build an identity provider, does not hand-roll the OIDC client, and does not let the identity provider's tokens become the app's session. They use code plus PKCE everywhere, run it in the BFF when there is a server tier, and convert the external identity into the platform's own short session at NestJS, so every login method shares one refresh, revocation and logout path. They check the flow under real browser conditions: Safari with tracking prevention, several tabs, the back button, an IdP clock five seconds off. When a vendor or an old library still offers the implicit flow or a silent-renew iframe as the default, the senior treats that as a reason to choose a different vendor or library.

Common mistakes

  • Using the implicit flow or response_type=id_token token because an old tutorial did.
  • Storing the PKCE verifier in localStorage where it persists after the flow, instead of a short-lived sealed cookie or sessionStorage.
  • Skipping state or nonce because "PKCE covers it"; they protect different things (callback CSRF and ID token replay).
  • Building redirect_uri from the incoming request, which breaks behind proxies and invites host-header tricks.
  • Linking accounts by email across providers.
  • Using the provider's access token as the app session, coupling every API to the provider's token format, lifetime and revocation.

Interview questions

  1. Explain authorization code with PKCE from the browser's point of view. What attack does PKCE stop? Expected answer: verifier and S256 challenge; the code is useless without the verifier, so interception of the redirect does not yield tokens. Follow-up: do state and nonce still matter? (Yes: callback CSRF and ID token binding.)
  2. Why is the implicit flow deprecated? Expected answer: tokens in URLs, no binding to the client, no refresh tokens, silent renew dependent on third-party cookies that browsers now block. RFC 9700 says not to use it.
  3. SPA as public client or BFF as confidential client? Expected answer: BFF when a server tier exists (tokens never reach JavaScript, refresh tokens held server-side); public client only when there is no server, with rotating or sender-constrained refresh tokens.
  4. Why should NestJS issue its own session after OIDC instead of using the IdP's tokens? Expected answer: one session model across login methods, short app-controlled lifetimes, local revocation, and no coupling of every API to the provider.
  5. Users in several tabs get "state mismatch". Why? Expected answer: one shared transaction cookie overwritten by parallel flows; key the transaction by state.
  6. The callback works in Chrome but not when the provider uses form_post. Why? Expected answer: a cross-site POST does not carry SameSite=Lax cookies.

Practical exercise

Add "Sign in with Keycloak" to the Next.js app through the BFF, ending in a NestJS-issued session.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The browser's Network panel never shows an identity-provider token in any response body or URL readable by page JavaScript.
  • Starting sign-in in three tabs at once results in three successful logins, not state mismatches.
  • An ID token with the wrong aud, an expired exp or a mismatched nonce is rejected, each with a distinct error code in the logs.
  • Pressing Back after a successful login lands on a signed-in page, not an error.
  • The resulting cookies are identical in name and attributes to a password login, and POST /api/auth/refresh works the same for both.

75.5 Protecting routes and UI: guards, role-based UI, and why hiding a button is not authorization

Concept

A browser app makes three different kinds of access decision, and only one of them is security:

  1. Route guards decide which pages a user is sent to: a logged-out user on /orders is redirected to /login; a customer on /admin sees "no access". In Next.js that is middleware plus the data access layer (73.9).
  2. Role-based UI decides which controls a user sees: the "Refund" button appears only for support supervisors, "Export" only for finance.
  3. Authorization decides which operations succeed: the API refuses a refund from anyone without the permission, and refuses to show order ord_42 to anyone who does not own it.

The first two are user experience. They keep honest users away from dead ends. The third is the security boundary, and it lives on the server: in NestJS, and in every Next.js Server Action and Route Handler that touches data. Hiding a button is not authorization, because the request the button would have sent can be sent without the button.

Why does it exist?

Everything in the browser is under the user's control. They can open DevTools, edit the React state that says role: 'customer', unhide the button, copy a request as curl from the Network panel, change ord_41 to ord_42, and send it again. In the App Router there is an extra trap: every Server Action is a public HTTP endpoint. Next.js compiles each action into an ID that the client posts to; anyone who can load a page that references the action can find its ID in the JavaScript and call it with any arguments, whether or not the button is rendered for them. Part 40.24 covered broken access control in APIs; this section is about the frontend habits that create it.

Mental model

Imagine a theatre. The usher who shows you to your row is the route guard and the role-based UI: helpful, and wrong seats are rare when ushers are good. The ticket check at the door is authorization. A theatre that removed the ticket check because "the ushers only show people to seats they paid for" would fill up with people who walked past the ushers.

How it works

The layers for one sensitive action, a refund on order ord_42:

flowchart LR
    ui["UI: Refund button shown if can orders refund"] --> sa["Server Action refundOrder"]
    sa --> c1{"requireSession and permission check"}
    c1 -->|"fails"| e1["Error: forbidden"]
    c1 -->|"passes"| api["NestJS POST /v1/orders/ord_42/refunds with user token"]
    api --> g{"JwtAuthGuard, PermissionsGuard, step-up check"}
    g -->|"fails"| e2["401 or 403 problem document"]
    g -->|"passes"| sql["UPDATE in a transaction, scoped by tenant and order"]
  1. The UI asks a question it cannot enforce. The permission list comes from /v1/me (71.3), computed by the server. The client renders <Can permission="orders:refund">. A tampered list only changes what the tampering user sees.
  2. The Server Action checks again, because it is an endpoint. It calls requireSession() and verifies the permission before calling the API, so a forged call fails fast with a clear error.
  3. NestJS decides. It verifies the token, checks the permission from its own data (not from anything the client sent), checks freshness of authentication for high-value actions (step-up), and scopes the query by tenant and owner (40.12).
  4. Step-up authentication asks a signed-in user to prove themselves again for a dangerous action: change email, add a payout account, refund over a threshold. The token carries auth_time (when the user last entered credentials) and amr (how: pwd, otp, hwk). If auth_time is older than five minutes, the API answers 401 with code: 'STEP_UP_REQUIRED', the client shows a re-authentication dialog, and retries. Step-up is the main defence against session riding (75.1): a malicious script can send the request, but cannot type the password.

What the browser must still be told: hide what users cannot do (fewer confusing 403s), and expect 403s anyway (permissions change while a page is open).

Practical example

A food delivery support console has three roles: agent (view orders, add notes), supervisor (refunds up to 50 USD), and finance (any refund, exports). A supervisor's console shows a "Refund" button; an agent's does not. When an agent's role is upgraded at 14:00, their open console still hides the button until /v1/me is refetched (five-minute stale time, or on focus). When a supervisor is downgraded at 14:00, their open console still shows the button until the refetch, and clicking it returns 403 FORBIDDEN, which the UI renders as "You no longer have permission for this action" and refetches /v1/me. Both cases are correct because the server decides.

React / Next.js example

The UI helper, display only:

// apps/web/src/auth/Can.tsx
'use client';
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';
import { useSession } from './SessionProvider';

export function Can({ permission, children, fallback = null }: { permission: string; children: ReactNode; fallback?: ReactNode }) {
  const session = useSession();
  // Display decision only. The Server Action and NestJS check again; this cannot grant anything.
  return <>{session?.permissions.includes(permission) ? children : fallback}</>;
}

The Server Action, which is an endpoint and checks like one:

// apps/web/app/(console)/orders/[id]/actions.ts
'use server';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';
import { requireSession } from '@/lib/session.server';
import { apiServer } from '@/lib/api.server';

const RefundInput = z.object({
  orderId: z.string().regex(/^ord_[A-Za-z0-9]{6,32}$/),
  amountMinor: z.string().regex(/^\d{1,9}$/),            // money as a string of minor units (80.7)
  reason: z.enum(['LATE', 'MISSING_ITEM', 'QUALITY', 'OTHER']),
  idempotencyKey: z.string().uuid(),
});

export async function refundOrder(input: unknown) {
  const session = await requireSession();                    // anyone can POST this action's ID
  if (!session.roles.some((r) => r === 'supervisor' || r === 'finance')) {
    return { ok: false as const, code: 'FORBIDDEN' };        // fail fast; NestJS would refuse anyway
  }
  const data = RefundInput.parse(input);                     // arguments are attacker-controlled too
  const res = await apiServer(session, `/v1/orders/${data.orderId}/refunds`, {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ amountMinor: data.amountMinor, reason: data.reason }),
    headers: { 'Idempotency-Key': data.idempotencyKey },
  });
  if (!res.ok) return { ok: false as const, code: (await res.json()).code as string }; // 403, STEP_UP_REQUIRED, ...
  revalidatePath(`/orders/${data.orderId}`);
  return { ok: true as const };
}

Two habits are visible. The action validates its own input with zod, because its parameters arrive from the network, not from your component. And the role check in the action is coarse (is this user staff at all), while NestJS makes the fine decision (refund limits, tenant, step-up), so the rule lives in one place.

Admin pages follow the same pattern as 73.9: requireSession() plus a role check in the page and in each data function, never only in a layout or in middleware.

Backend side (NestJS)

A permission decorator and guard, using Reflector.createDecorator (NestJS 10):

// apps/api/src/auth/permissions.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable, UnauthorizedException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Reflector } from '@nestjs/core';
import { PermissionService } from './permission.service';

export const RequirePermissions = Reflector.createDecorator<{ all: string[]; stepUpWithinSec?: number }>();

@Injectable()
export class PermissionsGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly reflector: Reflector, private readonly perms: PermissionService) {}

  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const rule = this.reflector.getAllAndOverride(RequirePermissions, [ctx.getHandler(), ctx.getClass()]);
    if (!rule) return true;
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user as { id: string; tenantId: string; authTime?: number };
    const granted = await this.perms.forUser(user.id, user.tenantId);   // server data, cached 60 s in Redis
    if (!rule.all.every((p) => granted.has(p))) {
      throw new ForbiddenException({ code: 'FORBIDDEN', title: 'Not allowed', status: 403 });
    }
    const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
    if (rule.stepUpWithinSec && (!user.authTime || now - user.authTime > rule.stepUpWithinSec)) {
      throw new UnauthorizedException({ code: 'STEP_UP_REQUIRED', title: 'Please confirm it is you', status: 401 });
    }
    return true;
  }
}

// usage on the controller method:
// @RequirePermissions({ all: ['orders:refund'], stepUpWithinSec: 300 })

The JwtStrategy from 75.1 maps the auth_time claim to user.authTime. A step-up 401 is not an expired session, so the guard from 75.3 must not label it UNAUTHENTICATED; authFetch then leaves it to the UI, which opens the re-authentication dialog instead of refreshing. Ownership is enforced in the query itself: UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2, and a zero-row result becomes 404, never "refund someone else's order".

Production scenario

A marketplace's seller dashboard served 40,000 sellers and had 61 Server Actions. A security review generated a list of every action ID from the production build's client manifest and called each one with a logged-in buyer account. Fifty-eight refused correctly through requireSession() plus a role check or through NestJS. Three succeeded: updateStoreHours, toggleListing and replyToReview, which called NestJS with a shared service token instead of the user's token, so NestJS saw "the web tier" and allowed it. The fix replaced the service token with the user's token for all user-initiated actions, and added a CI test that calls every exported action with a buyer session and asserts a refusal. Review time per release went up by about four minutes of CI.

Failure scenario

At 18:40 on a Friday, a merchant posted in a community forum that they could change the delivery fee of other merchants' stores. The store settings page rendered a saveDeliveryFee(storeId, feeMinor) Server Action. The page itself only listed the merchant's own stores, and the form only offered their own store ids. The action checked that a session existed and called PATCH /v1/stores/:id with the merchant's token. NestJS checked stores:write, which every merchant had, but did not check that the store belonged to the caller. Changing storeId in a replayed request was enough. Eleven stores had their fees changed before the endpoint was patched at 19:25 with WHERE id = $1 AND merchant_id = $2.

Nothing in the UI was wrong. The UI only ever showed the right stores. The bug was believing that what the UI offers limits what can be sent.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale permissions in open tabs: the UI shows or hides wrongly until /v1/me refetches; the server is right regardless. Refetch on 403.
  • Client bundles reveal admin code: an admin page's client components ship to anyone who can load the route's JavaScript. That reveals endpoints and action IDs, not data, but never put secrets or hidden "admin mode" switches in them.
  • server-only on modules that hold service credentials makes accidental import into a client component a build error.
  • Feature flags are not permissions: a flag that hides a beta feature from 95 % of users does not stop the other 95 % from calling it.
  • Step-up and session riding: without step-up, an XSS can change the account email and then reset the password, converting session riding into permanent takeover.
  • Prefetched or cached pages: a page rendered for an admin must not be cached in the Full Route Cache or a CDN and served to a customer (73.7, 81.9).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps one rule: the browser asks, the server decides. They use UI checks generously, because hiding impossible actions is good UX, and they never let one replace a server check. They treat Server Actions and Route Handlers as API endpoints with the same review checklist as a NestJS controller: authenticate, validate input, authorise with server data, scope by owner, use the user's token. They put step-up on the handful of actions that turn a stolen session into a stolen account. To a product manager: "The button is the menu; the kitchen still checks the order."

Common mistakes

  • Authorization only in the UI or only in middleware, with an API that trusts the web tier.
  • Treating Server Actions as private functions instead of public endpoints.
  • Calling NestJS with a service token for user actions, which hides the user from the API's authorization.
  • Trusting client-sent role, tenant or owner ids in request bodies.
  • No step-up on email change, password change, payout details and large refunds.

Interview questions

  1. Why is hiding a button not authorization? Expected answer: the request can be crafted without the button; only the server can enforce. Follow-up: what is the UI check for, then? (Usability: avoid dead ends and confusing errors.)
  2. What is special about Server Actions from a security point of view? Expected answer: each is a public POST endpoint addressable by its ID; arguments are untrusted; it must authenticate, validate and authorise itself.
  3. Where do permissions for role-based UI come from? Expected answer: a server-computed list (/v1/me), refreshed on focus and on 403; never decoded from a token and trusted.
  4. What is step-up authentication and which actions need it? Expected answer: fresh re-authentication for high-value actions, checked with auth_time; it blunts session riding and stolen sessions.
  5. How would you test that no Server Action is missing an authorization check? Expected answer: enumerate actions from the build, call each with the least-privileged session, assert refusal in CI.

Practical exercise

Add PermissionsGuard, <Can> and step-up to the refund flow.

Acceptance criteria:

  • An agent session calling the refundOrder action directly (by its ID, with curl) receives FORBIDDEN, and NestJS logs no refund attempt.
  • A supervisor whose last sign-in was 10 minutes ago gets a re-authentication dialog; after entering the password the refund succeeds once, with one idempotency key.
  • Downgrading a supervisor while their console is open results in a 403 on the next click and the button disappearing after the /v1/me refetch.
  • Changing the order id in a replayed request to another tenant's order returns 404.

75.6 CSRF in practice with cookies: SameSite, Fetch Metadata and double-submit

Concept

Part 40.22 explained CSRF: another site makes the victim's browser send a request to yours, and the browser attaches your cookies. This section is about what actually reaches your servers in 2026 and the minimum set of checks that closes the gaps, for this volume's architecture where NestJS accepts the session cookie through the rewrites proxy (75.1) and Next.js has its own Server Actions and Route Handlers.

The modern layered defence has four parts:

  1. SameSite=Lax cookies (75.2), which stop the browser from attaching the session to cross-site POSTs, fetches and iframes.
  2. Fetch Metadata: the Sec-Fetch-Site request header, sent by every current browser, which tells the server whether the request came from the same origin, the same site, another site, or the user typing a URL.
  3. An Origin check against an allow-list, for clients that do not send Fetch Metadata.
  4. A signed double-submit token for the cases the first three miss.

Why does it exist?

SameSite=Lax closed the classic attack but not every variant:

  • Same-site siblings. reviews.shop.example, a staging site, or a subdomain taken over through a dangling DNS record is same-site with shop.example. Cookies are attached; SameSite does nothing.
  • State changes on GET, which Lax sends on top-level navigations.
  • Browsers that do not default to Lax and cookies set without SameSite (75.2).
  • Login CSRF: the attacker logs the victim into the attacker's account. The victim then saves a card or an address into it. No session is needed to attack, so SameSite on the session cookie is irrelevant.
  • "Simple" requests that skip CORS: a cross-site form can POST with Content-Type: text/plain; if your API parses a text/plain body as JSON, the CORS preflight that would have blocked a JSON request never happens.

Mental model

Imagine a company mailroom. SameSite is the rule that letters from outside the building do not get the internal routing stamp. Fetch Metadata is a stamp the postal service adds to every envelope saying "posted from your building", "posted from the business park", or "posted from elsewhere". The Origin check reads the return address. The double-submit token is a code word printed on your own internal stationery, which outsiders have never seen.

How it works

The server-side decision for every request that carries the session cookie:

flowchart TB
    r["Request with session cookie"] --> m{"Method is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS?"}
    m -->|"yes"| ok["Allow, GET must not change state"]
    m -->|"no"| bearer{"Authenticated by Bearer header only?"}
    bearer -->|"yes"| ok2["Allow, not a CSRF vector"]
    bearer -->|"no"| sfs{"Sec-Fetch-Site present?"}
    sfs -->|"same-origin"| tok
    sfs -->|"same-site, cross-site"| deny["403 CSRF_REJECTED"]
    sfs -->|"absent"| org{"Origin in allow-list?"}
    org -->|"no"| deny
    org -->|"yes"| tok{"X-CSRF-Token matches signed cookie and session?"}
    tok -->|"no"| deny
    tok -->|"yes"| allow["Allow"]
  1. Safe methods pass, because they must not change state. That is a contract with yourself; enforce it in review.
  2. Bearer-only requests pass. A browser never attaches an Authorization header to a cross-site request on its own.
  3. Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin is required for cookie-authenticated writes. Note: same-origin, not same-site, so sibling subdomains are rejected. A value of none means the user typed the URL or used a bookmark, which never produces a POST with a body from your UI.
  4. Older clients without Fetch Metadata fall back to the Origin header, compared with an explicit list (https://shop.example). Behind the rewrites proxy, compare Origin with configured origins, not with the Host header, because the proxy changes Host to the API's internal name.
  5. The double-submit token: on login, the BFF sets __Host-csrf, a non-HttpOnly cookie containing a random value plus an HMAC of that value and the session id (sid). Client code reads it and sends it as X-CSRF-Token. The server recomputes the HMAC and compares. An attacker on another site cannot read your cookie, and the __Host- prefix stops a sibling subdomain from planting one.

Next.js specifics. Server Actions accept only POST, and Next.js compares the Origin header with the Host (or X-Forwarded-Host) header and rejects mismatches. If a proxy or a second domain legitimately sits in front, list it in experimental.serverActions.allowedOrigins in next.config.js (the option is still under experimental in Next.js 14 and 15). Route Handlers get no automatic protection: a POST handler that reads cookies needs the same checks as NestJS.

Practical example

The storefront's cookie-authenticated writes are: Server Actions (checkout, address book), Route Handlers under /api/auth (refresh, logout) and /api/bff/*, and NestJS endpoints reached through rewrites at /api/v1/* (cart updates, order cancellation). Each tier applies the decision above. Mobile apps call api.shop.example with Bearer tokens and skip the CSRF check entirely, because they never use the cookie.

React / Next.js example

The client side is one line in authFetch (75.3): attach the token on unsafe methods.

// apps/web/src/api/csrf.ts
export function csrfHeader(method: string = 'GET'): Record<string, string> {
  if (['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS'].includes(method.toUpperCase())) return {};
  const match = document.cookie.match(/(?:^|;\s*)__Host-csrf=([^;]+)/);
  return match ? { 'X-CSRF-Token': decodeURIComponent(match[1]) } : {};
}
// in authFetch: fetch(input, { ...init, credentials: 'include', headers: { ...init.headers, ...csrfHeader(init.method) } })

The Route Handler guard on the Next.js side:

// apps/web/lib/same-origin.server.ts
import 'server-only';

const ALLOWED = new Set((process.env.WEB_ORIGINS ?? '').split(',').filter(Boolean)); // e.g. https://shop.example

export function rejectCrossOrigin(req: Request): Response | null {
  const site = req.headers.get('sec-fetch-site');
  if (site) return site === 'same-origin' ? null : new Response(null, { status: 403 });
  const origin = req.headers.get('origin');                  // older clients without Fetch Metadata
  return origin && ALLOWED.has(origin) ? null : new Response(null, { status: 403 });
}
// usage: export async function POST(req: Request) { const denied = rejectCrossOrigin(req); if (denied) return denied; ... }

The auth endpoints in 75.10 use this guard; the refresh endpoint is the one place where GET must also work (for the navigation path), which is acceptable only because its sole effect is rotating the caller's own tokens and redirecting to a validated relative path.

Backend side (NestJS)

A global guard for cookie-authenticated writes:

// apps/api/src/security/csrf.guard.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, ForbiddenException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';
import type { Request } from 'express';

const SAFE = new Set(['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS']);
const ORIGINS = new Set((process.env.WEB_ORIGINS ?? '').split(','));

@Injectable()
export class CsrfGuard implements CanActivate {
  canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): boolean {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest<Request>();
    if (SAFE.has(req.method)) return true;
    if (!req.cookies?.['__Host-session']) return true;             // Bearer clients: not a CSRF vector
    const site = req.get('sec-fetch-site');
    if (site ? site !== 'same-origin' : !ORIGINS.has(req.get('origin') ?? '')) throw this.reject();
    if (!req.is('application/json') && req.headers['content-length'] !== '0') throw this.reject(); // no text/plain tricks
    const [value, mac] = String(req.get('x-csrf-token') ?? '').split('.');
    const sid = (req.user as { sessionId?: string } | undefined)?.sessionId ?? '';
    if (!value || !mac || !sid) throw this.reject();
    const expected = createHmac('sha256', process.env.CSRF_SECRET!).update(`${sid}.${value}`).digest('base64url');
    const a = Buffer.from(mac), b = Buffer.from(expected);
    if (a.length !== b.length || !timingSafeEqual(a, b)) throw this.reject();
    return true;
  }
  private reject() { return new ForbiddenException({ code: 'CSRF_REJECTED', title: 'Request blocked', status: 403 }); }
}

Register it with APP_GUARD after JwtAuthGuard so req.user.sessionId is available. Webhooks and machine endpoints authenticate differently and never carry the session cookie, so they pass the cookie check naturally. Log every rejection with Sec-Fetch-Site, Origin and the route; a spike right after a frontend deploy is usually a client that stopped sending the token, not an attack.

Production scenario

A retailer with 9,000 cookie-authenticated writes per minute deployed the guard in log-only mode for a week. Rejections that would have happened: 0.03 %, of which most were a partner's embedded widget on deals.shop.example (same-site, cross-origin) that had been posting to the cart API, unknown to the web team, and a browser extension replaying requests. Enforcement went live after the widget moved to its own Bearer-authenticated endpoint. The HMAC check costs about 5 microseconds per request.

Failure scenario

A food platform let restaurants host custom menu pages at <restaurant>.menus.shop.example, with a rich-text editor. A restaurant owner embedded a form that auto-submitted POST /api/v1/me/addresses on shop.example with an attacker's address marked as default. The request was cross-origin but same-site. The session cookie was SameSite=Lax, so the browser attached it. NestJS checked only Origin against a regular expression, /\.shop\.example$/, which matched. Customers who viewed that menu page and then ordered had food delivered to the attacker's address until a customer complained 26 hours later.

The fixes: user-generated pages moved to a separate registrable domain (shopmenus.example), which makes them cross-site; NestJS required Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin and an exact origin list; and the signed double-submit token became mandatory. Any one of the three would have stopped the attack.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Origin matching with regular expressions or endsWith accepts evilshop.example or sibling subdomains. Use an exact set.
  • Origin: null is sent from sandboxed iframes, some redirects and file: pages; never allow it.
  • Login and signup forms need CSRF protection too (login CSRF); use the same Sec-Fetch-Site check and a pre-session token.
  • Logout via GET can be triggered by any <img> on another site; logout is a POST.
  • CORS with credentials: true and a reflected origin turns every site into a trusted caller and defeats all of the above (Part 11.13).
  • Mobile webviews and old browsers may omit Fetch Metadata; the Origin fallback covers them.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior first asks whether the cookie authenticates the request at all; if not, CSRF is not in scope and they say so in the design doc. When it is, they layer cheap checks (SameSite, Sec-Fetch-Site, exact Origin, signed token), put them in one guard per tier rather than per endpoint, and test with a hostile page on a sibling subdomain, which is the case SameSite misses. They treat "user content on a subdomain of our site" as a CSRF and cookie-scoping risk, and move it to its own registrable domain.

Common mistakes

  • Relying on SameSite alone and forgetting same-site siblings and login CSRF.
  • Checking Origin with a suffix match.
  • Unsigned double-submit cookies without the __Host- prefix, which a sibling subdomain can overwrite.
  • Assuming Route Handlers are protected like Server Actions.
  • Accepting text/plain bodies on JSON endpoints.

Interview questions

  1. With SameSite=Lax cookies everywhere, do you still need CSRF tokens? Expected answer: usually yes as defence in depth; Lax misses same-site siblings, GET mutations, login CSRF and browsers without Lax defaults. Follow-up: which single check covers sibling subdomains? (Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin.)
  2. What is Fetch Metadata? Expected answer: Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Dest request headers set by the browser, not scriptable, describing the request's context.
  3. How do Next.js Server Actions defend against CSRF, and what do Route Handlers need? Expected answer: POST only plus Origin versus Host comparison; Route Handlers need explicit checks.
  4. Why must a double-submit cookie be signed and __Host- prefixed? Expected answer: so a sibling subdomain cannot plant a known value, and so the token is bound to the session.
  5. What is login CSRF and why does it matter for a store? Expected answer: victim is signed into the attacker's account and saves payment details or addresses into it.

Practical exercise

Deploy CsrfGuard and rejectCrossOrigin, then attack them.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A hostile page on a sibling subdomain (served locally as evil.shop.test) that auto-posts to /api/v1/me/addresses is rejected with 403 CSRF_REJECTED.
  • A text/plain form post to a JSON endpoint is rejected.
  • The real UI performs every write successfully, verified by an end-to-end test.
  • Mobile-style Bearer requests without cookies pass without a CSRF token.
  • Rejections are logged with route, Sec-Fetch-Site and Origin, and a dashboard shows their rate.

75.7 XSS from the frontend side: React escaping, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, CSP and Trusted Types

Concept

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is attacker-controlled data becoming code in your page. Part 40.21 covered it from the API's side: classify fields as plain or rich text, sanitise rich text with an allow-list, and send CSP as a backstop. This section is about the frontend, where the code actually runs.

React gives you a strong default: text you interpolate in JSX is escaped. <p>{order.note}</p> with a note of <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> renders those characters as text. So XSS in a React app does not come from ordinary rendering; it comes from a short list of sinks, places where a string is turned into HTML, a URL or code:

Sink Example Why it is dangerous
dangerouslySetInnerHTML <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: review.body }} /> Raw HTML, including event handlers
URL attributes <a href={profile.website}> with javascript:alert(1) Runs on click; React 18 only warns in development, React 19 blocks javascript: URLs at render
DOM APIs through refs ref.current.innerHTML = ..., insertAdjacentHTML Bypasses React entirely
Code from strings eval, new Function, setTimeout('...') Executes text
Inline <script> in server rendering JSON-LD built with JSON.stringify(product) </script> in data closes the tag early
Navigation window.location.href = params.get('next') javascript: URLs, and open redirects (75.9)
Libraries Markdown renderers with raw HTML enabled, chart tooltips, rich-text editors They use innerHTML internally

Two browser features turn "we were careful" into "the browser enforces it": Content Security Policy (CSP), which decides which scripts may run, and Trusted Types, which makes the dangerous DOM sinks refuse plain strings.

Why does it exist?

XSS is the attack that defeats almost every other control in this Part. It can ride HttpOnly sessions (75.1), read CSRF tokens from the page (75.6), click hidden buttons and change what the user sees. Escaping by default made XSS rarer, not impossible, and modern apps add sinks constantly: a CMS for marketing banners, markdown in product descriptions, HTML emails previewed in a support console, structured data for SEO. Each one is a place where one forgotten sanitiser call becomes a stored XSS on a page thousands of customers load.

Mental model

Imagine a printing press that sets every customer's text in a glass frame (React escaping): it can be read, never obeyed. dangerouslySetInnerHTML removes the glass for one frame. Sanitising is checking that frame's text before removing the glass. CSP is a rule at the door of the print shop that only staff with today's badge (a nonce) may give instructions. Trusted Types is a rule that the glass can only be removed by one named supervisor who always checks first.

How it works

Sanitise at the sink. When you must render HTML, pass it through an HTML sanitiser such as DOMPurify (version 3) immediately before rendering, with a named configuration. Sanitising on input at the API (40.21) is good; sanitising at the sink is mandatory, because data reaches the browser from more places than one API endpoint.

Validate URLs by scheme. Allow https: and mailto:, perhaps http:; reject everything else, including javascript:, data: and vbscript:. Parse with new URL(); do not use regular expressions on raw strings.

Escape inline JSON. When server-rendering <script type="application/ld+json">, replace < with < so the data can never contain </script>. The Next.js documentation's JSON-LD example does exactly this.

Strict CSP with nonces. A nonce is a random value generated per response. The policy says "only scripts carrying this nonce may run", and 'strict-dynamic' lets those trusted scripts load further chunks. An injected <script> or onerror handler has no nonce and is blocked. In the Next.js App Router, middleware generates the nonce, sets the CSP header, and passes the policy to rendering through a request header; Next.js reads the nonce from it and adds it to its own framework and page scripts.

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant M as Middleware
    participant R as ServerRender
    B->>M: GET /products/espresso-grinder
    M->>M: nonce = random, build CSP with nonce and strict-dynamic
    M->>R: request headers carry CSP and x-nonce
    R->>R: Next.js adds nonce to its script tags
    R-->>B: HTML plus Content-Security-Policy header
    B->>B: run scripts with matching nonce
    B->>B: block injected inline script, send violation report

The cost: a nonce must be different on every response, so every page that uses it is rendered dynamically. Static generation, ISR (73.2) and the Full Route Cache cannot serve a per-request nonce. For a storefront whose product pages are ISR, that is a real tradeoff. Options are a nonce-based policy on dynamic and account pages only, a hash-based policy for static pages (Next.js 15 added experimental Subresource Integrity support, experimental.sri, to generate hashes at build time), or a weaker allow-list policy on cached marketing pages while the strict one protects pages with sessions.

Report first. Ship Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only for two to four weeks, collect violations at a reporting endpoint, fix legitimate ones, then enforce. Part 40.33 showed this rollout for helmet; the browser side is the same.

Trusted Types. With the CSP directive require-trusted-types-for 'script', the browser makes sinks like innerHTML and eval throw when given a plain string. Code must pass a TrustedHTML object created by a named policy (trustedTypes.createPolicy('sanitize', { createHTML: (s) => DOMPurify.sanitize(s) })), and the trusted-types directive lists which policy names may exist. Every sink in the app, including those inside libraries, now goes through a function you can review. Support arrived in Chromium in 2020 and in other engines more recently; check current support before relying on it, and treat it as an enforcement layer that older browsers simply do not apply. Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: require-trusted-types-for 'script' to find every sink.

Practical example

A product page renders: the product name and description (description is markdown from the merchant CMS), customer reviews (plain text), a "visit the maker's website" link (merchant-supplied URL), and JSON-LD for search engines. The name and reviews are plain JSX text. The description is converted from markdown with raw HTML disabled, then sanitised. The website link passes through safeHref. The JSON-LD is escaped. CSP is enforced on account and checkout pages with nonces, and report-only on ISR product pages until the hash-based option is ready.

React / Next.js example

The three helpers every codebase should have exactly once:

// apps/web/src/security/safe-render.tsx
import DOMPurify from 'isomorphic-dompurify';             // DOMPurify that also runs during server rendering

const PROFILE = { USE_PROFILES: { html: true }, FORBID_TAGS: ['style', 'form'], FORBID_ATTR: ['style'] };

export function SafeHtml({ html, className }: { html: string; className?: string }) {
  // The only component allowed to use dangerouslySetInnerHTML; an ESLint rule bans it elsewhere.
  return <div className={className} dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(html, PROFILE) }} />;
}

export function safeHref(raw: string | null | undefined): string | undefined {
  if (!raw) return undefined;
  try {
    const url = new URL(raw, 'https://shop.example');     // relative links resolve against our origin
    return ['https:', 'http:', 'mailto:'].includes(url.protocol) ? url.toString() : undefined;
  } catch {
    return undefined;                                      // unparseable: render no link at all
  }
}

export function JsonLd({ data }: { data: unknown }) {
  // '<' becomes < so a product named "</script><script>..." cannot close the tag.
  const json = JSON.stringify(data).replace(/</g, '\\u003c');
  return <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: json }} />;
}

The CSP helper that middleware calls, following the pattern in the Next.js documentation:

// apps/web/lib/csp.ts  (called from middleware.ts, Next.js 14 Edge runtime; 81.10 shows the caller)
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';

export function withCsp(req: NextRequest): NextResponse {
  const nonce = btoa(crypto.randomUUID());
  const csp = [
    `default-src 'self'`,
    `script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'`,
    `style-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}'`,
    `img-src 'self' https://images.shop.example data:`,
    `connect-src 'self' https://rum.shop.example`,     // where scripts may send data: limits exfiltration
    `frame-ancestors 'none'`,                           // clickjacking (81.9)
    `form-action 'self'`,
    `base-uri 'none'`,
    `object-src 'none'`,
    `report-to csp`,
  ].join('; ');
  const requestHeaders = new Headers(req.headers);
  requestHeaders.set('x-nonce', nonce);
  requestHeaders.set('Content-Security-Policy', csp);  // Next.js reads the nonce from here while rendering
  const res = NextResponse.next({ request: { headers: requestHeaders } });
  res.headers.set('Content-Security-Policy', csp);
  res.headers.set('Reporting-Endpoints', 'csp="https://shop.example/api/csp-reports"');
  return res;
}

A server component that renders its own inline script reads the nonce with headers().get('x-nonce') (in Next.js 15 and later, (await headers()).get('x-nonce')) and passes it to next/script as the nonce prop. The middleware matcher for CSP should skip static files and prefetch requests (the Next.js docs exclude requests carrying the next-router-prefetch header), otherwise every image pays for a nonce it does not use. Add 'unsafe-eval' to script-src only in development, where React's tooling needs it, never in production.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API's part of frontend XSS defence:

  • Send text, not HTML, wherever possible. description as markdown or plain text, with the client choosing how to render it. If the API must send HTML, sanitise it with the same named policy as the client and name the field descriptionHtml, so nobody renders it as text or, worse, renders a text field as HTML.
  • JSON responses with Content-Type: application/json and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so a browser never interprets an API response as an HTML page (40.33).
  • Serve user uploads from another registrable domain (shopusercontent.example) with Content-Disposition: attachment for anything not an image, so an uploaded SVG or HTML file is never same-origin script (74.8, 22.30).
  • Collect CSP reports without letting the collector become a denial-of-service target:
// apps/api/src/security/csp-report.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Header, HttpCode, Logger, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';

@Controller('csp-reports')
export class CspReportController {
  private readonly log = new Logger('CSP');

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(204)
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 30, ttl: 60_000 } })     // per client: reports arrive in bursts from one bad page
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'no-store')
  receive(@Body() body: unknown): void {
    // Reporting API sends an array of { type: 'csp-violation', url, body: { blockedURL, effectiveDirective, ... } }.
    const reports = Array.isArray(body) ? body.slice(0, 20) : [body];
    for (const r of reports as Array<{ url?: string; body?: Record<string, unknown> }>) {
      this.log.warn({ page: r.url, directive: r.body?.effectiveDirective, blocked: r.body?.blockedURL }, 'csp violation');
    }
  }
}

The body parser must accept application/reports+json (Reporting API) and application/csp-report (the older report-uri format) for this route; in Express that is express.json({ type: ['application/json', 'application/reports+json', 'application/csp-report'], limit: '64kb' }). Most violations come from browser extensions; alert on a spike for one page and directive, not on the total.

Production scenario

A fashion retailer with 3 million monthly visitors rolled out a strict nonce CSP on account, cart and checkout pages. Report-only mode produced about 6,000 violations a day: 82 % from browser extensions, 15 % from an old inline A/B test snippet that was moved into a nonced script, and 3 % from a chat widget that injected inline styles and needed style-src adjustments. Enforcement shipped after three weeks. Turning those pages from static to dynamic rendering added 35 ms to median TTFB, which the team accepted for pages that were personalised anyway. Product pages stayed ISR with a report-only policy and a weekly review.

Failure scenario

At 21:10 a search engine's crawler alert showed that product pages for one merchant were redirecting to a gambling site. The merchant had named a product Espresso Cup</script><script src=//cdn-assets.example/x.js></script>. The product page built JSON-LD with JSON.stringify(product) inside dangerouslySetInnerHTML, without escaping <. The string closed the JSON-LD script tag and opened the attacker's. The pages were ISR, so the poisoned HTML was cached at the CDN and served to every visitor, about 41,000 page views in 90 minutes, until the merchant was disabled and the paths revalidated.

The fix was the JsonLd helper above, an ESLint rule (react/no-danger with an exception list of one file), product-name validation at the API (no < or > in names, which no real product needed), and a report-only CSP on product pages, which would have produced violation reports from the first page view.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Markdown with raw HTML enabled (rehype-raw in the remark and rehype ecosystem) silently reintroduces HTML injection.
  • Sanitiser configuration drift: two components with different DOMPurify options. One SafeHtml, one profile.
  • Mutation XSS: HTML that is safe when sanitised but changes meaning when the browser re-parses it; keep DOMPurify current, because its releases fix these.
  • href set through a ref or a third-party link component skips React's URL handling.
  • postMessage handlers that write event.data into the DOM without checking event.origin (75.9).
  • Nonce leakage: a nonce reused across responses (cached HTML) is as good as no nonce; dynamic rendering is the price.
  • CSP in a <meta> tag cannot use frame-ancestors or reporting; send it as a header.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior counts sinks. They keep one sanitised HTML component, one URL helper and one JSON-in-script helper, and enforce them with lint rules, so a reviewer can find every dangerous line with one search. They treat CSP as a project with a report-only phase, accept dynamic rendering where pages hold sessions, and are explicit about which pages run a weaker policy and why. They see Trusted Types as the long-term way to make sinks impossible to misuse, and they adopt it in report-only mode first. And they remember XSS is a full-stack bug: the API decides whether HTML or text crosses the wire.

Common mistakes

  • dangerouslySetInnerHTML "just for line breaks"; use CSS white-space: pre-line instead.
  • Trusting href values from users or merchants without checking the scheme.
  • JSON.stringify into a <script> without escaping <.
  • CSP with 'unsafe-inline' in script-src, which disables its XSS protection.
  • Assuming a static nonce works with ISR or a CDN cache.

Interview questions

  1. React escapes output. How do XSS bugs still happen in React apps? Expected answer: through sinks: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, URL attributes, refs and DOM APIs, inline script during SSR, libraries using innerHTML, navigation to user URLs. Follow-up: how do you find them in a codebase? (Lint rules and a search for the sinks.)
  2. How does a nonce-based CSP with 'strict-dynamic' work, and what does it cost in Next.js? Expected answer: per-response nonce on trusted scripts, which may load more; injected scripts lack it. It forces dynamic rendering, so no static or ISR caching of those pages.
  3. What are Trusted Types? Expected answer: a CSP-enforced mode where DOM sinks accept only typed objects created by named policies, making every sink go through reviewed code.
  4. How would you roll out CSP on an existing storefront? Expected answer: report-only, collect and classify, fix, enforce per page group, keep monitoring.
  5. Why serve user uploads from a separate domain? Expected answer: an uploaded HTML or SVG file on your origin is same-origin script; a separate registrable domain makes it cross-site.

Practical exercise

Add SafeHtml, safeHref, JsonLd and a report-only CSP to the product and account pages.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A product named </script><script>alert(1)</script> renders as text and the JSON-LD stays valid.
  • A merchant website of javascript:alert(1) renders no link.
  • react/no-danger fails the lint for any dangerouslySetInnerHTML outside safe-render.tsx.
  • With the CSP enforced on /account, an inline script injected through DevTools does not run, and a violation report reaches the collector.
  • The account pages' TTFB change after enabling nonces is measured and recorded.

75.8 Third-party scripts, supply-chain risk and Subresource Integrity

Concept

Every script that runs in your page has the same power as your own code: it can read the DOM, including what the user types into the card form; it can ride the session (75.1); it can send data anywhere CSP's connect-src allows. That includes three kinds of code you did not write:

  1. Third-party scripts loaded at runtime from another company's servers: analytics, tag managers, A/B testing, chat, reviews, ads, session replay.
  2. Libraries loaded from public CDNs by URL.
  3. npm dependencies bundled into your own JavaScript, which run in your origin with no separate URL at all.

Supply-chain risk is the chance that one of those is changed by someone hostile: a vendor is breached, a CDN domain changes owner, an npm maintainer's account is phished. Subresource Integrity (SRI) is the browser feature that refuses to run a fetched script whose bytes do not match a hash you published: <script src="..." integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous">.

Why does it exist?

Because it keeps happening. In 2018 attackers modified 22 lines of a JavaScript file on British Airways' site, sending card details typed into the payment page to a look-alike domain; about 400,000 customers were affected and the UK regulator fined the company 20 million GBP. In June 2024 the polyfill.io domain, embedded on more than 100,000 sites, came under new ownership and began serving code that redirected mobile users to scam sites. In September 2025, a phished maintainer account published versions of widely used npm packages (chalk, debug and others, billions of weekly downloads combined) with code that hooked browser fetch and wallet APIs to redirect cryptocurrency payments; any web app that built and deployed during the hours those versions were live shipped the payload in its own bundle. None of these needed a bug in the victim's code.

The payment industry made it a rule: PCI DSS 4.0 requirements 13.4.3 and 11.6.1, mandatory since 31 March 2025, require merchants to inventory and justify every script on payment pages, assure their integrity, and detect unauthorised changes to those pages and their security headers.

Mental model

Imagine your shop's front door has a lock and an alarm. Then you hand keys to the cleaning company, the security firm, the window cleaner and the coffee machine technician. Each is trustworthy, but each has their own keys, their own staff and their own suppliers. SRI is accepting a delivery only if the seal matches the one you recorded. CSP's connect-src is a rule that nothing may leave the shop except through the loading bay you watch. Isolation in an iframe is giving the coffee technician a door to a separate room instead of a key to the shop.

How it works

The trust chain on a typical checkout page:

flowchart LR
    page["shop.example checkout"] --> own["Your bundle: 1,400 npm packages"]
    page --> gtm["Tag manager container"]
    gtm --> a1["Analytics vendor script"]
    gtm --> a2["A/B testing script"]
    gtm --> a3["Marketing pixel added by a campaign manager"]
    page --> chat["Chat widget"]
    chat --> chatdeps["Widget's own CDN and dependencies"]
    page --> pay["Payment provider hosted fields in an iframe"]

Each arrow is a party who can change code that runs on your checkout. The controls, in order of strength:

  1. Remove. Every script on a payment or account page needs an owner and a reason. A tag manager container that marketing can edit without review is an unreviewed deploy pipeline into your checkout; keep it off payment pages.
  2. Isolate. Card entry belongs in the payment provider's hosted fields or hosted page (an iframe on the provider's origin). The card number never exists in your page's DOM, so no script in your page can read it. This is also what keeps most of your stack out of PCI scope.
  3. Pin and verify. For scripts with versioned, immutable URLs, add SRI. If the file changes, the browser refuses to run it and the page loses that feature instead of leaking data. SRI cannot protect "evergreen" URLs that vendors update in place, such as most analytics and tag manager scripts; for those, self-hosting a reviewed copy is the only way to pin.
  4. Contain. A strict CSP limits where scripts can send data (connect-src, img-src, form-action), which is the step every skimmer needs. With 'strict-dynamic', host allow-lists in script-src are ignored by supporting browsers, so connect-src and form-action are your exfiltration controls.
  5. Monitor. CSP reports, a scheduled job that fetches checkout pages and hashes every script, and alerts when a hash or header changes (what PCI 19.6.1 asks for).
  6. Dependency hygiene for the bundled code: commit lockfiles and install with npm ci or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile; delay adoption of brand-new releases (pnpm 10.16 added a minimumReleaseAge setting, and Renovate has an equivalent), so a malicious version is usually caught and pulled before you install it; pnpm 10 no longer runs dependencies' install scripts unless allowed; review lockfile diffs for unexpected new packages; and use npm audit signatures to check registry signatures and provenance.

Practical example

A grocery delivery checkout had 23 scripts. The inventory found: 6 owned by the web team (bundles), 2 required (payment SDK, fraud-detection device fingerprint), 4 analytics, 7 marketing pixels added through the tag manager over three years (two for campaigns that had ended), a chat widget, a heatmap tool, an accessibility overlay and a currency converter nobody remembered. After the review, checkout loaded 9: the bundles, payment hosted fields, the fraud script with SRI on a pinned version, and one self-hosted analytics script. Marketing pixels fired on the order confirmation page instead, after payment. Checkout JavaScript fell from 1.1 MB to 420 KB, and INP improved from 310 ms to 170 ms at p75 (Part 76 — Web Performance).

React / Next.js example

Loading a pinned third-party script with SRI and the CSP nonce:

// apps/web/app/(checkout)/layout.tsx
import Script from 'next/script';
import { headers } from 'next/headers';
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

export default function CheckoutLayout({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const nonce = headers().get('x-nonce') ?? undefined;         // set by the CSP middleware (81.7)
  return (
    <>
      {children}
      <Script
        src="https://cdn.fraudvendor.example/device/4.12.3/device.min.js"   // versioned, immutable URL
        integrity="sha384-8F5r1aYk3cP7mJt0eXk4M0u8m0Q7pD9yHq3o3o8cJYxk7W2tq9f4m1Jb6nYc2Lza" // illustrative; generate with the command below
        crossOrigin="anonymous"                               // required for SRI on cross-origin scripts
        strategy="afterInteractive"
        nonce={nonce}
      />
    </>
  );
}

Generate the hash from the exact file you reviewed, and pin it in code review:

curl -s https://cdn.fraudvendor.example/device/4.12.3/device.min.js \
  | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A

next/script passes integrity, crossOrigin and nonce through to the <script> element. If the vendor changes the file without changing the URL, the browser blocks it and logs an integrity error; your monitoring should treat that as an incident to investigate, not a bug to "fix" by updating the hash without looking at the diff.

For the bundled dependencies, a CI step that fails on unexpected changes:

# .github/workflows/web.yml (excerpt)
- name: Install with the committed lockfile only
  run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
- name: Verify registry signatures and provenance
  run: npm audit signatures
- name: Fail if new packages appeared without review
  run: git diff --exit-code pnpm-lock.yaml

Backend side (NestJS)

The API decides how much of the dangerous work happens in the browser at all:

  • Create payment intents on the server and send the browser only a client secret for the provider's hosted fields. The NestJS service never receives card numbers, and neither does your page's DOM.
  • Keep the CORS allow-list to your own web origins. A vendor domain in Access-Control-Allow-Origin with credentials lets that vendor's scripts, from their own pages, call your API as the user.
  • Collect and alert on CSP reports (75.7) and integrity failures reported by your RUM tool.
  • Rate-limit and anomaly-check sensitive endpoints, because a skimmer that cannot exfiltrate directly may try to change the account email through your own API from inside the page (step-up in 75.5 stops that).
  • Expose a script inventory: a small internal endpoint or a checked-in JSON file listing every allowed third-party script, its owner and hash, which the monitoring job compares with production.

Production scenario

A ticketing site serving 25 million page views a month ran a nightly headless browser job against its five checkout pages, recording every script URL, its SHA-384 and the CSP header. Over a year it raised 31 alerts: 24 were vendors publishing new versions at the same URL (each reviewed and either pinned or moved off checkout), 6 were marketing changes to the tag manager on pages it should not reach, and 1 was an analytics vendor's CDN briefly serving a file with an unexpected 2 KB appended, which the vendor confirmed as a compromise of their build. SRI had already blocked that file in browsers; the job told the team within six hours.

Failure scenario

On a Tuesday at 11:00 a campaign manager added a "conversion booster" pixel to every page through the tag manager. It came from a small vendor. Eight days later, a bank's fraud team contacted the retailer: cards used only on its site were being sold. The pixel's script had been replaced on the vendor's server two days after it was added; the new version read the card form on checkout (the retailer used its own card fields, not hosted fields) and posted the data to an image URL. The CSP allowed img-src * "for marketing". About 12,000 cards were exposed.

The remediation followed the list above: hosted payment fields, no tag manager on checkout, a strict connect-src and img-src, SRI on the remaining pinned scripts, the nightly integrity job, and a written rule that new third-party scripts need security review. The PCI forensic investigation cost more than the year's revenue from the campaign.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • SRI and evergreen URLs: a vendor that updates in place will break your pinned hash; that breakage is the feature working, and the vendor relationship decides whether you self-host.
  • Missing crossorigin="anonymous": SRI on a cross-origin script without CORS fails closed (the script is blocked).
  • Scripts loaded by scripts: SRI on a tag manager does not cover what it loads; CSP and inventory do.
  • Bundled dependency compromise bypasses SRI and CSP entirely, because the code is in your own file from your own origin. Lockfiles, release-age delays and review are the controls.
  • 'strict-dynamic' trusts whatever a nonced script loads, so a compromised nonced loader can load anything; containment is in connect-src.
  • Browser extensions inject scripts outside your control; CSP reports from them are noise to filter, not incidents.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats every third-party script as a production dependency with the access of a senior engineer and no code review. They keep an inventory with owners, keep payment data in provider iframes, pin what can be pinned, contain what cannot with CSP, and monitor what ships. They push back on "just add this tag" with numbers: performance cost, data exposure, PCI scope.
