They know the npm tree is the largest third party of all, and they want lockfile review and a release-age delay in CI before anyone argues about one analytics script.

Common mistakes

  • Tag managers on payment pages, editable by non-engineers.
  • Card fields in your own DOM when the provider offers hosted fields.
  • img-src * or connect-src *, leaving skimmers an open exit.
  • Updating an SRI hash without reviewing why the file changed.
  • Installing without a frozen lockfile in CI, so builds pick up whatever was published an hour ago.

Interview questions

  1. What does Subresource Integrity protect against, and what can it not protect? Expected answer: a modified file at a fixed URL; not evergreen URLs, not scripts loaded by scripts, not bundled npm code. Follow-up: what covers those? (Self-hosting, CSP containment, lockfiles and review.)
  2. How would you reduce the risk of a Magecart-style skimmer on checkout? Expected answer: hosted payment fields, minimal scripts, strict CSP exfiltration directives, SRI, integrity monitoring.
  3. What do PCI DSS 4.0 requirements 13.4.3 and 11.6.1 ask of a web team? Expected answer: inventory and authorise every payment-page script, assure integrity, detect changes to scripts and headers.
  4. How do you defend against a compromised npm package in a frontend bundle? Expected answer: frozen lockfiles, release-age delay, lockfile diff review, signature checks, fewer dependencies.
  5. Why does 'strict-dynamic' change how you think about CSP host allow-lists? Expected answer: supporting browsers ignore host lists in script-src; trust flows from nonced scripts, so exfiltration directives carry the containment.

Practical exercise

Inventory and lock down the checkout page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A checked-in third-party-scripts.json lists every script on checkout with owner, purpose, URL and hash.
  • Card entry uses the provider's hosted fields; searching the checkout DOM for an input with autocomplete="cc-number" finds none in your origin.
  • A pinned script with a deliberately wrong SRI hash is blocked by the browser and reported by monitoring.
  • CI fails when pnpm-lock.yaml changes without being committed, and when a dependency's registry signature is invalid.
  • connect-src and img-src on checkout list only your origins and the payment and fraud vendors.

75.9 Clickjacking, open redirects and other browser-only attacks

Concept

Some attacks exist only because a browser holds a logged-in session while it renders pages from many origins, follows redirects for you, keeps snapshots of pages you left, and lets windows talk to each other. None of them needs a bug in your SQL or your business logic. Each has a small, specific defence that is easy to forget:

Attack What the attacker does Defence
Clickjacking Loads your page in an invisible iframe over a decoy ("Click to win") so the user's click lands on your "Confirm" button Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (plus X-Frame-Options: DENY for very old browsers)
Open redirect Uses your trusted domain to bounce users to a phishing page: shop.example/login?next=https://evil.example Allow only relative paths on your origin; validate with new URL
Reverse tabnabbing A page you opened with target="_blank" uses window.opener to navigate your tab to a fake login rel="noopener noreferrer"; modern browsers imply noopener for target="_blank"
postMessage confusion Another window sends messages your listener trusts Check event.origin against an exact allow-list; validate event.data with a schema
Token leakage through Referer A reset-password URL with a token is sent to third parties as the Referer of the next request Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin site-wide, no-referrer on token pages
Back-button exposure after logout The next person on a shared computer presses Back and sees the previous user's orders from the back/forward cache Cache-Control: no-store on personal pages, re-check the session on pageshow, Clear-Site-Data on logout
Web cache deception Tricks a CDN into caching a personal page by requesting /account/orders/x.css Cache by explicit rules and Cache-Control, never by file extension; private, no-store on personal responses

Why does it exist?

The browser is designed to compose content from many sources: frames, windows, redirects, caches. Each composition feature was built for a legitimate use (embedding a map, a "Continue to your order" redirect after login, fast Back navigation) and each has a hostile use when a session is attached. Phishing in particular loves open redirects, because a link that starts with your real domain passes users' and email filters' checks.

Mental model

Imagine a bank branch. Clickjacking is someone holding a sheet of glass with a painted "Free coffee" button over the teller's "Approve transfer" button. An open redirect is the bank's own receptionist agreeing to escort any visitor to any address they name, including the con man's office across the road. Back-button exposure is leaving yesterday's customer's papers on the counter because the next customer might press the "show me what was here" bell.

How it works

The open redirect, which is the one most teams have somewhere:

sequenceDiagram
    participant V as Victim
    participant E as Email
    participant S as shop.example
    participant P as PhishingSite
    E->>V: Your order is delayed, sign in to see it
    V->>S: GET /login?next=//shop-example-help.example/verify
    S-->>V: login page on the real domain, real TLS padlock
    V->>S: POST credentials, success
    S-->>V: 303 to next, unvalidated
    V->>P: GET /verify on the look-alike domain
    P-->>V: Please re-enter your card to verify delivery

The steps to defend each attack:

  1. Framing: send frame-ancestors 'none' on every HTML response (or 'self' if you frame your own pages). It belongs in the CSP header, not a <meta> tag, which cannot carry it.
  2. Redirect targets: accept only a path that starts with a single /, parse it with new URL(raw, yourOrigin), and require the resulting origin to equal yours. The parser handles the tricks that string checks miss: //evil.example (protocol-relative), /\evil.example (browsers treat \ as /), and tabs or newlines inside the string, which URL parsing strips.
  3. New windows: rely on the implied noopener, and still set rel="noopener noreferrer" on user-supplied links so older browsers and window.open calls behave the same.
  4. Messages: in every message listener, compare event.origin with an exact string, then parse event.data with zod. When sending, always pass a target origin to postMessage, never '*' for anything sensitive.
  5. Logout on shared devices: the back/forward cache (bfcache) keeps a whole page in memory. Browsers have historically skipped bfcache for Cache-Control: no-store pages, and Chrome has been experimenting with relaxing that for pages whose cookies have not changed. So also listen for pageshow with event.persisted === true and re-check the session.

Practical example

A pharmacy delivery site sends "Your prescription is ready" emails linking to /login?next=/orders/ord_9. Its login handler, the OIDC start route (75.4), the refresh redirect (75.3) and the logout handler all accept a next parameter, so all four use one safeNextPath function. The account pages send Cache-Control: private, no-store, logout sends Clear-Site-Data, and every HTML response carries frame-ancestors 'none' from the CSP middleware (75.7). The prescription-upload page opens the pharmacist's help article with target="_blank" and rel="noopener noreferrer".

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/lib/safe-redirect.ts
const ORIGIN = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_ORIGIN ?? 'https://shop.example';

export function safeNextPath(raw: string | null | undefined, fallback = '/'): string {
  if (!raw || !raw.startsWith('/') || raw.startsWith('//') || raw.startsWith('/\\')) return fallback;
  try {
    const url = new URL(raw, ORIGIN);                       // strips tabs and newlines, resolves dot segments
    if (url.origin !== ORIGIN) return fallback;             // catches every remaining trick
    if (url.pathname.startsWith('/api/')) return fallback;  // never bounce into an endpoint
    return `${url.pathname}${url.search}${url.hash}`;
  } catch {
    return fallback;
  }
}
// apps/web/src/auth/BfcacheGuard.tsx
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';

export function BfcacheGuard() {
  useEffect(() => {
    const onShow = async (e: PageTransitionEvent) => {
      if (!e.persisted) return;                              // normal load: the server already checked
      const res = await fetch('/api/v1/me', { credentials: 'include', cache: 'no-store' });
      if (res.status === 401) window.location.replace('/login?reason=signed-out');
    };
    window.addEventListener('pageshow', onShow);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('pageshow', onShow);
  }, []);
  return null;
}

Mount BfcacheGuard in the (account) layout only. A message listener follows the same discipline: if (event.origin !== 'https://pay.provider.example') return; then PaymentEventSchema.safeParse(event.data).

Backend side (NestJS)

The API's share is headers and redirect discipline:

  • Frame protection on the API too. helmet's defaults (40.33) send X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN; set CSP frame-ancestors 'none' for any HTML the API serves (Swagger UI, email previews, OAuth consent pages).
  • No open redirects in the API. Endpoints such as GET /v1/email/click?to=... for tracking links must sign the target (HMAC(to), 40.18) or map an id to a stored URL; never redirect to a raw parameter.
  • Cache-Control: private, no-store on every cookie-authenticated response, and never let a CDN cache by extension. Web cache deception works when the CDN caches /account/orders/x.css because of .css while the origin ignores the suffix and returns the orders page. Configure the CDN to respect origin Cache-Control and make NestJS return 404 for unknown path suffixes.
  • Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin globally, and no-referrer on pages with tokens in the URL (password reset, email verification); the token in those links should be single-use and short-lived anyway.

Production scenario

A marketplace's security team ran a quarterly review of these "small" defences across 140 routes. Findings over a year: 6 open redirects (a returnTo in a promo page, two in legacy login variants, one in a logout GET, two in email click tracking), 2 pages missing frame-ancestors (an embedded seller help page and an old payment confirmation page), and 11 personal pages without no-store. Each fix was a few lines. The open redirects mattered most: the company's brand-protection vendor had linked 4 phishing campaigns to them in the previous year.

Failure scenario

At 08:30 on a Monday the support queue filled with customers saying the site had asked them to "re-verify their card" after signing in. A phishing email had linked to https://shop.example/login?next=/\shop-example-verify.example/card. The login page's check was next.startsWith('/') && !next.startsWith('//'). Browsers normalise \ to / in URLs, so /\host became //host, a protocol-relative URL to the attacker's domain. Customers saw the real login page with the real padlock, signed in successfully, and landed on a perfect copy of the payment page. About 1,900 customers entered card details before the email filter vendor blocked the campaign at 11:10.

The fix was the new URL origin comparison above, applied to every redirect parameter found by a search for next, returnTo, redirect, continue and url in route handlers and pages, plus a unit test table of 25 known bypass strings.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Legitimate framing: a partner widget or your own help centre may need to frame a page; allow exact origins in frame-ancestors, per route.
  • Login popups and COOP: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin breaks popup-based login flows that use window.opener (75.4); use same-origin-allow-popups on the opening page.
  • Redirects after OAuth must carry the next value through the sealed transaction (75.4), not through the provider's redirect URI.
  • Clear-Site-Data is broad: "cookies" clears every cookie for the registrable domain, including consent and A/B cookies, and "cache" can be slow on large caches. Send "storage" on every logout with explicit deletion of the auth cookies, and add "cookies" and "cache" for "this is a shared device" logouts.
  • Double-encoded paths (%2F%2Fevil.example) decode in some frameworks before your check runs; check after decoding, with the URL parser.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps a short list of browser-only attacks and a matching list of defaults: frame-ancestors on every HTML response, one redirect validator, noopener on new windows, origin checks on every message listener, no-store on personal pages, and a logout that clears what the browser keeps. They put each default in one place (middleware, a helper, a layout) so new routes inherit it. When they review a feature with a redirect, a popup, an iframe or a shared-device use case, they ask about these by name, because none of them shows up in an API test.

Common mistakes

  • Validating redirect targets with startsWith('/') alone.
  • Relying on X-Frame-Options only, without frame-ancestors.
  • postMessage(data, '*') with sensitive data, or listeners without an origin check.
  • Personal pages without Cache-Control: no-store, cached by a CDN or shown from bfcache after logout.
  • Logout as a GET link, which any page can trigger with an <img> tag.

Interview questions

  1. How do you prevent clickjacking today? Expected answer: CSP frame-ancestors 'none' or an exact allow-list, sent as a header; X-Frame-Options as a legacy fallback. Follow-up: why not a <meta> CSP? (It cannot carry frame-ancestors.)
  2. How would you validate a next redirect parameter? Expected answer: relative path only, parsed with new URL against your origin, origin equality, reject // and /\, and test known bypasses.
  3. What is reverse tabnabbing and is it still a risk? Expected answer: the opened page controlling window.opener; modern browsers imply noopener for target="_blank", but window.open and old browsers still need it set explicitly.
  4. What can a shared-computer user see after the previous user logged out, and how do you prevent it? Expected answer: bfcache or HTTP-cached personal pages; no-store, pageshow re-check, Clear-Site-Data, clearing client caches.
  5. What is web cache deception? Expected answer: a CDN caching a personal response because of a static-looking suffix; cache by explicit rules and origin headers, and return 404 for unknown suffixes.

Practical exercise

Harden the redirect, framing and logout behaviour of the storefront.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A table-driven test passes for 25 redirect inputs, including //evil.example, /\evil.example, /%2F%2Fevil.example, /\tevil.example and https://evil.example, all resolving to /.
  • Loading /checkout in an iframe on another origin shows a blocked frame in the browser console.
  • After logout, pressing Back on /orders shows the login page, verified in a Playwright test.
  • curl -I https://shop.example/account/orders/x.css returns 404 with Cache-Control: no-store, and the CDN logs show no cache entry for it.

75.10 Worked example: login, refresh and logout for a Next.js app against a NestJS auth service

This example assembles the Part into one flow for the storefront: shop.example (Next.js 14 App Router, the BFF) in front of a NestJS auth service and the NestJS order API, both on an internal network. It replaces the single 15-minute cookie of 73.9 with the full design: the BFF owns the cookies, NestJS issues and rotates tokens, and the browser holds nothing it can read except a CSRF token. Part 79 — Full-Stack Worked Project builds live order tracking on exactly these names and endpoints.

Requirements

  • Sign-in with email and password through a form that works before JavaScript loads (progressive enhancement), with next redirects that cannot leave the site.
  • Lifetimes: access JWT 15 minutes; refresh token 14 days idle, 30 days absolute, rotated on every use with reuse detection and a 20-second grace window.
  • Silent refresh on navigation and on client API calls, one rotation per expiry across tabs.
  • Logout of this browser immediately in every tab; logout everywhere effective on the next API call on any device.
  • Security: no token readable by page JavaScript; CSRF checks on every cookie-authenticated write; CSP with nonces on account pages; login rate-limited per email and per IP.
  • Performance budgets: middleware under 2 ms p95 with no network calls; refresh under 50 ms p95 at the BFF; login under 400 ms p95 (dominated by argon2id).

The flow

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant N as NextBFF
    participant A as NestJSAuth
    participant PG as PostgreSQL
    B->>N: POST login Server Action, email, password, next
    N->>A: POST /v1/auth/login, x-bff-key, x-forwarded-for
    A->>PG: SELECT user, argon2id verify
    A->>PG: INSERT refresh_tokens, new family
    A-->>N: accessToken, refreshToken, sessionId, lifetimes
    N-->>B: 303 to next, Set-Cookie session, refresh, csrf
    B->>N: GET /orders with session cookie
    N->>N: middleware verifies JWT locally, adds CSP nonce
    N->>A: server component fetches with Bearer access token
    A-->>N: orders
    N-->>B: HTML

The lifecycle of one browser session:

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SignedOut
    SignedOut --> Active: login sets cookies
    Active --> AccessExpired: 15 minutes pass
    AccessExpired --> Active: refresh rotates tokens
    AccessExpired --> SignedOut: refresh fails, expired or reused
    Active --> SignedOut: logout in any tab
    Active --> Revoked: logout everywhere on another device
    Revoked --> SignedOut: next API call returns SESSION_REVOKED

The contract

Caller to endpoint Method and path Auth Result
Browser to BFF Server Action login on /login Next.js Origin check 303 to next, three cookies
Browser to BFF GET /api/auth/refresh?next= Refresh cookie 303 to next, or to /login
Browser to BFF POST /api/auth/refresh Refresh cookie, Sec-Fetch-Site 204, or 401 problem with code
Browser to BFF POST /api/auth/logout and /logout-all Cookies, Sec-Fetch-Site 204, cookies cleared
BFF to NestJS POST /v1/auth/login, /refresh, /logout x-bff-key plus internal network Token pair or 401 problem
BFF to NestJS POST /v1/auth/logout-all x-bff-key plus user's Bearer token 204
Browser via rewrites to NestJS /api/v1/* __Host-session cookie, CsrfGuard Resource or 401 with X-Auth-Error

The token pair shape lives in @shop/contracts, so the BFF parses it with zod like any other response (74.1):

// packages/contracts/src/auth.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const TokenPairSchema = z.object({
  accessToken: z.string().max(3_800),            // must fit in a cookie (81.2)
  accessExpiresIn: z.number().int().positive(),  // seconds, 900
  refreshToken: z.string().min(43),              // opaque, 32 random bytes base64url
  refreshExpiresIn: z.number().int().positive(), // seconds, idle lifetime
  sessionId: z.string(),                         // the family id, also the JWT's sid claim
});
export type TokenPair = z.infer<typeof TokenPairSchema>;

Backend: the NestJS auth service

// apps/auth/src/auth/auth.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Header, HttpCode, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { z } from 'zod';
import type { TokenPair } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { BffClientGuard } from './bff-client.guard';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from './jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from './current-user.decorator';
import { LoginService } from './login.service';
import { RefreshService } from './refresh.service';

const Login = z.object({ email: z.string().email().max(254), password: z.string().min(1).max(256) });
const Refresh = z.object({ refreshToken: z.string().min(43).max(128) });

@Controller('v1/auth')
@UseGuards(BffClientGuard)                                  // only the Next.js tier holds the x-bff-key secret
export class AuthController {
  constructor(private readonly login_: LoginService, private readonly refresh_: RefreshService) {}

  @Post('login') @HttpCode(200) @Header('Cache-Control', 'no-store')
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 } })        // per IP; LoginService also limits per email
  login(@Body(new ZodValidationPipe(Login)) b: z.infer<typeof Login>): Promise<TokenPair> {
    return this.login_.login(b.email, b.password);          // generic INVALID_CREDENTIALS, constant-time path (22.25)
  }

  @Post('refresh') @HttpCode(200) @Header('Cache-Control', 'no-store')
  refresh(@Body(new ZodValidationPipe(Refresh)) b: z.infer<typeof Refresh>): Promise<TokenPair> {
    return this.refresh_.rotate(b.refreshToken);            // grace window and reuse detection (81.3)
  }

  @Post('logout') @HttpCode(204)
  logout(@Body(new ZodValidationPipe(Refresh)) b: z.infer<typeof Refresh>): Promise<void> {
    return this.refresh_.revokeFamilyOf(b.refreshToken);     // idempotent: unknown or revoked tokens are fine
  }

  @Post('logout-all') @HttpCode(204) @UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)
  logoutAll(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser): Promise<void> {
    return this.refresh_.logoutEverywhere(user.id);         // all families revoked, auth epoch bumped
  }
}

BffClientGuard compares x-bff-key with the configured secret using timingSafeEqual; the auth service also listens only on an internal load balancer, so the header is a second lock, not the only one. Throttling per IP works because trust proxy is set to exactly one hop and the BFF forwards the browser's address in X-Forwarded-For (73.8). The access JWT carries sub, sid, roles, auth_time, iat, exp, iss and aud: 'shop-web', signed RS256 with a kid, and is checked by assertCookieSafe (75.2) when issued.

Frontend: the login Server Action

// apps/web/app/login/actions.ts
'use server';
import { cookies, headers } from 'next/headers';
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { setAuthCookies } from '@/lib/auth-cookies';
import { setCsrfCookie } from '@/lib/csrf.server';
import { callAuth } from '@/lib/auth-api.server';
import { safeNextPath } from '@/lib/safe-redirect';

const Form = z.object({ email: z.string().email(), password: z.string().min(1), next: z.string().optional() });

export async function login(_prev: { error?: string } | undefined, formData: FormData) {
  const parsed = Form.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
  if (!parsed.success) return { error: 'Enter your email and password.' };
  const clientIp = headers().get('x-forwarded-for')?.split(',')[0]?.trim() ?? '';
  const result = await callAuth('login', { email: parsed.data.email, password: parsed.data.password }, clientIp);
  if (!result.ok) {
    return { error: result.code === 'RATE_LIMITED' ? 'Too many attempts. Try again in a minute.' : 'Email or password is incorrect.' };
  }
  setAuthCookies(cookies(), result.pair);                   // __Host-session and __Secure-refresh (81.2)
  setCsrfCookie(cookies(), result.pair.sessionId);          // __Host-csrf = value.HMAC(sid.value) (81.6)
  redirect(safeNextPath(parsed.data.next, '/orders'));      // 303 after a Server Action; only relative paths
}

The page renders <form action={formAction}> with useFormState(login, undefined) from react-dom (React 19 renames it useActionState and moves it to react), inputs with autoComplete="email" and autoComplete="current-password" so password managers work, and a hidden next field. Without JavaScript, the form posts to the action and the redirect still happens. Server Actions already reject cross-origin posts (75.6), which covers login CSRF. callAuth is a small fetch wrapper: AUTH_API_URL, the x-bff-key header, X-Forwarded-For, AbortSignal.timeout(3_000), TokenPairSchema.parse on success and the problem code on failure.

Frontend: middleware

// apps/web/middleware.ts  (Next.js 14, Edge runtime)
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { createRemoteJWKSet, jwtVerify } from 'jose';
import { withCsp } from './lib/csp';                       // 81.7

const JWKS = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(`${process.env.AUTH_ISSUER}/.well-known/jwks.json`));
const PROTECTED = ['/orders', '/account', '/checkout', '/cart'];

export async function middleware(req: NextRequest) {
  const { pathname, search } = req.nextUrl;
  if (!PROTECTED.some((p) => pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(`${p}/`))) return withCsp(req); // e.g. /login
  const token = req.cookies.get('__Host-session')?.value;
  if (token) {
    try {
      await jwtVerify(token, JWKS, { issuer: process.env.AUTH_ISSUER, audience: 'shop-web', clockTolerance: 5 });
      return withCsp(req);                                 // optimistic check passed; the DAL and NestJS check again
    } catch { /* expired or invalid: refresh below */ }
  }
  if (req.headers.get('next-router-prefetch')) return new NextResponse(null, { status: 204 }); // never rotate for prefetches
  const refresh = new URL('/api/auth/refresh', req.url);
  refresh.searchParams.set('next', `${pathname}${search}`);
  return NextResponse.redirect(refresh, 307);              // the refresh cookie is only sent to /api/auth
}

export const config = { matcher: ['/orders/:path*', '/account/:path*', '/checkout/:path*', '/cart', '/login'] };

Middleware cannot see __Secure-refresh (its Path is /api/auth), so it redirects whenever the session cookie is missing or invalid, and the refresh handler decides between "rotate" and "go to login". Logged-out users on a protected page pay one extra redirect; that is cheaper than sending the refresh token on every request. Static storefront pages are outside the matcher and get their headers (a report-only CSP, frame-ancestors 'none', Referrer-Policy) from headers() in next.config.js.

Frontend: the refresh handler

// apps/web/app/api/auth/refresh/route.ts  (Node.js runtime)
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { REFRESH_COOKIE, SESSION_COOKIE, setAuthCookies, clearAuthCookies } from '@/lib/auth-cookies';
import { secondsLeft } from '@/lib/session.server';
import { callAuth } from '@/lib/auth-api.server';
import { rejectCrossOrigin } from '@/lib/same-origin.server';
import { safeNextPath } from '@/lib/safe-redirect';

export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';
type Outcome = { kind: 'fresh' } | { kind: 'rotated'; pair: Parameters<typeof setAuthCookies>[1] }
  | { kind: 'signed-out'; code: string } | { kind: 'unavailable' };

async function rotate(req: NextRequest): Promise<Outcome> {
  if ((await secondsLeft(req.cookies.get(SESSION_COOKIE)?.value)) > 60) return { kind: 'fresh' }; // another tab won
  const raw = req.cookies.get(REFRESH_COOKIE)?.value;
  if (!raw) return { kind: 'signed-out', code: 'SESSION_EXPIRED' };
  const r = await callAuth('refresh', { refreshToken: raw }, req.headers.get('x-forwarded-for') ?? '');
  if (r.ok) return { kind: 'rotated', pair: r.pair };
  return r.status === 401 ? { kind: 'signed-out', code: r.code } : { kind: 'unavailable' };
}

export async function GET(req: NextRequest) {                // navigation path from middleware
  const next = safeNextPath(req.nextUrl.searchParams.get('next'), '/orders');
  const o = await rotate(req);
  if (o.kind === 'unavailable') return new NextResponse('Sign-in is temporarily unavailable. Retry in a moment.', { status: 503, headers: { 'Retry-After': '5' } });
  const target = o.kind === 'signed-out' ? `/login?reason=${o.code}&next=${encodeURIComponent(next)}` : next;
  const res = NextResponse.redirect(new URL(target, process.env.APP_ORIGIN), 303);
  if (o.kind === 'rotated') setAuthCookies(res.cookies, o.pair);
  if (o.kind === 'signed-out') clearAuthCookies(res.cookies);
  res.headers.set('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
  return res;
}

export async function POST(req: NextRequest) {               // client path from authFetch (81.3)
  const denied = rejectCrossOrigin(req);
  if (denied) return denied;
  const o = await rotate(req);
  if (o.kind === 'unavailable') return NextResponse.json({ code: 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE', status: 503, title: 'Try again' }, { status: 503 });
  if (o.kind === 'signed-out') {
    const res = NextResponse.json({ code: o.code, status: 401, title: 'Signed out' }, { status: 401, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/problem+json' } });
    clearAuthCookies(res.cookies);
    return res;
  }
  const res = new NextResponse(null, { status: 204, headers: { 'Cache-Control': 'no-store' } });
  if (o.kind === 'rotated') setAuthCookies(res.cookies, o.pair);
  return res;
}

secondsLeft verifies the session JWT with the same jose setup as the DAL and returns its remaining lifetime, or 0. The "fresh" short circuit is what makes the Web Locks single-flight in 75.3 produce one rotation instead of one per tab. A 503 from the auth service is not a logout: the user keeps their cookies and retries.

Frontend: logout

// apps/web/app/api/auth/logout/route.ts
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { REFRESH_COOKIE, clearAuthCookies } from '@/lib/auth-cookies';
import { clearCsrfCookie } from '@/lib/csrf.server';
import { callAuth } from '@/lib/auth-api.server';
import { rejectCrossOrigin } from '@/lib/same-origin.server';

export async function POST(req: NextRequest) {
  const denied = rejectCrossOrigin(req);                     // logout is a POST; a GET logout is CSRF-able
  if (denied) return denied;
  const raw = req.cookies.get(REFRESH_COOKIE)?.value;
  if (raw) await callAuth('logout', { refreshToken: raw }, '').catch(() => undefined); // best effort, 1.5 s timeout
  const sharedDevice = req.nextUrl.searchParams.get('device') === 'shared';
  const res = new NextResponse(null, { status: 204 });
  clearAuthCookies(res.cookies);
  clearCsrfCookie(res.cookies);
  res.headers.set('Clear-Site-Data', sharedDevice ? '"cookies", "storage", "cache"' : '"storage"');
  res.headers.set('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
  return res;
}

The client's logout button posts there, then calls queryClient.clear(), posts { type: 'logged-out' } on the auth BroadcastChannel so every other tab runs AuthBroadcastListener (75.3), and navigates with router.replace('/login?reason=signed-out'). "Log out everywhere" posts to /api/auth/logout-all, which calls NestJS with the user's Bearer token first and then does the same cleanup. If the NestJS call fails, the browser is still logged out; the response tells the UI that other devices may stay signed in until their refresh tokens are used, and the UI offers a retry.

Failure drills

Drill Expected behaviour What proves it
Auth service down for 10 minutes Existing sessions keep working until their access tokens expire; refresh returns 503 and navigation shows a retry page; new logins fail with a clear message Synthetic check of /orders stays green for active sessions; no cookies cleared
Laptop wakes with 6 tabs and 12 prefetches One rotation; prefetches get 204; no reuse revocation refresh_tokens shows one child row; reuse counter unchanged
Stolen refresh cookie replayed after the user refreshed Family revoked; attacker and user both signed out; security alert 401 REFRESH_REUSED; audit log entry with both IPs
Signing key rotated (new kid) jose fetches the JWKS once on the unknown kid; no logouts Middleware p95 spike under 50 ms for one request per isolate
Redis down Epoch check fails open for reads with an alert, closed for step-up actions; grace window off, so racing tabs may be signed out Dashboard shows auth_epoch_unavailable; error budget burn measured
Access token grows past 2 KB after a roles change CI fails on assertCookieSafe fixture Red build, not a silent cookie drop
Phishing link with next=/\evil.example Lands on /orders after login The redirect test table (75.9)

Numbers

At the evening peak of 60,000 concurrent sessions: about 67 rotations per second, NestJS refresh p50 6 ms and p95 18 ms, BFF refresh handler p95 31 ms including the internal hop. Middleware JWT verification with a cached JWKS takes about 0.4 ms. Login p95 is 290 ms, of which argon2id is about 70 ms and the rest network and PostgreSQL. The cookies cost about 850 bytes (session) plus 90 bytes (CSRF) on each page and API request, roughly 40 bytes after HTTP/2 header compression. "Logout everywhere" reaches another device's next API call through the Redis epoch check (0.3 ms per request).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps every responsibility in exactly one place: cookie attributes in auth-cookies.ts, rotation in the refresh handler, the decision to refresh in middleware and authFetch, token issuing and revocation in NestJS, redirect validation in safeNextPath. They separate "the auth service is unavailable" from "the user is signed out" everywhere, because conflating them turns a five-minute outage into a mass logout. They test the races (tabs, prefetches, sleep) and the hostile cases (replay, phishing redirects, cross-site posts) as named drills, and they measure rotations, reuse revocations and logout reach, so a frontend change that breaks auth shows up as a graph, not as support tickets.

Practical exercise

Build the flow end to end on the monorepo from Part 70, with a Playwright test suite (Part 77).

Acceptance criteria:

  • With JavaScript disabled, a user can sign in and land on the next page; a next of https://evil.example lands on /orders.
  • No response readable by page JavaScript contains an access or refresh token; document.cookie shows only __Host-csrf.
  • Deleting __Host-session in DevTools and navigating to /orders causes one redirect to /api/auth/refresh and back, with one new row in refresh_tokens.
  • Opening 5 tabs, expiring the session, and focusing all tabs produces one rotation.
  • Logging out in one tab sends the other four to /login within one second, and Back from /login does not show order data.
  • "Log out everywhere" on browser A makes browser B's next GET /api/v1/orders return 401 SESSION_REVOKED, and B lands on /login without a refresh attempt.
  • Stopping the auth service for two minutes does not sign anyone out.

Senior Checklist — Part 75

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain what XSS gets with each token storage option, and why HttpOnly limits theft but not session riding
  • I set session cookies with __Host-, no Domain, Secure, HttpOnly and an explicit SameSite, and I keep tokens under the 4 KB cookie limit
  • I can implement silent refresh with single-flight across tabs, a server-side grace window, and machine-readable 401 reasons
  • I can state how long "logout everywhere" takes in my system and how the auth epoch shortens it
  • I run OIDC as authorization code with PKCE, in a BFF where possible, and convert the external identity into our own session
  • I treat every Server Action and Route Handler as a public endpoint that authenticates, validates and authorises itself
  • I layer SameSite, Sec-Fetch-Site, exact Origin checks and a signed double-submit token on cookie-authenticated writes
  • I can list the XSS sinks in a React app and keep each behind one reviewed helper, with CSP nonces on pages that hold sessions
  • I keep an inventory of third-party scripts, isolate payment fields, pin with SRI where possible and contain the rest with CSP
  • I validate every redirect target with the URL parser and send frame-ancestors, no-store and Clear-Site-Data where they belong

Part 75 — Key Takeaways

  • No token storage defeats XSS; choose what XSS gets, and prefer that the browser holds nothing it can read.
  • The BFF pattern keeps tokens on the server and gives the browser one HttpOnly cookie; CSRF is the price, and it is cheap to pay.
  • __Host- cookies, no Domain, explicit SameSite, small tokens: cookie mistakes fail silently.
  • Refresh is a concurrency problem first: single-flight across tabs, an "already fresh" check, and a short grace window prevent false reuse alarms.
  • Every 401 needs a machine-readable reason, so the client knows whether to refresh, step up or sign out.
  • "Logout everywhere" has a delay; state it, and shorten it with an epoch check where data is sensitive.
  • Authorization code with PKCE is the only browser flow; the implicit flow and silent-renew iframes are gone.
  • The browser asks, the server decides: hidden buttons, route guards and middleware are UX, and every Server Action is an endpoint.
  • SameSite misses same-site siblings and login CSRF; Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin and a signed token close the gaps.
  • React escapes text; XSS lives in a short list of sinks, and CSP nonces cost you static rendering on the pages that use them.
  • Every third-party script and npm package runs with your origin's power; inventory, isolate, pin, contain and monitor.
  • Small browser-only attacks (open redirects, clickjacking, bfcache after logout) each need one default in one place.

Part 76 — Web Performance

Part 42 — Performance Engineering taught you to measure an API with percentiles, find the N+1 query, size the connection pool and keep p99 inside a budget. Part 11 — Networking and HTTP covered compression, HTTP/2 and cache headers; Part 46 — Cloud Architecture (46.3) put a CDN in front of everything; Part 51 — Cost-Aware Engineering priced the bytes. Part 69 — How the Browser Builds a Page then followed one product page from the first byte to interactive and showed you how to read a waterfall. This Part is about changing what you read: how to take a page that real users experience as slow and make it fast, and how to keep it fast after the next twenty deploys.

The backend engineer's instinct is that a page is slow because an API is slow. Sometimes that is true. More often the API answers in 80 ms and the user still waits four seconds, because the image the user is looking at was discovered late, the JavaScript that makes the button work is 900 KB, a third-party script hides the page while it decides which experiment to show, and the server rendered the HTML only after four sequential calls. Each of those has an owner, a number and a fix, and roughly half of them sit on the backend's side of the line. Every section of this Part therefore ends in the same place: what the NestJS API and the Next.js server must send, cache or aggregate so that the browser can be fast.

Stack and versions, as in the rest of the volume: Next.js 14 with the App Router (with notes where 15 and 16 differ), React 18, the web-vitals library v4 (with notes for v5), Lighthouse 12 and Lighthouse CI, current Chrome DevTools, and the NestJS API with @shop/contracts from Parts 73–75. The metrics are the current Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP) and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024; FID appears in this Part only as history. The worked example in 76.12 takes a real-world-shaped product page from a p75 LCP of 4.8 s to under 2.5 s, one measured step at a time, and Part 79 — Full-Stack Worked Project reuses the measurement pipeline and budgets defined here.

76.1 Why frontend performance is revenue

Concept

Web performance is how quickly a page shows the user what they came for, how quickly it responds when they act, and how stable it stays while they read. It is not one number. A page can show a price in 1.2 s and still ignore the "Add to cart" tap for 600 ms; another can be fully interactive and then jump the "Place order" button down by 80 pixels just as the user's thumb lands.

Performance is revenue because every one of those delays and jumps costs a fraction of users. Some leave before the page appears. Some tap twice and get annoyed. Some give up on a slow checkout step. On a storefront doing a million sessions a week, a fraction of a percent is real money, and on a cheap phone over a congested mobile network the fractions are much larger than on the laptop where the page was built.

Why does it exist?

Engineers optimise what they can see. The team that builds a page sees it on a recent MacBook, on office Wi-Fi, with a warm cache and a CDN edge 5 ms away. The median customer of an Indian, Brazilian or Indonesian e-commerce site sees it on a two- to four-year-old Android phone with four slow CPU cores, on a 4G connection whose round-trip time swings between 70 and 400 ms, often with a cold cache. The same JavaScript bundle that parses in 120 ms on the laptop takes 600 to 900 ms on that phone.

Without a discipline of measuring real users, nobody notices. The page "feels fine", the API dashboards are green, the Lighthouse score on the developer's machine is 92, and the conversion rate on mobile is 40% lower than on desktop for reasons the business attributes to "mobile users browse more". Web performance as a practice exists to make that invisible cost visible, attach it to money, and give each team a number it can move.

Mental model

Imagine a shop on a busy street. Customers walk in (navigation). If the door is heavy and the lights take a while to come on (slow first paint), some turn around on the pavement. If the shelves are visible but the shop assistant ignores them for a few seconds when they ask a question (slow interaction), some walk out. If the shelves slide around while they reach for a product (layout shift), they grab the wrong thing and leave annoyed. The shop never sees the people who turned around on the pavement; it only sees fewer sales. Web performance is putting a counter at the door that records how long each customer waited and what they did next.

How it works

The chain from milliseconds to money has four links, and a senior engineer can explain each one.

flowchart LR
    eng["Engineering change: bytes, requests, main-thread work"] --> metric["User-centric metric: LCP, INP, CLS"]
    metric --> behaviour["User behaviour: bounce, add to cart, checkout completion"]
    behaviour --> money["Business outcome: conversion rate, revenue per session"]
    money -->|"justifies"| eng
  1. An engineering change alters bytes on the wire, the number of round trips, server time or main-thread work. You control this.
  2. A user-centric metric measures what the user experiences: when the main content appeared (LCP), how long an interaction took to show a result (INP), how much the layout moved (CLS). These are defined in 76.2 to 76.5.
  3. User behaviour changes with the metric: bounce rate, pages per session, add-to-cart rate, checkout completion. The relationship is not linear. Going from 1.5 s to 1.2 s LCP rarely moves anything measurable; going from 5 s to 2.5 s often does.
  4. The business outcome is conversion rate and revenue per session, which is what the product manager and the finance team understand.

Published case studies give a sense of scale. Treat them as directional, not as promises for your site; most are correlations from the companies' own analysis.

Source What they reported
Deloitte and Google, "Milliseconds Make Millions" (2020) A 0.1 s improvement in mobile site speed went with about 8% higher retail conversion and about 10% higher travel conversion
Vodafone (web.dev case study, 2021) A 31% LCP improvement in an A/B test went with 8% more sales
Google and SOASTA research (2017) As mobile load time grows from 1 s to 3 s, bounce probability rises 32%; to 5 s, 90%
redBus (web.dev case study, 2023) Reducing INP went with roughly 7% higher sales
Akamai retail study (2017) A 100 ms delay in load time went with a conversion drop of up to 7%

The Vodafone result is the most useful kind, because it came from an A/B test: half the traffic got the faster page, so the difference in sales can be attributed to speed rather than to season or marketing. When you argue for performance work inside your own company, aim for the same: a holdout experiment, or at least a before-and-after on the same traffic mix.

The second half of the mechanism is who is slow. Performance problems are not evenly distributed:

  • Network: a 4G connection in a busy city centre often has 100 to 200 ms round-trip time and 2 to 10 Mbps of real throughput, with frequent stalls. Every extra round trip (a redirect, a new origin's handshake, a request chain) costs that RTT again. Part 11.5 explains why bandwidth rarely helps and latency always hurts.
  • CPU: JavaScript is parsed, compiled and executed on the device. A budget Android phone is commonly four to six times slower than a developer laptop at this. 500 KB of compressed JavaScript is roughly 1.5 to 2 MB uncompressed, and on that phone it can mean one to two seconds of main-thread work before the page responds.
  • Memory: low-end phones have 2 to 4 GB of RAM shared with the OS and other apps. Large images and heavy JavaScript heaps cause tab reloads and jank.
  • Cache state: a first-time visitor from a search result or a social link has nothing cached. Those are exactly the users you most want to convert, and they get the slowest experience.

This is why every performance number in this Part is quoted at the 75th percentile of real users on mobile, not at the median on desktop.

Practical example

A food delivery marketplace serves 3.2 million restaurant-menu page views a day, 78% on mobile. Its analytics team segments sessions by the LCP each user experienced on the first page:

LCP bucket (first page)   Share of mobile sessions   Order conversion
under 2.5 s               41%                        7.9%
2.5 s to 4.0 s            34%                        6.6%
over 4.0 s                25%                        4.8%

This table does not prove that speed causes conversion. Users with slow phones may also be users with less spending power, and users in areas with poor networks may have fewer restaurants available. But it frames the opportunity: if the "over 4 s" quarter converted like the middle group, the business would gain about 1.8 points of conversion on a quarter of mobile traffic. The team then runs a real experiment (76.12 shows the steps) to measure the causal part.

React / Next.js example

The first engineering step is to collect the metric per user and join it to behaviour. Part 69.10 showed useReportWebVitals sending raw values. For revenue analysis you also need the dimensions that let analysts segment: the route template (not the full URL), the device class, the connection type, and an id that joins the metric to the analytics session.

// apps/web/src/perf/WebVitalsReporter.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router, rendered once in app/layout.tsx)
'use client';
import { useReportWebVitals } from 'next/web-vitals';
import { usePathname } from 'next/navigation';
import { routeTemplate } from './route-template';           // '/p/trail-runner-gtx' -> '/p/[slug]'

type NetInfo = { effectiveType?: string; saveData?: boolean };

export function WebVitalsReporter({ sessionId, buildId }: { sessionId: string; buildId: string }) {
  const pathname = usePathname();
  useReportWebVitals((metric) => {
    const conn = (navigator as Navigator & { connection?: NetInfo }).connection; // Chromium only
    const body = JSON.stringify({
      name: metric.name,                    // 'LCP' | 'INP' | 'CLS' | 'FCP' | 'TTFB'
      value: Math.round(metric.name === 'CLS' ? metric.value * 1000 : metric.value), // CLS x1000 as an integer
      rating: metric.rating,                // 'good' | 'needs-improvement' | 'poor'
      id: metric.id,                        // unique per page load and metric
      navigationType: metric.navigationType,
      route: routeTemplate(pathname),       // low-cardinality label
      effectiveType: conn?.effectiveType ?? 'unknown',
      deviceMemory: (navigator as Navigator & { deviceMemory?: number }).deviceMemory ?? null,
      sessionId,                            // joins to analytics: conversion per LCP bucket
      buildId,                              // which deploy produced this experience
    });
    // A JSON Blob keeps the Content-Type as application/json, so NestJS parses it (82.11).
    navigator.sendBeacon('/api/v1/rum/vitals', new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' }));
  });
  return null;
}

Three choices are deliberate. The route template keeps the number of distinct values small, so dashboards and Prometheus labels stay cheap (76.11). The buildId lets you see a regression the hour it ships instead of a month later in CrUX. The sessionId is what turns a performance dashboard into a revenue argument.

Backend side (NestJS)

The backend's first job in a revenue conversation is to be measurable on the same timeline as the frontend. Three things make that possible:

  • Server-Timing on HTML and API responses (69.10), so a slow TTFB in the field can be split into "Next.js render", "NestJS product call" and "database" without opening a second tool.
  • A RUM ingestion endpoint that accepts beacons cheaply, validates them, and forwards them to the metrics and analytics pipeline. It must never be on the critical path: it answers 204 No Content without waiting for any downstream write. The full controller is in 76.11.
  • Stable identifiers in responses: the same X-Request-Id the frontend can attach to a slow-interaction report, and a build or deployment id in a response header so RUM data can be grouped by release.

The backend should also expose its own percentiles per route in a way that matches the frontend's segmentation. "p95 of GET /v1/products/:id is 85 ms" is far more useful when a dashboard next to it shows "p75 TTFB of /p/[slug] on mobile is 1.4 s", because the gap between those numbers is the part of the problem the API latency dashboard cannot see.

Production scenario

A fashion retailer with 9 million monthly mobile sessions found that its product listing pages had a p75 LCP of 3.9 s and its checkout a p75 INP of 420 ms. Engineering estimated three sprints of work. The product manager asked what it would earn. The team ran a 50/50 holdout for two weeks on listing pages only, after shipping image resizing and moving a tag manager off the critical path:

                         Control    Faster variant
p75 LCP, mobile          3.9 s      2.4 s
Bounce rate              47.1%      44.0%
Product page views/sess  3.1        3.4
Add-to-cart rate         9.2%       9.8%

The add-to-cart lift of 0.6 points on that traffic was worth about four times the cost of the remaining work over a year. The rest of the roadmap was approved in one meeting, because the argument was in the business's own units.

Failure scenario

At 10:30 on the first day of a summer sale, the marketing team launched a new homepage with an autoplaying hero video, a countdown timer and a personalised banner pulled from a recommendation service. On the office network it looked great. By 13:00 the operations dashboard showed orders 14% below forecast, although sessions were 20% above. Every backend dashboard was green: API p99 at 140 ms, no errors, Redis hit rate 97%.

The RUM dashboard, which nobody had open, told the story. p75 mobile LCP on the homepage had gone from 2.3 s to 6.1 s: the hero video's poster image was 1.4 MB, the recommendation call ran in the server render before any HTML was sent (adding 700 ms of TTFB under sale load), and the countdown's JavaScript ran a 30 ms layout-thrashing update every 100 ms, pushing INP to 650 ms. Users on mid-range phones were leaving the homepage before it rendered. The fix, a static poster at 90 KB, the banner moved behind a <Suspense> boundary so it streamed after the shell, and a CSS-only countdown, went out at 15:40. Orders recovered within the hour.

The postmortem's main action was not technical: the RUM dashboard was added to the launch checklist and to the on-call's sale-day view, with an alert on p75 LCP per top route.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Correlation is not causation. Slow users differ from fast users in device, location and intent. Use A/B tests or before-and-after on stable traffic to claim revenue impact.
  • Survivorship in RUM. Users who leave before the page loads may never send a beacon, so field data can look better than reality. sendBeacon on visibilitychange (which web-vitals uses) catches most, but not users whose browser never ran your script.
  • Bots and synthetic traffic inflate or deflate numbers. Filter known bots, your own monitoring agents and prerender services from RUM.
  • Mix shift. A marketing campaign that brings many new users on cheap phones makes p75 worse with no code change. Segment by device class and connection type before blaming a deploy.
  • Desktop hides mobile. An "all devices" p75 can be good while mobile p75 is poor. Always report mobile separately.
  • Average instead of percentile. A mean LCP of 2.1 s can hide a p75 of 3.4 s. Report p75 for Web Vitals and p95 for internal diagnosis.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior refuses to have the performance conversation in engineering units only. "We cut 400 KB of JavaScript" is a task; "we moved 18% of mobile sessions from poor to good LCP, and in the holdout that segment added to cart 0.6 points more often" is a business result. They set up the measurement before the optimisation, because without a baseline nobody will believe the improvement.

They also know where the leverage is. They look at the slowest quartile on the most valuable routes first: the product page, the listing page and checkout, on mobile. They do not chase a Lighthouse score of 100 on the About page.

To a product manager: "About a quarter of our mobile visitors wait more than four seconds to see the product. Those visitors buy less. We can measure how much less with a two-week experiment, and the fixes are mostly smaller images, less script and a faster server response."

Common mistakes

  • Measuring only on developer hardware and concluding the site is fast.
  • Using the Lighthouse score as the business metric. It is a lab diagnostic with a weighted formula; users and search ranking use field metrics.
  • Reporting averages or all-device numbers that hide the slow mobile tail.
  • Claiming revenue from correlation and losing credibility when a later experiment shows a smaller effect.
  • Treating performance as a one-off project instead of a budget that every change must respect (76.11).

Interview questions

  1. How would you convince a product manager to fund performance work? Expected answer: measure field metrics per route and device, join them to conversion, run a holdout on one route, and present the result in revenue terms. Why it matters: performance work competes with features. Follow-up: what if the experiment shows no effect? (Check that the change actually moved p75 for the affected users and that the metric is the one users feel; some pages are already fast enough.)
  2. Why quote web performance at the 75th percentile on mobile? Expected answer: it reflects the experience of most real users including slower devices and networks, it is the threshold Core Web Vitals use, and mobile is usually both slower and the majority of traffic.
  3. The API p99 is 120 ms but users say the page is slow. What could be happening? Expected answer: client-side waterfalls, late resource discovery, large JavaScript and hydration, render-blocking third parties, sequential server-side calls, uncached HTML. Follow-up: how do you prove it? (Waterfall plus Server-Timing plus RUM attribution.)
  4. What makes low-end devices disproportionately slow? Expected answer: JavaScript parse, compile and execute is CPU-bound and several times slower; memory pressure; the network RTT on mobile multiplies every round trip.
  5. How would you avoid survivorship bias in RUM? Expected answer: send on visibilitychange with sendBeacon, load the reporting snippet early and small, compare beacon counts to server-side page views to measure loss.

Practical exercise

Join performance to behaviour for one high-traffic route you own.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every page load on that route sends LCP, INP and CLS with route template, device memory, effective connection type, build id and analytics session id.
  • A query or dashboard shows conversion (or your route's key action) per LCP bucket (good, needs improvement, poor), for mobile only.
  • The beacon count is compared with server-side page views for the same route and day, and the loss rate is written down.
  • A one-paragraph note to your product manager estimates the opportunity and proposes a holdout experiment to measure the causal part.

76.2 Core Web Vitals: what they are, how they are judged, field vs lab

Concept

Core Web Vitals are three user-centric metrics Google defines and publishes thresholds for, each covering one part of the experience:

Metric Measures Good Needs improvement Poor
LCP, Largest Contentful Paint Loading: when the largest image or text block in the viewport was rendered ≤ 2.5 s 2.5 s to 4.0 s > 4.0 s
INP, Interaction to Next Paint Responsiveness: how long interactions take to produce the next frame, across the whole visit ≤ 200 ms 200 ms to 500 ms > 500 ms
CLS, Cumulative Layout Shift Visual stability: the largest burst of unexpected layout shift ≤ 0.1 0.1 to 0.25 > 0.25

A page passes when the 75th percentile of real page loads is in the "good" range for all three, measured separately for mobile and desktop. Around the core three sit diagnostic metrics that are not Core Web Vitals but explain them: TTFB (time to first byte, "good" at 800 ms or under), FCP (first contentful paint, "good" at 1.8 s or under) and, in the lab only, TBT (total blocking time).

Why does it exist?

Before Core Web Vitals, teams measured onload, "fully loaded", or a synthetic score, none of which matched what users felt. onload waits for every image below the fold and every iframe; a page can be usable long before it or unusable long after. Different tools reported different numbers for the "same" metric.

Core Web Vitals give everyone the same definitions, implemented in the browser itself, with public thresholds. They are also a ranking signal in Google Search (a modest one, as part of "page experience"), which made business stakeholders pay attention. For an engineer the value is simpler: three numbers with a precise meaning that can be measured identically in the field, in DevTools and in CI.

FID, the original responsiveness metric, measured only the input delay of the first interaction. A page could hydrate quickly enough to make the first tap feel fine and then take 700 ms on every filter click. INP replaced it in March 2024 because it covers every interaction and the full time to the next paint.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant inspector with three questions. How long until the food you ordered is on the table (LCP)? When you wave at the waiter during the meal, how long until they visibly respond, judged on almost your worst wait, not your first (INP)? Did the table get moved while you were eating (CLS)? The restaurant passes when three out of four diners would answer "fine" to each question.

How it works

The definitions you need to reason with:

  1. LCP is the render time of the largest image or text block visible in the viewport, reported by the browser through the largest-contentful-paint performance entry. Candidates are <img> elements, <image> inside SVG, <video> poster images (and the first frame of a video in recent Chrome), elements with a CSS background-image loaded through url(), and block-level elements containing text. The browser reports a new candidate whenever a larger one paints, and stops after the first user input (a tap, click or key press; scrolling stops it too). Invisible elements (opacity: 0) and placeholder-like low-entropy images are ignored. Detail in 76.3.
  2. INP observes every click, tap and key press during the visit (not hover or scroll). For each, it measures from the input to the next frame painted after the event handlers ran. The reported INP is the slowest interaction, except that on pages with many interactions one outlier is ignored per 50 interactions, so it approximates a high percentile of that visit's interactions. Detail in 76.4.
  3. CLS sums the layout-shift scores (impact fraction multiplied by distance fraction, 69.5) of shifts not caused by recent user input, groups them into session windows (shifts less than 1 s apart, up to 5 s per window), and reports the worst window. Detail in 76.5.
  4. Field data (real user monitoring, RUM) is collected from real visits. Google's public field dataset is the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX): Chrome users who opted into usage statistics, aggregated over a rolling 28 days, at origin level and for URLs with enough traffic. PageSpeed Insights, Search Console and the CrUX API all read it. Your own RUM (web-vitals or useReportWebVitals) gives you every browser that supports the APIs, real-time, with your own dimensions.
  5. Lab data comes from a controlled run: Lighthouse, WebPageTest or a DevTools Performance recording, on a fixed device profile and network. Lab data is reproducible and debuggable, but it is one load, on one profile, with no real interactions, so it cannot measure INP directly. TBT, the sum of the part of each long task beyond 50 ms between FCP and the page becoming quiet, is the lab proxy for main-thread responsiveness.
flowchart TB
    field["Field data: real users"] --> crux["CrUX: Chrome, 28-day rolling, p75"]
    field --> rum["Your RUM: web-vitals beacons, real-time, your dimensions"]
    lab["Lab data: one controlled load"] --> lh["Lighthouse and PageSpeed lab section"]
    lab --> wpt["WebPageTest: real devices and locations"]
    lab --> dt["DevTools Performance panel"]
    crux --> judge["Core Web Vitals assessment and search signal"]
    rum --> decide["Which route, device and release regressed"]
    lh --> debug["Why it is slow, before it ships"]
    wpt --> debug
    dt --> debug

The two kinds of data answer different questions, and confusing them causes most performance arguments:

Question Use Why not the other
Are real users having a good experience? Field (CrUX, RUM) Lab is one load on one profile
Did yesterday's deploy regress mobile LCP? Your RUM by build id CrUX lags by up to 28 days
Why is this page's LCP slow? Lab (DevTools, WebPageTest) plus RUM attribution Field gives the number, not the trace
Will this pull request make the page slower? Lab in CI (Lighthouse CI, bundle size) Field data does not exist yet
What is our INP? Field only Lab has no real interactions; TBT is a proxy

A good mental check: lab tells you what could happen, field tells you what did happen. When they disagree, field wins, and the lab profile is probably wrong for your users (76.11).

Practical example

A listing page's numbers from the three sources on the same day:

Source                         LCP       INP      CLS     Notes
CrUX, mobile, p75 (28 days)    3.1 s     260 ms   0.04    includes 3 weeks before last fix
Own RUM, mobile, p75 (today)   2.6 s     230 ms   0.03    after the image fix 6 days ago
Lighthouse mobile, one run     3.4 s     n/a      0.00    TBT 610 ms; simulated slow 4G
Developer laptop, DevTools     0.9 s     40 ms    0.00    no throttling, warm cache

All four are "correct". CrUX still averages in the slower weeks. RUM shows the fix working. Lighthouse's simulated profile is slower than the real median user, which is fine for catching regressions. The laptop number is irrelevant to customers. The team reports RUM p75 internally, watches CrUX for the external assessment, and uses Lighthouse in CI for relative changes.

React / Next.js example

useReportWebVitals in Next.js is a thin wrapper over the web-vitals library. When you need attribution, the "why" behind each value, use the library's attribution build directly in a client component:

// apps/web/src/perf/VitalsWithAttribution.tsx  (web-vitals v4; same function names in v5)
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS, onTTFB, onFCP, type Metric } from 'web-vitals/attribution';

function send(metric: Metric, extra: Record<string, unknown>) {
  const body = JSON.stringify({ name: metric.name, value: metric.value, rating: metric.rating,
    id: metric.id, navigationType: metric.navigationType, route: location.pathname, ...extra });
  navigator.sendBeacon('/api/v1/rum/vitals', new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' }));
}

export function VitalsWithAttribution() {
  useEffect(() => {
    onLCP((m) => send(m, {
      lcpTarget: m.attribution.target,                     // CSS selector of the LCP element
      ttfb: m.attribution.timeToFirstByte,                 // the four LCP subparts (82.3)
      loadDelay: m.attribution.resourceLoadDelay,
      loadDuration: m.attribution.resourceLoadDuration,
      renderDelay: m.attribution.elementRenderDelay,
    }));
    onINP((m) => send(m, {
      inpTarget: m.attribution.interactionTarget, type: m.attribution.interactionType,
      inputDelay: m.attribution.inputDelay, processing: m.attribution.processingDuration,
      presentation: m.attribution.presentationDelay, loadState: m.attribution.loadState,
    }));
    onCLS((m) => send(m, { clsTarget: m.attribution.largestShiftTarget, loadState: m.attribution.loadState }));
    onTTFB((m) => send(m, { dns: m.attribution.dnsDuration, conn: m.attribution.connectionDuration }));
    onFCP((m) => send(m, {}));
  }, []);
  return null;
}

Each on* function registers once and calls back when the value is final, typically when the page is hidden (visibilitychange), or on every change if you pass { reportAllChanges: true } for debugging. The attribution build is about 1.5 KB larger than the standard one; on most pages that is a good trade. Note the v4 field names: target, resourceLoadDuration and interactionTarget were renamed from v3's element, resourceLoadTime and eventTarget, and v5 removed onFID entirely. Pin the version in package.json and check the changelog when you upgrade.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API contributes directly to two of the three metrics and indirectly to the third:

  • LCP starts with TTFB. HTML rendered by Next.js waits for whatever NestJS calls the page makes; the API's latency, its cacheability and whether calls can run in parallel all land in the TTFB subpart (76.10).
  • CLS depends on the response shape: image width and height in the product DTO, stable list lengths, predictable banner slots (69.5).
  • INP depends on payload size and shape more than people expect. A 600 KB JSON response that the client parses, normalises and renders into 400 rows costs main-thread time on every filter change.

The API should also make field data trustworthy: answer the RUM beacon with 204 quickly, validate it with the same zod schema the client uses (WebVitalReportSchema in @shop/contracts, 76.11), and record the deployment id so the field can be grouped by release.

Production scenario

A travel booking site's CrUX report in Search Console showed 61% of mobile URLs "poor" on INP, and the SEO team escalated. The engineering team's own RUM, already sending INP with attribution, showed that 80% of poor interactions were on two elements: the date picker and the "Filter by price" slider on the results page. The loadState attribution said 70% of them happened during dom-content-loaded, before hydration had finished, so the interaction waited behind a 900 ms hydration task. Fixing hydration cost (76.7) and debouncing the slider moved p75 INP from 380 ms to 170 ms in their RUM within a week. CrUX caught up 28 days later, and Search Console moved the URLs to "good" a few days after that. The team had told the SEO lead in advance to expect the lag, which saved a week of anxious messages.

Failure scenario

A team set a release gate: "Lighthouse performance score of at least 90 on the product page". For six months every release passed. Then a quarterly CrUX review showed mobile p75 LCP of 3.6 s. The lab runs had been executing from a CI runner in the same AWS region as the origin, with a warm CDN, testing a product with a small hero image. Real users came from three continents, half hit CDN misses because HTML was personalised, and the top-selling products had 2,400-pixel hero images uploaded by merchandisers. The lab gate measured a page nobody visited, under conditions nobody had. The fix was to gate on RUM as well (alert on p75 per route per release) and to make the lab test representative (76.11): a CDN-miss run, the top five products by traffic, and a realistic throttling profile.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Browser support. LCP and INP are reported by Chromium-based browsers; Firefox supports LCP and, more recently, the Event Timing API needed for INP; Safari has been adding support behind the others. Your RUM numbers are therefore Chromium-heavy. CrUX is Chrome-only by definition.
  • Back/forward cache restores are page loads to the user but do not run your page scripts again. web-vitals reports them with navigationType: 'back-forward-cache' and a near-zero LCP; segment or you will think the site got faster when bfcache eligibility improved (76.9).
  • Prerendered pages (Speculation Rules, 76.6) report metrics relative to activation, not to the start of the hidden prerender. navigationType: 'prerender' distinguishes them.
  • Soft navigations in single-page apps (client-side route changes) are not page loads; LCP and CLS are attributed to the first page of the visit and INP accumulates across all routes. Chrome has an experimental soft-navigation API; until it ships, attribute interactions to the route that was active when they happened.
  • Long-lived tabs accumulate CLS and INP for hours. A dashboard opened all day will report its worst interaction from the afternoon.
  • Iframes: LCP and CLS inside cross-origin iframes are not visible to the parent page's APIs, though CrUX includes some of their effect.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats the three metrics as a contract with users and the diagnostic metrics as the tools to meet it. They state the target in the standard form ("p75 mobile LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 on the product, listing and checkout routes") and refuse vaguer goals like "make it faster". They know which data answers which question and do not let a lab score stand in for user experience, or a field number stand in for a diagnosis.

They are also honest about what Core Web Vitals do not cover: they say nothing about whether checkout's API errors, whether search results are relevant, or whether a skeleton screen is shown for nine seconds before real data arrives. Product-specific metrics ("time to first product price", "time until cart count is accurate") belong next to them, measured with performance.mark and sent through the same pipeline.

Common mistakes

  • Still talking about FID or tools that report it; it is no longer a Core Web Vital.
  • Treating Lighthouse as field data, or expecting Lighthouse to report INP.
  • Reading CrUX the day after a fix and concluding it did not work.
  • Mixing mobile and desktop in one percentile.
  • Ignoring navigation type, so bfcache and prerender loads distort the numbers.
  • Sending the full URL as a label, which explodes metrics cardinality and leaks query strings with personal data.

Interview questions

  1. Name the Core Web Vitals and their "good" thresholds. Expected answer: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, at the 75th percentile of page loads, mobile and desktop separately. Follow-up: why did INP replace FID? (FID measured only the first interaction's input delay; INP covers all interactions and the full time to next paint.)
  2. What is the difference between field and lab data, and when do you use each? Expected answer: field is real users, the source of truth for experience; lab is controlled and reproducible, used for diagnosis and pre-release checks.
  3. Why can't Lighthouse measure INP, and what does it use instead? Expected answer: no real user interactions in a page load test; TBT measures long-task blocking during load as a proxy. Follow-up: when do TBT and INP disagree? (INP from interactions long after load, or slow event handlers that do not show in load-time tasks.)
  4. Your CrUX LCP did not improve a week after a fix that your RUM shows working. Why? Expected answer: CrUX is a 28-day rolling window; it includes the old days. Also check that CrUX's population (Chrome, opted in) matches.
  5. Which elements can be the LCP element? Expected answer: images, SVG images, video posters or first frames, CSS background images, block-level text. Not invisible elements or low-entropy placeholders; reporting stops at first input.
  6. How would you get attribution for a poor INP from real users? Expected answer: the web-vitals/attribution build: interaction target, type, the three phases, load state and long animation frame entries.

Practical exercise

Build a "three sources" view for one route.

Acceptance criteria:

  • You pull the route's (or origin's) CrUX p75 for mobile from PageSpeed Insights or the CrUX API.
  • Your own RUM reports p75 LCP, INP and CLS for the same route on mobile for the last 7 days, excluding back-forward-cache and prerender navigations.
  • A Lighthouse mobile run and a DevTools recording with CPU and network throttling are recorded for the same URL.
  • A short note explains every difference between the four sets of numbers.

76.3 LCP: the four subparts and what moves each

Concept

LCP is one number, but it is the sum of four consecutive stages, and each stage has different owners and different fixes. Chrome's own guidance names them the LCP subparts:

  1. Time to first byte (TTFB): from the start of navigation until the first byte of HTML arrives. Redirects, DNS, TCP, TLS, CDN, server rendering and API calls all live here.
  2. Resource load delay: from TTFB until the browser starts fetching the LCP resource (usually an image). Zero for a text LCP element.
  3. Resource load duration: how long the LCP resource takes to download.
  4. Element render delay: from the end of the download until the element is actually painted. Render-blocking CSS, fonts, scripts that hide the page, and main-thread work all live here.

Optimising LCP without knowing which subpart dominates is guessing.

Why does it exist?

"LCP is 4.2 s" tells you nothing about what to do. Teams used to respond with a generic list: compress images, add a CDN, minify JavaScript. Sometimes that worked. Often the real problem was that the hero image was not in the HTML at all and only started downloading after 1.5 s of JavaScript, and shrinking it from 200 KB to 100 KB saved 150 ms of a 2,000 ms delay. The subpart breakdown exists so that each fix is aimed at the stage that is actually slow.

Mental model

Imagine ordering a pizza for delivery. TTFB is how long the shop takes to answer the phone and confirm the order. Load delay is how long until the driver actually leaves; perhaps the order sat on the counter because nobody saw the ticket. Load duration is the drive. Render delay is the time between the driver arriving and you eating: finding your keys, the dog in the way, a neighbour who insists on chatting. Buying a faster scooter only helps the drive.

How it works

flowchart LR
    nav["Navigation start"] --> ttfb["TTFB: redirects, connection, server, API calls"]
    ttfb --> delay["Load delay: until the LCP image request starts"]
    delay --> dur["Load duration: image download"]
    dur --> render["Render delay: until the element paints"]
    render --> lcp["LCP"]

The healthy shape, from Chrome's published guidance, is roughly 40% TTFB, under 10% load delay, about 40% load duration and under 10% render delay. A 2.5 s LCP budget therefore looks like about 1,000 ms TTFB, 250 ms delay, 1,000 ms download, 250 ms render. The two "delay" subparts should be close to zero; when they are large, the page is doing something wrong rather than doing something hard.

What moves each subpart:

Subpart Common causes when large Fixes
TTFB Redirect chains, CDN miss on dynamic HTML, sequential server-side API calls, cold serverless starts, no connection reuse to the origin Cache HTML at the CDN (ISR, static), parallelise or aggregate calls (76.10), stream the shell first (73.2), remove redirects, keep connections warm
Load delay LCP image injected by client JavaScript, set as a CSS background, lazy-loaded, on a new origin without preconnect, low default image priority Put the <img> in server HTML, fetchpriority="high", never loading="lazy" on it, serve from the same origin or preconnect (69.3)
Load duration Oversized image, wrong format, no responsive variants, bandwidth shared with large scripts AVIF or WebP, srcset and sizes, image CDN, fewer competing high-priority downloads (76.8)
Render delay Render-blocking CSS or sync scripts, web fonts blocking text, anti-flicker A/B snippets that hide the page, LCP element hidden until hydration, long main-thread tasks Inline or split critical CSS, font-display and fallback metrics, remove hiding snippets, render the element in HTML, break up long tasks (76.6, 76.7)

Two rules decide most cases:

  • The LCP resource must be discoverable from the HTML. The preload scanner (69.1) reads raw HTML bytes. If the image URL is only known after JavaScript runs, load delay includes the whole script download, parse, execution and often a data fetch.
  • The LCP element must not depend on JavaScript to become visible. If a carousel renders its first slide only after hydration, render delay includes hydration, even when the image downloaded early.

Practical example

RUM attribution for a product page, mobile, p75 of each subpart over a week:

Subpart              p75        Share   Verdict
TTFB                 1,320 ms   33%     high for a CDN-cacheable page
Resource load delay  1,410 ms   35%     should be under 10%: image found late
Resource load dur.     820 ms   20%     image is 290 KB JPEG at 1600 px
Element render delay   480 ms   12%     web font blocks the caption overlay
LCP (p75, measured)  3,980 ms

(The p75 of each subpart does not add up exactly to the p75 of LCP, because different page loads are at the 75th percentile for different subparts. The proportions are still the right guide.)

The biggest subpart is load delay, and the lcpTarget attribution says div.gallery > div.swiper-slide-active > img. The gallery is a client component; the image URL arrives in a JSON response after hydration. Image compression alone would cut at most a few hundred milliseconds. Making the first image part of the server HTML removes over a second.

React / Next.js example

Render the first gallery image as a server component with next/image, and let the interactive carousel take over after hydration:

// apps/web/app/p/[slug]/ProductHero.tsx  (server component, Next.js 14)
import Image from 'next/image';
import { GalleryCarousel } from './GalleryCarousel';            // 'use client' component
import type { ProductView } from '@shop/contracts';

export function ProductHero({ product }: { product: ProductView }) {
  const [first, ...rest] = product.images;                       // ordered by the API
  return (
    <div className="hero" style={{ aspectRatio: `${first.width} / ${first.height}` }}>
      {/* In the server HTML: the preload scanner sees it, no JavaScript needed to show it. */}
      <Image
        src={first.url}
