        alt={first.alt}
        width={first.width}
        height={first.height}
        priority                     // adds a preload link and fetchpriority="high", disables lazy loading
        sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw"                   // phones download a ~750 px variant
      />
      {/* Hydrates later; it reuses the first slide and adds the rest. */}
      <GalleryCarousel images={rest} />
    </div>
  );
}

In Next.js 16 the priority prop is deprecated in favour of preload (plus fetchPriority="high" and loading="eager" when you want them separately); the intent is the same. Check the rendered HTML with View Source, not the Elements panel: the <img> has fetchpriority="high" and no loading="lazy", and exactly one <link rel="preload" as="image"> matches its imagesrcset and imagesizes. A second preload with a different URL means a double download.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API decides two of the four subparts more than any frontend code does.

// apps/api/src/catalog/dto/product-image.dto.ts
import { Expose } from 'class-transformer';

export class ProductImageDto {
  @Expose() url!: string;      // image CDN URL without size params; the frontend loader adds w= and format
  @Expose() width!: number;    // intrinsic pixels, so the page reserves space (CLS) and picks srcset widths
  @Expose() height!: number;
  @Expose() alt!: string;      // required for accessibility (75.9); never empty for the hero
  @Expose() position!: number; // 0 is the hero: the frontend must not guess which image is the LCP
}
  • TTFB: the product endpoint must be fast and cacheable. If the page is ISR or statically rendered, the API's latency moves out of the user's path entirely; if the page is dynamic, every millisecond of the slowest sequential call is in every user's LCP (76.10).
  • Discoverability: return the hero image in the main product response, first, with dimensions. A separate GET /v1/products/:id/media that the client fetches after hydration guarantees a large load delay.
  • Image bytes: store originals, serve variants from an image CDN or the Next.js image optimiser, and reject 6,000-pixel uploads at ingestion or resize them then. A merchandising tool that lets 4 MB images through is an LCP bug in the backend.

Production scenario

An electronics retailer moved its product page from a client-rendered React app to the Next.js App Router, and p75 LCP improved only from 4.1 s to 3.4 s. Attribution showed load delay at 1.1 s: the old <ProductGallery> client component read the selected colour from the URL hash, which the server never sees, so it rendered no image. Moving the colour to a ?colour= search parameter let the server render the right hero. Load delay fell to 90 ms and p75 LCP to 2.2 s.

Failure scenario

At 11:00 after a routine design-system upgrade, a listing page's p75 LCP alert fired: 2.1 s to 3.7 s for builds after web@4.18.0. Nothing in the listing code had changed. The new version of the shared <ProductCard> component set loading="lazy" on every image by default, "for performance". The first two cards in the viewport were the LCP candidates; lazy images are not fetched until layout confirms they are near the viewport, so their requests started after layout, at low priority, behind 300 KB of JavaScript. The fix was a priority prop on the first row of cards and a lint rule rejecting lazy loading on the first N items of any list rendered by a server component. Default-lazy is right below the fold and wrong above it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The LCP element differs by viewport. On desktop it might be the hero image; on a narrow phone, a long product title paragraph. Check attribution per device class.
  • Text LCP waits for fonts. If the font blocks text rendering (font-display: block or a slow font with no fallback), render delay grows (76.8).
  • Background images in CSS are invisible to the preload scanner until the CSS is parsed and the element is styled.
  • Cookie consent banners can become the LCP element when they are the largest text block. That is "fine" for the metric and bad for the product; check what the element actually is.
  • Video heroes: the poster image is the candidate; make it small and preloaded, and do not autoplay a multi-megabyte video on mobile data.
  • Redirects (http to https, example.com to www, /p/123 to /p/123-slug) each add a round trip to TTFB, often 100 to 300 ms on mobile.
  • A/B testing on the client: swapping the hero after load creates a new, later LCP candidate.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior asks one question first: "Which subpart is biggest, on mobile, at p75, for this route?" Then they ask who owns it. TTFB belongs to the server, CDN and API teams together. Load delay is almost always a rendering architecture issue: the element is not in the HTML. Load duration is image pipeline work. Render delay is CSS, fonts, third parties and main-thread work. They refuse to approve "optimise images" as the first task when attribution says the image request starts 1.4 s after the HTML.

They also budget LCP the way they budget an API: a number per route, broken into the four subparts, with the API's share written down. "The product page gets 600 ms of TTFB on a CDN miss, of which the NestJS product call may use 150 ms" is a requirement a backend team can design to.

Common mistakes

  • Optimising image bytes when the problem is discovery.
  • Rendering the hero through a client-only carousel or a CSS background.
  • Lazy-loading the LCP image, often through a component default.
  • More than one fetchpriority="high" or preloads for images that are not the LCP element, which compete for bandwidth.
  • Ignoring TTFB on "fast" APIs whose calls are sequential or uncached in the server render.

Interview questions

  1. What are the four LCP subparts? Expected answer: TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration, element render delay. Why it matters: each needs a different fix. Follow-up: what are healthy proportions? (Roughly 40/10/40/10, with both delays near zero.)
  2. Your LCP image downloads quickly but LCP is late. Where do you look? Expected answer: render delay: render-blocking CSS, fonts, scripts hiding the page, the element waiting for hydration, long tasks.
  3. Why does a client-rendered carousel hurt LCP even if its images are small? Expected answer: the image URL is unknown to the preload scanner; the request waits for JavaScript and often a data fetch; the slide may only become visible after hydration.
  4. What can the backend change to improve LCP without touching frontend code? Expected answer: make HTML cacheable or faster to render (parallel calls, aggregated endpoints), remove redirects, return the hero image first with dimensions, serve resized images.
  5. Is priority on next/image always good? Expected answer: only for the LCP image; it preloads and raises priority, so on other images it steals bandwidth. Follow-up: what changed in Next.js 16? (priority deprecated in favour of preload.)

Practical exercise

Break down LCP for your highest-traffic route.

Acceptance criteria:

  • RUM with web-vitals/attribution reports the four subparts and the LCP target selector for at least one week, segmented by mobile and desktop.
  • You identify the largest subpart at p75 on mobile and name the cause with evidence (a waterfall or a Performance trace).
  • One fix aimed at that subpart is shipped, and the subpart's p75 moves by at least 30%.
  • The rendered HTML (View Source) contains the LCP <img> with fetchpriority="high", explicit dimensions and no loading="lazy".

76.4 INP: input delay, processing and presentation

Concept

Interaction to Next Paint measures how long the page takes to visibly respond to the user. For every click, tap or key press it records the time from the input until the browser paints the next frame after the event handlers have run, and it reports (approximately) the worst of these over the whole visit.

Each interaction has three phases:

  1. Input delay: from the input until event handlers start. Large when the main thread is busy with something else, such as hydration, a timer, or a third-party script.
  2. Processing duration: the time the event handlers themselves run (all pointerdown, pointerup, click or keydown, keyup handlers for that interaction).
  3. Presentation delay: from the end of the handlers until the frame is painted: React rendering work scheduled by the handler that runs before paint, style recalculation, layout, paint and compositing.

Why does it exist?

Users judge responsiveness by feedback. If they tap "Add to cart" and nothing changes for 400 ms, they tap again, or assume the site is broken. FID only measured the input delay of the first interaction, and most sites passed it easily while still feeling sluggish on every filter, tab and dropdown. INP measures what users actually notice: the time until they see that something happened, for all interactions, not just the first.

For backend engineers this is the least intuitive Core Web Vital: a click that shows a spinner at once has a good INP even if the API takes two seconds, while synchronously filtering 5,000 items has a bad INP with no network involved. The API's influence is indirect, through how much data the client must process.

Mental model

Imagine pressing a lift button. INP is not how long the lift takes to arrive; it is how long until the button lights up. A button that lights instantly feels fine even if the lift takes 40 seconds; one that stays dark for two seconds feels broken. Input delay is the controller busy with another floor; processing is its own decision; presentation is the bulb warming up.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant M as MainThread
    participant R as Renderer
    U->>M: tap at t=0
    Note over M: busy with hydration task, input delay 180 ms
    M->>M: pointerdown, pointerup, click handlers, processing 90 ms
    M->>R: style, layout, paint, presentation 60 ms
    R-->>U: next frame at t=330 ms
  1. The browser records each event through the Event Timing API. Events belonging to one user action share an interactionId.
  2. Durations are measured to the next paint and rounded to 8 ms. The interaction's latency is the longest duration among its events.
  3. The page keeps the slowest interactions. At the end of the visit (or when the page is hidden), INP is the slowest, ignoring the single highest for every 50 interactions. On a typical page with fewer than 50 interactions, it is simply the slowest one.
  4. To find what made an interaction slow, use the Long Animation Frames API (LoAF, Chrome 123+). A long animation frame is any frame that took more than 50 ms from the start of its work to paint, and its entry lists the scripts that ran in it: sourceURL, sourceFunctionName, invoker (for example BUTTON#add-to-cart.onclick or a setTimeout callback), their duration and how much of it was forced style and layout. web-vitals/attribution attaches the LoAF entries that overlapped the INP interaction.

What moves each phase:

Phase Typical causes Fixes
Input delay Hydration of a large tree, long tasks from third-party scripts, timers and polling doing heavy work, interaction during load Less JavaScript (76.7), split hydration with Suspense and lazy client components, defer third parties, break up long tasks (69.7)
Processing Synchronous filtering or sorting of big arrays, JSON parsing in handlers, synchronous localStorage writes, analytics calls in the click handler, large state updates that re-render a whole page Do the minimum before paint, useTransition for non-urgent updates, move analytics and storage to after paint, smaller payloads from the API, Web Workers for heavy compute
Presentation Huge DOM (10,000+ nodes), layout thrashing, expensive CSS (large blurs, many shadows), rendering long lists without virtualisation Virtualise lists (71.6), content-visibility: auto for offscreen sections, avoid reading layout after writing styles, smaller DOM

The core technique for processing time is "paint first, work later": in the handler, make the smallest state change that shows feedback, let the browser paint, and then do the rest in a later task.

Practical example

An order history page lists 300 orders loaded in one response. Typing in the search box filters by product name on every keystroke. RUM shows p75 INP of 340 ms on mobile, attributed to input#order-search with type: 'keyboard', processing duration 220 ms. The LoAF script attribution names OrdersTable render work inside the onChange handler: every keystroke re-filters 300 orders with nested items and re-renders all 300 rows synchronously.

Three changes, each with a measured effect: the input's own state stays urgent while the filtered list moves into a transition (INP 340 to 150 ms); the list is virtualised so only 20 rows render (150 to 90 ms); and the API gains ?q= search with cursor pagination, so the client never holds more than 50 orders (memory and parse time drop as well).

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/orders/OrderSearch.tsx
'use client';
import { useState, useTransition, useDeferredValue } from 'react';
import { OrdersTable } from './OrdersTable';
import type { OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';

function yieldToMain(): Promise<void> {
  const s = (globalThis as { scheduler?: { yield?: () => Promise<void> } }).scheduler;
  return s?.yield ? s.yield() : new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 0)); // scheduler.yield: Chrome 129+
}

export function OrderSearch({ orders, onSearchTracked }: {
  orders: OrderSummary[]; onSearchTracked: (q: string) => void;
}) {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');             // urgent: the input must echo the key at once
  const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query);      // the table renders with this, in the background
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  async function onChange(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {
    const q = e.target.value;
    setQuery(q);                                       // smallest update that gives feedback
    await yieldToMain();                               // let the browser paint the keystroke first
    startTransition(() => onSearchTracked(q));         // analytics and non-urgent state after paint
  }

  return (
    <>
      <input id="order-search" value={query} onChange={onChange} aria-busy={isPending} />
      <OrdersTable orders={orders} query={deferredQuery} />  {/* memoised; virtualised rows */}
    </>
  );
}

useDeferredValue lets React render the input with the new value first and the expensive table with the deferred value in an interruptible background render, so a second keystroke abandons the stale table render instead of queueing behind it. useTransition does the same for updates you trigger yourself. Neither makes a single slow component faster; the table still needs memoisation and virtualisation (71.6, 71.8).

To see which scripts are behind slow frames in the field, a small LoAF observer is enough:

// apps/web/src/perf/loaf.ts  (Chromium 123+; feature-detect elsewhere)
// TypeScript's DOM lib may not ship LoAF types yet, so declare the fields we read.
type LoafScript = { invoker: string; sourceURL: string; sourceFunctionName: string;
  duration: number; forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration: number };
type LoafEntry = PerformanceEntry & { scripts: LoafScript[] };

export function observeLongFrames(report: (s: object) => void) {
  if (!PerformanceObserver.supportedEntryTypes?.includes('long-animation-frame')) return;
  new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
    for (const f of list.getEntries() as LoafEntry[]) {
      if (f.duration < 150) continue;                       // keep only the worst frames
      for (const s of f.scripts) {
        report({ invoker: s.invoker, source: s.sourceURL, fn: s.sourceFunctionName,
          ms: Math.round(s.duration), layoutMs: Math.round(s.forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration) });
      }
    }
  }).observe({ type: 'long-animation-frame', buffered: true });
}

Aggregate by source in your RUM backend and you get a ranked list of the scripts, including third-party ones, that cause slow frames for real users.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API shapes INP through the data the client must handle during interactions:

  • Filter, sort and search on the server for anything larger than a few hundred items. Return a page (Part 15.5, 72.7), not the whole collection for client-side filtering.
  • Return view-shaped data. If the UI shows totalFormatted and statusLabel, consider returning the raw values plus what the client needs to render quickly; avoid nested structures the client must normalise on every update.
  • Keep payloads small. A 900 KB JSON response costs roughly 10 to 20 ms per 100 KB to parse on a mid-range phone, plus the rendering of everything in it. Trimming unused fields (76.10) is an INP fix.
  • Make mutations acknowledge fast and support optimistic UI with idempotency keys (72.6), so a tap can show its result immediately while the request completes.
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts  (excerpt)
@Get()
async list(@Query(new ZodValidationPipe(OrderListQuerySchema)) q: OrderListQuery, @CurrentUser() user: AuthUser) {
  // q: { q?: string; status?: OrderStatus; cursor?: string; limit: 1..50, default 20 }
  return this.orders.search(user.id, q);  // pg_trgm index on product names; returns { items, nextCursor }
}

Production scenario

A grocery delivery site's checkout had p75 INP of 470 ms on the "Choose delivery slot" step. Attribution showed input delay as the largest phase, with loadState: 'complete', so the page had finished loading. LoAF entries named a chat widget's setInterval callback that polled every 2 s and took 120 to 180 ms each time on mid-range phones, plus a slot grid that re-rendered 168 slots on every tap. Loading the chat widget only after a user opened "Help", and memoising slot cells, brought p75 INP to 160 ms. The share of users who completed the slot step rose from 88% to 91%.

Failure scenario

On a Monday morning, after a release that added a "recently viewed" feature, the support team reported that "Add to cart" sometimes added two items. The RUM dashboard showed INP on product pages up from 190 ms to 520 ms for the new build. The feature's click handler on "Add to cart" synchronously serialised the entire recently-viewed list (with product JSON) into localStorage, about 400 KB, before the optimistic cart update ran. On slow phones the button gave no feedback for half a second, users tapped again, and the second tap was a new request without an idempotency key. The fix was twofold: update the cart badge first and move the storage write into an idle callback, and send an Idempotency-Key per add-to-cart intent (Parts 14 and 728.6) so double taps were harmless regardless of speed.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Interactions during load are often the worst, because hydration blocks the main thread. Check loadState in attribution before optimising handlers.
  • Hover and scroll do not count, but a scroll handler that does heavy work still delays the next tap's input.
  • Keyboard interactions on text inputs fire for every key; a slow onChange is multiplied by typing speed.
  • Third-party scripts can attach their own listeners to your buttons (analytics auto-tracking) and add processing time you cannot see in your code.
  • Single-page apps: INP is reported for the whole visit; the worst interaction may be on a route different from the one where the page loaded. Record the active route with each interaction.
  • await does not yield to paint if the promise is already resolved (69.7); use scheduler.yield() or a macrotask.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior reads INP attribution in phases, like an API trace in spans. Large input delay means "the main thread was busy with something else": find it with LoAF, usually hydration or a third party. Large processing means "our handler does too much before paint": split it. Large presentation means "the DOM or CSS is too heavy": shrink it. They push large data operations to the server, and they insist every mutation shows immediate feedback and is idempotent, because slow feedback creates duplicate requests.

They profile before adding useMemo anywhere. To a product manager: "When people tap, the screen should react within a fifth of a second. On cheaper phones ours sometimes takes half a second, mostly because of a chat widget; loading it only when someone asks for help fixes most of it."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming slow APIs cause poor INP. INP ends at the next paint; a spinner shown immediately is a fast interaction.
  • Doing analytics, storage and logging inside click handlers before the visual update.
  • Loading every third-party widget on page load and blaming React for input delay.
  • Rendering hundreds of rows on each keystroke instead of deferring and virtualising.
  • Measuring INP in the lab with TBT only, missing slow interactions that happen after load.

Interview questions

  1. What are the three phases of an INP interaction? Expected answer: input delay, processing duration, presentation delay. Follow-up: which is usually large during page load? (Input delay, from hydration and scripts.)
  2. How does INP choose its value for a visit? Expected answer: the slowest interaction, ignoring one highest per 50 interactions; reported when the page is hidden.
  3. How would you find which script causes slow interactions for real users? Expected answer: Long Animation Frames API script attribution (invoker, sourceURL), collected through RUM, or the LoAF entries in web-vitals/attribution.
  4. What does useTransition change about INP? Expected answer: it marks the update as non-urgent and interruptible, so the urgent update can paint first; it does not make the expensive render cheaper.
  5. How can the backend improve INP? Expected answer: server-side filtering and pagination, smaller payloads, view-shaped data, fast acknowledgements and idempotent mutations for optimistic UI.
  6. Why does "paint first, work later" need a real yield? Expected answer: microtasks run before rendering; only a new task (or scheduler.yield()) lets the browser paint.

Practical exercise

Fix the worst interaction on one page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • RUM reports INP with interaction target, type, the three phases, load state and LoAF script attribution for that page.
  • You name the worst interaction at p75 on mobile and its largest phase, with a DevTools Performance recording that reproduces it under 4x CPU throttling.
  • After your change, that interaction's p75 INP is under 200 ms in RUM for the new build.
  • Any mutation triggered by the interaction shows feedback within one frame and sends an idempotency key.

76.5 CLS in the field: shifts the lab never sees

Concept

Part 69.5 explained what a layout shift is, how each shift is scored (impact fraction multiplied by distance fraction) and how CLS takes the worst session window of shifts. It fixed the classic load-time causes: images without dimensions, late fonts, and banners inserted above content. This section is about the gap between lab CLS and field CLS. A Lighthouse run sees only the first few seconds of one page load with no scrolling, no clicks and no consent banner decisions. Real users scroll, open drawers, wait for recommendations, return with the back button, and keep tabs open for an hour. Field CLS is usually higher than lab CLS, and the difference is where most remaining problems live.

Why does it exist?

Teams fix load-time shifts, see a lab CLS of 0.00, and stop. Meanwhile CrUX reports 0.18, because shifts happen after load: a "Customers also bought" row that arrives 3 s after the page and pushes the reviews down, an infinite list whose skeletons are shorter than the real cards, a toast that pushes the header, a sticky "Download our app" bar. Understanding when shifts happen and which ones count is how you close that gap.

Mental model

Imagine reading a newspaper while someone keeps sliding new clippings into the middle of the page. If you asked them to add something (you turned the page, clicked "show more"), you expect movement and do not mind. If they add it while you are reading, you lose your place. CLS counts only the unrequested slides, and only the worst burst of them.

How it works

  1. Every visible element that changes its start position between frames creates a layout-shift entry.
  2. A shift within 500 ms after a discrete user input (click, tap, key press) has hadRecentInput: true and does not count. Expanding an accordion the user clicked is fine. Scrolling is not a discrete input, so content that loads during scroll and shifts the page counts.
  3. Changes made with CSS transform (animations, slides) do not move layout positions and do not create shifts.
  4. Shifts are grouped into session windows (gaps under 1 s, windows up to 5 s); CLS is the largest window's sum, over the whole time the page is open.
  5. web-vitals reports CLS when the page is hidden, with attribution for the largest shift: largestShiftTarget, largestShiftTime and loadState.

Typical field-only causes, and where the fix belongs:

Cause When it happens Fix Owner
Late recommendation or promo row inserted above existing content 1 to 5 s after load Reserve the slot with a fixed min-height, or render below the fold, or stream it in a reserved <Suspense> fallback of the same height Frontend and API (slot exists or not, known at render)
Skeleton shorter than real content in infinite lists During scroll Skeleton heights from the same layout as real cards; append below the viewport only Frontend
Cookie consent or app banner pushing content After load Overlay with position: fixed, never push the document Frontend, consent vendor config
Ads and third-party embeds resizing Any time Fixed-size containers per ad slot, overflow: hidden Frontend, ad ops
Font swap with very different metrics First second next/font fallback adjustment, size-adjust (76.8) Frontend
Content that depends on client-only data (cart count, login state) changing header height After hydration Same height in both states; server-render the session view (75.1) Frontend and BFF
bfcache restore not available Back navigation Make pages bfcache-eligible (76.9); a restored page does not shift Both

Practical example

A product page has lab CLS 0.01 and field CLS p75 of 0.16 on mobile. Attribution: largestShiftTarget: 'section.reviews', largestShiftTime around 2,900 ms, loadState: 'complete'. The reviews section moves down when a "Frequently bought together" block, fetched by a client component from /api/bff/bundles/:productId, renders above it. Most users have not scrolled yet, so the shift is "unexpected". The bundle block appears on 60% of products, so a fixed placeholder would leave a gap on the other 40%.

The fix comes from the API: the product response gains hasBundles: boolean (cheap to compute from the same query), the server renders a placeholder of the right height only when it is true, and the bundle content streams into it. Field CLS p75 drops to 0.03.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/p/[slug]/page.tsx  (excerpt, server component)
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { BundlesSection, BundlesSkeleton } from './Bundles';

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  const product = await getProduct(params.slug);           // includes hasBundles
  return (
    <>
      <ProductHero product={product} />
      {product.hasBundles && (
        // Skeleton and real section share the same CSS min-height: no shift when content arrives.
        <Suspense fallback={<BundlesSkeleton />}>
          <BundlesSection productId={product.id} />         {/* async server component, streams in */}
        </Suspense>
      )}
      <Reviews productId={product.id} />
    </>
  );
}

Streaming the section from the server rather than fetching it after hydration has two benefits: the content often arrives before the user starts scrolling, and the reserved space is in the very first HTML, so no frame ever shows the page without it.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API can prevent most "will this block exist?" shifts by answering that question in the main response:

  • Booleans or counts for optional sections (hasBundles, reviewCount, promoSlot: 'none' | 'banner' | 'carousel'), computed in the same query, so the server renders the right placeholder.
  • Image and video dimensions in every media DTO (76.3, 75.5).
  • Stable page sizes for lists (limit honoured exactly), so skeleton counts match.
  • For personalised blocks served from a slower recommendation service, a timeout with a known empty shape: if recommendations are not ready in 150 ms, return { items: [], reason: 'timeout' } and let the frontend collapse the slot before the first paint, rather than filling it 2 s later.

Production scenario

A news-style marketplace homepage had field CLS p75 of 0.24, lab 0.02. Grouping CLS attribution by largestShiftTarget showed three selectors responsible for 85% of poor scores: the main article list (pushed by a consent banner), the "Deals" row (pushed by a late sponsor strip) and the footer (irrelevant: it shifted on infinite scroll append while offscreen and contributed little). The team changed the consent banner to a fixed overlay and gave the sponsor strip a fixed 96 px slot returned by the API as sponsorSlot: true | false. Field CLS p75 fell to 0.06 within two weeks of RUM data.

Failure scenario

An "A/B test that won" turned into a CLS incident. The variant added a "Free delivery over ₹499" bar that the experimentation script inserted at the top of the page after it fetched the assignment, about 1.2 s after load. Conversion in the variant rose slightly in the first week, and the variant shipped to 100%. A month later, CrUX moved the site's mobile CLS to "needs improvement" and the SEO team raised an alarm. RUM attribution named the main content container, shifted by 40 px about 1.2 s after load on every page. The bar was moved into the server-rendered layout, with the experiment assignment made at the edge (73.9) so the HTML already contained the right variant.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shifts during scroll count: scrolling is not a discrete input, so lazy content that resizes as it enters the viewport adds to CLS.
  • Long-lived tabs accumulate windows; one bad shift an hour in can be the reported value.
  • Elements entering or leaving the DOM do not shift by themselves; it is the other elements they push that shift.
  • content-visibility: auto without contain-intrinsic-size can cause shifts when offscreen sections render with their real height.
  • Hydration mismatches that re-render a different layout (73.10) shift content that the server rendered.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats unreserved space as a bug with an owner. For every block that can appear, disappear or change size after the first paint, they ask: is its existence known at render time? If yes, render the slot on the server. If no, can the API make it known (a boolean, a count, a timeout with an empty answer)? If still no, put it below the fold or in an overlay. They look at field CLS attribution, not the lab number, and they include CLS in the review of every experiment, because client-side experiments are a common source of late shifts.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting lab CLS and never looking at field attribution.
  • Skeletons that do not match the real content's height.
  • Client-side A/B tests that insert or swap above-the-fold content after load.
  • Pushing banners into the document instead of using fixed overlays.
  • Collapsing an empty slot after the first paint instead of deciding before it.

Interview questions

  1. Why is field CLS often worse than lab CLS? Expected answer: lab captures only load with no interaction; field includes post-load shifts from late content, scrolling, banners, ads and long-lived tabs.
  2. Which shifts are excluded from CLS? Expected answer: those within 500 ms of a discrete user input, and movement via transform. Follow-up: is scrolling an input for this purpose? (No.)
  3. How can an API prevent a layout shift? Expected answer: tell the renderer in advance whether optional sections exist and how big media is; time out slow optional data with an empty, known shape.
  4. How would you find which element causes CLS for real users? Expected answer: web-vitals/attribution largestShiftTarget and largestShiftTime, grouped across users.

Practical exercise

Close the lab-to-field gap on one page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • RUM reports CLS with largest-shift target, time and load state; the top three targets by contribution are listed.
  • For each, you identify whether its existence is known at render time and move the decision to the server or API where possible.
  • Field CLS p75 on mobile is under 0.1 for the new build, and lab CLS remains under 0.05.

76.6 The critical rendering path: render-blocking resources and resource hints

Concept

The critical rendering path is the minimum set of work between receiving HTML and painting the first useful pixels: download the HTML, discover and download render-blocking CSS (and any synchronous scripts), build the DOM and CSSOM, lay out and paint. Part 69.1 walked through each stage, and 69.3 introduced preconnect, preload, modulepreload, prefetch, fetchpriority and 103 Early Hints. This section turns that knowledge into an optimisation process: find what blocks first render, shorten the chain, and use hints and speculation to start work before the browser would discover it.

Three numbers describe a critical path: how many critical resources there are, how many bytes they total, and how many round trips deep the longest dependency chain is. A page whose first paint needs HTML, one CSS file and one font has a path two round trips deep. A page whose CSS @imports a third-party font stylesheet, which references a font file on a fourth origin, is four or five round trips deep before the first text paints.

Why does it exist?

On mobile, round trips dominate. At 150 ms RTT, every additional level in the chain costs at least 150 ms, plus connection setup for new origins (one to three more RTTs). Bytes matter second: a 200 KB render-blocking CSS file on a 1.6 Mbps link takes about a second on its own. The critical path is where FCP and the render delay part of LCP come from, and it is fully under your control.

Mental model

Imagine assembling flat-pack furniture. The instructions (HTML) say "see booklet B" (CSS), which says "use bracket kit C, sold separately" (font from another origin). Each "see elsewhere" is a trip to the shop. Optimising the critical path means putting everything needed for step one in the first box, and phoning ahead for anything that must come from the shop.

How it works

flowchart TB
    html["HTML, first byte"] --> css["app.css, render-blocking"]
    html --> img["LCP image, preloaded"]
    css --> imp["@import fonts.thirdparty.example/css"]
    imp --> font["font file on another origin"]
    css --> fcp["First paint possible after CSS"]
    font --> text["Text paints with web font"]
    html --> js["page JS, defer or module: not blocking"]

The process a senior runs:

  1. List render-blocking requests. Lighthouse's render-blocking insight and the Performance panel's network track mark them. In a Next.js App Router app, these are normally the route's CSS files (/_next/static/css/*.css) and anything added with next/script beforeInteractive or plain <script> tags in the head.
  2. Remove chains. Replace CSS @import with direct <link> tags or bundling; self-host fonts so they come from the page's own origin (next/font does this); avoid CSS that is only discovered by JavaScript.
  3. Shrink what blocks. Ship only the CSS the route uses. Next.js App Router splits CSS per route segment; large global stylesheets and CSS-in-JS libraries that inject at runtime defeat this. Use the DevTools Coverage panel to see unused bytes in each CSS file. For very small critical CSS, Next.js 15 added an experimental inlineCss option that inlines styles into the HTML instead of linking them; it removes a round trip but makes every HTML response bigger and the CSS uncacheable separately, so measure.
  4. Start critical work earlier. preconnect to the one or two origins the first paint needs, preload late-discovered critical files (fonts used above the fold, the LCP image if it is not a plain <img>), and fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image. Every hint has a cost: each preload competes for bandwidth with the HTML and CSS.
  5. Use server think time. 103 Early Hints (69.3) let the CDN or server send Link: rel=preload and rel=preconnect headers while the HTML is still being rendered, so the CSS and font downloads overlap with TTFB. They help most on dynamic pages with long server time.
  6. Make the next page instant. For the likely next navigation, fetch or render it ahead of time. Next.js <Link> already prefetches routes in the viewport in production builds (static routes fully, dynamic routes down to the nearest loading.js boundary). The browser's Speculation Rules API (Chromium 121+ for document rules and eagerness) can go further and prerender a whole page in a hidden tab, so the click shows it immediately.
Technique What it removes Cost and risk
Self-host fonts (next/font) 1 to 3 RTTs for a new origin plus the CSS hop Build-time download; licence check
Remove CSS @import One RTT per level None
Per-route CSS, remove unused Bytes before first paint Discipline in shared components
preconnect DNS, TCP, TLS for a known origin Idle sockets if unused; keep to 2 or 3
preload font or LCP image Late discovery Bandwidth competition; double download if attributes mismatch
103 Early Hints Overlaps downloads with server time Needs CDN or proxy support for 1xx; only for resources common to the route
Speculation Rules prerender Whole next navigation Server load and analytics for pages never visited; must avoid side effects

Practical example

A category page's first paint waits for HTML (TTFB 600 ms), globals.css (180 KB, of which Coverage shows 74% unused on this route), and a @import of a Google Fonts stylesheet that then fetches two font files from fonts.gstatic.com. FCP on Lighthouse mobile: 2.9 s. Changes: the font moves to next/font/google (self-hosted at build, preloaded, with fallback metrics), utility CSS is purged per route, and a hero banner's background image becomes an <img> with fetchpriority="high". The critical path drops from four round trips deep to two, render-blocking CSS from 180 KB to 38 KB, and FCP to 1.6 s.

React / Next.js example

Speculation rules for product pages from a listing page, inserted by a server component so they are in the HTML:

// apps/web/app/c/[category]/SpeculationRules.tsx  (server component)
export function SpeculationRules() {
  const rules = {
    prerender: [{
      where: { and: [{ href_matches: '/p/*' }, { not: { selector_matches: '[data-no-prerender]' } }] },
      eagerness: 'moderate',          // starts on hover (about 200 ms) or pointerdown on mobile
    }],
  };
  return (
    <script
      type="speculationrules"
      // Static JSON, no user data: safe to inline. Browsers without support ignore the script type.
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(rules) }}
    />
  );
}

Two cautions. Next.js App Router's client-side navigations between its own routes do not use a prerendered document (the router does a soft navigation), so prerendering helps most for full-page navigations: links into the app from marketing pages, or apps that deliberately use plain anchors for product pages. And a strict CSP (75.7) must allow inline speculation rules, with a nonce or the 'inline-speculation-rules' source keyword.

Backend side (NestJS)

Prerendering and prefetching create requests that no human has asked for yet. The backend must recognise them and stay safe:

// apps/api/src/common/speculative.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';

@Injectable()
export class SpeculativeRequestMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    // Chromium sends "Sec-Purpose: prefetch" or "prefetch;prerender" on speculative document requests.
    const purpose = req.header('sec-purpose') ?? '';
    res.locals.speculative = purpose.includes('prefetch');
    // Speculative requests must not count as product views or trigger rate-limit lockouts.
    next();
  }
}
  • GET must be safe. A prerender of a URL that marks a notification as read or adds a product to "recently viewed" has done it without the user. Keep side effects in POSTs (Part 15.3).
  • Analytics should count a prerendered page only when it activates. Client code can check document.prerendering and listen for prerenderingchange.
  • Capacity: speculation multiplies HTML requests. A moderate-eagerness rule on a listing page with 24 products might add 5 to 15% more product-page renders; that is cheap with ISR and expensive with fully dynamic rendering.
  • Early Hints: when the HTML is rendered by Next.js behind a CDN, the CDN is usually the right place to emit 103 responses, from Link headers it has seen on earlier responses. A NestJS server rendering HTML itself can call res.writeEarlyHints() (Node 18.11+), as 69.3 showed.

Production scenario

An online travel agency's search-results-to-hotel-page navigation had a p75 LCP of 2.7 s on the hotel page. Adding a moderate prerender rule for the first eight hotel links (selected by a CSS class the server added to the top results) made activated prerenders show LCP under 300 ms. About 38% of hotel page views became prerender activations. Server-side HTML renders rose 11%, and the team had to exclude prerenders from the "hotel viewed" event, which had briefly inflated the funnel. Net p75 LCP for the hotel page fell to 1.9 s.

Failure scenario

A team added <link rel="preload"> for "everything important": three fonts, two hero images (desktop and mobile versions), the main CSS and four JavaScript chunks. Mobile LCP got worse, from 2.6 s to 3.1 s. The waterfall showed eleven high-priority requests competing for a 1.6 Mbps link during the first second, the desktop hero (400 KB) downloading on phones, and two fonts preloaded without crossorigin, so the browser fetched them twice (69.3). Removing all but the one font and the one responsive LCP image preload (generated by next/image) restored LCP to 2.4 s.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Preload without use shows a console warning after a few seconds; treat it as a bug.
  • Font preloads need crossorigin, even for same-origin fonts, or the preloaded response is not reused.
  • Early Hints may be dropped by load balancers or proxies that do not forward 1xx responses.
  • Prerender of authenticated pages: the prerender runs with the user's cookies; any page that should not render speculatively (checkout, payment) must be excluded with a selector or href rule.
  • Speculation on metered connections: Chrome limits speculation when Data Saver or battery saver is on; do not depend on it for correctness.
  • CSS in JavaScript that injects styles at runtime moves style work onto the main thread and can delay first paint until hydration.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior counts round trips before bytes. They draw the dependency chain for the first paint and the LCP element and ask why each link exists. They are stingy with hints: one preconnect per truly critical origin, one image with high priority, preloads only for things the preload scanner cannot see. They see speculation as a capacity decision as much as a frontend one, and they talk to the backend owner before turning on prerendering for dynamic pages.

Common mistakes

  • Preloading many resources, which reorders priorities in the wrong direction.
  • Loading fonts from third-party CSS with @import.
  • One global stylesheet for every route, mostly unused.
  • Prerendering pages with side effects on GET.
  • Assuming Early Hints work without checking with curl -v through the real CDN.

Interview questions

  1. What makes a resource render-blocking? Expected answer: stylesheets in the head (for matching media) and classic synchronous scripts; defer, async and module scripts do not block rendering.
  2. How would you shorten a critical path four round trips deep? Expected answer: remove @import chains, self-host fonts, preconnect or preload what cannot be discovered early, inline very small critical CSS.
  3. When would a preload make LCP worse? Expected answer: when it competes with the LCP image or CSS for bandwidth, preloads the wrong variant, or mismatches attributes causing a double download.
  4. What are speculation rules and what must the backend do about them? Expected answer: a browser API to prefetch or prerender likely next pages; the backend must keep GET safe, recognise Sec-Purpose, avoid counting speculative views, and plan capacity.
  5. Where should 103 Early Hints be generated in a Next.js plus CDN setup? Expected answer: usually at the CDN or edge from known Link headers, since the hints must be sent before the origin finishes rendering and must survive every hop.

Practical exercise

Map and shorten the critical path for one route.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A diagram shows every resource needed for first paint and for the LCP element, with the round-trip depth of each.
  • Render-blocking CSS bytes and unused percentage (Coverage panel) are recorded before and after.
  • At most two preconnect hints and one high-priority image remain, and no preload warnings appear in the console.
  • If you add speculation rules, speculative product views are excluded from analytics and you have measured the change in server renders.

76.7 JavaScript cost: budgets, code splitting, lazy loading and third-party scripts

Concept

JavaScript is the most expensive byte on the web. An image byte is downloaded and decoded, often off the main thread. A JavaScript byte is downloaded, then parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread, and in a React app the execution includes hydration: rebuilding the component tree in the browser and attaching event handlers to server-rendered HTML. 300 KB of compressed JavaScript is roughly 1 MB of source, which on a mid-range phone can mean 1 to 2 seconds of main-thread work. During that time, taps wait (input delay, 76.4) and, if the LCP element depends on the code, LCP waits too.

A bundle budget is a hard limit on how much JavaScript a route may ship, enforced in CI. Code splitting divides the code so each route loads only what it needs. Lazy loading defers code until it is actually needed: on interaction or when it scrolls into view. Third-party scripts (analytics, tag managers, chat, A/B testing, reviews, ads) are JavaScript you did not write, do not review and cannot fully control, and they are usually the biggest single source of main-thread time on commercial sites.

Why does it exist?

JavaScript grows by accretion. Each feature adds a library; each library seems small; nobody removes the date library from the feature that was cut last year. Part 70.5 showed how bundlers split code at build time and tree-shake unused exports. That machinery only helps if someone decides what belongs in the first load and watches the number. Budgets exist because without a number that fails a build, the bundle grows by a few kilobytes every week until the product page needs 900 KB.

Third-party scripts need their own discipline because they are added by people outside engineering (marketing, analytics, sales), often through a tag manager that bypasses code review entirely.

Mental model

Imagine a delivery van with a fixed loading time per box, and every box must also be unpacked and assembled at the customer's door before they can use anything. Images are flat-packed posters: quick to unload. JavaScript boxes need assembly, by one person (the main thread), while the customer waits at the door. A budget is the van's capacity. Code splitting is sending only the boxes for today's room. Lazy loading is "we'll bring the garden furniture when you go into the garden". Third-party scripts are boxes your neighbours asked you to deliver on the same trip.

How it works

The cost of a script on the critical path:

download (network)  ->  parse + compile (main thread, or background for large scripts)
                    ->  execute module top level  ->  hydrate React tree  ->  handlers attached

What a Next.js App Router page ships:

  1. Framework and shared chunks used by every route (React, the router, shared components).
  2. Route chunks for the client components used by this route. Server components ship no component JavaScript; only components marked 'use client' and their imports go to the browser.
  3. The RSC payload: a serialised description of the server component tree plus the props passed to client components, inlined in the HTML in self.__next_f.push(...) script tags and parsed on load. Large props passed to client components are therefore paid for twice: once as HTML and once as payload.
  4. Lazy chunks loaded later with next/dynamic or import().

The tools to see it: @next/bundle-analyzer (a treemap of every chunk), the DevTools Coverage panel (how much of each downloaded script ran during load), and Lighthouse's "Reduce unused JavaScript" diagnostic. Next.js 14 and 15 print "First Load JS" per route in next build output; Next.js 16 removed those size columns, so use the analyzer or a dedicated size check (76.11) instead.

The levers, in order of usual impact:

Lever Typical saving Note
Move work to server components Whole components and their libraries Markdown rendering, date formatting, data mapping need not ship
Remove or defer third-party scripts 100 to 500 KB and hundreds of ms of main-thread time Governance more than code (table below)
next/dynamic for heavy, below-the-fold or on-click components 50 to 300 KB from first load Zoom viewers, 3D, maps, rich editors, charts
Replace heavy libraries 20 to 70 KB each Intl.DateTimeFormat instead of a date library, native fetch, small validators
Fix barrel imports 10 to 200 KB experimental.optimizePackageImports for icon and UI libraries
Modern browser targets 5 to 15% Fewer polyfills and transforms via browserslist (70.2)

Third-party scripts in Next.js are loaded with next/script:

strategy When it loads Use for
beforeInteractive In the initial HTML, before hydration Almost nothing: consent managers that legally must run first, bot detection
afterInteractive (default) After some hydration Tag managers, analytics that must count every page view
lazyOnload During browser idle time after load Chat widgets, social embeds, survey tools, retargeting pixels
worker (experimental) In a Web Worker via Partytown Pages Router only; not supported in the App Router 
flowchart TB
    tag["New third-party script request"] --> need{"Needed for first view or legally first?"}
    need -->|"yes"| before["beforeInteractive, rare"]
    need -->|"no"| count{"Must count every page view?"}
    count -->|"yes"| after["afterInteractive, or a server-side event API"]
    count -->|"no"| act{"Used only on user action?"}
    act -->|"yes"| facade["Facade: load on click"]
    act -->|"no"| lazy["lazyOnload"]

@next/third-parties wraps common ones (Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics, YouTube and Google Maps embeds) with sensible defaults. For heavy embeds, a facade is often better than any strategy: show a static image of the chat bubble or video thumbnail and load the real script only on click.

Practical example

A product page ships 612 KB compressed JavaScript on first load. The analyzer and Coverage show: 140 KB framework (fixed), 118 KB a 3D viewer used by 4% of visitors after a click, 64 KB a date library used to format "Delivery by Thu, 14 Nov", 92 KB a reviews widget's client bundle, 41 KB an icon library imported through its barrel, and 157 KB of third-party scripts (tag manager plus four tags it loads). Actions: the 3D viewer becomes next/dynamic, loaded on click; the delivery date is formatted on the server; the reviews section becomes a server component with a small client "helpful" button; optimizePackageImports is set for the icon library; the tag manager loses two dead tags and the chat widget becomes a facade. First load JS falls to 228 KB, hydration on a mid-range phone from 780 ms to 290 ms, and p75 INP from 260 to 170 ms.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/p/[slug]/ProductActions.tsx
'use client';
import dynamic from 'next/dynamic';
import { useState } from 'react';

// Separate chunk; nothing downloads until the component first renders. ssr: false is
// allowed here because this is a client component (Next.js 15 rejects it in server components).
const ModelViewer = dynamic(() => import('./ModelViewer'), {
  ssr: false,
  loading: () => <div className="viewer-placeholder" aria-busy="true" />,  // same size: no CLS
});

export function ProductActions({ modelUrl }: { modelUrl: string | null }) {
  const [show3d, setShow3d] = useState(false);
  return (
    <>
      {modelUrl && (
        <button
          type="button"
          onPointerEnter={() => void import('./ModelViewer')}   // warm the chunk on hover: free head start
          onClick={() => setShow3d(true)}
        >
          View in 3D
        </button>
      )}
      {show3d && modelUrl && <ModelViewer src={modelUrl} />}
    </>
  );
}
// apps/web/app/layout.tsx  (excerpt)
import Script from 'next/script';
import { GoogleTagManager } from '@next/third-parties/google';

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en-IN">
      <body>
        {children}
        <GoogleTagManager gtmId={process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_GTM_ID!} />
        {/* Survey tool: not needed for any first-visit task, so idle time only. */}
        <Script src="https://surveys.vendor.example/s.js" strategy="lazyOnload" />
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
// apps/web/next.config.mjs  (excerpt)
import bundleAnalyzer from '@next/bundle-analyzer';
const withBundleAnalyzer = bundleAnalyzer({ enabled: process.env.ANALYZE === 'true' });

export default withBundleAnalyzer({
  experimental: { optimizePackageImports: ['lucide-react', 'date-fns'] }, // rewrite barrel imports
});

Backend side (NestJS)

The API decides how much data ends up in JavaScript-land:

  • Props crossing the server/client boundary are serialised into the page. If a server component passes the full 40 KB ProductDetailDto to a client component that uses four fields, the HTML carries those 40 KB again as RSC payload. Shape view models in the BFF or ask the API for what the screen needs (76.10).
  • Formatting on the server (prices with currency, dates in the store's time zone, statusLabel) can remove whole client libraries. Part 74.7 kept money as minor-unit strings in the contract; formatting for display can still happen in a server component.
  • Third-party server-side alternatives: many analytics and marketing tags have server-to-server APIs. Sending conversion events from NestJS (after the order is committed, with an outbox, Part 28) is more accurate than a browser pixel and removes a script from the page.

Production scenario

A furniture retailer's tag manager had grown to 31 tags across six teams. A LoAF-based report (76.4) showed third-party scripts responsible for 58% of long animation frame time on product pages for real users. The team introduced a third-party budget: 120 KB compressed and 150 ms of main-thread time at p75, owned by a named person, with a quarterly review where each tag needed a business owner and a usage number. Eleven tags were removed (four belonged to campaigns that had ended over a year earlier), three moved to server-side event APIs and five to lazyOnload. Product page p75 INP went from 310 ms to 180 ms with no change to first-party code.

Failure scenario

On Black Friday at 09:05, mobile conversion dropped by a third. The A/B testing vendor's script, loaded synchronously in the head with an "anti-flicker" snippet that set body { opacity: 0 } until the experiment loaded or 4 s passed, was being served slowly by the vendor's CDN under global load. Every page was invisible for up to 4 s: LCP render delay jumped by that amount. The site's own servers were healthy. The emergency fix was removing the snippet through the tag manager, at 09:40. The permanent fix moved experiment assignment to the edge and server (73.9), so variants were in the HTML, and banned render-hiding snippets in the third-party policy.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Third-party script outages can block rendering (synchronous scripts) or hang load; anything in the head is a single point of failure.
  • Hydration of a huge tree is a long task no matter how the code is split; reduce client components on the page, not just bytes.
  • Over-splitting creates many tiny requests and request chains; a chunk loaded on click must still download on a slow network, so prefetch it on hover or when idle.
  • next/dynamic with ssr: false renders nothing on the server, which can harm SEO and cause layout shift if the placeholder size differs.
  • Shared chunks change on every deploy if a commonly used module changes, invalidating long-term caches for every user (76.9).
  • Polyfills for old browsers sent to every browser waste bytes; differential serving is mostly obsolete now that ES2020 support is near-universal.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior thinks of JavaScript as CPU time on the user's device, not as kilobytes. They set a budget per route type (for example, 170 KB compressed first-load JavaScript for landing routes like product and category pages, more for the logged-in dashboard), make it fail CI, and require a written exception to exceed it. Their default for a new component is "server component" and they need a reason to add 'use client'.

For third parties they act as a governance owner, not a gatekeeper: every tag has an owner, a purpose, a size and a review date, and the cheapest loading strategy that still meets its purpose. To a marketing lead: "Each tag costs us about this much speed, which costs about this much conversion; let's keep the ones that earn more than they cost."

Common mistakes

  • Marking a whole page 'use client' to use one hook, shipping everything below it.
  • Measuring bundle size only after compression, forgetting that parse and execute cost follows the uncompressed size.
  • Letting the tag manager bypass review and performance budgets.
  • Lazy loading above-the-fold content, trading LCP for a smaller bundle.
  • Passing whole DTOs to client components, doubling page weight through the RSC payload.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a kilobyte of JavaScript more expensive than a kilobyte of image? Expected answer: it must be parsed, compiled and executed on the main thread, plus hydration in React; images decode mostly off the main thread.
  2. How do server components reduce JavaScript, and where can they increase page weight? Expected answer: their code never ships; but props passed to client components are serialised into the RSC payload in the HTML.
  3. How would you choose next/script strategies for a tag manager, a chat widget and a consent manager? Expected answer: afterInteractive for the tag manager, lazyOnload or a facade for chat, beforeInteractive only where consent legally must run first. Follow-up: which strategy does not work in the App Router? (worker.)
  4. What does a bundle budget look like and how is it enforced? Expected answer: a per-route compressed size limit checked in CI with a size tool or Lighthouse CI assertions, with exceptions reviewed.
  5. What are the risks of a client-side A/B testing script? Expected answer: render blocking, anti-flicker hiding the page, late content swaps causing CLS and LCP changes, a third-party single point of failure.

Practical exercise

Put one route on a JavaScript diet.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The analyzer treemap and Coverage report for the route are saved, with the top ten modules by size and their usage during load.
  • At least one heavy component is moved to a server component or next/dynamic, and at least one third-party script changes strategy or becomes a facade.
  • First-load JavaScript for the route is under an agreed budget, enforced in CI (76.11).
  • p75 INP and hydration long-task duration are compared before and after on a mid-range device profile.

76.8 Images and fonts: formats, responsive images, lazy loading and font loading

Concept

Images are usually the largest bytes on a page and the most common LCP element. Fonts are small but sit on the critical path for text and can cause both render delay and layout shift. The engineering choices are few and well understood:

  • Format: AVIF (typically 40 to 50% smaller than JPEG at similar quality), WebP (25 to 35% smaller), JPEG or PNG as fallback. SVG for icons and logos.
  • Size: serve each device an image close to the pixels it will display, with srcset (the available widths) and sizes (how wide the image will be in the layout).
  • Loading: loading="lazy" for images below the fold, eager and fetchpriority="high" for the LCP image, decoding="async" for the rest.
  • Fonts: WOFF2, subsetted to the characters you use, self-hosted, at most two families, loaded with a font-display strategy and a fallback font adjusted to the same metrics.

Why does it exist?

A merchandiser uploads a 4,000 by 3,000 pixel, 3.8 MB photo. Without a pipeline it is served as-is to a phone that displays it 390 CSS pixels wide (about 1,170 device pixels at 3x density). That is fifteen times the needed pixels and one of the most common causes of poor LCP load duration. Fonts have the opposite problem: they are small, but the browser hides text while it waits for them (up to 3 s in most browsers with the default font-display: auto) or swaps them in late and shifts every line.

Mental model

Imagine printing a photo for a wallet, a frame and a billboard. You would not print the billboard and fold it into the wallet. srcset is the set of print sizes you keep in stock; sizes tells the shop how big the frame is; the browser picks the smallest print that still looks sharp. Fonts are the typeface on a shop sign: if the sign painter is late, you can leave the sign blank (block), put up a temporary sign in a similar typeface and repaint later (swap), or keep the temporary sign for today (optional).

How it works

The browser's image selection, for <img srcset="a-640.avif 640w, a-1080.avif 1080w, a-1920.avif 1920w" sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw"> on a 390 px wide phone at 3x density:

  1. Evaluate sizes: the viewport is under 768 px, so the slot is 100vw = 390 CSS px.
  2. Multiply by device pixel ratio: 390 x 3 = 1,170 device px needed.
  3. Pick the smallest candidate at least that wide. a-1080.avif is just short of 1,170, so the browser takes a-1920.avif, nearly three times the pixels it needs. Adding a 1,200 px candidate fixes that. Browsers may also pick a smaller candidate on slow connections, and many sites cap the effective density at 2x, because the visual difference above 2x is small and the bytes nearly double.

next/image generates this for you. Its loader requests /_next/image?url=...&w=1080&q=75, and the optimiser resizes, converts to the best format the browser's Accept header allows (configure images.formats to include image/avif), and caches the result. Without sizes, next/image assumes the image is full-viewport width on every device and generates a srcset of 1x and 2x for its fixed width, which is often far too large for responsive layouts.

Font loading:

font-display Text before the font loads Risk
block (and usually auto) Invisible for up to about 3 s Render delay on text LCP
swap Fallback immediately, swap when loaded Layout shift if metrics differ
fallback Invisible about 100 ms, fallback, swap only within about 3 s Compromise
optional Invisible about 100 ms, then the font is used only if already available Best for CLS and LCP; first visit may never show the web font

The CLS risk of swap is solved by fallback metric adjustment: CSS @font-face descriptors size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override make a local fallback (Arial, Roboto) occupy the same space as the web font. next/font computes and applies these automatically (adjustFontFallback defaults to true), self-hosts the font files at build time, and preloads them.

flowchart LR
    up["Merchant upload"] --> ingest["NestJS ingest: validate, cap, strip EXIF, store dimensions"]
    ingest --> s3["Object store, content-hash key"]
    s3 --> icdn["Image CDN: AVIF or WebP per width"]
    api["Product API: url, width, height, alt"] --> page["Next.js: next/image with sizes"]
    page -->|"srcset request"| icdn
    icdn -->|"immutable, 1 year"| browser["Browser"]

Practical example

A product listing page with 24 product cards on mobile: originals are 1,600 px JPEGs averaging 240 KB. With next/image, AVIF, sizes="(max-width: 640px) 50vw, 25vw" and lazy loading below the first row, the first viewport downloads four images at about 18 KB each instead of 240 KB, and the rest load as the user scrolls. Image bytes on initial load fall from 5.7 MB (all 24 eager) to 72 KB plus the hero. The brand font, previously two weights from a third-party host with display=block, moves to next/font/local with one variable font file subsetted to Latin (38 KB), display: 'swap' and an adjusted fallback; text appears at FCP and CLS from the font swap drops to near zero.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/fonts.ts
import localFont from 'next/font/local';

export const brand = localFont({
  src: './fonts/Brand-Variable-latin.woff2',   // one variable file for all weights, Latin subset
  display: 'swap',
  variable: '--font-brand',
  adjustFontFallback: 'Arial',                // size-adjust etc. so the swap does not shift layout
  preload: true,
});
// apps/web/next.config.mjs  (images excerpt)
export default {
  images: {
    formats: ['image/avif', 'image/webp'],     // AVIF first; falls back by Accept header
    remotePatterns: [{ protocol: 'https', hostname: 'img.shop-cdn.example', pathname: '/products/**' }],
    deviceSizes: [640, 750, 828, 1080, 1200, 1920], // drop 2048 and 3840 for a storefront
    minimumCacheTTL: 2678400,                  // 31 days: product image URLs are versioned
  },
};

For cards below the fold, next/image lazy-loads by default; pass priority (Next.js 16: preload) only to the LCP image. Set placeholder="blur" with a tiny blurDataURL from the API if you want a low-quality preview; it does not change LCP, which counts the full image.

Backend side (NestJS)

The image pipeline is backend work:

// apps/api/src/media/media.service.ts  (excerpt; uses the sharp library)
import sharp from 'sharp';
import { BadRequestException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
import { ObjectStore } from './object-store';        // thin wrapper over the S3 client (Part 33)

@Injectable()
export class MediaService {
  constructor(private readonly objects: ObjectStore) {}

  async ingest(buffer: Buffer, alt: string) {
    const meta = await sharp(buffer).metadata();
    if (!meta.width || !meta.height) throw new BadRequestException('UNREADABLE_IMAGE');
    if (meta.width * meta.height > 40_000_000) throw new BadRequestException('IMAGE_TOO_LARGE'); // 40 MP cap
    const master = await sharp(buffer)
      .rotate()                                   // apply EXIF orientation, then strip metadata
      .resize({ width: 2400, withoutEnlargement: true })
      .jpeg({ quality: 85, mozjpeg: true })
      .toBuffer({ resolveWithObject: true });
    // Content-hash key: the URL changes when the bytes change, so the CDN can cache it forever.
    const key = `products/${createHash('sha256').update(master.data).digest('hex').slice(0, 32)}.jpg`;
    await this.objects.put(key, master.data, 'image/jpeg');
    return { key, width: master.info.width, height: master.info.height, alt };
  }
}
  • Normalise at upload: cap dimensions, fix orientation, strip EXIF (which also removes GPS location, a privacy issue), record width and height.
  • Versioned URLs: a content-hash key lets the CDN cache images for a year with immutable (76.9).
  • Where to resize: the Next.js optimiser runs sharp on your Node servers; at high traffic or with many product images, that is real CPU and a cache-miss latency spike. A dedicated image CDN (or an image service behind CloudFront) moves that load off the web tier. remotePatterns must be strict, or anyone can use your optimiser to resize arbitrary internet images at your expense.
  • Vary: Accept when negotiating AVIF or WebP by Accept header, so a CDN does not serve AVIF to a browser that asked for JPEG.

Production scenario

A classifieds site with 40 million listing photos served originals averaging 410 KB through CloudFront. Moving to an image service that generated AVIF and WebP variants at four widths, keyed by content hash, cut image transfer by 71%, saved about 38 TB of CDN egress a month (Part 51 prices that), and moved p75 mobile LCP on listing pages from 3.3 s to 2.4 s, almost entirely through the load duration subpart.

Failure scenario

After enabling the Next.js image optimiser on a self-hosted Node deployment, the web tier's CPU went to 95% during a sale and HTML TTFB tripled. Each of 12 pods was resizing product images on cache misses, because the optimiser's cache lived on each pod's local disk and pods were replaced frequently by autoscaling. The team moved images to a separate image CDN path with its own cache and kept next/image with a custom loader that built CDN URLs, so the Node servers did no image work at all.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Missing sizes with responsive layouts makes phones download desktop images.
  • Art direction (a different crop on mobile) needs <picture> with <source media>, not just srcset.
  • AVIF encoding is slow; generate variants ahead of time or cache them aggressively.
  • Icon fonts are text to screen readers and block rendering; use inline SVG.
  • Too many font weights: each is a separate file unless you use a variable font.
  • Fonts for non-Latin scripts (Devanagari, Chinese) are large; use unicode-range subsets so pages download only the ranges they use.
  • Lazy images in a horizontal carousel may never be "near the viewport" by the browser's heuristic until scrolled; set eager for the first slides.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior sees images as a pipeline with a contract: the API returns a versioned URL, dimensions and alt text; the frontend declares how big the image is in the layout (sizes); an image service does the conversion; the CDN caches it forever. They make sure no single layer can undo the others (no 4 MB uploads, no missing sizes, no lazy LCP). For fonts their default is one self-hosted variable font, swap with adjusted fallback metrics, or optional where brand typography is not essential on first view.

Common mistakes

  • Serving originals and relying on CSS to shrink them.
  • Omitting sizes on next/image in responsive layouts.
  • Running image optimisation on the web tier without a shared cache at scale.
  • Third-party font CSS with display=block.
  • Forgetting width and height, causing layout shift (69.5).

Interview questions

  1. How does the browser choose an image from srcset and sizes? Expected answer: computes the slot width from sizes, multiplies by device pixel ratio, picks the smallest adequate candidate.
  2. What are the tradeoffs between font-display: swap and optional? Expected answer: swap always shows the web font eventually but can shift layout; optional avoids late swaps but may not show the web font on first visit.
  3. What should the backend do at image upload time? Expected answer: validate, cap dimensions, fix orientation, strip EXIF, store dimensions and a content-hashed URL.
  4. What can go wrong with the Next.js image optimiser at scale? Expected answer: CPU load and cache misses on the web tier, per-pod caches, and abuse if remotePatterns is too broad.

Practical exercise

Fix the image and font pipeline for one page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every image on the page is served as AVIF or WebP at a width within 1.5x of its displayed device pixels, verified in the Network panel on a phone profile.
  • Only the LCP image is eager and high priority; all others below the fold are lazy.
  • Fonts are self-hosted WOFF2, at most two files on first load, with adjusted fallback metrics; CLS from font swap is under 0.01.
  • The upload endpoint rejects oversized images and stores dimensions.

76.9 Caching for frontends: immutable assets, HTML caching, service workers and the bfcache

Concept

A frontend has four caches between the user and your servers, and each needs a different policy:

  1. Static assets (JavaScript chunks, CSS, fonts, images) with a content hash in the file name, such as /_next/static/chunks/app/p/page-3f9c1a2b.js. The name changes when the content changes, so the file can be cached forever: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.
  2. HTML documents, which have stable URLs (/p/trail-runner-gtx) and must change when content or code changes. They get short shared caching at the CDN, revalidation, or no caching at all, depending on whether they are personalised (73.1, 73.7).
  3. Service worker caches, a programmable cache inside the browser (the Cache API, 69.8) that your own script controls: it can serve repeat visits and offline pages without the network.
  4. The back/forward cache (bfcache), an in-memory snapshot of the whole page that the browser keeps when the user navigates away, so pressing Back restores it instantly without reloading anything.

Part 11.11 covered Cache-Control, ETag and revalidation, Part 27 the backend caches, and Part 73.7 the four Next.js caches. This section is about the policy for a frontend's own files and documents, and the two browser-side caches.

Why does it exist?

A returning visitor should download almost nothing: the framework and shared chunks have not changed since yesterday, the font has not changed in a year. Without hashed, immutable assets, the browser must either revalidate every file (a round trip each, even for 304s) or risk running yesterday's JavaScript with today's HTML. Without careful HTML caching, either every request hits the origin (slow TTFB) or users see stale prices. And the fastest navigation of all, Back, is often slow only because a page accidentally opted out of the bfcache.

Mental model

Imagine a library. Books with an edition number on the spine (hashed assets) can be shelved permanently: a new edition gets a new number and a new place. The daily newspaper (HTML) has the same title every day, so you must check the date before trusting the copy on the shelf. A service worker is a personal assistant who keeps copies at your desk and decides when to fetch fresh ones; helpful, but if they never check the date, you read last month's paper. The bfcache is leaving your book open on the desk when you step out, rather than shelving it.

How it works

The policy table most frontends should start from:

Resource Cache-Control Why
/_next/static/* (hashed JS, CSS, fonts, media) public, max-age=31536000, immutable (Next.js sets this) Name changes with content; never revalidate
Content-hashed product images public, max-age=31536000, immutable Same reason; URL from the API changes on re-upload
Unhashed files in public/ (logo.svg, robots.txt) public, max-age=3600 or explicit per file Next.js defaults to max-age=0; set headers or move them under hashed imports
Static or ISR HTML (product, category) public, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 at the CDN; browser max-age=0 Short shared freshness, instant responses while revalidating (73.2)
Personalised HTML (cart, account) private, no-cache (or no-store for sensitive pages, 75.9) Never shared; revalidate every time
Public API GETs called from the browser public, max-age=0, s-maxage=30 plus ETag CDN absorbs load; browser always revalidates
Personal API GETs private, no-cache plus ETag 304s save bytes; never shared 
flowchart LR
    b["Browser"] --> bf{"Back or forward?"}
    bf -->|"yes, eligible"| snap["bfcache snapshot, about 0 ms"]
    bf -->|"no"| sw{"Service worker?"}
    sw -->|"controls page"| swc["SW cache or network"]
    sw -->|"none"| http["HTTP cache: hashed assets hit, HTML revalidates"]
    swc --> cdn["CDN: s-maxage HTML, immutable assets"]
    http --> cdn
    cdn --> origin["Next.js and NestJS"]

Service workers are worth their complexity for apps used repeatedly (a delivery partner's app, an internal dashboard), offline-capable flows, and sites on very poor networks. For a typical storefront, hashed assets with immutable caching already give most of the repeat-visit benefit, and a service worker adds a new failure mode: a bad or stale worker can serve broken pages to every returning user until it updates. If you use one: precache only the app shell and hashed assets, use network-first or stale-while-revalidate for HTML, enable navigation preload so the network request for the page starts in parallel with the worker's startup, and ship a kill switch (a no-op worker at the same URL). For Next.js App Router, Serwist (@serwist/next) is the maintained successor to the older next-pwa plugin; Workbox provides the strategies underneath (CacheFirst, StaleWhileRevalidate, NetworkFirst).

The bfcache restores a page only if it is eligible. The common reasons a page is not: an unload event listener (use pagehide instead), Cache-Control: no-store on the document (Chrome has been relaxing this for some pages, but do not rely on it), and open connections or locks the browser cannot freeze. DevTools has a dedicated test under Application, Back/forward cache, that lists the blocking reasons for the current page. Code that must refresh data on restore listens for pageshow with event.persisted === true.

Practical example

A storefront's repeat-visit analysis: returning mobile users on a product page downloaded 410 KB per visit. The waterfall showed the JavaScript chunks were served from cache, but /public/fonts/brand.woff2 (unhashed, max-age=0) revalidated on every page, the hero image URLs included a ?v=timestamp that changed on every deploy, and HTML was no-store because a header component read cookies. Moving the font to next/font (hashed), using content-hash image keys from the API, and moving the personalised header to a client component (so HTML could be ISR) cut repeat-visit transfer to 38 KB and repeat-visit p75 LCP from 1.9 s to 0.9 s. Back navigations went from full reloads to bfcache restores once no-store was gone.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/next.config.mjs  (headers excerpt)
export default {
  async headers() {
    return [
      { source: '/brand/:file*', headers: [{ key: 'Cache-Control', value: 'public, max-age=86400' }] },
      { source: '/robots.txt', headers: [{ key: 'Cache-Control', value: 'public, max-age=3600' }] },
    ];
  },
};
// apps/web/src/perf/BfcacheRefresh.tsx
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

export function BfcacheRefresh() {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  useEffect(() => {
    const onShow = (e: PageTransitionEvent) => {
      // Restored from bfcache: the snapshot may be minutes old. Refetch volatile data only.
      if (e.persisted) void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['cart'] });
    };
