    window.addEventListener('pageshow', onShow);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('pageshow', onShow);
  }, [qc]);
  return null;
}

Backend side (NestJS)

// apps/api/src/catalog/products.controller.ts  (excerpt)
import { Controller, Get, Header, Param } from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('v1/products')
export class ProductsController {
  constructor(private readonly products: ProductsService) {}

  @Get(':slug')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300')
  @Header('Vary', 'Accept-Encoding')                    // never Vary on Cookie for public data
  findOne(@Param('slug') slug: string) {
    return this.products.findPublicBySlug(slug);        // no per-user fields in a shared response
  }
}
  • Public responses must contain nothing personal. One isFavourite field in a CDN-cached product response leaks one user's data to everyone (73.7 has the incident). Split personal fields into a separate private endpoint.
  • ETags on personal GETs let the browser and TanStack Query revalidate cheaply. Express generates weak ETags for responses by default; for streamed or very large responses compute them from a version column.
  • The bfcache and logout pull in opposite directions: no-store on authenticated pages prevents a restored page from showing data after logout (75.9), but disables bfcache for those pages. A senior compromise: no-store for pages with sensitive data (account, orders, payment), cacheable documents elsewhere, and a pageshow handler that rechecks the session on restore.

Production scenario

A media-heavy marketplace measured back-navigation from product to listing: 34% of all listing page views were Back navigations. Only 9% were bfcache restores. The DevTools bfcache test listed two blockers: an analytics library's unload listener and Cache-Control: no-store on listing HTML. Upgrading the library (it moved to pagehide) and serving listings with ISR headers raised bfcache restores to 71% of Back navigations, which RUM showed with navigationType: 'back-forward-cache' and near-zero LCP. Listing page server renders dropped by a fifth.

Failure scenario

A team shipped a service worker that cached HTML with CacheFirst "for offline support". A week later a pricing bug fix went out; support tickets about wrong prices kept arriving for days from returning customers. Their service worker served the old HTML, which referenced old hashed chunks that were still on the CDN, so everything "worked", just with stale prices. The fix was a new worker with NetworkFirst for navigations and a three-second timeout falling back to cache, skipWaiting plus clients.claim to take over quickly, and a server-side Clear-Site-Data: "cache" header on one release to clear the poisoned caches. Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends covers what happens to users on old bundles during deploys more generally.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Deleting old hashed assets on deploy breaks users who loaded yesterday's HTML and lazily request a chunk that no longer exists. Keep previous builds' assets for days (Part 78).
  • Query-string cache busting (app.js?v=2) is ignored by some caches and is not content-based; use hashed file names.
  • Vary: Cookie on a public response makes the CDN cache a copy per cookie value, which is effectively no caching.
  • Service worker scope and updates: a worker controls pages under its scope until a new one installs and activates; a byte-identical worker never updates.
  • bfcache and real-time connections: an SSE or WebSocket connection open at navigation time may block bfcache or be closed on freeze; reconnect on pageshow (72.8).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior separates versioned things (cache forever) from named things (revalidate or cache briefly) and refuses anything in between, such as unhashed scripts with long lifetimes. They treat a service worker as production infrastructure with its own rollout and kill switch, not as a checkbox, and they usually do not add one to a storefront without a specific offline or repeat-use requirement. They measure bfcache restore rate as a performance metric, because it is the cheapest page load there is.

Common mistakes

  • Long max-age on HTML without a purge strategy.
  • Unhashed assets in public/ with default max-age=0, revalidated on every page.
  • CacheFirst for HTML in a service worker.
  • unload handlers in your code or third-party libraries.
  • Personal data in CDN-cacheable responses.

Interview questions

  1. Why can hashed assets be cached forever but HTML cannot? Expected answer: the hash changes the URL when content changes; HTML has a stable URL and must reflect new content and new asset references.
  2. What blocks the bfcache, and how do you check? Expected answer: unload listeners, no-store, some open connections; DevTools Application panel bfcache test, and RUM navigation type.
  3. When is a service worker worth it for a web app? Expected answer: repeated use, offline needs, poor networks; with network-first HTML, navigation preload and a kill switch.
  4. What goes wrong if you delete old assets immediately on deploy? Expected answer: open tabs and cached HTML request old chunks and get 404s; lazy routes break.

Practical exercise

Audit caching for one route.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A table lists every resource on the page with its Cache-Control, whether its URL is content-hashed, and whether it is served from cache on a repeat visit.
  • Repeat-visit transfer for the page is under 50 KB, excluding API data.
  • The DevTools bfcache test passes for the page, and RUM shows bfcache restores as a share of Back navigations.
  • No public API response contains per-user fields.

76.10 The backend's share: TTFB, API waterfalls, over-fetching, chatty endpoints and BFF aggregation

Concept

The backend influences frontend performance through five mechanisms:

  1. TTFB of the HTML: everything the server does before sending the first byte, including every API call a server component awaits.
  2. API waterfalls: requests that wait for other requests, on the server (sequential awaits in a render) or on the client (a fetch inside the callback of another fetch).
  3. Over-fetching: responses that contain far more than the screen needs, costing transfer, parse time and memory.
  4. Chatty endpoints: screens that need many small requests because the API is shaped around resources rather than tasks.
  5. Cacheability: whether responses can be shared by a CDN or the Next.js Data Cache, which decides whether the API is in the user's path at all.

A BFF aggregation layer (73.8) is the main tool to fix the last three, and parallelism plus streaming fix the first two.

Why does it exist?

Backend engineers measure endpoint latency; users experience the critical path. An endpoint at 60 ms p95 can still cost a user 1.2 s if a page calls it after four other requests in sequence over a 200 ms mobile round trip. The backend's share of web performance is not "make the endpoint faster" alone; it is "make fewer, parallel, cacheable, right-sized calls possible at render time".

Mental model

Imagine sending someone to collect five documents from five offices in one building. If they must bring each document back to you before you tell them the next office (a waterfall), the trip takes five times as long. If you give them the full list at once (parallel), it takes as long as the slowest office. If one clerk gathers all five for them at a single counter (aggregation), they make one trip. If the documents are public and photocopied in the lobby (caching), they make no trip at all. Over-fetching is them bringing back the whole filing cabinet.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant N as NextServer
    participant P as ProductSvc
    participant R as PricingSvc
    participant I as InventorySvc
    Note over N: before: sequential awaits, 120 + 90 + 140 = 350 ms
    N->>P: GET product
    P-->>N: 120 ms
    N->>R: GET price
    R-->>N: 90 ms
    N->>I: GET stock
    I-->>N: 140 ms
    Note over N: after: Promise.all, max of three = 140 ms

TTFB itself has parts, visible in the Navigation Timing entry and in web-vitals TTFB attribution: waiting (redirects and queuing), cache (service worker or HTTP cache lookup), DNS, connection (TCP and TLS), and request duration (sending the request until the first response byte, which includes server time). Only the last is server-side; Server-Timing splits it further.

The fixes, by mechanism:

Mechanism Symptom in a trace Fix
Sequential server calls Server-Timing spans back to back Promise.all, start independent fetches before awaiting, or one aggregated BFF call
Slow non-critical data in render TTFB grows with the slowest call Stream it: put the slow component behind <Suspense> so the shell flushes first (73.2)
Client-side chains Initiator chain from request to request (69.10) Fetch on the server, or in parallel on the client, or include in one view model
Over-fetching Large JSON, low field usage View-shaped endpoints, field selection, @Expose serialisation groups, pagination
Chatty screens Many small requests per view BFF aggregation per screen, or batch endpoints (GET /v1/products?ids=)
Uncacheable responses Every render hits the API Split public from personal data; s-maxage, revalidate and tags
No compression or old protocol Large transfer for text Brotli or gzip at the CDN, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 (Part 11.10, 11.6)

Practical example

A product page in a Next.js server component awaits: product (120 ms), price (90 ms), stock (140 ms), recommendations (380 ms), reviews summary (70 ms), sequentially: 800 ms of server time, all in TTFB. The page cannot be cached because stock and price change often. Changes:

  1. Product, price, stock and reviews summary start in parallel: 140 ms.
  2. Recommendations move behind <Suspense>, so they stream after the shell; they no longer affect TTFB or LCP.
  3. The product response is split: a cacheable public part (title, images, description: s-maxage=300, tag-revalidated on edits) and a small volatile part (price and stock: 30 s). The page becomes ISR with a 30 s revalidate.

TTFB on a CDN miss falls from about 950 ms to about 260 ms; on a CDN hit, to about 60 ms.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/app/p/[slug]/page.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router)
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import { getProduct, getPrice, getStock, getReviewSummary } from '@/lib/catalog'; // fetch wrappers
import { Recommendations, RecommendationsSkeleton } from './Recommendations';

export const revalidate = 30;                                 // ISR: page cached, re-rendered at most every 30 s

export default async function ProductPage({ params }: { params: { slug: string } }) {
  // Start all independent calls before awaiting any of them.
  const [product, price, stock, reviews] = await Promise.all([
    getProduct(params.slug),            // fetch(..., { next: { revalidate: 300, tags: [`product:${params.slug}`] } })
    getPrice(params.slug),              // fetch(..., { next: { revalidate: 30 } })
    getStock(params.slug),
    getReviewSummary(params.slug),
  ]);
  return (
    <>
      <ProductHero product={product} />
      <PriceAndStock price={price} stock={stock} />
      <ReviewSummary summary={reviews} />
      <Suspense fallback={<RecommendationsSkeleton />}>
        {/* Slow (p95 380 ms) and not needed for LCP: streams after the shell. */}
        <Recommendations productId={product.id} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  );
}

In Next.js 15, params becomes a promise (const { slug } = await params) and fetch is no longer cached by default, so the next: { revalidate } options must be explicit (73.5).

Backend side (NestJS)

When several screens need the same aggregation, or mobile apps need it too, an aggregated endpoint in NestJS (or a dedicated BFF service) beats repeating Promise.all in every frontend:

// apps/api/src/product-page/product-page.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header, Param, UseInterceptors, ClassSerializerInterceptor, SerializeOptions } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ProductPageService } from './product-page.service';

@Controller('v1/product-pages')
@UseInterceptors(ClassSerializerInterceptor)
export class ProductPageController {
  constructor(private readonly pages: ProductPageService) {}

  @Get(':slug')
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=0, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=120')
  @SerializeOptions({ groups: ['page'], excludeExtraneousValues: true }) // only @Expose({ groups: ['page'] }) fields
  get(@Param('slug') slug: string) {
    return this.pages.view(slug);
  }
}
// apps/api/src/product-page/product-page.service.ts  (excerpt)
async view(slug: string): Promise<ProductPageView> {
  const product = await this.catalog.bySlug(slug);                 // needed for ids
  const [price, stock, reviews] = await Promise.all([
    this.pricing.current(product.id),
    this.inventory.availability(product.id).catch(() => ({ state: 'unknown' as const })), // degrade, do not fail
    this.reviews.summary(product.id),
  ]);
  return new ProductPageView(product, price, stock, reviews);      // about 6 KB instead of 48 KB of raw DTOs
}

The rules that make this work: one round trip per screen for the first render; independent calls in parallel with timeouts and degraded fallbacks (Part 29 for timeouts and circuit breakers); view models that contain what the screen renders; public and personal data in separate responses so the public one can be cached; Server-Timing spans for each downstream call (69.10). The Part 73.8 table still applies for deciding whether this aggregation lives in Next.js or NestJS: a single web frontend usually aggregates in Next.js; web plus mobile usually shares an aggregated endpoint.

Production scenario

A food delivery restaurant page called nine endpoints from the browser after hydration: restaurant, menu categories, menu items per category (four calls), offers, delivery estimate and favourites. On a 4G phone the last data arrived at 3.4 s. A GET /v1/restaurant-pages/:id endpoint returned one 22 KB view model (from 140 KB across the nine responses), the page rendered it on the server with the menu cached for 60 s at the CDN, and favourites and the delivery estimate (personal, location-based) came from one small client call. The menu was visible at 1.3 s p75, and API request volume for the page fell by 80%.

Failure scenario

At 19:30 on a Friday, peak dinner time, p75 TTFB for restaurant pages jumped from 300 ms to 2.8 s. Dashboards showed the menu service healthy. Server-Timing on the HTML showed a new span, promo;dur=2400: a promotions call added that week inside the aggregated endpoint, awaited before rendering, with no timeout. The promotions service was overloaded by a marketing push. Because the call was in the critical path of a non-streamed render, its tail latency became every user's TTFB. The fix was a 150 ms timeout with an empty-promotions fallback, and moving the promo banner behind <Suspense> so it could arrive late without blocking the page.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Aggregation amplifies failure: one slow dependency slows the whole view unless each call has a timeout and a fallback.
  • Aggregated responses are harder to cache if they mix volatility levels; split by freshness.
  • Over-aggregation: a "page endpoint" that returns everything for every variant of a screen becomes the new over-fetching.
  • N+1 behind the aggregate: a view endpoint that loops over items calling another service (Part 42.4) moves the waterfall inside the data centre, where it is faster but still adds up.
  • Streaming and status codes: once the shell is flushed with 200, a later failure cannot change the status; handle errors inside the streamed component (73.2).
  • Compression of tiny responses wastes CPU; compress above about 1 KB.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior budgets server time inside TTFB like any other dependency: "the product page has 300 ms of server time on a CDN miss; the slowest critical call gets 150 ms with a timeout; anything slower streams or loads later". They ask of every call in a render: is it needed for the first paint? Can it run in parallel? Can it be cached, and for how long? What happens if it times out? They choose the aggregation location by who else needs it, not by habit, and they keep business rules in the services, never in the BFF.

To a product manager: "The page waits for five lookups one after another. Doing them at the same time and moving the recommendations lower on the page saves about half a second for everyone, and the recommendations still appear before most people scroll to them."

Common mistakes

  • Sequential awaits for independent data in server components.
  • Blocking the whole render on non-critical data instead of streaming it.
  • Returning whole entities when the screen needs a few fields.
  • Mixing personal fields into public responses, which makes them uncacheable or leaks data.
  • Aggregating without timeouts, so the slowest dependency sets everyone's TTFB.

Interview questions

  1. How does a backend reduce LCP without touching frontend code? Expected answer: lower TTFB through caching and parallel calls, view-shaped responses, image metadata first, fewer redirects.
  2. What is an API waterfall and how do you find one? Expected answer: requests that depend on earlier ones; the Initiator chain in DevTools for the client, Server-Timing and traces for the server.
  3. Where should screen aggregation live: Next.js or NestJS? Expected answer: Next.js when only the web app needs it; a shared endpoint or BFF service when mobile and web need the same shape; never with business rules.
  4. How do you keep an aggregated endpoint from being as slow as its slowest dependency? Expected answer: parallelise, set per-call timeouts, return degraded fallbacks, stream non-critical parts, cache by freshness.
  5. What is over-fetching's cost in the browser beyond bytes? Expected answer: parse time, memory, RSC payload duplication, slower interactions when the client processes large data.

Practical exercise

Remove one waterfall end to end.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Server-Timing on the page's HTML shows each downstream call as a span; a before-trace shows at least two sequential independent calls.
  • After the change, independent calls run in parallel, each with a timeout and fallback, and non-critical data streams behind <Suspense>.
  • One client-side request chain is removed or parallelised, verified with the Initiator view.
  • p75 TTFB on a CDN miss and the page's total API payload are recorded before and after.

76.11 Measuring: Lighthouse, WebPageTest, real-user monitoring and performance budgets in CI

Concept

Performance work needs three kinds of measurement, each answering a different question (76.2):

  • Lab tools reproduce one page load under controlled conditions so you can see why it is slow. Lighthouse (in Chrome DevTools, PageSpeed Insights, the CLI and Lighthouse CI) runs a scripted load on an emulated mobile device and reports metrics, a score and diagnostics. WebPageTest runs loads on real browsers and devices from chosen locations and connection profiles, with filmstrips, request waterfalls and scripted journeys. The DevTools Performance panel records a trace you can step through.
  • Real-user monitoring (RUM) collects metrics from every real visit (web-vitals), and tells you what users actually experienced, by route, device, connection and release.
  • Performance budgets in CI turn agreed numbers into failing checks, so a pull request that adds 120 KB of JavaScript or pushes lab LCP past a threshold is stopped before it ships.

Part 42.11 built the backend version of this loop: load tests and latency budgets in CI. This is the frontend version, and the two should report into the same dashboards.

Why does it exist?

Performance decays silently. Each change is small, nobody owns the total, and the people adding weight (a feature team, a marketing tag) are not the people who see the RUM dashboard. Teams that fix performance once without a measurement loop are back where they started within two or three quarters. The loop exists to make regressions visible within hours (RUM by build) or before merge (CI budgets), and to make every fix provable.

Mental model

Imagine managing your weight. The lab test is the doctor's full check-up: precise, explains causes, but once a year in a controlled setting. RUM is the bathroom scale every morning: less detail, but it tells you the truth about your normal life and catches the trend early. The budget is the rule "no dessert if the scale says more than X". You need all three; the check-up alone does not stop the slow drift.

How it works

Lighthouse. The default mobile run emulates a mid-range phone with 4x CPU slowdown and a slow 4G network (150 ms RTT, about 1.6 Mbps down) using simulated throttling: it loads the page quickly and models how long it would have taken on the slow profile. The performance score (Lighthouse 10 and later) weights five lab metrics: TBT 30%, LCP 25%, CLS 25%, FCP 10% and Speed Index 10%. Single runs vary by 5 to 10 points with network and machine noise, so CI runs three to five times and asserts on the median. Lighthouse 12.6 and 13 have been reorganising diagnostics into "insights" shared with the DevTools Performance panel; audit ids used in CI assertions can change between major versions, so pin the Lighthouse CI version.

WebPageTest. Choose a real device class (for example a mid-range Android phone), a location close to your users and a connection profile. Run first view and repeat view. The filmstrip shows what the user saw at each 100 ms; the waterfall shows connection reuse, priorities and chains. Scripted tests can log in or add to cart before measuring. It is the best tool when the question is "what does this look like from Mumbai on a real phone?"

DevTools Performance panel and CrUX. For diagnosis on your own machine, the Performance panel's live metrics view shows LCP, CLS and INP as you click through the page, and can show the page's CrUX field values next to your local ones, so you can see at a glance whether your local run is representative. Set CPU throttling to match a mid-range phone (recent Chrome versions can calibrate a throttling preset to your machine) and a network preset such as Slow 4G, then record. The insights sidebar breaks LCP into the four subparts (76.3) and INP into its three phases (76.4) for that recording, and names the LCP element and the slow interaction's handlers. For field numbers outside your own RUM, the CrUX API (records:queryRecord with an origin or url and a formFactor) returns p75 values and good, needs-improvement and poor shares for the last 28 days, and the CrUX History API returns weekly values for trend lines. Both are free with an API key and are the fastest way to see a competitor's or a new acquisition's field performance, or your own for browsers your RUM does not reach.

RUM pipeline.

flowchart LR
    page["Page: web-vitals attribution"] -->|"sendBeacon on hide"| bff["Next.js same origin, rewrite"]
    bff --> api["NestJS POST /v1/rum/vitals, 204"]
    api --> prom["Prometheus histograms: route, device, build"]
    api --> store["Event store for attribution: ClickHouse or warehouse"]
    prom --> dash["Grafana: p75 per route, alert on release"]
    store --> dash

Two storage needs: histograms for cheap, real-time p75 per route and device with alerts, and raw events with attribution for diagnosis ("which LCP element, which script"). Bucket boundaries at the "good" and "poor" thresholds (2,500 and 4,000 ms for LCP; 200 and 500 for INP; 0.1 and 0.25 for CLS) make the share of good experiences exact even though the p75 is interpolated.

Budgets in CI. Three kinds, each failing the build:

Budget type Example Tool
Quantity First-load JS for /p/[slug] ≤ 170 KB compressed; images on first view ≤ 300 KB size-limit or a script over the build output; Lighthouse resource assertions
Lab timing Median of 3 Lighthouse mobile runs: LCP ≤ 2,500 ms, TBT ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 Lighthouse CI against the preview deployment
Field timing p75 mobile LCP per route for a new build ≤ 2.5 s and not worse than the previous build by > 10% RUM alert after deploy (Part 78 turns this into a frontend SLO)

Practical example

A team's measurement setup for its storefront: Lighthouse CI runs on every pull request against the preview deployment, testing three URLs (home, a top category, the top product) three times each; size-limit checks the product route's JavaScript; WebPageTest runs nightly from two locations on a real mid-range Android device to catch CDN and third-party regressions that CI cannot see; RUM alerts the owning team when a route's p75 mobile LCP or INP for the newest build crosses the threshold with at least 2,000 samples.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/lighthouserc.js  (Lighthouse CI; run with `lhci autorun` after the preview deploy)
module.exports = {
  ci: {
    collect: {
      url: [
        `${process.env.PREVIEW_URL}/`,
        `${process.env.PREVIEW_URL}/c/running-shoes`,
        `${process.env.PREVIEW_URL}/p/trail-runner-gtx`,
      ],
      numberOfRuns: 3,                                   // assertions use the median run; default mobile profile
    },
    assert: {
      assertions: {
        'largest-contentful-paint': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 2500 }],
        'total-blocking-time': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 200 }],
        'cumulative-layout-shift': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 0.1 }],
        'categories:performance': ['warn', { minScore: 0.85 }],   // the score is a hint, not the gate
      },
    },
    upload: { target: 'temporary-public-storage' },      // or an LHCI server for history
  },
};
{
  "size-limit": [
    { "name": "product page client JS", "path": ".next/static/chunks/app/p/[slug]/*.js", "limit": "60 kB" },
    { "name": "shared framework JS", "path": ".next/static/chunks/{framework,main-app,webpack}-*.js", "limit": "110 kB" }
  ]
}

The size-limit entry lives in apps/web/package.json; limit is compressed size by default. Glob paths depend on the Next.js version's chunk naming, so check them after each Next.js upgrade.

Backend side (NestJS)

The RUM endpoint, validated with the shared contract and cheap enough to take every beacon:

// packages/contracts/src/rum.ts
import { z } from 'zod';
export const WebVitalReportSchema = z.object({
  name: z.enum(['LCP', 'INP', 'CLS', 'FCP', 'TTFB']),
  value: z.number().nonnegative().max(120_000),       // CLS arrives x1000 as an integer
  rating: z.enum(['good', 'needs-improvement', 'poor']),
  id: z.string().max(64),
  navigationType: z.string().max(32),
  route: z.string().max(80).regex(/^\/[\w\-\[\]\/]*$/), // route template, never a raw URL with query
  effectiveType: z.string().max(16).optional(),
  buildId: z.string().max(40),
  attribution: z.record(z.string(), z.union([z.string().max(200), z.number()])).optional(),
});
export type WebVitalReport = z.infer<typeof WebVitalReportSchema>;
// apps/api/src/rum/rum.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post, Req } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { Histogram } from 'prom-client';
import type { Request } from 'express';
import { WebVitalReportSchema, type WebVitalReport } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { RumEventsProducer } from './rum-events.producer';

const vitals = new Histogram({
  name: 'web_vitals_value',
  help: 'Core Web Vitals from real users (ms; CLS x1000)',
  labelNames: ['metric', 'route', 'device'],            // no build label here: raw events carry it
  buckets: [100, 200, 250, 500, 800, 1000, 1800, 2500, 4000, 6000, 10000], // thresholds are edges
});

@Controller('v1/rum')
export class RumController {
  constructor(private readonly events: RumEventsProducer) {}

  @Post('vitals')
  @HttpCode(204)
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 60, ttl: 60_000 } })     // per IP; a page sends about 5 beacons
  ingest(@Body(new ZodValidationPipe(WebVitalReportSchema)) r: WebVitalReport, @Req() req: Request) {
    const device = /Mobi|Android/i.test(req.get('user-agent') ?? '') ? 'mobile' : 'desktop'; // coarse on purpose
    vitals.labels(r.name, r.route, device).observe(r.value);
    this.events.enqueue({ ...r, device, receivedAt: Date.now() }); // buffered, batched to Kafka; never awaited
  }
}

Points that matter in production:

  • Content type: sendBeacon with a plain string sends text/plain, which NestJS's JSON body parser ignores, leaving @Body() empty. Send a Blob typed application/json (same-origin, so no CORS preflight issue), as 76.1 does.
  • Cardinality: labels are route templates and a device class, never URLs, user ids or build ids. Prometheus cost grows with every label combination; builds belong in the raw event store.
  • Never on the critical path: respond 204 immediately; do the write asynchronously; drop under pressure rather than slowing down.
  • Abuse: the endpoint is public and unauthenticated. Validate strictly, cap sizes, rate-limit, and treat RUM data as untrusted when computing anything important.
  • Query: histogram_quantile(0.75, sum by (le, route) (rate(web_vitals_value_bucket{metric="LCP",device="mobile"}[1h]))) gives p75 LCP per route.

Production scenario

A marketplace with 600 deploys a quarter added Lighthouse CI and a RUM release alert in the same sprint. In the following quarter, CI blocked 14 pull requests: nine for JavaScript size (mostly accidental client imports of server-only libraries), three for TBT and two for CLS. The RUM alert fired four times; two were real regressions CI could not catch (a third-party script update and a CDN configuration change), and two were mix shifts from campaigns, which the team learned to recognise by checking device and connection segments first. Mobile p75 LCP for the top routes stayed within 100 ms of target for the whole quarter, against a drift of about 600 ms in the previous one.

Failure scenario

Lighthouse CI was introduced with a single run per URL and a hard performance-score threshold of 90. Within a week, developers learned to click "re-run" until it passed: scores varied from 82 to 95 for identical code because the CI runners shared CPU with other jobs. Then they asked for the check to be made optional. The team restored trust by running three times and asserting on the median, asserting on metrics instead of the score, moving the runs to dedicated runners, and testing against the deployed preview through the CDN instead of a local next start. Flaky gates are worse than no gates, because they teach people to ignore red.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Lab results depend on the runner: CPU contention, region and whether the CDN cache is warm. Fix the environment and record it with the results.
  • Testing next dev measures the development build, which is much larger and slower; always test a production build.
  • Logged-in pages need a scripted login (Lighthouse CI puppeteer script, WebPageTest scripting) with a test account.
  • Ad blockers and privacy browsers block RUM beacons; your field data under-represents those users.
  • Sampling: on very high traffic, sample RUM (for example 10% of page views) but sample by page view, not by beacon, so all metrics of a page view arrive together.
  • Third-party regressions happen without your deploy; only RUM and scheduled synthetic tests see them.
  • CrUX eligibility: URLs and origins below a traffic threshold have no CrUX data at all, and new pages take weeks to appear. Your own RUM is the only field signal for them.
  • Clock and timing differences: RUM values are relative to navigation start in the user's browser, so client clocks do not matter, but receivedAt on the server does for grouping by deploy time. Group by build id, not by arrival time.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

A senior builds the loop before the optimisation: RUM with attribution and a build id, a small set of lab tests on representative URLs, and budgets that fail the build. They choose few, stable assertions over many noisy ones, and they make the backend part of the same picture (Server-Timing, API p95 per route next to TTFB p75). They treat a budget breach like a failing test: fix it or record an explicit, time-limited exception, never quietly raise the limit.

Common mistakes

  • Gating on the Lighthouse score instead of specific metrics and sizes.
  • Single Lighthouse runs in CI, producing flaky results.
  • RUM without dimensions (route, device, build), so a regression cannot be located.
  • Raw URLs as metric labels, exploding cardinality and leaking personal data.
  • No owner for alerts, so RUM regressions sit unread on a dashboard.

Interview questions

  1. What does the Lighthouse performance score measure, and why should you not gate on it alone? Expected answer: a weighted blend of five lab metrics (TBT, LCP, CLS, FCP, Speed Index) on one emulated load; it varies between runs and does not represent field experience.
  2. How would you design a RUM pipeline for Core Web Vitals? Expected answer: web-vitals with attribution, beacons on page hide, a cheap validated endpoint, histograms for p75 and alerts, raw events for attribution, low-cardinality dimensions including build id in the event store.
  3. What kinds of performance budgets exist and where is each enforced? Expected answer: quantity (bytes, requests) and lab timing in CI; field timing as post-deploy alerts or SLOs.
  4. Why use WebPageTest when you have Lighthouse? Expected answer: real devices and locations, filmstrips, repeat views, scripted journeys, connection-level detail.
  5. How do you keep lab performance tests from being flaky? Expected answer: dedicated runners, multiple runs and medians, metric assertions, production builds, consistent CDN state.
  6. Your RUM says p75 LCP is 2.2 s but CrUX says 2.9 s. Which do you believe? Expected answer: both may be right: CrUX is Chrome-only, opted-in users, 28 days, and includes users your beacons miss; RUM includes other browsers and only recent builds. Compare the same window, browser and form factor before concluding. Follow-up: which one does search use? (CrUX.)

Practical exercise

Build the measurement loop for your web app.

Acceptance criteria:

  • RUM sends LCP, INP and CLS with attribution, route template, device and build id to a NestJS endpoint that validates with the shared schema and returns 204.
  • A Grafana panel shows p75 per route for mobile and the share of "good" experiences, using bucket boundaries at the thresholds.
  • Lighthouse CI runs three times per URL on the preview deployment with metric assertions, and size-limit checks the product route's JavaScript.
  • A deliberately bloated pull request (add a 100 KB library to the product page) fails CI with a clear message.

76.12 Worked example: a product page from LCP 4.8 s to under 2.5 s

Concept

This section applies the whole Part to one page, in the order a senior would work: measure in the field, attribute, fix the largest subpart, re-measure, repeat, then lock the result in with budgets. Every number is a p75 on mobile from RUM unless it says "lab".

The starting point

The page is https://shop.example/p/trail-runner-gtx, a Next.js 14 App Router product page in front of the NestJS catalogue, pricing and inventory services, behind CloudFront. It gets 140,000 mobile views a day, mostly first visits from search and ads. The goal: p75 mobile LCP under 2.5 s without regressing INP or CLS, and an estimate of the business effect.

RUM with web-vitals/attribution (76.2) over seven days, about 28,000 LCP samples:

Metric (p75, mobile)     Value      Rating
LCP                      4.8 s      poor
  TTFB                   1,450 ms
  Resource load delay    1,600 ms
  Resource load dur.     1,100 ms
  Element render delay     650 ms
INP                      260 ms     needs improvement
CLS                      0.14       needs improvement
LCP element              div.gallery img (82% of loads), h1.product-title (18%)
Lab (Lighthouse mobile)  LCP 6.9 s, TBT 940 ms, CLS 0.12

The process, repeated once per subpart:

flowchart LR
    m["Measure: RUM p75 with attribution"] --> a["Attribute: largest subpart, its cause"]
    a --> f["Fix: one change aimed at it"]
    f --> v["Verify: same metric, new build"]
    v --> m
    v --> l["Lock in: budget or build check"]

Step 0: find the cause of each subpart

A WebPageTest run on a real mid-range Android phone from a nearby location, plus a DevTools trace with 4x CPU throttling, explained every subpart:

  • TTFB 1,450 ms. x-nextjs-cache was absent and CloudFront reported Miss on every request. The root layout called cookies() to show "Hi, Priya" and the cart count, which made every route dynamic (73.5). Server-Timing showed four sequential awaits: product 120 ms, price 90 ms, stock 140 ms, recommendations 380 ms.
  • Load delay 1,600 ms. The gallery was a client-only carousel. Its image URLs came from GET /v1/products/:id/media, fetched in a useEffect after hydration of 610 KB of JavaScript.
  • Load duration 1,100 ms. The hero was a 1,600-pixel JPEG of 340 KB with no srcset, competing for bandwidth with the JavaScript.
  • Render delay 650 ms. An A/B testing script with an anti-flicker snippet hid the body until the experiment loaded (typically 400 ms, up to 2 s), and the brand font came from a third-party host with display=block.
  • CLS 0.14. Mostly the font swap shifting the title and price block, plus a reviews widget that grew after load.
flowchart LR
    subgraph Before
        b1["TTFB 1450"] --> b2["Delay 1600"] --> b3["Download 1100"] --> b4["Render 650"]
    end
    subgraph After
        a1["TTFB 380"] --> a2["Delay 120"] --> a3["Download 330"] --> a4["Render 140"]
    end
    b4 --> lcpb["LCP p75 4.8 s"]
    a4 --> lcpa["LCP p75 2.1 s"]

Step 1: TTFB, make the page cacheable and parallel

  1. The greeting and cart count moved into a client component fed by the session view and GET /api/bff/cart (73.8, 81.1). The layout no longer reads cookies, so product pages can be statically rendered and revalidated.
  2. The page got export const revalidate = 30, matching the freshness of price and stock; the product fetch uses revalidate: 300 and a product:<slug> tag, and the catalogue service's update event calls revalidateTag through the publisher from 73.13.
  3. Product, price and stock run in Promise.all; recommendations moved behind <Suspense> (76.10).
  4. CloudFront's HTML cache policy honours s-maxage from Next.js, capped at 60 s (73.7).

Result after a week: CDN hit rate for the route from 0% to 93%, TTFB p75 from 1,450 ms to 380 ms, LCP p75 from 4.8 s to 3.7 s. The backend's own latency barely changed; it simply left the user's path for 93% of views.

Step 2: load delay, put the hero in the HTML

  1. API change: the product response now includes images[] with url, width, height, alt and position, hero first (76.3). The separate media endpoint remains for the full gallery.
  2. The first image renders in a server component with next/image and priority; the carousel hydrates later around it (76.3).
  3. The 3D viewer (118 KB) moved to next/dynamic on click, and the reviews widget became a server component with a small client button (76.7). First-load JavaScript fell from 610 KB to 240 KB.

Result: load delay from 1,600 ms to 120 ms; LCP p75 from 3.7 s to 2.6 s. INP improved too, from 260 ms to 200 ms, because hydration got shorter.

Step 3: load duration, send the right bytes

  1. sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw", images.formats with AVIF first, and deviceSizes trimmed to six widths (76.8).
  2. Images moved to an image CDN path with content-hash keys and a one-year immutable policy, so the Next.js servers do no resizing.
  3. The ingest endpoint now caps uploads at 2,400 pixels and stores dimensions (76.8).

Result: the hero on a typical phone is a 58 KB AVIF instead of 340 KB; load duration from 1,100 ms to 330 ms; LCP p75 from 2.6 s to 2.25 s.

Step 4: render delay, stop hiding the page

  1. The experiment assignment moved to middleware at the edge, which sets a cookie and rewrites to the right variant (73.9), so the HTML already contains the variant. The anti-flicker snippet was deleted and banned in the third-party policy.
  2. The font moved to next/font/local: one variable WOFF2, Latin subset, display: 'swap' with an adjusted fallback (76.8).
  3. The reviews section got a reserved height from reviewCount in the API response (76.5).

Result: render delay from 650 ms to 140 ms; CLS p75 from 0.14 to 0.03.

Step 5: lock it in

  • Lighthouse CI on every pull request, three runs against the preview deployment, with LCP, TBT and CLS assertions (76.11).
  • size-limit for the product route's client chunks at 60 KB and the shared framework at 110 KB.
  • A RUM alert per build: p75 mobile LCP for /p/[slug] above 2.5 s or 10% worse than the previous build, with at least 2,000 samples.
  • A build check that fails if /p/[slug] is reported as dynamic in next build output, because Step 1's gain depends on it staying cacheable.

Results

28 days after the last change:

Metric (p75, mobile)         Before     After
LCP                          4.8 s      2.1 s     good
  TTFB                       1,450 ms   380 ms
  Resource load delay        1,600 ms   120 ms
  Resource load duration     1,100 ms   330 ms
  Element render delay         650 ms   140 ms
INP                          260 ms     170 ms    good
CLS                          0.14       0.03      good
First-load JS (compressed)   610 KB     240 KB
Hero image bytes             340 KB     58 KB
Origin HTML renders/day      140,000    about 11,000
Lab LCP (Lighthouse mobile)  6.9 s      2.3 s

Steps 2 to 4 shipped behind a feature flag with a 10% holdout for two weeks. In the holdout comparison the faster page had a 4.1% higher relative add-to-cart rate and a 2.6-point lower bounce rate. Step 1 could not be held out cleanly (it changed caching for everyone), so the team reported its effect only as a before-and-after, labelled as such.

What the team chose not to do

Three proposals were rejected, and the reasons matter as much as the fixes. A service worker to cache the product page was turned down: most visitors were first-time visitors from search, so it would not have helped them, and it added a stale-HTML risk (76.9). Moving to the edge runtime for rendering was postponed: with a 93% CDN hit rate, the remaining origin renders were a small share of page views, and the edge would have needed a rewrite of the data layer (73.9). Inlining all CSS was measured and dropped: it removed one round trip on first visits but made every HTML response 30 KB larger and uncacheable separately for repeat visits. Each was a reasonable idea aimed at a subpart that was no longer the largest.

Backend side (NestJS)

Change Owner Effect
Product response includes ordered images with dimensions and alt Catalogue API Load delay; CLS
reviewCount and hasBundles in the product response Catalogue API CLS: slots reserved at render
Public product data split from personal data; s-maxage headers Catalogue API and BFF HTML and API cacheable at the CDN
Tag revalidation on product update events Catalogue publisher Freshness without short TTLs
Promise.all with timeouts and fallbacks in the render BFF (Next.js server) TTFB on CDN misses
Image ingestion caps and content-hash keys Media service Load duration; CDN egress
RUM endpoint with zod validation and histograms Platform API The measurement loop

More than half of the improvement came from backend and BFF changes, even though the metric is "frontend".

Failure scenario

Three weeks later the RUM alert fired for build web@5.3.0: p75 TTFB for /p/[slug] back to 1.2 s and LCP to 3.4 s. The build check had been added after this pull request merged. A new currency selector in the shared header called cookies() in a server component to read the preferred currency, turning every page dynamic again. The CDN hit rate dropped to zero within minutes of the deploy, and the origin's HTML render rate went up thirteenfold. The fix moved the currency read into the client component (prices are converted for display on the client from the minor-unit strings, Part 74.7) and the dynamic-route build check went live the same day. Total time in the regressed state: 3 hours, because the alert was per build.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior did not start with images, even though "optimise images" was the team's first instinct. They started with attribution, fixed subparts in order of size, measured after each step, and assigned each fix to whoever owned it, backend included. They protected the gains with checks aimed at the specific mechanisms that produced them (cacheability, bundle size, the LCP element in HTML), not only with a generic score. They reported the business effect honestly, separating the experiment-backed part from the before-and-after part.

Interview questions

  1. Walk through how you would take a page from LCP 4.8 s to under 2.5 s. Expected answer: field data with attribution, the four subparts, fix the largest first (often TTFB through caching, or load delay through putting the image in HTML), re-measure each step, add budgets. Follow-up: why not start with image compression? (It addresses only load duration.)
  2. Why did removing a cookies() call improve TTFB so much? Expected answer: it made the route static or ISR, so the CDN and Full Route Cache could serve it; the API left the user's path.
  3. How would you prove the business effect? Expected answer: a holdout behind a flag on part of the traffic, with conversion compared; label non-experimental changes honestly.
  4. What would you add to CI after this project? Expected answer: Lighthouse CI metric assertions, bundle size limits, a check that the route stays static, a RUM alert per build.

Practical exercise

Run this process on a real page with poor LCP.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A before table like the one above, from at least 5,000 field samples, with the four subparts and the LCP element.
  • At least three steps, each aimed at one subpart, each with its own after-measurement.
  • At least one backend change in the list, with its effect measured.
  • Budgets and a build check that would catch a regression of each mechanism you fixed.
  • p75 mobile LCP under 2.5 s, with INP and CLS not worse than before.

Senior Checklist — Part 76

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can tie a Core Web Vitals change to a business metric and propose a holdout experiment to measure it
  • I can state the LCP, INP and CLS thresholds and explain why they are judged at p75 on mobile
  • I know which questions field data answers and which lab data answers, and I never gate on a Lighthouse score alone
  • I can break LCP into its four subparts with web-vitals/attribution and fix the largest one first
  • I can read INP attribution by phase and find the slow script with the Long Animation Frames API
  • I can close the gap between lab and field CLS by moving "will this block exist?" decisions to the server and API
  • I can map a critical path in round trips and use preconnect, preload, fetchpriority and speculation rules sparingly
  • I set a JavaScript budget per route, default to server components, and govern third-party scripts with owners and strategies
  • I serve images in modern formats at the right size from a pipeline that stores dimensions, and fonts self-hosted with adjusted fallbacks
  • I cache hashed assets forever, HTML briefly, and keep pages eligible for the bfcache
  • I keep the API out of the user's path with caching, parallel calls, streaming and view-shaped responses
  • I run a RUM pipeline with low-cardinality labels, and budgets in CI that fail the build

Part 76 — Key Takeaways

  • Performance is revenue, and the slow quartile on mobile is where the money is; measure it before you optimise it.
  • Core Web Vitals are LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms and CLS ≤ 0.1 at p75; INP replaced FID in 2024.
  • Field data says what happened, lab data says why; when they disagree, the lab profile is wrong.
  • LCP is four subparts; the two delays should be near zero, and a large one means an architecture problem, not a slow network.
  • INP ends at the next paint: show feedback first, do the work later, and keep third parties off the main thread.
  • Unreserved space is a bug; the API can prevent most layout shifts by saying in advance what will appear.
  • Count round trips on the critical path before bytes, and treat every resource hint as a cost.
  • JavaScript is CPU time on the user's phone: budget it per route, default to server components, and govern every tag.
  • Images need a pipeline with dimensions and variants; fonts need self-hosting and matched fallbacks.
  • Hashed assets are cached forever, HTML briefly, and the fastest page load is a bfcache restore.
  • The backend's biggest contribution is often not a faster endpoint but taking the endpoint out of the user's path.
  • A measurement loop with RUM by build and budgets in CI is what keeps a fast page fast.

Part 77 — Frontend Testing and Quality

Part 41 — Testing Backend Systems with Jest and NestJS built the backend's test practice: the pyramid and the trophy (41.1), test doubles (41.4), what to mock (41.5), integration tests against a real PostgreSQL (41.7), contract tests (41.14), flaky tests (41.18) and CI organisation (41.19). Part 74.10 added consumer-driven contracts between the web app and the API. This Part does the same job for the screens: what to test where, how to test components by their behaviour, how to fake the network without lying about it, how to run a browser against a real NestJS backend in CI, and what a backend engineer should look for when reviewing a frontend pull request.

Stack and versions, as in the rest of the volume: React 18 (notes for 19), Next.js 14 App Router (notes for 15), Vitest 3 (notes for 2 and 4), @testing-library/react 16 with @testing-library/dom 10 and @testing-library/user-event 14, @testing-library/jest-dom 6, MSW 2, Playwright 1.5x, @axe-core/playwright 4 and vitest-axe, and the NestJS 10 API with PostgreSQL 16 from the rest of the book. The feature under test throughout is the checkout of 71.13 and the order pages of 72.12.

77.1 The frontend testing pyramid and trophy: what to test where

Concept

A test level is how much of the real system a test runs. On the frontend there are four useful levels:

  • Static checks: TypeScript, ESLint and the shared contract types (70.8, 70.10, 80.3). They run in seconds and catch a whole class of mistakes without executing anything.
  • Unit tests: one pure function, reducer or hook, with no DOM layout and no network. Milliseconds each.
  • Component tests (often called integration tests on the frontend): render a component or a whole screen into a simulated DOM (jsdom), interact with it the way a user would, and fake only the network. Tens to hundreds of milliseconds each.
  • End-to-end (e2e) tests: a real browser, the real production build of the web app, and a real or nearly real backend. Seconds each.

The testing pyramid says "many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few e2e tests". Kent C. Dodds' testing trophy reshapes it for user interfaces: a wide base of static checks, a modest layer of unit tests, the largest layer of component/integration tests, and a thin top of e2e tests. Part 41.1 explained both shapes for the backend. On the frontend the trophy usually wins, for a reason specific to UIs: most frontend bugs live in how pieces are wired together (a form, its validation schema, the API client, the error mapper, the loading state), not inside any single function.

Why does it exist?

Because every level has a price and a blind spot, and a team without a deliberate split ends up at one of two extremes.

  • All unit tests. Every component is rendered with shallow mocks of its children and its hooks. Coverage reads 90 %. Then a renamed prop breaks the checkout and every test stays green, because each test mocked the thing that broke.
  • All e2e tests. Every behaviour is checked by clicking through a real browser. The suite takes 45 minutes, fails 3 % of the time for reasons nobody can reproduce, and developers learn to press "re-run" instead of reading failures.

The split exists so each question is asked at the cheapest level that can answer it honestly.

Mental model

Imagine checking a restaurant. You taste the sauce on its own (unit test): fast, and you learn whether the sauce is right. You order a full dish at the pass and eat it at the counter (component test): you learn whether the sauce, the pasta and the plating work together, without waiting for a table. Once a week you book a table as a stranger, arrive through the front door and pay (e2e test): slow and expensive, but it is the only way to learn that the door sticks and the card machine is offline. You do not book a table to check the salt.

How it works

flowchart TB
    st["Static: tsc, ESLint, shared zod types"] --> un["Unit: pure functions, reducers, hooks"]
    un --> co["Component: screens in jsdom, MSW for the network"]
    co --> e2e["E2E: Playwright, production build, real NestJS"]
    e2e --> prod["Production signals: RUM, error tracking, Part 78"]
    co --> ct["Contract: Pact against the API, 80.10"]

A working rule for deciding where a test goes:

  1. Is it a rule about data? Money formatting, date bucketing, a reducer's legal transitions, a URL builder. Unit test. If the rule is shared with the backend, it lives in @shop/contracts and is tested once there.
  2. Is it something a user sees or does on one screen? "A 422 for the postcode shows a message under the postcode field", "the Place order button is disabled while placing". Component test, with the network faked at the HTTP layer (77.5).
  3. Does it cross a boundary that a fake cannot represent honestly? Cookies and redirects through the BFF (Part 75), real CSS layout, a real database constraint stopping a duplicate order, the production bundle's code splitting. E2E test.
  4. Is it about the API's shape rather than its behaviour? Contract test (74.10), not e2e.
  5. Is it about how it looks? Visual regression (77.9), on a few stable screens.

Typical cost per level on a mid-size storefront (a laptop and a 4-vCPU CI runner):

Level Time per test Typical count Suite time in CI Flake rate if done well
Static (tsc, ESLint) n/a whole repo 20-60 s 0
Unit (Vitest) 1-20 ms 400-1,500 5-20 s ~0
Component (Vitest + Testing Library + MSW) 30-300 ms 300-1,000 30-120 s < 0.1 %
Contract (Pact consumer) 50-200 ms 10-40 10-20 s ~0
E2E (Playwright, 4 shards) 3-30 s 15-60 journeys 3-8 min < 0.5 % with the rules of 77.8
Visual (Playwright screenshots) 1-3 s 10-40 screens 1-2 min < 0.5 % in a pinned Docker image

Practical example

The checkout of 71.13 has these risks, each placed at one level:

Risk Level Why there
The reducer allows ORDER_PLACED from payment Unit Pure function, every transition in a table
formatMoney('129900', 'INR') shows ₹1,299.00 Unit Pure; also run in the API's tests via @shop/contracts
A 422 with path: "postcode" appears under the postcode input and takes focus Component Needs a rendered form and a faked response, not a database
A 409 CART_CHANGED on the coupon shows the notice and new totals Component Same
A double click on Place order sends one request Component Needs real event handling and a counted fake endpoint
A double click creates exactly one row in orders E2E Only the real API, idempotency interceptor and unique index can prove it
The confirmation page is reached and Back does not show a live payment form E2E Real browser history
POST /v1/orders still returns problem+json with code Contract Shape, not behaviour
The price summary did not move 40 px after a CSS refactor Visual Only pixels can tell

React / Next.js example

The scripts in apps/web/package.json make the split visible, so a developer knows which command answers which question:

{
  "scripts": {
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit",
    "lint": "next lint",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "test:watch": "vitest",
    "test:coverage": "vitest run --coverage",
    "test:pact": "vitest run --config vitest.pact.config.ts",
    "e2e": "playwright test",
    "e2e:ui": "playwright test --ui",
    "e2e:visual": "playwright test --project=visual"
  }
}

In Next.js 14 and 15, one more boundary decides the level: async Server Components cannot be rendered by Vitest and Testing Library today (the Next.js testing guide says so explicitly). Synchronous Server Components and all Client Components can be. So the senior split for an App Router page is: keep data fetching in a thin async page component, pass plain props into synchronous components, component-test those, and cover the async page in e2e.

// app/orders/[id]/page.tsx: thin async Server Component, covered by e2e
import { getOrderForPage } from '@/server/orders';      // calls NestJS through the BFF client (79.8)
import { OrderView } from './OrderView';

export default async function OrderPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  const order = await getOrderForPage(params.id);        // Next.js 15: params is a Promise, await it
  return <OrderView order={order} />;                     // synchronous, component-tested with plain props
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The API decides how testable the frontend can be. Four things make the split above possible:

  • Stable, documented error codes in one shape. Component tests fake { code: 'CART_CHANGED', issues: [...], requestId } (74.6). If the API sometimes returns { message: 'cart changed' } from a different filter, the fake and reality drift and the component test lies.
  • A shared schema package. @shop/contracts lets the frontend build fixtures through the same zod schemas the API validates with (77.6), so a fixture that the API could never produce fails at the fixture, not in production.
  • Deterministic seeding for e2e. A test-only module that creates a user, a cart and a product in one call, enabled only in the e2e environment (77.11).
  • A request ID on every response (X-Request-Id, exposed under CORS). When an e2e test fails, the Playwright trace shows the request ID, and the API log for that ID shows what the server thought.
// apps/api/src/common/request-id.middleware.ts
import { Injectable, NestMiddleware } from '@nestjs/common';
import type { NextFunction, Request, Response } from 'express';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

@Injectable()
export class RequestIdMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
    const incoming = req.header('x-request-id');
    const id = incoming && /^[\w-]{8,64}$/.test(incoming) ? incoming : randomUUID(); // never trust arbitrary input
    req.headers['x-request-id'] = id;
    res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', id);                    // the test report and the log line now share a key
    next();
  }
}

Production scenario

A grocery delivery web app had 2,100 frontend tests: 1,700 unit tests on hooks and components rendered with every child mocked, 380 component tests, and 22 Playwright journeys. The unit layer took 40 s, the component layer 95 s, e2e 6 minutes over 4 shards. An audit of the last 50 production frontend bugs found: 3 would have been caught by a unit test, 31 by a component test that did not exist (wrong error message, missing loading state, a field not cleared on step change), 9 only by e2e (cookie path, redirect loop, chunk splitting), and 7 only in production (a Safari 16 bug, a third-party script, a CDN header). The team stopped writing mocked-children unit tests for components, moved that effort into screen-level component tests with MSW, and kept e2e at 25 journeys. Six months later, escaped frontend bugs per release had fallen from 1.9 to 0.7, and the suite was 30 s faster because 900 low-value unit tests had been deleted.

Failure scenario

At 18:40 on a sale day, the "Apply coupon" button stopped working for every customer. All 2,100 tests were green. The coupon component's unit test rendered <CouponStep> with applyCoupon mocked by vi.mock, and the mock resolved with { totals }. A backend change two days earlier had wrapped the response as { cart: { version, totals } } behind an API version header the web app already sent. The real applyCoupon parsed it with PricedCartSchema, threw a ZodError, and the component showed "Could not apply the code" for every code.

The unit test had mocked the module that broke, so it could not see the break. A component test with MSW returning a fixture built through PricedCartSchema would have run the real client and parser. A Pact interaction for the coupon endpoint (74.10) would have stopped the API deploy. The postmortem added both, and a review rule: do not vi.mock your own API client in component tests.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mocking the thing under test. vi.mock('../api/checkout') in a test about checkout behaviour removes the client, the parser and the error mapper from the test.
  • Snapshot tests of whole component trees (toMatchSnapshot() on rendered HTML) change on every harmless markup edit; reviewers approve the diffs without reading them.
  • E2E as the only safety net for validation messages: 40 journeys for one form, each 20 s, and the suite is too slow to run on every pull request.
  • Coverage as a target. 90 % line coverage of components says nothing about whether the error states render; Part 41.16 explains what the number means.
  • Async Server Components pushed into component tests with hacks (calling the function and awaiting the JSX) test React internals, not the page.
  • Tests that only pass on a fast laptop: a waitFor with a 1 s timeout that passes locally in 200 ms and times out on a loaded CI runner.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks, for each risk, "what is the cheapest test that would fail if this broke, without lying?" They accept a small number of slow, honest tests over a large number of fast tests that mock the interesting parts. They treat the network boundary as the natural seam for frontend tests, because it is the boundary the backend owns and can describe precisely (zod schemas, OpenAPI, problem documents). They keep e2e for things only a real browser and a real backend can prove: cookies, redirects, the production bundle, database constraints. To a product manager they say: "Most of our tests check each screen in seconds with a fake server; about twenty slower tests walk the money paths through a real browser and a real database before every release."

Common mistakes

  • Writing component tests that assert on internal state (wrapper.state(), hook return values of a component) instead of what the user sees.
  • One e2e test per acceptance criterion, instead of component tests for most criteria and one journey for the path.
  • Mocking fetch with vi.fn() per test, so each test invents its own response shapes.
  • No static layer in CI: tsc --noEmit not run, because next build "already type-checks" (it does, but only for files it builds, and late in the pipeline).
  • Keeping tests that nobody would miss. A test that has never failed for a real bug and breaks on every refactor is a cost, not an asset.

Interview questions

  1. Why does the testing trophy fit frontends better than the pyramid? Expected answer: most UI bugs are in the wiring of components, hooks, schemas and the network client; component tests with a faked network catch them at low cost, while isolated unit tests with mocked children miss them. Why it matters: it decides where a team spends its testing effort. Follow-ups: when would you still write many unit tests? (Dense pure logic: pricing display, date bucketing, reducers.)
  2. Where would you test that a server field error appears under the right input? Expected answer: a component test with MSW returning the real problem document; not e2e (too slow for every field), not a unit test of applyServerErrors alone (misses the wiring).
  3. What can only an e2e test prove? Expected answer: real cookies, redirects and BFF behaviour, the production bundle, CSS layout, real database constraints and idempotency across the stack.
  4. How do you test an async Server Component in Next.js 14? Expected answer: you do not unit-render it; keep it thin, component-test the synchronous children with props, and cover the page in e2e.
  5. A team has 95 % coverage and frequent UI regressions. What do you look at first? Expected answer: what the tests mock and what they assert; likely mocked children and API modules, and assertions on implementation details.
  6. How does the backend make the frontend easier to test? Expected answer: one error shape with stable codes, shared schemas, deterministic seeding, request IDs.

Practical exercise

Take the order pages of 72.12 and write a one-page test plan.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every risk listed in the 72.12 failure-drill table is assigned to exactly one level, with one sentence on why.
  • At most 5 e2e journeys; each covers a boundary that a component test cannot (cookies, redirects, database, production bundle).
  • No test in the plan mocks the web app's own API client module.
  • The plan names the API features it depends on (error codes, seeding endpoint, request ID) and who owns each.

77.2 Unit tests with Vitest: utilities, reducers and hooks

Concept

A unit test runs one small piece of code with controlled inputs and checks its output. On the frontend the good candidates are pure functions (formatting, parsing, sorting, URL building), reducers (71.5), custom hooks with real logic (retry, debounce, idempotency keys), and schema refinements in the shared contracts.

Vitest is a test runner built on Vite (70.3). It reuses the app's Vite config, so TypeScript, JSX, path aliases and import.meta.env work in tests the same way they work in the app. Its API is deliberately close to Jest's: describe, it, expect, vi.fn(), vi.mock(), vi.useFakeTimers(). Jest (29 or 30) remains common, especially in older Create React App and Next.js projects; everything in this section applies to it with jest. in place of vi..

Why does it exist?

Pure logic is where combinatorics live. A money formatter has currencies, negative amounts, zero, very large values and locale differences. A reducer has every pair of state and action. Checking those through rendered components would take 50 times longer and say less about which case failed. A unit test runs each case in a millisecond and names it.

Mental model

Imagine testing a calculator's keys one at a time on a bench, before it is built into the till. You learn quickly and exactly which key is broken. You do not learn whether the till's drawer opens.

How it works

  1. Vitest reads vitest.config.ts (or the test block of vite.config.ts), transforms test files with the same plugins as the app (esbuild for TypeScript, the React plugin for JSX), and runs each test file in a worker (threads or forks; forks is the default since Vitest 2).
  2. The environment decides which globals exist. node (default) has no DOM. jsdom or happy-dom provide document, window, sessionStorage and events. Pure functions should run in node; hooks and components need a DOM.
  3. Module mocking (vi.mock(path, factory)) is hoisted to the top of the file and replaces a module for that file only.
  4. Fake timers (vi.useFakeTimers()) replace setTimeout, setInterval and Date, so a hook that waits 1 s and then 2 s can be tested in milliseconds with vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1000), which also flushes promise callbacks between timers.
  5. renderHook (from @testing-library/react, since v13.1) renders a hook inside a tiny test component and returns result.current; updates must happen inside act() so React applies state changes before you assert.

Vitest 3 versus Jest for a frontend repository:

Question Vitest 3 Jest 29/30
Uses the app's Vite config and aliases Yes, same pipeline Needs moduleNameMapper, a transformer (ts-jest, @swc/jest, babel-jest)
ESM support Native Experimental flags or transforms
Speed on 1,000 tests Typically 1.5-3x faster cold, much faster in watch Mature, slower start
Next.js Official guide with @vitejs/plugin-react Official next/jest preset (nextJest())
Browser Mode (real browser instead of jsdom) Experimental in 2 and 3, stable in Vitest 4 No
Multiple configs in one run test.projects (10.2+), replacing vitest.workspace projects

Practical example

Three unit-test targets from the checkout:

  • formatMoney(minor: string, currency: string, locale?): minor units arrive as strings (74.7); the formatter must not use floating point for large values.
  • checkoutReducer (71.5): every legal transition and every illegal one ignored.
  • usePlaceOrder (71.8): retries a timeout with the same idempotency key, backs off 1 s then 2 s, clears the key after a final answer, and refuses a second submit while one is in flight.

React / Next.js example

The configuration. The React plugin handles JSX; vite-tsconfig-paths reads the @/ alias from tsconfig.json, exactly as the Next.js Vitest guide recommends:

// apps/web/vitest.config.ts  (Vitest 3)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import tsconfigPaths from 'vite-tsconfig-paths';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), tsconfigPaths()],
  test: {
    environment: 'jsdom',                        // per-file override: // @vitest-environment node
    setupFiles: ['./src/test/setup.ts'],
    include: ['src/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}'],
    exclude: ['**/*.pact.test.ts', 'e2e/**'],     // Pact and Playwright have their own runners
    restoreMocks: true,                           // vi.spyOn restored after each test
    unstubGlobals: true,                          // vi.stubGlobal undone after each test
    coverage: { provider: 'v8', reporter: ['text', 'lcov'], include: ['src/**/*.{ts,tsx}'] },
  },
});
// apps/web/src/test/setup.ts
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';       // toBeInTheDocument, toHaveAccessibleName, ...
import { cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';
import { afterEach } from 'vitest';

afterEach(() => {
  cleanup();                                     // unmount after every test; automatic only with globals: true
  sessionStorage.clear();                        // idempotency keys from 77.8 must not leak between tests
});

A table-driven unit test of the money formatter. It runs in the node environment, so it starts in a few milliseconds:

// packages/contracts/src/money.test.ts
// @vitest-environment node
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { formatMoney } from './money';

describe('formatMoney', () => {
  it.each([
    ['129900', 'INR', 'en-IN', '₹1,299.00'],
    ['0', 'INR', 'en-IN', '₹0.00'],
    ['5', 'USD', 'en-US', '$0.05'],
    ['-2500', 'EUR', 'de-DE', '-25,00 €'],
    ['900719925474099312', 'INR', 'en-IN', '₹9,00,71,99,25,47,40,993.12'], // beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
  ])('formats %s %s in %s as %s', (minor, currency, locale, expected) => {
    // Intl may use a narrow no-break space in some locales; normalise for a readable expectation
    expect(formatMoney(minor, currency, locale).replace(/ | /g, ' ')).toBe(expected);
  });

  it('rejects a decimal string instead of guessing', () => {
    expect(() => formatMoney('12.99', 'INR')).toThrow(/minor units/);
  });
});

The last case of the table is the interesting one: if formatMoney did Number(minor) / 100, the value would round silently. The implementation must use BigInt and string slicing; this test proves it without reading the code.

A reducer test covers the transition table of 71.5 as data:

// apps/web/src/checkout/checkoutReducer.test.ts
// @vitest-environment node
import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { checkoutReducer, type CheckoutState } from './checkoutReducer';
import { aTotals, anAddress } from '../test/builders';     // builders parse through @shop/contracts (83.6)

const payment: CheckoutState = { step: 'payment', address: anAddress(), coupon: null, totals: aTotals(), error: null };

describe('checkoutReducer', () => {
  it('moves payment -> placing on PLACE_ORDER and clears the error', () => {
    const next = checkoutReducer({ ...payment, error: 'Declined' }, { type: 'PLACE_ORDER' });
    expect(next).toMatchObject({ step: 'placing', error: null });
  });

  it('ignores a second PLACE_ORDER while placing (double tap)', () => {
    const placing = checkoutReducer(payment, { type: 'PLACE_ORDER' });
    expect(checkoutReducer(placing, { type: 'PLACE_ORDER' })).toBe(placing);  // same object: no re-render
  });

  it.each(['address', 'coupon', 'payment'] as const)('ignores ORDER_PLACED from %s', (step) => {
    const state = step === 'payment' ? payment : ({ ...payment, step } as unknown as CheckoutState);
    expect(checkoutReducer(state, { type: 'ORDER_PLACED', orderId: 'A7K2Q9P' })).toBe(state);
  });

  it('returns to payment with the message on ORDER_FAILED', () => {
    const placing = checkoutReducer(payment, { type: 'PLACE_ORDER' });
    expect(checkoutReducer(placing, { type: 'ORDER_FAILED', message: 'Card declined' }))
      .toMatchObject({ step: 'payment', error: 'Card declined' });
  });
});

Asserting toBe(state) (same reference) for ignored actions is deliberate: React skips the re-render when a reducer returns the same object, so this is a performance property as well as a correctness one.

A hook test for usePlaceOrder with fake timers. Here mocking the API module is correct: the subject is the hook's retry policy, not the network, and the component tests of 77.3 cover the real client.

// apps/web/src/checkout/usePlaceOrder.test.ts
import { act, renderHook } from '@testing-library/react';
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { usePlaceOrder } from './usePlaceOrder';
import { placeOrder, ApiTimeoutError } from '../api/orders';
import { ApiError } from '../api/errors';

vi.mock('../api/orders', async (importOriginal) => {
  const actual = await importOriginal<typeof import('../api/orders')>();
  return { ...actual, placeOrder: vi.fn() };              // keep ApiTimeoutError real
});

describe('usePlaceOrder', () => {
  beforeEach(() => vi.useFakeTimers());
  afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());

  it('retries a timeout with the same idempotency key after 1 s', async () => {
    vi.mocked(placeOrder)
      .mockRejectedValueOnce(new ApiTimeoutError())
      .mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: 'A7K2Q9P' } as Awaited<ReturnType<typeof placeOrder>>);
    const { result } = renderHook(() => usePlaceOrder('cart-1', 9));

    let outcome: unknown;
    await act(async () => {
      const pending = result.current.submit('upi');
      await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1000);            // the backoff before attempt 2
      outcome = await pending;
    });

    expect(outcome).toEqual({ ok: true, orderId: 'A7K2Q9P' });
    const [first, second] = vi.mocked(placeOrder).mock.calls;
    expect(second[1]).toBe(first[1]);                      // same key: the server replays, never duplicates
    expect(sessionStorage.getItem('idem:checkout:cart-1:v9')).toBeNull(); // final answer clears it
  });

  it('refuses a second submit while the first is in flight', async () => {
    vi.mocked(placeOrder).mockReturnValue(new Promise(() => {}));   // never settles
    const { result } = renderHook(() => usePlaceOrder('cart-1', 9));
    let second: unknown;
    await act(async () => { void result.current.submit('upi'); second = await result.current.submit('upi'); });
    expect(second).toEqual({ ok: false, message: 'Already placing your order' });
    expect(placeOrder).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });

  it('keeps the key when the outcome is unknown, so a retry replays', async () => {
    vi.mocked(placeOrder).mockRejectedValue(new ApiError(503, 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE'));
    const { result } = renderHook(() => usePlaceOrder('cart-1', 9));
    await act(async () => { await result.current.submit('upi'); });
    expect(sessionStorage.getItem('idem:checkout:cart-1:v9')).not.toBeNull();
  });
});

Backend side (NestJS)

Pure rules shared by both sides belong in @shop/contracts and get their unit tests there, run by both pipelines (70.9). The money formatter above is one; others are the order status lifecycle (canCancel(status)), cursor encoding, and postcode syntax. The API's Jest suite and the web's Vitest suite both import the same package; the package's own Vitest suite runs once per change. What the API must not do is reimplement a shared rule with subtly different behaviour: if the API decides cancellability with status in ('PENDING','PAID') and the web with canCancel(), the "Cancel" button and the server disagree for PACKED.

// packages/contracts/src/order-status.ts: one rule, imported by NestJS and React
export const CANCELLABLE = ['PENDING', 'PAID'] as const;
export const canCancel = (status: string): boolean => (CANCELLABLE as readonly string[]).includes(status);
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.service.ts (excerpt)
import { canCancel } from '@shop/contracts';
// ...
if (!canCancel(order.status)) throw new ConflictException({ code: 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE' }); // same rule as the button

Production scenario

A storefront's unit layer is 900 tests in 11 s on CI: 340 in packages/contracts (formatters, schemas with refinements, status rules), 410 reducers and pure helpers in the web app, and 150 hook tests. They run first in the pipeline (after tsc) so a broken formatter fails a pull request in under a minute, before the slower component and e2e jobs start. Watch mode reruns only the tests affected by a saved file, typically 5 to 30 tests in under a second.

Failure scenario

A developer changed formatMoney to use Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: 'currency', currency }).format(Number(minor) / 100), because it was shorter. All component tests passed: their fixtures used amounts like 129900. Two weeks later a B2B customer placed a bulk order of 1,234,567,890,123.45 in Indonesian rupiah, and the confirmation page showed a total that differed from the invoice by 3 rupiah. The table-driven test with a value beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER existed in the API's repository but not in the web's. Moving the formatter and its tests into @shop/contracts, used by both, removed the duplicate and the gap.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Fake timers and promises. vi.advanceTimersByTime (sync) does not flush promise callbacks between timers; a retry loop with await stalls. Use vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync.
  • Fake timers and Testing Library. user-event waits with real timers by default; with fake timers create it with userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime }).
  • Intl differences between Node versions (ICU data, narrow no-break spaces in some locales) make formatter snapshots fail after a Node upgrade; normalise spaces or pin the CI Node version.
  • Module mocks leak between tests in the same file if return values are set with mockReturnValue and not reset; restoreMocks: true resets spies, vi.mocked(fn).mockReset() resets vi.fn() mocks created in factories.
  • Time zone dependence. A date-bucketing test passes in Bengaluru and fails on a UTC runner; set process.env.TZ in the config or pass the zone explicitly (74.7).
