  • jsdom is not a browser. It has no layout (getBoundingClientRect returns zeros), no IntersectionObserver, no matchMedia by default. Hooks that depend on them need small fakes or a real browser (Vitest Browser Mode, or Playwright component tests).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior writes unit tests where the logic is dense and the inputs are many, and keeps them in the package that owns the rule, so the backend and frontend share both the code and its tests. They prefer table-driven tests because a table is reviewable: a reviewer can spot the missing case (zero, negative, very large) without reading code. They mock a module only when the subject of the test is the code that calls it (a retry policy), never when the subject is the module itself. And they do not unit-test components by mocking their children: that is a component test's job, done without the mocks.

Common mistakes

  • Testing implementation details of hooks: asserting how many times an internal useState setter was called.
  • Forgetting act() around hook updates and silencing the warning instead of fixing it.
  • Using real timers in retry tests and waiting 3 real seconds per test.
  • Running pure-function tests in jsdom, paying 100-300 ms of environment start-up per file for nothing.
  • Duplicating shared rules in web and API code, each with its own tests that agree with themselves.

Interview questions

  1. When would you mock a module in a frontend unit test? Expected answer: when the subject is the caller's policy (retry, caching, sequencing) and the module's own behaviour is tested elsewhere; never your API client in a test about screen behaviour.
  2. How do you test a hook that retries with backoff? Expected answer: renderHook, fake timers, vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync inside act, assert calls and arguments (same idempotency key). Follow-up: why not the sync advanceTimersByTime? (It does not flush promise callbacks between timers.)
  3. Vitest or Jest for a new Vite or Next.js project? Expected answer: Vitest for shared Vite config, native ESM and speed; Jest remains fine where it is established, with next/jest for Next.js.
  4. Why test a money formatter with a value above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER? Expected answer: it proves no floating-point conversion happens; minor units travel as strings (74.7).
  5. What is jsdom missing, and what do you do about it? Expected answer: layout, observers, media queries and real rendering; fake the API minimally or move the test to a real browser.

Practical exercise

Write the unit layer for the order status rules and the checkout hook.

Acceptance criteria:

  • canCancel, formatMoney and encodeCursor/decodeCursor live in @shop/contracts with table-driven tests, including a value above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and an unknown status string.
  • The NestJS cancel endpoint and the web "Cancel" button both import canCancel; a test in each proves it.
  • usePlaceOrder tests cover: timeout then success with the same key, 409 IDEMPOTENCY_IN_PROGRESS retried, a 422 clearing the key, an unknown outcome keeping it, and a second submit refused, all in under 200 ms total with fake timers.
  • Pure-function test files run in the node environment.

77.3 Component tests with Testing Library: behaviour, not implementation

Concept

A component test renders a real component tree (a form, a dialog, a whole checkout step) into a simulated DOM and drives it the way a user would: find the input by its label, type, press the button, read what appears. Testing Library (@testing-library/react on top of @testing-library/dom) is the standard tool. Its guiding principle, in its author's words: the more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you.

In practice that means three habits:

  • Find elements the way a user or a screen reader would: by role and accessible name (getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })), by label, by visible text. Not by CSS class, component name or internal state.
  • Interact with real events through @testing-library/user-event, which types character by character, moves focus, fires pointerdown, mousedown, focus, pointerup, mouseup, click in the browser's order, and respects disabled.
  • Assert on the result a user could observe: text, focus, disabled state, the accessible description of an input, the request that was sent.

Why does it exist?

Older React testing tools (Enzyme) encouraged reaching inside components: read state, call instance methods, shallow-render and find children by component type. Those tests broke on every refactor (renaming a state variable, converting a class to hooks, splitting a component) while staying green when the user-visible behaviour broke. They tested the code's shape, not its job. Enzyme also never supported React 18. Testing Library replaced it by making the implementation unreachable on purpose: there is no API to read a component's state.

There is a bonus that matters to the whole team: a test that finds the Postcode field by getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Postcode' }) fails if the label is missing or not linked to the input. Accessibility bugs become test failures (69.9).

Mental model

Imagine a mystery shopper who is not allowed into the kitchen. They can only read the menu, order, and judge what arrives. If the chef reorganises the kitchen, the shopper's report does not change. If the dish arrives cold, it does. Testing Library is the rule that keeps your tests out of the kitchen.

How it works

  1. render(<AddressForm onSaved={onSaved} />) creates a container div in document.body, mounts the tree with createRoot, and wraps the mount in act(), so effects have run before you assert.

  2. Queries search document.body (via screen) or a container (via within(el)). There are three families:

    Prefix Not found More than one Async Use for
    getBy... throws throws no Elements that must be there now
    queryBy... returns null throws no Asserting absence: expect(queryByRole('alert')).toBeNull()
    findBy... rejects after timeout (1,000 ms default) rejects yes, retries Elements that appear after a request or a timer

    Each family has All variants (getAllByRole) that return arrays.

  3. Query priority (Testing Library's own guidance): getByRole (with name), then getByLabelText, getByPlaceholderText, getByText, getByDisplayValue; then getByAltText, getByTitle; and only as a last resort getByTestId. Role queries use the same accessibility tree a screen reader uses, computed by dom-accessibility-api.

  4. userEvent.setup() creates a user session. Every interaction returns a promise and must be awaited: await user.type(input, '560001'), await user.click(button), await user.tab(), await user.keyboard('{Enter}').

  5. Matchers from @testing-library/jest-dom read the DOM the way a user perceives it: toBeVisible, toBeDisabled, toHaveFocus, toHaveValue, toHaveAccessibleName, toHaveAccessibleDescription, toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true').

  6. Cleanup unmounts the tree after each test (77.2's setup file).

test code                 Testing Library                     React + jsdom
---------                 ---------------                     -------------
render(<Form/>)     ->    createRoot + act()            ->    DOM nodes in document.body
user.type(postcode) ->    keydown/keypress/input/keyup  ->    RHF register onChange, re-render
user.click(submit)  ->    pointer + mouse + click       ->    handleSubmit -> zod -> setError
findByRole('alert') ->    poll DOM every 50 ms          ->    <p role="alert">Postcode must be 6 digits</p>

Practical example

The address form of 71.7 has five behaviours worth a test, all observable without reading its code:

  1. Submitting empty shows field messages and does not call onSaved.
  2. A wrong postcode shows "Postcode must be 6 digits" after the field loses focus (mode: 'onTouched').
  3. A valid form calls onSaved once with trimmed values.
  4. A server 422 with path: "postcode" shows the server's message under the postcode and moves focus there.
  5. While saving, the submit button is disabled.

The form's input is a prop (onSaved), so the test passes a vi.fn(). That is not "mocking the network"; it is supplying the component's real input. The network version of the same flow, through the real client and MSW, is in 77.5.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/src/checkout/AddressForm.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { AddressForm } from './AddressForm';
import { ApiError } from '../api/errors';

async function fillValid(user: ReturnType<typeof userEvent.setup>) {
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Full name' }), '  Asha Rao ');
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Mobile number' }), '9876543210');
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'House number and street' }), '12 MG Road');
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'City' }), 'Bengaluru');
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Postcode' }), '560001');
}

describe('AddressForm', () => {
  it('shows field messages and does not save an empty form', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSaved = vi.fn();
    render(<AddressForm onSaved={onSaved} />);

    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save address' }));

    expect(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Full name' })).toHaveAccessibleDescription('Enter your full name');
    expect(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Postcode' })).toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
    expect(onSaved).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  it('validates the postcode when the field loses focus', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    render(<AddressForm onSaved={vi.fn()} />);
    const postcode = screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Postcode' });

    await user.type(postcode, '5600');
    expect(postcode).toHaveAccessibleDescription('');      // quiet while typing: mode 'onTouched'
    await user.tab();
    expect(postcode).toHaveAccessibleDescription('Postcode must be 6 digits');
  });

  it('saves trimmed values once', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSaved = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    render(<AddressForm onSaved={onSaved} />);
    await fillValid(user);
    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save address' }));

    expect(onSaved).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(onSaved.mock.calls[0][0]).toMatchObject({ fullName: 'Asha Rao', postcode: '560001' }); // zod trimmed it
  });

  it('puts a server field error under the field and focuses it', async () => {
    const user = userEvent.setup();
    const onSaved = vi.fn().mockRejectedValue(new ApiError(422, 'ADDRESS_REJECTED', [
      { path: 'postcode', code: 'NOT_SERVICEABLE', message: 'We do not deliver to 560001 yet' },
    ]));
    render(<AddressForm onSaved={onSaved} />);
    await fillValid(user);
    await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save address' }));

    const postcode = screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Postcode' });
    expect(postcode).toHaveAccessibleDescription('We do not deliver to 560001 yet');
    expect(postcode).toHaveFocus();                         // applyServerErrors: shouldFocus on the first issue
  });
});

Notice what the test never mentions: React Hook Form, register, the zod resolver, useState. The form could be rewritten with React 19 Actions (71.7) and these four tests would still be the specification.

Notice also the query getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Postcode' }). The input has inputMode="numeric" but no type="number", so its role is textbox; a type="number" input would be spinbutton. When a role query cannot find an element, Testing Library prints the accessibility tree it did find, which usually shows the problem at once ("you have a textbox named 'Pincode'").

Testing the presentational pieces of 71.10 is even simpler, because they take only props:

// apps/web/src/orders/CancelReasonPicker.test.tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { CancelReasonPicker } from './CancelReasonPicker';

it('reports the chosen reason and supports the keyboard', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  const onChange = vi.fn();
  render(<CancelReasonPicker value={null} onChange={onChange} />);

  const group = screen.getByRole('radiogroup', { name: 'Why are you cancelling?' });
  expect(group).toBeInTheDocument();
  await user.tab();                                          // focus enters the group
  await user.keyboard('{ArrowDown}');                        // native radios move with arrows
  expect(onChange).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith('ORDERED_BY_MISTAKE');
});

Backend side (NestJS)

The fourth address test depends on a contract the API must keep: a 422 problem document whose issues[].path matches the form's field names (postcode, not address.postcode or zip). The API's own e2e test should assert the same shape, so both sides hold the same example:

// apps/api/test/checkout-address.e2e-spec.ts  (Jest + supertest, Part 41.13)
it('rejects a non-serviceable postcode with a field path the form understands', async () => {
  const res = await request(app.getHttpServer())
    .post('/v1/checkout/address')
    .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`)
    .send({ ...validAddress, postcode: '560001' })            // seeded as not serviceable
    .expect(422)
    .expect('Content-Type', /application\/problem\+json/);

  expect(res.body).toMatchObject({
    code: 'ADDRESS_REJECTED',
    issues: [{ path: 'postcode', code: 'NOT_SERVICEABLE' }],  // path equals the RHF field name
    requestId: expect.any(String),
  });
});

When the frontend test and the backend test use the same literal example (postcode, NOT_SERVICEABLE), a reviewer can see the contract in both pull requests. Pact (74.10) makes that link mechanical.

Production scenario

A storefront's 420 component tests cover 31 screens and run in 68 s on a 4-vCPU runner (Vitest's default parallelism, one worker per core). The slowest 10 % are full-screen tests of checkout steps at 400-900 ms each, mostly user.type on long forms. Two changes halved them. userEvent.setup({ delay: null }) skips the macrotask pause user-event v14 inserts between keystrokes. And long fixed inputs that no test inspects per keystroke use await user.click(el) then await user.paste('12 MG Road'), which fires one input event instead of one per character. Tests that check per-keystroke behaviour (formatting a phone number as you type) keep type.

Failure scenario

A design-system upgrade changed the Button component to render <div role="button" tabIndex={0}> so it could hold a loading spinner. All 420 component tests still passed: getByRole('button') matched the div, and user.click fired click events on it. In production, keyboard users could no longer submit checkout: the div had no handler for Enter and Space, and the form's implicit submission on Enter stopped working because there was no submit button inside the form.

The tests had only used the mouse. Adding one keyboard path per form (await user.keyboard('{Enter}') in the postcode field, then expect onSaved called) failed immediately on the new Button. The fix restored a native <button type="submit"> with the spinner inside it, and an axe check (77.10) now flags role-button divs in forms.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • getByText for interactive elements passes when the text exists anywhere, even in a non-clickable span; prefer getByRole with name.
  • fireEvent instead of user-event: fireEvent.change sets a value without focus, key events or disabled checks; a test can "type" into a disabled field.
  • Not awaiting user calls produces assertions that run before React re-renders, and act warnings.
  • Multiple matches: two "Remove" buttons in a cart list; scope with within(row) instead of getAllByRole(...)[1].
  • Hidden elements: role queries ignore elements with display: none or aria-hidden by default (hidden: false); a modal behind another modal is invisible to them, which is usually what a user experiences too.
  • Translations: tests that query by English text break when copy changes; for i18n apps render with the real message catalogue of one locale and query by those strings, or by role plus the message key's output.
  • Portals: dialogs rendered into document.body via a portal are found by screen, not by the container returned from render.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior writes component tests as executable acceptance criteria, in the user's vocabulary. If a test needs a data-testid, they first ask whether the element is missing an accessible name, because a real user would have the same problem. They keep every test independent and short, and they read a failing test's printed DOM before reaching for a debugger. They test at least one keyboard path for every form and dialog. And they insist the server's error contract is part of the test, because the most common frontend bug in a checkout is not a crash, it is a correct server message shown in the wrong place.

Common mistakes

  • Asserting on CSS classes (toHaveClass('error')) instead of aria-invalid and the accessible description.
  • Testing third-party components (React Hook Form's internals, a date picker library) instead of your use of them.
  • Huge setup per test: 60 lines of providers and mocks before one assertion; extract a renderCheckout() helper (77.4).
  • Snapshotting rendered HTML instead of asserting behaviour.
  • Mouse-only tests, which miss the most common accessibility regressions.

Interview questions

  1. Why prefer getByRole over getByTestId? Expected answer: it finds elements by what users and assistive technology perceive, survives refactors, and fails when accessibility is broken; test IDs are invisible to users and prove nothing about them.
  2. getBy, queryBy or findBy: which for what? Expected answer: getBy for present now, queryBy to assert absence, findBy for elements that appear asynchronously.
  3. Why user-event rather than fireEvent? Expected answer: realistic event sequences, focus, keyboard, disabled handling; fireEvent dispatches one synthetic event.
  4. How do you test that a server error lands on the right field? Expected answer: return the problem document with path, assert the field's accessible description and focus, and keep the API's own test asserting the same path.
  5. What does a component test not prove? Expected answer: real layout, CSS, browser quirks, cookies, redirects, the production bundle.

Practical exercise

Write component tests for the coupon step of 71.13 using only props for its callbacks.

Acceptance criteria:

  • No query uses a CSS selector or test ID.
  • Tests cover: invalid code syntax (client), a server 422 with path: "code", a 409 CART_CHANGED banner, the button disabled while applying, and applying with the Enter key.
  • Each test runs in under 300 ms.
  • Renaming the internal state variables or replacing React Hook Form with plain useState requires no test change.

77.4 Async UI, providers and framework seams in component tests

Concept

Real screens are asynchronous and live inside providers: a TanStack Query client, a router, a session context, a Zustand store, sometimes the Next.js App Router. A component test must supply these the way the app does, wait for asynchronous UI correctly, and replace only the seams that a test environment cannot provide (the Next.js router, IntersectionObserver, the clock). Getting this wrong produces the two classic frontend test diseases: act() warnings and tests that pass or fail depending on machine speed.

Why does it exist?

Because "wait one second and check" is how flaky tests are born. A test that renders the order page and immediately asserts "Order A7K2Q9P" fails, because the data arrives after a request. A test that waits a fixed 500 ms passes on a laptop and fails on a busy CI runner. And a test that renders a component without the app's providers either crashes (No QueryClient set, use QueryClientProvider to set one) or, worse, uses a shared client from another test and sees its cached data.

Mental model

Imagine testing a vending machine. You must plug it in (providers) before pressing buttons, and after pressing "B4" you watch the slot until the can drops, up to a sensible limit, rather than counting to three and looking once. You also start every test with a freshly stocked machine, not the one the last tester half-emptied.

How it works

  1. A test render helper builds the providers per test: a new QueryClient each time (so no cache leaks), with retry: false so an error response shows the error state at once instead of after three retries with backoff.
  2. Waiting: findBy... and waitFor(() => expect(...)) poll the DOM every 50 ms until the assertion passes or a timeout (1,000 ms default) expires. They are the only correct way to wait for UI. waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByText('Loading...')) waits for a loading state to go away.
  3. act() warnings ("An update to OrderPage inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)") mean a state update happened after the test stopped waiting: usually a request that resolved after the last assertion. The fix is to wait for the final UI state, not to wrap things in act by hand.
  4. Framework seams are replaced at module level: next/navigation (useRouter, usePathname, useSearchParams) has no App Router context in Vitest, so the test mocks the module with vi.mock('next/navigation', ...). Browser APIs missing from jsdom (IntersectionObserver, matchMedia, ResizeObserver) get small fakes with vi.stubGlobal.
  5. Stores created at module level (Zustand) keep state between tests in the same file; reset them in beforeEach from their initial state.
  6. Render counts can be measured with React's <Profiler onRender>, which works in tests, so "typing in the coupon does not re-render the summary" (71.13) becomes an assertion.
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Test
    participant RTL as TestingLibrary
    participant R as React
    participant Q as QueryClient
    participant M as MSW
    T->>RTL: renderCheckout at /orders/A7K2Q9P
    RTL->>R: mount inside providers
    R->>Q: useQuery order A7K2Q9P
    Q->>M: GET /api/v1/orders/A7K2Q9P
    T->>RTL: findByRole heading Order A7K2Q9P
    RTL->>RTL: poll DOM every 50 ms
    M-->>Q: 200 order fixture
    Q-->>R: data, re-render
    RTL-->>T: heading found, assertion passes

Practical example

The order detail screen of 72.12 uses useQuery for the order, useMutation for cancel, useRouter from next/navigation to go back to the list, and a Zustand store for the "compact view" toggle. The tests need: fresh providers, the network faked with MSW (77.5 explains the handlers), the router mocked, the store reset, and waits on visible states.

React / Next.js example

The shared render helper:

// apps/web/src/test/render.tsx  (TanStack Query v5)
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { render, type RenderOptions } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import type { ReactElement, ReactNode } from 'react';
import { SessionProvider, type Session } from '@/session/SessionProvider';

export function makeTestQueryClient() {
  return new QueryClient({
    defaultOptions: {
      queries: { retry: false, gcTime: Infinity, staleTime: 0 },   // errors show at once; no GC timers during the test
      mutations: { retry: false },
    },
  });
}

type Options = RenderOptions & { session?: Session | null; queryClient?: QueryClient };

export function renderWithProviders(ui: ReactElement, { session = aSession(), queryClient = makeTestQueryClient(), ...rest }: Options = {}) {
  const Wrapper = ({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) => (
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <SessionProvider value={session}>{children}</SessionProvider>
    </QueryClientProvider>
  );
  return { user: userEvent.setup(), queryClient, ...render(ui, { wrapper: Wrapper, ...rest }) };
}

export const aSession = (overrides: Partial<Session> = {}): Session =>
  ({ userId: 'u1', name: 'Asha', roles: ['customer'], ...overrides });

The App Router seam. next/navigation hooks read a context that only the Next.js runtime provides, so the test replaces the module and keeps a handle on push:

// apps/web/src/test/next-navigation.ts
import { vi } from 'vitest';

export const router = { push: vi.fn(), replace: vi.fn(), back: vi.fn(), refresh: vi.fn(), prefetch: vi.fn() };
export let searchParams = new URLSearchParams();
export const setSearchParams = (q: string) => { searchParams = new URLSearchParams(q); };

vi.mock('next/navigation', () => ({
  useRouter: () => router,
  usePathname: () => '/orders/A7K2Q9P',
  useSearchParams: () => searchParams,       // a URLSearchParams is close enough to ReadonlyURLSearchParams for reads
  notFound: () => { throw new Error('NEXT_NOT_FOUND'); },
}));

A test of the order screen's three states, waiting correctly:

// apps/web/src/orders/OrderDetail.test.tsx
import '../test/next-navigation';                            // registers the vi.mock before the component imports it
import { screen, waitForElementToBeRemoved, within } from '@testing-library/react';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { beforeEach, describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { server } from '../test/msw/server';
import { anOrder } from '../test/builders';
import { renderWithProviders } from '../test/render';
import { router } from '../test/next-navigation';
import { useViewPrefs } from './viewPrefsStore';
import { OrderDetail } from './OrderDetail';

const API = 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1';

describe('OrderDetail', () => {
  beforeEach(() => useViewPrefs.setState(useViewPrefs.getInitialState(), true)); // Zustand 4.5+/5: reset the store

  it('shows the order once loaded', async () => {
    server.use(http.get(`${API}/orders/:id`, () => HttpResponse.json(anOrder({ displayId: 'A7K2Q9P', status: 'PAID' }))));
    renderWithProviders(<OrderDetail orderId="A7K2Q9P" />);

    await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByRole('status', { name: 'Loading order' }));
    expect(screen.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order A7K2Q9P' })).toBeVisible();
    expect(within(screen.getByRole('region', { name: 'Status' })).getByText('Paid')).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('shows a retryable error with the request ID on a 503', async () => {
    server.use(http.get(`${API}/orders/:id`, () => HttpResponse.json(
      { code: 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE', status: 503, title: 'Service unavailable', issues: [], requestId: 'req-42' },
      { status: 503, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/problem+json' } },
    )));
    const { user } = renderWithProviders(<OrderDetail orderId="A7K2Q9P" />);

    const alert = await screen.findByRole('alert');
    expect(alert).toHaveTextContent('We could not load this order');
    expect(alert).toHaveTextContent('req-42');                 // support can find the server log
    server.use(http.get(`${API}/orders/:id`, () => HttpResponse.json(anOrder({ displayId: 'A7K2Q9P' }))));
    await user.click(within(alert).getByRole('button', { name: 'Try again' }));
    expect(await screen.findByRole('heading', { name: 'Order A7K2Q9P' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  it('goes back to the list after a successful cancel', async () => {
    server.use(
      http.get(`${API}/orders/:id`, () => HttpResponse.json(anOrder({ displayId: 'A7K2Q9P', status: 'PAID' }))),
      http.post(`${API}/orders/:id/cancel`, () => HttpResponse.json(anOrder({ displayId: 'A7K2Q9P', status: 'CANCELLED' }))),
    );
    const { user } = renderWithProviders(<OrderDetail orderId="A7K2Q9P" />);
    await user.click(await screen.findByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel order' }));
    await user.click(screen.getByRole('radio', { name: 'Ordered by mistake' }));
    await user.click(within(screen.getByRole('dialog')).getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel order' }));
    await expect.poll(() => router.push.mock.calls.length).toBe(1);   // Vitest 1.3+: retries until it passes
    expect(router.push).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/orders?cancelled=A7K2Q9P');
  });
});

Measuring renders, for the 71.13 criterion "typing the coupon re-renders neither the address nor the summary":

// apps/web/src/checkout/CheckoutFlow.renders.test.tsx (excerpt)
import { Profiler, type ProfilerOnRenderCallback } from 'react';

const commits: string[] = [];
const onRender: ProfilerOnRenderCallback = (id) => { commits.push(id); };

it('typing a coupon does not re-render the price summary', async () => {
  const { user } = renderWithProviders(<CheckoutFlowAtCouponStep wrapSummary={(n) => <Profiler id="summary" onRender={onRender}>{n}</Profiler>} />);
  commits.length = 0;                                        // ignore the mount
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Coupon code' }), 'SAVE50');
  expect(commits.filter((id) => id === 'summary')).toHaveLength(0);
});

Backend side (NestJS)

Component tests wait for states; the API must make those states distinguishable and stable:

  • Error responses always carry requestId in the body and X-Request-Id in headers, so the error state can show it and a test can assert it.
  • Retry-After on 429 and 503, exposed with CORS exposedHeaders, so the client's "wait" treatment (74.6) is testable with a fixed value.
  • Mutation responses return the updated resource (POST /cancel returns the cancelled order), so the client can update its cache without a second request and the test needs one handler, not two.
  • Deterministic ordering for lists (ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC), so fixtures and screenshots are stable and the UI does not reorder rows between refetches.
// apps/api/src/orders/orders.controller.ts (excerpt)
@Post(':id/cancel')
@HttpCode(200)
async cancel(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
             @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(CancelOrderSchema)) body: CancelOrder): Promise<OrderSummary> {
  const order = await this.orders.cancel(user.id, id, body.reason); // 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE if shipped
  return toOrderSummary(order);                                     // the new state: the client needs no refetch
}

Production scenario

On a 4-vCPU runner, 420 component tests run in 68 s with a fresh QueryClient per test. An earlier version shared one module-level client "for speed"; it saved about 2 ms per test and produced 11 order-dependent failures a month, each costing an engineer 20 minutes to re-run and dismiss. Vitest's --sequence.shuffle flag, run nightly, now catches any new order dependence within a day.

Failure scenario

A test suite passed for months with await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 300)) after each render, "to let the query settle". A CI runner upgrade moved the jobs to shared ARM instances. Response times from MSW stayed under 5 ms, but React's rendering in jsdom slowed by about 40 % under contention, and 9 % of runs failed. The team deleted every fixed sleep (147 of them), replaced them with findBy and waitFor on the final visible state, and the flake rate fell to zero. The suite also got 44 s faster, because the sleeps had been waiting even when nothing was pending.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • waitFor with side effects inside: waitFor(() => user.click(...)) clicks many times; only assertions go inside waitFor.
  • Empty waitFor (await waitFor(() => {})) waits for nothing useful and hides act warnings without fixing them.
  • Retries on in tests: TanStack Query's default 3 retries with exponential backoff make an error state appear after about 7 s, past every timeout.
  • gcTime timers keep the process alive or warn after the test; gcTime: Infinity in the test client avoids scheduling them.
  • Mocking next/navigation after import: vi.mock is hoisted within its own file; importing a helper that calls vi.mock must happen before the component's import, or the mock must be in the setup file.
  • Server Components imported into a test fail on server-only imports or async rendering; test their synchronous children.
  • Fake timers with MSW: MSW's delay() uses timers; with fake timers active it never resolves unless you advance time.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior makes the correct test the easy test: one renderWithProviders helper, one router mock, builders for every fixture, and lint rules (testing-library/prefer-find-by, testing-library/no-wait-for-side-effects, testing-library/await-async-events from eslint-plugin-testing-library) that reject the flaky patterns in review. They wait for outcomes, never for time. They mock framework seams (router, observers) at their thinnest point and never the app's own data layer. And they treat a new act warning as a failing test, because it is a real asynchronous update the test did not account for.

Common mistakes

  • One QueryClient for the whole suite.
  • Fixed sleeps instead of findBy/waitFor.
  • Mocking useQuery to return { data } directly, which skips loading, error and the real fetch.
  • Forgetting to reset module-level stores, so test order matters.
  • Raising the global async timeout to 10 s to hide slow tests instead of finding what is slow.

Interview questions

  1. What does an act() warning tell you, and how do you fix it? Expected answer: a state update after the test stopped waiting; wait for the final UI state with findBy or waitFor rather than wrapping in act manually.
  2. How do you configure TanStack Query for tests, and why? Expected answer: a new client per test, retry: false, gcTime: Infinity; isolation and immediate error states.
  3. How do you test a Client Component that uses useRouter from next/navigation? Expected answer: mock the module and assert calls on push or replace; cover real navigation in e2e.
  4. How would you prove a keystroke does not re-render an expensive component? Expected answer: wrap it in <Profiler> and count commits during typing.
  5. Why are fixed sleeps in tests both slow and flaky? Expected answer: they wait even when nothing is pending, and they are too short on slow machines.

Practical exercise

Build the test harness for the order list of 72.12.

Acceptance criteria:

  • One renderWithProviders helper, one next/navigation mock, and a store reset; no test file creates its own QueryClient.
  • Tests cover loading, empty, filtered-empty, error with request ID and retry, and a successful optimistic cancel, using only findBy, waitFor and waitForElementToBeRemoved for waiting.
  • vitest run --sequence.shuffle passes 20 times in a row.
  • eslint-plugin-testing-library is enabled with its recommended React config and reports zero problems.

77.5 Mocking the network with MSW

Concept

Mock Service Worker (MSW) intercepts HTTP requests at the network layer and answers them with handlers you write. In the browser it registers a real Service Worker (69.8, 82.9) that catches fetch from the page; in Node (Vitest, Jest, Playwright's Node side) it patches the request modules (fetch, http, XMLHttpRequest) through its interceptors library. Either way, your application code runs unchanged: the real API client, the real parsers, the real error mapper (74.6). Only the server is fake.

MSW 2 (released in late 2023) changed the API completely from v1. Handlers are built with http.get(...), http.post(...) and return HttpResponse objects based on the Fetch API's Response. The v1 style, rest.get(path, (req, res, ctx) => res(ctx.json(...))), does not exist in v2; most blog posts and many Stack Overflow answers still show it.

Why does it exist?

The alternatives all cut the test somewhere worse:

  • vi.mock('../api/orders') removes the client, the zod parsing and the error mapping from the test (the coupon incident of 77.1).
  • vi.stubGlobal('fetch', vi.fn()) keeps the client but makes every test hand-build Response objects, and gives no protection against a request the test did not expect.
  • A real backend is right for e2e (77.11) but too slow and too stateful for 400 component tests, and cannot easily produce a 503, a timeout or a malformed body on demand.

MSW sits at the one boundary the backend team can describe exactly: method, path, headers, status and body.

Mental model

Imagine a film set where the actors (your components and client) perform exactly as they will in the cinema, but the street outside the window is a painted backdrop. The actors do not know it is painted. The crew can change the backdrop between takes: a sunny street, a storm, an empty road. MSW is the backdrop, and server.use(...) is changing it for one take.

How it works

flowchart LR
    comp["Component and real API client"] --> fetchcall["fetch POST /api/v1/orders"]
    fetchcall --> icpt["MSW interceptor in Node, or Service Worker in the browser"]
    icpt --> match{"Handler matches method and path?"}
    match -->|"yes"| handler["Handler builds HttpResponse"]
    match -->|"no"| unhandled["onUnhandledRequest: error, warn or bypass"]
    handler --> comp
  1. Handlers describe responses: http.get('http://localhost:3000/api/v1/orders/:id', ({ params, request }) => HttpResponse.json(...)). Paths support parameters (:id) and wildcards (*).
  2. The server (setupServer(...handlers) from msw/node) is started once per test file in the setup file with server.listen(), reset after each test with server.resetHandlers(), and stopped with server.close().
  3. Per-test overrides: server.use(handler) prepends handlers for the current test only; resetHandlers() removes them. { once: true } makes a handler answer one request and then fall through, which is how you test "first attempt fails, retry succeeds".
  4. Unhandled requests: onUnhandledRequest: 'error' turns a request no handler matched into a test failure, so a component that suddenly calls a new endpoint cannot pass by accident.
  5. Responses are real Response objects: HttpResponse.json(body, { status, headers }), HttpResponse.text(), new HttpResponse(null, { status: 204 }), and HttpResponse.error() for a network failure (the client sees TypeError: Failed to fetch).
  6. Timing: await delay(200) inside a handler; await delay('infinite') for a request that never answers (tests a timeout or a pending state).
  7. In the browser, npx msw init public/ --save writes mockServiceWorker.js into the static folder; setupWorker(...handlers).start() from msw/browser registers it. The same handler modules serve local development without a backend and Storybook (through msw-storybook-addon).

Two environment details catch most teams:

  • Absolute URLs in Node. In the browser, fetch('/api/v1/orders') resolves against the page's origin. Node's fetch has no page and throws TypeError: Failed to parse URL. The fix is in the app, not the test: route every request through one apiUrl(path) helper whose base is empty in the browser and http://localhost:3000 in tests (set from import.meta.env or a config module), and write handlers with the same absolute base.
  • Jest with jsdom. jest-environment-jsdom hides Node's fetch, Response, TextEncoder and streams, which MSW 2 needs. Use the jest-fixed-jsdom environment (from the MSW maintainers) or move to Vitest, whose jsdom environment keeps Node's globals.

Practical example

The checkout needs default handlers for the happy path (view, address, coupon, place order) and per-test overrides for each failure: 422 on the postcode, 409 CART_CHANGED on the coupon, 402 declined payment, a timeout followed by a replay, a 503 with a non-JSON body from a proxy. The handlers also enforce part of the contract: the place-order handler rejects a request without Idempotency-Key, exactly as the API does, and counts calls so a double-click test can assert "one request".

React / Next.js example

The setup and default handlers:

// apps/web/src/test/msw/server.ts  (MSW 2)
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { checkoutHandlers } from './checkout.handlers';
import { orderHandlers } from './orders.handlers';

export const server = setupServer(...checkoutHandlers, ...orderHandlers);
// apps/web/src/test/setup.ts (additions to 83.2)
import { afterAll, afterEach, beforeAll } from 'vitest';
import { server } from './msw/server';

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));   // a surprise request fails the test
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());                            // drop per-test overrides
afterAll(() => server.close());
// apps/web/src/test/msw/checkout.handlers.ts
import { http, HttpResponse, delay } from 'msw';
import { PlaceOrderRequestSchema, ApplyCouponSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { aCheckoutView, aPricedCart, aProblem } from '../builders';

export const API = 'http://localhost:3000/api/v1';
export const placeOrderCalls: { key: string | null; body: unknown }[] = [];

export const checkoutHandlers = [
  http.get(`${API}/checkout/view`, () => HttpResponse.json(aCheckoutView({ version: 7 }))),

  http.post(`${API}/checkout/coupon`, async ({ request }) => {
    const parsed = ApplyCouponSchema.safeParse(await request.json());
    if (!parsed.success) return HttpResponse.json(aProblem('VALIDATION_FAILED', 400), { status: 400 });
    return HttpResponse.json(aPricedCart({ version: parsed.data.cartVersion + 1, appliedCoupon: parsed.data.code }));
  }),

  http.post(`${API}/orders`, async ({ request }) => {
    const key = request.headers.get('Idempotency-Key');
    const body = await request.json();
    placeOrderCalls.push({ key, body });
    if (!key) return HttpResponse.json(aProblem('IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED', 400), { status: 400 }); // like the API
    if (!PlaceOrderRequestSchema.safeParse(body).success) {
      return HttpResponse.json(aProblem('VALIDATION_FAILED', 400), { status: 400 });
    }
    await delay(30);                                                 // enough for a double click to land
    return HttpResponse.json({ id: 'A7K2Q9P', status: 'PENDING' }, { status: 201 });
  }),
];

Per-test overrides for the failure paths:

// apps/web/src/checkout/CouponStep.msw.test.tsx
import { screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { beforeEach, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { server } from '../test/msw/server';
import { API } from '../test/msw/checkout.handlers';
import { aProblem, aPricedCart } from '../test/builders';
import { renderCheckoutAt } from '../test/render-checkout';         // renderWithProviders + CheckoutPage at a step

it('shows the server message under the code for an expired coupon', async () => {
  server.use(http.post(`${API}/checkout/coupon`, () => HttpResponse.json(
    aProblem('COUPON_REJECTED', 422, [{ path: 'code', code: 'EXPIRED', message: 'This code expired on 31 Oct' }]),
    { status: 422, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/problem+json' } },
  )));
  const { user } = await renderCheckoutAt('coupon');
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Coupon code' }), 'OCT50{Enter}');
  expect(await screen.findByText('This code expired on 31 Oct')).toBeVisible();
});

it('shows the cart-changed notice and the fresh totals on a 409', async () => {
  server.use(http.post(`${API}/checkout/coupon`, () => HttpResponse.json(
    { ...aProblem('CART_CHANGED', 409), cart: aPricedCart({ version: 12, totalMinor: '84900' }) },
    { status: 409, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/problem+json' } },
  )));
  const { user } = await renderCheckoutAt('coupon');
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Coupon code' }), 'SAVE50{Enter}');
  expect(await screen.findByText(/your cart changed in another tab/i)).toBeVisible();
  expect(screen.getByRole('complementary', { name: 'Order summary' })).toHaveTextContent('₹849.00');
});

it('treats an HTML 502 from a proxy as "service unavailable", not a crash', async () => {
  server.use(http.post(`${API}/checkout/coupon`, () =>
    new HttpResponse('<html><body>Bad Gateway</body></html>', { status: 502, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' } })));
  const { user } = await renderCheckoutAt('coupon');
  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Coupon code' }), 'SAVE50{Enter}');
  expect(await screen.findByText('Could not apply the code. Please try again.')).toBeVisible(); // toApiError handled it
});

it('recovers from a network failure on retry', async () => {
  server.use(http.post(`${API}/checkout/coupon`, () => HttpResponse.error(), { once: true }));  // then default handler
  const { user } = await renderCheckoutAt('coupon');
  const input = screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Coupon code' });
  await user.type(input, 'SAVE50{Enter}');
  expect(await screen.findByText('Could not apply the code. Please try again.')).toBeVisible();
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Apply' }));
  expect(await screen.findByText('SAVE50 applied.')).toBeVisible();
});

Counting requests for the double-click test uses the handler's own log. MSW's life-cycle events (server.events.on('request:start', ...)) are an alternative when you want to count every request regardless of handler:

it('sends one order request for a double click, with an idempotency key', async () => {
  placeOrderCalls.length = 0;
  const { user } = await renderCheckoutAt('payment');
  await user.dblClick(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));
  expect(await screen.findByText(/order A7K2Q9P/i)).toBeVisible();
  expect(placeOrderCalls).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(placeOrderCalls[0].key).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/);
});

Backend side (NestJS)

A handler is a claim about what the API does. Each claim should be traceable to the API's real behaviour:

Handler behaviour API behaviour that must exist Where the API proves it
400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED without the header IdempotencyInterceptor rejects missing keys (15.12) Supertest e2e (41.13)
409 CART_CHANGED with a fresh cart in the body Conditional UPDATE ... WHERE version = $n (71.13) Integration test with a real PostgreSQL (41.9)
problem+json with code, issues, requestId One global ProblemDetailsFilter (74.6) Pact verification (74.10)
HTML 502 from a proxy The load balancer, not Nest, returns it Not an API test: a resilience case the client must handle

The API can also make mocks safer by exporting what the mocks need from @shop/contracts: the request schemas (so handlers validate what they receive), the error codes as a zod enum (so a handler cannot invent CART_CHANGD), and example payloads used in its own OpenAPI document (74.2). When the backend renames an error code, the web's handler modules fail to type-check, which is the right moment to find out.

// packages/contracts/src/errors.ts: the known codes of 80.6 plus checkout's, as a closed enum for writers and fixtures
// (readers still accept any string in ProblemSchema.code, so a new code never crashes an old client)
import { z } from 'zod';

export const ErrorCodeSchema = z.enum([
  'VALIDATION_FAILED', 'IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED', 'IDEMPOTENCY_IN_PROGRESS', 'CART_CHANGED',
  'COUPON_REJECTED', 'ADDRESS_REJECTED', 'PAYMENT_DECLINED', 'ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE', 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE',
]);
export type ErrorCode = z.infer<typeof ErrorCodeSchema>;    // ProblemDetailsFilter and aProblem() both take ErrorCode

Production scenario

A storefront has 64 MSW handlers across 9 modules, used in three places: 420 Vitest component tests, 140 Storybook stories (through msw-storybook-addon, so designers can see every error state), and a "no backend" local mode (setupWorker started when NEXT_PUBLIC_API_MOCKING=enabled in development only). Handler maintenance costs about an hour a week. In one quarter onUnhandledRequest: 'error' caught 14 pull requests that added a new API call without a test for its failure states.

Failure scenario

A team's MSW handlers returned HttpResponse.json(...) for errors without a Content-Type: application/problem+json header, so Content-Type was application/json. The client's toApiError (74.6) accepted any JSON. Months later the API team made the global filter stricter and the client was changed to check for problem+json before parsing an error body, to avoid treating a JSON success payload from a misconfigured proxy as an error. Every component test of an error state now failed, but only in the web repository, two weeks after the API change, during an unrelated pull request. The real fix was shared: aProblem() in the fixtures package now returns a full HttpResponse with the right content type, and the API's Pact verification asserts the header.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Relative URLs in Node throw before MSW sees the request; use an absolute base in tests.
  • Handler order: the first matching handler wins; a wildcard http.all('*', ...) placed first hides everything after it.
  • resetHandlers() forgotten, so a 503 override from one test leaks into the next.
  • Reading the body twice: await request.json() consumes it; use request.clone() if two pieces of code must read it.
  • Fake timers with delay(): the delay never resolves unless time is advanced.
  • Timeouts with AbortSignal.timeout(15_000) are not controlled by Vitest's fake timers in Node; make the timeout configurable and use 50 ms in tests, with delay('infinite') in the handler.
  • The Service Worker in development keeps intercepting after you disable mocking until the page is reloaded and the worker is unregistered; gate it on an environment flag and call worker.stop().
  • Never ship MSW to production: import msw/browser only inside a development-only dynamic import.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats MSW handlers as a second, small implementation of the API's contract, and holds them to the same standard: they validate requests with the real request schemas, return responses built through the real response schemas, use the real error codes, and fail on any request nobody planned for. They keep one handler set for tests, Storybook and offline development so there is one place to update. And they remember what MSW cannot prove: that the real API behaves like the handler. That is the job of contract tests (74.10) and a few e2e journeys (77.7).

Common mistakes

  • Copying v1 examples (rest, res(ctx.json())) into an MSW 2 project.
  • onUnhandledRequest: 'bypass' in tests, which lets real requests leak out to the network or fail silently.
  • Handlers that accept anything, so a client sending the wrong body still gets a happy response.
  • Inline fixtures in every test, each shaped a little differently.
  • Mocking only the happy path, leaving error, empty and slow states untested.

Interview questions

  1. Why mock at the network layer rather than the module layer? Expected answer: the real client, parsing and error mapping run; tests break when the contract breaks, not when internals move.
  2. How do you test a retry that succeeds on the second attempt? Expected answer: server.use(http.post(url, () => HttpResponse.error(), { once: true })), then the default handler answers the retry.
  3. What does onUnhandledRequest: 'error' protect against? Expected answer: components calling endpoints no test planned for, and accidental real network calls.
  4. How do MSW mocks drift from the real API, and how do you limit it? Expected answer: hand-written shapes and codes; build fixtures through shared schemas, validate requests in handlers, share the error code enum, verify with Pact.
  5. What changed between MSW 1 and 2? Expected answer: http namespace and HttpResponse based on Fetch API types instead of rest and res(ctx...); Node 18+ required; msw/node and msw/browser entry points.

Practical exercise

Build the MSW layer for checkout and the order pages.

Acceptance criteria:

  • onUnhandledRequest: 'error' in tests; zero unhandled-request errors on main.
  • Every handler that accepts a body validates it with the shared request schema and returns the API's 400 VALIDATION_FAILED shape on failure.
  • Error fixtures are typed with ErrorCode; changing an error code in @shop/contracts breaks the web's type check.
  • Tests exist for: field 422, 409 CART_CHANGED, 429 with Retry-After: 30, HTML 502, network error then success, and a timeout using a configurable 50 ms timeout and delay('infinite').
  • The same handlers power Storybook and a development-only "no backend" mode.

77.6 Sharing mocks with the backend contract

Concept

A fixture is a canned example of data: an order, a cart, an error. A builder is a function that returns a valid fixture with sensible defaults and lets each test override only what it cares about (anOrder({ status: 'SHIPPED' }), Part 41.6). Sharing mocks with the backend contract means fixtures and handlers are derived from the same source of truth the API uses: the zod schemas in @shop/contracts (74.3), or the OpenAPI document generated from NestJS (74.2). A fixture that the API could never produce cannot be built.

Why does it exist?

Because mocks rot. A hand-written order fixture written in March still has totalAmount: 1299 (a number) in October, after the API moved to totalMinor: '129900' (a string, 74.7). The component tests are green, the UI renders NaN in production. Every mock is a copy of the contract, and copies drift unless something checks them.

Mental model

Imagine a bakery that makes display cakes for the window. If the display cakes are made from the same recipe cards as the real ones, a recipe change shows up in the window the next morning. If the window team keeps their own recipe cards, the window shows last year's cake forever.

How it works

flowchart LR
    contracts["@shop/contracts zod schemas"] --> api["NestJS ZodValidationPipe and response mappers"]
    contracts --> builders["Fixture builders parse through schemas"]
    builders --> msw["MSW handlers"]
    msw --> vt["Vitest component tests"]
    msw --> sb["Storybook stories"]
    msw --> dev["Local no-backend mode"]
    openapi["OpenAPI from @nestjs/swagger"] --> gen["orval mock: true, optional"]
    gen --> msw
    api --> pact["Pact verification, 80.10"]
    vt --> pact
  1. Builders parse. anOrder(overrides) merges defaults with overrides and returns OrderSummarySchema.parse(result). An override that breaks the schema throws in the test that wrote it, with zod's path and message.
  2. Builders live next to the contracts, in a packages/test-fixtures workspace package (dev dependency only), so both the web and the API's tests can use them. The API uses them for request bodies in supertest tests; the web uses them for responses in MSW.
  3. Handlers validate requests with the request schemas, so the mock rejects what the API would reject.
  4. Generated mocks are an alternative or a starting point: orval with mock: true (74.2) generates MSW handlers with faker-generated data from the OpenAPI document. Generated mocks are good for "every endpoint answers something"; hand-written builders are better for named scenarios ("an order that shipped yesterday").
  5. The contract test closes the loop: Pact (74.10) proves the API actually returns what the consumer tests expect, so the remaining risk is behaviour, not shape.

Practical example

The order fixture used by 140 tests and 30 stories:

  • defaults represent a typical order: PAID, 2 items, INR, placed 2 hours ago in Asia/Kolkata;
  • deliveryDate, deliveredAt, storeTimeZone, version and updatedAt are present because OrderSummarySchema requires them (74.7);
  • money is minor units as strings;
  • IDs are UUIDs with a readable displayId.

When the backend adds a required field to OrderSummarySchema, every builder call fails at once with invalid_type at "deliveryWindow", and one change to the builder's defaults fixes 140 tests.

React / Next.js example

// packages/test-fixtures/src/orders.ts  (dev dependency of apps/web and apps/api)
import { OrderSummarySchema, type OrderSummary } from '@shop/contracts';

const FIXED_NOW = '2026-11-05T09:30:00.000Z';                 // stable for screenshots and date text

export function anOrder(overrides: Partial<OrderSummary> = {}): OrderSummary {
  return OrderSummarySchema.parse({                           // throws with a path if the fixture is impossible
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),                                  // global in browsers and Node 19+: works in Storybook too
    displayId: 'A7K2Q9P',
    status: 'PAID',
    totalMinor: '129900',
    currency: 'INR',
    placedAt: FIXED_NOW,
    updatedAt: FIXED_NOW,
    deliveryDate: '2026-11-06',
    deliveredAt: null,
    storeTimeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata',
    version: 3,
    items: [
      { sku: 'TB-SONIC-01', name: 'Sonic toothbrush', quantity: 1, unitPriceMinor: '99900' },
      { sku: 'FL-MINT-50', name: 'Mint floss', quantity: 2, unitPriceMinor: '15000' },
    ],
    ...overrides,
  });
}

export const aShippedOrder = (o: Partial<OrderSummary> = {}) => anOrder({ status: 'SHIPPED', ...o });
// packages/test-fixtures/src/problems.ts
import { HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { ProblemSchema, type ErrorCode, type ApiIssue } from '@shop/contracts';

export function aProblem(code: ErrorCode, status: number, issues: ApiIssue[] = [], requestId = 'req-test-1') {
  return ProblemSchema.parse({ type: `https://errors.shop.example/${code}`, title: code, status, code, issues, requestId });
}

export const problemResponse = (code: ErrorCode, status: number, issues: ApiIssue[] = []) =>
  HttpResponse.json(aProblem(code, status, issues), {
    status,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/problem+json', 'X-Request-Id': 'req-test-1' }, // same as the real filter
  });

Using a recorded real response as a fixture is sometimes worth it for complicated payloads (a search result with facets). Record from staging once, then run it through the schema in a test, so the recording is also checked when the schema changes:

// apps/web/src/test/recorded.test.ts
// @vitest-environment node
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { SearchResultSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import recorded from './recordings/search-toothbrush.json';

it('the recorded search response still matches the contract', () => {
  expect(() => SearchResultSchema.parse(recorded)).not.toThrow();
});

Backend side (NestJS)

The API uses the same package in three ways:

  • Request bodies in supertest tests come from builders (aPlaceOrderRequest()), so the API's tests and the web's mocks agree on what a valid request is.
  • Response conformance: the API's e2e tests parse real responses with the response schemas. This is the backend half of the bargain: if the web's fixtures are built through OrderSummarySchema and the API's real responses are checked against OrderSummarySchema, the fixtures and reality can only differ in values, not in shape.
  • Error catalogue test: one test triggers each ErrorCode the API can return and checks the body with ProblemSchema and the content type.
// apps/api/test/orders.e2e-spec.ts (excerpt)
import { OrderSummarySchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { aPlaceOrderRequest } from '@shop/test-fixtures';

it('returns an order that matches the shared contract', async () => {
  const created = await request(app.getHttpServer())
    .post('/v1/orders').set(authHeaders).set('Idempotency-Key', randomUUID())
    .send(aPlaceOrderRequest({ cartId })).expect(201);
  const res = await request(app.getHttpServer()).get(`/v1/orders/${created.body.id}`).set(authHeaders).expect(200);
  expect(() => OrderSummarySchema.parse(res.body)).not.toThrow();   // the same schema the web fixtures parse through
});

Production scenario

After moving to schema-parsed builders, a storefront measured fixture-related escapes: in the 12 months before, 7 production bugs where a component test passed with a fixture shape the API no longer produced; in the 12 months after, zero. The cost was a one-off two-day migration of 210 inline fixtures into 18 builders, and about 4 ms extra per test for zod parsing.

Failure scenario

The API added PARTIALLY_REFUNDED to the order status enum. OrderSummarySchema used z.enum([...]) with the known statuses, so the web's builders were still valid, but the web had no fixture with the new status and no UI for it. The API shipped first, as the rollout table in 74.9 says it may only when clients have a fallback. The web's status badge did STATUS_LABELS[order.status].label, which threw for the new value, and the error boundary replaced the whole order page.

The schema should have been an open enum on the client side (74.7): known values plus a fallback. The test that would have caught it is a single builder call, anOrder({ status: 'SOMETHING_NEW' as never }), rendered on the order page with an assertion that a generic "Updated" badge appears. The team now adds an "unknown enum value" test for every enum the UI renders.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Random data in fixtures (faker without a seed) produces screenshots and text assertions that differ per run; seed it or use fixed defaults.
  • Fixtures with real personal data copied from production dumps; never, even in tests.
  • Builders that bypass the schema for "special cases" (as OrderSummary), which reintroduce drift.
  • Generated mocks only: every endpoint returns plausible noise, but nobody wrote the scenario that matters ("coupon expired").
  • Shared fixtures package pulling msw into the API's production dependencies; keep it a dev dependency on both sides.
  • Dates: fixtures with new Date() make "placed 2 hours ago" text change with the clock; use a fixed instant and fake timers or pass now explicitly.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior asks "what makes this mock true?" for every mock, and wants the answer to be a mechanism, not a person's memory. Builders parsing through shared schemas, request validation in handlers, a shared error enum, response conformance checks in the API's tests and Pact verification are five cheap mechanisms that together make most drift impossible. They keep builders boring and deterministic, named for business situations, and owned by both teams.

Common mistakes

  • Fixtures typed with as casts rather than parsed.
  • Each test file defining its own order shape.
  • Not testing unknown enum values that the API is allowed to add.
  • Builders that return the same object instance, so one test's mutation changes another test's fixture.
  • Fixtures package depending on app code, creating a cycle between apps and the package.

Interview questions

  1. How do you keep frontend mocks in sync with the API? Expected answer: build fixtures through shared schemas, validate requests in handlers, share error codes, check real responses against the same schemas in API tests, verify with Pact.
  2. Builders or generated mocks? Expected answer: generated mocks for breadth, builders for named scenarios; both through the schema.
  3. What test would have caught a new enum value crashing the UI? Expected answer: render with an unknown value and assert a fallback; the client schema should accept unknown values.
  4. Why should the API's tests use the frontend's fixture package? Expected answer: one definition of valid requests and responses on both sides; drift shows up in whichever pipeline runs first.

Practical exercise

Create packages/test-fixtures for the order and checkout domain.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Builders for order, cart, checkout view, priced cart, address and problem documents, each parsing through @shop/contracts.
  • The web's MSW handlers and the API's supertest tests both import from it; neither has inline fixtures for these types.
  • An API e2e test parses every order endpoint's response with the shared schema.
  • A web test renders the order page with an unknown status and asserts the fallback badge.
  • Adding a required field to OrderSummarySchema produces a builder error that names the field.

77.7 End-to-end tests with Playwright: locators, auto-waiting and test data

Concept

An end-to-end (e2e) test drives a real browser through the real production build of the web app, talking to a real backend, and checks what a user would see and what the system recorded. Playwright (Microsoft, @playwright/test) is the test runner and browser automation library most teams choose today. It controls Chromium, Firefox and WebKit through their own protocols, runs tests in parallel worker processes, and gives each test a fresh browser context: an isolated profile with its own cookies, storage and cache, created in milliseconds.

Three Playwright ideas do most of the work:

  • Locators describe how to find an element (page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })) and are evaluated lazily every time they are used, so they survive re-renders.
  • Auto-waiting: before clicking, Playwright waits until the element is attached, visible, stable (not animating), enabled and receiving events.
  • Web-first assertions: await expect(locator).toHaveText('Paid') retries until it passes or the assertion timeout (5 s by default) expires.

Why does it exist?

Component tests fake the network and run in jsdom, so they cannot see four classes of bugs:

  1. Integration across real boundaries: the BFF's cookies (75.2), redirects, CORS, the idempotency interceptor and the database's unique index.
  2. The production bundle: code splitting, tree shaking, environment variables baked at build time (70.6), CSS ordering. Part 70.3 tells the story of a bug visible only in vite build output.
  3. Real browser behaviour: layout, focus, history and the Back button, <dialog>, file inputs, Safari's differences.
  4. Deploy-shaped problems: a missing route, a 404 on a lazy chunk, a wrong basePath.

Older tools (Selenium WebDriver, early Cypress) made such tests slow and flaky enough that teams gave up on them. Playwright's isolation, auto-waiting and tracing made a small e2e layer cheap enough to run on every pull request.

Mental model

Imagine a secret shopper who visits the real shop, with real stock and a real till, at opening time. They follow a short script: pick a toothbrush, apply a coupon, pay twice by accident, check the receipt, check the stockroom ledger. Each shopper gets a fresh, empty basket and a fresh loyalty card, so two shoppers in the shop at the same time never see each other's baskets.

How it works

flowchart LR
    runner["Playwright test runner"] --> w1["Worker 1"]
    runner --> w2["Worker 2"]
    w1 --> ctx1["Browser context: own cookies and storage"]
    w2 --> ctx2["Browser context"]
    ctx1 --> web["Next.js production build, next start"]
    ctx2 --> web
    web --> api["NestJS API, e2e mode"]
    api --> pg[("PostgreSQL, seeded per test")]
    runner --> report["HTML report, traces, screenshots"]
  1. playwright.config.ts declares where tests live, which browsers (projects) to run, how many workers, retries, the base URL, and a webServer block that starts the app (and optionally the API) and waits for a URL to answer before tests start.
  2. Each test receives fixtures: page, context, request (an HTTP client for API calls that shares nothing with the page unless asked), and any custom fixtures you define with test.extend.
  3. Locators are built from roles, labels and text, in the same priority order as Testing Library (77.3). page.getByTestId('order-row') exists, reading data-testid by default (configurable with testIdAttribute).
  4. Actions (click, fill, press, selectOption, setInputFiles) auto-wait; assertions retry. There is almost never a reason for page.waitForTimeout(ms).
  5. Network control: page.route(pattern, handler) can fulfil, abort or modify requests in the browser, for failure drills; page.waitForResponse(predicate) waits for a specific API response.
  6. Tracing: with trace: 'on-first-retry', a failed test that is retried records a trace file: every action, DOM snapshot before and after, network requests with headers and bodies, console logs. npx playwright show-trace trace.zip (or the HTML report) replays it.

Practical example

The checkout journey for e2e, chosen because every step crosses a boundary component tests cannot:

  1. A fresh customer with a seeded cart (one toothbrush, ₹999.00) is signed in through the real BFF login.
  2. They enter an address; the API prices delivery (₹40.00).
  3. They apply SAVE50; the API recomputes totals (cart version moves from 8 to 9).
  4. They double-click "Place order".
  5. The browser lands on /orders/<id> with replace, so Back goes to the cart, not to a live payment form.
  6. The test asks the API, through the test-support endpoint, how many orders exist for the cart: exactly one.

React / Next.js example

The configuration:

// apps/web/playwright.config.ts  (Playwright 1.5x)
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

const CI = !!process.env.CI;
const BASE_URL = process.env.E2E_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  fullyParallel: true,                                 // tests in one file also run in parallel
  forbidOnly: CI,                                      // a stray test.only fails CI
  retries: CI ? 2 : 0,
  workers: CI ? 4 : undefined,
  reporter: CI ? [['blob'], ['github']] : [['html', { open: 'never' }]],
  timeout: 30_000,                                     // per test
  expect: { timeout: 5_000 },                          // per assertion retry window
  use: {
    baseURL: BASE_URL,
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure',
    locale: 'en-IN',
    timezoneId: 'Asia/Kolkata',                        // dates render the same on every runner
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
    { name: 'mobile-safari', use: { ...devices['iPhone 13'] }, grep: /@mobile/ },   // a tagged subset on WebKit
  ],
  webServer: process.env.E2E_BASE_URL ? undefined : {  // against a preview URL, start nothing (Part 78)
    command: 'pnpm build && pnpm start',               // the production build, never next dev
    url: `${BASE_URL}/api/health`,
    reuseExistingServer: !CI,
    timeout: 180_000,
  },
});

The journey. Test data comes from a fixture (defined in 77.8), and every assertion is web-first:

// apps/web/e2e/checkout.spec.ts
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { test } from './fixtures';                     // adds `customer` with a seeded cart and a signed-in page

test('places exactly one order for a double click @mobile', async ({ page, customer, api }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Delivery address' })).toBeVisible();

  await page.getByLabel('Full name').fill('Asha Rao');
  await page.getByLabel('Mobile number').fill('9876543210');
  await page.getByLabel('House number and street').fill('12 MG Road');
  await page.getByLabel('City').fill('Bengaluru');
  await page.getByLabel('Postcode').fill('560038');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save address' }).click();

  const summary = page.getByRole('complementary', { name: 'Order summary' });
  await expect(summary).toContainText('Delivery ₹40.00');            // priced by the real API

  await page.getByLabel('Coupon code').fill('SAVE50');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Apply' }).click();
  await expect(summary).toContainText('Total ₹989.00');              // 999 + 40 - 50
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to payment' }).click();

  const placed = page.waitForResponse((r) => r.url().endsWith('/api/v1/orders') && r.request().method() === 'POST');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).dblclick();
  const res = await placed;
  expect(res.status()).toBe(201);

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders\/[0-9a-f-]{36}$/);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /^Order [A-Z0-9]{7}$/ })).toBeVisible();

  expect(await api.ordersForCart(customer.cartId)).toHaveLength(1);  // the database agrees: one order
  await page.goBack();
  await expect(page).not.toHaveURL(/\/checkout/);                    // replace: no live payment form behind us
});

The test reads like the acceptance criteria in 71.13 because it is written in the same vocabulary: labels, roles and visible amounts. Nothing in it depends on component names, CSS or the order of DOM nodes.

Backend side (NestJS)

E2E tests need the API to support them without weakening production:

  • A test-support module, imported only when E2E_SUPPORT=enabled, exposing POST /__e2e/customers (creates a user, a cart and returns IDs), GET /__e2e/carts/:id/orders, and POST /__e2e/reset. It is guarded by a separate secret header and absent from production images by configuration and by a startup assertion.
  • A health endpoint the webServer can wait on (Part 31.12), returning 200 only when the database is reachable.
  • Production behaviour everywhere else: real guards, real idempotency, real throttling (with limits raised by config in e2e, not disabled).
// apps/api/src/e2e-support/e2e-support.module.ts
import { Module, type DynamicModule } from '@nestjs/common';
import { E2eSupportController } from './e2e-support.controller';
import { E2eSupportService } from './e2e-support.service';

@Module({})
export class E2eSupportModule {
  static register(): DynamicModule {
    if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' && process.env.E2E_SUPPORT === 'enabled') {
      throw new Error('E2E support must never run in production');   // fail the boot, loudly
    }
    return process.env.E2E_SUPPORT === 'enabled'
      ? { module: E2eSupportModule, controllers: [E2eSupportController], providers: [E2eSupportService] }
      : { module: E2eSupportModule };                                 // empty module: no routes exist
  }
}
// apps/api/src/e2e-support/e2e-support.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Get, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { E2eSecretGuard } from './e2e-secret.guard';                // compares x-e2e-secret with timingSafeEqual
import { E2eSupportService } from './e2e-support.service';

@Controller('__e2e')
@UseGuards(E2eSecretGuard)
export class E2eSupportController {
  constructor(private readonly support: E2eSupportService) {}

  @Post('customers')                                                // one transaction: user + cart + items
  createCustomer(@Body() body: { cart?: { sku: string; quantity: number }[] }) {
    return this.support.createCustomer(body.cart ?? [{ sku: 'TB-SONIC-01', quantity: 1 }]);
  }

  @Get('carts/:id/orders')
  ordersForCart(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string) {
    return this.support.ordersForCart(id);                         // SELECT id FROM orders WHERE cart_id = $1
  }
}

Production scenario

A storefront runs 26 Playwright journeys on every pull request: checkout (3 variants), login, refresh and logout (from 75.10), order list with filters and infinite scroll, live status, cancel, returns, address book, search. On 4 shards of 2 workers each, the suite takes 3 min 40 s; the slowest journey (checkout with payment retry) takes 21 s. Monthly cost on GitHub-hosted runners is about 4,000 runner-minutes. Over a year the suite blocked 38 pull requests for real bugs, 22 of which no component test could have caught (cookie paths, a missing await in a Server Action, a chunk that failed to load under basePath).

Failure scenario

A team wrote 140 e2e tests in their first month with Playwright, one per acceptance criterion, all against a shared staging environment with shared test accounts. By month three, the suite took 38 minutes and failed on 30 % of runs: two tests cancelled the same order in parallel, a test expected "3 orders" while another test added a fourth, a staging deploy restarted the API mid-run, and a coupon used by tests hit its global redemption limit. Developers stopped looking at results. The recovery took a quarter: move field-level criteria into component tests (140 became 24 journeys), run e2e against an ephemeral stack per job (77.11), create a fresh customer per test, and treat every flaky test as a bug with an owner (77.8).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Testing against next dev: different code (no minification, no static optimisation, on-demand compilation that makes the first navigation take seconds). Always test next build output.
  • page.waitForTimeout used as a fix for timing; it hides the race and adds seconds.
  • CSS selectors and nth-child: break on every layout change; use roles and labels.
  • Assertions without await (expect(locator).toBeVisible() without await) pass immediately and test nothing; the @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises lint rule catches them.
  • Shared accounts across workers: counts, carts and order lists collide.
  • Third-party scripts (analytics, chat, payment iframes) slow or break tests; block them with page.route in e2e or use the provider's test mode.
  • Time: "Delivers tomorrow" depends on the clock; set timezoneId and control time with page.clock (Playwright 1.45+) where the UI computes dates.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior keeps e2e tests few, valuable and boring. Each journey must cross a boundary only e2e can cross, and must check a business outcome (one order row), not only UI text. They insist on the production build, fresh data per test, roles and labels for locators, and traces on failure, so a red build can be diagnosed from the report without re-running it locally. They budget e2e time like any other resource: if the suite passes 5 minutes, something moves down to component tests. And they make the backend a partner: the test-support module is designed, reviewed and guarded like production code, because it is code that can create users.

Common mistakes

  • Writing e2e tests for every validation message.
  • Logging in through the UI in every test (77.8 shows storage state).
  • Asserting only on UI text when the risk is in the data (duplicates, wrong totals).
  • No traces or screenshots on failure, so every failure needs a local reproduction.
  • Disabling auth, CSRF or throttling for e2e, so the tested system is not the deployed one.

Interview questions

  1. What makes Playwright tests less flaky than older tools? Expected answer: isolated contexts per test, auto-waiting actionability checks, retrying web-first assertions, lazy locators; plus traces for diagnosis.
  2. Why run e2e against the production build? Expected answer: dev servers differ in bundling, splitting, env handling and compilation timing; bugs live in the build.
  3. How do you check a business outcome in an e2e test? Expected answer: query the system of record through a guarded test-support endpoint or the API, for example one order for the cart.
  4. How would you expose test-only backend endpoints safely? Expected answer: a dynamic module registered only under an explicit flag, a separate secret, a boot-time assertion that refuses production, and no such routes in production images.
  5. When is page.route appropriate in an e2e test? Expected answer: failure drills (API down, slow response) and blocking third parties; not for faking the happy path, which defeats the purpose.

Practical exercise

Write the checkout journey above against the monorepo from Part 70.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The suite starts next build output through webServer, or targets E2E_BASE_URL when set.
  • The journey creates its own customer through the test-support API and asserts exactly one order row after a double click.
  • No locator uses CSS selectors, XPath or nth; no waitForTimeout anywhere.
  • A failed run produces a trace with the network log, and the API's request ID is visible in it.
  • The API refuses to boot with NODE_ENV=production and E2E_SUPPORT=enabled.

77.8 Auth state, parallel runs and flakiness control

Concept
