Three practices make an e2e suite fast and trustworthy:

  • Authentication state reuse: sign in once, save the browser's cookies and storage to a file (storage state), and start each test's context from that file instead of logging in again.
  • Isolation for parallelism: every worker and every test owns its data (its own user, cart and orders), so tests can run in any order and at the same time.
  • Flakiness control: a flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Retries detect flakiness; they must not hide it. Each flaky test is diagnosed, fixed or quarantined with an owner.

Why does it exist?

Logging in through the UI takes 1-3 s; across 200 test runs per pipeline that is minutes of nothing. Shared data forces serial execution, so the suite gets slower with every test. And flaky tests destroy trust: Part 41.18 described the backend version; on the frontend, timing, animation, data collisions and third parties add more causes. A team that re-runs red builds until they go green has stopped testing.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel. Each guest gets a key card cut once at reception (storage state), not a new check-in every time they return to their room. Each guest has their own room (data isolation), so housekeeping can clean all rooms at once. And when a guest reports that the lift sometimes stops between floors, the hotel does not tell them to press the button again; it calls the engineer.

How it works

  1. Per-worker accounts. A worker-scoped fixture creates one customer per worker through the test-support API, signs in through the real login page once, and saves context.storageState() to playwright/.auth/worker-<n>.json. Tests in that worker start their context from that file.
  2. Per-test data. A test-scoped fixture creates the test's own cart (and anything else it changes) for that worker's customer, so tests in the same worker do not share mutable state.
  3. Cookies with prefixes. The BFF's __Host-session and __Secure-refresh cookies (75.2) require Secure. Chromium and Firefox accept Secure cookies from http://localhost; if a browser in your matrix does not, serve the e2e stack over HTTPS with a local certificate (a Caddy container in the compose file) rather than weakening the cookie attributes.
  4. Sharding splits the suite across CI machines: npx playwright test --shard=2/4. Each shard writes a blob report; a final job runs npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./blob-reports to produce one report.
  5. Flake detection: with retries: 2, a test that fails then passes is reported as flaky, not passed. New or changed tests run with --repeat-each=10 in a nightly job (or --only-changed=origin/main, Playwright 1.46+, on pull requests) to flush out flakiness before it reaches main.
  6. Quarantine is a tag (@quarantine), excluded from the blocking job with --grep-invert @quarantine and run in a non-blocking job, with a ticket, an owner and a deadline.

Common causes of e2e flakiness and their fixes:

Cause Symptom Fix
Shared data between tests "Expected 3 orders, got 4" Fresh customer and cart per test
Fixed waits Passes locally, fails on CI Web-first assertions, waitForResponse
Animations and transitions Click lands on a moving element Playwright waits for stability; disable animations in visual tests (77.9)
Clock and time zones "Delivers tomorrow" vs "today" at 23:59 timezoneId, page.clock, fixed seed dates
Third-party scripts Random timeouts Block with page.route in e2e
Server cold start First test times out webServer waits on a health URL; warm-up request in global setup
Background jobs Status not updated yet expect.poll on the API, with a bounded timeout
Test order dependence Fails only with --shard Isolation; run with fullyParallel locally too

Practical example

A suite of 26 journeys on 4 shards with 2 workers each uses 8 workers, so 8 customers are created per run, each signed in once (8 logins, about 12 s of total work, spread in parallel). Each test then creates its cart in about 60 ms through the API. Flaky rate over 30 days: 0.3 % of test runs, all reported in the weekly flake review.

React / Next.js example

The fixtures file:

// apps/web/e2e/fixtures.ts
import { test as base, expect, type APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';

type Customer = { userId: string; email: string; password: string; cartId: string };
type Api = { ordersForCart(cartId: string): Promise<{ id: string }[]>; placeSeedOrder(cartId: string): Promise<string> };

const API_URL = process.env.E2E_API_URL ?? 'http://localhost:4000';
const support = (request: APIRequestContext) => ({
  post: (p: string, data: unknown) => request.post(`${API_URL}/__e2e${p}`, { data, headers: { 'x-e2e-secret': process.env.E2E_SECRET! } }),
  get: (p: string) => request.get(`${API_URL}/__e2e${p}`, { headers: { 'x-e2e-secret': process.env.E2E_SECRET! } }),
});

export const test = base.extend<{ customer: Customer; api: Api }, { workerStorageState: string; workerCustomer: Omit<Customer, 'cartId'> }>({
  workerCustomer: [async ({ playwright }, use) => {
    const request = await playwright.request.newContext();
    const res = await support(request).post('/customers', {});
    expect(res.ok()).toBeTruthy();
    await use(await res.json());                                  // { userId, email, password }
    await request.dispose();
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  workerStorageState: [async ({ browser, workerCustomer }, use) => {
    const file = path.resolve(test.info().project.outputDir, `.auth/worker-${test.info().parallelIndex}.json`);
    if (!fs.existsSync(file)) {
      const page = await browser.newPage({ storageState: undefined, baseURL: test.info().project.use.baseURL }); // signed out
      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(workerCustomer.email);
      await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(workerCustomer.password);
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
      await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders$/);                 // the real BFF set __Host-session
      await page.context().storageState({ path: file });
      await page.close();
    }
    await use(file);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  storageState: ({ workerStorageState }, use) => use(workerStorageState),   // every context starts signed in

  customer: async ({ request, workerCustomer }, use) => {
    const res = await support(request).post(`/customers/${workerCustomer.userId}/carts`, { items: [{ sku: 'TB-SONIC-01', quantity: 1 }] });
    await use({ ...workerCustomer, cartId: (await res.json()).cartId });   // a fresh cart per test
  },

  api: async ({ request }, use) => {
    await use({
      ordersForCart: async (cartId) => (await support(request).get(`/carts/${cartId}/orders`)).json(),
      placeSeedOrder: async (cartId) => (await (await support(request).post(`/carts/${cartId}/orders`, {})).json()).id,
    });
  },
});

The session cookie in saved storage state is a 15-minute access JWT (75.3). Runs longer than that are covered by the refresh flow the app already has: the saved __Secure-refresh cookie lets the BFF rotate silently, which is itself worth exercising in e2e. If a single test outlives the refresh token (it should not), the test is too long.

Failure drills inside e2e use page.route in the browser, so the rest of the stack stays real:

// apps/web/e2e/order-live-status.spec.ts (excerpt)
test('shows an honest offline banner when the API is down, and recovers', async ({ page, customer, api }) => {
  await page.goto(`/orders/${await api.placeSeedOrder(customer.cartId)}`);
  await page.route('**/api/v1/orders/**', (route) => route.fulfill({
    status: 503, contentType: 'application/problem+json',
    body: JSON.stringify({ code: 'UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE', status: 503, title: 'Unavailable', issues: [], requestId: 'drill-1' }),
  }));
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Showing status from');      // stale but honest (78.10)
  await page.unroute('**/api/v1/orders/**');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).not.toContainText('Showing status from');
});

Backend side (NestJS)

Parallel e2e runs put concurrent load on the API that production rarely sees from one client: eight workers each creating customers and placing orders at once. The API should take it without special cases:

  • Throttling keyed by user, with e2e limits from configuration. ThrottlerModule.forRootAsync reads limits from ConfigService; e2e sets higher limits rather than removing the guard, so 429 handling is still exercised by one dedicated test.
  • No global state in the test-support service: each createCustomer uses unique emails (e2e+<uuid>@shop.test), so parallel workers never collide on a unique index.
  • Background work made observable: if order confirmation emails or status changes are done by a worker (Part 36), the test-support API exposes "jobs pending for this order", and tests poll it with expect.poll instead of sleeping.
// apps/api/src/app.module.ts (excerpt)  @nestjs/throttler v5+
ThrottlerModule.forRootAsync({
  inject: [ConfigService],
  useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => [{
    name: 'default',
    ttl: 60_000,
    limit: config.get<number>('THROTTLE_LIMIT_PER_MIN', 120),   // e2e sets 5000; the guard still runs
  }],
}),

Production scenario

After introducing per-worker accounts and per-test carts, a team moved from workers: 1 to 4 shards of 2 workers. Wall-clock time fell from 19 minutes to 3 min 40 s. They added a weekly 30-minute "flake review": the CI dashboard lists every test reported flaky that week; each gets an owner. Over two quarters the flaky rate fell from 2.1 % to 0.3 % of test runs, and "re-run" clicks on the e2e job fell from about 60 a week to 4.

Failure scenario

A test for "logout everywhere" (75.10) revoked all sessions for its user by bumping the Redis epoch. It used the worker's shared customer. Every other test in that worker, running afterwards, started from a storage state whose session was now revoked, and failed with a redirect to /login. The failures appeared random because they depended on which worker ran the logout test and when. The fix: tests that change the identity itself (logout everywhere, password change, account deletion) create their own customer and sign in inside the test, never using the worker's storage state.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Storage state committed to Git: it contains live session cookies for a test environment; add playwright/.auth to .gitignore.
  • Storage state reused across environments: cookies for localhost do not apply to a preview URL; key the file by base URL.
  • retries hiding real races: a test that fails 1 in 20 runs in CI may be a real race in the product (a double submit, a stale cache), not a test problem; read the trace before blaming the test.
  • Shards with uneven duration: one shard takes 6 minutes while others take 2; Playwright splits by test count, so split long files or balance by tagging.
  • test.describe.configure({ mode: 'serial' }) used to paper over shared data; when one test fails, the rest of the group is skipped.
  • Worker-scoped fixtures that leak data: a worker's customer accumulates hundreds of orders over a long run, slowing list pages; create carts and orders per test and reset per run.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior designs test data like a multi-tenant system: every worker is a tenant, every test a session within it, nothing shared that can be mutated. They treat retries as a sensor, not a cure, and they make flakiness visible with a number on a dashboard and an owner per test. When a test is flaky they first suspect the product (a race the user could also hit), then the test, then the environment, in that order, because the trace usually shows which.

Common mistakes

  • Logging in through the UI in every test.
  • One shared test account for the whole suite.
  • Using retries as the flakiness policy.
  • Quarantining without an owner or a deadline, so the quarantine becomes a graveyard.
  • Disabling the throttler instead of configuring its limits.

Interview questions

  1. How do you avoid logging in for every e2e test? Expected answer: save storage state once per worker (or per role) and start contexts from it; tests that change identity create their own user.
  2. How do you make e2e tests safe to run in parallel? Expected answer: per-worker accounts, per-test data, unique identifiers, no shared mutable fixtures, no serial mode.
  3. What is your policy for flaky tests? Expected answer: retries detect and report, a dashboard and owner per flaky test, quarantine with a deadline, suspect the product first.
  4. How do you shard Playwright in CI and still get one report? Expected answer: --shard=i/n with the blob reporter per shard, then merge-reports in a final job.
  5. How would you test behaviour that depends on a background job? Expected answer: poll an observable signal (expect.poll on an API) with a bounded timeout, never a fixed sleep.

Practical exercise

Convert a serial, shared-account e2e suite into a parallel one.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Worker-scoped customers and storage state; no test logs in through the UI except the auth tests and identity-changing tests.
  • The suite passes with --repeat-each=5 --workers=8 and with --shard=1/4 through --shard=4/4.
  • CI merges blob reports into one HTML report with traces for retried tests.
  • A flaky-test report lists each test that needed a retry in the last 7 days.
  • The throttler stays enabled, with one test that asserts the 429 and Retry-After behaviour.

77.9 Visual regression testing

Concept

A visual regression test takes a screenshot of a page or component and compares it, pixel by pixel, with an approved baseline image. If more pixels differ than a threshold allows, the test fails and produces a diff image highlighting the change. Playwright has this built in: await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(). Hosted services (Chromatic for Storybook, Percy, Applitools) add a review UI, cross-browser rendering and smarter diffing for a fee.

Why does it exist?

Because no other test sees CSS. A component test asserts that the "Place order" button exists and is enabled; it cannot see that a stylesheet change pushed it below the fold on a 360 px phone, or that it is now white text on a white background. Part 70.5 tells the story of a build setting that dropped checkout's CSS chunk; Part 69.4 the story of a global !important that moved the payment button. Both shipped with green tests.

Mental model

Imagine a "spot the difference" puzzle done by a machine every time someone changes the shop window. It does not know what a good window looks like; it only knows what yesterday's approved window looked like, and circles everything that changed. A person then decides whether each circle is a mistake or the new design.

How it works

  1. First run: toHaveScreenshot('checkout-payment.png') writes the baseline into a snapshots folder next to the test, named with the project and platform (checkout-payment-chromium-linux.png). Baselines are committed.
  2. Later runs render the same state and compare with pixelmatch. Options: maxDiffPixels, maxDiffPixelRatio, threshold (per-pixel colour tolerance, 0-1, default 0.2).
  3. Stabilisation: Playwright takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match before comparing, and by default disables CSS animations and transitions (animations: 'disabled') and hides the text caret.
  4. Masking: mask: [locator] paints dynamic regions (a timestamp, a carousel, a map) with a solid box; stylePath (1.41+) injects a stylesheet just for screenshots.
  5. Updating: an intended change is accepted with npx playwright test --update-snapshots, and the new PNGs are reviewed in the pull request like code.
  6. Determinism: fonts and anti-aliasing differ between macOS, Windows and Linux, so baselines are generated and compared in one place: the official Docker image, mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.5x.0-noble (pin the exact version matching @playwright/test).

Practical example

A storefront keeps 24 visual tests: the checkout's three steps in two viewports (375 x 812 and 1280 x 800), the order page in each status, the cart with 0, 1 and 30 items, and the error and empty states. Data comes from the e2e seed with fixed values (names, prices, a frozen clock), so screenshots are identical across runs.

React / Next.js example

// apps/web/e2e/visual/checkout.visual.spec.ts
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { test } from '../fixtures';

test.use({ viewport: { width: 375, height: 812 } });

test('payment step @visual', async ({ page, customer }) => {
  await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2026-11-05T09:30:00+05:30'));   // "Delivers tomorrow" is stable
  await page.goto('/checkout?step=payment');
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' })).toBeEnabled();
  await page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready);                         // web fonts loaded (82.8)

  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout-payment-mobile.png', {
    fullPage: true,
    mask: [page.getByTestId('promo-carousel')],                           // rotating content
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.002,                                             // about 800 pixels on this page
  });
});
# .github/workflows/web-visual.yml (job excerpt)
visual:
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.50.0-noble    # same image locally: identical fonts and rendering
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - run: corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
    - run: pnpm --filter web exec playwright test --project=visual
    - if: failure()
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with: { name: visual-diffs, path: apps/web/test-results }   # expected, actual and diff PNGs

Developers regenerate baselines with the same container: docker run --rm -v $PWD:/work -w /work mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.50.0-noble pnpm --filter web exec playwright test --project=visual --update-snapshots.

Backend side (NestJS)

Screenshots are only stable if the data is. The API's e2e mode should provide:

  • Fixed seed values: product names, prices and images that never change between runs.
  • Deterministic ordering of lists (ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC), or rows swap places.
  • An injectable clock: a Clock provider overridden in e2e so "placed 2 hours ago" and delivery dates are fixed, matching page.clock in the browser.
  • Stable image URLs for seeded products, served from a local fixture bucket, not a CDN that may change compression.
// apps/api/src/common/clock.ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class Clock { now(): Date { return new Date(); } }

@Injectable()
export class FixedClock extends Clock {                         // provided instead of Clock when E2E_FIXED_NOW is set
  constructor(private readonly at = new Date(process.env.E2E_FIXED_NOW ?? '2026-11-05T04:00:00Z')) { super(); }
  now(): Date { return this.at; }
}

Production scenario

The 24 visual tests take 70 s on one job. In six months they caught 11 real regressions (a z-index change hiding the coupon error behind the summary, a font fallback after a CDN change, a Tailwind upgrade changing default line heights) and produced 9 false positives, all from one rotating banner before it was masked. Baseline updates appear in about one pull request a week and take a minute to review in GitHub's image diff view.

Failure scenario

A team added 300 visual tests in a week, generated on developers' Macs and run on Linux CI. Every test failed on the first CI run because of font anti-aliasing. Someone raised maxDiffPixelRatio to 0.05 globally to "fix" it. Two months later a change made the checkout total's font 40 % lighter and moved the delivery fee line off-screen on small phones; both changes were under 5 % of pixels and passed. The recovery: regenerate all baselines in the Docker image, set the ratio back to 0.002, cut the suite to the 30 screens that matter, and mask the dynamic parts instead of loosening the threshold.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Different machines, different pixels: generate and compare in one pinned container.
  • Loose global thresholds hide real changes; mask dynamic regions instead.
  • Web fonts not loaded when the screenshot is taken; wait for document.fonts.ready.
  • Lazy images below the fold in fullPage shots; scroll or use loading="eager" in the visual test build.
  • Too many baselines: hundreds of near-identical screenshots that everyone updates without looking.
  • Third-party widgets (chat, payment iframes) render differently every time; mask or block them.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior uses visual tests for a small set of high-value screens and states, where a layout break costs money (checkout, product page, order confirmation), and never as a substitute for behaviour tests. They make determinism a backend and frontend responsibility together: seeded data, fixed clocks, stable ordering, pinned rendering environment. And they treat a snapshot update as a design review, not a chore.

Common mistakes

  • Baselines generated on a laptop.
  • Raising thresholds instead of masking.
  • Visual tests for every component in every state, so updates become rubber stamps.
  • No artifact upload, so the diff image is lost when CI fails.

Interview questions

  1. Why do visual tests fail between macOS and Linux, and how do you fix it? Expected answer: font rendering and anti-aliasing differ; generate and compare in one pinned Docker image.
  2. How do you handle dynamic content in screenshots? Expected answer: fixed data and clock, mask, a screenshot-only stylesheet; not looser thresholds.
  3. What can visual tests catch that component tests cannot? Expected answer: CSS, layout, overlap, contrast, fonts, responsive breakpoints.
  4. What does the backend contribute to stable screenshots? Expected answer: fixed seed data, deterministic ordering, an injectable clock, stable image URLs.

Practical exercise

Add visual tests for checkout and the order page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • At most 12 screenshots, covering two viewports.
  • Baselines generated and compared in the pinned Playwright container.
  • maxDiffPixelRatio at or below 0.002; dynamic regions masked.
  • Moving the "Place order" button by 8 px or changing the total's font weight fails the test.
  • Diff images are uploaded as CI artifacts on failure.

77.10 Accessibility testing with axe

Concept

axe-core (Deque) is an open-source engine that checks a rendered DOM against accessibility rules derived from WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines): missing form labels, images without alternative text, invalid ARIA, duplicate IDs, low colour contrast, missing document language, buttons without names. It runs in the page and returns a list of violations, each with a rule ID, an impact (minor, moderate, serious, critical), the offending elements and a help link. It plugs into Playwright (@axe-core/playwright), into component tests (vitest-axe or jest-axe), into Storybook, and into browser extensions.

Automated tools find a meaningful share of accessibility issues, not all of them. Deque's own studies put it at roughly half of issues by volume on real audits; whether a heading structure makes sense, whether the focus order is logical, or whether an error message is understandable needs a person with a keyboard and a screen reader (69.9).

Why does it exist?

Because accessibility regressions are invisible to sighted mouse users, who are most of the team. Part 69.9 tells the story of a live order status a screen reader never announced. A missing <label> costs nothing to fix in the pull request and a support call, a complaint, or in many countries a legal claim, after release. An automated check in CI turns the cheap half of accessibility into a test failure.

Mental model

Imagine a building inspector with a checklist: ramp present, handrail height, door width, fire exit signs lit. The inspector finds every missing handrail in minutes. The checklist cannot tell whether the building is pleasant to use in a wheelchair; for that you still need someone to try it.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Test
    participant P as Page
    participant AX as axe-core
    T->>P: navigate and reach the state to check
    T->>AX: inject and run with WCAG tags
    AX->>P: walk the DOM and computed styles
    AX-->>T: violations with rule, impact, nodes, help URL
    T->>T: fail if violations not empty
  1. Run at meaningful states: not only after page load, but with the error messages showing, the dialog open, the menu expanded. Each state is a new DOM.
  2. Choose rules by tag: wcag2a, wcag2aa, wcag21a, wcag21aa, wcag22aa, best-practice. Most teams enforce WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 level AA.
  3. Scope: .include('#checkout') or .exclude('#third-party-chat') to avoid failing on code you do not own (with a ticket to the vendor).
  4. jsdom limits: in component tests axe cannot compute colour contrast or anything layout-based, because jsdom has no rendering; jest-axe disables such rules or they give no results. Contrast belongs in the Playwright checks.
  5. Baselines for legacy pages: a page with 140 existing violations cannot be fixed in one pull request. Record known violations by rule and selector, fail only on new ones, and burn the list down.

Practical example

Checkout gets axe checks at five states: address step empty, address step with validation errors, coupon step with a server error, payment step, and the confirmation page. The order page gets checks with the cancel dialog open and with the live status region updated. Each check takes 150-400 ms in Playwright.

React / Next.js example

A Playwright fixture so every test can check accessibility in one line:

// apps/web/e2e/a11y.ts  (@axe-core/playwright 4)
import AxeBuilder from '@axe-core/playwright';
import { expect, type Page } from '@playwright/test';

export async function expectNoA11yViolations(page: Page, opts: { include?: string; exclude?: string[] } = {}) {
  let builder = new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa', 'wcag21a', 'wcag21aa', 'wcag22aa']);
  if (opts.include) builder = builder.include(opts.include);
  for (const sel of opts.exclude ?? []) builder = builder.exclude(sel);
  const { violations } = await builder.analyze();
  // A readable failure: rule, impact and the first selector of each violation
  expect(violations.map((v) => `${v.impact} ${v.id}: ${v.nodes[0]?.target.join(' ')}`)).toEqual([]);
}
// apps/web/e2e/checkout.a11y.spec.ts
import { test } from './fixtures';
import { expectNoA11yViolations } from './a11y';

test('address step is accessible, including its error state', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expectNoA11yViolations(page, { include: 'main' });
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save address' }).click();              // all fields invalid
  await expectNoA11yViolations(page, { include: 'main' });                        // error text contrast, aria-describedby
});

In component tests, vitest-axe checks structure (labels, roles, ARIA) quickly on every state a component can be in:

// apps/web/src/orders/CancelOrderDialog.a11y.test.tsx
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { axe } from 'vitest-axe';
import 'vitest-axe/extend-expect';                       // adds toHaveNoViolations
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { CancelOrderDialog } from './CancelOrderDialog';

it('has no structural accessibility violations when showing an error', async () => {
  const { container } = render(<CancelOrderDialog open reason={null} error="This order has already shipped" onClose={() => {}} />);
  expect(await axe(container)).toHaveNoViolations();   // contrast is not checked in jsdom: Playwright covers it
});

Playwright 1.49+ also offers ARIA snapshots: await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toMatchAriaSnapshot(...) compares the accessibility tree (roles, names, structure) with a stored YAML description. It catches a heading that became a div or a button that lost its name, without pixels.

Backend side (NestJS)

Accessibility looks like a frontend concern, but the API decides several things a screen reader user experiences:

  • Error messages are written for people. The problem document's issues[].message is shown under a field and read aloud; "must match /^\d{6}$/" is not a message. The API's error catalogue owns user-facing copy, or returns codes the frontend maps to copy (74.6), but never regex text.
  • Images come with alternative text. Product and review image fields in the API include alt (from the catalogue's admin tool), so the frontend has something meaningful to render.
  • Language and locale: the API returns Content-Language and localised copy consistently, so the page's lang attribute matches the text a screen reader pronounces.
  • Live status events carry a human summary ("Out for delivery, arriving by 7:40 pm") for the status region's announcement (69.9), in addition to the machine status.
// packages/contracts/src/catalog.ts (excerpt)
export const ProductImageSchema = z.object({
  url: z.string().url(),
  width: z.number().int().positive(),
  height: z.number().int().positive(),      // dimensions prevent layout shift (82.5)
  alt: z.string().min(1).max(160),          // required: the API refuses to publish an image without it
});

Production scenario

A storefront runs 32 axe checks in Playwright (about 9 s total) and 180 vitest-axe checks in component tests (about 6 s). In the first month the checks failed 17 pull requests: 9 missing labels on new inputs, 4 buttons with only an icon and no name, 3 colour-contrast failures on new badges, and 1 aria-hidden on a focusable element. An annual manual audit by an accessibility specialist still found 23 issues the tools could not see, mostly focus order in the new mega-menu and unclear error copy.

Failure scenario

A payment provider's new iframe widget failed axe on every page with three serious violations. To unblock the release, someone excluded iframe globally from the axe checks. Six months later the team's own embedded map iframe, without a title, shipped on the order tracking page, and screen reader users heard only "frame". The exclusion should have been the vendor's specific selector, with a ticket, an expiry date and a test that the exclusion still matched something.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Checking only the initial page: errors, dialogs and expanded menus are where most violations live.
  • Colour contrast in jsdom silently does nothing; run contrast checks in a real browser.
  • Global exclusions that hide your own regressions; scope exclusions to exact third-party selectors.
  • Treating "zero violations" as accessible: keyboard order, focus management and meaningful copy still need manual testing.
  • Legacy pages: failing on all existing violations blocks every change; baseline and burn down.
  • Dynamic regions: a live region announced on every SSE event floods a screen reader; test the announcement policy, not only the markup (Part 79).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior makes accessibility a definition-of-done item with automated enforcement for what machines can check and a scheduled manual audit for what they cannot. They run axe at the states that matter, keep exclusions narrow and dated, and treat component tests that query by role as the cheapest accessibility test of all (77.3). They also push accessibility into the backend contract: human error messages, required alt text, localised copy.

Common mistakes

  • One axe check on page load per route and nothing else.
  • Excluding whole element types to pass.
  • Relying on axe for keyboard and focus behaviour.
  • API error messages that are developer strings, read aloud to users.

Interview questions

  1. What can automated accessibility tools find, and what can they not? Expected answer: missing labels, names, ARIA errors, contrast, language; not focus order, meaningful copy or usability with a screen reader.
  2. Why does axe in jsdom miss colour contrast? Expected answer: jsdom does no layout or rendering, so computed colours and overlaps are unavailable.
  3. How do you introduce axe to an app with hundreds of existing violations? Expected answer: baseline existing violations, fail on new ones, burn down by priority.
  4. What does the API contribute to accessibility? Expected answer: human-readable error messages, required alt text, consistent language, human summaries for live updates.

Practical exercise

Add accessibility checks to checkout and the order page.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Playwright axe checks at the five checkout states and the two order-page states listed above, enforcing WCAG 2.1 AA tags.
  • vitest-axe checks for every dialog and form component in its error state.
  • Any exclusion names an exact third-party selector, links a ticket and has an expiry date checked by a test.
  • The API refuses to publish a product image without alt, and its error messages contain no regular expressions or field-type jargon.

77.11 Testing against a real NestJS backend in CI with Docker Compose

Concept

An ephemeral test stack is a complete, short-lived copy of the system started for one CI job and thrown away afterwards: PostgreSQL, Redis, the NestJS API in e2e mode, and the web app's production build. Docker Compose describes it in one file; the CI job starts it, waits for every service to be healthy, runs Playwright against it, collects logs and reports, and stops it. Each pull request gets its own stack, so no two runs share data or versions.

Why does it exist?

The alternatives fail in known ways. A shared staging environment is deployed by other people at random times, holds data other tests mutate, and runs whatever API version was merged last, not the one in your pull request (the 38-minute, 30 %-flaky suite of 77.7). Mocking the backend in e2e with page.route everywhere turns the slowest tests into expensive component tests. A stack per job costs 60-90 seconds to start and gives each run a known version of every component and an empty, seeded database.

Mental model

Imagine a flight simulator that is built fresh for each pilot, with the exact aircraft model they will fly, and dismantled after the session. No previous pilot's coffee cup in the cockpit, no surprise software update mid-flight.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant CI as GitHubActions
    participant DC as DockerCompose
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant API as NestJS
    participant WEB as NextStart
    participant PW as Playwright
    CI->>DC: docker compose up --build --wait
    DC->>PG: start, healthcheck pg_isready
    DC->>API: start after PG healthy, run migrations
    DC->>WEB: start after API healthy
    DC-->>CI: all services healthy
    CI->>PW: playwright test --shard=1/4
    PW->>WEB: journeys in browser
    WEB->>API: BFF calls with x-bff-key
    PW->>API: seed via __e2e routes
    CI->>DC: logs to artifact, compose down -v
  1. Images are built from the pull request's commit: the API's Dockerfile (Part 44.13) and the web's standalone Next.js image (73.11). In a monorepo, Turborepo's prune keeps each image to its own dependencies (70.12).
  2. Health checks gate start order: depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }. docker compose up --wait returns only when every service with a health check reports healthy, or fails the job.
  3. Migrations run before the API serves traffic, as in production (Part 24): a one-shot migrate service that the API depends on with condition: service_completed_successfully.
  4. Configuration mirrors production except for test-only flags: E2E_SUPPORT=enabled, raised throttle limits, a fixed clock if visual tests need it, a fake payment provider in test mode.
  5. Playwright runs on the CI host (or in the Playwright container) against http://localhost:3000, with E2E_BASE_URL set so its own webServer block starts nothing.
  6. On failure, the job uploads the Playwright report and docker compose logs, so the browser trace's request IDs can be matched to API log lines.
  7. Teardown: docker compose down -v removes containers and volumes.

GitHub Actions service containers (services: postgres:) are an alternative for the database alone; Compose is better when the stack includes your own images and their start order.

Practical example

The stack for the storefront: PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, the API (migrations, then node dist/main.js), the web (node server.js from Next.js standalone output) and a stub payment provider. Cold start on a GitHub-hosted 4-vCPU runner: image builds with the Docker layer cache 50-70 s, up --wait 18 s. Four Playwright shards each start their own stack, so shards never share a database.

React / Next.js example

# e2e/compose.yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: shop, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: shop, POSTGRES_DB: shop_e2e }
    tmpfs: [/var/lib/postgresql/data]                  # in memory: faster, and nothing survives the job
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U shop -d shop_e2e"], interval: 2s, retries: 30 }
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"], interval: 2s, retries: 30 }
  migrate:
    build: { context: .., dockerfile: apps/api/Dockerfile, target: runtime }
    command: ["node", "dist/migrate.js"]               # runs TypeORM migrations, then exits 0
    environment: { DATABASE_URL: postgres://shop:shop@db:5432/shop_e2e }
    depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }
  api:
    build: { context: .., dockerfile: apps/api/Dockerfile, target: runtime }
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://shop:shop@db:5432/shop_e2e
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      E2E_SUPPORT: enabled
      E2E_SECRET: ${E2E_SECRET}
      BFF_KEY: ${BFF_KEY}
      THROTTLE_LIMIT_PER_MIN: "5000"
      PAYMENTS_BASE_URL: http://payments-stub:8080
    ports: ["4000:4000"]
    depends_on:
      migrate: { condition: service_completed_successfully }
      redis: { condition: service_healthy }
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD", "wget", "-qO-", "http://localhost:4000/health/ready"], interval: 2s, retries: 60 }
  web:
    build: { context: .., dockerfile: apps/web/Dockerfile }
    environment: { API_INTERNAL_URL: http://api:4000, BFF_KEY: ${BFF_KEY}, NODE_ENV: production }
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    depends_on: { api: { condition: service_healthy } }
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD", "wget", "-qO-", "http://localhost:3000/api/health"], interval: 2s, retries: 60 }
  payments-stub:
    image: wiremock/wiremock:3.9.1
    volumes: ["./payments-stub:/home/wiremock"]        # canned approve and decline responses
# .github/workflows/web-e2e.yml
name: web-e2e
on: { pull_request: { paths: ['apps/**', 'packages/**', 'e2e/**'] } }
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy: { fail-fast: false, matrix: { shard: [1, 2, 3, 4] } }
    env: { E2E_SECRET: e2e-${{ github.run_id }}, BFF_KEY: bff-${{ github.run_id }}, E2E_BASE_URL: http://localhost:3000, E2E_API_URL: http://localhost:4000 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: docker compose -f e2e/compose.yaml up --build --wait
      - run: pnpm --filter web exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: pnpm --filter web exec playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/4
      - if: always()
        run: docker compose -f e2e/compose.yaml logs --no-color > compose-logs.txt
      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: e2e-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: |
            apps/web/blob-report
            compose-logs.txt
          retention-days: 7
      - if: always()
        run: docker compose -f e2e/compose.yaml down -v
  report:
    if: always()
    needs: e2e
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { pattern: e2e-shard-*, path: all-blob-reports, merge-multiple: true }
      - run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: e2e-html-report, path: playwright-report, retention-days: 14 }

The secrets are generated per run: nothing in this stack is a real credential, and the test-support secret dies with the job.

Backend side (NestJS)

What the API must provide so the stack starts reliably and the tests are honest:

  • Separate liveness and readiness (Part 31.12, @nestjs/terminus): /health/ready checks PostgreSQL and Redis; Compose waits on it.
  • Migrations as a separate command, not run inside main.ts on every boot, so a failed migration fails the migrate service with a clear log instead of a crash loop.
  • Configuration validated at boot (ConfigModule.forRoot({ validate })) so a missing BFF_KEY fails in 2 seconds with a message, not 20 minutes later as 401s in a trace.
  • Fast shutdown on SIGTERM (app.enableShutdownHooks()), so compose down takes 1 s, not the 10 s default kill timeout.
  • Structured logs with the request ID, so the uploaded compose logs can be searched for the ID shown in the Playwright trace.
// apps/api/src/health/health.controller.ts  (@nestjs/terminus 10)
import { Controller, Get } from '@nestjs/common';
import { HealthCheck, HealthCheckService, TypeOrmHealthIndicator } from '@nestjs/terminus';
import { RedisHealthIndicator } from './redis.health';           // small custom indicator: PING with 500 ms timeout

@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(private health: HealthCheckService, private db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator, private redis: RedisHealthIndicator) {}

  @Get('live') live() { return { status: 'ok' }; }               // process is up; no dependencies

  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([
      () => this.db.pingCheck('postgres', { timeout: 1000 }),
      () => this.redis.isHealthy('redis'),
    ]);
  }
}

Production scenario

A team running 26 journeys against per-shard Compose stacks measured, over a quarter: median e2e job time 5 min 10 s (stack start 1 min 25 s, tests 3 min 30 s, teardown and upload 15 s), 0.3 % flaky runs, and zero failures caused by "someone else's deploy". Moving from the shared staging environment cost about 1,500 extra runner-minutes a month and saved an estimated 30 engineer-hours a month previously spent re-running and investigating staging-caused failures.

Failure scenario

The e2e job passed for weeks while production checkout broke twice. The compose file used image: shop/api:latest from the registry instead of building from the pull request's commit, so e2e always tested the last image someone had pushed manually, sometimes days old. A web change that needed a new API field passed against an old API that happened to include it on an abandoned branch image. The fix: build both images from the commit under test (build: in compose, with the layer cache), tag them with the SHA, and print the SHA of each service in the test report header via a /version endpoint.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Images not built from the commit under test, testing a different version from the one being merged.
  • Health checks missing or checking the wrong thing (a port being open instead of the app being ready).
  • Persistent volumes reused between runs on self-hosted runners; use tmpfs or down -v.
  • Port clashes on self-hosted runners running two jobs; use a Compose project name per job (-p e2e-${{ github.run_id }}) and dynamic ports.
  • Real third parties called from the stack (payments, SMS); stub them (WireMock, a fake service) and keep one contract test against the provider's sandbox elsewhere.
  • ARM laptops versus x86 CI: images built locally on Apple Silicon differ from CI; build in CI, or use multi-platform builds.
  • Slow image builds: without a layer cache (docker/build-push-action with cache-from: type=gha), every run reinstalls dependencies.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior wants the e2e environment to be a function of the commit: same commit, same stack, same result. They build every image from the commit under test, start dependencies with health checks, keep test-only behaviour behind explicit flags, stub external parties, and collect logs automatically. They count the minutes and accept them, because a reproducible red build is worth more than a fast unreliable one. They also design the API's health, configuration and shutdown behaviour with this environment in mind, since a service that starts cleanly in Compose usually starts cleanly in Kubernetes too.

Common mistakes

  • Testing against shared staging.
  • image: latest in the e2e compose file.
  • No logs collected, so failures cannot be traced to the backend.
  • Disabling auth or CSRF in the e2e stack to make tests easier.
  • Running migrations inside the API's boot with no separate failure signal.

Interview questions

  1. Why an ephemeral stack per CI job instead of a shared staging environment? Expected answer: versions match the commit, data is isolated, no interference from other deploys, reproducible failures.
  2. How do you make sure services start in the right order? Expected answer: health checks plus depends_on conditions, up --wait, a one-shot migration service.
  3. How do you connect a failed browser test to a backend error? Expected answer: request IDs in responses and logs, the Playwright trace's network log, compose logs uploaded as artifacts.
  4. What do you do about third-party services in the stack? Expected answer: stub them with canned responses; test the real integration separately against the provider's sandbox.

Practical exercise

Build the Compose stack and the GitHub Actions job above for the monorepo of Part 70.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Images are built from the commit under test; the report shows each service's commit SHA.
  • docker compose up --wait fails the job within 60 s if the API cannot reach PostgreSQL.
  • Four shards each start their own stack; one merged HTML report is published.
  • On failure, the job uploads compose logs, and a request ID from a failed trace can be found in them.
  • The API refuses to boot with a missing BFF_KEY, with a clear message, in under 5 s.

77.12 Code review for frontend changes: what a backend reviewer should look for

Concept

Backend engineers are often asked to review frontend pull requests: in a full-stack team, in a monorepo where the change touches packages/contracts, or because the frontend change calls a new endpoint. A useful review does not require knowing every React idiom. It requires knowing where frontend changes break production, and those places overlap heavily with what a backend engineer already understands: contracts, errors, retries, caching, security, data volume and tests.

Why does it exist?

Because the most expensive frontend bugs are full-stack bugs, and a reviewer who only reads one side misses them. A frontend reviewer may approve a perfectly idiomatic component that retries a non-idempotent POST, shows a server error in the wrong place, or puts an access token in localStorage. A backend reviewer who knows what to look for catches those in minutes.

Mental model

Imagine an electrician inspecting a kitchen renovation. They do not judge the cabinet colours. They check every place where the new kitchen connects to the building's wiring: sockets, load, earthing, what happens when a fuse trips. The backend reviewer inspects every place where the screen connects to the API.

How it works

The review, in the order a senior reads a frontend pull request:

Area Questions Where in this book
Contract Does it use the shared schema or generated client, or a hand-written type? Does it handle unknown enum values and nullable fields? 74.3, 74.7
Errors Is every API error mapped (field, banner, toast, reauth, wait)? Is the request ID shown? Is "unknown outcome" distinguished from "failed"? 74.6, 77.8
Writes Is every write protected against double submit? Does every retried write send an Idempotency-Key? 71.8, 78.6
Retries and timeouts Are there timeouts (AbortSignal.timeout)? Are retries limited, with backoff, and only for safe or idempotent calls? 72.10, Part 31
Data volume Is a list paginated by cursor? Is the payload slim? Any N+1 request patterns (one request per row)? 72.7, 82.10
Caching Are query keys complete? Is personal data kept out of shared caches? Are revalidate and tags right on Next.js fetches? 72.2, 79.7
Security Tokens only in HttpOnly cookies? No dangerouslySetInnerHTML with API data? Redirect targets validated? Secrets not in NEXT_PUBLIC_*? 75.1, 75.7, 75.9, 76.6
Server and client boundary Does a Client Component import server-only code? Does a Server Component leak secrets into props? 73.4
Performance Does it add a large dependency to the entry chunk? Images sized? Layout shift? 76.7, 76.8
Accessibility Labels, roles, keyboard path, focus after errors? 69.9, 83.10
Tests Component tests for each new state with MSW? A journey only if a boundary is crossed? No mocks of the app's own client? This Part
Observability Are errors reported with release and request ID? Are new user actions measurable? Part 78

Practical example

A pull request adds "Reorder" to the order page: a button that calls POST /v1/orders/:id/reorder and navigates to the cart. A backend reviewer reads 140 lines of TSX and leaves four comments in ten minutes:

  1. "The mutation has retry: 2 (from a copied hook). This POST creates a cart; without an Idempotency-Key a timeout plus retry can create two. Add a per-attempt key or set retry: 0." (71.8)
  2. "On 409 ITEMS_UNAVAILABLE the toast says 'Something went wrong'. The API returns issues listing the unavailable SKUs; show them." (74.6)
  3. "The button has an icon and no text; add an accessible name." (69.9)
  4. "Tests mock reorderOrder with vi.mock; use the MSW handler so the real client and parser run, and add the 409 case." (77.5)

None of these needs deep React knowledge.

React / Next.js example

A diff that looks fine to a reader who does not think about the backend:

// apps/web/src/orders/ReorderButton.tsx (as submitted)
'use client';
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation';

export function ReorderButton({ orderId }: { orderId: string }) {
  const router = useRouter();
  const m = useMutation({
    mutationFn: () => fetch(`/api/v1/orders/${orderId}/reorder`, { method: 'POST' }).then((r) => r.json()),
    retry: 2,                                            // review: retried non-idempotent POST
    onSuccess: () => router.push('/cart'),
    onError: () => alert('Something went wrong'),        // review: drops code, issues and requestId
  });
  return <button onClick={() => m.mutate()}><CartIcon /></button>;   // review: no accessible name, no double-submit guard
}

And after review:

// apps/web/src/orders/ReorderButton.tsx (after review)
'use client';
import { useMutation } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation';
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { reorder } from '@/api/orders';                  // shared client: timeout, toApiError, schema parsing
import { useErrorTreatment } from '@/api/useErrorTreatment';

export function ReorderButton({ orderId }: { orderId: string }) {
  const router = useRouter();
  const key = useRef(crypto.randomUUID());               // one key per attempt; retries reuse it
  const treat = useErrorTreatment();                     // classify(): fields, banner, toast with request ID
  const m = useMutation({
    mutationFn: () => reorder(orderId, key.current),     // sends Idempotency-Key
    retry: (count, e) => count < 2 && isRetryable(e),    // only timeouts and 409 IDEMPOTENCY_IN_PROGRESS
    onSuccess: (cart) => router.push(`/cart?from=${encodeURIComponent(cart.sourceOrderId)}`),
    onError: treat,
  });
  return (
    <button type="button" onClick={() => m.mutate()} disabled={m.isPending}>
      <CartIcon aria-hidden /> {m.isPending ? 'Adding to cart...' : 'Reorder'}
    </button>
  );
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The review often ends with a backend change, and the backend reviewer is the right person to see it:

  • The new endpoint must accept Idempotency-Key (the interceptor from 15.12) and document it in OpenAPI.
  • 409 ITEMS_UNAVAILABLE must list SKUs in issues with stable codes, so the UI can show them.
  • The response should return the new cart, so the client does not need a second request.
  • The endpoint needs a rate limit and an ownership check (the order belongs to the caller, Part 40.12).

The pull-request template makes the full-stack questions explicit for both sides:

## Full-stack checklist
- [ ] Uses shared contracts or the generated client; unknown enum values handled
- [ ] Every API error code this screen can receive is mapped; request ID shown on unexpected errors
- [ ] Writes are idempotent (key sent) and double-submit safe; retries only for safe or idempotent calls
- [ ] Lists use cursor pagination; no request per row
- [ ] No tokens or secrets in client code or NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables; no unsanitised HTML
- [ ] Component tests with MSW for loading, empty, error and success; e2e only for new boundaries
- [ ] Accessible names, labels and a keyboard path for new controls

Production scenario

A team added a rotating backend reviewer to every frontend pull request that touched the API client or contracts, about 30 % of frontend pull requests. Review time per pull request rose by a median of 12 minutes. In the following two quarters, production incidents classified as "frontend-backend mismatch" (wrong error handling, duplicate writes, missing pagination, contract drift) fell from 9 to 2.

Failure scenario

A frontend pull request replaced the order history's cursor pagination with "load all orders and filter in the browser", because the new filter UI needed client-side filtering. Two frontend engineers approved it; the component was clean and well tested with a 20-order fixture. In production, customers with 2,000+ orders (B2B clinics) loaded a 6 MB response, the API's p99 for that endpoint went from 120 ms to 4.2 s, and the database's CPU doubled at 10:00 when clinics opened. A backend reviewer would have asked the first question in the checklist's data-volume row: "what is the largest list this can fetch?" The fix added server-side filter parameters to the cursor endpoint (Part 15.6).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Reviewing only the TSX and missing that the change requires an API change nobody made.
  • Approving tests that mock the client, so the new error codes are never exercised.
  • Missing the server/client boundary: an import that pulls a server secret into a Client Component's bundle.
  • Copied hooks carrying retry or cache settings that are wrong for the new call.
  • Fixtures with 3 rows hiding volume problems.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior reviews every connection between the screen and the system: what is sent, what can come back, what happens on retry, how much data moves, what is cached and for whom, what is exposed to the browser, and how anyone will know it broke. They leave idiom and style to frontend specialists and lint rules, and spend their attention where a mistake costs money. They ask for the backend half of the change in the same pull request or a linked one, and they treat the checklist as a conversation starter, not a gate to tick.

Common mistakes

  • Commenting on style while missing a retried POST.
  • Assuming the framework handles errors.
  • Not asking about the largest realistic data size.
  • Not checking what ends up in the client bundle (NEXT_PUBLIC_, server imports).

Interview questions

  1. You are a backend engineer reviewing a React pull request. What do you look at first? Expected answer: the API calls: contract types, error handling, idempotency and retries, pagination and volume, caching, security of tokens and HTML, tests at the network boundary.
  2. How can a frontend change cause a backend incident? Expected answer: removed pagination, retry storms, request-per-row patterns, polling too often, cache keys that defeat caching.
  3. What would you check in a Next.js pull request specifically? Expected answer: server and client boundary, secrets in props or NEXT_PUBLIC_, fetch caching and revalidation, Server Action authorisation.
  4. How do you make full-stack review routine? Expected answer: code owners for the API client and contracts, a pull-request checklist, paired backend reviewers on API-touching changes.

Practical exercise

Review three real frontend pull requests from your team's history using the table above.

Acceptance criteria:

  • For each, list every comment you would leave, labelled with the row of the table it belongs to.
  • At least one comment per pull request results in a backend change (idempotency, error codes, pagination, rate limit or ownership check).
  • Propose a CODEOWNERS rule that adds a backend reviewer to changes under apps/web/src/api/ and packages/contracts/.
  • Write the pull-request template for your repository, under 12 items.

77.13 Worked example: tests for the checkout flow from unit to end to end

This example builds the full test suite that 71.13 promised for the three-step checkout (address, coupon, payment), using every tool of this Part. The goal is not the most tests; it is the smallest suite where every serious way the checkout can break makes at least one test fail, at the cheapest level that can see it.

The test plan

# Risk Level File Time
1 Illegal step transitions, double PLACE_ORDER Unit checkoutReducer.test.ts 4 ms
2 Retry reuses the idempotency key; unknown outcome keeps it Unit usePlaceOrder.test.ts 30 ms
3 Money formatting, large values Unit packages/contracts/src/money.test.ts 3 ms
4 Field errors from zod and from the server land on the right input Component AddressForm.test.tsx 0.9 s
5 The cart version threads through every request Component CheckoutPage.flow.test.tsx 1.4 s
6 409 CART_CHANGED shows notice and fresh totals Component CouponStep.msw.test.tsx 0.4 s
7 Double click sends one request with a key Component PaymentStep.msw.test.tsx 0.3 s
8 Proxy 502 HTML and network errors degrade honestly Component CouponStep.msw.test.tsx 0.5 s
9 The API still returns what the web client reads Contract orders.pact.test.ts 0.6 s
10 Concurrent same-key requests create one order row API integration orders.idempotency.int-spec.ts 2.1 s
11 Full journey, double click, one row, Back safe E2E checkout.spec.ts 14 s
12 Payment declined, then approved with another method E2E checkout-decline.spec.ts 11 s
13 Layout of the payment step on mobile and desktop Visual checkout.visual.spec.ts 4 s
14 Accessibility at five checkout states Accessibility checkout.a11y.spec.ts 3 s

Fourteen files, about 40 seconds of test time in total, most of it in two e2e journeys. Every risk the 71.13 failure table listed has a row.

The pipeline

flowchart LR
    pr["Pull request"] --> stat["tsc and ESLint, 40 s"]
    stat --> unit["Vitest unit and component, 70 s"]
    stat --> apit["API Jest unit and integration, 90 s"]
    unit --> pact["Pact publish and verify, 60 s"]
    apit --> pact
    pact --> e2e["Playwright on Compose stack, 4 shards, 4 min"]
    e2e --> vis["Visual and a11y, 90 s"]
    vis --> merge["Merge allowed"]

The cheap jobs run first and in parallel; the expensive ones run only when the cheap ones pass. A typo in a zod schema fails in 40 s; a broken idempotency interceptor fails in under 3 minutes; a layout break in under 8.

Component level: the version thread

The most valuable new test is the one that walks all three steps in jsdom with MSW and checks the requests, not only the screen. The cart version (71.13) must move from 7 to 8 to 9 and every write must carry the latest one. A bug here applies a coupon to a cart the user never saw.

// apps/web/src/checkout/CheckoutPage.flow.test.tsx
import { screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { server } from '../test/msw/server';
import { API } from '../test/msw/checkout.handlers';
import { aCheckoutView, aPricedCart } from '../test/builders';
import { renderWithProviders } from '../test/render';
import { CheckoutPage } from './CheckoutPage';
import { fillAddress } from '../test/flows';                       // the five fields, by label

it('sends the latest cart version with every write', async () => {
  const seen: { path: string; version: unknown; key: string | null }[] = [];
  server.use(
    http.get(`${API}/checkout/view`, () => HttpResponse.json(aCheckoutView({ version: 7, totalMinor: '99900' }))),
    http.post(`${API}/checkout/address`, async ({ request }) => {
      const body = (await request.json()) as { cartVersion: number };
      seen.push({ path: 'address', version: body.cartVersion, key: null });
      return HttpResponse.json(aPricedCart({ version: 8, totalMinor: '103900' }));     // + delivery 40.00
    }),
    http.post(`${API}/checkout/coupon`, async ({ request }) => {
      const body = (await request.json()) as { cartVersion: number };
      seen.push({ path: 'coupon', version: body.cartVersion, key: null });
      return HttpResponse.json(aPricedCart({ version: 9, totalMinor: '98900', appliedCoupon: 'SAVE50' }));
    }),
    http.post(`${API}/orders`, async ({ request }) => {
      const body = (await request.json()) as { cartVersion: number };
      seen.push({ path: 'orders', version: body.cartVersion, key: request.headers.get('Idempotency-Key') });
      return HttpResponse.json({ id: 'A7K2Q9P', status: 'PENDING' }, { status: 201 });
    }),
  );
  const { user } = renderWithProviders(<CheckoutPage />);

  await fillAddress(user, await screen.findByRole('form', { name: 'Delivery address' }));
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save address' }));
  const summary = screen.getByRole('complementary', { name: 'Order summary' });
  expect(await screen.findByRole('heading', { name: 'Have a coupon?' })).toBeVisible();
  expect(summary).toHaveTextContent('₹1,039.00');                  // totals come only from the server

  await user.type(screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Coupon code' }), 'SAVE50{Enter}');
  expect(await screen.findByText('SAVE50 applied.')).toBeVisible();
  expect(summary).toHaveTextContent('₹989.00');
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Continue to payment' }));
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }));

  await expect.poll(() => seen.map((s) => `${s.path}@${s.version}`)).toEqual(['address@7', 'coupon@8', 'orders@9']);
  expect(seen[2].key).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/);
});

The test fails if any step sends a stale version, if PriceSummary ever computes a total itself, or if the order request loses its key. It needs no browser and no database, and runs in 1.4 s.

Contract level: what the client reads from POST /v1/orders

Two interactions added to the web's pact (74.10): the 201 body the client parses with OrderCreatedSchema, and the 409 CART_CHANGED problem document with a fresh cart. The API's provider verification seeds "cart exists at version 9" and "cart exists at version 10" through state handlers. If an API engineer changes 409 to 422 for stale carts, the API's pull request fails before merge, with the web's interaction named in the error.

API level: one row under concurrency

The component test proves the browser sends one request for a double click. It cannot prove that two requests with the same key, from a retry racing the original, create one order. Only the API with a real PostgreSQL can (41.9, 41.17):

// apps/api/test/orders.idempotency.int-spec.ts  (Jest, Testcontainers PostgreSQL 16)
import request from 'supertest';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';
import { aPlaceOrderRequest } from '@shop/test-fixtures';
import { bootTestApp, type TestApp } from './support/boot';        // configureApp() as in main.ts

let t: TestApp;
beforeAll(async () => { t = await bootTestApp(); });
afterAll(() => t.close());

it('creates one order for two concurrent requests with the same key', async () => {
  const { token, cartId } = await t.seed.customerWithCart({ version: 9 });
  const key = randomUUID();
  const send = () => request(t.http).post('/v1/orders')
    .set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`).set('Idempotency-Key', key)
    .send(aPlaceOrderRequest({ cartId, cartVersion: 9 }));

  const [a, b] = await Promise.all([send(), send()]);
  const statuses = [a.status, b.status].sort();
  // One request wins; the other replays the result (201) or sees the reservation (409 IDEMPOTENCY_IN_PROGRESS)
  expect([[201, 201], [201, 409]]).toContainEqual(statuses);
  const { rows } = await t.pg.query('SELECT count(*)::int AS n FROM orders WHERE cart_id = $1', [cartId]);
  expect(rows[0].n).toBe(1);                                          // the unique index on (user_id, idempotency_key) holds
});

E2E level: the two journeys

Journey 11 is the test in 77.7: a fresh customer, the real BFF login (storage state from 77.8), address, coupon, a double click on "Place order", exactly one row via the test-support API, and Back not returning to a live payment form.

Journey 12 adds the payment provider. The Compose stack's WireMock stub (77.11) declines card 4000 0000 0000 0002 and approves UPI. The test chooses card, sees the decline under the payment method with focus moved to it, switches to UPI and completes. It asserts one order and one failed payment attempt recorded against it. This is the only test that proves the idempotency key is cleared after a definite decline (71.8), so the second attempt is a new attempt and not a replay of the decline.

Visual and accessibility

Two screenshots of the payment step (375 px and 1280 px) in the pinned Playwright container, the promo carousel masked and the clock fixed (77.9). axe checks at five states: empty address, address with errors, coupon with server error, payment, confirmation (77.10). The vitest-axe checks of the three step components run in the component job.

Proving the suite works: break things on purpose

A suite is only as good as the bugs it catches. Before merging the suite, the team broke the checkout deliberately, one change at a time (a manual form of mutation testing, Part 41.15), and recorded which test failed:

Deliberate bug First failing test Level Time to red in CI
Remove the inFlight ref guard in usePlaceOrder #2, #7 Unit, component 1 min 50 s
Send view.version instead of the latest version to the coupon endpoint #5 Component 1 min 50 s
PriceSummary adds subtotal + deliveryFee - discount itself #5 (rounding on a 3-way split fixture) Component 1 min 50 s
Map server issues to address.postcode instead of postcode #4 Component 1 min 50 s
API returns 422 instead of 409 for a stale cart #9 (API pull request) Contract 2 min 30 s
Drop the unique index in a migration #10, #11 API integration, e2e 3 min, 6 min
Delete the Idempotency-Key header from the client #7, #10 (via #11) Component, e2e 1 min 50 s
navigate('/orders/..') without replace #11 E2E 6 min
A global CSS change pushes "Place order" below the fold on mobile #13 Visual 8 min
Postcode label removed, placeholder only #4, #14 Component, a11y 1 min 50 s
Payment decline keeps the idempotency key #12 E2E 6 min

Every deliberate bug failed at least one test, and 8 of the 11 failed in under two minutes. Two tests the team had planned (a snapshot of the coupon step and an e2e test for each coupon error) were dropped, because no deliberate bug was caught only by them.

Numbers

  • 14 test files for checkout: 3 unit, 5 component, 1 contract, 1 API integration, 2 e2e, 1 visual, 1 accessibility.
  • Pull-request feedback: first red signal in 40 s (types), most behaviour bugs red within 2 minutes, the full pipeline in about 8 minutes.
  • Flake rate for the checkout tests over 60 days: 0 for unit and component, 0.4 % for e2e (two cases, both a slow image build timing out the --wait; fixed by raising the health check's retries).
  • Cost: about 9 runner-minutes per pull request across all jobs.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior builds the suite from the risk table backwards, not from the components forwards. Each risk gets one honest test at the cheapest level, and each level answers a question the others cannot: the reducer's rules in milliseconds, the screen's behaviour against a faithful fake in a second, the API's promise to each consumer in a contract, the database's guarantee under concurrency, and the whole path through a real browser a handful of times. Then they prove the suite by breaking the product on purpose, and delete tests that catch nothing. The backend work is part of the testing work: error codes with field paths, a seeding module, request IDs, health checks, a fixed clock and a shared fixtures package are what make the frontend suite possible.

Practical exercise

Build this suite for your checkout, or for the order list of 72.12.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A risk table with one test per risk at the cheapest honest level, and no test without a risk.
  • The version-thread component test, the concurrency integration test and one e2e journey exist and pass.
  • The deliberate-bug table has at least 10 rows; every bug fails at least one test; at least 7 fail before e2e runs.
  • The full pipeline finishes in under 10 minutes on GitHub-hosted runners; unit and component feedback in under 2.
  • The flaky rate over 30 days is reported automatically and is under 1 % for e2e.

Senior Checklist — Part 77

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can place each frontend risk at the cheapest honest test level: static, unit, component, contract, e2e, visual or accessibility
  • I write unit tests for pure rules and hooks with Vitest, table-driven, with fake timers and advanceTimersByTimeAsync for retries
  • I write component tests with Testing Library that query by role and label, use user-event, and include a keyboard path
  • I wait for outcomes with findBy, waitFor and expect.poll, never fixed sleeps, and I treat act warnings as failures
  • I mock the network with MSW 2, fail on unhandled requests, and never mock the app's own API client in screen tests
  • I build fixtures through the shared zod schemas and keep mocks honest with request validation, a shared error enum and Pact
  • I know which Next.js pieces cannot be component-tested (async Server Components) and cover them in e2e
  • I write Playwright journeys against the production build with fresh data per test, storage state per worker and traces on failure
  • I control flakiness with isolation, retries as a sensor, a flake dashboard, owners and dated quarantine
  • I keep visual tests few, deterministic and generated in a pinned container
  • I run axe at meaningful states in a real browser and know what automated accessibility checks cannot find
  • I can run the whole stack per CI job with Docker Compose, health checks and images built from the commit under test
  • I can review a frontend pull request for contract, errors, idempotency, volume, caching, security and tests
  • I can prove a suite's value by breaking the product on purpose and seeing which test fails

Part 77 — Key Takeaways

  • Most frontend bugs live in wiring, so the testing trophy's wide middle of component tests beats a pyramid of mocked unit tests.
  • Test what the user perceives: roles, labels, text, focus and the request that was sent, never internal state.
  • The network is the right seam: fake it with MSW, keep the real client, parser and error mapper in every screen test.
  • Mocks are a second implementation of the contract; build fixtures through shared schemas and verify the real API with Pact.
  • Wait for outcomes, not for time; fixed sleeps are both slow and flaky.
  • E2E tests are few and must cross a boundary only a real browser and backend can: cookies, redirects, the production bundle, database constraints.
  • Parallel e2e needs tenant-style isolation: an account per worker, data per test, nothing shared that can change.
  • Retries detect flakiness; they do not fix it, and the product is the first suspect.
  • Visual and accessibility checks catch what behaviour tests cannot, if they are deterministic and run at the states that matter.
  • An ephemeral Compose stack built from the commit under test makes e2e failures reproducible and attributable.
  • The backend makes the frontend testable: stable error codes with field paths, request IDs, a guarded seeding module, health checks and a controllable clock.
  • A suite proves its worth only when you break the product on purpose and watch it fail.

Part 78 — Shipping and Operating Frontends

Part 47 — CI/CD and Deployment Strategies built the backend's delivery pipeline: continuous integration (47.1), artifacts (47.3), deployment strategies (47.7), feature flags (47.8), rollbacks (47.9) and post-deploy verification (47.10). Part 43 — Observability covered logs, metrics and traces (43.4), Part 44 containers, Part 46.8 CloudFront, and Part 49 SLOs and error budgets. This volume has already touched deployment from the frontend side: environment variables and runtime config (70.6), source maps (70.7), Next.js output modes and version skew (73.11), version telemetry and reload nudges (74.9), CSP (75.7) and caching for frontends (76.9).

A frontend deploy is different from a backend deploy in one way that drives most of this Part: the old version keeps running after you replace it. A NestJS deploy ends when the last old pod drains. A web deploy never quite ends, because the old JavaScript is running in thousands of open tabs, in CDN caches, in service workers, and in browsers that cached yesterday's HTML. This Part covers where to host, how to build once and configure per environment, how to keep old and new versions working together, how to roll out and roll back, how to see browser errors and connect them to backend traces, how to set frontend SLOs, which security headers belong at the edge, and one incident and one pipeline that put it together.

Stack and versions, as in the rest of the volume: Next.js 14 App Router (notes for 15) with output: 'standalone', a Vite 5 SPA for the admin app, AWS S3 and CloudFront, GitHub Actions, the Sentry JavaScript SDK v8 concepts (notes where v7 differs), OpenTelemetry for the NestJS side (Part 43.4), and the web-vitals library v4 from Part 76.

78.1 Hosting options: static hosting, managed platforms and Node servers for SSR

Concept

A web app's build produces up to three kinds of output, and each needs a different kind of host:

  • Static files: HTML, JavaScript, CSS, fonts and images. Any static host can serve them: S3 behind CloudFront, GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages. A Vite SPA (70.11) and a Next.js static export (73.11) produce only this.
  • Server-rendered responses: HTML or React Server Component payloads computed per request, Server Actions, Route Handlers, middleware. These need a running Node.js server (next start or the standalone server.js in a container on ECS or Kubernetes) or a serverless function platform.
  • Edge logic: small functions that run in CDN locations close to the user (CloudFront Functions, Lambda@Edge, Vercel or Netlify edge functions, Next.js middleware on an edge runtime). They rewrite URLs, add headers, pick a canary, check a cookie.

Managed frontend platforms (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, AWS Amplify Hosting) bundle all three behind a Git integration: every push becomes an immutable deployment with its own URL, production is an alias pointing at one of them, and rollback moves the alias.

Why does it exist?

Because the cost and risk profiles differ by a factor of a hundred. A static SPA on S3 and CloudFront serving 10 million page views a month costs a few tens of dollars, has no servers to patch, and cannot be overloaded by traffic in any practical sense. A Next.js storefront with SSR and ISR needs servers that scale with traffic, share a cache (73.11), and can fail like any backend service. A team that picks SSR for an internal admin tool pays for servers it does not need; a team that picks a static SPA for an SEO-dependent product catalogue loses search traffic (73.1).

Mental model

Imagine three ways to sell sandwiches. A vending machine (static hosting) is stocked once and serves anyone, any hour, at almost no cost, but every sandwich is pre-made. A deli counter (Node server) makes each sandwich to order with fresh ingredients, needs staff on shift, and can get a queue at lunchtime. A franchise with a head office (managed platform) gives you the counter, the machines, the staff rota and the delivery vans as a service, for a fee and on their rules.

How it works

flowchart LR
    user["Browser"] --> cdn["CloudFront distribution"]
    cdn -->|"/assets/*, /_next/static/*"| s3["S3 bucket, private, OAC"]
    cdn -->|"/admin/* SPA HTML"| s3
    cdn -->|"storefront HTML, RSC, actions"| alb["ALB"]
    alb --> next["Next.js standalone on ECS"]
    next --> api["NestJS on ECS, internal"]
    cdn --> fn["CloudFront Function: SPA rewrite, canary cookie"]

The common production shape on AWS for this book's stack:

  1. One CloudFront distribution per site, with cache behaviours by path pattern. /_next/static/* and /assets/* go to an S3 origin; everything else for the storefront goes to an ALB origin in front of Next.js; the admin SPA's HTML and assets come from S3 under /admin/.
  2. The S3 bucket is private. CloudFront reads it through Origin Access Control (OAC), the successor to Origin Access Identity, with a bucket policy that allows only that distribution. Public S3 website hosting is not used: it cannot use OAC and serves over HTTP only.
  3. SPA routing: a request for /admin/orders/123 has no file in S3. A CloudFront Function on viewer request rewrites paths without a file extension to /admin/index.html. The older trick, mapping S3's 403/404 to index.html with custom error responses, also turns genuinely missing assets into 200 HTML responses, which breaks chunk-error detection (78.3).
  4. Next.js servers run from the standalone output in containers (73.11), with readiness checks, a shared cache handler for ISR, and the same build ID and Server Actions key on every replica.
  5. Edge functions stay tiny: CloudFront Functions run in under a millisecond, have no network access and a 10 KB code limit; Lambda@Edge can make network calls but adds tens of milliseconds and deploys slowly to all regions.

Hosting options for the three apps in this volume:

Option Fits Strengths Costs and limits
S3 + CloudFront Vite SPA, Next.js static export, docs Cheapest, no servers, absorbs any spike, full control of headers and caching You build preview URLs, atomic switching and rollback yourself; no SSR
