Next.js standalone on ECS/Kubernetes behind CloudFront SSR storefront with ISR, Server Actions, BFF Same platform as NestJS, private network to the API, full control You run servers, shared cache, skew protection and scaling
Serverless adapters (OpenNext on Lambda) SSR with spiky traffic on AWS Scales to zero, per-request cost Cold starts (200-1,000 ms on first request), more moving parts, adapter lag behind Next.js releases
Vercel / Netlify Teams that want previews, rollbacks and edge features out of the box Immutable deployments, instant rollback, preview per PR, skew protection (Vercel) Price per seat and per usage at scale, platform-specific features, private network to your API needs extra setup
Amplify Hosting Small AWS-centric teams Git-connected, previews, SSR support Fewer controls than raw CloudFront, lags newest Next.js features

Practical example

The storefront company runs three frontends:

  • Storefront (shop.example): Next.js 14 with SSR and ISR, 2.5 million page views a day, peaks of 900 requests per second at the origin after CDN caching. Hosted as standalone containers on ECS Fargate (6-24 tasks, autoscaled on CPU and request count) behind CloudFront.
  • Admin (admin.shop.example): a Vite SPA used by 300 staff. Hosted on S3 + CloudFront. Hosting cost: about 4 dollars a month.
  • Docs (docs.shop.example): Next.js static export on S3 + CloudFront.

All three share one GitHub Actions setup (78.11), and the storefront's API calls go through its BFF to NestJS on the same private network.

React / Next.js example

The CloudFront Function that serves the admin SPA's HTML for client-side routes and leaves real files alone:

// infra/cloudfront/admin-spa-rewrite.js  (CloudFront Functions runtime 2.0; plain JavaScript in the console)
// Shown with types for readability; deploy the compiled JS. No network, under 1 ms, 10 KB limit.
function handler(event: { request: { uri: string } }) {
  const req = event.request;
  const uri = req.uri;
  // Paths with a file extension are real objects: /admin/assets/index-B7xQ2kLm.js, /admin/favicon.svg
  if (/\.[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,8}$/.test(uri)) return req;
  // Everything else is a client-side route: /admin/orders/123 -> /admin/index.html
  if (uri.startsWith('/admin')) req.uri = '/admin/index.html';
  return req;
}

A missing chunk (/admin/assets/Orders-OLDHASH.js) now returns S3's real 403/404, which the app can detect and handle (78.3), instead of an HTML page that fails to parse as JavaScript.

For the storefront, next.config.js keeps the settings from 73.11 and adds one that matters for multi-version hosting:

// apps/web/next.config.ts  (Next.js 15 supports a TypeScript config; on 14 use next.config.js / .mjs)
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const config: NextConfig = {
  output: 'standalone',
  generateBuildId: async () => process.env.GIT_SHA ?? 'local',
  deploymentId: process.env.GIT_SHA,       // tags asset and RSC requests with ?dpl=<sha> for skew handling (84.4)
  poweredByHeader: false,
  cacheHandler: require.resolve('./cache-handler.js'),
  cacheMaxMemorySize: 0,
};
export default config;

Backend side (NestJS)

Hosting choices change what the API must handle:

  • Same origin through the BFF (the storefront): the browser calls shop.example/api/v1/...; the BFF forwards to NestJS on the private network with x-bff-key (75.10). No CORS on the API at all; the API is not reachable from the internet.
  • Separate origin (the admin SPA calling api.shop.example directly): the API needs CORS for exactly https://admin.shop.example, credentials: true if cookies are used, exposedHeaders for X-Request-Id, Retry-After and X-App-Version (74.9), and a preflight cache (maxAge) to save a round trip per new URL.
  • CloudFront in front of the API: the API must read the client IP from X-Forwarded-For correctly (Express trust proxy set to the number of proxy hops), or rate limits apply to CloudFront's IPs instead of users (Part 40.35).
// apps/api/src/main.ts (excerpt): admin SPA on another origin
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import type { NestExpressApplication } from '@nestjs/platform-express';
import { AppModule } from './app.module';

const app = await NestFactory.create<NestExpressApplication>(AppModule);
app.set('trust proxy', 2);                                   // CloudFront + ALB: req.ip is the user's IP
app.enableCors({
  origin: ['https://admin.shop.example'],                    // exact origins, never '*' with credentials
  credentials: true,
  allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'Idempotency-Key', 'X-Client', 'X-Client-Version', 'traceparent'],
  exposedHeaders: ['X-Request-Id', 'Retry-After', 'X-App-Version'],
  maxAge: 600,                                               // browsers cache the preflight for 10 minutes
});
await app.listen(4000);

Production scenario

The storefront's CDN serves 94 % of requests (all hashed assets, ISR pages within s-maxage); the origin sees about 6 %. At a sale peak of 15,000 requests per second at the edge, the Next.js tasks handled 900 per second at p95 140 ms, with 24 tasks of 1 vCPU and 2 GB. The admin SPA's monthly CloudFront and S3 bill was 4.20 dollars. A brief evaluation of moving the storefront to a managed platform estimated a 6x higher hosting bill at their traffic, but also two engineer-weeks a quarter saved on preview environments and rollback tooling; the team stayed on ECS and built those features (78.11).

Failure scenario

A team hosted their SPA with S3 static website hosting and configured CloudFront's custom error responses to return /index.html with status 200 for every 403 and 404. After a deploy that removed old chunks, users with open tabs clicked "Orders"; the browser requested Orders-OLDHASH.js, received index.html with status 200 and Content-Type: text/html, and failed with SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'. Their error tracker grouped these as a JavaScript syntax error in a vendor file; nobody connected it to the deploy for two days. The fix: a CloudFront Function rewrite for extension-less paths only, so missing assets return a real 404 that the app's chunk-error handler recognises (78.4), plus keeping old assets (78.3).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Public S3 buckets for "simplicity"; use OAC and block public access.
  • Error-response mapping that turns missing JS into HTML, hiding chunk errors.
  • Trailing slashes and index.html in static exports: /docs/intro versus /docs/intro/ versus /docs/intro.html; set trailingSlash consistently and rewrite at the edge.
  • Lambda@Edge for tasks a CloudFront Function can do, adding latency and slow deploys.
  • SSR servers without a shared cache serving different ISR versions per task (73.11).
  • Managed platform limits: function timeouts, body size limits, and regions far from your API add latency to every server render.
  • API in a different region from the SSR servers: each server render pays 80-150 ms per API call (Part 46.14).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior chooses the least server that meets the requirement: static where possible, SSR where SEO, personalisation at first paint or the BFF demand it, and edge logic only for routing and headers. They price the options with real traffic and with engineer time, because a managed platform's bill buys features (previews, instant rollback, skew protection) that otherwise become a quarter of platform work. And they put the frontend's servers next to the API, because the slowest part of server rendering is almost always the network hop to the data.

Common mistakes

  • SSR for an internal SPA that has no SEO needs and 300 users.
  • Static export for pages that need per-user data at first paint, followed by loading spinners everywhere.
  • Serving the API cross-origin from the browser when a same-origin BFF already exists, adding CORS and preflights.
  • Forgetting trust proxy, so rate limiting and logs see the CDN's IPs.

Interview questions

  1. When would you host a frontend on S3 and CloudFront rather than a Node server? Expected answer: when the output is static (SPA, static export, docs): cheaper, simpler, overload-proof; not when you need SSR, ISR, Server Actions or middleware.
  2. How do you serve a client-routed SPA from S3 correctly? Expected answer: private bucket with OAC, and an edge rewrite of extension-less paths to index.html, so missing assets still return 404.
  3. What do managed platforms give you that you must build yourself on AWS? Expected answer: immutable deployments with URLs, preview per pull request, alias-based instant rollback, skew protection, integrated edge functions.
  4. What changes for the API when the SPA is on another origin? Expected answer: CORS with exact origins, credentials, exposed headers, preflight caching, and correct client IPs behind the CDN.
  5. Why put SSR servers in the same region and network as the API? Expected answer: each server render makes API calls; cross-region adds 80-150 ms per call to TTFB.

Practical exercise

Host the admin SPA and the storefront on AWS.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The admin SPA is served from a private S3 bucket through CloudFront with OAC; the bucket blocks public access.
  • /admin/orders/123 returns the SPA's HTML; /admin/assets/missing.js returns 404, not HTML.
  • The storefront runs from the standalone output on ECS behind CloudFront, with /_next/static/* served from S3 by a separate cache behaviour.
  • The API sees the user's IP in req.ip behind CloudFront and the ALB.
  • A one-page cost estimate compares this setup with a managed platform at 2.5 million page views a day.

78.2 Build once, deploy many: runtime configuration for frontends

Concept

Build once, deploy many means the pipeline builds one artefact per commit (a container image for the Next.js server, a dist/ folder for the SPA), tests that exact artefact, and promotes the same bytes through preview, staging and production. Nothing is rebuilt per environment. Whatever differs between environments (API base URL, Sentry environment, feature flag client key, analytics ID, allowed CSP origins) is supplied at runtime, not compiled in.

Part 70.6 introduced the problem from the tooling side: VITE_* and NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are inlined into the bundle at build time and are public, and a runtime config endpoint fixes the "frozen" problem. This section is about operating that pattern: what the artefact contains, where each value comes from in each hosting model, the Next.js traps that silently re-freeze runtime values, and how config changes are released and audited.

Why does it exist?

Because "it worked in staging" only means something if staging ran the same artefact. A team that runs next build three times, once per environment, has three different bundles: different chunk hashes, potentially different dependency resolutions if the lockfile moved, different inlined values. A bug that exists only in the production build cannot be reproduced in staging. Rebuilding also triples build time and makes rollback a rebuild of an old commit (slow, and not guaranteed to reproduce the same bytes). Part 47.3 made the same argument for backend artefacts; frontends add the inlining problem on top.

Mental model

Imagine a touring theatre production. The set, costumes and script are built once and travel in the same trucks to every city. What changes per city is a small card at the stage door: the venue's address, the local fire exit plan, the stage manager's phone number. If each city rebuilt the set from the drawings, no two performances would be the same show.

How it works

flowchart LR
    commit["Commit 3b9f412"] --> build["Build once: image web:3b9f412, assets uploaded"]
    build --> test["Unit, component, e2e on that image"]
    test --> prev["Preview: same image, preview config"]
    prev --> stg["Staging: same image, staging config"]
    stg --> prod["Production: same image digest, production config"]
    cfg["Config per environment: ECS task env, SSM, config.json"] --> prev
    cfg --> stg
    cfg --> prod

Where runtime values come from, by hosting model:

Hosting Server-only values Public values the browser needs Mechanism
Next.js server (container) process.env read at request time in server code Rendered by the root layout into a <script> or passed as props to a client provider ECS task definition env, SSM Parameter Store, Secrets Manager
Static SPA on S3 None (no server) /config.json per environment, fetched at boot Pipeline writes config.json per environment beside the immutable assets
SPA served by NestJS or nginx Server env Injected into index.html at start-up as window.__APP_CONFIG__ Template replacement at container start

The rules that make it work:

  1. Classify each value (70.6): public-by-design (analytics ID), environment-specific (API URL), or secret (never in the frontend). Only the first two reach the browser.
  2. One schema for the config, in code, validated at boot with zod. A missing or malformed value fails loudly at start, not as a blank screen for one user segment.
  3. Config is not cached like assets. config.json gets Cache-Control: no-cache (revalidate every time, cheap with an ETag), never the immutable header the hashed assets get.
  4. Next.js re-freezing trap: in the App Router, a page or layout that is statically rendered at build time evaluates process.env.X during next build, and the value is baked into the prerendered HTML. To read runtime values, the component must render dynamically: call noStore() from next/cache (Next.js 14), await connection() from next/server (Next.js 15), read headers()/cookies(), or set export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic' on that segment. The root layout that injects public config is usually dynamic anyway in a storefront with sessions.
  5. One release identity everywhere: the commit SHA is the image tag, the Next.js build ID (73.11), the deploymentId, the release sent to the error tracker (78.6), and the X-Client-Version header (74.9). When a browser error arrives, one string tells you which code and which source maps.

Practical example

The storefront's public runtime config has six values: apiBasePath (/api), sentryDsn, sentryEnvironment (preview, staging, production), flagsClientKey, analyticsId, and release. The server-only config has twelve, including API_INTERNAL_URL, BFF_KEY and the Redis URL for the cache handler. A preview environment for pull request 1842 runs the same image as production with sentryEnvironment=preview, a staging API, and the flag client key of the preview project.

React / Next.js example

The config schema and a server-side reader:

// apps/web/src/config/public-config.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const PublicConfigSchema = z.object({
  apiBasePath: z.string().startsWith('/'),
  sentryDsn: z.string().url().or(z.literal('')),           // empty disables reporting in local dev
  sentryEnvironment: z.enum(['local', 'preview', 'staging', 'production']),
  flagsClientKey: z.string().min(10),
  analyticsId: z.string().optional(),
  release: z.string().regex(/^web@[0-9a-f]{7,40}$|^web@local$/),
});
export type PublicConfig = z.infer<typeof PublicConfigSchema>;
// apps/web/src/config/server-config.ts
import 'server-only';                                       // importing this from a Client Component fails the build
import { PublicConfigSchema, type PublicConfig } from './public-config';

let cached: PublicConfig | null = null;
export function getPublicConfig(): PublicConfig {
  // Read at runtime from the container's environment, validated once per process
  cached ??= PublicConfigSchema.parse({
    apiBasePath: process.env.PUBLIC_API_BASE_PATH ?? '/api',
    sentryDsn: process.env.PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN ?? '',
    sentryEnvironment: process.env.PUBLIC_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT,
    flagsClientKey: process.env.PUBLIC_FLAGS_CLIENT_KEY,
    analyticsId: process.env.PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID,
    release: `web@${process.env.GIT_SHA ?? 'local'}`,
  });
  return cached;
}

Note the variable names: PUBLIC_*, not NEXT_PUBLIC_*. The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix tells Next.js to inline the value at build time, which is exactly what we are avoiding.

The root layout renders the values into a provider, dynamically:

// apps/web/app/layout.tsx  (Next.js 14; on 15 use `await connection()` from 'next/server')
import { unstable_noStore as noStore } from 'next/cache';
import { getPublicConfig } from '@/config/server-config';
import { PublicConfigProvider } from '@/config/PublicConfigProvider';   // 'use client' context provider

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  noStore();                                                // never prerender: config is read per request
  const config = getPublicConfig();
  return (
    <html lang="en-IN">
      <body>
        <PublicConfigProvider value={config}>{children}</PublicConfigProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

For the static admin SPA, the pipeline writes config.json per environment and the app loads it before rendering:

// apps/admin/src/main.tsx  (Vite 5 SPA)
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { PublicConfigSchema } from './config/public-config';
import { App } from './App';

async function boot() {
  const res = await fetch('/admin/config.json', { cache: 'no-cache' });  // revalidates; ETag makes it a 304
  const config = PublicConfigSchema.parse(await res.json());               // fail loudly on bad config
  createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(<App config={config} />);
}
boot().catch((e) => {
  document.getElementById('root')!.textContent = 'The admin app is misconfigured. Please contact the platform team.';
  console.error(e);
});

Backend side (NestJS)

The API takes part in the same discipline:

  • The API is configured the same way: one image, environment from ECS task definitions and SSM, validated at boot with ConfigModule.forRoot({ validate }) (77.11).
  • The API advertises the current web release (X-App-Version, 74.9) from configuration that the deploy pipeline updates when a new web release goes live, not from the API's own build.
  • Public config can come from the API for SPAs that have no server of their own (70.6's /api/public-config), with Cache-Control: no-cache and an ETag.
  • Config values that change behaviour are flags, not config. Turning on a new checkout belongs in the flag service (78.5), evaluated identically by the web and the API (74.9), not in a config file that needs a deploy.
// apps/api/src/config/public-config.controller.ts  (for the admin SPA when served without config.json)
import { Controller, Get, Header } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';

@Controller('public-config')
export class PublicConfigController {
  constructor(private readonly config: ConfigService) {}

  @Get()
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'no-cache')                       // revalidate every time; Express adds a weak ETag
  get() {
    return {
      apiBasePath: '/v1',
      sentryEnvironment: this.config.getOrThrow<string>('SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT'),
      sentryDsn: this.config.get<string>('ADMIN_SENTRY_DSN', ''),
      flagsClientKey: this.config.getOrThrow<string>('ADMIN_FLAGS_CLIENT_KEY'),
      release: this.config.getOrThrow<string>('ADMIN_RELEASE'),   // set by the admin deploy job
    };
  }
}

Production scenario

After moving to build once, deploy many, the storefront's pipeline went from three next build runs (4 min each) to one, and promotion from staging to production became a 40-second ECS service update with the same image digest. Over the next year the team had zero "works in staging, broken in production" incidents caused by build differences, compared with four the previous year (two from a lockfile change between builds, one from a NEXT_PUBLIC_ value typo in the production build only, one from a different Node version on the production build runner).

Failure scenario

A developer moved the Sentry environment from NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT to a runtime PUBLIC_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT read in app/layout.tsx, but the layout had no dynamic API call. next build prerendered the shell with process.env.PUBLIC_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT undefined in the CI build environment, the zod schema was not yet in place, and every environment reported errors as environment: undefined. Production errors mixed with preview errors for a week, and an alert keyed on environment:production never fired during a real incident. The fix: noStore() in the layout, schema validation that throws on a missing value, and a post-deploy smoke test that fetches the page and asserts the expected environment string in the rendered config.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • NEXT_PUBLIC_ on environment-specific values: frozen at build, and different per build if you rebuild.
  • Statically rendered layouts reading process.env: the value is from the build machine.
  • config.json cached with long max-age: a config fix takes a day to reach users.
  • Secrets in public config because "it is only the staging key".
  • Config schema drift: the pipeline writes a field the app no longer reads, or misses a new one; validate in the pipeline too, with the same schema.
  • Rollback with config: rolling back the image but not a config change that the old code cannot read; keep config backward compatible like an API (Part 25).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats the frontend artefact like any backend artefact: built once, identified by its commit, promoted unchanged, configured from outside, validated at start. They push every environment difference into a small, typed, validated config, and everything that changes behaviour for users into flags. They know the framework's traps (build-time inlining, static prerendering) and test for them in the post-deploy smoke test, because these bugs are silent: nothing crashes, the app just quietly uses the wrong value.

Common mistakes

  • Rebuilding per environment.
  • Using NEXT_PUBLIC_ for anything that differs between environments.
  • No validation, so a missing value becomes undefined deep in a component.
  • Putting feature switches in config files instead of the flag service.

Interview questions

  1. Why build a frontend once and promote it, rather than build per environment? Expected answer: the tested bytes are the deployed bytes; faster pipeline; reproducible rollbacks; no build-time drift.
  2. How do you give a Next.js app runtime public config? Expected answer: read non-NEXT_PUBLIC_ env vars in server code at request time, render them into a client provider from a dynamic layout, validate with a schema.
  3. Why might process.env.X in a Next.js layout still be frozen at build time? Expected answer: the layout was statically prerendered during next build; make it dynamic with noStore(), connection() or a dynamic API.
  4. How do you configure a static SPA per environment? Expected answer: config.json per environment beside immutable assets, served with no-cache, fetched and validated before render.

Practical exercise

Convert the storefront and the admin SPA to build once, deploy many.

Acceptance criteria:

  • One image per commit for the storefront and one dist/ per commit for the admin; no per-environment builds.
  • grep -r over the built output finds no environment-specific URL, key or environment name.
  • Public config is validated by one zod schema in the app and in the pipeline.
  • The same image digest runs in preview, staging and production, each reporting its own Sentry environment.
  • A post-deploy smoke test asserts the rendered environment name and release for each environment.

78.3 Cache busting and versioned assets

Concept

Cache busting is making sure browsers and CDNs fetch new files when the content changes, while caching unchanged files as long as possible. The modern approach is content-hashed file names: the bundler names each output file after a hash of its content (index-B7xQ2kLm.js, /_next/static/chunks/app/checkout/page-3f9c1a2b.js). A changed file gets a new name, so it can be cached forever with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The HTML that references those names has a stable URL and is cached briefly or revalidated on every request (76.9).

Part 76.9 covered which headers each resource class gets. This section covers how a deploy publishes a new version without breaking anyone: the order of uploads, asset retention, CDN invalidation, and how to check the result.

Why does it exist?

Because the two goals pull against each other. Long caching makes repeat visits fast and the CDN cheap: 94 % of the storefront's requests never reach an origin. But a long-cached file with a stable name (app.js) cannot be updated: users keep the old one for a year. Content hashes resolve the conflict for assets. HTML remains the one file that must change at a stable URL, and the deploy procedure is about getting HTML and assets to agree at every moment.

Mental model

Imagine a library that never changes a book once it is on the shelf. A new edition gets a new catalogue number and goes on the shelf beside the old one. Only the catalogue card at the front desk (the HTML) is updated to point to the new edition. Readers halfway through the old edition can finish it, because nobody took it off the shelf.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant CI as Pipeline
    participant S3 as S3Assets
    participant ORG as HtmlOrigin
    participant CF as CloudFront
    participant B as Browser
    CI->>S3: 1. upload new hashed assets, immutable, no deletes
    CI->>ORG: 2. deploy new HTML: new SPA index or new Next.js tasks
    CI->>CF: 3. invalidate HTML paths only
    B->>CF: GET /checkout
    CF-->>B: new HTML referencing page-3f9c1a2b.js
    B->>CF: GET page-3f9c1a2b.js
    CF->>S3: miss, fetch once
    CF-->>B: asset, cached for a year
    CI->>S3: 4. days later: lifecycle deletes assets older than 30 days
  1. Assets first. Upload the new build's hashed files before anything references them. If HTML went first, users would request files that do not exist yet.
  2. Never delete on deploy. Old assets stay, because old HTML in browsers, CDN caches and open tabs still references them (78.4). aws s3 sync --delete is the classic mistake.
  3. HTML second. For an SPA, upload index.html (and config.json) last, with Cache-Control: no-cache. For Next.js, rolling out the new tasks is the HTML switch: the new server renders HTML that references the new build's assets.
  4. Invalidate only what has a stable URL: /index.html, /admin/* HTML routes, ISR pages if needed. Never invalidate /* "to be safe": it costs money beyond the free tier (1,000 paths a month; a wildcard counts as one path, but every cached object is refetched), and it causes a thundering herd at the origin.
  5. Retention by lifecycle: an S3 lifecycle rule deletes objects under the assets prefix older than N days (30 is common), or a cleanup job keeps the last K builds' manifests and deletes files referenced by none of them.
  6. Hash scope: unhashed files in public/ (logo.svg, robots.txt) get short caching or must be imported through the bundler to get a hash (76.9).

Headers after a correct deploy, checked with curl:

$ curl -sI https://shop.example/_next/static/chunks/app/checkout/page-3f9c1a2b.js | grep -iE 'cache-control|x-cache|age'
cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
x-cache: Hit from cloudfront
age: 81234

$ curl -sI https://shop.example/checkout | grep -iE 'cache-control|x-cache'
cache-control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate
x-cache: Miss from cloudfront

$ curl -sI https://admin.shop.example/admin/index.html | grep -iE 'cache-control|etag'
cache-control: no-cache
etag: "9b2cf535f27731c974343645a3985328"

Practical example

The admin SPA's deploy:

  1. aws s3 sync dist/assets s3://shop-admin/admin/assets --cache-control 'public,max-age=31536000,immutable' (no --delete).
  2. aws s3 cp dist/index.html s3://shop-admin/admin/index.html --cache-control 'no-cache'.
  3. aws s3 cp config/production.json s3://shop-admin/admin/config.json --cache-control 'no-cache'.
  4. aws cloudfront create-invalidation --paths '/admin/index.html' '/admin/config.json' (often unnecessary with no-cache, but it removes any copy CloudFront cached under an older policy).

A lifecycle rule on the admin/assets/ prefix expires objects 30 days after creation. The bucket holds about 40 builds' worth of assets, 180 MB in total, costing a few cents a month.

React / Next.js example

Next.js names everything under /_next/static/ with content hashes (and a build ID directory for build manifests), and its server sends immutable for those paths. When CloudFront serves /_next/static/* from S3, the pipeline uploads the build's static folder before rolling out the new tasks:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/publish-web-assets.sh: run after the image is built, before the ECS rollout
set -euo pipefail
: "${GIT_SHA:?}" "${ASSET_BUCKET:?}"

# Extract .next/static from the built image so the uploaded files are exactly the image's files
cid=$(docker create "web:${GIT_SHA}")
docker cp "$cid:/app/apps/web/.next/static" ./static && docker rm "$cid"

aws s3 sync ./static "s3://${ASSET_BUCKET}/_next/static" \
  --cache-control 'public,max-age=31536000,immutable' \
  --no-progress                                 # never --delete: old tabs still need old chunks
echo "uploaded $(find ./static -type f | wc -l) files for ${GIT_SHA}"

Vite's equivalent check in the build: build.manifest: true writes .vite/manifest.json, listing every output file per entry. A cleanup job can keep the files referenced by the last 10 manifests and delete the rest, which is more precise than an age rule when releases are infrequent.

Backend side (NestJS)

The API's responses follow the same principle:

  • Versioned, hashed asset URLs from the API: product images uploaded to S3 get content-hashed keys (p/8f3a2c.webp), so the API can return URLs that the CDN caches as immutable; a re-upload produces a new URL (Part 33).
  • No long caching of anything with a stable URL unless there is a purge path: GET /v1/catalog/categories with s-maxage=60 and stale-while-revalidate, not a day.
  • Static files served by NestJS (ServeStaticModule from @nestjs/serve-static, for small internal tools) need explicit headers: immutable for hashed assets, no-cache for index.html. The defaults are neither.
// apps/api/src/app.module.ts (excerpt): an internal tool's SPA served by NestJS
import { ServeStaticModule } from '@nestjs/serve-static';
import { join } from 'node:path';

ServeStaticModule.forRoot({
  rootPath: join(__dirname, '..', 'ops-ui'),
  serveRoot: '/ops',
  serveStaticOptions: {
    setHeaders: (res, filePath) => {
      res.setHeader('Cache-Control', filePath.includes('/assets/')
        ? 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable'     // hashed by Vite
        : 'no-cache');                              // index.html and config.json
    },
  },
}),

Production scenario

The storefront deploys about 6 times a day. Each deploy uploads 30-60 new files (most chunks are unchanged and keep their hash, so the upload is incremental), about 2 MB. The /_next/static prefix holds roughly 30 days of builds: 9,000 files, 300 MB. CloudFront's hit ratio for hashed assets is 99.3 %; the first user after a deploy pays one origin fetch per new chunk per edge location. HTML invalidations are unnecessary for the SSR pages (they are private, no-cache) and limited to ISR paths that changed.

Failure scenario

A team's deploy script uploaded index.html first ("it's small") and then the assets. Uploads ran in parallel, and on a slow CI day the 400 asset files took 50 seconds. For those 50 seconds, users loading the admin received new HTML referencing chunks that did not exist yet, and got a blank page with 404s in the console. The error tracker showed 1,200 errors in under a minute, every deploy. Reversing the order (assets, then HTML) removed the window completely.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • aws s3 sync --delete on the assets prefix removes chunks open tabs still need.
  • HTML uploaded before assets, opening a window of broken pages.
  • Query-string busting (app.js?v=42): not content-based, and some caches ignore query strings (76.9).
  • Unhashed files with long caching: a changed logo.svg stays old for a year.
  • Invalidating /* on every deploy: cost, origin load spikes, and it masks wrong cache headers.
  • CDN caching error responses: CloudFront caches 404s for 10 seconds by default (configurable error caching minimum TTL); a request for a chunk just before it was uploaded can cache the 404.
  • Lifecycle rules too short for long-lived tabs (an operations dashboard open for a month).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior thinks of a deploy as adding files, never replacing them, with HTML as the single pointer that moves. They order the steps so every reference points to something that exists, keep old files long enough to cover the real tail of old tabs (measured by version telemetry, 74.9), and check the result with curl in the post-deploy smoke test rather than trusting the configuration. They also know that the same thinking applies to anything the API returns as a URL: content-addressed and immutable where possible, short-lived and purgeable where not.

Common mistakes

  • Deleting old assets on deploy.
  • Wrong upload order.
  • Global invalidations instead of correct headers.
  • Forgetting config.json and index.html need no-cache.

Interview questions

  1. Why can hashed assets be cached forever? Expected answer: the name changes when the content does; the old name always means the old content.
  2. In what order do you publish a frontend deploy, and why? Expected answer: assets first, HTML last, no deletes; every reference points to an existing file at every moment.
  3. How long do you keep old assets? Expected answer: long enough for the measured tail of old HTML and tabs (days to weeks), enforced by lifecycle rules or manifest-based cleanup.
  4. When do you need a CloudFront invalidation? Expected answer: for stable-URL resources cached at the edge (HTML with s-maxage, ISR pages, config) that must change now; not for hashed assets.

Practical exercise

Write the asset publish step for the storefront and the admin.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Assets are uploaded before HTML; no step deletes objects under an assets prefix.
  • curl -I in the post-deploy smoke test asserts immutable on a hashed asset and no-cache (or private, no-cache) on HTML and config.json.
  • A lifecycle or manifest-based cleanup keeps at least 30 days or the last 20 builds of assets.
  • An open tab from three deploys ago can still lazy-load a route chunk.

78.4 What happens to users on the old version during a deploy

Concept

Version skew is the period when a client runs code from one release and talks to servers, files or APIs from another. Part 73.11 named it for Next.js and Part 74.9 covered the API side (version headers, reload nudges, minimum versions). This section is the operations view: the four places old frontend code keeps living, the specific errors each produces after a deploy, and the handling that turns each error into a quiet reload instead of a broken page.

The four places:

  1. Open tabs. The JavaScript loaded at 09:00 is still running at 17:00. Lazy routes (70.5) are fetched only when the user clicks.
  2. Cached HTML. A CDN or browser copy of the old HTML references the old build's chunk names.
  3. The back/forward cache. Pressing Back restores a frozen snapshot of an old page, JavaScript and all (76.9).
  4. Service workers. A registered worker can keep serving an old app shell until a new worker installs and activates.

Why does it exist?

Because the browser, not the server, decides when code is replaced. The server can only offer new code; the tab picks it up on its next full page load, which may be hours away. The errors this causes are intermittent, affect only some users, cluster right after deploys, and look like random JavaScript errors in the error tracker unless you know their signatures.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant that changes its menu at noon. Diners seated at 11:50 still have the old menu in their hands. If the kitchen throws away every ingredient for old dishes at noon, those diners' orders fail. A good kitchen keeps cooking old dishes for a while, and a good waiter, seeing an old menu, offers the new one politely instead of letting the order fail.

How it works

The errors and their signatures:

What the old client does What fails Signature
Lazy-loads a route chunk deleted by the deploy Dynamic import Vite: TypeError: Failed to fetch dynamically imported module; webpack/Next.js: ChunkLoadError: Loading chunk 482 failed
Lazy-loads a chunk and gets HTML (bad SPA fallback, 78.1) Script parse SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'
Navigates client-side in the App Router after the server changed RSC payload from a different build Hard navigation fallback, or errors about missing client references
Posts to a Server Action removed or renamed by the new build Action lookup Failed to find Server Action "...". This request might be from an older or newer deployment. (73.11)
Calls the API with an old request shape Contract skew 400 VALIDATION_FAILED, CLIENT_OUTDATED (74.9)
A service worker serves the old shell Everything above, for days A user reports "still the old design" after a reload

The handling, layer by layer:

  1. Keep old assets (78.3). This alone removes most chunk errors.
  2. Catch chunk errors and reload once. Vite (11.4+) dispatches a vite:preloadError event on window when a dynamic import's preload fails; webpack-based apps catch ChunkLoadError in an error boundary (71.11). Either way: save any form draft (72.10), reload the page so the browser fetches the new HTML, and guard with sessionStorage so a genuinely broken deploy cannot cause a reload loop.
  3. Route old clients to old servers where the platform supports it. Next.js's deploymentId option tags asset requests with ?dpl=<id> and RSC and action requests with an x-deployment-id header; Vercel's Skew Protection uses this to route an old client to the old deployment for a configurable window. Self-hosted, the cheap version is: keep old assets, and treat a Server Action skew error as "reload".
  4. Nudge long-lived tabs to reload at a safe moment (74.9's X-App-Version check): switch client-side navigations to full page loads once a newer version is known.
  5. Update service workers deliberately: detect a waiting worker, ask the user, activate on consent, reload on controllerchange. Keep a kill switch.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Installing: register sw.js
    Installing --> Waiting: install event done, old worker still controls tabs
    Waiting --> Activating: all tabs closed, or skipWaiting on user consent
    Activating --> Active: activate event, clients.claim
    Active --> Redundant: replaced by a newer worker or unregistered
    Redundant --> [*]

A new worker waits until no tab is controlled by the old one. That is a safety feature: activating immediately (skipWaiting() on install) can leave a running page with old JavaScript fetching through a new worker's caches, which is version skew inside one tab.

Practical example

The storefront deploys at 14:00. At 14:10, 18 % of active sessions are still on the 11:00 build (from version telemetry). Over the next hour those users generate: 0 chunk errors (assets retained), 37 Server Action skew errors (a renamed action for "save address"), each turned into a reload with the address draft restored from sessionStorage, and 2 CLIENT_OUTDATED responses from an API endpoint whose old shape was removed too early. By 16:00, under 2 % of sessions are on the old build.

React / Next.js example

The admin SPA's chunk-error handler (Vite 5):

// apps/admin/src/boot/chunk-reload.ts
const KEY = 'chunk-reload-at';

export function installChunkReload(saveDrafts: () => void): void {
  window.addEventListener('vite:preloadError', (event) => {
    const last = Number(sessionStorage.getItem(KEY) ?? 0);
    if (Date.now() - last < 30_000) return;      // reloaded in the last 30 s: let the error surface, avoid a loop
    event.preventDefault();                       // stop Vite from throwing the error to the app
    sessionStorage.setItem(KEY, String(Date.now()));
    saveDrafts();                                 // form drafts to sessionStorage (78.10)
    window.location.reload();                     // fetch the new index.html and its new chunks
  });
}

The storefront's equivalent lives in the App Router's error boundary for a segment, plus the API client's handling of the action skew error:

// apps/web/app/(shop)/error.tsx  (Next.js 14 App Router segment error boundary)
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { reportError } from '@/observability/report';

const isSkew = (e: Error) =>
  e.name === 'ChunkLoadError' || /Failed to find Server Action|Loading chunk \d+ failed/.test(e.message);

export default function ShopError({ error, reset }: { error: Error & { digest?: string }; reset: () => void }) {
  useEffect(() => {
    if (isSkew(error) && !sessionStorage.getItem('skew-reloaded')) {
      sessionStorage.setItem('skew-reloaded', '1');      // cleared on the next successful page load
      window.location.reload();                         // new HTML, new build: the user barely notices
      return;
    }
    reportError(error, { tags: { boundary: 'shop', digest: error.digest } });   // 84.6
  }, [error]);
  return (
    <div role="alert">
      <p>Something went wrong on this page.</p>
      <button type="button" onClick={reset}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  );
}

The service worker update flow, for the delivery-partner app that does use one (76.9):

// apps/partner/src/sw/register.ts
export async function registerServiceWorker(onUpdateReady: (activate: () => void) => void) {
  if (!('serviceWorker' in navigator)) return;
  const reg = await navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js', { updateViaCache: 'none' }); // always fetch sw.js fresh
  const offer = (worker: ServiceWorker) => onUpdateReady(() => worker.postMessage({ type: 'SKIP_WAITING' }));

  if (reg.waiting) offer(reg.waiting);                          // an update was already waiting
  reg.addEventListener('updatefound', () => {
    const next = reg.installing;
    next?.addEventListener('statechange', () => {
      if (next.state === 'installed' && navigator.serviceWorker.controller) offer(next);  // update, not first install
    });
  });
  let reloading = false;
  navigator.serviceWorker.addEventListener('controllerchange', () => {
    if (!reloading) { reloading = true; window.location.reload(); }   // the new worker took over: load new code
  });
  setInterval(() => reg.update(), 60 * 60_000);                 // long-lived tabs check hourly
}
// apps/partner/public/sw.js (excerpt): only activates when the page asks
self.addEventListener('message', (event) => {
  if (event.data?.type === 'SKIP_WAITING') self.skipWaiting();
});

The kill switch for a broken worker is a new sw.js at the same URL that removes itself:

// apps/partner/public/sw.js (emergency version)
self.addEventListener('install', () => self.skipWaiting());
self.addEventListener('activate', async () => {
  await self.registration.unregister();                        // no worker after this
  const clients = await self.clients.matchAll({ type: 'window' });
  clients.forEach((c) => c.navigate(c.url));                   // reload every tab from the network
});

Backend side (NestJS)

The API's part in surviving skew (74.9 has the full rollout rules):

  • Accept the previous web build's requests for at least the measured old-tab window; expand-and-contract every change (Part 25).
  • Return machine-readable skew signals: CLIENT_OUTDATED as a problem document, so the client reloads instead of showing an error.
  • Send Clear-Site-Data only as a last resort: Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "storage" on a response (for example the logout or a special /reset route) tells the browser to drop caches and storage for the origin, which also removes service worker registrations when "storage" is included. It is a blunt tool: it logs users out and deletes drafts.
  • Serve sw.js with Cache-Control: no-cache if NestJS or the BFF serves it, so the browser's update check sees new versions promptly.
// apps/api/src/common/client-outdated.exception.ts
import { HttpException, HttpStatus } from '@nestjs/common';

export class ClientOutdatedException extends HttpException {
  constructor(minVersion: string) {
    super({ code: 'CLIENT_OUTDATED', status: 426, title: 'Please reload to continue', issues: [], minVersion },
          HttpStatus.UPGRADE_REQUIRED);              // 426; the client treats CLIENT_OUTDATED as "reload now"
  }
}

Production scenario

Version telemetry for the storefront over a month: after a deploy, 25 % of sessions are on the previous build at +5 minutes, 9 % at +1 hour, 1.5 % at +24 hours, and a tail of 0.1 % at +7 days (kiosk tablets in partner clinics that are never reloaded). Assets are retained for 30 days, which covers everyone except devices nobody restarts; those get the CLIENT_OUTDATED reload when an API change finally requires it.

Failure scenario

The delivery-partner app's first service worker called self.skipWaiting() in install and clients.claim() in activate, so each new worker took over open tabs immediately. One release changed the shape of the cached offline route data. Riders with the app open during the deploy kept running the old JavaScript, now served route data by the new worker's caches in the new shape; the map screen crashed for 640 riders in the evening peak. Riders had to force-close the browser to recover. The team moved to the consent-based flow above, versioned cache names per release (routes-v42), and deleted old caches only in activate.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Reload loops when the new build itself is broken; always guard reloads with a time-based flag.
  • Lost input on automatic reload; save drafts first.
  • Chunk errors from ad blockers or flaky networks, not deploys; a single reload attempt handles both, but measure them separately by checking whether a newer version exists.
  • skipWaiting() on install, mixing versions in one page.
  • sw.js cached by the CDN with a long max-age; browsers cap the HTTP cache for service worker scripts at 24 hours, but use no-cache anyway.
  • bfcache restores an old page after a deploy; listen for pageshow with event.persisted and run the version check.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior designs every deploy for the users who will not reload: old files stay, the API stays compatible, skew errors are recognised by signature and turned into a single safe reload, and long-lived tabs are nudged at a safe moment. They measure the old-version tail per release and set retention and compatibility windows from data. They are cautious with service workers, because a worker is a cache you cannot purge from the server, and they always ship a kill switch before they ship the worker.

Common mistakes

  • Treating chunk errors as random bugs instead of deploy symptoms.
  • Automatic reloads without a loop guard or draft saving.
  • Immediate skipWaiting() in service workers.
  • No kill switch for a service worker.

Interview questions

  1. Why does a frontend deploy cause errors for users who did nothing wrong? Expected answer: old code in open tabs, cached HTML and service workers references deleted chunks, removed Server Actions or old API shapes.
  2. How do you handle ChunkLoadError or vite:preloadError? Expected answer: keep old assets; on the error, save drafts and reload once with a loop guard; report it tagged as skew.
  3. How do you update a service worker safely? Expected answer: let the new worker wait, offer a reload, skipWaiting on consent, reload on controllerchange; versioned caches; a kill-switch worker.
  4. What does Next.js's deploymentId do? Expected answer: tags asset, RSC and action requests with the deployment so a platform can route old clients to the old deployment or detect skew.

Practical exercise

Make the storefront and admin survive three deploys in a row with an open tab.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A tab opened on build N can navigate to every lazy route after builds N+1, N+2 and N+3 are deployed.
  • A removed Server Action triggers one reload with the form draft restored, and no reload loop when the new build is broken.
  • Chunk-skew errors are reported with a skew tag and excluded from the error-rate alert.
  • The partner app's worker updates only after consent, and the kill-switch worker removes it from every tab within one navigation.

78.5 Rollouts for frontends: canaries, feature flags, kill switches and rollback

Concept

A rollout is how a new version reaches users: all at once, or gradually with checks along the way. For frontends there are four tools, each with a different blast radius and speed:

  • Canary release: a small share of users (1-10 %) get the new build while the rest stay on the old one; metrics decide whether to continue.
  • Feature flag: the new behaviour ships dark inside the build and is switched on per user, segment or percentage, without a deploy (Part 47.8).
  • Kill switch: a flag whose only job is to turn a feature or a third-party integration off instantly when it misbehaves.
  • Rollback: return everyone to the previous build.

Why does it exist?

Because some frontend failures only appear with real users: a Safari version the test matrix lacks, a low-end Android phone, a payment provider's widget, a CSS change that breaks a locale with long words. A canary limits who sees a bad build; a flag limits who sees a bad feature; a kill switch limits how long they see it; rollback is the last resort. And frontend rollback has a twist backend rollback does not: users who loaded the bad build keep running it after you roll back (78.4).

Mental model

Imagine opening a new kitchen layout in one branch of a restaurant chain before all of them (canary), adding a new dish to the menu but only offering it to regulars who ask (flag), keeping a big red button that pulls a dish off every menu at once (kill switch), and, if the new layout is a disaster, moving the cooks back to the old kitchen (rollback), knowing that the diners already served from the new kitchen still have their plates.

How it works

flowchart LR
    deploy["Deploy build N+1 as canary"] --> five["5 percent of sessions, sticky cookie"]
    five --> watch{"Error rate, Web Vitals, checkout success vs build N"}
    watch -->|"healthy for 30 min"| fifty["50 percent"]
    fifty --> watch2{"Healthy for 30 min?"}
    watch2 -->|"yes"| full["100 percent"]
    watch -->|"regression"| back["Route all to build N"]
    watch2 -->|"regression"| back
    full --> flags["Turn features on by flag, gradually"]

Canaries by hosting model:

  1. Next.js servers on ECS: run the new task set beside the old one and use ALB weighted target groups (for example 95/5). Enable target group stickiness so a session does not flip between versions on every request, which would create skew on every navigation. ECS blue/green deployments through CodeDeploy automate the shift and rollback on CloudWatch alarms.
  2. Static SPAs on CloudFront: CloudFront continuous deployment attaches a staging distribution to the production one and sends a percentage of traffic (up to 15 %) or requests with a specific header to it, with optional session stickiness. Alternatively a CloudFront Function assigns a sticky canary cookie and rewrites /index.html to /index-canary.html; because assets are content-hashed and retained, both versions' files coexist in one bucket.
  3. Managed platforms: rolling releases or traffic splitting between deployments are built-in features on some platforms.

Flags for frontends need two properties backend flags do not:

  • Evaluate on the server when the flag changes what renders first. A client-side flag evaluated after hydration produces a flicker (old UI, then new) and layout shift (76.5). In Next.js, evaluate in the server component or middleware and pass the result down; bootstrap the client SDK with the server's values.
  • Same answer in web and API (74.9): one flag service, one bucketing key (the user ID), and an API that accepts both the old and the new request shape while the flag is partial.

Kill switches default to "feature on" only when the flag service answers; if the flag service is down, the SDK uses the last known value or a safe default. Third-party widgets (chat, reviews, a new payment method) each get one.

Rollback by hosting model, assuming assets are retained:

Hosting Rollback action Time
SPA on S3 Copy the previous build's index.html (kept in an archive prefix) over the live one; invalidate it 10-30 s
Next.js on ECS Update the service to the previous task definition (same image digest as before) 2-5 min (task start, health checks, drain)
ECS blue/green with CodeDeploy Reroute the listener back to the blue target group Under 1 min
Managed platform Point the production alias at the previous deployment Seconds

Rollback does not reach tabs already running the bad build. For those, the options are the X-App-Version nudge (74.9), a kill switch for the broken feature, or, for a severe bug, a minimum version enforced by the API with CLIENT_OUTDATED.

Choosing the tool:

Situation Use
Risky new feature (new checkout) Flag, ramped by percentage with metrics per variant
Framework or dependency upgrade (React, Next.js major) Canary of the whole build
Third-party script or widget Kill switch
Bad deploy found after full rollout Rollback, plus nudge or kill switch for open tabs
Bug in a flagged feature Turn the flag off; no deploy

Practical example

The storefront upgrades from Next.js 14 to 15. The build goes out as a canary at 5 % on ECS with ALB weights and stickiness. After 30 minutes the canary's p75 INP is 12 % worse on Android (a hydration change in a product carousel); the error rate and checkout success are unchanged. The team holds at 5 %, fixes the carousel, ships a new canary, and completes the rollout the next day. Separately, the new "Reorder" button (77.12) ships behind a flag, off; it is turned on for staff, then 10 %, 50 % and 100 % of customers over a week while the API watches the reorder endpoint's error rate and latency.

React / Next.js example

Server-side flag evaluation in a server component, with the result passed to the client so there is no flicker:

// apps/web/app/(shop)/orders/[id]/page.tsx
import { getFlags } from '@/flags/server';                 // wraps the flag provider's server SDK, cached per request
import { getSession } from '@/auth/session';
import { OrderView } from './OrderView';
import { getOrderForPage } from '@/server/orders';

export default async function OrderPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  const session = await getSession();
  const [order, flags] = await Promise.all([
    getOrderForPage(params.id),
    getFlags({ userId: session.userId, keys: ['reorder-button', 'kill-reviews-widget'] }),
  ]);
  return <OrderView order={order} showReorder={flags['reorder-button']} reviewsEnabled={!flags['kill-reviews-widget']} />;
}
// apps/web/src/flags/server.ts
import 'server-only';
import { cache } from 'react';
import { flagClient } from './client';                       // the provider's server SDK, initialised once per process

type FlagKey = 'reorder-button' | 'kill-reviews-widget' | 'new-checkout';
const SAFE_DEFAULTS: Record<FlagKey, boolean> = { 'reorder-button': false, 'kill-reviews-widget': false, 'new-checkout': false };

export const getFlags = cache(async ({ userId, keys }: { userId: string; keys: FlagKey[] }) => {
  const out = {} as Record<FlagKey, boolean>;
  await Promise.all(keys.map(async (k) => {
    try {
      out[k] = await flagClient.getBooleanValue(k, SAFE_DEFAULTS[k], { targetingKey: userId }); // OpenFeature-style call
    } catch {
      out[k] = SAFE_DEFAULTS[k];                              // flag service down: safe default, never block the page
    }
  }));
  return out;
});

The admin SPA's rollback, in the pipeline:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/rollback-admin.sh <previous_sha>: assets are retained, so only the HTML pointer moves
set -euo pipefail
PREV="${1:?previous sha}"
aws s3 cp "s3://shop-admin/releases/${PREV}/index.html" s3://shop-admin/admin/index.html --cache-control 'no-cache'
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id "$ADMIN_DIST_ID" --paths '/admin/index.html' >/dev/null
echo "admin rolled back to ${PREV}; open tabs on the bad build will be nudged by X-App-Version"

Backend side (NestJS)

  • Accept both shapes while a flag is partial: the API's DTO accepts the old and new request (deliveryWindow or deliverySlotId, 74.9) until the flag is at 100 % and old tabs are gone.
  • Evaluate the same flag with the same key when the API's behaviour depends on it, through the same provider.
  • Tag metrics with the client version and variant: error rate and latency per X-Client-Version and per flag variant show a bad canary or a bad flag variant without waiting for averages to move.
  • Enforce a minimum version only for severe cases, with CLIENT_OUTDATED (78.4).
// apps/api/src/common/client-metrics.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Histogram } from 'prom-client';
import { tap } from 'rxjs/operators';

const httpDuration = new Histogram({
  name: 'http_server_duration_seconds', help: 'API latency by route and client build',
  labelNames: ['route', 'status', 'client', 'client_version'],   // client_version: a handful of live builds, bounded
  buckets: [0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5],
});

@Injectable()
export class ClientMetricsInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) {
    const req = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest();
    const end = httpDuration.startTimer({ route: req.route?.path ?? 'unknown', client: req.header('x-client') ?? 'unknown',
      client_version: (req.header('x-client-version') ?? 'unknown').slice(0, 12) });
    return next.handle().pipe(tap({
      next: () => end({ status: ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse().statusCode }),
      error: (e) => end({ status: e?.status ?? 500 }),
    }));
  }
}

Client version labels are bounded only if the number of live builds is: map anything older than the last five builds to old before recording, or the label's cardinality grows with every deploy (Part 43.3).

Production scenario

The storefront runs about 30 flags at any time: 8 release flags for features being ramped, 6 kill switches for third parties, the rest experiments. Release flags have an owner and an expiry; a weekly job lists flags at 100 % for more than 14 days, and their removal is a normal ticket. Over a year, 11 incidents were mitigated by turning a flag off (median time to mitigate 4 minutes), 3 by canary aborts before reaching 10 % of users, and 2 needed a full rollback.

Failure scenario

A new product-review widget from a third party was loaded on every product page without a kill switch. On a Saturday evening the vendor's CDN slowed to 8-second responses. The widget's script was loaded synchronously in the head by a tag manager. LCP on product pages went from 2.1 s to 9 s, and conversion dropped by a third. Removing the script needed a deploy through a frozen weekend pipeline; it took 2 hours and 10 minutes. The postmortem added a kill switch for every third-party script, loaded them with async after the main content (76.7), and added a synthetic check on the vendor's script latency.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Canary without stickiness: a user alternates between versions on each request, causing skew errors on every navigation.
  • Canary metrics compared to the wrong baseline: compare canary and control in the same time window, not canary today versus last Tuesday.
  • Client-side flag evaluation causing flicker and layout shift.
  • Flags evaluated differently by web and API, so the UI sends a request the API rejects.
  • Kill switch that fails closed: if the flag service is unreachable, the switch should keep the last known state or a safe default, not break the page.
  • Rollback without retained assets: the previous HTML references files the bad deploy deleted.
  • Rolling back the web but not a dependent API change, or the reverse.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior separates deploy from release: the code goes out continuously, the behaviour goes out by flag, gradually, with metrics per variant. They canary builds whose risk is in the platform (framework upgrades, build config) and flag features whose risk is in the product. Every third party gets a kill switch before it gets a contract. And they remember that rollback is not time travel for a frontend: tabs keep the bad code, so the plan for a bad release always includes how those tabs are reached.

Common mistakes

  • Big-bang releases of risky features without a flag.
  • Flags without owners or expiry, turning into permanent configuration.
  • No stickiness in canaries.
  • Assuming rollback fixes open tabs.

Interview questions

  1. How do you canary a static SPA on CloudFront? Expected answer: CloudFront continuous deployment with weighted or header-based routing, or an edge function with a sticky cookie choosing between two index.html files, with retained hashed assets.
  2. Why evaluate frontend flags on the server? Expected answer: no flicker or layout shift, same value as the API, secrets and targeting rules stay server-side.
  3. What does a kill switch need to be useful? Expected answer: fast propagation, a safe behaviour when the flag service is down, one per risky dependency, tested regularly.
  4. How is frontend rollback different from backend rollback? Expected answer: open tabs keep running the bad build; you need nudges, kill switches or minimum versions as well as moving the pointer.
  5. Flag or canary for a Next.js major upgrade? Expected answer: canary; the risk is in the whole build, not one feature.

Practical exercise

Add canaries, flags and kill switches to the storefront.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A canary at 5 % with sticky sessions on ECS (or CloudFront continuous deployment for the admin), promoted by a script that compares canary and control error rate, p75 INP and checkout success in the same window.
  • Flags evaluated server-side and passed as props; no client flicker in a Playwright screenshot test.
  • Every third-party script behind a kill switch that keeps working when the flag service is unreachable.
  • A rollback runbook for each hosting model, rehearsed, with measured time to restore.

78.6 Error tracking with source maps

Concept

Error tracking collects exceptions from real users' browsers, enriches each with context (release, environment, URL, browser, the user's recent actions), groups identical errors into issues, and alerts when an issue is new or spikes. Sentry is the most widely used tool; Datadog RUM, Bugsnag, Rollbar and Honeybadger work on the same concepts. Part 70.7 explained source maps and showed a home-grown reporter with NestJS-side symbolication. This section covers operating a real error tracker for the storefront: what the SDK captures, how releases and source maps connect, how to keep noise and personal data out, and how to alert on what matters.

The core concepts, in Sentry's vocabulary (the others use similar terms):

  • DSN: the public URL the SDK sends events to. It identifies a project; it is not a secret (anyone can read it from the bundle), so ingestion is protected by allowed domains, rate limits and quotas, not by hiding it.
  • Event: one captured error or message, with a stack trace, tags, breadcrumbs and context.
  • Issue: a group of events with the same fingerprint (by default derived from the stack trace).
  • Release: the version of the code that produced the event (web@3b9f412), used to find source maps and to tell "new in this release" from "old problem".
  • Breadcrumbs: the trail before the error: clicks, navigations, fetch calls with status codes, console messages.
  • Debug ID: an identifier injected into both a minified file and its map, so the tracker matches them without relying on file names and URLs.

Why does it exist?

Because browser errors are invisible by default. A NestJS exception is in your logs; a TypeError in a customer's Safari tab is not anywhere you can see, unless something sends it to you. Without error tracking, frontend incidents are detected by support tickets, hours late, described as "the page is broken". With it, a new error in the checkout appears within a minute of the first user hitting it, with the release, the browser, the original source line and the API call that preceded it.

Mental model

Imagine every customer's device has a small black-box recorder. When something crashes, the recorder sends you the last 30 seconds of what happened, stamped with which version of the software was running. A clerk sorts thousands of reports into piles by cause, and rings you only when a new pile appears or an old pile suddenly grows.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant CI as Pipeline
    participant ST as Sentry
    participant B as Browser
    participant APP as AppCode
    CI->>CI: build with hidden source maps, inject debug IDs
    CI->>ST: upload maps for release web@3b9f412
    CI->>CI: delete .map files from the deploy artefact
    B->>APP: user clicks Apply coupon
    APP->>APP: TypeError thrown
    APP->>ST: event with release, debug IDs, breadcrumbs, minified stack
    ST->>ST: match maps by debug ID, symbolicate, fingerprint
    ST-->>CI: alert: new issue in release web@3b9f412
  1. Initialise early with dsn, release, environment and sampling. The SDK installs global handlers (window.onerror, unhandledrejection) and wraps timers and event listeners to capture errors with better stacks.
  2. React boundaries report explicitly: an error caught by an error boundary is "handled" and does not reach the global handler, so boundaries call captureException (71.11). In React 19, createRoot(el, { onCaughtError, onUncaughtError }) is one place to report every error.
  3. Next.js has three runtimes (browser, Node server, edge); @sentry/nextjs initialises each (a client config file, plus instrumentation.ts with register() loading server and edge configs) and wraps the build with withSentryConfig to upload source maps.
  4. Source maps: the build creates hidden maps (70.7), the Sentry CLI or bundler plugin injects debug IDs and uploads maps for the release, and the maps are deleted from what gets deployed.
  5. Filtering: ignoreErrors and denyUrls drop known noise (browser extensions, ResizeObserver loop warnings); beforeSend scrubs data and can drop or re-fingerprint events.
  6. Sampling and quotas: errors usually at 100 %, performance traces at 5-20 %, session replays on error only. Spike protection and per-project rate limits stop one bad release from consuming the month's quota.
  7. Alerts: on new issues in production, on issues regressing (resolved, then seen again in a newer release), and on error rate per release crossing a threshold.

SDK versions differ in visible ways: in v7, integrations were classes (new Sentry.BrowserTracing()); in v8 they are functions (Sentry.browserTracingIntegration()), and the Node SDK moved onto OpenTelemetry under the hood. Copying v7 snippets into a v8 project fails at type-check.

Practical example

The storefront reports from browser, Node and edge runtimes into one Sentry project per app, with environments preview, staging, production. About 40,000 error events a day arrive from production, grouped into roughly 300 open issues; most are noise from extensions and old browsers, filtered before ingestion. Alerts go to the web on-call channel for: any new issue with more than 20 users in an hour, any issue tagged checkout with more than 5 users, and a release whose error-session rate is twice the previous release's in its first hour.

React / Next.js example

Client initialisation, reading runtime config (78.2). Because environment and release come from the runtime provider rather than NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables, the client SDK is initialised by a small Client Component rendered at the top of the root layout:

// apps/web/src/observability/SentryInit.tsx  (@sentry/nextjs 8)
'use client';
import * as Sentry from '@sentry/nextjs';
import { usePublicConfig } from '@/config/PublicConfigProvider';

let started = false;
export function SentryInit() {
  const cfg = usePublicConfig();
  if (!started && typeof window !== 'undefined' && cfg.sentryDsn) {
    started = true;                                          // once per page load, during the first client render
    Sentry.init({
      dsn: cfg.sentryDsn,
      environment: cfg.sentryEnvironment,
      release: cfg.release,                                  // web@<sha>: matches uploaded maps and X-Client-Version
      tunnel: '/monitoring',                                 // same-origin route: fewer ad-blocker losses, simpler CSP
      sendDefaultPii: false,
      tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
      tracePropagationTargets: [/^\/api\//],                 // trace headers only on our own BFF calls (84.7)
      replaysSessionSampleRate: 0,
      replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 0.2,                         // replay a fifth of sessions that hit an error
      integrations: [Sentry.browserTracingIntegration(), Sentry.replayIntegration({ maskAllText: true, blockAllMedia: true })],
      ignoreErrors: ['ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications'],
      denyUrls: [/^chrome-extension:\/\//, /^moz-extension:\/\//],
      beforeSend(event, hint) {
        const err = hint.originalException as Error | undefined;
        if (err && /ChunkLoadError|Failed to fetch dynamically imported module|Failed to find Server Action/.test(`${err.name} ${err.message}`)) {
          event.fingerprint = ['version-skew'];              // one issue for all skew errors (84.4)
          event.tags = { ...event.tags, skew: 'true' };
        }
        if (event.request?.url) event.request.url = event.request.url.replace(/([?&](token|code|email)=)[^&]+/g, '$1[redacted]');
        return event;
      },
    });
  }
  return null;
}

The tradeoff: errors thrown before hydration are not captured. If that matters, keep the DSN (public and the same for every environment) in the build-time client config file the Sentry wizard creates, and set only environment and release from the runtime provider with Sentry.getCurrentScope().setTag(...) and the event's release in beforeSend.

The reporting helper the error boundaries use, so every report carries the same tags:

// apps/web/src/observability/report.ts
import * as Sentry from '@sentry/nextjs';
import { ApiError } from '@/api/errors';

export function reportError(error: unknown, opts: { tags?: Record<string, string>; feature?: string } = {}) {
  Sentry.withScope((scope) => {
    if (opts.feature) scope.setTag('feature', opts.feature);       // checkout, orders, account
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(opts.tags ?? {})) scope.setTag(k, v);
    if (error instanceof ApiError) {
      scope.setTag('api.code', error.code);
      scope.setTag('api.status', String(error.status));
      if (error.requestId) scope.setTag('request_id', error.requestId);   // jump to the API log line (84.7)
      if (error.status < 500) scope.setLevel('warning');                  // 4xx are expected outcomes, not crashes
    }
    Sentry.captureException(error);
  });
}

Source maps for the Vite admin SPA, with the Sentry CLI and debug IDs:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ci/admin-sourcemaps.sh: after `vite build --sourcemap hidden`, before uploading dist/ to S3
set -euo pipefail
RELEASE="admin@${GITHUB_SHA}"
npx @sentry/cli sourcemaps inject apps/admin/dist                       # writes debug IDs into .js and .map
npx @sentry/cli sourcemaps upload --release "$RELEASE" apps/admin/dist  # needs SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN, SENTRY_ORG, SENTRY_PROJECT
find apps/admin/dist -name '*.map' -delete                              # never publish maps (76.7)

For the Next.js storefront, withSentryConfig(nextConfig, { org, project, authToken: process.env.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN, widenClientFileUpload: true, tunnelRoute: '/monitoring' }) does the same during next build. Because the image is built once (78.2), the maps are uploaded once, under the release that every environment reports.

Backend side (NestJS)

Three backend responsibilities:

  • Request IDs and codes in every error response (74.6), so a browser event tagged request_id and api.code leads straight to the API's log line.
  • A tunnel for apps without their own server. The Next.js storefront's tunnelRoute runs in the BFF. The admin SPA has no server, so NestJS forwards its envelopes, after checking they are for the expected Sentry project, which stops the endpoint becoming an open relay.
  • Rate limits and body limits on the tunnel: a crash loop in one release can send thousands of events per second per user.
// apps/api/src/monitoring/sentry-tunnel.controller.ts
import { BadRequestException, Controller, HttpCode, Post, Req } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import type { Request } from 'express';

const ALLOWED = { host: 'o123456.ingest.sentry.io', projectIds: new Set(['4507001']) };   // the admin project only

@Controller('monitoring')
export class SentryTunnelController {
  @Post()
  @HttpCode(200)
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 60, ttl: 60_000 } })            // per client IP: a crash loop cannot flood us
  async forward(@Req() req: Request & { rawBody?: Buffer }) {   // NestFactory.create(AppModule, { rawBody: true })
    const envelope = req.rawBody?.toString('utf8') ?? '';
    if (envelope.length > 200_000) throw new BadRequestException('envelope too large');
    const header = JSON.parse(envelope.split('\n', 1)[0] ?? '{}') as { dsn?: string };
    const dsn = new URL(header.dsn ?? 'http://invalid');
    const projectId = dsn.pathname.replace('/', '');
    if (dsn.hostname !== ALLOWED.host || !ALLOWED.projectIds.has(projectId)) throw new BadRequestException('unknown dsn');
    await fetch(`https://${ALLOWED.host}/api/${projectId}/envelope/`, {
      method: 'POST', body: envelope, headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-sentry-envelope' },
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(3000),                         // never hold API workers on a slow vendor
    });
  }
}

The tunnel's route must accept the envelope's content type (text/plain or application/x-sentry-envelope) as a raw body; enable rawBody: true in NestFactory.create and keep the JSON body parser from rejecting it.

Production scenario

On a normal day the storefront's production project receives 40,000 events; inbound filters (extensions, legacy browsers, known noise) drop about 55 % before they count against the quota. After a deploy, the "release health" view shows crash-free sessions for the new release within 10 minutes: typically 99.85 %. Median time from the first user hitting a new checkout error to an alert in the on-call channel: 3 minutes. With debug IDs, 99 % of production stack frames symbolicate to original TypeScript lines.

Failure scenario

A team uploaded source maps in a separate job that rebuilt the app "with maps on". The rebuild produced different chunk hashes from the deployed build (a dependency had a floating version). For a month, every production stack trace showed minified frames, and an intermittent checkout crash went undiagnosed: the trace said n is not a function at index-Bx91.js:1:48213. The fix was build once (78.2): the same build produces the deployed files and the maps, debug IDs tie them together, and a CI check fails if the release has no uploaded maps before deploy.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Maps uploaded for a different build than the one deployed; build once and use debug IDs.
  • Maps served publicly by forgetting to delete them from the artefact.
  • Ad blockers drop requests to well-known tracker domains; a same-origin tunnel recovers many of them.
  • CSP blocks reporting: connect-src must allow the tunnel route or the ingest host (78.9).
  • PII in events: URLs with tokens, form values in breadcrumbs, user emails; scrub in beforeSend and server-side data scrubbing, mask replays.
  • Error storms: a render loop in one release sends events per animation frame; SDK rate limits, spike protection and the tunnel's throttle contain it.
  • 4xx as errors: reporting every 422 as an exception floods the tracker with expected outcomes; report them as warnings or breadcrumbs.
  • Cross-origin scripts report only Script error. without details unless served with CORS headers and loaded with crossorigin="anonymous".

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats the error tracker as a production system with inputs to control: one release identity, maps from the deployed build, noise filtered at the edge, personal data scrubbed by default, quotas protected from storms. They alert on change (new issues, regressions, per-release rates) rather than on totals, and they tag events with the feature and the API's code and request ID, so a browser error becomes a backend investigation in one click. They would rather have 30 well-grouped, owned issues than 3,000 ignored ones.

Common mistakes

  • No release on events, so nothing can be tied to a deploy.
  • Maps from a separate build.
  • Everything reported at error level, including expected 4xx.
  • No scrubbing, sending tokens and emails to a third party.
  • Alerting on raw event counts, which fire on noise and miss a small new checkout bug.

Interview questions

  1. Why is a Sentry DSN not a secret, and how is ingestion protected? Expected answer: it ships in the bundle; protection comes from allowed origins, rate limits, quotas and inbound filters.
  2. How do source maps reach the error tracker without being public? Expected answer: build with hidden maps, inject debug IDs, upload for the release, delete maps from the deploy artefact.
  3. Why do errors caught by React error boundaries need explicit reporting? Expected answer: boundaries handle them, so global handlers never see them; call captureException in the boundary (or use React 19 root callbacks).
  4. What would you alert on for frontend errors? Expected answer: new issues above a user threshold, regressions, error-session rate per release versus the previous release, checkout-tagged issues.
  5. How do you stop a tunnel endpoint becoming an open relay? Expected answer: check the envelope's DSN host and project ID against an allow-list, size limits, rate limits.

Practical exercise

Set up error tracking for the storefront and the admin SPA.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every event carries release, environment and, for API errors, api.code and request_id.
  • Production stack traces show original TypeScript file and line for a deliberately thrown test error; no .map file is reachable on the CDN.
  • Version-skew errors group into one issue with a skew tag.
  • A URL containing ?token=abc appears as ?token=[redacted] in the event.
  • The admin's tunnel through NestJS rejects envelopes for any other DSN and is rate-limited.

78.7 Correlating a browser error with a backend trace

Concept

A distributed trace (Part 43.4) records one operation's journey across services as a tree of spans, linked by a shared trace ID that travels in a header. The W3C Trace Context standard defines that header: traceparent: 00-<32 hex trace id>-<16 hex parent span id>-<flags>. Part 43 traced requests from the API inward: NestJS, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka.
