This section extends the trace outward to the browser, so one trace starts with the user's click and ends with the database write, and a browser error report carries the same trace ID as the backend spans and logs.

Why does it exist?

Because the most frustrating frontend incidents are full-stack: "Apply coupon is slow for some users" or "Place order failed with no message". The browser sees a 9-second wait; the API's dashboards show p95 of 120 ms. Without correlation, the frontend team and the backend team look at different data and argue. With a shared trace ID, the browser event links to the exact backend trace, showing whether the 9 seconds were spent in the BFF, a cold Next.js task, a lock wait in PostgreSQL (Part 21), or before the request left the phone.

Mental model

Imagine a parcel with one tracking number from the moment the customer drops it at the counter. Every depot scans the same number. When the customer complains it took nine days, you type one number and see each depot and how long the parcel sat there, instead of asking each depot separately whether they remember a brown box.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant BFF as NextBFF
    participant API as NestJS
    participant PG as Postgres
    participant ST as ErrorTracker
    participant TR as TraceBackend
    B->>B: click Apply coupon, start span, trace id 4bf9
    B->>BFF: POST /api/v1/checkout/coupon, traceparent 00-4bf9...-01
    BFF->>API: POST /v1/checkout/coupon, traceparent continues 4bf9
    API->>PG: UPDATE carts ... span in trace 4bf9
    PG-->>API: lock wait 8.4 s
    API-->>BFF: 409 CART_CHANGED, X-Request-Id r-77
    BFF-->>B: 409 problem document
    B->>ST: event with trace_id 4bf9, request_id r-77
    API->>TR: spans for trace 4bf9
    BFF->>TR: spans for trace 4bf9
  1. The browser starts or joins a trace for a user action and sends traceparent on its API calls. Two common ways: the error tracker's tracing integration (Sentry's browserTracingIntegration sends sentry-trace and baggage headers to URLs matching tracePropagationTargets), or the OpenTelemetry web SDK (@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-web with the fetch instrumentation, configured with propagateTraceHeaderCorsUrls) sending W3C traceparent.
  2. The BFF continues the trace. Next.js has built-in OpenTelemetry spans for rendering and fetches; with an OpenTelemetry SDK registered in instrumentation.ts, incoming traceparent is extracted and outgoing fetch calls to NestJS carry it.
  3. NestJS continues it with the OpenTelemetry Node SDK and its HTTP, Express, pg and ioredis instrumentations (Part 43.4). Logs include trace_id and span_id (43.2).
  4. The error report carries the trace ID as a tag, so the error tracker links to the trace backend (Tempo, Jaeger, X-Ray, Datadog, or Sentry's own trace view if both ends use Sentry).
  5. Headers must be allowed: same-origin calls through the BFF need nothing; cross-origin calls need traceparent (and tracestate, or sentry-trace and baggage) in the API's CORS allowedHeaders, or the preflight fails and the request never happens.
  6. Sampling must agree: the sampled flag in traceparent tells downstream services the browser decided to sample this trace; the backend should respect the parent's decision (parent-based sampling) so a sampled browser trace is not cut off at the API.

Which header to use:

Backend tracing Browser side Header
Sentry SDK on BFF and NestJS Sentry browserTracingIntegration sentry-trace, baggage
OpenTelemetry on BFF and NestJS OpenTelemetry web SDK, or a small traceparent generator traceparent, tracestate
Mixed Choose W3C traceparent as the common language; configure each SDK to propagate it traceparent

Practical example

"Apply coupon is slow for some users." Sentry shows 140 events in an hour of a client-side timeout on POST /api/v1/checkout/coupon, all from users with large carts. Each event has a trace_id. Opening one in Tempo shows: browser span 9.2 s; BFF span 9.1 s; NestJS POST /v1/checkout/coupon 9.0 s; inside it, UPDATE carts waited 8.4 s on a row lock. Another span in the same second shows the cart-recalculation worker holding a transaction open across a call to the pricing service (Part 21, Part 31). One trace, one link, a diagnosis in five minutes instead of a two-team meeting.

React / Next.js example

The smallest vendor-neutral version: the API client creates a traceparent per user action, sends it on every request of that action, and attaches the trace ID to error reports. Sampling here is a simple 10 % decision per action; a full OpenTelemetry web SDK adds browser-side spans and timings on top of the same idea.

// apps/web/src/observability/trace.ts
const hex = (bytes: number) =>
  Array.from(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(bytes)), (b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join('');

export type TraceCtx = { traceId: string; traceparent: string; sampled: boolean };

export function newTrace(sampleRate = 0.1): TraceCtx {
  const traceId = hex(16);                                   // 32 hex chars, never all zeros in practice
  const sampled = Math.random() < sampleRate;
  return { traceId, sampled, traceparent: `00-${traceId}-${hex(8)}-${sampled ? '01' : '00'}` };
}
// apps/web/src/api/checkout.ts (excerpt): one trace per user action
import { newTrace } from '@/observability/trace';
import { reportError } from '@/observability/report';
import { apiFetch } from './client';                         // timeout, toApiError, schema parsing (80.6)
import { PricedCartSchema, type ApplyCoupon } from '@shop/contracts';

export async function applyCoupon(body: ApplyCoupon) {
  const trace = newTrace();
  try {
    return await apiFetch('/v1/checkout/coupon', PricedCartSchema, {
      method: 'POST', body, headers: { traceparent: trace.traceparent }, timeoutMs: 8000,
    });
  } catch (e) {
    reportError(e, { feature: 'checkout', tags: { trace_id: trace.traceId } });   // the link to the backend trace
    throw e;
  }
}

The BFF's server-side tracing, registered once:

// apps/web/instrumentation.ts  (Next.js 14: set experimental.instrumentationHook: true; stable in 15)
export async function register() {
  if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME === 'nodejs') {
    const { registerOTel } = await import('@vercel/otel');  // or a hand-built NodeSDK, as in Part 43.4
    registerOTel({ serviceName: 'shop-web-bff' });           // extracts incoming traceparent, propagates on fetch
  }
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The NestJS side is Part 43.4's setup plus three details that matter when the trace starts in a browser:

  • Parent-based sampling: ParentBasedSampler honours the browser's sampled flag, with a ratio sampler only for traces that arrive without a parent.
  • Treat incoming trace context as untrusted input: anyone can send traceparent. It must not change behaviour or authorisation; it only links telemetry. Some teams re-root traces at the edge for anonymous traffic to stop clients forcing 100 % sampling.
  • Expose the server's trace to the browser when useful: a Server-Timing header (Server-Timing: app;dur=118, traceparent;desc="00-4bf9...") lets RUM read server timing and the trace ID via PerformanceResourceTiming.serverTiming; cross-origin it also needs Timing-Allow-Origin.
// apps/api/src/tracing.ts  (loaded before the app: node -r ./dist/tracing.js dist/main.js)
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from '@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node';
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from '@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-http';
import { ParentBasedSampler, TraceIdRatioBasedSampler } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base';

new NodeSDK({
  serviceName: 'orders-api',
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter({ url: process.env.OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT + '/v1/traces' }),
  sampler: new ParentBasedSampler({ root: new TraceIdRatioBasedSampler(0.05) }),  // browser decides when it is the parent
  instrumentations: [getNodeAutoInstrumentations({ '@opentelemetry/instrumentation-fs': { enabled: false } })],
}).start();
// apps/api/src/common/server-timing.interceptor.ts
import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common';
import { trace } from '@opentelemetry/api';
import { tap } from 'rxjs/operators';

@Injectable()
export class ServerTimingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  intercept(ctx: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) {
    const started = performance.now();
    const res = ctx.switchToHttp().getResponse();
    return next.handle().pipe(tap({ finalize: () => {
      const span = trace.getActiveSpan()?.spanContext();
      const parts = [`app;dur=${(performance.now() - started).toFixed(1)}`];
      if (span) parts.push(`trace;desc="${span.traceId}"`);       // readable by RUM; no secrets in here
      if (!res.headersSent) res.setHeader('Server-Timing', parts.join(', '));
    } }));
  }
}

Production scenario

With browser-to-database traces at 10 % of user actions (100 % for checkout actions, which are fewer than 2 % of requests), the storefront stores about 3 million spans a day, roughly 40 dollars a month in the trace backend. In the following quarter, 9 of 14 frontend-reported performance incidents were diagnosed from a single linked trace; the median time from alert to root cause fell from 95 minutes to 22.

Failure scenario

The admin SPA called api.shop.example directly. A developer enabled the OpenTelemetry web SDK with propagateTraceHeaderCorsUrls: [/.*/]. The API's CORS configuration did not list traceparent in allowedHeaders. Every cross-origin request now carried a non-simple header, triggered a preflight, and the preflight was rejected: the admin app stopped loading data entirely. It had worked on the developer's machine because the local proxy made the calls same-origin. The fix: add traceparent and tracestate to allowedHeaders, restrict propagation to the API's exact origin, and add an e2e test against a cross-origin setup.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • CORS rejects trace headers on cross-origin calls; list them in allowedHeaders.
  • Propagating trace headers to third parties (payment providers, analytics) leaks internal IDs and can break their CORS; restrict propagation targets to your own origins.
  • Sampling mismatch: the browser samples, the API's root sampler drops the trace; use parent-based sampling.
  • Clients forcing sampling by sending the sampled flag on every request; cap or re-root at the edge.
  • Clock skew between the user's device and servers makes browser spans look like they start after their children; trace UIs handle it, but do not compute server latency from client timestamps.
  • Long-lived SSE connections (Part 79) as one span lasting an hour; trace individual events or reconnections instead.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior wants one identifier to follow a user action across every system it touches, and every report (error event, log line, trace, support ticket) to carry it. They choose W3C Trace Context as the common language, keep propagation to their own origins, honour the client's sampling decision within limits, and make sure the API's CORS and the BFF's forwarding never drop the header. They measure the value in incident minutes saved, which almost always pays for the spans stored.

Common mistakes

  • Two disconnected worlds: frontend errors in one tool, backend traces in another, no shared ID.
  • Trace headers sent to every origin.
  • Forgetting CORS allowedHeaders.
  • Root sampling in every service, so browser-started traces arrive incomplete.

Interview questions

  1. How do you connect a browser error to a backend trace? Expected answer: propagate W3C traceparent (or the vendor's headers) from the browser through the BFF to the API, and tag the error event with the trace ID.
  2. What breaks when you add traceparent to cross-origin requests? Expected answer: it is a non-simple header, so a preflight is required; the API must allow it in CORS.
  3. Why parent-based sampling? Expected answer: the first service's decision is honoured end to end, so sampled traces are complete.
  4. Is an incoming traceparent trustworthy? Expected answer: no; it is client input for telemetry only, never for logic; cap client-forced sampling.
  5. What is Server-Timing useful for here? Expected answer: exposing server duration and trace ID to RUM in the browser, readable via the Resource Timing API.

Practical exercise

Trace "Apply coupon" from click to database.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A deliberately slow coupon request (inject a 3-second pg_sleep in a test environment) produces one trace with browser or client, BFF, NestJS and PostgreSQL spans.
  • The resulting browser timeout event in the error tracker carries the same trace_id and the API's request_id.
  • Trace headers are sent only to the storefront's own /api/ routes and the API origin; a request to the payment provider carries none.
  • The admin SPA's cross-origin calls succeed with traceparent after the CORS change, verified by an e2e test.

78.8 Real-user monitoring and frontend SLOs

Concept

Real-user monitoring (RUM) measures what actual users experience in their browsers: page load timings and Core Web Vitals (Part 76), JavaScript errors, failed API calls as the browser saw them, and whether user journeys complete. Part 76.11 covered collecting Web Vitals with the web-vitals library and using them in performance budgets. This section turns RUM into frontend service level objectives (SLOs): targets for the user's experience, with error budgets and alerts, in the same discipline Part 49 applied to the backend (49.2 SLIs, 49.3 SLOs, 49.5 error budgets).

A frontend SLI (service level indicator) is a ratio of good events to all events, measured in the browser:

  • Page load availability: page loads that rendered the main content without a fatal error, out of all page loads.
  • Load performance: page loads with LCP at or under 2.5 s, out of all page loads with an LCP value.
  • Interaction responsiveness: page views with INP at or under 200 ms.
  • Journey success: checkout attempts (a click on "Place order") that reached the confirmation page or a definite, user-caused failure (declined card), out of all attempts.
  • Client-observed API success: browser API calls that got a non-5xx response within the timeout, including network failures and timeouts the server never saw.

Why does it exist?

Because the backend's SLOs can be green while users suffer. The API's availability counts requests that reached it. It cannot count the request that failed in a phone's flaky network, the checkout that broke because a JavaScript chunk failed to load, the 7-second LCP caused by a third-party font, or the button that did nothing because of an exception in a click handler. Frontend SLOs measure the product where the customer is, and their error budgets give the frontend team the same tool the backend team has for deciding between features and reliability work.

Mental model

Imagine a delivery company that measures on-time departures from its depots (backend SLOs) and also asks every customer whether the parcel arrived intact and on time (frontend SLOs). The depot numbers can be perfect while vans break down on the road. Only the doorstep number tells you what the customer got.

How it works

flowchart LR
    br["Browser: web-vitals, error handler, journey events"] --> beacon["sendBeacon /api/v1/rum/events on visibilitychange"]
    beacon --> ing["NestJS RUM ingest: validate, bucket, count"]
    ing --> prom["Counters: good and total per SLI, route group, device"]
    ing --> store["Raw events: ClickHouse or warehouse, sampled"]
    prom --> slo["SLO and burn-rate rules"]
    slo --> alert["Pager: fast burn"]
    slo --> ticket["Ticket: slow burn"]
    store --> dash["Dashboards by release, route, device, country"]
  1. Collect in the browser: Web Vitals via onLCP, onINP, onCLS (76.11); page load success when the main content's component mounts; fatal errors from the error boundary; journey events (checkout_attempt, checkout_confirmed, checkout_failed_user, checkout_failed_system); API call outcomes from the client's middleware.
  2. Send reliably: batch events and flush with navigator.sendBeacon on visibilitychange to hidden (not unload, which is unreliable and blocks the bfcache, 76.9).
  3. Validate and bucket on ingest: reject malformed or absurd values (LCP of 10 minutes), map URLs to route groups (/p/:slug, /checkout), device to classes (mobile, desktop), keep labels bounded.
  4. Count good and total events per SLI as counters. Percentiles (p75 LCP) are useful on dashboards; SLOs are cleaner as ratios ("90 % of loads have good LCP"), because ratios add up across time and instances and support error budgets.
  5. Define SLOs over a window (28 days) with an error budget: an SLO of 99.5 % for checkout page availability allows 0.5 % bad loads.
  6. Alert on burn rate (49.5): page when the budget is being spent fast (for example 14.4x the allowed rate over both 1 hour and 5 minutes), open a ticket on slow burns (for example 3x over 6 hours).
  7. Segment by release: every event carries the release (78.2), so a regression in one deploy shows as a step change for that release, and the canary comparison of 78.5 uses the same data.

The storefront's SLOs:

SLI Good event SLO (28 days) Owner
Checkout page availability Checkout step rendered without a fatal error 99.5 % Web team
Checkout journey success Attempt ends in confirmation or a user-caused failure 99.0 % Web and orders API
Product page LCP (mobile) LCP at or under 2.5 s 85 % Web team
INP (all pages, mobile) INP at or under 200 ms 85 % Web team
Client-observed API success Non-5xx within timeout, no network error 99.3 % Orders API, platform

Practical example

On a normal day the storefront records 2.5 million page loads and 41,000 checkout attempts. Checkout journey success runs at 99.6 %; the remaining 0.4 % are mostly payment-provider timeouts. The error budget for the 99.0 % SLO is 1 % of attempts, about 12,000 bad attempts in 28 days. A deploy that breaks the coupon step for Safari users (6 % of checkout traffic) would burn the budget at about 6x the allowed rate: a ticket, not a page, under a fast-burn threshold of 14.4x. That is why the checkout availability SLO is tighter and alerts faster, and why canaries (78.5) compare releases directly instead of waiting for SLO burn.

React / Next.js example

The journey events, sent through the same RUM queue as Web Vitals:

// apps/web/src/observability/rum.ts
import { onCLS, onINP, onLCP, type Metric } from 'web-vitals';   // v4

type RumEvent =
  | { t: 'vital'; name: 'LCP' | 'INP' | 'CLS'; value: number; rating: Metric['rating']; route: string }
  | { t: 'page'; ok: boolean; route: string }
  | { t: 'journey'; name: 'checkout_attempt' | 'checkout_confirmed' | 'checkout_failed_user' | 'checkout_failed_system'; code?: string }
  | { t: 'api'; route: string; outcome: 'ok' | 'http_5xx' | 'timeout' | 'network'; status?: number };

const queue: RumEvent[] = [];
let release = 'web@unknown';
let routeGroup = 'unknown';

export function initRum(opts: { release: string; routeGroup: string }) {
  release = opts.release;
  routeGroup = opts.routeGroup;                          // from the App Router segment, e.g. '/p/[slug]'
  const vital = (m: Metric) => queue.push({ t: 'vital', name: m.name as 'LCP' | 'INP' | 'CLS', value: m.value, rating: m.rating, route: routeGroup });
  onLCP(vital); onINP(vital); onCLS(vital);
  addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => { if (document.visibilityState === 'hidden') flush(); });
}

export const track = (e: RumEvent) => { queue.push(e); if (queue.length >= 20) flush(); };

function flush() {
  if (!queue.length) return;
  const body = JSON.stringify({ release, events: queue.splice(0, queue.length) });
  navigator.sendBeacon('/api/v1/rum/events', new Blob([body], { type: 'application/json' }));   // survives page hide
}

The checkout calls track({ t: 'journey', name: 'checkout_attempt' }) on submit, and one of the three outcome events when usePlaceOrder (71.8) returns. An "unknown outcome" counts as checkout_failed_system, because the user did not get an answer.

Backend side (NestJS)

The RUM ingest endpoint is a public, unauthenticated, high-volume write path. It must be cheap, defensive and bounded. It sits beside 76.11's POST /v1/rum/vitals (which keeps feeding the web_vitals_value histogram) and adds the SLI counters for availability, journeys and the LCP good/total ratio:

// apps/api/src/rum/rum-events.controller.ts  (next to 82.11's rum.controller.ts)
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { Counter } from 'prom-client';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';

const ROUTES = new Set(['/', '/p/[slug]', '/c/[slug]', '/cart', '/checkout', '/orders', '/orders/[id]']);
const Batch = z.object({
  release: z.string().max(60),
  events: z.array(z.object({ t: z.enum(['vital', 'page', 'journey', 'api']) }).passthrough()).max(50),
});

const sli = new Counter({ name: 'rum_sli_events_total', help: 'Frontend SLI events', labelNames: ['sli', 'route', 'good'] });

@Controller('v1/rum')
export class RumEventsController {
  @Post('events')
  @HttpCode(204)
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 30, ttl: 60_000 } })            // per IP; a beacon every few seconds at most
  ingest(@Body(new ZodValidationPipe(Batch)) batch: z.infer<typeof Batch>) {
    for (const e of batch.events as Record<string, unknown>[]) {
      const route = ROUTES.has(String(e.route)) ? String(e.route) : 'other';   // bounded label values
      if (e.t === 'vital' && e.name === 'LCP' && typeof e.value === 'number' && e.value < 120_000) {
        sli.inc({ sli: 'lcp', route, good: String(e.value <= 2500) });
      } else if (e.t === 'page') {
        sli.inc({ sli: 'page_availability', route, good: String(e.ok === true) });
      } else if (e.t === 'journey' && e.name !== 'checkout_attempt') {
        sli.inc({ sli: 'checkout_journey', route: '/checkout', good: String(e.name !== 'checkout_failed_system') });
      }
    }
    // Raw events go to a queue for the warehouse at a 10 % sample; the counters above are unsampled.
  }
}

The SLO and a fast-burn alert in Prometheus terms:

# prometheus/rules/frontend-slo.yaml
groups:
  - name: frontend-slo
    rules:
      - record: sli:checkout_journey:ratio_rate1h
        expr: sum(rate(rum_sli_events_total{sli="checkout_journey",good="true"}[1h]))
              / sum(rate(rum_sli_events_total{sli="checkout_journey"}[1h]))
      - record: sli:checkout_journey:ratio_rate5m
        expr: sum(rate(rum_sli_events_total{sli="checkout_journey",good="true"}[5m]))
              / sum(rate(rum_sli_events_total{sli="checkout_journey"}[5m]))
      - alert: CheckoutJourneyFastBurn
        expr: (1 - sli:checkout_journey:ratio_rate1h) > (14.4 * 0.01)
              and (1 - sli:checkout_journey:ratio_rate5m) > (14.4 * 0.01)
        labels: { severity: page, team: web }
        annotations: { summary: "Checkout journey SLO burning 14x budget; check the latest web release and orders API" }

The release is deliberately not a Prometheus label (it would add a series per deploy); per-release analysis uses the sampled raw events in the warehouse and the error tracker's release health.

Production scenario

Three months after introducing frontend SLOs, the storefront's error budget report showed: checkout availability 99.78 % (budget 44 % spent, mostly one bad deploy), journey success 99.41 % (budget 59 % spent, mostly a payment provider's degradation), mobile product LCP 87 % good (just above the 85 % target, after a hero image regression), INP 91 % good. The product manager used the LCP budget, close to exhausted, to schedule image work ahead of a new carousel feature, a decision that previously would have been an argument.

Failure scenario

The team's first availability SLI counted a page load as good if the HTML returned 200. A release broke hydration on the cart page for Chrome on Android: the server-rendered HTML looked right, but every button was dead because a client chunk threw during hydration. The SLI stayed at 99.9 % for six hours while cart-to-checkout conversion fell by 40 %. The SLI now requires a client-side "page ready" signal from the main content's component after hydration, plus no fatal error in the first 10 seconds.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Server-side definitions of good that miss client failures (hydration errors, dead buttons).
  • Beacons lost when sent on unload; use visibilitychange and sendBeacon.
  • Bots and synthetic traffic inflating good events; filter known bots and exclude your own monitoring.
  • Ad blockers blocking /rum endpoints with telltale names; same-origin, neutral paths help.
  • Unbounded labels (full URLs, release, user agent) exploding metric cardinality.
  • bfcache restores and soft navigations: client-side route changes produce no new LCP; measure route-change timings separately and do not count them as page loads.
  • Sampling bias: users on slow networks are the most likely to leave before the beacon; flush early as well as on hide.
  • SLOs nobody owns: an SLO without an owner and an action when the budget is spent is a chart.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior defines good events from the user's side of the screen, keeps the number of SLOs small (four or five that map to revenue and trust), and makes each one a ratio with a window, an owner and a policy for when the budget runs out. They connect frontend SLOs to backend ones without merging them: a payment provider's degradation burns the journey SLO and the API's dependency SLO at the same time, which is the point. And they segment by release, because the fastest frontend regression detector is comparing one build with the previous one.

Common mistakes

  • Using HTTP status as the only availability signal for a client-rendered app.
  • Percentile SLOs that cannot be added up or budgeted; prefer good/total ratios.
  • Alerting on every dip instead of on burn rate.
  • Too many SLOs, so none of them drives decisions.

Interview questions

  1. Why can backend SLOs be green while users suffer? Expected answer: they only see requests that arrived; client-side failures (network, chunk loads, hydration, script errors, third parties) are invisible to them.
  2. Define a frontend availability SLI. Expected answer: page loads where the main content rendered after hydration without a fatal error, over all page loads, measured in the browser.
  3. Why ratios rather than p75 for SLOs? Expected answer: ratios aggregate correctly over time and instances and map to error budgets and burn-rate alerts.
  4. How do you alert on a frontend SLO? Expected answer: multi-window burn-rate alerts on the good/total ratio; page on fast burn, ticket on slow burn.
  5. What must the RUM ingest endpoint defend against? Expected answer: volume, malformed or absurd values, label cardinality, abuse; validate, bound, throttle, sample raw events.

Practical exercise

Define and implement frontend SLOs for the storefront.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Four SLIs defined as good/total ratios measured in the browser, each with a 28-day SLO and an owner.
  • Page availability requires a post-hydration "ready" signal; a deliberately broken hydration in staging drops the SLI within 10 minutes.
  • The ingest endpoint validates with zod, bounds route labels to a fixed list and is throttled.
  • Burn-rate alerts exist for checkout availability and journey success, tested by replaying a synthetic failure.
  • A per-release dashboard shows each SLI for the current and previous release.

78.9 Frontend security headers at the edge

Concept

Security headers are HTTP response headers that tell the browser to enforce protections the page cannot enforce on its own: use HTTPS only, run only approved scripts, refuse to be framed, do not guess content types, send less referrer data, disable powerful features. Part 40.33 listed them for APIs, and Part 75.7 built a nonce-based Content Security Policy for the Next.js app. This section is about where these headers are set for frontends (CDN, Next.js middleware, origin), how to set them for a static SPA that has no server, how to roll out a CSP without breaking production, and how to keep the layers from contradicting each other.

The headers that matter for a storefront:

Header Typical value Protects against
Strict-Transport-Security max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload Downgrade to HTTP, cookie theft on first visit (with preload)
Content-Security-Policy Per app; nonce-based for SSR (75.7), hash or 'self'-based for static XSS impact, rogue scripts, data exfiltration
X-Content-Type-Options nosniff Browsers executing a non-script response as script
Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin Leaking full URLs (with tokens or order IDs) to third parties
Permissions-Policy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(self), payment=(self) Embedded or injected code using powerful features
frame-ancestors (CSP) or X-Frame-Options frame-ancestors 'none' / DENY Clickjacking (75.9)
Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin (or same-origin-allow-popups for payment popups) Cross-window attacks, enables process isolation
Reporting-Endpoints csp="/api/csp-reports" Where violation reports go (Reporting API)

Why does it exist?

Because the browser is the last line of defence and only does what it is told. A static SPA on S3 sends no security headers at all by default. A Next.js app sends some. If headers are set in three places (CloudFront, middleware, NestJS), they can contradict each other, and browsers apply the strictest CSP when more than one is present, which turns a harmless duplication into a production outage. Setting headers at the edge gives one place to see and change them for every response, including the static files no application code touches.

Mental model

Imagine a building's front door with a security desk. The desk hands every visitor the same badge rules (HTTPS only, no photography upstairs, escort required), whether they came for a meeting (dynamic page) or to pick up a parcel (static file). Some rooms need a special pass printed fresh for each visitor (a per-request CSP nonce), and only the room's own staff can print it.

How it works

flowchart LR
    br["Browser"] --> cf["CloudFront response headers policy: HSTS, nosniff, referrer, permissions, COOP"]
    cf --> s3["S3: SPA and hashed assets, CSP with hashes set by the policy"]
    cf --> next["Next.js middleware: per-request nonce CSP for HTML (81.7)"]
    next --> bff["BFF Route Handlers"]
    bff --> api["NestJS: helmet, CSP default-src none for JSON"]
    br --> rep["Reports to /api/csp-reports"]
    rep --> api
  1. Static, same-for-every-response headers (HSTS, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP) go in a CloudFront response headers policy attached to every cache behaviour. AWS provides a managed SecurityHeadersPolicy; a custom policy sets exact values. The policy's origin override setting decides whether CloudFront replaces a header the origin already sent.
  2. CSP for SSR HTML needs a fresh nonce per response, so it is set where the HTML is generated: Next.js middleware (75.7). The CloudFront policy must not override it.
  3. CSP for a static SPA cannot use nonces (the same index.html is served to everyone). Use script-src 'self' with no inline scripts, or 'sha256-...' hashes of the few inline scripts, set by the response headers policy for the HTML behaviour.
  4. Roll out in report-only mode first: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only with report-to csp (and the older report-uri for browsers without the Reporting API). Collect reports for one to two weeks, fix or allow-list legitimate sources, then switch to enforcing.
  5. HSTS preload is a one-way door: once shop.example is in browsers' built-in preload list, every subdomain must serve HTTPS, and removal takes months. Start with a short max-age, add includeSubDomains after auditing subdomains, and submit for preload last.
  6. Test headers in the post-deploy smoke test with curl -I against each behaviour (HTML, asset, API), so a CDN configuration change cannot silently drop them.

Practical example

The admin SPA on S3 gets all headers from one custom response headers policy, including an enforcing CSP: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: https://img.shop.example; connect-src 'self' https://api.shop.example; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; report-to csp. The storefront's HTML gets its CSP from middleware with a nonce; CloudFront adds the rest and is configured not to override CSP. NestJS responses carry helmet's defaults plus Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none', which is right for JSON that should never render as a page.

React / Next.js example

The response headers policy as infrastructure code (CloudFormation YAML, as used for the rest of the CDN):

# infra/cloudfront/admin-headers.yaml (excerpt)
AdminSecurityHeaders:
  Type: AWS::CloudFront::ResponseHeadersPolicy
  Properties:
    ResponseHeadersPolicyConfig:
      Name: admin-security-headers
      SecurityHeadersConfig:
        StrictTransportSecurity: { AccessControlMaxAgeSec: 63072000, IncludeSubdomains: true, Preload: true, Override: true }
        ContentTypeOptions: { Override: true }                                   # X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
        FrameOptions: { FrameOption: DENY, Override: true }
        ReferrerPolicy: { ReferrerPolicy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, Override: true }
        ContentSecurityPolicy:
          Override: true
          ContentSecurityPolicy: >-
            default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: https://img.shop.example;
            connect-src 'self' https://api.shop.example; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self';
            report-uri https://api.shop.example/csp-reports; report-to csp
      CustomHeadersConfig:
        Items:
          - { Header: Permissions-Policy, Value: "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()", Override: true }
          - { Header: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, Value: same-origin, Override: true }
          - { Header: Reporting-Endpoints, Value: 'csp="https://api.shop.example/csp-reports"', Override: true }

For the storefront, the middleware from 75.7 sets the nonce CSP; the CloudFront policy for the storefront's HTML behaviour omits ContentSecurityPolicy entirely so there is exactly one CSP header. A Playwright check (77.7) asserts it:

// apps/web/e2e/headers.spec.ts
import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

test('HTML responses carry exactly one CSP with a nonce, plus the edge headers', async ({ page }) => {
  const res = await page.goto('/checkout');
  const headers = await res!.allHeaders();                                // lower-cased; duplicates joined with ", "
  expect(headers['content-security-policy']).toMatch(/script-src 'self' 'nonce-[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{16,}' 'strict-dynamic'/);
  expect(headers['content-security-policy'].match(/default-src/g)).toHaveLength(1);   // not two merged policies
  expect(headers['strict-transport-security']).toContain('max-age=63072000');
  expect(headers['x-content-type-options']).toBe('nosniff');
});

Backend side (NestJS)

  • Headers for the API's own responses with helmet (Part 40.33): JSON responses get default-src 'none' and frame-ancestors 'none'; the API never serves HTML that needs a permissive policy.
  • The CSP report endpoint from 75.7, extended for operations: it must normalise both report formats: the older report-uri sends Content-Type: application/csp-report with one csp-report object; the Reporting API sends application/reports+json with an array. It must be throttled and size-limited, and it should drop reports from browser extensions (chrome-extension: source files), which are most of the noise.
  • Cookies depend on HTTPS: the __Host- and __Secure- cookies of 75.2 are only accepted over secure connections, so HSTS is a prerequisite for the auth design, not an extra.
// apps/api/src/security/csp-report.controller.ts  (81.7's controller, now normalising both formats and dropping noise)
import { Body, Controller, Header, HttpCode, Post } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { Logger } from '@nestjs/common';

type Legacy = { 'csp-report'?: { 'violated-directive'?: string; 'blocked-uri'?: string; 'document-uri'?: string; 'source-file'?: string } };
type Modern = { type: string; body?: { effectiveDirective?: string; blockedURL?: string; documentURL?: string; sourceFile?: string } }[];

@Controller('csp-reports')
export class CspReportController {
  private readonly log = new Logger('csp');

  @Post()
  @HttpCode(204)
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'no-store')
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 20, ttl: 60_000 } })
  receive(@Body() body: Legacy | Modern) {           // body parser configured for application/csp-report and reports+json, 16 KB limit
    const reports = Array.isArray(body)
      ? body.filter((r) => r.type === 'csp-violation').map((r) => r.body ?? {})
      : [{ effectiveDirective: body['csp-report']?.['violated-directive'], blockedURL: body['csp-report']?.['blocked-uri'],
           documentURL: body['csp-report']?.['document-uri'], sourceFile: body['csp-report']?.['source-file'] }];
    for (const r of reports) {
      if (r.sourceFile?.startsWith('chrome-extension:') || r.sourceFile?.startsWith('moz-extension:')) continue; // noise
      this.log.warn({ msg: 'csp_violation', directive: r.effectiveDirective, blocked: r.blockedURL, page: r.documentURL });
    }
  }
}

Production scenario

The storefront ran its CSP in report-only mode for 12 days and received about 180,000 reports. After dropping extension noise, 96 % came from two legitimate sources missing from the policy (the payment provider's fraud-detection script and a font CDN) and 4 % from a compromised browser extension injecting ads on 0.3 % of sessions. The team added the two sources, switched to enforcing, and the injected ads disappeared from those users' checkout pages. Enforcing reports now average 2,000 a day, mostly extensions, and a spike above 10,000 pages the web on-call, because it usually means a deploy added an inline script.

Failure scenario

A platform engineer attached AWS's managed security headers policy, which includes a Content-Security-Policy, to every behaviour of the storefront's distribution, with origin override on. CloudFront replaced the middleware's nonce-based CSP with a generic one that allowed no inline scripts and no nonces. Next.js's inline bootstrap scripts were blocked; the storefront rendered server HTML with no interactivity on every page. Because the error tracker's script was blocked too, the first signal was conversion dropping to near zero 14 minutes later. The rollback took 9 minutes (CloudFront propagation). The fix: a custom policy without CSP for the storefront's HTML behaviour, the header test above in the post-deploy smoke test, and CDN header changes treated as deploys with a canary.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two CSP headers from different layers: the browser enforces both, so the effective policy is the intersection.
  • Static SPA with inline scripts: no nonce is possible; remove inline scripts or use hashes, and remember a hash changes when the script does.
  • HSTS preload with an HTTP-only subdomain (an old marketing site): it becomes unreachable in every browser.
  • CSP blocking the error tracker or RUM: connect-src must include the tunnel or ingest origin (78.6, 78.8).
  • X-Frame-Options: DENY on a page legitimately embedded (a payment return page inside an iframe); use frame-ancestors with the exact allowed origin instead.
  • COOP same-origin breaking payment popups that need window.opener; use same-origin-allow-popups where the flow requires it.
  • Report floods: one bad page sends a report per violation per page view; throttle and sample.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior decides, for each header, the single layer that owns it: the CDN for headers that are the same on every response, the HTML generator for anything per-request, the API for its own JSON. They roll out CSP in report-only mode with a real report pipeline, treat CDN header changes as deploys with tests and canaries, and keep HSTS preload as a deliberate, audited step. They verify headers from the outside after every deploy, because configuration that is not tested is configuration that will drift.

Common mistakes

  • No headers on static hosting because "there is no server".
  • Managed policies applied blindly over application-set CSPs.
  • Enforcing CSP without a report-only phase.
  • HSTS preload before auditing subdomains.

Interview questions

  1. Where would you set security headers for a static SPA on S3? Expected answer: a CloudFront response headers policy, including a CSP based on 'self' and hashes, since S3 cannot add headers per response.
  2. Why can a CDN-level CSP break a Next.js app? Expected answer: it replaces or adds to the per-request nonce CSP; inline bootstrap scripts without the nonce are blocked; multiple CSPs intersect.
  3. How do you roll out CSP safely? Expected answer: report-only with a report endpoint, analyse and fix, then enforce, keep monitoring reports.
  4. What is the risk of HSTS preload? Expected answer: it is hard to undo, and every subdomain must support HTTPS.
  5. What headers should a JSON API send? Expected answer: nosniff, a restrictive CSP (default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'), HSTS, no caching of personal data; via helmet.

Practical exercise

Put security headers at the edge for the admin SPA and the storefront.

Acceptance criteria:

  • The admin SPA's responses carry HSTS, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP and an enforcing CSP from a CloudFront response headers policy; S3 sends none itself.
  • The storefront's HTML carries exactly one CSP, with a per-request nonce from middleware; a Playwright test fails if a second CSP appears.
  • CSP reports from both report formats reach NestJS, extension noise is dropped, and the endpoint is throttled.
  • The post-deploy smoke test checks headers on an HTML page, a hashed asset and an API response.

78.10 Incident story: a deploy that broke checkout only for users with a cached old bundle

This incident is a composite of several real ones. Every mechanism in it appears earlier in this volume; the incident is what happens when three small gaps line up.

What happened

On a Friday evening, about 11 % of checkout attempts failed with "We couldn't place your order. Please try again." for 85 minutes. Retrying did not help. Reloading the page did. New visitors were unaffected, so the team's own checks, run in fresh browsers, all passed.

18:05  Web release web@9c1e deploys: checkout sends deliverySlotId instead of deliveryWindow (behind no flag;
       the API had accepted both for 3 weeks, per 80.9's expand step).
18:06  Version dashboard (X-Client-Version at the API) shows 100 % of traffic on web@9c1e within a minute.
18:20  API release removes deliveryWindow support (the contract step), justified by the dashboard.
18:21  Users whose tabs loaded checkout before 18:05 (open tabs, home-screen web apps, bfcache restores)
       press "Place order". Old bundle sends deliveryWindow -> 400 VALIDATION_FAILED, issue path "deliverySlotId".
18:21  The old form has no deliverySlotId field. applyServerErrors maps nothing; the root error shows a generic message.
       The user retries: same 400, same message. Some reload and succeed; most give up.
18:40  RUM journey SLI (84.8) slow-burn ticket opens: checkout_failed_system at 2.3 %, 5x budget rate.
18:52  Support reports "order button broken" from 9 customers; on-call cannot reproduce in a fresh browser.
19:15  An engineer notices the error tracker issue "400 VALIDATION_FAILED deliverySlotId" is tagged
       release web@4d2a, the PREVIOUS release. The alert rule only watched the latest release.
19:28  Trace for one failure (84.7) shows the request body with deliveryWindow; the cause is clear.
19:40  API hotfix restores deliveryWindow (expand again); failures stop.
19:46  Incident closed. 1,930 failed attempts, about 640 customers, an estimated 4 % of the evening's checkout revenue.

Why it happened

Three gaps, each harmless alone:

  1. The version telemetry measured the wrong client. The browser sent X-Client-Version: web@4d2a. The BFF forwarded the request to NestJS and, in its shared fetch helper, set X-Client-Version to its own build ID, which became web@9c1e the moment the new BFF tasks took over. The API's dashboard therefore showed the BFF's version, not the bundle running in users' browsers. The old-bundle tail of 78.4 (25 % at 5 minutes, 9 % at 1 hour) was invisible.
  2. The contract step was gated by time and a dashboard, not by a contract test of deployed releases. The web pipeline ran Pact's record-deployment but not record-release (74.10), so the broker believed only web@9c1e was in use, and the API's verification of deployedOrReleased pacts passed.
  3. The client had no treatment for "your client is too old". A 400 VALIDATION_FAILED on a field the form does not have is, by definition, version skew. The error mapper (74.6) treated it as a generic failure; a CLIENT_OUTDATED signal (78.4) would have reloaded the page with the draft saved.

And one detection gap: the error-tracker alert rule filtered on the newest release, on the reasoning that old releases' errors are old news. After a deploy, the newest problems often live in the old release.

Detection, mitigation and what changed

The fastest signal existed: RUM's journey SLI moved within 20 minutes, but as a slow-burn ticket, because 11 % of checkout traffic at that hour burned the budget at 5x, under the 14.4x page threshold. Diagnosis was slow because the on-call reproduced in fresh browsers, which by construction ran the new bundle. The trace (78.7) and the release tag on the error event (78.6) together pointed at the cause in two minutes once someone looked at them.

The actions, each mapped to a section of this volume:

Action Prevents Section
BFF forwards the browser's X-Client-Version unchanged and sends its own as X-Bff-Version Wrong version telemetry 74.9
Contract steps require browser-version traffic below 0.1 % for 7 days, read from RUM, not the API Premature removal 74.9, 84.8
Web pipeline runs record-release per build and record-support-ended from telemetry Pact blind to old tabs 74.10
Client maps VALIDATION_FAILED with an unknown field path to the reload treatment, and the API sends CLIENT_OUTDATED for removed fields during a grace period Dead-end retries 74.6, 84.4
Error-tracker alerts on new issues in any release seen in the last 7 days Missed old-release errors 78.6
Checkout journey SLO gets a page-level alert at 3x burn during peak hours Slow detection 78.8
On-call runbook: "reproduce with an old build" using a pinned preview URL of the previous release Unreproducible bugs 78.11

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior reads this incident as one lesson: the frontend version that matters is the one running in the browser, and it is always older than you think. Every mechanism that decides compatibility (telemetry, contract tests, deploy gates, alerts, reproduction) must see browser versions, including old ones. They also notice that nothing here was exotic: an expand-and-contract migration done in the right order, a BFF helper with a sensible default, an alert rule that looked reasonable. Incidents at this level come from the gaps between correct parts, which is why the fix list touches the BFF, the API, the pipeline, the error tracker, RUM and the runbook.

Interview questions

  1. Why could the team not reproduce the bug? Expected answer: fresh browsers load the new bundle; the bug only existed in old bundles still running in tabs.
  2. What was wrong with the version dashboard? Expected answer: the BFF overwrote the browser's version header with its own, so the API saw the BFF's version.
  3. Which contract-testing step would have caught it? Expected answer: recording each web release in the broker so deployedOrReleased verification includes builds still open in tabs.
  4. How should a client react to a validation error on a field it does not have? Expected answer: treat it as version skew: save the draft and reload, ideally triggered by an explicit CLIENT_OUTDATED from the API.

Practical exercise

Run this incident as a game day (Part 49.12) on staging.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Open checkout in a browser on build N, deploy build N+1 with a renamed request field, then deploy an API that removes the old field.
  • Before the fixes, the old tab fails as described; after the fixes, the old tab reloads with its draft and the order succeeds.
  • The version dashboard shows the old browser build's traffic during the exercise.
  • The error tracker alerts on the old release's new issue within 5 minutes.

78.11 Worked example: a GitHub Actions pipeline with preview environments

This example assembles the Part into one pipeline for the storefront (Next.js 14 standalone on ECS behind CloudFront, assets on S3), reusing the test layers of Part 77 and the backend pipeline of Part 47.11.

Requirements

  • Build once: one image per commit, identified by its digest; the same image runs in preview, staging and production (78.2).
  • Preview per pull request at https://pr-<n>.preview.shop.example, ready within 10 minutes of a push, deleted when the pull request closes.
  • Tests at every gate: static and component tests before building; Playwright journeys, visual and accessibility checks against the preview (75.7-83.10); Pact gates before production (74.10).
  • Assets before HTML, never delete (78.3); maps uploaded privately (78.6).
  • Production by canary: 5 % for 20 minutes with automated comparison, then 100 % (78.5); rollback in under 5 minutes.
  • No long-lived cloud keys: GitHub's OIDC token assumes AWS roles per environment.
  • Bookkeeping: Sentry release deploys, Pact record-deployment and record-release, and the advertised web version (74.9) updated on production go-live.

The pipeline

flowchart LR
    pr["Pull request push"] --> verify["verify: tsc, lint, Vitest, Pact consumer"]
    verify --> build["build: image web:sha, push ECR, upload assets and maps"]
    build --> preview["preview: ECS service pr-n, host rule"]
    preview --> e2e["e2e on preview: Playwright, visual, axe"]
    e2e --> comment["comment preview URL and report on PR"]
    merge["Merge to main"] --> stg["staging: same digest, smoke"]
    stg --> gate["can-i-deploy production"]
    gate --> canary["production canary 5 percent, compare 20 min"]
    canary --> full["production 100 percent, record release"]
    close["PR closed"] --> teardown["delete preview service and rule"]

The pull-request workflow

# .github/workflows/web-pr.yml
name: web-pr
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ['apps/web/**', 'packages/**', 'pnpm-lock.yaml']
permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read, pull-requests: write }
concurrency: { group: web-pr-${{ github.event.number }}, cancel-in-progress: true }   # a new push cancels the old run
env:
  SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
  PREVIEW_HOST: pr-${{ github.event.number }}.preview.shop.example
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: pnpm }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm turbo run typecheck lint test --filter=web...        # unit, component, MSW (83.2-83.6)
      - run: pnpm --filter web test:pact && pnpm pact-broker publish apps/web/pacts --consumer-app-version "$SHA" --branch "${{ github.head_ref }}"
        env: { PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL: "${{ vars.PACT_BROKER_URL }}", PACT_BROKER_TOKEN: "${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }}" }

  build:
    needs: verify
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs: { digest: "${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}" }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with: { role-to-assume: "${{ vars.AWS_BUILD_ROLE }}", aws-region: ap-south-1 }   # OIDC, no stored keys
      - uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          file: apps/web/Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ${{ vars.ECR_REPO }}/web:${{ env.SHA }}
          build-args: GIT_SHA=${{ env.SHA }}
          secrets: sentry_auth_token=${{ secrets.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN }}   # maps uploaded inside the build, then deleted
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
      - run: GIT_SHA="$SHA" ASSET_BUCKET="${{ vars.ASSET_BUCKET }}" ci/publish-web-assets.sh   # 84.3: assets first, no deletes

  preview:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: { name: preview, url: "https://${{ env.PREVIEW_HOST }}" }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with: { role-to-assume: "${{ vars.AWS_PREVIEW_ROLE }}", aws-region: ap-south-1 }
      - run: ci/preview-up.sh "${{ github.event.number }}" "${{ vars.ECR_REPO }}/web@${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}"
      - run: ci/wait-healthy.sh "https://$PREVIEW_HOST/api/health" 300

  e2e:
    needs: preview
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.50.0-noble              # same image as the visual baselines (83.9)
    env:
      E2E_BASE_URL: https://${{ env.PREVIEW_HOST }}
      E2E_API_URL: ${{ vars.PREVIEW_API_URL }}                         # shared preview API with E2E support, synthetic data only
      E2E_SECRET: ${{ secrets.PREVIEW_E2E_SECRET }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm --filter web exec playwright test --project=chromium --project=visual
      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: playwright-report, path: apps/web/playwright-report, retention-days: 14 }

  comment:
    needs: [preview, e2e]
    if: always() && needs.preview.result == 'success'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: |
          gh pr comment ${{ github.event.number }} --repo ${{ github.repository }} --body \
          "Preview: https://${PREVIEW_HOST} (web@${SHA::7}). E2E: ${{ needs.e2e.result }}. Report: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}"
        env: { GH_TOKEN: "${{ github.token }}" }

What ci/preview-up.sh does, in four AWS CLI calls: register a task definition revision for web-preview with the image digest and the preview environment's configuration (78.2: PUBLIC_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT=preview, the preview API's internal URL, a preview BFF_KEY from Secrets Manager); create or update an ECS service web-pr-<n> with one Fargate task (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB); create a target group and an ALB listener rule matching Host: pr-<n>.preview.shop.example; and print the URL. A wildcard DNS record and certificate for *.preview.shop.example mean no DNS work per pull request. Previews run on Fargate Spot and cost about 0.6 dollars per pull request-day.

The teardown workflow runs on pull_request: types: [closed] and deletes the service, the listener rule and the target group. A nightly job deletes any preview service whose pull request is closed, in case a teardown failed.

Previews are behind the company's SSO at the ALB (an authenticate-oidc listener action) so unreleased features are not public, and they send X-Robots-Tag: noindex so search engines never index them.

The main-branch workflow

# .github/workflows/web-deploy.yml (jobs excerpt)
on: { push: { branches: [main], paths: ['apps/web/**', 'packages/**'] } }
concurrency: { group: web-deploy, cancel-in-progress: false }      # never cancel a production deploy halfway
jobs:
  staging:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with: { role-to-assume: "${{ vars.AWS_STAGING_ROLE }}", aws-region: ap-south-1 }
      - run: ci/ecs-deploy.sh web-staging "$(ci/digest-for.sh web "$GITHUB_SHA")"   # the PR build's digest: no rebuild
      - run: ci/smoke.sh https://staging.shop.example                            # headers, env name, release, health

  production:
    needs: staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production                                         # required reviewers and a deploy window
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm dlx @pact-foundation/pact-cli pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant web --version "$GITHUB_SHA" --to-environment production
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with: { role-to-assume: "${{ vars.AWS_PROD_ROLE }}", aws-region: ap-south-1 }
      - run: ci/ecs-canary.sh web-prod "$(ci/digest-for.sh web "$GITHUB_SHA")" --weight 5 --hold 20m   # sticky ALB weights
      - run: ci/compare-canary.sh --window 20m --max-error-ratio 1.5 --max-inp-regression 0.10 --min-checkout-success 0.99
      - run: ci/ecs-canary.sh web-prod --promote                     # 100 %, old task set drained, kept 1 hour for rollback
      - run: |
          npx @sentry/cli releases deploys "web@${GITHUB_SHA}" new -e production
          pnpm dlx @pact-foundation/pact-cli pact-broker record-deployment --pacticipant web --version "$GITHUB_SHA" --environment production
          pnpm dlx @pact-foundation/pact-cli pact-broker record-release --pacticipant web --version "$GITHUB_SHA" --environment production
          aws ssm put-parameter --name /shop/prod/latest-web-release --value "web@${GITHUB_SHA}" --overwrite   # X-App-Version (80.9)

ci/compare-canary.sh queries the RUM counters (78.8) and the error tracker's release stats for the canary and the control task sets in the same 20-minute window. If the canary's error-session rate is more than 1.5 times the control's, p75 INP is more than 10 % worse, or checkout journey success drops below 99 %, it exits non-zero; the next step never runs, and an if: failure() step sets the canary weight back to 0. The old task set stays registered for an hour after promotion, so a rollback is a listener-weight change (under a minute), not a new deployment.

Numbers

  • Pull request to preview URL: median 7 min 40 s (verify 2 min 10 s, build with cache 3 min 30 s, preview up and healthy 2 min).
  • E2E on preview: 26 journeys, 24 visual and 32 accessibility checks in 4 min 50 s.
  • Merge to production at 100 %: median 34 minutes, of which 20 are the canary hold.
  • Rollback during the canary: 40 s; after promotion, within the first hour: 55 s; later: a normal deploy of the previous digest, about 4 minutes.
  • Cost: about 14 runner-minutes per pull request push, 6 per production deploy, and about 90 dollars a month of preview Fargate Spot capacity for roughly 150 pull request-days.

Failure drills

Drill Expected behaviour
A pull request breaks a Pact interaction verify passes; the API's verification flags it; can-i-deploy blocks production
A canary raises INP by 25 % on Android compare-canary.sh fails; weight returns to 0; the release never reaches 100 %
A deploy step deletes old assets by mistake The asset-retention smoke check (a chunk from three builds ago returns 200) fails in staging
Preview teardown fails The nightly sweeper removes the orphaned service
A runner leaks the AWS role session It expires in one hour and can only deploy the preview environment
The error tracker is down during deploy The canary comparison falls back to RUM counters; the deploy can still be judged

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior builds the pipeline around one artefact and one question per stage: does the code compile and behave (verify), does it work as a whole (preview with e2e), does it keep every deployed consumer working (Pact gate), and do real users get a better or at least not worse experience (canary comparison)? They make previews cheap enough to be the default way of reviewing frontend changes, keep cloud access short-lived and scoped per environment, and treat the bookkeeping steps (release records, deployed versions, the advertised web version) as part of the deploy, because the next incident's diagnosis depends on them.

Practical exercise

Build this pipeline for the monorepo of Part 70.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Every pull request gets a preview URL within 10 minutes, behind SSO, with noindex, and it disappears within 10 minutes of closing.
  • The production image digest equals the preview and staging digest for the same commit.
  • Assets are published before HTML and never deleted by the pipeline; source maps never appear on the CDN.
  • A deliberately slowed canary (an artificial 300 ms main-thread task on button clicks) is rolled back automatically.
  • After a production deploy, the error tracker shows the deploy, Pact shows the version as deployed and released, and the API advertises the new web release.

Senior Checklist — Part 78

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can choose between S3 and CloudFront, a Node server for SSR, serverless adapters and a managed platform, with real cost numbers
  • I can serve a client-routed SPA from a private bucket without turning missing assets into HTML
  • I build one artefact per commit and configure it at runtime, and I know when Next.js freezes process.env into prerendered HTML
  • I publish assets before HTML, never delete on deploy, and keep old assets for the measured tail of old tabs
  • I can recognise version-skew errors by signature and turn them into one guarded reload with drafts saved
  • I can update and, if needed, kill a service worker safely
  • I can run canaries with sticky sessions, server-evaluated flags and kill switches, and I know rollback does not reach open tabs
  • I can set up error tracking with releases, debug IDs, private source maps, scrubbing and alerts on change
  • I can follow one trace from a browser click through the BFF and NestJS to PostgreSQL, with CORS and sampling right
  • I can define frontend SLIs as good/total ratios measured in the browser, with SLOs, error budgets and burn-rate alerts
  • I can place each security header in exactly one layer and roll out CSP through report-only
  • I can build a GitHub Actions pipeline with previews per pull request, OIDC to AWS, Pact gates and an automated canary

Part 78 — Key Takeaways

  • A frontend deploy never fully ends: old code keeps running in tabs, caches and service workers, so every deploy must work for them too.
  • Host with the least server that meets the requirement: static where you can, SSR where SEO, first-paint personalisation or a BFF need it.
  • Build once, promote the same bytes, and configure at runtime; NEXT_PUBLIC_ and static prerendering are how runtime values get frozen by accident.
  • Publish by adding files, never replacing them: assets first, HTML last, no deletes, retention measured against real old-tab tails.
  • Version-skew errors have signatures; recognise them and reload once, safely, instead of showing an error.
  • Separate deploy from release: canaries for platform risk, flags for product risk, kill switches for third parties.
  • Rollback moves the pointer, not the users; plan how open tabs on a bad build are reached.
  • Error tracking is only useful with one release identity, private source maps from the deployed build, scrubbing and alerts on change.
  • One trace ID from the click to the database turns a cross-team argument into a five-minute diagnosis.
  • Frontend SLOs must be measured on the user's side of the screen; backend SLOs cannot see client failures.
  • Each security header has one owning layer; a CDN that overrides an application's CSP can take the whole site down.
  • The browser version, not the server's, decides compatibility; telemetry, contract tests and alerts must see old builds.

Part 79 — Full-Stack Worked Project: Live Order Tracking

This Part builds one feature end to end, in the order a senior team would build it, and shows every decision along the way: a live order tracking page for the grocery storefront that has run through this whole volume. A customer places an order, opens shop.example/orders/<id>, and watches it move from "Paid" to "Packing" to "Out for delivery" to "Delivered", with an arrival window, a timeline, a delivery note they can edit, and a cancel button that works only while cancelling is still possible.

Nothing in this Part is new technology. Every mechanism was introduced earlier, and this Part cites where: the shared contracts package and error shape (Part 74), the BFF and its cookies (Parts 73 and 75), the query cache and the SSE merge rules (Part 72), Web Vitals budgets (Part 76), the test layers (Part 77), and the delivery pipeline (Part 78). On the backend it uses the transactional outbox (Part 30.10), optimistic concurrency (Part 21.5), Redis Streams and SSE (Parts 27 and 35). The point is to see them work together, and to see the places where they pull against each other.

Stack and versions, as in the rest of the volume: Next.js 14 App Router with notes for 15, React 18, TanStack Query v5, zod 3, NestJS 10 with TypeORM 0.3, PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7, Vitest 3, MSW 2, Playwright 1.5x, OpenTelemetry, and the AWS setup of Part 78 (ECS Fargate, ALB, CloudFront, S3).

79.1 Requirements and non-functional requirements

Concept

A requirement says what the feature does for the user. A non-functional requirement (NFR) says how well it must do it: how fast, how fresh, how available, at what scale, at what cost. For a live feature the NFRs decide the architecture more than the functional requirements do. "Show the order status" can be built with a page refresh; "show a status change within 2 seconds to 60,000 people watching at once" cannot.

Why does it exist?

Because without numbers, every design choice is an opinion. Polling or SSE? One stream per order or per customer? Cache the page at the CDN or not? Each question has a different answer at 500 viewers and at 60,000, at a 30-second freshness target and at a 2-second one. Writing the numbers down first is what lets a team argue about the design instead of about taste.

Mental model

Imagine commissioning a bridge. "It crosses the river" is the requirement. "It carries 40-tonne trucks, survives a 1-in-100-year flood, and costs under budget" are the NFRs, and they decide whether you build a footbridge or a suspension bridge.

How it works

Functional requirements, written as a product manager and an engineer would agree them:

  1. A signed-in customer can open the tracking page for their own order from the confirmation page, the order list (72.12), a push notification or an email link.
  2. The page shows: order number, items, total, delivery address, the current status in words, an arrival window ("Arriving 7:10 to 7:30 pm" in the store's time zone, 74.7), and a timeline of status changes with times.
  3. Status changes appear without a reload: Paid, Packing, Out for delivery, Delivered (or Cancelled).
  4. The customer can edit the delivery note ("Leave at the door, ring once") until the order is out for delivery. The change shows immediately.
  5. The customer can cancel while the order is Paid; once packing starts the button explains why it is gone.
  6. If live updates stop, the page says so honestly and keeps showing the last known status with its time (72.10, 72.11).
  7. Screen reader users hear status changes, but not every ETA tweak (69.9, 83.10).

Non-functional requirements, with the numbers that drive the design:

NFR Target Why this number
Orders per day 400,000; evening peak 18,000 per hour Current volume x 1.5 headroom
Concurrent tracking viewers at peak 60,000 (about 1 in 3 active orders has a tab open) RUM data from the old polling page
Status changes per order 5 on average (PAID, PACKING, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, plus ETA updates) Dispatch data
Events at peak about 120 per second, bursts to 600 when a dark store releases a batch of riders 18,000 orders/h x 5 / 3,600 x safety factor
Freshness p95 under 2 s from the database commit to the customer's screen; p99 under 5 s Customers stare at this page while waiting; support calls rise when it lags
Tracking page load TTFB p75 under 400 ms; LCP p75 under 2.0 s on mobile; INP p75 under 150 ms; CLS under 0.05 Volume budgets from 76.2, tighter LCP because the page is mostly text
Availability 99.9 % for reading tracking (page and stream combined), 28-day window One of the frontend SLOs of 78.8
Degradation API down: last known status stays visible; stream down: polling every 30 s within 10 s of detecting it 72.10 "honest stale data"
Security Customers see only their own orders; enumeration returns 404, not 403; delivery notes are personal data Part 40.12 IDOR, 40.31 data protection
Cost Under 0.02 cents per tracked order in compute and data transfer Finance's ceiling for the feature

What is out of scope, written down so nobody builds it by accident: a live rider map (the driver app and the WebSocket gateway of 35.13 own locations), chat with the rider, and native mobile apps (they consume the same API and events).

Practical example

Turning the NFRs into first estimates, before any code:

  • Connections: 60,000 concurrent SSE streams. A NestJS process holding idle SSE connections uses roughly 30-60 KB of memory per connection (socket buffers, the RxJS subscription, the Redis consumer bookkeeping). At 50 KB, 60,000 streams need about 3 GB of memory in total; spread over 6 tasks of 2 GB, that is 10,000 streams and 500 MB per task, comfortable.
  • Event fan-out: 120 events per second, each to exactly one customer stream. Fan-out is 1:1 per order, not broadcast, so the stream layer does about 120 writes per second at peak, trivial; the cost is the connections, not the events.
  • Page loads: 18,000 orders per hour, each tracking page opened about 4 times (notification, reopen, refresh): about 20 page loads per second at peak, each one server-rendered with one API call. Small.
  • Polling comparison: the old page polled every 10 s; at 60,000 viewers that was 6,000 requests per second, 95 % unchanged (the same numbers as 72.8's meal-kit story). SSE replaces it with 60,000 mostly idle connections and 120 events per second.
  • Bandwidth: an event is about 250 bytes on the wire with SSE framing; heartbeats every 20 s are 20 bytes. 60,000 x 20 bytes / 20 s = 60 KB/s of heartbeats. Negligible.

Backend side (NestJS)

The NFRs translate into backend commitments that shape every later section:

  • One source of truth for status: the orders row, changed only by conditional updates with a version (79.3), never by two services writing independently.
  • Events derived from committed state through an outbox (Part 30.10), so a status the customer sees always exists in the database, and no committed change is lost if Redis or the process dies.
  • Long-lived connections isolated from request/response traffic, so a reconnect storm cannot starve checkout (bulkheads, Part 31.6; deployment in 79.10).
  • Every endpoint bounded: rate limits, payload caps, timeouts and a connection cap per user (79.4).

Production scenario

The team that owned the polling page measured it for a week before starting: p50 freshness 5.1 s (half the poll interval plus processing), 6,000 requests per second at peak hitting the orders API, 31 % of the API's peak CPU spent on unchanged tracking responses, and 2,400 support contacts a week starting with "where is my order" while the page showed a stale status. Those four numbers became the success criteria: p95 freshness under 2 s, tracking API load down by 90 %, and "where is my order" contacts down by a third.

Failure scenario

A previous attempt, two years earlier, started from the code. A developer added a WebSocket gateway, one socket per order card, broadcast every status change to every connected client ("the client filters"), and shipped it on a Friday. At the evening peak, 40,000 connected clients each received every one of 120 events per second: 4.8 million messages per second, most of them discarded by the browser. The gateway pods ran out of CPU in nine minutes, the load balancer marked them unhealthy, every client reconnected at once, and the reconnect storm took down the orders API they shared. Nobody had written down "fan-out is 1:1 per order".

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Viewers per order greater than one: a customer with the page open on a phone and a laptop, plus a family member; plan for 1.3 streams per active order.
  • Batch releases: a dark store dispatching 200 orders at once produces a burst of 200 events in a second; the burst, not the average, sizes the relay.
  • Very long-lived tabs: a tab left open overnight after delivery must stop streaming (79.6).
  • Time zones: arrival windows are shown in the store's time zone, not the device's (74.7); a customer travelling still sees store time.
  • Orders from other channels (phone orders placed by support) must be trackable the same way.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior starts with a one-page brief: requirements, NFRs with numbers, out-of-scope items, and back-of-envelope estimates for connections, events, page loads and cost. They make freshness a measured SLO from day one, because a live feature that is sometimes 30 seconds late is worse than an honest refresh button. They notice the shape of the load (many idle connections, few events, 1:1 fan-out) and let it pick the transport. And they decide what the page does when each dependency fails before they decide how it looks when everything works.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing the transport first (WebSockets "because real-time") and the numbers later.
  • Averages instead of bursts for sizing.
  • No degradation requirement, so the first outage produces a blank page.
  • Forgetting authorization in the requirement: "my order", not "an order".

Interview questions

  1. What NFRs would you write for a live order tracking page? Expected answer: concurrent viewers, events per second at peak and in bursts, freshness percentiles, page load budgets, availability, degradation behaviour, security and cost. Follow-up: which of them decides SSE versus polling? (Freshness and viewer count together.)
  2. How do you estimate the cost of 60,000 SSE connections? Expected answer: memory per connection times count, spread across tasks; events per second are small because fan-out is 1:1.
  3. Why write out-of-scope items down? Expected answer: they stop scope creep and keep the design from being sized for features nobody asked for (a rider map needs a different transport and rate).

Practical exercise

Write the one-page brief for live tracking of your own product (a parcel, a ride, a food order).

Acceptance criteria:

  • Functional requirements as numbered user-visible behaviours, including what happens when live updates fail.
  • At least eight NFRs with numbers and a reason for each.
  • Back-of-envelope estimates for connections, events per second (average and burst), page loads per second and memory.
  • An out-of-scope list of at least three items.

79.2 API design and contract: REST, SSE and the shared types package

Concept

The feature needs four things from the API: read one order's tracking state, push changes to it, change the delivery note, and cancel. Following the volume's decisions, the reads and writes are REST endpoints (Part 15), the push is the per-customer SSE stream already used by the order list (72.8), and every shape lives in @shop/contracts as zod schemas (74.3), validated on both sides, with errors in the one problem-document shape (74.6) and the SSE payloads covered by Pact message contracts (74.10).

Why does it exist?

Because the contract is what lets three teams (web, orders API, dispatch) work in parallel. Once OrderTrackingSchema and the event schema are merged, the web team builds against MSW fixtures parsed through them (77.6), the API team builds the endpoints that must produce them, and Pact checks that what is deployed still matches. Without the contract first, the frontend waits for the backend, or guesses, and the guesses become production bugs.

Mental model

Imagine building a house where the plumber and the electrician work at the same time. They can, if the drawings show where every pipe and cable enters each room. The contract is the drawing. Change it, and both trades must see the change before they cut a hole in a wall.

How it works

Transport choice, from the browser's side (72.8) and the server's (35.1), applied to this feature's numbers:

Option Freshness Load at 60,000 viewers Complexity Verdict
Polling every 10 s p50 about 5 s 6,000 RPS, mostly unchanged Lowest Fails the 2 s freshness target
Polling every 2 s p50 about 1 s 30,000 RPS Low Meets freshness, fails cost
SSE, one stream per customer Sub-second 60,000 idle connections, 120 events/s Medium Chosen
WebSocket Sub-second Same connections Higher: own reconnection, upgrade support Not needed: the client sends nothing on this channel

The per-customer stream of 72.8 (GET /v1/orders/events) is reused rather than adding GET /v1/orders/:id/events, for three reasons: the order list and the tracking page share one connection per tab; a customer with two orders in flight needs one stream, not two (connections are the cost, 79.1); and the server-side replay already exists. The client filters by orderId, which is cheap because events are only for that customer.

Endpoints:

Method and path Purpose Notes
GET /v1/orders/:id/tracking Everything the page needs in one response private, no-cache with ETag; 404 for other customers' orders
GET /v1/orders/events Per-customer SSE stream (72.8) Event types order, reset, reauth, ping; replay from Last-Event-ID
PATCH /v1/orders/:id/delivery-note Change the note Idempotency-Key; expectedVersion; returns the new tracking state
POST /v1/orders/:id/cancel Cancel (72.12) Idempotency-Key; 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE once packing started

Through the BFF, the browser calls them as shop.example/api/v1/... (the rewrites proxy of 73.8), and the stream is routed by CloudFront straight to the API's realtime tasks (79.10), so no Next.js process buffers it.

New statuses, rolled out in the right order. The existing OrderStatusSchema (74.7) has PENDING, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED. Grocery delivery needs PACKING and OUT_FOR_DELIVERY (SHIPPED stays for parcel orders). A new response enum value is a change where the clients ship first (the table in 74.9): the web already reads statuses through openEnum (74.7), which maps unknown values to UNKNOWN and renders a generic "Updated" badge; mobile apps get a release with the new labels; only after version telemetry shows old mobile builds below the threshold does the API start emitting the new values.

Practical example — the contracts

// packages/contracts/src/orders.ts (additions)
import { z } from 'zod';
import { OrderSummarySchema } from './orders.summary';     // 80.11: id, displayId, status, totalMinor, currency, items,
