                                                           // placedAt, deliveryDate, deliveredAt, storeTimeZone, version, updatedAt
export const OrderStatusSchema = z.enum([
  'PENDING', 'PAID', 'PACKING', 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED',
]);                                                        // closed for writers; readers use openEnum (80.7)

const Instant = z.string().datetime({ offset: true });

export const EtaWindowSchema = z.object({ from: Instant, to: Instant })
  .refine((w) => Date.parse(w.from) <= Date.parse(w.to), 'from must not be after to');

export const TrackingStepSchema = z.object({ status: OrderStatusSchema, at: Instant });

export const OrderTrackingSchema = OrderSummarySchema.extend({
  status: OrderStatusSchema,
  etaWindow: EtaWindowSchema.nullable(),                   // null until dispatch has a window
  timeline: z.array(TrackingStepSchema).max(20),           // oldest first
  deliveryNote: z.string().max(200).nullable(),
  cancellable: z.boolean(),                                // computed by the server with canCancel() (83.2)
  noteEditable: z.boolean(),
});
export type OrderTracking = z.infer<typeof OrderTrackingSchema>;

export const UpdateDeliveryNoteSchema = z.object({
  note: z.string().trim().max(200).transform((s) => (s === '' ? null : s)),
  expectedVersion: z.number().int().nonnegative(),         // optimistic concurrency (Part 21.5)
});
export type UpdateDeliveryNote = z.infer<typeof UpdateDeliveryNoteSchema>;

The event schema of 72.8 grows by two optional fields. Adding optional fields to an event is backward compatible (Part 25.4): old clients' z.object parsers strip unknown keys, and the Pact message contract (74.10) keeps asserting the fields each consumer reads.

// packages/contracts/src/order-events.ts (78.8's schema, extended)
export const OrderEventSchema = z.object({
  orderId: z.string().uuid(),
  status: OrderStatusSchema,
  version: z.number().int().nonnegative(),                 // the orders.version column, as in OrderSummary
  updatedAt: z.string().datetime({ offset: true }),
  etaWindow: EtaWindowSchema.nullable().optional(),        // new: present when dispatch changed the window
  summary: z.string().max(160).optional(),                 // new: human text for the live region (83.10)
});
export type OrderEvent = z.infer<typeof OrderEventSchema>;

What the wire looks like for one status change on the stream:

id: 1730813127412-0
event: order
data: {"orderId":"1d6c0b6e-2f3a-4c55-9d1e-8a7b6c5d4e3f","status":"OUT_FOR_DELIVERY","version":7,
data:  "updatedAt":"2026-11-05T13:45:27.402Z","etaWindow":{"from":"2026-11-05T13:55:00Z","to":"2026-11-05T14:10:00Z"},
data:  "summary":"Out for delivery. Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm."}

(SSE allows a payload over several data: lines; the browser joins them with newlines before JSON.parse, which accepts the whitespace. In practice NestJS writes one line.) The id is the Redis Stream entry ID, which is what Last-Event-ID sends back on reconnect (72.8).

React / Next.js example

The web side reads the contract through the tolerant readers of 74.7, so a status this build does not know never crashes the page:

// apps/web/src/orders/tracking.read.ts
import { OrderTrackingSchema, OrderEventSchema, OrderStatusSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { openEnum } from '@/wire/decode';                       // 80.7: unknown values -> 'UNKNOWN', reported once

const status = openEnum(OrderStatusSchema, 'OrderStatus');

export const OrderTrackingRead = OrderTrackingSchema.extend({
  status,
  timeline: OrderTrackingSchema.shape.timeline.element.extend({ status }).array().max(20),
});
export const OrderEventRead = OrderEventSchema.extend({ status });
export type OrderTrackingView = ReturnType<typeof OrderTrackingRead.parse>;

The labels live in one place, with a fallback:

// apps/web/src/orders/status-copy.ts
import type { OrderTrackingView } from './tracking.read';

export const STATUS_COPY: Record<OrderTrackingView['status'], { label: string; step: number }> = {
  PENDING: { label: 'Waiting for payment', step: 0 },
  PAID: { label: 'Order confirmed', step: 1 },
  PACKING: { label: 'Packing your order', step: 2 },
  OUT_FOR_DELIVERY: { label: 'Out for delivery', step: 3 },
  SHIPPED: { label: 'Shipped', step: 3 },
  DELIVERED: { label: 'Delivered', step: 4 },
  CANCELLED: { label: 'Cancelled', step: -1 },
  UNKNOWN: { label: 'Updated', step: -1 },                     // a status this build has never heard of
};

Backend side (NestJS)

The API validates writes with the shared schemas through ZodValidationPipe (74.3), maps entities to the read shape in one mapper (so cancellable and noteEditable are computed in exactly one place), and documents everything in the OpenAPI spec generated from the same schemas (74.2):

// apps/api/src/orders/tracking.mapper.ts
import { canCancel, type OrderTracking } from '@shop/contracts';
import type { OrderEntity } from './order.entity';
import type { OrderStatusEventEntity } from './order-status-event.entity';
import { toOrderSummary } from './order-summary.mapper';         // 80.7: minor units, ISO instants, store time zone

const NOTE_EDITABLE = new Set(['PENDING', 'PAID', 'PACKING']);

export function toOrderTracking(order: OrderEntity, events: OrderStatusEventEntity[]): OrderTracking {
  return {
    ...toOrderSummary(order),
    etaWindow: order.etaFrom && order.etaTo ? { from: order.etaFrom.toISOString(), to: order.etaTo.toISOString() } : null,
    timeline: events.slice(-20).map((e) => ({ status: e.status, at: e.occurredAt.toISOString() })),
    deliveryNote: order.deliveryNote,
    cancellable: canCancel(order.status),                       // the same rule the API enforces on POST /cancel
    noteEditable: NOTE_EDITABLE.has(order.status),
  };
}

The consumer-side Pact for the event (74.10's MessageConsumerPact), written by the web team and verified by the API's event builder:

// apps/web/src/orders/order-events.pact.test.ts  (@pact-foundation/pact 12)
import { MatchersV3, MessageConsumerPact, synchronousBodyHandler } from '@pact-foundation/pact';
import { it } from 'vitest';
import { OrderEventRead } from './tracking.read';

const { like, uuid, integer, regex } = MatchersV3;
const pact = new MessageConsumerPact({ consumer: 'web', provider: 'orders-events', dir: './pacts' });

it('handles an order status event as the tracking page does', () =>
  pact
    .given('order 1d6c moves to OUT_FOR_DELIVERY')
    .expectsToReceive('an order event with status, version and eta window')
    .withContent({
      orderId: uuid('1d6c0b6e-2f3a-4c55-9d1e-8a7b6c5d4e3f'),
      status: like('OUT_FOR_DELIVERY'),
      version: integer(7),
      updatedAt: regex('^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}T.*Z$', '2026-11-05T13:45:27.402Z'),
      etaWindow: { from: like('2026-11-05T13:55:00Z'), to: like('2026-11-05T14:10:00Z') },
      summary: like('Out for delivery. Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm.'),
    })
    .verify(synchronousBodyHandler((body) => { OrderEventRead.parse(body); })));   // the page's real parser

Production scenario

The contract pull request was 140 lines and took two days of review between the three teams. It changed twice: dispatch asked for etaWindow instead of a single eta (a window is honest about uncertainty, and dispatch already computed one), and support asked for timeline so agents and customers would see the same history. After it merged, the web team worked against MSW fixtures for nine days while the API was built; the first integration on staging found two bugs, both in the API's mapper, both caught by the Pact verification before anyone opened a browser.

Failure scenario

In an earlier project, the team added OUT_FOR_DELIVERY to the server's enum and started emitting it the same day, reasoning that "the web is deployed with the API". The Android app, two releases behind for 18 % of users, parsed statuses with a strict enum, threw on the unknown value, and showed a blank tracking screen for every order that went out for delivery that evening. The contract said nothing about rollout order. The rule from 74.9, clients with a fallback first, then the server emits, would have avoided it, and a Pact verification of deployedOrReleased mobile versions would have failed the API deploy.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Events for orders the page has not loaded yet (another tab placed a new order): the client ignores them for this page; the order list invalidates (72.8).
  • Events older than the page's server-rendered state: the version guard drops them.
  • Payload growth: keep events small; the page fetches full details on a reset, never through the stream.
  • Optional fields that become required: never in place; a new event type or a versioned event name (Part 25.4).
  • Enum additions on the stream follow the same client-first rule as REST responses.
  • ETag on a personal resource must be private; a shared cache must never store it (76.9).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior writes the contract before the code, in the shared package, reviewed by every team that touches it, and treats it as the feature's real specification. They reuse what exists (the per-customer stream, the summary schema, the error shape) rather than inventing a parallel channel, and they plan enum and field changes as rollouts with an order, not as edits. Their one-sentence explanation to a product manager: "We agree the exact shape of the data first, so the app, the website and the API can be built at the same time, and a robot checks they still agree before every deploy."

Common mistakes

  • A separate stream per order when a per-customer stream already exists.
  • Shipping a new enum value from the server first.
  • Computing cancellable in the client from a status list that can drift from the server's rule.
  • Putting large or personal fields in events that may be logged or replayed.

Interview questions

  1. Why reuse a per-customer SSE stream instead of one per order? Expected answer: connections are the cost; one stream per tab serves the list and every order; replay already exists; client-side filtering is cheap because events are scoped to the customer.
  2. How do you add a new status value safely? Expected answer: clients that tolerate unknown values ship first, verified by contract tests against deployed and released versions; then the server emits it.
  3. What belongs in an event payload? Expected answer: identity, the new state's key fields, the version and timestamps, small optional extras; never large or sensitive data, which the client fetches.
  4. Where should cancellable be computed? Expected answer: on the server, with the same rule the cancel endpoint enforces, exposed as a field.

Practical exercise

Write the contract pull request for your tracking feature.

Acceptance criteria:

  • OrderTrackingSchema, the extended OrderEventSchema and the write schemas in @shop/contracts, with OpenAPI generated from them.
  • MSW fixtures for tracking built through the schemas (77.6), including an order with an unknown status.
  • A Pact message interaction for the event, verified by the API's event builder in CI.
  • A written rollout order for the new statuses, naming the telemetry threshold that allows the server to emit them.

79.3 NestJS backend: PostgreSQL schema, status transitions and the outbox

Concept

The backend has one job that everything else depends on: change an order's status correctly and tell the world exactly once per committed change. Three pieces do it:

  • The orders row holds the current status, a version that increases on every change, the arrival window and the delivery note. Changes use optimistic concurrency (Part 21.5): UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2.
  • order_status_events records the history (the timeline the page shows), one row per change, unique per (order_id, version).
  • The transactional outbox (Part 30.10): in the same transaction as the status change, a row is written to outbox. A separate relay reads unpublished rows and appends them to the customer's Redis Stream, from which the SSE controller of 72.8 replays and streams.

Why does it exist?

Because the obvious code, "update the row, then publish to Redis", has two failure windows (the dual-write problem, Part 30.9). If the process dies after the commit and before the publish, the customer never sees the change until they reload. If the publish happens before the commit and the transaction then rolls back, the customer sees a status that never happened. At 400,000 orders a day, "rarely" is several times a day. The outbox makes the event a consequence of the commit: if the change is committed, the event will be published, possibly twice, never zero times, and never for a change that did not commit.

Mental model

Imagine a bank clerk who, in the same stroke of the pen, updates your balance and writes a line in the "letters to send" book. A courier comes by every few moments, posts every unsent letter, and ticks it off. If the courier is ill, the letters wait in the book; nobody forgets them, and no letter is sent for a payment that was torn up before it was entered.

How it works

erDiagram
    ORDERS ||--o{ ORDER_STATUS_EVENTS : records
    ORDERS ||--o{ OUTBOX : emits
    ORDERS {
        uuid id PK
        uuid user_id
        text status
        int version
        timestamptz eta_from
        timestamptz eta_to
        text delivery_note
        timestamptz updated_at
    }
    ORDER_STATUS_EVENTS {
        bigint id PK
        uuid order_id FK
        int version
        text status
        timestamptz occurred_at
        text source
    }
    OUTBOX {
        bigint id PK
        uuid aggregate_id
        uuid user_id
        text type
        jsonb payload
        text traceparent
        timestamptz created_at
        timestamptz published_at
    }

The DDL, as a migration (Part 24: additive, safe on a live table):

-- migrations/1730800000000-order-tracking.sql (expand step: only additions)
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD COLUMN eta_from      timestamptz,
  ADD COLUMN eta_to        timestamptz,
  ADD COLUMN delivery_note text CHECK (char_length(delivery_note) <= 200),
  ADD CONSTRAINT eta_window_ordered CHECK (eta_from IS NULL OR eta_to IS NULL OR eta_from <= eta_to);
-- status is text with a CHECK listing allowed values; adding PACKING and OUT_FOR_DELIVERY replaces the CHECK
ALTER TABLE orders DROP CONSTRAINT orders_status_check,
  ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_check CHECK (status IN
    ('PENDING','PAID','PACKING','OUT_FOR_DELIVERY','SHIPPED','DELIVERED','CANCELLED')) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_status_check;   -- validates without blocking writes for long (Part 24)

CREATE TABLE order_status_events (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  version     integer NOT NULL,
  status      text NOT NULL,
  occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  source      text NOT NULL,                                  -- 'customer', 'warehouse', 'dispatch', 'support'
  UNIQUE (order_id, version)                                  -- one history row per version: replays cannot duplicate
);

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  id           bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  aggregate_id uuid NOT NULL,
  user_id      uuid NOT NULL,                                 -- which customer stream receives it
  type         text NOT NULL,                                 -- 'order.status_changed', 'order.note_changed'
  payload      jsonb NOT NULL,                                -- an OrderEvent, already shaped for the wire
  traceparent  text,                                          -- links the relay's span to the request (85.11)
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at timestamptz
);
-- The relay only ever reads unpublished rows, oldest first: a small partial index stays small forever.
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

Transitions are rules, shared and tested (77.2). The allowed moves live in @shop/contracts, so the API enforces them and the web can explain them:

// packages/contracts/src/order-transitions.ts
import type { z } from 'zod';
import type { OrderStatusSchema } from './orders';

type Status = z.infer<typeof OrderStatusSchema>;
const NEXT: Record<Status, readonly Status[]> = {
  PENDING: ['PAID', 'CANCELLED'],
  PAID: ['PACKING', 'CANCELLED'],
  PACKING: ['OUT_FOR_DELIVERY', 'SHIPPED'],
  OUT_FOR_DELIVERY: ['DELIVERED'],
  SHIPPED: ['DELIVERED'],
  DELIVERED: [],
  CANCELLED: [],
};
export const canTransition = (from: Status, to: Status): boolean => NEXT[from].includes(to);
export const allowedFrom = (to: Status): Status[] => (Object.keys(NEXT) as Status[]).filter((s) => NEXT[s].includes(to));

One transaction per change. The service applies a transition with a conditional UPDATE, writes the history row and the outbox row, all or nothing:

// apps/api/src/orders/order-status.service.ts  (TypeORM 0.3)
import { ConflictException, Injectable, NotFoundException } from '@nestjs/common';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { propagation, context } from '@opentelemetry/api';
import { allowedFrom, type OrderEvent } from '@shop/contracts';
import { statusSummary } from './status-summary';                 // "Out for delivery. Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm."

type Change = { orderId: string; to: OrderEvent['status']; source: string; eta?: { from: Date; to: Date } | null };

@Injectable()
export class OrderStatusService {
  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  async transition(c: Change): Promise<OrderEvent> {
    return this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
      // Conditional update: only from a status that allows this move. No SELECT ... FOR UPDATE needed.
      // TypeORM's query() on PostgreSQL returns [rows, rowCount] for UPDATE and DELETE, so destructure.
      const [rows]: [{ id: string; user_id: string; version: number; updated_at: Date; eta_from: Date | null; eta_to: Date | null;
                    store_time_zone: string }[], number] = await m.query(
        `UPDATE orders
            SET status = $2, version = version + 1, updated_at = now(),
                eta_from = COALESCE($4, eta_from), eta_to = COALESCE($5, eta_to)
          WHERE id = $1 AND status = ANY($3)
        RETURNING id, user_id, version, updated_at, eta_from, eta_to, store_time_zone`,
        [c.orderId, c.to, allowedFrom(c.to), c.eta?.from ?? null, c.eta?.to ?? null],
      );
      const row = rows[0];
      if (!row) {
        const exists = await m.query('SELECT status FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [c.orderId]);
        if (!exists.length) throw new NotFoundException({ code: 'NOT_FOUND' });
        throw new ConflictException({ code: 'INVALID_TRANSITION', issues: [{ code: exists[0].status, message: `Cannot move to ${c.to}` }] });
      }
      await m.query(
        'INSERT INTO order_status_events (order_id, version, status, source) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)',
        [row.id, row.version, c.to, c.source],
      );
      const event: OrderEvent = {
        orderId: row.id, status: c.to, version: row.version, updatedAt: row.updated_at.toISOString(),
        etaWindow: row.eta_from && row.eta_to ? { from: row.eta_from.toISOString(), to: row.eta_to.toISOString() } : null,
        summary: statusSummary(c.to, row.eta_from, row.eta_to, row.store_time_zone),
      };
      const carrier: Record<string, string> = {};
      propagation.inject(context.active(), carrier);              // W3C traceparent of the current request (85.11)
      await m.query(
        `INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, user_id, type, payload, traceparent) VALUES ($1, $2, 'order.status_changed', $3, $4)`,
        [row.id, row.user_id, JSON.stringify(event), carrier.traceparent ?? null],
      );
      return event;                                               // committed when this callback resolves
    });
  }
}

The WHERE status = ANY($3) makes the transition state-idempotent: the warehouse sending "PACKING" twice moves the order once; the second call finds no row in an allowed state and gets 409 INVALID_TRANSITION, which the warehouse integration treats as "already done". This matters because upstream systems retry (Part 30.12).

The relay. A small worker loop (Part 36) claims a batch of unpublished rows, appends each to the customer's Redis Stream, and marks them published, using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so several relay instances can run without double-claiming (Part 21.10):

// apps/api/src/orders/outbox.relay.ts
import { Injectable, Logger, OnApplicationShutdown, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRedis } from '@nestjs-modules/ioredis';             // or a small provider wrapping ioredis
import type Redis from 'ioredis';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';

const BATCH = 200;
const STREAM_MAXLEN = 500;                                         // per customer: about 15 minutes of history (78.8)

@Injectable()
export class OutboxRelay implements OnModuleInit, OnApplicationShutdown {
  private readonly log = new Logger(OutboxRelay.name);
  private running = true;

  constructor(private readonly ds: DataSource, @InjectRedis() private readonly redis: Redis) {}

  onModuleInit() { void this.loop(); }
  onApplicationShutdown() { this.running = false; }

  private async loop() {
    while (this.running) {
      const published = await this.tick().catch((e) => { this.log.error(e); return 0; });
      if (published < BATCH) await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, published ? 20 : 100)); // idle: poll every 100 ms
    }
  }

  async tick(): Promise<number> {
    return this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
      const rows: { id: string; user_id: string; payload: unknown }[] = await m.query(
        `SELECT id, user_id, payload FROM outbox
          WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, [BATCH]);
      if (!rows.length) return 0;
      const pipe = this.redis.pipeline();
      for (const r of rows) {
        const key = `orders:events:${r.user_id}`;
        pipe.xadd(key, 'MAXLEN', '~', STREAM_MAXLEN, '*', 'payload', JSON.stringify(r.payload));
        pipe.expire(key, 3600);                                     // idle customers' streams disappear after an hour
        pipe.publish(`orders:live:${r.user_id}`, '1');              // wake live SSE subscribers (78.8's subscribe)
      }
      await pipe.exec();                                            // if Redis fails, the transaction rolls back: retried
      await m.query('UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ANY($1)', [rows.map((r) => r.id)]);
      return rows.length;
    });
  }
}

If the process dies after pipe.exec() and before the commit, the rows are published again on the next tick: at least once. Duplicates are harmless because every consumer applies events by version (72.8). The order of events per customer is preserved because rows are claimed in id order and a customer's events land in one stream.

Practical example — one transition, timed

The warehouse system marks order 1d6c... as packed and handed to rider R-221 at 19:15:27 store time:

13:45:27.391Z  POST /internal/orders/1d6c.../status {to: OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, eta: 13:55-14:10}  (service auth)
13:45:27.394Z  BEGIN; UPDATE orders ... WHERE status = ANY('{PACKING}') RETURNING version=7      2.1 ms
13:45:27.396Z  INSERT order_status_events (version 7); INSERT outbox                             0.9 ms
13:45:27.402Z  COMMIT                                                                            1.8 ms
13:45:27.471Z  relay tick claims outbox id 88412311 (idle poll, waited 69 ms)
13:45:27.473Z  XADD orders:events:u-5f2... -> 1730813127412-0; PUBLISH orders:live:u-5f2...      0.6 ms
13:45:27.475Z  SSE controller writes "event: order" to the customer's connection
13:45:27.6xxZ  browser receives it (network 60-150 ms on 4G); cache patched; status heading re-renders

Commit to screen: about 200-300 ms, well under the 2 s p95 target. The idle poll interval (100 ms) is the largest controllable delay; PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY from a trigger could wake the relay instantly, at the cost of another moving part, and is not needed at this target.

Backend side (NestJS)

The internal endpoint that upstream systems call, separate from customer routes:

// apps/api/src/orders/internal-status.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, HttpCode, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Post, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { OrderStatusSchema } from '@shop/contracts';
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { ServiceAuthGuard } from '../auth/service-auth.guard';       // mTLS or a signed service token (Part 40.19)
import { OrderStatusService } from './order-status.service';

const InternalStatusChange = z.object({
  to: OrderStatusSchema,
  source: z.enum(['warehouse', 'dispatch', 'support']),
  eta: z.object({ from: z.coerce.date(), to: z.coerce.date() }).nullable().optional(),
});

@Controller('internal/orders')
@UseGuards(ServiceAuthGuard)                                         // never reachable with a customer cookie
export class InternalStatusController {
  constructor(private readonly status: OrderStatusService) {}

  @Post(':id/status')
  @HttpCode(200)
  change(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
         @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(InternalStatusChange)) body: z.infer<typeof InternalStatusChange>) {
    return this.status.transition({ orderId: id, to: body.to, source: body.source, eta: body.eta ?? null });
  }
}

The relay's query plan, with 40 million historical outbox rows and a few hundred unpublished:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id, user_id, payload FROM outbox
 WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 200 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

 Limit  (cost=0.29..18.71 rows=200 width=612) (actual time=0.031..0.402 rows=163 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=171
   ->  LockRows  (cost=0.29..39.12 rows=421 width=612) (actual time=0.030..0.388 rows=163 loops=1)
         ->  Index Scan using outbox_unpublished on outbox  (cost=0.29..34.91 rows=421 width=612)
               (actual time=0.017..0.211 rows=163 loops=1)
 Planning Time: 0.118 ms
 Execution Time: 0.431 ms

The partial index contains only unpublished rows, so it stays a few pages in size however large the table grows. A nightly job deletes published rows older than 7 days in batches (DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT 10000)), keeping vacuum cheap (Part 19).

Production scenario

At the evening peak the relay publishes 120 to 600 rows a second in batches of 20 to 200, using about 4 % of one vCPU on each of two instances. Outbox backlog (unpublished rows) averages 3 and peaked at 2,100 during a 40-second Redis failover; the relay caught up 6 seconds after Redis returned, and every event was delivered. The order_status_events table grows by 2 million rows a day; it is partitioned by month (Part 23) once it passes 500 million rows.

Failure scenario

During testing, a developer "optimised" the relay to publish first and update published_at in a separate statement without a transaction. When a relay instance was killed mid-batch during a deploy, 140 rows were published but never marked, and a second instance had already claimed overlapping rows because nothing held their locks. Customers received duplicated events, which the version guard absorbed, and a few events were stuck as "unpublished" until the next tick, which was also fine. The real damage was elsewhere: the analytics consumer of the same stream counted each event as a delivery milestone and double-counted 140 deliveries in a finance report. The rule written into the code review checklist: every consumer of order events must be idempotent by (orderId, version), not only the browser.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two upstream systems race (support cancels while the warehouse starts packing): the conditional UPDATE lets exactly one win; the other gets 409 INVALID_TRANSITION.
  • Redis down: the relay's transaction rolls back and retries; the outbox grows; SSE clients stop receiving events and the page falls back (79.12).
  • Relay down: same as Redis down, but nothing alerts unless outbox backlog and age are monitored (79.11).
  • Hot rows: an order changes at most a handful of times; no hot-row contention. The outbox insert is an append on a sequence, also fine at this rate.
  • Clock in events: updated_at comes from the database's now(), one clock for every writer, not the API task's clock.
  • Transaction scope: never call external services (dispatch, SMS) inside the transaction (Part 21.8); they consume the outbox stream too.
  • Long transactions block vacuum on outbox; keep the relay's transaction to one batch.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior makes the database row the only truth and every other representation (history, stream, cache, screen) a derivation of committed changes, carried by an outbox. They express transitions as data in the shared package, enforce them with one conditional UPDATE, and design every consumer to be idempotent by version. They size the relay from bursts, monitor backlog and age, and choose polling at 100 ms because it meets the target with fewer moving parts than triggers or CDC (Part 39), which they would adopt at 10x (79.13).

Common mistakes

  • Publishing to Redis in the request after commit (dual write).
  • SELECT then UPDATE for transitions, which races.
  • Outbox without a partial index, so the relay's query slows as the table grows.
  • Consumers that are not idempotent by version.
  • Calling external services inside the status transaction.

Interview questions

  1. Why an outbox instead of publishing after commit? Expected answer: a crash between commit and publish loses the event; publishing before commit can announce a change that rolls back; the outbox ties the event to the commit and gives at-least-once delivery.
  2. How do you make status transitions safe under concurrency? Expected answer: a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status = ANY(allowed) (and a version), checked by rows affected; one writer wins.
  3. What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED give the relay? Expected answer: several instances can claim disjoint batches without blocking each other.
  4. Why is at-least-once delivery acceptable here? Expected answer: every consumer applies events by (orderId, version), so duplicates are no-ops.
  5. How do you keep the outbox query fast with 40 million rows? Expected answer: a partial index on unpublished rows and regular deletion of old published rows.

Practical exercise

Build the schema, the transition service and the relay.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A migration that only adds (columns, tables, a replaced CHECK validated with NOT VALID then VALIDATE).
  • An integration test (Testcontainers, Part 41.7) firing two concurrent transitions from PAID (to PACKING and to CANCELLED): exactly one succeeds, one history row and one outbox row exist.
  • Killing the relay between XADD and commit, then restarting it, produces a duplicate stream entry and no missing one.
  • EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) of the relay query uses outbox_unpublished with 10 million published rows present.

79.4 NestJS backend: endpoints, the SSE stream, auth and rate limits

Concept

With the data model in place, the API exposes it through four routes (79.2). Each route gets the same treatment the rest of the book gives a production endpoint: authentication and ownership checks, input validation with the shared schemas, idempotency for writes, rate limits, bounded payloads and timeouts, and errors in the one problem-document shape. The SSE route gets three extra rules because it is long-lived: a cap on connections per user, an end at the access token's expiry, and a way to cut it when the session is revoked.

Why does it exist?

Because every route is an attack surface and a capacity cost. A tracking endpoint without an ownership check is an IDOR (Part 40.12): anyone can walk order IDs and read names and addresses. A stream without a connection cap lets one buggy client (or a script) hold thousands of sockets. A stream that never re-checks auth keeps delivering a customer's data after "log out everywhere" (75.3). A note endpoint without idempotency writes twice on a retry and burns a version, causing a spurious conflict.

Mental model

Imagine a hotel with a front desk (the REST routes) and an intercom in every room (the stream). The desk checks your key card on every visit. The intercom was connected when you checked in, so it needs its own rules: it switches off when your stay ends, it switches off if the hotel cancels your card, and no guest may have more than a few intercoms in their name.

How it works

The routes and their guards:

Route Guards and pipes Limits Errors
GET /v1/orders/:id/tracking JwtAuthGuard, ownership in the query 120/min per user 404 NOT_FOUND (also for other users' orders)
GET /v1/orders/events JwtAuthGuard, SseConnectionLimitGuard 6 concurrent streams per user; 20 connects/min per user 429 TOO_MANY_STREAMS; reauth event at expiry or revocation
PATCH /v1/orders/:id/delivery-note JwtAuthGuard, CsrfGuard (75.6), IdempotencyInterceptor (15.12), ZodValidationPipe 10/min per user 409 VERSION_CONFLICT with fresh state; 409 NOTE_LOCKED once out for delivery
POST /v1/orders/:id/cancel As above (72.12) 5/min per user 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE

Per-user limits use the user-keyed throttler guard of 75.10, not IP limits, because many customers share mobile carrier IPs.

The tracking read is one query for the order (scoped by user) and one for the last 20 history rows, mapped by toOrderTracking (79.2). Express adds a weak ETag to JSON responses and answers 304 Not Modified when the browser's If-None-Match matches, which turns TanStack Query's refetch-on-focus (72.3) into a 200-byte round trip when nothing changed.

// apps/api/src/orders/tracking.controller.ts
import { Controller, Get, Header, NotFoundException, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectDataSource } from '@nestjs/typeorm';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import type { OrderTracking } from '@shop/contracts';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { UserThrottlerGuard } from '../common/user-throttler.guard';   // 81.10
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { OrderEntity } from './order.entity';
import { OrderStatusEventEntity } from './order-status-event.entity';
import { toOrderTracking } from './tracking.mapper';

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, UserThrottlerGuard)
export class TrackingController {
  constructor(@InjectDataSource() private readonly ds: DataSource) {}

  @Get(':id/tracking')
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 120, ttl: 60_000 } })
  @Header('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache')               // never shared; revalidate with the ETag
  async get(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string): Promise<OrderTracking> {
    const order = await this.ds.getRepository(OrderEntity).findOne({ where: { id, userId: user.id } }); // ownership in the WHERE
    if (!order) throw new NotFoundException({ code: 'NOT_FOUND' });  // same answer for "missing" and "not yours"
    const events = await this.ds.getRepository(OrderStatusEventEntity)
      .find({ where: { orderId: id }, order: { version: 'ASC' }, take: 20 });
    return toOrderTracking(order, events);                    // about 2.1 KB of JSON, 0.9 KB gzip
  }
}

The delivery note write uses the version the page last saw (expectedVersion) in a conditional UPDATE, and emits an outbox event so other tabs learn about it. The event carries the status (unchanged) and the new version, not the note: notes are personal data and stay out of streams and logs (Part 40.31).

// apps/api/src/orders/delivery-note.service.ts (core)
async updateNote(userId: string, orderId: string, body: UpdateDeliveryNote): Promise<OrderTracking> {
  return this.ds.transaction(async (m) => {
    const [rows]: [{ id: string; version: number; status: string; updated_at: Date }[], number] = await m.query(
      `UPDATE orders SET delivery_note = $3, version = version + 1, updated_at = now()
        WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2 AND version = $4 AND status IN ('PENDING','PAID','PACKING')
      RETURNING id, version, status, updated_at`,
      [orderId, userId, body.note, body.expectedVersion],
    );
    if (!rows.length) throw await this.explainNoteConflict(m, userId, orderId, body.expectedVersion); // 404, NOTE_LOCKED or VERSION_CONFLICT
    const r = rows[0];
    await m.query(
      `INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate_id, user_id, type, payload) VALUES ($1, $2, 'order.note_changed', $3)`,
      [r.id, userId, JSON.stringify({ orderId: r.id, status: r.status, version: r.version, updatedAt: r.updated_at.toISOString() })],
    );
    return this.tracking.load(m, userId, orderId);            // the fresh tracking state, so the client needs no refetch
  });
}

explainNoteConflict reads the order once more (inside the same transaction) to return the precise problem document: NOT_FOUND, NOTE_LOCKED (status moved past packing) or VERSION_CONFLICT with the current tracking state in an extra current member, so the client can show what changed without another request (74.6).

The SSE stream is 72.8's controller with three additions: a connection cap, an end at token expiry, and a revocation check on the heartbeat.

// apps/api/src/orders/order-events.controller.ts (78.8, extended)
import { Controller, Headers, MessageEvent, Query, Sse, UseGuards } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Observable, filter, finalize, interval, map, merge, mergeMap, race, share, take, takeUntil, timer } from 'rxjs';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { SseConnectionLimitGuard, SseConnections } from './sse-connection-limit';
import { SessionEpochs } from '../auth/session-epochs';             // reads auth:epoch:<userId> (81.3)
import { OrderEventsStream } from './order-events.stream';        // 78.8's merge(concat(replay, live), heartbeat)

const ACCESS_TTL_S = 15 * 60;                                       // the access JWT lifetime (81.10)

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, SseConnectionLimitGuard)
export class OrderEventsController {
  constructor(private readonly streams: OrderEventsStream, private readonly epochs: SessionEpochs,
              private readonly conns: SseConnections) {}

  @Sse('events')
  stream(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser, @Headers('last-event-id') headerId?: string,
         @Query('lastEventId') queryId?: string): Observable<MessageEvent> {
    // EventSource sends the header only on its own reconnects; a stream the page reopens passes ?lastEventId= (85.6)
    const lastEventId = headerId ?? (queryId && /^\d+-\d+$/.test(queryId) ? queryId : undefined);
    const msLeft = Math.max(0, (user.issuedAt + ACCESS_TTL_S) * 1000 - Date.now());
    const expired$ = timer(msLeft).pipe(map((): MessageEvent => ({ type: 'reauth', data: { reason: 'EXPIRED' } })));
    const revoked$ = interval(20_000).pipe(                         // piggybacks on the heartbeat cadence
      mergeMap(() => this.epochs.isRevoked(user.id, user.issuedAt)), // one Redis GET, about 0.3 ms
      filter(Boolean),
      map((): MessageEvent => ({ type: 'reauth', data: { reason: 'REVOKED' } })),
    );
    const end$ = race(expired$, revoked$).pipe(take(1), share());
    return merge(this.streams.forUser(user.id, lastEventId).pipe(takeUntil(end$)), end$)
      .pipe(finalize(() => void this.conns.release(user.id)));    // runs on client disconnect too
  }
}
// apps/api/src/orders/sse-connection-limit.ts
import { CanActivate, ExecutionContext, HttpException, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';
import { InjectRedis } from '@nestjs-modules/ioredis';
import type Redis from 'ioredis';

const MAX_STREAMS = 6;

@Injectable()
export class SseConnections {
  constructor(@InjectRedis() private readonly redis: Redis) {}
  async acquire(userId: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const key = `sse:conn:${userId}`;
    const n = await this.redis.multi().incr(key).expire(key, 16 * 60).exec();   // every stream ends within 15 min,
    const count = Number(n?.[0]?.[1] ?? 0);                                     // so a crashed task's count self-heals
    if (count > MAX_STREAMS) { await this.redis.decr(key); return false; }
    return true;
  }
  async release(userId: string) { await this.redis.decr(`sse:conn:${userId}`); }
}

@Injectable()
export class SseConnectionLimitGuard implements CanActivate {
  constructor(private readonly conns: SseConnections) {}
  async canActivate(ctx: ExecutionContext): Promise<boolean> {
    const user = ctx.switchToHttp().getRequest().user as { id: string };
    if (await this.conns.acquire(user.id)) return true;
    throw new HttpException({ code: 'TOO_MANY_STREAMS', title: 'Too many live connections' }, 429);
  }
}

Three operational details for the stream tasks:

  1. No buffering on the path: NestJS's @Sse() sets Content-Type: text/event-stream and Cache-Control: no-cache; the response also needs compression disabled for this route (a global compression() middleware buffers), and CloudFront's cache behaviour for the path uses caching disabled and an origin response timeout above the 20 s heartbeat (79.10).
  2. Reconnect hint: the first message sets retry (NestJS's MessageEvent has a retry field) to 3,000 ms plus random jitter up to 2,000 ms, so 60,000 clients do not reconnect in the same second after a blip.
  3. Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, each stream sends a ping with a randomised retry between 1 and 10 s and completes, so a deploy spreads reconnections over ten seconds instead of creating a spike (Part 31.13).

Practical example — the stream at work

$ curl -N -H "Cookie: __Host-session=$SESSION" https://staging.shop.example/api/v1/orders/events
retry: 4120

event: ping
data:

id: 1730813127412-0
event: order
data: {"orderId":"1d6c0b6e-...","status":"OUT_FOR_DELIVERY","version":7,"updatedAt":"2026-11-05T13:45:27.402Z",...}

event: ping
data:

event: reauth
data: {"reason":"EXPIRED"}
$                                                   # stream completed at the token's expiry

curl -N disables curl's own buffering, so events print as they arrive. Opening a seventh stream for the same user returns HTTP/2 429 with {"code":"TOO_MANY_STREAMS",...}.

Backend side (NestJS)

The module wiring keeps the stream route in a module that the realtime deployment loads and the request/response deployment does not (79.10), using one image and two entry points:

// apps/api/src/main.realtime.ts: the same codebase, only the stream and its dependencies
import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core';
import { RealtimeAppModule } from './realtime-app.module';     // AuthModule, RedisModule, OrderEventsModule, HealthModule
import { configureApp } from './configure-app';

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = configureApp(await NestFactory.create(RealtimeAppModule, { bodyParser: false })); // streams take no bodies
  app.enableShutdownHooks();
  await app.listen(4001);
}
bootstrap();

Production scenario

At the evening peak the realtime service runs 8 tasks of 1 vCPU and 2 GB, holding 58,000 to 64,000 streams (about 7,500 per task, 420 MB of memory per task for connections), with CPU under 20 %. Reauth events close about 70 streams a second (every stream ends within 15 minutes); clients refresh and reconnect with Last-Event-ID within 1-2 s and replay what they missed. The tracking read handles 25 requests per second at p95 18 ms, with 61 % answered 304.

Failure scenario

The first staging load test opened 20,000 streams and then restarted all realtime tasks at once. Every client reconnected within the default EventSource retry of about 3 seconds, and all 20,000 replays hit Redis and the auth middleware in the same second; p99 connect time went to 9 seconds, and 3 % of clients hit the per-user connect rate limit because the browser retried quickly after errors. The fixes: the jittered retry hint, rolling restarts with a 30-second gap between tasks (ECS minimumHealthyPercent 100, maximumPercent 125), and a connect-rate limit counted per user per minute rather than per 10 seconds.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Ownership by a separate query (load by ID, then compare userId) is easy to forget in one route; put the user in the WHERE.
  • 403 for other users' orders reveals that the ID exists; return 404.
  • Long-lived auth: a stream authorised at 10:00 must not deliver after a 10:05 revocation; the epoch check on the heartbeat bounds it to 20 s.
  • Connection counter drift after a crash; the TTL equal to the maximum stream lifetime heals it.
  • Global compression middleware buffering SSE; exclude the route.
  • EventSource treats any non-200 as final: a 429 or 401 closes it for good; the client must decide what to do next (79.6).
  • Notes in events or logs: keep personal data out of streams, outbox payloads and access logs.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior applies the same checklist to every route (auth, ownership, validation, idempotency, limits, error shape) and then asks what is different about the long-lived one. A stream holds authority for as long as it is open, so it gets an expiry, a revocation check and a cap. It holds memory for as long as it is open, so it lives on its own tasks with its own scaling metric. And it reconnects in herds, so the server tells clients when to come back, with jitter.

Common mistakes

  • Authenticating the stream once and never again.
  • No per-user connection cap.
  • Serving streams from the same tasks as checkout.
  • Default retry for every client, so reconnects synchronise.
  • Returning the note in the outbox payload "for convenience".

Interview questions

  1. How do you stop an SSE stream from outliving a revoked session? Expected answer: end it at the token's expiry with a reauth event, check a revocation epoch on the heartbeat, and let the client refresh and reconnect.
  2. Why return 404 instead of 403 for someone else's order? Expected answer: 403 confirms the ID exists; 404 gives an enumerator nothing.
  3. How do you cap SSE connections per user across many tasks? Expected answer: a shared counter in Redis incremented on connect and decremented on teardown, with a TTL equal to the maximum stream lifetime.
  4. Why does the delivery-note event not contain the note? Expected answer: notes are personal data; events are replayed and may be logged; the client refetches when the event's status did not change.

Practical exercise

Implement the four routes with their guards and limits.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Requesting another user's order returns 404 with the same body as a missing order.
  • A second PATCH with the same Idempotency-Key returns the first response; a stale expectedVersion returns 409 VERSION_CONFLICT with current.
  • A seventh concurrent stream for one user returns 429 TOO_MANY_STREAMS; closing one stream allows a new one.
  • After "log out everywhere", an open stream receives reauth with REVOKED within 25 s and completes.
  • A rolling restart of the realtime tasks shows reconnections spread over at least 10 s.

79.5 Next.js frontend: the server-rendered order page shell

Concept

The tracking page is a server-rendered shell with one live island. The App Router page (a Server Component, 73.4) fetches the tracking state from NestJS on the server and renders everything a customer needs to read immediately: the status heading, the arrival window, the timeline, items, address and total. One Client Component, TrackingLive, takes that state as its initial data, opens the stream and keeps the status, window and timeline current. Everything else stays server-only and ships no JavaScript.

Why does it exist?

Because the most important moment on this page is the first second. A customer who taps a push notification wants "Out for delivery, arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm" on the screen, not a spinner while a JavaScript bundle loads, fetches and renders (73.1). Server rendering puts the answer in the HTML, which makes it the LCP element (76.3) and readable even if JavaScript fails. The live island then makes it current.

Mental model

Imagine a printed departure board at a train station that also has one small electronic panel for the platform and delay. The printed parts (the train, its stops) never change, so they are printed once. Only the panel updates. Printing the whole board electronically would be slower and more fragile for no gain.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant CF as CloudFront
    participant MW as Middleware
    participant RSC as OrderPage
    participant API as NestJS
    participant RT as Realtime
    B->>CF: GET /orders/1d6c...
    CF->>MW: forward, cookies included
    MW->>MW: verify __Host-session JWT, 0.4 ms
    MW->>RSC: render the page
    RSC->>API: GET /v1/orders/1d6c.../tracking, Bearer from cookie
    API-->>RSC: 200 tracking, 18 ms
    RSC-->>B: streamed HTML with status heading, timeline, initial state
    B->>B: hydrate TrackingLive, about 14 KB gzip
    B->>CF: GET /api/v1/orders/events
    CF->>RT: forward to realtime tasks, no caching
    RT-->>B: retry hint, replay, then live events
  1. Middleware (75.10) verifies the session JWT for /orders/:path* and redirects to the refresh route when it is missing or expired, before any rendering.
  2. The page calls a server-only data function, getOrderTracking(id), which reads the access token from the cookie and calls NestJS on the private network with a 1.5 s timeout. It is dynamic by nature (it reads cookies), so nothing is cached between users (73.7).
  3. notFound() for a 404 renders not-found.tsx; any other failure throws to the segment's error.tsx (79.6), which shows a retry with the request ID.
  4. Formatting happens once, deterministically: dates are formatted with Intl.DateTimeFormat and the store's time zone (74.7) through the same helper on the server and the client, so hydration never mismatches (73.10) and a later live update formats exactly as the server did.
  5. Streaming: the main content renders immediately; a slower "Buy again" strip is wrapped in Suspense so it never delays the status (73.2).
  6. loading.tsx shows a skeleton with the same dimensions as the real heading and window, so nothing shifts when the content arrives (76.5).

Practical example

What the customer receives in the first HTML response, before any JavaScript runs (about 11 KB gzip): a heading "Out for delivery", the line "Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm", a four-step progress bar with the current step marked with aria-current="step", the timeline with times, items and total, and the address with the delivery note. A customer on a slow connection or with JavaScript blocked still sees the correct status as of page load, plus a "Refresh" link.

React / Next.js example

The server-only data function:

// apps/web/lib/orders.server.ts
import 'server-only';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
import { OrderTrackingRead, type OrderTrackingView } from '@/orders/tracking.read';
import { toApiError } from '@/api/errors';

const API = process.env.API_INTERNAL_URL!;                       // server-only runtime config (84.2)

export async function getOrderTracking(id: string): Promise<OrderTrackingView | null> {
  const token = cookies().get('__Host-session')?.value;          // Next.js 15: (await cookies()).get(...)
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/v1/orders/${encodeURIComponent(id)}/tracking`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, 'X-Client': 'web-ssr' },
    cache: 'no-store',                                           // personal data: never in the Data Cache (79.7)
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1500),                           // a slow API must not hold the HTML forever
  });
  if (res.status === 404) return null;
  if (!res.ok) throw await toApiError(res);                      // error.tsx shows code and requestId
  return OrderTrackingRead.parse(await res.json());              // open enums: an unknown status renders "Updated"
}

The page:

// apps/web/app/(shop)/orders/[id]/page.tsx  (Next.js 14; in 15, params is a Promise: const { id } = await params)
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation';
import { Suspense } from 'react';
import type { Metadata } from 'next';
import { getOrderTracking } from '@/lib/orders.server';
import { getFlags } from '@/flags/server';                       // 84.5
import { getSession } from '@/auth/session';
import { TrackingLive } from './TrackingLive';                   // 'use client'
import { OrderItems } from './OrderItems';                       // server component, no JS
import { BuyAgain } from './BuyAgain';                           // server component, slower, streamed
import { BuyAgainSkeleton } from './BuyAgainSkeleton';

export const metadata: Metadata = { title: 'Track your order', robots: { index: false } };

export default async function OrderTrackingPage({ params }: { params: { id: string } }) {
  const session = await getSession();
  const [tracking, flags] = await Promise.all([
    getOrderTracking(params.id),
    getFlags({ userId: session.userId, keys: ['live-tracking'] }),
  ]);
  if (!tracking) notFound();

  return (
    <main className="tracking">
      <TrackingLive initial={tracking} live={flags['live-tracking']} />   {/* status, window, timeline, note, cancel */}
      <OrderItems items={tracking.items} totalMinor={tracking.totalMinor} currency={tracking.currency} />
      <Suspense fallback={<BuyAgainSkeleton />}>
        <BuyAgain orderId={tracking.id} />
      </Suspense>
    </main>
  );
}

TrackingLive is a Client Component, but it is still server-rendered on the first request (Client Components render on the server too, 73.4), so the status heading is in the HTML. Its props are plain JSON (OrderTrackingView and a boolean), which is the rule for crossing the server/client boundary.

The shared formatter, used by server and client:

// apps/web/src/orders/format.ts
const windowFmt = new Map<string, Intl.DateTimeFormat>();

export function formatEtaWindow(from: string, to: string, timeZone: string, locale = 'en-IN'): string {
  const key = `${locale}|${timeZone}`;
  if (!windowFmt.has(key)) windowFmt.set(key, new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { hour: 'numeric', minute: '2-digit', timeZone }));
  const f = windowFmt.get(key)!;
  return `Arriving ${f.format(new Date(from))} to ${f.format(new Date(to))}`;   // the store's zone, never the device's
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The server render depends on three API behaviours:

  • Bearer or cookie: JwtStrategy accepts the session JWT from the cookie or the Authorization header (75.1), so the server component can forward the same token over the private network.
  • Fast, bounded reads: the tracking read is two indexed queries (orders by primary key and user, order_status_events by (order_id, version)), p95 under 20 ms, so the 1.5 s SSR timeout is a safety net, not a budget.
  • Request IDs on every response, which the error page shows and the Next.js server logs alongside its own trace ID (79.11).

Production scenario

Field data after launch (p75, mobile, 28 days): TTFB 310 ms (CloudFront to the Next.js task about 40 ms, middleware 1 ms, the API call 22 ms, rendering 35 ms, the rest network), LCP 1.4 s (the status heading, text, no web font blocking thanks to font-display: swap and a preloaded subset, 76.8), CLS 0.01, INP 70 ms. The page's JavaScript is the shared framework chunks (cached from earlier visits for 80 % of loads) plus 14 KB gzip for TrackingLive.

Failure scenario

An early version fetched the tracking state in TrackingLive with useQuery on mount, and the server rendered only a skeleton. In the lab it looked fine. In the field, customers tapping a notification on a mid-range Android phone over 4G waited 3.8 s at p75 for the status, because the bundle had to download, parse and run before the fetch even started (the waterfall of 76.10). Support saw no change in "where is my order" contacts. Moving the fetch into the Server Component cut LCP to 1.4 s and put the answer in the HTML.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Formatting with the device's time zone on the client and the server's on the server causes hydration mismatches and wrong times; pass the store's zone explicitly.
  • Fetching with the Data Cache (cache: 'force-cache') for personal data can serve one customer's order to another in Next.js 14's default caching (73.7); always no-store for personal reads.
  • Slow API: without a timeout, a stuck API call holds the response until the platform times out; with one, error.tsx renders quickly with a retry.
  • Params from the URL are input: encode them when building the API URL; validate the UUID before calling.
  • Search engines and link previews must not index the page; noindex, and personal data only after authentication.
  • The Back button: authenticated pages and the bfcache pull in opposite directions (76.9, 81.9); the page uses private, no-cache plus 81's BfcacheGuard, which reloads a restored page after logout, and TrackingLive reconnects on pageshow.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior puts the answer to the user's question in the first HTML response and adds interactivity only where the page changes. They draw the server/client boundary around the smallest component that needs state, pass it plain data, and keep formatting deterministic so the server and client agree. They give server data fetching a timeout and treat the API's latency as part of the page's TTFB budget. And they measure the result in the field, because the lab hides the network and device costs that motivated server rendering in the first place.

Common mistakes

  • Client-side fetching for the main content of a page users open from notifications.
  • A Client Component at the page root, shipping JavaScript for static parts.
  • Device time zone formatting.
  • No timeout on server fetches.
  • Data Cache on personal reads.

Interview questions

  1. Why server-render the tracking page instead of fetching on the client? Expected answer: the status is in the first HTML (LCP, no waterfall, works without JavaScript); the live island takes over afterwards.
  2. How do you pass server data into a Client Component? Expected answer: as serializable props from the Server Component; the client seeds its cache with them.
  3. How do you avoid hydration mismatches with dates? Expected answer: format with an explicit locale and time zone through one helper used on both sides, or render the formatted string from the server.
  4. What should happen when the API is slow during server rendering? Expected answer: a bounded timeout and an error boundary with retry and request ID, not an unbounded wait.

Practical exercise

Build the page shell.

Acceptance criteria:

  • With JavaScript disabled, the page shows the correct status, window and timeline for a seeded order.
  • The LCP element in a Lighthouse mobile run is the status heading; LCP under 2.0 s on the staging preview.
  • Another customer's order ID renders not-found.tsx; an API 503 renders error.tsx with the request ID and a retry button.
  • No hydration warnings in the console with the device time zone set to America/New_York and the store in Asia/Kolkata.

79.6 Next.js frontend: live status, optimistic actions and error states

Concept

TrackingLive is the page's one interactive island. It does four jobs:

  1. Seed the TanStack Query cache with the server-rendered state, so the cache, not component state, is what the UI reads (72.1).
  2. Stay live through the per-customer stream, merging events into the cache with the version guard of 72.8, and tell the user honestly when live updates stop.
  3. Edit the delivery note optimistically: show the new note at once, send it with an idempotency key and the expected version, and reconcile with the server's answer.
  4. Cancel pessimistically: cancelling touches money and races with packing, so the button waits for the server's answer before the page says "Cancelled".

Why does it exist?

Because live UIs fail in ways static pages do not. The stream drops on a train through a tunnel; the session expires while the page is open; another tab changes the note; an event for version 8 arrives before the response for version 7; packing starts in the second between "Cancel" and the request reaching the API. A live page that handles only the happy path shows wrong information with confidence, which is worse than a page that shows old information honestly.

Mental model

Imagine an airport arrivals board connected to the control tower by a radio link. The board shows the latest message it received, with the time it received it. If the radio goes quiet, a small light says "last update 2 minutes ago" and an attendant phones the tower every half minute. When a passenger asks the attendant to change their pickup note, the attendant writes it on the board straight away in pencil and inks it when the tower confirms.

How it works

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Connecting
    Connecting --> Live: open event
    Live --> Reconnecting: network error, EventSource retries
    Reconnecting --> Live: open event, replay from Last-Event-ID
    Live --> Reauth: reauth event
    Reauth --> Connecting: refreshOnce ok, reopen with lastEventId
    Reauth --> SignedOut: refresh fails
    Connecting --> Polling: three failures in two minutes
    Reconnecting --> Polling: still closed after 10 s
    Polling --> Connecting: every 2 minutes, or tab visible again
    Live --> Paused: tab hidden 5 min, or no live orders left
    Paused --> Connecting: tab visible and a live order needs it
    SignedOut --> [*]

The rules, in order of importance:

  1. One stream per tab, shared by every subscriber. A LiveOrdersProvider mounted in the (shop)/orders layout owns the EventSource (72.8's hook, moved into a provider) and reference-counts the components that need it: the order list, the tracking page. When nothing needs live data (no subscriber, or every tracked order is DELIVERED or CANCELLED), it closes the stream, so a tab left open overnight costs the server nothing.
  2. Merge by version, by field. An event updates status, version, updatedAt and etaWindow only if event.version is greater than the cached version; if the status changed it also appends to the timeline. If the event's status equals the cached status (a note change from another tab, 79.4), the event carries nothing to merge, so the tracking query is invalidated and refetched (one 1 KB GET, usually a 304).
  3. reauth means refresh, then reopen. The stream ends at token expiry or revocation (79.4). The provider calls refreshOnce() (75.3, single-flight across tabs), and on success opens a new EventSource with ?lastEventId= set to the last ID it saw, because a new EventSource object does not send the Last-Event-ID header; only its own automatic reconnects do. If the refresh fails, the auth broadcast of 75.3 sends every tab to sign-in.
  4. EventSource hides HTTP status codes. When it closes for good (readyState === 2), the page cannot tell a 401 from a 429 or a 503. The provider treats every permanent close the same way: try refreshOnce(), reopen with backoff (2, 4, 8 s with jitter), and after three failures in two minutes switch to polling the tracking query every 30 s, with a banner.
  5. Honest staleness. When not Live, the status line shows "Last updated 7:12 pm" from the cached updatedAt, and the banner explains what is happening. Nothing pretends to be live.
  6. Announce status, not noise. A visually hidden role="status" region announces the event's summary only when the status changes, not on ETA adjustments (77.10, 77.9).
  7. Back/forward cache: on pageshow with event.persisted, the provider reopens the stream and the tracking query refetches (76.9).

Practical example

A customer on a commuter train has the page open. Timeline of what they see:

  • 19:12:40: "Packing your order", status line "Live".
  • 19:13:05: the train enters a tunnel; the connection drops. EventSource retries silently; after 10 s still closed, the banner shows "Reconnecting. Showing status from 7:12 pm" and polling starts.
  • 19:15:27: the order goes out for delivery while they are in the tunnel; the poll at 19:15:35 fails (offline).
  • 19:16:10: out of the tunnel; online fires, the provider reopens with ?lastEventId=1730812960113-0; the server replays the OUT_FOR_DELIVERY event; the heading changes, the screen reader announces "Out for delivery. Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm", the banner disappears.

React / Next.js example

The provider, with the connection state machine reduced to its essentials:

// apps/web/src/orders/LiveOrdersProvider.tsx  (React 18, TanStack Query v5)
'use client';
import { createContext, useCallback, useContext, useEffect, useRef, useState, type ReactNode } from 'react';
import { useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { refreshOnce } from '@/api/auth-fetch';                      // 81.3
import { applyOrderEvent } from './applyOrderEvent';                // version-guarded merge, below
import { OrderEventRead } from './tracking.read';

type Conn = 'connecting' | 'live' | 'reconnecting' | 'polling' | 'paused';
const Ctx = createContext<{ conn: Conn; subscribe: () => () => void }>({ conn: 'paused', subscribe: () => () => {} });
export const useLiveOrders = () => useContext(Ctx);

export function LiveOrdersProvider({ enabled, children }: { enabled: boolean; children: ReactNode }) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  const [conn, setConn] = useState<Conn>('paused');
  const [subscribers, setSubscribers] = useState(0);
  const lastId = useRef<string | null>(null);
  const failures = useRef<number[]>([]);

  const subscribe = useCallback(() => { setSubscribers((n) => n + 1); return () => setSubscribers((n) => n - 1); }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!enabled || subscribers === 0 || document.visibilityState === 'hidden') { setConn('paused'); return; }
    let source: EventSource | null = null;
    let stopped = false;
    let retry: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;

    const open = () => {
      setConn('connecting');
      const qs = lastId.current ? `?lastEventId=${encodeURIComponent(lastId.current)}` : '';
      source = new EventSource(`/api/v1/orders/events${qs}`, { withCredentials: true });
      source.onopen = () => setConn('live');
      source.addEventListener('order', (m) => {
        const msg = m as MessageEvent<string>;
        lastId.current = msg.lastEventId || lastId.current;
        const parsed = OrderEventRead.safeParse(JSON.parse(msg.data));
        if (parsed.success) applyOrderEvent(qc, parsed.data);
      });
      source.addEventListener('reset', () => void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] }));  // gap too old (78.8)
      source.addEventListener('reauth', () => { source?.close(); void reconnect(true); });
      source.onerror = () => {
        if (source?.readyState === EventSource.CONNECTING) { setConn('reconnecting'); return; }   // browser is retrying
        source?.close(); void reconnect(false);                                                  // closed for good
      };
    };

    const reconnect = async (expected: boolean) => {
      if (stopped) return;
      const now = Date.now();
      if (!expected) failures.current = [...failures.current.filter((t) => now - t < 120_000), now];
      if (failures.current.length >= 3) { setConn('polling'); retry = setTimeout(open, 120_000); return; } // try again in 2 min
      const ok = await refreshOnce();                             // a 401 is the most likely permanent close
      if (!ok) return;                                            // the auth broadcast sends every tab to sign-in (81.3)
      const backoff = expected ? 0 : 2 ** failures.current.length * 1000 + Math.random() * 1000;
      retry = setTimeout(open, backoff);
    };

    open();
    const onOnline = () => { if (conn !== 'live') { source?.close(); open(); } };
    addEventListener('online', onOnline);
    return () => { stopped = true; clearTimeout(retry); source?.close(); removeEventListener('online', onOnline); };
  }, [enabled, subscribers, qc]);                                 // eslint: conn read only in onOnline, deliberately

  return <Ctx.Provider value={{ conn, subscribe }}>{children}</Ctx.Provider>;
}

A separate small effect (not shown) sets subscribers-independent visibility state: when the tab has been hidden for five minutes it closes the stream, and visibilitychange back to visible reopens it and refetches. The polling fallback is not in the provider at all: TrackingLive sets refetchInterval: conn === 'polling' ? 30_000 : false on its query, so the cache stays the only source the UI reads.

The merge, shared by the list (72.8) and the tracking page:

// apps/web/src/orders/applyOrderEvent.ts
import type { QueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { orderKeys } from './orderKeys';                          // 78.2, with tracking: (id) => [...details(), id, 'tracking']
import type { OrderTrackingView } from './tracking.read';
import type { z } from 'zod';
import type { OrderEventRead } from './tracking.read';

type Ev = z.infer<typeof OrderEventRead>;

export function applyOrderEvent(qc: QueryClient, e: Ev) {
  let needsRefetch = false;
  qc.setQueryData<OrderTrackingView>(orderKeys.tracking(e.orderId), (old) => {
    if (!old || e.version <= old.version) return old;            // unknown here, duplicate or out of order: no-op
    if (e.status === old.status) { needsRefetch = true; return old; } // a change the event does not carry (note)
    return {
      ...old,
      status: e.status, version: e.version, updatedAt: e.updatedAt,
      etaWindow: e.etaWindow === undefined ? old.etaWindow : e.etaWindow,
      timeline: [...old.timeline, { status: e.status, at: e.updatedAt }].slice(-20),
      cancellable: e.status === 'PENDING' || e.status === 'PAID',  // display hint; the server enforces (85.4)
      noteEditable: ['PENDING', 'PAID', 'PACKING'].includes(e.status),
      lastSummary: e.summary,                                     // client-only field for the live region, never sent back
    } as OrderTrackingView;
  });
  if (needsRefetch) void qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: orderKeys.tracking(e.orderId) });
  // ...plus 78.8's patch of the detail and list caches, unchanged
}

The two display hints duplicate canCancel and the note rule for the moment between the event and the next refetch; the server's answer to an action is still final. In the codebase they import the same canCancel from @shop/contracts (77.2); they are spelled out here for readability.

The island itself:

// apps/web/app/(shop)/orders/[id]/TrackingLive.tsx
'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useQuery } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useLiveOrders } from '@/orders/LiveOrdersProvider';
import { orderKeys } from '@/orders/orderKeys';
import { fetchTracking } from '@/orders/api';                     // apiGet + OrderTrackingRead.parse (78.2, 80.7)
import { STATUS_COPY } from '@/orders/status-copy';
import { formatEtaWindow, formatTime } from '@/orders/format';
import type { OrderTrackingView } from '@/orders/tracking.read';
import { ConnectionBanner } from './ConnectionBanner';
import { DeliveryNote } from './DeliveryNote';
import { CancelOrder } from './CancelOrder';
import { Timeline } from './Timeline';

export function TrackingLive({ initial, live }: { initial: OrderTrackingView; live: boolean }) {
  const { conn, subscribe } = useLiveOrders();
  const terminal = (s: string) => s === 'DELIVERED' || s === 'CANCELLED';
  const { data: t } = useQuery({
    queryKey: orderKeys.tracking(initial.id),
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetchTracking(initial.id, signal),
    initialData: initial,                                         // the server-rendered state seeds the cache
    staleTime: 30_000,
    refetchInterval: (q) => (conn === 'polling' || !live) && !terminal(q.state.data?.status ?? '') ? 30_000 : false,
  });

  useEffect(() => (live && !terminal(t.status) ? subscribe() : undefined), [live, t.status, subscribe]);

  return (
    <section aria-labelledby="status-h" className="tracking-live">
      <h1 id="status-h">{STATUS_COPY[t.status].label}</h1>
      <p className="eta">{t.etaWindow ? formatEtaWindow(t.etaWindow.from, t.etaWindow.to, t.storeTimeZone) : ' '}</p>
      <ConnectionBanner conn={live ? conn : 'polling'} updatedAt={formatTime(t.updatedAt, t.storeTimeZone)} terminal={terminal(t.status)} />
      <p className="visually-hidden" role="status" aria-live="polite">{(t as { lastSummary?: string }).lastSummary ?? ''}</p>
      <Timeline steps={t.timeline} timeZone={t.storeTimeZone} current={t.status} />
      <DeliveryNote orderId={t.id} note={t.deliveryNote} editable={t.noteEditable} version={t.version} />
      {t.cancellable && <CancelOrder orderId={t.id} />}
    </section>
  );
}

The ETA line always renders (a non-breaking space when empty) so its height is reserved and a late window does not shift the page (76.5). ConnectionBanner renders nothing when live, a one-line notice otherwise, in a container with a fixed minimum height for the same reason.

The optimistic note, with version-aware, field-level rollback (72.6, 72.12):

// apps/web/app/(shop)/orders/[id]/useSaveNote.ts
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { useRef } from 'react';
import { orderKeys } from '@/orders/orderKeys';
import { saveDeliveryNote } from '@/orders/api';                  // authFetch PATCH with Idempotency-Key and x-csrf-token
import { ApiError } from '@/api/errors';
import type { OrderTrackingView } from '@/orders/tracking.read';

export function useSaveNote(orderId: string) {
  const qc = useQueryClient();
  const key = useRef<string | null>(null);
  const k = orderKeys.tracking(orderId);

  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: async (note: string) => {
      key.current ??= crypto.randomUUID();                         // one key per attempt; retries reuse it
      const expectedVersion = qc.getQueryData<OrderTrackingView>(k)!.version;
      return saveDeliveryNote(orderId, { note, expectedVersion }, key.current);
    },
    onMutate: async (note) => {
      await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: k });
      const before = qc.getQueryData<OrderTrackingView>(k)!;
      qc.setQueryData<OrderTrackingView>(k, { ...before, deliveryNote: note || null });   // show it now
      return { previousNote: before.deliveryNote };
    },
    onSuccess: (fresh) => {
      key.current = null;                                          // final answer: the next save is a new attempt
      qc.setQueryData<OrderTrackingView>(k, (old) => (!old || fresh.version >= old.version ? fresh : old));
    },
    onError: (e, _note, ctx) => {
      key.current = e instanceof ApiError && e.status < 500 ? null : key.current;          // keep the key on unknown outcomes
      if (e instanceof ApiError && e.code === 'VERSION_CONFLICT' && e.current) {
        qc.setQueryData(k, e.current as OrderTrackingView);       // server's truth, including the other tab's note
        return;
      }
      // Roll back only the field we changed: an SSE event may have advanced the status meanwhile.
      qc.setQueryData<OrderTrackingView>(k, (old) => old && { ...old, deliveryNote: ctx?.previousNote ?? null });
    },
  });
}

current is the extra member of the VERSION_CONFLICT problem document (79.4). 74.6's toApiError parses only the standard members, so this feature extends it by one line: it keeps parsed.data.current (validated with OrderTrackingRead) on a new optional ApiError.current field. Problem documents may carry extension members (RFC 9457), and clients that do not know them ignore them.

Cancel stays pessimistic: a confirmation dialog, then POST /v1/orders/:id/cancel with an idempotency key through 72.12's useCancelOrder with onMutate removed. On 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE the dialog says "Packing has already started, so this order can't be cancelled. You can refuse the delivery at the door" and the tracking query refetches; the SSE event moving the order to PACKING usually arrives first anyway.

Error states

Situation What the customer sees Mechanism
Stream reconnecting (under 10 s) Nothing different EventSource auto-retry; banner only after 10 s
Stream down longer "Reconnecting. Showing status from 7:12 pm" ConnectionBanner, polling every 30 s
Session expired mid-page Nothing; a reconnect within 2 s reauth, refreshOnce, ?lastEventId=
Logged out everywhere Sign-in page in every tab reauth REVOKED, failed refresh, auth broadcast (75.3)
API down when saving the note Note shown, then "Couldn't save your note. Try again", old note restored Field-level rollback
Another tab changed the note The other tab's note appears with "Updated in another window" VERSION_CONFLICT with current, or invalidate on a same-status event
Cancel too late Dialog explains; status shows Packing 409 ORDER_NOT_CANCELLABLE, refetch
Unknown status from a newer API "Updated" badge, timeline still correct openEnum (74.7)
Offline "You're offline. Showing status from 7:12 pm" navigator.onLine, online event reopens
Tracking page for someone else's order "We couldn't find that order" 404, not-found.tsx

Backend side (NestJS)

What the client logic above relies on from the API, each a deliberate design decision:

  • Event IDs that are stable replay cursors (Redis Stream entry IDs) and a replay window long enough for a tunnel or a lock screen: MAXLEN ~ 500 per customer covers far more than 15 minutes for one customer's orders.
  • reset when the gap is too old, so the client never silently misses a change.
  • A VERSION_CONFLICT body that includes the current state, saving a round trip at the exact moment the user is confused.
  • Idempotent writes with keys stored for 24 hours (15.12), so a note saved offline and retried on reconnect cannot apply twice.
  • 304 responses for refetches, so the polling fallback costs about 200 bytes per poll per viewer when nothing changed.

Production scenario

In the first month: 12 % of tracking sessions saw at least one reconnect (mostly mobile networks), 0.8 % fell back to polling at some point, and the median time in polling was 50 s before the stream recovered. Reauth reconnects happened about once per 15 minutes per open page, invisible to users (median gap 0.9 s, events replayed). Delivery-note saves: 9,000 a day, 0.3 % conflicts (two devices), 0.1 % rolled back after network errors and saved on the user's retry.

Failure scenario

The first release opened the EventSource inside TrackingLive and another inside the order list's hook. Customers who opened the list and then a tracking page in the same tab held two streams; with React Strict Mode in development the double mount (71.4) briefly made four, and the per-user cap of 6 was reached by customers with three tabs open. The seventh connection got 429, which EventSource reported only as a closed stream, and those tabs dropped into polling with a "Reconnecting" banner that never went away. Moving the stream into one reference-counted provider per tab, and closing it when no live order needs it, fixed both the cap and the banner.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Two EventSources in one tab, from separate components; one provider per tab.
  • Manual reopen without ?lastEventId= loses events between the close and the reopen.
  • Status-based hints drifting from the server's rules; import them from @shop/contracts and treat them as hints.
  • Rolling back a whole snapshot after a failed save erases a status that arrived by SSE meanwhile; roll back the field.
