  • Announcing every event floods screen reader users; announce status changes only.
  • Strict Mode double effects opening two streams; the effect's cleanup must close the stream (71.4).
  • Terminal orders kept live for hours; close when nothing needs the stream.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior treats the stream as one more writer to the query cache, with the same rules as mutations: versioned, idempotent, field-level. They design the connection as a state machine with an honest UI for every state, and they assume the transport will hide the information they want (status codes) and plan around it. They make optimistic updates only where being briefly wrong is harmless (a note) and keep money-touching actions pessimistic (cancel). And they count connections per tab and per user, because a live feature's cost and its failure modes both live in the connection count.

Common mistakes

  • Reading pushed data into component state next to a cache that disagrees.
  • No polling fallback, so a failed stream means a frozen page.
  • "Live" indicators that lie when the stream is down.
  • Optimistic cancel for an action that races with the warehouse.
  • Forgetting pageshow and online events, so a restored or reconnected page stays stale.

Interview questions

  1. How do you handle a session expiring while an SSE stream is open? Expected answer: the server ends the stream with a reauth event; the client refreshes once (single-flight), then reopens with the last event ID as a query parameter, because a new EventSource does not send Last-Event-ID.
  2. EventSource closed for good. What happened, and what do you do? Expected answer: you cannot see the status code; try a refresh, reopen with backoff, and fall back to polling with an honest banner after repeated failures.
  3. Why roll back only the changed field after a failed optimistic update? Expected answer: other writers (SSE events, other mutations) may have changed other fields meanwhile; a full snapshot rollback erases them.
  4. When should an action not be optimistic? Expected answer: when it races with other actors and being wrong costs money or trust, like cancelling an order that may already be packing.
  5. How do you stop a tab left open overnight from holding a stream? Expected answer: reference-count subscribers, close when every tracked order is terminal or the tab has been hidden for a while, reopen on visibility.

Practical exercise

Build LiveOrdersProvider, TrackingLive, the optimistic note and the pessimistic cancel.

Acceptance criteria:

  • One EventSource per tab across the list and tracking pages, verified in DevTools with Strict Mode on.
  • Duplicate and out-of-order events change nothing; a same-status event triggers exactly one tracking refetch.
  • Expiring the session while the page is open reconnects within 3 s with no missed events.
  • With the realtime service stopped, the banner appears within 10 s, polling runs every 30 s, and the stream returns within 2 minutes of the service coming back.
  • A note saved while offline is retried with the same idempotency key and saved once.
  • A screen reader (VoiceOver or NVDA) announces each status change once and no ETA-only changes.

79.7 Auth across both sides: cookies, refresh and guards

Concept

The tracking feature adds no new authentication; it uses the design of Part 75 exactly, and this section checks every path the feature opens against it. The decisions being reused (75.10): the Next.js BFF owns the cookies; __Host-session holds a 15-minute access JWT with audience shop-web; __Secure-refresh is scoped to Path=/api/auth and rotated by the BFF's /api/auth/refresh route; __Host-csrf is a double-submit token bound to the session ID; NestJS accepts the session JWT from the cookie or a Bearer header, answers 401 with an X-Auth-Error code, and checks a Redis epoch (auth:epoch:<userId>) so "log out everywhere" takes effect on the next request.

The feature has five paths into the system, and each must be authenticated, authorised and protected against cross-site requests:

Path Who authenticates Authorisation CSRF
Page load GET /orders/:id Next.js middleware (optimistic JWT check), then the server component's API call NestJS: the order must belong to the user (in the SQL WHERE) Not needed: a GET that changes nothing
Refetch GET /api/v1/orders/:id/tracking NestJS JwtAuthGuard, cookie via the rewrites proxy Same ownership query Not needed
Stream GET /api/v1/orders/events NestJS JwtAuthGuard at connect; expiry and epoch while open (79.4) Stream key is the user's own ID; no order ID from the client is trusted Not needed; SameSite=Lax cookies are not sent on cross-site subresource requests
Note PATCH and cancel POST NestJS JwtAuthGuard Ownership in the conditional UPDATE CsrfGuard: X-CSRF-Token must equal __Host-csrf and match the session ID (75.6)
Status changes from the warehouse ServiceAuthGuard (service token or mTLS) Service scopes Not reachable by browsers

Why does it exist?

Because live features tend to open side doors. A stream endpoint written in a hurry takes ?orderId= from the client and streams that order's events to whoever asks. A refetch route added "just for the page" skips the ownership check because "the page already checked". A note endpoint called from a client component forgets the CSRF header because the developer tested it from the same origin. Each one is an incident: an IDOR leaking addresses, or a cross-site request changing someone's delivery note.

Mental model

Imagine a building with several entrances: the main door, the car park lift, a loading bay and a side gate for staff. Securing the main door does nothing if the lift goes straight to every floor. Part 75 built the badge system; this section walks every entrance of the new wing and checks that each one reads the badge.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant N as NextBFF
    participant A as NestJS
    participant R as Redis
    B->>N: GET /orders/1d6c with __Host-session
    N->>N: middleware verifies JWT, audience shop-web
    N->>A: GET /v1/orders/1d6c/tracking, Bearer token
    A->>R: GET auth:epoch:u-5f2
    A-->>N: 200, order belongs to u-5f2
    B->>A: GET /api/v1/orders/events, cookie, via CloudFront
    A-->>B: stream for u-5f2 only
    B->>A: PATCH note with X-CSRF-Token and Idempotency-Key
    A-->>B: 200 fresh tracking
    Note over A,B: 15 min later the stream sends reauth EXPIRED
    B->>N: POST /api/auth/refresh with __Secure-refresh
    N-->>B: new __Host-session
    B->>A: GET /api/v1/orders/events?lastEventId=...

Three points that are easy to get wrong:

  1. Middleware is not authorisation. It verifies that a session exists and redirects when it does not (75.10); it cannot know who owns order 1d6c. The ownership check lives in NestJS, in the SQL, on every route that takes an order ID. The Next.js server component trusts the API's 404.
  2. The stream takes no order ID. It streams the authenticated user's own events (orders:events:<userId>). The client filters by order ID for display only; filtering is not security.
  3. Refresh happens in one place. Client-side fetches go through authFetch (75.3), which refreshes on 401 UNAUTHENTICATED and retries once; the stream's reauth path calls the same refreshOnce. There is no second refresh implementation for "the live part".

Practical example — the attacker's view

A security review tried five attacks against staging:

Attempt Result Why
Change the order ID in the URL to another customer's 404 page Ownership in the WHERE
curl the stream with another user's ID as a parameter The caller's own events The stream ignores client-supplied identity
A page on evil.example posts a form to PATCH /api/v1/orders/:id/delivery-note 403 CSRF_FAILED SameSite=Lax blocks the cookie on cross-site POST and the CSRF header is missing
Replay a stolen expired session cookie 401 with X-Auth-Error: UNAUTHENTICATED 15-minute JWT; the refresh cookie is never sent outside /api/auth
"Log out everywhere" on another device while the stream is open reauth REVOKED within 20 s, then sign-in Epoch checked on the heartbeat

React / Next.js example

The client write helper, which is the only way the page calls the note endpoint:

// apps/web/src/orders/api.ts (excerpt)
import { authFetch } from '@/api/auth-fetch';                     // 81.3: refresh on 401, retry once
import { csrfHeader } from '@/api/csrf';                          // 81.6: { 'X-CSRF-Token': <__Host-csrf> }
import { toApiError } from '@/api/errors';
import { OrderTrackingRead } from './tracking.read';
import type { UpdateDeliveryNote } from '@shop/contracts';

export async function saveDeliveryNote(orderId: string, body: UpdateDeliveryNote, idempotencyKey: string) {
  const res = await authFetch(`/api/v1/orders/${encodeURIComponent(orderId)}/delivery-note`, {
    method: 'PATCH',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Idempotency-Key': idempotencyKey, ...csrfHeader() },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),                                   // a string, so authFetch can resend it after a refresh
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw await toApiError(res);
  return OrderTrackingRead.parse(await res.json());
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The note controller shows the full guard stack in one place:

// apps/api/src/orders/delivery-note.controller.ts
import { Body, Controller, Param, ParseUUIDPipe, Patch, UseGuards, UseInterceptors } from '@nestjs/common';
import { Throttle } from '@nestjs/throttler';
import { UpdateDeliveryNoteSchema, type UpdateDeliveryNote, type OrderTracking } from '@shop/contracts';
import { JwtAuthGuard } from '../auth/jwt-auth.guard';               // cookie or Bearer, epoch check (81.3)
import { CsrfGuard } from '../security/csrf.guard';                  // 81.6
import { UserThrottlerGuard } from '../common/user-throttler.guard';
import { IdempotencyInterceptor } from '../common/idempotency.interceptor'; // 8.12
import { ZodValidationPipe } from '../common/zod-validation.pipe';
import { CurrentUser, type AuthUser } from '../auth/current-user.decorator';
import { DeliveryNoteService } from './delivery-note.service';

@Controller('v1/orders')
@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard, CsrfGuard, UserThrottlerGuard)              // order matters: who, then cross-site, then rate
export class DeliveryNoteController {
  constructor(private readonly notes: DeliveryNoteService) {}

  @Patch(':id/delivery-note')
  @Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 } })
  @UseInterceptors(IdempotencyInterceptor)                           // replays the first response for a repeated key
  update(@CurrentUser() user: AuthUser, @Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
         @Body(new ZodValidationPipe(UpdateDeliveryNoteSchema)) body: UpdateDeliveryNote): Promise<OrderTracking> {
    return this.notes.updateNote(user.id, id, body);                 // ownership inside the UPDATE (85.4)
  }
}

Because the browser reaches NestJS through the same origin (the rewrites proxy and the CloudFront path behaviour), the API needs no CORS configuration for this feature; adding enableCors "to be safe" would only widen what other origins can do.

Production scenario

The feature's security review took half a day because there was nothing new to design: the review was the table of paths above, each mapped to an existing guard, plus the five attack attempts. One finding: the first version of the internal status endpoint lived under /v1/orders/:id/status, reachable through the public rewrites proxy and protected only by ServiceAuthGuard. It was moved under /internal, which CloudFront and the BFF do not route at all, so a mistake in the guard could not expose it.

Failure scenario

In another company's tracking feature, the stream endpoint was GET /orders/:id/events, authenticated but without an ownership check, "because the order ID is a UUID nobody can guess". Order IDs appeared in tracking links shared by customers on social media and in support screenshots. A scraper collected 30,000 IDs from public posts and subscribed to all of them, receiving names, delivery windows and rider first names in real time. UUIDs are identifiers, not secrets; the fix was the same ownership check every other route had, and a per-user stream instead of per-order streams.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Shared tracking links ("share my delivery with a friend") need a separate, scoped, expiring token and a reduced view, not the customer's session (a future feature, designed as such).
  • Support agents viewing an order use a different audience and role, checked by the API (75.5), never the customer route with a flag.
  • The refresh cookie never reaches the stream or the API: its Path=/api/auth keeps it out of every other request (75.2).
  • Cookie size: the session JWT must stay small (75.2); the stream sends it on every reconnect.
  • CSRF on GET: none needed as long as GET routes never change state; a "mark notifications read on view" side effect would break that rule.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior lists every path a new feature opens and maps each to an existing control, adding new controls only where the feature truly differs (the stream's lifetime). They keep authorisation in the API and in the data query, treat identifiers as public, keep internal endpoints off the public routing table entirely, and refuse "temporary" CORS. Reusing the auth design unchanged is the goal, not a shortcut: every reuse is one less thing to get wrong.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting middleware or the page for authorisation.
  • Order-scoped streams without ownership checks.
  • Internal endpoints routed through the public proxy.
  • A second refresh implementation for the live connection.

Interview questions

  1. Where is "this order belongs to this user" checked, and why there? Expected answer: in the API, inside the SQL of every route that takes an order ID; it is the only layer that cannot be bypassed.
  2. Why does the stream not take an order ID? Expected answer: identity comes from the session; the stream is the user's own events; client-side filtering is display only.
  3. Does the SSE GET need CSRF protection? Expected answer: no state change, and SameSite=Lax cookies are not sent on cross-site subresource requests; the writes need it.
  4. Why no CORS for this feature? Expected answer: everything is same-origin through the BFF and CloudFront; CORS would only add exposure.

Practical exercise

Run the attack table against your staging environment.

Acceptance criteria:

  • All five attempts behave as listed, recorded with request IDs.
  • A test fails if any route under /v1/orders/:id lacks the user in its query (a unit test over the repository calls, or an integration test with two users).
  • /internal/* is unreachable from the public CloudFront distribution.
  • "Log out everywhere" cuts an open stream within 25 s, verified in Playwright (79.9).

79.8 Performance: caching, payload size and a Core Web Vitals check

Concept

Performance for this feature has three parts. Load performance: the first view of the page (TTFB, LCP, CLS) on a mid-range phone over 4G. Interaction performance: INP when the customer saves a note or opens the cancel dialog. Steady-state cost: what 60,000 open pages cost the servers and the network while nothing happens. Part 76 gave the tools and budgets; this section applies them and records the numbers.

Why does it exist?

Because live pages have a performance failure mode static pages do not: they get worse the longer they are open. A page that re-renders the whole timeline on every event, or leaks a listener per reconnect, has a fine Lighthouse score and a terrible INP after twenty minutes. And the steady-state cost (connections, heartbeats, refetches) is paid by the backend for every open tab, all evening.

Mental model

Imagine a taxi company's dispatch screen. It must come on quickly when a dispatcher sits down (load), respond instantly when they click (interaction), and still be responsive at the end of an eight-hour shift without the office's network groaning (steady state).

How it works

What is cached where (76.9):

Resource Where cached Policy
/_next/static/* (framework and TrackingLive chunks) CloudFront and browser public, max-age=31536000, immutable, content-hashed (78.3)
Tracking HTML Nowhere shared private, no-cache (dynamic, personal); bfcache allowed, guarded (79.5)
GET /v1/orders/:id/tracking Browser HTTP cache and TanStack Query private, no-cache plus ETag; staleTime 30 s
Stream Nothing Caching disabled at CloudFront; no-cache
Product images in the item list CloudFront and browser Hashed URLs, immutable, sized srcset (76.8)

Payload budget:

Item Size Note
HTML (first response, streamed) 11 KB gzip Status, window, timeline, items, address
TrackingLive client chunk 14 KB gzip Provider, merge, banner, note form; cancel dialog lazy-loaded (5 KB)
Tracking JSON 2.1 KB, 0.9 KB gzip Refetch is usually a 304 of about 200 bytes
Stream event about 250 bytes Heartbeat 20 bytes every 20 s

Rendering cost per event: applyOrderEvent replaces only the tracking object; Timeline and OrderItems are memoised by their props (items never change), so an event re-renders the heading, the ETA line, the banner and the timeline's last step. Measured with the React Profiler (71.12): 1.8 ms per event commit on a Moto G Power class device.

Steady-state cost at 60,000 open pages: 60,000 connections on 8 realtime tasks; 3,000 heartbeats per second in total (60 KB/s); about 70 reauth reconnects per second (each a refresh at the BFF, p95 31 ms in 75.10, and a stream reconnect with a short replay); about 40 refetch 304s per second from focus events. Compared with the polling page's 6,000 full responses per second, the API's tracking load fell by about 99 %.

Practical example — the Core Web Vitals check before launch

The team ran three checks, matching 76.11's practice:

  1. Lighthouse CI on every preview (78.11), mobile emulation, against a seeded order, with a session cookie for the test customer:
// apps/web/lighthouserc.js (excerpt)  Lighthouse CI 0.14; plain JS config file
module.exports = {
  ci: {
    collect: {
      url: [`${process.env.PREVIEW_URL}/orders/${process.env.SEEDED_ORDER_ID}`],
      numberOfRuns: 3,
      settings: { preset: 'perf', extraHeaders: JSON.stringify({ Cookie: process.env.LHCI_SESSION_COOKIE }) },
    },
    assert: {
      assertions: {
        'largest-contentful-paint': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 2000 }],
        'cumulative-layout-shift': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 0.05 }],
        'total-blocking-time': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 150 }],          // lab proxy for INP
        'resource-summary:script:size': ['error', { maxNumericValue: 180_000 }],
      },
    },
  },
};

The session cookie for a test customer comes from the test-support API (77.7) in the preview environment only.

  1. A long-session test in Playwright: open the page, push 200 status and ETA events through the test-support API over 10 minutes, force 30 reconnects with page.route aborts, then measure: JS heap growth under 2 MB (performance.memory in Chromium), event listener count on window and document stable (CDP's DOMDebugger.getEventListeners through page.context().newCDPSession(page)), and an interaction (open and close the cancel dialog) under 100 ms in a performance trace.

  2. RUM after a 5 % flag rollout (78.5): p75 mobile LCP 1.4 s, INP 70 ms, CLS 0.01 for the tracking route, compared with the old polling page's LCP 3.8 s, INP 180 ms (it re-rendered the whole page every poll), CLS 0.12 (the ETA line appeared late).

React / Next.js example

The timeline only re-renders the steps that changed, and keys are stable (71.3):

// apps/web/app/(shop)/orders/[id]/Timeline.tsx
'use client';
import { memo } from 'react';
import { STATUS_COPY } from '@/orders/status-copy';
import { formatTime } from '@/orders/format';
import type { OrderTrackingView } from '@/orders/tracking.read';

type Step = OrderTrackingView['timeline'][number];

const StepRow = memo(function StepRow({ step, timeZone, current }: { step: Step; timeZone: string; current: boolean }) {
  return (
    <li aria-current={current ? 'step' : undefined}>
      <span>{STATUS_COPY[step.status].label}</span> <time dateTime={step.at}>{formatTime(step.at, timeZone)}</time>
    </li>
  );
});

export function Timeline({ steps, timeZone, current }: { steps: Step[]; timeZone: string; current: string }) {
  return (
    <ol className="timeline">
      {steps.map((s) => (
        <StepRow key={`${s.status}-${s.at}`} step={s} timeZone={timeZone} current={s.status === current} />  // stable keys
      ))}
    </ol>
  );
}

Backend side (NestJS)

The backend's share of the page's speed (76.10):

  • One request for the page: the tracking endpoint returns everything the shell needs (summary, timeline, flags for the UI), so server rendering makes one API call, not four.
  • Indexes for the two reads: orders by primary key (with user_id in the predicate) and order_status_events (order_id, version) from the unique constraint, both under 1 ms.
  • ETag and 304 on refetches.
  • Small events: the stream never carries items, addresses or notes.
  • SSE over HTTP/2 at CloudFront, so a tab's stream shares one connection with its other requests (72.8's six-connection problem does not apply).
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT status, version, occurred_at FROM order_status_events
 WHERE order_id = '1d6c0b6e-2f3a-4c55-9d1e-8a7b6c5d4e3f' ORDER BY version ASC LIMIT 20;

 Limit  (cost=0.57..12.83 rows=6 width=29) (actual time=0.021..0.026 rows=6 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=5
   ->  Index Scan using order_status_events_order_id_version_key on order_status_events
         (cost=0.57..12.83 rows=6 width=29) (actual time=0.020..0.024 rows=6 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (order_id = '1d6c0b6e-2f3a-4c55-9d1e-8a7b6c5d4e3f'::uuid)
 Planning Time: 0.092 ms
 Execution Time: 0.041 ms

Production scenario

Two weeks after full rollout, the tracking route was the fastest authenticated page on the site by p75 LCP. The realtime tasks cost about 230 dollars a month at the evening peak's scale (8 Fargate tasks of 1 vCPU and 2 GB, scaled down to 3 overnight), about 0.002 cents per tracked order, a tenth of the cost ceiling. The orders API's peak CPU fell by 28 % because the polling traffic was gone.

Failure scenario

A later change added a countdown ("Arriving in 12 minutes") that updated every second with setInterval and setState at the top of TrackingLive. Every second the whole island re-rendered, including the timeline and the note form; on low-end Android phones INP rose to 340 ms because a keypress in the note field often landed during a render, and battery drain complaints followed. The countdown moved into its own tiny component with its own state, updating every 30 seconds (minutes do not need second precision), and INP returned to 70 ms.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Long-open pages: leaks of listeners or timers per reconnect; test with long sessions, not only Lighthouse.
  • Re-rendering everything per event; memoise stable regions and keep live state low in the tree.
  • Fonts or icons arriving late and shifting the status heading; preload the subset, reserve space.
  • Large timelines for orders with many ETA changes; cap at 20 steps.
  • Heartbeat frequency: too frequent wastes battery and bandwidth; too rare lets proxies and NATs drop idle connections (35.8); 20 s fits CloudFront and ALB timeouts.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior budgets the three kinds of performance separately: first view in the lab and the field, interactions with a profiler on a slow phone, and steady state as a server-and-network cost per open page per hour. They keep the live part of the tree small, measure long sessions as well as first loads, and count the backend savings, because a live feature done well should make the system cheaper than the polling it replaced.

Common mistakes

  • Only measuring first load for a page people keep open.
  • Live state at the top of the tree.
  • Caching personal responses in shared caches "for speed".
  • Second-by-second timers for minute-level information.

Interview questions

  1. How do you measure performance for a page users keep open for 30 minutes? Expected answer: first-load Web Vitals plus a long-session test (memory, listeners, interaction latency after many events and reconnects) and RUM INP over the whole visit.
  2. What does the backend contribute to this page's LCP? Expected answer: one fast aggregated read, indexed queries, an ETag, and server rendering's API latency inside TTFB.
  3. How did SSE change the backend cost compared with polling? Expected answer: from thousands of full responses per second to idle connections, heartbeats and a few hundred small events and reconnects per second.

Practical exercise

Run the three checks on your preview environment.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Lighthouse CI assertions as above pass on three runs against a seeded order.
  • The long-session test shows heap growth under 2 MB and a stable listener count after 200 events and 30 reconnects.
  • A Profiler recording shows each event commit under 4 ms on a throttled CPU (4x slowdown).
  • A one-paragraph cost note compares the realtime tasks with the polling traffic they replaced.

79.9 Tests: backend unit and integration, frontend component, one journey across both

Concept

The test suite follows Part 77's rule: every serious risk gets one honest test at the cheapest level that can see it (77.1), and the suite is proved by breaking the product on purpose (77.13). Live features add two kinds of risk that need care: time (events arrive later, out of order, twice, or not at all) and connections (streams drop, expire and reconnect). Most of both can be tested without a browser; one Playwright journey proves the whole path.

Why does it exist?

Because the bugs that matter here are sequences, and sequences are where manual testing is weakest. "An event for version 8 arrives while a note save for version 7 is in flight" is easy to describe, hard to reproduce by hand, and trivial to script with a fake event source and MSW.

Mental model

Imagine testing a train signalling system. You test each signal's logic on a bench, the interlocking between signals in a simulator where you can make trains arrive in any order, and you run one real train down the real line before opening it. You do not test signal timing by running real trains.

How it works

The plan:

# Risk Level Tool
1 Illegal transitions accepted Unit Vitest table over canTransition in @shop/contracts
2 Two concurrent transitions both succeed API integration Jest, Testcontainers PostgreSQL (41.7)
3 A committed change produces no event (or a rolled-back one does) API integration Relay test with a real PostgreSQL and Redis
4 Stream delivers other users' events; misses replay API integration Node fetch reading the SSE body
5 Stream outlives expiry or revocation API integration Same, with a short token and an epoch bump
6 Cache merge applies duplicates or out-of-order events Unit applyOrderEvent with a real QueryClient
7 Live UI shows stale data as live; no fallback Component Vitest, Testing Library, a fake EventSource, MSW
8 Note rollback erases a status that arrived meanwhile Component Same
9 The event contract drifts Contract Pact message (79.2)
10 Whole path: commit to screen, reconnect, logout everywhere E2E Playwright on the Compose stack (77.11)
11 Page budgets Performance Lighthouse CI (79.8)
12 Accessibility of every state Accessibility axe at four states (77.10)

Practical example — the stream, tested without a browser

An SSE response is a text stream. Node's fetch exposes it as a ReadableStream, so an integration test can read events directly:

// apps/api/test/order-events.int-spec.ts  (Jest, the app booted with configureApp, Testcontainers PG and Redis)
import { bootTestApp, type TestApp } from './support/boot';

async function readEvents(res: Response, until: (events: { event: string; data: string; id?: string }[]) => boolean, ms = 5000) {
  const reader = res.body!.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
  const events: { event: string; data: string; id?: string }[] = [];
  let buf = '';
  const deadline = Date.now() + ms;
  while (Date.now() < deadline && !until(events)) {
    const { value, done } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    buf += value;
    let i: number;
    while ((i = buf.indexOf('\n\n')) >= 0) {                    // an SSE message ends with a blank line
      const block = buf.slice(0, i); buf = buf.slice(i + 2);
      const f = Object.fromEntries(block.split('\n').map((l) => [l.slice(0, l.indexOf(':')), l.slice(l.indexOf(':') + 1).trim()]));
      if (f.event || f.data) events.push({ event: f.event ?? 'message', data: f.data ?? '', id: f.id });
    }
  }
  await reader.cancel();                                         // closes the stream: exercises the server's teardown
  return events;
}

let t: TestApp;
beforeAll(async () => { t = await bootTestApp({ withRelay: true }); });
afterAll(() => t.close());

it('streams only the caller\'s events, in version order, after a commit', async () => {
  const asha = await t.seed.customerWithOrder({ status: 'PAID' });
  const ravi = await t.seed.customerWithOrder({ status: 'PAID' });
  const res = await fetch(`${t.url}/v1/orders/events`, { headers: { Cookie: `__Host-session=${asha.token}` } });
  expect(res.headers.get('content-type')).toMatch(/text\/event-stream/);

  await t.status.transition({ orderId: ravi.orderId, to: 'PACKING', source: 'warehouse' });   // someone else's
  await t.status.transition({ orderId: asha.orderId, to: 'PACKING', source: 'warehouse' });
  await t.status.transition({ orderId: asha.orderId, to: 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY', source: 'dispatch' });

  const events = await readEvents(res, (es) => es.filter((e) => e.event === 'order').length >= 2);
  const orders = events.filter((e) => e.event === 'order').map((e) => JSON.parse(e.data));
  expect(orders.map((o) => [o.orderId, o.status])).toEqual([
    [asha.orderId, 'PACKING'], [asha.orderId, 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY'],
  ]);                                                             // nothing of Ravi's
  expect(orders[1].version).toBeGreaterThan(orders[0].version);
});

it('replays from lastEventId and ends with reauth when the session is revoked', async () => {
  const c = await t.seed.customerWithOrder({ status: 'PAID' });
  const first = await fetch(`${t.url}/v1/orders/events`, { headers: { Cookie: `__Host-session=${c.token}` } });
  await t.status.transition({ orderId: c.orderId, to: 'PACKING', source: 'warehouse' });
  const [e1] = (await readEvents(first, (es) => es.some((e) => e.event === 'order'))).filter((e) => e.event === 'order');

  await t.status.transition({ orderId: c.orderId, to: 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY', source: 'dispatch' });  // while disconnected
  const second = await fetch(`${t.url}/v1/orders/events?lastEventId=${e1.id}`, { headers: { Cookie: `__Host-session=${c.token}` } });
  await t.auth.logoutEverywhere(c.userId);                       // bumps auth:epoch (81.3)
  const events = await readEvents(second, (es) => es.some((e) => e.event === 'reauth'), 30_000);
  expect(events.find((e) => e.event === 'order')?.data).toContain('OUT_FOR_DELIVERY');            // replayed
  expect(JSON.parse(events.find((e) => e.event === 'reauth')!.data)).toEqual({ reason: 'REVOKED' });
}, 40_000);

The second test waits up to one heartbeat interval (20 s) for the revocation check; in the test configuration the heartbeat is 1 s so the test takes about 2 s.

React / Next.js example — the live island with a fake stream

jsdom has no EventSource. A small fake gives the test full control over timing:

// apps/web/src/test/fake-event-source.ts
type Listener = (e: MessageEvent<string>) => void;

export class FakeEventSource {
  static instances: FakeEventSource[] = [];
  static readonly CONNECTING = 0; static readonly OPEN = 1; static readonly CLOSED = 2;
  readyState = FakeEventSource.CONNECTING;
  onopen: (() => void) | null = null;
  onerror: (() => void) | null = null;
  private listeners = new Map<string, Listener[]>();
  constructor(public url: string) { FakeEventSource.instances.push(this); }
  addEventListener(type: string, fn: Listener) { this.listeners.set(type, [...(this.listeners.get(type) ?? []), fn]); }
  removeEventListener(type: string, fn: Listener) { this.listeners.set(type, (this.listeners.get(type) ?? []).filter((f) => f !== fn)); }
  close() { this.readyState = FakeEventSource.CLOSED; }
  // test helpers
  open() { this.readyState = FakeEventSource.OPEN; this.onopen?.(); }
  emit(type: string, data: unknown, id = `${Date.now()}-0`) {
    const e = new MessageEvent(type, { data: JSON.stringify(data), lastEventId: id });
    (this.listeners.get(type) ?? []).forEach((fn) => fn(e));
  }
  fail(permanently: boolean) { this.readyState = permanently ? FakeEventSource.CLOSED : FakeEventSource.CONNECTING; this.onerror?.(); }
}
// apps/web/app/(shop)/orders/[id]/TrackingLive.test.tsx
import { act, screen, within } from '@testing-library/react';
import { http, HttpResponse, delay } from 'msw';
import { beforeEach, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { server } from '@/test/msw/server';
import { API } from '@/test/msw/checkout.handlers';
import { aTracking } from '@/test/builders';                    // parses through OrderTrackingRead (83.6)
import { renderWithProviders } from '@/test/render';
import { FakeEventSource } from '@/test/fake-event-source';
import { LiveOrdersProvider } from '@/orders/LiveOrdersProvider';
import { TrackingLive } from './TrackingLive';

vi.mock('@/api/auth-fetch', async (orig) => ({ ...(await orig<object>()), refreshOnce: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(true) }));

beforeEach(() => { FakeEventSource.instances = []; vi.stubGlobal('EventSource', FakeEventSource); });

const initial = aTracking({ id: 'o-1', status: 'PACKING', version: 6, deliveryNote: 'Ring once' });
const renderPage = () => renderWithProviders(
  <LiveOrdersProvider enabled><TrackingLive initial={initial} live /></LiveOrdersProvider>);

it('applies newer events, ignores old ones, and announces status changes', async () => {
  renderPage();
  const es = FakeEventSource.instances[0];
  act(() => es.open());
  act(() => es.emit('order', { orderId: 'o-1', status: 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY', version: 7, updatedAt: '2026-11-05T13:45:27Z',
    summary: 'Out for delivery. Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm.' }));
  expect(screen.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveTextContent('Out for delivery');
  expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toHaveTextContent('Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm');

  act(() => es.emit('order', { orderId: 'o-1', status: 'PACKING', version: 6, updatedAt: '2026-11-05T13:40:00Z' }));
  expect(screen.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveTextContent('Out for delivery');   // stale event ignored
  expect(FakeEventSource.instances).toHaveLength(1);                                          // one stream per tab
});

it('keeps a status that arrived during a failed note save', async () => {
  server.use(http.patch(`${API}/orders/o-1/delivery-note`, async () => { await delay(50); return HttpResponse.error(); }));
  const { user } = renderPage();
  const es = FakeEventSource.instances[0];
  act(() => es.open());
  const field = screen.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Delivery note' });
  await user.clear(field); await user.type(field, 'Leave with security');
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save note' }));
  act(() => es.emit('order', { orderId: 'o-1', status: 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY', version: 7, updatedAt: '2026-11-05T13:45:27Z' }));

  expect(await screen.findByText("Couldn't save your note. Try again")).toBeVisible();
  expect(field).toHaveValue('Ring once');                                                    // note rolled back
  expect(screen.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveTextContent('Out for delivery');  // status kept
});

it('says honestly when live updates stop, and polls', async () => {
  let polls = 0;
  server.use(http.get(`${API}/orders/o-1/tracking`, () => { polls++; return HttpResponse.json(initial); }));
  vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });
  renderPage();
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    await act(async () => { FakeEventSource.instances.at(-1)!.fail(true); await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(10_000); });
  }
  expect(within(screen.getByRole('region', { name: /out for|packing/i })).getByText(/Showing status from/)).toBeVisible();
  await act(() => vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(31_000));
  expect(polls).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

The journey across both

One Playwright test on the Compose stack (77.11), using the test-support API to move the order the way the warehouse would:

// apps/web/e2e/live-tracking.spec.ts
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { test } from './fixtures';                               // 83.8: per-worker customer and storage state

test('status changes appear live, survive a disconnect, and stop at logout everywhere', async ({ page, customer, api, browser }) => {
  const orderId = await api.placeSeedOrder(customer.cartId);     // PAID
  let documents = 0;
  page.on('request', (r) => { if (r.resourceType() === 'document') documents++; });
  await page.goto(`/orders/${orderId}`);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveText('Order confirmed');

  await api.advance(orderId, 'PACKING');                         // POST /__e2e/orders/:id/status
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveText('Packing your order', { timeout: 2000 }); // the freshness target

  await page.context().setOffline(true);
  await api.advance(orderId, 'OUT_FOR_DELIVERY', { eta: { from: '2026-11-05T13:55:00Z', to: '2026-11-05T14:10:00Z' } });
  await expect(page.getByText(/Showing status from/)).toBeVisible({ timeout: 15_000 });
  await page.context().setOffline(false);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 })).toHaveText('Out for delivery', { timeout: 10_000 }); // replayed
  await expect(page.getByText('Arriving 7:25 to 7:40 pm')).toBeVisible();
  expect(documents).toBe(1);                                     // no reload happened

  const other = await browser.newContext({ storageState: await page.context().storageState() });
  const otherPage = await other.newPage();
  await otherPage.goto('/account/security');
  await otherPage.getByRole('button', { name: 'Log out everywhere' }).click();
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/, { timeout: 25_000 });  // the stream's REVOKED reauth, then a failed refresh
  await other.close();
});

The last part changes the identity, so this test uses its own customer (77.8's rule), not the worker's.

Backend side (NestJS)

The test-support module of 77.7 gains one route, guarded and absent from production like the rest:

// apps/api/src/e2e-support/e2e-support.controller.ts (addition)
@Post('orders/:id/status')
advance(@Param('id', ParseUUIDPipe) id: string,
        @Body() body: { to: OrderEvent['status']; eta?: { from: string; to: string } }) {
  return this.status.transition({                                // the real service: real transaction, real outbox
    orderId: id, to: body.to, source: 'support',
    eta: body.eta ? { from: new Date(body.eta.from), to: new Date(body.eta.to) } : null,
  });
}

Using the real OrderStatusService matters: the journey then proves the outbox, the relay, Redis and the stream, not a shortcut that writes to Redis directly.

Production scenario

The tracking suite: 46 unit tests (2 s), 14 API integration tests (38 s, most of it container start-up shared with other suites), 22 component tests (6 s), 2 Pact interactions, 1 Playwright journey (24 s) plus the long-session performance test (10 minutes, nightly only), axe at four states. Breaking the product on purpose (77.13) before launch: removing the version guard failed tests 6 and 7; removing ownership from the stream failed test 4; publishing in the request instead of the outbox failed test 3 (a rolled-back transaction still produced an event); removing ?lastEventId= from the client's reopen failed test 10; removing the epoch check failed tests 5 and 10.

Failure scenario

The first version of the journey asserted the live update with await page.waitForTimeout(3000) followed by a text check, "to give the stream time". It passed for weeks. Then the relay's idle poll interval was raised from 100 ms to 1 s to save database load, freshness p95 went from 0.3 s to 1.4 s, and the test still passed because three seconds was generous. Nobody noticed that the freshness target had nearly been used up. Rewriting the assertion as a web-first toHaveText(..., { timeout: 2000 }) made the test encode the requirement (79.1) rather than a guess, and it caught the next regression: a CloudFront cache policy change that added 1.5 s of buffering.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Testing streams with fixed sleeps hides freshness regressions; assert with the NFR as the timeout.
  • Fakes that never fail: a fake EventSource must support permanent and temporary failures, or the fallback code is untested.
  • Journeys that bypass the outbox (writing straight to Redis) prove the UI but not the system.
  • Long heartbeat intervals in tests: make them configurable so revocation tests run in seconds.
  • Shared customers in tests that log out everywhere (77.8).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior turns each NFR into an assertion: the 2 s freshness target becomes a Playwright timeout, the "one stream per tab" rule becomes a count of fake instances, "never another customer's events" becomes an integration test with two customers. They test time and connections with fakes they control, and keep exactly one journey for the full path. And they treat the test-support API as part of the product, routed through the real services, because a shortcut in the test is a gap in the proof.

Common mistakes

  • No test for out-of-order or duplicate events.
  • No test for the fallback path.
  • E2E for every live behaviour, making the suite slow and flaky.
  • Mocking the stream at the module level so the provider's reconnection logic never runs.

Interview questions

  1. How do you test an SSE endpoint without a browser? Expected answer: read the response body as a text stream with Node fetch, parse messages on blank lines, assert events, and cancel the reader to test teardown.
  2. How do you test a client's handling of out-of-order events? Expected answer: a controllable fake EventSource emitting events in a chosen order, with a real query client, asserting the UI.
  3. What should the one end-to-end journey prove? Expected answer: commit to screen within the freshness target, recovery after a disconnect without a reload, and the auth cut-off, through the real outbox and stream.

Practical exercise

Build the twelve tests in the plan.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Each deliberate bug listed in the production scenario fails at least one test.
  • The Playwright journey's live assertion uses the 2 s freshness target as its timeout and passes 20 times with --repeat-each=20.
  • The fake EventSource covers open, events with IDs, temporary failure and permanent failure.
  • The suite adds under 90 s to the pull-request pipeline, excluding the nightly long-session test.

79.10 Deployment: containers, CDN, environment config and a flagged rollout

Concept

The feature ships as three containers built once per commit (78.2): the web image (Next.js standalone), and one API image run with two entry points, api (request/response) and realtime (streams only, 79.4). CloudFront routes each path to the right origin with the right caching and timeouts. Configuration differs per environment, the image does not. And the user-visible behaviour is released by a server-evaluated flag (78.5), ramped while the SLOs are watched, with a kill switch that falls back to polling.

Why does it exist?

Because the stream changes the operational profile of the system. Request/response tasks scale with requests per second; stream tasks scale with open connections and memory, and they must drain slowly on deploys. Mixing them means a reconnect storm competes with checkout for CPU, and a checkout deploy drops 60,000 streams. And because a live feature can fail in ways no test predicted, it needs a way to switch off in seconds without a deploy.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant that adds a phone line for order updates. You do not ask the chefs to answer it; you hire a separate person with their own headset, sized for how many calls are open, not how many dishes are cooked. And you keep a sign ready that says "Call back later, check the board" in case the phone system fails.

How it works

flowchart LR
    user["Browser"] --> cf["CloudFront shop.example"]
    cf -->|"/_next/static/*"| s3["S3 assets, immutable"]
    cf -->|"/api/v1/orders/events"| rtalb["ALB realtime target group"]
    cf -->|"/api/*, pages"| webalb["ALB web target group"]
    rtalb --> rt["realtime tasks: main.realtime.js"]
    webalb --> web["web tasks: Next.js standalone"]
    web -->|"rewrites /api/v1/*, SSR fetches"| api["api tasks: main.js, internal ALB"]
    rt --> redis[("Redis: streams, epochs, counters")]
    api --> pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    api --> redis
    relay["relay inside api tasks"] --> pg
    relay --> redis

CloudFront behaviours, most specific first:

Path pattern Origin Cache policy Origin request policy Timeouts
/_next/static/* S3 (OAC) Caching optimised, immutable None Default
/api/v1/orders/events Realtime ALB Caching disabled All viewer headers except Host, all cookies, all query strings (lastEventId) Origin response timeout 60 s (above the 20 s heartbeat); keep-alive 60 s
/api/* Web ALB Caching disabled All cookies, headers, query strings Response timeout 30 s
Default (*) Web ALB Caching disabled for personal pages; ISR pages use the origin's s-maxage All cookies 30 s

The ALB in front of the realtime tasks has its idle timeout raised from the default 60 s to 120 s; heartbeats every 20 s keep connections well inside both limits. CloudFront serves HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 to browsers, so a tab's stream shares one connection with its other requests.

Scaling and draining:

  • api: ECS target tracking on CPU at 55 %, 4 to 24 tasks.
  • realtime: target tracking on a custom CloudWatch metric, ActiveStreams per task (published every 30 s from the connection counter), target 7,500; memory as a second policy at 70 %. 3 tasks overnight, 8 to 10 at peak.
  • Deploys for realtime: rolling, minimumHealthyPercent 100 and maximumPercent 125, so new tasks come up before old ones stop; the target group's deregistration delay is 30 s; on SIGTERM the task sends jittered retry hints and completes its streams (79.4), so clients reconnect over about 10 s to the new tasks.

Environment configuration (78.2): the web image reads API_INTERNAL_URL, PUBLIC_SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT, PUBLIC_FLAGS_CLIENT_KEY and the release at runtime; the API image reads DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, JWT_PUBLIC_KEY, AUTH_ISSUER, SSE_HEARTBEAT_MS (20,000 in production, 1,000 in tests) and RELAY_ENABLED (true on api tasks, false on realtime tasks, so exactly one kind of task runs the relay). Secrets come from Secrets Manager into the task definitions (Part 46.11).

Rollout order, the expand and contract plan of Part 25 applied to this feature:

Step Change Safe because
1 Migration: new columns, tables, widened status CHECK Additive; old code ignores it
2 API: outbox and relay on, tracking endpoint, stream extensions; still emitting only old statuses Nobody calls the new endpoints yet
3 Web: tracking page and openEnum readers, behind flag live-tracking off (polling page shown) Dark launch
4 Mobile apps: release with new status labels Old apps keep working on old statuses
5 Flag ramp: staff, then 1 %, 10 %, 50 %, 100 % of customers over 9 days Each step gated on SLOs (below)
6 Warehouse and dispatch start sending PACKING and OUT_FOR_DELIVERY Only after old mobile builds fall below 1 % (74.9 telemetry)
7 Old polling page removed After 14 days at 100 % without a kill-switch use

Each ramp step waits for 24 hours of: tracking availability SLO burn under 1x (78.8), freshness p95 under 2 s, realtime task memory under 70 %, error-tracker issues for the tracking route not above baseline (78.6).

Practical example — the flag and its kill switch

The flag is evaluated on the server (78.5), so the first HTML already reflects it and nothing flickers. With live-tracking off, TrackingLive gets live={false} and polls every 30 s through the same query; the provider never opens a stream. That fallback is the kill switch: if the realtime tier fails, turning the flag off moves every new page view to polling within the flag service's propagation time (seconds). Pages already open need nothing extra: when their stream fails, the provider has already fallen back to polling (79.6), so the flag only has to stop new streams being opened.

// apps/web/src/flags/server.ts (addition to 84.5's SAFE_DEFAULTS)
const SAFE_DEFAULTS = {
  'live-tracking': false,          // if the flag service is unreachable, poll: slower, never broken
  // ...
} as const;

Backend side (NestJS)

The realtime task publishes its connection count for autoscaling, using the counter it already keeps per user plus a per-task gauge:

// apps/api/src/orders/stream-metrics.ts (realtime tasks only)
import { Injectable, OnModuleDestroy, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common';
import { CloudWatchClient, PutMetricDataCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-cloudwatch';

@Injectable()
export class StreamMetrics implements OnModuleInit, OnModuleDestroy {
  private active = 0;
  private timer?: NodeJS.Timeout;
  private readonly cw = new CloudWatchClient({});
  opened() { this.active++; }
  closed() { this.active--; }
  onModuleInit() {
    this.timer = setInterval(() => void this.cw.send(new PutMetricDataCommand({
      Namespace: 'Shop/Realtime',
      MetricData: [{ MetricName: 'ActiveStreams', Value: this.active, Unit: 'Count',
                     Dimensions: [{ Name: 'Service', Value: 'orders-realtime' }] }],   // averaged across tasks by the policy
    })).catch(() => undefined), 30_000);
  }
  onModuleDestroy() { clearInterval(this.timer); }
}

The same number is exported to Prometheus as a gauge (Part 43.3) for dashboards; CloudWatch is used here only because ECS target tracking reads it natively.

Production scenario

The 9-day ramp went: staff (300 users) found a timezone bug in the ETA for one store with a misconfigured zone; 1 % ran a weekend peak with no SLO burn; 10 % exposed the reconnect spike on realtime deploys (fixed with jittered retry hints before 50 %); 50 % and 100 % were uneventful. At 100 %, 64,000 peak streams ran on 9 realtime tasks. The kill switch was used once in the first quarter, for 22 minutes, during a Redis maintenance event that went wrong; customers saw "checking every 30 s" banners and no errors, and the tracking availability SLO burned 0.4 % of its budget.

Failure scenario

On staging, the first CloudFront configuration had a single behaviour for /api/* pointing at the web ALB, so the stream went through the Next.js rewrites proxy (73.8). Events arrived in bursts every 30 to 60 seconds, the CloudFront origin response timeout fired on quiet streams, and the Next.js tasks' memory grew with every held connection. The edge case had been written down in 73.8 ("streaming responses through rewrites may be held"), and the architecture had been designed to avoid it; only the CDN configuration had not been written to match. A specific behaviour for /api/v1/orders/events straight to the realtime ALB, added to the infrastructure code with a test that curls the stream through CloudFront and checks the first ping arrives within 25 s, closed it.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Behaviour ordering in CloudFront: the more specific stream path must come before /api/*.
  • Origin response timeout below the heartbeat cuts quiet streams.
  • ALB idle timeout default 60 s; raise it for streams.
  • Relay running on both task types doubles the claimers; harmless with SKIP LOCKED but wasteful; one flag decides.
  • Deregistration delay too long for streams that never finish; streams end on SIGTERM, so 30 s is enough.
  • Kill switch untested: rehearse it on staging monthly (Part 49.12).
  • Mobile enum order: emitting new statuses before old apps are gone breaks them (79.2).

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior deploys one artefact per service, gives long-lived connections their own tasks and scaling metric, writes the CDN routing as code with a test that the stream actually streams, and releases the behaviour separately from the code with a flag whose off position is a working product. They sequence the rollout so every step is reversible and gated on measurements, and they rehearse the kill switch before they need it.

Common mistakes

  • Streams on the same tasks as request/response traffic.
  • Scaling realtime tasks on CPU, which stays low while memory and connections run out.
  • One CDN behaviour for all API paths.
  • A flag whose off state is a broken page.

Interview questions

  1. Why run SSE on separate tasks from the API? Expected answer: different resource profile (connections and memory), different scaling metric, deploys and reconnect storms isolated from checkout (a bulkhead).
  2. What CDN and load balancer settings matter for SSE? Expected answer: caching disabled, all cookies and the query string forwarded, origin response and idle timeouts above the heartbeat, a specific path behaviour that bypasses buffering proxies, HTTP/2 to browsers.
  3. How do you roll out a live feature safely? Expected answer: additive migration, backend first, dark launch behind a server-evaluated flag with a working fallback, ramp on SLOs, emit new enum values only after old clients are gone.
  4. What metric do you autoscale stream servers on? Expected answer: active connections per task (and memory), not CPU.

Practical exercise

Deploy the feature to staging behind the flag.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Three services from two images, each image built once and promoted by digest.
  • A CloudFront test proves the stream's first ping arrives within 25 s through the CDN and that /api/v1/orders/*/tracking is never cached.
  • Realtime tasks scale out when 10,000 synthetic streams are opened (k6 or a small Node script) and scale in afterwards.
  • A rolling deploy of realtime tasks drops no events (replay), and reconnections spread over at least 10 s.
  • Turning live-tracking off makes new page views poll, with no errors, within one minute.

79.11 Observability: one trace from a browser click to a database write

Concept

Part 78.7 connected browser errors to backend traces with W3C traceparent. This feature has two journeys worth tracing. The write path: the customer clicks "Save note", the request crosses CloudFront, the BFF's proxy and NestJS, and ends in a PostgreSQL UPDATE and an outbox INSERT. The push path: a committed change travels from the outbox through the relay and Redis to the stream and the screen. The write path is one trace. The push path starts in a different process at a different time, so it is a second trace linked to the first through the traceparent stored in the outbox row (79.3).

Why does it exist?

Because "the note took ages to save" and "the status was late" are the two complaints this feature will get, and both cross five systems. Without a trace, the web team sees a slow request and the database team sees fast queries, and nobody sees the 900 ms the request spent queued behind a cold Next.js task. Without freshness metrics, a relay falling behind looks like nothing at all until support calls rise.

Mental model

Imagine a parcel tracking number that is printed on the customer's receipt, scanned at every depot, and also written on the delivery van's job sheet the next morning. The receipt and the job sheet are separate documents created at different times, but the shared number lets you follow the parcel from the shop counter to the doorstep.

How it works

sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant CF as CloudFront
    participant N as NextBFF
    participant A as NestJS
    participant P as Postgres
    participant RL as Relay
    participant RT as Realtime
    B->>CF: PATCH note, traceparent 00-4bf9...-01
    CF->>N: forwards headers
    N->>A: rewrites proxy keeps traceparent
    A->>P: UPDATE orders, INSERT outbox with traceparent
    P-->>A: COMMIT
    A-->>B: 200 fresh tracking, X-Request-Id
    RL->>P: claim outbox row, span linked to 4bf9
    RL->>RT: XADD and PUBLISH via Redis
    RT-->>B: event: order, about 300 ms after commit
  1. The browser starts the trace for the user action with the small generator of 78.7 (or the OpenTelemetry web SDK), sending traceparent only to its own /api/ paths, and tags any error event with the trace ID.
  2. The BFF's rewrites proxy forwards request headers, so traceparent reaches NestJS unchanged. If the BFF's OpenTelemetry setup (78.7) instruments the proxy hop, it appears as a span; if not, NestJS's server span is the browser span's direct child. Either way the trace ID is the same.
  3. NestJS continues the trace with auto-instrumentation (Part 43.4): the HTTP server span, the Redis GET for the auth epoch, the pg spans for UPDATE, INSERT and COMMIT. Parent-based sampling honours the browser's decision.
  4. The outbox row stores traceparent (79.3). The relay starts its publish span with an OpenTelemetry span link to that context, so the trace UI can jump from the write to the publish.
  5. The stream does not create a span per event. At 120 events a second, the useful signal is a freshness histogram: at the moment the realtime task writes an event, it records now - updatedAt in order_event_lag_seconds. The browser records the same age on arrival as a RUM value, corrected for clock skew with the response Date header.

The relay's linked span:

// apps/api/src/orders/outbox.relay.ts (inside tick(), per row)
import { ROOT_CONTEXT, propagation, trace, type Link } from '@opentelemetry/api';

const tracer = trace.getTracer('orders-relay');

function linkFrom(traceparent: string | null): Link[] {
  if (!traceparent) return [];
  const ctx = propagation.extract(ROOT_CONTEXT, { traceparent });   // rebuild the stored request context
  const sc = trace.getSpanContext(ctx);
  return sc ? [{ context: sc }] : [];
}

// for each claimed row r:
tracer.startActiveSpan('outbox.publish', { links: linkFrom(r.traceparent), attributes: {
  'order.id': r.aggregate_id, 'outbox.id': r.id, 'outbox.age_ms': Date.now() - r.created_at.getTime(),
} }, (span) => { /* pipe.xadd(...) as in 85.3 */ span.end(); });

The freshness metric at the edge of the system:

// apps/api/src/orders/order-events.stream.ts (where an event is turned into a MessageEvent)
import { Histogram } from 'prom-client';

const lag = new Histogram({
  name: 'order_event_lag_seconds',
  help: 'Database commit to SSE write, per event',
  buckets: [0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 30],                  // 2 s is the freshness target (85.1)
});

export function observeLag(updatedAtIso: string): void {
  lag.observe(Math.max(0, (Date.now() - Date.parse(updatedAtIso)) / 1000));
}

Practical example — one "Save note", end to end

The trace for a note saved at the evening peak, as the trace UI shows it:

trace 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736                                total 182 ms (browser view)
browser  click "Save note" -> fetch PATCH                            ├──────────────────────────── 182 ms
  network + CloudFront (edge POP Mumbai)                             ├─ 41 ms
  web-bff  proxy /api/v1/orders/:id/delivery-note                    │  ├── 96 ms
    orders-api  PATCH /v1/orders/:id/delivery-note                   │  │  ├── 88 ms
      JwtAuthGuard + Redis GET auth:epoch                            │  │  │  ├ 1.1 ms
      CsrfGuard, UserThrottlerGuard (Redis INCR)                     │  │  │  ├ 0.9 ms
      IdempotencyInterceptor reserve (Redis SET NX)                  │  │  │  ├ 0.6 ms
      pg BEGIN; UPDATE orders ... WHERE version = $4                 │  │  │  ├ 2.4 ms
      pg INSERT outbox                                               │  │  │  ├ 0.8 ms
      pg SELECT tracking (order + 20 events)                         │  │  │  ├ 1.3 ms
      pg COMMIT                                                      │  │  │  ├ 2.0 ms
      serialise + idempotency store                                  │  │  │  ├ 1.2 ms
      (unexplained gap: event loop lag)                              │  │  │  └ 77 ms   <- the finding
linked: outbox.publish (relay)  outbox.age_ms=94                     └ +94 ms after commit, 0.7 ms

Fourteen milliseconds of real work, 77 ms of unexplained time inside the NestJS span. The API's event loop lag metric (Part 10.27) for that task showed 70 to 90 ms spikes every few seconds: a synchronous JSON.stringify of a large export job running on the same tasks. Moving the export to a worker (Part 36) brought the PATCH p95 from 210 ms to 60 ms. Without the trace, the database would have been blamed.

Backend side (NestJS)

What the backend emits for this feature, beyond the generic HTTP metrics:

Signal Type Alert
order_event_lag_seconds Histogram p95 above 2 s for 10 minutes (freshness SLO burn)
Outbox backlog (count(*) WHERE published_at IS NULL) and oldest age Gauges, sampled every 15 s Oldest unpublished row older than 30 s
ActiveStreams per task (79.10) Gauge Above 9,000 per task for 10 minutes
Stream connects, reauth closes, 429 TOO_MANY_STREAMS Counters 429 rate above 0.5 % of connects
Replay requests that returned reset Counter Above 2 % of reconnects (replay window too short)
INVALID_TRANSITION from internal callers Counter by source Spike after an upstream deploy
Tracking availability and journey SLIs (78.8) RUM counters Burn-rate alerts

Logs carry requestId, trace_id and the order ID, never the delivery note (Part 40.31). The relay logs one line per batch (count, oldest age), not per row.

Production scenario

The tracking dashboard has six panels: freshness p50/p95/p99, outbox backlog and age, active streams per task with memory, connects and reauths per second, the RUM tracking availability SLI, and error-tracker issues for the tracking route by release. In the first quarter, freshness alerts fired three times: a Redis failover (40 s), a relay deploy that started with RELAY_ENABLED=false on every task (12 minutes; the backlog alert caught it before customers called), and a PostgreSQL vacuum stall on outbox (79.12). Each was diagnosed from the dashboard and one linked trace in under ten minutes.

Failure scenario

For the first two weeks, the freshness histogram was recorded in the relay at publish time, not at the stream write. It showed p95 0.2 s throughout an evening when customers on one realtime task saw updates 40 seconds late: that task's Redis subscriber connection had silently stalled after a network blip, and events piled up in its stream while the relay, correctly, kept publishing. The metric measured the part of the path that worked. Moving the measurement to the last server-side step, the SSE write, and adding a RUM measurement in the browser, made the stall visible; a subscriber health check (a self-published probe every 10 s that must arrive within 2 s) now restarts a stuck subscriber.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Measuring freshness too early in the path hides stalls downstream; measure at the last step you control, and in the browser.
  • Clock skew between the database and the realtime tasks distorts lag; use database time (updatedAt from now()) and keep hosts on NTP; in the browser, correct with the server's Date header.
  • Span per event at high rates costs more than it tells; histograms and sampled linked spans are enough.
  • Trace headers to third parties: propagate only to your own origins (78.7).
  • Personal data in span attributes: order IDs yes, notes and addresses never.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior instruments the feature around its promise: freshness is a histogram measured at the last step, the write path is one trace from the click, and the asynchronous hop is joined by a stored context and a span link. They alert on symptoms customers feel (lag, availability) and on the leading indicators that predict them (backlog age, subscriber health), and they test that every alert can fire. The trace that found the event-loop problem is the typical payoff: the slow part was not where anyone was looking.

Common mistakes

  • No link between the request trace and the asynchronous publish.
  • Freshness measured at the producer instead of the consumer.
  • Alerting on stream count alone, which changes with traffic, instead of lag and backlog age.
  • Logging payloads of personal fields.

Interview questions

  1. How do you trace work that continues asynchronously after the request? Expected answer: store the trace context with the work (here in the outbox row) and start the later span with a link to it.
  2. Where do you measure freshness for a live feature? Expected answer: at the last server-side step (the stream write) and in the browser, both against the commit time from the database.
  3. What would you alert on to catch a stuck relay before customers notice? Expected answer: the age of the oldest unpublished outbox row, plus freshness p95.

Practical exercise

Instrument the write and push paths.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A note save produces one trace with browser, NestJS and PostgreSQL spans, and the relay's publish span links to it.
  • order_event_lag_seconds is recorded at the SSE write; a deliberately paused relay makes the backlog-age alert fire within one minute.
  • A browser error during a note save carries the same trace_id as the backend spans.
  • No span attribute or log line contains a delivery note.

79.12 Failure drills: backend down, SSE disconnects, stale bundle, slow database

Concept

A failure drill (Part 49.12) breaks one dependency on purpose, in staging or in a controlled production window, and checks that the system behaves as designed and that the people on call can see it. Each drill states the expected behaviour in advance, so the drill either confirms the design or finds the gap. The four drills the outline requires, plus two more this design depends on, all have the same goal: the customer always sees the last known status, labelled honestly, and nothing is lost.

Why does it exist?

Because the degradation paths in 79.6 and 79.10 are code that runs only when something is broken, which means it almost never runs. Untested fallbacks fail the first time they are needed: the polling interval was never wired, the banner has a typo, the kill switch flag was renamed. Drills turn "we designed for that" into "we watched it work".

Mental model

Imagine a fire drill in an office. Nobody expects a fire on Tuesday, but on Tuesday everyone walks out by the planned route while someone times it and notes the door that sticks. The real fire is not the time to discover the door.

How it works

flowchart TB
    full["Live: SSE stream, sub-second freshness"] --> recon["Reconnecting: auto retry, replay from Last-Event-ID"]
    recon --> poll["Polling every 30 s, honest banner"]
    poll --> stale["Showing last known status with its time"]
    stale --> err["Error page with retry and request ID, only if the first load fails"]
    full -.->|"kill switch"| poll

The drills, with what was expected and what was measured on staging at production scale (60,000 synthetic streams):

Drill Expected Measured Gap found
Orders API down 5 min (all api tasks stopped) Open pages keep status; banner; note save fails with rollback; new page loads show error.tsx with retry As expected; streams stayed up (realtime tasks independent) and kept delivering replays error.tsx retry hammered the API on recovery: added jittered retry
Realtime tasks killed Clients reconnect; after 10 s, polling; streams return within 2 min of recovery Reconnect p95 3.1 s with jitter; 0 events lost None
Network flap (CloudFront to ALB, 30 s) Auto reconnect, replay All events replayed; 0.4 % got reset and refetched Replay window raised from 15 min to 30 min for slow customers
Stale bundle (tab on build N while N+2 emits a new status) Old tab shows "Updated" badge, timeline intact; nudge to reload As expected via openEnum Nudge appeared only after 30 min (74.9 default); set to 5 min for tracking
Slow database (pg_sleep injected in the tracking read; lock held on one order row) Reads time out at 2 s; SSR shows error.tsx; open pages unaffected; relay backlog grows; freshness alert SSR timed out at 1.5 s as designed; relay blocked on the locked row only Relay batch blocked behind one locked row: added SKIP LOCKED was already there, but the transition UPDATE waited 30 s; set lock_timeout = 2s on API transactions
Redis primary failover Relay retries; streams drop and reconnect; replay fails over to reset if the stream was lost 38 s outage; backlog peaked at 2,100; caught up in 6 s; clients refetched Connection counter keys lost: limits briefly unenforced, acceptable

Practical example — the four required drills in detail

Backend down. At 19:00 on staging the api service is scaled to zero. Open tracking pages: the stream is served by the realtime tasks, which do not depend on the api tasks, so live status keeps working for changes already in the outbox; the relay runs inside api tasks, so new changes stop flowing and the freshness alert fires after 30 s. Customers who reload see error.tsx: "We couldn't load your order. Try again", with the request ID, after 1.5 s (the SSR timeout). A note save shows the optimistic note, then rolls it back with "Couldn't save your note. Try again". At 19:05 the service returns; the relay drains the backlog in 4 s; streams deliver the queued events. Lesson recorded: the relay should run on its own small service so an api outage does not also stop status events (done in the next sprint).

SSE disconnects. A CloudFront origin is made unreachable for 90 s by blocking the realtime ALB's security group. EventSource retries silently; after 10 s, banners read "Reconnecting. Showing status from 7:12 pm" and polling starts against the api tasks (which are healthy). Polling load: 60,000 / 30 s = 2,000 requests per second, 95 % 304. When the block is lifted, reconnects arrive spread over 8 s thanks to the jittered retry, each replaying from Last-Event-ID.

Stale bundle. A tab is opened on build N. Build N+1 adds a READY_FOR_PICKUP status for click-and-collect, and the API starts emitting it for one test order (the drill skips the "mobile first" gate on purpose). The old tab receives the event, openEnum maps the status to UNKNOWN and reports it once to the error tracker with a skew tag (78.4), the heading reads "Updated", the timeline adds a step labelled "Updated", and within 5 minutes the version nudge (74.9) shows "A new version is available. Reload". Nothing crashes. The same drill on a build without openEnum (kept as a negative control) throws in STATUS_COPY[...] and shows the segment error boundary, which is exactly the incident the rollout order prevents.

Slow database. A test transaction holds a row lock on order 1d6c for 60 s while the warehouse simulator tries to move it to OUT_FOR_DELIVERY. Before the fix, the transition waited 30 s (the default statement timeout on that pool) and the warehouse integration retried three times, stacking waiters. After setting lock_timeout = '2s' for API transactions (SET LOCAL lock_timeout at the start of transition()), the transition fails fast with 55P03 lock_not_available, mapped to 409 RETRY_LATER, and the warehouse retries with backoff (Part 31.4). Other orders are unaffected: the relay's SKIP LOCKED passes over the locked outbox rows, and tracking reads for other orders stay at p95 18 ms.

Backend side (NestJS)

The two settings the slow-database drill added, in the transition transaction:

// apps/api/src/orders/order-status.service.ts (start of the transaction callback)
await m.query(`SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '2s'`);          // fail fast instead of queueing behind a held lock
await m.query(`SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '3s'`);     // bound any single statement (Part 19)
// apps/api/src/common/api-exception.filter.ts (addition): map PostgreSQL lock timeouts to a retryable 409
if (exception instanceof QueryFailedError && (exception.driverError as { code?: string }).code === '55P03') {
  return reply(409, 'RETRY_LATER', 'The order is being updated. Try again shortly.', { retryAfterSec: 1 });
}

Production scenario

The team runs one drill a month in staging at production scale and the "realtime tasks killed" drill quarterly in production during a quiet hour, announced to support. The production drill in month three took 9 realtime tasks down one at a time over 15 minutes: 64,000 streams moved without a single lost event, the freshness p99 rose to 4.1 s for 30 seconds per task, and no customer contacted support.

Failure scenario

Before the drills, the polling fallback had never run in production. The first real stream outage came from a CloudFront configuration change that set the stream behaviour's origin response timeout to 10 s. Every quiet stream was cut after 10 s; clients reconnected, were cut again, and after three failures in two minutes switched to polling, as designed. But polling used refetchInterval from a conn value captured in a stale closure (a bug no test exercised), so the pages never actually polled. For 50 minutes customers saw "Reconnecting" and a status that never changed. The fix was one line; the lesson was the monthly drill, and a component test for the polling path (79.9, the third test).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Drills that skip the people part: check that the alert fired, the right person was paged and the runbook was right.
  • Fallbacks that overload a healthy dependency: 60,000 pages polling every 5 s would be 12,000 requests per second; 30 s and 304s keep it at 2,000 mostly empty responses.
  • Recovery stampedes: retries without jitter turn recovery into a second outage.
  • Shared fate: the relay inside api tasks tied event flow to api health; drills reveal such coupling.
  • Negative controls: run the old behaviour once to prove the drill can detect the failure.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior writes the expected behaviour of every dependency failure before building the fallbacks, then proves it with scheduled drills at real scale, including the alerting and the humans. They look especially for shared fate (two features failing together because they share a process) and for recovery behaviour, which is where a second outage usually starts. A drill that finds nothing is good news; a drill that is never run is a guess.

Common mistakes

  • Fallback code without tests or drills.
  • No lock_timeout, so one held lock queues every writer.
  • Polling fallbacks with aggressive intervals.
  • Drills only in tiny staging environments, where scale effects never appear.

Interview questions

  1. What should a live tracking page do when the API is down? Expected answer: keep showing the last known status with its time, label it honestly, roll back optimistic writes with a clear message, and show a retryable error only when there is no data at all.
  2. How do you stop one locked row from stalling a status pipeline? Expected answer: lock_timeout on writers, SKIP LOCKED in the relay, and retryable errors with backoff for callers.
  3. How do you test that an old bundle survives a new enum value? Expected answer: keep a tab on build N, emit the new value from build N+2, check the fallback label, the skew report and the reload nudge.
  4. Why drill at production scale? Expected answer: reconnect storms, polling load and backlog drain only appear with realistic connection counts.

Practical exercise

Run the six drills on staging.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A written expected behaviour for each drill before it runs.
  • Each drill's alert fires and reaches the on-call channel within the expected time.
  • No events are lost in any drill (verified by comparing outbox rows with events received by a synthetic client).
  • At least one gap found and fixed, with a test added for it.

79.13 Senior review: what you would change at 10x scale

Concept

A senior review looks at a working system and asks what breaks first if load grows by an order of magnitude, and what should not change. At 10x, this feature means 600,000 concurrent viewers, 1,200 events per second on average, bursts of 6,000, and 4 million orders a day. Some parts scale by adding tasks; some hit hard limits and need a different design; and some decisions are worth keeping exactly as they are.

Why does it exist?

Because the cheapest time to know the next architecture is before you need it, and the most expensive mistake is building it now. The current design meets today's numbers with a lot of headroom and few moving parts (79.1). The review documents where the headroom ends, so the team watches the right metrics and starts the next step a quarter before it is urgent, not during an outage.

Mental model

Imagine a bakery that sells 1,000 loaves a day planning for 10,000. More ovens is easy. The single front door, the one delivery van and the owner doing every order by hand are the real limits. And the recipe, which customers love, should not change at all.

How it works

What breaks first, in order:

Component Today At 10x Change
Realtime tasks (memory per connection) 9 tasks, 64,000 streams about 80 tasks, 600,000 streams Scales out as is; consider a dedicated gateway on a runtime with cheaper idle connections, or a managed service (AWS API Gateway WebSocket, AppSync Events) after a cost comparison
Redis, single primary: streams, pub/sub, counters Under 5 % CPU Pub/sub fan-out to 80 subscribers per message becomes the bottleneck Redis Cluster with sharded pub/sub (SSUBSCRIBE, Redis 7) keyed by user, so a message goes only to the shard and tasks that hold that user
Relay polling one outbox 600 rows/s burst 6,000 rows/s burst Partition the outbox by user_id hash across N relays, or replace polling with CDC (Debezium on the WAL, Part 39) publishing to Kafka
orders and order_status_events writes Comfortable 4 million orders, 20 million history rows a day Monthly partitions for history and outbox (Part 23); archive delivered orders' history after 90 days
Reauth reconnects every 15 min 70/s 700/s, each a refresh at the BFF Stagger with jitter already; consider a longer-lived, stream-only token minted by the BFF with a narrow audience (shop-stream), revocable by the same epoch
Mobile apps keeping streams open in the background Not an issue Large share of connections from backgrounded phones Close streams when apps background; use push notifications (APNs, FCM) for status changes instead
Single region One AWS region Customers in several countries Regional stacks with customers pinned to their home region; the contract and events unchanged 
flowchart LR
    pg[("PostgreSQL, partitioned outbox")] --> cdc["CDC: Debezium on the WAL"]
    cdc --> kafka["Kafka topic order-events, keyed by userId"]
    kafka --> gw["Stream gateway tier, 80 or more tasks"]
    gw --> rc[("Redis Cluster: replay streams, sharded pub/sub")]
    gw --> browsers["Browsers: same SSE contract"]
    kafka --> push["Push notification service for backgrounded apps"]
    kafka --> analytics["Analytics, idempotent by orderId and version"]

What not to change, because it is what makes the system correct:
