  • The contract: OrderTrackingSchema, the event schema, the problem documents, the rollout rules for enums. Browsers and apps do not care how events reach them.
  • Versioned, idempotent consumers: every consumer applies events by (orderId, version); at-least-once delivery stays safe whatever the transport.
  • The outbox semantics: events derive from committed state. CDC is the same idea with a different reader.
  • The honest fallback: polling with a banner, behind a flag. At 10x the kill switch matters more, not less.
  • Server rendering of the shell: the first view does not depend on the live tier at all.

Practical example — the cost check before building anything

The team priced the 10x options with real numbers. Staying on Fargate with SSE: about 80 tasks at the evening peak, roughly 2,100 dollars a month, plus Redis Cluster at about 900 dollars. A managed WebSocket service: priced per connection-minute and per message, it came to about 6,500 dollars a month at 600,000 peak connections with typical evening session lengths, without counting the work to move the browser from SSE to WebSockets. The decision: stay on SSE and Fargate, move to Redis Cluster with sharded pub/sub at 3x, introduce CDC at 5x, and revisit managed services if connection costs or operational load change. The thresholds became alerts on the metrics of 79.11.

Backend side (NestJS)

The change at 3x is small because the stream code already has one seam: OrderEventsStream.forUser(userId, lastEventId) (72.8, 85.4). Moving from SUBSCRIBE on a single Redis to SSUBSCRIBE on a cluster changes the implementation behind that method, not the controller, the contract or the client. The relay's seam is the same: the outbox row is the input, the customer's stream is the output; CDC replaces the loop, not the semantics. Keeping these seams narrow was a deliberate choice in 79.3 and 79.4.

Production scenario

Eighteen months later, at 3.4x, the team made the first planned change: Redis Cluster with sharded pub/sub, behind the existing interface, rolled out one realtime task at a time. Freshness p95 stayed at 0.4 s through the migration. CDC was prototyped but not yet needed: the partitioned relay (four relays, each owning a hash range of user_id) handled bursts of 2,500 rows per second at 15 % of one vCPU each.

Failure scenario

A different company, seeing a similar feature succeed, rebuilt it at 1x for "web scale": Kafka, a custom WebSocket gateway in another language, a separate tracking database fed by CDC, and a GraphQL subscription layer. It took two quarters, introduced four new on-call rotations, and at launch delivered freshness of 3 s p95 (worse than the simple version) because events crossed five systems. The review that followed recommended returning to the outbox, Redis and SSE design for their scale, which they did. Scaling ahead of need is a cost, not insurance.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Changing the contract during a scale migration: two risky changes at once; keep the wire format fixed.
  • Fan-out patterns that break at scale: broadcast designs (every message to every gateway) fail long before 1:1 designs.
  • Regional splits with users travelling: pin by home region, never by request location, or a customer's stream and orders disagree.
  • Push notifications as a replacement for open tabs: they complement, they do not deliver to an open web page.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

The senior names what breaks first, at what multiple, with which metric warning in advance, and what the next design is, then deliberately does not build it yet. They protect the decisions that make the system correct (contract, versions, outbox, fallback) and keep narrow seams around the parts that will change (the stream source, the relay). And they price options with real numbers, because "it scales" is not a decision until someone has written down what it costs.

Common mistakes

  • Building the 10x architecture at 1x.
  • Changing the client protocol to scale the server.
  • Broadcast fan-out "for simplicity".
  • No written thresholds, so the scale work starts during an incident.

Interview questions

  1. What breaks first if live tracking grows tenfold? Expected answer: pub/sub fan-out on a single Redis and the relay's burst capacity, then partition sizes; stream tasks simply scale out.
  2. What would you not change, and why? Expected answer: the contract, versioned idempotent consumers, outbox semantics, the honest fallback and server-rendered shell; they make the system correct regardless of transport.
  3. When would you move from an outbox poller to CDC? Expected answer: when relay throughput or database load from polling becomes the limit; CDC keeps the same semantics with lower latency and load, at the cost of new infrastructure.
  4. Managed realtime service or your own? Expected answer: compare real connection-minute and message costs and operational load at your numbers; at moderate scale your own SSE tier is often cheaper and simpler.

Practical exercise

Write the 10x review for your own live feature.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A table of components with today's load, the load at 10x and the first component to hit a hard limit.
  • A list of decisions not to change, each with the reason.
  • Costed options for the two most likely changes, with the metric and threshold that triggers each.
  • The code seams where each change would happen, identified in your codebase.

Senior Checklist — Part 79

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can write requirements and NFRs with numbers and derive connection, event and cost estimates from them
  • I can design a REST plus SSE contract in a shared package and roll out enum and field changes in the right order
  • I can change status with conditional updates and publish events through a transactional outbox with idempotent consumers
  • I can build an SSE endpoint with ownership, a connection cap, an end at token expiry and a revocation check
  • I can server-render the page shell with the answer in the first HTML and one small live island
  • I can merge pushed events into the query cache by version and field, and fall back to honest polling
  • I can make a write optimistic only where being briefly wrong is harmless, with field-level rollback
  • I can map every path of a feature to the existing auth design without adding side doors
  • I can measure load, interaction and steady-state performance for a page users keep open
  • I can test streams without a browser and prove the whole path with one journey that encodes the freshness target
  • I can deploy streams on their own tasks behind a CDN configured for them, and release by flag with a working off state
  • I can follow one trace from a click to a database write and link the asynchronous publish to it
  • I can run failure drills at realistic scale and turn the gaps into tests
  • I can review a system for 10x, naming what breaks first and what must not change

Part 79 — Key Takeaways

  • Write the numbers first; for live features the NFRs (viewers, bursts, freshness, degradation) pick the architecture.
  • The contract comes before the code, lives in the shared package, and changes follow a rollout order: clients that tolerate new values ship first.
  • The database row is the only truth; history, streams, caches and screens are derived from committed changes through an outbox.
  • Every consumer applies events by entity and version, so at-least-once delivery, duplicates and reordering are harmless.
  • A long-lived connection holds authority and memory: give it a cap, an expiry, a revocation check and its own tasks.
  • Put the answer in the first HTML; make live only the part that changes.
  • The query cache is the one source the UI reads; pushed events are one more writer with the same rules as mutations.
  • Optimistic for harmless changes, pessimistic for money and races; roll back fields, not snapshots.
  • A live page must say honestly when it is not live, and keep working by polling behind a server-evaluated flag.
  • Test time and connections with fakes you control, and keep one end-to-end journey whose timeout is the freshness target.
  • Trace the click to the database write, link the asynchronous hop, and measure freshness at the last step.
  • Drill every failure at realistic scale; fallbacks that never run do not work.
  • At 10x, scale the parts that limit you and keep the contract, the versions, the outbox and the fallback exactly as they are.

Part 80 — Frontend and Full-Stack Interview Preparation

Part 59 prepared you for a senior backend loop and Part 68 gave you the playbook for any loop: the funnel, the coding round, the system design procedure, take-homes, offers. This Part covers the rounds those two do not: the JavaScript fundamentals round, the browser round, the React round, the UI machine-coding round, frontend system design, and the full-stack design round where the interviewer cares most about the line between the browser and your API. It also adds what the rest of the book lacks: a junior and entry-level track.

Every answer here points to the section that teaches the idea properly. Use this Part as a question bank and a method, and go back to Volume 7 (Parts 69–79), Volume 0 (Parts 0–7) and Volume 1 when an answer feels thin. A model answer you have memorised but cannot extend with one number and one failure mode is not ready.

80.1 How frontend and full-stack interview loops work

80.1.1 The rounds and what each one signals

Concept

A frontend or full-stack loop is built from seven kinds of round. Most companies run four or five of them in three to five hours, plus a recruiter screen at the start and a hiring-manager conversation at the end.

Round Typical length What you do The real signal
JavaScript and TypeScript fundamentals 45–60 min Explain and predict: closures, this, the event loop, promises, coercion, types Do you have an accurate model of the language, or folklore?
Browser and web platform Often folded into another round Explain rendering, CORS, cookies, caching, security, accessibility Can you debug what happens outside your own code?
UI machine coding 60–90 min Build a working component in a browser editor: typeahead, infinite list, form Can you ship a small, correct, accessible feature under time pressure?
React (or the team's framework) 45–60 min, or part of machine coding Explain re-renders, effects, state placement, server components, hydration Do you know why the framework behaves as it does, or only the API?
Frontend system design 45–60 min Design the client of a feed, a chat, a product page Can you structure a large UI: components, state, data, performance, failure?
Full-stack system design 45–60 min Design one feature end to end: browser, BFF, API, database, cache Can you own a contract between frontend and backend?
Behavioural 45 min Stories: design and product, a performance win, an incident Do people want to build with you?

Some loops replace machine coding with a take-home (Part 68, 68.4) or replace the fundamentals round with a classic algorithms round (Part 68, 68.2). Ask the recruiter which rounds you will get; it is a normal question and the answer saves you weeks.

Why does it exist?

A backend loop can test most of the job with a coding round and a system design. A frontend job has a different failure surface: the code runs on a slow phone you do not control, the user is a person with a keyboard, a screen reader and a flaky train connection, and the bugs are race conditions between a click, a fetch and a re-render. The rounds above exist because each one catches a different way a frontend engineer fails in production:

  • The fundamentals round catches engineers who cannot explain why their await inside forEach did not wait.
  • Machine coding catches engineers who can talk about React but leave a typeahead that shows results for "ap" after the user typed "apple".
  • Frontend system design catches engineers who put every API response into one global store and then cannot invalidate anything.
  • Full-stack design catches engineers who design a beautiful UI against an API that cannot serve it in under 2 seconds.

Mental model

Imagine hiring a chef. You ask them to explain why bread rises (fundamentals), you watch them cook one dish in 60 minutes in an unfamiliar kitchen (machine coding), you ask them to plan a 200-cover wedding menu (system design), and you ask how they handled a supplier who sent the wrong fish (behavioural). Each test is cheap compared with hiring the wrong chef, and no single test is enough.

How it works

flowchart TB
  R["Recruiter screen<br/>30 min"] --> T["Technical phone screen<br/>JS fundamentals or a small UI task"]
  T --> L["Onsite or virtual loop"]
  L --> MC["UI machine coding<br/>60-90 min"]
  L --> FE["React and browser deep dive<br/>45-60 min"]
  L --> SD["Frontend or full-stack design<br/>45-60 min"]
  L --> BH["Behavioural<br/>45 min"]
  MC --> D["Debrief and hiring decision"]
  FE --> D
  SD --> D
  BH --> D

Interviewers write evidence against a rubric for each round, then a debrief combines them (Part 87, 87.5 shows how rubrics are written from the other side of the table). Two consequences matter to you. First, a strong round cannot fully rescue a weak one, because the debrief looks for "no concerns" across signals. Second, the interviewer can only score what they saw or heard, so narrating your reasoning is not optional.

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

They treat each round as a sample of a real day at work. In machine coding they behave as they would on a feature ticket: clarify, build the smallest working slice, then handle loading, error, empty and keyboard states. In system design they start from the user and the numbers, not from a library name. They prepare stories with numbers because "made it faster" is not evidence and "LCP from 4.1 s to 2.2 s at the 75th percentile" is.

Common mistakes

  • Preparing only LeetCode for a loop that has no algorithms round and two UI rounds.
  • Learning React APIs without the JavaScript underneath; every React question eventually becomes a closure or reference-equality question.
  • Treating frontend system design as "draw the backend". The interviewer wants the client: component tree, state, cache, rendering strategy, accessibility.
  • Not asking the recruiter which framework the machine-coding round allows. Many allow React, some require vanilla DOM.

80.1.2 What changes by level: junior, mid, senior

Concept

The same question is graded differently by level. "Build a typeahead" is a junior question if you only need it to work, a mid question if it must handle races and debouncing, and a senior question if you are expected to raise accessibility, caching, request cancellation and what the API should look like.

Signal Junior (0–2 years) Mid (2–5 years) Senior (5+ years)
Fundamentals Correct basics: scope, arrays, promises, HTTP methods, status codes Event loop order, closures in React, async error handling Explains mechanisms and their production symptoms, reads a trace
Coding A small task works; code is readable Handles edge cases, loading and error states, uses types well Clean structure, accessibility, cancellation, tests, says what is cut
React Components, props, state, lists with keys Effects done right, state placement, memoisation trade-offs Server vs client components, hydration, cache invalidation, profiling
Design Not usually asked; maybe "how would you structure this page" Component tree and data flow for one feature Full frontend or full-stack design with numbers, rollout, observability
Behavioural Learning, asking for help, one project in depth Owning a feature end to end, working with design Influence, trade-offs with product, incidents, raising the bar for others

Part 58 — Junior to Principal: What Is Expected at Each Level describes the same ladder for backend work; 58.1 and 58.6 transfer directly.

Production scenario

A mid-level candidate builds a working typeahead in 40 minutes and stops. A senior candidate builds the same thing in 35 minutes, then says: "I have not added a results cache, and I want the API to accept a limit so we never ship 500 results to a phone. I also need aria-activedescendant so a screen reader announces the highlighted option." Same code, different level, because the second candidate showed they know what production will ask next.

Failure scenario

A senior candidate with eight years of backend experience applies for a full-stack role, aces the system design round, and fails the machine-coding round because they spent 25 minutes setting up a state management library for a component with three pieces of state. The debrief note reads "over-engineers; did not deliver a working UI". Seniority is judged partly on knowing what not to build.

80.1.3 Choosing what to prepare: a decision table

Not everyone needs every round. Use the job description and the recruiter's answer to weight your time.

You are interviewing for Weight your preparation Can mostly skip
Junior frontend or full-stack Volume 0 fundamentals (80.8), one portfolio project, small UI tasks, Git, HTTP, basic SQL Frontend system design at scale
Mid frontend (product team) JS bank (80.2), React bank (80.4), machine coding (80.5) Deep database internals
Senior frontend All of 80.2–80.6, plus performance and accessibility stories Low-level algorithms beyond medium difficulty
Full-stack at a product company 80.2, 80.4, 80.5, 80.7, plus Part 59's API and SQL sections Frontend system design of very large apps
Full-stack at a startup Machine coding, full-stack design, one deployed project, speed Perfect pixel styling
Backend engineer moving to full-stack 80.3 browser, 80.4 React, 80.5 machine coding; you already have Part 59 Re-learning backend design

80.1.4 Preparing in four weeks and in eight weeks

Concept

A plan beats a pile of bookmarks. Both plans below assume about 90 minutes on weekdays and three hours on one weekend day. Keep the same log Part 68 recommends (68.9): question or problem, date, time taken, what went wrong. Anything that appears twice in "what went wrong" gets extra practice the following week.

How it works

Four-week plan (you already work in frontend or full-stack):

Week Fundamentals Building Design and stories
1 80.2 JS and TS bank, out loud; the event loop exercise until you get it right twice Typeahead (80.5.2) from a blank file, timed at 60 min Write four STAR stories (80.9) with numbers

Eight-week plan (moving from backend, or rusty):

Week Focus Read or redo Output

2 The browser Part 69, then 80.3 Trace one page in the Performance panel (69.10)

Common mistakes

  • Reading model answers without first answering out loud. Recognition feels like knowledge; recall under pressure is the skill being tested.
  • Practising machine coding in your own configured editor only. Interview editors (CodeSandbox, StackBlitz, CoderPad) have no autocomplete for your utilities and sometimes no TypeScript types. Practise there at least twice.
  • Booking the top-choice company in week one.

Practical exercise

Fill in the plan that matches you with real dates, book one mock machine-coding round and one mock design round with real people for the last week, and start the log today. Acceptance criteria: every week has dated sessions; both mocks are booked; after week two the log names your two weakest topics and what you did about each.

80.2 JavaScript and TypeScript question bank

Part 59, 59.1 already covers TypeScript from a backend view (type vs interface, generics, discriminated unions, unknown, utility types, narrowing). The questions here are the ones frontend loops ask, framed around the browser and the UI. Each has a model answer, what a strong answer adds, and where the topic is taught.

Q1. What is a closure, and where have you seen one cause a bug?

  • Model answer — A closure is a function together with the variables from the scope where it was created. The function keeps access to those variables after the outer function has returned, because the variables live as long as something references them, not as long as the call that created them (1.4.2). Every event handler and every React callback is a closure. The classic bug is a stale closure: the function captured a value at creation time and keeps using it after the value changed.

    function OrderTimer({ orderId }: { orderId: string }) {
  const [seconds, setSeconds] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      setSeconds(seconds + 1); // bug: `seconds` is always 0 inside this closure
    }, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, []); // the effect ran once, so the callback captured the first render's `seconds`
  return <p>Order {orderId}: waiting {seconds}s</p>;
}

    The display goes 0, 1, 1, 1. The fix is the functional update setSeconds((s) => s + 1), which reads the latest value from React instead of from the closure.

  • What a strong answer adds — That each render of a component creates new closures over that render's props and state, so "stale" means "from an older render". Mentions the var-in-a-loop version (for (var i...) with setTimeout prints the final value three times because there is one i for the whole function; let creates a new binding per iteration). Mentions that closures also keep memory alive: a handler attached to window that closes over a large array keeps that array until the handler is removed.

  • Where it is taught — 1.4.2 Scope, closures and the call stack; 71.4 Effects; 71.6 for callbacks and custom hooks.

Q2. How is this decided in JavaScript?

  • Model answer — this is decided by how a function is called, not where it is written, with one exception: arrow functions have no this of their own and use the this of the scope they were written in. The rules, in order of priority:

    1. new Fn(): this is the new object.
    2. fn.call(obj), fn.apply(obj), or a function made with fn.bind(obj): this is obj.
    3. obj.method(): this is obj, the thing before the dot.
    4. A plain call fn(): this is undefined in strict mode (all ES modules and classes are strict), or the global object in old sloppy scripts.
    class CartService {
  private items: string[] = [];
  add(sku: string) { this.items.push(sku); }
}
const cart = new CartService();
button.addEventListener('click', () => cart.add('SKU-1')); // fine: called as cart.add
const add = cart.add;
add('SKU-2'); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')

  • What a strong answer adds — That passing cart.add as a callback (onClick={cart.add}, setTimeout(cart.add)) is the same as the plain call, and the three fixes: wrap in an arrow, bind once in the constructor, or define the method as an arrow class field (add = (sku: string) => {...}), which costs one function per instance instead of one on the prototype. Knows that in a DOM addEventListener callback written as a normal function, this is the element (event.currentTarget), and that function components in React made most this questions disappear from UI code.

  • Where it is taught — 1.4.1 and 1.5.1 for functions and objects; 59.1 for TypeScript class details.

Q3. Explain prototypes. What does class actually create?

  • Model answer — Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype. When you read a property that the object does not have, the engine looks on the prototype, then on its prototype, until it reaches null. That chain is how methods are shared. class Order { total() {} } creates a constructor function Order and puts total on Order.prototype; each new Order() gets its own fields, and a link to Order.prototype for methods. extends links one prototype to another. Classes are mostly syntax over this mechanism, with real differences: class bodies are strict, classes cannot be called without new, and private #fields are truly private.

    class Order { constructor(public id: string) {} label() { return `Order ${this.id}`; } }
const o = new Order('ORD-1001');
Object.getPrototypeOf(o) === Order.prototype;      // true
Object.hasOwn(o, 'label');                          // false: it is on the prototype

  • What a strong answer adds — Why it matters in practice: structuredClone and JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) return plain objects, so a cloned Order has lost its methods; data from an API is never a class instance unless you build one; adding methods to built-in prototypes (Array.prototype.last = ...) can collide with future standard methods, which is why that practice is banned. Can mention that instanceof checks the prototype chain and fails across iframes or duplicated library copies.

  • Where it is taught — 1.5.1 Objects; 1.7.2 Interfaces, type aliases and unions for typing plain data instead of classes.

Q4. The event loop: predict the output

This is the most common fundamentals exercise in frontend loops. Part 59, Q14 has the Node.js version with process.nextTick and setImmediate; this is the browser version.

console.log('1 script start');

setTimeout(() => console.log('2 timeout'), 0);

Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log('3 then A'))
  .then(() => console.log('4 then B'));

queueMicrotask(() => console.log('5 microtask'));

(async () => {
  console.log('6 async body');
  await null;
  console.log('7 after await');
})();

requestAnimationFrame(() => console.log('8 animation frame'));

console.log('9 script end');

  • Model answer — 1, 6, 9, 3, 5, 7, 4, then 2 and 8. The reasoning, step by step:

    1. The script itself is one task. Synchronous code runs to completion: 1, then the async function body runs synchronously up to its first await, printing 6, then 9.
    2. While running, it queued microtasks in this order: then A (the promise was already resolved, so its callback is queued at once), the queueMicrotask callback, and the continuation after await null.
    3. When the call stack empties, the browser drains the whole microtask queue before doing anything else: 3 (which resolves the next promise and queues then B at the back), 5, 7, then 4.
    4. Only then does the event loop move on. The setTimeout callback is a task (often called a macrotask); the requestAnimationFrame callback runs in the rendering step, just before the next paint.
    call stack:      1 6 9
microtasks:      3 5 7 4        (drained completely, including newly added ones)
then, order not fixed by the spec:
task:            2              (timer task, usually first)
render step:     8              (before the next paint, roughly every 16.7 ms at 60 Hz)

  • What a strong answer adds — That the order of 2 and 8 is not guaranteed: the timer usually wins, but a render opportunity can come first, and a background tab may not render at all, so requestAnimationFrame can wait indefinitely. That because microtasks drain completely, a microtask that keeps queueing microtasks starves rendering and input, which is a frozen tab with no long setTimeout in sight. That a long task (over 50 ms) blocks input, which is what INP measures (76.4). Strong candidates draw the loop: one task, all microtasks, maybe render, next task.

  • Where it is taught — 2.1.1 The single thread and the event loop; 10.16 and 10.17 for the runtime view; 69.7 The main thread, the browser event loop and long tasks.

Q5. How do errors work with promises and async/await? Where do they get lost?

  • Model answer — An async function always returns a promise. A throw inside it rejects that promise; await on a rejected promise throws at that line, so try/catch works as you expect, but only around an await. Errors are lost in four common ways:

    1. A promise that is never awaited or given a .catch (a "floating" promise). The browser fires an unhandledrejection event and logs it; your UI shows nothing.
    2. array.forEach(async (x) => ...): forEach ignores the returned promises, so nothing waits and nothing catches.
    3. try { return fetchOrder(id); } catch {} without await: the function returns the promise before it rejects, so the catch never runs. Use return await inside try.
    4. fetch resolves on HTTP 404 and 500. It only rejects on network failure or abort. You must check res.ok.
    async function loadDashboard(userId: string) {
  const results = await Promise.allSettled([
    api.getOrders(userId),
    api.getRecommendations(userId), // optional panel: may fail without breaking the page
  ]);
  const [orders, recs] = results;
  if (orders.status === 'rejected') throw orders.reason; // the page cannot work without orders
  return { orders: orders.value, recs: recs.status === 'fulfilled' ? recs.value : [] };
}

  • What a strong answer adds — The combinators and their failure semantics: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection but does not cancel the others (they keep running and their later rejections are ignored), allSettled never rejects, any resolves with the first success, race settles with the first to settle. Cancellation is a separate mechanism (AbortController, 72.10). Mentions reporting unhandledrejection to error tracking (78.6), and that the backend version of this policy is in Part 59, Q21.

  • Where it is taught — 2.3.1 What a promise is; 2.4.1; 2.5.1 Errors, timeouts and cancellation; 2.7.1 Reading the clues.

Q6. == versus ===, and the coercion questions

  • Model answer — === compares without converting types. == converts first, with rules that surprise people: 0 == '' is true, '1' == 1 is true, null == undefined is true but null == 0 is false, [] == false is true. Use === everywhere, with one accepted exception some teams allow: value == null to check for both null and undefined. NaN is not equal to anything including itself; use Number.isNaN. Object.is is === except that Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true and Object.is(0, -0) is false, and it is what React uses to decide whether state changed.
  • What a strong answer adds — Where coercion bites in UI code: input values are always strings, so quantity + 1 from an input gives "21"; if (count) hides a legitimate 0 (render {count && <Badge />} and React prints a literal 0 on the page); typeof null === 'object'; and money must never be a float (0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3), which is why the contract sends minor units (74.7). Uses ?? instead of || when 0 or '' are valid values.
  • Where it is taught — 1.1.3 Equality, truthiness and coercion; 74.7 Dates, money, IDs and enums across the wire.

Q7. How do you copy objects and arrays, and why does immutability matter in React?

  • Model answer — Assignment copies the reference, not the object. Spread ({ ...order }, [...items]) makes a shallow copy: the top level is new, nested objects are shared. structuredClone(value) makes a deep copy of plain data, Map, Set, Date and typed arrays, but throws on functions and DOM nodes and drops class prototypes. JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) is worse: it turns Date into strings and drops undefined. React decides whether to re-render by comparing references with Object.is, so mutating state in place (cart.items.push(item); setCart(cart)) gives React the same reference and the UI does not update.

    type Cart = { id: string; items: { sku: string; qty: number }[] };
function setQty(cart: Cart, sku: string, qty: number): Cart {
  return {
    ...cart,                                   // new cart object
    items: cart.items.map((i) => (i.sku === sku ? { ...i, qty } : i)), // new array, one new item
  };                                           // unchanged items keep their identity, so memoised rows skip re-render
}

  • What a strong answer adds — That structural sharing (copy only the path you change) is what makes immutability cheap and what lets React.memo rows skip work. That Object.freeze is shallow. That the newer non-mutating array methods (toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with) avoid the classic bug of items.sort() mutating state. That Immer (used inside Redux Toolkit, 72.9) lets you write mutating code that produces immutable updates.

  • Where it is taught — 1.5.1 and 1.5.2; 71.2 State and re-rendering; 72.9 Client state stores.

Q8. ES modules versus CommonJS. What does a bundler do with them?

  • Model answer — ES modules (import/export) are the language standard and are static: imports are declared at the top level, so tools can see the whole dependency graph without running code. That is what makes tree shaking possible (70.5). Imports are live bindings: if the exporting module changes the value, importers see the change. CommonJS (require, module.exports) is Node's older system, resolved at runtime, so a bundler cannot always tell what is used. import() is a dynamic import that returns a promise and is how code splitting works: the bundler emits a separate chunk loaded on demand.
  • What a strong answer adds — Circular imports give undefined (or a temporal-dead-zone error) at module-evaluation time, which shows up as "works in dev, crashes in production build". Side-effectful modules (those that patch globals or register CSS) must be listed under sideEffects in package.json or tree shaking may drop them. Top-level await exists in ES modules and blocks modules that import it. After a deploy, a lazy chunk that was deleted from the server produces "ChunkLoadError" for users on the old version (78.4).
  • Where it is taught — 1.7.1 Modules; 69.6 Script loading; 70.5 Tree shaking and code splitting at build time.

Q9. Write a generic TypeScript helper for the UI and explain the constraint

  • Model answer — A typical one is a typed groupBy used to render orders by status:

    function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(items: readonly T[], keyOf: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]> {
  const out = {} as Record<K, T[]>;
  for (const item of items) {
    const k = keyOf(item);
    (out[k] ??= []).push(item);              // create the bucket on first use
  }
  return out;
}

type Order = { id: string; status: 'placed' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' };
const byStatus = groupBy(orders, (o) => o.status); // Record<'placed' | 'shipped' | 'delivered', Order[]>

    K extends PropertyKey restricts the key to string | number | symbol, the only types usable as object keys. Inference does the rest: the caller never writes the type parameters.

  • What a strong answer adds — Notices the honest gap: the return type claims every status key exists, but a status with no orders has no bucket, so byStatus.shipped.length can throw. A strong candidate either returns Partial<Record<K, T[]>> or pre-fills the known keys. Mentions the built-in Object.groupBy (available in current browsers; check your targets, 70.2) and that its TypeScript type is already Partial. Links to the generic component pattern: function Select<T>({ options, getLabel }: SelectProps<T>).

  • Where it is taught — 1.7.3 Generics; 59.1, Q2 for constraints; 70.8 TypeScript configuration for frontends.

Q10. How does narrowing work, and how do you model UI states with it?

  • Model answer — Narrowing is the compiler following your checks: after typeof x === 'string', 'error' in r, x instanceof Date, or a check on a literal field, it knows a more specific type in that branch. For UI, the best use is a discriminated union for request state, which makes impossible combinations (loading and error at once, data without success) unrepresentable:

    type Remote<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string; requestId?: string };

function assertNever(x: never): never { throw new Error(`Unhandled state: ${JSON.stringify(x)}`); }

function render(s: Remote<Order[]>) {
  switch (s.status) {
    case 'idle': return null;
    case 'loading': return <Spinner />;
    case 'success': return s.data.length ? <OrderList orders={s.data} /> : <EmptyState />;
    case 'error': return <ErrorBanner message={s.message} requestId={s.requestId} />;
    default: return assertNever(s); // compile error if a new status is added and not handled
  }
}

  • What a strong answer adds — User-defined type guards (function isProblem(x: unknown): x is Problem) for API errors, and the warning that a guard is a promise to the compiler that nothing checks; for data crossing the network, use a runtime schema (zod) so the type and the check cannot drift (74.3). Narrowing of a let variable may not survive into a callback if the variable is reassigned later, and TypeScript is optimistic about object properties: it keeps a narrowed order.status across a function call that might have changed it. Empty is its own state, not a special case of success (72.11).

  • Where it is taught — 1.7.2 Interfaces, type aliases and unions; 59.1, Q3 and Q9; 72.11 Loading, empty and error states as a design requirement.

Q11. Which utility types do you use in React code?

  • Model answer — Partial<T> for patch payloads and form drafts, Pick and Omit to derive component props from a domain type, Record<K, V> for lookup tables, ReturnType and Awaited to type what a function or API call produces, NonNullable to strip null. React adds its own: React.ComponentProps<'button'> to accept every native button prop, and React.ReactNode for children.

    type ButtonProps = React.ComponentProps<'button'> & { variant?: 'primary' | 'danger'; loading?: boolean };

function Button({ variant = 'primary', loading = false, disabled, children, ...rest }: ButtonProps) {
  return (
    <button {...rest} className={`btn btn-${variant}`} disabled={disabled || loading} aria-busy={loading}>
      {loading ? 'Please wait' : children}
    </button>
  );
}

  • What a strong answer adds — satisfies to check a config object against a type without widening it (for example, a route table where each key must exist but literal values stay literal). That deriving types from one source (the contracts package, or z.infer) beats hand-written duplicates that drift. That Omit on a union type does not distribute, which surprises people.

  • Where it is taught — 59.1, Q6 for the full list; 70.8; 74.3 Shared zod schemas.

Q12. What is debouncing versus throttling? Implement debounce.

  • Model answer — Debounce waits until calls stop for a given time, then runs once with the last arguments: right for a search box (search after the user pauses for 250 ms). Throttle runs at most once per interval while calls keep coming: right for scroll or resize handlers.

    function debounce<A extends unknown[]>(fn: (...args: A) => void, waitMs: number) {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  const debounced = (...args: A) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), waitMs);
  };
  debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timer); // so a component can clean up on unmount
  return debounced;
}

  • What a strong answer adds — That debouncing reduces requests but does not fix races: two slow requests can still return out of order, so you also need cancellation or a latest-request check (80.5.2). That a debounced function created inside a component body is recreated every render, so each keystroke gets a fresh timer, the old timers still fire, and nothing is debounced; create it once (useMemo or useRef) or debounce the value instead (a useDebouncedValue hook). That for scroll-linked visual work, requestAnimationFrame is usually better than a time-based throttle.

  • Where it is taught — 72.10 Offline and flaky networks: timeouts, retries, AbortController; 71.6 Custom hooks.

80.3 Browser and web platform questions

These questions separate engineers who write components from engineers who can debug a page. Many loops do not run a separate browser round; the questions appear inside the React round, the design round, or as follow-ups ("why is this slow?", "why does the API call fail only from the browser?"). Volume 0's Part 7 — Your First Frontend meets several of these for the first time; Part 69 is the full treatment.

Q13. What happens between receiving HTML and seeing pixels?

  • Model answer — The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM. It combines them, computing the style of every visible element (style), then works out each box's size and position (layout), then fills in pixels for text, colours, borders and images, usually into several layers (paint), then the compositor thread assembles the layers on the GPU (composite). CSS is render-blocking: the browser will not paint until the stylesheets in the <head> have loaded. A classic <script> without defer or async blocks the parser, because the script might change the document.

    HTML bytes → DOM ─┐
                  ├→ style → layout → paint → composite → pixels
CSS bytes → CSSOM ┘

  • What a strong answer adds — Connects stages to costs and metrics: a large render-blocking stylesheet delays first paint and LCP; changing width re-runs layout, changing color re-runs paint, changing transform or opacity can be done by the compositor alone, which is why animations should use those two properties. Uses defer for app scripts and <link rel="preload"> for the LCP image (69.3, 76.6). Mentions that the backend owns the first step: a 900 ms TTFB delays everything after it (76.10).

  • Where it is taught — 3.6.1 From URL to rendered page; 69.1 From URL to pixels; 69.6 Script loading; 76.6 The critical rendering path.

Q14. Reflow versus repaint. What is layout thrashing?

  • Model answer — A reflow (layout) recalculates geometry: it happens when something that affects size or position changes, such as width, font size, adding DOM nodes, or the window resizing. A repaint redraws pixels without changing geometry, such as a colour change. Reflow is more expensive because a change can ripple to parents, siblings and children. Layout thrashing is forcing many reflows in one frame by alternating writes and reads: reading offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect() after a style write forces the browser to do layout immediately to give you a correct answer.

    // Thrashing: one forced layout per row (1,000 rows = 1,000 layouts in one frame)
rows.forEach((row) => { row.style.height = `${row.offsetHeight + 8}px`; });

// Batched: all reads, then all writes = one layout
const heights = rows.map((row) => row.offsetHeight);
rows.forEach((row, i) => { row.style.height = `${heights[i] + 8}px`; });

  • What a strong answer adds — How you would find it: the Performance panel shows purple "Layout" blocks with a "Forced reflow" warning (69.10). Long tasks from thrashing hurt INP (76.4). Fixes beyond batching: transform instead of top/left, CSS contain to limit how far layout spreads, and virtualisation for very long lists (71.9).

  • Where it is taught — 69.1; 69.5 Layout shift; 69.7 long tasks; 76.4 INP.

Q15. Explain CORS and the preflight request.

  • Model answer — Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: a page from https://shop.example may send requests to https://api.shop.example, but its JavaScript may not read the response unless the API says so. CORS is the protocol for the API to say so, with Access-Control-Allow-Origin and related response headers. For requests that could not have been sent by an old HTML form (a method other than GET, HEAD or POST; custom headers such as Authorization; or a Content-Type such as application/json), the browser first sends a preflight: an OPTIONS request asking "may I send this method with these headers?". Only if the preflight response allows it does the real request go out.

    OPTIONS /v1/orders                         ← preflight
Origin: https://shop.example
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, idempotency-key

204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.example
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PATCH
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type, idempotency-key
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600                ← cache the answer for 10 minutes

  • What a strong answer adds — CORS protects users' data in the browser; it is not server security, because curl and Postman ignore it (that is why "it works in Postman" means nothing). With cookies (credentials: 'include'), the server must echo a specific origin, * is refused, and Vary: Origin must be set so a CDN does not serve one origin's headers to another. Preflights add a round trip, which matters on mobile: Access-Control-Max-Age or serving the API from the same origin through a BFF or proxy path (73.8) removes them. A CORS error in the console often hides a real 500 that lacked the CORS headers.

  • Where it is taught — 11.13 CORS; Part 7 — Your First Frontend for the first encounter; 73.8 The BFF pattern.

Q16. Cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB: what goes where?

  • Model answer —

    Store Sent to server automatically Readable by JS Size (approximate) Lifetime Use for
    Cookie with HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax Yes, to matching domain and path No About 4 KB each Until expiry Session identifiers, refresh tokens
    Cookie without HttpOnly Yes Yes About 4 KB Until expiry Non-secret preferences the server needs (locale)
    localStorage No Yes, synchronously About 5 MB per origin Until cleared Non-sensitive preferences, drafts
    sessionStorage No Yes, synchronously About 5 MB Per tab, until closed Per-tab wizard state
    IndexedDB No Yes, asynchronously Large, quota-based Until cleared or evicted Offline data, large caches

    Tokens that grant access should live in HttpOnly cookies, because anything JavaScript can read, an XSS bug can steal.

  • What a strong answer adds — The trade-off is honest: HttpOnly cookies resist token theft but bring CSRF, handled with SameSite, Fetch Metadata headers and, where needed, a double-submit token (75.6); access tokens kept in memory vanish on reload and need silent refresh (75.3). localStorage is synchronous and blocks the main thread on large reads, and Safari can evict script-written storage after a period without visits. Storing personal data in localStorage survives logout unless you clear it.

  • Where it is taught — 11.8 Cookies and sessions; 69.8 Browser storage; 75.1 Where tokens live; 75.2 Session cookies done right.

Q17. What is XSS and how does CSP help? Does React prevent XSS?

  • Model answer — Cross-site scripting is an attacker getting their script to run in your origin, usually by getting text they control rendered as HTML. Once it runs, it can do anything the user can: read non-HttpOnly storage, call your API with the user's cookies, change the page. React escapes values rendered in JSX, so <p>{comment.body}</p> is safe. It does not protect dangerouslySetInnerHTML, URLs in href or src (a javascript: URL from user input), direct DOM APIs such as innerHTML, or HTML you build outside React. Content Security Policy is a response header that tells the browser which scripts may run; a strict policy with per-response nonces blocks injected inline scripts even when an escaping bug slips through.

    Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'

  • What a strong answer adds — Sanitise rich text with a maintained library (DOMPurify) on output, validate URL schemes (https: only) for user-supplied links, and treat Markdown rendering as HTML rendering. Roll CSP out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first and collect reports, because a strict policy breaks third-party tags. Trusted Types make DOM sinks reject plain strings. XSS defeats CSRF defences, so it is the bug to prevent first.

  • Where it is taught — 75.7 XSS from the frontend side; 75.8 Third-party scripts; 78.9 Frontend security headers at the edge.

Q18. How does HTTP caching work for a frontend? What headers do you set?

  • Model answer — The browser and CDNs cache by URL and obey Cache-Control. Two kinds of file need opposite rules:
    • Hashed static assets (app.3f9a1c.js): the name changes when the content changes, so cache forever: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.
    • HTML and the entry point: must always be revalidated so users pick up new deploys: Cache-Control: no-cache (which means "store but check first"), with an ETag so the check returns a cheap 304 Not Modified.
    • Personal API responses: Cache-Control: private, no-store or private, max-age=0, never cached by a shared CDN.
    • Public API data: s-maxage for the CDN, plus stale-while-revalidate so users get an instant response while the CDN refreshes in the background.
  • What a strong answer adds — no-cache is not no-store; mixing them up is a classic answer error. Caching the HTML for an hour while assets are hashed means users keep loading old HTML that references deleted chunks after a deploy (78.3, 78.4). The client has its own cache layers above HTTP (TanStack Query, the Next.js caches), and each needs its own invalidation story (72.4, 73.7). The back/forward cache is broken by Cache-Control: no-store on the HTML and by unload handlers (76.9).
  • Where it is taught — 11.11.1 ETags and conditional requests; 11.11.2 Cache-Control; 76.9 Caching for frontends; 78.3 Cache busting and versioned assets.

Q19. What are the accessibility basics you check in every component?

  • Model answer — Five checks catch most problems:
    1. Semantic elements first: a <button> for actions, an <a href> for navigation, real <label> elements tied to inputs, headings in order, lists as lists. A <div onClick> is not focusable, not announced as a button and does not respond to Enter or Space.
    2. Keyboard: everything works with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Escape and arrow keys where expected, and focus is visible.
    3. Focus management: a dialog moves focus in, traps it, and returns it to the trigger on close; a route change moves focus to the new heading.
    4. Text alternatives: meaningful alt on content images, empty alt="" on decorative ones, accessible names on icon buttons (aria-label="Remove item").
    5. Contrast and state: text contrast at least 4.5:1 for normal text, and state not shown by colour alone (an error has text, not just a red border).
  • What a strong answer adds — "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA": ARIA changes what assistive technology announces but adds no behaviour. Live regions (aria-live="polite") announce async results such as "8 results" or "Added to cart". Automated tools (axe in tests, 77.10) catch roughly a third to a half of issues, so a keyboard-only pass and a quick screen reader pass are still needed. Accessibility is often a legal requirement, and accessible forms convert better for everyone.
  • Where it is taught — 69.2 Semantic elements and forms; 69.9 Accessibility as engineering; 77.10 Accessibility testing with axe.

Q20. What are the Core Web Vitals and how do you improve each?

  • Model answer — Three field metrics judged at the 75th percentile of real page loads:
    • LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): when the largest image or text block appears. Good is 2.5 s or less. Improve with a faster TTFB, a preloaded and prioritised hero image (fetchpriority="high"), no lazy-loading of the LCP image, and less render-blocking CSS and JavaScript.
    • INP (Interaction to Next Paint): the latency from a click, tap or key press to the next frame, taken from close to the worst interaction on the page. Good is 200 ms or less. Improve by breaking long tasks, shipping less JavaScript, deferring non-urgent updates (startTransition), and avoiding huge re-renders on input.
    • CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): how much visible content jumps unexpectedly. Good is 0.1 or less. Improve with width and height (or aspect-ratio) on images and embeds, reserved space for ads and banners, and font loading that does not reflow text.
  • What a strong answer adds — Lab tools (Lighthouse) and field data (RUM, the Chrome UX Report) disagree, and the field is what counts: a fast developer laptop hides a mid-range phone's INP (76.2). LCP splits into four subparts (TTFB, resource load delay, resource load duration, element render delay) and you fix the biggest one first (76.3). INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in 2024. A strong candidate tells one story with numbers (80.9).
  • Where it is taught — 76.2 Core Web Vitals; 76.3 LCP; 76.4 INP; 76.5 CLS in the field; 76.12 Worked example.

80.4 React and Next.js questions

The React round is where backend engineers moving to full-stack are most often caught out, because the API is small and the behaviour underneath is subtle. Every question here ends up testing one of three ideas: a render is a function call, state is a snapshot per render, and identity (references and keys) decides what React keeps.

Q21. What does "render" mean in React, and what triggers a re-render?

  • Model answer — Rendering is React calling your component function to get a description of the UI. Then React compares the new description with the previous one (reconciliation) and applies the minimal DOM changes in the commit phase. A component re-renders when its state changes (setState with a value that is not Object.is-equal to the current one), when its parent re-renders (by default, whether or not props changed), or when a context it reads changes. Re-rendering is not the same as touching the DOM: if the output is identical, nothing is committed.
  • What a strong answer adds — State updates are batched (since React 18, also inside promises and timeouts) and state is a snapshot: after setCount(count + 1) the variable count in that render does not change. Reconciliation rules: a different element type at the same position unmounts the old subtree (losing its state); the same type updates in place. Re-renders are usually cheap; the problem is a re-render that is expensive or very frequent, found with the React Profiler (71.12), not guessed.
  • Where it is taught — 71.2 State and re-rendering; 71.3 Reconciliation and keys; 71.12 Performance basics.

Q22. Why do lists need keys, and what goes wrong with the array index as a key?

  • Model answer — A key tells React which item is which between renders, so it can keep the right component state and DOM node with the right data. With the index as key, inserting at the top, deleting, or re-sorting shifts every index, so React reuses component instances for different items: a half-typed quantity input or an expanded row "moves" to the wrong product. Use a stable unique id from the data (order.id).

    {cartItems.map((item) => (
  <CartRow key={item.sku} item={item} />   // stable: state follows the item, not the position
))}

  • What a strong answer adds — Index keys are acceptable only for static lists that never reorder and hold no state. Keys must be unique among siblings, not globally. Changing a key on purpose is a tool: <OrderForm key={orderId} /> resets all state inside the form when the user switches orders, which is simpler than an effect that resets fields. Generating keys with Math.random() remounts every row on every render.

  • Where it is taught — 71.3 Reconciliation and keys; 71.9 Lists, tables and large lists.

Q23. When should you use useEffect, and when should you not?

  • Model answer — An effect is for synchronising with something outside React: a subscription, a timer, a WebSocket or SSE connection, a non-React widget, a manual DOM measurement. You do not need an effect to compute values from props or state (compute them during render), to respond to a user event (do it in the event handler), or to reset state when a prop changes (use a key). Every effect that subscribes must return a cleanup.

    function useOrderEvents(orderId: string, onEvent: (e: OrderEvent) => void) {
  const latest = useRef(onEvent);
  latest.current = onEvent;                      // always call the newest handler without resubscribing
  useEffect(() => {
    const source = new EventSource(`/v1/orders/events?orderId=${encodeURIComponent(orderId)}`, { withCredentials: true });
    source.onmessage = (msg) => latest.current(JSON.parse(msg.data) as OrderEvent);
    return () => source.close();                 // runs on unmount and before re-subscribing to a new orderId
  }, [orderId]);
}

  • What a strong answer adds — In development, Strict Mode mounts, unmounts and remounts components to expose missing cleanups, so an effect that runs twice is a hint, not a bug in React. Fetching in an effect needs race handling (an ignore flag or AbortController) and usually belongs in a data library (TanStack Query, 72.2) or a server component instead. An effect that sets state that its own dependencies read is an infinite loop. The dependency list is not an optimisation knob: lying to it creates stale closures (80.2 Q1). Updating a ref during render as above is a common pattern, though React's documentation prefers doing it in an effect or using the newer useEffectEvent hook where your React version has it.

  • Where it is taught — 71.4 Effects: useEffect done right; 72.8 Real-time data in the UI.

Q24. Where should a piece of state live?

  • Model answer — Put state as close as possible to where it is used, and in the place whose lifetime matches it. A decision table:

    Kind of state Example Where it lives
    Derived from other state or props Cart total, filtered list Not state at all: compute during render
    Local UI Is this dropdown open useState in that component
    Shared by siblings Selected address used by two panels Lift up to the nearest common parent
    Should survive reload and be shareable Filters, sort, page, selected tab The URL (search params)
    Data from the server Orders, products, the user A server-state cache (TanStack Query, SWR) or server components
    Truly global client state Theme, feature flags, auth status Context for rarely changing values; a small store (Zustand, Redux Toolkit) for frequently changing ones
    Form draft Fields being typed The form library or the form component

  • What a strong answer adds — The most expensive mistake is copying server data into a global client store: now you own caching, deduplication, staleness and invalidation by hand, and two copies disagree (72.1). Context is a dependency-injection tool, not a state manager: every consumer re-renders when the value changes, so a context holding a fast-changing object re-renders the whole app. Duplicated state (storing both items and itemCount) eventually disagrees.

  • Where it is taught — 71.10 Component patterns; 72.1 Server state vs client state; 72.9 Client state stores.

Q25. React.memo, useMemo, useCallback: when are they worth it?

  • Model answer — All three trade memory and comparison work for skipped work. React.memo(Component) skips re-rendering when props are shallow-equal. useMemo caches a computed value between renders until dependencies change. useCallback caches a function's identity. They pay off when a render is measurably expensive (a 2,000-row table, a chart) or when identity matters (a memoised child, or a dependency of an effect). Elsewhere they add noise and can hide bugs with wrong dependency lists.
  • What a strong answer adds — React.memo is defeated by a new object, array or inline function in the props on every render, which is why useCallback exists at all. Fix structure before memoising: move state down, or pass expensive children as children so they are not re-created. Measure with the Profiler first. The React Compiler, where a team adopts it, inserts this memoisation automatically, which changes the advice to "write plain code and let the compiler handle it" (71.12).
  • Where it is taught — 71.6 useMemo, useCallback and custom hooks; 71.12 Performance basics.

Q26. Server components versus client components in Next.js

  • Model answer — In the App Router, components are server components by default: they run on the server (at build time or per request), can read the database or call internal APIs directly, and send rendered output to the browser with no component JavaScript. They cannot use state, effects, or browser APIs. A file starting with 'use client' marks a client component boundary: it and everything it imports become part of the browser bundle, are pre-rendered to HTML on the server, then hydrated so they become interactive. Props passed from a server component to a client component must be serialisable (no functions, no class instances).
  • What a strong answer adds — Push the 'use client' boundary down to the leaves (the "Add to cart" button, not the whole product page) to keep bundles small. A server component can pass a server component to a client component as children, which keeps the child on the server. Secrets in a server component stay on the server, but anything passed as a prop to a client component is visible to the user. Server-side fetch and data caching behaviour has changed between Next.js major versions, so say which version you mean (73.5, 73.7).
  • Where it is taught — 73.3 The App Router; 73.4 Server components and client components: the boundary.

Q27. What is a hydration error, and how do you fix one?

  • Model answer — Hydration is React attaching event handlers to server-rendered HTML by rendering the same tree in the browser and matching it to the existing DOM. A hydration error means the first client render produced different output from the server's HTML. Common causes: values that differ between server and client (Date.now(), Math.random(), new Date().toLocaleString() with a different time zone or locale), branching on typeof window during render, reading localStorage during render, invalid HTML nesting that the browser silently repairs (a <div> inside a <p>), and browser extensions that inject markup.
  • What a strong answer adds — Fixes by cause: format dates on the server with an explicit time zone and locale, or render them in the client after mount; move browser-only reads into useEffect and render a placeholder first; for a truly client-only widget use next/dynamic with ssr: false, called from a client component (the App Router does not allow it in a server component); use suppressHydrationWarning only on a single element whose text legitimately differs, such as a timestamp. A mismatch is not only a console warning: React may discard the server HTML for that subtree and re-render it on the client, which costs LCP and can cause layout shift.
  • Where it is taught — 73.10 Hydration and hydration errors.

Q28. How do you fetch data and keep it fresh? How do you invalidate after a mutation?

  • Model answer — On the client, use a server-state library. TanStack Query caches by query key (['orders', { status: 'open' }]), deduplicates concurrent requests for the same key, refetches stale data in the background, and retries failures. staleTime says how long data counts as fresh; garbage-collection time says how long unused data stays in memory. After a mutation, invalidate the affected keys so they refetch, or write the server's response into the cache directly.

    const queryClient = useQueryClient();
const cancelOrder = useMutation({
  // The key comes in with the variables, so TanStack's automatic retries reuse it: one key per user action.
  mutationFn: ({ orderId, idempotencyKey }: { orderId: string; idempotencyKey: string }) =>
    api.cancelOrder(orderId, { idempotencyKey }),
  onSuccess: (updated) => {
    queryClient.setQueryData(['order', updated.id], updated);          // the detail view updates at once
    return queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] });    // every list containing it refetches
  },
});
// In the click handler: a new key per click, generated once, outside mutationFn.
cancelOrder.mutate({ orderId, idempotencyKey: crypto.randomUUID() });

    On the server in Next.js, data fetched in server components is cached by Next's own layers, and a Server Action invalidates them with revalidatePath or revalidateTag.

  • What a strong answer adds — Name every cache between the database and the pixel and how each is invalidated: Redis on the backend, the CDN, the HTTP cache, Next's data and route caches, the client query cache (72.4, 73.7). Optimistic updates need a rollback path and an idempotency key so a retry does not cancel twice (72.6). For lists, invalidating a prefix key refetches every filtered variant. Real-time events can be merged into the cache instead of refetching (72.8).

  • Where it is taught — 72.2 TanStack Query; 72.3 Stale time and background refetch; 72.5 Mutations and invalidation; 73.7 Next.js caching layers.

Q29. How do you handle errors and loading states in a React tree?

  • Model answer — Each region of the page owns its own loading, empty and error states, so one failing panel does not blank the page. Error boundaries catch errors thrown during rendering in their subtree and show a fallback; they do not catch errors in event handlers or async code, which you handle where they happen. Suspense shows a fallback while a child is waiting for data or code; in Next.js, loading.tsx and error.tsx are route-level Suspense and error boundaries.
  • What a strong answer adds — Place boundaries by business importance: the recommendations panel can fail silently, the checkout summary cannot. Show the requestId from the error contract in the fallback so support can find the trace (74.6, 78.7). Avoid spinners that flash for 80 ms (delay them about 200 ms) and skeletons that shift layout when content arrives.
  • Where it is taught — 71.11 Error boundaries and Suspense; 72.11 Loading, empty and error states; 74.6 Error contracts.

Q30. A list page is slow to type into. How do you investigate?

  • Model answer — Reproduce with CPU throttling (4x or 6x) in DevTools, record a Performance trace while typing, and look for long tasks on each keypress. Then open the React Profiler to see which components re-render and why. Typical findings: the input state lives at the top of a page that re-renders a 3,000-row list per keystroke; an inline object prop defeats React.memo on every row; filtering runs on every render instead of being memoised. Fixes in order: move the input state down or debounce the filter value, render the list from a deferred value (useDeferredValue) so typing stays responsive, memoise the rows, and virtualise the list so only about 30 rows exist in the DOM.
  • What a strong answer adds — Gives the before-and-after metric (INP from 450 ms to 120 ms on a mid-range phone) and checks it in field data after release, not only in the lab. Considers moving filtering to the server for very large lists, with a debounced query and cancellation.
  • Where it is taught — 71.9 Virtualisation; 71.12 The React Profiler; 76.4 INP.

80.5 The UI machine-coding round

80.5.1 How to approach it

Concept

In a UI machine-coding round you build a small working feature in 60 to 90 minutes, in a browser-based editor, usually in React and TypeScript, with a mock API or a provided fetch endpoint. It is the frontend cousin of the low-level design round in Part 67 — Low-Level Design and Machine Coding: the problem is small enough to finish, and the grade is mostly about how you finish it.

Why does it exist?

Because it is the closest thing to a real ticket that fits in an hour. An interviewer learns more from watching you build a typeahead than from any question about hooks: do you get a working slice early, do you think of the user typing faster than the network, does the keyboard work, do you name things well, do you know when to stop.

Mental model

Imagine a carpenter's trial: build a small stool in an hour with someone else's tools. Nobody expects carving. They expect it to stand, to hold weight, to have no splinters, and to be built in a sensible order: legs and seat first, sanding last.

How it works

A time-boxed procedure for a 60-minute round:

Minutes Step What you say or do
0–5 Clarify Inputs, outputs, API shape, required states, keyboard and accessibility expectations, what "done" means, whether libraries are allowed
5–8 Plan out loud The component tree, the state (and its type), the data flow, the one or two hard parts
8–30 Working slice The happy path end to end, ugly but correct; render real data as early as possible
30–45 Hard parts Races, cancellation, double submit, keyboard navigation, loading, empty and error states
45–55 Polish Accessibility attributes, naming, extract a hook, remove dead code
55–60 Wrap up What you would test, what you cut and why, what production would need 
flowchart LR
  A["Clarify<br/>states and API"] --> B["Plan<br/>tree, state type, data flow"]
  B --> C["Happy path<br/>working end to end"]
  C --> D["Hard parts<br/>races, errors, keyboard"]
  D --> E["Polish<br/>a11y, names, hooks"]
  E --> F["Wrap up<br/>tests, cuts, production"]

What interviewers look for, roughly in this order: it works; state is modelled clearly (a discriminated union beats five booleans); async edge cases are handled; it is usable with a keyboard and a screen reader; the code is readable; you communicated throughout. Styling is almost never graded beyond "usable".

A rubric you can practise against (interviewers use something close to it; 87.5 explains how such rubrics are built):

Dimension Weak Meets bar Strong
Working software Does not run, or only the first case Main flow works Main flow plus edge cases work, verified by trying them
State modelling Many booleans that can contradict Clear state, some duplication Minimal state, derived values computed, impossible states unrepresentable
Async correctness Races, no error handling Errors shown, loading shown Cancellation, latest-wins, double-submit guard, retries considered
Accessibility Clickable divs, no labels Semantic elements, labels Keyboard support, ARIA where needed, live announcements, focus management
Code quality One 200-line component Reasonable components Small hooks and components with good names, typed props
Communication Silent, or talks without building Explains decisions Plans, narrates trade-offs, states what is cut and why

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

They get something on screen by minute 20, because a beautiful half-built architecture scores below an ugly working feature. They model state before writing JSX. They ask about the API because half of the hard problems (pagination, search limits, idempotency) are decided there. And they say out loud what production would add (tests, analytics, error tracking), which shows awareness without spending time on it.

Common mistakes

  • Installing a state library or a form library before anything renders.
  • Building the whole UI with hard-coded data and running out of time before the fetch.
  • Ignoring the error path because the mock API never fails. Ask; or add a "fail" toggle to the mock yourself.
  • Long silences. Narrate: "I am choosing a reducer here because there are four states with clear transitions."

80.5.2 Worked problem: typeahead search with debouncing and race handling

The prompt. "Build a product search box. As the user types, show up to 8 matching products from GET /api/products/search?q=. The user can pick one with the mouse or keyboard."

Clarifying questions worth asking. Minimum query length? (2 characters.) Debounce? (Yes, your choice.) Does the API support limit? (Yes.) What happens on error? (Show a message, keep typing working.) Is a screen reader user in scope? (Always say yes.)

The hard parts. Out-of-order responses ("ap" returning after "apple"), too many requests, keyboard navigation, and announcing results.

import { useEffect, useId, useRef, useState } from 'react';

type Product = { id: string; name: string; priceMinor: number };
type SearchState =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; items: Product[] }
  | { status: 'error' };

function useDebouncedValue<T>(value: T, delayMs: number): T {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delayMs);
    return () => clearTimeout(timer);               // every keystroke cancels the previous timer
  }, [value, delayMs]);
  return debounced;
}

function useProductSearch(query: string): SearchState {
  const [state, setState] = useState<SearchState>({ status: 'idle' });
  const cache = useRef(new Map<string, Product[]>());

  useEffect(() => {
    if (query.length < 2) { setState({ status: 'idle' }); return; }
    const cached = cache.current.get(query);
    if (cached) { setState({ status: 'success', items: cached }); return; }

    const controller = new AbortController();
    setState({ status: 'loading' });
    fetch(`/api/products/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}&limit=8`, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(async (res) => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        const items = (await res.json()) as Product[];
        cache.current.set(query, items);
        setState({ status: 'success', items });
      })
      .catch((err: unknown) => {
        if (err instanceof DOMException && err.name === 'AbortError') return; // superseded, not a failure
        setState({ status: 'error' });
      });
    return () => controller.abort();                 // a newer query aborts the older request: latest wins
  }, [query]);

  return state;
}

The component handles the combobox pattern: the input owns focus, the highlighted option is announced through aria-activedescendant, and a live region reads out the result count.

export function ProductSearch({ onSelect }: { onSelect: (p: Product) => void }) {
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  const [active, setActive] = useState(-1);
  const query = useDebouncedValue(text.trim().toLowerCase(), 250);
  const state = useProductSearch(query);
  const listId = useId();
  const items = state.status === 'success' ? state.items : [];

  useEffect(() => setActive(-1), [query]);           // a new result set starts with nothing highlighted

  function choose(p: Product) { onSelect(p); setText(p.name); setOpen(false); }

  function onKeyDown(e: React.KeyboardEvent<HTMLInputElement>) {
    if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') { e.preventDefault(); setOpen(true); setActive((i) => Math.min(i + 1, items.length - 1)); }
    else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') { e.preventDefault(); setActive((i) => Math.max(i - 1, 0)); }
    else if (e.key === 'Enter' && active >= 0 && items[active]) { e.preventDefault(); choose(items[active]); }
    else if (e.key === 'Escape') { setOpen(false); }
  }

  const expanded = open && items.length > 0;
  return (
    <div className="search">
      <label htmlFor={`${listId}-input`}>Search products</label>
      <input
        id={`${listId}-input`}
        role="combobox"
        aria-autocomplete="list"
        aria-expanded={expanded}
        aria-controls={listId}
        aria-activedescendant={active >= 0 ? `${listId}-opt-${active}` : undefined}
        value={text}
        onChange={(e) => { setText(e.target.value); setOpen(true); }}
        onKeyDown={onKeyDown}
        onBlur={() => setOpen(false)}
      />
      {expanded && (
        <ul id={listId} role="listbox">
          {items.map((p, i) => (
            <li
              key={p.id}
              id={`${listId}-opt-${i}`}
              role="option"
              aria-selected={i === active}
              onMouseDown={(e) => e.preventDefault()}  // keep focus in the input so blur does not close first
              onClick={() => choose(p)}
            >
              {p.name}
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
      <div aria-live="polite" className="visually-hidden">
        {state.status === 'loading' && 'Searching'}
        {state.status === 'success' && `${items.length} results`}
        {state.status === 'error' && 'Search failed. Keep typing to try again.'}
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

What interviewers look for.

  • Race handling, explained. Debounce reduces requests from about 10 per word to 1 or 2; AbortController plus the effect cleanup guarantees the screen only ever shows the latest query's results. A strong candidate says both are needed and why: debounce alone still allows a slow "ap" response to arrive after "apple".
  • State as a union, not isLoading, isError, data booleans that can contradict.
  • The cache turns backspacing into instant results. A strong candidate notes it is unbounded and would cap it (an LRU of 50 entries) or hand it to TanStack Query with placeholderData to keep the old list visible while loading.
  • Accessibility: the WAI-ARIA combobox pattern, onMouseDown preventing blur, and the live region. Most candidates skip this; it is the cheapest way to stand out.
  • API awareness: the limit parameter, trimming and lower-casing so "Apple " and "apple" share a cache entry, and asking whether the backend search is prefix-based or full-text (34.7).

Follow-ups to expect. "Highlight the matched text" (split the name on the query, wrap matches in <mark>, never inject HTML). "Results flicker while loading" (keep previous results with a dimmed style). "How would you test it?" (Testing Library with fake timers and MSW returning delayed responses out of order, 77.4, 77.5).

80.5.3 Worked problem: an infinite-scroll order list

The prompt. "Show the user's orders, newest first, loading 20 more when they reach the bottom. The API is GET /api/orders?cursor= returning { items, nextCursor }."

The hard parts. Not loading the same page twice, stopping at the end, recovering from an error, not duplicating rows when new orders arrive between pages, and keeping the page usable for keyboard users who cannot "scroll to the bottom".

import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react';

type Order = { id: string; placedAt: string; totalMinor: number; status: string };
type Page = { items: Order[]; nextCursor: string | null };

function useOrderPages() {
  const [items, setItems] = useState<Order[]>([]);
  const [cursor, setCursor] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [done, setDone] = useState(false);
  const [status, setStatus] = useState<'idle' | 'loading' | 'error'>('idle');
  const inFlight = useRef(false);                  // a ref, because state updates are not visible until next render

  const loadMore = useCallback(async () => {
    if (inFlight.current || done) return;          // guard against the observer firing twice
    inFlight.current = true;
    setStatus('loading');
    try {
      const qs = cursor ? `?cursor=${encodeURIComponent(cursor)}` : '';
      const res = await fetch(`/api/orders${qs}`, { credentials: 'include' });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      const page = (await res.json()) as Page;
      setItems((prev) => {
        const seen = new Set(prev.map((o) => o.id));
        return [...prev, ...page.items.filter((o) => !seen.has(o.id))]; // dedupe across page boundaries
      });
      setCursor(page.nextCursor);
      setDone(page.nextCursor === null);
      setStatus('idle');
    } catch {
      setStatus('error');
    } finally {
      inFlight.current = false;
    }
  }, [cursor, done]);

  return { items, status, done, loadMore };
}

function Sentinel({ onVisible, disabled }: { onVisible: () => void; disabled: boolean }) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
  useEffect(() => {
    const el = ref.current;
    if (!el || disabled) return;
    const observer = new IntersectionObserver(
      (entries) => { if (entries[0]?.isIntersecting) onVisible(); },
      { rootMargin: '600px 0px' },                 // start loading before the user reaches the end
    );
    observer.observe(el);                          // observe() reports the current state at once
    return () => observer.disconnect();
