  }, [onVisible, disabled]);
  return <div ref={ref} aria-hidden="true" />;
}

export function OrderHistory() {
  const { items, status, done, loadMore } = useOrderPages();
  return (
    <section aria-labelledby="orders-heading">
      <h2 id="orders-heading">Your orders</h2>
      <ul aria-busy={status === 'loading'}>
        {items.map((o) => <li key={o.id}><OrderRow order={o} /></li>)}
      </ul>
      {status === 'error' && (
        <p role="alert">Could not load more orders. <button onClick={loadMore}>Try again</button></p>
      )}
      {!done && status !== 'error' && (
        <button onClick={loadMore} disabled={status === 'loading'}>
          {status === 'loading' ? 'Loading' : 'Load more orders'}
        </button>
      )}
      {done && items.length === 0 && <p>You have no orders yet.</p>}
      <Sentinel onVisible={loadMore} disabled={done || status !== 'idle'} />
    </section>
  );
}

What interviewers look for.

  • Cursor pagination, and why. Offset pagination (?page=3) skips or repeats rows when new orders are inserted at the top between requests; a cursor ("orders older than this one") does not, and it is cheaper for the database at depth (15.5, 18.4.1). A strong full-stack candidate says what the cursor encodes (placed_at plus id, to break ties) and that the index must match.
  • The in-flight guard in a ref, because two observer callbacks in the same frame would both see the old status.
  • The re-observe detail. When a short page leaves the sentinel still visible, the observer will not fire again by itself. Because loadMore changes identity when the cursor changes and disabled flips back to false, the effect reconnects, and observe() reports the current intersection immediately, loading the next page. Candidates who notice this impress.
  • A real button. Infinite scroll alone traps keyboard users and makes the footer unreachable. The "Load more" button doubles as the retry path.
  • Scale. Past a few hundred rich rows, the DOM itself becomes slow; mention virtualisation (71.9) and that useInfiniteQuery (72.7) gives caching, retries and refetch for free in production code.

Follow-ups to expect. "Keep the scroll position when the user goes to an order and comes back" (cache pages in a query cache or sessionStorage, restore position after render). "New orders arrive live" (show a "2 new orders" button at the top rather than inserting rows that shift the page; CLS, 76.5).

80.5.4 Worked problem: a refund form with validation and double-submit protection

The prompt. "Build a refund request form: order, amount, reason, and details. Details are required when the reason is 'other'. Submit to POST /api/refunds. Make sure a customer cannot accidentally create two refunds."

The hard parts. Validation timing that is helpful rather than noisy, mapping server errors to fields, and double-submit protection that survives a fast double click, a slow network and a retry.

import { useRef, useState } from 'react';

type Reason = 'damaged' | 'not_received' | 'wrong_item' | 'other';
type Values = { amount: string; reason: Reason | ''; details: string };
type Errors = Partial<Record<keyof Values | 'form', string>>;

function validate(v: Values, maxMinor: number): Errors {
  const e: Errors = {};
  const minor = Math.round(Number(v.amount) * 100);
  if (!v.amount || Number.isNaN(minor) || minor <= 0) e.amount = 'Enter an amount greater than 0.';
  else if (minor > maxMinor) e.amount = `You can refund at most ${(maxMinor / 100).toFixed(2)}.`;
  if (!v.reason) e.reason = 'Choose a reason.';
  if (v.reason === 'other' && v.details.trim().length < 20) e.details = 'Tell us a little more (at least 20 characters).';
  return e;
}

export function RefundForm({ orderId, maxMinor, onDone }: { orderId: string; maxMinor: number; onDone: (id: string) => void }) {
  const [values, setValues] = useState<Values>({ amount: '', reason: '', details: '' });
  const [touched, setTouched] = useState<Partial<Record<keyof Values, boolean>>>({});
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState<Errors>({});
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);
  const submittingRef = useRef(false);                       // synchronous guard: state is not updated until re-render
  const idempotencyKey = useRef(crypto.randomUUID());        // one key per refund attempt, reused on retry

  const shown = (f: keyof Values) => (touched[f] ? errors[f] : undefined);
  function update<K extends keyof Values>(field: K, value: Values[K]) {
    const next = { ...values, [field]: value };
    setValues(next);
    setErrors(validate(next, maxMinor));
  }

  async function onSubmit(e: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const found = validate(values, maxMinor);
    setErrors(found);
    setTouched({ amount: true, reason: true, details: true });
    if (Object.keys(found).length > 0) {
      document.getElementById(`refund-${Object.keys(found)[0]}`)?.focus(); // move focus to the first problem
      return;
    }
    if (submittingRef.current) return;
    submittingRef.current = true;
    setSubmitting(true);
    try {
      const res = await fetch('/api/refunds', {
        method: 'POST',
        credentials: 'include',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Idempotency-Key': idempotencyKey.current },
        body: JSON.stringify({ orderId, amountMinor: Math.round(Number(values.amount) * 100), reason: values.reason, details: values.details.trim() }),
      });
      if (res.status === 201 || res.status === 200) { onDone(((await res.json()) as { id: string }).id); return; }
      const problem = (await res.json().catch(() => ({}))) as { issues?: { path: string; message: string }[]; detail?: string };
      if (res.status === 422 && problem.issues?.length) {
        setErrors(Object.fromEntries(problem.issues.map((i) => [i.path === 'amountMinor' ? 'amount' : i.path, i.message])));
      } else {
        setErrors({ form: problem.detail ?? 'We could not submit your request. Please try again.' });
      }
    } catch {
      setErrors({ form: 'Network problem. Your request may not have been sent; trying again is safe.' });
    } finally {
      submittingRef.current = false;
      setSubmitting(false);
    }
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={onSubmit} noValidate aria-describedby={errors.form ? 'refund-form-error' : undefined}>
      {errors.form && <p id="refund-form-error" role="alert">{errors.form}</p>}
      <label htmlFor="refund-amount">Amount</label>
      <input id="refund-amount" inputMode="decimal" value={values.amount}
        aria-invalid={!!shown('amount')} aria-describedby={shown('amount') ? 'refund-amount-err' : undefined}
        onChange={(e) => update('amount', e.target.value)} onBlur={() => setTouched((t) => ({ ...t, amount: true }))} />
      {shown('amount') && <p id="refund-amount-err">{shown('amount')}</p>}
      {/* reason (a <select>) and details (a <textarea>) follow the same pattern */}
      <button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>{submitting ? 'Submitting' : 'Request refund'}</button>
    </form>
  );
}

What interviewers look for.

  • Three layers of double-submit protection, each for a different failure: the disabled button (visual, but a second click can land before the re-render); the submittingRef guard (synchronous, stops a double click in the same frame); and the idempotency key, created once per attempt and sent on every retry, so even a retry after a timeout cannot create a second refund. Only the third one protects money; the server must store the key and return the first result for a repeat (15.12, 30.12, 71.8).
  • Validation timing: errors appear after a field is touched or on submit, not while the user types their first character; focus moves to the first error; aria-invalid and aria-describedby connect messages to inputs.
  • Money as integer minor units on the wire, never floats (74.7). A strong candidate notes Math.round(Number('10.10') * 100) is safe for two decimals but would parse with a decimal library or a string split in production, and that currencies differ in decimal places.
  • Server errors mapped to fields using the problem-details issues array from the error contract (74.6), and an honest network-error message: the request may have succeeded, so retry with the same key.
  • Client validation is convenience. The server checks the amount against the real order, and the shared zod schema (74.3) keeps both sides' rules identical.

Follow-ups to expect. "When do you reset the idempotency key?" (After success, or when the user changes the payload meaningfully, since a key reused with a different body should be rejected by the server.) "Use React Hook Form" (fine; show register, handleSubmit, formState.isSubmitting and setError, 71.7). "What if the user refreshes during submit?" (The server has the key; on reload, the order page shows the refund as pending.)

80.5.5 Worked problem: an order status stepper as a small state machine

The prompt. "Show an order's progress: placed, confirmed, packed, shipped, delivered. An order can be cancelled before it is packed. Updates arrive from a live stream. Show a Cancel button only when cancelling is allowed."

The hard parts. Modelling legal transitions, handling events that arrive late, duplicated or out of order, and not letting the UI's opinion override the server's truth.

import { useReducer } from 'react';

type Status = 'placed' | 'confirmed' | 'packed' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled';
const STEPS = ['placed', 'confirmed', 'packed', 'shipped', 'delivered'] as const;

const NEXT: Record<Status, readonly Status[]> = {
  placed: ['confirmed', 'cancelled'],
  confirmed: ['packed', 'cancelled'],
  packed: ['shipped'],
  shipped: ['delivered'],
  delivered: [],
  cancelled: [],
};
const canCancel = (s: Status) => NEXT[s].includes('cancelled');

type View = { status: Status; version: number; pendingCancel: boolean; notice?: string };
type Action =
  | { type: 'server_update'; status: Status; version: number }
  | { type: 'cancel_requested' }
  | { type: 'cancel_failed'; message: string };

function reducer(view: View, action: Action): View {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'server_update': {
      if (action.version <= view.version) return view;              // duplicate or out-of-order event: ignore
      if (!NEXT[view.status].includes(action.status)) {
        console.warn('Skipped transition', view.status, '->', action.status); // we missed an event; the server wins
      }
      return { status: action.status, version: action.version, pendingCancel: false };
    }
    case 'cancel_requested':
      return canCancel(view.status) ? { ...view, pendingCancel: true, notice: undefined } : view;
    case 'cancel_failed':
      return { ...view, pendingCancel: false, notice: action.message };
  }
}

export function OrderStepper({ initial, onCancel }: { initial: { status: Status; version: number }; onCancel: () => Promise<void> }) {
  const [view, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { ...initial, pendingCancel: false });
  // In the real page, the SSE hook from 80.4 Q23 dispatches { type: 'server_update', ... } for each event.

  async function cancel() {
    dispatch({ type: 'cancel_requested' });
    try { await onCancel(); }                                       // the stream delivers the 'cancelled' update
    catch { dispatch({ type: 'cancel_failed', message: 'This order can no longer be cancelled.' }); }
  }

  if (view.status === 'cancelled') return <p role="status">This order was cancelled.</p>;
  const current = STEPS.indexOf(view.status as (typeof STEPS)[number]);
  return (
    <div>
      <ol className="stepper">
        {STEPS.map((step, i) => (
          <li key={step} data-state={i < current ? 'done' : i === current ? 'current' : 'todo'}
              aria-current={i === current ? 'step' : undefined}>
            {step}
          </li>
        ))}
      </ol>
      {canCancel(view.status) && (
        <button onClick={cancel} disabled={view.pendingCancel}>{view.pendingCancel ? 'Cancelling' : 'Cancel order'}</button>
      )}
      {view.notice && <p role="alert">{view.notice}</p>}
    </div>
  );
}

What interviewers look for.

  • An explicit transition table instead of scattered if statements. The same table drives which buttons appear, so the UI cannot offer an action the domain forbids. It mirrors the backend's status machine (79.3), ideally generated from the same contracts package.
  • Versions, not timestamps, for ordering. Events can arrive twice (at-least-once delivery) or out of order after a reconnect; a monotonically increasing version from the server makes the reducer idempotent (35.10.1).
  • The server is the authority. If the client missed "packed" and receives "shipped", it does not reject the update for being an illegal transition; it logs the gap and shows the truth. The table is for affordances, not for vetoing the source of record. This is the point most candidates miss.
  • Pending state for the cancel without pretending it succeeded: the button is disabled, and the real cancelled state arrives from the stream. If the order was packed a second ago, the API returns a 409 and the UI says so honestly.
  • Semantics: an ordered list with aria-current="step", and the cancelled state announced with role="status".

Follow-ups to expect. "Make cancel optimistic" (set a provisional cancelled state with rollback on failure, and an idempotency key, 72.6). "Add an estimated delivery time" (comes from the server, formatted with Intl.DateTimeFormat in the user's time zone). "Test it" (the reducer is a pure function: unit-test every transition, duplicate and out-of-order case with Vitest, 77.2).

80.6 Frontend system design

80.6.1 A framework for the round

Concept

A frontend system design round asks you to design the client side of a product: "Design the news feed", "Design a comment thread with live updates", "Design a product page with a cart." The backend is a box you talk to through an API you define. The 45-minute procedure from Part 68 (68.3) still applies (clarify, estimate, design, deep dive, trade-offs), but the content of each step is different.

Why does it exist?

Large frontends fail in ways that are architectural, not syntactic: state duplicated in three stores, a page that ships 900 KB of JavaScript, a feed that janks on a mid-range phone, a real-time view that shows a message twice, a design that cannot be translated. The round checks that you can see those problems before they are built.

Mental model

Imagine designing a restaurant's dining room rather than its kitchen. The kitchen (backend) exists; your job is the flow of guests: where they wait, how orders reach the pass, what happens when a dish is late, how a guest in a wheelchair gets to a table. Same discipline, different room.

How it works

Walk through ten areas, spending most time on the two or three that matter for this product.

flowchart TB
  R["1 Requirements<br/>functional, non-functional, devices"] --> C["2 Component tree"]
  C --> S["3 State and data flow"]
  S --> A["4 API contract"]
  A --> K["5 Caching and freshness"]
  K --> P["6 Performance"]
  P --> X["7 Accessibility and i18n"]
  X --> E["8 Loading, empty and error states"]
  E --> O["9 Observability"]
  O --> L["10 Rollout"]
Area Questions you answer out loud
Requirements Who uses it, on what devices and networks? Which features are in v1? Is SEO needed? What are the latency and size budgets?
Component tree What are the main components, which are server-rendered, which are interactive? Where are the boundaries for loading and errors?
State and data flow What is server state, URL state, local UI state, global state? Where does each live (80.4 Q24)?
API contract Which endpoints, with what shapes, pagination, errors and real-time channel? Does a BFF aggregate them?
Caching Which caches exist (CDN, HTTP, query cache), what are their keys and how is each invalidated?
Performance Rendering strategy per region, bundle budget, images, virtualisation, Core Web Vitals targets
Accessibility and i18n Keyboard model, screen reader announcements, focus, right-to-left layouts, number, date and currency formatting
States Loading, empty, partial, error, offline, stale; what the user sees in each
Observability RUM for Web Vitals, error tracking with source maps, a trace ID from click to database
Rollout Feature flags, canary, old-bundle compatibility, kill switch

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

They anchor on numbers early ("a feed on a 4G phone; budget 170 KB of compressed JavaScript for the route; LCP under 2.5 s at p75"), pick a rendering strategy per region of the page rather than per app, and spend their deep-dive minutes on the part that is genuinely hard for this product: for a feed it is list performance, for a comment thread it is real-time consistency, for a product page it is caching and the cart.

Common mistakes

  • Designing the backend in depth and never drawing a component.
  • Naming libraries instead of decisions ("Redux and React Query") without saying what each holds.
  • No error, empty or offline states.
  • Treating accessibility and internationalisation as a closing sentence rather than a constraint that shapes components.

80.6.2 Worked design: a news feed

Requirements. Infinite feed of posts (text, up to four images, link previews); like and comment counts; like a post; see "new posts" without losing your place. Mobile-first web; 60% of users on mid-range Android over 4G. v1 excludes post creation. Targets: LCP 2.5 s, INP 200 ms, CLS 0.1 at p75.

Component tree and rendering. The shell and the first page of posts are server-rendered for fast LCP; the list is a client component because it scrolls, paginates and updates.

flowchart TB
  Page["FeedPage - server component"] --> Shell["AppShell: header, nav"]
  Page --> Feed["FeedList - client component"]
  Feed --> Banner["NewPostsBanner"]
  Feed --> V["VirtualisedList"]
  V --> Card["PostCard"]
  Card --> Media["MediaGrid with reserved aspect ratio"]
  Card --> Actions["ActionBar: like, comment, share"]
  Feed --> Sentinel["LoadMore sentinel and button"]

State and data flow. Pages of posts live in a query cache (useInfiniteQuery under the key ['feed']). Posts are stored once by ID so a like on a post that appears twice (a share and the original) updates both. The like toggle is an optimistic mutation with rollback and an idempotency key. The scroll position and loaded pages survive navigation to a post and back because they live in the cache, not in component state.

API contract.

// GET /v1/feed?cursor=<opaque>&limit=20
type FeedPage = {
  items: Post[];
  nextCursor: string | null;   // opaque: encodes (rank, postId) so inserts never cause skips or repeats
};
type Post = {
  id: string;
  author: { id: string; name: string; avatarUrl: string };
  text: string;                // plain text; links detected on the client, never HTML from the server
  media: { url: string; width: number; height: number; alt: string }[];
  likeCount: number;
  likedByMe: boolean;
  createdAt: string;           // ISO 8601 UTC
};
// POST /v1/posts/:id/like and DELETE /v1/posts/:id/like are idempotent by design (PUT-like semantics)
// GET /v1/feed/new-count?since=<postId> for the banner, polled every 60 s while the tab is visible

Performance deep dive. The feed is the hard part:

  • Virtualisation keeps about 15 cards in the DOM instead of 600 after ten minutes of scrolling. Variable-height cards need measurement; the library measures on render and caches heights by post ID.
  • Images carry width and height from the API, so space is reserved (no CLS); the first card's image is fetchpriority="high", the rest loading="lazy", in responsive sizes from an image CDN (76.8).
  • New posts go into a banner ("12 new posts") that the user clicks, rather than being inserted above the reading position. Inserting rows above the viewport is the most common feed CLS bug.
  • JavaScript budget: the like animation, share sheet and comment drawer are lazy-loaded on first interaction (76.7).

Accessibility. The ARIA feed pattern: a container with role="feed" and aria-busy while loading, each post an <article> with aria-posinset and aria-setsize (use -1 when the total is unknown), keyboard shortcuts to move between posts, and a visible "Load more" button as an alternative to scrolling.

States, observability, rollout. Skeleton cards of fixed height for the first load; an inline retry row when a page fails; "You are offline, showing saved posts" when navigator.onLine is false and the cache has data. RUM reports INP and CLS for the feed route separately; a long-animation-frame or long-task metric during scroll flags jank. The new feed ships behind a flag to 5% of users, compared on scroll depth and INP before widening.

What a strong answer adds. Ranking is a backend concern, but cursor design is shared: a ranked feed cannot use created_at alone as a cursor. Server-side, a feed is a fan-out problem (54.12); the frontend's job is to never ask for more than it shows.

80.6.3 Worked design: a comment thread with live updates

Requirements. Comments under an article, one level of replies, newest first; post, edit within 10 minutes, delete own comments; new comments from others appear live; 2,000 concurrent readers on a popular article, about 5 new comments per second at peak.

Transport. The client only receives updates and sends occasional writes through normal POST requests, so Server-Sent Events fit better than WebSockets: plain HTTP, automatic reconnection, and Last-Event-ID for resume (35.1.1, 35.3.1). Writes stay as REST calls with idempotency keys.

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant UI as Thread
  participant API as CommentsAPI
  participant S as Stream
  U->>UI: Types comment and presses Post
  UI->>UI: Insert pending comment with tempId
  UI->>API: POST /v1/articles/a1/comments with Idempotency-Key
  API-->>UI: 201 with id c900 and seq 4521
  UI->>UI: Replace tempId with c900
  API->>S: Publish comment.created seq 4521
  S-->>UI: event id 4521 comment.created c900
  UI->>UI: Already have c900, ignore duplicate
  Note over UI,S: After a dropped connection the browser reconnects with Last-Event-ID 4521

State. A normalised map commentsById plus an ordered list of top-level IDs and, per parent, a list of reply IDs. Every event carries the article's monotonically increasing seq. The client applies an event only if seq is greater than the last applied one for that comment, so duplicates and replays are harmless. Optimistic inserts carry a client-generated tempId; the POST response or the stream event, whichever arrives first, reconciles it to the real ID.

API contract.

type Comment = {
  id: string;
  parentId: string | null;
  author: { id: string; name: string };
  body: string;                 // plain text; rendered with React escaping, never as HTML
  status: 'visible' | 'deleted' | 'hidden_by_moderator';
  editedAt: string | null;
  createdAt: string;
  version: number;              // for edit conflicts: PATCH sends If-Match with this version
};
type CommentEvent =
  | { type: 'comment.created'; seq: number; comment: Comment }
  | { type: 'comment.updated'; seq: number; comment: Comment }
  | { type: 'comment.deleted'; seq: number; id: string };
// GET /v1/articles/:id/comments?cursor=   (newest first, 20 per page; replies collapsed with a count)
// GET /v1/articles/:id/comments/stream    (SSE; supports Last-Event-ID)

Deep dives.

  • Live insertion without disruption. If the reader is at the top, new comments slide in; if they are reading further down, show "3 new comments" instead of shifting the page.
  • Edit conflicts. Two tabs editing the same comment: PATCH with If-Match: <version> returns 412 for the stale one, and the UI offers to reload the latest text (optimistic concurrency, Part 21 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control).
  • Moderation and deletion. A deleted comment with replies becomes a tombstone ("This comment was deleted") so replies keep their context.
  • Security. User text is rendered as text; links become anchors only after scheme validation; rate limits on POST are enforced by the server and surfaced as a clear 429 message with a retry time (15.13).
  • Scale. 2,000 readers is 2,000 idle SSE connections per article, which the backend fans out through pub/sub across pods (35.5); the frontend keeps one stream per tab and closes it when the tab is hidden for more than a few minutes, catching up with Last-Event-ID on return.

Accessibility and i18n. New comments are announced politely and in batches ("3 new comments"), not one by one; relative times ("2 minutes ago") use Intl.RelativeTimeFormat and update at most once a minute; the reply form returns focus to the new reply after posting.

What a strong answer adds. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent application is the whole consistency model, and the same seq makes resume, deduplication and ordering one mechanism. For collaborative editing of one document (not a thread), the problem becomes operational transforms or CRDTs (66.2.10), which is a different design.

80.6.4 Worked design: an e-commerce product page with a cart

Requirements. Product details, images, price, stock status, variant picker (size, colour), reviews summary, "Add to cart" with a mini-cart. SEO matters. 50,000 products; prices change a few times a day; stock changes constantly during sales. LCP under 2.5 s at p75 on mobile.

Rendering per region, because one page mixes data with very different freshness and personalisation:

Region Freshness need Personal? Strategy
Title, description, images, specs Hours No Static or ISR, cached at the CDN, revalidated by tag on publish
Price Minutes, must be correct at checkout Sometimes (member pricing) Server-rendered per request or streamed; re-checked at checkout
Stock status Seconds during sales No Client fetch with a short staleTime, or streamed
Reviews summary Hours No ISR, streamed below the fold
Cart and mini-cart Immediate Yes Client component; server is the source of truth
Recommendations Minutes Yes Client-rendered after load, lazily 
flowchart LR
  B["Browser"] --> CDN["CDN<br/>cached HTML shell and assets"]
  CDN --> N["Next.js server<br/>ISR product page"]
  B -->|"cart and stock calls"| BFF["Next.js route handlers<br/>BFF"]
  N --> CAT["Catalog API"]
  BFF --> CART["Cart API"]
  BFF --> INV["Inventory API"]
  CART --> PG[("PostgreSQL")]
  CAT --> R[("Redis")]

State and data flow. Product data arrives from the server render. The selected variant lives in the URL (?variant=blue-m) so it can be shared and survives reload; changing it swaps images and price without a navigation. The cart is server state: useQuery(['cart']) with optimistic "Add to cart" that bumps the mini-cart count at once, sends POST /v1/cart/items with an idempotency key, and rolls back with a message if stock ran out.

Contract decisions. Money in minor units with a currency code (74.7); availability as an enum (in_stock, low_stock, out_of_stock, preorder) with a display message chosen by the client; the cart response returns the full recalculated cart (totals, discounts, line errors) so the client never computes totals itself.

Performance. The hero image is the LCP element: preloaded, correctly sized with srcset, not lazy. The variant picker and Add to cart button are the only client components above the fold (73.4). Third-party tags (analytics, chat widget) load after interaction or idle (75.8, 76.7). Space is reserved for the price and stock line so streaming them in does not shift layout. Part 76's worked example (76.12) takes a page like this from LCP 4.8 s to under 2.5 s; Part 73's (73.13) builds the ISR listing with a client cart.

Accessibility and i18n. The variant picker is a radio group (one Tab stop, arrow keys within); out-of-stock variants are announced as unavailable rather than hidden; the price uses Intl.NumberFormat with the user's locale and the product's currency; "Added to cart" is announced in a live region and focus stays on the button.

What a strong answer adds. The price on the page is a display, the price at checkout is a contract: the order API recalculates it, and the page must handle "price changed since you added this" gracefully. Cache invalidation is the real design: a price change must purge the CDN page by tag and update the Redis entry, or two caches disagree for an hour.

80.7 Full-stack system design: the contract is the design

80.7.1 Worked design: checkout with stock reservation

Concept

In a full-stack design round, the interviewer wants one feature end to end: browser, BFF or API, database, cache. The best candidates spend the most time on the contract between frontend and backend, because that is where full-stack engineers add value that neither a pure frontend nor a pure backend engineer brings. Part 74 — Frontend–Backend Contracts is the toolkit; Part 79 — Full-Stack Worked Project: Live Order Tracking is a complete worked build. This section shows how to present one in 45 minutes.

The prompt. "Design checkout for a food-delivery app: the user reviews the cart, applies a coupon, picks an address, pays, and sees the order confirmed. Restaurants have limited stock of some dishes."

How it works

Requirements and numbers. 2 million daily users, 150,000 orders a day, peak 15 orders per second at dinner (about 3x average), checkout p95 under 800 ms excluding the payment provider. A dish must not be sold beyond its stock. Payments can time out.

flowchart LR
  W["Browser<br/>Next.js client"] --> E["CDN and edge"]
  E --> B["Next.js BFF<br/>session cookie to token"]
  B --> O["Orders API - NestJS"]
  O --> PG[("PostgreSQL<br/>carts, reservations, orders")]
  O --> RD[("Redis<br/>menus, idempotency keys")]
  O --> PAY["Payment provider"]
  O --> Q["Outbox to queue"]
  Q --> N["Notifications and restaurant app"]

The contract first. Write the shapes before drawing boxes; they decide the rest.

// Shared in @shop/contracts as zod schemas; validated in the BFF, the API and the client (74.3)
type Money = { amountMinor: number; currency: 'INR' | 'USD' };

type CheckoutSession = {
  id: string;
  version: number;                         // optimistic concurrency: every PATCH sends If-Match
  lines: { dishId: string; name: string; qty: number; unitPrice: Money; issue?: 'out_of_stock' | 'price_changed' }[];
  coupon: { code: string; discount: Money } | null;
  addressId: string | null;
  totals: { subtotal: Money; delivery: Money; discount: Money; total: Money };  // always computed by the server
  reservationExpiresAt: string;            // stock held for 10 minutes
};

// POST  /v1/checkout-sessions                      create from cart; reserves stock
// PATCH /v1/checkout-sessions/:id   If-Match: 7    coupon or address; returns the full recalculated session
// POST  /v1/checkout-sessions/:id/orders  Idempotency-Key: <uuid>   place the order and start payment
// Errors: application/problem+json with code, issues[], requestId (74.6)
//   409 OUT_OF_STOCK (issues point at lines[i]), 412 VERSION_MISMATCH, 422 COUPON_INVALID, 402 PAYMENT_DECLINED

Why each choice matters:

  • The server computes every total. The client renders totals and never adds prices, so coupon rules live in one place.
  • Full-object responses to every PATCH remove a class of bugs where the client patches local state differently from the server.
  • If-Match with version stops two tabs from applying conflicting coupons silently; the stale tab gets 412 and refetches.
  • The idempotency key on order placement is created when the user lands on the pay step and reused on every retry, so a double click, a refresh or a timeout retry cannot create two orders or two charges (30.12, 71.8).
  • Typed error codes with issues paths let the UI put "Paneer tikka is sold out" on the right line instead of a toast (74.6).

Data and consistency. Reservations are rows with an expiry: UPDATE dish_stock SET reserved = reserved + $qty WHERE dish_id = $id AND available - reserved >= $qty in the same transaction that inserts the reservation; zero rows updated means out of stock (Part 21). A scheduled job releases expired reservations. Order placement writes the order and an outbox row in one transaction (30.10), then calls the payment provider; an unknown payment outcome leaves the order in payment_pending, resolved by the provider's webhook or a reconciliation job (30.13). The user-visible states are designed, not accidental (30.14): "Confirming payment" is a real screen.

Caching. Menus and dish details are cached in Redis and at the CDN (public, minutes). Checkout sessions are never cached by shared caches (private, no-store). The client query cache holds the session under ['checkout', id] and replaces it with each server response.

Frontend behaviour. The pay button is disabled while a submission is in flight and the idempotency key is reused on retry; on payment_pending the page subscribes to the order's status (SSE, as in 79.2) instead of polling every second; on 409 the cart page highlights the affected line and offers alternatives.

Rollout and observability. The new checkout ships behind a flag per city. A trace ID travels from the browser click through the BFF to the API and database (78.7, 79.11). Dashboards: checkout conversion, p95 latency per step, 409 and 412 rates, payment_pending older than 5 minutes.

sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant B as BFF
  participant O as OrdersAPI
  participant P as Payments
  C->>B: POST orders with Idempotency-Key k1
  B->>O: Forward with user token and k1
  O->>O: Insert order and outbox in one transaction
  O->>P: Create charge
  P--xO: Timeout
  O-->>C: 202 order o77 status payment_pending
  C->>O: Subscribe to o77 status
  P->>O: Webhook charge succeeded
  O-->>C: Event o77 confirmed
  C->>B: Retry with k1 after a network error
  B->>O: Same key k1
  O-->>C: 202 same order o77, no second charge

How a Senior Full-Stack Engineer thinks about this

They draw the contract before the boxes, design the error and pending states as carefully as the happy path, and make sure every retry anywhere in the chain is safe. They name what they would not build in v1 (split payments, scheduled orders) and why that is safe to defer.

Common mistakes

  • Letting the client compute totals or decide stock.
  • A generic { error: "Something went wrong" } contract that the UI cannot map to fields.
  • Treating a payment timeout as a failure and letting the user pay again.
  • Designing the database in detail and never saying what the user sees during each state.

Interview questions

  1. Why return the full session from every PATCH instead of a diff? Expected: one source of truth, no client-side recalculation drift, simpler caching; the cost is a slightly larger payload, which is trivial here.
  2. Where do you generate the idempotency key and when do you reset it? Expected: on the client, once per placement attempt; reset only after a definitive result or a meaningful change to the session.
  3. How does a breaking change to CheckoutSession reach production safely? Expected: additive changes first, both versions supported while old bundles are in the wild, contract tests in CI (74.9, 74.10, 78.4).
  4. What happens if the reservation expires while the user is on the payment page? Expected: the order endpoint re-checks stock atomically and returns 409; the UI shows the affected lines; the timer is shown to the user so it is not a surprise.

Practical exercise

Pick one feature from your current job and write its contract in the style above: shapes, endpoints, error codes with issues paths, idempotency and concurrency rules, and the user-visible states for each failure. Acceptance criteria: a frontend engineer could build the UI against MSW mocks from your contract alone (77.6), and every retry in your design is safe.

80.8 The junior and entry-level track

80.8.1 What juniors are asked, and how it is graded

Concept

Junior and entry-level loops (internships, graduate roles, first jobs, career changers) test whether you can learn quickly and work safely on a team. Nobody expects you to design a feed. They expect correct fundamentals, a small working piece of code, the everyday tools (Git, HTTP, a little SQL), and one project you understand all the way down.

A typical junior loop:

Round What happens What they look for
Fundamentals Questions on JavaScript, HTML, CSS, HTTP Correct basics in your own words; honesty about gaps
Small coding task 30–45 minutes: transform data, render a list, call an API Working code, readable names, testing your own output
Tools Git workflow, the terminal, reading an error You can work in a team repository without breaking things
Project walkthrough 15–20 minutes on something you built You made the decisions, you know why, you know what is weak
Behavioural Learning, asking for help, handling feedback Coachability, curiosity, reliability

Why does it exist?

A junior engineer costs the team mentoring time for months. The loop estimates two things: how much support you will need, and how fast you will grow. Fundamentals predict the first; the project walkthrough and how you react to hints predict the second.

Mental model

Imagine a driving test. The examiner does not expect racing skills. They expect you to check mirrors every time, follow the rules, stay calm when something unexpected happens, and admit when you are unsure of the route. Safe and teachable beats fast and flashy.

How it works — the small coding task

A typical task: "Given this array of orders, render them grouped by status with a total per group, and add a filter by customer name." Work in this order: restate the task, write the data transformation as a plain function and print its output, then render it, then add the filter. Say what you are checking as you go.

import { useState } from 'react';

type Order = { id: string; customer: string; status: 'placed' | 'shipped' | 'delivered'; totalMinor: number };

export function totalsByStatus(orders: Order[]): Record<Order['status'], number> {
  const totals = { placed: 0, shipped: 0, delivered: 0 };       // every status present, even with no orders
  for (const o of orders) totals[o.status] += o.totalMinor;
  return totals;
}

export function OrdersSummary({ orders }: { orders: Order[] }) {
  const [name, setName] = useState('');
  const visible = orders.filter((o) => o.customer.toLowerCase().includes(name.trim().toLowerCase())); // derived, not state
  const totals = totalsByStatus(visible);
  return (
    <section>
      <label htmlFor="customer-filter">Filter by customer</label>
      <input id="customer-filter" value={name} onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)} />
      <ul>
        {Object.entries(totals).map(([status, total]) => (
          <li key={status}>{status}: {(total / 100).toFixed(2)}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
      {visible.length === 0 && <p>No orders match.</p>}
    </section>
  );
}

What gets a junior hired here: a separate pure function that is easy to test, an empty state, a real label, a stable key, money kept in minor units, and saying "the filtered list is derived, so I did not put it in state".

How it works — presenting a portfolio project

Prepare a two-minute walkthrough and be ready for ten minutes of questions. Use this shape:

  1. The problem, in one sentence. "A small app for a local bakery to take pre-orders for pickup."
  2. The stack and why. "React with Vite for the frontend, a NestJS API, PostgreSQL. I chose Postgres because orders and items are relational."
  3. One hard thing you solved. "Two customers could book the last pickup slot at once. I fixed it with a unique constraint on slot and date, and the API returns a clear 409 the UI turns into a message."
  4. What you would change. "I store the session token in localStorage; I now know an HttpOnly cookie is safer, and I would move to that."
  5. Proof. A live link, a README with setup steps, a few tests, and a clean commit history.

Interviewers will open your repository. They look at the README, whether the app runs, whether commits have meaningful messages, and whether there is at least one test. A project you deployed and maintained for two months beats five tutorial clones.

Common mistakes

  • Memorising definitions and being unable to give an example.
  • Saying "we" for a team project and being unable to say what you built.
  • Presenting a tutorial project as your own design; one follow-up question exposes it.
  • Not testing your own code in the coding task: run it with an empty array and one odd input before saying "done".
  • Bluffing. "I have not used that yet; here is how I would find out" is a good junior answer (59.0.4 shows the pattern).
  • Ignoring the hint. When the interviewer nudges, they are helping; take it and say thank you.

Practical exercise

Pick one project. Write the two-minute walkthrough in the five-part shape above, record yourself saying it, and fix the README so a stranger can run the project in under ten minutes. Acceptance criteria: the recording is under two and a half minutes; it names one hard problem and one thing you would change; a friend can clone and run the app from the README alone.

80.8.2 A six-week junior plan

Week Study Build Practise
1 Part 1 — Programming Fundamentals in JavaScript and TypeScript Ten small data-transformation functions on an orders array Answer J1–J8 aloud
2 Part 2 — Asynchronous JavaScript; Part 3 — How the Web Works Fetch a public API and render it with loading and error states J9–J20
3 Part 5 — Git Basics and the Development Workflow; Part 4 — Linux and the Command Line Put your project on GitHub with branches and pull requests J25–J28
4 Part 7 — Your First Frontend Add a form with validation to your project J21–J24
5 Part 6 — Your First Backend, with its SQL section Add a small API and a table behind your frontend J29–J30
6 Review your log Deploy the project; write the README Two mock interviews with friends

80.8.3 Thirty junior questions with short answers

Each answer is the short version you should be able to say in under a minute. The pointer tells you where Volume 0 teaches it properly.

JavaScript and TypeScript

  • J1. What is the difference between let, const and var? const cannot be reassigned, let can, both are block-scoped; var is function-scoped and hoisted, which causes bugs, so modern code avoids it. A const object can still be changed inside. (1.1.2)
  • J2. What are the primitive types? string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol; everything else is an object, including arrays and functions. Primitives are copied by value, objects by reference. (1.1.1)
  • J3. Why use === instead of ==? === does not convert types, so '1' === 1 is false; == converts and gives surprises like 0 == '' being true. (1.1.3)
  • J4. What is a closure? A function that remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that outer function has finished. Event handlers use them all the time. (1.4.2)
  • J5. What do map, filter and reduce do? map turns each item into a new item, filter keeps items that pass a test, reduce combines all items into one value such as a total. None of them change the original array. (1.5.2)
  • J6. When would you use a Map or a Set? A Set for unique values (seen order IDs); a Map for key-value lookups where keys are not just strings or the order of insertion matters. (1.5.3)
  • J7. What does TypeScript add? Types checked before the code runs, so many mistakes (wrong property name, missing argument) are caught in the editor. The types are removed when the code is compiled to JavaScript. (1.2.1)
  • J8. What is a union type? A value that can be one of several types, such as 'placed' | 'shipped'; TypeScript makes you handle each possibility. (1.7.2)

Asynchronous code

  • J9. Why is JavaScript code asynchronous? It runs on one thread; waiting for the network without blocking means starting the request and continuing, then handling the result later through the event loop. (2.1.1)
  • J10. What is a promise? An object for a value that will arrive later: pending, then fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. (2.3.1)
  • J11. What does await do? It pauses the async function until the promise settles, then gives you the value or throws the error, without blocking the rest of the page. (2.4.1)
  • J12. How do you handle errors with async/await? Wrap the await in try/catch; and with fetch, check response.ok, because a 404 or 500 does not throw. (2.5.1)
  • J13. How do you run two requests at the same time? Start both and await Promise.all([a, b]); it fails if either fails, so use Promise.allSettled when one is optional. (2.3.1, 2.4.1)

HTTP and the web

  • J14. What happens when you type a URL and press Enter? DNS finds the server's address, the browser opens a connection (with TLS for HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, receives HTML, then fetches CSS, JavaScript and images and renders the page. (3.6.1)
  • J15. What are the main HTTP methods? GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates part, DELETE removes. GET must not change data. (3.2.1)
  • J16. What do status codes 200, 201, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 500 mean? OK, created, bad request, not logged in, logged in but not allowed, not found, server error. 2xx success, 4xx client problem, 5xx server problem. (3.3.1)
  • J17. What is a header? Name two. Extra information sent with a request or response: Content-Type says the body format, Authorization carries credentials, Cache-Control says how long to cache. (3.3.2)
  • J18. What is JSON and what can go wrong parsing it? A text format for data with objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null; parsing an HTML error page as JSON throws "Unexpected token <". (3.4.1)
  • J19. What is a REST API? An API organised around resources (/orders/42) and HTTP methods, returning JSON and status codes. (3.5.1)
  • J20. What is CORS, in one sentence? The browser's rule that a page may only read responses from another origin if that server allows it with CORS headers. (Part 7 — Your First Frontend; 11.13)

HTML, CSS and the browser

  • J21. Why does semantic HTML matter? Elements like <button>, <nav> and <label> give keyboard support, screen reader meaning and better SEO for free; a clickable <div> gives none of that. (Part 7 — Your First Frontend; 69.2)
  • J22. Explain the CSS box model. Every element is content, then padding, then border, then margin; box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border, which is easier to reason about. (Part 7 — Your First Frontend; 69.4)
  • J23. Flexbox or grid? Flexbox for laying out items in one direction (a toolbar, a row of buttons); grid for two-dimensional layouts (a page or a card gallery). (Part 7 — Your First Frontend; 69.4)
  • J24. What is the DOM? The browser's tree of objects built from the HTML, which JavaScript can read and change; React changes it for you. (Part 7 — Your First Frontend; 69.1)

Git and tools

  • J25. What is a commit, and what makes a good one? A saved snapshot of changes with a message; a good commit is small, does one thing and says why. (5.1.1)
  • J26. Describe the pull request workflow. Create a branch, commit, push, open a pull request, get review, fix feedback, merge into main. (5.3.1, 5.5.1)
  • J27. How do you resolve a merge conflict? Open the conflicted files, choose or combine the changes between the markers, run the tests, then commit the resolution. (5.4.1)
  • J28. How do you undo a commit that is already pushed? git revert <commit> creates a new commit that undoes it, which is safe for shared branches; do not rewrite shared history with reset. (5.7.1)

SQL basics

  • J29. Write a query for the ten most recent orders of one customer. SELECT id, total_minor, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10; and mention that an index on (customer_id, created_at) makes it fast. (6.3.1; Part 18 — SQL Mastery for Backend Engineers, 18.4.1, when you are ready for more)
  • J30. What is the difference between an inner join and a left join? An inner join returns only rows that match in both tables; a left join returns every row from the left table, with nulls where the right table has no match, for example customers with no orders. (6.3.1; 18.2.1)

What a strong junior answer adds, for any of the thirty: one concrete example from something you built, and one thing that can go wrong. "A left join, for example to show customers with zero orders, and I learned to count orders.id rather than * or every customer shows at least 1."

80.9 Behavioural rounds for frontend and full-stack engineers

80.9.1 Four stories to prepare, with STAR examples

Concept

STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) is the shape. Part 59, 59.21 covers the general behavioural questions (incidents, disagreement, mentoring, saying no); this section covers the four stories frontend and full-stack interviewers ask for most. Keep each to about two minutes, put the numbers in the Result, and spend most of the time on Action: what you did.

Practical example — working with design and product

Situation. Design delivered a checkout redesign with a multi-step carousel of offers before the payment step. Task. I was the engineer on the checkout team, and the release was four weeks out. Action. I built a quick prototype on a throttled mid-range phone and showed the designer and product manager that the carousel added 380 KB of JavaScript and pushed INP to 340 ms. Instead of saying no, I proposed two options: a static offers row with the same content, or the carousel lazy-loaded after payment. We ran the static version as an A/B test behind a flag. Result. The static version kept offer click-through within 2% of the design's estimate, checkout INP stayed at 150 ms, and the designer added a "performance budget" note to the design system template.

What makes it strong: you brought evidence instead of opinion, offered options, and left the decision with the right person.

Practical example — accessibility advocacy

Situation. A customer complaint said our checkout could not be completed with a keyboard. Task. I was not on the checkout team, but I owned the shared component library. Action. I reproduced it: our custom select trapped focus. I fixed the component, added axe checks to the component tests and a keyboard-only Playwright journey to CI (77.7, 77.10), and ran a 30-minute session for two teams on the five checks from 80.3 Q19. Result. Critical axe violations went from 41 to 0 across the library in six weeks; the keyboard journey has caught three regressions since; support tickets mentioning keyboard or screen reader dropped from about 12 a month to 1.

Practical example — a performance win

Situation. Our product page LCP was 4.1 s at the 75th percentile on mobile, and the page was the entry point for 60% of paid traffic. Task. I was asked to get it under 2.5 s within a quarter. Action. RUM showed most of the time was resource load delay: the hero image was discovered late because it was set by client-side JavaScript. I moved the image into the server-rendered HTML with fetchpriority="high" and correct srcset sizes, cut the API waterfall from three sequential calls to one BFF call (76.10), and deferred two third-party tags. Result. LCP went to 2.2 s at p75 in field data within three weeks; mobile conversion on the page rose 6% in the following month's A/B comparison, and I added a performance budget to CI so it stayed there (76.11).

Practical example — a bug in production

Situation. After a Friday deploy, error tracking showed a spike in "ChunkLoadError" and checkout completions fell 18% within 40 minutes. Task. I was on call for the web app. Action. The source-mapped stack traces showed users on the old HTML requesting JavaScript chunks the deploy had deleted (78.4, 78.10). I rolled back first, which restored conversion in 6 minutes, then fixed the cause: we kept the previous two releases' assets on the CDN, set the HTML to no-cache, and added a handler that reloads the page once on a chunk load failure. Result. Total impact was about 50 minutes and roughly 300 failed checkouts; we have had zero chunk errors in eleven deploys since, and the blameless review added an "old bundle" check to the deploy checklist.

What makes it strong: mitigation before diagnosis, the cause in one sentence, a fix to the system rather than a promise to be careful, and honest numbers including the cost.

Common mistakes

  • Stories with "we" throughout and no clear action of yours.
  • No numbers, or numbers with no baseline ("made it 50% faster" from what?).
  • Blaming design, product or the backend team. Describe their constraint, then what you did.
  • Choosing a story where nothing was at stake.

80.10 Mock interviews and rubrics

80.10.1 A React deep-dive transcript, with rubric notes

Interviewer: This component shows the wrong user's orders for a moment when I switch users quickly. Why?

Candidate: Can I see how it fetches? ... It fetches in a useEffect keyed on userId and sets state when the response arrives. If I switch from user A to user B, both requests are in flight; if A's response is slower, it arrives last and overwrites B's data. It is a race.

Interviewer: How do you fix it?

Candidate: Minimal fix: an AbortController created in the effect and aborted in the cleanup, so A's request is cancelled when userId changes, and I ignore AbortError. In production code I would move this to TanStack Query with the key ['orders', userId], because each user's data then has its own cache entry and the race cannot happen; it also gives me caching when switching back.

Interviewer: And the flash of the old user's data?

Candidate: With separate cache keys, switching to B shows B's loading state or B's cached data, never A's. If they want the previous data to stay visible while loading, placeholderData does that, but for different users I would not, because showing A's orders under B's name is a privacy problem, not a UX nicety.

Rubric notes. Strong: named the race precisely, gave a minimal fix and a production fix, and raised the privacy angle unprompted. A mid-level answer stops at "add a loading spinner", which hides the bug instead of fixing it.

80.10.2 The first five minutes of a frontend system design round

Interviewer: Design the comment section for our news site.

Candidate: Before I design, a few questions. Who are the readers and on what devices? ... Mostly mobile, fine. Do comments need to appear live, or is refresh acceptable? ... Live, okay. Replies: one level or unlimited nesting? ... One level. Do we need SEO for comments? ... No, so the thread can be client-rendered below the article, which keeps the article's LCP unaffected. Scale: how many readers on a popular article? ... About 2,000 at once and a few comments per second. Then I will spend most time on real-time consistency (ordering, duplicates, reconnects) and on not disrupting someone who is reading. Is that the right focus for you?

Rubric notes. Strong: requirements drive decisions immediately (no SEO, so client-rendered; live, so a transport choice), and the candidate proposes where to go deep and checks with the interviewer. The rest of the round follows 80.6.3.

80.10.3 A scoring sheet for your own mocks

Round Score 1 (weak) Score 3 (meets bar) Score 5 (strong)
JS fundamentals Folklore, wrong order in the event loop exercise Correct answers Correct answers plus mechanism plus a production symptom
Machine coding Not working at the end Working with main states Working, accessible, race-safe, with stated cuts
React API recall only Correct behaviour explained Explains why, picks state placement and caching deliberately
Frontend design Library names, no states Component tree, data flow, API Numbers, rendering per region, failure states, rollout
Full-stack design Boxes with no contract Contract and data model Contract with errors, idempotency and concurrency; user-visible states
Behavioural Vague, "we" Clear STAR STAR with baselines, numbers, and what you learned

Ask your mock interviewer to fill this in honestly, then put the two lowest rows into your log as next week's focus.

Senior Checklist — Part 80

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I know which rounds my target loop has, what each one signals, and how grading changes by level
  • I have a dated four-week or eight-week plan with booked mock interviews and a log
  • I can predict the browser event loop output (sync, all microtasks, then tasks and the render step) and explain why
  • I can explain closures, this, prototypes, promise error handling, coercion, copying and modules with a UI example each
  • I can explain the rendering pipeline, layout thrashing, CORS preflight, cookie and storage trade-offs, CSP, HTTP caching, accessibility basics and Core Web Vitals
  • I can explain re-renders, keys, effects, state placement, memoisation, server and client components, hydration errors and cache invalidation
  • I can build a typeahead with debouncing and AbortController, an infinite list with cursor pagination, a form with three layers of double-submit protection, and a status stepper driven by a transition table, each in under an hour
  • I can run a frontend system design with the ten-area framework and pick a rendering strategy per region
  • I can present a full-stack design contract-first, with error codes, idempotency, concurrency control and user-visible pending states
  • I can present one portfolio project in two minutes and answer the thirty junior questions (if I am early in my career, or when I interview juniors)
  • I have four STAR stories with baselines and numbers: design and product, accessibility, performance, production bug

Part 80 — Key Takeaways

  • Frontend and full-stack loops test different failure surfaces from backend loops: the language, the browser, the framework, building UI under time pressure, and the contract between client and server.
  • The same question is graded by level; seniority shows in what you raise unprompted (races, accessibility, caching, the API shape) and in what you choose not to build.
  • Most React questions reduce to three ideas: a render is a function call, state is a snapshot per render, and identity (references and keys) decides what React keeps.
  • In the event loop exercise, run the synchronous code, then drain every microtask, then tasks and the render step; say which orders the spec does not guarantee.
  • In machine coding, get a working slice on screen by minute 20, model state as a union, then handle races, errors, empty states and the keyboard.
  • Debouncing reduces requests; only cancellation or latest-wins checks fix races. Disabled buttons reduce double submits; only idempotency keys make them safe.
  • A transition table drives UI affordances, but the server remains the source of truth; versions make live updates idempotent.
  • Frontend system design is a rendering and state decision per region of the page, plus loading, error, accessibility and rollout plans; library names are not a design.
  • In full-stack design, write the contract first: full-object responses, server-computed totals, typed error codes mapped to fields, If-Match for concurrency and idempotency keys for every retry.
  • Juniors are hired for correct fundamentals, a small working task, safe use of Git, and one project they understand deeply and can criticise honestly.
  • Behavioural stories need a baseline, an action that was yours, and a measured result; mitigation before diagnosis is the shape of a good incident story.
  • Practise out loud, in an interview editor, with real people, and let a log of what went wrong decide next week's work.
